en: The Carakasamhitā of Agniveśa, Revised by Caraka and Dṛḍhabala,
with the Āyurvedadīpikā Commentary of Cakrapāṇidatta, edited by Vaidya Jādavaji Trikamji Āchārya.
3rd ed., Nirnaya Sagar Press, Bombay, 1941;
4th ed., Munshiram Manoharlal, New Delhi, 1981.
*Sūtrasthāna*.
The First Chapter.
1.1.1ab: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on Longevity (Dīrghañjīvitīya).
1.1.2ab | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
1.1.3ab | Desiring long life, Bharadvāja approached; 1.1.3cd | Indra, the lord of the immortals, knowing him to be a refuge due to his fierce asceticism.
1.1.4ab | For, as Āyurveda was proclaimed by Brahmā, so did Pajāpati receive it in its entirety at the beginning; and from him, the two Aśvins received it in turn.
1.1.5ab | From the two Aśvins, the blessed Śakra received [the knowledge] in its entirety;
1.1.5cd | Bharadvāja, who was proclaimed by the Ṛṣis, then approached Śakra.
1.1.6ab | When diseases arise as obstacles for embodied beings, [they obstruct] asceticism, fasting, study, celibacy, vows, and lifespan.
1.1.6cd | [They obstruct] asceticism, fasting, study, celibacy, vows, and lifespan.
1.1.7ab | Then, placing compassion for all beings foremost, the great seers of meritorious deeds 1.1.7cd | assembled on an auspicious slope of the Himalayas.
1.1.8ab | Aṅgiras, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Bhṛgu;
1.1.8cd | Ātreya, Gautama, Sāṅkhya, Pulastya, Nārada, and Asita.
1.1.9ab | Agastya, Vāmadeva, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Āśvalāyana;
1.1.9cd | Pārikṣi, Bhikṣu, Ātreya, Bharadvāja, and Kapiñjala.
1.1.10ab | Viśvāmitra, Āśmarathya, Bhārgava, Cyavana, and Abhijit;
1.1.10cd | Gārgya, Śāṇḍilya, Kauṇḍilya, Vārkṣi, Devala, and Gālava.
1.1.11ab | Sāṅkṛtya, Baijavāpi, Kuśika, and Bādarāyaṇa; 1.1.11cd | Baḍiśa, Śaralomā, and both Kāpya and Kātyāyana.
1.1.12ab | Kāṅkāyana, Kaikaśeya, Dhaumya, Mārīca, and Kāśyapa;
1.1.12cd | Śarkarākṣa, Hiraṇyākṣa, Lokākṣa, and Paiṅgi as well.
1.1.13ab | Śaunaka, Śākuneya, Maitreya, and Maimatāyani; 1.1.13cd | as well as the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, and other great ṛṣis.
1.1.14ab | They were treasuries of the knowledge of Brahman, of self-control, and of restraint; 1.1.14cd | blazing with the splendor of asceticism, like fires into which oblations are being poured.
1.1.15ab | Seated there in comfort, they engaged in this meritorious discourse:
1.1.15cd | Health is the supreme root of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
1.1.16ab | Diseases are the snatchers away of that well-being and life. 1.1.16cd | This great obstacle has appeared for human beings.
1.1.17ab | Having asked, "What might be the means for their pacification?", they became absorbed in meditation.
1.1.17cd | Then, with the eye of meditation, they beheld Śakra as their refuge.
1.1.18ab | That lord of the immortals will explain the means to peace exactly as it is.
1.1.18cd | Who would go to the abode of the Thousand-Eyed One to ask the Lord of Śacī?
1.1.19ab | "I am to be employed here in the sense of the first-person pronoun"—this was the first statement.
1.1.19cd | Bharadvāja spoke thus; therefore, he was appointed by the sages.
1.1.20ab | Having gone to the abode of Śakra, he beheld the slayer of Bala in the midst of the assembly of celestial sages; 1.1.20cd | [he saw him] shining like a blazing fire.
1.1.21ab | Having approached and greeted the Lord of the Gods with blessings of victory, 1.1.21cd | the wise one spoke with humility the excellent words of the sages.
1.1.22ab | For diseases that have arisen are terrifying to all living beings. 1.1.22cd | Therefore, O Lord of the Immortals, tell me properly the means for their pacification.
1.1.23ab | To him, the Lord Śatakratu proclaimed the Āyurveda; 1.1.23cd | having perceived the vast intellect of that supreme ṛṣi through his few words.
1.1.24ab | Knowledge of causes, symptoms, and medicines is the ultimate refuge for both the healthy and the sick.
1.1.24cd | This eternal and meritorious work, consisting of three aphorisms, was understood by the Grandfather (Brahmā).

1.1.25ab | That sage of great intelligence, with his mind fixed upon it, quickly understood in its entirety that Āyurveda, which has no end or limit and consists of three branches. 1.1.25cd | He understood it all exactly as it is, without delay.

1.1.26ab | By that [means], Bharadvāja obtained immeasurable life, endowed with happiness. 1.1.26cd | And he recounted it to the sages, leaving nothing out, as something not superior to what they themselves possessed.
1.1.27ab | And the sages received that [work] for the welfare of all beings from Bharadvāja; 1.1.27cd | desiring long life, they took up this Veda which increases longevity.
1.1.28ab | Those great seers beheld them correctly with the eye of knowledge:
1.1.28cd | both the general and the particular, as well as qualities, substances, and actions.
1.1.29ab | And having understood the *samavāya* (inherent connection), those who have followed the procedure taught in the Tantra,
1.1.29cd | obtained supreme bliss and a life that is not subject to decay.
1.1.30ab | Then Punarvasu, devoted to loving-kindness, [taught] the meritorious Ayurveda; 1.1.30cd | out of compassion for all living beings, he gave it to six disciples.
1.1.31ab | Agniveśa, Bhela, Jatūkarṇa, Parāśara,
1.1.31cd | Hārīta, and Kṣārapāṇi received those words of the Sage.
1.1.32ab | Therein, there was a distinction in the intellect [of Agniveśa], but no other instruction from the Sage.
1.1.32cd | For Agniveśa was the first author of this treatise (tantra).
1.1.33ab | Then Bhela and the others, being highly intelligent, composed their respective treatises. 1.1.33cd | Having completed them, they recited them to Ātreya along with the assembly of sages.
1.1.34ab | Having heard the outlining of the meanings by those of meritorious deeds, 1.1.34cd | the ṛṣis, delighted that it had been correctly outlined, gave their approval.
1.1.35ab | All those who desired the welfare of all beings praised them; 1.1.35cd | they spoke aloud and in unison, "Excellent is this compassion toward all living beings!"
1.1.36ab | The celestial sages, stationed in heaven, heard that holy sound. 1.1.36cd | Having heard it from the supreme ṛṣis, they, together with the gods, rejoiced exceedingly.
1.1.37ab | "Aha! How excellent!"—this resounding cry echoed throughout the three worlds;
1.1.37cd | it was uttered by beings out of joy in the sky, smooth and deep.
1.1.38ab | Auspiciously, the wind blew and all the directions were illuminated by rays of light; 1.1.38cd | And divine showers of flowers fell, accompanied by water.
1.1.39ab | Then the deities of knowledge entered [the body] of Agniveśa and the others:
1.1.39cd | Intellect, accomplishment, memory, wisdom, fortitude, fame, forbearance, and compassion.
1.1.40ab | And those tantras were approved by the supreme sages;
1.1.40cd | they attained a firm footing on earth for the welfare of the multitudes of living beings.

1.1.41ab | That which is beneficial and harmful, pleasure and pain, and the lifespan along with what is beneficial and harmful for it; 1.1.41cd | as well as its measurement—that in which these are taught is called Āyurveda.
1.1.42ab | The conjunction of the body, the senses, the mind (sattva), and the self is the sustainer; it is life.
1.1.42cd | It is called by the synonyms "the ever-moving" and "the continuous connection," as well as "life-span" (āyus).
1.1.43ab | Of that lifespan, the Veda is considered the most meritorious by those who know the Vedas;
1.1.43cd | for it will be declared what is beneficial for human beings in both worlds.
1.1.44ab | Universality (*sāmānya*) is always the cause of the increase of all entities;
1.1.44cd | Particularity (*viśeṣa*) is the cause of their decrease, while activity (*pravṛtti*) pertains to both.
1.1.45ab | Generality brings about unity, while particularity effects distinction.
1.1.45cd | For generality consists in having the same meaning, whereas particularity is its opposite.
1.1.46ab | Sattva, the self (ātman), and the body—these three are like a triple-staff (tridaṇḍa).
1.1.46cd | The world exists through their conjunction; everything is established therein.
1.1.47ab | He is the Puruṣa, and that is consciousness, and that is remembered as the substratum;
1.1.47cd | for this Veda has been revealed for his sake, and he is the purpose of this Veda.
1.1.48ab | Earth and the other elements, the self, mind, time, and space constitute the collection of substances.
1.1.48cd | A substance possessing sense organs is sentient; one devoid of sense organs is insentient.

1.1.49ab | Meaningful [entities] beginning with the teacher and ending with the intellect, as well as those beginning with the supreme (parā) and ending with effort (prayatna), are declared to be qualities (guṇas). 1.1.49cd | Action (karman) is said to be that which is characterized by effort and so forth, namely, purposeful movement.
1.1.50ab | Inherence (samavāya) is considered the non-separateness of the earth and other elements with their qualities.
1.1.50cd | It is eternal; for wherever there is a substance, there the quality is not non-eternal.

1.1.51ab | That in which the qualities of action reside, and which is the inherent cause; 1.1.51cd | that is substance (dravya); however, the inherent cause is a quality (guṇa) that is devoid of motion.
1.1.52ab | Substance, residing in conjunction and disjunction, is the cause [of these].
1.1.52cd | Action is the performance of what is to be done; action does not depend on anything else.
1.1.53ab | Thus has the cause been stated; the effect here is said to be the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātusāmya).
1.1.53cd | And the activity of maintaining that equilibrium of the constituents is declared to be the purpose of this treatise.
1.1.54ab | The association of time, the intellect, the sense organs, and their objects may be improper or excessive;
1.1.54cd | this constitutes the threefold collection of causes for diseases that depend on both [the body and the mind].
1.1.55ab | The body and that which is designated as the mind (sattva) are considered the substratum of diseases.
1.1.55cd | Likewise, their union is the cause of happiness; [and] equilibrium is the cause of happiness.
1.1.56ab | The supreme Self, however, is changeless with respect to the qualities of the elements, the constituents, and the senses.
1.1.56cd | Being the eternal cause of consciousness, the Seer perceives all activities.
1.1.57ab | Vāyu, pitta, and kapha are declared to be the collection of bodily doṣas. 1.1.57cd | Furthermore, the mental [doṣas] are specified as rajas and tamas alone.

1.1.58ab | The former [disease] is pacified by medicines based on divine and rational means; 1.1.58cd | the mental [disease] is pacified by knowledge, specialized understanding, fortitude, mindfulness, and meditative concentration.
1.1.59ab | Dry, cold, light, subtle, mobile, clear, and rough;
1.1.59cd | the wind (māruta) is pacified by substances possessing qualities opposite to its own.

1.1.60ab | Pitta is unctuous, hot, sharp, liquid, sour, mobile, and pungent; it is quickly pacified by substances possessing qualities opposite to these. 1.1.60cd | [It is quickly pacified] by substances with contrary properties.
1.1.61ab | Heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, sweet, stable, and slimy;
1.1.61cd | the qualities of phlegm (śleṣman) are pacified by qualities that are their opposites.
1.1.62ab | By means of medicines possessing contrary qualities, administered according to the appropriate place, measure, and time, 1.1.62cd | disorders considered curable are brought to cessation.
1.1.63ab | A therapeutic means is not taught for diseases that cannot be cured.
1.1.63cd | Furthermore, hereafter the qualities and actions of substances will be described according to their respective materials.
1.1.64ab | Taste is that which has the sense organ of the tongue as its object; its substance consists of water and earth.
1.1.64cd | Furthermore, the three [elements] beginning with space (ākāśa) serve as the causal conditions for its manifestation and its specific qualities.
1.1.65ab | Sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and indeed,
1.1.65cd | astringent— this is remembered as the collection of the six tastes.
1.1.66ab | Sweet, sour, and salty [tastes] conquer Vāyu; astringent, sweet, and bitter [tastes] conquer Pitta; 1.1.66cd | Astringent, pungent, and bitter [tastes] conquer Śleṣman.
(1.1.66.1ab) Pungent, sour, and salty [tastes] increase *pitta*; sweet, sour, and salty increase *kapha*.
(1.1.66.1cd) And pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes] provoke *samīraṇa* (vāta).
1.1.67ab Some [substances] pacify the *doṣas*, while others corrupt the *dhātus*.
1.1.67cd | Regarding the regimen for those in good health, some consider that the substance [of treatment] is of three kinds.
1.1.68ab | That [food] is further said to be of three kinds: mobile, vegetable, and mineral. 1.1.68cd | Honey, cow-products, bile, fat, marrow, blood, and flesh.
1.1.69ab | Excrement, urine, skin, semen, bone, sinew, horn, nail, and hoof; 1.1.69cd | from mobile beings are derived: hair, body hair, and bile-stone (rocanā).
1.1.70ab | Gold, the five impure metals, sand, and lime; 1.1.70cd | Realgar, orpiment, gems, salt, red ochre, and collyrium.
1.1.71ab | Terrestrial medicine has been described; that which is produced from the earth (audbhida) is of four kinds:
1.1.71cd | the tree (vanaspati), the creeper (vīrudh), the shrub (vanaspatya), and the herb (oṣadhī).
1.1.72ab | A *vanaspati* bears fruit; a *vānaspatya* bears flowers and also fruit.
1.1.72cd | Plants that end with the ripening of their fruit are called *oṣadhi*; those with spreading creepers are known as *vīrudh*.
1.1.73ab | Root, bark, pith, resin, stalk, fresh juice, and sprouts;
1.1.73cd | Alkaline substances, milk, fruit, flower, ash, oils, and thorns.
1.1.74ab | The group of plants propagated by cutting consists of leaves, shoots, tubers, and sprouts.
1.1.74cd | It is recorded that there are fifteen root-bearing plants and twenty fruit-bearing plants.
1.1.75ab | There are four great unctuous substances (mahāsneha) and five salts;
1.1.75cd | eight urines are enumerated, as well as eight milks.
1.1.76ab | Furthermore, six trees indicated by Punarvasu are for the purpose of purification. 1.1.76cd | He who knows how to apply these in various disorders is a knower of the Veda.
1.1.77ab | Hastidantī, haimavatī, śyāmā, trivṛt, and adhoguḍā;
1.1.77cd | Saptalā, śvetanāmā, pratyakśreṇī, and gavākṣī as well.
1.1.78ab | Jyotiṣmatī, bimbī, śaṇapuṣpī, and viṣāṇikā;
1.1.78cd | ajagandhā, dravantī, and kṣīriṇī is the sixteenth among these.
1.1.79ab | Śaṇapuṣpī, bimbī, and haimavatī are also used for emesis.
1.1.79cd | Śvetā and jyotiṣmatī should likewise be employed for head-purgation (śirovirecana).
1.1.80ab | Those eleven remaining [drugs] are to be employed for purgation.
1.1.80cd | Thus have been described the root-bearing plants by name and action; now hear about those that bear fruit.
1.1.81ab | Śaṅkhinī, viḍaṅga, trapuṣa, and madana;
1.1.81cd | dhāmārgava, ikṣvāku, jīmūta, and kṛtavedhana; 1.1.81ef | And klītaka is known to be of two kinds: that which grows in marshy land (ānūpa) and that which grows on dry land (sthalaja).
1.1.82ab | Prakīryā, codakīryā, pratyakpuṣpā, and likewise abhayā;
1.1.82cd | antaḥkoṭarapuṣpī, and hastiparṇī constitute the autumnal group.
1.1.83ab | The fruit of kampillaka, āragvadha, and kuṭaja; 1.1.83cd | as well as dhāmārgava, ikṣvāku, jīmūta, and kṛtavedhana.
1.1.84ab | Madana, kuṭaja, trapuṣa, and hastiparṇinī; 1.1.84cd | these are to be employed both for emesis and for enemas.
1.1.85ab | Pratyakpuṣpā is prescribed for administration through the nose (nastaḥ) and for emesis (pracchardana).
1.1.85cd | Those ten which remain are stated to be used for purgation (virecana).
1.1.86ab | Nineteen fruits have been described according to their names and actions.
1.1.86cd | Unctuous substance (sneha) is declared to be of four kinds: ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow.
1.1.87ab | For the purpose of drinking, massage, enemas, and likewise for nasal administration, according to their application;
1.1.87cd | [these oils] are emollient, life-sustaining, complexion-enhancing, and promoters of strength and nourishment.
1.1.88ab | Indeed, these unctuous substances are prescribed as removers of vāta, pitta, and kapha.
1.1.88cd | [These include] sauvarcala, saindhava, viḍa, and audbhida salts.
1.1.89ab | Together with sea salt (sāmudra), these constitute the five types of salts.
1.1.89cd | They are unctuous, hot, sharp, and most effective as digestive stimulants (dīpanīya).
1.1.90ab | They are employed for the purpose of external application, as well as in the procedures for oleation and sudation;
1.1.90cd | [They are used] in downward and upward purgatives, in non-unctuous enemas, and in unctuous enemas.
1.1.91ab | For the purpose of anointing, for food, and for the purgation of the head; 1.1.91cd | For surgical procedures, for wicks, and for collyrium and massage.

1.1.92ab | In cases of indigestion, intestinal distension due to wind, abdominal tumors, colic, and abdominal diseases, the salts have been described. Now, learn from me the eight types of urine. 1.1.92cd | [The salts] have been stated; hereafter, understand the eight urines from me.
1.1.93ab | All those which are declared as the primary [urines] in the teaching of Ātreya,
1.1.93cd | namely, the urine of the sheep, the urine of the goat, the urine of the cow, and that of the buffalo.
1.1.94ab | The urine of the elephant, the camel, the horse, and the donkey;
1.1.94cd | is hot, sharp, non-unctuous, pungent, and endowed with saltiness.
1.1.95ab | Urine is appropriate for use as a rubbing powder, and it is also appropriate for use as an ointment.
1.1.95cd | Urine is appropriate for use in enemas, and it is also appropriate for use as a purgative.

1.1.96ab | This [application] is also indicated for sudations, for diseases associated with them, for abdominal distension (ānāha), and for medicinal formulations; 1.1.96cd | as well as for abdominal enlargements (udara), hemorrhoids (arśas), abdominal tumors (gulma), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and leprosy (kilāsa).

1.1.97ab | That [oil] is prescribed for poultices (upanāha) as well as for affusions (pariṣeka). 1.1.97cd | It is taught as being digestive-stimulant (dīpanīya), anti-toxic (viṣaghna), and anthelmintic (krimighna).
1.1.98ab | It is said that this is the best remedy for those afflicted by anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
1.1.98cd | When drunk, it pacifies the phlegm (śleṣman) and restores the downward movement of the wind (māruta).
1.1.99ab | "It draws down the pitta to the lower part"—this is a summary of its qualities.
1.1.99cd | Though stated by me in general terms, it shall now be explained in detail.
1.1.100ab | Goat's urine is slightly bitter, unctuous, and non-contrary to pitta;
1.1.100cd | that of the goat is astringent and sweet, wholesome, and destroys the [three] doṣas.
Cow's milk is slightly sweet, destroys the [three] doṣas, cures worms and skin diseases, and when drunk, pacifies itching; it is beneficial for abdominal disorders caused by the doṣas.
1.1.102ab | Buffalo urine, which contains alkali and is laxative, destroys hemorrhoids, swellings, and abdominal enlargements.
1.1.102cd | Elephant urine, being salty, is beneficial for those suffering from worms and skin diseases.
1.1.103ab | Camel’s milk is praised for those suffering from bound feces, urine, poison, phlegm, diseases, and hemorrhoids.
1.1.103cd | That which is slightly bitter is said to cure asthma and cough, and it also destroys hemorrhoids.
1.1.104ab | For horses, [a diet] that is bitter and pungent removes skin diseases, wounds, and poisons.
1.1.104cd | Donkey urine destroys epilepsy, insanity, and demonic possession.
1.1.105ab | Thus, the urines have been described here according to their respective capacities; 1.1.105cd | hereafter, the milks shall be discussed, along with their actions and qualities.
1.1.106ab | Goat’s milk, cow’s milk, and that which is buffalo’s milk;
1.1.106cd | as well as the milk of female camels, female elephants, mares, and likewise of women.
1.1.107ab | Milk is generally considered to be sweet, unctuous, and cold; it is regarded as galactagogue.
1.1.107cd | It is nourishing, bulk-promoting, aphrodisiac, intellect-enhancing, strengthening, and mind-soothing.
1.1.108ab | It is vitalizing, removes fatigue, and subdues dyspnea and cough.
1.1.108cd | It destroys hemorrhagic fever (rakta-pitta) and promotes the healing of fractured joints.
1.1.109ab | It is wholesome for all living beings, and likewise acts as a pacifier and a purifier;
1.1.109cd | it quenches thirst, stimulates the digestive fire, and is supreme for those suffering from emaciation and wasting.
1.1.110ab | In cases of anemia (pāṇḍuroga), acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), consumption (śoṣa), abdominal tumors (gulma), and likewise abdominal enlargements (udara);
1.1.110cd | as well as in diarrhea (atīsāra), fever (jvara), burning sensations (dāha), and especially in edema (śvayathu).
1.1.111ab | In cases of vitiation of the female reproductive tract or semen, when urine is scanty,
and when stool is knotted, [these are] wholesome for those suffering from disorders of Vāta and Pitta.
1.1.112ab | In nasal therapy, external applications, and immersions, as well as in emesis and non-unctuous enemas;
1.1.112cd | and in purgation and oleation—milk is employed in all these instances.

1.1.113ab | I shall describe the qualities of milk for each [animal] individually and in their proper order; 1.1.113cd | I shall explain them further and in their entirety in the chapter concerning food, drink, and so forth.
1.1.114ab | Now, there are three other trees, distinct from those with fruits and roots: the Snuhī, the Arka, and the Aśmantaka. 1.1.114cd | Their application is described individually, one by one.
1.1.115ab | One should know that *aśmantaka* is for emesis, and the milk of *snuhī* is for purgation.
1.1.115cd | The milk of *arka* is to be understood as being for both emesis and purgation.
1.1.116ab | They say that there are these three other trees whose barks are beneficial:
1.1.116cd | namely, the pūtīka, the kṛṣṇagandhā, and likewise the tilvaka tree.
1.1.117ab | Pūtīka and likewise Tilvaka are to be employed for purgation.
1.1.117cd | Kṛṣṇagandhā is prescribed for erysipelas, swellings, and hemorrhoids.
A wise physician should also recognize these six purifying trees as being effective for ringworm, abscesses, swellings of the cheeks, skin diseases, and alajī.
1.1.119ab | Thus have been described the plants that bear fruit and roots, as well as the fats and salts; 1.1.119cd | the urines, the milks, the trees, and those six whose bark yields milk.
1.1.120ab | For those who do not recite prayers know the medicinal herbs by both name and form in the forest— 1.1.120cd | namely, the shepherds, the cowherds, and others who dwell in the woods.
1.1.121ab | Neither by the mere knowledge of names nor again by the knowledge of forms,
1.1.121cd | can anyone truly know the supreme attainment of medicinal herbs.
1.1.122ab | Even one who knows the application [of these] but does not know their forms is called a knower of their true nature.
1.1.122cd | How much more so the physician who would understand the medicinal herbs in every respect?
1.1.123ab | But he who knows their application as it is brought about by place and time,
1.1.123cd | examining each individual person— that one should be known as the best of physicians.
1.1.124ab | Just as poison, just as a weapon, just as fire, and just as a thunderbolt; 1.1.124cd | so too is medicine when unknown; when known, it is like nectar.
For a medicine that is unknown by way of its three aspects— name, form, and quality—
even if it is known, if it is improperly administered, leads to harm.
1.1.126ab | Even a sharp poison may become an excellent medicine through proper application.
1.1.126cd | And even a medicine, if improperly administered, turns into a sharp poison.

1.1.127ab | Therefore, it is not proper for a physician who desires life and health to administer any medicine that is contrary to reason. 1.1.127cd | Nothing at all should be accepted by a wise man who longs for life and freedom from disease.
1.1.128ab | Even the thunderbolt of Indra, when it falls upon the head, may leave something remaining;
1.1.128cd | But medicine prescribed by one who does not know leaves the patient afflicted, for it does not leave anything remaining [of his disease].

1.1.129ab | To one who is suffering, lying down, full of faith, and afflicted by disease, 1.1.129cd | he who, considering himself wise, administers medicine without possessing the necessary knowledge; ||
1.1.130ab | Even by conversing with one who has abandoned dharma, who is sinful, who is like death itself, and who is evil-minded, 1.1.130cd | a man may fall into hell.
1.1.131ab | Better indeed is the venom of a poisonous snake, or even molten copper,
1.1.131cd | drunk, or iron balls heated by an intense fire, consumed.
But one who merely assumes the dress of those learned in the Vedas should not accept food,
drink, or wealth from one who has sought refuge and is afflicted by disease.

1.1.133ab | Therefore, an intelligent person desiring to become a physician should apply supreme effort toward the perfection of his own qualities, so that he may become a giver of life to men. 1.1.133cd | [He should strive] so that he may become a giver of life to men.
1.1.134ab | That alone is a proper medicine which conduces to health. 1.1.134cd | And he alone is the best among physicians who can deliver one from diseases.
1.1.135ab | Success in all medical procedures proclaims correct application. 1.1.135cd | And success proclaims the best of physicians as one endowed with all virtuous qualities.
1.1.136 | Regarding this, there are these verses:
1.1.136ab | The source of Āyurveda, the cause, the commencement of the tradition,
1.1.136cd | the authorization for the aphoristic composition, and the definitive determination of Āyurveda.
1.1.137ab | The complete cause and the effect constitute the purpose of Āyurveda. 1.1.137cd | As well as the causes, the humors (doṣas), and the medicine, in brief.
1.1.138ab | The tastes together with their associated substances constitute the threefold collection of substances.
1.1.138cd | These are the root-yielding plants, the fruit-yielding plants, the oleaginous substances, and the salts.
1.1.139ab | Urine, milks, and trees—those six which have their bark as a source;
1.1.139cd | And the actions of all these, along with the qualities and defects resulting from their proper or improper application.
1.1.140ab | Where the censure of physicians occurs, and all the qualities of physicians;
1.1.140cd | all this has been fully explained by the Great Sage in the preceding chapter.
Thus ends the first chapter, named "The Longevity Chapter," in the Section on General Principles (*Sūtrasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The Second Chapter:
1.2.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter concerning the grains of *Apāmārga*.
1.2.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
1.2.3ab | The seeds of Apāmārga, long peppers (pippalī), and black peppers (marica);
1.2.3cd | Viḍaṅga, Śigru, mustard seeds (sarṣapa), and Tumburu.
Ajājī, ājagandhā, pīlu, elā, hareṇukā, pṛthvīkā, surasā, śvetā, kuṭheraka, and phaṇijjhaka.
1.2.5ab | One should administer the seeds of *śirīṣa*, garlic, the two types of *haridrā*, the two salts, *jyotiṣmatī*, and ginger for head-purgation (*śīrṣavirecana*).
1.2.5cd | [One should give] *jyotiṣmatī* and ginger for head-purgation.
1.2.6ab | In cases of heaviness of the head, headache, coryza, hemicrania, 1.2.6cd | intestinal worms, epilepsy, loss of smell, and delusion;
1.2.7ab | Madana, madhuka, nimba, jīmūta, and kṛtavedhana;
1.2.7cd | pippalī, kuṭaja, ikṣvāku, elā, and dhāmārgava.
1.2.8ab | When the disease of kapha and pitta has arisen and is localized in the stomach (āmāśaya),
1.2.8cd | the physician should administer emetics for the purpose of vomiting, without further vitiating the body.

1.2.10ab | Pīlu, āragvadha, drākṣā, dravantī, and nicula—one should employ these for the purpose of purgation when the doṣa has reached the colon (pakvāśaya).
1.2.10cd | [One should employ these] for the purpose of purgation when the doṣa has reached the colon (pakvāśaya).
1.2.11ab | Pāṭalā, agnimantha, bilva, and śyonāka;
1.2.11cd | kāśmarya, śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, and nidigdhikā.
1.2.12ab | Balā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, bṛhatī, eraṇḍa, and punarnavā;
1.2.12cd | barley, kulattha, kola, guḍūcī, and madana.
1.2.13ab | Palāśa, kattṛṇa, unctuous substances (snehas), and salts;
1.2.13cd | These one should employ in non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpanas) for upward movement of wind (udāvarta) and obstructions (vibandha).
1.2.14ab | From this very group of medicinal herbs, the oil for non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) is to be prepared.
1.2.14cd | This compendium of the five purificatory procedures (pañcakarma) is declared to be "Mārutaghna" (the destroyer of wind).

1.2.15ab | For those in whom these [doshas] have become manifest, one should administer the five purificatory procedures (pañcakarma) by means of oleation and sudation; 1.2.15cd | doing so while carefully considering the appropriate dosage and timing.
1.2.16ab | Reasoning (yukti) is based on the time of the dose; success (siddhi) is established upon reasoning.
1.2.16cd | One who knows reasoning always stands above those who merely possess knowledge of substances.

1.2.17ab | Hereafter, I shall describe various medicinal gruels (yavāgū) for the purpose of curing diverse disorders that are treatable by them. 1.2.17cd | [These are intended] for the alleviation of various morbid conditions.

1.2.18ab | A gruel prepared with long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), chaba pepper (cavya), leadwort (citraka), and dry ginger (nāgara) is digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya). 1.2.18cd | When properly prepared, it also destroys colic (śūlaghnī).
1.2.19ab | A gruel prepared with *dadhittha*, *bilva*, *cāṅgerī*, sour gruel (*takra*), and pomegranate is digestive and constipating.
1.2.19cd | A gruel prepared with the five roots (*pañcamūla*) is likewise used for the treatment of abdominal distension caused by wind (*savāta*).
1.2.20ab | A gruel prepared with śālaparṇī, balā, bilva, and pṛśniparṇī,
1.2.20cd | and made sour with pomegranate, is beneficial for those suffering from diarrhea caused by pitta and kapha.
1.2.21ab | A gruel prepared with half water and half curd from a goat, along with hrīvera, utpala, nāgara, and pṛśniparṇī, destroys bloody diarrhea.
1.2.21cd | [This] peyā, when prepared with these, cures blood-stained dysentery.

1.2.22ab | One should administer a gruel (peyā) containing ativiṣā, along with sour substances and nāgara, when there is āma; 1.2.22cd | When there is dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), one should give it with śvadaṃṣṭrā and kaṇṭakārī, together with phāṇita.
1.2.23ab | A gruel prepared with viḍaṅga, pippalīmūla, śigru, and marica,

1.2.24ab | Prepared with raisins, sārivā, laja, long pepper, honey, and ginger, it destroys thirst; 1.2.24cd | and that which is cooked with *somarājī* destroys poison.
1.2.25ab | A gruel prepared with the decoction of boar meat is considered nourishing.
1.2.26cd | A gruel made from roasted *gavedhukā* seeds mixed with honey is emaciating.
1.2.26ab | Rich in ghee and abundant in sesame seeds, it is unctuous when combined with salt.
1.2.26cd | In a decoction of kuśa grass and āmalaka, it is a desiccant for śyāmāka grains.
1.2.27ab | Decoction prepared with the ten roots (daśamūlī) cures cough, hiccup, dyspnea, and phlegm.
1.2.27cd | When cooked in "yamaka" (a mixture of two fats) and processed with wine (madirā), it cures pain in the colon (pakvāśaya).

1.2.28cd | With rose-apple, mango stones, sour wood-apple, and bilva, it is considered constipating (aṅgrāhikī).
1.2.29ab | It is considered a purgative when prepared with alkali, *citraka*, asafoetida, and *amlavetasa*.
1.2.29cd | With *abhayā*, long pepper root, and ginger, it facilitates the downward movement of wind (*vāta*).
1.2.30ab | Gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with buttermilk (*takra*) destroys complications arising from the improper administration of ghee.
1.2.30cd | In the event of complications involving oil, a preparation of parched grain flour cooked with buttermilk is recommended.
1.2.31ab | A preparation of cow's meat broth with sour ingredients destroys irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
1.2.31cd | A decoction of barley cooked in a mixture of two liquids (yamaka), along with long pepper (pippalī) and emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), is beneficial for the throat.
1.2.32ab | Prepared with the juice of *tāmracūḍa* (cock), it removes pain from the seminal passage.
1.2.32cd | When prepared with split black gram (*māṣavidala*), clarified butter, and milk, it is aphrodisiac.
1.2.33ab | Prepared with upodikā and curd, it destroys intoxication. 1.2.33cd | Boiled with apāmārga, milk, and the broth of a monitor lizard, it destroys hunger.
1.2.34 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
1.2.34ab | These twenty-eight types of gruels (yavāgū) have been proclaimed;
1.2.34cd | and the compendium of medicinal formulations has been taught in reliance upon the five therapeutic procedures (pañcakarma).

1.2.35ab | Previously, the medicinal substances were mentioned for the purpose of understanding roots and fruits; 1.2.35cd | they are now proclaimed again for the purpose of understanding the basis of the five therapeutic procedures (pañcakarma).

1.2.36ab | Possessing memory, skilled in causes and reasoning, and self-controlled; 1.2.36cd | such a physician, endowed with practical wisdom, is fit to perform medical treatment through the application of medicines.
Thus ends the second chapter, named "The Chapter on Apāmārga Seeds," in the Section on Verses (*Ślokasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.

Chapter Four:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter entitled "The Chapter on the Six Hundred Purificatory Procedures" (Ṣaḍvirecanaśatāśritīya).
1.4.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.4.3 | Indeed, here there are six hundred purgatives, six substrates for purgation, five sources of decoctions, five types of decoction preparation, fifty major decoctions, and five hundred decoctions; such is the summary.

1.4.4 | Regarding what was stated as "six hundred purgative formulations," we shall here present them in summary and explain them in detail in the *Kalpopaniṣad* section: (in that regard,) three hundred and thirty formulations have been prepared for *phala*; thirty-nine formulations for *jīmūtaka*; forty-five for *ikṣvāku*; *dhāmārgava* becomes sixtyfold when employed in formulations; *kuṭaja* undergoes eighteen formulations; and *kṛtavedhana* becomes sixtyfold when employed in formulations.

One hundred formulations of Śyāmā and Trivṛt have been prescribed, and there are ten other formulations here as well; Caturaṅgula enters into twelve formulations, Lodhra is joined with sixteen formulations in its procedure, Mahāvṛkṣa has twenty formulations, there are thirty-nine formulations of Saptalā and Śaṅkhinī, and forty-eight of Dantī and Dravantī; thus, there are six hundred purgative formulations.
1.4.5 | There are six bases for purgation: milk, roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

1.4.6 | There are five sources of astringents (kaṣāya), namely: sweet-astringent, sour-astringent, pungent-astringent, bitter-astringent, and astringent-astringent; these are the designations used in this treatise.

1.4.7 | There are five types of pharmaceutical preparations of decoctions (*kaṣāya*), namely: fresh juice (*svarasa*), paste (*kalka*), boiled decoction (*śṛta*), cold infusion (*śīta*), and hot infusion (*phāṇṭa*).
(1) The juice extracted by pressing a substance with a machine is called *svarasa*. A lump consisting of substances ground with their own juice is proclaimed as *kalka*.
Physicians say that a substance boiled in fire is called *śṛta*;
[this applies to] water that has been drawn from a source, heated, and left to stand overnight.
A decoction (kaṣāya) that is extracted by boiling is declared to be "cold" (śīta).
That which is crushed after being thrown into hot water is proclaimed as a "hot extract" (phāṇṭa).

Among these, there is an increasing degree of potency in the order mentioned; therefore, the preparation of decoctions depends upon the strength of the disease and the patient. Indeed, not all of them are suitable for use in every case.

1.4.8 | We shall now provide a detailed explanation of what was stated as "the fifty great groups of decoctions" (*pañcāśan-mahā-kaṣāyā*); namely: the group of six decoctions consisting of those that are vitalizing (*jīvanīya*), bulk-promoting (*bṛṃhaṇīya*), scraping (*lekhanīya*), purgative (*bhedanīya*), healing (*sandhānīya*), and digestive-stimulant (*dīpanīya*); the group of four decoctions consisting of those that are strength-giving (*balya*), complexion-enhancing (*varṇya*), beneficial for the throat (*kaṇṭhya*), and beneficial for the heart (*hṛdya*); and the group of six decoctions consisting of those that destroy satiation (*tṛptighna*), cure hemorrhoids (*arśoghra*), cure skin diseases (*kuṣṭhaghna*), cure itching (*kaṇḍūghna*), kill worms (*krimighna*), and neutralize poisons (*viṣaghna*).

The group of four decoctions consists of: galactagogue, galacto-purifier, spermatogenetic, and semen-purifier; the group of seven decoctions consists of: adjuncts to oleation, adjuncts to sudation, adjuncts to emesis, adjuncts to purgation, adjuncts to non-unctuous enema, adjuncts to unctuous enema, and adjuncts to head-evacuation; and the group of three decoctions consists of: arrestors of vomiting, arrestors of thirst, and arrestors of hiccough.

The group of five decoctions consists of those that consolidate feces, those that purify feces, those that consolidate urine, those that purify urine, and those that purge urine. The group of five decoctions consists of those that alleviate cough, those that alleviate dyspnea, those that alleviate edema, those that alleviate fever, and those that alleviate fatigue. The group of five decoctions consists of those that pacify burning sensations, those that pacify coldness, those that pacify urticaria, those that pacify body aches, and those that pacify colic.

The group of five decoctions consists of: that which stabilizes the blood, that which stabilizes pain, that which stabilizes consciousness, that which stabilizes progeny, and that which stabilizes youth. Thus, these fifty great decoctions (*mahākaṣāya*) have been explained for the purpose of illustrating the characteristics and examples of the major decoctions.
Within each of those great decoctions, we shall further explain ten constituent decoctions; thus, they constitute exactly five hundred decoctions.

1.4.9 | They are as follows: *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *medā*, *mahāmedā*, *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *mudgaparṇī*, *māṣaparṇī*, *jīvantī*, and *madhuka*—these ten are the vitalizers (*jīvanīya*). (1) *Kṣīriṇī*, *rājakṣavaka*, *aśvagandhā*, *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *vāṭhyāyanī*, *bhadraudanī*, *bhāradvājī*, *payasyā*, and *ṛṣyagandhā*—these ten are the bulk-promoters (*bṛṃhaṇīya*). (2) *Mustā*, *kuṣṭha*, *haridrā*, *dāruharidrā*, *vacā*, *ativiṣā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *citraka*, *cirabilva*, and *haimavatī*—these ten are the scraping agents (*lekhanīya*). (3)
1. *Suvahā*, *arkapuṣpikā*, *agnimukhī*, *citrā*, *citraka*, *cirabilva*, *śaṅkhinī*, *śakulādanī*, *svarṇakṣīriṇī*—these ten are the drugs that cause purging (4).
2. *Madhuka*, *madhuparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *ambaṣṭhakī*, *samaṅgā*, *mocarasa*, *dhātakī*, *lodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, *kaṭphala*—these ten are the drugs that promote healing (5).
3. *Pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *cavya*, *citraka*, *śṛṅgavera*, *amlavetasa*, *marica*, *ajamodā*, *bhallātakāsthi*, *hiṅguniryāsa*—these ten are the drugs that stimulate digestion (6).
Thus ends the sixth section, the group on the afflictions (kaṣāya).
1.4.10 | These ten—aindrī, ṛṣabhī, atirasā, ṛṣyaproktā, payasyā, aśvagandhā, sthirā, rohiṇī, balā, and atibalā—are strengthening (balya) [drugs] (7).
These ten—candana, tuṅga, padmaka, uśīra, madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, sārivā, payasyā, sitālatā, and [the tenth implied by the list]—are complexion-enhancing (varṇya) [drugs] (8).
These ten—sārivā, ikṣumūla, madhuka, pippalī, drākṣā, vidārī, kaiṭarya, haṃsapādī, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā—are throat-beneficial (kaṇṭhya) [drugs] (9).
Mango, hog-plum, *kalikuca*, *karamarda*, wood-apple, *amlavetasa*, *kuvala*, jujube, pomegranate, and citron—these ten are heart-pleasing (10).
Thus ends the fourth group of decoctions (*kaṣāya-varga*).
1.4.11 | These ten—*gāgara*, *cavya*, *citraka*, *viḍaṅga*, *mūrvā*, *guḍūcī*, *vacā*, *musta*, *pippalī*, and *paṭola*—are destroyers of satiation (11).
These ten—*kuṭaja*, *bilva*, *citraka*, *nāgara*, *ativiṣā*, *abhayā*, *dhanvayāsaka*, *dāruharidrā*, *vacā*, and *cavya*—are destroyers of hemorrhoids (12).
These ten—*khadira*, *abhayā*, *āmalaka*, *haridrā*, *aruṣkara*, *saptaparṇa*, *āragvadha*, *karavīra*, *viḍaṅga*, and the tender shoots of *jātī*—are destroyers of skin diseases (13).
These ten—sandalwood (*candana*), *nalada*, *kṛtamāla*, *naktamāla*, *nimba*, *kuṭaja*, mustard (*sarṣapa*), *madhuka*, *dāruharidrā*, and *mustā*—are destroyers of itching (*kaṇḍūghna*).
(14) These ten—*akṣīva*, black pepper (*marica*), *gaṇḍīra*, *ebuka*, *viḍaṅga*, *nirguṇḍī*, *kiṇihī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *vṛṣaparṇikā*, and *ākhuparṇikā*—are destroyers of worms (*krimighna*).

(15) These ten—*haridrā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *suvahā*, small cardamom (*sūkṣmailā*), *pālindī*, sandalwood (*candana*), *kataka*, *śirīṣa*, *sindhuvāra*, and *śleṣmātaka*—are destroyers of poison (*viṣaghna*). (16)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Section on Astringents.
1.4.12 | These ten—the roots of vīraṇa, śāli, ṣaṣṭika, ikṣuvālikā, darbha, kuśa, kāśa, gundra, itkaṭa, and kattṛṇa—are galactagogues (17).
These ten—pāṭhā, mahauṣadha, suradāru, musta, mūrvā, guḍūcī, vatsaka-phala, kirātatiktaka, kaṭurohiṇī, and sārivā—are purifiers of breast milk (18).
These ten—jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, medā, vṛddharuhā, jaṭilā, and kuliṅgā—are semen-producers (19).
Kuṣṭha, elavāluka, kaṭphala, samudraphena, kadamba-niryāsa, ikṣukāṇḍa, ikṣu, ikṣuraka, vasuka, and uśīra—these ten are the purifiers of semen (20). Thus ends the fourth group of decoctions.
1.4.13 | These ten are the adjuncts to oleation (snehopaga): *mṛdvīkā*, *madhuka*, *madhuparṇī*, *medā*, *vidārī*, *kākolī*, *kṣīrakākolī*, *jīvaka*, *jīvantī*, and *śālaparṇī*.
(21) These ten are the adjuncts to sudation (svedopaga): *śobhāñjanaka*, *airaṇḍa*, *arka*, *vṛścīra*, *punarnavā*, *yava*, *tila*, *kulattha*, *māṣa*, and *badara*.
(22) These ten are the adjuncts to emesis (vamanopaga): *madhu*, *madhuka*, *kovidāra*, *karbudāra*, *nīpa*, *vidula*, *bimbī*, *śaṇapuṣpī*, *sadāpuṣpā*, and *pratyakpuṣpā*. (23)
These ten—grapes (*drākṣā*), *kāśmarya*, *parūṣaka*, *abhayā*, *āmalaka*, *bibhītaka*, water-lily (*kuvala*), *badara*, *karkandhu*, and *pīlu*—are the adjuncts for purgation (24).

These ten—*trivṛt*, *bilva*, long pepper (*pippalī*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), *vacā*, the fruit of *vatsaka*, *śatapuṣpā*, licorice (*madhuka*), and the fruit of *madana*—are the adjuncts for non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) (25).
These ten—*rāsnā*, deodar (*suradāru*), *bilva*, *madana*, *śatapuṣpā*, *vṛścīra*, *punarnavā*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *agnimantha*, and *śyonāka*—are the adjuncts for unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) (26).
Jyotiṣmatī, kṣavaka, marica, pippalī, viḍaṅga, śigru, sarṣapa, apāmārga-taṇḍula, śvetā, and mahāśvetā—these ten are the adjuncts for head-purgatives (śirovirecana).
Thus ends the seventh group of decoctions (kaṣāya-varga).
1.4.14 | These ten—jambu, mango sprouts, mātuluṅga, sour jujube, pomegranate, barley, liquorice, kushtha, clay, and parched grain—are the suppressors of vomiting (28).
These ten—ginger, dhanvayavāsa, musta, parpaṭaka, sandalwood, kirātatikta, gudūcī, hrīvera, dhānyaka, and paṭola—are the suppressors of thirst (29).
These ten—śaṭī, puṣkara root, jujube seeds, kaṇṭakārī, bṛhatī, vṛkṣaruhā, abhayā, pippalī, durālabhā, and kulīraśṛṅgī—are the suppressors of hiccups (30).
Thus ends the group of three astringent decoctions.
1.4.15 | Priyaṅgu, anantā, āmrāsthi, kaṭvaṅga, lodhra, mocarasa, samaṅgā, dhātakīpuṣpa, padmā, and padmakeśara—these ten are the astringents that bind the feces (31).
Jambu-tvak, śallakī-tvak, kacchurā, madhūka, śālmalī, śrīveṣṭaka, bhṛṣṭamṛd, payasyā, utpala, and tilakaṇā—these ten are the astringents that cleanse the feces (32).
Jambu, āmra, plakṣa, vaṭa, kapītana, udumbara, aśvattha, bhallātaka, aśmantaka, and somavalka—these ten are the astringents that bind the urine (33).
The flowers of the padma, utpala, nalina, kumuda, saugandhika, puṇḍarīka, śatapatra, madhuka, priyaṅgu, and dhātakī—these ten are purifiers of the urine (mūtra-virajanīya).
(34) The roots of vṛkṣādanī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, vasuka, vaśira, pāṣāṇabheda, darbha, kuśa, kāśa, gundra, and itkaṭa—these ten are laxatives for the urine (mūtra-virecanīya).
(35) Thus ends the fifth group of decoctions (kaṣāya-varga).
1.4.16 | These ten—*drākṣā*, *abhayā*, *āmalaka*, *pippalī*, *durālabhā*, *śṛṅgī*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *vṛścīra*, *punarnavā*, and *tāmalakī*—are alleviators of cough (36).
These ten—*śaṭī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *amlavetasa*, *elā*, *hiṅgu*, *aguru*, *surasā*, *tāmalakī*, *jīvantī*, and *caṇḍā*—are alleviators of dyspnea (37).
These ten—*pāṭalā*, *agnimantha*, *śyonāka*, *bilva*, *kāśmarya*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *bṛhatī*, *śālaparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, and *gokṣuraka*—are alleviators of edema (38).
Sārivā, śarkarā, pāṭhā, mañjiṣṭhā, drākṣā, pīlu, parūṣaka, abhayā, āmalaka, and bibhītaka—these ten are fever-alleviating (39).
Drākṣā, kharjūra, priyāla, badara, dāḍima, phalgu, parūṣaka, ikṣu, yava, and ṣaṣṭika—these ten are fatigue-alleviating (40).
Thus ends the fifth group of decoctions.
1.4.17 | These ten—lāja, candana, kāśmarya-phala, madhūka, śarkarā, nīlotpala, uśīra, sārivā, guḍūcī, and hribera—are alleviators of burning sensations (41).
These ten—tagara, aguru, dhānyaka, śṛṅgavera, bhūtīka, vacā, kaṇṭakārī, agnimantha, śyonāka, and pippalī—are alleviators of cold sensations (42).
These ten—tinduka, priyāla, badara, khadira, kadara, saptaparṇa, aśvakarṇa, arjuna, asana, and arimedā—are alleviators of urticaria (43).
Vidārīgandhā, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, eraṇḍa, kākolī, candana, uśīra, elā, and madhuka—these ten are the alleviators of bodily aches (44).
Pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, śṛṅgavera, marica, ajamoda, ajagandhā, jīraka, and gaṇḍīra—these ten are the alleviators of colic pain (45).
Thus ends the fifth group of decoctions.
1.4.18 | Honey, madhuka, blood, mocarasa, earth, potsherd, lodhra, gairika, priyaṅgu, and sugar—these ten are the restorers of the blood (46).
Śāla, kaṭphala, kadamba, padmaka, tumba, mocarasa, śirīṣa, vañjula, elavāluka, and aśoka—these ten are the restorers of sensation (47).
Hiṅgu, kaiṭarya, arimedā, vacā, coraka, vayasthā, golomī, jaṭilā, palaṅkaṣā, and aśokarohiṇī—these ten are the restorers of consciousness (48).
*Aindrī*, *brāhmī*, *śatavīryā*, *sahasravīryā*, *amoghā*, *avyathā*, *śivā*, *ariṣṭā*, *vāṭyapuṣpī*, and *viṣvaksenakāntā*—these ten are the "establishers of progeny" (49).
*Amṛtā*, *abhayā*, *dhātrī*, *muktā*, *śvetā*, *jīvantī*, *atirasā*, *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *sthirā*, and *punarnavā*—these ten are the "establishers of youth" (50).
Thus ends the group of five decoctions.
1.4.19 | Thus, having summarized the five hundred pentads, these fifty great pentads have been explained for the purpose of defining and illustrating the great pentads.

1.4.20 | For there is no limit to expansion, nor does extreme brevity suffice for the capacity of those with small intellects; therefore, they have been taught neither too briefly nor too extensively.

Indeed, this much is sufficient for the practical application of those with small intellects, and for the knowledge of the unspoken meaning by the wise who are skilled in the specific characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), inference (*anumāna*), and reasoning (*yukti*).

1.4.21 | To the Blessed Ātreya who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, these five hundred groups of decoctions do not suffice; for those very same constituent parts recur excessively within each of those great decoction groups."
1.4.22 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, this should not be viewed in such a manner by one who possesses intelligence.

For even a single entity receives multiple designations while performing various functions. For example, a man is capable of performing many actions; whatever action he performs, he receives a specific secondary name associated with that particular action—whether as the agent, the instrument, or the result. In the same way, medicinal substances should also be understood."

And if we were to find some single substance endowed with such qualities that it would be capable of performing all actions, who then would desire to investigate or teach anything other than that to their disciples?

1.4.23 | Regarding this, there are these verses: 1.4.23ab | Since six hundred purgatives have been described here in summary—along with the number of substances from which they are derived—and likewise their six bases; 1.4.23cd | [these are stated].
1.4.24ab | The tastes, excluding the saline (lavaṇa), are designated as "decoctions" (kaṣāya).
1.4.24cd | Therefore, the source of decoctions is said to be fivefold.
1.4.25ab | Likewise, their preparation is said to be fivefold again;
1.4.25cd | and fifty [preparations] of the great astringents (kaṣāya) are proclaimed.
1.4.26ab | Furthermore, five hundred decoctions have been described according to their respective parts; 1.4.26cd | this is for the sake of definition, for there is no limit to their full extent.
1.4.27ab | Nor is excessive brevity sufficient for the sake of comprehension; 1.4.27cd | therefore, this [work] is neither too brief nor too extensive for one of limited intelligence.
1.4.28ab | For the practical application of the dull-witted, and for the increase of the intellect of the wise;
1.4.28cd | this group of fifty decoctions has indeed been set forth.

1.4.29ab | He who knows the application of these [therapies] to external actions and their conjunction and employment in internal ones, he is the best of physicians. 1.4.29cd | [He who knows] both the combination and the practical application [of therapies], he is the most excellent physician.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "The Chapter on the Six Hundred Purgatives," in the Section on Verses of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
This concludes the group of four on medicinal substances.
Chapter Five.
1.5.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on eating in measured quantities.
1.5.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.5.3 | One should eat in moderation; furthermore, the quantity of food depends upon the strength of the digestive fire.

1.5.4 | Indeed, as long as the food eaten by him undergoes digestion without impairing its natural state and reaches full maturation at the proper time, so much should be understood as the measure of his proper quantity.

1.5.5 | In this regard, food substances such as *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, partridge, grey partridge, black buck, rabbit, *śarabha*, *śambara*, and others, although light by nature (*prakṛti-laghu*), depend upon the quantity (*mātrā*) [consumed].

Likewise, food substances such as flour products, sugarcane, milk preparations, green gram, *māṣa* beans, the meat of marshy or aquatic animals, and so forth, although heavy by nature (*prakṛti-guru*), depend solely upon the quantity.

1.5.6 | Nor should one consider weight and lightness to be irrelevant when a substance has been thus described; for light substances abound in the qualities of air and fire, while others abound in the qualities of earth and water. Therefore, even when consumed to satiety, light substances are said to be of little fault because their very nature is to kindle the digestive fire. Heavy substances, however, by their very nature do not kindle the fire due to their dissimilarity [to it], and consequently they are excessively harmful when consumed to satiety, except in cases where there is strength of the digestive fire resulting from physical exercise. This, then, is the measure that depends upon the strength of the digestive fire.

1.5.7 | Nor does it disregard the substance [of the food]; for, with regard to the substance, it is taught that heavy foods should be taken to a third or a half of fullness, while even light foods should not be eaten to excessive fullness, for the sake of maintaining the digestive fire through proper reasoning.
1.5.8 | Indeed, food consumed in the proper measure, without impairing the natural constitution, necessarily endows the consumer with strength, complexion, happiness, and longevity.
1.5.9 | Furthermore, there are verses on this point:
Therefore, one who has ever eaten heavy food made of flour, or even flattened rice (pṛthuka), should never eat it; rather, one should eat only in moderation when truly hungry.
1.5.10 | One should not habitually consume dried meat, dried vegetables, lotus roots, or lotus stalks because of their heaviness; nor should one ever consume lean meat.
1.5.11 | One should not habitually consume fish, curd, mung beans, and barley-gruel.
1.5.12 | One should habitually consume flour preparations, śāli rice, mung beans, rock salt, āmalaka, barley,
rainwater, milk, ghee, meat from wild animals, and honey.
1.5.13 | One should employ that [regimen] constantly by which health is maintained and which prevents the arising of disorders not yet born.
1.5.14 | Hereafter, the duties pertaining to the body, such as the application of collyrium to the eyes and so forth,
will be fully explained according to their qualities with reference to the regimen for maintaining health.
1.5.15 | One should daily apply sauvīra collyrium for the benefit of the eyes;
or, for the purpose of inducing lacrimation, one should use rasāñjana every five or eight nights.
1.5.16 | The eye consists of fire (tejas); therefore, it is particularly susceptible to harm from phlegm (śleṣman).
Consequently, treatment that removes phlegm is beneficial for clarifying the vision.
1.5.17 | A sharp collyrium should not be applied to the eyes during the day;
for the vision, weakened by purgation, fails when it encounters the sun.
1.5.18 | Therefore, it is certainly desired that the collyrium be washed away at night;
for just as in the case of gold and other substances that have become variously defiled, [they must be purified].
1.5.19 | The purification of washed [objects] is by means of oil, cloth, hair, and so forth, rendering them stainless;
likewise, for the eyes of mortals, it is by means of collyrium, eye-drops, and the like.
1.5.20 | Vision appears undisturbed, like the moon in a cloudless sky.
[One should use] hareṇukā, priyaṅgu, pṛthvīkā, keśara, and nakha.
1.5.21 | Hrivera, candana, patra, tvak, elā,
uśīra, padmaka, dhyāmaka, madhuka, māṃsī, guggulu, aguru, and śarkara.
1.5.22 | The auspicious barks of the nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, and lodhra trees;
sarjarasa from the forest, musta, śaileya, and the white and blue lotuses (kamala and utpala).
1.5.23 | Having ground together śrīveṣṭaka, śallakī, and śukabarha,
one should smear that wick, which resembles a blade of barley, onto a reed shaft.
1.5.24 | The physician should prepare that wick to the size of a thumb and eight finger-breadths long;
once it is dried and its core removed, a person should insert it into the smoking pipe.
1.5.25 | One should comfortably inhale the smoke from a wick soaked in fat, ignited by fire,
prepared with muscle fat (vasā), ghee, beeswax, and excellent medicinal herbs combined according to the proper method.
1.5.26 | Having prepared an unctuous wick with the drugs of the sweet group (madhuraka), one should employ medicated smoking (dhūma).
[The ingredients include] śvetā, jyotiṣmatī, yellow orpiment (haritāla), and realgar (manaḥśilā).
1.5.27 | Scents such as aguru, patra, and others are used for fumigation to clear the head;
they alleviate heaviness of the head, headache, chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), and hemicrania (ardhāvabhedaka).
1.5.28 | Earache, eyeache, cough, hiccup, dyspnea, throat obstruction,
weakness of the teeth, and discharge arising from defects of the ears, nose, and eyes [are symptoms of vāta].
1.5.29 | Foul odor from the nose and mouth, toothache, loss of appetite, lockjaw,
stiffness of the neck, itching, worms, and pallor of the face [arise].
1.5.30 | Excessive salivation, hoarseness of voice, uvulitis, and ranula;
as well as baldness, graying of the hair, and its falling out.
1.5.31 | Sneezing, excessive drowsiness, confusion of the intellect,
and hypersomnia are alleviated by the inhalation of smoke, and physical strength becomes increased.
1.5.32 | The hair of the head, the skull, the sense organs, and the voice— these,
though located above the clavicle, do not consist of wind and phlegm, even when they are strong.
1.5.33 | Diseases of the head may arise from inhaling the smoke through the mouth.
Eight times for its administration and drinking have been fully described.
1.5.34 | Indeed, the provocation of vāta and śleṣman is observed at these times:
after bathing, after eating, after scraping the tongue, after sneezing, and after brushing the teeth.
1.5.35 | A self-controlled person should smoke after using nasal drops, collyrium, or upon waking from sleep;
thus, diseases of the supraclavicular region caused by wind and phlegm do not arise.
1.5.36 | However, for one suffering from disease, three draughts of gruel (peyā) should be taken at each of the three meals;
moreover, the wise person should drink [only] twice a day at the proper times.
1.5.37 | In practice, however, one should administer a single unctuous enema, but three or four purgative enemas;
[the signs of successful treatment are] purification of the heart, throat, and senses, lightness of the head, and alleviation [of symptoms].
1.5.38 | The symptoms of one who has properly drunk [the emetic] regarding the aforementioned defects are deafness,
blindness, muteness, internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), and vertigo of the head.
1.5.39 | Smoke that is inhaled at the wrong time or in excess causes complications.
In such cases, the drinking of ghee, as well as nasal drops (nasya), collyrium (añjana), and eye-satiation (tarpaṇa), are desired.
1.5.40 | If, in a disorder arising from smoke, the Vāyu is not overcome by Pitta, an unctuous (snaihika) treatment should be used;
however, in cases of Raktapitta, it should be cooling, and in cases of Kapha-Pitta, it should be drying (virūkṣaṇa).
1.5.41 | Next, however, I shall declare for whom the inhalation of smoke is forbidden:
one who has undergone purgation (virikta) should not drink smoke, nor should one after the administration of an enema (bastikarma).
1.5.42 | Not one afflicted by passion, nor one afflicted by poison, nor one grieving, nor a pregnant woman;
nor one exhausted, nor intoxicated, nor hungry, nor suffering from bile-fever, nor one suffering from insomnia.
1.5.43 | Not during fainting, giddiness, or thirst; not when emaciated, nor when there is a wound;
not after drinking wine or milk, nor after consuming unctuous substances (sneha), nor honey.
1.5.44 | One should not smoke after eating, nor with curd, nor when one is emaciated, nor when angry, nor when there is dryness of the palate,
nor in cases of cataract, nor when the head is afflicted.
1.5.45 | A man who, out of delusion, drinks smoke at improper times— neither during the Śaṅkhaka fever, nor Rohiṇī, nor Meha, nor in cases of intoxication— [incurs harm].
1.5.46 | His diseases increase, becoming severe, due to the improper use of smoke. One who is fit for smoking should inhale it when the morbid humors (doṣas) are localized in the head, nose, or eyes.
1.5.47 | When [the smoke] is located in the throat, one should exhale it through the nose and mouth;
while drinking mouthfuls of smoke through the mouth, one should not expel it through the nose.
1.5.48 | For smoke ascending in the reverse direction quickly injures the eyes;
therefore, with straight limbs and eyes, one-pointed in mind, and well-seated, [one should practice] for three cycles.
1.5.49 | The self-controlled practitioner should drink the smoke while closing one nostril with his fingers;
for purgation, the nozzle should be twenty-four finger-breadths long.
1.5.50 | In the application of oleation therapy, a pipe thirty-two finger-breadths long is desired;
it should be straight, provided with three bulbous joints, and its tip should be the size of a jujube seed.
1.5.51 | A smoking pipe (dhūmanetra) is recommended as having materials identical to those of the enema nozzle (bastinetra);
[the smoke] should emerge from a distance, be cut at its joints, and be thinned by the tube.
1.5.52 | Smoke, when used for the proper duration and at the right time, does not impair the sense organs;
it is so when the chest, the throat, and the head attain lightness.
1.5.53 | When the phlegm has become thin and the smoke is well-drunk, one should declare [the treatment] successful;
however, if the voice remains impure and the throat remains coated with phlegm, [it is not yet complete].
1.5.54 | When the head becomes motionless and the smoke has thus been fully inhaled, one should recognize that it has reached its limit;
at that point, the palate, the crown of the head, and the throat become parched and intensely heated.
1.5.55 | The living being becomes thirsty and faints, and blood flows excessively;
the head spins excessively, and fainting (mūrchā) arises in him.
1.5.56 | When smoke is used in excess, the sense organs are afflicted.
One should not apply *aṇutaila* every year, nor at the three [specified] times.
1.5.57 | He who practices nasal therapy (nasya-karma) at the appropriate time, as prescribed, when the sky is free of clouds during the rainy season, autumn, and spring;
1.5.58 | His sight, his sense of smell, and his hearing are not impaired;
nor shall his hair or beard ever turn white or tawny.
1.5.59 | Furthermore, the hair does not fall out but grows excessively;
there is stiffness of the neck, headache, facial paralysis, and lockjaw.
1.5.60 | Chronic rhinitis, hemicrania, and tremors of the head are pacified;
[as are disorders of] the vessels, the sutures of the cranial bones, the ligaments, and the tendons.
1.5.61 | And those who have been nourished by his inhalation (nāvana) obtain superior strength;
their face becomes bright and full, and their voice is smooth, steady, and great.
1.5.62 | All the sense organs attain clarity, and his strength increases;
moreover, diseases arising above the clavicle do not suddenly afflict him.
1.5.63 | Furthermore, old age does not gain strength over the upper parts of the body of one who is decaying.
[One should apply] sandalwood, agallochum, *patra*, the bark of *dārvī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*.
1.5.64 | Prapauṇḍarīka, sūkṣmailā, viḍaṅga, bilva, utpala, hrībera, abhaya, vanya, tvak, musta, sārivā, and sthirā.
1.5.65 | Jīvantī, pṛśniparṇī, suradāru, śatāvarī,
hareṇu, bṛhatī, vyāghrī, surabhī, and padmakeśara.
One should cook [the paste] in one hundred times its quantity of pure *māhendra* water;
when ten times the amount of oil remains, one should remove the decoction from the heat.
1.5.67 | One should cook oil with that decoction ten times;
then, during its tenth cooking, an equal portion of goat's milk [should be added].
1.5.68 | This is the procedure for administering *aṇutaila* for nasal drops (*nāvana*).
One should employ a dose of this oil measuring half a *pala*.
1.5.69 | For one whose head has been lubricated and fomented,
one should perform this procedure for seven days, administering three nasal drops with a cotton swab every third day.

1.5.70 | One who lives in a sheltered place, avoids heat, follows a wholesome regimen, eats salutary food, and has controlled senses— this oil destroys the three *doṣas* and bestows strength upon the sense organs.
1.5.71 | One who employs [these drugs] at the proper time attains the qualities as described:
[one should take them] twice a day, with the tips crushed, consisting of decoctions that are pungent and bitter.
1.5.72 | One should chew the tooth-cleansing twig without injuring the gums;

Chapter Six:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter titled "The Eighty [Verses] on Eating."
1.6.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

1.6.3ab | For one who knows seasonal suitability (ṛtusātmya) regarding activities and diet, strength and complexion increase from food such as that which has been eaten. 1.6.3cd | [This applies] to him whose seasonal suitability is understood as being based on conduct and diet.

1.6.4 | Here, indeed, one should understand the year as having six parts according to the division of seasons. Among these, one should determine the three seasons beginning with Śiśira and ending with Grīṣma as the northern course (udagayana) and the period of accumulation (ādāna) of the sun; whereas the three seasons beginning with Varṣā and ending with Hemanta are the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) and the period of release (visarga).

1.6.5 | Furthermore, during the period of emission (*visarga*), the winds blow without being excessively dry; whereas during the period of withdrawal (*ādāna*), the Moon, its strength unimpeded, constantly nourishes the world by filling it with cool rays. Therefore, the period of emission is characterized by the nature of Soma (*saumya*). The period of withdrawal, however, is characterized by the nature of Fire (*āgneya*). These two—the Sun and Wind, and the Moon—governed by the path of the inherent nature of Time (*kāla-svabhāva-mārga-parigṛhīta*), are taught to be the causal conditions for the manifestation of time, seasons, tastes, humors (*doṣa*), and the bodily strength.

1.6.6 | In that regard, the sun, taking away the moisture of the world with its rays, and the winds, which are intense and dry, causing desiccation during the seasons of early winter, spring, and summer respectively, produce dryness; by increasing the dry tastes—bitter, astringent, and pungent—they bring about weakness in human beings.

1.6.7 | During the rainy season, autumn, and early winter, when the sun faces south and its heat is diminished by time, the path of the wind, clouds, and rain, while the moon’s power remains unimpeded and the world’s heat is pacified by the waters of Indra, the non-arid tastes—sour, salty, and sweet—increase respectively; therein, the strength of men is augmented.
And there is a verse on this point:
"1.6.8ab | At the beginning and at the end, men have weakness during exhalation and inhalation;
1.6.8cd | But one should indicate that in the middle there is moderate strength, while at the end it is best and at the beginning [best] as well."

1.6.9ab | In the cold season of Hemanta, the digestive fire of strong individuals becomes even stronger, being restrained by the touch of cold winds. 1.6.9cd | It then becomes capable of digesting food that is heavy both in quantity and in substance.
1.6.10ab | When that [wind] does not find suitable fuel produced from the body, then it destroys the *rasa*. Therefore, the cold wind becomes aggravated in the cold season.
Therefore, during the season of frost, one should consume unctuous, sour, and salty tastes,
as well as the fatty meat of aquatic and marshy animals.
1.6.12ab | A man should eat the meat of hole-dwelling animals and that of those who seize their prey by force; 1.6.12cd | he should drink wine, rum, or honey-mead as an after-drink.

1.6.13ab | Cow’s milk products, preparations of sugarcane, muscle fat, oil, and freshly cooked rice; 1.6.13cd | for one who practices these in the winter and drinks warm water, his lifespan does not diminish.
1.6.14ab | One should resort to oil massage, rubbing the body, oil for the head, the *jentāka* bath, and sunlight;
1.6.14cd | as well as a warm underground chamber and likewise a warm inner room.
1.6.15ab | In cold weather, one should use enclosed vehicles, beds, and seats; 1.6.15cd | covered with woolen cloaks, skins, silken fabrics, blankets, and rugs.

1.6.16ab | Always wearing heavy, warm clothing, with his limbs smeared with thick *aguru* paste; 1.6.16cd | on his bed, he should lie with a full-bodied woman whose breasts are large and well-developed.
1.6.17ab | Embracing her whose limbs are anointed with agallochum, he should sleep, his passion kindled by intoxication.
1.6.17cd | And he should indulge in sexual union to his heart's content at the onset of the cold season.

1.6.18ab | One should avoid foods and drinks that increase wind (vāta) and those that are light; 1.6.18cd | as well as exposure to strong winds, eating in moderation, and diluted flour-drinks during the onset of winter.
1.6.19ab | The Hemanta and Śiśira seasons are equal; however, there is a slight distinction regarding Śiśira.
1.6.19cd | [This distinction consists of] dryness born of the period of extraction (Ādāna), and cold produced by clouds, wind, and rain.

1.6.20ab | Therefore, the entire regimen prescribed for the winter season is recommended for the early spring (śiśira). 1.6.20cd | However, during the early spring, one should especially resort to a warm house that is free from drafts.
1.6.21ab | One should avoid pungent, bitter, and astringent foods and drinks that increase *vāta* and are light; 1.6.21cd | as well as those that are cold, during the winter season.
1.6.22ab | Phlegm, accumulated during the spring, being stirred up by the rays of the sun, 1.6.22cd | afflicts the bodily fire and thereby produces many diseases.
1.6.23ab | Therefore, one should perform therapeutic procedures such as emesis and others during the spring season.
1.6.23cd | One should avoid heavy, sour, unctuous, and sweet foods, as well as sleeping during the day.

1.6.24ab | During the onset of spring, one should practice physical exercise, dry massage, medicinal smoking, gargling, and the application of collyrium. 1.6.24cd | One should also habitually perform the rules for cleansing with lukewarm water.

1.6.25ab | With his limbs anointed with sandalwood and aloe, and subsisting on barley and wheat; 1.6.25cd | [he may eat] the meat of the śarabha, the śaśa, the eneya deer, the quail, and the partridge.

1.6.27cd | At that time, food and drink that are sweet, cold, liquid, and unctuous are beneficial.

1.6.28cd | [One who partakes of] ghee, milk, and śāli rice does not suffer in the summer.
1.6.29ab | One should drink wine either in small quantities or not at all, or else with a great deal of water.
1.6.29cd | One should avoid salt, sourness, pungency, heat, and physical exercise.

1.6.30ab | During the day he should sleep in a cool chamber, and at night, being attended by those cooled by the rays of the moon; 1.6.30cd | adorned with pearls and gems, he should resort to this [lifestyle].
1.6.31ab | Fanned with fans and touched by hands cooled with sandalwood water, 1.6.31cd | Adorned with pearls and gems, he should enjoy her company.

1.6.32ab | During the summer season, a man who abstains from sexual intercourse should frequent cool forests, waters, and flowers. 1.6.32cd | [He should frequent] cool forests, waters, and flowers. 1.6.32cd | During the summer season, a man who abstains from sexual intercourse should frequent [them].
1.6.33ab | When the body is weakened by improper intake, the digestive fire (paktā) becomes weak.
1.6.33cd | It is then further afflicted during the rainy season by the vitiating factors of wind (anila) and the other humors.
1.6.34ab | From the earth's vapors, from the discharge of clouds, and from the sourness resulting from the ripening of water;
1.6.34cd | during the rainy season, when the strength of the digestive fire has diminished, the wind and the other humors become aggravated.

1.6.36cd | One should generally partake of drinks and foods prepared with honey.

1.6.39ab | One should drink a small amount of *mādhvīkāriṣṭa* mixed with honey, or water;

1.6.40ab | He should be devoted to rubbing the body, massaging with unguents, bathing, perfumes, and garlands. 1.6.40cd | Wearing clean garments, he should occupy a dwelling that is not damp during the rainy season.

1.6.41ab | For those whose bodies have become accustomed to the cold of the rainy season, when they are suddenly heated by the rays of the sun, 1.6.41cd | the accumulated *pitta* generally becomes aggravated in the autumn.
1.6.42ab | In that condition, food and drink that are sweet, light, cold, and slightly bitter; 1.6.42cd | which pacify pitta, should be consumed in the proper measure by those who desire recovery.

1.6.43ab | Quails, francolin partridges, antelopes, rabbits, wild sheep, and hares; 1.6.43cd | as well as rice, barley, and wheat—these they call the foods to be enjoyed at the end of the rainy season.
1.6.44ab | The drinking of bitter ghee, purgation, and bloodletting; 1.6.44cd | [these] should be performed at the end of the rainy season, as well as the avoidance of the sun's heat.
1.6.45ab | One should avoid fat, oil, frost, the meat of aquatic and marshy animals, 1.6.45cd | alkali, curd, sleeping during the day, and the eastern wind in this case.
1.6.46ab | Scorched by the rays of the sun during the day and cooled by the rays of the moon at night;
1.6.46cd | ripened by time, free from defects, and rendered non-venomous by Agastya.
1.6.47ab | Known as *haṃsodaka*, the autumnal water is pure and stainless;
1.6.47cd | for bathing, drinking, and immersion, this water is beneficial like nectar.
1.6.48ab | And autumnal garlands and spotless garments,
1.6.48cd | are praised in the autumn season, as are the rays of the moon at twilight.

1.6.49ab | Thus has been described seasonal suitability (ṛtusātmya), which is based on activity and diet. 1.6.49cd | That which is conducive due to appropriateness is called environmental suitability (okasātmya).

1.6.50ab | Those who know what is wholesome (*sātmya*) maintain that wholesomeness consists in qualities that are the opposite of those of the [local] regions and diseases, as well as of one's own habitual qualities. 1.6.50cd | They also consider the first [instance of] consumption and conduct to be wholesome.

1.6.51ab | Whatever should or should not be practiced by men during each respective season,
1.6.51cd | has been explained, along with its causes and what constitutes suitability (*sātmya*), in the chapter on the "Eighty" (*Aśitīya*).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, named "The Eighty," in the Section on Verses (*Ślokasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Seven.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the non-suppression of natural urges (*Navegāndhāraṇīya*).
1.7.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.7.3cd | nor those of semen, nor of wind, nor of vomiting, nor of sneezing.

1.7.4cd | nor tears, nor sleep, nor sighing caused by fatigue.

|) (1.7.33.1cd | as well as the constriction of the heart and other organs—this is the characteristic of physical exercise.

(1.7.35.1cd) those men who are overcome by anger, grief, fear, or exhaustion;

1.7.40cd | for their bodily constitution is said to be one that follows the latent tendencies of the *doṣas*.
1.7.41ab | For those whose qualities are contrary [to their constitution], the regimen for maintaining health is beneficial.
1.7.41cd | A balanced diet containing all tastes and that which is congenial is recommended for one with balanced *dhātus*.

One should recognize the presence of impurity by its heaviness and the depletion of impurity by its lightness; furthermore, one should discern the state of the channels of impurity through excessive obstruction or discharge.

1.7.45ab | These and other diseases arise in those who lead an irregular life while in a state of health; therefore, one should be devoted to the regimen for maintaining health while healthy.
In the first month of Mādhava, again in the first month of Nabhasya,
and likewise in the first month of Sahasya, one should eliminate the accumulation of impurities.

1.7.47ab | For those whose bodies have been lubricated and fomented, the wise physician should always first administer enemas (basti) and nasal therapies (nasya), both upwards and downwards. 1.7.47cd | Thereafter, he should perform the enema procedure and the nasal treatment.

1.7.48ab | From this point forward, one who knows the proper time should employ, in due order and according to suitability, 1.7.48cd | proven rejuvenative formulations (rasāyana) and aphrodisiac preparations (vṛṣyayoga).
1.7.49ab | Likewise, diseases do not arise when the bodily constituents (dhātus) remain in their natural state. 1.7.49cd | The constituents flourish, and old age approaches with diminished vigor.
1.7.50ab | This rule has been demonstrated regarding the non-occurrence of disorders;
1.7.50cd | but for those that are innate and others, it will be taught separately.
1.7.51ab | Those exogenous diseases of humans which arise from spirits, poisons, wind, fire, combat, and so forth; 1.7.51cd | in these, it is the intellect that commits the transgression.
1.7.52ab | Envy, grief, fear, anger, pride, hatred, and so forth—
1.7.52cd | all these mental afflictions are said to arise from intellectual error (prajñāparādha).
1.7.53ab | The abandonment of errors of judgment, the tranquility of the senses, and mindfulness;
1.7.53cd | Knowledge of place, time, and the self, and the following of the conduct of the virtuous.
1.7.54ab | This path has been shown for the non-arising of adventitious [afflictions]. 1.7.54cd | A wise person should therefore perform beforehand that which he knows to be beneficial for himself.

1.7.55ab | The knowledge of authoritative instruction and its practical application are the causes for the non-arising of disorders and for the pacification of those already arisen. 1.7.55cd | [These are the causes] for the non-arising of disorders and for the pacification of those that have arisen.
1.7.56ab | Those of evil conduct, speech, and disposition are informers, fond of quarreling,
1.7.56cd | who mock at others' vital points, greedy, envious of the prosperity of others, and deceitful.

1.7.57ab | Those who delight in slandering others, the fickle, those who serve their enemies, 1.7.57cd | the merciless, and those who have abandoned righteousness— these lowest of men are to be avoided.
1.7.58ab | By means of their intelligence, learning, age, character, fortitude, memory, and concentration;
1.7.58cd | The elders who serve the aged are themselves aged, knowing the true nature [of things] and free from distress.

1.7.59ab | Those who are well-disposed toward all beings, tranquil, and firm in their praised vows; 1.7.59cd | Those who speak of the true path and whose hearing and sight are meritorious—these are to be served.
1.7.60ab | One who desires happiness both in this world and after death, regarding diet, conduct, and activities,
1.7.60cd | should apply the greatest effort toward the practice of what is beneficial, being possessed of intelligence.
1.7.61ab | One should not eat curd at night, nor without ghee and sugar;
1.7.61cd | nor without green gram soup, nor without honey, nor when hot, nor without *āmalaka* fruits.
One who is fond of curd but neglects the prescribed regimen may suffer from fever, hemorrhagic disorders, biliousness, erysipelas, leprosy, anemia, vertigo, and even severe jaundice.
1.7.63 | Regarding this, there are these verses:
1.7.63ab | The urges, the diseases arising from those urges, and their remedies;
1.7.63cd | which urges should be restrained, for what purpose, and what is beneficial or harmful [in each case].
