1.7.64ab | There is a sequential order regarding what is appropriate and harmful, what is to be avoided and what is to be practiced, as well as what is improper.
1.7.64cd | Likewise, diet, the cleansing of the channels, and medicinal drugs follow their respective natural orders.
1.7.65ab | That which is the medicine for the non-arising of future diseases,
and 1.7.65cd | those persons who are to be avoided or served by a wise man seeking his own welfare.
In this chapter on the suppression of natural urges, the sage, the son of Atri, has explained everything regarding the manner and the reason why curd should be consumed.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Non-Restraint of Natural Urges," in the Section on General Principles of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.8.0 | Eighth Chapter | 1.8.1ab | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the examination of the sense organs (indriyopakramaṇīya).
1.8.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.8.3 | It has been stated in the section on the sense organs that there are indeed five sense organs, five substantial entities of the sense organs, five bases of the sense organs, five objects of the sense organs, and five cognitions of the sense organs.

1.8.4 | Furthermore, some say that the mind (*manas*), which is beyond the senses, is designated as *sattva* or *cetas*; its activity depends upon the attainment of its objects and the self, and it serves as the causal condition for the activity of the sense organs.

1.8.5 | Furthermore, because of the deviation from its own object, the objects of the senses, and volitional intentions, the *sattva* (mental faculty) within a single person is manifold. Moreover, due to its association with the qualities (*guṇas*) of *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*, it is not manifold [in its essence]. For it is not the case that one [entity] functions toward many [objects] simultaneously; therefore, the activity of all the sense organs does not occur at one and the same time.
1.8.6 | The sages teach that the *sattva* which constantly follows a person according to its qualities is indeed that very *sattva*, because of the predominance of its latent tendencies.
1.8.7 | The sense faculties, preceded by the mind, become capable of grasping their respective objects.
1.8.8 | Therein, the five sense faculties are the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
1.8.9 | The five elemental substances are ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
1.8.10 | The seats of the five sense-faculties are the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the tongue, and the skin.
1.8.11 | The objects of the five sense faculties are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

1.8.12 | The cognitions of the five sense organs—beginning with visual cognition—are produced from the contact of the sense organ, the sense object, the self, and the mind; they are momentary and determinate in nature. This constitutes the "five pentads."

1.8.13 | Mind, the objects of the mind, intellect, and the self—this is the summary of the qualities of the internal substances; it is also the cause for the engagement in or withdrawal from the auspicious and inauspicious, as well as that which is called action (kriyā), which is dependent upon substance.

1.8.14 | In that regard, although the sense organs are composed of a collection of transformations of the five great elements and are thus inferable, fire is specifically present in the eye, space in the ear, earth in the nose, water in the tongue, and air in the organ of touch.
Therein, whatever element a sense organ is predominantly composed of, it perceives its corresponding object by virtue of that specific nature and its pervasive power.

1.8.15 | Through excessive application, non-application, or improper application toward their respective objects, the sense organ, together with the mind, undergoes a morbid change and leads to the impairment of its corresponding faculty of cognition; conversely, through the restoration of its capacity, it returns to its natural state and nourishes its corresponding faculty of cognition.
1.8.16 | Regarding the mind, however, the object is that which is to be thought about.
In that regard, those same forms of association—equal, excessive, deficient, and erroneous—are the causes of the natural state and its transformation for both the mind and the mental faculty.

1.8.17 | In this regard, one should strive by these means for the natural state of the senses together with the mind so that they do not suffer affliction when they are afflicted; namely, through the appropriate union of the self, the senses, and their objects; by the repeated right examination of actions with the intellect; and by the practice of measures contrary to the qualities of place, time, and the self.
Therefore, everyone who desires to achieve their own welfare should always adhere to mindfulness and practice virtuous conduct in every respect and at all times.

1.8.18 | By practicing that, one simultaneously achieves two goals: health and mastery over the senses. O Agniveśa, we shall teach you that entire code of right conduct (sadvṛtta) in its entirety. It is as follows: one should worship the gods, cows, Brahmins, teachers, elders, perfected beings (siddhas), and preceptors; one should tend the sacred fire; one should wear auspicious medicinal herbs; one should perform ablutions twice a day; one should frequently cleanse the excretory orifices and the feet; and every three fortnights, one should have the hair of the head, beard, body, and nails trimmed.

He should always wear untorn garments, be cheerful and fragrant, maintain a dignified appearance, and keep his hair well-groomed. He should regularly apply oil to his head, ears, nose, and feet; he should inhale medicinal smoke, be the first to speak, and possess a pleasant countenance. He should assist those in distress, act as a priest (*hotṛ*), perform sacrifices, give gifts, pay homage at crossroads, offer oblations (*bali*), honor guests, present funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to the ancestors, and speak at the proper time words that are beneficial, measured, and sweet. He should be self-controlled, righteous in nature, free from envy regarding the cause, and free from envy regarding the result.

Free from anxiety, fearless, modest, wise, highly energetic, skillful, patient, righteous, and a believer; one who serves those who are advanced in discipline, intellect, learning, lineage, and age, as well as perfected masters and teachers; carrying an umbrella and a staff, wearing a turban and sandals, he should walk looking only a yoke’s length ahead; being habituated to auspicious conduct, he should avoid tattered clothes, bones, thorns, impurities, heaps of hair and chaff, ashes, potsherds, bathing grounds, and places where offerings are made; and until he becomes fatigued, he should refrain from strenuous physical exercise, remaining a friend to all living beings.

He may be one who conciliates the angry, encourages the frightened, and assists the distressed; one who is true to his word, primarily employs conciliation, endures the harsh speech of others, destroys resentment, perceives the virtue of tranquility, and is a destroyer of the causes of passion and hatred.

1.8.19 | One should not speak untruth; one should not take what belongs to another; one should not desire the wife of another nor the wealth of another; one should not take pleasure in enmity; one should not commit sin; one should not be a sinner even toward a sinner; one should not speak of the faults of others; one should not discover the secrets of others; one should not sit with the unrighteous, nor with those who hate the king, nor with the insane, nor with the outcaste, nor with killers of embryos, nor with the base, nor with the wicked; one should not mount defective vehicles; one should not sit upon a hard seat that is level with the knees.

One should not resort to a bed that is not spread with various coverings, not well-supported, not spacious, or uneven; one should not wander upon mountain peaks or rugged terrain; one should not climb trees; one should not plunge into the swift current of water; one should not sit in the shade of a funeral pyre; one should not walk about amidst a fire-eruption; one should not laugh loudly; one should not release sound-filled wind (flatus); one should not yawn, sneeze, or laugh with the mouth uncovered; one should not pick at the nose; one should not grind the teeth; and one should not snap the nails.

One should not strike bones, nor scratch the ground, nor cut grass, nor crush clods of earth; one should not move the limbs in an improper manner; one should not gaze at celestial bodies, nor at anything undesirable, impure, or inauspicious; one should not utter the sound "hum" toward a corpse; one should not step on the shadow of a shrine, a banner, a teacher, or those worthy of worship, nor on anything inauspicious; one should not frequent at night temples, shrines, crossroads, burial grounds, parks, cemeteries, or places of execution; one should not enter an empty house or a forest alone, nor [associate with] those of evil conduct.

One should associate with women, friends, and servants; one should not oppose superior persons, nor attend upon those who are inferior; one should not take pleasure in crookedness, nor resort to the ignoble; one should not cause fear, nor indulge in rashness, excessive sleep, staying awake at night, bathing, drinking, or eating; one should not stand for long with the knees raised; one should not approach predatory beasts, nor animals with fangs or horns; one should avoid headwinds, the heat of the sun, frost, and violent gusts; one should not initiate quarrels; one should not attend to the sacred fire without being composed, nor while impure from food remnants, nor while holding it below.

One should perform the ablution while exerting oneself; one should not touch water while still fatigued, nor with a face that has not been immersed, nor while naked. One should not touch the head with the bathing-cloth, nor strike the tips of the hair. Having performed the ablution, one should not wear those same two garments. Without having touched gems, clarified butter, objects of worship, auspicious items, and flowers, one should not go outside. One should not pass by objects of worship and auspicious things keeping them to the left, nor other objects keeping them to the right.

1.8.20 | One should not eat without wearing jewels on the hand, nor without having bathed, nor while wearing soiled garments; nor without having recited prayers (*japa*), nor without having offered oblations to the deities, nor without having presented offerings to the ancestors (*pitṛs*); nor without having given to teachers, nor to guests, nor to those who have sought refuge; nor without wearing auspicious perfumes, nor without wearing garlands; nor without having washed one's hands, feet, and face; nor with an impure mouth; nor facing north; nor with a distracted mind; nor when the attendants are undevoted, undisciplined, impure, or hungry; nor in unholy vessels, nor in an improper place, nor at an improper time, nor in a crowded place; nor without first giving a portion to the fire, nor that which has not been sprinkled with consecrated water (*prokṣaṇa*).

One should not consume food that has not been consecrated with mantras, nor food that is contemptible, nor food that is loathsome or served in a repugnant manner; one should not eat stale food, except for meat, green vegetables, dried vegetables, fruits, and snacks; one should not eat everything on one’s plate, except for curd, honey, salt, barley-meal, and ghee; one should not eat curd at night; one should not eat barley-meal alone, nor at night, nor after having already eaten, nor in large quantities, nor twice [in one sitting], nor from what is separated by water; and one should not eat it after having cut it up by the twice-born.

1.8.21 | One should not eat while not upright; one should not eat, nor sleep, nor attend to other duties while suffering from the urge to void; one should not eject phlegm, feces, or urine facing the wind, fire, water, the moon, the sun, a twice-born person, or a teacher; one should not urinate on a path, nor in a populated place, nor at the time of eating; and one should not discharge mucus or nasal secretions while engaged in recitation, fire-offerings, study, ritual offerings, or auspicious rites.
1.8.22 | One should not despise a woman, nor place excessive confidence in her, nor disclose secrets to her, nor entrust her with authority.

One should not engage in sexual intercourse with a woman who is menstruating, nor one who is ill, nor one who is impure, nor one who is inauspicious, nor one whose appearance, conduct, or hospitality are disagreeable; nor one who is unskilled, nor one who is not generous, nor one who is unwilling, nor one who desires another, nor another’s wife, nor one of a different species, nor in a non-vaginal opening; nor at a shrine, a crossroads, a four-way junction, a grove, a cemetery, an execution ground, or in water; nor among medicinal herbs, nor near Brahmins, teachers, or temples of the gods; nor during the two twilights, nor while guests are present; nor when one is impure, nor when one has not taken medicine, nor when one has not formed a firm resolve, nor when one’s joy has not been aroused, nor when one has not eaten, nor when one has overeaten, nor when one is in an unstable position.
One who is oppressed by the urge to urinate or defecate, nor one afflicted by fatigue from exertion, physical exercise, or fasting, should not engage in sexual intercourse.

1.8.23 | One should not speak ill of the virtuous or of one's teachers; being impure, one should not perform rites of sorcery, worship at shrines, honor those worthy of veneration, or engage in Vedic study.

1.8.24 | One should not practice the study [of the Veda] during lightning storms or unseasonable winds; nor when the quarters of the sky are ablaze; nor during a conflagration, an earthquake, or a great festival; nor during the fall of meteors or the approach of a great planetary conjunction; nor on a lunar day when the moon has disappeared; nor during the two twilights; nor without the Guru being present before one; nor that which is dropped, nor excessive, nor exhausted, nor discordant, nor with unstable words, nor too fast, nor too slow, nor too weak, nor uttered with sounds that are excessively high or low.

1.8.25 | One should not abandon established conventions, nor should one break a rule of conduct. One should not wander about at night or in improper places; during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*), one should not engage in eating, Vedic study, sexual intercourse, or sleep. One should not form friendships with children, the elderly, the greedy, the foolish, the afflicted, or the impotent. One should have no fondness for intoxicants, gambling, or association with prostitutes. One should not disclose secrets, nor should one despise anyone. One should not be conceited, nor incompetent, nor lacking in courtesy, nor envious. One should not revile Brahmins, nor [cows].

He may raise the rod of punishment, but he must not insult the elderly, teachers, assemblies, or kings; nor should he speak excessively, nor should he cast out kinsmen, those who are devoted to him, those who have shared his hardships, or those who know his secrets.

1.8.26 | He should not be lacking in fortitude, nor excessively haughty in spirit; he should not fail to support his dependents, nor lack trust in his own kin; he should not seek pleasure alone, nor follow a disposition, conduct, or practice characterized by misery; he should not place his confidence in everyone, nor suspect everyone, nor deliberate at all times.

1.8.27 | One should not let the time for action pass by; one should not persist in what has not been examined; one should not be a slave to the senses; one should not allow the restless mind to wander; one should not impose an excessive burden upon the organs of perception and action; one should not be a procrastinator; one should not follow after anger or joy; one should not dwell in sorrow; one should not yield to arrogance upon success nor to dejection upon failure; one should constantly remember one's true nature; one should be certain of the power of causes and ever intent on initiating causal actions; one should not rest content merely with what has been done; one should not abandon vigor; and one should not dwell upon criticism.

1.8.28 | One who is impure shall not offer oblations into the fire with the finest clarified butter, unbroken grains, sesame seeds, *kuśa* grass, and mustard seeds while seeking blessings for himself. [He should instead recite: "May Agni not depart from my body; may Vāyu bestow the vital breaths upon me; may Viṣṇu bestow strength upon me; may Indra bestow valor upon me; may the auspicious waters enter me. He should touch water while reciting the hymn *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. Having wiped his lips twice and sprinkled water on his feet, he should touch the apertures of his head, as well as his own self, heart, and head, with water.
1.8.29 | He should be devoted to celibacy, the giving of knowledge, friendliness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and tranquility.

1.8.30 | Regarding this, there are these verses: 1.8.30ab | "The five pentads have been taught, as well as the mind and the fourfold causes; 1.8.30cd | [all of this], along with good conduct, has been explained in its entirety in this chapter on the sense organs."
1.8.31ab | He who properly follows the regimen for the healthy as it has been prescribed, 1.8.31cd | remains free from disease for a hundred years and is not deprived of his lifespan.
1.8.32ab | Honored by the virtuous, he fills the world of men with his fame; 1.8.32cd | He attains both dharma and artha and becomes a kinsman to all living beings.
1.8.33ab | One who performs meritorious deeds attains the worlds of those who have done good.
1.8.33cd | Therefore, this conduct should be practiced by everyone at all times.
1.8.34ab | And whatever else there may be that is not mentioned here but is worthy of honor,
1.8.34cd | Ātreya always approves of that conduct as well.
1.8 Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Introduction to the Senses," in the Section on General Principles (*Ślokasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
This concludes the second section, the "Quadruplet on the Healthy Person" (*Svasthacatuṣka*).
1.9.0 Ninth Chapter.
1.9.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the "Minor Four Pillars" (Khuḍḍākacatuṣpāda).
1.9.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.9.3ab | The physician, the medicinal substances, the attendant, and the patient constitute the four pillars. 1.9.3cd | When endowed with their respective qualities, they should be known as the causes for the pacification of disease.
1.9.4ab | Morbid alteration (vikāra) is the disequilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātu), while their equilibrium is called the natural state (prakṛti).
1.9.4cd | Health is designated as happiness, and morbid alteration is indeed suffering.

1.9.5ab | When there is a disorder of the bodily constituents (dhātu), the activity of the four praised factors beginning with the physician, directed toward the restoration of the equilibrium of those constituents, is designated as "treatment" (cikitsā).
1.9.5cd | [This activity] is called treatment because its purpose is the re-establishment of the balance of the constituents.
1.9.6ab | Thorough mastery of the scriptures, having observed medical procedures many times, 1.9.6cd | Dexterity, and purity— these are to be known as the four qualities of a physician.
1.9.7ab | Abundance, suitability for that [purpose], manifold conceptualization,
and excellence— this fourfold set is said to be the quality of substances.
1.9.8ab | Knowledge of proper conduct, dexterity, and affection for her husband; 1.9.8cd | and purity—this fourfold quality is [required] in a person who attends to one.
1.9.9ab | Retentiveness, compliance with instructions, and likewise fearlessness;
1.9.9cd | as well as the capacity to provide information regarding diseases—these are recorded as the qualities of a patient.
1.9.10ab | The cause for success consists of sixteen qualities and four pillars.
1.9.10cd | The knower, the instructor, the applicator, and the primary factor—these constitute the physician here.

1.9.11ab | For just as the cooking vessel, fuel, and fire are the causes for a cook in the act of cooking; 1.9.11cd | so too are the terrain, the army, and weapons the means for a victor in his conquest.
1.9.12ab | Likewise, the patient and the others are the factors designated as causes for success.
1.9.12cd | Therefore, among these, the physician is the primary cause in medical treatment.

1.9.13ab | Just as clay, the staff, the wheel, the string, and so forth, do not produce their effect without a potter; 1.9.13cd | so too the three components [of medicine] do not bring about their quality without a physician.
1.9.14ab | Just like a city of the Gandharvas, their most dreadful transformations go to destruction;
1.9.14cd | whereas others, awaiting the proper means, quickly attain growth.

1.9.15ab | When the three factors are present, both the wise and the ignorant may act as physicians; however, it is better that the ignorant person sacrifice himself than that he should practice medicine.
1.9.15cd | It is preferable for the ignorant one to offer up his own life than to engage in medical treatment.

1.9.16ab | Just as one who is blind and ignorant moves like someone terrified by the movements of his own hands; 1.9.16cd | so does an ignorant physician proceed in his medical practices, driven like a boat by the force of the wind.
1.9.17ab | Having rescued one whose life span is fixed by chance,
1.9.17cd | a physician who fancies himself a healer quickly kills hundreds of those whose life spans are not fixed.

1.9.18ab | Therefore, a physician who is engaged in the fourfold application—namely, in the knowledge of the meaning of the treatise, in its practical application, and in the observation of clinical procedures—is called a "rescuer of life. 1.9.18cd | [A physician] who is endowed with this quartet is termed a *prāṇābhisara*.
1.9.19ab | He who possesses fourfold knowledge regarding the cause, the symptoms, the pacification, and the non-recurrence of diseases; 1.9.19cd | that king-deserving physician is the best of all.

1.9.20ab | Weapons, scriptures, and water act according to the virtues or defects of the recipient. 1.9.20cd | Therefore, for the sake of medical treatment, one should purify one's wisdom by taking the patient into account.
1.9.21ab | Knowledge, deliberation, discernment, mindfulness, devotion to that [goal], and action— 1.9.21cd | for one who possesses these six qualities, nothing remains unachievable.
1.9.22ab | Knowledge, intelligence, practical experience, repeated practice, success, and a [worthy] refuge—
1.9.22cd | each one of these is sufficient for the accomplishment of the title "physician."

1.9.23ab | But he in whom all these auspicious qualities, such as knowledge and the rest, are present; 1.9.23cd | he, being a bestower of happiness to living beings, deserves the title of "physician" in its true sense.
1.9.24ab | The scripture is for the purpose of illumination, and insight is the intellect of the self.
1.9.24cd | A physician who treats with these two properly employed does not commit an error.
1.9.25ab | Since three quarters of medical treatment depend upon the physician,
1.9.25cd | therefore the physician should exert effort toward the perfection of his own qualities.

1.9.26ab | Friendliness toward those who are suffering, compassion for the afflicted, affection for those who are capable [of improvement], and equanimity toward those established in their natural state— 1.9.26cd | such is the fourfold conduct of a physician.
1.9.27 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
1.9.27ab | The physician’s victory has four pillars; each pillar consists of four qualities.
1.9.27cd | The physician is the most important among the pillars, for such are the qualities of the healer.
1.9.28ab | The various types of knowledge and the fourfold divine intellect of physicians—
1.9.28cd | all of this has been fully elucidated in the *Khuḍḍākacatuṣpāda* chapter.
1.9 | Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Minor Four Pillars," in the Section on Verses (*Ślokasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.10.0 | The Tenth Chapter.
1.10.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the "Great Four Pillars" (*Mahācatuṣpāda*).
1.10.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.10.3 | "Medicine has four pillars and sixteen components," so say the physicians; that which was described in the previous chapter as possessing sixteen qualities—that medicine, when applied with proper reasoning, is sufficient for health—thus spoke the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya.

1.10.4 | "No," says Maitreya. "For what reason? Because we see some who are afflicted with disease, yet possessing the necessary means, provided with attendants, self-controlled, and treated by skilled physicians, and thus recovering; while others, though similarly situated, are dying. Therefore, medicine is of no avail, just as: a small amount of water poured into a chasm or a lake, or a handful of dust scattered upon a flowing river or a heap of sand."

Likewise, others are seen who, lacking resources and attendants, being devoid of self-control, and treated by unskilled physicians, recover even while undergoing such treatment; yet others, though treated in the same manner, die. Furthermore, there are cases where one recovers by receiving treatment and dies despite it, while another recovers without treatment and dies without it. Therefore, it is considered that medicine is not distinct from non-medicine.

1.10.5 | "Maitreya! It is wrongly thought," said Ātreya, "for what reason? That which was stated—that those patients who die despite being provided with this medicine endowed with sixteen qualities—is untenable. For medicine is never a non-cause for diseases that are curable by medicine. Furthermore, as for those patients who recover even without medicine alone, it is not the case that they lack the specific conditions for recovery that would have been met by the provision of complete medicine."

For just as a person might provide strength to a man who has fallen along with his chariot in order to raise him up, so that he might rise more quickly and without exhaustion, even so it is for the sick upon obtaining the complete medicine.

Furthermore, there are those who are ill and die even from the best of medicines; yet it is not the case that all those provided with medicine would recover. For not all diseases are curable by means; nor is there success through lack of means for diseases that are curable by means; nor does this collection of medicines exist for diseases that are incurable. Indeed, a wise physician is not able to raise up a patient who is about to die; for it is the experts who act after due examination.

For just as an archer who knows the art of yoga and is constant in practice, taking up his bow and shooting an arrow at a large target that is not too distant, does not fail and accomplishes his intended task, so too a physician endowed with his own qualities and equipped with the necessary instruments, having observed [the patient] and commencing the treatment, does not fail regarding a curable disease and certainly establishes the patient in health; therefore, medicine is not indistinguishable from non-medicine.

1.10.6 | Furthermore, this is evident to us: when we treat the diseased with medicine that is not itself diseased, the emaciated with what is not emaciated, and we nourish the thin and weak, deplete the obese and fatty, treat with cold that which is overcome by heat, and with heat that which is overcome by cold; when we replenish deficient tissues and diminish those that are excessive, and by treating diseases through the reversal of their roots, we establish them properly in their natural state—for us who act in this manner, this collection of medicines becomes most desirable.
And there are verses on this point:
1.10.7ab | A physician who understands the distinction between the curable and the incurable, and who acts with prior knowledge,
1.10.7cd | undertakes his work at the proper time and certainly achieves success.
1.10.8ab | A physician who treats an incurable patient will certainly suffer the loss of wealth, knowledge, and reputation, as well as censure and the failure to gather followers.
1.10.8cd | He shall surely incur these misfortunes if he attempts to treat one whose condition is beyond cure.
1.10.9ab | That which is curable is considered to be either easily curable or difficult to cure;
1.10.9cd | and the incurable is of two kinds: that which is palliable and that which is untreatable.
1.10.10ab | Regarding the curable [diseases], there is a threefold distinction according to their being slight, moderate, or severe.
1.10.10cd | However, there is no such variation for the incurable; for those [diseases] that are certain [to be fatal], there is no alternative.

1.10.11ab | For one whose causes, premonitory symptoms, and signs are slight, 1.10.11cd | and for whom the affected constituent (dūṣya) does not possess qualities identical to those of the humor (doṣa), that humor shall not become the primary constitution (prakṛti).
1.10.12ab | Neither is the quality of the time equal [to the disease], nor is the location difficult to treat;
1.10.12cd | there is only one course [of action], the disease is not chronic, and there are no complications.

1.10.13ab | Furthermore, there is a single condition for the onset [of curability]: the body is capable of withstanding all medicinal treatments. 1.10.13cd | And the presence of the four therapeutic pillars (catuṣpāda) is the characteristic of that which is easily curable.
1.10.14ab | When the signs, premonitory symptoms, and manifest forms possess moderate strength;
1.10.14cd | And when there is a commonality among the season, the constitution, and the affected tissue, or among any one of them.
1.10.15ab | For pregnant women, the elderly, and children, [a disease] that is not excessively afflicted by complications;
1.10.15cd | one that is not amenable to surgical, caustic, or thermal treatments, and which arises in a difficult location.

1.10.16ab | One should recognize a disease as curable with difficulty when it follows a single path, is not fully developed in all four stages, or follows two paths; or when it is not excessively chronic, or is produced by two doṣas.
1.10.17ab | Because some portion of life remains, it is palliative and incurable through the observance of wholesome regimens;
1.10.17cd | it yields little pleasure, and with a slight cause, it quickly recurs.

1.10.18ab | A disease that is deep-seated, located in many tissues, and dependent upon the vital points (marmans) and joints; 1.10.18cd | which is constantly persistent and remains for a long duration.
1.10.19ab | One should know that [the disease] arising from two doṣas is likewise [incurable], as is that arising from all three doṣas;
1.10.19cd | as well as that which has transcended the path of treatment and that which follows all pathways.
1.10.20ab | It causes anxiety, aversion, and delusion, and destroys the sensory faculties;
1.10.20cd | it is especially fatal for one who is weak, and it constitutes a disease accompanied by fatal signs (ariṣṭa).

1.10.21ab | Having first thus examined the specific characteristics of the disorders, the wise physician should thereafter undertake the commencement of treatment for those conditions that are curable.

1.10.22ab | He who knows the distinction between the curable and the incurable and possesses correct understanding, 1.10.22cd | would not entertain a false notion regarding those who are equal to Maitreya.
1.10.23 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
1.10.23ab | Herein are the medicinal herbs, the qualities of the quarters, the sources, and the basis of therapeutics;
1.10.23cd | the intellects of Ātreya and Maitreya, and the determination regarding the two-fold nature of the intellect.

1.10.24ab | Furthermore, the fourfold classifications of diseases, each with its own specific characteristics, have been described in the *Mahācatuṣpāda*; upon these depends the physician’s success in treatment.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, named "The Great Fourfold Division," in the Section on General Principles of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.11.0 | Chapter Eleven.
1.11.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the three pursuits (*tisraiṣaṇīya*).
1.11.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.11.3 | Indeed, here in this world, a person whose strength, intellect, manliness, and prowess are unimpaired, perceiving what is beneficial both in this world and in the world beyond, must pursue three kinds of quests.
Namely: the quest for life, the quest for wealth, and the quest for the world beyond.
1.11.4 | Of these pursuits, one should first attend to the pursuit of life.

Why? Because when life is abandoned, everything is abandoned. Its preservation consists in the following: for one who is healthy, the adherence to the regimen for health; for one who is afflicted, vigilance in the pacification of disorders. Both of these have been stated and will be further explained. By not deviating from what has been prescribed and by preserving life, one attains a long lifespan; thus, the first pursuit has been explained.

1.11.5 | Now, one might turn to the second pursuit, the desire for wealth; for after life itself, it is wealth that must be sought. Indeed, there is nothing more wretched than a long life devoid of the means of subsistence; therefore, one should strive to acquire the necessary resources.

In this regard, we shall explain the means of acquiring resources: namely, agriculture, animal husbandry, trade, service to the king, and so forth; as well as whatever other actions one may know to be blameless among the virtuous and conducive to the nourishment of one's livelihood, those one should undertake to perform. By acting thus, a man lives a long life and becomes free from distress.
Thus, the second pursuit, the quest for wealth, has been explained.
1.11.6 | Now, one might enter upon the third pursuit, that of the world beyond.

And here there arises a doubt: "Shall we exist after passing away from this world, or not? Why, then, this doubt? It is said in reply: For there are some who rely solely on direct perception and, because rebirth is imperceptible, have resorted to nihilism; yet others accept rebirth based solely on the authority of scripture. Furthermore, due to conflicting Vedic texts: "Some consider the mother and the father to be the cause of birth. [And so forth.]
"Others [hold that it arises from] inherent nature, the creation of another, or chance.
Thus, there is doubt: does rebirth indeed exist, or does it not?
1.11.7 | In this regard, a wise person should abandon both the mindset of nihilism and doubt.

Why? Because that which is perceptible is indeed limited, whereas there exists a non-perceptible reality that is not limited, which is apprehended through scripture, inference, and reasoning. Furthermore, even those very sense organs by which something is perceived as perceptible exist in a non-perceptible state.

1.11.8 | Furthermore, there is non-perception through direct perception of existing forms due to extreme proximity, extreme distance, obstruction, weakness of the sense organs, non-steadiness of the mind, blending with similar objects, being overwhelmed, and extreme subtlety. Therefore, it is said without examination that only the directly perceived exists and nothing else exists.
1.11.9 | Furthermore, these [scriptural] passages are not authoritative, because they contradict reason.
1.11.9ab | If that self which belongs to the mother or the father were to migrate into the offspring;
1.11.9cd | would that self migrate in its entirety, or by means of a single part?
1.11.10ab | If the entire [subtle body] were to move away, there would be the death of the mother or the father.
1.11.10cd | There is not any part whatsoever of the subtle self that is not continuous [with the gross body].
1.11.11ab | Intellect and mind are determined to be exactly like the self;
1.11.11cd | for those who hold this view, there is no fourfold origin.
1.11.12ab | One should know that the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the six elements is innate; 1.11.12cd | yet in their conjunction and their separation, action alone is the cause.

1.11.13ab | The creation by another is not admitted for the beginningless element of consciousness. 1.11.13cd | If the Supreme Self is accepted as its cause, then let it be considered a creation by another.
1.11.14ab | There is no examination, nor that which is to be examined; there is no agent, nor any cause.
1.11.14cd | There are no gods, no seers, and no perfected ones (siddhas); there is neither action nor the fruit of action.
1.11.15ab | For the nihilist whose mind is struck by caprice, there is no self at all.
1.11.15cd | And this possession by nihilism is a sin greater than all other sins.
Therefore, the wise man, having abandoned this mindset that has strayed onto an improper path,
should perceive everything as it truly is by means of the lamp of the intellect of the virtuous.
1.11.17 | Indeed, everything is of two kinds: existent and non-existent. Its examination is fourfold: authoritative testimony, perception, inference, and reasoning.
1.11.18 | First, those who are authoritative (āpta) are as follows:
1.11.18ab | Those who are liberated from passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) by the power of austerity and knowledge;
1.11.18cd | Whose stainless knowledge is always unimpeded at all times.
1.11.19ab | Those who are authoritative, disciplined, and awakened—their word is undoubtedly true. 1.11.19cd | Why would they speak untruth, being free from passion and darkness?
1.11.20ab | That cognition which arises from the contact of the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects; 1.11.20cd | being manifest at that very moment, it is defined as perception (pratyakṣa).

1.11.21ab | That which was previously perceived is inferred in three ways and across the three times. 1.11.21cd | Hidden fire is inferred by smoke; sexual intercourse is inferred from the sight of a pregnancy.
1.11.22ab | Thus do the wise determine that the future fruit arises from the past seed, 1.11.22cd | having observed here in this very world that the fruit produced from a seed is similar [to it].

1.11.23ab | From the conjunction of water, tilling, seed, and season, the production of crops occurs; 1.11.23cd | likewise, through the conjunction of the six elements, there is the production of embryos.
1.11.24ab | From the conjunction of the fire-drill, the wood to be drilled, and the act of drilling, fire is produced.
1.11.24cd | Likewise, a combination of the four pillars of treatment, when applied with reason, is the destroyer of disease.
1.11.25ab | That intellect which perceives phenomena born from the conjunction of many causes,
1.11.25cd | is to be known as *yukti* (reasoning) pertaining to the three times, by which the three aims of life (*trivarga*) are accomplished.
1.11.26ab | This is the examination; there is no other by which everything is examined.
1.11.26cd | That which is to be examined consists of both the existent and the non-existent; and by this [examination], rebirth exists.

1.11.27 | In this regard, authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) is first the Veda; furthermore, any other discourse on the scriptures composed by investigators that is not contrary to the meaning of the Veda, which is approved by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and directed toward the welfare of the world, is also authoritative scripture. From authoritative scripture it is understood that generosity, austerity, sacrifice, truthfulness, non-violence, and celibacy bring about both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
1.11.28 | Nor is rebirthlessness taught through the gateways of dharma for those who have not transcended the defects of their mental essence by means of being free from defects.

1.11.29 | One should thus resolve that rebirth was seen and taught by the ancient and more ancient great seers (maharṣis)—those who were intent upon the gateway of dharma, free from fear, passion, hatred, greed, delusion, and pride, devoted to Brahman, authoritative, knowers of action, whose movement of being and intellect was unimpaired, and who possessed divine vision.

1.11.30 | Furthermore, it is perceived even through direct observation: children who are dissimilar to their parents; differences in complexion, voice, form, temperament, intellect, and fortune among those born of similar origins; birth into high or low families; slavery or sovereignty; happiness or unhappiness; longevity or its lack; the attainment here of what was not performed [in this life]; the spontaneous occurrence of crying, suckling, laughing, fear, and so forth in those who have not been taught; the manifestation of bodily marks; and the variation in results despite similarity in action, as well as the presence of intelligence in some cases and its absence in others.
Skill in action, memory of past births—including the return here after passing away from this world—and the perception of the pleasant and unpleasant as equal.

1.11.31 | For this very reason, it is inferred as follows: that which is self-performed, unavoidable, indestructible, pertaining to a previous body, designated as "fate" (daiva), and continuous—this is its fruit; and from this, another [fruit] will arise in the future. From the fruit, the seed is inferred, and from the seed, the fruit.

1.11.32 | And this is the reasoning: the birth of an embryo results from the collection of the six elements; action arises from the conjunction of the agent and the instrument; the fruit belongs to the deed performed, not to one not performed; there is no production of a non-existent thing from what is not its seed; the fruit corresponds to the action; and nothing is produced from a seed other than that which is appropriate to it—this is the reasoning.

1.11.33 | Thus, when rebirth has been taught by means of these four authorities, one should apply oneself to the gateways of dharma, as follows: in service to the teacher, in study, in the observance of vows, in the taking of a wife, in procreation, in the maintenance of dependents, in the honoring of guests, in giving, in freedom from covetousness, in austerity, in freedom from malice, in unafflicted action of body, speech, and mind, in the investigation of the body, the senses, the objects, the intellect, and the self, and in the concentration of the mind.

Furthermore, whatever other such actions there may be that are not censured by the virtuous, which lead to heaven and promote one's livelihood, he should know them and undertake to perform them; by acting thus, he gains fame in this world and heaven after death.
Thus, the third desire for the next world has been explained.
1.11.34 | Now, indeed, there are three supports, three types of strength, three bases, three diseases, three pathways of disease, three kinds of physicians, and three types of medicine.

1.11.35 | "The three supports" refers to: diet, sleep, and celibacy. Supported by these three when they are applied according to reason, the body—strengthened and augmented by these supports—endures for as long as the force of its life-span (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) lasts, provided one does not neglect the regimen that will be taught right here.

1.11.36 | Strength is threefold: innate, seasonal, and produced by application. That which belongs to the body and the mind by nature is innate; that which arises from the divisions of time, such as the seasons, and from age is seasonal; furthermore, that which is born from the application of diet and activity is produced by application.

1.11.37 | Regarding the "three bases"—namely, objects, actions, and time—their excessive application (*atiyoga*), non-application (*ayoga*), and perverse application (*mithyāyoga*) [are the causes]. Among these, the excessive viewing of visible objects that possess extreme brilliance is *atiyoga*; the total absence of viewing them is *ayoga*; and the viewing of forms that are excessively close, excessively distant, fierce, terrifying, wonderful, hateful, loathsome, deformed, or frightening, and so forth, is *mithyāyoga*. (Note: *darśanam* is supplied).

Likewise, excessive hearing of sounds such as those of thunder, drums, or shouting constitutes *atiyoga* (excessive application); total non-hearing is *ayoga* (non-application); and hearing harsh sounds, or sounds that cause the destruction of what is desired, injury, assault, or terror, constitutes *mithyāyoga* (perverse application). Similarly, excessive smelling of extremely sharp, pungent, or obstructing odors is *atiyoga*; total non-smelling is *ayoga*; and smelling putrid, loathsome, impure, moist, poisonous, windy, or corpse-like odors is *mithyāyoga*. (Omission of *śravaṇam* and *ghrāṇam*).

Likewise, excessive consumption of tastes is *atiyoga* (excessive application); total non-consumption is *ayoga* (lack of application); and improper application (*mithyāyoga*) will be taught in the specific section concerning the rules for food, excluding the categories [of quantity]. Similarly, the excessive indulgence in tactile objects that are extremely cold or hot—such as bathing, anointing, and massage—is *atiyoga*; the total non-indulgence in them is *ayoga*; and the improper application (*mithyāyoga*) consists of indulging in tactile objects such as bathing, cold, or heat out of sequence, as well as injuries from uneven positions and contact with impure beings.

1.11.38 | Among these, one [quality]—touch—is pervasive among the sense organs and inherent in the mind (*cetas*); furthermore, the mind is also pervasive due to its pervasion by touch. Therefore, that specific state produced by the pervasive quality of touch, which arises from non-conduciveness (*anupaśaya*), constitutes the fivefold and threefold variety of unwholesome contact between the senses and their objects (*asātmyendriyārthasaṃyoga*); for the meaning of "conducive" (*sātmya*) is indeed the meaning of "conducive to well-being" (*upaśaya*).
1.11.39 | Action (*karma*) is the activity of speech, mind, and body.

Among these, excessive activity of speech, mind, and body is *atiyoga* (excessive application); total non-activity is *ayoga* (lack of application); and improper activity of the body—such as suppressing natural urges, forcing them out, stumbling, falling, contorting the limbs, injuring the limbs, striking, massaging, obstructing the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and causing affliction—is *mithyāyoga* (wrong application). Improper activity of speech—such as slandering, lying, quarreling at the wrong time, speaking what is unpleasant, incoherent, unrefined, or harsh words—is *vāṅmithyāyoga*. Improper activity of the mind—such as fear, grief, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, and false views—is *mānaso mithyāyoga*.

1.11.40 | In brief, one should understand that improper application (mithyāyoga) consists of all unwholesome actions born of speech, mind, and body—whether previously mentioned or not—that are characterized by either excessive application (atiyoga) or deficient application (ayoga).
1.11.41 | Thus, one should determine that the threefold action, which consists of the threefold conceptualization, is indeed "intellectual error" (*prajñāparādha*).
1.11.42 | Furthermore, the year consists of the seasons characterized by cold, heat, and rain—namely, winter, summer, and the rainy season—and that is time (*kāla*).

Among these, time characterized by excessive features is "excessive application of time" (*kālātiyoga*); time characterized by deficient features is "non-application of time" (*kālāyoga*); and time characterized by features contrary to its own natural characteristics is "perverse application of time" (*kālamithyāyoga*).
Moreover, time is said to be transformation (*pariṇāma*).

1.11.43 | Thus, unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects, intellectual error, and transformation—these three, each having three varieties, are the causes of disorders; however, when joined with wholesome contact, they become the causes of the natural state.

1.11.44 | The existence and non-existence of all things are not perceived apart from proper application (yoga), lack of application (ayoga), excessive application (atiyoga), and wrong application (mithyāyoga); for existence and non-existence depend upon their respective proper methods of application.

1.11.45 | There are three types of diseases: endogenous (nija), exogenous (āgantu), and mental (mānasa). Among these, the endogenous arises from the bodily humors (doṣas); the exogenous arises from spirits, poisons, wind, fire, physical assault, and so forth; whereas the mental arises from the attainment of the desired or the non-attainment of the undesired.

1.11.46 | In this regard, even one who is afflicted by mental disease should strive, with an intelligent mind, to repeatedly discern through his intellect what is beneficial and what is harmful; he should endeavor to avoid those things among virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) that are harmful, and to cultivate those that are beneficial. For in this world, nothing—whether happiness or suffering—is accomplished without these three mental factors. Therefore, this should be practiced: one should strive to attend upon those who possess knowledge of these matters, and to understand accurately one's own self, country, family, time, strength, and capacity.
And there is a verse on this point:

47ab | Regarding the mind, the remedy is the contemplation of the three aims of life; 47cd | as well as service to those who possess that knowledge, and full understanding of the self and so forth in every respect.

1.11.48 | Regarding the "three pathways of disease": they are the peripheral tissues (*śākhā*), the vital points, bones, and joints (*marmāsthisandhi*), and the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*). Among these, the peripheral tissues consist of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) such as blood and the skin; this is the external pathway of disease. Furthermore, the vital points include the bladder, heart, head, and so forth; the bones and joints refer to the unions of bones and the tendons and ligaments attached to them; this is the intermediate pathway of disease. Finally, the visceral cavity is referred to in the treatise by synonymous terms such as the great channel (*mahāsrotas*), the middle of the body, the great depression, and the receptacles for undigested and digested food (*āmapakvāśaya*); this is the internal pathway of disease.

1.11.49 | In that regard, diseases such as swellings, pustules, alaji, apacī, skin tags (carmakīla), fleshy growths (adhimāṃsa), moles (maṣaka), leprosy (kuṣṭha), and freckles (vyaṅga), as well as visarpa, swelling, abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids (arśas), and abscesses (vidradhi), follow the external path; whereas diseases such as hemiplegia (pakṣavadha), seizures (graha), facial paralysis (apatānaka), facial distortion (ardita), wasting (śoṣa), consumption (rājayakṣman), pain in the bones and joints, prolapse of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa), and diseases of the head, heart, and bladder follow the middle path.

Diseases such as fever, diarrhea, vomiting, indigestion, choleraic pain, cough, dyspnea, hiccups, abdominal distension, splenic disorders, and others arising in the internal channels; as well as erysipelas, edema, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, abscesses, and others following the path of the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), come into being.

1.11.50 | "Physicians are of three kinds" (1.11.50ab). There are those who practice under the pretext of being physicians; some are those who have attained success through [secret] means; 1.11.50cd | there are those endowed with the true qualities of a physician; thus are physicians of three kinds on earth.
1.11.51ab | Those who obtain the title of physician through medical instruments, medicines, books, [medical] plants, or mere appearances; 1.11.51cd | being ignorant, they are merely impostors.

1.11.52ab | Those who acquire the title of "physician" by means of their reputation for fame, honor, or knowledge, though they do not possess those qualities; 1.11.52cd | they should be known as "those who have attained success through artificial means."
1.11.53ab | Those who are perfected in the knowledge of application, specialized knowledge, and spiritual attainments, bestowing happiness;
1.11.53cd | they are the followers of life, and within them the state of true medical science is established.

1.11.54 | Medicine is of three kinds: that which relies on divine power (*daivavyapāśraya*), that which relies on rational application (*yuktivyapāśraya*), and the subjugation of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*).

Among these, that which relies on divine power consists of mantras, medicinal herbs, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, burnt sacrifices, observances, expiations, fasts, benedictions, prostrations, pilgrimages, and so forth. That which relies on rational application is the systematic administration of food and medicinal substances. The subjugation of the mind is the restraint of the mind from unwholesome objects.

1.11.55 | Indeed, when the bodily humors (doṣas) are provoked, physicians generally prescribe three types of therapy directed toward the body itself: internal cleansing, external cleansing, and the application of surgical instruments.

Among these, internal cleansing (*antah-parimārjana*) refers to that which, having entered the interior of the body, removes diseases through medicinal substances and dietary preparations; whereas external cleansing (*bahiḥ-parimārjana*) refers to that which, relying on external contact, removes ailments through massage, fomentation, ointments, affusions, rubbing, and so forth. Furthermore, the application of instruments (*śastra-praṇidhāna*) consists of excision, incision, puncturing, splitting, scraping, lancing, scarifying, suturing, probing, cauterization with alkali (*kṣāra*), and leeches (*jalaukas*).
1.11.56 | Furthermore, there are verses on this point:
1.11.56ab | When a disease has arisen, whether external or internal, a wise person attains relief through medical treatment or by the application of surgical instruments.
1.11.56cd | [He attains relief] through action or by the employment of a weapon.
1.11.57ab | Indeed, the fool, through either delusion or negligence, does not perceive;
1.11.57cd | the first disease as it arises, like an ignorant man [failing to see] an enemy.
1.11.58ab | For a disease, having first become minute, subsequently increases in magnitude.
1.11.58cd | Once it has taken root, it robs the fool of both strength and life.
1.11.59ab | One who is deluded does not regain consciousness as long as he is not afflicted.
1.11.59cd | But once afflicted, he subsequently applies his mind toward the suppression of the disease.
1.11.60ab | Then, having summoned his sons, wives, and kinsmen, he says:
1.11.60cd | "Let someone bring a physician for me, even at the cost of my entire fortune."
And who is capable of protecting such a person— one who is weak, afflicted by disease,
emaciated, with failing senses, miserable, and whose life has reached its end?
1.11.62ab | Not finding a protector, that fool gives up his life,
1.11.62cd | like a monitor lizard whose tail has been caught and is being dragged away by a stronger force.
Therefore, one who desires his own well-being should apply remedies even before diseases arise, or while they are still in their early stages.
Regarding this, there are two verses (1.11.64):
The desires, the supports, the strength, the causes, and the diseases;
the paths of the physician and the medicines—these are [the subjects] in the chapter on the Three Desires (Tisraiṣaṇīya).
1.11.65ab | Eight factors have been taught as being threefold by the wise Kṛṣṇātreya, who is unattached to worldly objects; 1.11.65cd | in these, everything is established.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Threefold Quest," in the Section on General Principles of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.12.0 | Chapter Twelve.
1.12.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the Vātakalākalīya (the classification of the powers of wind).
1.12.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.12.3 | Desiring to know each other’s opinions regarding the knowledge of the qualities and functions of Vāta, the great sages sat together and asked one another: "What are the qualities of Vāyu? What are its aggravating factors, or what are its pacifying measures? How do aggravating and pacifying factors provoke or pacify it, given that it is not a composite substance, is without a fixed location, and is intangible? And what are the actions of this wind—both when it is agitated and when it is unagitated—as it moves within bodies or outside of bodies?"
1.12.4 | Regarding this, Kuśa Sāṅkṛtyāyana said: "Roughness, lightness, coldness, harshness, coarseness, and clarity—these six are the qualities of vāta."

1.12.5 | Having heard those words, Bharadvāja Kumāraśiras said: "It is exactly as the Blessed One has said; these indeed are the qualities of vāta. However, when actions possessing such qualities, such substances, and such potencies are practiced repeatedly, vāyu undergoes provocation (prakopa). For the practice of things with similar qualities is the cause of the increase of the bodily constituents (dhātus)."

1.12.6 | Having heard those words, Kāṅkāyana, the physician of the Bāhlīkas, said: "It is exactly as the venerable one has stated; these very factors are indeed provokers of vāta, and those opposite to them are the pacifiers of vāta, for the reversal of what provokes the dhātus is the cause of their pacification."

1.12.7 | Having heard those words, Baḍiśa Dhāmārgava said: "It is exactly as the Blessed One has stated; these indeed are the factors that pacify the provocation of Vāta. For we shall explain how the factors that provoke or pacify [Vāta] do so by reaching this [Vāta], which is non-composite and unstable. The factors that provoke Vāta in the bodies are those that produce dryness, lightness, coldness, harshness, roughness, clarity, and porosity; in such bodies, Vāta, having found its substrate and becoming nourished, undergoes provocation."

Furthermore, those things which pacify wind (vāta) are unctuous, heavy, hot, smooth, soft, slimy, and dense; when moving within bodies of such a nature, the wind, no longer becoming obstructed, attains pacification.

1.12.8 | Having heard those words of Baḍiśa—which were truthful and approved by the hosts of ṛṣis—the royal sage Vāryovida said: "It is exactly so; all this is beyond reproach, just as the Blessed One has said."

Now, having established through direct perception, inference, and authoritative instruction the various functions—whether occurring within bodies or outside of bodies—of Vāyu, who moves both within and without the body when provoked or unprovoked, we shall describe them to the best of our ability after paying homage to Vāyu. Vāyu is the sustainer of the body's systems and mechanisms; he consists of Prāṇa, Udāna, Samāna, Vyāna, and Apāna; he is the initiator of all high and low movements; the restrainer and director of the mind; and the stimulator of all the sense organs.

When unagitated, it carries all the objects of the senses; it arranges the constituents of the entire body; it provides cohesion for the body; it sets speech in motion; it is the source of touch and sound; it is the root of the ears and the sense of touch; it is the origin of joy and enthusiasm; it fans the fire of digestion; it dries up the morbid humors (doṣas); it expels external impurities; it opens the large and minute channels; it fashions the forms of the embryo; and it serves as the sustaining condition for the continuity of life.

When indeed provoked within the body, it afflicts the body with various disorders for the destruction of strength, complexion, happiness, and lifespan; it agitates the mind, impairs all the sense organs, destroys fetuses, causes deformities, or causes them to be retained for an excessive period; it generates fear, grief, delusion, dejection, and excessive lamentation, and it obstructs the vital breaths.

Indeed, for him who exists as the primordial nature (prakṛti) moving through the world, these activities occur: namely, the supporting of the earth, the kindling of fire, the regulation of the continuous movement of the sun, moon, constellations, and the hosts of planets, the creation of clouds, the discharge of waters, the setting in motion of streams, the production of flowers and fruits, the sprouting of plants, the differentiation of the seasons, the division of the elements, and the manifestation of the forms and dimensions of those elements.
The preparation of the seed, the growth of the crop without over-wetting or drying out, and the absence of harmful transformation.

When the self has become agitated and moves through the worlds, these are its actions: namely, the crushing of mountain peaks, the uprooting of trees, the churning of the oceans, the overflowing of lakes, the reversing of rivers, the shaking of the earth, the swelling of clouds, the emission of mist, frost, dust, sand, fish, crocodiles, snakes, alkaline matter, blood, stones, and thunderbolts, the disruption of the six seasons, and the destruction of crops and living beings.
He is the one who brings about calamities and the cause of the non-existence of beings; he is the emission of clouds, the sun, fire, and wind—the destroyers at the end of the four ages.

For that Blessed One is both the source and the imperishable; he is the creator of the existence and non-existence of beings, the ordainer of pleasure and pain, death, Yama, the restrainer, Prajāpati, Aditi, Viśvakarman, Viśvarūpa, the omnipresent, the ordainer of all systems, the subtle atom of all entities, the pervasive Lord, Viṣṇu who has traversed the worlds, and indeed the Blessed Wind of the worlds.

1.12.9 | Having heard those words of Vāryovida, Marīci said: "Even if this is so, what capacity does this [knowledge] have for either explaining or understanding the purpose of medical science? This discussion has been undertaken with reference to the science of medicine."

1.12.10 Vāryovida said: If a physician does not first examine the wind (vāyu)—which is exceedingly powerful, extremely harsh, very swift in its action, and life-threatening—how could he, even with great care, speak of protecting it when it has suddenly become provoked? Indeed, he would do so even earlier out of fear of a fatal crisis. Furthermore, praise of the wind according to its true nature leads to health, the increase of strength and complexion, brilliance, nourishment, the attainment of knowledge, and the excellence of the supreme lifespan.

1.12.11 | Marīci said: It is fire itself, situated within the body as bile (pitta), which—whether provoked or unprovoked—produces both auspicious and inauspicious effects. These include: digestion and indigestion, vision and blindness, moderation and excess of heat, natural state and morbid change, and the colors of health and disease; as well as courage, fear, anger, joy, delusion, clarity, and other such pairs of opposites.

1.12.12 | Having heard those words of Marīci, Kāpya said: "It is Soma itself, situated within the phlegm (śleṣman) in the body, which—whether agitated or unagitated—produces good and evil effects; namely, firmness, looseness, growth, emaciation, energy, laziness, virility, impotence, knowledge, ignorance, intellect, delusion, and other such pairs of opposites."

1.12.13 | Having heard those words of Kāpya, the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya said: "All of you have spoken correctly, with the exception of your absolute certainty; for indeed, all the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman*, when in their natural state (*prakṛtibhūta*), endow a person with unimpaired senses, strength, complexion, and happiness, and with a long life—just as dharma, artha, and kāma, when properly practiced, endow a person with great ultimate well-being in this world and the next."
Indeed, the three seasons themselves, having undergone a great transformation, bring about a change in him through a vast reversal, so that the world is struck by misfortune at a time of calamity.
1.12.14 | All the sages approved of those words of the venerable Ātreya and rejoiced in them.
And on this point there is a verse:
1.12.15ab | Having heard those words of Ātreya, everyone indeed agreed; 1.12.15cd | and the farmers rejoiced, just as the gods did at the word of Indra.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
1.12.16ab | There are six qualities, two types of causes, and furthermore, three types of actions;
1.12.16cd | the fourfold action of vāyu, and separately, those of kapha and pitta.
Whatever is the opinion of the great seers and whatever is the wisdom of Punarvasu,
all of that has been fully elucidated in this section on the subtle and gross aspects of wind (Kalākalīya).

1.12 | Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Enumeration of the Qualities of Vata," in the Section on General Principles (*Ślokasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
(12) This concludes the "Quadripartite Instruction" (*Nirdeśacatuṣka*).
1.13.0 | The Thirteenth Chapter.
1.13.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on oleation therapy (sneha).
1.13.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.13.3ab | To Punarvasu, who was seated together with the Sāṃkhyas who had calculated all that is to be calculated, 1.13.3cd | Vahniveśa asked his own doubt for the sake of the welfare of the world.

1.13.4 | What are the sources of the fats, how many are they, and what are their individual properties? What are the times for post-drink administration, for whom are they indicated, how many are there, and what are the considerations?

1.13.5 | How many measures are there, how are they measured, and what [measure] is prescribed for whom? What kind of unctuous substance is beneficial for whom, and what is the maximum dose for oleation?

1.13.6 | Who are those who require oleation and who do not? What are the signs of one who is unoleated, properly oleated, and excessively oleated? What is beneficial before the drink, when it has been drunk, and when it has been digested? What is wholesome and what is unwholesome?
1.13.7 | Who possess soft or hard bowels? What are the complications and what are the successes? What is the desired procedure regarding clear [therapies], purification, and oleation?
1.13.8 | O Lord of immeasurable wisdom, in what things are these investigations to be employed, and by what method? I desire to know this knowledge regarding affection.
1.13.9 | Then Punarvasu, the dispeller of that doubt, replied:
"O gentle one, the source of oily substances is twofold: immobile and mobile."
1.13.10 | Sesame, priyāla, abhiṣuka, bibhītaka, citrā, abhayā, eraṇḍa, madhūka,
mustard, kusumbha, bilva, āruka, mūlaka, atasī, nikocaka, akṣoḍa, karañja, and śigru;
1.13.11 | Likewise, those known as stationary sources of fat include [plants], while mobile ones consist of fish, wild animals, and birds.
Among these, curd, milk, ghee, meat, muscle fat, and marrow are likewise prescribed as sources of fat.
1.13.12 | Of all varieties of oil, sesame oil is the most excellent;
castor oil is the foremost for strength, for oleation, and for purgation.
Castor oil is pungent, hot, heavy, and removes vāta and kapha;
when combined with astringent, sweet, and bitter [substances], it also destroys pitta.
Ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow are considered the best among all unctuous substances.
And among these, clarified butter is indeed the best, because it conforms to the requirements of refinement.
1.13.14 | Ghee alleviates pitta and vāta; it is beneficial for the plasma, semen, and ojas. It is cooling, softening, and clarifies the voice and complexion.
1.13.15 | This oil destroys wind, does not increase phlegm, increases strength,
is beneficial for the skin, hot in potency, provides stability, and cleanses the female reproductive tract.
1.13.16 | Fat is desired for those suffering from wounds, fractures, blows, or injuries to the vagina, ears, or head;
for increasing virility, for oleation therapy, and for physical exercise.
1.13.17 | Bone marrow increases strength, semen, plasma, phlegm, fat, and marrow;
it especially provides strength to the bones and is beneficial for oleation.

1.13.18 | Ghee should be drunk in autumn; muscle fat and marrow in spring; and oil in the rainy season. A person should drink unctuous substances when it is neither excessively hot nor excessively cold.
1.13.19 | A person with a predominance of vāta and pitta should drink it at night or during the heat;
one with a predominance of śleṣman should drink it by day or when the sun is cool.
1.13.20 | If drunk when it is excessively hot, or during the day, or by one in whom vāta and pitta predominate,
it may provoke fainting, thirst, insanity, or jaundice.
1.13.21 | A man who drinks unctuous substances at night during the cold season, even if he has a predominance of phlegm (śleṣman), may suffer from abdominal distension (ānāha),
loss of appetite (aruci), colic (śūla), or jaundice (pāṇḍutā).
1.13.22 | Warm water should be drunk after ghee; vegetable broth is recommended after oil;
after muscle fat or marrow, the scum (maṇḍa) should be taken; or else, warm water may be used after all of them.
1.13.23 | Boiled rice, gruel, meat broth, meat, milk, curd, barley gruel,
soup, vegetables, vegetable broth, *kāmbalika*, and *khaḍa*.
1.13.24 | Barley meal, sesame paste, fermented liquors, electuaries,
as well as solid foods, unguents, enemas, and urethral enemas.
1.13.25 | Mouth-rinsing, oil for the ears, nasal therapy, and the saturation of the ears and eyes—
these twenty-four are the applications of oleaginous substances (sneha). 1.13.26 | However, that oleaginous substance which is to be drunk clear is not called an application (vicāraṇā).
This method for oleation observed by the physician is considered the primary or foremost procedure.
1.13.27 | Fat (sneha), when combined with the six tastes—both individually and in combination—attains sixty-three varieties; and when taken alone, it constitutes one.
1.13.28 | Thus, these sixty-four formulations of oleaginous substances (sneha) should be applied by one who possesses knowledge, according to the place, season, disease, and the individual patient.
1.13.29 | The large, medium, and small doses of unctuous substance are expected to take a full day and night, a full day, and half a day respectively to reach digestion.
1.13.30 | Thus, three measures of unctuous substance have been specified according to their quantity;
I shall now describe their administration for each individual person.
1.13.31 | Those men who are constantly accustomed to abundant fats, who endure hunger and thirst,
whose digestive fire is of supreme strength, and who are preeminent in physical power;
1.13.32 | Those suffering from abdominal tumors, those bitten by snakes, those afflicted with erysipelas (visarpa),
the insane, those with difficult urination, and those with constipation;
1.13.33 | One should drink it in the highest dose; hear now the benefits of drinking it.
When properly administered, this quickly pacifies all disorders.
The dose that draws out the humors follows all pathways;
it is strengthening and restores the body, the senses, and the mind to youthfulness.
1.13.35 | Those afflicted by eruptions, boils, pustules, itching, and similar symptoms;
those suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders, and gout (vātaśoṇita).
1.13.36 | Those who do not eat excessively, those with a mild digestive tract,
and likewise those of moderate strength, should drink a medium dose.
1.13.37 | This dose is characterized by a mild impairment [of the senses] and does not excessively deplete strength;
it emolliates easily and is employed for the purpose of purification (śodhana).
1.13.38 | However, those who are elderly or young, those who are delicate and accustomed to comfort,
those for whom an empty stomach is unwholesome, and those with weak digestive fire— [for them, this is not recommended].
1.13.39 | Those who suffer from fever, diarrhea, or cough that have persisted for a long time,
as well as those who are small in stature or deficient in strength, should drink a small dose of unctuous substance (sneha).
1.13.40 | This dose is pleasant during elimination; it provides oleation and nourishment, is aphrodisiac, strengthening, free from complications, and its effects persist for a long time.
1.13.41 | Those of vāta-pitta constitution, those afflicted by vāta-pitta disorders,
those desiring clear vision, the wounded, the emaciated, the elderly, children, and likewise the weak;
Those who desire the prolongation of life, those seeking strength, complexion, and a clear voice; those desiring nourishment, those desiring progeny, and those seeking delicacy of body.
Those who desire luster, vigor, memory, intelligence, digestive fire, the faculties of perception, and strength,
as well as those afflicted by burning sensations, weapons, poisons, or fire, should drink ghee.
Those whose phlegm and fat are increased, whose throats and bellies are unstable and large, those afflicted by wind-related diseases, and those of a windy temperament; ||| 1.13.44 ||
1.13.45 | Those embodied beings who desire strength, leanness, lightness, firmness, stability of the limbs, and smooth, supple, and thin skin [should resort to this].
1.13.46 | Those with worms in the digestive tract, those with a harsh digestive tract, those afflicted by fistulas,
and those accustomed to oil should drink oil during the cool season.
1.13.47 | Those who endure wind and heat, those who are parched, those emaciated by carrying loads and traveling long distances,
whose semen and blood have dried up, and whose phlegm and fat have been consumed;
1.13.48 | Those in whom the powerful Vāyu remains, having obstructed the channels and causing great pain in the bones, joints, veins, ligaments, vital points (marmans), and the abdominal cavity;
1.13.49 | For those men who possess great digestive power and for whom fat is wholesome, the drinking of muscle fat is prescribed as a means of oleation.
1.13.50 | Those with a keen digestive fire, who can endure hardship, who are voracious eaters,
who consume fats, those afflicted by Vata, and those with a hard bowel, should receive oleation therapy using marrow.

1.13.51 | That specific unctuous substance (sneha) which is beneficial for each particular individual has been thus described. Regarding the maximum duration of oleation therapy, it is seven nights or three nights.

1.13.52 | Those who require sudation or purification, those who are dry, those suffering from disorders of Vata, those constantly engaged in physical exercise, wine, or women, and those who are given to excessive thinking, should be treated with oleation.
1.13.53 | For those for whom drying therapy is prescribed instead of purification,
oleation is not recommended, as their phlegm and fat are excessively increased.
1.13.54 | Those whose mouths and rectums are constantly discharging secretions, those with chronically weak digestive fire,
those overcome by thirst and fainting, pregnant women, and those suffering from dryness of the palate— [should not undergo emesis].
1.13.55 | Those who loathe food, those vomiting, those afflicted by stomach ailments or poisons,
the weak, the exhausted, those debilitated by oleation therapy, and those intoxicated with wine;

1.13.56 | Those undergoing nasal therapy (nastaḥ), bladder enemas (basti), or rectal enemas (varti) should not be given unctuous substances. From the intake of such unctuous substances during these procedures, very severe diseases arise in them.
1.13.57 | Feces that are knotted or dry, wind that is displaced and weak,
and a digestive fire characterized by harshness and dryness— these are the signs of lack of unctuousness (asnigdha) in the body.
1.13.58 | The downward movement of wind, a stimulated digestive fire, non-adherent and unctuous stools,
and softness and oiliness in the limbs arise from those who have been treated with oleation.
1.13.59 | Pale complexion, heaviness, dullness, undigested stools,
drowsiness, loss of appetite, and horripilation are the signs of excessive unctuousness (atisnigdha).

1.13.60 | One who wishes to drink oil the following day should eat food that is liquid, warm, non-obstructive to the channels, in the proper quantity, not excessively unctuous, and unmixed with other substances.
1.13.61 | When desiring food at mealtime, one should drink pacifying oil;
for the sake of purification, however, a person should drink it after the evening meal has been digested and before the next meal.
1.13.62 | One should use warm water for attendance, observe celibacy, and sleep at night;
one should not suppress feces, urine, flatus, or eructations when they have arisen.
1.13.63 | One should avoid physical exertion, loud speaking, anger, grief, cold, and heat; one should resort to a sleeping place and seat that are sheltered from the wind.
1.13.64 | A man who, after drinking oil, consumes oil again,
develops severe diseases due to the improper administration of oil.
1.13.65 | A person with a soft bowel habit becomes oleated after three nights by the consumption of clear [medicinal] liquids;
however, a person with a hard bowel habit becomes oleated after seven nights.
Molasses, sugarcane juice, whey, milk,
churned curd, milk-rice, kṛśarā, ghee, and the decoction of kāśmarya and triphalā.
1.13.67 | Having drunk grape juice, or the juice of the *pīlu* fruit, or even warm water,
or fresh wine, a person with a soft bowel is purged.
1.13.68 | These [purgatives] never cause purgation in one with a hard bowel;
in one with a hard bowel, the *grahaṇī* is characterized by excessively aggravated wind (*vāta*).
1.13.69 | When the *grahaṇī* has aggravated *pitta*, diminished *kapha*, and mild *vāyu*, it belongs to one with a soft bowel; therefore, such a person is considered easy to purge.
1.13.70 | In one whose *grahaṇī* is dominated by *pitta* yet possesses great digestive fire-power,
the ingested fat is quickly reduced to ashes by the intensity of that fire.
1.13.71 | Having consumed that dose of unctuous substance, the powerful digestive fire, while spreading its vital energy (ojas),
may provoke an intense thirst accompanied by complications.
Even very heavy food is not sufficient to pacify one who is saturated with passion;
if he does not obtain cool water, he is consumed by fire,
just as a venomous serpent dwelling in the midst of dry grass is consumed by the fire of its own poison.
1.13.73 | If thirst should arise while the unctuous substance (sneha) is undigested, the physician should induce emesis;
having drunk cold water again and eaten dry food, he should then vomit.
1.13.74 | Ghee alone is not [indicated] in cases of pitta, especially when accompanied by āma; for it would color the entire body, destroy consciousness, and cause death.
1.13.75 | Lassitude, nausea, constipation, fever, stiffness, loss of consciousness,
skin diseases, itching, pallor, swelling, hemorrhoids, anorexia, and thirst.
