1.13.76 | Abdominal enlargement, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, numbness, suppression of speech, colic,
and complications from undigested matter (*āma*) arise from the improper administration of oleation (*sneha*).
In that case as well, scraping (ul lekha na) is recommended, as are sudation (sveda), waiting for the appropriate time,
and purgation (sraṃsana), having assessed the strength of each respective disease.
1.13.78 | The administration of *takrāriṣṭa*, the consumption of dry foods and drinks,
the various urines, and *triphalā* are the remedies for complications arising from oleation therapy.
1.13.79 | Oil that is administered at the wrong time, or that which is unwholesome, or not applied in the proper measure,
or due to improper treatment, may cause harm even when used excessively.
1.13.80 | After three nights have passed since the application of unctuous substances, the person should drink the enema fluid;
having eaten unctuous, warm liquid food and rice with meat broth for three days, he should undergo the procedure.
1.13.81 | Likewise, having fasted for one day and then eaten, one should drink an emetic;
however, in the case of an un-purificatory oil enema, the regimen should be like that for one who has undergone purgation.
For those men who hate fatty substances yet crave them, who have a soft bowel, who cannot endure hardship, and who are addicted to wine— for them, the *vicāraṇā* (clarified butter) is recommended.

The juices of the quail (*lāva*), partridge (*taittira*), peacock (*māyūra*), swan (*haṃsa*), boar (*vārāha*), cock (*kukkuṭa*), cow (*gavya*), goat (*āja*), *airbhra*, and fish (*matsya*) are beneficial for oleation (*snehana*).
Barley, jujube, and horse-gram, along with fats mixed with jaggery and sugar;
pomegranate, curd, and the three pungents (vyoṣa)—this is a compendium of combinations of meat broths.
1.13.85 | Sesame seeds eaten first with oil and molasses cause oleation,
as do kṛsarā porridge with much oil, and likewise *tilakāmbalikā*.
1.13.86 | One who is dry [of humors] should drink molasses, ginger, and oil together with wine; once that is digested, he should eat a meal consisting of well-cooked meats.
A man suffering from vāta disorders becomes lubricated by drinking oil with the scum of wine, or muscle fat or marrow, or milk mixed with treacle.
1.13.88 | Having drunk milk that is warm from the cow, mixed with fat and sugar,
or having drunk the liquid from curd combined with molasses, a man becomes oleated.
1.13.89 | A gruel prepared with five handfuls of ingredients, along with milk-rice mixed with mung beans,
cooked in milk and containing abundant fat, will soon cause a person to become oleated.
1.13.90 | A *pañcaprasṛtikī* gruel, prepared with one *prasṛta* each of ghee, oil, muscle fat, marrow, and rice, should be drunk by one desiring oleation.
Alternatively, a fatty pork broth mixed with ghee and salt,
when drunk diligently twice a day, will soon cause a person to become oleated.
The meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals, along with jaggery, curd, milk, and sesame seeds—
One suffering from skin diseases, edema, or urinary disorders should not employ oleation therapy.
1.13.92 | One should oleate them with appropriate, proven, and non-vitiating unctuous substances,
prepared either with pippalī and harītakī, or with triphalā.

1.13.93 | A physician should prepare a medicated oil containing the three pungents (vyoṣa) along with grape juice, emblic myrobalan juice, and sour curd; by drinking that, a person becomes lubricated.
The juices of barley, jujube, and horse gram, along with alkali, wine, curd, milk, and ghee— this preparation, when processed, is an excellent unctuous medicated ghee (snehanīya-ghṛta).

1.13.95 | Having prepared oil with marrow, muscle fat, ghee, and the juices of jujube and the three myrobalans, one should administer it in cases of disorders of the female reproductive tract and the semen.
1.13.96 Just as cloth absorbs water and then releases it in excess,
and just as oil digests within fire, so too does [the medicine] flow out in excess.
1.13.97 | Or just as water, having moistened a lump of clay,
flows away and the moisture slips off when poured with haste, so too does [the medicine] administered with haste.
1.13.98 | Fatty substances mixed with salt oleate a person quickly;
for they are unctuous, non-drying, subtle, hot, and pervasive.

1.13.99 | One should first administer oleation (sneha), followed immediately by sudation (sveda). For one who has been prepared with oleation and sudation, purification (saṃśodhana) or other [therapies] should then be applied.
1.13.100 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
The oleaginous substances, the procedure for oleation, the complete success in treating complications along with their remedies—
all this has been explained by the Blessed One, the son of Candrabhāgā, in response to the questions asked.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, named "The Chapter on Oleation," in the Section on Verses (*Ślokasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Fourteen:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on sudation (*Svedādhyāya*).
1.14.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.14.3 | Therefore, the methods of sudation shall now be explained, by which, when properly applied,
diseases caused by Vata and Kapha that are curable by sudation are pacified.
1.14.4 | When the wind has been subdued by sudation preceded by oleation,
feces, urine, and semen will not become obstructed in any way whatsoever.
1.14.5 | For even dry pieces of wood can be bent according to the proper method by means of lubrication and steaming; how much more so, then, living men?

Sudation that takes into account the disease, the season, and the patient's condition; which is neither too hot nor too mild; which possesses the appropriate substances and is properly prepared for the specific location, is considered effective in achieving its purpose.
1.14.7 | When there is fever, cold, or when the body possesses great strength, a strong sudation is beneficial;
when weak, a weak sudation; and when moderate, a moderate sudation is recommended.
1.14.8 | Fomentation is desired in cases of vāta-śleṣman, or vāta alone, or kapha alone;
it is prepared as unctuous-dry, as well as unctuous or dry.
1.14.9 | When vāta is located in the stomach (āmāśaya) and kapha is situated in the large intestine (pakvāśaya),
sudation preceded by dry measures is beneficial, as is that preceded by unctuous measures.
1.14.10 | One should gently foment the testicles, the heart, and the eyes, or not at all;
the groins with moderate heat, and the remaining parts of the body as desired.
1.14.11 | Having covered the eyes with well-cleaned cotton pads, or with balls of wheat flour, or with the petals of lotuses or water-lilies, one should apply fomentation.
1.14.12 | With cool strings of pearls, with cooling vessels,
and with hands moistened by water and adorned with lotuses, he should touch the heart of one who is perspiring.
1.14.13 | When the cold and pain have subsided, when stiffness and heaviness have been overcome,
and when softness and perspiration have arisen, it is considered the time to cease from sudation.
1.14.14 | Excess of bile (pitta), fainting, lassitude of the body, thirst, burning sensations, weakness of voice and limbs— these are the signs of one who has been excessively sweated.
1.14.15 | The entire regimen for the summer season that was described in the chapter on "The Eighty" (Aśitīya) [should also be followed].
For one who has sweated excessively, a sweet, unctuous, and cooling [treatment] should be administered.
1.14.16 | For those who habitually consume astringents and wine, for pregnant women, those suffering from *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders),
those with a predominance of *pitta*, those with diarrhea, those who are dry, and those with diabetes mellitus;
1.14.17 | For those with inflamed or prolapsed rectums, and those afflicted by disorders of irregular wine consumption.
For those who are exhausted, those who have lost consciousness, those who are corpulent, and those suffering from bilious urinary disorders.

1.14.18 | For those who are thirsty and hungry, for the angry and the grieving, for those with consumption, for those with abdominal dropsy, for the wounded, and for those afflicted by chronic disease;
1.14.19 | The physician should not apply sudation to those who are weak, excessively emaciated, whose ojas has been depleted, nor to those suffering from taimira (visual disorders).
1.14.20 | In cases of coryza, cough, hiccup, dyspnea, and lack of lightness; in pain of the ears, neck, and head; in hoarseness of voice, and constriction of the throat.
1.14.21 | In cases of facial paralysis, paralysis of a single limb or the entire body, hemiplegia, loss of consciousness, abdominal distension, constipation, urinary retention, and yawning;
1.14.22 | In cases of contraction of the sides, back, waist, and flanks; in sciatica (gṛdhrasī);
in dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra); in enlargement of the scrotum; and in body aches (aṅgamardaka).
1.14.23 | Also in cases of pain in the feet, knees, thighs, and calves; in swelling; in chronic ulcers (khallī);
in undigested states (āmavāta); in coldness; in shivering; and in "pins" of wind (vātakaṇṭaka).
1.14.24 | Fomentation is said to be beneficial in cases of contraction, extension, and pain; in stiffness, heaviness, and numbness; and in disorders affecting all parts of the body.
1.14.25 | One should apply poultice-fomentation (piṇḍasveda) using sesame, black gram, horse gram, sour substances, ghee, oil, meat, boiled rice, milk-porridge, kṛśara, and various meats.
1.14.26 | With the dung of cows, donkeys, camels, pigs, and horses; with barley grains along with their husks; and with sand, dust, stones, dried cow-dung, and iron filings.

1.14.27 | One should cause those with kapha disorders to sweat using the aforementioned methods, and one should treat those with vata disorders accordingly; these same substances are also recommended for use in bed-sweating (prastara-sveda) according to their respective indications.
1.14.28 | Well-anointed, one perspires comfortably in underground chambers, in *jentāka* (dry steam baths), and in warm inner rooms heated by smokeless embers.
1.14.29 | Meat from domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals; milk; the head of a goat;
the fat, marrow, bile, and blood of a boar; and oily sesame seeds with rice.

1.14.30 | Having boiled these together, the most excellent physician— one who understands the distinctions of place and time and acts with due consideration— should apply tube-fomentation (nāḍīsveda).
1.14.31 | With the leaves of *vāruṇī*, *amṛta*, *eraṇḍa*, *śigru*, *mūlaka*, and *sarṣapa*; and with those of *vāsā*, *vaṃśa*, *karañja*, *arka*, and *aśmantaka*.
1.14.32 | Having boiled water with the leaves of *śobhāñjana*, *sairēya*, *mālatī*, *surasa*, and *arjaka*, one should apply it as tubular fomentation (*nāḍīsveda*).
1.14.33 | One should administer nāḍīsveda (tube-sudation) using bhūtīka and pañcamūla with wine, the whey of curd, urine, sour liquids, and fats.
1.14.34 | These same decoctions (niryūhas) should also be used in a water-vat for the purpose of sudation; one should also cause vats for ghee, milk, and oil to be prepared.
1.14.35 | An poultice (upanāha) made from wheat fragments and powdered barley mixed with sour liquids, along with oil, yeast-leaven (kiṇva), and salt, is highly recommended.
1.14.36 | One should apply a poultice (upanāha) consisting of fragrant substances, *surā* liquor, *kiṇva* yeast, *jīvantī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *umā*, and *kuṣṭha* oil, combined together.
1.14.37 | It should be bound with skins that have their hair on and are not putrid;
in their absence, however, with silken or woolen cloths of heating potency.
1.14.38 | One should release what was bound during the day at night, and release what was done at night during the day;
this is for the purpose of avoiding burning sensations, though greater effort should be made when it is cool.
1.14.39 | Saṅkara, prastara, nāḍī, pariṣeka, avagāhana, jentāka,
aśmaghana, karṣū, kuṭī, bhū, and kumbhikā.
1.14.40 | These thirteen—the *kūpa*, the *holāka*, and so forth—are methods of sudation.
I shall describe them all in their proper order, one after another.

1.14.41 | In that regard, one should know that fomentation performed with the aforementioned boluses, whether separated by a cloth or not separated by a cloth, is called *saṅkarasveda* (mixed fomentation).

1.14.42 | One should know that *prastara-sveda* (bed-sudation) consists of the following: while the patient lies down with all limbs well-anointed upon a bed covered with awns, *śamī*, grain-particles, or *pulāka*; or with *veśavāra*, milk-pudding (*pāyasa*), *kṛśara*, *utkārikā*, and so forth; and with an upper cover made of silk or wool, or with leaves of the *pañcāṅgula*, *uruvūka*, or *arka* plants. This is called *prastara-sveda*.

1.14.43 | Furthermore, for sudation substances—such as roots, fruits, leaves, and sprouts; or the flesh, heads, and feet of wild animals and birds; or other items of hot nature combined with appropriate acids, salts, and fats; or urine, milk, and so forth—one should boil them in a cauldron that does not emit steam. Then, using a tube made from any one of reed, *iṣīkā* grass, bamboo, split bamboo, or *karaja* and *arka* leaves, shaped like the trunk of an elephant's foreleg, and measuring either one *vyāma* or half a *vyāma* in length, [the steam is applied].

One should administer steam by means of a tube whose circumference at the base is one-fourth of a *vyāma* and at the tip is one-eighth, with its lumen covered on all sides by wind-dispelling leaves, and bent two or three times; the patient’s body should be anointed with oil processed with wind-dispelling drugs. For steam, when directed obliquely, has its fierce force checked and, without burning the skin, provides a comfortable fomentation; this is known as *nāḍīsveda*.

1.14.44 | Furthermore, for those suffering from vāta disorders or predominant vāta (vātikottaravātika), one should fill jars, sprinkling-basins, or conduits with lukewarm decoctions of roots and other [vāta-alleviating] ingredients; then, having anointed the patient's body with the appropriate processed fats and covered it with cloth, one should sprinkle [the liquid]. This is known as *pariṣeka* (affusion).

1.14.45 | Immersion in a tub containing a decoction that removes wind (vāta), along with milk, oil, ghee, meat broth, and warm water, is indeed the same as the previously described method of immersion.

1.14.46 | Now, one desiring to construct a *jentāka* (a steam-bath house) should examine the ground: on a superior and auspicious plot of land in the eastern or northern direction, consisting of black-sweet soil or golden soil; on the bank of any water-reservoir such as a pond or lotus-pool, on the southern or western side where there is a good landing-place (*sūpatīrtha*); on a level and well-proportioned plot of land, starting seven or eight *aratnis* from the water, one should construct a gabled chamber facing east or north, with its entrance toward the landing-place.

One should have it constructed, measuring sixteen *ratni*s in height and width, perfectly circular all around, finished with plaster work, and provided with many windows. Inside this gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*), one should have a pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) constructed all along the walls, equal in width and height to one *aratni*, extending up to the door. And in the center of this gabled chamber, one should have a charcoal-receptacle pillar constructed out of clay, four *kīśuka*s in measure—equivalent to the height of a man—shaped like a *kandu* (a shallow bowl), with many very fine holes, and provided with a lid.

Having filled it with wood of *khadira* or *aśvakarṇa* and other such trees, he should set it ablaze. When he knows that the wood is well-burnt, smokeless, and no longer glowing, but that the fire-chamber is permeated solely by fire and by a heat suitable for inducing perspiration, then he should have this man—whose body has been anointed with wind-dispelling ointments and covered with a cloth—enter therein, instructing him thus: "O gentle one, enter for the sake of well-being and health," and having entered it...

Having ascended the pedestal, you may lie down comfortably on either side as you please; however, even when overcome by sweat and fainting, you must not let go of this pedestal until your last breath. For if you were to fall from this space of the pedestal and fail to reach the door, you would instantly lose your life due to being overwhelmed by sweat and fainting; therefore, you must not release this pedestal under any circumstances.

When you perceive yourself to be free from excessive moisture, with sweat and mucus properly discharged, all the channels released, the body lightened, and the sensations of obstruction, stiffness, numbness, pain, and heaviness gone—then, following that steam-chamber (*piṇḍikā*), you should proceed to the door. Having emerged, do not touch cold water suddenly for the sake of protecting your eyes; rather, once the heat and fatigue have subsided, you should bathe appropriately with pleasantly warm water after a short while and then eat.
This is the procedure for *jentāka-sveda* (steam-bath therapy).
Having heated a solid stone slab made of rock to the size of a reclining person by means of well-kindled wood that wards off the wind, [he placed it upon the bed].
1.14.48 | Having removed all coals and sprinkled that stone with warm water, one should then prepare a bed for it using silk and woolen cloths.
1.14.49 | With all his limbs well-anointed with oil, the person lying upon that [bed] perspires comfortably, well-covered by Kaurava skins, silks, woolens, and other such garments.
1.14.50 | Thus has been described perspiration by means of stone-heats (aśmaghana-sveda); now perspiration by means of a pit (karṣū-sveda) shall be explained.
One who knows the divisions of the site should dig a trench beneath the bed.
1.14.51 | Then, one should fill that trench with glowing, smokeless charcoal;
lying upon a bed over it, a person sweats comfortably.
Having constructed a small hut with thick walls, neither too high nor too wide, circular in shape, and without windows, one should plaster it inside with kuṣṭha and other such substances.
1.14.53 | The physician should prepare a well-spread bed within the cottage,
using coverlets, skins, silken cloths, rugs, woolen blankets, and cushions.
1.14.54 | Having surrounded her on all sides with small charcoal-heaters filled with embers,
one who has been anointed may enter within and sweat comfortably.
1.14.55 | That same procedure for sweating with stone-masses which was prescribed for the ground is also taught for a level, windless plot of land that is well-prepared.
1.14.56 | One should bury a jar filled with a decoction that dispels wind (vāta) into the ground,
leaving half or one-third of it above the surface as a bed.
1.14.57 | Or one may prepare a seat that is not overly crowded with furnishings;
then, one should cast well-heated iron balls into a cauldron.
1.14.58 | Standing upon those stones, he sweats comfortably by their heat;
his limbs well-covered and well-anointed with unctuous substances that destroy the wind (vāyu).

1.14.59 | One should construct a well with a width equal to the length of the bed and twice that in depth, in a commendable location sheltered from the wind, and it should be thoroughly cleaned inside.

1.14.60 | When a pit has been filled with the dung of elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, and camels and set on fire, a man who is well-covered, well-stretched out upon it, and anointed with oil, perspires easily.
1.14.61 | One should ignite a fire of the aforementioned dried cow-dung cakes (dhītīkā) there upon the bed, with a size equal to the dimensions of the interior of the sleeping chamber.
1.14.62 | When the fire has been well-kindled and smokeless, one should prepare it as described.
There, covered by his own cloth and having anointed himself with oil while lying down, a person sweats comfortably.
1.14.63 | This is called *holāka-sveda*, declared by the Great Sage to be easy to perform.
Thus, there are thirteen types of sudation that rely upon the qualities of fire.
1.14.64 | Physical exercise, staying in a warm room, heavy clothing, hunger,
excessive drinking, fear, anger, poultices, wrestling, and exposure to the wind.
1.14.65 | These ten cause perspiration in a person even without the quality of fire;
thus has been described the two-fold sudation, both that which is associated with the qualities of fire and that which is not.
1.14.66 | Moisture (snigdha) may pertain to a single part or to the entire body, and likewise, it may be dry (rūkṣa);
thus, this threefold dual combination is proclaimed with reference to sudation (sveda).
1.14.67 | One who has been treated with oleation should be approached with sudation; once sweated, he should consume wholesome food.
On that day, however, a person whose limbs have been sweated should avoid physical exercise.
1.14.68 | Regarding this, there are these verses:—
how sudation acts as a therapeutic agent, for whom it is beneficial, and of what kind;
in which region it is appropriate, and how that region must be protected.

1.14.69 | The signs of properly sudated and excessively sudated states, as well as the medicinal substances for excessive sudation; those unfit for sudation, those suitable for sudation, the sudation materials, and their pharmaceutical preparations.
1.14.70 | There are thirteen types of sudation without the use of fire, and ten types with fire;
in summary, six types of sudation have been demonstrated in this chapter on sudation.
1.14.71 | Whatever was to be said regarding the subject of sudation has thus been stated by the Great Sage.
The disciples must practice accordingly, while Punarvasu shall be the instructor.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, named "Sudation," in the *Ślokasthāna* of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Fifteen:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on "Preparations" (*Upakalpanīya*).
1.15.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.15.3 | In this world, indeed, when a physician intends to administer emesis or purgation to a king, a member of the royal family, or anyone else possessing abundant wealth, the necessary materials must be prepared well in advance of the administration of the medicine. For these are for the purpose of providing substitutes should the medicine fail to act properly; for it is not easy to procure the medicinal substances quickly and in the correct proportions when a crisis has already arisen at such a close-proximity time, even if one possesses the means to purchase them.

1.15.4 | To the Blessed One Ātreya, who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "Indeed, O Blessed One, a wise person should provide such countermeasures at the very outset that once they have been applied, the medicine will invariably succeed; for the success of all actions is held to be caused by correct application, while failure is caused by incorrect application. If, however, an action undertaken either correctly or incorrectly succeeds or fails without certainty, then knowledge becomes equal to ignorance."

1.15.5 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, it is possible for us, as well as for those like us, to provide such a remedy so that when applied, the medicine will certainly succeed. Furthermore, we can correctly instruct you in the excellence of its administration; yet there is no one who would be able to comprehend what has been thus instructed, or having comprehended it, to practice or apply it accordingly."

For the subtle variations in the states of the humors, medicines, place, time, strength, body, diet, suitability, mental disposition, constitution, and age are such that, when contemplated, they would confuse even the intellect of one possessed of pure and vast intelligence, let alone one of small intellect. Therefore, we shall duly teach both of these—proper application of medicines and the remedies for complications arising from those that have failed—in the subsequent section on Success (Siddhi).

1.15.6 | Now, first of all, we shall briefly describe the various requisites: namely, one who is skilled in the science of architecture should first prepare a commendable house that is sturdy, sheltered from the wind, with a single opening for ventilation, easy to move about in, not situated in a valley, inaccessible to smoke, heat, water, and dust, free from undesirable sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells, and provided with a well, a mortar and pestle, a privy, a bathing area, and a kitchen.

1.15.7 | Then, he [should appoint] attendants endowed with virtue, purity, proper conduct, affection, dexterity, and courtesy, who are skilled in service and proficient in all tasks—namely, cooks of soups and rice, bath-attendants, massagers, those who help one rise, those who help one lie down, and those who grind medicines—and who are not adverse to any work; as well as courtiers who are skilled in song, instrumental music, conversation, verses, stanzas, tales, histories, and Purāṇas, who understand intentions, are agreeable, and know the proper place and time. And likewise...

He provided quails, francolins, hares, deer, antelopes, black-tailed deer, mṛgamātṛkā, and rams; a milch cow that was well-behaved, healthy, with her calf living, and well-provided with grass, shelter, and water;

as well as vessels for washing and rinsing, water-jars, pitchers, pots, pans, bowls, large jars, small jars, basins, platters, ladles, buckets, cooking vessels, churns, skins, clothes, thread, cotton, wool, and so forth; and beds and seats equipped with censers and receiving-stands, furnished with well-spread rugs, upper covers, pillows, and bolsters.

The comforts for lying down, sitting, oleation, sudation, massage, affusion, sprinkling, anointing, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema, unctuous enema, head-purgation, and the voiding of urine and feces; as well as well-washed pillows and stones of smooth, medium texture.

And surgical instruments for the purpose of accessories, a smoking pipe (*dhūmanetra*), a bladder nozzle (*bastinetra*), a urethral enema nozzle (*uttarabastika*), a bundle of *kuśa* grass, a balance scale, and measuring vessels; as well as ghee, oil, muscle fat (*vasā*), marrow (*majjā*), honey, molasses, salt, fuel, water, honey-wine (*madhusīdhu*), *surā* wine, *sauvīraka*, *tuṣodaka*, *maireya*, *medaka*, curd, whey (*dadhimaṇḍa*), buttermilk (*udasvit*), fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*), and urine; likewise, *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans (*mudga*), black gram (*māṣa*), barley, sesame, horse-gram (*kulattha*), jujube (*badara*), raisins (*mṛdvīkā*), *kāśmarya*, *parūṣaka*, chebulic myrobalan (*abhayā*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), and beleric myrobalan (*bibhītaka*).

One should prepare various types of materials for oleation and sudation, as well as medicinal drugs designated as emetic, purgative, both-acting, astringent, digestive-stimulant, carminative, palliative, and wind-alleviating;
furthermore, whatever other instruments one might know to be necessary for counteracting complications, and whatever else is required for their use, all that should be collected.

1.15.8 | Thereafter, one should treat that person with the aforementioned oleation and sudation therapies as appropriate. If, however, during this interval some acute mental or physical disease should suddenly assail him, one should strive to alleviate that first; then, having alleviated it, one should treat him for the same duration with the very same procedure.

1.15.9 | Then, having observed that the person has been treated with oleation and sudation, is of unimpaired mind, has slept well, has properly digested his food, has bathed his head, has anointed his body, wears a garland, is clothed in unblemished garments, and has worshipped the deities, fire, the twice-born, teachers, elders, and physicians; and having had the Brahmins recite auspicious prayers at a favorable constellation, lunar day, karana, and muhurta, one should cause him to drink a dose of the decoction of *madana* fruit, consecrated by the benedictions uttered by those Brahmins and mixed with honey, *madhuka*, rock salt, and treacle.

1.15.10 | Regarding the dosage for the decoction of *madanaphala* and indeed the dosages for all purificatory procedures (*saṃśodhana*), these must be determined according to each individual. For the dosage of one should be understood as that amount which, when drunk, is effective for removing morbid humors (*doṣa*) without resulting in either excessive action (*atiyoga*) or insufficient action (*ayoga*).

1.15.11 | One should wait for a moment after he has drunk it; when one recognizes that the *doṣa* is undergoing liquefaction through the appearance of perspiration, has moved from its locations due to horripilation, has entered the abdomen due to abdominal distension, and has turned upward due to nausea and salivation, then one should have him sit upon a seat that is knee-high, unobstructed, provided with well-applied rugs, upper covers, and pillows, and equipped with a backrest.

One should offer gifts and perform services; in the matter of receiving a gift upon the forehead, supporting the sides, pressing the navel, and massaging the back, approved friends who are not to be shunned should exert themselves.

1.15.12 | Then he should instruct him as follows: "With your lips, palate, and throat wide open, without excessive exertion, inducing the urges that have already arisen; slightly bending the neck while keeping the body erect; and, if the urges do not emerge spontaneously, stimulating them by touching the throat with two fingers whose nails are well-trimmed, or with the stalks of blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*kumuda*), or fragrant water lilies (*saugandhika*), you should discharge [the semen] comfortably. He should act accordingly; thereafter, the physician should attentively observe the urges as they enter the receptacle.

For by observing the specific nature of the force (*vega*), the skilled physician may discern the distinctions between proper application (*yoga*), deficient application (*ayoga*), and excessive application (*atiyoga*); and by discerning these specific forces, he shall understand the required action as it truly is through its characteristics. Therefore, he should observe the forces with focused attention.

1.15.13 | In this regard, these are the specific signs for knowing deficient application (ayoga), proper application (yoga), and excessive application (atiyoga): non-occurrence [of the purgative effect] due to some cause, or the failure of the medicine alone; and the downward displacement of the doshas, or their obstruction—these are the signs of deficient application. Occurrence at the proper time, moderate pain, the sequential elimination of the doshas, and the natural subsiding [of the action] are the signs of proper application. Furthermore, the classification of [proper application] as sharp, mild, or moderate should be understood according to the specific quantity of the doshas eliminated by that application. However, regarding excessive application:
The symptoms of excessive administration (atiyoga) include the appearance of frothy blood and the onset of a moon-like pallor.

In that regard, one should recognize these complications caused by both excessive and deficient administration: flatulence (ādhmāna), cutting pain (parikartikā), discharge (parisrāva), distress of the heart (hṛdayopasaraṇa), stiffness of the limbs (aṅgagraha), loss of vitality (jīvādāna), displacement (vibhraṃśa), rigidity (stambha), and exhaustion (klama)—these are the complications.

1.15.14 | Having observed that he has indeed vomited by means of this yoga, and having had his hands, feet, and mouth well washed, one should comfort him for a moment; then, after administering one of the unctuous, purgative, or pacifying medicated smokes according to his capacity, one should again have him touch water.

1.15.15 | Having had him sip water and enter a windless room, and having laid him down, one should instruct him: "Spend the entire day avoiding even in thought these conditions: speaking loudly, overeating, standing too long, walking excessively, anger, grief, cold, heat, frost, mist, strong winds, riding in vehicles, sexual intercourse, staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, and the consumption of food that is incompatible, undigested, unwholesome, untimely, measured in excess, deficient, heavy, or irregular; as well as the suppression or premature arousal of natural urges.
He should act accordingly.

1.15.16 | Then, in the evening or on the following day, once he has been sprinkled with comfortable water, one should have him drink lukewarm gruel (*yavāgū*) made from old red rice grains, well-cooked and preceded by the scum (*maṇḍa*), after carefully considering the strength of his digestive fire. In this same manner during the second and third meal-times; however, at the fourth meal-time, one should feed him a thick porridge (*vilepī*) made from the same kind of rice grains, well-boiled and served with warm water, either without fat or salt, or with only a little fat and salt. In this same manner during the fifth and sixth meal-times.

At the seventh mealtime, one should feed him two *prasṛta* measures of well-cooked rice made from the same kind of *śāli* grains, with warm water as a drink, along with a thin lentil soup (*mudgayūṣa*) seasoned with a small amount of fat and salt.

Likewise at the eighth and ninth mealtimes. At the tenth mealtime, however, one should feed him the meat broth of any bird such as the common quail (*lāva*) or the grey partridge (*kapiñjala*), prepared with water and salt but not too thick, with warm water as a drink. Likewise at the eleventh and twelfth mealtimes. From that point onward, gradually consuming the qualities of solid food, he should return to his normal diet within seven nights.

1.15.17 | Then, having again treated him with oleation and sudation, and having observed that his mind is unimpaired, that he has slept comfortably and digested his food well, and that the *homa*, offerings, auspicious rites, recitations, and expiations have been performed; on an auspicious lunar day, asterism, division of the day (*karaṇa*), and moment (*muhūrta*), after having had the Brahmins pronounce blessings, one should administer a dose of the three-fold paste (*trivṛt-kalka*) the size of an *akṣa* fruit, mixed with a suitable liquid, after carefully considering the variations in the doshas, the medicine, the location, the time, strength, the body, dietetic suitability, mental temperament (*sattva*), constitution (*prakṛti*), and age.

Once he has been properly purged, one should treat him according to the procedure described for emesis—excluding the use of medicated smoke—until he regains his strength, complexion, and natural constitution.

When he has regained his strength and complexion, and is observed to be mentally untroubled, well-rested, and having fully digested his food, one should have him bathe his head, anoint his body, wear garlands, dress in unblemished garments, and adorn himself with suitable ornaments. Having shown him to his friends and kinsmen, one should then allow him to indulge in his desires.
1.15.18 | And there are verses on this point:
1.15.18ab | By this method, a king or even one of royal rank, 1.15.18cd | or whoever possesses abundant wealth, is worthy of the purificatory treatment.
1.15.19ab | But a poor man, having encountered a calamity for which purification is timely,
1.15.19cd | may drink as much as he desires even without gathering the necessary materials, however difficult they may be to obtain.
1.15.20ab | For not all human beings possess every kind of requisite;
1.15.20cd | nor do terrible diseases fail to afflict even the poor.
1.15.21ab | Whatever medicine can be prepared by a man in times of distress, 1.15.21cd | that should be used according to his ability, as well as clothing and food.

1.15.22ab | Having properly drunk a purifying agent that removes impurities, cures diseases, and clarifies strength and complexion, one is endowed with a long life. 1.15.22cd | [Having properly drunk a purifying agent that removes impurities, cures diseases, and clarifies strength and complexion, one is endowed with a long life.]
1.15.23 | Regarding this, there are these verses:
1.15.23ab | For lords of great wealth, one should administer emesis along with purgation;
1.15.23cd | having collected whatever materials are required and for whatever purpose, one should employ them.

1.15.24ab | Just as the dosage to be administered and the characteristics of its proper application [are described], 1.15.24cd | so too are the signs of deficient and excessive application, as well as the complications and secondary disorders.
1.15.25ab | That which is unfit to be consumed by one who is pure, and the procedure for readmission;
1.15.25cd | all that Punarvasu has declared in the chapter on medical formulations (kalpanādhyāya).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, named "The Preparation of Requisites," in the Section on General Principles of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.16.0 | Chapter Sixteen.
1.16.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the "Introduction to Therapeutics" (Cikitsāprābhṛtīya).
1.16.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

1.16.3ab | The wise physician, possessing the medical treatises and devoted to his practice, who purges a person by means of proper application, causes him to enjoy happiness. 1.16.3cd | [The patient] enjoys happiness through that correct application.
1.16.4ab | When an ignorant person who considers himself a physician causes a man to undergo purgation,
1.16.4cd | that man suffers pain due to both excessive application and lack of application.
1.16.5ab | Weakness, lightness, lassitude, attenuation of diseases, and a relish for food;
1.16.5cd | purity of the heart and complexion, hunger, thirst, and the timely discharge of natural urges.
1.16.6ab | Purity of the sense organs, the intellect, and the mind; the downward movement of the vital air (māruta);
1.16.6cd | These are the signs of one who has been properly purged, as well as the restoration of the digestive fire (kāyāgni).
1.16.7ab | Spitting, impurity of the heart, and nausea due to phlegm and bile;
1.16.7cd | Distension of the abdomen, loss of appetite, diarrhea, weakness, and lack of lightness.
1.16.8ab | Weakness of the calves and thighs, lassitude, a sense of stiffness, and the onset of chronic rhinitis;
1.16.8cd | these are the signs of those who have not been purged, as well as the suppression of the bodily wind (vāta).
1.16.9ab | When bile, phlegm, and wind have arrived [in the body] in their respective order,
1.16.9cd | the blood that subsequently flows out resembles the water from fat and flesh.
1.16.10ab | Water that is free from phlegm and bile, or blood, or even black;
1.16.10cd | [This is the result] for one who is thirsty and afflicted by wind, and who is losing consciousness due to excessive [drinking].
1.16.11ab | Indeed, these very same symptoms occur when emesis is performed excessively; 1.16.11cd | as well as upward-moving diseases of wind (vāta) and an excessive impairment of speech.

The Eighteenth Chapter.
1.18.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the three types of swelling (Triśothīya).
1.18.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.18.3 | There are three types of swelling caused by vāta, pitta, and śleṣman; these, moreover, are of two kinds, distinguished as endogenous (nija) and exogenous (āgantu).

1.18.4 | In that regard, exogenous swellings arise through cutting, piercing, tearing, breaking, crushing, grinding, striking, killing, binding, wrapping, lancing, or squeezing; or by contact with the juice of the *bhallātaka* flower or fruit, or with *ātmaguptā*, *śūka*, insects, thorns, poisonous leaves, creepers, or shrubs; or by sweating, crawling over, or urinating upon [the body]; or by the falling of the fangs, teeth, horns, or claws of venomous creatures; or by contact with oceanic poison, wind, cold, or fire.

1.18.5 | Furthermore, these [afflictions] are first perceived through their respective causes and symptoms, which are partially contrary to their own specific manifestations; and when treated with remedies such as binding, mantras, antidotes, ointments, heating, and cooling, they attain pacification.

1.18.6 | Furthermore, endogenous [diseases] arise from the improper administration of oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas, unctuous enemas, or head-evacuants; or from incorrect dietary rehabilitation; or from vomiting, alasaka, visūcikā, dyspnea, cough, diarrhea, consumption, anemia, abdominal dropsy, fever, menorrhagia, fistula-in-ano, or hemorrhoids; or from excessive emaciation; or from skin diseases, itching, pustules, and the like; or from the suppression of the urges of vomiting, sneezing, belching, semen, flatus, urine, or feces; or from sudden [exertion] in one who is already exhausted by labor, disease, fasting, or travel.

"Swelling (śopha) arises from the consumption of excessively heavy, sour, salty, or flour-based foods; fruits, vegetables, curd, and myrobalan; fermented liquors, unripened milk, sprouted grains, new grain, awned cereals, and *śamī* beans; meat from marshy or aquatic animals; from eating clay, mud, or clods of earth; from excessive salt intake; from injuring the fetus; from miscarriage; from improper postpartum care; and from the aggravation of the bodily humors (*doṣas*). Thus has the general cause been stated."

1.18.7. However, this is the distinction here: Vāyu, provoked by cold, roughness, lightness, dryness, fatigue, fasting, excessive emaciation, depletion, and so forth, overcomes the skin, flesh, blood, and other tissues to produce swelling. This swelling arises and subsides quickly; it is dark or reddish in color, or of its natural hue; it is mobile, pulsating, and characterized by rough, coarse, and cracked skin and hair; it feels as if it is being cut, split, pressed, pierced by needles, crawled upon by ants, or scraped.
When it feels as if smeared with mustard paste, causing a tingling sensation, contraction, or stretching, it is *vāta-śotha* (swelling caused by wind).

Pitta, provoked by the consumption of hot, sharp, pungent, alkaline, salty, and sour foods, by indigestion, and by the heat of fire and sunlight, overcomes the skin, flesh, and blood to produce a swelling. This swelling arises and subsides quickly; it has a black, yellow, blue, or coppery appearance, is hot and soft, and its hair becomes brownish-copper. It is characterized by burning, aching, fuming, radiating heat, sweating, and moistening, and it cannot tolerate touch or heat. This is *pitta-śotha* (swelling caused by bile).

1.18.7.(3) Kapha, aggravated by heavy, sweet, cold, and unctuous substances, as well as by excessive sleep, lack of exercise, and other such factors, overcomes the skin, flesh, blood, and other tissues to produce swelling. This swelling is characterized by slow onset and resolution; it has a pale-white appearance, is heavy, unctuous, smooth, firm, dense, with hair at its tip that is white, and it is tolerant of touch and heat. This is known as kaphaja-swelling (śleṣma-śotha).

1.18.7 | Just as three types of swellings arise from two doṣas due to the combination of their respective causes and forms, and one type arises from the combination of all [three] doṣas due to the convergence of their respective causes and forms; thus, there is a sevenfold classification.

1.18.8 | Swelling (śotha) is observed to be divided into two types, three types, four types, seven types, and eight types according to their respective constituent causes (prakṛti); yet, it is again considered as one alone due to the commonality of its characteristic—namely, elevation (utsedha).
Regarding this, there are verses: 1.18.9ab | If a person's limbs swell, feel as if they are falling asleep, and ache;
1.18.9cd | and if, when pressed, they quickly rebound, one should designate that as *vāta-śotha* (edema caused by wind).

1.18.10cd | and which subsides through the application of unctuous substances, heat, and massage— that is of the Vāta type.

That very same dosha, when aggravated by specific causes and having moved to other locations, gives rise to many diseases.
Therefore,

For that physician who, having understood this triad, undertakes medical actions with prior knowledge and according to the proper method, does not falter in his professional duties.

The Nineteenth Chapter.
1.19.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the eight types of abdominal enlargements (aṣṭodarīya).
1.19.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

1.19.3 | Herein, indeed, there are eight types of abdominal enlargements (udara), eight urinary obstructions (mūtrāghāta), eight defects of breast milk (kṣīradoṣa), and eight defects of semen (retodoṣa); seven types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), seven types of carbuncles (piḍakā), and seven types of erysipelas (visarpa);

six types of diarrhea (atīsāra), six types of upward displacement of wind (udāvarta), five types of abdominal tumors (gulma), five defects of the spleen (plīhadoṣa), five types of cough (kāsa), five types of dyspnea (śvāsa), five types of hiccups (hikkā), five types of thirst (tṛṣṇā), five types of vomiting (chardi), five causes for the non-eating of food (bhaktasyānaśanasthāna), five types of head diseases (śiroroga), five types of heart diseases (hṛdroga), five types of anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and five types of insanity (unmāda).

There are four types of epilepsy, four diseases of the eyes, four diseases of the ears, four types of coryza, four diseases of the mouth, four disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), four types of intoxication, four types of fainting, four types of consumption (śoṣa), and four types of impotence; there are three types of swelling, three types of leucoderma (kilāsa), and three varieties of internal hemorrhage (lohitapitta).

There are two types of fever, two types of ulcers, two types of spasms, two types of sciatica, two types of jaundice, two types of indigestion (āmavikāra), two types of vātarakta, and two types of hemorrhoids; one type of thigh-stiffness (ūrustambha), one type of paralysis (saṃnyāsa), and one great disease (mahāgada); twenty species of worms, twenty types of urinary disorders (prameha), and twenty types of gynecological disorders (yonivyāpad). Thus, forty-eight bases of diseases are enumerated in this compendium.
1.19.4. We shall now explain these in accordance with their enumeration:

there are eight types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*), namely those caused by *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, *sannipāta* (combined humors), splenic enlargement (*plīha*), intestinal obstruction (*baddha*), perforation (*chidra*), and *dakodara* (ascites). There are eight types of urinary obstructions (*mūtrāghāta*), namely those born of *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, *sannipāta*, urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), gravel (*śarkarā*), semen (*śukra*), and blood (*śoṇita*). There are eight defects of milk (*kṣīradoṣa*), namely discoloration, foul odor, bad taste, sliminess, frothiness, dryness, heaviness, and excessive unctuousness. There are eight defects of semen (*retodoṣa*), namely that which is thin, dry, frothy, non-white, putrid, excessively mucilaginous, contaminated by other bodily tissues (*dhātu*), and oily (*avasā*).

1.19.4.(2) There are seven types of *kuṣṭha*: *kapāla*, *udumbara*, *maṇḍala*, *ṛṣyajihva*, *puṇḍarīka*, *sidhma*, and *kākaṇa*. There are seven types of *piḍaka*: *śarāvikā*, *kacchapikā*, *jālinī*, *sarṣapī*, *alajī*, *vinatā*, and *vidradhī*. There are seven types of *visarpa* known as those caused by *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, *agni*, *kardama*, *granthi*, and *sannipāta*. 1.19.4.(3) There are six types of *atīsāra*: those born of *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, *sannipāta*, fear, and grief. There are six types of *udāvarta*: those born of the suppression of flatus (*vāta*), urine, feces, semen, vomiting, and sneezing.

1.19.4. There are five types of *gulma* (abdominal tumors): those born of *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, *sannipāta* (combined humors), and blood. The five types of splenic disorders (*plīhadoṣa*) are explained by the same [classification] as the *gulmas*. There are five types of cough (*kāsa*): those born of *vāta*, *pitta*, *kapha*, injury (*kṣata*), and wasting (*kṣaya*). There are five types of dyspnea (*śvāsa*): the great (*mahā*), the upward (*ūrdhva*), the interrupted (*chinna*), the darkening (*tamaka*), and the minor (*kṣudra*). There are five types of hiccups (*hikkā*): the great (*mahatī*), the deep (*gambhīrā*), the intermittent (*vyapetā*), the minor (*kṣudrā*), and those born of food (*annajā*). There are five types of thirst (*tṛṣṇā*): those consisting of *vāta*, *pitta*, phlegm (*āma*), wasting (*kṣaya*), and complications (*upasarga*). There are five types of vomiting (*chardi*): that born from contact with disagreeable objects.

And those arising from the excess of wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination; the five causes of abstaining from food regarding meals—namely, aversions to wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination; the five types of head diseases—which, summarizing the previous enumeration, are born of wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, and parasites; the five types of heart diseases—which are explained by the [same] head diseases; the five types of jaundice—which are born of wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, and the eating of earth; and the five types of insanity—which have wind, bile, phlegm, their combination, and external causes as their origins (4).

1.19.4. There are four types of epilepsy (*apasmāra*), caused by wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*kapha*), and their combination (*sannipāta*). Four types of eye diseases, four types of ear diseases, four types of coryza, four types of mouth diseases, four types of disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī-doṣa*), four types of intoxication (*mada*), and four types of fainting (*mūrchā*) are explained in the same manner as the [four] epilepsies. There are four types of consumption (*śoṣa*), arising from violence, suppression of natural urges, wasting (*kṣaya*), and irregular eating. There are four types of impotence (*klaibya*), resulting from injury to the seed, failure of the penis (*dhvajabhaṅga*), old age, and depletion of semen (*śukrakṣaya*).

1.19.4. There are three types of swelling caused by vāta, pitta, and śleṣman; three types of vitiligo—red, copper-colored, and white; and three types of internal hemorrhage (lohitapitta)—affecting the upper part, the lower part, and both parts.

1.19.4. There are two types of fever: that characterized by a desire for heat arising from cold, and that characterized by a desire for cold arising from heat; two types of ulcers: endogenous and exogenous; two types of stretching pains (āyāma): external and internal; two types of sciatica (gṛdhrasī): from Vāta and from Vāta-Kapha; two types of jaundice (kāmalā): localized in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha) and localized in the peripheral tissues (śākhā); two types of undigested matter (āma): intestinal torpor (alasaka) and choleraic gastroenteritis (visūcikā); two types of gout (vātarakta): deep-seated and superficial; and two types of hemorrhoids (arśas): dry and moist.

1.19.4. (8) One is "stiffness of the thigh" (*ūrustambha*), arising from the three *doṣas* in their undigested state (*āmāt*); one is "paralysis" (*saṃnyāsa*), consisting of the three *doṣas* and having its seat in the mind and body; and one is the "great disease" (*mahāgada*), which is the dogmatic adherence to what is not reality (*atattvābhiniveśa*). (8)

1.19.4. There are twenty types of creeping organisms (*kramijāti*). Those born from external filth (*bahirmalaja*) are of two kinds: lice (*yūkā*) and ants (*pipīlikā*). Those born from blood (*śoṇitaja*) are six: hair-eaters (*keśāda*), body-hair-eaters (*lomāda*), loma-dvīpas, saurasas, audumbaras, and mothers of creatures (*jantumātṛ*). Those born from phlegm (*kaphaja*) are seven: intestine-eaters (*antrāda*), stomach-writhers (*udarāveṣṭa*), heart-eaters (*hṛdayāda*), curavas, darbha-flowers (*darbhapuṣpa*), saugandhikas, and great-rectums (*mahāguda*). Those born from feces (*purīṣaja*) are five: kakerukas, makerukas, lalihās, saśūlakas, and sausurādas.

There are twenty types of *prameha*: ten caused by *śleṣman* (phlegm), namely—*udakameha*, *ikṣubālikārasameha*, *sāndrameha*, *sāndraprasādameha*, *śuklameha*, *śukrameha*, *śītameha*, *śanairmeha*, *sikatāmeha*, and *lālāmeha*; and four caused by *vāta* (wind), namely—*kṣārameha*, *kālameha*, *nīlameha*, *lohitameha*, *mañjiṣṭhāmeha*, *haridrāmeha*, *hastimeha*, and *madhumeha*. Thus, there are twenty *pramehas*.

There are twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract (*yonivyāpad*). Four are born of the *doṣas*: those caused by *vāta*, *pitta*, *śleṣman*, and *sannipāta*. The remaining sixteen are specified according to the combinations of the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas* (vitiated tissues) along with their specific characteristics; they are as follows: *raktayoni*, *arajaskā*, *acaraṇā*, *aticaraṇā*, *prākcaraṇā*, *upaplutā*, *pariplutā*, *udāvartinī*, *karṇinī*, *putraghnī*, *antarmukhī*, *sūcīmukhī*, *śuṣkā*, *vāminī*, *ṣaṇḍhayoni*, and *mahāyoni*.
Thus, there are twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract. (9)
1.19.4 | This enumeration, moreover, has been explained according to its respective order.

1.19.5 | All internal disorders whatsoever do not arise apart from vāta, pitta, and kapha. Just as a bird, even while flying all day long, never passes beyond its own shadow, so too all disorders caused by the imbalance of one's own constituent elements (dhātus) do not transcend vāta, pitta, and kapha.

Furthermore, having carefully examined the specific locations, configurations, and natural dispositions of vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, the wise designate all disorders as being composed of those very same factors.
And on this point, there are these two verses:

"Those numerous collections of disorders in the body that arise from an imbalance of one's own constituent elements (dhātus) are not distinct from pitta, kapha, and vāyu; rather, they are merely specific manifestations of those [three]."
1.19.7ab | An exogenous disorder follows an endogenous one, and likewise, an endogenous disorder that has increased may follow an exogenous one.
1.19.7cd | Having correctly understood the secondary association (anubandha) and the primary nature (prakṛti) therein, one should then commence the treatment.
Regarding this, there are two verses: 1.19.8ab | Three groups of twenty, three groups of one, and three groups of three have been declared;
1.19.8cd | Eight groups of two, ten groups of four, and twelve groups of five.
In the chapter on diseases titled "The Eight Abdominal Diseases," four groups of eight, two groups of six, and three groups of seven diseases have been elucidated.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Eight Abdominal Diseases," in the Section on General Principles of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.20.0 | Chapter Twenty. 1.20.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the major diseases (mahārogādhyāya).
1.20.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.20.3 | There are four types of diseases: those caused by external factors (*āgantuka*), and those caused by wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*). The state of being a disease (*rogatva*) is of one kind for all four of these, due to the commonality of their nature as suffering (*ruksāmānyāt*). Furthermore, their origin (*prakṛti*) is twofold, through the division into exogenous (*āgantuka*) and endogenous (*nija*). Their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is also twofold, distinguished by mind (*manas*) and body (*śarīra*). However, the specific disorders (*vikāra*) are innumerable, because of the innumerability of the variations in their origins, substrata, symptoms (*liṅga*), and locations (*āyatana*).

1.20.4 | Pleasures, however, consist for a stranger of nails, teeth, falls, sorcery, curses, possession, assaults, blows, piercings, bonds, wrappings, pressings, ropes, fire, weapons, thunderbolts, and the afflictions of spirits, and so forth; whereas for one's own [body], pleasure consists of the imbalance of wind, bile, and phlegm.
1.20.5 | Indeed, the etiological factors for both exogenous and endogenous diseases are unwholesome contact of the senses with their objects, intellectual error, and the effects of time.
1.20.6 | However, all these four fully developed diseases indeed follow one another and do not enter into a state of confusion with each other.

1.20.7 | For an exogenous (āgantuja) disease first arises with pain and subsequently brings about an imbalance of the wind, bile, and phlegm; however, in an endogenous (nija) disease, the wind, bile, and phlegm first fall into a state of imbalance and subsequently produce the pain.

1.20.8 | The distribution of the locations of these three doshas within the body will now be taught as follows: the bladder, the receptacle for feces (purīṣādhāna), the waist, the thighs, the feet, the bones, and the colon (pakvāśaya) are the locations of vāta; among these, the colon is specifically the location of vāta. Sweat, plasma (rasa), lymph (lasīkā), blood, and the stomach (āmāśaya) are the locations of pitta; among these, the stomach is specifically the location of pitta. The chest, head, neck, joints, stomach, and fat are the locations of śleṣman;
among these, the chest is specifically the location of śleṣman.

1.20.9 | Vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, which circulate throughout the entire body, produce both auspicious and inauspicious effects within the whole body depending on whether they are in their normal or provoked states. When existing in their natural state (prakṛtibhūta), they produce auspicious results such as growth, strength, complexion, and clarity; however, when they undergo morbid change (vikṛti) and are designated as disorders (vikāra), they produce inauspicious results.
1.20.10 | In that regard, there are disorders arising from the humors collectively (*sāmānyaja*) and those arising from individual humors (*nānātmaja*).

Among these, those arising from the humors collectively have been previously explained in the chapter on the eight abdominal enlargements (*aṣṭodarīya*); we shall now explain here in this chapter those arising from individual humors.
They are as follows: eighty disorders of *vāta*, forty disorders of *pitta*, and twenty disorders of *śleṣman*.
1.20.11 | First, we shall explain the disorders of *vāta* (wind).

They are as follows: splitting of the nails, cracking of the feet, pain in the feet, drooping of the feet, numbness of the feet, *vātakhuḍḍatā* (stiffness of the legs), stiffness of the ankles, cramps in the calves, sciatica (*gṛdhrasī*), splitting of the knees, looseness of the knees, stiffness of the thighs, weakness of the thighs, deformity of the fingers, prolapse of the rectum, pain in the rectum, upward displacement of the testicles, stiffness of the penis, distension of the groin, splitting pain in the hips, diarrhea, and upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*).
Lameness, hunchbackedness, dwarfism, seizing of the neck, seizing of the back, crushing of the sides, and constriction of the abdomen.

Delusion of the heart, flaccidity of the heart, aching sensation in the chest, oppression in the chest, piercing pain in the chest, emaciation of the arms, stiffness of the neck, stiffness of the nape of the neck, hoarseness of the throat, splitting pain in the jaw, cracking of the lips, tearing of the eyes, splitting pain in the teeth, looseness of the teeth, muteness, impediment of speech, an astringent taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth, loss of the sense of taste, loss of the sense of smell, earache, and hearing sounds that do not exist.

Deafness, hard-of-hearing, stiffness of the eyelids, contraction of the eyelids, cataract, pain in the eyes, drooping of the eyes, drooping of the eyebrows, splitting pain in the temples, splitting pain in the forehead, headache, cracking of the scalp, facial paralysis, disease of a single limb, disease of all limbs, hemiplegia, convulsions, tetanus, darkness of vision, vertigo, trembling, yawning, hiccups, and despondency.

Excessive prattle, roughness, harshness, a dark-red complexion, insomnia, and instability of mind—these eighty disorders of wind (vāta) have been explained as the most manifest among the innumerable disorders of wind.

1.20.12 | Indeed, among all these aforementioned disorders of vāta, as well as others not mentioned, this is the unchanging essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of vāta and the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of its action, by perceiving which—whether in its entirety or in part—the skilled physicians determine with certainty that it is indeed a disorder of vāta. These are as follows: dryness, coldness, lightness, clarity, mobility, formlessness, and instability are the essential natures of vāta.

And because the action of Vāyu is of such a nature, its specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is as follows when it enters various parts of the body: namely—drooping, falling away, expansion, contraction, splitting, exhaustion, exhilaration, thirst, trembling, whirling, movement, pricking pain, distress, and various types of activity; likewise, roughness, hardness, clarity, porosity, redness, dustiness, astringency, a bad taste in the mouth, dryness, piercing pain, numbness, contraction, stiffness, lameness, and so forth are the actions of Vāyu. One should diagnose a disorder of Vāta as being accompanied by these very symptoms.

1.20.13 | One should treat that [condition] with therapies that are sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, and hot—such as oleation, sudation, non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), nasal therapy (nastaḥkarma), diet, massage, rubbing, and affusion—all of which alleviate Vāta, while taking into account the proper dosage and timing. Among all these treatments for Vāta, physicians consider non-unctuous and unctuous enemas to be the most important; for these, having entered the colon from the very beginning, cut away the root of the purely morbid Vāta.

In that state, even when the external wind has been conquered, the disorders of wind within the body attain pacification; just as when the root of a tree is cut, the trunk, branches, sprouts, flowers, fruits, leaves, and so forth are inevitably destroyed, so it is here.

1.20.14 | Hereafter, we shall explain the forty disorders of *pitta*: burning sensation (*oṣa*), scorching (*ploṣa*), burning heat (*dāha*), inflammation (*davathu*), fuming sensation (*dhūmaka*), acidity (*amlaka*), acid eructation (*vidāha*), internal burning (*antardāha*), burning in the shoulders (*aṃsadāha*), excessive heat (*ūṣmādhikya*), excessive sweating (*atisveda*), body odor (*aṅgagandha*), cracking of the limbs (*aṅgāvadaraṇa*), moisture of the blood (*śoṇitakleda*), moisture of the flesh (*māṃsakleda*), burning of the skin (*tvagdāha*), cracking of the skin (*tvagavadaraṇa*), and peeling of the skin (*carmadalana*).

Red urticaria, red eruptions, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), red circular patches, greenish discoloration, yellowish discoloration, bluish skin, axillary eruption, jaundice, a bitter taste in the mouth, a blood-like odor from the mouth, fetid breath, excessive thirst, lack of satiety, burning of the mouth, inflammation of the throat, inflammation of the eyes, inflammation of the anus, inflammation of the penis, consumption of vital tissues, and entering into darkness.

And there is yellowness or turmeric-yellow coloration of the eyes, urine, and feces; thus, these forty disorders of pitta have been explained as the most manifest among the innumerable disorders of pitta.

1.20.15 | Indeed, among all these aforementioned disorders of pitta and others that have not been mentioned, this is the essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of pitta—immutable—and the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of its action, by perceiving which, or even a part thereof, skilled physicians determine with certainty that it is indeed a disorder of pitta. Namely: heat (*auṣṇya*), sharpness (*taikṣṇya*), liquidity (*dravatva*), lack of excessive unctuousness (*anatisneha*), a color excluding white and reddish-brown, a raw-flesh-like odor (*visra*), pungent and sour tastes (*rasa*), and mobility (*sarattva*); these are the essential natures of pitta.
Because bile (*pitta*) is of such a nature, these are its specific characteristics as it enters various parts of the body:

namely, burning, heat, digestion (*pāka*), perspiration, moisture, suppuration, itching, exudation, and redness, as well as the production of its own characteristic odor, color, and taste. One should diagnose a disorder of bile (*pittavikāra*) by identifying these qualities associated with it.

1.20.16 | One should treat that [condition] with sweet, bitter, astringent, and cold therapeutic measures—such as oleation, purgation, plasters, affusions, and massages—that alleviate pitta, taking into account the proper dosage and the appropriate time; indeed, physicians consider purgation to be the most important of all treatments for pitta.

For that [remedy], having entered the stomach from the very beginning, removes only the root of the morbid pitta; once the pitta has been conquered therein, the disorders of pitta located within the body also attain pacification, just as when the fire is removed, the fire-room alone becomes cool.

1.20.17 | Hereafter we shall explain the twenty disorders of *śleṣman* (phlegm), namely: satiety, drowsiness, excessive sleep, stiffness, heaviness of the limbs, laziness, sweetness of the mouth, salivation, spitting of phlegm, excess of waste matter, *balāsaka*, indigestion, coating of the heart, coating of the throat, thickening of the vessels, goiter, and extreme obesity.

Coldness of the digestive fire, urticaria, a whitish complexion, and whiteness of the urine, eyes, and feces—these twenty disorders of phlegm (śleṣman) are explained as the most manifest among the innumerable disorders of phlegm.

1.20.18 | Indeed, among all these aforementioned disorders of *śleṣman* as well as others not mentioned, this is the unchanging essential nature (*ātmarūpa*) of *śleṣman* and the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of its action, by perceiving which—whether in its entirety or in part—the experts, free from doubt, diagnose it as a disorder of *śleṣman*. Namely: unctuousness, coldness, whiteness, heaviness, sweetness, stability, sliminess, and smoothness are the essential natures of *śleṣman*.

Because phlegm (*śleṣman*) is of such a nature, these are its specific characteristics as it enters various parts of the body: namely—whiteness, coldness, itching, stability, heaviness, unctuousness, numbness, moisture, coating, binding, sweetness, and slowness of action are the functions of phlegm; one should diagnose a disorder of phlegm as being endowed with these very qualities.

1.20.19 | One should treat that [condition] with therapeutic measures consisting of pungent, bitter, astringent, sharp, hot, and dry substances, such as sudation, emesis, head-purgation, physical exercise, and other phlegm-subduing therapies, taking into account the proper dosage and the appropriate time.

Physicians consider emesis (vamana) to be the most important of all therapeutic procedures for the treatment of kapha, because it enters the stomach from the very beginning and, once the state of disease has subsided, expels the purely morbid kapha upwards. When that kapha has been conquered, even the internal disorders caused by kapha reach a state of pacification; just as when the embankment of a field is broken, rice, barley, ṣaṣṭika rice, and other crops dry up without being further saturated by water, so it is in this case.
1.20.20 | And there are verses on this point:
1.20.20ab | First, the physician should examine the disease, and immediately thereafter the medicine; 1.20.20cd | Subsequently, he should perform the treatment, preceded by knowledge.
But that physician who undertakes treatments without having understood the disease—
even if he is knowledgeable in the application of medicines— achieves success only by chance.
But he who knows the specific characteristics of diseases, is skilled in all medicinal remedies, and understands place, time, and dosage— for him, success is beyond doubt.
1.20.23 | Regarding this, there are these verses:
1.20.23ab | Summary, constitution, location, the gateway of transformation, and the onset;
1.20.23cd | As well as the absence of doubt and the sequelae of diseases have been fully elucidated.
1.20.24ab | The locations of the doshas that give rise to diseases, the various groups of diseases born from them, 1.20.24cd | the specific signs of each dosha, and their immutable functions.
1.20.25ab | And the therapeutic measures for the individual doshas have been specified; 1.20.25cd | correctly [taught] in this extensive chapter on diseases by the seer of reality.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Great Diseases," in the Section on General Principles of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The group of four diseases is concluded.
1.21.0 | Chapter Twenty-one.
1.21.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the Eight Things Not to Be Despised.
1.21.2 Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

1.21.3 | Here, indeed, with reference to the body, eight types of persons are censured; namely: one who is too tall, one who is too short, one who has excessive hair, one who is hairless, one who is too dark, one who is too fair, one who is too stout, and one who is too emaciated.
1.21.4 | In that regard, there are further specific censures concerning those who are excessively obese or excessively emaciated.

For the excessively obese person, there are eight defects: diminution of lifespan, obstruction of speed, difficulty in sexual intercourse, debility, foul odor, affliction by perspiration, excessive hunger, and excessive thirst. This excessive obesity arises from over-satiation, the consumption of heavy, sweet, cold, and unctuous foods, lack of exercise, lack of sexual activity, sleeping during the day, constant indulgence in joy, lack of mental concern [for one's health], and the nature of the seed (genetic predisposition).

For in one who has excessive fat (*medas*), it is fat alone that accumulates, and not the other *dhātus* in the same way; therefore, there is a decrease in his lifespan. Due to the flaccidity, softness, and heaviness of the fat, there is an obstruction of speed (*java*). Due to the paucity of semen (*śukra*) and because its path is obstructed by fat, sexual intercourse is difficult. There is debility due to the inequality of the *dhātus*, and foul odor due to the defects of the fat, the inherent nature of fat, and its tendency toward perspiration.

Due to the association with phlegm (śleṣman), its tendency to flow, its abundance, its heaviness, and its inability to withstand physical exertion, there is affliction by perspiration; and due to a sharp digestive fire and abundant abdominal wind, there is excessive hunger and an excess of thirst.
And there are verses on this point:
1.21.5ab | Because its pathways are obstructed by fat, the vāyu in the abdominal cavity specifically...
1.21.5cd | ...as it moves about, kindles the digestive fire and even dries up the food.
1.21.6ab | Therefore, he quickly digests his food and craves more; 1.21.6cd | and due to the lapse of time, he suffers certain terrible disorders.
1.21.7ab | These two, Agni and Māruta, especially cause affliction;
1.21.7cd | for these two burn the massive [trees], just as forest fires burn forests.

1.21.8ab | When fat has increased excessively, the [disorders] such as wind (anila) and the others, having suddenly produced severe morbidities, quickly destroy life. 1.21.8cd | [They] bring about dreadful disorders and swiftly take away vitality.

1.21.9ab | Due to the excessive growth of fat and muscle, one whose buttocks, abdomen, and breasts are unstable; 1.21.9cd | and whose nourishment and vigor are disproportionate—such a man is said to be excessively obese.
1.21.10ab | Thus have been specified the defects, the causes, and the symptoms of obesity. 1.21.10cd | Hereafter, that which is to be said regarding extreme emaciation will be explained.
1.21.11ab | The consumption of dry foods and drinks, fasting, eating in moderation; 1.21.11cd | excessive application of medical procedures, grief, and the suppression of natural urges and sleep.

1.21.12ab | Dryness, the use of rubbing powders, the habitual practice of bathing, natural constitution, and old age; 1.21.12cd | The persistence of morbid humors and anger—these afflict a man who is excessively emaciated.
A person who is emaciated cannot endure physical exertion, excessive satiety, hunger, thirst, disease, or medicine; likewise, such a person cannot withstand extreme cold, heat, or sexual intercourse.

Spleen disease, cough, wasting, dyspnea, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and abdominal enlargements— these diseases, as well as those affecting the digestive tract, generally afflict the emaciated person.
1.21.15ab | One who has shriveled buttocks, belly, and neck, covered with a network of veins;
1.21.15cd | who is extremely emaciated, reduced to skin and bone, and has thickened joints, is considered a *sthūlaparvan* man.
1.21.16ab | These two types of men—the excessively obese and the excessively emaciated—are constantly afflicted by disease.
1.21.16cd | Therefore, they must be constantly treated with both depleting and nourishing therapies.
1.21.17ab | Between obesity and emaciation, emaciation is preferable, for those two are balanced in their requirements.
1.21.17cd | If disease should afflict both, it would afflict the obese person far more severely.
A man whose flesh and body proportions are balanced,
who possesses firm sense organs, is not overcome by disorders through his strength.
1.21.19ab | Enduring hunger, thirst, heat, cold, and physical exertion, 1.21.19cd | He is considered to have balanced digestion, balanced aging, and a balanced accumulation of muscle mass.
1.21.20ab | For those who are obese, heavy food that is depleting is desired for the purpose of emaciation;
1.21.20cd | whereas for those who are lean, light food that is nourishing is intended for the purpose of building up the body.
1.21.21ab | Foods and drinks that subdue Vāta and remove Kapha and fat;
1.21.21cd | Dry and hot enemas, sharp [medicines], and dry massages.

1.21.22ab | The administration of *guḍūcī* and *bhadramustā*, as well as that of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*); 1.21.22cd | The administration of *takrāriṣṭa* and the administration of honey (*mākṣika*).
Viḍaṅga, ginger, alkali, iron filings, honey,
and the powder of barley and āmalaka— this formulation combined with honey [is used].
The formulation of the five roots beginning with bilva (bilvādi-pañcamūla), combined with honey, [is also used].
1.21.24cd | And the administration of *śilājatu*, as well as the juice of *agnimantha*, is supreme.
1.21.25ab | *Praśātikā*, *priyaṅgu*, *śyāmāka*, *yavaka*, and *yava*;
1.21.25cd | *jūrṇāhvā*, *kodrava*, *mudga*, *kulattha*, and *cakramudgaka*.
The seeds of *jāḍhakī* should be used for food together with *paṭola* and *āmalaka*, followed by honey-water as a drink.
One should administer non-toxic (ariṣṭa) preparations as after-drinks to remove fat, muscle tissue, and phlegm;
these should be applied in appropriate combinations for the destruction of excessive corpulence.
One who desires to abandon obesity should gradually increase staying awake, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, and mental exertion.
1.21.29ab | Sleep, joy, a comfortable bed, tranquility of mind, and peace; 1.21.29cd | cessation of anxiety, sexual intercourse, and physical exertion, and the sight of what is dear.
Fresh grains, fresh wine, the juices of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals,
as well as seasoned meats, curd, clarified butter, and milks.
1.21.31ab | Sugarcane, śāli rice, mung beans, wheat, and preparations of jaggery;
1.21.31cd | Enemas that are unctuous and sweet, and the constant application of oil massage.
1.21.32ab | Anointing with unctuous substances, massage, bathing, and the use of perfumes and garlands; 1.21.32cd | white clothing, and the timely elimination of the bodily humors (doṣas).
The practice of elixirs (*rasāyana*), aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya*),
and medicinal formulations destroys extreme emaciation and bestows upon men the highest degree of corpulence.
By not thinking about his affairs, by constant gratification,
and through indulgence in sleep, a man thrives like a boar.
But when the mind is weary and the faculties whose nature is action are overcome by fatigue, they withdraw from their objects; then the human being sleeps.
1.21.36ab | Happiness and suffering, nourishment and emaciation, strength and weakness; 1.21.36cd | virility and impotence, knowledge and ignorance, and even life itself depend upon sleep.
Sleep indulged in at the wrong time and to excess would destroy both happiness and longevity, like another Kālarātri (the Night of Doom).
That very sleep, when properly applied, again unites the body with happiness and long life,
just as true wisdom, having arrived, unites a yogin with spiritual perfection.
1.21.39ab | Those exhausted by singing, Vedic study, liquor, women, labor, carrying heavy loads, or walking long distances;
1.21.39cd | those suffering from indigestion, those with chest wounds, the emaciated, the elderly, children, and likewise the weak.
1.21.40ab | Those afflicted by thirst, diarrhea, and colic; those suffering from dyspnea, hiccups, and emaciation;
1.21.40cd | Those who have fallen, been struck, or are insane; and those exhausted by travel or staying awake at night.
1.21.41ab | Those who are exhausted by anger, grief, or fear, and those accustomed to sleeping during the day; 1.21.41cd | all these should practice daytime sleep at all times.
1.21.42ab | For thus, the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus) and their strength arise;
1.21.42cd | phlegm (śleṣman) nourishes the limbs, and stability of life is attained.
1.21.43ab | In the summer, however, when the winds are drying due to the onset of heat and the vital air (māruta) is increasing,
1.21.43cd | sleeping during the day for very short durations is recommended, as the nights are exceedingly brief.
In seasons other than summer, daytime sleep provokes *śleṣman* and *pitta*; therefore, daytime sleep is not recommended during those times.
Those who are obese, those who constantly use unctuous substances, those with a predominance of *kapha*, those suffering from *kapha*-related diseases,
and those afflicted by *dūṣīviṣa* poisoning should never sleep during the day.
1.21.46ab | Halīmaka, headache, a sense of numbness, heaviness of the limbs, 1.21.46cd | body ache, loss of digestive fire, and a coating over the heart.
1.21.47ab | Swelling, anorexia, nausea, coryza, and hemicrania;
1.21.47cd | Eruptions, skin lesions, pustules, itching, drowsiness, cough, and diseases of the throat.
1.21.48ab | Confusion of memory and intellect, obstruction of the channels, fever, 1.21.48cd | incapacity of the sense organs, and the onset of the force of the poison.
1.21.49ab | From the habitual practice of sleeping during the day, which is unwholesome, there arises [disease] in men.
