1.21.49cd | Therefore, having understood sleep to be either beneficial or harmful, the wise man should sleep comfortably.
1.21.50ab | Waking at night is parching, while sleeping during the day is unctuous.
1.21.50cd | However, sitting and dozing is neither parching nor obstructive to the channels.

1.21.51ab | Just as food is for the maintenance of the body, so is sleep considered to be for its well-being. 1.21.51cd | Obesity and emaciation arise specifically from the nature of one's sleep and diet.
1.21.52ab | Oil massage, rubbing the body, bathing, the juices of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals;
1.21.52cd | Shali rice, curd, milk, unctuous substances, wine, and mental pleasure.
1.21.53ab | Fragrances, sounds, and massages that are agreeable to the mind;
1.21.53cd | Anointing of the eyes, and anointment of the head and the face.
1.21.54ab | A well-spread bed, a dwelling, comfort, and likewise a suitable time—
1.21.54cd | These bring about sleep before long, even when it has been lost due to some cause.
1.21.55ab | Purging of the body and the head, emesis, fear, 1.21.55cd | anxiety, anger, as well as smoking, physical exercise, and bloodletting.
Fasting, an uncomfortable bed, nobility of character, and mastery over darkness ward off the harmful onset of excessive sleepiness.
1.21.57ab | These very factors should be known as the causes of insomnia:
1.21.57cd | the action, the time, the morbid transformation, the constitution, and indeed the wind.
Sleep arises from *tamas*, from phlegm (*śleṣman*), and from exhaustion of mind and body;

it may also be adventitious, following upon disease, or produced by the very nature of night. Those who know the truth declare that sleep produced by the nature of night is the sustainer of living beings (*bhūtadhātrī*).
They say that sleep arising from *tamas* is the root of sin, while they designate the remaining types as occurring within the context of diseases.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
1.21.60ab | Among those censured persons, the two who are especially censured,
1.21.60cd | the reason for their censure, their defects, and the treatment for those defects.

1.21.61ab | For those to whom sleep is beneficial at certain times, and for those to whom it is harmful at others; 1.21.61cd | that which serves as the remedy for excessive sleep and for insomnia is itself [sleep].
1.21.62ab | Whatever sleep there may be, and whatever its specific power, all that the son of Atri,
Punarvasu, proclaimed within the enumeration of the eight irreproachable [sleeps].
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Eight Things Not to Be Condemned," in the Section on General Principles of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Twenty-Two.
1.22.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on lightening and nourishing therapies.
1.22.2 | Thus said the venerable Ātreya.
1.22.3 | Ātreya spoke, exhorting his six most excellent disciples, Agniveśa and the others, who were devoted to austerity and the study of the sacred texts.

1.22.4 | He who understands the proper timing for lightening therapy (laṅghana), nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa), drying therapy (rūkṣaṇa), oleation therapy (snehana), sudation therapy (svedana), and astringent therapy (stambhana)— he indeed is a physician.
1.22.5 | When Ātreya had spoken thus, Agniveśa said to him:

1.22.6 | O Blessed One, what is fasting (laṅghana), and who are those fit for fasting? What is nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa), who are those fit for nourishment, and who are those fit for drying therapy (rūkṣaṇa)? What is drying therapy itself?

1.22.7 | O Teacher, you should explain: what are the unctuous substances and who are considered fit for oleation? What are the sudorifics and who are considered fit for sudation? And what is the astringent therapy, and who are fit for it?

1.22.8 | You should describe, in brief, the characteristics of these six [therapeutic measures] beginning with fasting (laṅghana), when they have been properly administered, under-administered, or over-administered.
1.22.9 | Having heard those words of Agniveśa, the Teacher said:
"Whatever causes lightness in the body is known as *laṅghana* (fasting/lightening therapy)."
That which produces bulkiness of the body is *bṛṃhaṇa* (nourishing);
that which produces dryness, roughness, and clarity is indeed *rūkṣaṇa* (desiccating).
1.22.11 | Oleation (snehana) produces unctuousness, lubrication, softness, and moisture; it overcomes stiffness, heaviness, and cold.
Fomentation (svedana) produces perspiration and overcomes stiffness, heaviness, and cold.
1.22.12 | Stambhana (astringent) is that which makes the mobile and unstable firm and steady;
it is light, hot, sharp, clear, dry, subtle, rough, and mobile.
1.22.13 | A substance that is generally hard is considered *laṅghana* (lightening therapy). [Substances that are] heavy, cold, soft, unctuous, thick, gross, and slimy [are the opposite].
1.22.14 | Generally, a substance that is mild, stable, and smooth is said to be nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa).
That which is dry, light, rough, sharp, hot, stable, and non-slimy [is said to be depleting].
1.22.15 | Generally, that substance which is hard is indeed drying (rūkṣaṇa).
That which is liquid, subtle, mobile, unctuous, slimy, heavy, cold,
and generally mild or soft is considered unctuous (snehana).
1.22.16 | A substance that is generally hot, sharp, mobile, unctuous, dry, subtle, liquid, stable,
and heavy is said to be sudorific (svedana).
1.22.17 | That substance which is described as cold, mild, soft, smooth, dry, subtle, liquid,
and stable is generally considered to be astringent (stambhana).
1.22.18 | There are four types of purification: thirst, wind, and heat;
digestive stimulants, fasting, and physical exercise—these constitute lightening therapy (laṅghana).
Those with abundant phlegm (śleṣman), bile (pitta), blood (asṛj), and waste products (mala), whose bodily humors (māruta) are combined,
and who possess large bodies and strength, should be treated with lightening therapies (laṅghana) through purificatory procedures (viśuddhi).
1.22.20 | Those whose diseases of moderate strength arise from phlegm and bile—
namely vomiting, diarrhea, heart disease, choleraic disorders, intestinal torpor, and fever— [should be treated with emetics].
1.22.21 | Constipation, heaviness, eructation, nausea, anorexia, and other such symptoms— the wise physician should generally treat these first with digestive (pācana) measures.
1.22.22 | Those very same diseases for which the humors have become weak should be conquered by the suppression of thirst and by fasting.

1.22.23 | One may conquer diseases of moderate strength through physical exercise, exposure to the sun, and wind; how much more so those whose strength is inferior, especially for those who possess great strength?

1.22.24 | For those suffering from skin diseases, for those with excessive urination, and for those who have been treated with unctuous, fluid-retaining, and nourishing therapies— even for those with disorders of Vata— lightening therapy (laṅghana) is recommended during the winter season.

1.22.25 | The meat of deer, fish, and birds that have been killed by poisoned arrows, are unexhausted, are in the prime of their youth, and live in their natural habitats, is said to be nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa*).
1.22.26 | Those who are emaciated, wounded, lean, aged, weak, constant travelers,
those habitually addicted to women and wine, and persons in the summer heat— these men are said to require nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa).
1.22.27 | For those who have been emaciated by wasting diseases, hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), and other ailments,
the light meat-soups of carnivorous animals serve as nourishing therapy.
1.22.28 | Bathing, massage, sleep, sweet unctuous enemas,
sugar, milk, and ghee— these are all promoters of intelligence and nourishers of the intellect.

1.22.29 | The consumption of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances; lack of restraint with women; and the intake of oil-cakes, oil-cakes from sesame, buttermilk, honey, and similar items, which cause dryness.
1.22.30 | Those conditions characterized by excessive secretions, those involving the major doṣas, those located in vital spots (marmans),
and diseases such as ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs) are indicated for drying therapy (rūkṣaṇīya).

1.22.31 | Those oils that are to be used for oleation and those persons who are to be subjected to sudation have been described by me in detail in the chapter on oleation and in the one called sudation.
1.22.32 | All that medicine which is liquid, thin, and cooling,
and which is sweet, bitter, or astringent, is entirely styptic (stambhana).
1.22.33 | Those who have been burnt by bile, alkali, or fire; those afflicted by vomiting and diarrhea;
and those suffering from the excessive administration of poison or sudation—these are indicated as cases requiring astringent (stambhana) treatment.
1.22.34 | When there is the discharge of flatus, urine, and feces; lightness in the limbs; purification of the heart, eructations, throat, and mouth; and when drowsiness and fatigue have passed; ||

1.22.35 | When perspiration has arisen, when there is a relish for food, when hunger and thirst manifest themselves, and when the inner self is free from distress, the fasting regimen should be declared as accomplished.
1.22.36 | Splitting pain in the joints, aching of the limbs, cough, dryness of the mouth,
loss of appetite, anorexia, thirst, and weakness of the ears and eyes.
1.22.37 | Excessive mental agitation, frequent upward movement of wind (ūrdhvavāta), darkness in the heart,
and the destruction of the body's digestive fire and strength occur when fasting is practiced to excess.
1.22.38 | Strength, the attainment of nourishment, and the elimination of the defects of emaciation are the characteristics of one who has been nourished;
whereas excessive thickness is the characteristic of one who has been excessively nourished.

When the signs of "done" (kṛta) or "over-done" (atikṛta) appear upon the emesis being bypassed or when it has become parched, the patient becomes stiff; this occurs once strength is regained and the aforementioned diseases have been conquered.
1.22.40 | A darkish complexion, stiffness of the limbs, agitation, lockjaw,
and suppression of the heart and bowels are the symptoms of excessive immobilization (atistambhita).
1.22.41 | Briefly stated, the characteristic of these six unprocessed medicinal substances is simply the subsiding or the increase of the bodily constituents (dhātus).

1.22.42 | Thus, six effective therapeutic measures for all diseases have been correctly described; they are proven for the successful treatment of curable conditions when administered in accordance with the proper dosage and timing.
And there is a verse on this point:
"Due to the extensive combination of the humors (doṣas), the therapeutic measures indeed become intermingled;
yet they do not exceed the number six, just as the humors such as Vāta and the others do not exceed the number three."

1.22.44 | Regarding this, there are these verses: Thus, in this chapter on fasting (laṅghana), the six therapeutic measures have been explained by the Blessed One, by means of which medical treatment proceeds in accordance with the questions asked.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Lightening and Nourishing," in the Section on General Principles (Ślokasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Twenty-three:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on "Excessive Satiation" (Santarpaṇīya).
1.23.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.23.3 | He who satiates himself with unctuous, sweet, heavy, and slimy foods, with fresh grains, fresh wines, and the meats of marshy and aquatic animals;
1.23.4 | Indulging excessively in dairy products, foods made with molasses, and those made from flour;
loathing physical exertion; and being devoted to the pleasures of sleeping by day and reclining on beds and seats.
1.23.5 | Diseases arising from the cause of over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa) arise in him:
urinary disorders (prameha), carbuncles (piḍakā), urticaria (koṭha), itching (kaṇḍū), anemia (pāṇḍu-āmaya), and fever (jvara).
1.23.6 | Skin diseases (kuṣṭha), disorders of undigested matter (āma-pradoṣa), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), and anorexia (arocaka).
Drowsiness, impotence, excessive corpulence, laziness, and heaviness of the limbs.
1.23.7 | There is a coating of the channels of the senses, delusion of the intellect, lethargy,
swellings, and other such conditions for one who does not apply a remedy quickly.
In that condition, scraping (ullekhana), purgation (vireka), bloodletting (raktamokṣaṇa),
physical exercise (vyāyāma), fasting (upavāsa), medicated smoking (dhūma), and sudation therapies (svedana) are recommended.
1.23.9 | The consumption of *abhayā* with honey, generally the use of dry foods,
and the powders and ointments that have been described as destroyers of itching and urticaria [are recommended].
1.23.10 | One should drink the decoction of triphalā, āragvadha, pāṭhā, saptaparṇa, vatsaka, musta, madana, and nimba, boiled with water.

1.23.11 | By that [practice], when applied according to the proper measure and time, disorders arising from over-satiation such as urinary disorders (*meha*) and others will certainly be destroyed for one who practices it.
1.23.12 | Mustā, āragvadha, pāṭhā, triphalā, and devadāru;
śvadaṃṣṭrā, khadira, nimba, the two types of haridrā, and the bark of vatsaka.
1.23.13 | A man who drinks their juice every morning according to his specific dosha is completely liberated from all diseases caused by over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa).
1.23.14 | By employing these in the form of body rubs, massages, and medicinal baths, skin disorders are pacified; likewise, when combined with oleation therapies.
1.23.15 | Kuṣṭha, gomedaka, hiṅgu, krauñca-bone, trikaṭu, vacā, vṛṣaka, elā,
śvadaṃṣṭrā, kharāhvā, and aśmabheda;
1.23.16 | This, when drunk with buttermilk, whey from curd, or the sour juice of jujube, cures dysuria and urinary disorders (prameha).
1.23.17 | By the administration of buttermilk with *abhayā*, as well as with *triphalā*,
and by the use of fermented medicinal liquors (*ariṣṭas*), urinary disorders and other ailments are pacified.
1.23.18 | This churned drink (mantha), consisting of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), honey, viḍaṅga (krimighna), and ajamodā,
along with parched grain flour (saktu) and oil, is beneficial when prepared by being steeped in iron-water.
1.23.19 | Vyōṣa, viḍaṅga, śigru, triphalā, kaṭurohiṇī,
the two types of bṛhatī, the two types of haridrā, pāṭhā, ativiṣā, and sthirā.
1.23.20 | One should powder asafoetida, roots of *kebuka*, *yavānī*, coriander, *citraka*, black salt, cumin, and *hapuṣā*.
1.23.21 | The portions of powder, oil, ghee, and honey should be equal in measure;
one should drink this satiation mixture with sixteen times the portion of roasted grain flour (saktu).
1.23.22 | By the application of this [oil], diseases arising from over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa) are pacified,
as are urinary disorders (prameha), obstructed winds (mūḍhavāta), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas), and jaundice (kāmalā).
1.23.23 | Splenic enlargement, anemia, edema, dysuria, anorexia,
heart disease, pulmonary consumption, cough, asthma, and throat obstruction.
1.23.24 | Worms, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), excessive paleness, and extreme corpulence [are cured];
furthermore, the digestive fire of men is kindled, and memory and intellect increase.
One who is constant in physical exercise, eats old *śyāmāka* grain and barley or wheat,
is freed from obesity and released from the disorders caused by over-nutrition (*saṃtarpaṇa*).

1.23.26 | It has been stated that for diseases arising from over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa), the remedy is under-nutrition (apatarpaṇa). Hereafter, the diseases born of under-nutrition, along with their remedies, will be described.
1.23.27 | Wasting away of the body, digestive fire, strength, complexion, vitality, semen, and muscle;
fever accompanied by cough, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite.
1.23.28 | Weakness of hearing, insanity, delirium, pain in the heart,
retention of feces and urine, and colic localized in the calves, thighs, and sacrum.
1.23.29 | The joints of the bones, the marrow, and whatever other diseases are born of Vāta—
such as Ūrdhvavāta and others— all arise from under-nourishment (apatarpaṇa).

1.23.30 | Regarding them, the experts have further declared a medicinal treatment for nourishment (saṃtarpaṇa) which is desired whether it be effective for immediate use or for regular practice. 1.23.31 | For one who has become emaciated immediately [due to depletion] is indeed restored immediately by means of nourishing therapy.
It does not dance [with agitation], but through the practice of nourishment, it flourishes even when long depleted.

1.23.32 | For one who has been weak for a long time, the physician should administer medicine without haste, acting in accordance with the patient's body, the digestive fire, the humors, the dosage, and the season.
1.23.33 | Meat broths, milks, and ghees are beneficial for him,
as are baths, enemas, massages, and nourishing drinks.
1.23.34 | For those afflicted by fever and cough, those who are emaciated, those suffering from dysuria,
those with excessive thirst, and those with upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), nourishing draughts (tarpaṇa) will now be described as beneficial.
1.23.35 | A churned drink (mantha) made from equal parts of sugar, long pepper, oil, ghee, and honey,
with double the amount of roasted grain flour (saktu), is praised as an aphrodisiac for them.
1.23.36 | A satiation drink (tarpaṇa) consisting of roasted grain flour (saktu), wine (madirā), honey (kṣaudra), and sugar (śarkarā) should be drunk;
it facilitates the downward movement of wind (māruta), feces, urine, phlegm (kapha), and bile (pitta).
One should drink a satiating mixture of treacle, roasted grain flour (saktu), ghee, whey, and sour gruel;
it cures dysuria and alleviates upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
1.23.38 | A churned drink (mantha) prepared with dates, grapes, vṛkṣāmla, amlīka, pomegranates,
parūṣaka, and āmalaka cures disorders caused by alcohol.
1.23.39 | A *mantha* (thick drink) made with water, whether sweet, sour, oily, or even dry,
provides immediate satiation and bestows stability, complexion, and strength.

1.23.40 | Regarding this, there is a verse: The diseases arising from over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa) and those arising from under-nutrition (apatarpaṇa), along with their remedies, have been fully described in this chapter on Saṃtarpaṇīya.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, named "On Satiation," in the Section on Verses (*Ślokasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Twenty-four: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules regarding blood (*Vidhiśoṇitīya*).
1.24.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules regarding blood.
1.24.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.24.3 | When blood has arisen [as a result of injury], it becomes pure for embodied beings through the prescribed method;
that method which has been fully elucidated according to place, time, and individual suitability.
1.24.4 | For that pure blood endows living beings with strength, complexion, happiness, and longevity;
indeed, life follows the state of the blood.
1.24.5 | By excessively corrupted, numerous, sharp, and hot liquors, as well as by other substances of that kind,
and likewise by those that are very salty, alkaline, sour, and pungent.
1.24.6 By the consumption of horse gram, black gram, flat beans, and sesame oil,
and by all kinds of greens such as the root of the elephant-foot yam and radish;
1.24.7 | From the consumption of aquatic, marshy, and wild animals, as well as those that seize their prey, and from the use of curd, sour liquids, whey, fermented gruel, wine, and sauvīraka;
1.24.8 By eating incompatible foods, or those that are damp and putrid;
by sleeping during the day after eating; and by consuming liquids, oily, and heavy substances [at improper times].
1.24.9 | Likewise, for those who eat excessively and indulge in anger, the heat of the sun and fire,
due to the suppression of the urge to vomit and from not drinking water at the proper time, [arises].
1.24.10 | Blood becomes severely vitiated by exhaustion, injury, and heat, as well as by indigestion and overeating,
and by the very nature of the autumn season.
1.24.11 | Thereafter, various diseases born of blood arise:
inflammation of the mouth, redness of the eyes, and a foul odor from the nose and mouth.
1.24.12 | Gulma, upakuśa, visarpa,
raktapitta, pramīlaka, abscess (vidradhi), raktameha, pradara, and vātaśoṇita.
1.24.13 | Discoloration, loss of digestive fire, thirst, heaviness of the limbs, burning sensations,
extreme debility, loss of appetite, and pain in the head.
1.24.14 | There is a burning sensation in the food and drink, bitter and sour eructations, exhaustion, an abundance of anger, confusion of the intellect, and a salty taste in the mouth.
1.24.15 | Perspiration, foul odor of the body, intoxication, trembling, loss of voice,
excessive drowsiness and sleep, and the frequent perception of darkness;
1.24.16 | Itching, eruptions, pustules, leprosy, skin-scaling, and so forth—
all these disorders are to be understood as having their seat in the blood.

1.24.17 | Those diseases which, though treated with cold, hot, unctuous, dry, and other remedies, are not properly cured when they ought to be curable— one should recognize them as being born of blood (rakta).
1.24.18 | In cases of blood disorders, one should employ treatments that alleviate raktapitta (hemorrhagic diseases),
as well as purgation, fasting, and the draining of blood.

1.24.19 | One should cause the blood of a person to flow out by considering the strength of the disease, the measure of the bodily humors, the degree of purification, or the state of the blood itself, or by carefully examining the internal seat of the disorder.
1.24.20 | From vāta, the blood becomes reddish-brown, clear, frothy, and thin;
from pitta, it is yellowish-black or red, and due to its heat, it clots slowly.
1.24.21 | Slightly pale due to vitiated *kapha*, slimy, fibrous, and thick;
characterized by combined symptoms (*saṃsarga*), it possesses the signs of all three [doshas] in the case of *sānnipātika* (combined morbidity).
1.24.22 | Know that pure blood has the luster of refined gold and the indragopa insect, resembles the color of lotus-juice and lac, and is the same hue as the guñjā fruit.
1.24.23 | When blood has been removed, food and drink that are neither too hot nor too cold, light, and digestive-stimulating are beneficial.
For at that time, the body—having its blood unstable—and especially the digestive fire, must be protected.

1.24.24 | They praise the man whose complexion and senses are clear, who does not crave the objects of the senses, whose digestive fire is unimpeded, who is endowed with happiness, contentment, and strength, and whose blood is pure.
1.24.25 | When, however, the aggravated humors (malas) enter the channels that carry blood and those designated as carrying rasa— either individually or all together— then [the following occurs].
1.24.26 | In one whose habit is impure food, whose self is shrouded by passion and delusion, the humors remain obstructed, and then diseases arise.
1.24.27 | A wise physician should recognize intoxication (mada), fainting (mūrchā), and coma (saṃnyāsa) among these [conditions];
in their causes, symptoms, and subsidence, there is an increasing degree of severity in each subsequent one.
1.24.28 | When Vāyu enters that weak station of the mind,
agitating the mind of the living being, it then causes the loss of consciousness.
1.24.29 | In this same way, pitta and likewise kapha, by agitating the mind of men, bring about confusion of consciousness; the specific details regarding this will now be explained.

One should recognize one possessed by the intoxication of wind (vātamada) as having speech that is stuck, not infrequent, and rapid; with movements that are wavering and faltering; having a dry, dark-brown, or reddish appearance;
speaking with anger and harshness; and being fond of fighting and quarreling.
One should recognize a person overcome by pitta-intoxication by its appearance, which is reddish, yellowish, or blackish.

One should recognize that a person afflicted by intoxication caused by *kapha* speaks very little and incoherently, is possessed of drowsiness and laziness, is pale, and is constantly absorbed in deep reflection.
1.24.33 | All these symptoms arise from intoxication caused by the combination [of all three humors];
this intoxication, which has the appearance of liquor-induced intoxication, arises quickly and is quickly pacified.
1.24.34 | That which is called intoxication caused by liquor, that caused by poison, and that caused by blood—
all these intoxications do not occur without the triad of vāta, pitta, and kapha.
1.24.35 | Seeing the sky as blue, or black, or even reddish, he enters into darkness and awakens quickly. 1.24.36 | There is trembling, aching of the limbs, and pain in the heart.
Emaciation and a dark-red complexion occur when fainting is caused by Vata.
Seeing the sky as red, green, yellow, or even white,
he enters into darkness and awakens covered in sweat.
1.24.38 | Thirsty and afflicted with heat, with eyes turbid from blood and bile, with loose stools and a yellowish complexion— these are the signs when fainting arises from Pitta.
Seeing the sky covered with dense masses of darkness like clouds,
he enters into that darkness and awakens only after a long time.
1.24.40 | When fainting arises from phlegm (kapha), it is accompanied by salivation and nausea, as if the limbs were covered with heavy, moist hides.
1.24.41 | Manifesting every form, like an epilepsy (apasmāra) arising from a derangement of the humors (sannipāta),
it swiftly casts down a person even without loathsome movements.
1.24.42 | When the [three] humors (*doṣa*) have produced intoxication and fainting in embodied beings,
they subside by themselves once their impulse has spent, even without medicines or ritual renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
1.24.43 | The exceedingly powerful impurities, having seized the activity of speech, body, and mind,
abandon the weak creature who has taken refuge in the abodes of the vital breaths.
1.24.44 | Having renounced everything through formal renunciation, becoming like a piece of wood and resembling one who is dead,
he is swiftly deprived of his life-breaths, having abandoned actions that yield immediate results.
1.24.45 | Just as a wise man would swiftly seize a vessel sinking in deep water before it reaches the bottom, so too should he grasp the one afflicted by renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
1.24.46 | Collyriums, expressed juices, medicinal smokes, insufflations,
pricking with needles, cauterization, and pressure between the nails are recommended [for the treatment of eye diseases].
1.24.47 | Plucking out the hair of the head and body, biting with the teeth,
and rubbing against a female animal (ātmaguptā) are beneficial for awakening him.
One should repeatedly pour into his mouth various strong intoxicants that have been concentrated and mixed with abundant pungent substances.
1.24.49 | Likewise, one should administer the juice of *mātuluṅga* combined with *mahauṣadha*; similarly, one should give *sauvarcala* salt mixed with wine, sour gruel, and *kāñjika*.
1.24.50 | One should administer asafoetida and trikaṭu until consciousness is restored;
once consciousness has returned, one should treat the patient with light foods.
By means of wonders that cause amazement, reminders, and things pleasant to hear; by the sharp sounds of songs and musical instruments, and by various spectacles.
1.24.52 | By means of emetics, purgatives, fumigations, collyriums, gargles,
bloodletting, as well as physical exercise and friction massage.
1.24.53 | When consciousness has been restored, the wise physician should initiate supportive treatment;
for his mind must be protected from the causes of relapse.

1.24.54 | For those who have been prepared with oleation and sudation, one should perform the five therapeutic procedures according to the specific dosha and the patient's strength, in cases of fainting and intoxication.
1.24.55 | Likewise, the administration of the twenty-eight-ingredient bitter ghee (tikta-sarpis),
or similarly that of the great six-pala ghee (mahat-ṣaṭpala), is recommended.
1.24.56 | Alternatively, there is the use of triphalā combined with ghee, honey, and sugar;
or the use of śilājatu; or even the use of milk.
1.24.57 | The use of long pepper with milk, or of chitraka with milk,
or of the kumbha-sarpis elixir is highly recommended.
1.24.58 | Through bloodletting, through the study of the scriptures, and by attending upon virtuous and courageous people, intoxication and fainting are pacified in embodied beings.
1.24.59 | Regarding this, there are two verses:— The pure and the impure blood, their causes, the diseases arising from the vitiation of the blood, and the medicinal treatment for those diseases.

In this chapter on the [proper] procedure regarding bloodletting, all of this— the causes, symptoms, and treatments for intoxication (mada), fainting (mūrchā), and collapse (saṃnyāsa)— has been elucidated.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, named "The Regulation of Blood," in the Section on General Principles of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The group of four chapters on Application is completed.
Chapter Twenty-Five.
1.25.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the origin of man (Yajjapuruṣīya).
1.25.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.25.3ab | Long ago, when the great seers—whose nature was directly perceived—had assembled before the venerable Punarvasu, this conversation arose.
1.25.3cd | This conversation appeared among those gathered great sages.

1.25.4ab | That which is designated as the "Person" (puruṣa), consisting of the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects; 1.25.4cd | and this aggregate of diseases—[this is the subject] for the determination of their prior origin.
1.25.5ab | In the meantime, Vāmaka, the lord of Kāśī, who was skilled in the meaning of words,
1.25.5cd | approached the assembly of seers and, having offered his salutations, spoke these words.
1.25.6ab | "O sirs, is it true that whatever kind of person one is born as, that same kind of diseases are said to afflict him?
1.25.6cd | When the king had spoken thus, Punarvasu replied to the sages:
1.25.7ab | All of you, whose doubts have been severed by immeasurable knowledge and discernment, 1.25.7cd | ought to dispel the doubt of the King of Kāśī.
1.25.8ab | Having examined that thoroughly, Pārīkṣi first spoke these words to Maudgalya:
1.25.8cd | "The person is born of the self, and diseases are born of the self; for he is the cause."
1.25.9ab | He accumulates and experiences both action and the fruits of action;
1.25.9cd | for without the element of consciousness, there is no engagement with pleasure and pain.
1.25.10ab | But Śaraloman said, "No; for one who hates suffering would never, by means of the self, join the self with diseases and sufferings."
1.25.11ab | But the mind, when enveloped by rajas and tamas, is designated as sattva;
1.25.11cd | it is the cause for the production of the body and of its modifications.
1.25.12ab | But the knower of water said, "No; for the mind alone is not the cause.
1.25.12cd | Without the body there are no bodily diseases, nor does the mind persist."
1.25.13ab | Living beings and various kinds of diseases are born from rasa (flavor/nutrient essence).
1.25.13cd | For water possesses rasa; it is traditionally held to be the cause of their manifestation.
1.25.14ab | Hiraṇyākṣa, however, said "No," for the self is not considered to be born of rasa.
1.25.14cd | The mind is not beyond the senses; likewise, there are diseases born from sound and other [objects].
1.25.15ab | A person is born from the six elements, and likewise diseases are born from the six elements.
1.25.15cd | For this aggregate is proclaimed by the primordial Sāṃkhyas to be composed of the six elements.
To Kuśika who was speaking thus, Kauśika said, "No;
for how could one born of the six elements exist without mother and father?"
1.25.17ab | A man is born from a man, a cow from a cow, and a horse from a horse.
1.25.17cd | Diseases such as urinary disorders (meha) are said to be hereditary; these are the causes in this case.
1.25.18ab | Bhadrakāpya, however, said "No," for a blind person is not born from one who is blind.
1.25.18cd | Furthermore, your [theory] that the parents themselves were produced prior [to the child] is not tenable.
1.25.19ab | A living being is considered to be born of karma, and its diseases are likewise born of karma.
1.25.19cd | There is no birth of diseases or of a person without the performance of karma.
1.25.20ab | Bharadvāja, however, said "No," for the agent is prior to the action.
1.25.20cd | An unperformed action is not seen; how could a person be the fruit of that which has not been done?

1.25.21ab | The cause of the manifestation [of disease] is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of both diseases and the person; 1.25.21cd | just as hardness, liquidity, mobility, and heat are indeed the inherent natures of earth, water, wind, and fire respectively.
1.25.22ab | Kāṅkāyana, however, said "No," for there would be no fruit of an undertaking.
1.25.22cd | There would be neither the non-establishment nor the establishment of entities by way of their own nature.

1.25.23ab | You are the creator of boundless resolve, Brahmā, the progenitor, and the lord of creatures; 1.25.23cd | [the master] of this world of sentient and insentient beings, and of their pleasure and pain.
1.25.24ab | "Not so," said the mendicant Ātreya; for Prajāpati is not one's offspring.
1.25.24cd | Desiring the constant welfare of his subjects, he would not, like an unrighteous man, yoke them to sufferings.
1.25.25ab | Man indeed is born of time, and his diseases are likewise born of time.
1.25.25cd | The entire world is subject to time; time is the cause everywhere.
1.25.26ab | Then Punarvasu spoke this to the ṛṣis as they were disputing:
1.25.26cd | "Do not speak thus; for truth is difficult to attain through reliance on partisan positions."
1.25.27ab | For those who speak arguments along with counter-arguments as if they were certain, 1.25.27cd | do not reach the end of the position, moving like a sesame presser.
1.25.28ab | Having thus abandoned the clash of disputations, let the inner self be contemplated.
1.25.28cd | As long as the mass of darkness has not been shaken off, knowledge does not proceed toward the object of knowledge.
For those very same conditions that produce prosperity in a man,
those very same conditions may also bring forth various calamities and diseases.

1.25.30 | Then, having heard the words of the venerable Ātreya, Vāmaka, the lord of Kāśī, spoke again to the venerable Ātreya: "Venerable sir, what is the cause for the increase of a person born with favorable signs and of diseases born from unfavorable signs?"

1.25.31 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "The consumption of wholesome food alone brings about the growth of a person, whereas the consumption of unwholesome food, on the other hand, is the cause of disease."

1.25.32 | To the Blessed One Ātreya, who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, how may we understand here the unmistakable characteristics of the various types of food designated as wholesome and unwholesome? For we observe that those very types of food designated as wholesome or unwholesome produce opposite effects due to differences in dose, time, processing, soil (terrain), body, humor (doṣa), and the individual's state."

1.25.33 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, know that whatever collection of food maintains the bodily constituents (dhātus) in their natural equilibrium when they are balanced, and restores them to balance when they are disturbed, is wholesome; conversely, that which does the opposite is unwholesome. This definition of the wholesome and the unwholesome is beyond exception."
1.25.34 | To the Blessed Ātreya who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, if this were taught in such a manner, most physicians would not understand it."

1.25.35 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, those who have understood the true nature of food in terms of its qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), actions (*karman*), and all its constituent parts, as well as factors such as quantity (*mātrā*) and so forth—they alone are capable of comprehending what has been thus taught.

However, we shall teach this in such a way that even physicians of the most common type will understand it, without citing every instance of factors like quantity; for these possess many various variations.
We shall, however, explain the specific rules for the regimen of food according to their characteristics and their constituent parts."

1.25.36 | For example: food has a single nature as food because there is no difference in its essential purpose; it has two origins, consisting of the immobile and the mobile; it has two types of effects, distinguished by whether their results are beneficial or harmful; it has four modes of administration, through the consumption of drinks, edibles, foods, and linctuses; it has six tastes, due to the sixfold variety of flavors; and it possesses twenty qualities.

Due to the accompaniment of heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, dry, dull, sharp, stable, mobile, soft, hard, clear, slimy, smooth, rough, subtle, gross, dense, and liquid qualities, as well as the great variety of substances, combinations, and preparations, [taste] has innumerable variations.

1.25.37 | We shall now duly explain those various modifications and constituent parts which are most frequently employed, which are by their very nature most beneficial or most harmful for the majority of human beings.

1.25.38 | For example: among awned grains (*śūkadhānya*), red rice (*lohitaśāli*) is the most wholesome and best; among pulses (*śamīdhānya*), mung beans (*mudga*); among waters, rainwater; among salts, rock salt (*saindhava*); among leafy vegetables (*śāka*), *jīvantī*; among the meat of deer, that of the black antelope (*aiṇeya*); among birds, the common quail (*lāva*); among burrowing animals, the monitor lizard (*godhā*); among fish, the *rohita*; among clarified butters (*sarpiḥ*), cow's ghee; among milks, cow's milk; among vegetable oils, sesame oil; and among animal fats, the fat of the wild boar is superior to the fat of marshy animals.

The fat of the *culukī* fish, among the fats of fish; the fat of the *pākahaṃsa*, among the fats of aquatic birds; the fat of the domestic cock, among the fats of gallinaceous birds; the fat of the goat, among the fats of branch-eating animals; ginger, among tubers; the grape, among fruits;
and sugar, among products of sugarcane—thus have the substances that are, by their very nature, most wholesome among the various types of food been explained in their primary forms.

1.25.39 | We shall now describe those things that are most harmful: among awned grains (*śūkadhānya*), barley (*yavaka*) is the most excellent by virtue of being the most unwholesome; among legumes (*śamīdhānya*), black gram (*māṣa*); among waters, rainwater collected during the rainy season; among salts, saline soil (*ūṣara*); among leafy vegetables (*śāka*), mustard greens (*sarṣapaśāka*); among the meat of wild animals (*mṛgamāṃsa*), beef; among birds, the one-eyed pigeon (*kāṇakapota*); among hole-dwelling creatures, the frog; among fish, the *cilicima*; among clarified butters (*sarpiṣ*), sheep's ghee; among milks, ewe's milk; among vegetable oils (*sthāvarasneha*), the oil of *kukkuṃbha*; and among animal fats, buffalo fat.

The fats of marsh-dwelling animals, the fat of crocodiles, the fat of fish, the fat of water-fowls such as the cāṣa and madgu, the fat of sparrows, the fat of birds that scratch for food, the fat of elephants, the fat of branch-eating animals, the fruit of the *nikuca*, the tubers of the *āluka*, and the inspissated juice (*phāṇita*) of sugarcane products—these are explained as the most excellent substances among the various types of food preparations that are most wholesome by nature. Thus, the section on the wholesome and unwholesome components of food preparations has been explained.
1.25.40 | Hereafter, we shall further explain in detail the substances that are primarily medicinal actions along with their associated properties.

For example: food is the best among those things that provide sustenance; water is the best among those that provide relief; wine is the best among those that remove fatigue; milk is the best among those that promote life; meat is the best among those that promote corpulence; broth is the best among those that provide nourishment; salt is the best among those that improve the relish of food substances; sourness is the best among those that are pleasing to the heart; chicken is the best among those that are strengthening; the semen of the crocodile is the best among those that are aphrodisiacs; honey is the best among those that pacify phlegm and bile; ghee is the best among those that pacify wind and bile; oil is the best among those that pacify wind and phlegm; emesis is the best among those that remove phlegm; and purgation is the best among those that remove bile.

Enema is the best among those that remove vāta; sudation among those that produce softness; physical exercise among those that produce stability; alkali among those that destroy virility; tinduka among those that create an appetite for food; and raw wood-apple among those that clear the throat.

Sheep’s ghee is for those things that are unwholesome to the heart; goat’s milk is for those things that cure consumption, are wholesome for breast milk, are astringent for the blood, and thoroughly pacify *rakta-pitta*; sheep’s milk is for those things that generate *kapha* and *pitta*; buffalo’s milk is for those things that induce sleep; slightly-curdled curd (*mandaka-dadhi*) is for those things that cause secretions (*abhiṣyandi*); grain of *gavedhukā* is for those things that cause emaciation; grain of *uddālaka* is for those things that cause dryness (*virūkṣaṇīya*); sugarcane is for those things that increase urine; barley is for those things that increase semen; the fruit of the rose-apple (*jāmbava*) is for those things that increase *vāta*; fried cakes (*śaṣkulī*) are for those things that generate *kapha* and *pitta*; and horse-gram (*kulattha*).

Among those that generate *amlapitta*, black gram (*māṣa*) is the best; among those that generate *śleṣmapitta*, the fruit of the *madana* tree is the best; among those useful for emesis, non-unctuous enema, and unctuous enema, *trivṛt* is the best; among mild purgatives, *caturaṅgula* is the best; and among sharp purgatives, the latex of *snuk* is the best.

Pratyakpuṣpā is the best among head-purgatives; viḍaṅga among anthelmintics; śirīṣa among anti-toxins; khadira among anti-leprotic agents; rāsnā among wind-alleviators; āmalaka among those that maintain youthfulness; harītakī among wholesome tonics; eraṇḍa root among aphrodisiacs and wind-alleviators; pippalī root among digestive stimulants, carminatives, and removers of anal swelling, hemorrhoids, and colic; puṣkara root among removers of hiccups, dyspnea, cough, and side-ache; and musta among astringents, digestive stimulants, and carminatives. Udīcya [is the best among...]

Katvaṅga is the best among those that cause cooling, stimulate digestion, promote maturation, and cure vomiting and diarrhea; amṛtā is the best among those that are astringent, pacify raktapitta, are digestive stimulants, and alleviate wind disorders; and [guḍūcī] is the best among those that are astringent, remove vāta, stimulate digestion, and pacify obstructions of phlegm and blood.

Ativiṣā is the best among those that stimulate digestion, promote digestion, are constipating, and remove all the *doṣas*; the filaments of the blue lotus (*utpala*), white lotus (*kumuda*), and red lotus (*padma*) are the best among those that are constipating and pacify *rakta-pitta*; durālabhā is the best among those that pacify *pitta* and *śleṣman*; *gandha-priyaṅgu* is the best among those that pacify the excessive discharge of blood and *pitta*; the bark of *kuṭaja* is the best among those that are constipating, dry up, and pacify *śleṣman*, *pitta*, and blood; the fruit of *kāśmarya* is the best among those that are constipating and pacify *rakta-pitta*; and *pṛśniparṇī* is the best among those that are constipating, remove *vāta*, stimulate digestion, and act as aphrodisiacs.

Vidārigandhā is the best among those that are aphrodisiacs and removers of all the *doṣas*; balā is the best among those that are astringent, strengthening, and removers of *vāta*; gokṣuraka is the best among those that remove dysuria and *vāta*; and asafoetida (hiṅgu) is the best among those that are excising, digestive stimulants, carminatives, and pacifiers of *vāta* and *kapha*.

Amlavetasa is the best among those things that are purgative, digestive stimulants, carminatives, and removers of Vāta and Kapha; Yavaśūka is the best among those that are laxatives, digestives, and cures for hemorrhoids; the habitual use of buttermilk is the best among those that pacify disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), edema, hemorrhoids, and complications arising from ghee; the habitual use of the meat-juice of carnivorous animals is the best among those that cure disorders of the duodenum, consumption, and hemorrhoids; the habitual use of milk and ghee is the best among rejuvenatives (rasāyana); the habitual consumption of roasted barley flour with equal parts ghee is the best among aphrodisiacs and removers of Udāvarta; the habitual practice of oil gargles is the best among those that strengthen the teeth and improve the relish for food; and sandalwood is [the best among cooling agents].

Rāsnā and agaru are the best among those used for removing foul odors, burning sensations, and as cooling ointments; lāmajjaka and uśīra are the best among those used as ointments to remove heat, skin disorders, and perspiration; and kuṣṭha is the best among those used for massage and poultices that alleviate vāta.

Madhuka is the foremost among those things that are beneficial for the eyes, the voice, the hair, the throat, the complexion, and for cleansing and healing; wind is the foremost among the causes for providing vitality and consciousness; fire is the foremost among those that pacify coldness, stiffness, pain, and shivering; water is the foremost among astringent (stambhana) agents; water in which a heated clod of earth has been extinguished is the foremost among those that pacify excessive thirst and vomiting; eating in excess is the foremost among the causes of the disorder of undigested matter (āma); eating according to one's digestive fire is the foremost among those that kindle the fire; and activity and diet according to what is wholesome (sātmya) are the foremost among those things to be cultivated.

Eating at the proper time is the foremost among things that produce health; satiety is the foremost among the qualities of food; the suppression of natural urges is the foremost among things that produce ill-health; liquor is the foremost among things that generate mental pleasure; the abuse of liquor is the foremost among things that destroy intelligence, fortitude, and memory; and heavy food is the foremost among things that cause difficult digestion.

Eating a single meal [per day] is among things that cause easy digestion; excessive indulgence with women is among things that cause emaciation; suppression of the urge to ejaculate semen is among things that cause impotence; causing injury to others is among things that produce a lack of faith in food; fasting is among things that diminish life-span; eating in measured amounts is among things that cause emaciation; eating when the previous meal is undigested is among things that afflict the *grahaṇī*; irregular eating is among things that cause irregularity of the digestive fire (*agni*); eating foods of incompatible potencies (*viruddhavīrya*) is among things that produce loathsome diseases; the cessation [of activity] is among things that cause indigestion; physical exertion is among all unwholesome things; and improper application (*mithyāyoga*) is among things that cause disease.

Approaching a woman during her menses is among those things that cause disease; celibacy is among those things that bring misfortune; approaching another's wife is among those things that shorten life; mental resolve is among those things that act as aphrodisiacs; dejection is among those things that are non-aphrodisiacs; and undertaking tasks beyond one's strength is among those things that obstruct life.

Despair is the foremost among things that increase disease; bathing, among things that remove fatigue; joy, among things that cause gratification; grief, among things that cause emaciation; cessation of activity, among things that cause nourishment; nourishment, among things that cause sleep; excessive sleep, among things that cause drowsiness; the practice of all tastes, among things that increase strength; the practice of a single taste, among things that cause weakness; the fetus, among things that must be extracted; indigestion, among things that must be expelled; the child, among those who require mild remedies; the elderly, among those for whom palliative treatment is appropriate; the pregnant woman, among those who must avoid sharp medicines, sexual intercourse, and physical exercise; and mental well-being is the foremost among things that promote health.

The combination of the three humors (*sannipāta*) is the foremost among those difficult to treat; undigested matter (*āma*) among those difficult to treat due to irregularity; fever among diseases; leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) among chronic diseases; consumption (*rājayakṣmā*) among clusters of diseases; urinary disorder (*prameha*) among persistent ailments; leeches among instruments other than surgical tools; and the bladder (*basti*) among medical procedures.

The Himalaya is among the lands of medicinal herbs; the moon is among herbs; a desert land is among unhealthy regions; a marshy region is among unhealthy regions; obedience to instructions is among the qualities of a patient; a physician is among the components of medical treatment; atheism is among things to be avoided; greed is among causes of affliction; disobedience to instructions is among fatal signs; lack of despondency is among the characteristics of a livelihood; a group of physicians is among those who provide certainty; the application [of knowledge] is among the qualities of a physician; a group of physicians is among the means of discernment; reasoning accompanied by scripture is among the instruments of proof; and consensus is among the means of success.

Lack of resolve regarding the purposes of knowing the proper time is the cause of the transgression of time; the visibility of actions is what causes certainty; incapacity is the cause of fear; conversation with those who possess that knowledge is the means for increasing the intellect; the teacher is the cause for the mastery of the scriptures; Ayurveda is the nectar among immortals; the practice of wholesome speech is the means for what should be performed; the grasping of what is unwholesome is the cause of all harm; and the renunciation of everything is the cause of happiness.
Regarding this, there are verses:
1.25.41ab | One hundred and fifty-two of the foremost [therapies] have been specified;
1.25.41cd | these are taught as sufficient for the alleviation of disorders.

1.25.42ab | Regarding those things that perform the same function, the characteristic of the best among them is as follows: 1.25.42cd | Superiority in the performance of the task and excellence have also been declared [as its marks].
1.25.43ab | Whatever is beneficial for the pacification of vāta, pitta, and kapha,
and 1.25.43cd | whatever has been specifically designated as the most excellent remedy for disease;
1.25.44ab | Having understood this thoroughly, one should apply the medical treatment.
1.25.44cd | By acting thus, the physician always attains both dharma and pleasure.

1.25.45ab | That which is wholesome (pathya) because it does not deviate from the right path, and whatever is said to be pleasing to the mind; 1.25.45cd | as well as that which is unpleasant and unwholesome—one should certainly not take note of that.
1.25.46ab | Having encountered differences in measure, time, action, soil, body, and the qualities of the humors (doṣas),
1.25.46cd | those various conditions are indeed seen to manifest in such and such ways.
1.25.47ab | Therefore, the inherent nature has been specified, as well as the substratum consisting of the [five] elements and so forth.
1.25.47cd | Desiring success, one who seeks accomplishment should apply both types of action in dependence upon that.

1.25.48 | Having heard those words of the venerable Ātreya, Agniveśa spoke again to the venerable Ātreya: "This entire subject has been explained by your lordship exactly as it was introduced, and we have heard it.
Now, we wish to hear the definition of the substances used for *āsava* (fermented liquors) taught without exception and not too concisely."

1.25.49 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, in brief, there are eight sources of *āsava* (fermented liquors)—grain, fruit, root, heartwood, flower, stalk, leaf, and bark—with sugar as the ninth.
Since these become innumerable through the various combinations of substances, learn now of the eighty-four *āsava*s that are most wholesome among them.
They are as follows: *surā*, *sauvīra*, *tuṣodaka*, *maireya*, *medaka*, and *dhānyāmla*—these six are the *dhānya-āsava*s."

There are twenty-six fruit-based fermented liquors (*phalāsava*) made from grapes, dates, *kāśmarya*, *dhānvana*, *rājādana*, *tṛṇaśūnya*, *parūṣaka*, chebulic myrobalan (*abhayā*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*), *mṛgaliṇḍikā*, rose-apple (*jāmbava*), wood-apple (*kapittha*), *kuvala*, jujube (*badara*), *karkandhū*, *pīlu*, *priyāla*, jackfruit (*panasa*), banyan (*nyagrodha*), holy fig (*aśvattha*), *plakṣa*, *kapītana*, *udumbara*, *ajamoda*, horned water-lily (*śṛṅgāṭaka*), and *śaṅkhinī*.

There are eleven root-based fermented liquors (*mūlāsava*) made from the roots of *vidārigandhā*, *aśvagandhā*, black fragrant grass (*kṛṣṇagandhā*), *śatāvarī*, *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *dravantī*, *bilva*, castor-oil plant (*urubūka*), and *citraka*.

There are twenty types of spirituous liquors extracted from heartwood (*sārāsava*), made from *śāla*, *priyaka*, *aśvakarṇa*, *candana*, *syandana*, *khadira*, *kadara*, *saptaparṇa*, *arjuna*, *āsana*, *arimeda*, *tinduka*, *kiṇihī*, *śamī*, *śukti*, *śiṃśapā*, *śirīṣa*, *vañjula*, *dhanvana*, and *madhūka*.
There are ten types of floral spirits (*puṣpāsava*), made from the flowers of the *padma*, *utpala*, *nalina*, *kumuda*, *saugandhika*, *puṇḍarīka*, *śatapatra*, *madhūka*, *priyaṅgu*, and *dhātakī*.
There are four types of cane spirits (*kāṇḍāsava*), made from *ikṣu*, *kāṇḍekṣu*, *ikṣuvālikā*, and *puṇḍraka* as the fourth.

There are two fermented liquors made from the leaves of the *paṭola* and *tāḍaka*; there are four fermented liquors made from the bark of the *tilvaka*, *lodhra*, *elavāluka*, and *kramuka*; and there is one fermented liquor made from sugar alone.
Thus, eighty-four types of these fermented liquors (*āsava*) have been specified as distinct substances from one another.
They are designated as "fermented liquors" (*āsava*) because they have been fermented.
Furthermore, the detailed combinations and divisions of these substances, as well as their various preparations and refinements, are manifold.
For fermented liquors (*āsava*), when refined by their respective combinations and processing methods, perform their own specific functions.
Furthermore, factors such as the combination, processing, place, time, and dosage are prescribed for each of those various fermented liquors after having duly considered their particular effects.
And there is a verse on this point:
"Bestowing strength upon the mind, the body, and the digestive fire, destroying sleeplessness, grief, and loss of appetite,
and providing exhilaration— these eighty-four excellent fermented liquors (āsava) have been described."
1.25.51 | Regarding this, there is a verse:

1.25.51ab | In this chapter beginning with "The Origin of Man" (Yajjaḥpuruṣa), the Sage has declared the opinions concerning the nature of the body and diseases, as well as the determination of diet in its true essence; 1.25.51cd | and likewise the foremost medicinal wines and excellent liquors.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Origin of Man," in the Section on Verses (Ślokasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.26.0 | Chapter Twenty-Six.
1.26.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter concerning Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya.
1.26.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
Ātreya, Bhadrakāpya, and likewise Śākunteya;
Pūrṇākṣa Maudgalya and Hiraṇyākṣa Kauśika.
1.26.4ab | He who was named Kumāraśiras, the son of Bharadvāja, was likewise sinless;
1.26.4cd | as was the illustrious Vāryovida, the king and best among the wise.
1.26.5ab | And Nimi, the king of Videha, and the high-minded Baḍiśa;
1.26.5cd | Kāṅkāyana, the Bāhlīka, who was the best among the Bāhlīka physicians.
1.26.6ab | These great seers, advanced in learning and age, self-conquered,
1.26.6cd | gathered together in the delightful Caitraratha forest, desiring to sport.

1.26.7ab | As they sat there, this meaningful conversation arose among those who were well-versed in the principles, concerning the proper determination of the essence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). 1.26.7cd | [It occurred] regarding the definitive classification of the components that constitute that flavor.

1.26.8 | Bhadrakāpya said that there is only one taste, which the experts describe as the state pertaining to the tongue among the objects of the five senses, and which is not different from water. Śākunteya, the Brahmin, said there are two tastes: the incising (chedanīya) and the pacifying (upaśamanīya).
Pūrṇākṣa Maudgalya said there are three tastes: the incising, the pacifying, and the intermediate (sādhāraṇa).
There are four tastes, says Hiraṇyākṣa Kauśika: the pleasant and wholesome, the pleasant and unwholesome, the unpleasant and wholesome, and the unpleasant and unwholesome.

There are five tastes, says Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja: those of earth, water, fire, wind, and space. There are six tastes, says the royal seer Vāryovida: heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, and dry. There are seven tastes, says Nimi Vaideha: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent, and alkaline.

"There are eight tastes," says Baḍiśa: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, astringent, alkaline, and unmanifest. "Tastes are innumerable," says the Bāhlīka physician Kāṅkāyana, because the substrates, qualities, actions, and specific nuances of their relish are innumerable.
1.26.9 | The venerable Punarvasu Ātreya declared that there are exactly six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.

Water is the source of those six tastes; cutting and pacification are their two actions; through their combination, they attain commonality; palatability and non-palatability are their application; wholesomeness and unwholesomeness are their potencies; the modifications of the five great elements are their substrata; these substrata, designated as substances (*dravya*), are subject to nature, transformation, processing, place, and time. Within those substrata known as substances, there are qualities such as heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, and dry. Alkali (*kṣāra*) is so called because of its caustic flow; it is not a taste, but a substance produced from many tastes and possessing many tastes.

It is predominantly pungent and salty, endowed with many sensory objects, and produced by the instruments [of digestion]. Now, the non-manifestation of tastes indeed occurs in their primary state (*prakṛti*), or in a substance that possesses a secondary taste (*anurasa*) or is endowed with various secondary tastes. Furthermore, it is not logical to say they are "innumerable" based on the factors such as their substrates (*āśraya*), because those specific variations of the factors like the substrate are themselves innumerable. For each one of these factors—substrate and so forth—possesses innumerable specific variations, and yet no distinctness from them is possible, owing to the fact that they are for the most part mutually intermingled.
Because the qualities and natures arising from these [flavors] are innumerable, the wise do not prescribe the effects of flavors that have been mixed together.
Considering that very reason, we shall now teach the distinct characteristics of the six flavors when they are unmixed with one another.

1.26.10 | First, however, we shall say something with reference to the classification of substances (*dravyabheda*). In this context, all substances are composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*); they are either sentient (*cetana*) or insentient (*acetana*). Their qualities (*guṇa*) are sound and so forth, as well as heaviness and so forth; these extend up to the substances themselves. Action (*karman*) is said to be of five kinds, beginning with emesis (*vamana*).

1.26.11 | Among these, substances that abound in the qualities of heaviness, coarseness, hardness, slowness, stability, clarity, density, and grossness are of the earth (pārthiva); they produce accumulation, cohesion, weight, and stability. Substances that abound in the qualities of fluidity, unctuousness, coldness, slowness, softness, and sliminess are of the water (āpya); they produce moistening, oiliness, binding, trickling, softness, and refreshment. Substances that abound in the qualities of heat, sharpness, subtlety, lightness, dryness, and clarity are of the fire (āgneya); they produce burning, cooking, luster, illumination, and coloration.

Those substances that abound in the qualities of touch—lightness, coldness, roughness, hardness, clarity, and subtlety—are of the nature of air (*vāyavya*); they produce dryness, exhaustion, movement, clarity, and lightness. Those that abound in the qualities of softness, lightness, subtlety, smoothness, and sound are of the nature of space (*ākāśātman*); they produce softness, porosity, and lightness.
1.26.12 | By this instruction, there is no substance whatsoever to be found in the world that does not become a medicine, depending on the particular application and the specific purpose intended.

1.26.13 | However, substances do not become effective merely through the power of their qualities (*guṇa*). For substances act—having reached various specific substrates (*adhikaraṇa*) at various times—by means of the power of the substance itself, the power of the qualities, or the power of both substance and qualities; with reference to a particular application (*yukti*), purpose (*artha*), and objective. That which they perform is the action (*karma*); that by which they perform it is the potency (*vīrya*); where they perform it is the substrate (*adhikaraṇa*); when they perform it is the time (*kāla*); how they perform it is the method (*upāya*); and what they accomplish is the result (*phala*).
1.26.14 | Furthermore, their classification consists of sixty-three varieties based on the influence of substance, location, and time; we shall explain that.
The sweet [taste] undergoes combination with the sour and the others, and the sour and the rest likewise undergo combination individually with the remaining tastes;
thus, these fifteen substances consist of two tastes each.
1.26.16ab | There should be a separate combination of each [taste]—such as the sour and others—with the remaining [tastes]. 1.26.16cd | Likewise for the sweet, the sour, the salty, and the pungent.
1.26.17ab | Twenty substances with three tastes have been stated in their respective order;
1.26.17cd | fifteen substances will now be described by means of groups of four.
Sweet and sour, when combined with salt and the other [tastes] individually, form combinations;
when combined with the remaining [tastes] individually, they reach a number of fourfold combinations.

1.26.19ab | Sweet and salty flavors, when combined, as well as pungent and the others separately; 1.26.19cd | When joined with the remaining [flavors], sweet and bitter likewise undergo separate combinations.
1.26.20ab | Bitter and the other [tastes], when combined with sour and salty, are joined with them both separately;
1.26.20cd | having proceeded to separate combinations with the remaining [tastes], so too do sour and bitter with the rest.
1.26.21ab | However, salt and pungent [tastes] are combined with astringent and bitter [tastes].
1.26.21cd | But they say there are six [tastes], by excluding one from each of the five [groups].
1.26.22ab | Six [types of substances] have only one taste, while one has all six tastes.
1.26.22cd | Thus, sixty-three substances have been specified according to the enumeration of their tastes.

1.26.23ab | There would be sixty-three [tastes] if one were to calculate them by including both primary and secondary tastes (rasānurasas). 1.26.23cd | For the primary tastes transcend that number through their degrees of intensity (taratama).
1.26.24ab | There are fifty-seven combinations, but the formulations are sixty-threefold.
1.26.24cd | These have been devised by experts in rasa according to the suitability of the tastes therein.

1.26.25ab | In some cases, a single rasa should be prescribed, and in others, combined rasas; 1.26.25cd | by a physician desiring success, after having carefully considered the doshas, the medicines, and other factors.
1.26.26ab | Wise physicians prescribe substances such as those with two tastes and combinations of tastes; 1.26.26cd | or they may also formulate individual tastes for the sake of specific diseases.
1.26.27ab | He who is knowledgeable regarding the various combinations of tastes and is a knower of the various combinations of the humors (doṣas),
1.26.27cd | shall not be deluded concerning the causes, symptoms, and pacification of disorders.
1.26.28ab | The manifest taste of a dry substance is perceived at the beginning; 1.26.28cd | by contrast, there is a secondary taste (anurasa); indeed, there is no seventh [primary] taste.
1.26.29ab | Priority and posteriority, as well as conjunction, number, and indeed conjunction;
1.26.29cd | disjunction, separateness, and also dimension.
1.26.30ab | Saṃskāra and abhyāsa—these qualities, beginning with para, should be known.
1.26.30cd | We shall now describe them by their characteristics as the means for achieving success in medical treatment.

1.26.31ab | Regarding place, time, age, measure, digestion, potency, taste, and so forth; 1.26.31cd | [the determination of] superiority and inferiority, as well as the reasoning and the application that are appropriate.

1.26.32ab | Number is calculation; conjunction is said to be union with another. 1.26.32cd | It arises from the combination of two substances, or all [substances], or a single action, and it is indeed non-eternal.
1.26.33ab | Division (*vibhāga*) is indeed disjunction (*vibhakti*); it is separation and the taking [of a portion] part by part.
1.26.33cd | Separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*), as well as distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) and manifoldness (*anekatā*).
Furthermore, measurement (parimāṇa) is considered to be meting out (māna), refinement (saṃskāra), and instrumental means (karaṇa).
Practice (abhyāsa) is the repeated cultivation of states (bhāva), which is constant application (śīlana) and continuous performance (satatakriyā).

1.26.35ab | Thus have all the qualities, beginning with *para*, been described according to their own specific characteristics. 1.26.35cd | Without knowledge of these, medical treatment cannot be carried out properly.

1.26.36ab | Qualities are not said to reside in qualities; therefore, the physician should understand the qualities of tastes [as residing] in substances. 1.26.36cd | For the intentions of the author are manifold.
Therefore, having understood the subject matter at hand, as well as other places and times,
one should determine the meaning by considering the intention of the author of the treatise and the methods employed.
1.26.38ab | Hereafter, I shall declare the sixfold divisions of the tastes; 1.26.38cd | as well as how the six tastes are enumerated as originating from the five elements.

1.26.39 | Water is indeed gentle, originating from the atmosphere, naturally cold, light, and of unmanifest taste; however, as it falls from the atmosphere and having fallen, endowed with the qualities of the five great elements, it nourishes the forms of moving and stationary beings, and within those forms, tastes become fully manifested.

1.26.40 | Of these six tastes, the sweet taste arises from the predominance of the qualities of *soma* (the lunar principle); the sour taste from the abundance of earth and fire; the salty taste from the abundance of water and fire; the pungent taste from the abundance of air and fire; the bitter taste from the excess of air and space; and the astringent taste from the distinction of air and earth. Thus, the sixfold nature of these tastes is established through the specific variations of deficiency and excess among the great elements (*mahābhūtas*), just as there are various distinctions of color and form among stationary and moving beings due to the same principle. Furthermore, the specific variations of deficiency and excess among the great elements are established by the sixfold nature of time (*kāla*).

1.26.41 | In that regard, the *rasas* whose nature consists primarily of fire and wind generally move upward, due to the lightness and upward-ascending quality of wind, and the upward-flaming quality of fire. Those whose nature consists primarily of water and earth generally move downward, due to the heaviness of earth and the downward-flowing quality of water. Those whose nature is a mixture of both, however, move in both directions.
1.26.42 | We shall now explain the qualities and actions of each one of those six tastes according to their respective substances.

1.26.43.1 | Among these, the sweet taste (madhura-rasa), due to its suitability for the body, increases the plasma, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, ojas, and semen; it promotes longevity, clarifies the six senses, produces strength and complexion, subdues pitta, poison, and vāta, alleviates thirst and burning sensations, is beneficial for the skin, hair, throat, and strength; it is pleasing, life-sustaining, nourishing, bulk-promoting, bestows stability, heals wounds and fractures, refreshes the nose, mouth, throat, lips, and tongue, pacifies burning and fainting, is most beloved by bees and ants, and is unctuous, cold, and heavy.

Even though it possesses such qualities, when consumed in excess, that very substance produces obesity, flabbiness, laziness, excessive sleep, heaviness, lack of desire for food, weakness of the digestive fire, hypertrophy of the flesh in the mouth and throat, dyspnea, cough, catarrh, alasaka, cold fever, flatulence, sweetness of the mouth, vomiting, loss of consciousness and voice, goiter, scrofula, elephantiasis, swelling of the throat, coating of the bladder and vessels, diseases of the eyes, ophthalmia, and other such disorders born of kapha.

1.26.43.2 | Sour taste makes food palatable; it kindles the digestive fire, nourishes the body, provides energy, awakens the mind, strengthens the sense organs, increases strength, directs the wind (vāta) downward, satisfies the heart, causes salivation, draws out what has been eaten, moistens, digests, and brings gratification; it is light, hot, and unctuous.

Although it possesses such qualities, when used excessively on its own, it exhilarates the teeth, parches the mouth, causes the eyes to close, agitates the body hairs, dissolves phlegm, increases bile, vitiates the blood, burns the flesh, and makes the body flaccid; furthermore, it induces swelling in those who are emaciated, wounded, thin, or weak.

Due to its fiery nature, it causes wounds, blows, bites, burns, fractures, swellings, dislocations, urination over the body, crawling sensations, crushing, cuts, splits, separations, piercings, and bruises to suppurate; it also causes a burning sensation in the throat, chest, and heart.

1.26.43.3 | Salt taste is digestive, moistening, appetizing, laxative, excising, and splitting; it is sharp, mobile, downward-moving, and creates space; it removes wind (vāta), destroys stiffness, binding, and congestion, and acts as an antagonist to all other tastes. It causes salivation, liquefies phlegm (kapha), cleanses the channels, softens all parts of the body, and makes food palatable. When used in conjunction with food, it is not excessively heavy, but is unctuous and hot.

Even though it possesses such qualities, when used excessively on its own, it agitates the *pitta*, increases the blood, causes thirst, induces fainting, produces heat, tears [the tissues], erodes the flesh, brings about skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), increases poison, causes swellings to burst, loosens the teeth, destroys virility, obstructs the sense organs, and brings on wrinkles, gray hair, and baldness;
moreover, it gives rise to disorders such as hemoptysis (*lohitapitta*), acid gastritis (*amlapitta*), erysipelas (*vīsarpa*), gout (*vātarakta*), scabies (*vicarcikā*), and alopecia (*indralupta*).

1.26.43.4 | The pungent taste cleanses the mouth, kindles the digestive fire, dries up what has been eaten, causes the nose to flow, clears the eyes, and makes the sense organs distinct. It overcomes alasaka (intestinal torpor), swelling, obesity, urticaria, ophthalmia, unctuousness, sweat, moisture, and impurities. It stimulates the appetite, destroys anemia, settles ulcers, kills worms, scrapes the flesh, breaks up clots of blood, severs bonds, opens the channels, pacifies phlegm, and is light, hot, and dry.

Even though it possesses such qualities, when used excessively by itself, it destroys virility through the power of its post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*); and through the power of its taste (*rasa*) and potency (*vīrya*), it causes delusion, exhaustion, debility, emaciation, fainting, bending, darkness of vision, dizziness, irritation of the throat, and generates bodily heat; it diminishes strength, produces thirst, and furthermore, due to the predominance of the qualities of wind (*vāyu*) and fire (*agni*), it produces wind-born disorders in the feet, arms, sides, back, and so forth, characterized by vertigo, burning sensations, tremors, pricking, and piercing pains.

1.26.43.5 | Bitter taste (tikta-rasa), though itself lacking in palatability, destroys anorexia, is anti-toxic, and kills worms; it alleviates fainting, burning sensations, itching, skin diseases, and thirst; it stabilizes the skin and flesh, cures fever, stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, purifies breast milk, is scarifying, and dries up moisture, fat, muscle-fat, marrow, lymph, pus, sweat, urine, feces, bile, and phlegm; it is dry, cold, and light.

Even though it possesses such qualities, when used excessively and alone, because of its dryness and its harsh, pungent nature, it dries up the rasa, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; it produces roughness in the channels, robs strength, emaciates, causes exhaustion, induces delusion, causes vertigo, dries the mouth, and gives rise to other disorders of vāta.

1.26.43.6 | Astringent taste (kaṣāya-rasa) is pacifying, astringent in action, promotes healing of fractures, causes compression, heals wounds, is desiccant, and is styptic; it pacifies phlegm (śleṣman) and blood-bile (rakta-pitta), dries up bodily moisture, is dry, cold, and not heavy.

Even though it possesses such qualities, when consumed in excess by itself, it dries up the mouth, afflicts the heart, distends the abdomen, suppresses speech, obstructs the channels, induces a darkish discoloration, impairs virility, and undergoes digestion with flatulence; it arrests the flow of wind, urine, feces, and semen, causes emaciation, exhaustion, thirst, and stiffness, and—due to its harsh, clear, and dry nature—gives rise to vāta disorders such as hemiplegia, convulsions, facial paralysis, and facial distortions.

1.26.44 | Thus, these six tastes, whether used individually or collectively and in the proper measure, are beneficial to the world of the self; however, when used otherwise than this, they become harmful. Therefore, the wise person, for the sake of benefit alone, should employ them properly and in the correct measure.
And there are verses on this point:

45ab. A substance that is cold in its potency (vīrya) but sweet in both taste (rasa) and post-digestive effect (pāka), 45cd. Or one that is sour in those two and hot, as well as one that is pungent in those two; [these are exceptions].

1.26.46ab | The collection of their qualities is to be specified by means of instruction on their tastes (rasa); 1.26.46cd | [it shall also be taught] according to their potencies (vīrya) when they are not contradictory, and according to their post-digestive transformations (pāka).
1.26.47ab | Just as milk, as ghee, or as the two drugs chavya and citraka; 1.26.47cd | so too should the physician indicate other such substances according to their taste.
1.26.48ab | It may be sweet, slightly hot, astringent, and even bitter;
1.26.48cd | as for example the great five roots (mahat-pañcamūla), or the meat of aquatic and marshy animals.
1.26.49ab | Rock salt (saindhava) is not hot; likewise, the sour emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) is not hot.
1.26.49cd | The bitter substances—namely arka, aguru, and guḍūcī—are said to be hot.

1.26.50ab | For some sour substances are constipating, while some sour substances are purgative; 1.26.50cd | just as the wood-apple (kapittha) is constipating, so too is the emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) purgative.
1.26.51ab | Long pepper and ginger are aphrodisiacs, yet pungent substances are said to be non-aphrodisiac.
1.26.51cd | Astringent substances are styptic and cold; however, this is otherwise in the case of *abhayā*.
1.26.52ab | Therefore, one should not prescribe every substance solely on the basis of its taste.
1.26.52cd | For it is observed that even among substances with identical tastes, there exist distinct differences in their qualities.
1.26.53ab | Due to its dryness, the astringent taste is the best among dry substances; the pungent is middling;
1.26.53cd | and the bitter is inferior. Likewise, due to its heat, the salty taste is the foremost among hot substances.
1.26.54ab | Among unctuous substances, the middle one is sour, the last is pungent, and the sweet is supreme.
1.26.54cd | The middle one is sour, and the last taste is salty; thus is unctuousness described.
1.26.55ab | In terms of coolness, those that are astringent, sweet, and bitter are respectively medium, superior, and inferior.
1.26.55cd | Due to its own heaviness, salt is inferior even to the astringent.
