1.26.56ab | From sour comes pungent, and from that bitter; due to its lightness, it is the best of the best. 1.26.56cd | Some authorities maintain that among the light tastes, the salty taste is inferior.
1.26.57ab | He is inferior in both heaviness and lightness as well.
1.26.57cd | Furthermore, the characteristics of the post-digestive effects (vipāka) will now be fully explained.
1.26.58ab | The post-digestive transformation (vipāka) of pungent, bitter, and astringent [rasas] is generally pungent.
1.26.58cd | The sour [rasa] transforms into sour, the sweet into sweet, and likewise the salty.

1.26.59ab | The three tastes—sweet, salty, and sour—are considered pleasant for the discharge of wind, urine, and feces because of their unctuous nature. 1.26.59cd | They are generally regarded as conducive to the easy elimination of flatus, urine, and excrement.
1.26.60ab | Furthermore, the three tastes— pungent, bitter, and astringent— due to their dry nature,
1.26.60cd | are seen to cause distress during the discharge of wind, feces, urine, and semen.
1.26.61ab | That which is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka) diminishes semen, binds the feces and urine, and increases vāta.
1.26.61cd | That which is sweet in its post-digestive effect promotes the passage of feces and urine and increases kapha and semen.
1.26.62ab | That which produces bile causes the discharge of feces and urine; its digestion is sour, and it destroys semen.
1.26.62cd | Among these, the sweet is heavy, while the pungent and sour are otherwise (light).
1.26.63ab | Regarding the mild, moderate, or predominant nature of the characteristics of the post-digestive transformation (vipāka) of substances;
1.26.63cd | one should observe that [variation] in each specific case due to the particularity of the qualities (guṇa) of the substances.
1.26.64ab | Mild, sharp, heavy, light, unctuous, dry, hot, and cold—
1.26.64cd | some maintain that potency (*vīrya*) is of eight kinds, while others hold it to be of two kinds.
1.26.65ab | Potency (vīrya), whether cold or hot, is that by which an action is performed; 1.26.65cd | nothing is accomplished without potency; every action is brought about by potency.
1.26.66ab | Taste is perceived at the moment of contact; post-digestive transformation (vipāka) is established through the completion of the action.
1.26.66cd | Potency (vīrya) is perceived from the time of infusion until the moment of contact.
1.26.67ab | Where a similarity in taste, potency, and post-digestive effect is observed,
1.26.67cd | as well as a distinction in their actions, that is known as *prabhāva* (specific power).
1.26.68ab | Citraka is considered pungent in taste, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and hot in potency (vīrya).
1.26.68cd | Similarly, Dantī causes purgation through its specific inherent power (prabhāva).

1.26.69ab | Regarding poison and that which is said to be an antidote for poison, their specific potency (*prabhāva*) is the cause. 1.26.69cd | Likewise, that which acts as an emetic or a purgative is brought about by its specific potency.
1.26.70ab | Whatever various kinds of effects belong to gems that are to be worn, 1.26.70cd | those are produced by their power; their power is said to be inconceivable.
1.26.71ab | Their correct post-digestive transformations (*vipāka*), potencies (*vīrya*), and even their specific powers (*prabhāva*) have been declared.
1.26.71cd | A certain [substance] performs its action through its taste (*rasa*), and another through its potency (*vīrya*).
1.26.72ab | Some substance [overcomes] another by its quality, its post-digestive effect (vipāka), or its specific potency (prabhāva).
1.26.72cd | Post-digestive effect overcomes taste; specific potency overcomes both those [taste and post-digestive effect].
1.26.73ab | When there is equality of strength among the tastes (rasas) and the rest, this is their innate (naisargika) strength.
1.26.73cd | Hereafter, I shall teach the knowledge of the six tastes.
1.26.74ab | It is perceived through its lubricating, pleasing, exhilarating, and softening qualities.
1.26.74cd | When placed in the mouth, the sweet [taste] pervades the oral cavity and seems as if it were coating it.

From chattering of the teeth, salivation from the mouth, perspiration, numbness of the face, burning sensation in the mouth and throat, and by the very act of tasting a sour flavor, one should declare [the presence of fever].
1.26.76ab | That which, dissolving, produces moisture, salivation, and softness in the mouth,
is to be known as salt (lavaṇa), because it quickly causes a burning sensation in the mouth.
1.26.77ab | That which causes a sensation of agitation upon its application, feels as if it stings, and burns the mouth, nose, and eyes while flowing out, is known as *kaṭu* (pungent).
1.26.77cd | It is remembered as *kaṭu* because it causes a burning sensation and flows from the mouth, nose, and eyes.
1.26.78ab | That which checks the flow of saliva upon contact and does not taste sweet, 1.26.78cd | is bitter; it produces clarity of the mouth, dryness, and a refreshing sensation.
1.26.79ab | That rasa which, through clarity, astringency, and numbness, engages the sense of taste;
1.26.79cd | and which, as it were, binds the throat, is astringent (kaṣāya), even though it is expanding (vikāsī).

1.26.80 | When the venerable Ātreya had spoken thus, Agniveśa said to him: "Venerable sir, we have heard these words of yours regarding the subject of substances, qualities, and actions exactly as they are—unfailing and endowed with meaningful content. However, we wish to hear an instruction that is not overly concise concerning the characteristics of incompatible food combinations (*āhāra-vikāra-vairodhika*)."

1.26.81 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "Substances that are antagonistic to the bodily constituents (dhātus) enter into conflict with those constituents. Some do so because their qualities are mutually opposed; others through combination (saṃyoga); still others through processing (saṃskāra); others again due to place, time, quantity, and so forth; and others yet through their very nature."

1.26.82 | Among those foods which are most frequently consumed in relation to diet, we shall now teach concerning a portion of them that are antagonistic (*vairodhika*). One should not consume fish together with milk; for both of these are sweet and have a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), they cause great obstruction of the channels (*mahābhiṣyandi*), and because one is cold and the other hot, they possess contradictory potencies (*viruddhavīrya*). Due to this contradiction of potencies, they lead to the vitiation of the blood (*śoṇita*), and due to their great obstructiveness, they cause the blockage of the bodily passages.

1.26.83 | Having heard those words of Ātreya, Bhadrakāpya said to Agniveśa: "One may consume all fish together with milk, with the single exception of the cilicima. This fish is scaled, red-eyed, marked all over with red stripes, shaped like a rohita, and generally moves on the ground. If one were to consume it with milk, he would undoubtedly suffer from either one of the diseases born of blood or born of constipation, or even meet his death."

"No," said the venerable Ātreya, "one should not consume any fish at all with milk, and especially not the *cilicima* fish; for because it causes excessive secretions (*abhiṣyandi*), it produces these very severe diseases and excites the poison of the stomach (*āmaviṣa*).

Furthermore, one should not eat the flesh of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals together with honey, sesame, molasses, milk, black gram, radish, *kiṃśāru* (awned grain), or sprouted grains; for that is the root cause by which one incurs deafness, blindness, trembling, numbness, dumbness, nasal speech, or even death."

One should not consume *pauṣkara* or *rohiṇīka* potherbs, nor pigeons fried in mustard oil, together with honey and milk; for that is the root cause of contracting any one of the following: hemorrhagic ophthalmia (*śoṇitābhiṣyanda*), dilation of the vessels (*dhamanīpravicaya*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), *śaṅkhaka*, goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), or *rohiṇī*, or even death. Furthermore, after eating radish, garlic, *kṛṣṇagandha*, *ārjaka*, *sumukha*, *surasā*, and similar plants, one must not consume milk out of fear of the affliction of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).

One should never consume *jātuka* leaf-vegetable or ripe *nikuca* fruit together with honey and milk; for this leads to death, or else to the obstruction of strength, complexion, luster, and vigor, to a chronic illness, and to impotence.

That same ripe *nikuca* fruit should not be consumed together with black gram soup, molasses, or ghee, because of their mutual incompatibility (*virodhika*). Likewise, mango, hog-plum, citron, *nikuca*, *karamarda*, *moca*, *dantaśaṭha*, jujube, *kośāmra*, *bhavya*, rose-apple, wood-apple, tamarind, *pārāvata*, *akṣoḍa*, breadfruit, coconut, pomegranate, and emblic myrobalan—these and other substances of this kind, as well as all sour liquids and non-liquids, are incompatible with milk.
Similarly, *kaṅgu*, wild rice, *makuṣṭhaka*, horse-gram, black gram, and *niṣyāva* millet are incompatible with milk.
The leaf-vegetable *padmottarikā* consumed together with sugar-cane wine (*śārkara-maireya*) or honey is incompatible and excessively aggravates the wind (*vāta*).

*Hāridraka* fried in mustard oil is incompatible and excessively aggravates the bile (*pitta*). Rice pudding (*pāyasa*) followed by a stirred drink (*mantha*) as a post-consumption beverage is incompatible and excessively aggravates the phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Upodikā prepared with sesame paste is a cause of dysentery.
A crane together with *vāruṇī* liquor and boiled grains (*kulmāṣa*) is incompatible; that same crane, when fried in pig fat, causes instantaneous death.
Peacock meat, when placed on a spit of castor wood and iron, roasted over a castor-wood fire, and served with castor oil, causes instantaneous death.

The meat of a yellow dog, when smeared with turmeric and lead and scorched by a fire of turmeric, causes instantaneous death; that same meat, when covered with ashes and dust and taken with honey, likewise leads to immediate death. Pippalī peppers prepared with the scales of fish, as well as *kākamācī* and honey, cause death.
Honey for one afflicted by heat, or honey consumed while hot, leads to death.

Honey and ghee taken in equal proportions; honey and rainwater from the atmosphere taken in equal proportions; honey and lotus seeds; drinking hot water after honey; *bhallātaka* with hot water; *kampillaka* prepared with buttermilk; stale *kākamācī*; and the meat of a vulture roasted on charcoal—these are incompatible combinations.
Thus, these have been explained according to the questions asked.
And there are verses on this point:
Whatever kind of food one consumes that causes the humors (doṣas) to flow but does not expel them from the body— all that results in harm.
Furthermore, [the effects of substances] depend upon place, time, fire (digestive power), measure, suitability, wind (and other humors),
as well as processing, potency, the state of the digestive tract, and the sequence [of administration].

1.26.87ab | Due to avoidance, modification, digestion, and even through combination; 1.26.87cd | that which is contradictory, or not beneficial, or contrary to the rules for the excellence of the heart [is not to be used].

1.26.88ab | First, that which is contrary by way of location (*deśataḥ*) is as follows: dry, sharp, and so forth [medicines] in a desert (*dhanvan*); 1.26.88cd | whereas unctuous, cold, and so forth are the medicines employed in a marshy region (*ānūpa*).

1.26.89ab | That which is contrary even in terms of time is the practice of cold, dry, and similar [qualities] during the cold season; 1.26.89cd | as well as the practice of pungent, hot, and similar [qualities] during the hot season.

1.26.90ab | Likewise, food and drink of four kinds that are incompatible with fire [are incompatible] when taken together; 1.26.90cd | honey and ghee, when held in equal proportions, are incompatible with one another in those quantities.

1.26.91ab | For one accustomed to pungent, hot, and similar qualities, the consumption of sweet, cold, and similar qualities; 1.26.91cd | that which is contrary to one's habituation (*sātmya-viruddha*), as well as that which is contrary to the [doshas] such as *vāta* (*anila-ādi-viruddha*).

1.26.92ab | That food which is contrary to the habitual practice of similar qualities, or contrary to medicinal treatment; 1.26.92cd | that which is contrary by way of processing (saṃskāra) becomes like poison when eaten.
Just as meat of a peacock combined with castor oil and lead is known to be contrary in its potency, so too [this] is to be understood as being cold in its potency.
1.26.94ab | That [purgative] is administered together with a substance of hot potency;
1.26.94cd | for one with a hard bowel, it is too small in dose, of weak potency, and non-purging.
1.26.95ab | For one with a soft bowel, that which is heavy, purgative, and likewise excessive;
1.26.95cd | this is contrary to the state of the bowel, yet it may be considered contrary [to health] depending on the condition.
1.26.96ab | For one addicted to fatigue, sexual intercourse, and physical exertion, there is provocation of vāyu (wind).
1.26.96cd | For one who is drowsy and lazy, food causes provocation of kapha (phlegm).

1.26.97ab | That which one eats without having first voided feces and urine, and that which one eats while not hungry; 1.26.97cd | as well as that which follows the dictates of excessive hunger—all this would be contrary to the proper sequence.

1.26.98ab | But that which is contrary to the rule of exclusion is when, after consuming wild boar and other such [meats], one partakes of hot things; or having drunk ghee and other [medicines], one resorts to cold things.
1.26.98cd | [And] having consumed hot things, one partakes of ghee and so forth, and then resorts to cold things.
1.26.99ab | That which is incompatible by way of its digestion, or prepared from corrupted or inferior wood; 1.26.99cd | that which consists of undercooked rice, or excessively overcooked, or burnt;
1.26.99ef | that which is incompatible due to combination, such as sour [food] taken with milk.

1.26.100ab | That which is not pleasing to the mind is said to be contrary to the heart (hṛdviruddha). 1.26.100cd | One should know that which is contrary to prosperity (saṃpadviruddha) to be that in which the aesthetic flavor (rasa) has not yet arisen.
1.26.101ab | Even that which has lost its flavor, or indeed that whose flavor has been spoiled;
1.26.101cd | That which is known to be contrary to the rules, and which is eaten without being properly concealed;
1.26.101ef | Such food as this would be "contrary" when consumed.

For those suffering from impotence, blindness, erysipelas, ascites, eruptive boils, insanity, fistula-in-ano, fainting, intoxication, flatulence, throat-obstruction, jaundice, and even from āma-poisoning; (1.26.102)

1.26.103ab | They declare that incompatible food (viruddhānna) is the cause of kilāsa, kuṣṭha, and grahaṇī diseases, as well as swelling, amlapitta, fever, and chronic catarrh; 1.26.103cd | and likewise of the defects of progeny and even death.

1.26.104 | Indeed, for these and other diseases caused by antagonistic factors, the following measures serve as remedies: namely, emesis and purgation; the administration of substances that counteract those [antagonistic factors] for the purpose of pacification; and the prior preparation of the body with such substances.
And on this point, there are these two verses: 1.26.105ab | Evacuation counteracts diseases born of incompatible food.
1.26.105cd | Likewise, emesis, pacification, or first of all, the adoption of wholesome practices [are effective].

1.26.106ab | Due to suitability, or even due to small quantity, [a diet] may become ineffective for one with a stimulated digestive fire, for a young person, 1.26.106cd | and for those who are unctuous, habituated to exercise, and strong; in such cases, even a contradictory diet becomes harmless.
1.26.107 | Regarding this, there are these verses:
1.26.107ab | Whatever opinions the great sages held concerning the determination of tastes;
1.26.107cd | [The enumeration of] substances according to their qualities and sequence, and the number of substances based on their substrates of taste.

1.26.108ab | The cause for the enumeration of tastes, and the definitions of primary and secondary tastes; 1.26.108cd | And the individual definitions of the qualities (guṇas) such as heaviness and so forth.
1.26.109ab | By whatever cause the fivefold elements possess the state of being six flavors,
and 1.26.109cd | by which excellence of qualities the flavors partake of upward or downward movement.
1.26.110ab | The sixfold nature of the six tastes and their respective divisions;
1.26.110cd | The general rules and exceptions regarding the qualities and actions of substances.

1.26.111ab | The superior, inferior, and middling nature of tastes among cow's milk and other substances; 1.26.111cd | The signs of their post-digestive effect (pāka) and potency (prabhāva), and the determination of the number of potencies (vīrya).
1.26.112ab | Whatever is the specific characteristic of each of the six flavors being tasted;
1.26.112cd | whichever is opposed by which, and by which, and whatever effect it produces.
In the chapter on Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya, the Sage has explained all the remedies for those diseases caused by incompatible factors and those that have been neglected.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Ātreya and Bhadrakāpya," in the Section on Verses (Ślokasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.27.0 | Chapter Twenty-Seven | 1.27.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the rules for food and drink.
1.27.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.27.3 | Experts declare that food and drink—possessing desirable color, odor, taste, and touch, and prepared according to the rules—are the very life-force (*prāṇa*) of living beings, so called because their fruits are directly perceived. For it is by means of this fuel that the internal fire is maintained; it invigorates the *sattva* (vitality), and when consumed as prescribed, it promotes the proper organization of the bodily tissues, strength, complexion, and clarity of the sense organs. Conversely, when consumed otherwise, it leads to harm.
1.27.4 | Therefore, O Agniveśa, for the purpose of discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful, we shall teach the entire rule regarding food and drink.

By its very nature, water moistens; salt dissolves; alkali digests; honey binds; ghee lubricates; milk nourishes; meat builds up; meat broth refreshes; wine causes decay; *śīdhu* intoxicates; grape wine stimulates digestion; molasses accumulates [phlegm]; curd produces swelling; oil-cake and greens cause exhaustion; and bean soup contains abundant internal waste. Alkali generally destroys vision and semen.

Pungent [taste] is generally bile-producing, except for pomegranate and emblic myrobalan; sweet [taste] is generally phlegm-producing, except for honey and aged *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, barley, and wheat; bitter [taste] is generally wind-producing and non-aphrodisiac, except for *vegāgra*, *amṛtā*, and *paṭola* leaves; and acrid [taste] is generally wind-producing and non-aphrodisiac, except for long pepper and ginger.
1.27.5 | Hereafter, we shall provide a detailed exposition of the dietary substances according to their classification into groups.
1.27.6 | Groups based on awned grains, pulse-grains, meat, vegetables, and fruits;
green herbs, wines, water, cow products, and sugarcane preparations.

1.27.7 | We shall now describe two further groups of ten concerning the preparation and administration of prepared foods, according to their tastes, potencies, post-digestive effects, and specific properties.
1.27.8 | Now, the group of awned grains (śūkadhānya): red rice (raktaśāli), great rice (mahāśāli), kalama, that which is brought by birds (śakunāhṛta),
tūrṇaka, long-awned rice (dīrghaśūka), white rice (gaura), pale rice (pāṇḍu), and kalāṅgula.
1.27.9 | Sugandhaka, lohavāla, that which is called sārivā, pramodaka, pataṅga, tapanīya, and whatever other auspicious śāli rice varieties there may be.
They are cold in potency and in post-digestive effect, sweet, and they produce little wind; they bind the stool and cause slight constipation, are unctuous, nourishing, and increase semen and urine.
1.27.11 | Among those, red śāli rice is the best; it quenches thirst and removes the three impurities (tridoṣa).
The *mahā-śāli* is inferior to it, followed by *kalama*, and after that, the others.
1.27.12 | The *yavaka*, *hāyana*, *pāṃsuvāpya*, *naiṣadhaka*, and other varieties of rice imitate the qualities and defects of the *śāli* rice.
1.27.13 | Śāli rice that is cold, unctuous, not heavy, sweet, pacifies the three doṣas, and is stable in nature is the best;
among these, the white variety is superior, followed by the black-white variety.
1.27.14 | Varaka, koddālaka, cīna, śārada, ujjvala, dardura, gandhana, and kuruvinda— these varieties of *ṣaṣṭika* rice differ only slightly in their qualities.

1.27.15 | Rice (*vrīhi*) is sweet, has an acidic post-digestive effect (*pāka*), increases *pitta*, and is heavy; it produces copious urine, feces, and heat. However, *pāṭala* rice possesses all three *doṣas*.
1.27.16 | Śyāmāka, when mixed with koradūṣa, is astringent-sweet, light, increases vāta,
subdues kapha and pitta, is cold, constipating, and drying.
1.27.17 | Elephant-grass, śyāmāka, nīvāra, toyaparṇī, gavedhukā,
praśāntikā, ambhaḥśyāmāka, lauhitya, aṇu, and priyaṅgu; 1.27.18 | mukunda, kṣiṇṭigarmūṭī, varukā, and likewise varaka.
Śibira, utkaṭa, and jūrṇāhvā are similar to śyāmāka in their qualities.
Barley is dry, cold, heavy, sweet, and increases wind and feces;
it provides stability, is astringent, strengthening, and cures disorders of phlegm.
1.27.20 | Bamboo grain (veṇuyava) is considered to be dry, astringent in taste, sweet, a destroyer of phlegm and bile,
a remover of fat, worms, and poison, and strengthening.
1.27.21 | Wheat heals fractures, alleviates wind, and is sweet and cooling;
it is vitalizing, nourishing, aphrodisiac, unctuous, stabilizing, and heavy.
1.27.22 | Nāndīmukhī and Madhūlī are sweet, unctuous, and cooling.
Thus ends this first section on awned grains (śūkadhānya).

1.27.23 | Now, the group of pulse-cereals (śamīdhānyavarga): Mudga is considered the best of pulses; it is astringent-sweet, dry, cold, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), light, clear, and destroys phlegm and bile.
1.27.24 | Māṣa is highly aphrodisiac, an excellent subduer of vāta, unctuous, hot, sweet, and heavy; it is strengthening, produces abundant waste, and quickly bestows virility.

1.27.25 | The rājamāṣa bean is palatable, pleasing to the taste, and alleviates phlegm, semen disorders, and acid dyspepsia (amlapitta). It is sweet, increases wind (vāta), is parching, astringent, clear, and heavy.
1.27.26 | Kulattha beans are hot in potency, astringent in taste, and sour upon digestion; they subdue kapha, semen, and vāta.
They are constipating and beneficial for cough, hiccup, dyspnea, and hemorrhoids.

1.27.27 | Makuṣṭhaka beans are sweet in taste and sweet in digestion; they are astringent, dry, and cold. They are highly recommended for conditions such as internal hemorrhage (raktapitta) and fever.
1.27.28 | Chickpeas, lentils, peas,
and vetches are light, cold, sweet, slightly astringent, and drying.
1.27.29 | These [legumes] are recommended for use in soups and as plasters in cases of pitta and kapha disorders. Among them, masūra is constipating, while kalāya is excessively provocative of vāta.
1.27.30 | Sesame is unctuous, hot, sweet, bitter, astringent, and pungent;
it is beneficial for the skin, hair, and strength; it subdues Vāta and increases Kapha and Pitta.
Various types of pulses (śimbijātayaḥ), which are sweet, cooling, heavy, strength-depleting, and parching in nature,
should be eaten with fats by those who possess physical strength.
1.27.32 | The legume (śimbī) is parching and astringent; it provokes wind in the digestive tract, is neither aphrodisiac nor beneficial for the eyes, and undergoes digestion with flatulence.
1.27.33 | Āḍhakī destroys kapha and pitta but increases vāta; avalguja and iḍagaja destroy kapha and vāta; niṣpāva increases vāta and pitta.
1.27.34 | One should prescribe the fruits of *kākāṇḍī*, *umā* (or *mālā*), and *ātmaguptā* as being like those of the *māṣa*.
This second group of pulse-grains (*śamīdhānya*) has been proclaimed by the Great Sage.
1.27.35 | Now, the section on meat: the cow, donkey, mule, camel, horse, leopard, lion, bear, monkey,
wolf, tiger, hyena, brown mongoose, cat, and mouse.
1.27.36 | The jackal, the jackal (jambuka), the hawk, the vomit-eater, the blue jay, the crow,
the hare-killer, the honey-hunter, the vulture, the owl, and the sparrow;
1.27.37 | The *dhūmikā* and the *kurara* are among the predatory beasts and birds;
as are the white, the dark, the variegated-backed, the black, and the *kākulī* deer.
1.27.38 | The lizard, the *cillaṭa*, the frog, the monitor lizard, the porcupine, the rhinoceros, the iguana, the mongoose, and the hedgehog— these are known as the burrowers of the earth.

1.27.39 | The *sṛmara*, the yak (*camara*), the rhinoceros, the buffalo, the gayal, the elephant, the *nyaṅku* antelope, the boar, and likewise the *ruru* deer— all these are forest animals of the marshy regions (*anūpa*).
The tortoise, the crab, the fish, the porpoise, the timiṅgila,
the pearl-oyster, the conch, the udra, the kumbhīra, the culukī, the makara, and others.
1.27.41 | Thus have been described those that dwell in the water; now those that move about in the water will be mentioned:
the swan (*haṃsa*), the crane (*krauñca*), the egret (*balākā*), the heron (*baka*), the *kāraṇḍava*, and the *plava*.
1.27.42 | The *śarāri*, the *puṣkarāhva*, the *keśarī*, the *maṇituṇḍaka*, the *mṛṇālakaṇṭha*, the *madgu*, the *kādamba*, and the *kākatuṇḍaka*.
The *utkrośa*, the *puṇḍarīkākṣa*, the *megharāva*, the *ambukukkuṭī*,
the *ārā*, the *nandīmukhī*, the *vāṭī*, and the *sumukha* birds are companions that travel together.
1.27.44 | Rohiṇī, Kāmakālī, Sārasa, and Raktaśīrṣaka.
There are ruddy geese and other birds that frequent the water.
1.27.45 | The spotted deer (pṛṣata), the śarabha, the rāma, the śvadaṃṣṭra, the mṛgamātṛkā,
the hare (śaśa), the uraṇa, the kuraṅga, the gokarṇa, and the koṭṭakāraka.
The cāruṣka, the hariṇa, the eṇa, the śambara, the kālapucchaka, the ṛṣya, and the varapota are to be known as the jāṅgala deer.
1.27.47 | The lāva, the vartīraka, the vārtīka along with the kapiñjala,
the cakora, the upacakra, the kukkubha, and the raktavartmaka;

1.27.48 | These, beginning with the quail (*lāva*), are the *viṣkira* birds; those beginning with the partridge (*vartaka*) will now be described: the male partridge (*vartaka*), the female partridge (*vartikā*), the peacock (*barhin*), the partridge (*tittiri*), and the cock (*kukkuṭa*).
1.27.49 | The kaṅka, śāra, padendra, ābhoga, nardagiri, vartaka, krakara, avakara, and vāraḍa are the viṣkira birds.
1.27.50 | The hundred-petaled [lotus], the *bhṛṅgarāja*, the *koyaṣṭi*, the *jīvajīvaka*, the *kairāta*, the cuckoo (*kokila*), the *atyūha*, the *gopāputra*, and the *priyātmaja*.
1.27.51 | Laṭṭā, laṭṭa(ṭū)ṣaka, babhru, vaṭahā, ḍiṇḍimānaka,
jaṭī, dundubhi, pākkāra, lohapṛṣṭha, and kuliṅgaka.
1.27.52 | The pigeon, the parrot, the śāraṅga, the ciraṭī, the kaṅku, the yaṣṭikā, the sārikā, the kalaviṅka, the sparrow, and the aṅgāracūḍaka;
1.27.53 | The pigeon and the *pāṇḍavika* are called "pecking birds" (*pratuda*). They are designated as "forcible eaters" (*prasaha*) because they consume their prey by force.

1.27.54 | Those that dwell on the ground are called *bhūśaya* because they live in holes; those that frequent marshy lands are *ānūpa* because they take refuge in such areas; those born in water are *jalaja* because they reside in water; and those that move in water are *jalecara* because they roam within the water.

1.27.55 | Animals that live on land are called *jāṅgala*; those that roam in the *jāṅgala* region are likewise so designated. Those that scatter their food are known as *viṣkira*, and those that peck at it are known as *pratuda*.
1.27.56 | This eightfold classification of meat is proclaimed:
the Prasahas, the Bhūśayas, the Ānūpas, the Vārijas, and the Vāricāris.
1.27.57 | They are heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet; they increase strength and nourishment, are highly aphrodisiac, alleviate Vāta, and increase Kapha and Pitta.

1.27.58 | The physician [prescribes] the meat of carnivorous animals specifically for those men who are habitually engaged in physical exercise, who possess a keen digestive fire, and who are powerful.

1.27.59 | One should administer the group of birds beginning with the common quail (lāva), the Vaiṣkira group, and the Jāṅgala animals that are pecking birds (pratuda) for those suffering from chronic hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa), and consumption (śoṣa).
Light, cold, sweet, and slightly astringent, they are beneficial for people in cases where pitta is predominant,
vāta is moderate, and kapha is subordinate within a sannipāta disorder.
1.27.61 | The *viṣkira* birds, such as the quail (*vartaka*) and others, are only slightly different from the *prasaha* birds in their qualities.
Goat meat is neither excessively cold, heavy, nor unctuous, and it does not aggravate the bodily humors (*doṣa*).
1.27.62 | Meat is non-obstructive and nourishing because its constituent elements are similar to those of the human body;
mutton is heavy and nourishing due to its sweetness and cold potency.
1.27.63 | Since goats and sheep are not distinguished when mixed together in one pen, the meats taught here in general shall now be described individually according to their own specific qualities.
1.27.64 | A distinction will be taught for some individuals based on the excellence of their qualities regarding vision,
hearing, intellect, digestive fire, age, complexion, voice, and lifespan.
Barley is most beneficial, strengthening, a destroyer of wind, and increases muscle mass and semen;
it is heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet, and it bestows clarity of voice, complexion, and strength.
Swans are said to be nourishing, semen-prolific, and destroyers of wind (vāta);
they are unctuous, hot, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and restorers of the voice.
1.27.67 | The cock is supremely strengthening, dispels wind, and induces perspiration;
it is heavy, hot, and sweet, owing to its frequent resort to arid and marshy lands.
The partridge quickly subdues the three humors when wind is predominant;
the grey partridge is beneficial in disorders of bile and phlegm accompanied by blood.
1.27.69 | In mild winds, quails (lāva) are recommended because of their coolness, sweetness, and lightness;
they are astringent-sweet, light, and increase the digestive fire.
1.27.70 | They pacify the *sannipāta* (combined) disorder and are pungent in their post-digestive effect (*vipāka*).
The iguana (*godhā*) is sweet in its post-digestive effect, while being astringent and pungent in its taste (*rasa*).
The śallakī is known to pacify vāta and pitta, to be nourishing, and to increase strength;
it is sweet and sour, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka).
They destroy wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as curing cough and dyspnea;
they are astringent, clarifying, cooling, and eliminate hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta).
Doves that dwell in houses are sweet in their post-digestive effect (vipāka);
wild forest-dwelling doves are slightly lighter than them.
They are cooling, constipating, and cause very little urination.
The flesh of the parrot is astringent and sour, and it is dry and cold in its post-digestive effect.
1.27.75 | Sparrows are beneficial for emaciation, cough, and consumption; they are astringent, light, and digestive stimulants. They are sweet, unctuous, and increase strength and semen.
1.27.76 | The decoction (kaṣāya) pacifies the combination of the three humors (sannipāta) and also pacifies Vāta;
it is clear, dry, cold, pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), and light.
The rabbit is delicious and highly recommended in cases of *saṃnipāta* where wind (*vāta*) is predominant;
it is sweet, sweet in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), pacifies the three *doṣas*, and is auspicious.
1.27.78 | Deer meat is declared to be light, binding for the stool and urine, and cooling;
it is unctuous, nourishing, aphrodisiac, fatiguing, and subdues Vāta.
1.27.79 | Boar meat is strengthening, appetizing, sudorific, and heavy;
it is indicated for simple vāta disorders, chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), and irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
1.27.80 | Buffalo meat is beneficial for dry cough, fatigue, excessive digestive fire, and the wasting of muscle tissue; it is unctuous, hot, sweet, aphrodisiac, heavy, and satiating.
They produce firmness, bulk, enthusiasm, and even sleep;
they are heavy, hot, sweet, strengthening, nourishing, and subdue the wind (vāta).
1.27.82 | Fishes are declared to be unctuous, aphrodisiac, and productive of many doṣas,
due to their feeding on moss and young grass, and because they abstain from sleep.
The rohita fish is digestive-stimulant, light in digestion, and very strengthening;
it improves the complexion, alleviates vāta, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and increases physical strength.
1.27.84 | The meat of the tortoise (kūrma) is said to promote intelligence and memory, is wholesome, and cures consumption (śoṣa).
The meat of the rhinoceros (khaḍga) is known to be heavy for the channels (abhiṣyandi), strength-promoting, and sweet.
The meat of the dhārtarāṣṭra, cakora, duck, and peacock is emollient, nourishing, complexion-enhancing, fatiguing, and subdues vāta.
1.27.86 | And whatever eggs of sparrows there may be that are beneficial [should be used] for those with diminished semen, coughs, heart diseases, and chest wounds.
1.27.87 | Nothing among edible foods excels meat in being sweet, non-burning, immediately strength-promoting, and nourishing to the body.
1.27.88 | Thus, this third group of meats has been fully described. Now, the group of vegetables (śākavarga): pāṭā, āśuṣā, śaṭī, vāstuka, and suniṣaṇṇaka.
One should know that vāstuka is constipating and destroys the three doṣas;
kākamācī pacifies the three doṣas, is aphrodisiac, and is a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
The Rājakṣavaka vegetable is neither excessively hot nor cold in potency; it is laxative, destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha), pacifies the three doṣas, and is light.

1.27.91 | Kālaśāka is especially recommended for those suffering from disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī) and hemorrhoids; it is pungent, stimulates digestion, and overcomes artificial poisons and edema.
The kālāya vegetable is said to be light, hot, wind-increasing (vātala), and dry;
it is digestive, hot in potency, and astringent for kapha and vāta.
1.27.93 | The sour cāṅgerī is praised; it is beneficial for disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids.
It is sweet, sweet in its post-digestive effect, a laxative, and increases phlegm.
1.27.94 | Upodika is aphrodisiac, unctuous, cooling, and it destroys intoxication;
it is dry, counteracts intoxication and poison, and is recommended for those suffering from internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta).
1.27.95 | *Taṇḍulīyaka* is sweet and sweet in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), and it is cooling; so too are *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, the tips of *vetra* reeds, *kucelā*, and *vanatiktaka*.
1.27.96 | Karkoṭaka, avalguja, paṭola, śakulādanī, vṛṣapuṣpa, śārṅgeṣṭā, kembūka, and kaṭhillaka.
1.27.97 | Nāḍī, kalāya, gojihvā, vārtāka, tilaparṇikā,
kaulaka, kārkaśa, naimba, and that which is pārpaṭaka— these are the leaf-vegetables (śāka).
All pulses and vegetables—phanji, chilli, and kutumbaka—are bitter, cold, and pungent in their post-digestive effect; they alleviate kapha and pitta.
All varieties of *ālukā* along with their leaves, *kuṭiñjara*,
the flowers of *śaṇa* and *śālmalī*, *karbudāra*, and *suvarcalā*.
1.27.100 | Niṣpāva, kovidāra, pattūra, cuccūparṇikā, kumārajīva, loṭṭāka, pālaṅkyā, and likewise māriṣa.
1.27.101 | Kalamba, nālikā, sūrya, kusumbha, vṛkadhūmaka,
lakṣmaṇā, prapunnāḍa, nalinīkā, and kuṭheraka.
1.27.102 | Loṇikā, yavaśāka, kuṣmāṇḍaka,
avalguja, yātuka, śālakalyāṇī, triparṇī, and pīluparṇikā.
1.27.103 | Vegetables are generally heavy, dry, cause flatulence during digestion,
are sweet, cold in potency, and loosen the stool.
1.27.104 | It is recommended that [the pulp] be steamed, its juice squeezed out, and enriched with fats—
[using the fibers] of hemp, kovidāra, karbudāra, and śālmali.

The flowers of the Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Padma, and other such trees are astringent and highly recommended, especially in cases of internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta). These include the tender leaves as well.
1.27.106 | Astringent decoctions that are stabilizing and cooling are beneficial for those suffering from pitta-type diarrhea.
Vatsādanī destroys vāyu, while gaṇḍīra and citraka destroy kapha.
1.27.107 | Bilvaparṇī is even more excellent; the bilva leaf, however, subdues wind (vāta).
So too are bhaṇḍī, śatāvarī greens, balā, and jīvantika.
The flowers of *parvaṇī* and *parvapuṣpī*, as well as those of *lāṅgalakī* and *uruvūka*, are known to alleviate wind and bile; they are light, purgative, and bitter.
1.27.109 | Sesame, vetasa, and the vegetable of pañcāṅgula increase vāta; they are pungent, bitter, and sour, and they promote downward movement through the lower passage.
1.27.110 | The safflower (kausumbha) is dry, sour, and hot; it destroys phlegm and increases bile.
The cucumber (trapusa) and gourd (ervārūka) are sweet, heavy, constipating, and cold.
1.27.111 | Trapusa, when fully ripe, is pleasant to the palate yet dry; it promotes urination and relieves burning sensations, thirst, exhaustion, and distress.
Ervāruka, when fully ripe, likewise removes burning sensations, thirst, fatigue, and pain.
1.27.112 | Alābu (bottle gourd) causes the breaking of stool and is dry, cold, and heavy;
however, *cirbhaṭa* and vāruka are similar in that respect, but they are beneficial for breaking the stool.
1.27.113 | 1. Ripe kūṣmāṇḍa, when prepared with alkali, is sweet and sour, light, promotes the evacuation of urine and feces, and subdues all the doṣas.
Kelūṭa, kadamba, nadīmāṣaka,
and ainduka are said to be clear, heavy, cold, and highly obstructive to the channels (abhiṣyandi).
1.27.115 | Blue lotuses (utpala) are astringent and alleviate blood-bile (raktapitta).
Likewise, tālapralamba removes the pain of chest wounds.
1.27.116 | Date palm fruit and the kernel of the palmyra palm cure hemorrhagic disorders and consumption;
likewise do tarūṭa, lotus stalks, lotus roots, krauñcādana, and kaśeruka.
Śṛṅgāṭaka, when stirred with sugar, is heavy, constipating, and cooling.
The stalks of the kumuda and utpala lotuses are known to be beneficial when accompanied by their flowers and fruits.
Cold, sweet, and astringent, they aggravate phlegm and wind;
being slightly astringent and causing slight constipation, they are known to alleviate blood-bile (raktapitta).
The seed of the Pauṣkara, however, is sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect;
it is strengthening, cooling, heavy, unctuous, satiating, and nourishing in nature.
The muñcātaka is excellent for alleviating vāta and pitta; it is sweet, aphrodisiac, life-sustaining, nourishing, and beneficial for the throat; it is highly recommended as a rejuvenative (rasāyana).
The tuber of the vidārī is strengthening, diuretic, sweet, and cooling.
The tuber of the amlikā is considered beneficial for the digestive tract and for hemorrhoids, and it is light.
Not too hot, it subdues phlegm and wind, is constipating, and is recommended in cases of alcoholism (*madātyaya*).
Mustard greens (*sārṣapa-śāka*) are said to aggravate the three *doṣas* and cause the retention of feces and urine.
Likewise, the red-stalked [lotus] is especially dry and sour.
One should know that the *piṇḍāluka* is similar, being pleasant to the palate because it is a bulbous root (*kanda*).
However, there are many other species of mushrooms (*chatra*) besides the *sarpacchatraka*.
1.27.124 | Cold, causing catarrh, sweet, and heavy—
this is the fourth group of vegetables, consisting of leaves, tubers, and fruits.
1.27.125 | Now, the group of fruits (phalavarga):
[They cure] thirst, burning sensations, fever, dyspnea, hemorrhagic disorders, chest wounds, consumption,
disorders of wind and bile, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), hoarseness of voice, and alcoholism.
1.27.126 | The grape quickly removes a bitter taste in the mouth, dryness of the mouth, and cough;
it is nourishing, aphrodisiac, sweet, unctuous, and cooling.
1.27.127 | Date is sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, heavy, and cooling;
it is beneficial in cases of wasting, injury, burning sensations, and in disorders of wind and bile.
1.27.128 | Parūṣaka and Madhūka are nourishing, bulk-promoting, light, constipating, and cooling;
they are recommended for vāta and pitta disorders.
The āmrātaka fruit is sweet, nourishing, strengthening, satiating, and heavy;
it is unctuous, increases phlegm, is cold, aphrodisiac, and digests with difficulty due to causing flatulence.
1.27.130 | Mature palm fruits and coconut fruits are nourishing,
unctuous, cooling, strengthening, and sweet.
The Bhavya fruit is sweet, sour, and astringent; it causes constipation, is heavy and cold, increases Pitta and Kapha, is astringent, and cleanses the mouth.
1.27.132 | Tamarind, parūṣaka, grapes, jujubes, and āruka fruits,
as well as karkandhu and nikuca, provoke pitta and śleṣman.
1.27.133 | Āruka (gourd) that is neither too hot, heavy when well-cooked, predominantly sweet, and pleasant to the palate is nourishing,
digests quickly, and does not excessively increase the *doṣas*.
1.27.134 | The pigeon (pārāvata) is known to be of two kinds—cold and hot—and is sweet and sour; it is heavy, causes loss of appetite, and destroys excessive digestive fire.
The fruit of the *kāśmarya* is said to have qualities only slightly different from those of the *bhavya*; likewise, the sour *tūda* has qualities only slightly different from those of the *parūṣaka*.
1.27.136 | The unripe *kaṭphala* (ṭaṅka) is astringent-sweet, increases *vāta*, is heavy, and cold.
Raw *kapittha* destroys the throat, is anti-toxic, constipating, and increases *vāta*.
1.27.137 | Due to its sweet, sour, and astringent qualities, as well as its fragrance, it promotes the appetite.
When fully matured, it destroys humors and neutralizes poison; though heavy, it is constipating.

1.27.138 | Mature bilva is difficult to digest, aggravates the humors, and produces foul-smelling flatus; however, when young, it is unctuous, hot, and sharp, stimulates digestion, and conquers kapha and vata.
1.27.139 | Raw mango causes bleeding disorders and increases pitta;
ripe mango subdues vāyu and bestows muscle tissue, semen, and strength.
Jāmbara fruit is predominantly astringent and sweet, heavy, constipating, and cold;
it subdues phlegm and bile, is astringent, and is highly provocative of wind.
The jujube fruit (badara) is sweet, unctuous, laxative, and subdues wind and bile.
When dried, it destroys phlegm and wind and is not incompatible with bile.
The fruit of *simbi* (or *siñcitikā*) is astringent-sweet, cooling, and constipating;
so too are *gāṅgerukī*, *karīra*, *bimbī*, *todana*, and *dhanvana*.
The ripe jackfruit (panasa), the mango (moca), and the fruits of the rājādana tree are sweet, slightly astringent, cooling, and alleviate pitta and kapha.
Sweet, slightly astringent, unctuous, cold, and heavy;
due to their astringency and clarity, as well as their fragrance, they stimulate the appetite.
The fruit of the *lavalī* is suitable for use as a snack (*avadanśa*), is pleasing to the heart, and increases wind (*vātala*).
So too are the *nīpa*, *śatāhvaka*, *pīlu*, *tṛṇaśūnya*, and *vikaṅkata*.
Prācīnāmalaka destroys the bodily humors (doṣas) and removes poison;
Aiṅguda is bitter and sweet, unctuous and hot, and conquers phlegm and wind.
1.27.147 | Tinduka destroys phlegm and bile; it is astringent, sweet, and light.
One should know that āmalaka possesses all tastes except for the salty.
1.27.148 | Bibhītaka is dry, sweet, astringent, and sour; it is supreme in removing kapha and pitta, and it destroys the defects arising from the rasa, blood, muscle, and fat tissues.
It destroys hoarseness of voice, excessive phlegm, and diseases of bile;
it is sour, astringent, and sweet, subdues wind, is constipating, and stimulates digestion.
1.27.150 | The unctuous and hot pomegranate is pleasing to the heart and does not aggravate kapha or pitta;
however, that pomegranate which is dry and sour provokes pitta and vāta.
Among those, the sweet pomegranate (dāḍima) is the best for alleviating pitta;
the tree-sour (vṛkṣāmla) is astringent, dry, and hot, and is recommended for disorders of vāta and kapha.
The ripe fruit of the *amlikā* is slightly different from that [sour gruel] in its qualities;
however, *amlavetasa* is similar to it in those very same qualities, yet it is specifically a laxative.
