In all cases arising from vāta and kapha, the filaments (kesara) of the mātuluṅga are prescribed; the rest [of the fruit] is otherwise [heavy].
Karcūra is brightening, digestive-stimulant, cordial, fragrant, and devoid of bark;
it destroys phlegm and wind and is beneficial for asthma, hiccup, and hemorrhoids.
The fruit of the nāgaraṅga is sweet, slightly sour, pleasing to the heart, and stimulates the appetite; it is heavy to digest, pacifies vāta, and is substantial.
Vāta, mābhiṣuka, akṣoṭa, mukūlaka, and nikocaka—these, along with urumāṇa, are heavy, hot, unctuous, and sweet; they bestow strength.

1.27.158 | One should know that *priyāla* is similar to these [in its properties], except for the quality of heat; it subdues wind (*vāta*), is nourishing, aphrodisiac, and increases phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*).
The fruit of the *śleṣmātaka* is phlegm-increasing, sweet, cold, and heavy;
the fruit of the *aṅkoṭa* increases phlegm, is heavy, causes flatulence, and subdues the digestive fire.
The fruit of the *śamī* is heavy, hot, sweet, dry, and destroys the hair;
the fruit of the *kārañja* causes constipation and is not antagonistic to *vāta* and *śleṣman*.
One should know that āmrātaka, dantaśaṭha, sour karamardaka,
and airāvataka cause the aggravation of blood and bile (raktapitta).
1.27.162 | One should know that the fruit of the *parpaṭakī* is wind-alleviating, digestive-stimulating, pungent, and bitter; it increases wind and subdues phlegm and bile.
The fruit of the *akṣikī* is sour, destroys *pitta* and *śleṣman*, and increases *vāta*.
Those that are sweet and ripen sourly destroy *pitta* and *śleṣman*.
1.27.164 | The fruits of the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and nyagrodha are astringent, sweet, and sour; they increase vāta and are heavy.
The seed of the *bhallātaka* is like fire, while its flesh is sweet and cooling. This fifth group of fruits has been described as generally useful for consumption.
1.27.166 | Now, the group of green vegetables (haritavarga):
Ginger (ārdraka) and common ginger (viśvabheṣaja) are appetizing, digestive stimulants, and aphrodisiacs;
its juice is prescribed for obstructions caused by vāta and śleṣman.
The jambīra fruit is brightening, digestive-stimulant, sharp, fragrant, and cleanses the mouth;
it destroys phlegm and wind, kills worms, and digests food.
1.27.168 | Young radish removes the [specific] doṣas; mature radish aggravates all three doṣas;
processed with unctuous substances it alleviates vāta; but dried radish conquers kapha and vāta.
1.27.169 | Surasa destroys hiccup, cough, poison, dyspnea, and pain in the flanks;
it increases pitta, subdues kapha and vata, and removes foul odors.
1.27.170 | Yavānī, arjaka, śigru, śāleya,
and mṛṣṭaka are pleasing to the heart and palatable, yet they aggravate pitta.
1.27.171 | Gaṇḍīra, jalapippalī, tumbaru, and śṛṅgaverikā are sharp, hot, pungent, and dry; they alleviate kapha and vāta.
1.27.172 | Bhūstṛṇa (Cyperus rotundus) destroys virility; it is pungent, dry, and hot, and cleanses the mouth.
Kharāhvā (Mucuna pruriens) destroys kapha and vāta, and removes the pain of diseases of the bladder.
1.27.173 | Dhānyaka, ajagandhā, and sumukha are digestive stimulants (rocanas);
they are fragrant, not excessively pungent, and do not aggravate the bodily humors.
1.27.174 | Gṛñjanaka is astringent and sharp; it is beneficial for wind, phlegm, and hemorrhoids.
One should employ it in sudation and as food for those who do not have pitta disorders.
Onion increases phlegm, subdues wind, but does not alleviate bile;
it is suitable for food, strengthening, heavy, aphrodisiac, and appetizing.
Garlic destroys worms, skin diseases, and leucoderma; it subdues wind, cures abdominal tumors, is unctuous, hot, aphrodisiac, pungent, and heavy.
1.27.177 | These dried fruits destroy kapha and vāta, as do their seeds.
This sixth group concerning green vegetables is hereby concluded.

1.27.178 | Now, the section on alcoholic liquors (madyavarga): By nature, liquor is sour and hot, and it is said to be sour in its post-digestive transformation (vipāka). Generally, this is its common property; its specific characteristics will now be taught.

Surā is recommended for those who are emaciated, those with obstructed urine, and those suffering from disorders of the *grahaṇī* or hemorrhoids; it subdues *vāta* and is beneficial in cases of deficiency of breast milk or blood.
In cases of hiccups, dyspnea, catarrh, cough, constipation,
loss of appetite, vomiting, abdominal distension, and obstruction, wine that subdues Vāta is beneficial.
Jagala is beneficial for dysentery with piercing pain, colic, phlegm, wind, and hemorrhoids;
it is astringent, dry, and hot, it destroys swelling, and it digests food.

This *ariṣṭa* destroys consumption, hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, anemia, anorexia, and fever; it cures diseases caused by *kapha*, acts as an appetizer, and stimulates digestion. It is pleasant to the mouth, produces a mild intoxication, is fragrant, and alleviates diseases of the bladder.
Sugar-based food is digestible, transformative, pleasing to the heart, and improves the complexion.

1.27.184 | Matured juice (pakvarasa) is considered to be appetizing, digestive-stimulant, cordial, beneficial for emaciation, edema, and hemorrhoids; it destroys disorders of unctuousness and phlegm, and improves the complexion.
It is digestive, relieves constipation, purifies the voice and complexion,
is scraping, has a cooling taste, and is beneficial for swellings, abdominal enlargements, and hemorrhoids.
1.27.186 | Gauda liquor, which causes the discharge of stool and flatus, is nourishing and digestive.
It is considered beneficial for anemia and ulcers, and the Akshiki variety is regarded as digestive.
1.27.187 | Surasava liquor causes intense intoxication, subdues Vata, and is pleasant to the palate.
The Chedi liquor is a honey-based spirit that is sharp; the Maireya is sweet and heavy.
1.27.188 | Distilled with *dhātakī*, the fermented liquor from *mṛdvīkā* and sugarcane juice is pleasing to the heart, parching, appetizing, and digestive; like *mādhvīka*, it is not excessively hot.
Honey is brightening, digestive-stimulating, cordial, strengthening, and non-contrary to pitta;
it removes constipation, subdues kapha, is light, and produces little wind.
1.27.190 | Surā with its scum (maṇḍa) is dry, hot, derived from barley, and increases vāta and pitta; it is heavy and causes flatulence during digestion. Madhūlikā, however, increases kapha.
Sauvīraka and tuṣodaka are digestive stimulants and carminatives; they cure heart disease, anemia, and worms, are beneficial for malabsorption syndrome and hemorrhoids, and are laxative.
Sour gruel (amlakāñjika) removes burning fever through its touch and vāta and kapha through its consumption;
it relieves constipation, is laxative, and stimulates the digestive fire.
1.27.193 | Fresh liquor generally increases heavy humors and vāta; aged liquor cleanses the channels, stimulates digestion, is light, and improves the appetite.
Wine is exhilarating, pleasing, and dispels fear, grief, and fatigue; it bestows confidence, virility, eloquence, contentment, nourishment, strength, and energy.
1.27.195 | When drunk by those of sattvic nature according to the rules and with proper method, it becomes like nectar. This seventh chapter has been proclaimed concerning liquor.
1.27.196 | Now, the section on water (jalavarga):
All water is of a single kind; it falls from the vault of heaven as the rain of Indra.
Whether falling or already fallen, it depends upon place and time.
1.27.197 | Falling from the sky, it is touched by the moon, wind, and sun, which follow their respective courses;
and by the qualities of the earth—cold, heat, oily, dry, and so forth—according to its proximity.
1.27.198 | Celestial water is by nature cool, pure, auspicious, delicious, stainless, and light—possessing these six qualities; however, once fallen [to earth], it depends upon its receptacle.
In white soil, there is an astringent taste; in pale soil, it is bitter;
in brown soil, it is mixed with alkaline; and in saline soil, it is endowed with saltiness.
1.27.200 | Bitter water is found on mountain plateaus, while sweet water is found in black soil;
these are declared to be the six qualities of water situated upon the earth. Likewise, one should know that water which is of unmanifest taste belongs to Indra, as does that which is cold.
Whatever water falls from the sky, sent forth by Indra and caught in the vessels mentioned, the wise call that "belonging to Indra"; this is the preeminent water fit for the King to drink.
Water that is slightly astringent and sweet, very subtle, clear, light,
non-drying, and non-obstructive to the channels is considered the best of all.
The rainwater of the monsoon season is heavy, causes internal secretions, and is sweet when fresh;
however, that which falls generally in autumn is thin, light, and does not cause secretions.

1.27.204 | However, for those who are delicate and whose diet consists mostly of unctuous foods, this [ghee] is recommended as their food, whether in the form of solid food, snacks, things to be licked, or drinks.
In the winter, water is unctuous, aphrodisiac, beneficial for strength, and heavy;
in the late winter (śiśira), it is slightly lighter than that and subdues phlegm and wind.
One should know that the water of spring is astringent-sweet and dry;
it is certain that the water of summer is non-obstructive to the channels.
But when the clouds pour forth water during times of disorder, that water leads to calamity; of this there is no doubt.
1.27.208 | Water collected in autumn should be used especially by kings, royal officials, and persons of delicate constitution.
1.27.209 | Rivers originating from the Himalayas— whose waters are broken, agitated, and struck by rocks— are wholesome, sacred, and frequented by gods and sages.
1.27.210 | Rivers that carry stones and sand and possess clear water,
as well as those originating from the Malaya mountains— their water is like nectar.
Those rivers which flow toward the west are wholesome and possess clear waters; those that flow toward the eastern ocean generally move slowly and are heavy.
Those [waters] originating from the Pāriyātra mountains, as well as those from the Vindhya and Sahya ranges,
are the cause of diseases of the head and heart, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and elephantiasis (ślīpada).
1.27.213 | Rivers carrying rainwater are defiled by earth, insects, snakes, mice, and filth; they stir up all manner of impurities.
1.27.214 | One should discern the qualities and defects of water in ponds, wells, tanks, springs, lakes, cascades, and the like, as well as in marshy lands, mountains, and arid plains.
Water that is slimy, infested with worms, stagnant, covered with leaves, moss, and mud, discolored, tasteless, thick, and foul-smelling is not beneficial.
1.27.216 | That water which is from the abode of Varuṇa is pungent-smelling, possesses the three doṣas, and is saline.
Thus, this eighth group, the section on waters, has been declared with complete certainty.
1.27.217 | Now, the group of bovine products: Cow's milk possesses ten qualities: it is sweet, cold, mild, unctuous, thick, smooth and slimy, heavy, slow-digesting, and clear.
1.27.218 | Thus, one should increase this very *ojas* through substances possessing similar qualities;
milk is said to be the foremost among those that promote vitality (*jīvanīya*) and is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
The milk of buffalo-cows is heavier than that of cows and is cooler; it is less oily, beneficial for those who cannot sleep, and for those with excessive digestive fire.
The milk of camels is dry, hot, slightly salty, and light;
it is recommended for disorders of wind and phlegm, abdominal distension, worms, swelling, abdominal enlargements, and hemorrhoids.
The milk of single-hoofed animals is strengthening, stabilizing, and entirely hot;
it is slightly sour, salty, dry, light, and cures disorders of the limbs and wind (vāta).
1.27.222 | Goat's milk is astringent and sweet, cooling, constipating, and light;
it cures hemorrhaging and diarrhea, and removes consumption, cough, and fever.
1.27.223 | Goat's milk causes hiccup and dyspnea, and is hot; it increases pitta and kapha. The milk of female elephants is strengthening, heavy, and supremely bestows stability.
Human milk is life-sustaining, nourishing, wholesome, and emollient;
it is used as nasal drops for hemorrhaging and as a satiating treatment for those with eye pain.
Curd is brightening, digestive-stimulant, aphrodisiac, unctuous, and strength-increasing;
it is sour in its post-digestive transformation, hot in potency, subdues wind, auspicious, and nourishing.
Curd is recommended in cases of catarrh, diarrhea, chills, irregular fever,
loss of appetite, dysuria, and emaciation.
1.27.227 | Curd is generally forbidden in autumn, summer, and spring;
furthermore, it is unwholesome in disorders arising from blood, bile, and phlegm.
Curd produced from milk affected by all three doṣas is mild, yet it destroys vāta and is aphrodisiac;
its whey (sara) destroys kapha and vāta, while the scum (maṇḍa) cleanses the channels.

In cases of swelling, hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract, urinary retention, abdominal enlargement, anorexia, complications arising from oleation therapy, jaundice, and artificial poisons, one should administer buttermilk.
Freshly extracted butter is constipating, digestive-stimulant, and beneficial for the heart;
it cures disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids, and destroys facial paralysis and loss of appetite.
1.27.231 | It increases memory, intellect, digestive fire, semen, vigor, phlegm, and fat;
it removes wind, bile, poison, insanity, emaciation, misfortune, and fever.
1.27.232 | It is the best of all fats, cooling, and sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect.
Clarified butter, when prepared according to the prescribed rites, possesses a thousandfold potency and accomplishes a thousandfold of deeds.
1.27.233 | This aged ghee cures intoxication, epilepsy, fainting, consumption, insanity, chronic fever, and pain in the female reproductive tract, ears, and head.
1.27.234 | One should designate the butters of goats, sheep, and buffaloes as being like their respective milks;
so too are colostrum (*pīyūṣa*), *moraṭa*, and the various kinds of *kilāṭas*.
1.27.235 | All [these] when served with lamps, fire, and without sleep, bestow happiness;
they are heavy, satiating, aphrodisiac, nourishing, and subdue the wind (vāta).
1.27.236 | Curd-cakes made from buttermilk are clear, heavy, dry, and constipating. This ninth group is proclaimed as the section on cow products.
1.27.237 | Now, the section on sugarcane (ikṣuvarga):
The juice of sugarcane is aphrodisiac, cooling, laxative, unctuous, nourishing, and sweet in taste;
it increases phlegm (kapha), whereas that which is extracted from the crushed cane (yāntrika) causes burning acidity when consumed.
1.27.238 | Due to its coolness, clarity, and sweetness, vaṃśaka is superior to pauṇḍraka;
whereas jaggery (guḍa) produces an abundance of worms, marrow, blood, nodules, and flesh.
1.27.239 | When one-fourth, one-third, or one-half of the molasses remains, it is called *kṣudra-guḍa*.
As for the juice, the more it is washed (*dhauta*), the heavier it becomes; the molasses with very little impurity is as described before.
1.27.240 | Thereafter come candied sugar, granulated sugar, and pure sugar;
the more their purity, the greater their coolness.
Jaggery sugar (guḍa-śarkarā) is aphrodisiac, beneficial for those who are emaciated or suffering from chest wounds, and is oily;
while sugar made from the yaṣṭimadhu plant (yāsa-śarkarā) is astringent-sweet, cold, and slightly bitter.
1.27.242 | Honey-sugar (madhuśarkarā) is dry, it cures vomiting and diarrhea, and acts as a depletive.
All types of sugar are recommended for thirst, blood disorders, pitta, and burning sensations.
Honey derived from *mākṣika*, *bhrāmara*, and *kṣaudra* are the types of honey that increase *pitta*.
Among these, *mākṣika* is the best, while *bhrāmara* is specifically heavy.

1.27.244 | Honey from the *mākṣika* bee is the color of oil; that from the *pauttika* bee is the color of ghee; honey from the *kṣudra* bee is tawny in color; and that from the *bhrāmara* bee is said to be white.
Honey is wind-increasing (vātala), heavy, cold, and it subdues blood-bile (raktapitta) and phlegm (kapha).
It is a unifier of tissues, a cutter [of secretions], dry, astringent, and sweet.
Honey that is warm destroys [the disease] when one is afflicted by heat, or due to its association with poison.
Honey is beneficial in small quantities because of its heavy, rough, and astringent qualities, as well as its cold potency.
1.27.247 | There is nothing more painful than this: honey in an undigested state, for it destroys the human being instantly, like poison, because it opposes the initial digestive process.
In the case of undigested food (*āma*), warm treatment should be administered; however, that [warm treatment] is contraindicated when the *āma* is associated with honey.
Therefore, honey combined with *āma* is dreadful, as it kills instantly, just like poison.

1.27.249 | And because it consists of various substances, honey is a supreme vehicle of medicinal action (yogavāhin). Thus, this tenth group is considered to consist primarily of preparations of sugarcane.
1.27.250 | Now, the group of prepared foods (kṛtānnavarga):
Peysā (thin gruel) removes hunger, thirst, exhaustion, debility, abdominal diseases, and fever;
it generates perspiration and digestive fire, and promotes the downward movement of wind and feces.
1.27.251 | *Maṇḍa* (scum) is satiating, constipating, light, pleasing to the heart, and also used as a thick gruel;
it kindles the digestive fire and promotes the downward movement of flatus.
It softens the channels and also generates perspiration;
it is indicated for those who have undergone fasting or purgation, for those whose oleaginous substances have been digested, and for those suffering from thirst.
1.27.253 | Because it stimulates digestion and is light, *maṇḍa* sustains life;
however, *lājapeyā* removes fatigue for a person whose throat is parched.
1.27.254 | Barley-gruel (lājamaṇḍa) pacifies thirst and diarrhea, restores the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus), is auspicious,
kindles the digestive fire, and wards off burning sensations and fainting.
1.27.255 | For those with weak digestion or irregular digestion, for children, the elderly, women,
and those of delicate constitution, well-prepared rice-gruel made from parched grain (lājamaṇḍa) should be administered.

Boiled with long pepper (pippalī) and dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and combined with parched grain (lāja), sour substances (amla), and pomegranate (dāḍima), it relieves hunger and thirst, is wholesome, and removes the impurities of those who have undergone purification.
1.27.257 | Roasted grain flour (lāja-saktu) is astringent, sweet, cooling, and light.
Well-washed, drained, steamed, and heated rice is also light.
1.27.258 | They also prescribe fried rice for disorders caused by *gara* (poison) and phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Rice that is unwashed, unstrained, unsweated, and cold is heavy.
Meat, vegetables, fat, oil, ghee, marrow, fruits, and boiled rice are strengthening, nourishing, pleasing to the heart, heavy, and promote corpulence.
Similarly, *kulmāṣa* (half-cooked grains) prepared with a combination of black gram,
sesame, milk, and mung beans are heavy, dry, increase *vāta*, and cause loose stools.
1.27.261 | Regarding whatever foods are eaten after being steamed— whether made of mung beans, wheat, or sheep’s wool—
the physician should prescribe their heaviness or lightness according to the specific ingredients used.
1.27.262 | One should know that unseasoned soup, seasoned soup, thin soup, prepared broth, and meat broth, as well as sour and non-sour soups, are progressively heavier.
1.27.263 | Barley flour (saktu) increases wind, is dry, promotes the downward movement of abundant feces,
and when drunk, immediately satisfies a person and provides immediate strength.
1.27.264 | Barley flour derived from śāli rice is sweet, light, and cooling;
it is constipating, cures hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta), and removes thirst, vomiting, and fever.
Barley cakes, barley gruel, or even barley-meal alone may destroy diseases such as upward movement of wind (udāvarta),
catarrh, cough, urinary disorders, and throat obstructions.
1.27.266 | Those foods known as *dhānās* (parched grains) are generally scraping (*lekhanātmaka*) in nature;
due to their dryness, they are parching (*tarpaṇa*), and because they cause constipation (*viṣṭambhitva*), they are difficult to digest.
1.27.267 | Sprouted grains, *śaṣkulī* cakes, honey-filled sweets with lumps, *pūpa* cakes, *pūpalikā* cakes, and other such flour-based foods are exceedingly heavy.
Fruits, meat, fat, vegetables, sesame paste, and honey— when prepared together,
these foods are aphrodisiac, strengthening, heavy, and nourishing in nature.
Veśavāra is heavy, unctuous, and increases strength and nourishment. Cakes made with milk, sugarcane juice, jaggery, sesame, milk, honey, and sugar are heavy, satiating, and aphrodisiac.
They are considered edible, aphrodisiac, and strengthening, but they are also known to be extremely heavy.

1.27.271 | Products made from wheat are considered to be wholesome when prepared with fats; they possess various characteristics, are heavy to digest, nourishing, aphrodisiac, and pleasing to the heart.
1.27.272 | There are light foods prepared from wheat flour, such as parched grains, flat cakes, and cakes; having understood these, one should prescribe them accordingly.
One should eat pṛthuka grains that have been fried with ghee, but only in small quantities;
they should be digested while causing flatulence, being moist, and resulting in loose stools.
1.27.274 | Foods prepared from pulses, which are light for eating, increase wind (vāta), and are dry and cold,
should be eaten sparingly along with pungent, oily, and salty substances.
1.27.275 | Those foods that are soft-cooked, as well as those that are thick and hard, are heavy; when they have passed the stage of cooking, they bestow nourishment and strength.

Having understood the specific heaviness or lightness of each substance, one should prescribe for foods the combination of substances, their processing, and their individual weights according to their respective natures.
1.27.277 | (Vimardaka, prepared with various ingredients— cooked, raw, moistened, and roasted— is heavy, pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, and beneficial for those who possess strength.
1.27.278 | Rasālā is nourishing, aphrodisiac, unctuous, strengthening, and provides a relish for food.
Curd mixed with jaggery is emollient, nourishing, pleasing to the heart, and subdues Vata.
1.27.279 | A syrup made from grapes, dates, and jujubes is heavy and causes constipation; the same applies to that made from *parūṣaka* fruits, honey, and various preparations of sugarcane.

1.27.280 | Having understood the individual substances, their proportions, and their specific qualities and actions, one should prescribe those syrups (pānaka) which consist of combinations of pungent and sour ingredients.
1.27.281 | Pungent, sour, sweet, and salty *rāga-ṣāḍavas* are light, pleasing to the palate, agreeable to the heart, digestive stimulants, and appetizers.
1.27.282 | Pomegranate-based syrups are nourishing, strength-promoting, appetizing, and satiating, owing to their oiliness, sweetness, and heaviness.
Having understood the combinations, the processing, and the measurement of the substances used therein, one should likewise describe the qualities and actions of each of those electuaries.

1.27.284 | Śukta causes the secretion of blood, pitta, and kapha, and it facilitates the downward movement of vāta; one should know that fermented preparations made from bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like have the same properties.
The physician should know that *śiṇḍākī*, *āsuta*, and other sour preparations made with time (*kālāmla*), which are appetizing and light,
constitute the eleventh group among prepared foods (*kṛtānna*).
It has an astringent aftertaste, is sweet, subtle, hot, and pervasive;
it increases pitta, binds the feces and urine, and does not increase kapha.

Oil is considered the best among wind-alleviating substances, strengthening, and an enhancer of intellect and digestive fire; through its specific combinations and processing, it is regarded as a remedy for all diseases.
In ancient times, through the application of oil, the lords of the Daityas became free from old age, devoid of physical change, overcame fatigue, and possessed extraordinary strength in battle.
Castor oil is sweet, heavy, and increases phlegm (kapha);
it is an excellent remedy for vātarakta, abdominal tumors (gulma), heart disease, and chronic fever.
1.27.290 | Mustard oil is pungent and hot; it vitiates blood and bile (*raktapitta*), yet it removes phlegm, semen, and wind (*vāta*), and destroys itching and urticaria.
1.27.291 | *Priyāla* oil is sweet, heavy, and increases phlegm (*śleṣman*).
They desire what is beneficial, for excessive heat arises from the conjunction of wind and bile.
Ātasya is sweet and sour, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), hot in potency (uṣṇavīrya); it is beneficial for vāta but aggravates blood and pitta (raktapitta).
1.27.293 | Kusumbha oil is hot, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), heavy, causes a burning sensation,
and especially provokes all the doṣas.

1.27.294 | Furthermore, regarding those other oils from fruits that are employed in the preparation of food, one should describe them according to their qualities and actions, or else state that they are fruitless.
1.27.295 | Marrow and likewise fat are sweet, nourishing, aphrodisiac, and strengthening;
however, one should determine the coldness or heat of fat and marrow according to the nature of the animal from which they are derived.

1.27.296 | Viśvabheṣaja (ginger) is unctuous, digestive, aphrodisiac, hot, and alleviates vāta and kapha; it is sweet in its post-digestive effect, pleasing to the heart, appetizing, and a universal medicine.
Fresh long pepper (pippalī) is phlegm-forming, sweet, moist, heavy, and unctuous.
When dried, it destroys phlegm and wind; it is pungent, hot, and considered an aphrodisiac.
Black pepper (marica) is not excessively hot, is non-aphrodisiac, light, and improves the appetite.

Because it cuts, dries, and kindles [the digestive fire], asafoetida (hiṅgu) conquers phlegm and wind. One should know that asafoetida destroys obstructions caused by wind and phlegm, is pungent and hot, stimulates digestion, is light, pacifies colic, and acts as a digestive and an appetizer.
Saindhava salt is the best of salts; it is brightening, digestive, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, non-burning, and destroys the three doṣas while being sweet in taste.
1.27.301 | Sauvarcala salt, due to its subtlety, heat, lightness, and fragrance, is appetizing; it relieves constipation, is pleasing to the heart, and clarifies the eructation.
Due to its sharpness, heat, and penetrating nature, *viḍa* salt is digestive, destroys colic,
and promotes the downward and upward movement of the bodily winds (*vāta*).
1.27.303 | Rock salt (*audbhida*) is slightly bitter, pungent, alkaline, sharp, and liquefacient;
it lacks the aroma of black salt (*kālalavaṇa*), yet possesses the qualities of sochal salt (*sauvarcala*).
Sea salt is sweet and slightly bitter; that produced from earth is pungent.
All varieties of salt are appetizing, digestive when cooked, laxative, and alleviate Vāta.
Yavaśūka removes heart disease, anemia, disorders of the grahaṇī, splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, throat obstruction,
cough caused by phlegm, and hemorrhoids.
1.27.306 | All alkali (kṣāra) is sharp, hot, light, dry, moistening, digestive, fissuring, burning, appetizing, and excising; it resembles fire.
Kāravī, kuñcikā, ajājī, yavānī, and dhānyatumburu are appetizing,
digestive stimulants, and destroyers of wind, phlegm, and foul odors.
1.27.308 | There is no certainty regarding the devotion of those who practice the yoga of food.
This twelfth section concerning those who practice the yoga of food is now concluded.
1.27.309 | Spike-grain and leguminous grain that has been stored for a year is recommended;
generally, old grain is dry, whereas fresh grain is usually heavy.
1.27.310 | Whatever comes quickly is considered lighter.
Pulse that is dehusked and roasted with proper technique is light and digests easily.
One should discard the meat of an animal that is dead, emaciated, excessively fatty, old, young, killed by poisons, nourished on improper food, or slain by a predator.
1.27.312 | Therefore, meat is beneficial in other circumstances; it is nourishing, strength-increasing, pleasing to all beings, and the essence of meat is supremely heart-pleasing.
One should know that meat broth is like nectar for those who are emaciated, those freed from disease, the lean, those with diminished semen, and those seeking strength and a healthy complexion.
One should know that the specific taste prescribed for the pacification of all diseases promotes the voice,
bestows strength, and enhances age, intellect, the senses, and longevity.
Those men who are constantly devoted to physical exercise, those who are constantly devoted to women, those who are constantly devoted to wine,
and those who always consume meat broth, shall neither be diseased nor weak.
One should avoid vegetables that are infested with worms, damaged by wind or heat, dried out, stale, out of season, cooked without oil or fat, and those that have not been properly strained.
1.27.317 | Fruit that is old, unripe, spoiled by worms, predators, frost, or heat;
grown in an improper place or season, or moldy—that fruit is unsound.

1.27.318 | Just as there is no specific instruction for green vegetables apart from their preparation, so too is the determination of liquors, water, milk, and other substances made according to their respective groups.

1.27.319 | That drink which is contrary to the qualities of the food is considered improper; however, a post-prandial drink is seen as acceptable when it does not conflict with the bodily tissues (dhātus).
Having identified the eighty-four types of fermented liquors (āsava) that have been described,
one should drink water— examining both what is fit to be drunk and what is unfit— and then drink the beneficial [liquor] after it.
1.27.321 | Meat broth is recommended as a post-drink (anupāna) that is unctuous and hot for disorders of Vāta; sweet and cold for Pitta;
dry and hot for Kapha; and it is supreme in cases of wasting (kṣaya).
For those exhausted by fasting, travel, speaking, women, wind, heat,
and physical labor, milk is as wholesome for the purpose of a drink as nectar.
1.27.323 | Surā is prescribed as a post-drink for the nourishment of those who are emaciated;
honey-water is recommended after meals for those with stout bodies to induce leanness.
For those with weak digestive fire, for those suffering from insomnia due to drowsiness, grief, fear, or exhaustion,
and for those accustomed to wine and meat, wine alone is recommended.

1.27.325 | Now we shall describe the actions and qualities of after-drinks (anupāna). An after-drink satiates, pleases, invigorates, nourishes, brings about fullness, settles what has been eaten, breaks up the mass of food, produces softness, moistens, digests, and generates easy digestion and rapid elimination of the food.
And there is a verse on this:
An appropriate and beneficial after-drink (anupāna) quickly satisfies a person;
it facilitates the easy digestion of food and promotes both longevity and strength.

1.27.327ab | Not those afflicted by upward-moving wind (ūrdhvāṅgamāruta), nor those suffering from hiccups, dyspnea, or cough; 1.27.327cd | Nor those addicted to singing, talking, or study, nor those with chest wounds.

1.27.328ab | Having eaten, they should drink water, for that [water] remains in the throat and chest; 1.27.328cd | having destroyed the oily essence (sneha) produced from food, it leads once again to the aggravation of the humors (doṣa).
1.27.329ab | This has been stated as a single portion of food and drink that is generally used. 1.27.329cd | For it is not possible to specify all substances in their entirety by name.

Just as there is no medicinal herb that does not exist, and just as there are words for things produced in various regions, so too should each substance be described here according to its nature, even if it has not been explicitly mentioned.
1.27.331ab | The channels, the bodily constituents, the natural constitution, the tissues, and the activities;
1.27.331cd | The signs, the dimensions, the purification, and the measures are examined in this [chapter].
1.27.332ab | The preparation of food consists of meat from marshy regions, water, sky, desert, and so forth;
1.27.332cd | as well as those born in water, those born in marshy regions, and those that frequent water and marshes.
1.27.333ab | Those beings that eat heavy food are all considered to be heavy;
1.27.333cd | whereas those that eat light food are light, as are those born in arid regions and those that roam in arid regions.
1.27.334ab | Likewise, the limbs of the body include the thighs, the head, the shoulders, and so forth.
1.27.334cd | Of these, the shoulder is heavier than the flesh of the thigh; the chest is heavier than that, and the head is the heaviest of all.

1.27.335ab | The two testicles, the skin, the penis, the hips, the kidneys, the liver, and the rectum— 1.27.335cd | one should know these to be heavier than flesh, as well as the respective intermediate bones.
1.27.336ab | By their very nature, mung beans are light, as are the common quail and the grey partridge. 1.27.336cd | By their very nature, black gram is heavy, as are the boar and the buffalo.
1.27.337ab | One should know that among the bodily constituents (dhātus), beginning with blood, each subsequent one is heavier than the preceding.
1.27.337cd | Living beings who engage in much activity are superior to those who are indolent.
1.27.338ab | Among those of the same gender, males possess heaviness while females possess lightness;
1.27.338cd | within their own species, those of great size are heavy, and otherwise they are light.
1.27.339ab | One should understand that lightness results from the processing of heavy substances, and the opposite occurs otherwise.
1.27.339cd | Just as rice becomes parched grain (*lāja*), so too does flour become a prepared ball (*siddhapiṇḍikā*).
1.27.340ab | In the case of taking small amounts of heavy substances and excessive consumption of light ones,
1.27.340cd | the quantity (mātrā) is declared to be the determining factor for the heaviness or lightness of substances.
1.27.341ab | From heavy foods, only a small amount should be taken; from light foods, satiety is desired.
1.27.341cd | Substances depend upon the proper measure, and that measure depends upon the digestive fire.
1.27.342ab | Strength, health, longevity, and the vital breaths are all established in the digestive fire.
1.27.342cd | The fire blazes through the fuel of food and drink, and it subsides otherwise.
1.27.343ab | This consideration of relative severity and mildness generally applies to those who are weak;
1.27.343cd | namely, those of sluggish activity, those who are unwell, the delicate, and those accustomed to comfort.

1.27.344ab | Those men who have a keen digestive fire, eat coarse food, are constantly engaged in work, and have large bellies— 1.27.344cd | regarding them, one need not necessarily consider the relative heaviness or lightness [of their actions].
1.27.345ab | With a concentrated mind, one should constantly offer oblations into the internal fire with wholesome things;
1.27.345cd | using food and drink as fuel, without regard for quantity or time.
1.27.346ab | He who maintains the sacred fires always offers auspicious oblations into the internal fire; 1.27.346cd | who day after day mutters the Veda and likewise bestows gifts.
No diseases whatsoever afflict a man who is devoted to his own ultimate welfare and who understands what is wholesome in food and drink,
unless they are destined to arise from within [the body].

1.27.348ab | A person who eats wholesome food, who is free from disease, who has conquered his self, and who is esteemed by the virtuous, lives for thirty-six thousand nights. 1.27.348cd | [He lives] as one who is honored by the good.
1.27.349ab | Food is the life-breath of living beings; all the world runs after food.
1.27.349cd | [It provides] complexion, clarity, a melodious voice, vitality, intuition, and happiness.
1.27.350ab | Contentment, nourishment, strength, and intelligence—all these are established in food.
1.27.350cd | Whatever worldly action exists for one's livelihood, and whatever Vedic action leads to heaven;
1.27.351ab | Furthermore, that which was stated regarding the completion of ritual acts is also established in food (anna).
1.27.351 | On this point, there is a verse:
1.27.351cd | The qualities of food and drink are preeminent; twelve groups have been determined.
1.27.352ab | Adjuvant drinks with their qualities, and the summary of heaviness and lightness;
1.27.352cd | as described in the rules for food and drink, that must be examined with particular care.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rules for Food and Drink," in the Section on General Expositions of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
1.28.0 | Chapter Twenty-Eight | 1.28.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on various kinds of food and drink (Vividhāśitapītīya).
1.28.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

1.28.3 | The various kinds of food—eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed—which are beneficial to a living being, are properly digested by their respective internal heat, aided by the strength kindled by the internal fire (*antaragni*). When digested at the proper time, they mature all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) without causing instability, provided the channels of the *dhātus*, *samāna* wind, and the *srotas* are unimpaired. This process bestows solely prosperity through nourishment, strength, complexion, happiness, and longevity, and invigorates the bodily constituents. For the constituents, having the constituents as their nourishment, follow their own natural state (*prakṛti*).
1.28.4 | Therein, from food, that which is called *rasa* (nutritive essence) and waste matter known as *kiṭṭa* (dross) are produced.

From the *kiṭṭa*, sweat, urine, feces, vāta, pitta, and śleṣman (phlegm), as well as the impurities of the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, hair follicles, and the generative organ, and the body parts such as hair of the head, beard, body hair, nails, and so forth, are nourished.

However, from the *rasa* of food, the following are nourished: *rasa*, blood, muscle, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and *ojas*; the substances of the five sense organs known as the pure essences (*prasāda*) of the tissues; and body parts such as the ligaments, joints, and mucous secretions.

All these elements (dhātus), both those termed *prasāda* (pure) and those termed *mala* (impure), being nourished by the nutrient essence (*rasa*) and waste (*mala*), maintain their own respective proportions according to the age and body.
Thus, when the nutrient essence and waste remain within their own measures, they maintain the equilibrium of the elements in a person whose constituent parts are balanced.

However, due to specific causes, when the *prasāda*-named elements have become diminished or increased, the nutrient essence—rooted in food—produces equilibrium through its own increase or decrease for the sake of health; and the waste likewise produces equilibrium for the impurities.

Furthermore, the impurities (malas), which exceed their own measure and undergo successive transformations through the qualities of cold and heat, are observed to bring about equilibrium among the constituent elements (dhātus) of the body.
1.28.5 | Furthermore, the channels are the pathways for those elements known as impurity (*mala*) and clarity (*prasāda*).
They fill their respective elements according to their specific divisions.
Thus, this body originates from what is eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed.
Furthermore, diseases arise in this body originating from what is eaten, drunk, licked, and chewed;
however, it is the specific nature of the consumption of what is wholesome or unwholesome that produces the distinction between health and illness.

To the Blessed Ātreya who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, we observe that even those who consume food designated as wholesome may be diseased or free from disease, and likewise for that which is designated as unwholesome. This being so, how can we perceive the distinction between the auspicious and the inauspicious, which consists of the specific effects of consuming the wholesome and the unwholesome?"

1.28.7 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, diseases caused by that [unwholesome diet] do not arise in those who consume wholesome food; nor, however, does one transcend the fear of all diseases through the consumption of wholesome food alone. For there exist predispositions for disease even in the absence of the consumption of unwholesome food, namely: the reversal of seasons, intellectual error, and unwholesome sound, touch, form, taste, and smell."

Furthermore, those predispositions for disease bring about misfortune even to a person who consumes tastes properly; therefore, even those who employ wholesome food are seen to be afflicted by illness.
On the other hand, for those who consume unwholesome food, a transgression does not immediately become "defiled" (doṣavat) due to various causes.
For not all unwholesome things possess equal defects, nor do all defects have equal strength, nor are all bodies equally capable of withstanding disease.

For that very same unwholesome thing becomes even more unwholesome through excessive application in terms of place, time, combination, potency, and quantity. That same *doṣa* (humoral disorder) becomes most difficult to treat and most rapidly acting when it arises from a combined source, is subject to contradictory treatments, has spread deeply, has persisted for a long time, has originated in a vital organ (*prāṇāyatana*), and strikes a vital point (*marman*). Furthermore, bodies that are excessively obese, excessively emaciated, lacking flesh, blood, and bone, weak, nourished by unwholesome food, under-nourished, or possessing little mental fortitude are unable to withstand disease; conversely, those with the opposite qualities are able to withstand disease.
And from these very factors—unwholesome diet, the specific humors (doṣas), and the particularities of the body—diseases arise, whether they be mild or severe, acute or chronic.
It is those same vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, O Agniveśa, that, when provoked in specific locations, bring about specific diseases.

Adhimāṃsa, arbuda, kīla, galaśālūka, and śuṇḍikā;

1.28.22ab | Depressed by the impurities, the doshas cause their fragmentation, drying, and corruption; 1.28.22cd | and they also excessively cause the retention or excessive discharge of those impurities.
1.28.23ab | From various kinds of unwholesome things eaten, drunk, licked, or chewed,
1.28.23cd | these aforementioned disorders arise in human beings.

1.28.37ab | Learning, intelligence, memory, dexterity, fortitude, and the practice of what is beneficial;
1.28.37cd | Purity of speech, tranquility, and steadfastness attend upon the discerning man.

The distinction between the wise and the ignorant, as well as what is beneficial for the healthy and the afflicted— all that has been fully elucidated in the chapter on "Various Foods and Drinks."

1.29.0 | Chapter Twenty-Nine | 1.29.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the ten seats of the vital breaths (daśaprāṇāyatanīya).
1.29.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.29.3ab | They say there are exactly ten seats upon which the vital breaths (prāṇas) are established:
1.29.3cd | the two temples, the three vital points (marmans), the throat, the blood, the semen, the ojas, and the anus.
He who understands those sense organs, consciousness, the cause of volition,
and the diseases— he indeed is the wise one and is called a physician for the vital breaths.
1.29.5 | "O Agniveśa, physicians are indeed of two kinds: some are pursuers of life and destroyers of diseases, while others are pursuers of diseases and destroyers of life."
To the Blessed One Ātreya, who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "Blessed One, how are they to be understood by us?"

The Blessed One said: Those who are of noble birth, whose learning is purified, who have witnessed clinical practice, who are skillful, pure, dexterous, self-controlled, possessed of all necessary instruments, endowed with all their senses, and who understand both nature and the methods of treatment—they should be known as the rescuers of life and the destroyers of diseases. For such individuals are free from doubt regarding the knowledge of the body, the knowledge of the body's formation, and the knowledge of its natural state and its transformations.

They were free from doubt regarding the specific knowledge of the etiology, prodromal signs, symptoms, pain, and palliative factors of diseases that are easily curable, difficult to cure, manageable for life, or incurable.

They are the expounders of the threefold aphorism of Āyurveda, along with its compendium and exposition, and the collection of the three types of medicinal substances; they are the practitioners of the thirty-five roots and fruits, the four oleaginous substances, the five salts, the eight urines, the eight milks, the six milk-bark trees, the group of medicinal plants based on the five purificatory procedures beginning with head-evacuation, the twenty-eight gruels, the thirty-two powders and plasters, the six hundred purgatives, and the five hundred decoctions.

They were experts in the proper conduct of life, including the rules for food and drink, standing, walking, lying down, and sitting; they were skilled in the application of dosage, medicinal substances, collyrium, fumigation, nasal drops, massage, and cleansing; they knew how not to suppress natural urges and when to do so, as well as the proper exercise, suitability, examination of the senses, and the commencement of treatment according to virtuous conduct. They were free from doubt regarding medicine governed by its four pillars, consisting of sixteen components, with its definitive determination, its threefold search, and its knowledge of the proportions of the Vāta humor. Furthermore, they were establishers of the four types of oleation therapy, its twenty-four applications, its preparations, and its sixty-four variations.

They are skilled in various types of therapeutic procedures, as well as in the administration of diverse medicinal treatments for those requiring oleation, sudation, emesis, and purgation; they are experts in the classification of diseases arising from the specific proportions of the humors, such as diseases of the head, as well as fevers, carbuncles, abscesses, the three types of swellings (śopha) along with their various complications, the forty-eight bases of disease, the one hundred and forty diseases of diverse origins, and likewise those who are censured for being excessively obese or excessively emaciated.

[The chapter] on the causes, characteristics, and treatments of dreams, as well as the beneficial and harmful effects of sleep and excessive sleep along with their causes and treatments; the six types of treatments beginning with fasting (laṅghana); diseases arising from over-nutrition and under-nutrition together with their symptoms and pacification; and blood-born diseases.

They were experts in the causes and medicinal treatments for intoxication, fainting, and coma; skilled in the determination of dietary rules; proficient in the primary collection of wholesome and unwholesome food preparations and their transformations; knowledgeable in the eighty-four types of fermented liquors (*āsava*) and the determination of their substances, qualities, and actions; well-versed in the primary and secondary tastes and their combinations; familiar with the twelve categories of food and drink along with their specific contradictions; and conversant with the qualities and potencies of food and drink, including their after-drinks (*anupāna*), the ninefold summary of purposes, and the courses of digestion.

And [the knowledge] of the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome consisting in the specific application of what is beneficial and harmful, of diseases based on the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), of the collections of medicines, of the ten seats of life (*prāṇāyatana*), and that which I shall explain in the thirtieth chapter, the *Arthadaśamahāmūlīya*.

And therein, O Agniveśa, those who are skilled in the grasping, retention, comprehension, application, action, effect, time, agent, and instrument of the entire treatise—including its summary and its definitions—and who are likewise skilled in memory, intelligence, knowledge of the scriptures, and reasoning; who have perfected themselves through their qualities of conduct and by being non-contradictory in practice; and whose minds are filled with loving-kindness toward all living beings, like that toward a mother, father, brother, or kinsman—those endowed with such qualities are the "Rescuers of Life" (Prāṇābhisara), the destroyers of diseases.

1.29.8 | Conversely, those who are the adversaries of diseases and destroyers of life, yet are disguised under the mask of physicians—acting as thorns to the world and possessing the nature of impostors—they roam through kingdoms due to the negligence of kings.

1.29.9 | This is their specific modus operandi: boasting excessively under the guise of being physicians, they wander through the streets out of greed for profit; upon hearing that someone is ill, they rush toward him from all sides; in his presence, they loudly proclaim their own medical virtues; they repeatedly point out the faults of whatever physician is actually treating him; and they seek to win over the patient's friends by means of flattery, instigation, and service.

They proclaim their own lack of desire for much, yet having undertaken a task, they look back at it again and again; wishing to conceal their own ignorance through a display of skill, and being unable to turn back a disease, they declare themselves to be truly ill, lacking resources, without attendants, and helpless.

Having observed that he has reached his end, they resort to another place, making it a mere pretext for their own minds; in an assembly of common people, they describe their own skill as if it were unskillful, and they proclaim their lack of fortitude like those who are timid, even while they are actually steadfast. And having observed an assembly of wise men, they avoid it from afar like travelers avoiding a terrifying wilderness. Furthermore, whatever fragment of a sūtra they have mastered, they constantly cite it out of context or in connection with an entirely different subject.
They do not wish for inquiry, nor do they wish to engage in it; they tremble at inquiry as if at death, and among them no teacher, pupil, fellow-student, or disputant is known.
And there are verses on this point: Those who, having entered the guise of physicians, thus prey upon the diseased,
are like bird-catchers who, having taken refuge in a thicket, lie in wait for birds in the forest.
Excluded from the knowledge of the proper time for actions as heard and seen, they are indeed to be avoided; for they wander upon the earth as the followers of Death.
1.29.12 | A wise patient should avoid those physicians who are full of pride for the sake of their livelihood and who are fools posing as experts; they are like snakes that have just drunk air.
But to those who know the scriptures, who are skillful, pure, and experts in ritual action,
whose hands are steady and whose minds are self-controlled— to them I offer constant salutation.

1.29.14 | This summary of the meaning of the Section on Verses (Ślokasthāna) concerns the ten seats of the vital breath (prāṇa).
1.29.14 | Two types of physicians have been described, as well as the seats of the vital breath.

Chapter Thirty.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the ten great roots for the sake of wealth.
1.30.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
1.30.3ab | Ten great roots are attached to the object (artha) and yield great fruit.
1.30.3cd | The wise say that "the great," "the object," and "the heart" are synonyms.

1.30.4ab | The six limbs, the [inner] organ, discernment, the senses, and the five objects; 1.30.4cd | the self together with its qualities, the mind, and the object of thought—these are situated within the heart.
1.30.5ab | For the heart is held by those who contemplate the meaning to be the foundation for these states of being; 1.30.5cd | like the central beam at the corner of a house for the rafters.
From its impairment one suffers fainting, and from its destruction one meets death;
for that consciousness of touch is supported by it as its sustainer.
1.30.7ab | That is the seat of supreme vitality, and therein lies the concentration of consciousness. 1.30.7cd | Therefore, it is called the "great heart" (mahat-hṛdaya) by physicians.

1.30.9ab | By whose vital energy all embodied beings, being gratified, subsist; 1.30.9cd | without which the life of all creatures does not endure.
That which was the essence of the embryo at the beginning, that which was the quintessence of the embryo's fluids, and that which formerly entered the heart as it was developing— [that is this].
1.30.11ab | Through the destruction of which there is destruction; that which is the sustainer and resides within the heart;
1.30.11cd | That which is the essence and moisture of the body, and wherein the vital breaths (prāṇas) are established.
1.30.12ab | They bear fruit in many ways, as it were, yielding great results.
1.30.12cd | They are called *dhamanīs* because of being blown upon (*dhmāna*), *srotas* because of flowing (*sravaṇa*), and *sirās* because of coursing (*saraṇa*).
1.30.13ab | Therefore, those [pleasures] are great, rooted in greatness, and they preserve one's vital energy; 1.30.13cd | yet the causes of mental suffering must be especially avoided.
1.30.14ab | Whatever is beneficial to the heart, whatever promotes vigor, and whatever clarifies the channels—
1.30.14cd | each of those should be cultivated with effort, as well as tranquility and knowledge itself.

1.30.15 | Now, indeed, there is one [practice] that is the most excellent among those that increase life-force (*prāṇa*), one among those that increase strength, one among those that nourish, one among those that delight, one among those that gladden, and one among those that lead away from worldly existence.

In this regard, non-violence toward living beings is the supreme vigor among those that increase life-force; knowledge is the best among those that increase strength; mastery of the senses is the best among those that nourish; realization of reality is the best among those that delight; and celibacy is the best among those that lead away from worldly existence. Thus do the experts in Āyurveda consider it.

1.30.16 | In this regard, those who know Āyurveda should be considered as teachers who explain the treatise (*tantra*), its sections (*sthāna*), chapters (*adhyāya*), and questions (*praśna*) individually—by way of the sentence (*vākya*), the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), and the components of the meaning (*arthāvayava*).
To this, he asks: "How are the treatise and the others explained by way of the sentence, the meaning of the sentence, and the components of the meaning?"
1.30.17 | Here it is said: the *tantra* of the seers, being stated in its entirety according to tradition, has been declared word by word.

1.30.18 | Having thoroughly penetrated the reality of the matter with the intellect, it is spoken according to the meaning of the sentences—endowed with the methods of detailed exposition and summary, proposition, reason, example, application, and conclusion—and made intelligible to the three types of student intellects. Thus has it been stated.

1.30.19 | For difficult points of meaning that have been determined through systematic treatises, the meaning becomes clearly articulated through further analytical investigations, as it has been stated.

1.30.20 | If there should be questioners therein, [they might ask]: "Of the four Vedas—the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda, and Atharvaveda—which Veda do those who know Āyurveda declare it to be? What is *āyus* (life)? Why is it called *āyurveda*? For what purpose is *āyurveda*? Is it eternal (*śāśvata*) or non-eternal (*aśāśvata*)? How many and what are its ancillary sciences (*aṅga*)? By whom should this be studied, and for what purpose?"

1.30.21 | In that case, when questioned by the physician, he should declare his devotion to the Atharvaveda among the four Vedas—Ṛg, Sāman, Yajus, and Atharvan—for the Atharvaveda indeed teaches medical treatment through its inclusion of mantras for giving gifts, rites for well-being, offerings, auspicious ceremonies, burnt oblations, observances, expiations, fasts, and so forth; and medical treatment is taught for the benefit of life.

1.30.22 | Having taught the Veda, one must speak of the lifespan (*āyus*). In this context, lifespan, consciousness (*cetana*), continuity (*anuvṛtti*), life-force (*jīvita*), connection (*anubandha*), and sustainer (*dhārin*) have one and the same meaning.

1.30.23 | It is called Āyurveda because it causes one to know that [life-span]. If it is asked how so, it is said: it is Āyurveda because it makes known things according to their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), according to pleasure and pain, according to what is beneficial and harmful, and according to what is valid and invalid; furthermore, it is Āyurveda because it makes known those substances, qualities, and actions that are conducive to life and those that are not. Among these, the substances, qualities, and actions conducive to life and those not conducive to life will be taught exclusively by this treatise (*tantra*). 1.30.24 | Therein, life-span has been correctly described according to its specific characteristics both here and in the preceding chapter.

In this regard, the life of one who is not afflicted by physical or mental diseases—especially one in the prime of youth, endowed with capability, support, strength, vigor, fame, manliness, and prowess; existing in a state where knowledge, discernment, the senses, their objects, and power are fully assembled; possessing supreme prosperity and various delightful enjoyments; having all undertakings successful; and moving about according to his will—is called a happy life.

This is the opposite of what is considered "unpleasant. Furthermore, it belongs to one who desires the welfare of living beings, who refrains from the property of others, who speaks the truth, who is devoted to tranquility, who acts with circumspection, who is vigilant, who pursues the three aims of life without allowing them to conflict with one another, who honors those worthy of honor, whose character is defined by wisdom, higher knowledge, and peace, who serves the elders, who has well-restrained the impulses of passion, anger, envy, intoxication, and pride, who is constantly intent on various forms of giving, who is ever-devoted to austerity, knowledge, and self-control, who knows the inner self, and who is dedicated to that [knowledge].
For one who considers both this world and the next, and possesses mindfulness and intelligence, life is said to be beneficial; conversely, it is harmful for one who acts otherwise.

1.30.25 | The measure of life is perceived through signs of abnormality—though without apparent cause—in respect to objects, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and physical activities, such that one knows: "This person will return to his own nature (death) from this moment, or after a muhūrta, a day, three, five, seven, ten, or twelve days, a fortnight, a month, six months, or a year. In this context, "own nature" (*svabhāva*), the cessation of activity, death, impermanence (*anityatā*), and destruction (*nirodha*) are synonymous. This is the measure of life; the opposite of this is the non-measure [of life], as treated in the section on fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*).
Furthermore, the measure of the lifespan has been taught in Āyurveda with reference to the characteristics of the body's constitution.
1.30.26 | And its purpose is the preservation of health for one who is healthy, and the alleviation of disorders for one who is diseased.

1.30.27 | This very Āyurveda is understood to be eternal because it is beginningless, because its characteristics are established by its own nature, and because the essential nature of existence is constant.

Indeed, there has never been a time when the continuum of life or the continuum of consciousness did not exist; the knower of life is eternal, and pleasure and pain are beginningless, characterized by substantial causes through their successive conjunctions.
This summary of the subject matter is thus analyzed as the definition of Āyurveda.

The increase and decrease of substances—such as heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, dry, and so forth—occur through their general and specific properties, as it has been stated: "By the repeated use of heavy things, there is an accumulation of the heavy and a diminution of the light; and the same applies to the others. This nature of entities is eternal, as is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of substances such as earth and the rest. However, while substances and qualities exist, they may be either eternal or non-eternal.

Indeed, in Āyurveda, the arising of something that did not previously exist is not observed, except for the arising of understanding and instruction; some teachers teach this process of arising with reference to these two alone.
Its essential characteristic (*svābhāvika-lakṣaṇa*) is unconditioned (*akṛtaka*), as was stated here in the first chapter, just like the heat of fire or the fluidity of water.

Furthermore, its permanence as the intrinsic nature of an entity (*bhāva-svabhāva-nityatva*) has been explained by the Teachers: "When heavy [substances] are practiced upon, there is an increase [in heaviness], while for light [substances] there is a decrease."

1.30.28 | That Āyurveda has eight branches, namely: internal medicine (kāyacikitsā), surgery of the head and neck (śālākya), extraction of foreign bodies (śalyāpahartṛka), the pacification of poisons, artificial and natural toxins, and incompatible substances (viṣagaravairodhikapraśamana), demonology (bhūtavidyā), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtyaka), rejuvenation therapy (rasāyana), and aphrodisiac therapy (vājīkaraṇa).

1.30.29 | And it should be studied by Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, and Vaiśyas. Among them, it is for the sake of favoring living beings that it is studied by Brāhmaṇas; for the sake of protection, by Rājanyas; for the sake of livelihood, by Vaiśyas; or generally, for the sake of embracing dharma, artha, and kāma, by all.

In this regard, that which consists of making an effort to pacify the afflictions of those who know the self, who stand upon the path of Dharma, who illuminate the Dharma, or of one's mother, father, brothers, kinsmen, and elders; and that which consists of contemplating, teaching, or practicing the inner science (adhyātma) as declared in Ayurveda—this is his supreme Dharma. Furthermore, the acquisition of wealth and protection obtained from lords or wealthy persons by means of excellent offerings, as well as the protection of living beings under one's own care from disease—this is his Artha.

2.1.16 | Indeed, among all diseases, fever alone is taught first here, because it is the foremost of bodily disorders.

2.1.17 | Now, indeed, fever arises in human beings from eight causes; namely: from vāta, from pitta, from kapha, from vāta and pitta, from vāta and kapha, from pitta and kapha, from vāta, pitta, and kapha, and from the eighth cause, which is exogenous (āgantu).
2.1.18 | We shall now explain in detail its specific etiology, premonitory symptoms, clinical signs, and therapeutic palliation.

2.1.19 | Vāyu becomes aggravated by the excessive consumption of dry, light, and cold substances; by excessive administration of emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), and head-purgatives (śirovirecana); by physical exercise; by the suppression of natural urges; by fasting; by trauma; by sexual intercourse; by agitation, grief, and bloodletting; and by staying awake at night or by improper postures of the body.

2.1.20 | When that [Vāta] becomes aggravated, it enters the stomach (āmāśaya) and, mixing with the heat (ūṣman), reaches the first constituent of food transformation known as rasa. Having obstructed the channels carrying rasa and sweat, impaired the digestive fire (agni), and expelled the heat from the site of digestion, it pervades the entire body and thereby brings about fever.

2.1.21 | These are its signs: namely—irregularity in the onset and subsidence [of the fever], irregularity of body heat, and instability in the intensity or mildness of the fever; the arrival or increase of the fever at the end of digestion, at the end of the day, at the end of the night, or at the end of the summer heat; and especially a reddish-brown discoloration of the nails, eyes, face, urine, feces, and skin, along with excessive emaciation.

They experience various kinds of shifting and unshifting sensations in their respective limbs and members; namely: numbness in the feet, cramps in the calves, a loosening of the knees and all the joints, a sinking sensation in the thighs, and in the waist, sides, back, shoulders, arms, collarbones, and chest, a feeling as if they were broken, pained, crushed, pulled apart, cracked, split open, or pushed upward; furthermore, there is a loss of function in the jaws, ringing in the ears, a piercing pain in the temples, and an astringent taste or a bad taste in the mouth.

Dryness of the mouth, palate, and throat; thirst; a gripping sensation in the heart; dry vomiting; dry cough; suppression of sneezing and flatus; aversion to the taste of food; salivation, anorexia, and indigestion; despondency, yawning, depression, tremors, fatigue, giddiness, delirium, insomnia, horripilation, and sensitivity of the teeth; a desire for warmth; and the lack of relief from factors mentioned as causes, while finding relief in their opposites—these are the signs of vāta-type fever.

2.1.22 | Pitta becomes aggravated by the excessive consumption of hot, sour, salty, alkaline, and pungent foods, as well as by eating during indigestion, and likewise by exposure to sharp sunlight, heat from fire, physical exertion, anger, and irregular diet.

2.1.23 | When that [vitiated humor], having become aggravated, spreads from the stomach (āmāśaya) toward the heat (ūṣman), follows the first constituent of food-transformation known as rasa, obstructs the channels carrying rasa and sweat, impairs the digestive fire (agni) due to its fluidity, and expels the heat from the site of digestion (paktisthāna) to the exterior, it pervades the entire body while causing distress; at that time, it brings about fever (jvara).

2.1.24 | Its signs are as follows: the simultaneous onset or aggravation of fever throughout the entire body, especially during the digestion of food, at midday, at midnight, or in the autumn; a bitter taste in the mouth; inflammation of the nose, mouth, throat, lips, and palate; thirst, intoxication, vertigo, fainting, vomiting of bile, diarrhea, aversion to food, lassitude, exhaustion, delirium, and the appearance of red eruptions on the body.

The symptoms of fever caused by pitta (pittaja-jvara) are as follows: a yellowish-green or turmeric-yellow discoloration of the nails, eyes, face, urine, feces, and skin; an excessive intensity of heat; extreme burning sensations; a desire for cold things; lack of relief from the factors mentioned as causes (nidāna), and relief from their opposites. These are the signs of pitta-fever.

2.1.25 | Kapha becomes aggravated by the excessive consumption of unctuous, heavy, sweet, slimy, cold, sour, and salty substances, as well as by daytime sleep, sexual excitement, and lack of physical exercise.

2.1.26 | When that [Vata], being provoked, enters the stomach (āmāśaya) and, mixing with the heat (ūṣman), reaches the first constituent of food-transformation known as rasa, it obstructs the channels carrying rasa and sweat, impairs the digestive fire (agni), and, having expelled the heat from the site of digestion, spreads throughout the entire body while afflicting it; at that time, it brings about fever.

2.1.27 | Its signs are as follows: the simultaneous onset or increase of fever throughout the entire body, especially immediately after eating, in the forenoon, during the early part of the night, or in the spring season; heaviness of the limbs, lack of desire for food, excessive salivation, sweetness in the mouth, nausea, a sense of coating in the heart, stiffness, horripilation, weak digestion, excessive sleep, rigidity, drowsiness, cough, dyspnea, and coryza.

Coldness and whiteness of the nails, eyes, face, urine, feces, and skin; the appearance of extremely cold pustules on the limbs; a desire for warmth; lack of relief from the factors mentioned as causes, and relief from their opposites; these are the signs of fever caused by phlegm (kapha).

2.1.28 | From irregular eating, fasting, changes in diet, derangement of the bodily elements (*dhātu*), smelling unwholesome odors, using water contaminated by poison, contact with mountainous minerals (*gara*), improper application of oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas (*āsthāpana*), unctuous enemas (*anuvāsana*), and head-purgatives (*śirovirecana*); from incorrect post-dietary regimen (*saṃsarjana*), from abnormal delivery in women, from improper care of those who have delivered, and from the combination of the aforementioned causes according to their respective etiological factors.
Either one of the pairs of humors, or all three humors together, simultaneously undergo provocation; once provoked, they bring about fever by that very same sequence.

2.1.29 | In that regard, by observing the specific combinations of the aforementioned symptoms of fever, one should recognize a particular dual-type (dvandvika) fever or a fever of the combined type (sānnipātika).

Among these, that born of injury is associated with *vāyu* acting upon vitiated blood; that born of possession is associated with *vāyu* and *pitta*; while those born of malevolent magic and curses are associated with *sannipāta* (the combination of all three *doṣas*).

Among these, physicians state that the endogenous type is of two, three, four, or seven kinds, according to the variations of *vāta* and the other [humors].

2.1.33 | Its premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) are as follows: distaste in the mouth, heaviness of the body, lack of desire for food, agitation of the eyes, lacrimation, excessive sleep, restlessness, yawning, bending of the body, trembling, fatigue, vertigo, delirium, insomnia, horripilation, sensitivity of the teeth, inability to endure sound, cold, wind, or heat, anorexia, indigestion, debility, aching of the limbs, lassitude, diminished vitality, procrastination, and laziness.

The neglect of habitual duties, opposition toward one's own tasks, malice toward the words of elders, hatred toward children, lack of concern for one's own religious obligations, aversion to garlands, ointments, and fine food, loathing for sweet edibles, and a fondness for sour, salty, and pungent things—these are the premonitory symptoms of fever that appear before the onset of heat; moreover, they persist even when the patient is afflicted by that heat.
2.1.34 | Thus, these symptoms of fever have been explained individually, both in detail and in summary.

2.1.35 | Fever indeed originates from the wrath of Maheśvara; it is the taker of life for all living beings, the cause of affliction to the body, the senses, and the mind, the reducer of wisdom, strength, complexion, joy, and enthusiasm, and the producer of exhaustion, fatigue, delusion, and the obstruction of food. It is called *jvara* because it "fevers" (torments) the bodies; no other diseases are as terrible, accompanied by so many complications, or difficult to treat as this one.
It is the sovereign of all diseases and is designated by many different names among the various animal species.

All living beings are born with fever and die with fever; that is great delusion (mahāmoha). Overwhelmed by it, embodied beings do not remember even the slightest of their actions pertaining to a previous life. Furthermore, among all living beings, fever alone seizes the vital breaths at the end.

2.1.36 | In that case, when the premonitory symptoms appear or at the onset of fever and other diseases, light food or fasting is beneficial, because fever originates in the stomach (āmāśaya). Thereafter, the administration of decoctions, internal massages, oleation, sudation, plasters, affusions, ointments, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas, unctuous enemas, palliative measures, nasal therapy, fumigation, medicinal smoking, collyrium, milk, and dietary regimens should be applied according to their respective indications and with due discretion.

2.1.37 | In all cases of chronic fevers (jīrṇajvara), the drinking of ghee prepared with appropriate medicinal herbs is recommended. For ghee pacifies vāta through its unctuousness (sneha), kapha through its processing (saṃskāra), and pitta as well as heat (ūṣman) through its coldness (śaitya). Therefore, in all chronic fevers, ghee is beneficial, just as water is for objects scorched by fire.
2.1.38 | And there are verses on this point: Just as men, desiring to extinguish it, sprinkle water upon a burning house, so too is clarified butter used in chronic fever.
2.1.39 | Ghee pacifies vāta due to its unctuousness (sneha) and subdues pitta due to its coldness (śaitya);
however, it overcomes kapha through processing (saṃskāra), as its qualities are otherwise similar to that of kapha.
2.1.40 | No other unctuous substance follows the process of refinement as well as ghee does; therefore, ghee is considered the best of all unctuous substances.
2.1.41 | When a matter already stated in prose is subsequently sung again in verses, that repetition is not to be censured, as it serves the purpose of clarifying the meaning.
2.1.42 | Regarding this, there are these verses:
[The author describes] the threefold nature of disease through its synonyms, the fivefold cause,
the synonyms for the characteristics of disease, and the fivefold onset of illness.
2.1.43 | Fever is of eight types; its remote and proximate causes, its premonitory symptoms, its clinical signs, and its treatment shall be described in summary.
2.1.44 | Free from fever, Punarvasu spoke before Agniveśa, who was bowed down in reverence, concerning the etiology of fever.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Fever," in the Section on Diagnosis of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Two:
2.2.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of internal hemorrhage (raktapitta).
2.2.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
2.2.3 | We shall now explain how pitta receives the designation "lohitapitta" (blood-bile) according to its actual nature.

2.2.4 | When a person eats foods consisting mostly of barley (*yavaka*), wild millet (*uddālaka*), and *koradūṣa*, as well as other types of food that are extremely hot and pungent, accompanied by *niṣpāva* beans, black gram (*māṣa*), horse-gram (*kulattha*), and alkaline soups; or with curds, whey (*dadhimaṇḍa*), buttermilk (*udaśvit*), sour gruel (*kaṭvarāmla*), and *kāñjika* as condiments; or with the meat of boar, buffalo, sheep, fish, and cow; or with oil-cakes (*piṇyāka*), tubers (*piṇḍālu*), dried vegetables (*śuṣkaśāka*), radish, mustard, garlic, *karañja*, *śigru*, and *madhuśigru* (or *khaḍayūṣa*).

It should be accompanied by side-dishes such as bhūstṛṇa, sumukha, surasa, kuṭheraka, gaṇḍīra, kālamālaka, parṇāsa, kṣavaka, and phaṇijjhaka; or it may be followed by a post-prandial drink consisting primarily of *surā*, *sauvīra*, *tuṣodaka*, *maireya*, *medaka*, *madhūlaka*, *śukta*, or the sour juices of *kuvala* and *badara*; and it should consist for the most part of food made from flour.

If one who is oppressed by heat drinks raw milk in excessive or immoderate quantities, or eats with milk *rauhiṇīka* or *kāṇakapota* prepared with mustard oil and alkali; or if, oppressed by heat, he drinks milk together with *kulattha*, oil-cakes, or the ripe fruits of *jāmbava* and *lakucha*, or with fermented liquors (*śauktika*); for him who acts in this manner, the *pitta* becomes aggravated and the blood exceeds its normal measure.

When that [dosha] has exceeded its normal measure, the aggravated pitta, spreading through the body, reaches the openings of the channels originating from the liver and spleen as well as those carrying blood; having reached those openings which are heavy due to the congestion of blood, it obstructs them and thereby vitiates that very blood.
2.2.5 | Due to its association with blood, its corruption of the blood, and its conformity to the smell and color of blood, pitta is called *lohitapitta*.

2.2.6 | These are its premonitory symptoms, namely: lack of desire for food, burning sensation after eating, eructations with a sour or acidic smell and taste, frequent onset of vomiting, a sense of repulsiveness toward what has been vomited, hoarseness of voice, lassitude of the limbs, a general burning sensation, a sensation as if smoke is issuing from the mouth, and a metallic, bloody, fishy, or raw odor in the mouth.

The premonitory symptoms of *raktapitta* are as follows: a reddish, greenish, or yellowish discoloration of the limbs, excretions, feces, urine, sweat, saliva, nasal mucus, earwax, pustules, and boils; pain in the limbs; and the frequent sight in dreams of red, blue, yellow, or dark-colored objects that appear as if flaming. These are the prodromal signs of *raktapitta*.
2.2.7 | The complications (upadrava), moreover, are indeed debility, anorexia, indigestion, dyspnea, cough, fever, diarrhea, edema, consumption, anemia, and hoarseness of voice.
2.2.8 | Furthermore, its two pathways are upward and downward.

When the body has an abundance of phlegm (*śleṣman*), it moves upward due to contact with phlegm and is discharged through the ears, nose, eyes, and mouth; however, when the body has an abundance of wind (*vāta*), it moves downward due to contact with wind and is discharged through the urinary and fecal passages. But when the body has an abundance of both phlegm and wind, it follows both pathways due to the combined contact of phlegm and wind; moving along those two pathways, it is discharged from all the aforementioned orifices of the body.
