2.2.9 | Among these, that which moves upward is curable, because it is treatable by purgation and because there are many medicines for it; that which moves downward is palliable, because it is treatable by emesis and because there are few medicines for it; and that which moves both ways is incurable, because it is unsuitable for either emesis or purgation and because there are no medicines for it.

2.2.10 | Indeed, the provocation of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic fever) first occurred following the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, as a consequence of the fever that arose from the fire of Rudra’s wrath and indignation among living beings whose bodies were overwhelmed by it.

2.2.11 | One must strive for the immediate pacification of that [condition], which is as sudden as a forest fire that has broken out, by carefully considering the dosage, the place, and the time—whether through nourishing or depleting measures, with foods that are mild, sweet, cold, bitter, or astringent, or through applications such as plasters, affusions, baths, and tactile contact, or by means of emesis and other therapies, remaining vigilant therein.
2.2.12 | And there are verses on this point:
That *lohitapitta* (hemorrhagic disorder) which manifests through the upper channels is curable,
because it responds to purgation and because of the abundance of medicinal remedies available for it.
2.2.13 | Purgation, however, is the supreme medicine for the conquest of pitta;
and as for the kapha that is associated with it therein, purgation is considered its inferior [remedy].
2.2.14 | In that case, the medicine should be sweet and conducive to yoga (union). Therefore, blood that moves upward is considered curable.
2.2.15 | However, that [blood] which moves in the downward direction is determined to be palliable (yāpya),
because of the limited utility of emesis and the small quantity of the medicine used.
2.2.16 | Indeed, emesis is not said to be the best for the removal of pitta;
furthermore, it is considered inferior for pacifying the vāyu that is associated with it.

2.2.17 | That [excessive purgation] brings about complications; in that case, one should administer astringent and bitter [decoctions]. Therefore, it is declared to be palliable (yāpya), as has been stated regarding that which moves in the natural direction (anulomaga).
2.2.18 | That raktapitta which involves both pathways should be known as incurable for the very reason previously stated.
2.2.19 | Indeed, there is no purificatory therapy for this [condition] that follows the natural course of the disease;
and in the case of *raktapitta*, removal [of blood] along the natural course is prescribed.
2.2.20 | In this very way, a complete pacification of it is not found;
however, when the *doṣas* are combined, a remedy that conquers all is prescribed.
2.2.21 | Thus it has been stated that blood [disorders] have three types of outcomes depending on the specific path [of the disease].
However, due to these very causes, some curable conditions do not reach a successful conclusion.
2.2.22 | Due to the absence of attendants and instruments, the physician's own wickedness, his professional deficiencies,
or the failure to perform the treatment, even a curable disease may become incurable.
2.2.23 | In that regard, there may be one case of incurability due to the failure of the therapeutic measures for the curable types;
this is the diagnosis of rakta-pitta as it is taught.
2.2.24 | That which is black or blue, or has the luster of Indra’s bow (a rainbow),
or that which dyes clothing red, is incurable raktapitta.
2.2.25 | That blood which is extremely foul-smelling, excessive in quantity, accompanied by all complications,
and present during the wasting of strength and flesh, is considered unsuccessful in treatment.
2.2.26 | Furthermore, when a person afflicted by Rakta-pitta sees whatever is visible as red, and even the sky appears so, that condition is undoubtedly incurable.
2.2.27 | Among these, the incurable should be abandoned; the palliable should be managed with effort;
and the curable, the physician should treat with diligence using proven medicines.
2.2.28 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
[The author has described] the cause, the etymology of the name, the premonitory symptoms,
the complications, the two pathways, the association with the humors, the curability, and the reasons for it.
2.2.29 | Punarvasu, who was free from delusion, passion, defects, greed, pride, intoxication, and longing, spoke again on the etiology of *raktapitta*.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Etiology of Raktapitta," in the Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Three.
2.3.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of abdominal tumors (gulma).
2.3.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
2.3.3 | Indeed, there are five types of abdominal tumors (gulma) here; namely: vātagulma, pittagulma, śleṣmagulma, nicayagulma, and śoṇitagulma.

2.3.4 | To the Blessed Ātreya who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, how may we recognize the specific distinctions among the five types of gulma? For a physician, even if he knows medicines, is not capable of pacifying diseases if he does not know their specific distinctions."

2.3.5 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, the specific diagnosis of abdominal tumors (gulma) and other diseases arises from the distinctions in their etiology, premonitory symptoms, clinical signs, pain, and therapeutic suitability; however, listen now as that [diagnosis] is being explained specifically regarding abdominal tumors."

2.3.6 | When a person who is particularly prone to vāta is emaciated by one or another of the following—fever, emesis, purgation, or diarrhea—and consumes vāta-aggravating food, or especially cold food in excessive measure; or undergoes emesis or purgation without prior oleation; or induces vomiting when it has not yet arisen; or suppresses the urges of wind, urine, and feces when they have arisen; or drinks an excessive amount of fresh water after overeating; or travels in a very jolting vehicle; [then his vāta becomes provoked].

Whether due to excessive sexual indulgence, physical exertion, alcohol, grief, or lack of appetite; or if one suffers a traumatic injury; or if one habitually engages in irregular postures of sitting, lying down, standing, or walking; or if one undertakes some other such irregular and excessive form of physical activity—through such misconduct, the *vāta* becomes aggravated.

2.3.7 | That aggravated Vāyu, having entered the great channel (mahāsrotas), becomes solidified due to its dryness (raukṣya); having overflowed and coagulated, it establishes itself in the heart, the bladder, the flanks, or the navel. It produces pain and various kinds of nodules (granthi), and remains in a massed state; because of this massed condition, it is designated as "gulma. It repeatedly distends and repeatedly returns to a state of diminution.

Furthermore, due to the mobility of the wind (*vāyu*), there occurs a pervasive and intense sensation throughout the body, like the constant crawling of ants upon the limbs; it is characterized by frequent piercing, splitting, throbbing, stretching, contraction, numbness, horripilation, and the onset and subsiding of pain. At that time, the afflicted person feels as if his very self were being pierced by needles or spikes; moreover, he develops fever at the end of the day, his mouth becomes parched, his breathing is obstructed, and his hair stands on end at the manifestation of the pain.

Spleen enlargement, flatulence, intestinal gurgling, indigestion, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), body aches, and pain in the neck, head, temples, and groin afflict this patient; furthermore, his skin, nails, eyes, face, urine, and feces become blackish, reddish-brown, and rough. The factors mentioned as causes do not provide relief, whereas their opposites do; such is vāta-gulma. ||2.3.8||

Furthermore, when one who has already been emaciated by those very depletions consumes sour, salty, pungent, alkaline, hot, sharp, fermented, spoiled liquor, green fruits, acidic fruits, and burning vegetables, grains, meats, and so forth; or due to indigestion, overeating, or dryness in the stomach (āmāśaya); or for one who excessively practices vomiting, suppresses natural urges, or exposes himself to wind and sun—the pitta, together with the vāta, undergoes provocation.

2.3.9 | That aggravated wind, having become localized in a portion of the stomach (āmāśaya), produces those very types of pain already described in the context of vātagulma; whereas the bile (pitta) causes a burning sensation in this [gulma] in the abdomen, heart, chest, and throat. Being thus burned, it emits eructations accompanied by smoke and sourness; and the site of the gulma feels as if it is being burned, pained, fumed, heated, perspiring, and moistened. It becomes flaccid, intolerant to touch, and characterized by slight horripilation.

Fever, giddiness, burning sensations, thirst, dryness of the throat, palate, and mouth, delusion, and diarrhea afflict him; his skin, nails, eyes, face, urine, and feces become greenish-yellow; and things mentioned as causes [of Pitta disorders] do not agree with him, while their opposites are agreeable—this is Pittaja Gulma.

2.3.10 | However, in one who has been emaciated by those very same methods of depletion, phlegm (śleṣman), together with wind (māruta), becomes provoked due to overeating; due to the consumption of excessively unctuous, heavy, sweet, and cold foods; due to the habitual use of preparations of flour, sugarcane juice, milk, sesame, black gram, and molasses; due to the excessive drinking of weak wine; due to the excessive intake of green vegetables; due to the excessive eating of the meat of marshy, aquatic, and domestic animals; due to the suppression of hunger; due to the excessive drinking of water when not thirsty; or due to the violent agitation of the body.

2.3.11 | When that [wind] is aggravated, the *māruta* (vata), having become localized in a portion of the *āmāśaya* (stomach/intestines), produces those very types of pain already described in the context of *vātagulma*. However, the *śleṣman* (kapha) produces cold fever, anorexia, indigestion, body ache, horripilation, heart disease, vomiting, drowsiness, lassitude, a sense of being wrapped in a wet cloth, heaviness, and headache; furthermore, it causes stability, heaviness, hardness, deep-seated numbness, and whiteness in the *gulma*, as well as cough, dyspnea, catarrh, and consumption (*rājayakṣmā*) when it is excessively increased.

It produces [discoloration] on the skin, nails, eyes, face, urine, and feces; the factors mentioned as causes do not agree with it, while their opposites do—this is śleṣmagulma (kapha-type abdominal tumor).
2.3.12 | When there is a combination of the causes and signs of all three doṣas, experts designate that as sannipātika gulma.
Because its treatment involves mutually contradictory measures, this nicaya-gulma is incurable.

2.3.13 | Indeed, blood-gulma (śoṇitagulma) occurs only in women and not in men, due to the specific nature of the uterus and the non-discharge of the menses (ārtava). In a woman who suppresses her arisen urges due to dependence on others, lack of self-knowledge, or constant compliance with medical treatment; or in one whose immature fetus has recently been expelled, or who has recently given birth, or who indulges in things that aggravate vāta during her menstrual period—vāta quickly becomes provoked.

2.3.14 | That [vāta], becoming aggravated, enters the opening of the womb and obstructs the menstrual flow; that menstrual blood, being thus obstructed month after month, causes the abdomen to enlarge.

In her, piercing pain, cough, diarrhea, vomiting, anorexia, indigestion, body ache, drowsiness, lassitude, a sense of being wrapped in a wet cloth, and excessive salivation of phlegm arise; there is milk in the breasts, blackness of the lips and the areolae of the breasts, extreme exhaustion of the eyes, fainting, nausea, pregnancy-longings (dohada), and swelling of the feet; there is a slight emergence of the line of hair (romarājī) and a stretching of the vagina, and moreover, foul odor and discharge appear from the vagina; and her *gulma* alone throbs as a solid mass—fools call such a woman, though she is not pregnant, "pregnant."

2.3.15 | Now, these are the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) that occur prior to the manifestation of these five types of abdominal tumors (gulma): namely—lack of desire for food, anorexia, and indigestion; irregularity of the digestive fire (agni-vaiṣamya); a burning sensation after eating; vomiting and eructation at the time of digestion due to improper conduct; non-appearance of the urges for flatus, urine, and feces, or their appearance followed by non-discharge or only slight discharge; wind-pain (vāta-śūla), flatulence (āṭopa), rumbling in the intestines (antra-kūjana), horripilation (aparihṛṣaṇa), and excessive hardness of stool; lack of hunger, weakness, and intolerance to the feeling of fullness.

2.3.16 | Indeed, among all these types of gulma, no gulma occurs without vāta. Knowing that the sannipātika (combined) type is incurable, one should not undertake its treatment; however, in the case of those born from a single doṣa, one should apply the appropriate therapeutic measures. As for those involving two combined doṣas, one should treat them with general (common) procedures.

Whatever else one considers non-contradictory, that too should be applied after weighing the relative severity of the complications; one should treat the severe complications with urgency, while the others may be treated later.

If one acts with haste without perceiving any specific [contraindications], one should administer the treatment for Vata in cases of Gulma or urgent conditions: namely, oleation and sudation which alleviate Vata, mild purgatives combined with oleation, and enemas; and one should judiciously employ sour, salty, and sweet tastes.
For when the Vata has been pacified, even with minimal effort, it is possible to subdue other Doshas in cases of Gulma.
2.3.17 | And there is a verse on this point:
For those suffering from gulma, the pacification of the wind (vāta) should be carried out in every way according to the prescribed rules.
When the wind (māruta) is conquered by physical exercise, it destroys even a slight increase in other humors (doṣas) and [excessive] activity.
2.3.18 | Regarding this, there is a verse:— The number, the causes, the forms, as well as the premonitory symptoms,
have been taught in the section on the etiology (nidāna) of abdominal tumors (gulma), along with a portion of their treatments.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Gulma," in the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Four:
2.4.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of Prameha (urinary disorders).
2.4.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
2.4.3 | There are twenty types of prameha caused by the provocation of the three doṣas, as well as other disorders that are innumerable.
We shall now explain in detail how the provocation of the three doṣas brings about these pramehas.

2.4.4 | Indeed, in this context, the specific variations regarding the presence or absence of the impairment of a disorder arise from the particularities of the etiological factors (nidāna), the morbid humors (doṣa), and the affected tissues (dūṣya).

For when these three specific factors—etiology and the rest—do not mutually reinforce one another, or when they are weakened by the passage of time, or even if they do reinforce one another, then the manifestation of the disorder does not occur; or it manifests after a long delay, or it becomes mild, or its symptoms are incomplete as previously described. Conversely, in the opposite case, the reverse occurs. Thus, the cause for the manifestation of the specific variations regarding the presence or absence of the impairment of all disorders has been explained.

2.4.5 | Now, these three specific causes lead to the rapid manifestation of pramehas caused by kapha; namely: the excessive and frequent consumption of fresh grains such as hāyanaka, yavaka, cīnaka, uddālaka, naiṣadha, itkaṭa, mukundaka, mahāvrīhi, pramodaka, and sugandhaka; likewise, the consumption of fresh, ghee-rich pulses such as hareṇu and māṣa; and the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals.

The consumption of vegetables, sesame paste, flour-based foods, milk-rice, kṛśara, vilepī, and products of sugarcane; the intake of substances consisting mostly of milk, fresh wine, curdled whey, liquid curd, and very sweet, fresh [foods]; the avoidance of cleansing and physical exercise; indulgence in sleep, reclining, and sitting; and whatever other regimen there may be that generates phlegm, fat, and urine—all this constitutes the specific etiology.
2.4.6 | Phlegm (śleṣman) is a specific humor characterized by its great liquidity.
2.4.7 | 1 Excessively accumulated fat, muscle, body fluids, semen, blood, muscle-fat, marrow, lymph, and plasma—counted as *ojas*—are the specific types of tissues that may become vitiated (*dūṣya*).

2.4.8 | When these three specific factors—the etiological factors (nidāna) and so forth—converge, phlegm (śleṣman) quickly undergoes provocation due to its initial predominance. Once provoked, it rapidly attains diffusion throughout the body because of the body's laxity. As it spreads through the body, it first enters into a state of mixture with the fat (medas), both because fat is abundant and loosely bound within the body and because its qualities are most similar to the qualities of phlegm. By mixing with the fat, it vitiates it, owing to the fat’s own state of morbid transformation.

That vitiated [dosha], joined with corrupted fat, comes into contact with the body's moisture and flesh due to the excessive increase of that moisture and flesh; through this corruption of the flesh, it produces carbuncles of putrid flesh such as the *śarāvikā* and *kacchapikā*, because of its departure from its natural state.

Furthermore, by vitiating the moisture of the body, it transforms it into urine; reaching the heavy openings of the urine-carrying channels—which originate in the groin and bladder and are affected by the moisture of fat—it becomes obstructed therein. Consequently, it produces urinary disorders (pramehas) in those channels, leading to their stabilization or incurability, because it has become both a natural and a morbid state.

2.4.9 | However, the bodily moisture (śarīrakleda), mixed with phlegm (śleṣman) and fat (medas), upon entering the bladder (mūtrāśaya) and undergoing the state of urine, becomes affected by these ten phlegmatic qualities (ślaiṣmikaguṇa) which are characterized by imbalance: namely, white, cold, solid, slimy, clear, unctuous, heavy, sweet, thick, and slow. Therein, according to whichever quality—whether one or more—it is predominantly affected, it acquires a corresponding secondary (gauṇa) specific name.

2.4.10 | These ten types of prameha, moreover, exist according to their specific names; namely: udakameha, ikṣuvālikārasameha, sāndrameha, sāndraprasādameha, śuklameha, śukrameha, śītameha, sikatāmeha, śanairmeha, and ālālameha.

2.4.11 | These ten types of prameha are curable, because they share the same qualities as the site of the disease (the bladder), because of the predominance of kapha, and because they require similar therapeutic measures.
2.4.12 | In this regard, there are verses for the purpose of specifically identifying the various types of *śleṣmaprameha* (phlegmatic urinary disorders):
2.4.13 | A person with udameha, due to the provocation of phlegm (śleṣman), passes urine that is clear, copious, white, cold, odorless, and resembles water.
2.4.14 | Due to the provocation of phlegm (śleṣman), one passes urine that is excessively sweet, cold, slightly slimy, turbid, and resembling the juice of raw sugarcane.
2.4.15 | That man whose urine becomes thick when left overnight in a vessel is called a *sāndramehin* due to the provocation of *kapha*.
2.4.16 | When a person's urine is partially concentrated and partially clear,
they are said to have *sāndraprasādameha* due to the provocation of *śleṣman*.
2.4.17 | That man who frequently voids urine that is white and resembles flour paste due to the provocation of *kapha* is called a *śuklamehin*.
2.4.18 | That man who frequently passes urine that has the appearance of semen or is mixed with semen is said to have śukrameha (semenuria) due to the provocation of kapha.
2.4.19 | That man who voids urine that is excessively sweet and cold in great quantity is said to have śītameha, arising from the provocation of kapha.
2.4.20 | That man who voids urine containing minute, solidified morbid humors (doṣas) resembling sand should be known as a *sikatāmehin*, caused by the provocation of phlegm (*śleṣman*).
2.4.21 | If a person voids urine very slowly and without force, with difficulty and gradually,
they are called a *śanairmehī* (one who voids slowly) due to the provocation of *śleṣman* (phlegm).
2.4.22 | One who passes urine that is slimy and resembles saliva bound by threads should be known as an *ālālamehin*, caused by the provocation of *śleṣman* (phlegm).
2.4.23 | Thus, these ten types of prameha, caused by the provocation of kapha, have been explained.

2.4.24 | Pitta quickly becomes aggravated in one who consumes hot, sour, salty, alkaline, pungent, and undigested food, as well as in one who indulges in excessive exposure to sharp sunlight, heat from fire, physical exertion, anger, and irregular diet; and in such a body, that aggravated pitta, following that same sequence, very swiftly brings about these six types of prameha.

2.4.25 | Furthermore, indeed, their specific names arise solely from the particular qualities of the *pitta* humor; namely: *kṣārameha*, *kālameha*, *nīlameha*, *lohitameha*, *māñjiṣṭhameha*, and *hāridrameha*.
2.4.26 | These [qualities] are endowed with the six qualities of pitta—alkaline, sour, salty, pungent, viscid, and hot—in the same manner as previously described.
2.4.27 | All of these are merely palliative, because the humors (doṣas) are mixed and located in the fat (medas), and because their treatments are mutually contradictory.
2.4.28 | Regarding this, there are verses for the purpose of specifically identifying the various types of Pitta-type urinary disorders (pittaprameha):
2.4.29 | A person suffering from kṣārameha passes urine that possesses the smell, color, taste, and touch of an alkaline substance (kṣāra) due to the provocation of pitta.
2.4.30 | One who passes urine that is constantly black like ink and hot due to the excessive provocation of pitta should be known as suffering from kālameha.
2.4.31 | The man who voids sour urine resembling the wing of a blue jay should be known as a *nīlamehin* due to the excessive provocation of *pitta*.
2.4.32 | That man who passes urine that is fishy-smelling, salty, and hot,
due to the excessive provocation of pitta, one should know as a raktamehin.
2.4.33 | One who passes urine resembling the water of madder (mañjiṣṭhā), which is extremely foul-smelling,
due to the severe provocation of pitta, should be known as a māñjiṣṭha-mehin (one suffering from madder-like urinary disorder).
2.4.34 | One who passes urine that resembles the water of turmeric and is pungent,
due to the severe provocation of pitta, should be known as a patient suffering from *dhāridra-meha*.
2.4.35 | Thus, these six types of prameha have been explained as being caused by the provocation of pitta.

2.4.36 | In one who consumes astringent, pungent, bitter, dry, light, and cold substances, and engages in sexual intercourse, physical exercise, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas, head-purgatives, excessive straining, suppression of natural urges, fasting, injury, exposure to the sun, agitation, grief, bloodletting, staying awake at night, and improper postures of the body—indeed, in such a person with such a constitution, the Vata quickly becomes aggravated.

2.4.37 | When that [dosha], thus aggravated in such a body, spreads and reaches the urine-carrying channels after taking up the muscle fat (vasā), it brings about vasāmeha; furthermore, when it draws the marrow (majjā) into the urinary bladder, it brings about majjameha.

When, however, the lymph (lasīkā), flowing into the bladder, follows the urine and causes it to trickle excessively due to the excessive abundance of lymph and the dispersing action of the wind (vāyu), it indeed produces an obstruction to the flow of urine; then, like an intoxicated elephant, one discharges urine incessantly and without urge, which is called *hastimeha*. Furthermore, the vital essence (*ojas*) is sweet by nature; when the wind, through dryness, mixes it with an astringent quality and carries it into the bladder, it then produces *madhumeha*.
2.4.38 | Physicians declare these four types of prameha to be incurable because of their extreme severity and because they require contradictory treatments.

2.4.39 | Of these as well, specific names arise according to their particular qualities, as follows: vasāmeha (fat-urine), majjameha (marrow-urine), hastimeha (elephant-urine), and madhumeha (honey-urine).
2.4.40 | Regarding this, there are verses for the purpose of specifically identifying the various types of *vātaprameha*:
2.4.41 | That man who frequently passes urine mixed with fat or resembling fat is said to have vasāmeha;
this condition is incurable due to the provocation of vāta.
2.4.42 | That man who repeatedly passes urine mixed with marrow along with the urine is said to have majjameha; this condition is incurable due to the provocation of Vāta.
2.4.43 | He who constantly and excessively discharges urine like an elephant in rut is said to have hastimeha; this condition, arising from the provocation of vāta, is incurable.
2.4.44 | That man who voids urine that is astringent-sweet, pale, and dry, one should recognize him as a case of Madhumeha (diabetes) due to the provocation of Vāta; it is incurable.
2.4.45 | Thus, these four types of prameha are explained as being caused by the provocation of vāta.
2.4.46 | Thus, the twenty types of prameha caused by the provocation of the three doṣas have been explained.

2.4.47 | Furthermore, when the three *doṣas* are aggravated and about to bring about *prameha*, they manifest these premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*); namely: the matting of the hair, sweetness in the mouth, numbness and burning sensations in the hands and feet, dryness of the mouth, palate, and throat, thirst, lassitude, impurity of the body, a coating on the bodily orifices, a general burning sensation and numbness in the limbs, the attraction of bees and ants toward the body and urine, urinary defects in the urine, a fishy odor from the body, excessive sleep, and constant drowsiness.

2.4.48 | Furthermore, the complications (upadrava) of those suffering from prameha are indeed thirst, diarrhea, fever, burning sensation, debility, anorexia, indigestion, putrid flesh, carbuncles (piḍaka), alaji, abscesses (vidradhi), and so forth; these arise as consequences of that [disease].
2.4.49 | Therein, one should treat the curable types of prameha by applying purification and palliative therapies as appropriate.
2.4.50 | And there are verses on this point:
Prameha quickly approaches one who is greedy for foods, who hates bathing and walking, just as a bird flies to its nest in a tree.
2.4.51 | Death, taking the form of prameha, swiftly departs after seizing one who is of dull energy, dull intellect, excessively unctuous, and a great eater.
2.4.52 | That man who consumes food that maintains the equilibrium of the bodily constituents and engages in various other activities enjoys happiness.
2.4.53 | Regarding this, the Ślokas state: The cause of specific diseases and the etiology of the pramehas,
as well as the combination of the doṣas and dhātus and their various manifestations, [are described here].
2.4.54 | Since ten types of prameha are caused by kapha and six are born from pitta,
and since the powerful vāyu likewise produces four types of prameha.
2.4.55 | In this etiology of prameha, the distinctions between curable and incurable cases, the premonitory symptoms, the complications, and the outline of the treatment have been described.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Classification of Prameha," in the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Five:
2.5.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of skin diseases (Kuṣṭhanidāna).
2.5.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
2.5.3 | Seven substances constitute the basis for the various types of *kuṣṭha* when they undergo pathological transformation (*vikṛti*).

They are as follows: the three *doṣas*—vāta, pitta, and śleṣman—which are transformed through provocation; and the four bodily constituents (*dūṣya*) that serve as the substrates—skin, muscle, blood, and fat—which are transformed by the injury caused by the *doṣas*.
This sevenfold combination of the seven elements is the origin of the *kuṣṭhas*; arising from this source, they afflict the body exclusively.

2.5.4 | There is no leprosy whatsoever that is caused by the provocation of only a single *doṣa*; rather, even among leprosies of identical constitution (*prakṛti*), there exists a distinction in treatment based on the specific proportions of the *doṣas*, their variations, their persistence, and their locations, as well as differences in pain, color, shape, manifestation, and name.
It may be of seven types, eighteen types, or indeed an innumerable number of types.
For the *doṣas*, when differentiated by various combinations, produce differentiated disorders, except in the case of those conditions that are incurable.
Having observed that an enumeration of the varieties and transformations of these [skin diseases] would lead to excessive prolixity, we shall set forth only the seven specific types of kuṣṭha.

2.5.5 | Here, when the three [doshas], vāta and the others, are aggravated and corrupt the four [tissues] beginning with the skin (tvak), if vāta is predominant, *kapālakuṣṭha* arises; in pitta, *audumbara*; in śleṣman, *maṇḍalakuṣṭha*; in vāta and pitta, *ṛṣyajihva*; in pitta and śleṣman, *puṇḍarīka*; in śleṣman and māruta, *sidhmakuṣṭha*; and when all the doṣas are increased, *kākaṇaka* arises. Thus, this sevenfold classification of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) occurs.
And this very [pradhāna], when its constituent nature is further analyzed in greater and greater detail, arrives at an even more numerous enumeration of its various modifications.

2.5.6 | Herein, we shall briefly set forth the etiology of all types of kuṣṭha: for one who partakes of cold and hot things in an irregular sequence; likewise, for one who alternates between over-nutrition and under-nutrition, and between various types of food; for one who constantly and excessively consumes honey, molasses, fish, *lakucha*, radish, and *kākamācī* while suffering from indigestion; for one who eats *cilicima* with milk; and for one whose diet consists primarily of *hāyanaka*, *yavaka*, *cīnaka*, *uddālaka*, and *koradūṣa* grains.

When one consumes milk, curd, buttermilk, jujube, horse-gram, black gram, linseed, and safflower oil; or when one who is excessively satiated by these very items indulges in sexual intercourse, physical exercise, and heat; or when one afflicted by fear, fatigue, and heat suddenly enters cold water; or when one consumes burning foods without first eliminating the partially digested food (vidagdha); or when one suppresses vomiting; or when one over-indulges in unctuous substances—the three doshas simultaneously reach a state of provocation.

The four [tissues] beginning with the skin become flaccid; when they have become flaccid, the aggravated doshas, having reached their location and remaining there, vitiate those very same tissues—skin and the rest—and bring about the various types of leprosy (kuṣṭha).

2.5.7 | Their premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) are as follows: absence of perspiration, excessive perspiration, roughness, excessive smoothness, discoloration, itching, pricking pain, numbness, burning sensation, horripilation, stiffness, heat, heaviness, swelling, the creeping of ants [over the body], frequent accumulation of secretions in the bodily orifices, excessive pain in cases of ripening, burns, bites, fractures, wounds, or slips, and the corruption and non-healing of even minor ulcers.

2.5.8(1) Immediately thereafter, the various types of *kuṣṭha* manifest; regarding them, this is the specific knowledge of their sensations, colors, shapes, origins, and characteristics: namely, one should recognize *kapālakuṣṭha* as being dry, reddish, rough, irregularly spread, with coarse margins, thin, with slightly raised surfaces, numb as if asleep, covered with bristling hair, characterized by frequent pricking pain (*nistoda*), with little itching, burning, or discharge of pus and serous fluid, appearing quickly and arising suddenly, breaking rapidly, infested with small organisms, and having the color of blackish-red potsherds.

2.5.8(2) One should recognize *audumbara* kuṣṭha as being copper-colored, covered with copper-hued rows of hair, thick, and filled with abundant and copious pus, blood, and lymph; it is characterized by itching, moisture, sloughing, burning, and suppuration; it spreads rapidly, arises suddenly, and breaks open; it is accompanied by a burning sensation and worms, and has the color of a ripe *udumbara* fruit.

2.5.8(3) One should recognize Maṇḍala-kuṣṭha as being unctuous, heavy, elevated, smooth, firm, with yellowish margins, appearing white and red, marked by rows of white hair, discharging a profuse, thick, white, and slimy secretion, accompanied by much moisture, itching, and worms, characterized by restricted movement, arising, and breaking open, and circular in shape.

2.5.8(4) One should recognize those [skin diseases] as *ṛṣyajihva* which have rough surfaces, are reddish in color, dark-brown externally and internally, and appear blue, yellow, or coppery; which arise with rapid onset and subsidence; which have little itching, discharge, or worms; which abound in burning, tearing, pricking, and suppuration; which have pain comparable to that of being struck by a thorn; which are elevated in the center and thin at the edges; which are covered with hard pustules; and which are long and circular, shaped like the tongue of a Rishi.

2.5.8(5) One should recognize *puṇḍarīka* ulcers as those which have a white and red appearance, are red at their margins, are covered with red streaks and veins, are elevated, contain abundant and thick blood, pus, and lymph, are accompanied by itching, worms, burning, and suppuration, are characterized by rapid onset and progression, and are prone to bursting; they resemble the petals of a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).

2.5.8(6) One should recognize *sidhma* kuṣṭha as follows: it is rough and reddish-brown, with the outer skin shattered while the interior remains smooth; it appears white and red, is numerous, associated with little pain, little itching, burning, pus, or serous discharge (*lasīkā*), arises easily, contains few fissures or worms, and resembles the flower of the *alābu* gourd. One should recognize *kākaṇa* kuṣṭha as being initially the color of the *kākaṇantikā* fruit, but subsequently endowed with all the symptoms of every type of kuṣṭha. Due to the emergence of all the symptoms of every kuṣṭha through a most malignant process, it possesses many colors and is known as *kākaṇa*.
These two types are incurable, whereas the others are curable.
2.5.9 | In that regard, what is incurable does not transcend its state of incurability; however, some curable conditions may at times transcend their curability due to improper conduct.
For the six curable types, excluding the *kākaṇaka*, become incurable if they are left untreated or if they are overwhelmed by the *doṣas* through improper conduct.

2.5.10 | For even in those ulcers that are being treated, if they are neglected, worms born from the skin, flesh, blood, lymph, slough, moisture, and sweat emerge. As these worms consume the skin and other tissues, the *doṣas* further vitiate them, producing the following complications individually: therein, *vāta* produces a dusky-red or reddish-brown color, roughness, as well as dryness, pain, emaciation, pricking, trembling, horripilation, contraction, exhaustion, stiffness, numbness, piercing pain, and breaking pain; *pitta* produces burning, sweating, moisture, sloughing, discharge, suppuration, and redness.

Phlegm, however, produces whiteness, coldness, itching, stability, heaviness, swelling, unctuousness, and coating; whereas worms consume the four [tissues] beginning with the skin, as well as the vessels, the ligaments, and even the cartilages.

2.5.11 | Furthermore, in this very stage, complications afflict the leper; namely—excessive discharge, splitting pain in the limbs, falling off of the members and parts of the body, thirst, fever, diarrhea, burning sensation, debility, anorexia, and indigestion. One should recognize such a case as incurable.
2.5.12 | And there are verses on this point: "The man who, thinking 'this is curable,' previously neglects his disease, realizes he is as good as dead only after some time has passed."
2.5.13 | However, he who applies medicine properly before diseases arise, or while they are still in their early stages, enjoys happiness for a long time.
2.5.14 | Just as a young tree is cut with little effort, yet that very same tree when it has grown excessively large is cut only with great exertion; so it is here.
2.5.15 | In this very way, a disorder (vikāra) that is young is easily cured;
one that has increased is cured with difficulty, or it may even become incurable.
2.5.16 | Regarding this, there is a verse: The number, the substances, the doshas, the causes, the premonitory symptoms,
the clinical forms, and the complications of the skin diseases (kuṣṭha) have been described individually in the Kauṣṭhika chapter.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Kuṣṭha," in the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Six:
2.6.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of consumption (śoṣa).
2.6.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
2.6.3 | In this context, there are indeed four causes of wasting (śoṣa); namely: violence, suppression [of natural urges], depletion, and irregular eating.

2.6.4 | Regarding that which was stated—that violence (*sāhasa*) is the primary cause of consumption (*śoṣa*)—we shall now explain it in detail: when a man, being weak, engages in conflict with one who is strong; or exerts himself with an excessively heavy bow; or speaks excessively; or carries an excessive load; or swims for too great a distance in water; or excessively indulges in massage or stamping; or runs swiftly along a very long road; or is struck.
Or if one undertakes some other such activity, or an excessive amount of strenuous exertion, the chest is injured by that excessive action.
Vāyu then afflicts the injury in the chest;
remaining there, it seizes the phlegm located in the chest, vitiates the bile, and moves upward, downward, and across.

That portion of it which enters the joints of the body causes yawning, aching of the limbs, and fever to arise in him; that which reaches the stomach causes diseases of the chest and loss of appetite; that which arrives at the throat causes the throat to become hoarse and the voice to fail; that which follows the channels carrying the vital breath (prāṇa) causes dyspnea and catarrh; and that which remains in the head causes affliction of the head.

Then, due to the sudden exertion, the irregular movement of the *vāyu*, and the upward displacement of the throat, a persistent cough arises in him. From this persistence of coughing, blood is expectorated when the chest is wounded; and from the flow of blood, weakness is produced in him. Thus, these complications arising from rashness afflict the reckless man. Consequently, afflicted by these wasting complications, he gradually withers away.

Therefore, a wise person, having examined his own strength, should undertake to perform actions that are commensurate with it; for the body is the vessel of strength, and the person has the body as his foundation.
2.6.5 | And there is a verse on this point:
One should avoid rash action while protecting one's own life;
for it is by living that a person enjoys the desired fruit of his actions.

2.6.6 | We shall now provide a detailed explanation of what was stated—that suppression is the cause of consumption (śoṣa): When a person, having entered the presence of a king, a master, or at the feet of a teacher; or having entered a gambling hall, or another assembly of the virtuous, or the midst of women; or while traveling in various kinds of vehicles—suppresses the urges of flatus, urine, and feces that have arisen out of fear, addiction, modesty, or shame, then, due to that suppression, his *vāyu* (bodily wind) becomes aggravated.

That aggravated [wind], having stirred up the *pitta* and *kapha*, circulates upwards, downwards, and transversely; then, entering specific parts of the body in particular proportions as previously described, it produces pain, breaks up the feces, or dries them up, causes intense pain in the flanks, crushes the shoulders, strikes the throat and chest, afflicts the head, and produces cough, dyspnea, fever, hoarseness of voice, and catarrh.
Thereupon, afflicted by these complications of wasting, he gradually withers away.

Therefore, a wise person should especially strive for those matters pertaining to his own body that ensure its security and well-being; for the body is his foundation, and it is upon the foundation of the body that a person stands.
2.6.7 | And there is a verse on this point: Having abandoned everything else, one should preserve the body;
for in its absence, there is the total non-existence of all things for embodied beings.

2.6.(1) We shall now provide a detailed explanation of what was stated—that wasting (kṣaya) is the primary seat of consumption (śoṣa): When a person’s heart is overwhelmed by excessive grief and anxiety, or is possessed by envy, longing, fear, anger, and the like; or when, being emaciated, he indulges in dry food and drink; or when, being of a weak constitution, he abstains from food or eats very little—then the *rasa* (nutritive essence) residing in his heart undergoes depletion.
Due to that depletion, he suffers from consumption, and if no remedy is applied, he becomes afflicted by *yakṣman* (wasting disease) in the form that will be described hereafter.
2.6.8 | When a man, out of excessive passion, being intensely attached, begins an excessive indulgence with women, his semen undergoes depletion due to that excessive indulgence.

Furthermore, even if his semen reaches exhaustion, if his mind does not turn away from women, then for him—whose resolve is excessively intense and who engages in sexual intercourse—the semen does not flow because it has been utterly depleted. Consequently, as he exerts his body, the vital air (vāyu) enters the blood-carrying channels; from those channels it displaces the blood. Due to that depletion of semen, blood then flows out through his seminal passage, characterized by signs following the nature of wind.
Then, due to the depletion of semen and the discharge of blood, his joints become lax, dryness arises, the body further succumbs to weakness, and the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated.

That aggravated wind, as if enraged, coursing through the powerless body, excites the phlegm and bile and dries up the flesh and blood; it displaces the phlegm and bile, causes pain in the flanks, crushes the shoulders, and agitates the throat; having afflicted the head with phlegm, it fills it with phlegm; and by pressing upon the joints, it produces aching of the limbs, loss of appetite, and indigestion; and due to the provocation of bile and phlegm and because it moves in a contrary direction, the wind causes fever, cough, dyspnea, and hoarseness of voice.

It also produces catarrh; due to the resulting chronic cough, when the chest is wounded, he spits blood, and from the loss of blood, weakness arises in him. Then, afflicted by these wasting complications, he gradually withers away.
Therefore, a wise man, desiring to protect his own body, should protect his semen;
for this is the ultimate fruition of food.
2.6.9 | And there is a verse on this point: Semen is the supreme abode of one's food;
it must be protected by oneself, for its depletion brings about many diseases or even death.

2.6.10 | Regarding what was stated—that irregular eating is a cause of emaciation—we shall now explain it in detail: when a person consumes drinks, foods, edibles, and linctuses that are irregular in terms of their nature (*prakṛti*), processing (*karaṇa*), combination (*saṃyoga*), quantity (*rāśi*), location (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), application (*upayoga*), preparation (*saṃsthā*), and wholesomeness (*upaśaya*), then, because of those factors, his *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* fall into a state of imbalance (*vaiṣamya*).

When those morbid humors (doṣas), having followed the body, block the openings of the channels (srotas) and remain there, then whatever food a person consumes is produced almost entirely as urine and feces, and not as other bodily constituents (dhātus). He subsists by being supported by feces; therefore, for one who is wasting away, the feces must be specifically protected, as must those of others who are excessively emaciated and weak. As he fails to gain nourishment, the humors accumulated by his irregular diet, each manifesting its own complications, further desiccate the body.

In this condition, Vāta produces colic, body ache, hoarseness of the throat, pain in the sides, aching of the shoulders, loss of voice, and coryza; Pitta produces fever, diarrhea, and internal burning; while Kapha produces coryza, heaviness of the head, anorexia, and cough. Due to the persistence of this cough, when the chest is injured, he spits out blood, and from the loss of blood, weakness arises in him.
Thus, these three Doshas, accumulated through irregular diet, bring about Rājayakṣman (consumption).
Afflicted by those debilitating complications, he gradually withers away.

Therefore, a wise person should consume food that is not irregular, taking into account its natural properties, processing, combination, quantity, place, time, application, consistency, and post-digestive effect.
2.6.11 | And there is a verse on this point:
A wise person, seeing many painful diseases arising from irregular eating, should eat wholesome food, eat in moderation, eat at the proper time, and keep the senses under control.
2.6.12 | When these four bases of wasting are indulged in, vāta, pitta, and śleṣman undergo provocation. These provoked humors dry up the body with various complications.

Physicians designate this condition as *rājayakṣmā* because it is the most difficult of all diseases to cure; or else, because it formerly belonged to the blessed Soma, the king of the stars (*uḍurāja*), it is called *rājayakṣmā*.

2.6.13 | Its premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) are as follows: catarrh, frequent sneezing, excessive salivation of phlegm, sweetness in the mouth, lack of desire for food, exhaustion at mealtime, finding fault with things that are not defective or have only slight defects—such as the vessel, water, rice, soup, cakes, side dishes, or the server—and nausea after eating, as well as occasional vomiting of food and swelling of the mouth and feet.

Excessive gazing at his own hands; an extreme whiteness appearing in his eyes; a desire to know the measurements of his arms; a longing for women; cruelty; and a loathsome appearance on his body. Furthermore, in dreams, there is the frequent sight of waterless reservoirs, empty villages, towns, market-towns, and provinces; and of forests that are withered, burnt, or broken; as well as contact with, climbing upon, or traveling in vehicles drawn by lizards, peacocks, monkeys, parrots, snakes, crows, owls, and the like.
Mounting upon camels, donkeys, and boars, as well as climbing heaps of hair, bones, ashes, husks, and charcoal—these are the prodromal symptoms of consumption.

2.6.14 | Hereafter, there are eleven symptoms of this [disease], namely: fullness of the head, cough, dyspnea, hoarseness of voice, vomiting of phlegm, spitting of blood, pain in the sides, aching of the shoulders, fever, diarrhea, and loss of appetite.

2.6.15 | In that regard, one whose strength, muscle, and blood are not yet depleted, who is strong, and in whom no fatal signs (ariṣṭa) have appeared, should be known as curable even if afflicted by all the symptoms of wasting (śoṣa).

For a strong and well-nourished person, due to their capacity to withstand the force of both the disease and the medicine, should be considered as having few symptoms despite actually having very many symptoms.

2.6.16 | However, one should recognize that a weak patient—whose strength, muscle, and blood are excessively depleted—may exhibit many symptoms even when the signs [of approaching death] are few, or may exhibit signs of death even though no fatal prognostic signs (ariṣṭa) have yet appeared; this is due to his inability to withstand the force of the disease or the medicinal treatment. Such a patient should be abandoned, for fatal signs manifest in an instant, and the appearance of such fatal signs occurs without any apparent cause.
2.6.17 | Regarding this, there is a verse: He who understands the etiology, the symptoms, and the premonitory signs of wasting (śoṣa) in their true nature, he is worthy to attend upon the king.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Wasting," in the Section on Diagnosis of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Seven:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of insanity (unmāda).
2.7.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
2.7.3 | Indeed, there are five types of insanity here; namely: those caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, their combination (sannipāta), and exogenous factors (āgantu).

2.7.4 | In that regard, four types of persons for whom these [conditions] arise quickly due to the influence of the *doṣas* are as follows: those who are timid, those of afflicted temperament, those whose *doṣas* are aggravated, those who consume various kinds of food that are impure, corrupted, contaminated, or unsuitable according to an irregular method of consumption, those who practice medical treatment (*tantra*) improperly, those who engage in other irregular physical activities, those whose bodies are excessively depleted, those who are agitated by the onset of disease, and those whose minds are impaired.

Or, when the mind is afflicted by desire, anger, greed, joy, fear, delusion, exhaustion, grief, anxiety, agitation, and the like; or when it is repeatedly struck by these blows, and while the mind is impaired and the intellect is shaken, the provoked humors (doṣas) arise in force, enter the heart, obstruct the channels that carry the mind, and produce insanity.
2.7.5 | Furthermore, one should recognize insanity (unmāda) as a derangement of the mind, intellect, perception, knowledge, memory, devotion, character, activity, and conduct.

2.7.6 | These are its premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa), namely: emptiness of the head, agitation of the eyes, ringing in the ears, excessive respiration, salivation from the mouth, lack of desire for food, anorexia, indigestion, cardiac oppression, and meditation, fatigue, delusion, and anxiety at inappropriate times; constant horripilation, frequent fever, insanity of mind, 1) urticaria, the production of symptoms resembling facial paralysis (ardita) by the disease, and frequent visions in dreams.

The mounting of a sesame-press wheel by those who are deluded, agitated, unstable, and of ignoble form; being churned by whirlwinds and submerged in turbid waters in a whirlpool; and the withdrawal of the eyes—these are the premonitory symptoms of insanity caused by physical humors (*doṣa*).

2.7.7(1) Immediately following that, there is the manifestation of insanity. In this regard, the specific knowledge of insanity is as follows: constant wandering about; sudden twitching and tossing of the eyes, eyebrows, lips, jaws, hands, feet, and limbs; the continuous utterance of incoherent speech; frothing at the mouth; frequent smiling, laughing, dancing, singing, and playing musical instruments out of place; imitating the sounds of the lute, flute, conch, cymbals, and clapping without reason; mounting vehicles that are not vehicles; and adorning oneself with objects that are not ornaments.

Greed for foods not yet obtained, contempt for those already obtained, intense envy, emaciation, harshness, protruding reddened eyes, and lack of relief from factors that aggravate vāta—these are the symptoms of insanity caused by vāta.

2.7.7(2) Impatience, anger, and agitation out of place; striking oneself or others with weapons, clods of earth, whips, sticks, or fists; charging forward; a craving for shade, cold water, and food; excessive feverishness; coppery, green, or yellowish-red, bloodshot eyes; and lack of relief from things that aggravate pitta while finding relief from their opposites—these are the signs of insanity caused by pitta.

2.7.7(3) Staying in one place, silence, walking about only slightly, the flowing of saliva and nasal mucus, lack of desire for food, longing for solitude, loathsomeness, aversion to cleanliness, constant sleepiness, swelling of the face, eyes that are white, fixed, and smeared with impurities, and aggravation by factors contrary to those that pacify *kapha*—these are the symptoms of *śleṣman* (phlegm) insanity. When there is a combination of the symptoms of all three *doṣas*, one should recognize it as *sānnipātika* (combined); the experts declare that to be incurable.

2.7.8 | The therapeutic measures for the three types of curable diseases are as follows: oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema, unctuous enema, pacification, nasal therapy, medicated smoke, fumigation, collyrium, eye-drop, insufflation, blowing into the nose, massage, external application, affusion, anointing, beating, binding, confinement, frightening, startling, causing forgetfulness, depletion, and venesection; as well as the administration of diet according to the specific requirements and by proper means, and whatever other medicine may be necessary that is contrary to the etiological factors. These should also be employed.
2.7.9 | And there is a verse on this point: An excellent physician should cure curable insanity arising from the humors by means of this prescribed procedure that has been described.
2.7.10 | That insanity which is accompanied by specific distinctions in its etiology, prodromal signs, clinical symptoms, pain, and therapeutic suitability is called exogenous (*āgantuka*).
Some, however, maintain that its cause is improper past action (*karma*).
But the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya holds that its cause is solely the transgression of wisdom (*prajñāparādha*).

Indeed, due to a transgression of wisdom, he disregards the gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, gurus, elders, siddhas, teachers, and those worthy of worship, and commits harmful acts or undertakes some other such improper deed; then the gods and others, striking down that one who is already destroyed by himself, render him insane.

2.7.11 | In that regard, for one afflicted by adventitious insanity caused by the provocation of gods and other beings, these premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) arise: namely, a fondness for harming gods, cows, Brahmins, and ascetics; irritability; cruelty of intent; restlessness; a decline in vital essence (ojas), complexion, luster, strength, and the body; and, in dreams, being threatened or driven away by gods and other such beings. Immediately following this, the full manifestation of insanity occurs.

2.7.12 | In this regard, the specific modes of onset for these spirits who cause insanity and intend to produce it are as follows: the gods produce insanity by their mere glance; the teachers, elders, perfected ones (siddhas), and great seers (maharṣis) by their curses; the ancestors (pitṛs) by their appearance; the Gandharvas by their touch; the Yakṣas by their possession; the Rākṣasas by making one smell their own odor; and the Piśācas by mounting [the person] and driving them about.

2.7.13 | These are its symptoms, namely: excessive self-confidence, strength, energy, manliness, prowess, grasping, retention, recollection, knowledge, speech, and discernment; and the onset of insanity is not restricted to a specific time.

2.7.14 | Indeed, even among gods, sages, ancestors, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, or among teachers, elders, and perfected beings (siddhas), there are men who are to be approached during these intervals for the purpose of inducing madness.

Namely: at the commencement of an evil deed; or at the time of the ripening of a previously committed karma; or while dwelling alone in an empty house or standing at a crossroads; or during the twilight hours in a state of impurity; or during the junctions of the lunar phases (*parvan*) while engaged in sexual intercourse; or by approaching a woman in her menses; or when the practice of recitation, offerings, auspicious rites, or fire-oblations is defective; or upon the violation of restrictive observances (*niyama*), vows (*vrata*), or celibacy (*brahmacarya*); or in a great battle; or during the destruction of a country, a family, or a city; or when a great planetary affliction approaches.

Or during a woman’s time of childbirth; or upon contact with various beings that are inauspicious or impure; or during vomiting, purging, or the flow of blood; or when one is impure or lacks self-restraint yet approaches a *caitya* or a temple of a deity; or when one has consumed the remnants of meat, honey, sesame, molasses, or liquor; or when one is naked; or at night when one approaches a city, a market town, a crossroads, a grove, a cemetery, or a place of execution; or when one insults Brahmins, teachers, gods, ascetics, or those worthy of worship; or when one transgresses the proclamation of Dharma; or when one undertakes any other act that is not praised—these are explained as the times of affliction.

2.7.15 | Indeed, there are three purposes for spirits (bhūtas) in causing insanity: namely, violence (hiṃsā), pleasure (rati), and worship (abhyarcana). One should recognize these specific purposes through the specific characteristics of the patient's behavior during the state of madness. Among them, one who is driven insane by a spirit seeking violence enters fire, drowns in water, falls from a height or into a pit, strikes himself with weapons, whips, wood, clods of earth, or his own fists, or undertakes some other act intended to take his own life; such a case should be known as incurable. However, the other two types are curable.

2.7.16 | Their means of accomplishment are: mantras, medicinal herbs, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, religious observances, vows, expiatory rites, fasting, benedictions, prostrations, pilgrimage, and so forth.
2.7.17 | Thus, these five types of insanity have been explained.

2.7.18 | Indeed, when these [diseases] are classified according to the specific nature of the endogenous (nija) and exogenous (āgantu) factors, and according to the distinction between those that are curable and those that are incurable, although there are five types, they become only two.
And these two sometimes bind one another due to the combination of the aforementioned causes.
In their case, the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) are exclusively combined, and the clinical signs (liṅga) are likewise exclusively combined.

In that regard, one should know that an incurable [disease] is characterized by a combination with what is incurable, as well as a combination with both the curable and the incurable; however, a curable [disease] is characterized by a combination with what is curable.
One should know that its treatment consists precisely in a combination with the means of treatment.
2.7.19 | And there are verses on this point:
Neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas,
nor any others can afflict a man who is himself free from affliction.
2.7.20 | But for those who follow him while he is suffering due to his own karma, that suffering is not caused by them; for there is no such thing as having already accomplished what was to be done.
2.7.21 | When a disease arises from one's own past actions due to an error of judgment,
a wise person should not blame the gods, nor the ancestors, nor even the Rākṣasas.
2.7.22 | One should consider oneself alone as the agent of pleasure and pain;
therefore, one should follow the path that leads to the highest good and not tremble.
2.7.23 | Reverence toward the gods and others, the service of those who are beneficial,
and the opposition to them— all this depends upon the self.

2.7.24 | Regarding this, there is a verse:— The number, the cause, the premonitory symptoms, the clinical characteristics, the curability or otherwise, and the summary of treatment for insanity have been explained in this etiological chapter.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Insanity," in the Section on Diagnosis of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Eight:
2.8.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnosis of epilepsy (apasmāra).
2.8.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
2.8.3 | Indeed, in this regard, there are four types of epilepsy (apasmāra), caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, and their combination (sannipāta).

2.8.4 | These [diseases] quickly manifest in such living beings; namely, in those whose consciousness is afflicted by *rajas* and *tamas*, whose humors (*doṣas*) are agitated and excessively deranged, who consume various kinds of impure foods that are contaminated and corrupted, who employ methods of consumption characterized by irregularity, who practice unwholesome medical procedures (*tantra-prayoga*), who perform other irregular bodily activities, or whose humors are provoked due to excessive depletion.

When the internal self (*antarātman*) has its consciousness afflicted by the provoked *rajas* and *tamas*, they take up residence above the heart—the most excellent seat—and likewise above the seats of the senses.

Remaining there, when they suddenly fill the heart and the seats of the senses with desire, anger, fear, greed, delusion, joy, grief, anxiety, agitation, and so forth, then the living being suffers from epilepsy (*apasmāra*).

2.8.5 | Furthermore, they describe epilepsy (apasmāra) as a state characterized by the collapse of memory, intellect, and mental essence, involving loathsome movements and an intermittent entry into darkness.

2.8.6 | These are its premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa), namely: constant knitting of the eyebrows, deformity of the eyes, hearing sounds that do not exist, excessive flow of saliva and nasal mucus, lack of desire for food, anorexia, indigestion, oppression of the heart, rumbling in the abdomen, weakness, splitting pain in the bones, aching of the limbs, delusion, seeing darkness, fainting, and frequent giddiness; and in dreams, intoxication, dancing, piercing, pricking, trembling, falling, and so forth.
2.8.7 | Immediately after that, the manifestation of apasmāra (epilepsy) itself occurs.

2.8.8(1) | In this regard, the following is the specific diagnostic knowledge of apasmāra (epilepsy): one should recognize that a person suffers from apasmāra due to vāta when they experience frequent seizures, regain consciousness in an instant, have swollen eyes, speak incoherently, foam at the mouth, have an excessively distended neck, a twisted head, unevenly bent fingers, unsteady hands and feet, and reddish, harsh, or dark-brown nails, eyes, face, and skin; and who perceives unstable, flickering, harsh, and rough forms, finds relief through vāta-aggravating factors, and lacks relief through their opposites.

2.8.8(2) One should recognize epilepsy caused by *pitta* as characterized by frequent seizures, regaining consciousness in an instant, moaning, striking the ground, having green, yellow, copper-colored nails, eyes, face, and skin, exhibiting a fierce, terrifying, and blazing form smeared with blood, being aggravated by *pitta*-inducing factors, and relieved by their opposites.

2.8.8(3) One should recognize that a person is suffering from epilepsy due to *kapha* (phlegm) if they experience seizures after a long interval, regain consciousness after a long time, fall down, exhibit movements that are not excessively distorted, vomit saliva, have white nails, eyes, face, and skin, perceive white, heavy, and unctuous forms, find relief through *kapha*-aggravating factors (*anupaśaya*), and find no relief through their opposites.

2.8.8(4) One should recognize apasmāra characterized by all the symptoms combined as being of the sannipātika type; they declare that to be incurable. Thus, the four types of apasmāra have been explained.

2.8.9 | An exogenous (āgantuka) complication may indeed sometimes occur among these; we shall explain that in the subsequent section. Its specific diagnosis consists of an excess of symptoms as previously described, along with some signs that do not correspond to the symptoms of the [doshas].

2.8.10 | For those suffering from epilepsy, sharp purificatory and pacifying therapies should be administered according to the specific dosha involved; furthermore, when there is an association with extrinsic factors, mantra and other such measures should be employed.

2.8.11 | Indeed, during that destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, as embodied beings fled in various directions, the agitation of their bodies through running toward, fleeing from, rushing, swimming, leaping, and other such movements gave rise to abdominal tumors (gulma). From the consumption of the sacrificial oblation (havis), urinary disorders (prameha) and skin diseases (kuṣṭha) arose; from fear, terror, and grief, insanity (unmāda); from contact with various impure spirits, epilepsy (apasmāra); fever (jvara), moreover, originated from the forehead of Maheśvara; from his intense heat, hemorrhagic disease (raktapitta); and from excessive sexual indulgence by the King of Stars (the Moon), pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) arose.
2.8.12 | And there are verses on this point:
Epilepsy indeed arises from vāta, from pitta, and from kapha;
the fourth type, caused by the combination of all three (sannipāta), is likewise incurable.
2.8.13 | Wise physicians, being composed, bring to cure those diseases that are curable,
by means of strong purificatory therapies and also by appropriate palliative measures as required.
2.8.14 | When there is a concomitant association with an exogenous factor (āgantu) for that which is caused by the humors (doṣa),
then those learned in medicine declare it to be a common (sādhāraṇa) treatment.
2.8.15 | A physician who knows the specific nature of all diseases and is expert in all medicinal remedies destroys all ailments and does not fall into delusion.
2.8.16 | Thus has this excellent Section on Etiology (Nidānasthāna) been explained in its entirety.
A disease that acts as the cause of another disease is also observed.
2.8.17 | For example: from the heat of fever, *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorder) is provoked;
from *raktapitta*, fever arises; and from both of these, consumption (*śoṣa*) is also produced.
2.8.18 | From the enlargement of the spleen arises abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara), and from abdominal enlargement, swelling;
from hemorrhoids (arśas) arises painful abdominal enlargement, and also gulma is produced.
2.8.19 | Cough arises from catarrh, and from cough, consumption (kṣaya) is produced.
Consumption is also observed to be the cause of the disease of wasting (śoṣa).
2.8.20 | Those [factors] were previously described as purely diseases; subsequently, they are observed to act as causes, to act for both purposes, and likewise to act for a single purpose.
2.8.21 | For some disease, having become the cause of another disease, subsides;
yet another does not subside, even though it performs the function of a cause.
2.8.22 | Thus, the most difficult complications of diseases are seen among men,
due to the impurity of medical treatment as well as from their mutual interaction.
2.8.23 | A therapeutic application that pacifies one disease while provoking another is not pure;
however, that which is pure pacifies without causing provocation.
2.8.24 | Indeed, a single cause may produce many effects, and likewise, a single effect may arise from a single cause alone;
a single disease may have multiple causes, and many diseases may also have many causes.
2.8.25 | Fever, vertigo, delirium, and other such symptoms are seen to arise from dry causes;
moreover, fever alone may also be produced by dryness alone.
2.8.26 | A single fever may arise from many causes, such as dryness (rūkṣa) and so forth;
indeed, fevers and other diseases originate from such factors as dryness.
2.8.27 | A single sign may be observed for many [diseases], and likewise for a single disease;
there may be many signs for a single disease, and there may also be many signs for many diseases.
2.8.28 | Fever is considered the single characteristic sign of those diseases rooted in irregular onset;
and for fever alone, the single sign is said to be a generalized heat.
2.8.29 | Fever alone is said to have its roots in irregular onset;
by these symptoms, diseases such as fever, dyspnea, hiccup, and others are characterized.
2.8.30 | Just as one pacification is observed for many [diseases], so too is it observed for a single disease;
furthermore, there may be many pacifications for a single disease, and indeed many for many diseases.
2.8.31 | Fasting is the pacification for diseases arising from the stomach;
indeed, fasting alone is said to be the sole pacifier of fever.
2.8.32 | Likewise, light meals and similar measures are the pacifiers for fever alone;
these very same measures are also the pacifiers for fever, dyspnea, hiccup, and other such conditions.
2.8.33 | That which is easily curable (sukhasādhya) is accomplished by easy means in a short time;
however, that which is difficult to cure (kṛcchrasādhya) is accomplished with great effort over a long period.
2.8.34 | A disease designated as "palliable" (yāpya) does not reach total destruction;
however, the other type, the "incurable" (asādhya), transcends all therapeutic measures and must be rejected.
2.8.35 | An incurable disease may become curable, while a curable one may turn into an incurable one;
diseases undergo such changes in their state due to improper treatment or through destiny.

2.8.36 | A wise physician should observe the states of increase, stability, and decrease of diseases, as well as even the most subtle conditions of the body, the digestive fire, strength, and the mind.
2.8.37 | For having repeatedly understood the specific stages of the disease, the wise physician attains the fourfold excellence in each respective stage.
2.8.38 | Generally, the doshas that have moved horizontally afflict the patients for a long time;
therefore, one who understands the strength of the body and the digestive fire should not perform treatment with haste in these cases.
2.8.39 | One should either exhaust them through therapeutic applications or bring them comfortably into the digestive tract;
once the wise physician has ascertained that they have reached the digestive tract, he should eliminate them according to their proximity.

2.8.40 | Those which have been described in the summary as the signs of disease for the purpose of knowledge are, at that very time, the diseases themselves; they are not merely the signs of the ailments.
2.8.41 | Both the transformation and its source—this entire duality in brief—is subject to the power of a cause; in the absence of that cause, it does not continue.

2.8.42 | Regarding this, there are these verses: The causes, the premonitory symptoms, the symptoms, the therapeutic suitability, the pathogenesis, and first the origin [of diseases], along with a mere outline of their treatment.
2.8.43 | Furthermore, the curability of the eight disorders beginning with fever has been stated,
along with their causes, symptoms, and methods of pacification, both individually and collectively.
2.8.44 | The synonyms for causes, the names of diseases, and their characteristics—
this much is taught as the Nidāna-sthāna (the Section on Etiology) in summary.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Epilepsy," in the Section on Diagnosis (Nidānasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The Section on Diagnosis is completed. Now begins the Section on Specific Determination (Vimānasthāna).
The First Chapter.
3.1.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the specific determination of tastes (rasavimāna).
3.1.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

3.1.3 | In this treatise, indeed, after having entered into the specific details of the causes, premonitory symptoms, clinical signs, therapeutic suitability, enumeration, predominance, procedures, and variations of diseases, the physician must subsequently understand correctly—by means of an attentive mind—the measurement of the humors (doṣa), the medicine, the location, the time, the strength, the body, the essence (sāra), diet, suitability, the mind (sattva), the constitution (prakṛti), and age; for successful treatment depends upon the knowledge of the measurement of the humors and other factors. For a physician who does not know the measurement of the humors and so forth is not capable of suppressing disease. Therefore, O Agniveśa, we shall expound the Section on Measurement (Vimānasthāna) for the purpose of knowing the measurement of the humors and other factors.
3.1.4 | First, we shall describe the effects of tastes (rasa), substances (dravya), humors (doṣa), and disorders (vikāra).

There are six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent. When these are used properly, they sustain the body; however, when used improperly, they indeed lead to the provocation of the humors.
3.1.5 | Furthermore, the humors (doṣas) are three: vāta, pitta, and śleṣman.

When they are in their natural state (prakṛti), they are beneficial to the body; however, when they have undergone morbid change (vikṛti), they indeed afflict the body with various kinds of disorders.

3.1.6 | In this regard, three tastes each produce one of the *doṣas*, while three tastes each pacify it. Namely: pungent (*kaṭu*), bitter (*tikta*), and astringent (*kaṣāya*) produce *vāta*, whereas sweet (*madhura*), sour (*amla*), and salty (*lavaṇa*) pacify it; pungent, sour, and salty produce *pitta*, whereas sweet, bitter, and astringent pacify it; sweet, sour, and salty produce *śleṣman*, whereas pungent, bitter, and astringent pacify it.

3.1.7 | However, when there is a combination of tastes and doshas, those tastes which possess qualities identical to, or predominantly similar to, particular doshas will increase those doshas; whereas those with opposite qualities, or predominantly opposite qualities, pacify them when practiced repeatedly.
It is for the sake of this systematic arrangement that the number of tastes is taught as six when they are unmixed with one another, and the number of doshas as three.
3.1.8 | For the expansion of the conceptual constructions regarding their associations is indeed incalculable, because the distinctions among those conceptual constructions are incalculable.

3.1.9 | In that regard, concerning substances that possess multiple tastes and disorders that consist of multiple doṣas, one should determine the true nature of the potency of both substances and disorders by examining the influence of each taste and doṣa individually.
3.1.10 | But this is certainly not the case everywhere.

For it is not possible to determine the true nature of the power of a whole merely by inferring it from the power of its parts, when those parts are combined in unequal proportions, possess diverse natures, are mutually impaired, and are further conceptualized by other distinctions.

3.1.11 | For when the aggregate is thus engaged, having perceived the very reality of the power of the aggregate in this manner, one should then determine the reality of the power of the transformation of substances.

3.1.12 | Therefore, we shall teach the true nature [of substances] by way of their influence on the tastes, their influence on the substances themselves, their influence on the doshas, and their influence on the resulting disorders.
3.1.13 | In this regard, the influence of tastes has been taught.
We shall now teach the influence of substances.
Oil, ghee, and honey are substances intended for the pacification of vāta, pitta, and śleṣman respectively.

3.1.14 | In that regard, oil conquers Vāta when practiced continuously, because it is endowed with unctuousness (sneha), heat (uṣṇya), and heaviness (gaurava). For Vāta is endowed with dryness (raukṣya), coldness (śaitya), and lightness (lāghava), and thus possesses contrary qualities; for when substances of contrary qualities meet, the greater overcomes the lesser. Therefore, oil conquers Vāta when practiced continuously. Clarified butter (sarpiḥ) likewise conquers Pitta due to its sweetness (mādhurya), coldness (śaitya), and mildness (mandatva); for Pitta is non-sweet, hot (uṣṇa), and sharp (tīkṣṇa).

Honey conquers phlegm due to its dryness, sharpness, and astringency; for phlegm is indeed unctuous, mild, and sweet. Furthermore, whatever other substance there may be that is qualitatively opposite to wind, bile, and phlegm, it too conquers them when practiced habitually.
3.1.15 | Now, indeed, one should not consume three substances in excess compared to other substances; namely: long pepper (pippalī), alkali (kṣāra), and salt (lavaṇa).

3.1.16 | Pippalī fruits are indeed pungent, sweet in their post-digestive transformation (vipāka), heavy, not excessively unctuous or hot, moistening, and considered beneficial as medicines; yet they produce both wholesome and unwholesome effects immediately. They appear auspicious at first because of the excellence of their initial application, but they lead to the accumulation of the humors (doṣa). When used constantly, due to their heaviness and moistening nature, they aggravate phlegm (śleṣman); due to their heat, they aggravate bile (pitta); and they are not conducive to pacifying wind (vāta) because of their slight unctuousness and heat.
Indeed, they become carriers of the yoga; therefore, one should not consume long peppers in excess.

3.1.17 | Furthermore, alkali (kṣāra), being endowed with heat, sharpness, and lightness, first moistens and subsequently dries up; it is employed for the purposes of cooking, burning, and cleaving. When used in excess, it becomes harmful to the hair, eyes, heart, and virility. Indeed, those villages, cities, towns, and districts that use it constantly become afflicted with blindness, impotence, baldness, and premature greying, and suffer from heart disease—such as the people of Prācya and Cīna. Therefore, one should not use alkali in excess.
