3.1.18 | Salt, moreover, is endowed with heat and sharpness; it is neither too heavy nor too unctuous. It is moistening, capable of causing disintegration, and creates a relish for food substances. It is beneficial at first because its qualities are consistent with its application, yet it leads to the accumulation of the *doṣas*. It is employed for the purpose of stimulating the appetite, digestion, moistening, and disintegration [of morbid matter]. When used in excess, it brings about exhaustion, flaccidity, and weakness of the body.
For those villages, cities, market towns, and districts that constantly consume this [salt], their inhabitants mostly become weak, with diminished flesh and blood, and unable to endure hardship.
For example—the Bāhlīkas, Saurāṣṭrikas, Saindhavas, and Sauvīrakas; for they eat even salt together with milk.

Furthermore, in those regions of this earth that are excessively saline, medicinal herbs, creepers, trees, and forest giants do not grow, or they become of little vitality, because they are afflicted by salt.
Therefore, one should not consume salt in excess.
For even those persons who have become habituated to excessive salt, baldness, graying of the hair, and wrinkles appear prematurely.
3.1.19 | Therefore, it is better for them to gradually abandon those habits;
for even that which is habitual, when being discontinued gradually, results in no harm or only slight harm.
3.1.20 | That which is agreeable to one's own self is called *sātmya*; for the meaning of *sātmya* is the same as the meaning of *upaśaya* (therapeutic suitability).

It is threefold according to the division into superior, inferior, and intermediate; it is sevenfold, however, according to each individual taste and the consumption of all tastes combined. Among these, that which contains all tastes is superior, that which has only a single taste is inferior, and that which lies between the superior and the inferior is intermediate.
In this regard, one should gradually bring about a superior state of *sātmya* by means of inferior and intermediate states of *sātmya*.

Furthermore, even when all tastes are available, one should employ that which is wholesome; having duly considered all the eight factors of the specific rules for dietary practice—beginning with the constitution (prakṛti) and ending with the consumer—one should pursue only what is beneficial.

3.1.21 | In this regard, there are indeed these eight specific bases for the rules of diet: namely—nature, preparation, combination, quantity, place, time, method of consumption, and the consumer as the eighth.

3.1.22–1 | In this context, "nature" (prakṛti) is said to be that which is inherent (svabhāva). Furthermore, it is the natural endowment with qualities such as heaviness and so forth belonging to foods, medicinal herbs, and substances; for example, [the natural qualities] of black gram and mung bean, or of the pig and the antelope.
3.1.22–2 | Furthermore, *karaṇa* (processing) is the refinement (*abhisaṃskāra*) of natural substances. For refinement is said to be the imparting of another quality (*guṇāntarādhāna*).

Those qualities are imparted by means of contact with water and fire, purification, churning, place, time, seasoning (*vāsana*), fermentation (*bhāvanā*), and so forth, as well as by the passage of time, vessels, and other such factors.

3.1.22–3 | Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), moreover, is the state of cohesion of two or many substances; it initiates a specific quality (*viśeṣa*) which the substances do not initiate individually. For example: the conjunction of honey and clarified butter, and the conjunction of honey, fish, and milk.

3.1.22–4 | *Rāśi* (the heap), however, refers to the grasping of all [food] (*sarvagraha*) and the grasping of portions (*parigraha*), for the purpose of determining the results of both measured and unmeasured [intake].

In this context, "grasping of all" (*sarvagraha*) is the taking of the measure of the entire food as a single mass; "portion-grasping" (*parigraha*), on the other hand, is the taking of the measure of individual food substances one by one.
For "grasping of all" (*sarvagraha*) is the grasping of everything, and "grasping from everywhere" (*sarvataśca grahaḥ*) is called "portion-grasping" (*parigraha*).
3.1.22–5 | Furthermore, *deśa* (place) is location; it denotes the origin and distribution of substances, as well as regional suitability (*deśasātmya*).
3.1.22–6 | Time is indeed both constantly moving and situational; therein, the situational depends on transformation, while the constantly moving depends on seasonal suitability.
3.1.22–7 | Restriction regarding utilization (upayoga-saṃsthā), however, is the regulation of utilization; it depends upon the signs of digestion.
3.1.22 | Furthermore, the consumer is he who partakes of that food; it is dependent upon him that the suitability of the diet (sātmya) exists.
Thus, the eight specific bases for the rules regarding food have been explained.

3.1.23 | The specific variations of these [foods] yield auspicious or inauspicious results and act as mutual auxiliaries; one should desire to understand them, and having understood them, one should seek only what is beneficial; and one should never, out of delusion or negligence, consume any food or anything else that is pleasant yet harmful and results in unhappiness.

3.1.24 | In this regard, this is the rule for the preparation of food: for those who are healthy and for certain patients as well, it is most beneficial when consumed at the proper time according to one's constitution—warm, unctuous, in the correct quantity, not antagonistic to the digestive power once digested, in a pleasant place, with all desired accessories, neither too fast nor too slow, without talking, without laughing, with full attention, having properly observed oneself.

3.1.25–1 | We shall now teach its sixfold excellence: one should eat what is warm. For food eaten while warm is palatable; once consumed, it stimulates the digestive fire within the abdomen, undergoes digestion quickly, directs the wind (vāta) in its natural downward course, and diminishes phlegm (śleṣman). Therefore, one should eat what is warm.

3.1.25–2 | One should eat unctuous food; for when eaten unctuous, it tastes pleasant, and once consumed, it stimulates the non-digested digestive fire, undergoes digestion quickly, directs the *vāta* downward, nourishes the body, strengthens the sense organs, produces an increase in strength, and brings about clarity of complexion; therefore, one should eat unctuous food.

3.1.25–3 | One should eat in the proper measure; for food eaten in the proper measure does not afflict the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*, but increases *āyus* alone, passes easily through the rectum, does not impair the digestive heat (*ūṣman*), and reaches full digestion without distress. Therefore, one should eat in the proper measure.

3.1.25–4 | One should eat when [the previous meal] is digested; for if one eats while the previous meal is undigested, the ingested mass of food mingles with the undigested essence (*rasa*) of the prior meal and quickly provokes all the *doṣas*. However, for one who eats when the meal is digested—when the *doṣas* are situated in their own locations, the digestive fire is kindled, hunger has arisen, the openings of the channels are open, the belching is pure, the heart is clear, the downward movement of wind (*vātānulomya*) is established, and the bowels have been evacuated—the [new] food is properly assimilated.

Food consumed during the urges of flatus, urine, or feces corrupts all the tissues (dhātus) of the entire body and increases life-span alone; therefore, one should eat only when [the previous meal] is digested.

3.1.25–5 | One should eat food that is not antagonistic in its potency (vīrya); for by eating food that is non-antagonistic in potency, one is not afflicted by disorders born of food that is antagonistic in potency. Therefore, one should eat food that is not antagonistic in its potency.

3.1.25-6 | One should eat in a desired place and with all desired accessories; for while eating in a desired place, one does not suffer mental distress caused by factors arising from an undesired place that disturb the mind, and likewise with all desired accessories. Therefore, one should eat in a desired place and with all desired accessories.

3.1.25–7 | One should not eat too quickly; for one who eats too quickly, there occurs excessive salivation, depression, and instability of the food in the mouth, and the perception of the qualities or defects of the food is not certain. Therefore, one should not eat too quickly.

3.1.25–8 | One should not eat too slowly; for one who eats too slowly does not achieve satiety, eats excessively, and the food becomes cold and is digested irregularly. Therefore, one should not eat too slowly.

3.1.25–9 | One should eat without talking or laughing, with the mind fixed on that [act of eating]; for the very same faults that arise from eating too quickly occur when one eats while talking, laughing, or with the mind elsewhere. Therefore, one should eat without talking or laughing, with the mind fixed on that.

3.1.25 | One should eat properly after having carefully observed oneself; for when one knows, "this is wholesome for me" and "this is not wholesome for me," such is the self-concordance (ātmasātmya) of that person. Therefore, one should eat properly after having carefully observed oneself.
3.1.26 | And there is this [verse] here:
He who knows the tastes, the substances, the doshas, and the disorders by their specific potencies (prabhāva),
as well as place, time, and the body— he is our physician.
3.1.27 | Regarding this, there are two verses concerning the subject matter of the Vimāna-sthāna: the tastes, substances, and humors, along with diseases, according to their specific potencies;
substances that should not be consumed excessively; and the threefold nature of suitability (sātmya).
3.1.28 | The eight bases of food, as well as the excellence of the qualities of what is eaten—
all this has been elucidated in the Vimāna chapter titled "The Enumeration of Tastes."

Thus ends the first chapter, named "The Specific Determination of Tastes" (*rasavimāna*), in the Section on Specific Determinations (*vimānasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Two:
3.2.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the specific determination concerning the three parts of the stomach (*trividhakukṣīya-vimāna*).
3.2.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

3.2.3 | One who consumes food should allot three parts of space within the stomach: namely, one part for solid food preparations, one part for liquids, and one part for vāta, pitta, and kapha. For by consuming such a quantity of food, one does not incur any ill effect arising from immoderate eating.

3.2.4 | Furthermore, it is not possible to obtain the full excellence of the fruit of food merely through its being possessed of the proper quantity, because the eight specific bases for the rules of diet—beginning with constitution (*prakṛti*)—each have their own distinct results.
3.2.5 | In this regard, first, with reference to the mass of food, this is for the purpose of determining the results of moderation and immoderation:
for the classification of the rules concerning the mass of food consists precisely of these two—moderation and immoderation.
3.2.6 | Regarding that, the principle of moderation has been previously indicated through the division of the stomach into portions; we shall now explain it further in detail.

Namely: not overfilling the stomach with food; not constricting the heart; not splitting the sides; no excessive heaviness of the abdomen; satisfaction of the sense organs; the cessation of hunger and thirst; comfort during standing, sitting, lying down, walking, breathing in and out, laughing, and conversation; easy digestion in the evening and morning; and the promotion of strength, complexion, and growth—these are the characteristics of food taken in the proper measure.

3.2.7 | Furthermore, they describe immoderation as being of two kinds: deficient and excessive. Among these, they declare a deficient quantity of food to be the cause of the destruction of strength, complexion, and corpulence; it causes lack of satiety, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), loss of longevity, and lack of virility; it is devoid of vital energy (ojas); it causes injury to the body, mind, intellect, and senses; it destroys the essential tissues (sāra); it brings about misfortune, and it is the abode of more than eighty disorders of wind (vāta). On the other hand, the experts maintain that an excessive quantity excites all the bodily humors (doṣas).

For when one has reached satiety with solid foods and subsequently attains fullness through liquids, the wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman) located in the stomach become excessively oppressed by that overindulgence in food; they all simultaneously fall into a state of provocation. Being provoked, they enter that very mass of undigested food, remaining localized in a portion of the belly, and cause obstruction; or else, suddenly displacing it through the upper and lower passages, they produce various distinct disorders in the person who eats in excess.

In that condition, Vāta produces colic, flatulence, body ache, dryness of the mouth, fainting, giddiness, irregularity of digestion, and stiffness or contraction of the sides, back, waist, and vessels; Pitta, moreover, causes fever, diarrhea, internal burning, thirst, intoxication, giddiness, and delirium; while Śleṣman causes vomiting, anorexia, indigestion, cold-fever, lassitude, and heaviness of the limbs.

3.2.8 | Furthermore, it is not only an excessively large quantity of food that they consider to cause the disorder of *āma*; rather, the consumption of food and drink that is heavy, dry, cold, parched, loathsome, obstructive, burning, impure, or incompatible, as well as that consumed at the wrong time, or that which is consumed by one whose mind is afflicted by desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, shamelessness, grief, pride, agitation, or fear—that too causes the corruption of *āma* itself.
3.2.9 | Furthermore, it occurs here that even wholesome food, when consumed in the proper measure, does not digest due to anxiety,
grief, fear, anger, physical suffering, an uncomfortable bed, or staying awake at night.
3.2.10 | Physicians describe that twofold disorder of undigested matter (āmapradoṣa) as visūcikā and alasaka.
3.2.11 | In that regard, one should recognize visūcikā as having its morbid humors (doṣas) moving both upwards and downwards, possessing the characteristics already described.

3.2.12 | We shall now describe alasaka: In a person who is weak, has weak digestive fire, and an abundance of phlegm (śleṣman), who suppresses the urges of flatus, urine, and feces, and who consumes food that is stable, heavy, excessively dry, cold, and parched—his food and drink, oppressed by wind (anila) and its passage obstructed by phlegm, becomes excessively dissolved due to its sluggish nature and does not move toward the exterior; consequently, it exhibits excessive symptoms of the disorders of undigested matter (āmadoṣa), with the exception of vomiting and diarrhea.

Furthermore, when the humors (doṣas) become excessively aggravated and, moving through corrupted and obstructed channels, travel obliquely, they sometimes merely cause the body to become rigid like a staff; this condition is then called *daṇḍālasaka* and is declared incurable.

On the other hand, physicians designate the accumulation of undigested humors (*āmadoṣa*) resulting from the habit of eating incompatible foods, overeating, or eating before the previous meal is digested as *āmaviṣa*, because its symptoms resemble those of actual poison; that is ultimately incurable due to its rapid onset and the incompatibility of treatments required.

3.2.13 | In that case, if the undigested matter (āma) is severely corrupted and has become stagnant, one should first induce emesis by having the patient drink warm water mixed with salt; thereafter, one should treat the patient with fomentation and the application of suppositories, and also prescribe fasting.
In the case of visūcikā, however, fasting alone is the primary treatment, followed by the same sequence as for purgation.

In cases of complications arising from undigested matter (*āma-pradoṣa*), however, when the previous meal has been digested at the time of eating, one should observe that the patient’s stomach (*āśaya*) is coated with residual morbid humors (*doṣa*), the abdomen is numb and heavy, and there is no desire for food. At such a time, one should administer medicine both to digest the remaining morbid matter and to kindle the digestive fire (*agni-saṃdhukṣaṇa*); but one must never administer food while it is still undigested. For the digestive fire, weakened by the complication of *āma*, is incapable of simultaneously digesting the morbid matter, the medicine, and the mass of food.

Furthermore, a confusion between the undigested matter, the food, and the medicine—due to their excessive strength—might suddenly cause the patient, whose bodily fire has ceased to function, to fall into a state of extreme weakness.

Furthermore, disorders born from the defects of undigested matter (āma) are alleviated by fasting alone; however, when a persistent residue remains, for those diseases treated with fasting, one should set aside the remedy that is contrary to the cause and instead apply a medicine that is contrary to the specific affliction itself, according to its nature.

Moreover, experts maintain that in the treatment of all disorders, the medicine should be contrary to both the cause and the disease, or it should at least accomplish the same purpose as such a remedy.

Furthermore, for one whose doshas have been liberated but not yet fully matured, and when the digestive fire is blazing, oleation therapy (abhyaṅga), non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), and the internal drinking of fats (sneha-pāna) should be administered according to the rules and with due consideration, having correctly observed the various states of the doshas, the medicines, the region, the season, the strength, the body, dietary suitability, the mind, the constitution, the age, and the specific disorders.
3.2.14 | Furthermore, there is this verse:
Having thoroughly examined the eight bases for the rules of diet, one should act for one's own welfare;
and whatever other path exists here regarding the application of wholesome things, one should also follow that.
3.2.15 | Where do that which is eaten, chewed, drunk, and licked undergo digestion? O wise one, we ask this of you; tell us that, O intelligent one.
3.2.16 | Thus questioned by his disciples headed by Agniveśa, Punarvasu then explained to them where food is digested.
3.2.17 | The region between the navel and the breasts of a living being is known as the *āmāśaya* (receptacle of undigested food).
Whatever is eaten, chewed, drunk, or licked is digested here.
3.2.18 | Food, having reached the stomach, undergoes digestion entirely there;
once digested, it subsequently enters all the other receptacles via the vessels.
3.2.19 | Regarding this, there is a verse: The signs and the results of that [food] when it is possessed of proper measure have been stated as they truly are;
likewise, the signs and the results of food lacking in measure have been stated according to their respective divisions.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Three Parts of the Stomach," in the Section on Determinations (*Vimānasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Three:
3.3.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the determination concerning the destruction of inhabited regions (*Janapadoddhvaṃsanīya-vimāna*).
3.3.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

3.3.3 | In the district of Janapada, within the field of Pañcāla inhabited by the best of the twice-born, at the capital city of Kāmpilya, the Blessed Punarvasu Ātreya, surrounded by a circle of disciples, while wandering through the forest on the bank of the Gaṅgā during the last month of summer, spoke to his disciple Agniveśa.

3.3.4 | Indeed, O gentle one, abnormalities are observed among the constellations, the hosts of planets, the moon, the sun, wind, fire, and the directions; and due to seasonal disturbances, the earth will soon no longer properly provide the taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and specific action of medicinal herbs. Consequently, a state of widespread affliction is certain upon their loss.

Therefore, O gentle one, before this destruction occurs and before the earth becomes devoid of its essence, you must collect the medicines while their taste, potency, post-digestive effect, and specific action remain unimpaired.
We ourselves shall employ their tastes, potencies, post-digestive effects, and specific actions, as well as those who desire us and those whom we desire.

For indeed, my dear friend, when medicines have been properly extracted, properly prepared, and properly administered, there is no difficulty whatsoever in countering those disorders that cause the destruction of a country.

3.3.5 | To the Blessed Ātreya who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, indeed the medicines have been extracted, properly prepared, and properly administered; yet, why is it that the destruction of an entire region occurs simultaneously through a single disease among men whose constitution, diet, body, strength, suitability, mental nature, and age are all dissimilar?"

3.3.6 | The Blessed Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa, although humans are thus dissimilar by virtue of these factors such as their constitution (*prakṛti*) and so forth, those other factors which are common to them—through the impairment of these, diseases that arise at the same time and with the same symptoms destroy the population.
Indeed, these following factors are common to populations: namely, air, water, place, and time."

3.3.7-(1) In that regard, one should recognize wind (*vāta*) as being of such a nature that it causes ill health; namely: when it is irregular according to the season, excessively still, excessively moving, excessively harsh, excessively cold, excessively hot, excessively dry, excessively moist, possessing an excessively terrifying roar, having an excessively obstructed or mutually conflicting movement, excessively swirling, and when it is afflicted by unwholesome odors, vapors, sand, dust, and smoke.

3.3.7-(2) One should recognize water as being characterized by an excessive alteration of its odor, color, taste, and touch; as being abundant in moisture; as having aquatic creatures and birds departed from it; as having its aquatic inhabitants diminished; as being unpleasant; and as having lost its [beneficial] qualities.

Furthermore, the region is characterized by natural and unnatural colors, odors, tastes, and textures; it is excessively moist and infested with reptiles, beasts of prey, mosquitoes, locusts, flies, rats, owls, scavengers, birds, jackals, and the like; it is filled with thickets of grass and groves of trees, abounding in spreading creepers; its crops are as if never sown before, yet have withered and perished; the winds are smoky, the flocks of birds are cackling in distress, and the various herds of wild animals and birds are wandering about in agitation; and the people of that land have abandoned the eightfold duties, truth, shame, right conduct, and virtuous qualities.

One should recognize as harmful a sky that has a reservoir of water constantly agitated and overflowing, where there is continuous falling of meteors, thunderclaps, and earthquakes; which possesses a most terrifying form of sound; which is covered by a network of clouds that are rough, copper-colored, reddish, and white, obscuring the sun, moon, and stars; which appears to be in a state of constant agitation and distress, as if filled with fearful weeping, as if enveloped in darkness, as if haunted by *guhyakas*, and abounding in the sounds of lamentation.
Furthermore, one should determine a time to be harmful when its characteristics are contrary to those of the season, or when they are excessive, or when they are deficient.
3.3.7 | Experts declare that these four conditions, when possessed of such defects, bring about the ruin of the country; however, they say that those which are otherwise are beneficial.
3.3.8 | Even when these factors that cause the destruction of a country are deficient in their qualities, those who are treated with medicine attain freedom from fear of diseases.
3.3.9 | Furthermore, there are verses on this point: The specific reasons for the relative heaviness of place, time, wind, and water when they have become deficient will now be explained.

3.3.10 | A knower of the subject matter should understand that water is more significant than wind, place is more significant than water, time is more significant than place, and natural disposition is more significant than time,
because they are increasingly difficult to avoid.

3.3.11 | Furthermore, one who understands the specific characteristics of the aforementioned sheaths (koṣas) within the air and other elements should recognize lightness as the characteristic of ease in treatment.
3.3.12 | However, when men are treated with medicine even when all four [humors] are deranged at the end of their time, they do not become afflicted by disease.
3.3.13 | For those who share no commonality of death and no commonality of actions,
the fivefold treatment of action is declared to be the supreme remedy.
3.3.14 | The systematic administration of rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana) is highly commended;
likewise, the maintenance of bodily function through medicines previously extracted [from plants] is praised.
3.3.15 | Truthfulness, compassion for living beings, charity, offerings, worship of the deities,
following the conduct of the virtuous, tranquility, and self-protection.
3.3.16 | It is beneficial for the people to resort to auspicious places,
as well as to practice celibacy and to associate with those who observe celibacy.

3.3.17 | He should constantly engage in conversation with righteous, sattvic persons esteemed by the elders, concerning the treatises on dharma and the great sages who have conquered their own selves.
3.3.18 | This has been declared as the medicine for the preservation of life for those whose death is not predetermined during that most terrible time.

3.3.19 | Having heard these causes for the destruction of the population, Agniveśa spoke again to the Blessed Ātreya: "Now then, O Blessed One, from what root does the impairment of these [factors] such as wind arise, by which, when they are affected, they destroy the population?"

3.3.20 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "O Agniveśa! Whatever deficiency arises among all things, such as the wind and the rest, its root is unrighteousness (adharma), or its root is improper action performed in a previous life; the source of both of these is indeed intellectual error (prajñāparādha)."

For example: when the leaders of foreign cities, towns, market-towns, and districts transgress the Dharma and govern the people unrighteously, then those who depend on them and those who subsist on their legal proceedings further increase that unrighteousness. Consequently, that unrighteousness forcibly causes the Dharma to disappear; and once the Dharma has disappeared, they are abandoned even by the deities.

When their dharma has thus vanished, when they have become lawless and dominated by unrighteousness, and when the deities have departed from them, the seasons go astray. Consequently, the rain-god does not pour forth rain at the proper time, or he does not rain at all, or he rains in a distorted manner; the winds do not blow correctly, the earth becomes afflicted, the waters dry up, and the medicinal herbs, abandoning their natural state, fall into corruption. Thereafter, the inhabited regions perish due to the defects of what is touched and what is consumed.

3.3.21 | Likewise, even in the case of destruction of the country caused by weapons, unrighteousness alone is the cause. Those whose greed, anger, delusion, and pride have become excessively intense, having disregarded the weak, attack one another with weapons for the sake of harming themselves, their own kin, or others; or they attack others, or are attacked by others.
3.3.22 | Or else, having perceived that unrighteousness or some other transgression, they are struck down by various hosts of beings, such as the throngs of Rākṣasas.
3.3.23 | Likewise, even in the case of that which arises from a curse, unrighteousness (*adharma*) alone is the cause.

Those whose dharma has been lost and who have deviated from dharma, having disregarded their teachers, elders, perfected ones (*siddha*), sages (*ṛṣi*), and those worthy of honor, commit harmful acts; consequently, those subjects, cursed by their teachers and others, are reduced to ashes before the destruction of many generations of their families, while others [perish] at other times due to the perception of certain conditions.

3.3.24 | Furthermore, even prior to unrighteousness (*adharma*), no arising of evil occurred from any other cause. For in the primordial age (*ādikāla*), men possessed vigor equal to the sons of Aditi, with exceedingly pure and vast majesty; they performed the rituals and ordinances of sacrifices according to the dharma witnessed by the gods and divine seers (*devarṣi*); their bodies were firm, solid, and compact like the essence of mountains; their complexions and senses were serene; they possessed speed, strength, and prowess equal to the wind; they had beautiful hips and were endowed with handsome proportions, physical grace, and full development; and they were devoted to truth, uprightness, compassion, charity, self-restraint, discipline, austerity, fasting, and the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).

And those men became free from fear, passion, hatred, delusion, greed, anger, grief, pride, disease, sleep, drowsiness, fatigue, exhaustion, laziness, and possessiveness; they possessed immeasurable lifespans.

For them—whose natures, virtues, and actions were noble—crops appeared at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga, endowed with inconceivable qualities of taste, potency, maturation, and power, because the earth and other elements were possessed of all excellent qualities.

But as the Kṛta Yuga declined, due to excessive greed on the part of certain prosperous beings, there arose heaviness of body; from heaviness of body, fatigue; from fatigue, laziness; from laziness, accumulation; from accumulation, possessiveness; and from possessiveness, greed appeared during the Kṛta. Then, in the Tretā, from greed came malice; from malice, false speech; and from false speech, desire, anger, pride, hatred, harshness, assault, fear, distress, grief, anxiety, agitation, and so forth, came into being.
Thus, in the Tretā, one quarter of Dharma disappeared.

Due to the disappearance [of the dharma], there was a reduction by one quarter of the duration of the Yugas and the years; likewise, there occurred a destruction by one quarter of the qualities of the earth and the other elements.

And because of that destruction, there was a loss by one quarter of the qualities of crops—namely their moisture, purity, taste, potency, post-digestive transformation (vipāka), and specific efficacy (prabhāva).

Consequently, the bodies of living beings, being supported by food and conduct whose qualities were diminished by one quarter and thus not as they were before, were overcome by fire and wind and afflicted by diseases such as fever and the like. Therefore, living beings gradually underwent a decline in lifespan.
And there are these two verses on this point: "In each successive age, the quarter of dharma is diminished by this sequence;
and likewise, the quality-quarter of living beings [is diminished], whereby the world dissolves."
3.3.26 | When a full hundred years have passed, a year undergoes diminution;
this occurs at the time when the lifespan of embodied beings is intended to reach its measure.
3.3.27 | Thus, the cause for the prior production of modifications has been stated.
3.3.28 | To the Blessed One who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, is the lifespan of all beings indeed determined by a fixed duration, or not?"
3.3.29 | The Blessed One said to him:
"In this world, O Agniveśa, the lifespan of living beings depends upon the application of means;
for its strength or weakness is established in both destiny and human effort."
3.3.30 | One should know that "fate" (daiva) is the action performed by oneself in a previous body;
whereas "human effort" (puruṣakāra) is said to be that other [action] which is performed here in this life.
3.3.31 | There is indeed a distinction of strength between those two types of action as well;
for action is seen to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
3.3.32 | The conjunction of those two—nobility and long-lasting happiness—is the cause of a fixed lifespan; the opposite [conjunction] is the cause of the other.
3.3.33 | The middling [action] is held to be the cause of the middling; hear another [reason]:
for destiny is indeed overcome by human effort when it is weak.
3.3.34 | If another action is obstructed by a superior destiny,
then some, having observed this, consider that the lifespan is fixed.
3.3.35 | Some karma is fixed as to its ripening at a certain time and is great;
some, however, is not fixed as to time and is awakened by conditions.
3.3.36 | Therefore, because both possibilities are observed, the adoption of an absolute position is incorrect.

Furthermore, we shall provide an illustration here: for if the entire lifespan were of a fixed duration and measure, then those desiring long life would not employ such actions and rites as mantras, medicinal herbs, gems, auspicious ceremonies, offerings, oblations, observances, expiations, fasts, benedictions, prostrations, pilgrimages, and so forth; nor would sacrifices be performed.

Neither wild, fierce, and restless cattle, elephants, camels, donkeys, horses, buffaloes, and the like, nor harmful winds and such, would need to be avoided; nor precipices, mountains, treacherous fortresses, or the force of water; likewise, neither those whose minds are distracted, insane, agitated, fierce, fickle, deluded, or overwhelmed by greed; nor enemies; nor a raging fire; nor various venomous reptiles, serpents, and the like; nor rashness; nor conduct at improper places and times; nor the wrath of a king.
For such conditions as these would not cause the destruction of life, because the duration of every lifespan has a fixed measure of time.

Furthermore, the fear of untimely death would not come upon living beings if they did not practice those means that ward off the fear of untimely death; the efforts, discourses, applications, and insights of the great seers regarding elixirs (*rasāyana*) would be in vain; Indra would not strike down an enemy of fixed lifespan with his thunderbolt; the Aśvins would not restore a sick person with medicine; the great seers would not attain their desired lifespan through austerity; and the great seers—who have known all that is to be known—along with the lords of the gods, would neither perceive correctly, nor teach, nor practice [these truths].

Moreover, this is the supreme among all eyes, namely the eye of Indra, and this is directly perceived by us: just as there is an inequality of lifespan among thousands of men who repeatedly engage in battle and those who do not, and likewise an inequality of lifespan among those who are newborn due to the absence of medical treatment versus its presence, and even among those who consume poison and those who do not; and just as there is no equality in the acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) of water-jars and painted vases when they are being destroyed;
therefore, life is rooted in beneficial treatment, and from the opposite of that comes death.

Moreover, we perceive the cause for our being well-instructed, well-observing, and well-seeing as follows: the proper sequential application of actions and dietary modifications that are contrary to place, time, self, and the qualities [of the elements]; the total avoidance of excessive, deficient, and improper application; the restraint of all excesses; the non-restraint of those moving entities that have been provoked; and the avoidance of rash acts, all of which follow the traditional teachings of the Āryas.
3.3.37 | Thereafter, Agniveśa said: "Lord, this being so, how does timely death or untimely death occur for those whose lifespan has no fixed duration or measure?"

3.3.38 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "Listen, Agniveśa! Just as an axle fitted to a vehicle, though naturally endowed with the qualities of an axle and possessed of all excellent attributes, reaches its end when being drawn at the proper time solely through the exhaustion of its own measure; even so, life residing in the body, though strong by nature and properly maintained, reaches its end solely through the exhaustion of its own measure—that is death in due time."

And just as that very axle, due to being overloaded, or because of an uneven path, or a wrong path, or the breaking of the axle or wheel, or through the fault of the driver, or from the unyoking of the linchpin, or from lack of lubrication, or from overturning, meets with its end prematurely;

Likewise, life also meets its end prematurely due to exertion beyond one's strength, eating in a manner inconsistent with one's digestive fire, irregular eating habits, improper bodily postures, excessive sexual indulgence, association with the wicked, suppression of natural urges when they have arisen, non-suppression of urges that ought to be restrained, affliction by spirits, poisons, wind, or fire, injury, and the neglect of food and remedies; this is untimely death. Similarly, we observe that diseases such as fever, when improperly treated, also become causes of untimely death.

3.3.39 | Then Agniveśa asked: "O Blessed One, why indeed do physicians mostly prescribe hot water for those suffering from fever, and not cold water in that way, even though there is a bodily constituent (dhātu) that causes fever which is curable by cold?"

3.3.40 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "Physicians administer hot water to one suffering from fever for the purpose of promoting digestion (pācana), having duly considered the origin of the body's disease, the location, and the time.

For fever arises from the stomach (āmāśaya), and generally, the medicines for disorders originating in the stomach are capable of inducing digestion, emesis, and lightening (apatarpaṇa). Since hot water serves to promote digestion, physicians most frequently prescribe it for those afflicted by fever."

For it harmonizes their wind (vāta), stimulates the digestive fire in the stomach, undergoes digestion quickly, dries up phlegm (śleṣman), and even when drunk in small quantities, it serves to alleviate thirst. Nevertheless, this should not be administered in a fever where bile (pitta) is excessively increased, or in cases accompanied by burning sensations, vertigo, delirium, or diarrhea; for burning sensations, vertigo, delirium, and diarrhea increase further with heat, whereas they are pacified by cold.
3.3.41 | And it is said in this regard:
"Physicians who know the truth pacify diseases caused by heat with cold;
however, for those diseases caused by cold, heat is the physician's remedy."

3.3.42 | Likewise, for other diseases as well, the medicine is that which is contrary to their cause; for example—just as there is no pacification of diseases caused by depletion (apatarpaṇa) without replenishment (pūraṇa), so too there is no pacification of diseases caused by over-replenishment (pūraṇa) without depletion.
3.3.43 | Depletion therapy is also threefold: fasting, fasting with digestive processing, and the elimination of morbid humors.

Furthermore, for those with many defects, only the draining away of the defects should be performed; for as long as the embankment of a field is not breached, there can be no filling of the pond—just so it is with the draining away of defects.

one who does not acknowledge or remedy his faults; one who is destitute; one who lacks attendants; one who merely fancies himself a physician; one who is violent; one who is envious; one who has an intense aversion to righteousness (*dharma*); one whose strength, flesh, and blood are excessively depleted; one afflicted by an incurable disease; and one who exhibits the signs of approaching death.

The premonitory symptoms are general causes, while the specific characteristics are the actual causes;

Chapter Four:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the determination concerning the specific knowledge of the three types of diseases (*Trividharoga-viśeṣa-vijñānīya-vimāna*).
3.4.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
3.4.3 | Indeed, the specific knowledge of diseases is threefold; namely: authoritative instruction, direct perception, and inference.

3.4.4 | In this context, authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*) is the word of an authority (*āpta*). For authorities are those who possess unerring memory and discernment, and who perceive freedom from both joy and affliction. Because their speech is endowed with such qualities, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, that which is spoken by those who are intoxicated, insane, foolish, passionate, or wicked is not authoritative; indeed, perception is that which is apprehended by oneself through the senses and the mind, while inference is reasoning based upon logical connection.

3.4.5 | Indeed, having first examined the disease in every respect by means of this triad of cognitions, the subsequent determination becomes faultless; for knowledge does not arise regarding the entirety of the object of knowledge through only a single part of cognition.

In this triad of cognitions, knowledge first arises from the instruction of an authoritative person (*āptopadeśa*); thereafter, examination by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) becomes possible.

What has not been taught before is that which one should know by examining it through perception and inference. Therefore, the examination for those possessing knowledge is twofold: perception and inference; or it is threefold, including authoritative instruction.

3.4.6 | In this regard, the wise teach as follows: one should know each individual disease according to its specific provocation, its source, its origin, its nature, its location, its manifestation, its configuration, its sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, its complications, its progression through the stages of increase, stability, and decrease, its prognosis, its name, and its treatment; from such instruction, it is understood whether there should be an active engagement for the sake of remedy or a cessation thereof.

3.4.7 | Furthermore, one who desires to know the true nature of a disease through direct perception should examine all objects of the senses within the patient’s body using all the sense organs, with the exception of the sense of taste. For example—one should examine with the sense of hearing such things as the rumbling of the intestines, the cracking of joints and finger-joints, variations in the voice, and whatever other sounds may arise from the body.

One should examine with the eye the colors, shapes, dimensions, and shadows, as well as the natural state and morbid changes of the body, and whatever other things are perceptible to the eye that have not been specifically mentioned. Regarding taste, however, one should understand that which pertains to the patient's body—even though it is an object of the sense organ—through inference, for its direct perception is not possible. Therefore, one should ascertain the taste on the patient's mouth through questioning the patient; furthermore, one may infer a bad taste in the body from the crawling away of lice, and from the swarming of flies.

Regarding the sweetness of the body: when there is doubt as to whether the blood is *dhāri-lohita* (sustaining blood) or *lohita-pitta* (blood-bile), one should infer that it is *dhāri-lohita* from its being eaten by dogs and crows, and *lohita-pitta* from its not being eaten; in this way, one should also infer other tastes present in the patient's body. Furthermore, one should examine with the sense of smell all the odors present in the patient's body, both those pertaining to their natural state (*prakṛti*) and those resulting from morbid change (*vaikārika*). And one should examine with the hand the tactile sensations associated with the natural state and morbid change. Thus, examination has been described according to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative instruction (*upadeśa*).
3.4.8 | Furthermore, indeed, these other entities as well are likewise to be known primarily through inference.

For example: one should examine fire by its power of digestion; strength by its capacity for exertion; the ear and other senses by their apprehension of objects such as sound; the mind by its non-deviation from objects; consciousness (*vijñāna*) by its determination; passion (*rajas*) by attachment; delusion (*moha*) by lack of discernment; anger by malice; sorrow by dejection; joy by exhilaration; affection by contentment; fear by despondency; righteousness by its lack of despondency; vigor (*vīrya*) by its arousal; steadfastness by its lack of wavering; faith (*śraddhā*) by its intention; and intelligence (*medhā*)— [The text continues: ...by its retention. One should examine the quality of goodness (*sattva*) by its illumination, passion (*rajas*) by its activity, and darkness (*tamas*) by its obscuration. One should examine the body by its support [of the senses], the sense organs by their specific functions, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) by their movement, the life-force (*jīva*) by its connection with the vital breaths, the intellect (*buddhi*) by its comprehension, egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) by its conceit, the mind (*manas*) by its volition, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) by its subtlety, primordial matter (*prakṛti*) by its modification, and the Puruṣa by its being beyond the qualities (*guṇa*). Thus, one should examine each thing by its own characteristic mark. Furthermore, one should examine the self (*ātman*) by means of inference. And what is that inference? It is this: "I exist," because there is the experience of pleasure and pain. For it is not possible for pleasure and pain to be experienced without an experiencer. Just as Devadatta is the experiencer of the pleasure and pain arising from contact with cold and heat, so too is the self the experiencer of the pleasure and pain arising from contact with virtue and vice. Therefore, the self exists. Moreover, the self exists because it is the agent of actions. For it is not possible for an action to be performed without an agent. Just as Devadatta is the agent of the act of walking, so too is the self the agent of the acts of virtue and vice. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the enjoyer of the fruits of action. For it is not possible for the fruit of action to be enjoyed without an enjoyer. Just as Devadatta is the enjoyer of the fruit of the act of eating, so too is the self the enjoyer of the fruit of the acts of virtue and vice. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). For it is not possible for the field to be known without a knower of the field. Just as Devadatta is the knower of the field of a house, so too is the self the knower of the field of the body. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the witness (*sākṣin*). For it is not possible for there to be a witness without an object of witnessing. Just as Devadatta is the witness of a lawsuit, so too is the self the witness of the qualities (*guṇa*). Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the seer (*draṣṭṛ*). For it is not possible for there to be seeing without a seer. Just as Devadatta is the seer of forms, so too is the self the seer of the qualities. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the hearer (*śrotṛ*), the smeller (*ghrātṛ*), the taster (*rasayitṛ*), the feeler (*spraṣṭṛ*), and the thinker (*mantṛ*). For it is not possible for these functions to exist without an agent. Just as Devadatta is the agent of hearing and so forth, so too is the self the agent of hearing and so forth. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the knower (*jñātṛ*). For it is not possible for knowledge to exist without a knower. Just as Devadatta is the knower of the Vedas and so forth, so too is the self the knower of the field. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*). For it is not possible for the body, senses, and mind to function without a controller. Just as Devadatta is the controller of his chariot, so too is the self the controller of the body. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). For it is not possible for enjoyment to exist without an enjoyer. Just as Devadatta is the enjoyer of food and drink, so too is the self the enjoyer of the objects of the senses. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who departs, stays, and experiences (*apasarpaṇopasarpaṇasthānasaṃsthānaviśeṣajña*). For it is not possible for these states to exist without an agent. Just as Devadatta is the one who knows how to depart, stay, and occupy a particular position, so too is the self the one who knows how to depart from the body at death, stay during life, and occupy various positions. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who remembers. For it is not possible for memory to exist without a rememberer. Just as Devadatta is the rememberer of things seen and heard, so too is the self the rememberer of past lives. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who desires. For it is not possible for desire to exist without a desirer. Just as Devadatta is the desirer of women and wealth, so too is the self the desirer of liberation. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who resolves. For it is not possible for resolution to exist without a resolver. Just as Devadatta is the resolver of what is to be done and what is not to be done, so too is the self the resolver of what is to be attained and what is not to be attained. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who perceives. For it is not possible for perception to exist without a perceiver. Just as Devadatta is the perceiver of the six objects of sense, so too is the self the perceiver of the sixfold objects. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who acts. For it is not possible for action to exist without an actor. Just as Devadatta is the actor of various crafts, so too is the self the actor of various actions. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who enjoys. For it is not possible for enjoyment to exist without an enjoyer. Just as Devadatta is the enjoyer of the fruits of his labor, so too is the self the enjoyer of the fruits of its actions. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who is conscious. For it is not possible for consciousness to exist without a conscious one. Just as Devadatta is the conscious one regarding his own body, so too is the self the conscious one regarding the body of another. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who is aware. For it is not possible for awareness to exist without an aware one. Just as Devadatta is the aware one of his own thoughts, so too is the self the aware one of the thoughts of others. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who is mindful. For it is not possible for mindfulness to exist without a mindful one. Just as Devadatta is the mindful one of his own duties, so too is the self the mindful one of its own duties. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who is attentive. For it is not possible for attention to exist without an attentive one. Just as Devadatta is the attentive one of his own speech, so too is the self the attentive one of its own speech. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who is intelligent. For it is not possible for intelligence to exist without an intelligent one. Just as Devadatta is the intelligent one regarding the acquisition of wealth, so too is the self the intelligent one regarding the acquisition of liberation. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who is wise. For it is not possible for wisdom to exist without a wise one. Just as Devadatta is the wise one regarding the avoidance of danger, so too is the self the wise one regarding the avoidance of rebirth. Therefore, the self exists. Furthermore, the self exists because it is the one who is learned. For it is not possible for learning to exist without a learner. Just as Devadatta is the learner of the sciences, so too

One discerns perception by the grasping of names, mindfulness by recollection, modesty by shame, ethical conduct by constant practice, hatred by its prohibition, the underlying substrate by its persistence, fortitude by lack of agitation, submissiveness by obedience; the age, dietary habits, suitability, and the onset of disease by the specific characteristics of time, place, palliative factors, and pain; a disease with hidden signs by means of what is beneficial and what is harmful; the specific measure of the humors by the specific nature of the transgression; and the exhaustion of the lifespan by the fatal signs (*ariṣṭa*).

One should know that the presence of auspiciousness is indicated by an inclination toward what is beneficial; a pure disposition by its lack of change; and the mildness or severity of the digestive fire (*grahaṇī*), as well as dreams, intentions, and the pleasant or painful sensations of those who are disliked or liked, by means of the fourfold interrogation alone.
3.4.9 | Furthermore, there are verses on this point: A discerning physician should correctly understand diseases through authoritative tradition, instruction, direct perception, and inference.
3.4.10 | Having thoroughly examined everything in every way according to what is possible,
the knower of the matter should then immediately resolve upon both the truth and the course of action.
3.4.11 | One who knows the specific nature of what is to be done does not falter in practice;
being undeluded, he attains the fruit that arises from the absence of delusion.
3.4.12 | He who, though knowing reality, does not enter the inner self of the afflicted by means of the lamp of knowledge and intellect, does not treat his diseases.
3.4.13 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
The threefold compendium of knowledge concerning the specific varieties of all diseases—
how the authorities teach it, and how it is perceived through direct observation.
3.4.14 | Furthermore, the sage of noble intellect has declared in the Vimāna section on the knowledge of diseases those entities which are to be known through inference, and how they are to be known.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Specific Characteristics of the Threefold Diseases," in the Section on Determinations (*Vimānasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Fifth Chapter.
3.5.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the determination of the channels (*srotas-vimāna*).
3.5.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
3.5.3 | As many specific manifestations of conditioned states as there are within the person, so many specific types of channels (srotas) exist in this body.
Indeed, no conditioned states whatsoever can be produced or even undergo decay within the person without the channels;
for the channels serve as the carriers of the transforming elements (dhātus) in the sense of being their pathways.

3.5.4 Furthermore, some maintain that the person (*puruṣa*) is merely a collection of channels (*srotas*), because these channels pervade everything and flow everywhere, thereby provoking and pacifying the humors (*doṣa*). However, this is not so; for that which possesses the channels, that which they carry, that which they bring forth, and where they are situated—all that is distinct from them.
Indeed, some declare the channels to be innumerable due to their extreme multiplicity, while others provide a specific enumeration.
3.5.5–6 | [Absence?

3.5.7 | We shall now explain, according to their gross categories, some of the types of these channels from their origins, as well as the knowledge of their provocation, which will be sufficient for the wise to understand the meaning not yet stated, and for the ignorant to gain true insight.

Namely: those carrying breath, water, food, chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, urine, feces, and sweat. Furthermore, for wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*), which circulate throughout the entire body, all channels (*srotas*) serve as their pathways. Likewise, for the subtle principles (*sattva*, etc. that transcend the senses, the body alone—which possesses consciousness—serves as their pathway and their substratum. Because this [body] is the natural substrate of these channels, it is not afflicted by morbid transformations (*vikāra*).

3.5.8 | In that regard, the heart and the great channel (mahāsrotas) are the roots of the channels carrying the vital breath (prāṇa). When these are vitiated, the specific signs of their affliction are as follows: seeing a person breathing excessively, or with obstruction, or with agitation, or very shallowly and repeatedly, or with sound and pain, one should know that his channels carrying the vital breath are vitiated.

The root of the palate and the *kloma* are the sites of the water-carrying channels. When these are indeed vitiated, this is the specific diagnostic knowledge: namely, observing the drying up of the tongue, palate, lips, throat, and *kloma*, as well as excessive thirst, one should know that his water-carrying channels are vitiated.

The root of the food-carrying channels is the stomach and the left side of the body. When these are vitiated, the following is the complete diagnostic knowledge: namely, one should know that a person's food-carrying channels are vitiated upon observing a lack of desire for food, aversion to food, indigestion, and vomiting. The root of the rasa-carrying channels is the heart and the ten vessels (dhamanīs).
The root of the blood-carrying channels is the liver and the spleen.
The roots of the channels carrying flesh are the tendons and the skin;
the roots of the channels carrying urine are the kidneys and the omentum;
the roots of the channels carrying bone are the fat and the hips.

The bones and the joints are the roots of the channels that carry marrow; the testicles and the penis are the roots of the channels that carry semen. Regarding the signs of vitiation of these channels carrying rasa and the other tissues, they have been described in the chapter on "Various Foods and Drinks" (Vividhāśitapītīya); for indeed, the very same signs that indicate the vitiation of the tissues themselves apply to their respective vitiated tissue-channels.

The bladder and the groins are the roots of the urine-carrying channels (*srotas*); indeed, when these are afflicted, the specific signs of their disorder are as follows: one should know that a person's urine-carrying channels are disordered upon seeing him urinating excessively, or with extreme retention, or with provoked [urine], or in very small quantities, or frequently, or in large quantities, or accompanied by pain.

The receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) and the thick bowel (sthūlaguda) are the roots of the channels that carry feces. When these are vitiated, the specific signs of their disorder are as follows: one should know that a person's fecal-carrying channels are vitiated upon seeing him void stool with difficulty, in small quantities, accompanied by sound and pain, excessively liquid, excessively hard, or in excessive amounts.

The root of the sweat-carrying channels is fat and the hair follicles; when these are indeed vitiated, this is their specific clinical knowledge: namely, one should know that a person's sweat-carrying channels are vitiated upon observing the absence of perspiration, excessive perspiration, roughness, excessive smoothness of the body, a burning sensation, and horripilation.

3.5.9 | *Srotas*, *sirās*, *dhamanīs*, *rasāyanīs*, *rasavāhinīs*, *nāḍīs*, *pathins*, *mārgas*, the cavities of the body (*śarīracchidrāṇi*), whether closed or open, the locations (*sthānas*), the receptacles (*āśayas*), and the abodes (*niketas*)—these are the names for the visible and invisible spaces within the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). Through their provocation, the bodily constituents situated in their own locations as well as those moving through the channels (*mārga-gas*) undergo provocation; and through the provocation of others, the others likewise do so. When provoked, the channels corrupt only the channels, and the constituents corrupt only the constituents.
In all of these cases, it is the vitiated wind, bile, and phlegm that act as the corrupters, due to the inherent nature of the doshas.

Through wasting, suppression [of natural urges], dryness, physical exercise, hunger,
and other severe afflictions, the channels carrying the vital breath (prāṇa) become vitiated.
3.5.11 | The water-carrying channels become impaired by heat, undigested matter (āma), fear, excessive drinking, the consumption of overly dry food,

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Classification of Channels" (*srotovimāna*), in the Section on Specific Determinations (*vimānasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Six:
3.6.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the specific determination of the groups of diseases (*rogānīkavimāna*).
3.6.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

3.6.3 | There are two groups of diseases according to their efficacy: the curable and the incurable; two groups according to their intensity: the mild and the severe; two groups according to their location: those located in the mind and those located in the body; two groups according to their cause: those caused by the imbalance of one's own constituent elements (dhātus) and those caused by external factors; and two groups according to their site of origin: those arising from the stomach (āmāśaya) and those arising from the large intestine (pakvāśaya).

Thus, this [reality], being twofold due to the distinctions of power (*prabhāva*), empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), cause (*nimitta*), and intention (*āśaya*), may—when divided by means of another fundamental nature (*prakṛti*)—either be differentiated or, alternatively, be unified; it may thus be either one or many.

First, regarding unity: there is indeed only one category of disease (*rogānīka*), because suffering is common to all. Regarding plurality, however, there are ten categories of disease due to differences in their specific powers and so forth. Furthermore, this plurality may be either numerable (*saṃkhyeya*) or innumerable (*asaṃkhyeya*). Among these, the numerable is as stated in the *Aṣṭodarīya* chapter; the innumerable, on the other hand, is as described in the *Mahārogādhyāya*, because the descriptions of the symptoms, origins, and other characteristics of diseases are beyond counting.

3.6.4 | Nor can there be any faulty proposition here on the grounds that there is contradiction regarding the number of divisions when they are of different natures; nor can it be faultless on the grounds that there is no contradiction.

For the divider divides the object to be divided in one way, but by dividing that same divided thing again through another nature of division, he brings about a specific numerical distinction of divisions in many ways, and does not destroy the previous total of divisions.
Indeed, even when the nature of the division is the same, another application of the process must be taken into account.
There are meanings that are distinct yet expressed by identical words, and there are meanings that are not distinct yet expressed by synonymous words.

For the word "roga" (disease) is common to both the *doṣas* (humors) and the *vyādhis* (manifest diseases). Indeed, the *doṣas* also receive the names *roga*, *ātaṅka*, *yakṣman*, *doṣaprakṛti*, and *vikāra*; and the *vyādhis* likewise receive the names *roga*, *ātaṅka*, *yakṣman*, *doṣaprakṛti*, and *vikāra*.
In this regard, the term *roga* is common to both the *doṣas* and the *vyādhis*, whereas it is specific to the others.

3.6.5 | In this regard, diseases are innumerable due to their extreme multiplicity; however, the doshas are indeed numerable because they are not so numerous. Therefore, we shall explain the various types of disorders by way of illustration, and the doshas without exception.
Rajas and tamas are the two mental doshas.
The modifications of these two are desire, anger, greed, delusion, envy, pride, intoxication, sorrow, mental agitation, fear, joy, and so forth.
Furthermore, wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman) are indeed the bodily humors (doṣas).
Their modifications as well include fever, diarrhea, swelling, wasting, asthma, urinary disorders, leprosy, and so forth.
Thus have the defects (doṣas) alone and a portion of the disorders (vikāras) been explained.

3.6.6 | In this regard, there are indeed three types of provocation for both these groups of doshas; namely: unwholesome contact of the sense organs with their objects, intellectual error, and the effects of time (metabolic transformation).
3.6.7 | Indeed, when provoked by specific aggravating factors and specific corruptible elements, they bring about innumerable specific disorders.
3.6.8 | And those modifications, following one another, sometimes bind together, such as desire and the like, or fever and the like.
3.6.9 | However, the connection between rajas and tamas is constant with one another; for tamas does not proceed without rajas.

3.6.10 | Generally, when the bodily doshas occupy a single location, there occurs either a sannipāta (combined aggravation) or a saṃsarga (conjunction), due to their having similar qualities; for the doshas are indeed identical in their corrupting properties.

3.6.11 | Regarding that, the distinction between the primary disorder (*anubandhya*) and the secondary disorder (*anubandha*) is as follows: in an independent case, the primary disorder (*anubandhya*) is one whose symptoms are manifest and which exhibits the aforementioned onset and subsidence; the secondary disorder (*anubandha*), however, possesses characteristics contrary to that.
If the doshas present there are endowed with the characteristics of the primary disorder, they call it a triad (*trika*), i.e., *sannipāta*, or a pair, i.e., *saṃsarga*.
However, the differentiation of the doshas is manifold, being caused by the specific distinctions between the primary and secondary disorders.
Thus, this arrangement of various specific natures regarding the humors and diseases is based on conceptualization by physicians.

3.6.12 | Regarding the bodily fires (*agni*), there is a fourfold distinction based on the variation in their strength. Namely: sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), dull (*manda*), even (*sama*), and irregular (*viṣama*). Among these, the sharp fire tolerates all types of improper conduct; the dull fire possesses characteristics opposite to that; the even fire, however, falls into a state of disorder through improper conduct but remains in its natural state when there is no improper conduct; and the irregular fire possesses characteristics opposite to those of the even fire.

These are the four types of digestive fires (agni) belonging to the four types of persons. Among them, the fires of those whose *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* are in equilibrium and established in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*) are balanced (*sama*). However, in those of a *vāta* constitution, the fires become irregular (*viṣama*) because the seat of the fire (*agnyadhiṣṭhāna*) is overwhelmed by *vāta*. In those of a *pitta* constitution, the fires become sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) because the seat of the fire is overwhelmed by *pitta*. In those of a *śleṣman* constitution, the fires become weak (*manda*) because the seat of the fire is overwhelmed by *śleṣman*.

3.6.13 | Regarding this, some say: there are no living beings whose vāta, pitta, and śleṣman are in equilibrium, because humans consume irregular food; therefore, some are of vāta constitution (prakṛti), some are of pitta constitution, and others are of śleṣman constitution.

And that is untenable. For what reason? Physicians maintain that health consists in the equilibrium of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*); since health is the natural state (*prakṛti*) and medical treatment is undertaken for the sake of health, and that [health] is the desired condition, therefore there exist those with balanced *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman*. Indeed, there are no such things as "wind-natures," "bile-natures," or "phlegm-natures."

It is said that due to the predominance of this or that specific humor (*doṣa*), each particular temperament (*prakṛti*) is designated for human beings; however, since the state of being established in one's natural constitution (*prakṛtisthatva*) is not possible when the humors are in a state of disorder (*vikṛta*), these [temperaments] are not actually constitutions. Rather, there certainly exist those who are of windy (*vātalāḥ*), bilious (*pittalāḥ*), and phlegmatic (*śleṣmalāḥ*) natures, but they should be known as being non-constituted (*aprakṛtistha*).

3.6.14 | Indeed, for these four types of persons, there are four corresponding therapeutic applications (*anupraṇidhāna*) that lead to well-being. Among them, for those whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are all in equilibrium, [the application] should be balanced in every respect. For the other three, who have an excess of humors (*doṣa*), three therapeutic applications—each acting as an antidote to their respective predominant humor—are beneficial, until equilibrium is reached; once equilibrium is attained, however, the treatment must be balanced. Other such activities and medicinal applications shall be explained in detail below.
3.6.15 | There are three types of persons who are prone to illness, yet they are not ill according to the physicians of other medical systems.
They are as follows: those of a windy temperament (vātala), those of a bilious temperament (pittala), and those of a phlegmatic temperament (śleṣmala).

Their specific characteristics are as follows: in one of windy temperament, diseases caused by wind are predominant; in one of bilious temperament, those caused by bile; and in one of phlegmatic temperament, those caused by phlegm—these generally being more severe.

3.6.16 | In that regard, in a person of vāta constitution who indulges in factors that aggravate vāta, vāta quickly reaches a state of provocation, whereas the other two doṣas do not do so to the same extent; having become provoked, it afflicts the body with the aforementioned disorders, leading to the impairment of strength, complexion, happiness, and lifespan.

The method for its conquest is as follows: the application of oleation and sudation according to the prescribed rules; mild purificatory measures combined with unctuous, warm, sweet, sour, and salty substances; likewise, suitable foods; massage, poultices, wrapping, rubbing, affusion, immersion baths, gentle stroking, pressing, frightening, startling, and diverting the mind; the preparation of wines and fermented liquors; various types of unctuous substances processed with digestive, carminative, wind-alleviating, and purgative agents; as well as those cooked a hundred times or a thousand times for general use; enemas; the rules for administering enemas; and a pleasant lifestyle.

3.6.17 | Even in one who is of a bilious temperament (*pittala*), if they indulge in things that provoke bile (*pitta-prakopaṇa*), the bile quickly reaches a state of provocation, whereas the other two humors (*doṣas*) do not do so to the same extent. Once provoked, it afflicts the body with the aforementioned disorders, leading to the impairment of strength, complexion, happiness, and lifespan.

The means for its subjugation are as follows: drinking ghee, oleation with ghee, downward elimination of the morbid humors (doṣas), the consumption of medicinal herbs and foods that are sweet, bitter, astringent, and cooling; the enjoyment of fragrances that are mild, sweet, pleasant-smelling, cool, and heart-pleasing; and the wearing upon the chest of strings of pearls and gems that have been kept in extremely cold water, at every moment.

Sprinkling with water cooled by *aguru*, sandalwood, *priyaṅgu*, *kālīya*, lotus stalks, and cool breezes, and with waters scented by blue lotuses, white lotuses, red lotuses, fragrant lilies, and lotuses; listening to songs and instrumental music that are pleasant to the ear, soft, sweet, and agreeable to the mind; hearing of auspicious events; association with friends; and union with beloved women wearing cool garments and garlands, dwelling in palatial mansions cooled by the rays of the moon and gentle breezes.

[This includes] resorting to mountain interiors, riverbanks, cool dwellings, clothing, and the breeze from fans; frequenting delightful groves where pleasant, cool, and fragrant breezes prevail; attending to lotuses—*padma*, *utpala*, *nalina*, *kumuda*, *saugandhika*, *puṇḍarīka*, and *śatapatra*—held in the hands; and [cultivating] all gentle dispositions. (3.6.18) Even for one of phlegmatic temperament (*śleṣmala*), if they indulge in factors that aggravate phlegm, their phlegm quickly becomes provoked, whereas the other two *doṣas* do not [become so provoked] in the same way.
Having become provoked, it afflicts his body with the aforementioned disorders for the purpose of destroying his strength, complexion, happiness, and lifespan.

The method for its subjugation is as follows: purificatory therapies (saṃśodhana) prepared with sharp and hot substances; foods consisting mostly of dry matter, seasoned with pungent, bitter, and astringent tastes; likewise, running, leaping, swimming, walking about, staying awake, wrestling, sexual intercourse, physical exercise, massage, bathing, and rubbing the body; specifically, the consumption of sharp wines that have stood for a long time; the practice of smoking (dhūmapāna); fasting in all respects; wearing warm clothing; and the avoidance of comforts for the sake of comfort itself.
And there is a verse on this point:
"One who knows the specific nature of all diseases, who understands the specific requirements of every task,
and who knows the true essence of all medicinal substances— such a person shall become the lord of the king's life."
3.6.20 | Regarding this, there are these verses:—The classification of the groups of diseases according to the distinctions among the different constitutions (prakṛti);
their mutual non-contradiction; and the commonality between diseases and the humors (doṣa).
3.6.21 | The enumeration of the humors (doṣas), a portion of the disorders (vikāras), their aggravating factors (prakopaṇa),
concern regarding digestion (jaraṇa), and the factors that diminish the digestive fire (kāyāgni).

3.6.22 | Furthermore, the means for restoring the natural state of individuals with constitutions characterized by an excess of *vāta* and other humors have been expounded by the Great Sage in this Vimāna-section on the Classification of Diseases.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Classification of the Multitude of Diseases," in the Section on Specific Determination (*Vimānasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Seven:
3.7.1 Now, we shall expound the specific determination concerning the appearance of those who are afflicted by disease (*Vyādhitarūpīya-vimāna*).
3.7.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
3.7.3 | Indeed, in this world there are two types of persons who appear ill: one who is severely ill and one who is mildly ill.

Among them, the severely ill person may appear as if mildly ill because he is endowed with excellence of mind (*sattva*), strength, and body; whereas the other, the mildly ill person, may appear as if severely ill because of the inferiority of his mind and other qualities.
Unskilled physicians, judging solely by what they see with the eye, fall into error regarding the severity or mildness of their illnesses.
3.7.4 | Indeed, complete knowledge regarding the entirety of what is to be known does not arise through a mere fragment of knowledge.
For those who are mistaken indeed err even in their knowledge of diseases and the application of therapeutic measures.

When they encounter a patient with a severe illness appearing as one with a mild illness, they consider him to have few morbid humors (doṣas) and, by administering a mild purification (saṃśodhana) at the time of cleansing, they further aggravate his humors.

When, however, those who are slightly ill manifest the appearance of being severely ill, physicians consider that a great fault; at the time of purification, they administer a sharp purgative to him, and by excessively eliminating the humors (doṣas), they emaciate his body.
In this way, those who imagine they possess knowledge of the whole field of knowledge through a mere fragment of it stumble.

But physicians who have mastered what is to be known, having examined everything in every way as far as possible, reach a firm conclusion and never err; thus, they accomplish their intended purpose exactly as desired.
3.7.5 | Furthermore, there are verses on this point:
Having observed the manifestation of disease in a patient through the variations of the *sattva* and other factors,
the ignorant misjudge the strength and weakness of that disease.
3.7.6 | Deluded by ignorance, they employ these medicines improperly,
leading to the destruction or even the great suffering of those who are afflicted with disease.
3.7.7 | But the wise, having understood everything and examined it here in every way,
never falter in the application of medicines.

3.7.8 | Having thus heard from the venerable Ātreya, in this section on the forms of disease, the enumeration of the forms of disease, the possibility of their occurrence, the causes for discrepancies regarding the forms and etiology of diseases along with their exceptions, and the causes for consensus that are without exception, Agniveśa, having clasped the feet of the venerable Ātreya, asked what follows concerning the specific origins, locations, shapes, colors, names, potencies, and treatments of all worms that reside in the feces.
