3.7.9 | Then the venerable Ātreya spoke to him: "In this matter, Agniveśa, twenty types of parasites have previously been mentioned, distinguished by various classifications, with the exception of those that are congenital (*sahaja*). When further divided according to their origins (*prakṛti*), they become fourfold: namely, those born of feces (*purīṣaja*), those born of phlegm (*śleṣmaja*), those born of blood (*śoṇitaja*), and those born of impurities (*malaja*)."

3.7.10 | In this regard, impurity (mala) is both external and internal. Among these, we shall describe those born from external impurities. Their origin is the avoidance of cleansing; their habitat is the hair of the head, beard, body hair, eyelashes, and clothing; their form is minute, shaped like sesame seeds, and many-legged; their color is black and white; their names are lice (yūkā) and nits (pipīlikā); their effect is the production of itching and the manifestation of eruptions and pustules; and their treatment consists of extraction, the destruction of impurity, and the avoidance of substances that cause impurity.

3.7.11 | Indeed, the etiology of those [diseases] born of blood is the same as that of skin diseases (kuṣṭha). Their location is the blood-carrying vessels (dhamanīs). Their configuration is minute, circular, and rootless; some are invisible due to their subtlety. Their color is coppery. Their names are: keśādā, lomādā, lomadvīpā, saurasā, auḍumbarā, and jantumātaraḥ.

Their specific manifestations are the falling out of hair, beard, nails, body hair, and eyelashes; the itching, crawling sensations, and discharge from ulcers; and, when excessively advanced, the devouring of the skin, vessels, ligaments, flesh, and cartilage. Their treatment is also similar to that of the *kuṣṭha* diseases, which we shall explain later.

3.7.12 | Those born of *śleṣman* (phlegm) arise from the consumption of milk, jaggery, sesame, fish, meat of marshy animals, flour-based foods, fine rice preparations, safflower oil, as well as undigested food, putrid, moist, mixed, incompatible, and unwholesome meals; their site is the stomach (*āmāśaya*), and as they increase, they spread upwards, downwards, or in both directions.

As for the specific variations in their shape and color: some are white, broad, and shaped like a *bradhna* (the glans penis); some are circular in circumference, shaped like earthworms, white with a coppery luster; and some are minute, long, thread-like, and white. The names of these three types of worms caused by *śleṣman* are: *antrādāḥ*, *udarādāḥ*, *hṛdayacarāḥ*, *curavaḥ*, *darbhapuṣpāḥ*, *saugandhikāḥ*, and *mahāgudaḥ*.

The symptoms are: loss of luster, nausea, salivation from the mouth, anorexia, indigestion, fever, fainting, yawning, sneezing, abdominal distension, body ache, vomiting, emaciation, and roughness of the skin.

3.7.13 | Those born from feces have the same origin as those born from phlegm (*śleṣman*); their location is the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*). As they grow, they spread downward; however, if they should move toward the stomach (*āmāśaya*), then during that interval, his eructations and breaths will smell of feces. As for the specific distinctions of their shape and color: some are thin, round, and broad, white, long, and resemble the fibers of wool; others, however, are thick, round, and broad, and are dark-brown, blue, green, or yellow.

Their names are Kakerukas, Makerukas, Lelihās, Śaśūlakas, and Sausurādās. Their effects are: breaking of the stool, emaciation, roughness, and the production of horripilation. Furthermore, these very worms remain at the opening of the anus, biting it and producing itching; when they become excited, they repeatedly emerge from the anus. Such is the distinction regarding the origin and other characteristics of the worms born of phlegm (śleṣma) and those born of feces (purīṣa).
3.7.14 | Having taught the treatment for these [parasites] in brief, we shall hereafter teach it in detail.
In that regard, first of all, the extraction of all parasites must be performed; thereafter, the destruction of their habitat; and subsequently, the avoidance of those factors mentioned as causes.

3.7.15 | Regarding that, extraction (*apakarṣaṇa*) consists of removing [the parasites] by grasping them with the hand and examining them, using an instrument or without one; however, for parasites located in their specific sites, extraction should properly be performed by means of medicine, and that is of four kinds: namely, head-evacuation (*śirovirecana*), emesis (*vamana*), purgation (*virecana*), and non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*); such is the procedure for extraction.

As for the destruction of their natural constitution (*prakṛtivighāta*), it is the administration of substances that are pungent, bitter, astringent, alkaline, and hot, as well as anything else that is antagonistic to phlegm (*śleṣman*) and feces; such is the destruction of their natural constitution.

Next is the non-indulgence in those factors mentioned in the section on etiology—that is, the avoidance of what was described in the rules for etiology, as well as other substances of a similar nature.
Thus has treatment been explained according to its characteristics;
this very same subject shall now be taught again in detail.

3.7.16 | Now, having first treated a patient with worms in the digestive tract (krimikoṣṭha) for six or seven nights with oleation and sudation, the physician, intending to administer a purgative on the following day, should provide the patient with meals in the morning and evening consisting of milk, jaggery, curd, sesame, fish, meat of marshy animals, flour-based foods, fine rice, and safflower oil, in order to agitate the worms and cause them to move toward the digestive tract.

Then, when the night has dawned, having ascertained that the patient has slept comfortably and digested his food well, one should administer non-unctuous enemas, emetics, and purgatives on that very day, provided they are indicated, after thoroughly examining all specific contraindications.

3.7.17 | Then he should say, "Bring [the following]": radish, mustard, garlic, *karañja*, *śitru*, *madhuśigru*, *kharapuṣpā*, *bhūstṛṇa*, *sumukha*, *surasā*, *kuṣṭha*, *erakā*, *gaṇḍīra*, *kālamālaka*, *parṇāsa*, *kṣavaka*, and *phaṇijjhaka*; either all of these or as many as are available.

Having observed those [drugs] brought together, having cut them into pieces, washed them with water, and placed them in a well-washed vessel, one should cook them by pouring over them cow’s urine mixed with half as much water, stirring constantly with a ladle. When most of the water has been consumed and the medicinal substances have lost their juice, one should remove the vessel from the fire; then, having strained the decoction thoroughly, one should pour it—while still lukewarm—into the enema bag (basti), adding a paste of madanaphala, pippalī, and viḍaṅga, along with oil and svarjika salt.

One should administer this enema according to the prescribed rules; likewise, one may administer it with a decoction of arka, alarka, kuṭaja, āḍhakī, kuṣṭha, and kaiḍarya; or with a decoction of śigru, pīlu, kustumburu, kaṭukā, and sarṣapa; or with a decoction of āmalaka, śṛṅgavera, dāruharidrā, and picumarda, prepared with the addition of the group of drugs beginning with madanaphala—one should administer it three times or for seven nights.

3.7.18 | When the final enema has returned and the patient has recovered, one should on that very day skillfully administer a purificatory agent that acts as a dual-evacuant (both upward and downward). Its procedure shall be taught as follows: having stirred one akṣa measure of the paste of *trivṛt* into half-an-āñjali measure of a decoction of *madana* fruit and *pippalī*, one should give it to him to drink; this effectively eliminates his morbid humors from both channels.
In the same manner, the physician, observing all specific details with his intellect, should administer emetics and purgatives mentioned in the Kalpa section by combining them appropriately.
3.7.19 | Then, having recognized that he has been properly purged, one should sprinkle him with lukewarm decoction of *śaikharika* in the afternoon.

One should constantly perform all water-related activities, both external and internal, with that same decoction; in its absence, one should sprinkle him with decoctions of pungent, bitter, and astringent medicinal herbs, or with urine and alkaline preparations.

Having sprinkled him with water and led him into a windless chamber, one should treat him gradually with gruels (yavāgū) and other foods prepared with long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), chaba pepper (cavya), leadwort (citraka), and dry ginger (śṛṅgavera). Once he has reached the stage of thin gruel (vilepī), one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with vidanga oil every other day, twice or thrice.

3.7.20 | If, however, one should perceive that the worms have become excessively increased and are occasionally crawling within the head itself, then, having prepared the patient's head with oleation and sudation, one should purge it by means of a head-purgative (śirovirecana) using the seeds of *apāmārga* and similar substances.

3.7.21 | Now we shall explain that dietary regimen for worms which was prescribed for the destruction of their natural state: having gathered the *mūlakaparṇī* plant together with its roots, tips, and tendrils, one should cut it into pieces, pound it in a mortar, press it with the hands, and extract the juice. Having mixed red *śāli* rice flour with that juice, one should form a cake (*pūpalikā*), bake it on smokeless embers, and administer it, seasoned with *viḍaṅga* oil and salt, for a person suffering from intestinal worms to eat.

One should administer [the medicine], and immediately thereafter, one should have the patient drink sour gruel (*amlakāñjika*) or whey (*udaśvit*) mixed with the five groups of drugs beginning with *pippalī*, along with salt. According to this same method, one may prepare cakes (*pūpalikā*) using the juice of any one of the following: *mārka-va*, *arka*, *sahacara*, *nīpa*, *nirguṇḍī*, *sumukha*, *surasā*, *kuṭheraka*, *gaṇḍīra*, *kālamālaka*, *parṇāsa*, *kṣavaka*, *phaṇijjhaka*, *bakula*, *kuṭaja*, or *suvarṇakṣīrī*.

Likewise, one should prepare cakes (pūpalikās) using the expressed juices of kiṇihī, kirātatiktaka, suvahā, āmalaka, harītakī, and bibhītaka; and one should give these juices—either individually, in pairs, or all together, mixed with honey—to the patient in the morning on an empty stomach to drink.

3.7.22 | Now, having collected horse dung and spread it out on a large mat, one should dry it in the sun, pound it in a mortar, and then have it ground into fine powder on a grinding stone. Having thoroughly impregnated it eight or ten times with a decoction of *viḍaṅga* or a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) while in the sun, and having again had it ground into fine powder on a grinding stone, one should place it in a new jar and store it in a protected place.
Of these powders, one should give a palmful, or as much as seems appropriate, mixed with honey, for the patient suffering from intestinal worms to lick.

3.7.23 | Likewise, having collected the seeds of *bhallātaka* and crushed them to the measure of a *kalaśa*, one should place them in a strong *kalaśa* jar that has been treated with oil and fitted with a lid containing many fine holes. Having wrapped the body [of the patient] in clay, covered it with a wooden board (*uḍupa*), and placed it upon another strong jar that has likewise been treated with oil and buried up to its neck in the ground, one should pile cow-dung around it on all sides and set it on fire. When one knows that the cow-dung is well-burnt and the *bhallātaka* seeds have lost their oiliness, then one should remove that jar.

Then, having taken oil from that second jar and mixing it with powdered *viḍaṅga* seeds in a quantity equal to half the oil, one should leave it in the sun for the entire day. After that, one should give a dose of it to him to drink; by this, he is properly purged, and for one who has been purged, the subsequent regimen is as previously stated.
In exactly the same manner, one should prepare the oils from the heartwood of *bhadradāru* and *sarala* and give them to him to drink.
3.7.24 | And one should administer an unctuous enema to this patient at the proper time for an unctuous enema.

3.7.25 | Then he should say, "Bring [the following]": autumnal new rice and sesame seeds that have reached full maturity. Having brought them, he should thoroughly winnow them, cleanse them until they are perfectly pure, and place them in lukewarm decoction of *viḍaṅga* until their impurities are gone. Observing that the impurities have departed, he should pluck them well, winnow them again until thoroughly winnowed, and cleanse them until perfectly pure. Then, having infused them twenty-one times with the decoction of *viḍaṅga*, he should dry them in the sun.

Having crushed [the seeds] in a mortar and ground them finely again on a grinding stone, one should place them in a wooden tub (droṇī) and, repeatedly sprinkling them with a decoction of *viḍaṅga*, massage them with the hands alone. While they are being pressed, whatever oil rises to the surface should be collected by both hands, placed in a clean and sturdy jar, and stored in a protected place.

3.7.26 | Then he should say, "Bring these": two bilva-sized boluses of *tilvaka* and *uddālaka*, finely ground with a decoction of *viḍaṅga*; half that amount each of *śyāmā* and *trivṛt*; half that amount each of *dantī* and *dravantī*; and half that amount each of *cavya* and *citraka*.

Having mixed this collection of ingredients with half an āḍhaka measure of viḍaṅga decoction, having added that one-prastha measure of oil, and having stirred everything together, one should pour it into a large vessel, place it over the fire, and sitting comfortably on a seat, observing the oil from all sides, one should cook it continuously with a gentle fire, constantly stirring it with a ladle.

When he knows that the sound has ceased, the froth has subsided, the oil has become clear, the fragrance, color, and taste have each arisen as they should, and the medicinal preparation, when being kneaded with the two fingers, is neither too soft nor too hard and does not stick to the fingers—this is the time for its administration.

Then, having removed it and cooled it, having strained it through a large cloth, having poured it into a clean, sturdy jar, having covered it with a lid, and having wrapped it with a white cloth-strip, he should store it well-secured and well-guarded with a string.

Then one should give him the proper dose for drinking; by that, he is properly purged. For one whose morbid humors have been correctly eliminated, the subsequent regimen is as previously described. Then, at the time for an unctuous enema, one should administer an unctuous enema to him.
And by this very same method of preparation, having prepared the oils of mustard, linseed, *karanja*, and *kosātaki*, one should cause him to drink them, disregarding all specific variations.
Therefore, he becomes unattached.
3.7.27 | Thus, the specific origins, shapes, colors, names, potencies, and treatments of the two types of worms arising from phlegm and feces have been explained in general.

Specifically, for worms born of feces, the treatment should consist primarily of non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), and purgatives (anulomaharaṇa) using those very same medicinal substances in small doses. Furthermore, for worms born of phlegm (śleṣman), the treatment should be performed with those same medicinal substances in larger doses, consisting primarily of head-purgatives (śirovirecana), emetics (vamana), and palliative measures (upaśamana). Thus, this therapeutic procedure for destroying worms has been explained.
One who follows it must strive to avoid the respective causes [of each type of worm].
Thus, this treatment for intestinal worms has been explained correctly, exactly as it was set forth.
3.7.28 | And there are these verses on the subject:
The initial medicinal treatment for worms is considered to be their extraction;
thereafter follows the destruction of their habitat and the avoidance of their causative factors.
3.7.29 | This very same threefold procedure which has been proclaimed with reference to parasites is seen to be the method for the suppression of all disorders as well.
3.7.30 | Purification, pacification, and the avoidance of the causative factors—
these are the duties to be performed by a skilled physician for each disease according to the prescribed rules.
3.7.31 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
Two types of diseased persons—the knowledgeable and the ignorant—and two types of physicians with their respective purposes;
twenty types of parasites, and for them, the group of seven beginning with the etiology (hetu).
3.7.32 | This has been declared by the supreme seer in the Vimāna section on the nature of disease,
for the purpose of enlightening the disciples and for the alleviation of diseases.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Forms of Disease," in the Section on Determination (*Vimānasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Eight:
3.8.1 Now, we shall expound the determination concerning the physician’s victory over disease (*rogabhiṣagjitīya-vimāna*).
3.8.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

3.8.3 | A wise person, desiring to become a physician, should first examine the scripture itself by means of logical reasoning, having understood for himself the relative importance of tasks, the fruits of actions, their consequences, as well as place and time.

Indeed, various treatises of physicians circulate in the world; among them, one should consider that which is highly renowned, practiced by wise men, rich in meaning, honored by authoritative persons, beneficial for the intellects of the three types of students, free from the defect of redundancy, authored by a sage (*ārṣa*), possessing a well-arranged sequence of aphorisms, commentaries, and summaries, self-sustaining, with words that do not fall into error, using unstrained terminology, abundant in expression, conveying its subject matter through traditional succession, and primarily dedicated to the ascertainment of the true nature of reality.
One should resort to that treatise which has a coherent meaning, whose chapters are not confused, which provides quick awakening, and which is endowed with both definitions and illustrations;
for such a treatise, like the stainless sun, dispels darkness and illuminates everything.

3.8.4 | Immediately thereafter, one should examine the teacher (*ācārya*). He should be as follows: one whose learning is purified, who has witnessed the performance of medical acts, who is skillful, upright, pure, with a steady hand, provided with necessary equipment, endowed with all his faculties, knowledgeable of nature (*prakṛti*), knowledgeable of the proper course of treatment (*pratipatti*), free from hypocrisy, devoid of egoism, not envious, not prone to anger, patient with afflictions, affectionate toward students, a capable instructor, and able to impart knowledge.
For a teacher possessing such qualities quickly endows a good student with the qualities of a physician, just as a seasonal cloud endows a fertile field with the qualities of a harvest.
3.8.5 | Having approached him with the desire to please him, one should serve him vigilantly as if he were fire, a god, a king, a father, and a master.

Then, having mastered the entire treatise through his favor, one should repeatedly and correctly exert oneself toward the firmness of the treatise, the excellence of its expression, the understanding of its meaning, and the power of speech.
3.8.6 | Regarding this, we shall explain the means: study, teaching, and discussion with those learned in that science—these are the means.

3.8.7 | In this regard, the rule for study is as follows: being healthy and having made leisure time, rising early in the morning or at dawn, having performed his necessary duties and sipped water, and having paid homage to the gods, sages, cows, Brahmins, teachers, elders, perfected ones (*siddhas*), and preceptors, he should sit comfortably in a level, clean place. With speech preceded by the mind, reciting the aphorism (*sūtra*) over and over again, he should repeatedly turn it over in his mind after having understood and correctly entered into the true nature of its meaning, both for the purpose of avoiding his own faults and for the purpose of weighing the faults of others.
In this manner, one should constantly practice the study [of the Veda] at midday, in the afternoon, and at night, never neglecting the recitation. Thus ends the rule for study.

3.8.8 | Now, the procedure for teaching: An ācārya who has resolved to teach should first examine the student. This is as follows: one who is tranquil, of noble disposition, not prone to mean actions, with straight eyes, face, nose, and bridge of the nose; with a thin, red, and clear tongue; with undamaged teeth and lips; not stammering; possessed of fortitude and free from arrogance; intelligent, endowed with reasoning and memory, of noble character, born into a family of that [medical] science, or at least one whose conduct conforms to that science.

They say that one who possesses these combined qualities is fit to be taught: one who is intent upon reality (*tattva*), free from physical defects, with senses not distracted by other things, composed, not arrogant, contemplating the true nature of things, free from anger, devoid of vices, endowed with virtue, purity, good conduct, devotion, dexterity, and courtesy; one who is eager for study, focused on the understanding of meaning and the observation of ritual action without other pursuits, free from greed, untiring, a well-wisher of all beings, one who carries out all the instructions of the teacher, and is devoted to him. Such a person, endowed with this collection of virtues, they declare to be worthy of instruction.

3.8.9 | When such a seeker of study has approached, desiring to please the teacher, the teacher should address him as follows: "During the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day when the blessed moon is in conjunction with any one of the lunar mansions—Tiṣya, Hasta, Śravaṇa, or Aśvayuj—and during an auspicious Karaṇa and at a Maitra Muhūrta, [the student], having shaved his head, observed the fast, bathed, and put on saffron-colored garments, with fragrant substances in his hand, [should bring] sacrificial fuel, fire, clarified butter, ointment, and water-pots."

"Taking garlands, lamps, gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, silk garments, and enclosures; as well as kusha grass, unhusked rice, mustard seeds, and grains of rice; white flowers, both strung and unstrung; pure foods fit for sacrifice, and powdered perfumes—approach [the fire] with these."
3.8.10 | He should act accordingly.

3.8.11 | Having recognized that he has arrived, one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring four cubits (*kuṣkura*), on level ground that slopes toward the east or the north. It should be smeared with cow-dung and water, strewn with *kuśa* grass, well-enclosed by boundary-sticks (*paridhi*) on all four sides, and adorned as prescribed with sandalwood, water-jars, linen, gold, silver, gems, pearls, and coral; and it should be beautified with pure food offerings, perfumes, white flowers, parched grain (*lāja*), mustard seeds, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). Then, having done so, there—

Having kindled the fire with fuel-sticks of *pālāśa*, *aiṅguda*, *audumbara*, or *mādhuka* wood, facing east and being pure, he should perform the rules for study and offer oblations three times each with honey and clarified butter into the fire, using mantras associated with blessings, while addressing Brahmā, Agni, Dhanvantari, Prajāpati, the Aśvins, Indra, the ṛṣis, and the authors of the Sūtras, beginning first with "Svāhā."
3.8.12 | The disciple should touch him [the teacher] in turn.
Having offered the oblation, he should circumambulate the fire keeping it to his right.
Having completed the circumambulation, he should cause the Brāhmaṇas to pronounce auspicious blessings; he should also honor the physicians.

3.8.13 | Then, in the presence of the fire, the Brāhmaṇa, and the physician, he should instruct him as follows: "You must remain a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), maintain a beard, speak the truth, abstain from meat, consume only pure substances, be free from envy, and not carry weapons. Furthermore, nothing should be done by you against my word, except for that which is forbidden by the king, or that which would cause loss of life, or that which is vast, unrighteous, or associated with harm."

You must always remain one who has offered himself to me, who makes me his primary concern, who is dependent on me, and who follows what is dear and beneficial to me. You should attend upon and dwell with me by serving me like a son, like a slave, and like a petitioner; you should move about with humility, attentiveness, single-mindedness, discipline, and careful deliberation before acting, and without malice. Whether permitted or unpermitted to move about, you should first strive according to your ability to provide for the needs of the teacher.

O physician, desiring the accomplishment of your duties, the fulfillment of your goals, the acquisition of fame, and heaven after death, you must daily—whether rising or sitting—seek the welfare of all living beings, beginning with cows and Brahmins. You must strive with your whole being for the recovery of the sick; even for the sake of your own life, you must not harm patients, nor should you, even in thought, approach the wives of others, nor any property belonging to another, maintaining a modest appearance and attire.

One must be free from intoxication, sinless, and without sinful companions; one whose speech is gentle, pure, righteous, comforting, auspicious, truthful, beneficial, and measured; one who considers place and time, possesses mindfulness, and is always diligent in the excellence of knowledge, exertion, and the necessary means.

Furthermore, one should never administer medicine to those who are hated by the king or who hate the king, nor to those who are hated by the public or who hate the public; likewise, it should not be given to anyone whose conduct, character, behavior, or social dealings are excessively deceitful, wicked, or characterized by suffering, nor to those who do not acknowledge their faults or seek remedy for them, nor to those who are on the verge of death, nor similarly to women who lack a guardian or who are without supervision.

And one must never accept food given by a woman if it has not been authorized by her husband or her guardian. Furthermore, when entering the house of a sick person, one should do so having been announced, with permission granted for entry, accompanied by a man, well-covered, with head bowed, mindful, composed, and acting with constant mental vigilance after repeatedly inspecting everything; and having entered, one’s speech, mind, intellect, and senses must not be directed toward anything else.

One should make aspirations for others except for the sick person—except for the sake of helping the sick person—regarding other states of being that have occurred to the sick person or others; nor should the internal affairs of the sick person's family be disclosed to outsiders. Even though you know it, you must not describe the shortened lifespan of the sick person if such a description would result in distress to the sick person or anyone else. Furthermore, even if one possesses knowledge, one should not boast excessively about one's own wisdom, for many people become greatly agitated by someone who boasts, even if they are trustworthy.

3.8.14 | Furthermore, there is truly no further shore to Āyurveda; therefore, one should constantly apply oneself to it with vigilance, for this is what must be done. Moreover, one should acquire excellence of conduct from others as well, without being envious, for the entire world is a teacher to the wise and an enemy to the unwise. Therefore, having reflected upon this, a wise person should listen to and follow the words even of an adversary when they teach that which is beneficial, conducive to fame, life-prolonging, nourishing, and worldly.

Beyond this, he should say: "You must always behave properly toward the deities, the sacred fire, the twice-born, your guru, the elders, and the perfected teachers (siddhācāryas). For you who behave properly toward them, this fire, all fragrances, tastes, jewels, and seeds, as well as the deities as they have been described, shall lead to your welfare; otherwise, for one who behaves differently, they shall lead to misfortune. When the teacher speaks thus, the disciple should say, "So be it. One who acts according to the instruction is fit to be taught; one who acts otherwise is unfit to be taught.

Indeed, by teaching those who are to be taught, the teacher attains union with the fruits of teaching as previously described, and through other unmentioned qualities that promote welfare, he unites both the student and himself with them.
Thus, the rule for teaching has been stated.
3.8.15 | Hereafter, we shall explain the rules for discussion: a physician should engage in discussion with another physician.

For conversation with those who possess that same knowledge produces joy through the application of wisdom; it brings about self-confidence, bestows the power of speech, and illuminates one's fame. It removes doubts regarding what was previously heard by hearing it again, and for one who has no doubt regarding what has been heard, it further establishes firm conviction. It also brings certain matters not yet heard within the range of the ear—whatever an instructor, being pleased, imparts to a disciple who is eager to learn.

He teaches the collection of meanings intended as secrets in due order; even while conversing with one another, the seeker of victory speaks out of joy through concise summaries. Therefore, the wise praise discourse with those who possess such knowledge.
3.8.16 | Indeed, discourse with those who possess that same knowledge is of two kinds: discourse by way of conciliation and discourse by way of opposition.

3.8.17 | In that regard, a formal discussion is conducted with one who is endowed with the power of knowledge, specialized understanding, speech, and reply; who is free from anger; whose learning is not artificial; who is without envy; who is conciliatory; who is skilled in conciliation; who is patient with afflictions; and who speaks with kindness.

When conversing with such a person, one should speak with confidence and also inquire with confidence; to him who asks with confidence, one should explain the matter clearly. One should not be agitated by the fear of being defeated, nor should one rejoice upon defeating him, nor boast before others, nor, out of delusion, become a partisan of an extreme view, nor describe a matter that is unknown. One should properly conciliate him with conciliation and remain attentive therein. This is the rule for favorable conversation.
3.8.18 | Thereafter, when engaging in a debate with another, one should speak while perceiving for oneself the connection to what is beneficial.
Even before the debate begins, one should thoroughly examine the other debater, the alternative positions, the relative strengths and weaknesses, and the specific characteristics of the assembly.
For thorough examination indicates to the wise the proper times for engagement in or withdrawal from an action; therefore, experts praise thorough examination.

Indeed, while examining the difference between the superior and the inferior, one should properly investigate these qualities of a debater, both those that are conducive to excellence and those that are defective. They are as follows: learning, discernment, retention, eloquence, and the power of speech—these qualities they say are conducive to excellence. These, however, are the defective ones: irritability, lack of confidence, timidity, lack of retention, and lack of attentiveness. One should weigh these qualities according to their relative importance, both for the opponent and for oneself.
3.8.19 | In that regard, the other [the opponent] turns out to be of three kinds—superior, inferior, or equal—due to the distribution of qualities; but never in their entirety.
3.8.20 | The assembly is indeed of two kinds: the knowledgeable assembly and the ignorant assembly.
That same twofold assembly is further divided into three types by this distinction of causes: the friendly assembly, the neutral assembly, and the hostile assembly.

In that regard, when an assembly is hostile, or when it is endowed with the power of knowledge, discernment, speech, and rebuttal, or when it is deluded, debate is not conducted by anyone with anyone at all. However, when the assembly is deluded but friendly or neutral, debate may be conducted even without the powers of knowledge, discernment, speech, and rebuttal—even with one who lacks radiant fame and is despised for his great speed of thought.

When conversing with such a person, one should speak using long, rambling sentences filled with convoluted arguments; laughing excessively and repeatedly, one should mock him while observing the assembly through facial expressions and not granting him any opportunity to speak. And while uttering words of reproach, one should say: "He is being defeated," or else, "Your proposition is inferior."

Furthermore, when being challenged, one should reply: "Your Honor has been [studying] for a full year; you have surely not attended upon a teacher, or perhaps this much is sufficient for you. For they say that even a single instance of a defeat is a total defeat; therefore, one should never engage in debate with him under any circumstances.
Some say that one may speak thus even after having entered into a dispute with a superior; however, those who are skilled do not praise engaging in a dispute with one who is truly greater.

3.8.21 | When debating with one who is inferior or considered equal, one should speak in an assembly of friends; or else, speaking in an assembly of neutral persons—one endowed with the capacity for attentive listening, comprehension, discernment, retention, and the ability to formulate and respond to arguments—one must, with focused attention, observe the opponent’s strength in terms of merits and defects. Having observed this, where one considers the opponent superior, one should not engage him in debate, avoiding any manifestation of such engagement; however, where one considers the opponent inferior, there one should quickly subdue him.

In that regard, these indeed are the means for the swift suppression of inferior opponents: namely, one should overwhelm one deficient in learning with a recitation of extensive sūtras; one deficient in discernment with a statement containing difficult terminology; one deficient in retaining statements with long, rambling, and convoluted strings of sentences; one deficient in presence of mind with a single type of expression that conveys multiple meanings; one deficient in the power of speech by interrupting a sentence before it is half-finished; one lacking confidence by causing embarrassment; one prone to anger by provoking him; one who is timid by terrifying him; and one who is inattentive by restraining him.
In this way, by these means, one shall quickly overcome the supreme and the inferior.
3.8.22 | Regarding this, there are two verses: One should speak with skill after having initiated a debate, and one should not suppress what is appropriate.
For speech that initiates a debate may bring about intense hostility in some.
3.8.23 | There is nothing that an angry man will not do, nor is there anything he will not say. The wise do not welcome quarreling in the assembly of the virtuous.
3.8.24 | When the debate has proceeded in this manner, one should act as follows.

3.8.25 | First of all, one should strive to do this: having formed an alliance with the assembly, one should cause them to appoint a topic for oneself that is favorable, or one that would be extremely difficult for the opponent, or one that would bring the opponent's position into sharp opposition. Then, when the assembly has been convened, one should say, "It is impossible for us to speak [on this]; this very assembly shall establish the debate and the rules of debate according to your wish, as is appropriate, and according to their own inclination," and having said this, one should remain silent.
3.8.26 | In this regard, the definition of the boundaries of debate is as follows: "This is to be stated; this is not to be stated; in this manner one becomes defeated."

3.8.27 | These categories, indeed, are to be mastered for the purpose of understanding the path of medical discourse (*bhiṣagvāda*); namely: proposition (*vāda*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), inherence (*samavāya*), thesis (*pratijñā*), establishment (*sthāpanā*), counter-establishment (*pratiṣṭhāpanā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), application (*upanaya*), conclusion (*nigamana*), rejoinder (*uttara*), tenet (*siddhānta*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), tradition (*aitihya*), analogy (*aupamya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), the erratic (*savyabhicāra*), inquiry (*jijñāsā*).

Resolution, attainment of the goal, possibility, the censurable, the non-censurable, interrogation, counter-interrogation, fault of speech, praise of speech, quibble, non-reason, mistimed, censure, rebuttal, loss of the proposition, admission, shifting the reason, irrelevance, and the point of defeat.

3.8.28 | Debate (*vāda*) is that which one discusses with another by means of formal treatises (*śāstra*), after having entered into a dispute. It is twofold in brief: disputation (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*). Therein, the speech of two parties who have taken up opposing sides is disputation; cavil is the opposite of disputation. For example: one side maintains that rebirth exists, while the other maintains it does not; these two establish their respective positions through reasons for their own sides and expose the weaknesses in the opponent's position—this is disputation.
Sophistry (*vitaṇḍā*) is the perversion of argumentation;
sophistry consists merely in stating faults in the opponent's position.
3.8.29 | Substance, quality, generality, particularity, and inherence have been previously explained with their own defining characteristics in the *Ślokasthāna*.
3.8.30 | Now, the proposition (*pratijñā*): a proposition is the statement of that which is to be proven; for example—"The self (*puruṣa*) is eternal."

3.8.31 | Now, regarding establishment (*sthāpanā*): establishment is the formal proof of that very proposition (*pratijñā*) by means of the reason (*hetu*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). For the proposition comes first, and the establishment comes afterwards; for what indeed could be established that has not been proposed? For example: the proposition is "the self (*puruṣa*) is eternal"; the reason is "because it is uncreated" (*akṛtakatvāt*); the example is "just like space (*ākāśa*)" (*yathā ākāśam*); the application is "and just as space is uncreated and that [space] is eternal, so too is the self"; the conclusion is "therefore, it is eternal."

3.8.32 | Now, regarding *pratiṣṭhāpanā* (re-establishment): *pratiṣṭhāpanā* is the establishment of a contrary meaning for that very same proposition (*pratijñā*) of the opponent. For example: the proposition is "The self (*puruṣa*) is impermanent"; the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is perceptible by the senses" (*aindriyakatvāt*); the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like a jar" (*yathā ghaṭa*); the application (*upanaya*) is "just as a jar is perceptible by the senses and it is impermanent, so too is this [self]"; and the conclusion (*nigamana*) is "therefore, it is impermanent."

3.8.33 | Now, as for the means of knowledge (*hetu*): a means of knowledge is the cause of apprehension; it consists of perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), tradition (*aitihya*), and analogy (*aupamya*). That which is apprehended by these means of knowledge is reality (*tattva*).

3.8.34 | Now, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*): An illustration is that wherein there is a consensus of understanding between the ignorant and the learned, which describes what is to be described. For example—"Fire is hot, water is liquid, the earth is stable, and the sun is illuminating"; just as the sun is illuminating, so too is the knowledge of Sāṃkhya illuminating.
3.8.35 | The means (upāya) and the conclusion (nigamana) have been explained in the exposition of the proof (sthāpanā) and the counter-proof (pratiṣṭhāpanā).

3.8.36 | Now, the "counter-argument" (uttara): A counter-argument is defined as stating a dissimilarity when a similarity has been presented as a reason, or stating a similarity when a dissimilarity has been presented as a reason.

For example, when someone says, "The morbid changes (vikāra) share the same nature as their causes; for instance, cold diseases share a similarity with their causes in the contact of snow, frost, and cold winds," another might reply: "The morbid changes are dissimilar to their causes; for instance, the burning, heat, suppuration, and suppuration of the body's parts are dissimilar to their cause, which is the contact of snow, frost, and cold winds.
This is the counter-argument, along with its opposite.

3.8.37 | Now, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*): An established doctrine is that conclusion which, having been examined in various ways by investigators and proven through logical reasons, is firmly settled.

It is of four kinds: the established doctrine common to all systems (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*), the established doctrine specific to a particular system (*pratitantra-siddhānta*), the established doctrine by implication (*adhikaraṇa-siddhānta*), and the established doctrine by provisional acceptance (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*). Among these, the established doctrine common to all systems refers to that which is well-known in every respective system; for example: "There are causes of disease," "There are diseases," and "There are means of cure for those [diseases] that are curable."

The tenet established in its own specific system (pratitantrasiddhānta) is that which is well-known within each respective tantra. For example: elsewhere there are eight tastes, whereas here there are six; elsewhere there are five sense organs, whereas in this tantra there are six; and while all disorders caused by Vāta and the others are described elsewhere as being caused solely by Vāta and so forth, here they are established as being caused both by Vāta and the like, as well as by the primary elements (bhūta).

The *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion by implication) is that wherein, when a particular topic is being introduced, other topics are also established; for example, when it is stated, "One who is liberated does not perform actions connected with [karmic] consequences because of his lack of desire," it follows as established that there are the results of action, liberation, the self, and existence after death.

The *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (presumptive tenet) is that which one accepts at the time of debate as an object that is unestablished, unexamined, untaught, or even without a logical reason; for example: "Having taken it that substance (*dravya*) is primary, we shall speak"; "Having taken it that quality (*guṇa*) is primary, we shall speak"; "Having taken it that potency (*vīrya*) is primary, we shall speak"—and so forth.
Thus is the fourfold tenet.

3.8.38 | Now, regarding "word" (śabda): a word is a collection of phonemes (varṇas). It is of four kinds: that which has a perceptible object, that which has an imperceptible object, the true, and the false.

Among these, that which has a perceptible object is as follows: "The humors (doṣas) become aggravated by three causes, they are pacified by six therapeutic measures, and there is the perception of sound and other objects when the ear and other senses are present.
That which has an imperceptible object, however, is: "There is an afterlife; there is liberation."

"Truth" (satya) means that which is in accordance with reality: Ayurvedic instructions exist; there exist means for the successful treatment of curable diseases; and there exist fruits resulting from undertakings. Untruth (anṛta) is the opposite of truth.

3.8.39 | Now, perception (*pratyakṣa*): perception is that which is apprehended by oneself through both the self and the sense organs. Among these, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and so forth are perceived by the self, whereas sound and the other [objects] are perceived by the sense organs.

3.8.40 | Now, inference (anumāna)—inference is reasoning based on logical connection; for example: [inferring] fire by the power of digestion, strength by the power of exertion, the sense organs such as hearing by the perception of sound and so forth, and so on.
3.8.41 | Now, regarding tradition (aitihya): tradition is the instruction of a reliable authority, such as the Vedas and so forth.

3.8.42 | Now, comparison (*aupamya*): comparison is the manifestation of the similarity of one thing with another by means of the latter; for example—as that of Daṇḍaka by means of Daṇḍin, of Dhanuḥstamba by means of Dhanu, and of Ārogyada by means of Iṣvāsa.

3.8.43 | Now, regarding doubt (*saṃśaya*): doubt is defined as a lack of certainty concerning objects that are characterized by uncertainty; for example—since we observe men who possess the marks of longevity and those who do not, as well as those who practice [regimen] and those who do not, some who die quickly and others who live long—because both states are observed, there arises doubt: "Does untimely death (*akālamṛtyu*) truly exist, or does it not?"

3.8.44 | Now, as for the purpose (prayojana): the purpose is that for the sake of which undertakings are commenced; for example: "If untimely death exists, then I shall treat myself with life-prolonging measures and avoid those that shorten life, so that untimely death may not overcome me."
3.8.45 | Now, regarding the "erroneous" (savyabhicāra): the erroneous is that which deviates [from certainty]; for example—whether this medicine will be effective for this disease or not.
3.8.46 | Now, regarding inquiry (jijñāsā)—inquiry means examination; for example, as will be taught following the examination of medicines.
3.8.47 | Now, determination (*vyavasāya*): determination is defined as certainty; for example—"This disease is indeed caused by wind (*vāta*), and this alone is its remedy."

3.8.48 | Now, implication (*arthaprāpti*): implication is that wherein, when one matter has been stated, another matter—though unstated—is established. For example, when it is said, "This disease is not to be treated with nourishment," the implication arises: "This is to be treated with depletion. When it is said, "He should not eat during the day," the implication arises: "He should eat at night."

3.8.49 | Now, regarding origin (*saṃbhava*): that from which something originates is its origin; for example—the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*) are the origin of the embryo, unwholesome factors are the origin of disease, and wholesome factors are the origin of health.

3.8.50 | Now, that which is to be questioned (*anuyojya*): a statement is called "to be questioned" when it is possessed of a defect of speech. Alternatively, a statement made for the purpose of ascertaining a specific detail regarding matters that have been stated in general terms is also "to be questioned"; for example, when it is said, "This disease is to be treated by purification," one asks in return, "Is this to be treated by emesis, or is it to be treated by purgation?"
3.8.51 | Now, that which is not to be questioned (ananuyojya): "not to be questioned" is defined as the opposite of what has been stated above; for example: "This is incurable."

3.8.52 | Now, regarding *anuyoga* (interrogation): interrogation (*anuyoga*) is that which consists of a question or a partial question posed by those learned in a particular science to others equally learned in that same science—whether concerning the whole treatise (*tantra*) or a portion of it—for the purpose of examining knowledge, specialized understanding, the statement, and the response.
For example, when it has been asserted that "the person (*puruṣa*) is eternal," if another asks, "What is the reason?", that is interrogation.
3.8.53 | Now, regarding *pratyanuyoga* (counter-interrogation): *pratyanuyoga* is the interrogation of an interrogation; for example: "What, again, is the reason for this interrogation?"

3.8.54 | Now, the defect of the sentence (*vākyadoṣa*): the so-called defect of the sentence consists in being deficient (*nyūna*), meaningless (*anarthaka*), irrelevant (*apārthaka*), or contradictory (*viruddha*) with respect to the intended meaning; for without these [defects], the subject matter under discussion would not fail.

Among these, "deficient" means that it becomes deficient by lacking even one of the five members—thesis (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*); or, when a matter requiring many stated reasons is established by only one reason, that too is deficient.

Now, regarding the *adhika* (redundant): that which is called *adhika* is what is contrary to brevity (*nyūna*), or when, while the science of Ayurveda is being expounded, something from the teachings of Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, or any other source is stated that is irrelevant to the subject; or when even a relevant point is stated twice, it is *adhika* because of the fault of repetition (*punarukta*). This repetition is of two kinds: repetition of meaning (*arthapunarukta*) and repetition of words (*śabdapunarukta*).

Among these, an example of repetition of meaning is "medicine" (*bheṣaja*), "remedy" (*auṣadha*), and "means of cure" (*sādhana*); whereas an example of repetition of words is "medicine, medicine" (*bheṣajaṃ bheṣajam*).

Now, the meaningless (*anarthaka*): that which is called "meaningless" is speech that consists merely of a collection of syllables, like the five groups of consonants (*pañcavarga*), and is not grasped as having a meaning.

Now, the incoherent (*apārthaka*): that which is called "incoherent" is that which, although possessing words with meanings, has meanings that do not connect with one another; for example: *cakra-takra-vaṃśa-vajra-niśākarāḥ*.

Now, regarding the contradictory (*viruddha*): that which is called "contradictory" is what is contradicted by examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), established tenets (*siddhānta*), and conventions (*samaya*). Among these, examples and established tenets have been explained previously. Conventions, moreover, are of three kinds: namely, the medical convention (*āyurvaidika-samaya*), the sacrificial convention (*yājñika-samaya*), and the convention of the treatises on liberation (*mokṣaśāstrika-samaya*). Among these, the medical convention is that "medicine consists of four pillars"; the sacrificial convention is that "animals are to be sacrificed by the sacrificers"; and the convention of the treatises on liberation is that "there shall be no harm toward any living beings. In this context, that which is stated in opposition to one's own convention becomes contradictory.
Thus end the defects of speech.

3.8.55 | Now, the praise of the sentence (*vākyapraśaṃsā*): that which is called the praise of the sentence is as follows—indeed, in this matter, a sentence is praised as being "not deficient," "not excessive," "significant in meaning," "not meaningless," "not contradictory," and "having its word-meanings understood," such that it is not subject to further questioning.
3.8.56 | Now, regarding *chala* (quibble): *Chala* is that which is deceptive, appearing to have meaning while being meaningless, consisting merely of the substance of speech.
It is of two kinds: quibble with respect to words (*vākchala*) and quibble with respect to generalities (*sāmānyacchala*).

Among these, verbal quibble (*vākchala*) is as follows: Suppose someone says, "This physician is *navatantra*," and the physician replies, "I am not *navatantra*; I am *ekatantro* (a master of one treatise). The other person says, "I do not say that you have nine treatises (*tantrāṇi*), but rather that your treatise has been studied nine times. The physician replies, "My treatise has not been studied nine times by me; it has been studied many times by me. This is verbal quibble.

Quibble based on commonality (*sāmānyacchalam*) is as follows: when it is said, "medicine for the alleviation of disease," another might object: "What did you say? 'The existent [alleviates] the existent'? For the disease is existent, and the medicine is existent. And if the existent [alleviates] the existent, then since cough is existent and consumption is existent, by virtue of this commonality of being existent, your cough will lead to the alleviation of consumption. This is quibble based on commonality.

3.8.57 | Now, the "non-reason" (*ahetu*): the non-reason consists of the "equal-to-the-issue" (*prakaraṇasama*), the "equal-to-doubt" (*saṃśayasama*), and the "equal-to-the-subject-of-inquiry" (*varṇyasama*).

Among these, the non-reason called "equal-to-the-issue" is as follows: [the claim] that "the self is distinct from the body and is eternal. An opponent might say: "Because the self is distinct from the body, therefore it is eternal; for the body is non-eternal, and thus the self must be of a different nature (*vidharmin*). This, however, is not a valid reason; for that which is the very subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*) cannot itself be the reason.

The "equal-to-doubt" (saṃśayasama) fallacious reason is that which is itself the cause of doubt and yet is claimed to be the cause for cutting off that doubt. For example, when there is the doubt, "Since he speaks a portion of Āyurveda, could he perhaps be a physician or not?", another person might say: "Because he speaks a portion of Āyurveda, therefore he is a physician. This does not provide a specific qualification for the cause that cuts off the doubt; thus, it is a fallacious reason. For indeed, that which is the cause of doubt cannot be the very same thing that is the cause for cutting off that doubt.

The "equal to the subject" (*varṇyasama*) is a fallacious reason (*ahetu*); it is a reason that is not distinct from the subject (*varṇya*). For example, someone might say: "Intellect is non-eternal because it is intangible, like sound. In this case, the subject is sound, and intellect is also a subject; since [the reason] is not distinct from both these subjects, it is a fallacious reason called "equal to the subject."

3.8.58 | Now, regarding "mistimed" (*atītakāla*): that which is called "mistimed" is when what ought to have been stated first is stated later; because it has passed its proper time, it becomes ungraspable. Or, having failed to censure when a point of defeat had already been reached, but instead taking up another side and subsequently censuring [the original position], that statement of defeat becomes ineffective because it is mistimed for him.
3.8.59 | Now, refutation (upālambha): refutation is the statement of a fault in the reason (hetu); for example: "The fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) have already been explained as being non-reasons."

3.8.60 | Now, the rebuttal (parihāra): A rebuttal is the refutation of that very statement regarding a fault; for example: "The signs of life are perceived as long as the self resides eternally in the body, and they are not perceived upon its departure; therefore, the self is distinct from the body and eternal."

3.8.61 | Now, the abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*): Abandonment of the proposition is that wherein one, when questioned, relinquishes a proposition previously accepted; for example, having first made the proposition that "the self (*puruṣa*) is eternal," being questioned, one says: "It is non-eternal."
3.8.62 | Now, permission (abhyanujñā)—permission is that which consists in the acceptance of what is desired and what is undesired.
3.8.63 | Now, the "different reason" (hetvantara): "Different reason" is the statement of a different reason when the intended reason for the subject at hand has already been stated.
3.8.64 | Now, the "irrelevant" (arthāntara): "Irrelevant" means when, instead of stating one thing that ought to be said, one says something else.
For example, when the symptoms of fever ought to be stated, one states the symptoms of urinary disorder (prameha).

3.8.65 | Now, regarding the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): a point of defeat is the attainment of loss. It consists of the failure to understand a statement that has been stated three times in an assembly of knowledgeable persons; or the questioning of what should not be questioned, and the failure to question what should be questioned. Furthermore, the points of defeat are: abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), admission (*abhyanujñā*), statement at the wrong time (*kālātītavacana*), lack of reason (*ahetu*), deficiency (*nyūna*), redundancy (*adhika*), the meaningless (*vyartha*), the nonsensical (*anarthaka*), the repetitive (*punarukta*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the shifting of the reason (*hetvantara*), and the irrelevant (*arthāntara*). These are the points of defeat.
3.8.66 | Thus, the terms for the paths of discourse have been explained according to their enumeration.

3.8.67 | Indeed, when a debate among physicians proceeds, it should proceed only within the scope of Ayurveda and not elsewhere; for here, in all topics, there are extensive arguments and counter-arguments as well as pure logical justifications. Having examined all of these, one should state every word [of the argument], and not that which is irrelevant to the subject, unscriptural, unexamined, non-probative, confused, or non-comprehensive.
And one should state everything as being based on reason.

For all debates and disputes, when free from impurity, are indeed rational and serve as causes for medical treatment, because they increase excellent intelligence; for an unimpaired intellect brings about the successful accomplishment of every undertaking.
3.8.68 | Indeed, we shall now set forth here certain sections for the sake of the physicians' knowledge.

For the skilled praise the undertaking of actions preceded by knowledge. For, having correctly understood the cause, the instrument, the source of the action, the action itself, the fruit of the action, the consequence, the place, the time, the engagement, and the means, the agent—while performing the task—accomplishes the work with its desired fruit and consequence with no great effort.
3.8.69 | Therein, that which is called the cause (*kāraṇa*) is that which performs [an action]; it is itself the motive (*hetu*), and it is the agent (*kartṛ*).
3.8.70 | Furthermore, the instrument (karaṇa) is that which serves as an auxiliary for the agent who is striving toward the accomplishment of an action.
3.8.71 | But that which, undergoing transformation, attains the state of being an effect, is the source of the effect.
3.8.72 | But that [object] is a "kārya" (to-be-accomplished) with respect to which the agent proceeds, having intended its production.
3.8.73 | Furthermore, the fruit of the action is that for the sake of which the accomplishment of the action is intended.

3.8.74 | Indeed, that is called a *anubandha* (concomitant) which necessarily follows the agent after the action has been performed, being a state—whether auspicious or inauspicious—induced by that action.
3.8.75 | Place, however, is the substratum.
3.8.76 | Furthermore, time is transformation.

3.8.77 | Activity (pravṛtti), indeed, is effort directed toward an object to be accomplished; it is itself action (kriyā), work (karman), exertion (yatna), and the undertaking of a task (kāryasamārambha).

3.8.78 | Furthermore, *upāya* (the means) is the excellence and thorough application of the three—beginning with the cause (*kāraṇa*)—excluding the effect (*kārya*), the fruit (*phala*), and the consequence (*anubandha*). It is called *upāya* because it brings about the effects; once [the effect] has been accomplished, there is no further purpose for the means, nor does it exist at that moment. From the accomplishment comes the fruit, and from the fruit comes the consequence.
3.8.79 | This tenfold [set] is to be examined first; immediately thereafter, the engagement for the sake of the task is desired.
Therefore, a physician desiring to perform a task should, prior to the commencement of the task, examine only that which is to be examined through examination, and then begin to perform the action.

3.8.80 | If, in that regard, a physician or a non-physician should ask a physician as follows: "By how many kinds of examination should a physician who intends to administer emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema, unctuous enema, and head-evacuation examine the patient? What are the various objects of examination? What is the specific nature of these objects of examination? How should they be examined? What is the purpose of examination? Where is the application of emesis and the other therapies indicated, and where is their contraindication? And when there is a combination of indications for application and contraindications, what [should be done]?"
The definitive [treatment], and which medicinal substances for emesis and so forth are employed.

3.8.81 | If, being thus questioned, he should wish to delude [the questioner], he should say to him: "For examination is of many kinds, as is the variety of methods for examining. By which specific methodological variation of a different nature do you ask, through which distinct examination, or by which other methodological variation regarding the object of examination, you seek to determine the limit of the distinctions of that which is being distinguished?"

I shall not now fulfill your desire by analyzing the object of inquiry—which is distinct through another distinction of method or another nature of method—by means of a different analysis or another distinction of method or nature of method, and then explaining it otherwise.

3.8.82 | Whatever he may say in reply, that should be considered before responding, having regard for the rule for replying as it has been stated. But if he speaks correctly and one does not wish to confuse him, and considers the time for speaking to have arrived, one may, at will, tell him the truth in its entirety.
3.8.83 | Indeed, for those possessing knowledge, examination (parīkṣā) is of two kinds: perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna).
For these two, together with authoritative instruction (upadeśa), constitute examination.
Thus, this examination is twofold, or threefold when including authoritative instruction.

3.8.84 | We shall now demonstrate, by applying them to the physician and the other factors, that tenfold set of things to be examined—beginning with the cause—which was previously mentioned: here, in the attainment of the objective, the cause is the physician; the instrument is the medicine; the source of the effect is the disharmony of the bodily constituents (*dhātuvaiṣamya*); the effect is the equilibrium of the constituents (*dhātusāmya*); the fruit of the effect is the attainment of happiness; the consequence is indeed life itself; the place consists of both the environment and the patient; time, moreover, consists of both the year and the stages of the patient's condition; and the undertaking is the commencement of the therapeutic action.
The means (*upāya*), however, consists of the excellence and the proper application of the physician and the other factors.
Here too, the scope of this means has been explained by the very same specific means mentioned previously.

Thus, the ten factors beginning with the cause (*kāraṇa*) have been demonstrated by being distributed among the ten [factors] beginning with the physician; likewise, these ten kinds of objects of examination (*parīkṣya*) have been stated in that same sequence.
3.8.85 | Whatever specific feature of it is to be examined in whatever manner, that will be explained accordingly.

3.8.86 | The physician has been described as the primary cause [of treatment] previously; his examination follows: A physician is one who practices medicine, who is skilled in the application of the meaning of the aphorisms, and for whom the lifespan is known correctly in every respect.

Desiring to effect the equilibrium of all the bodily constituents (dhātus), he should first examine himself, observing the accomplishment of the task through qualities among those possessing qualities, considering: "Am I capable or not of accomplishing this task? In this regard, these are the qualities of a physician, endowed with which a physician becomes capable of effecting the equilibrium of the bodily constituents.

Namely: purity of learning, thorough observation of one's work, skillfulness, cleanliness, mastery of the hand, possession of necessary implements, perfection of all faculties, knowledge of the nature [of things], and knowledge of the means of accomplishment.
3.8.87 | Furthermore, the instrument (karaṇa) is the medicine (bheṣaja).
Medicine is that which serves as an auxiliary for a physician striving to achieve the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātu-sāmya), especially when compared to other means.
It is of two kinds, according to the distinction of reliance: reliance on divine power (daiva-vyapāśraya) and reliance on rational application (yukti-vyapāśraya).

Among these, that which relies on destiny (*daivavyapāśraya*) consists of mantras, medicinal herbs, gems, auspicious rites, offerings, oblations, religious observances, expiatory acts, fasting, benedictions, prostrations, pilgrimages, and so forth. That which relies on reason (*yuktivyapāśraya*) consists of purification, pacification, and physical activities whose results are perceptible.
Furthermore, this very medicine is of two kinds according to its constituent parts: substantial (*dravyabhūta*) and non-substantial (*adravyabhūta*).
Of these, that which is non-substantial is permeated by means (*upāyābhipluta*).

What is called a "means" (*upāya*) is an immaterial specific state (*bhāvaviśeṣa*), such as the display of fear, causing amazement, causing forgetfulness, agitation, exhilaration, threatening, killing, binding, dreams, or massage, as well as the aforementioned means for attaining success (*siddhi*); these are said to be "overwhelmed by means.
However, that which is material (*dravyabhūta*) enters into conjunction (*yoga*) with emetics and the like.

This is the examination of that [medicine] as well: "This [medicine] is of such a nature, possesses such qualities, and has such power; it was produced in this region, gathered in this season, stored in this manner, prepared in this way, and joined with this specific measure. When administered to a person of such a type, it removes or pacifies a disease of such a magnitude; furthermore, whatever other medicine of this kind there may be, it should be endowed with these same specific characteristics."
3.8.88 | The source of disease is the imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-vaiṣamya*); its characteristic sign is the onset of morbid change (*vikāra-āgama*).

Its examination consists of observing the specific signs of deficiency or excess in both the primary cause and the nature of the morbid change, as well as observing the specific signs of curability or incurability, and mildness or severity, of that morbid change.
3.8.89 | The goal is the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus). Its characteristic sign is the subsiding of morbid alterations (vikāra).

Its examination consists of: the alleviation of disease, the proper restoration of voice and complexion, the nourishment of the body, the increase of strength, a desire for food, a relish for meals at the proper time, the correct digestion of ingested food at its appropriate time, obtaining sleep at the right hour, the absence of abnormal dreams, awakening with ease, the unimpeded discharge of flatus, urine, feces, and semen, and the non-impairment of the mind, intellect, and sense organs in all their aspects.
3.8.90 | The fruit of action is the attainment of happiness; its characteristic is the satisfaction of the mind, the intellect, the senses, and the body.
3.8.91 | Furthermore, life is indeed the consequence; its characteristic is conjunction with the vital breaths.
3.8.92 | *deśa* (place), however, refers to both the earth and the patient.

3.8.93 | In that regard, the examination of the soil may be for the purpose of understanding the patient or for the purpose of understanding the medicine. First, this is for the purpose of understanding the patient.

For example: in which region of the earth was this person born, raised, or afflicted with disease? And in that region of the earth, what is the usual dietary intake of humans, what is their lifestyle, what is their conduct, what is their strength, what is their temperament, what is their constitution, what is their susceptibility to morbidity, what are their preferences, what are their diseases, what is beneficial, and what is harmful—this is determined by means of general observation.
However, for the sake of thoroughly understanding medicinal herbs, the examination of the ground will be described in the ritual manuals (kalpas).

3.8.94 | The patient, indeed, is the site of action. His examination may be for the purpose of knowing the measure of his lifespan, or for the purpose of knowing the measure of the strength and the [dosic] morbidity. Of these, this [examination] is first for the purpose of knowing the measure of the strength and the morbidity; for the determination of the appropriate dosage of medicine is dependent upon the specific measure of the patient's strength and corresponds to the measure of the morbidity.

For a medicine that is excessively strong, if administered by one who has not examined the patient, may suddenly cause the death of a weak patient. Indeed, very powerful medicines—whether of fiery or windy nature—or procedures involving fire, caustic alkali, and surgery, cannot be endured by those of little strength; for, due to their unbearable and extremely sharp force, they would instantly take away life.

Considering this very reason, they treat those who are weak and afflicted with medicines that do not cause despondency—medicines that are for the most part mild and delicate, progressively more potent, non-confusing, and not excessively harsh. This is especially true for women, for their hearts are generally unstable, tender, open, and distressed; they are mostly delicate, weak, and dependent on others. Likewise, in one who is strong but overcome by a powerful disease, medicine of little strength, when administered by an unexamining physician, becomes simply ineffective.

Therefore, one should examine the patient with respect to their constitution (*prakṛti*), morbid transformation (*vikṛti*), essence (*sāra*), compactness of the body (*saṃhanana*), stature (*pramāṇa*), suitability (*sātmya*), mental disposition (*sattva*), capacity for food (*āhāra-śakti*), capacity for exercise (*vyāyāma-śakti*), and age (*vayas*), for the purpose of ascertaining the specific measure of their strength.
3.8.95 | We shall now explain the various factors, beginning with the primary constituents (*prakṛti*), that influence the embryo.

They are as follows: the embryo depends upon the nature of the semen and ovum, the nature of the time and the uterus, the nature of the patient's diet and lifestyle, and the nature of the transformations of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Indeed, whichever of these factors is associated with a predominance of one or more of the humors (*doṣa*), the embryo becomes bound by that very humor; consequently, that specific humor-nature is said to be established in humans from the moment of conception.
Therefore, some are by nature phlegmatic (ślaiṣmala), some are bilious (pittala), some are windy (vātala), some are combinations of these, and some have balanced humors (samadhātu).
We shall now explain their characteristics.
3.8.96 | For phlegm (śleṣman) is unctuous, smooth, soft, sweet, substantial, thick, slow, steady, heavy, cold, moist, and clear.

Due to its oiliness (*sneha*), they have phlegmatic constitutions and glossy limbs; due to its smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*), they have smooth limbs; due to its softness (*mṛdutva*), their bodies are pleasant to behold, delicate, and bright-white; due to its sweetness (*mādhurya*), they possess abundant semen, sexual vigor, and offspring; due to its essence (*sāra*), they have bodies that are substantial, compact, and firm; due to its density (*sāndratva*), all their limbs are well-developed and complete; due to its slowness (*mandatva*), their movements, eating, and speech are slow; due to its inertia (*staimitya*), they are not quick in undertaking tasks nor in agitation or transformation; and due to its heaviness (*gurutva*), their movements are established and steady, being grounded in strength.

Due to its coldness, there is little hunger, thirst, heat, perspiration, or affliction; due to its viscidity, the joints and ligaments are well-knit; and likewise, due to its clarity, they possess a serene appearance and face, as well as a clear, glossy complexion and voice.
By virtue of possessing these qualities, those of a phlegmatic constitution (ślaiṣmala) are strong, wealthy, learned, vigorous, peaceful, and long-lived.
3.8.97 | Pitta is hot, sharp, liquid, with a raw-flesh smell, sour, and pungent.

Due to its heat (*auṣṇya*), those with a predominance of bile (*pitta*) are unable to endure heat, have a hot mouth, possess delicate and fair-limbed bodies, and are prone to abundant eruptions, moles, freckles, and pustules; they suffer from hunger and thirst, and are subject early to the defects of wrinkles, graying hair, and baldness; generally, their body hair, facial hair, and head hair are soft, sparse, and reddish-brown. Due to its sharpness (*taikṣṇya*), they possess fierce prowess, have a keen digestive fire, consume large quantities of food and drink, are intolerant of hardships, and are prone to biting. Due to its fluidity (*dravatva*), they have loose and soft joints and flesh, and produce copious excretions of feces, sweat, urine, and stool.

Due to their state of putrefaction, they possess a strong odor of pus from the armpits, mouth, head, and body; due to their pungent and sour nature, they have little semen, sexual intercourse, and offspring; and by virtue of these qualities, those who are of bilious temperament (pittala) are of moderate strength, moderate lifespan, and possess moderate knowledge, discernment, wealth, and means.

3.8.98 | Vāta, however, is dry, light, mobile, abundant, swift, cold, rough, and clear. Due to its dryness (raukṣya), those of a vāta-dominant constitution (vātalāḥ) are dry, emaciated, and small-bodied; they possess a constant, dry, thin, weak, faltering, or broken voice; and they are prone to wakefulness. Due to its lightness (laghutva), their gait, movements, diet, and speech are light and fickle. Due to its mobility (calatva), their joints, eyes, eyebrows, jaws, lips, tongue, head, shoulders, hands, and feet are unstable. Due to its abundance (bahutva), they engage in much prattle and have a profusion of tendons (kaṇḍarā) and veins (sirā). Due to its swiftness (śīghratva), they initiate activities quickly, undergo agitation and disorders rapidly, and experience sudden fear, passion, and detachment; yet they are capable of retaining what they have heard.

They have poor memory; due to coldness, they are intolerant of cold and suffer from constant shivering and stiffness caused by cold; due to roughness, their hair, beard, body hair, nails, teeth, face, hands, and feet are coarse; and due to clarity, their limbs and joints are cracked and they walk with a constant creaking sound in their joints. By virtue of these qualities, those who are dominated by Vāta are generally of little strength, short lifespan, few offspring, meager resources, and small wealth.
3.8.99 | Through association, they possess the characteristics of what is associated.
3.8.100 | "But those who possess all qualities and have balanced *dhātus*—
thus one should examine them according to their natural constitution (*prakṛti*)."
3.8.101 | Regarding the phrase "and from the transformation" (*vikṛtitas*), "transformation" (*vikṛti*) is said to mean "modification" (*vikāra*).

In that regard, one should examine the modification by means of the specificities of the cause (*hetu*), the affected humor (*doṣa*), the tissue (*dūṣya*), the constitution (*prakṛti*), the place (*deśa*), the time (*kāla*), and the strength (*bala*), as well as by its symptoms (*liṅga*); for indeed, without [knowledge of] the specificities of the strength of the causes and so forth, there can be no perception of the specific strength of the disease.

For that disease in which there is a similarity of strength among the doshas, the dushyas, the constitution, the location, and the time, and in which the strength of the cause and the symptoms is great, that disease becomes powerful; by the opposite of this, it is of little strength; whereas a disease of moderate strength is recognized through the commonality of some among the doshas, dushyas, and so forth, as well as the moderate strength of the cause and the symptoms.

3.8.102 | Regarding the "essence" (*sāra*): eight essences are taught for the purpose of knowing the specific measures of strength in men; namely—skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and the mind (*sattva*).
3.8.103 | In that regard, the skin of those possessing the essence (tvaksāra) is glossy, smooth, soft, clear, fine, thin, deep, and delicate-haired, as if radiant;
that state of possessing the essence indicates happiness, good fortune, sovereignty, enjoyment, intelligence, learning, health, joy, and longevity.

3.8.104 | The ears, eyes, mouth, tongue, nose, lips, palms, soles of the feet, nails, forehead, and penis—when these are glossy, red in color, beautiful, and radiant, they possess the quality of "red-essence" (rakta-sāra).
That quality of essence indicates happiness, elevated intelligence, mental nobility, delicacy, moderate strength, intolerance of hardship, and intolerance of heat.

3.8.105 | The joints of the temples, forehead, nape of the neck, eyes, cheeks, jaw, neck, shoulders, abdomen, armpits, chest, hands, and feet—when these are firm, heavy, and well-developed with auspicious flesh, they constitute the essence of flesh (*māṃsasāra*).
That essence indicates capacity for endurance, fortitude, lack of greed, wealth, learning, happiness, straightforwardness, health, strength, and long life.
