3.8.106 | In those whose essence is fat (medas), there is especially an abundance of oiliness in the complexion, voice, eyes, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, lips, urine, and excrement.
That state of being "essence" (sāratā) indicates wealth, sovereignty, the enjoyment of pleasures, generosity, straightforwardness, and a delicate mode of living.

3.8.107 | Those whose heels, ankles, knees, wrists, collarbones, chins, and heads are thick, as well as those with thick bones, nails, and teeth, possess the essence of bone (*asthisāra*). They are highly energetic, active, capable of enduring hardship, possessed of firm and solid bodies, and long-lived.
3.8.108 | Those whose limbs are soft, who are strong, whose complexion and voice are glossy, and whose joints are thick, long, and rounded, possess marrow as their essence.
They are long-lived, powerful, and become recipients of sacred learning, wealth, wisdom, progeny, and honor.

3.8.109 | Those with a *saumya* (lunar) constitution have a gentle appearance; their eyes seem as if filled with milk; they are full of great joy; their teeth are glossy, rounded, substantial, even, and closely set at the tips; their complexion and voice are clear and smooth; they are radiant and possess large buttocks; and they have the essence of *śukra* (semen).
They are fond of women and sensual enjoyments, are strong, and possess happiness, sovereignty, health, wealth, honor, and offspring.

3.8.110 | Those who possess memory, devotion, gratitude, wisdom, purity, and great energy; who are skillful, steadfast, and warriors who fight with valor in battle; who have abandoned despondency, whose movements, intellect, and actions are well-composed and profound; and who are intent upon what is auspicious—these are the ones whose essence is *sattva*.
Their qualities are explained by their very individual characteristics.

3.8.111 | Therein, men endowed with all the *sāras* become exceedingly strong, possessed of supreme happiness, capable of enduring hardships, confident in themselves regarding all undertakings, devoted to what is auspicious, with stable and well-composed bodies, with very steady gaits, and with great voices that are resonant, smooth, deep, and loud; they enjoy happiness, sovereignty, wealth, pleasures, and honor; they are slow to age and have few afflictions; their offspring are generally equal to them in qualities and abundant; and they are long-lived.
3.8.112 | But those which are the opposite of these are insubstantial.
3.8.113 | By means of the specific qualities of the middling [materials] through the specific essences of the middling [substances], the specific qualities [of the others] are explained.
3.8.114 | Thus, these eight types of men are taught for the purpose of knowing the specific measures of their strength.

3.8.115 | How indeed can a physician infer from the mere observation of the body alone that "this person is strong because he is well-nourished," "this one has little strength because of his emaciation," "this one is of great strength because of his large body," or "this one has little strength because of his small body"? For some who are small-bodied and emaciated are seen to be strong; in such cases, success is achieved like the carrying of a load by an ant.
Therefore, it is said that one should examine [the patient] according to their essence (*sāra*).

3.8.116 | Regarding "by way of bone-structure" (*saṃhananataḥ*): *saṃhanana* means compactness or conjunction; these are synonymous. In this context, a body is said to have a well-proportioned skeletal structure, well-knit joints, and well-set flesh and blood when it is very compact.
Among these, persons with a very compact body are strong; conversely, those with the opposite [structure] are weak; and due to a middling bone-structure, they possess middling strength.
3.8.117 | Regarding "according to measurement," the measurement of the body shall be taught according to its own finger-measure (aṅgula), by way of height, breadth, and length, respectively.

Therein, the two feet are fourteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length; the two shanks are eighteen aṅgulas long and sixteen aṅgulas in circumference; the two knees are four aṅgulas long and sixteen aṅgulas in circumference; the two thighs are eighteen aṅgulas long and thirty aṅgulas in circumference; the two testicles are six aṅgulas long and eight aṅgulas in girth; the penis is six aṅgulas long and five aṅgulas in girth; the vulva is twelve aṅgulis in circumference; the waist is sixteen aṅgulas wide; and the top of the bladder is ten aṅgulas.

The chest is ten fingers in width and twelve fingers in depth; the sides are ten fingers wide and twelve fingers long; the space between the breasts is twelve fingers; the extent of the breasts is two fingers; the chest is twenty-four fingers broad and twelve fingers high; the heart is two fingers; the shoulders are eight fingers; the shoulder-blades are six fingers; the upper arms are sixteen fingers; the forearms are fifteen fingers; the hands are twelve fingers; the armpits are eight fingers; and the sacrum—

The height [of the neck] is twelve finger-breadths; the back is eighteen finger-breadths in height; the neck (śirodharā) is four finger-breadths in height and twenty-two finger-breadths in circumference; the face is twelve finger-breadths in height and twenty-four finger-breadths in circumference; the mouth is five finger-breadths; the chin, lips, ears, the midpoint of the eyes, the nose, and the forehead are each four finger-breadths; and the head is sixteen finger-breadths in height and thirty-two finger-breadths in circumference. Thus, the measurement of the individual limbs and parts has been stated. Furthermore, the entire body consists of eighty-four finger-joints; it is said to be equal in length and breadth.

In that regard, longevity, strength, vigor, happiness, sovereignty, wealth, and other desired states depend upon a body of proper proportions; however, the opposite occurs when it is deficient or excessive.
3.8.118 | Regarding "and by way of suitability" (*sātmyataḥ*): suitability (*sātmya*) refers to that which, when consumed continuously, conduces to well-being.

Among these, those for whom ghee, milk, oil, meat broth, and all tastes are suitable are strong, capable of enduring hardship, and long-lived; however, those for whom dry substances are suitable, or who are suitable for only a single taste, are generally of little strength, incapable of enduring much hardship, short-lived, and possess few resources. Those, on the other hand, who are suitable for a mixture [of tastes] possess moderate strength due to the influence of suitability.
3.8.119 | "And [it is] according to *sattva*. By *sattva* is meant the mind (*manas*). It is the governing principle (*tantraka*) of the body due to its conjunction with the self (*ātman*).

It is threefold according to the distinction of strength—namely, superior (*pravara*), middling (*madhyama*), and inferior (*avara*). Consequently, persons possess superior, middling, or inferior *sattva*.

Among them, the most excellent beings—the essence of all beings—are taught to be those who abide in that essence; for even when they possess very small bodies, they are seen to be free from pain even amidst great afflictions, whether innate or adventitious, due to the preeminence of their essential qualities. As for those of middling nature, having placed others within themselves, they steady themselves by means of the self, or they are steadied by others.

But those of inferior nature cannot be supported by either themselves or others in their strength of being; for even though they possess large bodies, they are seen to be unable to endure even slight sensations. With fear, grief, greed, delusion, and pride ever-present, and upon hearing even fierce, terrifying, hateful, loathsome, or distorted accounts, or upon seeing the flesh and blood of animals or humans, they fall into one of the states of despair, discoloration, fainting, insanity, dizziness, or falling down, or else they meet death.
3.8.120 | "And also by the capacity for food": the capacity for food is to be examined by the power of ingestion and the power of digestion; for both strength and lifespan are dependent upon food.
3.8.121 | "And by the capacity for exertion": the capacity for exertion (*vyāyāma-śakti*) is also to be examined by means of the capacity for action (*karma-śakti*).
For the threefold nature of strength (*bala*) is inferred through the capacity for action.

3.8.122 | Regarding "according to age" (*vayastaḥ*): a specific state of the body dependent on the measure of time is designated as "age. That age is, in its broad divisions, threefold: childhood (*bāla*), middle age (*madhya*), and old age (*jīrṇa*). Among these, childhood lasts until sixteen years; it is characterized by immature bodily constituents (*dhātu*), unmanifested sexual characteristics, delicacy, intolerance of hardship, incomplete strength, and a predominance of the phlegm constituent (*śleṣma-dhātu*). Furthermore, up to thirty years is taught as middle age, during which the qualities of the bodily constituents increase, yet the mental state (*sattva*) is generally unstable.

Furthermore, the middle [period] is taught to last up to sixty years, during which one has attained equilibrium in strength, vigor, manliness, prowess, grasping, retention, memory, speech, and consciousness, as well as all the qualities of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), remaining established in strength with stable vital constituents and unimpaired qualities of the *dhātus*, though it is predominantly characterized by the bile constituent (*pitta-dhātu*).

Beyond this, it is called "decayed," lasting up to a hundred years, wherein the constituents, faculties, strength, vigor, manliness, prowess, grasping, retention, memory, speech, and consciousness progressively decline, and the qualities of the constituents fall away, being predominantly characterized by the wind constituent (*vāyu-dhātu*).

In this age, the measure of the lifespan is indeed one hundred years; however, there are also humans who live for more than a hundred years. Having ascertained the measure of their lifespan through the specific strengths of their constitution and so forth—excluding any morbidities—and by means of the signs of longevity, one should divide the stages of life into three.

3.8.123 | Thus, one should distinguish the specific strength of the factors beginning with the primary cause (*prakṛti*), excluding the morbid transformation (*vikṛti*), by dividing them into superior, intermediate, and inferior categories. Furthermore, the threefold strength of the humors (*doṣa*) is inferred from the threefold strength of the morbid transformation. Then, having divided the medicine into three types—sharp, mild, and moderate—one should administer the medicine according to the specific humor involved.
3.8.124 | Furthermore, the characteristics for the purpose of knowing the measure of lifespan will be taught in the sections on the sense organs and on the signs of birth.
3.8.125 | Time (*kāla*), moreover, consists of the year (*saṃvatsara*) and its various states (*avasthā*).
Among these, the year is divided into two, three, six, twelve, and further still, according to the requirements of specific tasks.

Here, however, the task will be taught by dividing [the year] into six parts: winter (*hemanta*), summer (*grīṣma*), and the rainy season (*varṣā*)—these are the three seasons characterized by cold, heat, and rain; and within the intervals between them are the other three seasons with common characteristics: the monsoon (*prāvṛṭ*), autumn (*śarad*), and spring (*vasanta*).
"Prāvṛṣ" (the rainy season) is the first period, for "varṣāḥ" (the rains) are its continuation;
thus these six seasons are divided with reference to purification.
3.8.126 | In those seasons characterized by common features (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*), the administration of emesis and other therapies is prescribed; in the others, it is prohibited.

For the seasons with common characteristics, being neither excessively cold, hot, nor rainy, are most comfortable and cause no disturbance to the body or the medicinal substances; whereas the others, due to being excessively cold, hot, or rainy, are most painful and do cause such disturbances.

3.8.127 | For in that winter season, because it is afflicted by excessive cold, the body becomes uncomfortable, puffed up by extremely cold winds, becomes very rigid, and its humors (doṣas) become obstructed. Furthermore, the medicine intended for purification, being hot by nature, attains a state of diminished potency due to the excessive cold. Therefore, when these two are combined, the purification therapy results in inadequate action (ayoga), and the body also suffers from complications of vāta.

Furthermore, in summer, because the body is afflicted by intense heat, it becomes uncomfortable; swollen by hot winds and sunlight, it is extremely relaxed and its humors (doṣas) are excessively liquefied. Moreover, the purificatory medicine, being hot by nature, attains even greater sharpness due to the influence of the heat. Therefore, when these two meet, the purification leads to excessive action (atiyoga), and the body also suffers from the complication of thirst.

During the rainy season, however, when the sky is overspread with clouds and water, with the sun, moon, and stars hidden, and filled with torrents of rain; when the earth is covered by layers of mud and water; when living beings have their bodies excessively moistened and their natural vigor impaired; and when the entire collection of medicinal plants has lost its potency due to contact with winds accompanied by water and clouds—the administration of emetics and other therapies becomes heavy in its action, and the bodies of patients become heavy in their response. Therefore, the cessation of emetics and such treatments is prescribed during the seasons following the rains, unless there is an urgent medical emergency.

Furthermore, in an urgent matter, one may certainly disregard the season; by applying artificial qualities that are contrary to the natural qualities of the season, and having prepared the medicine through variations in combination, processing, and dosage, making it equal in strength to the original measure, one should then administer it with the utmost effort and careful attention.

3.8.128 | Furthermore, even regarding the conditions of the patient, there is the designation of "proper time" and "improper time" with respect to what should and should not be done. For example: "In this condition, this medicine is at the wrong time; however, it is the right time for another. This too occurs according to specific conditions; therefore, even regarding the conditions of the patient, there is the designation of "proper time" and "improper time. The examination thereof consists in repeatedly observing all the specific conditions of the patient in order to apply the medicine correctly.

For medicine that is administered either after the proper time has passed or before it has arrived does not become effective; indeed, it is time that brings about the full efficacy of the medicinal application.

3.8.129 | Activity (*pravṛtti*), however, is the undertaking of each specific therapeutic action. Its definition is the coordinated application of the activities of the physician, the medicine, the patient, and the attendant.
3.8.130 | Furthermore, the means (*upāya*) consists of the excellence of the physician and the other factors, as well as the correct application (*abhividhāna*).

Its definition is: the possession by the physician and others of the aforementioned qualities, and the administration of medicine that has been properly prepared through the causes of success, such as place, time, dosage, suitability, and therapeutic action.
3.8.131 | Thus, these ten specific objects of examination must be examined individually.
3.8.132 | Indeed, the purpose of examination is the knowledge of how to act.
"Acting" (pratipatti) means the knowledge of how to perform a modification in accordance with how it ought to be performed.

3.8.133 | Furthermore, we shall explain in detail later in the Siddhisthāna (the section on successful treatments) where the application of emesis and other therapies is indicated, and where their cessation is required.

3.8.134 | However, when there is a conflict between the characteristics of proceeding with treatment and desisting from it, one should determine correctly by weighing the relative importance (guru-lāghava) regarding the final decision on either course.
For indeed, in the medical scriptures, diseases are described in relation to their treatment through general rules (utsarga) and exceptions (apavāda).
Therefore, it has been stated that one should determine correctly after having weighed the relative importance.
3.8.135 | Now, we shall explain in detail those medicinal substances that are employed in emesis and other such procedures.

Namely: with the fruits of *phalajīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *dhāmārgava*, *kuṭaja*, and *kṛtavedhana*; with the leaves and flowers of *phalajīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *dhāmārgava*, and *āragvadha*; with the decoctions of the roots of *vṛkṣaka*, *madana*, *svādukaṇṭaka*, *pāṭhā*, *pāṭalā*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *mūrvā*, *saptaparṇa*, *naktamāla*, *picumarda*, *paṭola*, *suṣavī*, *guḍūcī*, *citraka*, *somavalka*, *śatāvarī*, *dvīpī*, and *śigru*; and with the decoctions of *madhuka*, *madhūka*, *kovidāra*, *karvudāra*, *nīpa*, *vidula*, *bimbī*, *śaṇapuṣpī*, *sadāpuṣpā*, and *pratyakpuṣpā*.
And with decoctions of cardamom, elāhara, priyaṅgu, pṛthvīkā, kustumburu, tagara, nalada, hrīvera, tālīśa, and uśīra.

And with decoctions of *ikṣukāṇḍa*, *ikṣu*, *ikṣuvālikā*, *darbha*, *poṭagala*, and *kālaṅkṛtaka*; and with decoctions of *sumanā*, *saumanasyāyanī*, *haridrā*, *dāruharidrā*, *vṛścīra*, *punarnavā*, *mahāsahā*, and *kṣudrasahā*; and with decoctions of *śālmali*, *śālmalika*, *bhadraparṇī*, *elāparṇī*, *upodikā*, *uddālaka*, *ghanvana*, *rājādana*, *paci*, *trāga*, *gopī*, and *śṛṅgāṭikā*; and with *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *cavya*, *citraka*, *śṛṅgavera*, mustard seeds, molasses, milk, alkaline water, salt water, and so forth—either according to availability or as desired.

Having thus prepared [the drugs] and fashioned various types of foods—such as wicks, powders, electuaries, fats, decoctions, meat broths, gruels, soups, *kāmbalika*, milk-based preparations, sweetmeats (*modaka*), and other diverse kinds of edibles—one should administer emesis according to the prescribed method to a patient fit for emesis. This is the summary of the pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpa*) for emetic substances. We shall explain their detailed pharmaceutical processing (*kalpa*) later on.

3.8.136 | The purgative substances are as follows: the milk, roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits of *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *caturaṅgula*, *tilvaka*, *mahāvṛkṣa*, *saptalā*, *śāṅkhinī*, *dantī*, and *dravantī*, used according to their respective requirements—whether processed or unprocessed—with those various milks, roots, barks, leaves, flowers, and fruits; and with the decoctions of *ajagandhā*, *aśvagandhā*, *ajaśṛṅgī*, *kṣīriṇī*, *nīlinī*, and *klītaka*; and with the decoctions of *prakīryā*, *udakīryā*, *masūravidalā*, *kampillaka*, *viḍaṅga*, and *gavākṣī*.

And having prepared [the oil] with decoctions of *pīlu*, *priyāla*, *mṛdvīkā*, *kāśmarya*, *parūṣaka*, *badara*, *dāḍima*, *āmalaka*, *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, *vṛścīra*, *punarnavā*, *vidārigandhā*, and so forth; and with *sīdhu*, *surā*, *sauvīraka*, *tuṣodaka*, *maireya*, *medaka*, *madirā*, *madhu*, *madhūlaka*, *dhānyāmla*, *kuvala*, *badara*, *kharjūra*, *karkandhu*; and with curd, whey, and buttermilk; and with the milk and urine of cows, buffaloes, goats, and sheep—using these as available or as desired.

Having prepared pills, powders, fermented liquors (*āsava*), electuaries (*leha*), fats, decoctions, meat juices, soups, *kāmbalika*, gruels, milk-based preparations, sweetmeats (*modaka*), and various other kinds of foodstuffs and medicinal formulations, one should administer a purgative to a patient who requires it according to their specific needs. This is the summary of the pharmaceutical preparations of purgative substances. We shall explain the detailed method for these [substances] correctly at a later time.

3.8.137 | Regarding the substances used in enemas (*āsthāpana*) which undergo various preparations for application in different conditions of life, those substances, if taught by name in detail, would be innumerable due to their extreme multitude. Furthermore, in this treatise, instruction that is neither too concise nor too detailed is desired, as is pure knowledge alone. Therefore, we shall explain them here solely according to their tastes (*rasa*). For the expansion of the permutations of the combination of tastes among these [substances] is indeed innumerable, owing to the extreme multiplicity of the variations in the relative strength of the parts of the combined tastes.

Therefore, having divided a portion of substances for the sake of illustration among the tastes, and having further divided them according to each individual taste for the purpose of defining their names and characteristics, the six groups of enemas (āsthāpanaskandha) will be explained by means of their respective tastes.

3.8.138 | Regarding that which physicians call the sixfold non-uniform enema (*āsthāpana*), it is extremely difficult to obtain because medicinal substances are for the most part composed of blended tastes (*saṃsṛṣṭarasa*).

Therefore, in this section on sweet substances, those items that are sweet, predominantly sweet, have a sweet post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and possess a sweet specific action (*prabhāva*) will be taught as being simply "sweet"; the same applies to other substances as well.

3.8.139 | For example: jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, jīvantī, vīrā, tāmalakī, kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, śālaparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, asanaparṇī, medā, mahāmedā, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, śṛṅgāṭikā, chinnaruhā, chattrā, aticchattrā, śrāvaṇī, mahāśrāvaṇī, sahadevā, viśvadevā, śuklā, kṣīraśuklā, balā, atibalā, vidārī, kṣīravidārī, kṣudrasahā, mahāsahā, ṛṣyagandhā, aśvagandhā, vṛścīra, and punarnavā.

Bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, urubūka, moraṭa, śvadaṃṣṭrā, saṃharṣā, śatāvarī, śatapuṣpā, madhūkapuṣpī, yaṣṭīmadhu, madhūlikā, mṛdvīkā, kharjūra, parūṣaka, ātmaguptā, puṣkarabīja, kaśeruka, rājakaśeruka, rājādana, kataka, kāśmarya, śītapākī, odanapākī, tāla, kharjūramastaka, ikṣu, ikṣuvālikā, darbha, kuśa, kāśa, śāli, gundra, itkaṭaka, śaramūla, rājakṣavaka, ṛṣyaproktā, and dvāradā.

Bhāradvājī, vanatrapusī, abhīrupatrī, haṃsapādī, kākanāsikā, kuliṅgākṣī, kṣīravallī, kapolavallī, kapotavallī, somavallī, gopavallī, and madhuvallī—of these and other medicinal substances enumerated in the sweet group (madhuravarga), those that are to be cut should be cut into pieces, and those that are to be broken should be broken into fine fragments, and then [washed].

Having thoroughly washed a vessel with water and placed [the drugs] therein, one should pour in milk mixed with half as much water and cook it, stirring constantly with a ladle. When most of the water has been absorbed, when the medicinal herbs have lost their juice, and while the milk is not yet burnt, one should remove the vessel. Then, having strained the milk well until lukewarm, and having added ghee, oil, muscle fat, marrow, salt, and treacle, a physician who knows the procedure should duly administer this enema to one suffering from disorders of Vāta.
However, for one suffering from disorders of Pitta, it should be administered according to the procedure after mixing it with honey and ghee while cold.
Thus ends the Sweet Group (Madhuraskandha).

3.8.140 | The fruits of the *āmra*, *āmrātaka*, *lakuca*, *karamarda*, *vṛkṣāmla*, *amlavetasa*, *kuvala*, *badara*, *dāḍima*, *mātuluṅga*, *gaṇḍīra*, *āmalaka*, *nandītaka*, *śīta*, *tintiḍīka*, *dantaśaṭha*, *airāvataka*, *kośāmra*, and *dhanvana*; the leaves of the *āmrātaka*, *aśmantaka*, and *cāṅgerī*; the four kinds of *āmlīkā*; the two types of *kola*—fresh and dried; the two types of *śuṣkāmlikā*—wild and cultivated; and substances used for preparing *āsava*.

Surā, sauvīraka, tuṣodaka, maireya, medaka, madirā, madhu-śukta, śīdhu, dadhi, dadhi-maṇḍa, udaśvit, dhānyāmla, and so forth—of these and other medicinal substances enumerated in the sour group (amlavarga), having cut those that are to be sliced into pieces and broken those that are to be crushed into fine bits, one should pour them into a vessel with liquids, cook them, and prepare them. Then, according to the rules, the expert should duly administer this to one suffering from disorders of Vāta, combined with oil, muscle fat, marrow, salt, and treacle, while lukewarm. This concludes the sour category.

3.8.141 | Saindhava, sauvarcala, kāla, viḍa, pākya, ānūpa, kūpya, vālukaila, maulaka, sāmudra, romaka, audbhida, auṣara, pāṭeyaka, pāṃśuja, and other such varieties enumerated in the group of salts (lavaṇavarga)—these, when combined with unctuous substances and administered either with sour liquids or warm water, should be given by one who knows the procedure according to the rules as a comfortably warm enema (sukhoṣṇa-basti) for those suffering from disorders of Vāta. Thus ends the section on salts.

3.8.142 | Long pepper, long pepper root, elephant pepper, chaba pepper, leadwort, ginger, black pepper, bishop’s weed, fresh ginger, false black pepper, coriander, pīlu, tejavatī, cardamom, costus, marking nut seeds, asafoetida, resin, kilima, radish, mustard, garlic, karañja, śigru, madhuśigru, kharapuṣpa, bhūstṛṇa, sumukha, surasa, kuṭheraka, arjaka, gaṇḍīra, kālamālaka, parṇāsa, kṣavaka, phaṇijjhaka, alkali, urine, and bile; these are [the pungent group].

Of these and other medicinal substances enumerated in the pungent group (kaṭukavarga), having cut those that are to be cut into pieces and broken those that are to be broken into small fragments, one who knows the procedure should cook them with cow’s urine, prepare them, and duly administer a comfortably warm enema (basti) mixed with honey, oil, and salt to a patient suffering from disorders of phlegm (śleṣman). Thus ends the section on the pungent group.

3.8.143 | Sandalwood, *nalada*, *kṛtamāla*, *naktamāla*, *nimba*, *tumburu*, *kuṭaja*, turmeric, *dāruharidrā*, *musta*, *mūrvā*, *kirātatiktaka*, *kaṭukarohiṇī*, *trāyamāṇā*, *kāravellikā*, *karīra*, *karavīraka*, *rebuka*, *kaṭhillaka*, *vṛṣa*, *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *karkoṭaka*, *vārtāku*, *karkaśa*, *kākamācī*, *kākodumbarikā*, *suṣavī*, *ativiṣā*, *paṭola*, *kulaka*, *pāṭhā*, *guḍūcī*, the tips of *vetra*, *vetasa*, *vikaṅkata*, *bakula*, *somavalka*, *saptaparṇa*, *sumanā*, *arka*, *avalguja*, *vacā*, *tagara*, *aguru*, *vālaka*, and *uśīra*— these are [the plants].

Of these and other medicinal substances enumerated in the bitter group (tikta-varga), the physician who knows the procedure should cut those that require cutting into pieces, and break those that require breaking into small fragments; having washed them and sprinkled them with water, he should prepare and process them, and then duly administer a comfortably warm enema (basti) mixed with honey, oil, and salt to one suffering from disorders of phlegm (kapha). However, for one suffering from disorders of bile (pitta), the physician who knows the procedure should duly administer it cold, mixed with honey and ghee.
Thus ends the bitter section (tiktaskandha).
3.8.144 | [The suffix *cha* (i.e., *iya*) is applied after the following stems:

priyaṅgu, ananta, āmrātasthi, ambaṣṭhakī, kaṭvaṅga, lodhra, mocarasa, samaṅgā, dhātakīpuṣpa, padmā, padmakeśara, jambū, āmra, plakṣa, vaṭa, kapītana, udumbara, aśvattha, bhallātakāsthi, aśmantaka, śirīṣa, śiṃśapā, somavalka, tinduka, priyāla, badara, khadira, saptaparṇa, śvakarṇa, syandana, arjuna, arimeda, elavāluka, paripelava, kadamba, śallakī, jiṅginī, kāśa, kaśeruka, rājakaśeruka, kaṭphala, vaṃśa, padmaka, aśoka, śāla, dhava, sarja, bhūrja, and śaṇa.

Arapuṣpa, apāmārga, śamī, ācīkavara, tuṅga, ajakarṇa, sphūrjaka, bibhītaka, kumbhī, puṣkarabīja, lotus stalks, lotus fibers, lotus roots, tāla, and date palms—having cut these and other such medicinal substances enumerated in the group of astringents (kaṣāyavarga) into pieces where they are to be cut, and having broken them into fine fragments where they are to be broken, and having washed them, sprinkled them with water, boiled them, and prepared them properly, one should administer a comfortably warm enema (basti) supplemented with honey, oil, and salt.

One who knows the procedure should administer it according to the rules to one suffering from a disorder of phlegm; however, for one suffering from a disorder of bile, one should administer it after mixing it with honey and ghee while it is cold. Thus ends the section on decoctions.

3.8.145 | Regarding this, there are these verses: These six groups that have been enumerated according to the distinctions of taste— one should know them as universally applicable with respect to non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana).
3.8.146 | For indeed, those who know [the procedure] apply enemas for all diseases;
they subdue all diseases for which the non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) is beneficial.
3.8.147 | Those groups of substances which have not been prescribed for the pacification of particular disorders are, for those very disorders, provocative.
3.8.148 | Thus, these six groups of āsthāpana enemas have been explained by dividing them according to their tastes (rasas).

3.8.149 | From these [lists], a wise physician should exclude whatever substance, even if enumerated, he considers unsuitable; and he should prescribe whatever, even if not mentioned, he considers suitable. He may combine one group with another, whether by one with one or one with many, taking clinical reasoning as his authority.

Just as the alms-round of a mendicant, the seed of a farmer, or a thread for the wise, even a small amount serves to produce vast knowledge; therefore, for the intelligent, there is the exercise of inference, exclusion, and deliberation, whereas for the dull-witted, merely following what has been stated is better.

For as it has been said: "A physician who follows the prescribed path accomplishes his task; because the procedure is not too extensive, he does not fail, and because the illustration is not too brief."
3.8.150 | Hereafter, we shall explain the substances for oil enemas (anuvāsana).
An oil enema, however, consists of unctuous substances (sneha) alone.
Unctuous substances are of two kinds: those of vegetable origin and those of animal origin.
Among those, the unctuous substances derived from immobile sources are oil (*taila*) and non-oil (*ataila*).
We shall treat both of these as simply "oil" (*taila*), because of the predominance of oil in all respects.
Those derived from mobile sources, however, are muscle fat (*vasā*), marrow (*majjā*), and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).

Among these—oil, muscle fat, marrow, and clarified butter—the preceding ones are superior for oil enemas (anuvāsana) in disorders of Vāta and Kapha, while each subsequent one is superior in disorders of Pitta; however, all of them may be employed in all disorders through specific methods of processing.

3.8.151 | Furthermore, the substances for head-purgation (śirovirecana) are the fruits of apāmārga, pippalī, marica, viḍaṅga, śigru, śirīṣa, tumburu, pilu, ajājī, ajamodā, vārtākī, pṛthvīkā, elā, hareṇukā, as well as the leaves of sumukha, surasa, kuṭheraka, gaṇḍīra, kālamālaka, parṇāsa, kṣavaka, phaṇijjhaka, haridrā, śṛṅavera, mūlaka, laśuna, tarkārī, and sarṣapa.

The roots of arka, alarka, kuṣṭha, nāgadantī, vacā, apāmārga, śvetā, jyotiṣmatī, gavākṣī, gaṇḍīra, puṣpī, vākpuṣpī, vṛścikālī, vayasthā, and ativiṣā; the tubers of haridrā, śṛṅgavera, mūlaka, and laśuna; the flowers of lodhra, madana, saptaparṇa, nimba, and arka; the exudations of devadāru, aguru, sarala, śallakī, jiṅginī, asana, and hiṅgu; and the barks of tejovatī, varāṅga, iṅgudī, śobhāñjanaka, bṛhatī, and kaṇṭakārikā—these constitute the sevenfold head-purgative (śirovirecana), categorized according to their source: fruit, leaf, root, tuber, flower, exudation, and bark.

Saline, pungent, bitter, and astringent substances, as well as other unmentioned drugs that are beneficial to the sense organs, are prescribed for the purpose of head-purgation (śirovirecana) when administered according to their appropriate application.
3.8.152 | Regarding this, there are these verses:—The examination of the teacher, the student, and the subject matter; the reasons for it;
the rules for studying and teaching; and likewise the rules for discourse.
3.8.153 | There are fifty words for the path of debate diminished by six,
and ten other words, such as "reason" (kāraṇa) and so forth, according to their true nature.

3.8.154 | Furthermore, the ninefold [set] beginning with interrogation and examination regarding emesis and other therapies has been fully elucidated in the Vimāna on diseases within the Bhiṣagjitīya [section].
3.8.155 | This multitude of meanings has been spoken in many ways, variegated by diverse expressions and beautiful in its sense;
it is joined with various auspicious word-combinations and serves as the destroyer of the arguments of opponents.
Having understood this wisdom, which relies upon manifold reasons and crushes the doctrines of other schools,
he is not entangled by the refutations of others' words, nor can he be crushed by the arguments of others.
3.8.157 | However, for all entities beginning with the doshas,
the correct measurements have been explained in detail according to their divisions, based on the existence of causes.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of Disease and the Physician," in the Section on Determinations (Vimānasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
(In the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka,
the section on Vimāna has been established according to this limit.
The commentary on the Vimānasthāna is completed.
The Section on the Body (Śārīrasthāna)
The First Chapter.
4.1.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical treatise entitled "The Human Being in Its Various Aspects" (Katidhāpuruṣīya).
4.1.2 Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
4.1.3ab | O wise one, in how many ways is the person (puruṣa) divided according to the classification of the constituent elements (dhātu)?
4.1.3cd | Why is the person the cause, and what is the source of the person?

4.1.4ab | Is he ignorant or wise? Is he eternal, or is he shown to be non-eternal? 4.1.4cd | What is primordial nature (prakṛti)? What are the transformations (vikāras)? And what is the characteristic mark (liṅga) of the person (puruṣa)?
4.1.5ab | Those who know the Self describe the Self as actionless, independent, sovereign, omnipresent, and all-pervading; 4.1.5cd | likewise as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Witness.
4.1.6ab | O Blessed One, how can there be activity for that which is devoid of action?
4.1.6cd | If it were independent, why would it be born in undesirable wombs?
4.1.7ab | If he is a master [of himself], why is he forcibly overcome by unpleasant states?
4.1.7cd | And because they are all-pervasive, why does he not experience all sensations?
4.1.8ab | Why does the all-pervading Lord not see that which is obstructed by mountains or walls?
4.1.8cd | Is it the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) or the Field (kṣetra)? This is the doubt.
4.1.9ab | Without a prior field (kṣetra), the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is indeed not tenable. 4.1.9cd | And if the field were prior, the knower of the field would be non-eternal.
4.1.10ab | And for whom is this [soul] a witness, since no other agent is found?
4.1.10cd | And how could there be a distinction caused by cognition in that which is changeless?
4.1.11ab | Now, O Blessed One, which of the three does the physician treat for the afflicted person: 4.1.11cd | the past sensation, the present one, or the future one?

4.1.12ab | There is no attainment of that which is yet to come, nor any arrival of that which has passed. 4.1.12cd | Even for that which is present, there is no stability; therefore, there is indeed doubt.
4.1.13ab | What is the cause of the sensations, and what is said to be their basis?
4.1.13cd | And where do all these sensations go to their cessation without remainder?
4.1.14ab | By what marks is he perceived—the all-knowing, the renouncer of everything, who has emerged from all attachments; 4.1.14cd | the solitary, tranquil self of beings?
4.1.15ab | Having heard these words of Agniveśa, Punarvasu, the best among the wise, 4.1.15cd | whose mind was perfectly tranquil, explained everything exactly as it is.

4.1.16ab | The elements beginning with the ether (ākāśa), with consciousness as the sixth, are considered the person (puruṣa). 4.1.16cd | Furthermore, the single element of consciousness is also designated by the term "person."
[The reading 'khādayaścetanādhātuṣaṣṭhāstu' is preferred.
4.1.17ab | Furthermore, by way of the division of elements (dhātu), it is remembered as being twenty-fourfold:
4.1.17cd | the mind, the ten sense organs, their objects, and the eightfold primordial nature (prakṛti).
4.1.18ab | The definition of the mind is the non-occurrence and the occurrence of cognition;
4.1.18cd | for even when there is contact between the self, the sense organs, and the objects, [cognition] does not arise [in the absence of the mind].
4.1.19ab | Knowledge arises from the proximity of the mind, and it functions through its withdrawal.
4.1.19cd | Furthermore, two qualities of the mind are traditionally taught: its atomicity and its singularity.
4.1.20ab | That which is to be thought of, deliberated upon, inferred, meditated upon, and even intended;
4.1.20cd | whatever is to be known by the mind—all that indeed bears the designation of "object" (artha).
4.1.21ab | The function of the mind is the apprehension of the senses; its own restraint is self-control.
4.1.21cd | Discernment and deliberation follow, after which the intellect (buddhi) operates.
4.1.22ab | For an object of the senses is perceived by the sense organ together with the mind;
4.1.22cd | but thereafter it is conceptualized by the mind as possessing either qualities or defects.
4.1.23ab | In that regard, whatever cognition arises concerning an object which is determinative in nature,
4.1.23cd | by means of that [cognition], one resolves to speak or to act intentionally.
4.1.24ab | The sense organs of the elements, beginning with ether, are indeed joined with an increase of one [element] at each stage.
4.1.24cd | These five are to be inferred from their functions, from which cognition proceeds.
4.1.25ab | The two hands, the two feet, the anus, the generative organ, and also the organ of speech;
4.1.25cd | these are the five organs of action; the two feet are for the act of going.
4.1.26ab | The anus and the generative organ are for the purpose of excretion; the hands are for grasping and holding.
4.1.26cd | The tongue is the organ of speech, and speech consists of truth, which is light, and falsehood, which is darkness.
4.1.27ab | The great elements are space, wind, fire, water, and earth;
4.1.27cd | sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their respective qualities.
4.1.28ab | Of these, the first has one quality; there is an increase of qualities in each subsequent one. [Note:
"Of these, the first has one quality" is an alternative reading.
4.1.28cd | And the preceding [element] and its preceding quality are likewise recorded in sequence among the possessors of qualities.

[Variation: *‘pūrvo guṇaścaiva’*] 4.1.29ab | Hardness, fluidity, mobility, and heat are the qualities of earth, water, air, and fire, respectively. 4.1.29cd | Non-obstruction is observed as the characteristic mark of space, in due order.
4.1.30ab | All this [previously mentioned] is indeed the domain of the sense-organ of touch.
4.1.30cd | For touch, along with its opposites, is to be known by the sense-organ of touch.

4.1.31ab | The qualities (guṇas) in the body, as well as the indicators of those possessing qualities (guṇins), have been specified. 4.1.31cd | Objects such as sound and the rest should be known as the spheres of perception; they are the objects (viṣayas) that are the qualities.

4.1.32ab | Whatever cognition arises in a living being depending upon a particular sense organ, 4.1.32cd | it receives its designation from that [organ], while that which arises from the mind is designated by the mind.
4.1.33ab | Due to the diversity of effects, organs, and objects, many cognitions are indeed recorded.
4.1.33cd | Each single [cognition] arises from the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object.

[Variation: *‘ekaikasannikarṣajāḥ’*] 4.1.34ab | Just as sound produced by the contact of a finger, the thumb, the palm, the strings, the lute, and the fingernail is observed, so too is cognition observed to be born from conjunction (saṃyoga). 4.1.34cd | [End of verse]
4.1.35ab | One should know that which sustains yoga as the supreme among the intellect, the senses, the mind, and the objects.
4.1.35cd | For this aggregate of twenty-four principles is designated as "Puruṣa."
4.1.36ab | For one joined with rajas and tamas, this connection is endless;
4.1.36cd | but when those two are cast off through the increase of sattva, it ceases.
[With the reading "sattvabuddhyā" as an alternative:
4.1.37ab | Herein is action, and herein its fruit; herein is knowledge established.
4.1.37cd | Herein is delusion, pleasure, pain, life, death, and selfhood.
4.1.38ab | He who knows this in its true essence, he knows both dissolution and emergence. [Note: some manuscripts read "etadyo veda" instead of "evaṃ yo veda.
4.1.38cd | [He knows] the lineage, the medical treatment, and whatever else is to be known.

4.1.39ab: "And whatever is knowable here... [Alternative reading: *vedyaṃ yaccātra*] 4.1.39cd: Light and darkness, truth and falsehood, the Vedas, and auspicious and inauspicious actions—these would not exist if the Person (puruṣa), who is both the agent and the knower, did not exist.
[The reading 'kartā veditā' is preferred.
4.1.40ab | There is no locus, no pleasure, no pain, no going, no coming, and no speech;
4.1.40cd | no consciousness, no scriptures, and neither birth nor death.
4.1.41ab | If the Puruṣa did not exist, there would be neither bondage nor liberation.
4.1.41cd | Therefore, the Puruṣa is declared by those who know the cause to be the cause.
4.1.42ab | If the self were not the cause [of the elements], then space and the other elements would be without a cause.
4.1.42cd | Furthermore, cognition could not arise within them, nor would there be any purpose served by them.
4.1.43ab | A jar is made from clay, a staff, and a wheel, yet without a potter; 4.1.43cd | A house is made from clay, grass, and wood, yet without a builder.
4.1.44ab | Whoever might say that the body is produced by the instruments coming together,
4.1.44cd | does so out of ignorance, being devoid of both reasoning and scripture, for he asserts it to be without a creator.
4.1.45ab | Puruṣa is apprehended as the cause by all means of valid cognition.
4.1.45cd | From all those scriptures (āgama) by which the object of knowledge (prameya) is cognized.

4.1.46ab | Those others who have arisen through a continuous succession are not identical to him; 4.1.46cd | yet, because of their similarity in form, those ever-new individuals are designated as being "the very same."
4.1.47ab | Their collection of states is the Lordless [aggregate] designated as "sentient being" (sattva).
4.1.47cd | Some maintain that it is neither an agent nor an enjoyer; it is not a person (puruṣa).
4.1.48ab | By means of other states, others experience new states as the fruit of what was done by those [others].
4.1.48cd | Those who have not taught themselves experience what they have obtained, even though they are similar [to those who did the deeds].
4.1.49ab | The instruments are seen to be different [from one another], yet the agent is indeed that same one.
4.1.49cd | For the agent, when joined with the instruments, is the cause of all actions.
4.1.50ab | Time in the destruction of entities is swifter than the time it takes for an eye to blink;
4.1.50cd | there is no rebirth for those who are destroyed, and what has been done does not pass to another.
[With the reading *ca* as in the Pāṭha:
4.1.51ab | This is the opinion of those who know reality; therefore, he is the cause. 4.1.51cd | [He is] the eternal one, designated as the *puruṣa*, in the experience of activity by living beings.
4.1.52ab | Egoity, the fruit [of action], karma, the transition to another body, and memory—
4.1.52cd | exist for living beings while the cause [the Self] remains within the body.
4.1.53ab | For there is no origin for the Supreme Self, because it is beginningless.
4.1.53cd | But the Person, designated as a "heap," is born from delusion, desire, aversion, and karma.
4.1.54ab | The self is a knower; through its connection with the instruments, knowledge arises for it.
4.1.54cd | Due to the impurity of the instruments or due to their non-connection, [knowledge] does not arise.
4.1.55ab | Just as there is no vision of reality even for one who looks into a defiled mirror, 4.1.55cd | so it is when the mind is impaired, as with turbid water.
[Variation: *'yadvajjale'*, cf. pā+] 4.1.56ab | The instruments are the mind, the intellect, and the organs of cognition and action;
4.1.56cd | as well as the action arising from the conjunction with the agent, sensation, and the intellect itself.
4.1.57ab | The self of beings does not act alone, nor does it enjoy the fruit;
4.1.57cd | everything proceeds from conjunction; without that, nothing exists.
4.1.58ab | For no entity exists as a single [unit], nor does it exist without a cause.
4.1.58cd | Due to its rapid movement and its inherent nature, it does not transcend non-existence.

[“But an entity does not deviate from its own nature” (pā+)] 4.1.59ab | The person (*puruṣa*) is beginningless and eternal, whereas that which is born from a cause is the opposite. 4.1.59cd | That which exists without a cause is seen to be eternal; that which is born from a cause is otherwise.
4.1.60ab | That very [Self] is ungraspable because of its existence; it is not non-eternal for any reason.
4.1.60cd | Because of its existence, that Unmanifest is to be known as inconceivable; otherwise, it is manifest.
4.1.61ab | The Unmanifest is the Self, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), eternal, all-pervading, and immutable.
4.1.61cd | That which is other than this is the Manifest; furthermore, another pair will be described.
4.1.62ab | That which is manifest and perceptible by the senses is grasped by the senses.
4.1.62cd | On the other hand, that which is different from this is unmanifest, graspable through its mark (liṅga), and beyond the senses.

4.1.63ab | The elements beginning with ether, intellect, the unmanifest, and likewise the ego as the eighth; 4.1.63cd | are declared to be the eightfold primordial nature (prakṛti) of the elements, as well as the sixteen transformations (vikāra).
4.1.64ab | There are exactly five organs of cognition and five organs of action; 4.1.64cd | together with the mind and the five objects, these are designated as the "evolutes."
4.1.65ab | Thus the entire field has been described, excluding the Unmanifest.
4.1.65cd | The sages know the Unmanifest to be the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) of this field.
4.1.66ab | Intellect (buddhi) arises from the unmanifest; through intellect, one conceives "I am.
4.1.66cd | From egoism (ahaṅkāra), the elements beginning with space arise in their proper order.
"Then the ego grasps the elements beginning with space" (4.1.67ab).
Thereafter, having been born with all its limbs complete, it is said to have "arisen. At the time of dissolution, the person is separated once again from the desired states of existence (4.1.67cd).
4.1.68ab | From the unmanifest it goes to the state of manifestation, and again from the manifest to the state of the unmanifest;
4.1.68cd | possessed by rajas and tamas, it revolves like a wheel.

4.1.69ab | For those who have supreme attachment to dualistic pairs and those who are devoted to the ego-sense, there is rising and dissolution; but for those who are otherwise than this, there is neither.
4.1.70ab | Inhalation and exhalation, the opening and closing of the eyes, and so forth, life, and the movement of the mind;
4.1.70cd | the transition between different sense organs, as well as impulsion and retention—[these are the functions of the self].
4.1.71ab | Traveling to another country in a dream, as well as perceiving one's own death; 4.1.71cd | likewise, seeing with the right eye what was previously seen with the left eye.
4.1.72ab | Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, effort, consciousness, and fortitude;
4.1.72cd | intellect, memory, and ego—these are the marks of the Supreme Self.
4.1.73ab | Since these signs of a living being are perceived from [the body],
4.1.73cd | and not the signs of the self in one who is dead, therefore the great sages have so declared.

4.1.74ab | For when that [soul] has departed, the body is like an insentient empty house; 4.1.74cd | because it remains as nothing but the five elements, it is said to have "gone to the state of the five" (pañcatva).
4.1.75ab | The mind is insentient and possesses activity, while the Supreme is the conscious agent.
4.1.75cd | The activities of that all-pervading Lord are designated [only] when He is joined with the mind.
4.1.76ab | Since the self possesses consciousness, it is therefore designated as the agent.
4.1.76cd | And because the mind lacks consciousness, it is not called an agent, even though it possesses activity.
4.1.77ab | Just as every living being, by means of its own self, governs itself through the vital breaths in all wombs; 4.1.77cd | for there is no other governor for it.
4.1.78ab | The master performs that action by performing which he enjoys the fruit;
4.1.78cd | the master composes the mind; the master casts everything aside.
4.1.79ab | Although the embodied self is omnipresent, [it perceives] through its own respective sense organs of touch; [variant reading:
"The self is omnipresent in the body"].
4.1.79cd | But all sensations reside in all their respective substrates; therefore, the self does not experience them [all].
4.1.80ab | For this very reason, he possesses omnipresence, since he is all-pervading and great;
4.1.80cd | and through the concentration of the mind, the self perceives even that which is concealed.
4.1.81ab | One should know that [the soul] is eternally bound by the mind, which follows the actions of the body;
4.1.81cd | it exists within all wombs, even while remaining in a single womb.
4.1.82ab | There is no beginning for the Self; the succession of the field is beginningless. [Note: The reading 'anādirātmā kṣetrasya pāramparyamanādikam' is preferred.
4.1.82cd | Therefore, because both are beginningless, it cannot be said which came first.
4.1.83ab | One who knows is called a witness, not one who does not know; for the Self is traditionally held to be the witness.
4.1.83cd | Indeed, all states of being of all living beings have the Self as their witness.
4.1.84ab | The single self of beings is never perceived by means of defining characteristics;
4.1.84cd | for that which is unperceivable as a single entity, no particularity exists.
4.1.85ab | A distinction based on sensation is accepted for the person who is a conjunction [of body and mind].
4.1.85cd | Wherever sensation is determinate, there the distinction is produced by it.
4.1.86ab | "The physician treats all sensations belonging to the three times," so it is said.
4.1.86cd | That reasoning by which some explain this should now be understood.
4.1.87ab | Again that headache returns, and that fever has come back;
4.1.87cd | Again that cough is powerful, and that vomiting has returned.
4.1.88ab | By these well-known expressions, the arrival from the past is intended;
4.1.88cd | and this is the time when those who have passed away return once more.

4.1.89ab | That medicine which is administered with reference to that specific time [of onset] is called the pacifier of pains that have already passed. 4.1.89cd | It is said to be the alleviator of sensations that have already occurred.
4.1.90ab | Those waters have returned to me, by which the grain was struck down in the past.
4.1.90cd | Just as a dam is constructed for each specific task, so too do I take refuge [in this practice].
4.1.91ab | Having observed the premonitory signs of disorders about to manifest,
4.1.91cd | whatever therapeutic action is performed, that too destroys the pain before it has arrived.
4.1.92ab | Furthermore, the continuous succession of sufferings is brought to an end.
4.1.92cd | And pleasure also proceeds through the application of the causes of pleasure.
4.1.93ab | Those that are balanced do not become unbalanced, nor do those that are unbalanced attain balance.
4.1.93cd | The bodily constituents (dhātus) are constantly produced in accordance with their respective causes.

4.1.94ab | Having placed this reasoning forward, the physician destroys sensation pertaining to the three periods of time; 4.1.94cd | thus it is said that treatment is that which is final and free from ulterior motives (upadhā).
4.1.95ab | For an ulterior motive is the supreme cause that provides both suffering and the locus of suffering.
4.1.95cd | And the renunciation of all mental acquisitions is the remover of all suffering.
4.1.96ab Just as a silkworm produces threads for its own destruction,
4.1.96cd so the ignorant man, ever afflicted, draws greed from his objects of desire.
4.1.97ab | But he who, being wise, recognizes objects that are like fire and turns away from them;
4.1.97cd | because of his non-undertaking and non-association with them, suffering does not afflict him.
4.1.98ab | The impairment of intellect, fortitude, and memory; the onset of time and karma; 4.1.98cd | and the encounter with unwholesome objects—these are to be known as the causes of suffering.

4.1.99ab | That which is an uneven attachment to what is eternal and what is non-eternal, and to what is beneficial and what is harmful, 4.1.99cd | should be known as a derangement of the intellect; for the intellect that perceives correctly views things with equanimity.

4.1.100ab | The mind, being inclined toward sense objects, cannot be restrained from unwholesome matters due to the loss of fortitude. 4.1.100cd | For fortitude consists essentially in self-restraint.
4.1.101ab | For one whose self is shrouded by passion and delusion, there occurs a loss of memory regarding the knowledge of reality.
4.1.101cd | This is "loss of memory" (*smṛtibhraṃśa*), for that which is to be remembered resides within memory.
4.1.102ab | Deprived of intelligence, fortitude, and memory, whatever inauspicious action he performs—
4.1.102cd | One should know that to be intellectual error (prajñāparādha), which provokes all the [humoral] defects.
4.1.103ab | Provoking those who are mobile and suppressing those who have been provoked;
4.1.103cd | Indulging in rash acts and excessive indulgence with women.
4.1.104ab | The neglect of duties and the passing of the proper time for actions, as well as the improper commencement of undertakings;
4.1.104cd | The abandonment of discipline and proper conduct, and the assault upon those worthy of honor.
4.1.105ab | The intentional indulgence in things known to be harmful;
4.1.105cd | and the indulgence in causes that are supremely conducive to insanity.
4.1.106ab | Moving about at improper times and places, and friendship with those of afflicted conduct; 4.1.106cd | And the abandonment of right conduct as prescribed for the restraint of the senses.
4.1.107ab | Envy, pride, fear, anger, greed, delusion, intoxication, and confusion; 4.1.107cd | Or the afflicted action born from them, as well as any afflicted bodily action.
4.1.108ab | Furthermore, whatever other action of this kind arises from passion (rajas) and delusion (moha),
4.1.108cd | the learned call that a transgression of wisdom (prajñāparādha), which is the cause of disease.

[The variant reading is 'vyādhikāriṇam'. 4.1.109ab: One should recognize that incorrect cognition through the intellect and improper engagement [with objects] constitute *prajñāparādha* (intellectual error), for that is indeed within the domain of the mind. 4.1.109cd: [End of verse].

4.1.110ab | The timing of the onset of diseases has been specified in the summary of diseases. 4.1.110cd | As previously described, [the stages of] accumulation, aggravation, and pacification of pitta and the other doshas have also been explained.
4.1.111ab | Falsehood, excessive emaciation, and physical deformities, as well as those ending with [excessive] rain, are causes of disease.
4.1.111cd | So too are the states of food that is undigested, recently eaten, or fully digested, and the timing of its digestion—whether occurring at the proper or improper time.

[The variant reading is: *'bhuktajīrṇaprajīrṇānnakālāḥ' (4.1.112ab)] The forenoon, midday, and afternoon, as well as the three watches of the night— those diseases which are restricted to these times are known as "time-born" (*kālaja*).
4.1.113ab | Anyedyuṣka (occurs every other day), dvyahagrāhī (occurs every two days), tṛtīyaka (occurs every third day), and caturthaka (occurs every fourth day).
4.1.113cd | They manifest at their respective times, for it is at those times that their strength arises.

4.1.114ab | These and whatever other various diseases arise from time, [namely, those such as hemicrania, epilepsy, and so forth], 4.1.114cd | should be treated before they manifest by one who understands the strength [of the patient] and the [nature of the] time.

4.1.115ab | Diseases arising from the transformation of time, caused by old age and death, are seen as natural (svābhāvika). Nature (svabhāva) is beyond remedy. 4.1.115cd | That which is the action (karman) belonging to a previous body is designated by the term "fate" (daiva). 4.1.116ab | [Fate is] that which was indicated by the word "divine" (daiva), namely the karma of a prior existence.
4.1.116cd | That too is observed as the cause of diseases over time.
4.1.117ab | Indeed, there is no action so great that its fruit is not experienced.
4.1.117cd | Diseases born of past actions, which obstruct one's activities, come to an end through the exhaustion of those actions.
4.1.118ab | [Diseases arise] from hearing excessively loud sounds, or from not hearing at all.
4.1.118cd | And from hearing words that are excessively low, people become dull-witted.

4.1.119ab | Contact with the sense of hearing through sounds that are harsh, terrifying, inauspicious, unpleasant, or indicative of misfortune is called "false contact" (mithyā-saṃyoga). 4.1.119cd | [This] is described as such.
4.1.120ab | Non-contact, excessive contact, and likewise deficient contact; 4.1.120cd | these are stated in brief as the types of contact with tangible objects that impair the sense of touch.
4.1.121ab | That which [arises] from spirits, poisons, or winds, and that which occurs at an improper time;
4.1.121cd | Contact with unctuous, cold, or hot [objects] is called a false application (*mithyāyoga*).
4.1.122ab | The vision of radiant forms perishes from excessive looking.
4.1.122cd | And because of the perception of extremely subtle things, and because of their non-perception in every respect [otherwise].
4.1.123ab | From the sight of what is hated, terrifying, loathsome, distant, or excessively close;
4.1.123cd | And from the forms of tamasic [objects], a false conjunction is said to arise.

4.1.124ab | Excessive intake, non-intake, and that which results from unsuitability to one's constitution (*sātmya*) and so forth; 4.1.124cd | as well as the irregular intake and the insufficient intake of the tastes (*rasa*), cause vitiation.
4.1.125ab | The use of excessively mild or excessively sharp fragrances, 4.1.125cd | or the total avoidance of all fragrances, leads to the destruction of the sense of smell.
4.1.126ab | Putrid, putrefied, poisonous, or loathsome odors, as well as those that are out of season;
4.1.126cd | contact of the nose with such odors is called a false application (mithyāyoga).

4.1.127ab | Thus, the association with unwholesome objects is threefold and provokes the *doṣas*. 4.1.127cd | One should know that which does not attain the state of being one's own nature (*sahātmatā*) is "unwholesome" (*asātmya*). 4.1.128ab | The disease that arises from improper, excessive, or deficient application [of sense objects] is [caused by this].
4.1.128cd | That disease of sound and the other [objects] should be understood by the wise as being related to the sense organs (aindriyaka).
4.1.129ab | These are remembered as the causes of sensations that are not pacified;
[the reading 'asātmyānām' is an alternative].
4.1.129cd | However, the single cause of happiness is balanced application (samyoga), which is very difficult to obtain.
4.1.130ab | Neither the sense organs nor their objects are the causes of pleasure and pain;
4.1.130cd | rather, the cause of pleasure and pain is seen to be a fourfold contact.
4.1.131ab | The sense faculties exist, the objects exist, there is yoga, and yet there is no pain.
4.1.131cd | Nor is there pleasure; therefore, yoga alone is the fourfold cause.

4.1.132ab | Neither pleasure nor pain arises without the self, the sense organs, the mind, the intellect, the object, or the action; [an alternative reading is "Neither the self, the sense organs, the mind, the intellect, nor the object... 4.1.132cd | And whatever else is to be understood, that is explained accordingly.
4.1.133ab | Contact with the tactile organ and that which is purely mental—contact is of these two kinds. 4.1.133cd | It is the instigator of the experiences of pleasure and pain.
4.1.134ab | Thirst, consisting of desire and aversion, proceeds from pleasure and pain.
4.1.134cd | And thirst is further said to be the cause of pleasures and pains.
4.1.135ab | For it (consciousness) takes up those states designated as the basis of feeling;
4.1.135cd | it is not touched when there is no taking up, and that which is not touched does not experience feelings.
4.1.136ab | The basis of sensations is the mind and the body together with its sense organs;
4.1.136cd | excluding the hair of the head, body hair, the tips of the nails, food, excrement, and the properties of fluids.
4.1.137ab | In yoga and in liberation, there is the non-occurrence of all sensations.
4.1.137cd | In liberation, cessation is complete; yoga is that which leads to liberation.
4.1.138ab | [Cognition] arises from the contact of the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects.
4.1.138cd | Pleasure and pain do not arise when the mind is steady and established in the self.
4.1.139ab | Both of those cease and mastery arises;
4.1.139cd | the sages who know yoga recognize that as yoga for one still possessing a body.
4.1.140ab | Possession of the mind, knowledge of objects, and the performance of actions at will;
4.1.140cd | Sight, hearing, memory, radiance, and also invisibility according to one's desire.
4.1.141ab | Thus, this eightfold sovereign power of the yogis has been described.
4.1.141cd | All of that arises from the concentration of pure *sattva*.
4.1.142ab | Liberation arises from the absence of rajas and tamas and from the complete exhaustion of powerful karma;
4.1.142cd | it is called the disjunction from all associations and the state of non-rebirth.
4.1.143ab | The proper service of the virtuous and the complete avoidance of the wicked;
4.1.143cd | The practice of vows, fasting, and various kinds of observances.
4.1.144ab | Retention of the Dharmaśāstras, discernment, delight in solitude; 4.1.144cd | lack of attachment to sense-objects, resolve for liberation—this is supreme fortitude.
4.1.145ab | The non-commencement of actions and the complete exhaustion of those already performed;
4.1.145cd | Renunciation, absence of egoism, and seeing danger in worldly attachment;
4.1.146ab | Steadfastness of mind and intellect, and the investigation into the true nature of reality.
4.1.146cd | All this proceeds from the presence of the mindfulness of reality.
4.1.147ab | Memory arises through the service of the virtuous and other means, ending with fortitude.
4.1.147cd | By remembering the true nature of all things, one who remembers is liberated from suffering.
4.1.148ab | Eight causes will be described by which memory is produced.
4.1.148cd | Because of the apprehension of the form of the cause, and because of similarity along with its opposite.
4.1.149ab | Memory is said to arise from the persistence of mental substance (*sattva*), from repeated practice, from knowledge acquired through yoga, and furthermore, from what has been heard;
4.1.149cd | it is also called memory due to the recollection of things seen, heard, or experienced.
4.1.150ab | This is shown by the liberated as the sole path to liberation;
4.1.150cd | it is the power of the recollection of reality, by which those who have gone do not return.

4.1.151ab | Furthermore, this is declared by yogins to be the path (ayana) of yoga; 4.1.151cd | and by the Sāṃkhyas, who possess the knowledge of the enumerated categories (saṃkhyātadharmāḥ), it is the path of liberation for those who are liberated.
4.1.152ab | All suffering is caused by a condition, is without self, and is indeed impermanent.
4.1.152cd | Nor is it created by a self, for therein its own-nature arises.
4.1.153ab | As long as the true awakening has not arisen by which one realizes, "This am not," 4.1.153cd | and "This is not mine"— having understood this, the knower transcends everything.
4.1.154ab | In that final renunciation, all sensations, together with their roots,
| 4.1.154cd | along with perception, cognition, and discernment, come to cease without remainder.

[Variation: *‘from the cessation of the cognition of all objects of knowledge’*] 4.1.155ab | Thereafter, having become Brahman, the self of beings is no longer perceived; 4.1.155cd | it has emerged from all states of being, and no sign of it exists.

"Brahman is the goal of those who know Brahman, and that is the imperishable, which is without defining characteristics. (By Gaṅgādhara Ed., 4.1.155) Knowledge belongs to those who know Brahman; one who is ignorant is not capable of knowing it.
4.1.156 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
4.1.156ab | Twenty-three excellent questions concerning the person (puruṣa) 4.1.156cd | have been resolved in this chapter on "The Person" (Katidhāpuruṣīya) by the Seer of Reality.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Human Being in Its Many Aspects" (Katidhāpuruṣīya Śārīra), in the Section on Anatomy (Śārīrasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka. ||1||
The Second Chapter.
4.2.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the body concerning those of unequal lineages (atulyagotrīya).
4.2.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
4.2.3 | At the end of the destruction of passion, for one of unequal lineage who has engaged in union and discharged his secret [semen],
what would be the origin of the four-footed from the six? [The reading "catuṣpadaṃ ṣaḍprabhavaṃ kimasya" is preferred over "kiṃ syāccatuṣpātprabhavaṃ ca ṣaḍbhyaḥ"].
That which a man attains as the state of being an embryo within women.
4.2.4 | The wise call that semen of his which is deposited for the production of the embryo;
it possesses the four qualities of air, fire, earth, and water.
And its origin is from the six tastes.
4.2.5 | How and by what means is a fetus born with a complete body, comfortably and at the proper time? And why does a woman, though capable of bearing children, conceive only after a long delay?
Or having come into being, by what means does the embryo perish?

4.2.6 | When there is excellence of the semen, the blood, the self, the uterus, and the time, and when the treatment is carried out with wholesome foods— and not with unwholesome things— the fetus is born at the proper time, healthy, comfortably, and with a fully developed body.
4.2.7 | Due to disorders of the womb, mental distress, defects in semen, blood, diet, or lifestyle,
from untimely sexual union, or from the depletion of strength, even a woman who is capable of conceiving may not conceive for a long time.
4.2.8 | Sometimes the ignorant diagnose a woman’s fetus as being obstructed by wind (*vāta*), even though it is actually the blood that is obstructed.
For that blood, as it increases, produces the very appearance of a fetus within her.
4.2.9 | When [the fetus] has been set in motion by fire, the sun, physical exertion, grief, disease, or hot food and drink, some men—
seeing only blood and not recognizing it as the embryo— declare that it has been carried off by spirits.
4.2.10 | For night-rangers who subsist on vital energy (*ojas*), the body is not desired as food;
if they do not find an opening in the mother's womb, they would carry off the fetus, but if they do not find such an opportunity, they would take away the vital energy.
4.2.11 | Why does a maiden or a son give birth to twins— whether together or separately,
or sons and daughters, or many daughters—
and why does one [of them] remain in the womb for a very long time while the other attains full growth?

4.2.12 | When the female seed (rakta) is in excess, a daughter is born; when the male seed (śukra) is in excess, a son is born; and by that seed being made twofold, she gives birth to both a daughter and a son.
According to whichever among their own seeds is predominant.
4.2.13 | If the seed of one woman becomes divided such that the semen is in excess, she gives birth to two sons together;
or if it becomes divided such that the blood is in excess, [she gives birth to two daughters].
In the Suta [chapter], she is born in two ways when joined with Prasūti.
4.2.14 | To whatever extent the excessively aggravated *vāyu* (wind), having entered, divides the semen and menstrual blood into many parts,
to that same number of offspring it gives birth, according to their respective portions.
It brings forth [beings] consisting of karma by its own power.
4.2.15 | When the fetus does not receive nourishment, yet neither undergoes emaciation nor suffers from discharge,
the woman gives birth to that fetus after a very long time.
When he has become nourished even by many years, [then...]
4.2.16 | Due to the nature of karma and the unequal division of the portions of semen and blood, one grows larger within the womb while the second becomes smaller;
thus, even in the case of twins, there is this distinction of one being greater. (*Note: In some readings, it says "even when the [semen] is greater, this distinction occurs.")
4.2.17 | Why are there those with double seed, those with wind-like organs, those who carry impressions, and those who are eunuchs among men and women?
Or how is it that there are those who are crooked and those whose pleasure consists of envy?
Or he is born as a eunuch afflicted by wind.

4.2.18 | From seeds that have been scorched and are present in equal proportions, one becomes a hermaphrodite possessing both female and male characteristics and two types of semen; this occurs by [the embryo] reaching and damaging the receptacle of the semen (*śukrāśaya*). (*Note: The reading 'gatvā' is preferred over 'hatvā'.*)
The wind performs the function of the organ of smelling.

4.2.19 | And the wind (anila) produces [the condition] by obstructing the gateway of the seminal receptacle (*śukrāśaya*), thereby carrying away the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); [as it is said: "The wind indeed carries away the latent impressions.
It results in dullness, scanty semen, weakness, and lack of sexual excitement.
And the eunuch is the cause of both types of transformation.

4.2.20 | Due to the mother's obstruction during sexual intercourse and the weakness of the father's seed, the child may become crooked; even when both parents are overcome by jealousy, they are said to have little joy, for jealousy itself is the cause of such a condition. (Note: Some read 'vīrṣyāhvayasyaiva' instead of 'vīrṣyāratereva'.)
4.2.21 | He whose testicles have perished due to the disorder of wind (vāyu) and fire (agni) is a *vātika-ṣaṇḍaka*.
Thus, there are eight varieties of morbid conditions (*vikṛti*).
It is to be characterized by those whose nature is karma.

4.2.22 | What are the characteristics of a fetus that has recently entered the womb, whether it be female, male, or neuter as it resides in the abdomen? What is considered the cause [of these differences]?
And by which the offspring attains similarity of form.
4.2.23 | Spitting, heaviness, lassitude of the limbs, drowsiness, horripilation, pain in the heart, satiety,
and the retention of semen in the womb are the signs of a fetus that has immediately entered.
4.2.24 | A woman who desires a male child exhibits movements with her left limbs; she has the disposition for dreaming, drinking, eating, and activities characteristic of women;
she carries the fetus on the left side, yet her abdomen is not distended.
A woman whose milk flows from the left breast gives birth to a female child alone.
4.2.25 | But from this [seed], by the reversal of the characteristic marks, a third nature of mixed characteristics arises as a son;
however, at the time of conception, whichever [nature] the woman's mind [is directed toward]...
A living being goes toward that [state] and is born resembling it.
4.2.26 | There are four types of elements in the embryo, each consisting of fourfold: those derived from the mother and father,
those produced from food, and those produced by the self.
All [elements] exist within the body of everyone.
4.2.27 | Among these, those factors arising from the mother, the father, and past actions are the most powerful;
one should determine them to be the cause of resemblance.
One should also determine one's own strength according to one's capacity.
4.2.28 | Why does a woman give birth to an offspring that is deformed— either with deficient or extra limbs, or with impaired sense organs?
How does the self (ātman) pass from one body to another body, and by what is it eternally bound?
4.2.29 | Through defects in the seed, the self, karma, and time, as well as through defects in the mother’s diet and lifestyle,
the vitiated humors produce various deformities of shape, complexion, and the sense organs.
4.2.30 | Just as the force of wood, stone, clouds, and water during the rainy season might cause damage to a tree standing in the current of a river,
even so do the bodily humors (doṣas) cause deformity to the embryo situated within the womb.
4.2.31 | Accompanied by the four extremely subtle elements, the soul, possessing the speed of thought, departs from one body and enters another;
because its nature is determined by karma, it has no visible form, except for that which is seen through divine vision.
4.2.32 | He is all-pervading and the sustainer of all bodies;
he is the architect of the universe and possesses universal form;
he is the element of consciousness and transcends the senses.
He is ever-yoked and possessed of latent tendencies; he alone [is such].
4.2.33 | One should know that there are sixteen elements in the body— ten derived from the essence [of food] and six arising from the mother and father;
among these, four are dependent upon the self (ātman).
And the Self likewise abides within those four.

4.2.34 | They say that the elements (*bhūta*) produced from the mother and father in the womb are the *rajas* (ovum) and the *śukra* (semen). Those elements by which the semen and blood are nourished are known as the "elements born of the body" (*rasaja*); one should know them to be produced from the nutrient essence (*rasa*).
4.2.35 | But the four elements born of karma, which are merged within the self, enter the womb;
for that [self] possesses the nature of a seed with respect to each successive [body].
It goes from one body to another within the self.
4.2.36 | For the arising of form from form is well-established, as is that of mental entities from the mind;
yet those various distinctions of configuration and cognition [arise]...
And there, rajas and tamas are the cause of action.
4.2.37 | The Self is never separated from those subtle forms which transcend the senses;
nor is it separated from karma, nor from the mind and intellect, nor even from the defects resulting from the transformations of the ego.
4.2.38 | For the mind is bound by rajas and tamas; indeed, all defects reside therein in the absence of knowledge.
The cause for its movement and activity has been stated.
The mind is accompanied by defects, and action is powerful.
4.2.39 | From what do diseases arise? What is their pacification? What is the cause of joy and sorrow?
These disorders originate from the body and the mind (sattva).
How might those who have attained peace not fall back again?
4.2.40 | Intellectual error, unwholesome objects, and thirdly, the time of transformation are the causes of all diseases;
their pacification is threefold: through knowledge, wholesome objects, and the proper application of time.

4.2.41 | Ritual acts performed in accordance with dharma are said to be causes of joy; when performed otherwise, they lead to the power of sorrow. Diseases, however, arise from the body and the mind (sattva); through the non-occurrence of these two, they do not arise again.

4.2.42 | There is no such thing as the beginning of the continuity of form and of sentient existence that has not been previously stated; the non-occurrence of these two is brought about by the two higher faculties of concentration and mindfulness, and by the supreme wisdom.
4.2.43 | When the two types of truth-based treatment previously described have been administered according to the disease,
diseases do not afflict one who has conquered the senses, provided that fate is not adverse at that time.
4.2.44 | That which was performed in the past is called destiny (*daiva*); whereas that which is seen here as action is human effort (*pauruṣa*).
This [latter] is observed to be the cause for the commencement of activity, though it is uneven.
For that very same [equanimity] is the cause of cessation.
4.2.45 | By inducing the accumulation of *doṣas* from the winter season in spring, that from the summer in the rainy season,
and that from the rainy season promptly and correctly at the end of autumn, [one maintains health].
A living being never contracts diseases born of the improper seasons.
4.2.46 | A man who partakes of wholesome food and conduct, acts with circumspection, is unattached to sense objects,
is generous, impartial, devoted to truth, patient, and serves those who are authoritative, remains free from disease.
4.2.47 | Intellect, speech, and action accompanied by happiness; a disciplined mind, clear understanding,
knowledge, austerity, and devotion to yoga.
Diseases do not afflict him who possesses this.
4.2.48 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
Here, the Great Sage [addressed] Agniveśa’s collection of thirty-six questions, which are endowed with great significance.
The Blessed One, having determined his name exactly as it is, [spoke] for the sake of increasing knowledge in one of incomparable lineage.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Body with Unequal Limbs," in the Section on Anatomy (*Śārīrasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The Third Chapter.
