4.3.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the minor discourse on the descent of the embryo, which is part of the anatomy of the body.
4.3.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

4.3.3 | When there is union between a man whose semen is unimpaired and a woman whose womb, blood, and uterus are not corrupted, occurring during the fertile period (*ṛtukāla*), and when their union is thus appropriately joined—when the living soul (*jīva*), through its association with the mental constituents (*sattva*), descends into the mixture of semen and blood within the uterus, then the embryo (*garbha*) is produced; that [is as follows]:

Through the consumption of congenial tastes and being attended with proper regimens, the fetus grows free from disease; then, when the time has arrived, it is born in comfort, endowed with all the sense organs, with a fully developed body, and possessed of the excellence of strength, complexion, mental vigor (*sattva*), and physical integration. This embryo arises from the combination of these factors—it is derived from the mother, from the father, from the self (*ātman*), from congeniality, and from the essence of food (*rasa*). Furthermore, there exists a mental faculty (*sattva*) that is spontaneously generated (*aupapāduka*).
Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya.

4.3.4-(1) Bharadvāja says: "No. For what reason? Because neither the mother, nor the father, nor the self, nor suitability, nor the consumption of drinks, foods, edibles, and linctuses produces the embryo; nor does a sentient being (sattva) come from the other world and enter the embryo."

4.3.4-(2) For if indeed parents were to produce an embryo, then since there are many women and many men who desire sons, all of them—engaging in sexual intercourse with the intention of producing a son—would produce only sons; or those desiring daughters would produce only daughters. Yet, no women or men who desire offspring would remain childless, nor would they lament [as it is said: "Those who desire offspring do not lament"].
4.3.4-(3) Furthermore, the self does not produce itself.
For if the self were to produce itself, it would have to do so either as something already born or as something currently being born, or as something unborn; yet both of these cases are untenable.

Indeed, that which is already born does not produce [itself] because it already exists, and that which is unborn does not produce [itself] because it does not exist. Therefore, production is impossible in either case.
Let this matter rest for now.

If this self were capable of producing itself, why would it not produce itself in desirable wombs—[producing] one who is self-controlled, whose movement is unimpeded, who can assume any form at will, and who is endowed with splendor, strength, speed, beauty, courage, and firmness, being free from old age, disease, and death? For the self desires such a self, or even more than this.
4.3.4-(4) Furthermore, this embryo is born from unwholesome factors (*asātmyaja*).

For if it were born solely from wholesome factors (*sātmyaja*), then offspring would belong exclusively to those who practice what is wholesome, and those who practice what is unwholesome would be entirely childless; yet both conditions are observed in both cases.
4.3.4-(5) Furthermore, this embryo is not produced from rasa (nutritive essence).

For if it were produced from rasa, there would be no men or women who remained childless, since there is no one among them who does not consume rasa. If it were intended that embryos are born only to those who consume the best rasas, then offspring would belong exclusively to those who subsist on the milk, curd, ghee, honey, oil, rock salt, sugarcane juice, mung beans, and śāli rice of goats, sheep, deer, peacocks, and cows; whereas those who subsist entirely on śyāmāka, varaka, uddālaka, koradūṣaka, tubers, and roots would be entirely childless.
And both of these are observed in both cases.

4.3.4-(6) Furthermore, a being does not indeed descend into the womb having come from the next world. For if it were to descend [from there], there would be nothing pertaining to its previous body that remained unknown, unheard, or unseen to it; yet it does not remember even the slightest thing of that.

4.3.4 | Therefore, we say this: this embryo is not born of the mother, nor born of the father, nor born of the self, nor born of suitability, nor born of the tastes; furthermore, there is no spontaneously born being (*sattva-aupapāduka*). Thus spoke Bharadvāja (*this reading is disapproved by Yogīndranāthasena*).
4.3.5 | "No," said the venerable Ātreya; "the embryo is produced from all these factors combined."
4.3.6 | This embryo is born from the mother;
for without a mother, there would be no conception of an embryo, nor birth for those born from a womb.

We shall now explain those parts of this embryo which are derived from the mother and which arise from its origin from the mother; namely: the skin, blood, flesh, fat, the umbilicus, the heart, the *kloma*, the liver, the spleen, the kidneys, the bladder, the receptacle for feces, the stomach (*āmāśaya*), the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*), the upper rectum, the lower rectum, the small intestine, the large intestine, the omentum, and the mesentery—these are the parts derived from the mother.
4.3.7 | This embryo is also derived from the father.
Indeed, without a father there would be no production of an embryo, nor birth for those born from a womb.

We shall now explain those parts of this embryo which are derived from the father, and those which arise from the father during its formation; they are as follows: hair of the head, beard, nails, body hair, teeth, bones, veins, ligaments, arteries, and semen—these are the paternal constituents.
4.3.8 | This embryo is born of the self (*ātman*).

For that which is the inner self (*antarātman*) within the embryo is what they call the "living being" (*jīva*): eternal, free from disease, undecaying, immortal, imperishable, indivisible, uncuttable, unshakeable, universal in form, the architect of all, unmanifest, without beginning, without end, and even imperishable.
Having entered the womb and attained union with the semen and the blood, it generates itself as an embryo by means of itself; for the designation "self" applies to the embryo.
Furthermore, because that self is beginningless, [birth] is not tenable; therefore, this one, while unborn, produces the unborn embryo—for he, being unborn, produces the unborn embryo.

And that very embryo, over the course of time, attains the states of childhood, youth, and old age. In whichever state it exists, it is "born" in that state; yet, in the state projected for it, it is "about to be born. Therefore, that same entity is simultaneously both born and unborn.

And in that wherein both these conditions—being born and being about to be born—are possible, it is born as something already born; and likewise, in future different states, being unborn, it causes itself to be born by means of itself.

For indeed, birth is said to be merely the transition to another state at various stages of life and in various conditions. Just as for those very semen, blood, and living beings, the state of being an embryo does not exist prior to their union, but it comes into existence from that union; and just as for that same person, the status of being a father does not exist prior to having offspring, but it comes into existence from the offspring;
so too, for that very embryo, the states of being born and not yet born are spoken of according to each respective stage.

4.3.9 | Indeed, neither for the embryo, nor for the mother, nor for the father, nor for oneself, does there exist the power to act at will regarding all things. They perform some things by their own volition, and some by the power of karma; in some cases they possess the capacity for action, and in others they do not. Where there is a perfection of the instruments such as the *sattva* and so forth, there is the power to act at will precisely according to one's strength; hence, the opposite is suffering. Furthermore, it is not possible that the self fails to bring about the birth of an embryo due to a defect in the instruments; for those who know the self have observed that effort, procreation, sovereignty, and liberation depend upon the self.
For there is no other agent of pleasure and pain;
nor is a fetus produced from another when it is being born, just as a sprout does not arise without a seed.

4.3.10 | We shall now explain those qualities which are born of the self (*ātman*) for this embryo, and those which arise from its own self as it comes into being; namely: birth in various wombs, life-span, knowledge of the self, mind, the sense organs, inhalation and exhalation, propulsion, maintenance, specific features of form, voice, and complexion, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, consciousness, fortitude, intellect, memory, ego-sense, and effort—these are the qualities born of the self.

4.3.11 | This embryo is born of suitability (*sātmyaja*). Indeed, without the consumption of unsuitable things (*asātmya*), there is neither sterility in the man and woman, nor any undesirable state regarding their offspring.

As long as the three *doṣas*, though aggravated in men and women who consume unsuitable things, do not reach the body to cause injury to the semen, the blood, or the uterus, they remain capable of producing an embryo.

Furthermore, for men and women who follow a wholesome regimen, whose semen, blood, and uterus are unimpaired, yet who fail to conceive when they unite during the fertile period, embryos do not manifest due to the non-descent of the *jīva* (vital principle).
This embryo is produced not by wholesome factors alone; rather, it is said that a combination of causes is required here.

We shall now explain those qualities of the embryo which are born of suitability (*sātmyaja*), and those which arise from its development through suitability; namely: health, freedom from lethargy, lack of greed, clarity of the sense organs, excellence of voice, complexion, and seed, and an abundance of great joy—these are the qualities born of suitability.

4.3.12 | This embryo is born from the *rasa* (nutritive essence). For, without *rasa*, even the maintenance of the mother’s life would not be possible, let alone the birth of the embryo. Furthermore, *rasas* do not produce an embryo when they are consumed improperly; nor does the production of the embryo result from the proper consumption of *rasas* alone. In this matter, it is said that the totality [of factors] (*samudāya*) is also a cause.

We shall now explain those products of the embryo's essence (*rasa*), as well as those that arise from its very production through the essence; namely: the formation of the body, its growth, the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), satiety, nourishment, and vigor—these are the products of the essence.

4.3.13 | There indeed exists a sentient being of spontaneous birth (*aupapāduka*), which connects itself to a body through its vital principle (*jīva*). When its departure is imminent, its character changes, its devotion is reversed, all the sense faculties are tormented, strength declines, diseases increase, and deprived of this [principle], one abandons the life-breaths (*prāṇa*); that which governs the sense faculties is designated as "mind" (*manas*).
It is described as being of three kinds: pure (*śuddha*), passionate (*rājasa*), and dark (*tāmasa*).

Indeed, by whatever [mental state] his mind is predominantly occupied, through that he enters into conjunction in a second birth (or, as some read: "in a second birth"); but when he is conjoined with that very same pure [state], then he remembers even what has passed beyond birth.

For the knowledge of remembrance follows that very self due to the persistence of that same mind; and by prioritizing the persistence of which, a person is called a "rememberer of past births" (*jātismara*).

We shall now explain those qualities of this embryo which are born of *sattva*, which arise from its very nature as a sentient being. They are as follows: devotion, conduct, purity, aversion, mindfulness, delusion, renunciation, envy, heroism, fear, anger, lassitude, enthusiasm, sharpness, gentleness, profundity, and instability, along with others such as these. These are the modifications of *sattva*, which we shall describe later in detail according to the various classifications of *sattva*.

Indeed, there are many kinds of beings; all of them exist within a single person, yet they do not exist at one and the same time. However, [the author] speaks of "one" by way of general prevalence (*prāyovṛttyā*). [Note: An alternative reading is *prāyo 'nuvṛttyā*.]

4.3.14 | Thus, this embryo is produced from the combination of these various factors that form the embryo; just as a gabled house is formed from a combination of various materials, or as a chariot is formed from a combination of various chariot parts. Therefore, we have said this: this embryo is derived from the mother, derived from the father, derived from the self (ātman), derived from suitability (sātmya), and derived from nutritional essence (rasa); and there exists a spontaneously arising being (sattva aupapāduka). (Thus spoke the venerable Ātreya.)

4.3.15 | Bharadvāja said: "If this embryo is produced from the combination of these various factors that cause conception, how is it joined together? And even if it is joined, why does an embryo originating from such a combination arise with a human form, given that a human is said to originate from a human?"

In that regard, if it is accepted that because a human originates from a human, he is therefore born with a human form—just as a cow originates from a cow, or a horse from a horse—then the statement made previously that [the self] consists of an aggregate (*samudaya*) is untenable.

Furthermore, if a human originates from a human, why is it that those born from the dull-witted, the blind, the humpbacked, the mute, the dwarfed, the squinting, the deformed, the insane, the lepers, or those afflicted with skin diseases do not possess forms resembling their parents?

Now, in this case too, the following thought might occur: "This self perceives forms with its own eye, sounds with the ear, odors with the nose, tastes with the tongue, tangibles with the body of touch, and the object of cognition with the intellect; for this reason, they do not become like their parents, born from those who are insentient and so forth."

"In this case as well, there would be the fault of abandoning one's own proposition (*pratijñāhāni*). For if it were stated thus, the Self would be a knower when the sense organs exist and a non-knower when they do not exist. And where both of these—knowing and non-knowing—are possible, the Self would be subject to modification (*savikāra*). Furthermore, if the Self perceives objects through seeing and so forth, then when devoid of sense organs, it would be a non-knower due to the absence of seeing and so forth; being a non-knower, it would be without causal agency (*akāraṇa*); and because it lacks causal agency, it would not be the Self. Thus, this statement would be a mere verbal assertion and meaningless. So said Bharadvāja.

4.3.16 | Ātreya said: This was previously asserted—that the *sattva* (the conscious principle) binds itself to a body that touches the *jīva*. However, because that embryo, arising from a composite [of causes], is born with a human form, and is thus called "human" as it originates from a human, we shall explain that: there are four types of origins (*yoni*) for living beings—namely, those born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat (moisture), and from sprouting.
Indeed, each one of these four modes of birth has innumerable subdivisions, because the specific forms of living beings are innumerable.

In this regard, for viviparous and oviparous living beings, these embryonic factors take on whatever form they assume in whichever womb they enter; they become of such-and-such a form in each respective womb. Just as gold, silver, copper, tin, or lead, when poured into various molds made of beeswax, take the shape of those molds—so too, when they enter a human mold, they are born with a human form. Therefore, although the embryo arises from a combination [of factors], it is born with a human form;
and a human is said to arise from a human because that is its source.

4.3.17 | Regarding what was said—"If a human being is born from a human, why is it that those born from the dull-witted and others do not possess forms resembling their fathers?"—to this it is replied: For whichever specific limb or member the seed-portion within the seed is afflicted, a deformity arises in that very limb or member, but it does not arise in the absence of such affliction. Therefore, both possibilities are established here. Furthermore, all sense organs are derived from the self (ātman), and the cause for their presence or absence is destiny (daiva). Consequently, it is not the case that those born from the dull-witted and others must invariably possess forms resembling their fathers.

4.3.18 | Nor does the Self become a knower when the senses are present, nor an ignorant one when they are absent; for the Self is never non-existent, and it is observed that the particularity of knowledge arises from the particularity of the internal organ (sattva).
4.3.19 | And there are verses on this point:
"Because the agent lacks sense organs, knowledge of the effect does not arise.
Whatever action proceeds by means of entities, it does not proceed without them. [Note: The reading 'yaiḥ kriyā vartate yā tu' is preferred over 'yā kriyā vartate yā tu'.]
4.3.20 | Even though he knows [how to make it], a potter does not proceed to act due to the absence of clay.

Listen now to this great power of self-knowledge regarding the inner self (*adhyātma*): [Yogīndranāthasena reads "vedaṃ" and explains it as "vedaṃ vedamiva atathajñānaṃ śrūyatām" (listen to this knowledge of reality, like the Veda)].
4.3.21 | Having withdrawn the senses and having withdrawn the flickering mind,
the knower of the Self, entering into the inner self, remains established in his own knowledge.
4.3.22 | With his knowledge attentive in all respects, he examines all states of being.
And grasp this other definitive conclusion, O Bharadvāja.

4.3.23 | When one whose sensory faculties, speech, and movements have ceased is asleep and has entered a dream state, he perceives objects as well as pleasure and pain; therefore, even such a person is not considered ignorant.
4.3.24 | No single cognition whatsoever proceeds apart from self-knowledge;
for no entity exists as a solitary one, nor does it exist without a cause.
4.3.25 | Therefore, O Bharadvāja, know that the Self is both the primordial nature and the witness, as well as the cause; all this has been determined—abandon your doubt.
4.3.26 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
The cause for the conception, growth, and birth of the fetus;
the opinion of Punarvasu and the opinion of Bharadvāja.
4.3.27 | The refutation of the opponent's thesis, the clear determination of one's own position,
and the Lesser Discourse on Entry into the Womb have been elucidated therein.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Minor Treatise on the Descent of the Embryo," in the Section on Anatomy (Śārīrasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Four.
4.4.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the major treatise on the descent of the embryo (Mahatī Garbhāvakrānti Śārīra).
4.4.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

4.4.3 | We shall now explain in detail from what the embryo originates, that which is designated as the embryo, the modifications of the embryo, the sequence by which it is produced in the womb, the cause of its growth, the reason for its non-birth, the reason why it meets with destruction while being born in the womb, and the reason why, without being completely destroyed, it undergoes deformity.
4.4.4 | The embryo arises from the combination of these factors: the mother, the father, the self, suitability, the rasa (nutritive essence), and the *sattva* (psychic constitution).
Having analyzed which specific parts arise from which of these sources, the maternal and other constituent parts will be described individually below.
4.4.5 | Indeed, when there is a conjunction of semen, blood, and the living soul (jīva), the designation "embryo" (garbha) occurs once it has entered the womb.
4.4.6 | The embryo, moreover, is a modification of space, air, fire, water, and earth, serving as the substratum for consciousness.

Thus, by this reasoning, the embryo—which consists of a collection of modifications of the five great elements—is the substratum for consciousness; for it is declared to be its sixth constituent element (dhātu).

4.4.7 | We shall now explain the sequence by which [the embryo] is produced in the womb: When the old menses have passed and the new has not yet established itself, we call a woman who has bathed after her purification, whose genital tract and uterus are unimpaired, and who is in her fertile period, "ṛtumatī" (one in season). When a man with unimpaired seed enters into union with such a woman, then his supreme bodily constituent, excited by joy and transformed into semen, arises from every limb.

Thus, impelled and presided over by the self filled with joy—and [with the reading 'adhiṣṭhitabījadhātuḥ', "the seed-element being presided over"]—the element in the form of the seed, having emerged from the male body, enters the womb through the appropriate path and comes into union with the menstrual blood.

4.4.8 | In that regard, first, the element of consciousness (*cetanā-dhātu*)—which is the agent of sentient beings [the reading "instrument of non-sentient beings" is an alternative]—proceeds for the sake of grasping the qualities (*guṇas*). For it is the cause, the instrument, the motive, the imperishable, the doer, the thinker, the feeler [the reading "the awakener" is an alternative], the knower, the seer, the sustainer, Brahmā, Viśvakarman, the one of universal form, the Person (*puruṣa*), the source, the undecaying, the eternal, the possessor of qualities, the grasper, the primary matter (*pradhāna*), the unmanifest, the individual soul (*jīva*), the knower, the person (*pudgala*), the conscious being, the pervasive one, the self of the elements, the self of the senses, and the inner self.

At the time of taking up the qualities (*guṇa*), it first takes up space (*antarikṣa*) before the other qualities. Just as at the end of the dissolution, the imperishable Self (*akṣarabhūta ātmā*), desiring to emit beings and taking up the quality of *sattva*, first creates space, and then sequentially the four elements—wind and the others—whose qualities become increasingly manifest; so too, when proceeding to assume a body, it first takes up space alone, and then sequentially the four elements—wind and the others—whose qualities become increasingly manifest.
Indeed, all this taking up of qualities occurs in a very brief period of time.

4.4.9 | Endowed with all the [primordial] qualities (*guṇa*), having entered the state of the embryo, it becomes congealed in the first month; made turbid by all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), it exists as a mass of mucus (*kheṭa*), its form unmanifest, with its limbs and parts being both existent and non-existent.
4.4.10 | In the second month, it becomes a solid mass (*ghana*), or a fleshy lump (*peśī*), or a tumor-like mass (*arbuda*).
Among these, the *ghana* is male, the *peśī* is female, and the *arbuda* is neuter.
4.4.11 | In the third month, all the sense organs and all the limbs and parts of the body are produced simultaneously.

4.4.12 | Regarding this, some of its bodily parts have already been correctly described by distinguishing them as those derived from the mother and so forth. Now, however, we shall further explain some of these bodily parts and others again by means of different synonyms, according to their classification as modifications of the great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Indeed, even those parts derived from the mother and so forth are merely modifications of the great elements.

In this regard, its etheric (ākāśātmaka) qualities are sound, the sense of hearing, lightness, subtlety, and discernment; its airy (vāyvātmaka) qualities are touch, the sense of touch, roughness, propulsion, the arrangement of bodily constituents (dhātuvyūhana), and physical movements; its fiery (agnyātmaka) qualities are form, vision, illumination, digestion, and heat; its watery (abātmaka) qualities are taste, the sense of taste, coldness, softness, unctuousness, and moisture; and its earthy (pṛthivyātmaka) qualities are smell, the sense of smell, heaviness, stability, and material form.

4.4.13 | Thus, this person (puruṣa) is commensurate with the world. For as many specific embodied entities as there are in the world, so many are there in the person; and as many as there are in the person, so many are there in the world. The wise, however, desire to see it in this way.

4.4.14 | Thus, his sense organs and limbs are produced simultaneously, with the exception of those factors that arise for him at a later time after birth; such as, for example, the teeth, the secondary sexual characteristics (*vyañjanas*), the manifestation of distinct features, and other such things. Whichever constituent parts of that [embryo] are fully established, they themselves assume either the female gender, the male gender, or the neuter gender.

In this regard, whichever specific qualities—whether dependent on the primary cause (*pradhāna*) or dependent on the secondary qualities (*guṇa*)—predominate in the case of the female or the male, from that predominance arises the state of one or the other.

Namely: impotence, timidity, lack of confidence, delusion, instability, heaviness of the lower body, intolerance, laxity, softness, the portion of the seed in the womb, and other such factors that produce femininity; those opposite to these produce masculinity; and those possessing parts belonging to both categories produce neuter characteristics.

4.4.15 | At the very moment his sense organs become established, at that same moment a sensation arises with intensity in the mind; from that point onward, the embryo begins to throb and yearns for whatever was experienced in a previous birth. His heart, which is born of the mother, becomes connected to the mother's heart by means of the channels that carry the essence (*rasa*); therefore, through those channels, their affection flows together.

Observing this very reason, they do not wish to cause the fetus to be insulted by a state of divided heart [or, as another reading suggests, "insulted by one who has been treated with a divided heart"]. For when it is insulted, its destruction or deformity is observed;
for at that time, the mother shares the same welfare and security as the fetus in certain respects.
Therefore, the skilled physicians treat the pregnant woman especially with what is both pleasant and beneficial.
4.4.16 | We shall now briefly set forth the signs for the purpose of recognizing conception and the state of *dvaihṛdya* (the two hearts).

They are as follows: the appearance of menstrual blood, salivation from the mouth, a lack of desire for food, vomiting, loss of appetite, and especially a craving for sour things; a change in one's inclinations toward various objects, heaviness of the body, weakness of the eyes, the appearance of milk in the breasts, and a darkening of the lips, the nipples, and the areolae; excessive swelling of the feet, the slight emergence of a line of hair (the linea nigra), and the dilation of the vulva—these are the signs that occur when the fetus has reached maturity.
4.4.17 | Whatever she might desire, that one should give to her, except for things that cause injury to the fetus.

Therefore, at that time, the birth of the fetus is fraught with danger due to the instability of the vital vigor.

When the seed-portion of the uterus within her blood becomes vitiated, she gives birth to a barren woman (*vandhyā*); when, however, a portion of the seed-portion of the uterus within her blood becomes vitiated, she gives birth to one whose offspring is putrid (*pūtiprajā*).

However, for each of these three types of *sattva*, the number of its subdivisions is incalculable, due to their varying degrees of intensity, the specific differences in bodily origins, and their mutual interdependence.

therefore, we shall provide an explanatory exposition by way of illustrating several varieties of *sattva* through descriptions of their corresponding types.

4.4.37-(1) For example—one who is pure, devoted to truth, self-conquered, sharing with others, endowed with knowledge, realization, and the skill of speech and reply, possessed of mindfulness, free from desire, anger, greed, pride, delusion, envy, joy, and impatience, and equal toward all beings—such a one should be known as a Brāhmaṇa.

4.4.37-(5) One should recognize as belonging to Varuṇa a person who is brave, steadfast, pure, and a hater of impurity; who is a performer of sacrifices, delights in sporting in water, whose actions are untiring, and whose anger and favor are well-founded.

Regarding the cognition of that subject matter, there is the efficacy of the factors that produce the embryo and the concordance of those factors, as well as the obstruction by those factors that cause obstruction. 4.4.42 | On this point, there are these verses: The cause, the self, the primary nature, growth, and the gradual process within the womb—these five factors, which are the causes of the embryo's growth, are designated as auspicious.
4.4.43 | That which is the cause of non-conception, as well as that which causes destruction or deformity—
these three inauspicious conditions are said to be destroyers of the embryo.
4.4.44 | That physician who knows in every respect all these eight conditions designated as auspicious and inauspicious is worthy of serving the king.
4.4.45 | He, being of noble intellect, ought thus to know the means for obtaining a fetus, as well as those factors that have been described as causing the destruction of the fetus.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Great Discourse on the Descent of the Embryo," in the Section on Anatomy (*Śārīrasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Five.
4.5.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical discourse on the investigation of the person (*Puruṣavicaya-śārīra*).
4.5.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
4.5.3 | "This person (puruṣa) is identical with the world," so said the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya.

For as many specific entities as there are in the world—whether they possess form or are formless (the reading 'amūrtimantaḥ' is supported by Gaṅgādhara)—so many are there in the person; and as many as there are in the person, so many are there in the world. To the venerable Ātreya who spoke thus, Agniveśa said: "We do not fully grasp the meaning of the statement from this much alone; we wish to hear it further explained by the venerable one through his wisdom."

4.5.4 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "The specific components of the world are innumerable, and the specific components of the person are also innumerable. We shall, however, illustrate some of these entities according to their grosser aspects, considering them in their general nature; listen with an attentive mind, Agniveśa, as they are correctly described.

The six elements (dhātus), when combined, receive the designation 'person' (puruṣa); namely: earth, water, fire, air, space, and the unmanifest Brahman. It is these very same six elements, when combined, that receive the designation 'person'."
4.5.5 | Of that person, the earth is the body, water is the moisture, fire is the heat, wind is the breath, space is the cavities, and Brahman is the inner self.

Just as there is the manifestation of Brahmā in the world, so too is there the internal manifestation within the person. The manifestation of Brahmā in the world is Prajāpati; the manifestation of the inner self within the person is *sattva*. That which is Indra in the world is the *ahaṃkāra* (ego) in the person; Āditya is the faculty of grasping (*ādāna*); Rudra is anger; Soma is serenity; the Vasus are happiness; the Aśvins are beauty; Marut is enthusiasm; the Viśvedevas are all the sense organs as well as their objects; darkness is delusion; and light is knowledge—just as [in the macrocosm].

The creation of the world and so forth corresponds to the conception of the person; as is the Kṛta Yuga, so is childhood; as is the Tretā, so is youth; as is the Dvāpara, so is old age; as is the Kali, so is illness; and as is the end of the Yuga, so is death.
Thus, O Agniveśa, by this inference one should understand the similarity between the world and the person even regarding those specific parts that have not been explicitly mentioned.

4.5.6 | To the Blessed Ātreya who was speaking thus, Agniveśa said: "All this that has been stated by the Blessed One regarding the similarities between the world and the Puruṣa is indeed without exception. But what is the purpose of this instruction on their similarity?"
4.5.7 | The Blessed One said: "Listen, Agniveśa! For one who perceives the entire world within oneself and oneself within the entire world equally, true knowledge arises.

For one who sees the entire world within oneself, it occurs that the self alone is the agent of pleasure and pain, and nothing else. And because the world consists of action, having realized through reasoning and other means that 'I am the entire world,' knowledge is first raised for the sake of liberation."
In this context, the word "world" (loka) refers to a combination;
for, in general, the entire world consists of an aggregate of the six elements.
4.5.8 | Its causes are: arising, growth, affliction, and separation.

Among these, "cause" (hetu) is the cause of arising; "arising" (utpatti) is birth; "growth" (vṛddhi) is nourishment; "affliction" (upaplava) is the onset of suffering; and "separation" (viyoga) is the division of the six elements, the departure of the vital soul, the cessation of life-force, dissolution, and the very nature of the world. Its root is the activity (*pravṛtti*) that underlies all afflictions, while cessation (*nivṛtti*) is their stopping.
The knowledge that arises—that activity is suffering and cessation is happiness—is the truth.
The cause of that is knowledge common to all the world;
this is the purpose of the general instruction.
4.5.9 | Then Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, what is the root of worldly activity, and what is the means for its cessation?"

4.5.10 | The Blessed One said: "Activity is rooted in delusion, desire, hatred, and karma. Born from that, indeed, are egoism, attachment, doubt, flooding, falling away, misconception, lack of distinction, and lack of means; these, like trees with exceedingly vast branches, overwhelm a person as they grow, and having enveloped him, they stand firm. Overcome by these, one does not transcend mere existence."

In this context, *ahaṅkāra* (egoism) is the notion "I am endowed with such birth, form, wealth, conduct, intellect, character, learning, lineage, age, vigor, and power. *Saṅga* (attachment) is that mental, vocal, or physical action which does not lead to liberation (*apavarga*). *Saṃśaya* (doubt) is the uncertainty as to whether the fruits of action, liberation, the person, the state after death (*pretyabhāva*), and so forth, exist or do not exist. *Abhisaṃplava* (confusion) is the grasping [of the self] in all states as being non-different from it, thinking: "I am the creator; I am established by my own nature; I am the aggregate of body, senses, intellect, memory, and particularities. This is [the sense of] "mine" (*mama*).

The identification with the group consisting of mother, father, brothers, wife, children, kinsmen, friends, and servants, thinking "I am the group," is *abhyavapāta*. The perverse insistence on what is right and wrong, beneficial and harmful, auspicious and inauspicious, is *vipratyaya*. The perception of identity between the knower and the ignorant, the primary nature and its transformations, and activity and cessation, is *aviśeṣa*. Furthermore, ritual acts such as sprinkling, fasting, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, bathing three times a day, ritual ablutions, invoking deities, sacrificing for oneself or others, begging, entering water or fire, and so forth, are proclaimed to be *anupāya*, or non-means.

Thus, this person—clinging to egoism, attached, full of doubt, with a mind overwhelmed, fallen into error, holding wrong views, grasping at non-distinctions, and following a mistaken path—becomes a tree of residence for all sufferings rooted in the defects of the body and the nature of sentient beings.
Thus, being deluded by defects such as egoism and the like, he does not transcend worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), and that activity is the root of evil.
4.5.11 | Cessation is liberation; that is the supreme, the tranquil, that is the imperishable, that is Brahman—that is emancipation.

4.5.12 | In this regard, we shall explain the stages of advancement for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*). For such a seeker who perceives the defects of the world, there is first of all the approach to a teacher (*ācārya*), followed by the practice of his instructions, the proper service of the sacred fire, conformity with the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), the comprehension of their meaning, reliance upon that [knowledge], the performance of actions as prescribed therein, the honoring of the virtuous, the avoidance of the wicked, non-attachment to people, truthfulness, speech that is beneficial to all beings, gentle, not harsh, examined, and timely; regard for all living beings as for oneself; and the non-recollection, non-willing, and non-praying for all [objects of desire].

Not addressing women with familiarity, renunciation of all possessions, wearing a loincloth for the sake of modesty, clothing dyed with mineral pigments, a needle and thread for the purpose of sewing rags, and [implements] for maintaining purity.

A water-pot and a water-strainer; the carrying of a staff; a bowl for the purpose of wandering for alms; at one time a day, food that is not from a village and such as happens to be available for the sake of sustaining life; a bed, pillow, and covering made of withered, dry leaves and grass for the removal of fatigue; a girdle for the body for the sake of meditation; dwelling without a fixed home in the forests; the avoidance of activities such as sloth, sleep, and laziness; and the restraint of attachment and torment regarding the objects of the senses.

Engagement preceded by mindfulness in all undertakings—whether sleeping, standing, walking, looking, eating, moving about, or in the movements of the minor limbs; endurance of honor, praise, censure, and insult; fortitude in the face of hunger, thirst, fatigue, exhaustion, cold, heat, wind, rain, pleasure, and pain; remaining unshaken by grief, dejection, pride, agitation, intoxication, greed, passion, envy, fear, anger, and the like; perceiving egoism and other such states as obstacles; observing the commonalities between the world and the Puruṣa regarding creation and so forth; and the fear of missing the proper time for action during the commencement of yoga.

Constant lack of despondency, vigor of being (*sattva-utsāha*), and the strengthening of intelligence, fortitude, memory, and power for the sake of liberation; the restraint of the senses in the mind, of the mind in the self (*ātman*), and of the self [in the supreme Self]; the frequent enumeration of the parts of the body according to the division of its elements; the acceptance that all suffering is caused by a source, is insubstantial, and impermanent; the perception of evil in all activities; and the firm resolve that happiness lies in total renunciation—this is the path to liberation; otherwise, one is bound. Thus the "Upward Steps" (*udayanāni*) have been explained.
4.5.13 | And there are these verses on this point:
By these means of purification, the impure *sattva* becomes pure,
just as a mirror is polished by means of oil, cloth, hair, and so forth.
4.5.14 Just as the orb of the sun shines when it is not completely obscured by planets, clouds, dust, smoke, or mist, so too does the pure *sattva* shine.
4.5.15 | When that sattva is restrained within the self, its channels being closed,
it becomes pure, steady, and clear-rayed, like a lamp in a lamp-stand.
4.5.16 | That pure and true intellect which arises in one of purified being,
by which one pierces the exceedingly powerful darkness consisting of great delusion.
4.5.17 | By means of that [knowledge] one who knows the intrinsic nature of all things becomes free from longing;
by means of it one accomplishes yoga, and by means of it the follower of Sāṃkhya attains perfection.
4.5.18 | By which one does not resort to egoism, by which one does not worship a cause,
by which one does not cling to anything— by that [wisdom] everything is renounced.
4.5.19 | By which one constantly goes to Brahman— which is undecaying, peaceful, and immutable—
that is considered to be learning (vidyā), accomplishment (siddhi), thought (mati), intelligence (medhā), wisdom (prajñā), and knowledge (jñāna).
4.5.20 | For one who perceives the Self as spread throughout the world and the world within the Self—
the seer of both the higher and the lower— peace rooted in knowledge never perishes.
4.5.21 | For one who perceives all existents at all times and in all conditions,
being established in Brahman and pure, union [with the world] is no longer possible.
4.5.22 | Because of the absence of the mind and the instruments, even the subtle body (liṅga) is no longer perceived.
Due to the disjunction from all instruments, he is designated as "liberated."
4.5.23 | Free from evil, stainless, tranquil, supreme, imperishable, and undecaying;
immortal, Brahman, and Nirvana—peace is expressed by these synonyms.
4.5.24 | This, O gentle one, is that knowledge, knowing which the sages— freed from doubt and devoid of delusion, passion, and longing— attained perfect peace.

4.5.25 | Regarding this, there are two verses: The common root for the origin, the cessation, and indeed the path, has been indicated along with its purpose for both the world and the individual self.
4.5.26 | The concentration of pure sattva, true intellect, and the final state—
these have been declared by the Supreme Seer as the culmination regarding the discernment of the Puruṣa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Investigation of the Person," in the Section on Anatomy (*Śārīrasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Six:
4.6.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical section on the investigation of the body (*Śarīravicaya*).
4.6.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
4.6.3 | The investigation of the body is intended for the sake of benefiting the body.
For once the true nature of the body is known, knowledge arises regarding those factors that are beneficial to the body. Therefore, the experts praise the investigation of the body.

4.6.4 | In this context, what is called the "body" (*śarīra*) is the substratum for consciousness, consisting of a composite of transformations of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*), which functions through their balanced conjunction.
For when the constituent elements (*dhātu*) within this body fall into a state of imbalance (*vaiṣamya*), it then undergoes either affliction or destruction.
Furthermore, the movement toward imbalance among the elements consists of their increase or decrease, whether by way of deficiency or by way of their inherent nature (*prakṛti*).
4.6.5 | However, the increase and decrease of mutually contradictory elements occur simultaneously.
For that which causes the increase of one element becomes the cause of the diminution of another element possessing opposite qualities.

4.6.6 | Therefore, that very same medicine, when properly administered, simultaneously brings about the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus) that are either deficient or excessive; it diminishes what is in excess and replenishes what is deficient.

4.6.7 | Indeed, this alone is the desired fruit in the application of medicine and in the practice of the regimen for the healthy: that there should be equilibrium of the constituent elements (dhātus). For even those who are healthy, for the sake of maintaining the equilibrium of the elements, desire to consume in turn wholesome tastes, qualities, and dietary modifications known to be habit-forming (sātmya); and they seek to maintain balance by employing activities known to produce effects opposite to those resulting from consuming too much of a single type.

4.6.8 | Indeed, the application of actions and dietary modifications that are contrary to the qualities of place, time, and the self; the proper avoidance of all excessive application (atiyoga) and suppression (saṃdhāraṇa); the non-suppression of those [bodily urges] that have already arisen and possess a natural course; and the avoidance of rash acts—this much is taught as the regimen for the healthy (svasthavṛtta) for the purpose of favoring the equilibrium of the constituent elements (dhātus).

4.6.9 | Furthermore, the bodily elements (dhātus) attain increase when nourished by dietary modifications that possess similar qualities or are predominantly composed of similar qualities; however, they undergo decrease when nourished by dietary modifications that possess contrary qualities or are predominantly composed of contrary qualities.

4.6.10 | Now, these are the qualities of the bodily elements (*dhātu*) that determine their number and capacity; namely: heavy, light, cold, hot, unctuous, dry, dull, sharp, stable, mobile, soft, hard, clear, slimy, smooth, rough, subtle, gross, dense, and liquid. Among them, those that are heavy are nourished by the repeated application of heavy qualities of food and its transformations, while they consume those that are light; conversely, those that are light are nourished by light qualities, while they diminish those that are heavy.
In this same way, the increase of all elemental qualities occurs through similarity of association, and their decrease through the opposite.

Therefore, flesh is nourished by flesh more than by any other bodily constituents; likewise, blood is nourished by blood, fat by fat, muscle-fat by muscle-fat, bone by cartilage, marrow by marrow, semen by semen, and the fetus by the raw fetal tissue.

4.6.11 | In that case, there may be an absence of dietary preparations possessing qualities similar to those [required] for increasing that particular tissue (dhātu), or even when such preparations are present, they may not be used because they are unsuitable, due to a sense of disgust, or for some other reason; and since that tissue is to be increased, one should employ dietary preparations that possess qualities similar to it, even if they are of a different nature, provided they are otherwise wholesome and not prohibited.

For example: in the case of depletion of semen (*śukra*), the use of milk, ghee, and other substances described as sweet, unctuous, and cold; in the case of depletion of urine (*mūtra*), however, sugarcane juice, *vāruṇī* wine, scum, and liquids that are sweet, sour, salty, and moistening; in the case of depletion of feces (*purīṣa*), half-cooked grains, black gram, *kuṣkuṇḍa*, goat's dung, barley, vegetables, and fermented grain-liquids (*dhānyāmla*); in the case of depletion of *vāta*, substances that are pungent, bitter, astringent, dry, light, and cold; in the case of depletion of *pitta*, substances that are sour, salty, pungent, alkaline, hot, and sharp; and in the case of depletion of *śleṣman* (phlegm), substances that are unctuous, heavy, sweet, dense, and slimy.
Whatever action increases a particular bodily constituent (dhātu) should be practiced for that purpose.
In this manner, for all other bodily constituents as well, their increase and decrease should be managed through general principles and their opposites according to the appropriate time.
Thus, the factors that cause the increase and decrease of all constituents have been explained both individually and by way of general application.
4.6.12 | These factors bring about the complete growth of the body; namely: the influence of time, the natural perfection of constitution, excellence of diet, and the absence of obstacles.
4.6.13 | These factors increase strength:

namely—birth in a region inhabited by strong people and at a time when strong people prevail; a favorable seasonal conjunction; excellence of the qualities of the seed and the field; excellence of diet; excellence of the body; excellence of suitability (sātmya); excellence of the mind (sattva); perfection of one's innate nature; youth; past actions (karma); and exhilaration.

4.6.14 | These factors bring about the transformation of food: namely—heat, wind, moisture, unctuousness, time, and proper combination. (*Note: 'saṃyogaśca' is the reading preferred over 'samayogaśca'.*)
4.6.15 | Now, indeed, these are the specific functions of these factors—heat and the rest—which bring about the transformation of food:

namely, heat digests; wind draws [the food] apart; moisture brings about softness; unctuousness produces pliability; time effects the completion [of the process]; and their proper combination results in the transformation and equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

4.6.16 | When food is being digested, its qualities attain the state of bodily qualities according to their respective non-contradictory natures; those that are contradictory cause harm, and once harmed by their opposites, they afflict the body.

4.6.17 | Furthermore, the qualities of the body (*śarīraguṇāḥ*)—[alternatively read as "the bodily constituents" (*śarīradhātavaḥ*)]—are, in brief, of two kinds: those that are waste products (*malabhūtāḥ*) and those that are refined essences (*prasādabhūtāḥ*).
Among these, the waste products are those which cause affliction to the body.

For example: the coatings within the orifices of the body, those [secretions] that arise separately and flow outward, the fully matured bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*), the aggravated wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*), and whatever other factors reside in the body that lead to its impairment—all these we designate as waste products (*mala*).

But the others—namely those beginning with clarity (*prasāda*) and ending with fluidity (*drava*), categorized by their qualities (*guṇa*), as well as those beginning with taste (*rasa*) and ending with semen (*śukra*), categorized by their substances (*dravya*)—are [to be understood] from the teacher and so forth.
4.6.18 | In all of these [diseases], it is the vitiated *vāta*, *pitta*, and *śleṣman* that act as the corruptors, due to the inherent nature of the *doṣas*.

Furthermore, the various ways in which *vāta* and the others become corrupted when they have entered other tissues (*dhātu*) at different times are explained in the chapter on "Various Things Eaten and Drunk" (*Vividhāśitapītīya*).
This is the extent of the corruption of the *doṣas* and their movement, up until their contact with the bodily tissues (*dhātu*).
Indeed, the fruit of the humors—vata and the others—when they remain in their natural state is health;
therefore, the wise should strive to maintain them in that natural state.
And there is a verse on this point:
"The physician who knows the body in every way, in its entirety, and at all times,
knows Āyurveda in its completeness— that which bestows happiness upon the world."

4.6.20 | To the Blessed One Ātreya, who was speaking thus—[the variant reading is "to him who had spoken thus"]—Agniveśa said: "I have heard these words which were spoken by the Blessed One in the section concerning the body."

What part of the embryo indeed first develops within the womb; from what direction does its face turn, and how does it remain situated inside? What food does it subsist upon, and in what manner does it emerge? By what dietary regimens is it destroyed immediately after birth, and by what does it grow free from disease? Do disorders arise in it due to the provocation of the gods, or not? Furthermore, regarding its timely and untimely death, or its existence and non-existence, what does the Blessed One determine?
And what is its maximum lifespan, and what are the signs of that maximum lifespan?

4.6.21 | To Agniveśa, who had spoken thus, the venerable Punarvasu Ātreya said: "This has already been stated in the section on *garbhāvakrānti* (conception), namely, how this [embryo] is produced in the womb and when each of its bodily parts is formed."

In this regard, there are many kinds of conflicting views among all the sages who composed the aphorisms; listen now as these are being stated: Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja maintains that the head is first produced in the womb, considering it to be the seat of all the sense organs; Kāṅkāyana, the physician from Bāhlīka, holds that it is the heart, because it is the seat of consciousness; Bhadrakāpya holds that it is the navel, considering it to be the point of entry for food.

Bhadraśaunaka says it is the large intestine and the rectum, because they are the seat of the vital air (māruta); Baḍiśa says it is the hands and feet, because they are the instruments of the person (puruṣa); Janaka Vaideha says it is the sense organs, on the grounds that they are the seats of his intellect (buddhi); Mārīci Kaśyapa says it is inconceivable due to its being beyond perception; and Dhanvantari says it is the simultaneous manifestation of all the limbs. That [last view] is correct, because all the limbs, beginning with the heart, are manifested at the same time.

For the heart is the root and the foundation for some of its constituent parts; yet these do not arise prior to it. Therefore, all the limbs, beginning with the heart, arise simultaneously, since all phenomena are mutually dependent. Thus, seeing things as they truly are is correct.
4.6.22 | The embryo indeed remains within the womb with its back toward the mother's back, its head upward, its limbs contracted, and enveloped by the fetal membrane (jarāyu).

4.6.23 | Indeed, the embryo, having its thirst and hunger dispelled, exists dependent on the mother, subsisting through moisture and warmth within the womb while its limbs and organs are both formed and unformed; thereafter, some of its nourishment comes through the pores of the skin and some through the umbilical cord.

For a channel is connected to his navel, and another to that channel; and another is connected to his mother’s heart. Indeed, his mother’s heart merges with that other [channel] through the flowing vessels (*sirābhiḥ syandamānābhiḥ*). That essence of hers becomes the producer of his strength and complexion, and it is food containing all essences.
For in a woman who has conceived, the essence is distributed in three ways: for the nourishment of her own body, for the breast milk, and for the growth of the fetus.
Supported by that food, it remains within the womb, subsisting in dependence upon the mother.

4.6.24 | And when the time for birth has arrived, through the action of the winds of parturition, it emerges from the birth canal by turning head-downward; this is the natural course, whereas any other way is a deviation.
Beyond this, however, its activity becomes independent.
4.6.25 | Her diet and regimen, as prescribed in the section on the science of childbirth (jātisūtrīya), are non-disruptive to her health and promote her growth.

4.6.26 | Moreover, one born from those two [parents] when they have indulged in unwholesome practices is destroyed immediately, like a tree recently transplanted that has not yet established its roots and is struck down by wind and sun.

4.6.27 | Disorders caused by the provocation of gods and other deities are observed to correspond to the aggravation of the humors (doṣas), based on authoritative instruction, the sight of wondrous forms, and specific signs of onset and treatment.

4.6.28 | Regarding the existence or non-existence of timely and untimely death, this is our settled conclusion: "Whoever dies does so only at the [proper] time; for there is no gap in time," so some say. But that is incorrect.
For neither the absence of gaps nor the presence of gaps in time is tenable, because of the very nature of the specific characteristic of time.
Regarding this, others say: "When someone dies, that is his fixed time of death; it is true for all beings because of the equality of their actions.
This too is a misinterpretation of the meaning.
For no one is equal in action simply by the fact that no one does not die.
For "time" is spoken of with reference to the measure of the lifespan.

If it were held that for any person, whenever they die, that is their "time of death," then all things would occur for them at their own fixed times; but that is not tenable, for it is directly perceived that the fruit of eating at the wrong time, speaking at the wrong time, or acting at the wrong time is undesirable, whereas the opposite is desirable.

Indeed, the manifestation of the right time (*kāla*) and the wrong time (*akāla*) is perceived directly through observation of various circumstances in their respective states, as follows: "This is the right time for this disease, for food, for medicine, for treatment, or for evacuation," or "it is the wrong time.

This is also observed in the world: the rain falls at the right time, the rain falls at the wrong time; there is cold at the right time, cold at the wrong time; it is hot at the right time, it is hot at the wrong time; flowers and fruit appear at the right time, and flowers and fruit appear at the wrong time.
Therefore, both exist—death at the right time and death at the wrong time; there is no absolute certainty in this matter.

For if untimely death did not exist, then all life would have a fixed duration and measure; this being the case, the knowledge of what is beneficial and what is harmful would be causeless, and direct perception, inference, and authoritative instruction—which are regarded as valid means of knowledge in all treatises and by which things conducive to longevity and those detrimental to it are discerned—would become invalid. This claim that "there is no untimely death" is considered by the sages to be mere empty words.
4.6.29 | Indeed, the measure of the lifespan in this age is one hundred years.
4.6.30 | Its causes are the excellence of the qualities of nature, the self, and the practice of what is wholesome to one's constitution.

4.6.31 | Regarding this, there are these verses:— How the body exists and how it functions when afflicted by diseases; how it undergoes suffering and destruction; and what its constituent elements (dhātus) are.

4.6.32 | Their increase and decrease, as well as the medicine for those who are emaciated, [are explained]; likewise, the factors that cause the growth of the body and the factors that cause the increase of strength when it has diminished.

4.6.33 | The factors that cause transformation and their distinct functions, those known as impurities (*mala*), those known as clarity (*saṃprasāda*), the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and the question itself.

4.6.34 | The definitive conclusion regarding this [body], consisting of nine [or ten] parts, has been correctly revealed by the Supreme Sage in the Śārīra [chapter], which investigates the body, in accordance with the rules.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, named "The Anatomy of the Investigation of the Body," in the Section on Anatomy (Śārīrasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The Seventh Chapter.
4.7.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical section entitled "The Enumeration of the Body" (Śarīrasaṃkhyā-śārīra).
4.7.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

4.7.3 | Having divided the entire body part by part according to its enumeration, Agniveśa questioned the venerable Ātreya for the purpose of gaining knowledge regarding the measurement and enumeration of the whole body.
4.7.4 | The venerable Ātreya said to him: "Listen to me with an undistracted mind, Agniveśa, as I explain the entire body according to your question and in its true nature."

In the body there are six layers of skin (tvac); namely: the outermost is the water-bearing layer; the second is the blood-bearing layer; the third is the substratum for the arising of sidhma and kilāsa; the fourth is the substratum for the arising of dadru and kuṣṭha; the fifth is the substratum for the arising of alajī and vidradhi; and the sixth is that which, when severed, causes one to faint as if entering darkness, and which, being the site of origin, gives rise to blackish-red ulcers on the joints that have thick roots and are most difficult to treat—these are the six layers of skin.
These six remain, having pervaded the body with its six limbs.
4.7.5 | Now, this is the division of the limbs of the body: namely, two arms, two thighs, the head-and-neck, and the trunk; thus, there are six major limbs.

4.7.6 | There are three hundred and sixty bones, together with the teeth, the sockets of the teeth, and the nails. They are as follows: thirty-two teeth, thirty-two sockets of the teeth, twenty nails, sixty bones of the fingers and toes, twenty long bones of the hands and feet, four bases for the long bones of the hands and feet, two bones of the heels, and four [bones of the ankles].

In the two feet are the two ankle-bones; in the two hands are the two wrist-bones (*maṇibandhakau*); there are four bones in the two forearms, four in the two shanks, two in the knees, two in the kneecaps, two in the thigh-shafts, two in the arm-shafts, two in the shoulders, two in the shoulder-blades, two collarbones (*akṣakau*), one clavicle (*jatru*), two palates, two hip-blades, one pubic bone, forty-five bones in the back, fifteen in the neck, and fourteen in the chest—thus [there are] two hundred bones in total.

On each side there are twenty-four ribs, as many costal sockets, and as many tubercles of the costal sockets; there is one jawbone, two ligaments for the root of the jaw, one bone for the nose, cheeks, and forehead, two temples, and four cranial plates—thus, including the teeth, the mortar-like nails, and the rest, there are three hundred and sixty bones.
4.7.7 | The five bases of the sense-faculties; namely: the skin, the tongue, the nose, the eyes, and the ears.
The five faculties of cognition; namely: touch, taste, smell, sight, and hearing.
The five organs of action; namely: the hands, the feet, the anus, the generative organ, and the tongue.
4.7.8 | The heart is the single locus of consciousness.
4.7.9 | There are ten seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); namely: the head, the throat, the heart, the navel, the anus, the bladder, *ojas*, semen, blood, and flesh.
Among these, the first six are reckoned as vital points (*marman*).

4.7.10 | There are fifteen components of the visceral cavities (*koṣṭha*), namely: the navel, the heart, the *kloma*, the liver, the spleen, the two kidneys, the bladder, the receptacle for feces, the stomach (*āmāśaya*), the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*), the upper rectum, the lower rectum, the small intestine, the large intestine, and the omentum.

4.7.11 | There are fifty-six secondary members (*pratyaṅga*) attached to the six primary members; those which were not enumerated previously when the primary members were being enumerated shall now be elucidated here by means of other synonyms. [Note: The variant reading 'aprakāśya vyākhyātāni' (not having been elucidated) is noted.]

Namely: two calves, two thighs, two buttocks, two testicles, one penis, two groins, two knees, two hollows of the knees (*kukundarau*), one bladder-head (*bastiśīrṣam*), one abdomen, two breasts, two shoulders (*bhujau*), two upper-arm masses, one chin, two lips, two corners of the mouth, two gums, one palate, one uvula, two sub-tongues, one dewlap, and two [ears].
The two cheeks, the two ear-cavities, the two earlobes, the two eye-sockets, the four eyelids, the two pupils, the two eyebrows, the one nape of the neck, and the four palms, soles, and heart.
4.7.12 | There are nine great apertures: seven in the head and two below.
4.7.13 | This much of the visible world can indeed be pointed out.
4.7.14 | Beyond this, it is indeed to be inferred as indescribable.
For example: nine hundred ligaments, seven hundred vessels, and two hundred arteries.

There are four hundred [or five hundred, according to another reading] *peśīs*, one hundred and seven vital points (*marmans*), two hundred joints (*sandhis*), and twenty-nine thousand nine hundred and fifty-six vessels (*sirās* and *dhamanīs*) when divided into their minute parts; such is the measurement of the openings at their tips, and the same number applies to the hairs of the head, beard, and body.
This enumeration of the visible parts beginning with the skin has been stated exactly as it is; beyond this, it must be inferred through reasoning.

Both of these [alternatives] are not subject to doubt, because the body is of the nature of its primary material cause (*prakṛti*). [Note: Some do not distinguish between these two, stating, "Because the body is of the nature of its primary material cause"; and some state, "From the skin onwards, that which is visible is indeed inferable," and thus do not distinguish between those two either, because the body is of the nature of its primary material cause.]

4.7.15 | Now we shall explain that which is to be counted by the measure of the añjali; that is to be known as the supreme standard, and it is subject to increase and decrease, and is indeed to be inferred.

Namely: ten handfuls of water in the body according to the measure of one's own hand; that which, when excessively discharged, adheres to the feces, as well as the urine, blood, and other bodily constituents; that which, circulating throughout the entire body, supports the outer skin; that which, located within the skin in the form of a wound, receives the name *lasīkā*; and that which, bound by heat, issues forth from the pores of the hair and acquires the name *sveda* (perspiration).

That water measures ten handfuls (*añjali*): nine handfuls belong to the element of the transformation of food, which they call "nutritive essence" (*rasa*); eight belong to blood; seven to feces; six to phlegm (*śleṣman*); five to bile (*pitta*); four to urine; three to muscle fat (*vasā*); two to marrow (*medas*); one to bone marrow (*majjan*); half a handful to the brain; and semen is of that same measure, as is the *ojas*. [According to another reading: "In women, the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) is four handfuls; this is the *ojas* pertaining to phlegm."]
Thus, the true nature of the body has been explained.

4.7.16 | In that regard, whatever is specifically gross, stable, corporeal, heavy, rough, and hard—such as the limbs, nails, bones, teeth, flesh, skin, feces, hair of the head, beard, body hair, and tendons—that is of the earth element (*pārthiva*), along with smell and the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*). Whatever is liquid, flowing, slow, unctuous, soft, and slimy—such as lymph, blood, fat, phlegm, bile, urine, and sweat—that is of the water element (*āpya*), along with taste and the sense of taste (*rasana*).

That which is bile (*pitta*) and that which is heat (*ūṣman*), as well as whatever luster (*bhās*) there is in the body—all that is of the nature of fire (*āgneya*), consisting of form (*rūpa*) and sight (*darśana*). That which consists of inhalation and exhalation, opening and closing the eyes, contraction and expansion, movement, impulsion, and retention, etc.—that is of the nature of air (*vāyavīya*), consisting of touch (*sparśa*) and the sense of touch (*sparśana*). That which is distinct, namely what are called the large and minute channels (*srotas*), is of the nature of space (*āntarīkṣa*), consisting of sound (*śabda*) and hearing (*śrotra*). That which is the agent is Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), as well as the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*).
Thus has the enumeration of the parts of the body been set forth according to their gross divisions.

4.7.17 | The parts of the body, however, are incalculable due to their division into ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), because of their extreme multiplicity, extreme subtlety, and being beyond the reach of the senses.
Regarding their conjunction and disjunction, the cause is wind and the inherent nature of action (*karman*).
4.7.18 | This body, though observed to consist of many parts, is perceived as a unity; this is attachment. Separation [from it] is liberation.
In that regard, the Pradhāna, being unattached, ceases when all existence has ceased (or, according to another reading, when all continuity has ceased).
4.7.19 | There are two verses on this subject: The physician who knows the enumeration of the body in all its constituent parts is not afflicted by that delusion which arises from ignorance of them.
4.7.20 | One who is undeluded is not overcome by defects rooted in delusion;
being free from defect, desireless, and tranquil, he attains peace, never to be born again.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Anatomy of the Enumeration of the Body," in the Section on Anatomy of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The Eighth Chapter.
4.8.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the anatomical treatise concerning the birth of offspring.
4.8.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
4.8.3 | We shall now teach the procedure for the accomplishment of that purpose, for a man and a woman whose semen and ovum and womb are unimpaired, who desire excellent offspring.

[‘*tannirvṛttikaraṃ’ is an alternative reading] 4.8.4 | Furthermore, having prepared this woman and man with oleation and sudation, and having purified them through emesis and purgation, one should gradually restore them to their natural state.

Once they have been thoroughly purified, one should treat them with non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana). One should treat the man with ghee and milk processed with sweet medicinal herbs, while treating the woman with oil and black gram (māṣa) similarly prepared.

4.8.5 | Thereafter, for three nights beginning from the day of the *puṣpa*, she should remain celibate, sleeping on the ground, eating her food with her hands from an undamaged vessel, and not undergoing any cleansing of the body. Then, on the fourth day, having rubbed her down and bathed her including her head, he should clothe both her and himself in white garments. Then, dressed in white, wearing garlands, cheerful, and desiring one another, they should cohabit—beginning from the time of the bath—on even days if they desire a son, and on odd days if they desire a daughter.
4.8.6 | Nor should one have intercourse with her while she is lying face down or on her side.

In the case of a woman lying face down, the *vāta* becomes powerful and afflicts the womb (*yoni*). In the case of a woman on her side, *śleṣman* (phlegm) is displaced on the right side and obstructs the uterus (*garbhāśaya*); on the left side, *pitta* is displaced and, being afflicted, it causes a burning sensation in the blood and semen. Therefore, she should receive the seed while lying on her back (*uttānā*), for in this way the humors (*doṣas*) remain in their proper places.
When she has finished, one should sprinkle her with cold water.

In this regard, a woman who has overeaten, or is hungry, thirsty, frightened, dejected, afflicted by grief, angry, desiring another man, or excessively lustful for sexual intercourse does not conceive, or she gives birth to an abnormal offspring.
One should avoid a woman who is too young, too old, chronically ill, or afflicted by some other disorder.
These same defects apply to the man as well.
Therefore, a man and a woman, free from all defects, should unite.

4.8.7 | When both have experienced arousal and are mutually favorable during sexual union, they should prepare a pleasant, comfortable bed that is well-spread and permeated with agreeable fragrances; having eaten wholesome, appetizing food in moderation, neither should eat too much, and the man should mount from the right foot while the woman mounts from the left foot.

4.8.8 | Therein one should employ the mantra: "Thou art a serpent; thou art life; thou art the support from all sides. May Dhātṛ place thee; may Vidhātṛ place thee. Be possessed of the luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa).
"May Brahmā, Bṛhaspati, Viṣṇu, Soma, Sūrya, as well as the two Aśvins, Bhaga, and Mitra and Varuṇa, grant me a heroic son."
Having spoken thus, they should dwell together.

4.8.9 | If she should desire thus—"I wish for a son who is large, fair-complexioned, with tawny eyes, vigorous, pure, and endowed with courage"—then from the time of her ritual purification, one should give her to drink, at the proper times throughout seven days, a continuous supply of *mantha* made by mixing white barley flour with honey and clarified butter, stirred into the milk of a white cow whose calf is of the same color, served in a silver or bronze vessel.

In the morning, she should eat preparations of rice and barley mixed with curd, honey, clarified butter, or milk; likewise, in the evening, her shelter, bed, seat, drink, clothing, and ornaments should be pure white. Morning and evening, she should constantly gaze upon a large, white bull or a noble horse adorned with yellow sandalwood paste and armlets.
She should attend to her with gentle stories that are pleasing to the mind.
She should look upon other men and women who possess gentle appearance, speech, conduct, and gestures, as well as other objects of the senses that are pure and bright.
Her companions should constantly attend to her with what is pleasing and beneficial, as should her husband; yet they must not fall into a state of mutual intimacy.

Having remained according to this rule for seven nights, on the eighth day, having bathed with water including the head together with her husband, she should put on new, white garments, and wear white garlands and ornaments.

4.8.10 | Then the officiating priest (ṛtvij), having observed a site to the northeast of the house that slopes toward the east or the north, and having smeared the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) with cow-dung and water and sprinkled it with water, should establish the altar (vedi) upon this spot. To the west of that, one commissioned by a Brāhmaṇa should sit upon a heap of unwashed cloth or on the skin of a white bull; one commissioned by a Rājanya, however, on a tiger skin or the hide of a bull; and one commissioned by a Vaiśya, on the skin of a Ruru deer or a goat.

Seated there, having kindled the fire with fuel-sticks of *pālāśa*, *aiṅguda*, *audumbara*, or *mādhūka* wood; having strewn it around with *kuśa* grass and encircled it with enclosing sticks (*paridhi*); he should scatter parched grain and white, fragrant flowers.

Having brought a water-pot purified by strainers (*pavitra*) and prepared therein, he should place on all sides animals of the colors prescribed for the clarified butter (*ājya*), such as those of noble breed (*ājāneya*), for the purpose of the ghee-offering.

4.8.11 | Then, desiring a son, she should sit to the west of the fire and to the south of the Brāhmaṇa, and touch him together with her husband, while praying for a son according to her desire. Then, while she is thus praying, the officiating priest (ṛtvij), having addressed Prajāpati, should perform the optional sacrifice (kāmyeṣṭi) for the fulfillment of her wish in her womb by means of this verse: "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb.
Thereafter, having sprinkled the cooked rice-mess (sthālīpāka) with clarified butter, he should offer it three times according to the traditional injunction.
One should give her a water-pot consecrated with mantras, saying, "Perform all the purposes for which water is used.
Then, when the rite is completed, she should circumambulate the fire together with her husband, stepping forward with her right foot first.

Having performed the circumambulation and caused the Brahmins to pronounce auspicious blessings (*svasti*), she should consume the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*)—the man first, the woman afterwards—and she should leave no residue behind.
Then they two should dwell together for eight nights, and they should remain with exactly the same kind of retinue; in this manner, they shall procreate a desired son.

4.8.12 | But for a woman who desires a son who is dark-complexioned, red-eyed, broad-chested, and long-armed; or one who is black, with soft and long hair, white eyes, white teeth, radiant, and self-controlled—this same procedure for the oblation applies to these two as well. However, the ritual equipment (paribarha) should be devoid of color. Nevertheless, the other ritual equipment should be prepared according to their specific desire, corresponding to the characteristics of the son they wish for.

4.8.13 | A Śūdra, however, should perform only a salutation (namaskāra) [to the gods, the sacred fire, the twice-born, teachers, ascetics, and perfected beings]. (*Yogīndranāthasena does not read this passage.*)
4.8.14 | Having observed whatever specific blessing for a son each woman may desire, one should mentally traverse those various regions [corresponding to those desires].

Then, having traversed them, she who desires a son suitable to the people of whichever particular region should be told: "Adopt the food, recreation, conduct, and attire of the people of those respective regions.
Thus, this entire procedure for the fulfillment of blessings for a son has been explained.

4.8.15 | Indeed, it is not only this karma that produces specific colors; rather, the fire element, when predominant over the water and space elements, produces a bright white color; when predominant over the earth and wind elements, it produces a black color; and when all the elements are present in equal measure, it produces a dark (śyāma) color.

4.8.16 | Furthermore, the causes for the specific qualities of the *sattva* (disposition) of various living beings are: the *sattva* of their respective parents, the impressions (*śrutayaḥ*) of the pregnant mother, repeated action appropriate to oneself, and the habitual practice of specific *sattvas*.

4.8.17 | When a woman and a man, whose bodies have been refined by the prescribed method, enter into union, the semen, having come into contact with the blood, unimpaired and uniting with the unimpaired, invariably brings about the formation of the embryo in an unimpaired womb within a non-defective uterus.

Just as, for example, when a dye is applied to a well-prepared, stainless cloth, it immediately brings about a coloration endowed with its full quality; or just as milk, when mixed with curdling agents, abandons its own nature through that process of churning and attains the state of curd—so too is the semen.
4.8.18 | Thus, the cause for the determination of the fetus as female or male has been stated previously.

For just as a seed, when sown without being scorched, conforms to its own respective nature—whether it be rice conforming to the state of rice, or barley conforming to the state of barley—in the same way, the female and male also conform to the aforementioned classification of causes.
