4.8.19 | The transformation (*vivartana*) of these two [the mother and the embryo] by means of the ritual prescribed in the Vedas is taught; that is, their development into a different state through the proper application of rituals prior to the manifestation [of the fetus].
For rituals performed when the proper place and time are perfected invariably yield the desired fruit, whereas for others, the opposite is true.
Therefore, having observed that a woman has conceived, one should administer the *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child) to her before the fetus becomes manifest.

Having taken two unblemished sprouts from the north-eastern branches of a *nyagrodha* tree grown in a cow-pen, and having mixed them with curds along with two well-prepared grains—either *dhānyamāṣa* beans or white mustard seeds—one should drink it under the asterism Puṣya. Likewise, one should drink the paste of *aparājitā*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *apāmārga*, and *sahacara*, either combined together, individually, or as desired, with milk under the asterism Puṣya. Similarly, having thrown a *kuḍyakīṭaka* insect or a small fish into a handful of water, one should drink it under the asterism Puṣya. And so forth.

One should, under the asterism Puṣya, cast into curds, milk, or a handful of water small, fire-colored human figurines made of gold, silver, or iron, and drink them without leaving any remainder. Under the same asterism Puṣya, one should inhale the steam of rice-flour as it is being cooked, and having placed the juice of that same flour mixed with water upon the threshold, one should oneself pour it into the right nostril using a cotton swab.
Furthermore, whatever other rites for male-conception (*puṃsavana*) learned Brahmins or trustworthy women may recommend, those should also be performed.
Thus end the rites for male-conception.

4.8.20 | Hereafter we shall explain the methods for stabilizing the embryo: the holding of these herbs—Aindrī, Brāhmī, Śatavīryā, Sahasravīryā, Amoghā, Avyathā, Śivā, Ariṣṭā, Vāṭyapuṣpī, and Viṣvaksenakāntā—with the head or with the right hand; the drinking of milk or clarified butter prepared with these same herbs; bathing under the Puṣya asterism while using these same herbs; and always applying these [herbs] to the body. (*The reading "and always with these" is preferred over "sadā caitābhiḥ".*)
Likewise, there should be the constant use of all the life-prolonging medicinal herbs mentioned, according to their respective methods of administration.
Thus, the measures for stabilizing the fetus have been explained.

4.8.21 | These factors cause injury to the fetus; namely: by one who resorts to high, uneven, or hard seats; by one who suppresses the urges of flatus, urine, or feces; by one who engages in harsh or unaccustomed physical exercise; by one who consumes excessively sharp and hot substances; or by one who eats insufficient food—the fetus dies within the womb, or is expelled prematurely, or becomes emaciated.

Likewise, the fetus may be delivered prematurely from the mother due to blows and crushing pressures, or by frequent gazing at places such as chasms, pits, and precipices; or likewise by traveling in excessively jolting vehicles, or by hearing extremely unpleasant sounds.

If she lies constantly on her back, the umbilical cord attached to the fetus encircles its neck; if she sleeps with her limbs extended or wanders at night, she gives birth to one who is insane; if she is habitually quarrelsome, he will suffer from epilepsy; if she is habitually promiscuous, he will be deformed, shameless, or effeminate; if she is constantly grieving, he will be fearful, emaciated, or short-lived; if she is covetous (*abhidhyātrī*), he will be a tormentor of others, envious, or effeminate; if she is a thief... [the text continues].

One who eats excessively of *tvāya* (a type of grain) becomes excessively hostile and inactive; one who eats excessively of *amarṣiṇī* (a type of grain) becomes irascible, fierce, deceitful, and envious; one who eats excessively of *svapnanityā* (a type of grain) becomes prone to sleep, lethargic, dull-witted, and has weak digestion; one who eats excessively of *madyanityā* (a type of grain) becomes thirsty, short-tempered, and of unstable mind; one who eats primarily *godhā* meat (monitor lizard) becomes afflicted with gravel, urinary stones, or slow urination; one who eats primarily *varāha* meat (boar) becomes red-eyed, gasping for breath, and has very coarse hair; and one who eats fish constantly becomes characterized by long blinking.

If she constantly consumes sweet [substances], the woman with *prameha* becomes mute or excessively obese; if she constantly consumes sour [substances], she gives birth to one afflicted by *raktapitta* or diseases of the skin and eyes; if she constantly consumes salty [substances], she gives birth to one with early wrinkles and gray hair, or suffers from baldness; if she constantly consumes pungent [substances], she gives birth to one who is weak, has scant semen, or is childless; if she constantly consumes bitter [substances], she gives birth to one who is emaciated, weak, or underdeveloped; if she constantly consumes astringent [substances], she gives birth to one who is dark-complexioned, suffers from abdominal distension (*ānāha*), or from upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*). Whatever has been declared as the etiological factor (*nidāna*) for any particular disease, by habitually consuming that very thing, the pregnant woman gives birth to an offspring abounding in disorders caused by those same factors.
The defects arising from the father’s semen are explained by the same [principles] as those arising from the mother’s misconduct.

Thus, the factors that cause injury to the embryo have been described. Therefore, a woman desiring excellence of progeny should especially avoid unwholesome food and activities; she should conduct herself virtuously and attend to herself with wholesome food and activities.

4.8.22 | One should treat her diseases with medicines, food, and regimens that are predominantly mild, sweet, cooling, pleasant, and gentle; one should not administer emesis, purgation, or head-evacuation (errhines) to her, nor should one perform bloodletting. Furthermore, one should never administer non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) or unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) at any time, except in the case of an emergency disease. From the eighth month onwards, however, if emergency conditions arise that are curable by emesis and the like, the treatment should consist of mild emetics and so forth, or measures that serve the same purpose.
She should be attended to like a vessel full of oil, without causing agitation, as if she were pregnant.

4.8.23 | If, due to some transgression, she should see menstrual flow (puṣpa) after two or three months, one should know that her fetus will not remain; for at that time, the fetus has not yet acquired its essential strength (sāra).

4.8.24 | If, from the fourth month onwards, she should see menstrual flow due to the excessive indulgence in anger, grief, malice, envy, fear, terror, sexual intercourse, physical exertion, agitation, suppression [of natural urges], irregular eating, sleeping, or standing, or due to hunger and thirst, or from unwholesome food, we shall describe the procedure for stabilizing the embryo in her case. Immediately upon seeing the flow, one should tell her: "First, lie down on a bed spread with soft, comfortable, and cool coverings, with your head slightly lowered."

Then, having soaked a cotton pad with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and clarified butter that have been placed in extremely cold water, one should apply it near her vulva. Likewise, one should smear everything below the navel with clarified butter that has been washed a hundred or a thousand times; and one should sprinkle everything below the navel with very cold cow’s milk, or with honey-water (*madhukāmbu*), or with a decoction of the *nyagrodha* group of trees. Alternatively, she should be immersed in very cold water, or in a decoction of milky trees and astringent trees.

One should have her take medicated oils that have been infused with their own juices; or one should have her take a cotton-wool applicator (*picu*) soaked in milk and ghee prepared with the sprouts (*śuṅgā*) of the *nyagrodha* and other trees; and from this [mixture], one should have her consume a dose the size of an *akṣa*. Alternatively, one may have her consume milk and ghee alone. One should give her the filaments (*kiñjalka*) of the *padma*, *utpala*, and *kumuda* flowers mixed with honey and sugar for the purpose of licking (*lehārtha*), and *śṛṅgāṭaka*, lotus seeds, and *kaśeruka* for the purpose of eating. Or else, one may give her fragrant *priyaṅgu*, white *utpala*, lotus roots (*śālūka*), unripe figs (*audumbara-śalāṭu*), and *nyagrodha* sprouts.

One should have her drink goat’s milk, or milk boiled with balā, atibalā, śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, sugarcane root, and kākolī, mixed with honey and sugar. She should be fed soft, fragrant, and cool red śāli rice, or she should be fed the broth of common quail, grey partridge, deer, śambara antelope, rabbit, hariṇa deer, eṇa deer, or black-tailed deer, well-prepared with ghee. She should be kept away from anger, grief, exertion, sexual intercourse, and physical exercise, and one should attend to her with gentle stories that are pleasing to her mind; in this way, her fetus remains stable.

4.8.25 | Furthermore, if a woman should experience the appearance of menses due to the persistence of the *āma* (undigested morbid matter), it will generally cause injury to the embryo, because of the mutual incompatibility of those two conditions.

4.8.26 | Furthermore, if a pregnant woman who has consumed hot and sharp substances experiences the appearance of flowers or other vaginal discharges when the fetus has reached a great degree of development, her fetus will not attain growth due to such discharge; it remains for an excessively long time, which some call *upaviṣṭaka*.

Furthermore, when a woman is devoted to the practice of fasting vows, eats irregularly, hates oily substances, or indulges in things that provoke the wind (*vāta*), the fetus does not attain growth due to its extreme dryness. It remains for an excessively long time and becomes motionless; this condition is called *nāgodara*.

4.8.27 | We shall now describe the specific medical treatment for both of these women: the administration of ghees prepared with *bhautika*, *jīvanīya*, *bṛhaṇīya*, sweet, and *vāta*-alleviating drugs, as well as milks containing raw medicinal pastes (*āmagarbha*), promotes the growth of the fetus; likewise, they should be nourished with meals prepared with these same ghees and other substances, and provided with frequent use of vehicles, carriages, massage, and stretching exercises.

4.8.28 | Furthermore, for a woman whose fetus is dormant and does not move, one should feed her soft, sweet, and cool red *śāli* rice with the meat-broth of any one of the following—hawk, fish, gayal, peacock, cock, or partridge—mixed with plenty of ghee; or with black gram soup (*māṣayūṣa*) containing abundant ghee; or with radish soup (*mūlakayūṣa*) containing abundant ghee.
She should also be treated frequently with an oil massage on the regions of the abdomen, bladder, groins, thighs, hips, sides, and back using slightly warm oil.

4.8.29 | Furthermore, for a woman who suffers from upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and constipation in the eighth month, and if one considers it not treatable by unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), then one should prepare a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to pacify that disorder. For if udāvarta is neglected, it may suddenly cause the miscarriage of the fetus or even the death of the pregnant woman herself.

In that case, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) prepared by boiling the roots of vīraṇa, śāli, ṣaṣṭika, kuśa, kāśa, ikṣuvālikā, vetasa, and parivyādha, along with bhūtīka, anantā, kāśmarya, parūṣaka, madhuka, and mṛdvīkā, in milk mixed with half water; this decoction should be combined with a paste of the marrow of priyāla and bibhītaka, sesame, and a small amount of salt, and it should be neither too hot nor excessively salty.

Once her constipation has been relieved and she has eaten a stabilizing, non-burning diet while her limbs have been sprinkled with lukewarm water, one should perform an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using oil processed with madhuraka.
One should treat her while she is in the prone position with the administration of non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).

4.8.30 | Furthermore, when a fetus dies within the womb due to an excessive accumulation of morbid humors (*doṣa*), or from the excessive use of sharp and hot substances, or from the suppression of the urges of flatus, urine, and feces, or from irregular sitting, lying down, standing, compression, or injury, or from anger, grief, envy, fear, terror, and the like, or from other rash acts—then her abdomen becomes motionless, rigid, distended, cold, and as if containing a stone; the fetus is without movement.

Excessive pain arises, the afterbirth (āvyā) does not emerge, the birth canal (yoni) does not dilate, her eyes become sunken, she faints, suffers distress, feels giddy, pants heavily, and becomes full of restlessness; furthermore, the onset of the [birth] impulse is not perceived as it normally would be—one should recognize a woman with such symptoms as one whose fetus is dead.

4.8.31 | Regarding that fetus-thorn (*garbha-śalya*), some say the procedure for inducing the expulsion of the placenta (*jarāyu-prapātana*) is the pacifying treatment (*saṃśamana*); others say it consists of mantras and other rites prescribed in the *Atharvaveda*; and others say it is the extraction by means of a skilled surgeon (*śalyahartṛ*) using proven techniques.

Once the woman has been cleared of the fetal fragments, if she has delivered a stillborn fetus, one should first have her drink, according to her capacity, any one of the following—surā, sīdhu, ariṣṭa, madhu, madirā, or āsava—for the purpose of cleansing the womb, for the sake of relieving her distress, and to induce joy. Thereafter, she should be treated with nourishing, strength-preserving foods that do not contain fats, such as gruels (yavāgū) and the like, which are appropriate for that time, until the moisture of the humors and tissues has merely dried up.

From this point forward, one should treat the patient with the drinking of medicated fats (sneha), enemas (vasti), and dietary regimens known as digestive (dīpanīya), vitalizing (jīvanīya), nourishing (bṛṃhaṇīya), sweet (madhura), and wind-alleviating (vātahara).

For a woman whose fetus has reached maturity but whose fetal "thorn" (the placenta) has not yet been released, there should be treatment with oleation on that very day. Hereafter, we shall describe the monthly regimen for the fetus as it develops without abnormality. If, in the first month, she suspects she has conceived, she should drink unadulterated milk in a moderate quantity, cooled, at the appropriate times, and she should eat only wholesome food both morning and evening. In the second month, she should drink milk processed with sweet medicinal herbs.

In the third month, one should take milk mixed with honey and ghee; in the fourth month, one should eat a portion the size of an akṣa of fresh butter with milk; in the fifth month, milk and ghee; in the sixth month, milk and ghee processed with sweet medicinal herbs; and the same in the seventh month.

Regarding this, women say that the hair growing on the fetus causes a burning sensation in the mother; however, the Blessed Ātreya says this is not so. Rather, due to pressure from the fetus, the vāta, pitta, and śleṣman reach the chest and produce a burning sensation, from which itching arises, and from the root of that itching, the appearance of *kikkisā* (itching rashes) occurs.

In that regard, one should give her from time to time a palmful of fresh butter prepared with sweet medicinal herbs to drink; and one should massage her breasts and abdomen with a paste of sandalwood and lotus stalks, or with the powder of *śirīṣa*, *dhātakī*, mustard, and *madhuka*; or with a paste of *kuṭaja*, *ārjaka* seeds, *musta*, and turmeric; or with a paste of *nimba*, *kola*, *surasā*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*; or with *triphalā* mixed with the blood of a spotted deer, a black antelope, or a hare; and an oil massage should be performed with oil prepared from *karavīra* leaves.

Furthermore, sprinkling [of the body] should be done with water prepared from *mālatī* and *madhuka*. One should avoid scratching when itching arises, in order to prevent skin lesions and deformity; however, if the itching is unbearable, relief may be obtained through rubbing and friction. One should consume a diet consisting primarily of sweet foods that alleviate *vāta*, in small quantities, with little oil, salt, and with water as the only post-meal drink.

In the eighth month, however, she should drink milk-gruel mixed with ghee at the appropriate times. Regarding this, Bhadrakāpya says: "No, for jaundice (paiṅgalya) might afflict her fetus. The venerable Punarvasu Ātreya says: "Let there be jaundice in this case; nevertheless, this must not be done. For by acting thus, she gives birth to a healthy child, endowed with the excellence of health, strength, complexion, voice, and firmness—one who is the best even among his kinsmen. In the ninth month, indeed, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) to her with oil prepared from sweet medicinal herbs.

Therefore, one should insert a cotton swab (*picu*) into her vagina with this oil for the purpose of lubricating the passage to the site of the fetus. This procedure, which is taught starting from the first month up to the ninth month, ensures that at the time of delivery, the womb, hips, sides, and back of the pregnant woman become softened; the wind (*vāta*) becomes downward-moving; urine and feces follow their natural course easily through the passages; and the skin and nails attain softness.
Her strength and complexion increase, and she gives birth in due time to a desired son, endowed with prosperity and happiness, through her own well-being.

4.8.33 | Before the ninth month, one should have the maternity chamber constructed in a place where bones, gravel, and potsherds have been removed, on ground possessing excellent form, taste, and smell, with its door facing either east or north, made of wood from the *bilva*, *tinduka*, *iṅguda*, *bhāllātaka*, *vāraṇa*, or *khadira* trees; or whatever other woods the Brahmins learned in the Atharvaveda might recommend.

It was endowed with an abundance of bedding, ointments, coverings, and curtains; and it possessed dwellings constructed according to the principles of architecture, as well as fire-places, water-cisterns, mortars, latrines, bathing grounds, and kitchens, all comfortable according to the seasons.

4.8.34 | In that regard, ghee, oil, honey, rock salt (*saindhava*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), black salt (*kālalavaṇa*), *viḍa* salt, *viḍaṅga*, costus (*kuṣṭha*), *kilima*, ginger (*nāgara*), long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), elephant pepper (*hastipippalī*), *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *elā*, *aṅkolī*, *vacā*, *cavya*, *citrika*, *cirabilva*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), garlic (*laśuna*), *kataka*, *kaṇa*, *kaṇikā*, *nīpa*, linseed (*atasī*), *balvaja*, birch bark (*bhūrja*), horse gram (*kulattha*), *maireya* liquor, *surā* wine, and *āsava* spirits should be kept on hand.

Likewise, there were two stones, two small pestles and mortars, two large mortars, a donkey and a bull, two sharp needles and awls made of gold and silver, weapons of keen steel, two couches made of *bilva* wood, firewood from *tinduka* and *iṅguda* trees for kindling the fire, and many women who had borne many children, who were full of kindness, ever devoted, and of auspicious conduct.

Those who are skilled in practice, naturally affectionate, free from despondency, capable of enduring hardships, and esteemed; likewise Brahmins learned in the Atharvaveda; and whatever else one might consider appropriate for that occasion, as well as whatever other Brahmins and elderly women may say—that should be performed.

4.8.35 | Then, when the ninth month has begun, on an auspicious day, when the moon has entered into conjunction with a recommended constellation, during a favorable period of the moon, in an auspicious and propitious *karaṇa*, and at a friendly (*maitra*) moment, having offered a peace-oblation (*śānti-homa*), and having first caused a cow, a Brahmin, fire, and water to enter [the house], having given grass, water, honey, and parched grain to the cows, and having given unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), flowers, "joyful-faced" (*nāndīmukha*) fruits, and desired offerings to the Brahmins; having saluted them as they sit upon their seats and having sipped water again, he should cause them to pronounce a blessing (*svasti*).
Then, accompanied by the sound of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and followed by cows and Brahmins, she should enter the lying-in chamber (sūtikāgāra) by circling it clockwise;
staying there, she should await the time of delivery.

4.8.36 | Indeed, these are the signs that appear around the time of delivery: namely—lassitude of the limbs, pallor of the face, looseness of the eyes, a sensation as if the chest has been released from its binding, sagging of the abdomen, heaviness in the lower body, pricking pain in the groins, bladder, waist, belly, sides, and back, discharge from the vagina, and a lack of desire for food;
immediately following this, the appearance of the *āvi* (false labor pains) and the flow of amniotic fluid.

4.8.37 | When she has given birth, one should provide for her a bed upon the ground, furnished with a soft mattress. She should lie upon it. Then, women endowed with the qualities previously mentioned should surround her on all sides and attend to her, comforting her with words that are persuasive, instructive, and consoling.

4.8.38 | If she does not give birth while being afflicted by labor pains, then one should say to her: "Rise up, take up one of the pestles, and with this repeatedly strike this mortar filled with grain; repeatedly yawn, and walk back and forth from time to time. Thus some instruct.
Regarding this, the venerable Ātreya says: "No."

Indeed, the constant avoidance of strenuous exertion is advised for a pregnant woman, especially at the time of childbirth when all the bodily elements (dhātus) and humors (doṣas) are agitated. In such a delicate woman, the wind (vāyu), impelled by the exertion of using a pestle, might find an opening and destroy her life-force (prāṇas). For at that particular time, the pregnant woman is especially difficult to treat; therefore, the sages consider the use of a pestle to be something to be avoided, whereas yawning and walking should be practiced.

Then one should give her a powder of kuṣṭha, elā, lāṅgalikī, vacā, cikatraka, cirabilva, and cavya to smell; she should smell it repeatedly. Likewise, [one should give her] the smoke of birch bark or the sap of the śiṃśapā tree.
From time to time, one should anoint her waist, sides, back, and thighs with slightly warm oil and massage them gently.
By this procedure, the fetus turns downward.

4.8.39 | When she should perceive that her heart has loosened and entered her abdomen, that it seizes the head of the bladder, and that the female attendants urge her on, and the fetus turns downward—then, having placed her upon a couch in this state, one should begin the delivery.
And a sympathetic woman should whisper this mantra into her ear:
"Earth, water, space, fire, air, Viṣṇu, and Prajāpati."
May they always protect you, who are with child, and may they grant you freedom from all affliction.
"O fair-faced one, you who are untiring, give birth to an untiring son, possessing the splendor of Kārttikeya and protected by Kārttikeya! [The word 'indraḥ' is a variant reading.]

4.8.40 | And women possessing the qualities previously described should instruct her as follows: "Do not deliver prematurely. For if one who has not reached her time delivers prematurely, her labor becomes entirely futile; her offspring will be deformed or suffer from deformity, or she herself may become afflicted by dyspnea, cough, consumption, or splenic enlargement."

Just as one who exerts oneself to suppress the urges of sneezing, belching, wind, urine, or feces when their time has not yet arrived does not obtain relief, or obtains it only with great difficulty, so too is the case for a fetus whose time has not yet come when one attempts to induce its delivery. And just as the suppression of these very urges—sneezing and the rest—results in injury, so too does the failure to deliver a fetus whose time has arrived. She should be told: "Act according to the instructions given."

And while doing so, she should first breathe out slowly, and immediately thereafter, even more forcefully. While she is thus breathing out, women should make a sound, saying, "She has given birth! She has given birth! Blessed, blessed is the son!
In this way, her vital breaths are nourished by joy.
4.8.41 | And when she has given birth, one should examine her immediately—whether any [membrane] remains or not.
If no [membrane] remains, then another woman, having pressed firmly with her right hand above the navel and grasped from behind with her left hand, should shake her thoroughly.
Then, one should strike her hip with the heel of the foot.
Having grasped her buttocks, one should press them firmly.
Then, one should rub her throat and palate with a lock of her hair.
Furthermore, one should fumigate her vulva with birch bark, glass beads, and the sloughed skin of a snake.

One should cause her to drink a paste of *kuṣṭha* and *tālīsa*, having soaked it in either a decoction of *balvaja*, or in the scum of *maireya* or *surā* liquor, or in a sharp *kaulattha* soup, or in a preparation of *maṇḍūkaparṇī* and *pippalī*.

Likewise, having prepared a paste of *sūkṣmailā*, *kilima*, *kuṣṭha*, *nāgara*, *viḍaṅga*, *pippalī*, *kālāguru*, *cavya*, *citraka*, and *upakuñcikā*, one should cut off the right ear of either a living donkey or an old bull (as per the variant reading), crush it on a grinding stone, and throw it into one of the various decoctions such as that of *balvaja*. Having soaked it and let it stand for a moment, one should remove it and give this decoction to her to drink.

One should have her take a cotton swab (*picu*) of oil prepared with *śatapuṣpā*, *kuṣṭha*, *madana*, and *hiṅgu*. After this, one should administer an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*). Furthermore, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (*āsthāpana*) using the same aforementioned decoctions, supplemented with *phala*, *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *dhāmārgava*, *kuṭaja*, *kṛtavedhana*, and *hastipippalī*. This enema expels her other obstructed [fetus] along with wind, urine, and feces, because it causes the wind to move in its natural direction (*anuloma*). *Note: The variant reading "vāyoranulomagamanāt" (because of the downward movement of the wind) is preferred over "vāyorapratilomagatvāt" (because of the wind not moving upward).*
For others indeed become obstructed by wind, urine, feces, and other internal or external passages (or, according to another reading, "internal or external openings").

4.8.42 | Furthermore, when the ritual for the delivery of that other [child] is being performed, these following rites must be carried out for the newborn boy: namely, the clashing of two stones at the roots of his ears, and the sprinkling of his face with cold water or warm water, so that he may regain the life-breaths that were obstructed by distress.
If he should become motionless, they should winnow him with a winnowing basket containing black potsherds, continuing all these actions until the return of his vital breaths.
Then, having observed that his vital breaths have returned and he has regained his natural state, one should attend to him by providing bath-water and food.

4.8.43 | Next, one should begin the cleansing of his palate, lips, throat, and tongue with a finger whose nails have been well-trimmed and which is provided with a cotton wick (*picu*) from a well-washed pillow-case and smeared with ghee.
Having first wiped his mouth, one should cover his head and palate with a cotton wick soaked in oil.
Immediately thereafter, emesis (*pracchardana*) should be induced using ghee mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*).

4.8.44 | Next is the preparation of the tube. Therefore, we shall teach the method for its preparation: having made a mark eight finger-breadths from the attachment of the navel, one should grasp the two ends of the incision site gently and cut it with one of the sharp cutting instruments made of gold, silver, or iron—specifically one with a half-blade [variant reading: "with an upward blade"]. Having tied it at the tip with a thread, one should let it hang loosely around the patient's neck.

If its umbilicus should suppurate, one should anoint it with oil prepared from a paste of lodhra, madhuka, priyaṅgu, suradāru, and haridrā; one should also dust it with the powder of these very same medicinal herbs used for the oil.
Thus, the procedure for the preparation of the tube has been correctly explained.
4.8.45 | For if the vein is improperly prepared, there is danger of complications such as distension, exhaustion, protrusion, nodular swelling, bending, and yawning.

In that case, one should treat the patient with non-burning applications that pacify vāta and pitta—namely, massages, rubs, affusions, and medicated ghees—after carefully considering the relative severity of the condition.
4.8.46 | Immediately following this, the birth-rite (jātakarma) for the boy must be performed.

It is as follows: one should first give him honey and clarified butter, consecrated with mantras according to the traditional injunctions, for him to consume. After that, by this same procedure, one should first offer his right breast for him to suck.
Now, therefore, one should place a water-pot, consecrated with mantras, at the head [of the deceased].

4.8.47 | Now, one should provide protection for her: one should surround her house on all sides with the branches of the ādānī, khadira, karkandhu, pīlu, and parūṣaka trees. Furthermore, they should scatter mustard seeds, linseed, rice grains, and husks all around the maternity chamber.
Likewise, an offering of rice (tandula-bali) and oblations (homa) should be performed constantly at both times [morning and evening] until the naming ceremony (*nāmakarman*) has taken place.

And at the door, one should place a pestle across the threshold. Having tied a small bundle (poṭṭalikā) of medicinal herbs known as "demon-slayers"—namely vacā, kuṣṭha, kṣauma, hiṅgu, sarṣapa, atasī, garlic (laśuna), kaṇa, and kaṇikā—one should hang it on the northern threshold of the maternity chamber, and likewise around the neck of the woman who has given birth along with her child, and also upon the cooking pot, the water-jar, and the bed; and in the same manner, on both sides of the doorway. Inside the maternity chamber, there should always be a fire fueled by kaṇaka thorns and fuel of tinduka wood.
Women possessing the aforementioned qualities and her friends and female attendants should keep watch over her for ten or twelve days.
Her residence must be kept free from the cessation of gifts, auspicious prayers, hymns, songs, and instrumental music, and filled with food, drink, and people who are devoted and joyful.
Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Atharvaveda should constantly perform propitiatory oblations (*śānti*) at both times of day for the sake of the well-being of the child as well as the mother.
Thus, this method of protection has been explained.

4.8.48 | Furthermore, having ascertained that the woman who has recently given birth is hungry, one should have her drink a fatty substance—either ghee, oil, muscle fat, or marrow—to the best of her capacity, after considering what is habitually agreeable to her, mixed with the powder of long pepper, long pepper root, chaba pepper, leadwort, and fresh ginger.

After she has drunk the unctuous substance, one should massage her abdomen with ghee and oil and wrap it with a large, clean cloth; thus, because there is no space left, the wind will not produce any disorder in her abdomen. Once the unctuous substance is digested, one should have her drink a very unctuous and liquid gruel prepared with the *pippalyādi* group of drugs in the proper dose.
She should also be sprinkled with warm water twice a day—both before and after drinking the unctuous gruel.
Having observed this regimen for five or seven nights, one should gradually restore her strength.
This much constitutes the regimen for the healthy state of the woman who has recently given birth.

4.8.49 | Indeed, whatever disease arises in her becomes difficult to cure or even incurable, because all her tissues (dhātus) have been weakened and loosened by the growth and loss of the fetus, and because her body has become particularly depleted due to the pain of labor, discharge, blood loss, and exhaustion; therefore, one should treat her according to the prescribed method. One should especially treat her with procedures involving massage, rubbing, affusion, immersion baths, and regimens of food and drink prepared with elemental (bhautika), life-promoting (jīvanīya), nourishing (bṛṃhaṇīya), sweet, and wind-alleviating (vātahara) substances;
for women who have given birth are especially characterized by an empty body.

4.8.50 | On the tenth day—when the night of the tenth lunar day has passed—the woman, together with her son, having bathed with all kinds of fragrant herbs, white mustard seeds, and *lodhra* wood, and having put on light, unwashed, pure garments, adorned with pure, desirable, and light variegated ornaments, having touched auspicious objects, having worshipped the appropriate deity, and having caused Brahmins who possess topknots, wear white robes, and are free from physical defects to pronounce blessings (*svasti*), [she should perform the rites] for the child... of those who are not yet grown.

Having laid the child upon a heap of clothes with his head toward the east or the north—[the variant reading is "having covered the child with a large cloth, having laid him with his head toward the east or the north"]—and having said, "He bows first to the deities and then to the twice-born," the father of the child should cause two names to be made for him: one based on the lunar asterism (*nakṣatrika*) and one based on his wishes (*abhiprāyika*).

In that regard, the name should be intentional (*abhiprāyika*), beginning with a voiced consonant, ending with a semivowel (*antastha*) or a sibilant (*ūṣman*), not containing a *vṛddhi* vowel, inherited from three generations, and not based on a fixed [astrological] position (or, according to another reading: "not separated by more than three generations"). However, it should not be astrological (*nākṣātrika*), nor should it bear the same name as a lunar mansion deity (*nakṣatradevatā*), and it should consist of either two or four syllables. (4.8.51) Once the naming ceremony (*nāmakarman*) has been performed, one should begin to examine the boy for the purpose of knowing the measure of his lifespan.
In this matter, these are the characteristics of long-lived boys.

Namely: hair that grows one by one, soft, sparse, glossy, well-rooted, and black is praised; the skin is firm and thick; the head is naturally well-proportioned, slightly exceeding the standard measure, symmetrical, and resembling an umbrella [variant reading: "exceeding in measure"]; the forehead is broad, firm, even, with well-knit sutures of the temples, endowed with upward-pointing marks, full, wrinkled, and crescent-shaped; and the two ears are thick, with broad and level bases, and symmetrical.

The ears are low-set, large, drooping at the back, with well-knit earlobes and large openings; the eyebrows are slightly drooping, even, well-joined, broad, and thick; the eyes are even, with a composed gaze, clearly defined parts and divisions, powerful, endowed with brilliance, and possessed of beautiful eyelashes and outer corners; the nose is straight, with large nostrils, well-positioned, with its tip slightly curved; the mouth has large, straight, and well-set teeth; and the face is endowed with length and breadth, smooth, slender, and possessed of a natural complexion.

The tongue is naturally endowed with the color of the *pāṭala* flower; the palate is smooth, well-proportioned, possessed of warmth, and red; the voice is like that of a great river—unctuous, resonant, deep-sounding, and steady; the lips are red, neither too thick nor too thin, and provided with a wide expanse that covers the mouth; the jaws are large; the neck is rounded and not excessively long; the chest is broad and well-developed; the collarbones and the spinal column are hidden; the breasts are set far apart and are firm without being pressed together.

The sides [of the chest] are rounded, full, and long; the arms, thighs, and fingers are likewise; the hands and feet are large and well-developed; the nails are firm, rounded, glossy, copper-colored, prominent, and shaped like tortoise shells; the navel is clockwise-rotating and has a central depression; the chest is three parts less than the hips; the waist is level and well-fleshed; the buttocks are rounded, firm, well-fleshed, neither too high nor too low; the thighs are gradually tapering, rounded, and well-developed; and the calves are neither too thick nor too thin, like those of an antelope.

The shanks have veins, bones, and joints that are well-concealed; the ankles are neither excessively fleshy nor excessively emaciated; the feet possess the qualities previously described and are shaped like tortoises; the wind, urine, feces, and private parts are naturally proportioned; likewise, sleep, waking, exertion, smiling, crying, and the grasping of the breast [are normal]; and whatever else has not been mentioned, if it is all endowed with natural proportions, it is desirable, whereas the opposite is undesirable.
These are the characteristics of long life.
4.8.52 | Next, we shall explain the examination of the wet-nurse (*dhātrī*).

Now, one should say: "Bring a wet-nurse who is of the same caste, in her youth, modest, free from disease, without physical deformities, free from vices, not misshapen, not loathsome, born in the country, not mean, not of mean conduct, born of a good family, affectionate, healthy, whose own offspring are living, whose children are male, who gives much milk, is vigilant, does not sleep on the ground, is not of the lowest caste, is skilled in attendance, pure, a hater of impurity, and endowed with excellent breasts and breast-milk."

4.8.53 | Herein is the excellence of the breasts: they are neither too high nor too pendulous, neither too thin nor too full, possessing well-proportioned nipples, and easy to drink from—this is the excellence of the breasts.

4.8.54 | Excellence of breast milk consists in its having the natural color, smell, taste, and touch; furthermore, when it is poured into a vessel of water, the water assumes its own natural state because the milk is in its natural condition. That [milk] promotes nourishment and brings about health. (Excellence of breast milk)
4.8.55 | If it is otherwise than this, it should be known as spoiled.

Its specific characteristics are as follows: milk affected by vāta should be recognized as having a dark-red (śyāvāruṇa) color, an astringent aftertaste (kaṣāyānurasa), being clear (viśada), lacking a perceptible odor, dry (rūkṣa), liquid, frothy, light, not producing satiety, emaciating, and causing disorders of vāta. [The reading "kṣīram iti jñeyam" is preferred over "kṣīram abhijñeyam"].

Milk that appears black, blue, yellow, or copper-colored; has a bitter, sour, or pungent aftertaste; smells like a corpse or blood; is very hot; and causes disorders of bile (pitta) should be recognized as milk afflicted by pitta. Milk that is exceedingly white, possesses extreme sweetness, has a salty aftertaste; smells like ghee, oil, fat, or marrow; is slimy and fibrous; sinks when placed in a vessel of water; and causes disorders of phlegm (kapha) should be recognized as milk afflicted by kapha.

4.8.56 | Having carefully observed the specific characteristics of each of these three defects of breast milk, emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enemas, and unctuous enemas—administered according to the individual constitution and the specific disorder—become effective for pacification.

As for the regimen of food and drink for a woman with vitiated milk, it should consist primarily of barley, wheat, *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, *hareṇuka*, horse gram, *surā* liquor, *sauvīraka*, *maireya*, *medaka*, garlic, and *karañja*.
Furthermore, having repeatedly examined the particular defects of the milk, the corresponding therapeutic measures should be applied.

The drinking of decoctions of pāṭhā, mahauṣadha, suradāru, musta, mūrvā, guḍūcī, vatsaka-phala, kirātatiktaka, kaṭukarohiṇī, and sārivā is recommended; likewise, the application of other substances that are predominantly bitter, astringent, pungent, or sweet—after carefully considering the specific milk disorder, the dosage, and the time.
Thus end the purifications of milk.

4.8.57 | Factors that promote the production of breast milk (*kṣīrajanana*) include: wines excluding *sīdhu*; vegetables, grains, and meats from domestic, marshy, and aquatic sources; diets consisting predominantly of liquids, sweets, acids, and salts; milky plants; drinking milk and avoiding physical exertion; and the drinking of decoctions made from the roots of *vīraṇa*, *ṣaṣṭika*, *śāli*, *ikṣuvālikā*, *darbha*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *gundra*, and *utkaṭa*. (These are the factors that produce milk.)

4.8.58 | When the wet-nurse has abundant, sweet, and pure milk, she should bathe, apply unguents, and put on white garments. Then, bearing an herb such as the aindrī, brāhmī, śatavīryā, sahasravīryā, amoghā, avyathā, śivā, ariṣṭā, vāṭyapuṣpī, or viṣvaksenakāntā, she should first cause the child, who is facing east, to suckle from her right breast. This is the procedure for the wet-nurse.

4.8.59 | Immediately following this, we shall explain the rules for the nursery (*kumārāgāra*): one skilled in the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*) should construct it on an auspicious site—delightful, free from darkness, sheltered from winds yet with a portion open to the breeze, sturdy, and devoid of wild beasts, domestic animals, fanged creatures, rats, and insects; it should have well-distributed water sources and separate areas for the mortar, urination, defecation, bathing, and the kitchen; it should be comfortable according to the seasons and provided with beds, seats, and coverings appropriate to each season; furthermore, it should be well-provided with protective measures, offerings (*bali*), auspicious rites (*maṅgala*), burnt oblations (*homa*), and expiatory ceremonies (*prāyaścitta*), and filled with pure, elderly physicians and devoted attendants. Thus ends the rule for the nursery.

4.8.60 | The beds, seats, coverlets, and upper garments of the prince should be soft, light, clean, and fragrant; those that are full of sweat, dirt, or insects, or contaminated by urine and feces, should be avoided. In the absence of others, these very same items may be used after being thoroughly washed, well-perfumed, and properly dried.

4.8.61 | Furthermore, for fumigating garments, bedspreads, and coverlets, there should be fumigants consisting of barley, mustard, linseed, asafoetida, guggulu, vacha, coraka, vayaḥsthā, golomī, jaṭilā, palaṅkaṣā, aśokarohiṇī, and snake sloughs, combined with clarified butter.

4.8.62 | And gems should be worn by the prince; they should consist of the tips taken from the right horns of living rhinoceroses, ruru deer, gavayas, and bulls; as well as medicinal herbs such as aindrī and others, and jīvaka and ṛṣabhaka, and whatever other [herbs] those Brahmins learned in the Atharvaveda might recommend.

4.8.63 | Indeed, the toys for the prince should be variegated, resonant, delightful, light, with non-sharp points, incapable of entering the mouth, not life-threatening, and free from fear-inducing qualities.
4.8.64 | For it is not right to terrify him.

Therefore, while he is crying or refusing to eat, one should not utter the names of Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Pūtanas, and so forth, calling them out for the purpose of frightening the child, lest he fall under their control.

4.8.65 | If some ailment should befall the child, one should understand its true nature through specific observations of its constitution, etiology, prodromal symptoms, clinical signs, and therapeutic suitability; then, considering all particular factors related to the patient, the medicine, the place, and the time, one should begin the treatment by employing measures that are sweet, mild, light, fragrant, cold, and wholesome. For children are habituated to such things, and thus they obtain relief for a long time.

A healthy person should maintain a disease-free state by acting in opposition to the qualities of place, time, and self; by gradually substituting unwholesome things with wholesome ones and avoiding all harmful factors.
In this way, one attains the perfection of strength, complexion, body, and lifespan.
4.8.66 | Thus he should protect this prince until he reaches youth and until he has acquired skill in matters of dharma and artha.

4.8.67 | Thus the rite that brings about the fulfillment of blessings for sons has been explained. Performing it according to the prescribed rules, one who is free from malice obtains worship as desired.
4.8.68 | There are two verses on this point:
"This rite for the blessing of sons, which has been described as bringing about great prosperity and endowed with profound significance— "
Practicing that according to the rules as they truly are, the wise man who is free from envy obtains worship as he desires.
4.8.69 | The entire body is considered through its divine and human components;
because it consists of all these states of being, it is therefore called the "corporeal" (śārīra) station.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Anatomy of Procreation," in the Section on Anatomy (Śārīrasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka. The Section on Anatomy is complete. Now begins the Section on the Sense Organs (Indriyasthāna).
The First Chapter.
5.1.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the [diagnostic] signs of complexion and voice.
5.1.2 Thus said the venerable Ātreya.

5.1.3 | In this context, indeed, there are color, sound, smell, taste, touch, the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the sense of touch, vitality, devotion, purity, conduct, behavior, memory, form, natural constitution, morbid transformation, strength, exhaustion, intelligence, joy, dryness, unctuousness, drowsiness, exertion, heaviness, lightness, qualities, and food.

The physician, desiring to know the remaining measure of life through direct perception, inference, and authoritative instruction, must examine the following: the patient's state of residence, the transformation of food, the therapeutic measures employed, the complications, the disease itself, the premonitory symptoms of the disease, the sensations, the secondary afflictions, the complexion, the counter-complexion, the observation of dreams, the role of messengers, portents on the road, the conditions within the family of the patient, the stages of the disease, the preparation of medicines, and the rationale for the modification of medicines.
5.1.4 | Furthermore, among these objects of examination, some are independent of the person, while others depend upon the person.

Of those that are independent of the person, one should examine them through authoritative instruction and through reasoning; those that depend upon the person, however, one should examine by means of their natural state and their pathological transformation.
5.1.5 | In that regard, nature (prakṛti) is attached to genus, attached to family, following place, following time, following age, and fixed for each individual.
For those various specific dispositions of those various persons arise as being fixed by genus, family, place, time, age, and the individual.
5.1.6 | Furthermore, modification (vikṛti) is caused by the defining characteristic, caused by the thing to be defined, and conforms to its cause.

5.1.7(1) Among these, that which is called "caused by bodily characteristics" (lakṣaṇanimittā) is that for which the bodily characteristics themselves become the cause by chance; for certain characteristics are indeed inherent to the body, which, having taken hold at various times and locations, produce this or that pathological change.
5.1.7(2) But that [non-perception] which has a perceptible cause is one for which a cause is found, as has been stated in the *Nidānas*.

5.1.7 | That which conforms to the signs and imitates the meaning of the signs, yet is itself signless—physicians regard this as the sign for the knowledge of the measure of life. Furthermore, they describe it as the cause of the exhaustion of life, resembling the symptoms of the deceased; that which the wise teach for the purpose of knowing life that has reached its end. And with reference to this, we shall explain the signs pertaining to the person of those about to die. This is the brief outline.
We shall explain that in detail.
5.1.8 | In this regard, first of all is the section on complexion (*varṇa*).

It is as follows: black, dark, dark-fair, and fair—these are the natural complexions of the body; and one should also recognize other [complexions] which experts may describe according to the individual's constitution (*anūka*) or otherwise.

5.1.9 | Blue, dark, coppery, green, and white are the colors that constitute the morbid changes of the body; and one should recognize those other [colors] which, having not previously been abnormal, have arisen anew. Thus, the colors of the body in their natural and morbid states have been described.

5.1.9 | Having observed that in one half of the body there is the natural color while in the other half there is a changed color, and that both colors are demarcated by a distinct boundary—whether this occurs through a left-right division, an east-west division, an upper-lower division, or an internal-external division—one should know that it is a fatal sign (ariṣṭa) for the patient; likewise, such a variation in color occurring elsewhere on the face also leads to death.
5.1.10 | Exhaustion, exhilaration, dryness, and unctuousness are explained according to the distinction of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
5.1.11 | Likewise, the appearance of moles, freckles, black spots, or pustules on the face of a newborn should be understood as equally inauspicious for the mother.

5.1.12 | Furthermore, the appearance of any of the colors mentioned as indicative of morbid change on the nails, eyes, face, urine, feces, hands, feet, lips, and so forth, in those whose strength, complexion, and senses have diminished, is a sign of the exhaustion of life.

5.1.13 | Furthermore, whatever other unprecedented alteration of the complexion should suddenly arise without any apparent cause in a patient who is constantly declining, one should know that to be an *ariṣṭa* (a fatal sign).
Thus ends the section on complexion (*varṇa*).

5.1.14 | Regarding the section on voice (*svarādhikāra*): The natural voices (*prakṛtisvara*) are those that imitate the sounds of the swan, the curlew, the ocean-shore, the drum, the sparrow, the crow, the pigeon, and the jarjara-bird; these one should recognize even without observing others, or as they are described otherwise by experts.

The morbid voices (*vaikārikasvara*) of the diseased are those that are bleating like a sheep, choked, faltering, weak, dejected, or scattered; these one should recognize even without observing others, as having arisen suddenly without having been previously altered.
Thus, the natural and morbid voices have been explained.

5.1.15 | In that regard, the swift manifestation of both primary (*prakṛti*) and modified (*vaikārika*) vowels occurs; however, the multiplicity of vowels for a single [consonant] and the multiplicity of a single vowel are considered improper.
Thus concludes the section on vowels (*svarādhikāra*).
5.1.16 | Thus, the sections on the vowels of the letters have been correctly explained for the purpose of identifying the signs of those who are about to die.
5.1.17 | And there are verses on this point: He whose complexion becomes abnormal in half or even in the whole of his body, and for whom no cause can be found, [is destined to die].
5.1.18 | Whether it be blue, or dark brown, or copper-colored, or reddish—
when one half of the face is otherwise than the other, such a crowing of the cock is called a portent of misfortune.
5.1.19 | Excessive oiliness on one half of the face, extreme dryness on the other half of the face,
as well as exhaustion on one side and exhilaration on the other half of the face— these are the signs of a preta.
5.1.20 | Various types of tilakas, pipilavas, moles,
and streaks quickly appear on the face of a patient who is about to relinquish his life.
5.1.21 | Flowers on the nails or teeth, or mud adhering to the teeth,
or even powder upon the teeth— these are the signs of death.
5.1.22 | Pallor of the lips, feet, hands, eyes, urine, feces,
and even the nails— this discoloration in one whose strength is depleted brings about death.
5.1.23 | A wise man should know that one whose two lips are both blue, resembling ripe *jambū* fruits, is a person whose life has departed and who is about to die.
5.1.24 | Whether it be one or many, that person whose modifiable tone arises suddenly while they are declining does not exist [as a living being].
5.1.25 | Furthermore, whatever other abnormality there may be regarding the voice or the complexion of one who is deprived of strength and flesh— all that portends death.
5.1.26 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
Thus have the complexion and voice been described for the purpose of identifying those who are about to die;
he who understands these two correctly does not become deluded in the knowledge of life-span.
Thus ends the first chapter, named "The Chapter on Complexion and Voice," in the Section on the Examinations (*Indriyasthāna*) within the *Tantra* composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Two:
5.2.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the "Flowering" examination (*Puṣpitakam Indriyam*).
5.2.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
5.2.3 | Just as a flower here is the precursor of the fruit that is yet to come,
so too is the sign known as *ariṣṭa* the precursor of one who is about to die.
5.2.4 | Even so, there might be a flower that is not followed by fruit,
or there might be some fruit whose flower did not precede it.
5.2.5 | There is no destruction for one born who has not been marked by ill omens, except through death;
and even that death does not exist which is not preceded by ill omens.

5.2.6 | This [misdiagnosis] arises from an error of judgment: either by one who does not recognize a fatal sign (ariṣṭa) as such when it appears like a non-fatal sign, or by one who fails to perceive a fatal sign even when it is present.

5.2.7 | However, for the purpose of awakening knowledge regarding those who are about to die, we shall describe many men in various ways by means of the signs that precede death. 5.2.8 | He whose fragrance, resembling various flowers, manifests day and night—
Like a blossoming forest filled with various trees and creepers.
5.2.9 | The wise call that man "flowered" by the signs of death;
it is certain that he shall cast off his body within a year.
5.2.10 | Likewise, he whose fragrance becomes equal to that of each individual flower—
whether they be desirable or undesirable— is said to be "flowered."
5.2.11 | Or else, by smelling the foul odors on a person's limbs either collectively or individually,
the physician should recognize that he has reached the "flowering" stage of the disease.
5.2.12 | He whose auspicious and inauspicious bodily odors appear in a reversed manner without any apparent cause, whether his body has been bathed or not, is said to be "flowering."
5.2.13 | For example: sandalwood, costus, tagara, and aloe-wood; honey; garlands; urine and excrement; and even corpses that have died.
5.2.14 | Furthermore, whatever other various substances there are with diverse natures and diverse origins,
they too are to be understood as having undergone transformation by means of this same inference.
5.2.15 | Furthermore, we shall describe this characteristic pertaining to odor for the purpose of extension; by understanding which, the physician may predict the outcome for a man.
5.2.16 | He upon whose limbs a fishy odor arises—
whether it be pleasant or unpleasant— he does not live through that year.
5.2.17 | This much is the knowledge of smell; hereafter, the knowledge of taste regarding the bodies of the afflicted shall be explained according to the prescribed method.
5.2.18 | That rasa which is produced in the bodies of men who abide in their natural state undergoes a twofold transformation at the final stage of their lives.
5.2.19 | Some [taste] becomes exceedingly insipid for this person,
while another taste attains a vast sweetness.
5.2.20 | One should know that he has undergone a transformation by this inference:
for how could one man obtain the essence of another man?
5.2.21 | Flies, lice, and mosquitoes alike depart from the body of a living being who is about to die, driven away by its loss of vitality.
5.2.22 | Flies swarm from all sides toward a body that is excessively attached to sensual pleasures, even if it belongs to one who has bathed and anointed himself, once that body is ripened by time.
5.2.23 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
"I have described the general signs of taste and smell;
one should predict death as the fruit for a man who is 'in flower' (i.e., at the peak of his vitality)."
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Flowering Diagnostic Sign," in the Section on the Diagnostic Signs (Indriyasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The Third Chapter.
5.3.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the sense of touch (the Palpable Organ).
5.3.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
5.3.3 | The signs of those about to die have been described individually regarding complexion, voice, smell, and taste; now learn correctly of them also regarding touch.

5.3.4 | Desiring to know the remaining measure of a patient's lifespan primarily through the sense of touch, the physician should either touch his body with his own hand while it is in its natural state, or have it examined by another.

Indeed, by examining the body of the patient, these conditions should be recognized in their respective locations: namely, the loss of pulsation in parts of the body that are normally constantly pulsating; the cooling of those that are normally perpetually warm; the hardness of what is normally soft; the roughness of what is normally smooth; the disappearance of what is normally present; the loosening, breaking, or falling away of the joints; the depletion of flesh and blood, or their hardness, or the persistence of perspiration, or rigidity;
and whatever other such characteristic of tactile sensations may be severely disordered and without apparent cause.
Thus has the definition of tangible objects been stated in brief.

5.3.5 | We shall explain that in detail: if, upon being palpated individually, his feet, calves, thighs, buttocks, abdomen, sides, back, shoulders, hands, neck, palate, lips, or forehead should be found to be perspiring, cold, rigid, harsh, or devoid of flesh and blood, one should know that this person has lost his life-force and will die before long.

If, when being palpated individually, his ankles, knees, groin, anus, testicles, penis, navel, shoulders, breasts, wrists, ribs, jaw, nose, ears, eyes, eyebrows, temples, and so forth, should be found to be sagging, displaced, fallen from their places, or loosened, one should know that this person has lost his life-force and will die before long.

5.3.6 | Likewise, one should examine his exhalation, the temples, the eyelashes, the eyes, the hair of the head, the body hair, the abdomen, the nails, and the fingers. If his exhalation should be either excessively long or excessively short, one should know that he is devoid of life. If, when his temples are being palpated, they do not throb, one should know that he is devoid of life.

If his teeth should become scattered, white, and covered with tartar, one should know that he is about to die. If his eyelashes should become matted together like locks of hair, one should know that he is about to die.

If his eyes are naturally deficient or afflicted by deformity—being excessively bulging, excessively sunken, excessively squinting, excessively uneven, with eyelids that are too loose, excessively watery, constantly open, constantly closed, or characterized by excessive opening and closing; or if the gaze is wandering, inverted, depressed, or distorted; or if he is blind like a mongoose or a pigeon; or if they have the color of a firebrand; or if they are excessively overwhelmed by any one of the following colors: black, yellow, blue, dark-brown, coppery, green, turmeric-yellow, or white—then one should know him to be on the verge of death.
Then, one should pull out his hair and body hair; if, while being pulled, the hair and body hair fall out without causing pain, one should know that he is dead.

If veins should appear on his abdomen, whether they be dark-blue, copper-colored, blue, yellow, or white, one should know that he is dead. If his nails should become devoid of flesh and blood and take on the color of a ripe jambu fruit, one should know that he is dead.
Then one should stretch its fingers; if its fingers, while being stretched, do not break, one should know that it is dead.
5.3.7 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
He who, while touching these many tangible objects, perceives them correctly with respect to the patient,
does not fall into delusion concerning the knowledge of life-span.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Diagnostic Sign of Palpation," in the Section on the Diagnostic Signs (*Indriyasthāna*) within the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Four:
5.4.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnostic sign concerning the array of the senses (*Indriyānīka*).
5.4.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
5.4.3 | Listen now to how a physician who desires to know the lifespan of a person should examine their sense organs, as one skilled in discernment would do.
5.4.4 | One should examine perception and the other [faculties] according to their true nature through inference;
for knowledge that transcends the senses is indeed truly known [only] by means of the senses.
5.4.5 | When one observes a change in the cognition dependent on the sense organs of a person who is otherwise healthy, without any apparent cause, that is a sign of death.
5.4.6 | Thus has been correctly described the characteristic of the arising of the unwholesome regarding the sense-faculties. Now, understand that very same thing once again in further detail.
5.4.7 | Seeing both of these as being censured— space as if it were solidified matter, and the earth as if it were space— one meets with death.
5.4.8 | For one who sees the wind moving through the sky,
yet the blazing fire does not come [to him], one should declare that his life has reached its end.
5.4.9 | Having seen a man standing or moving in water that is very clear, free from nets, and devoid of aquatic creatures, he is liberated from life.
5.4.10 | He who, while awake, sees ghosts, various kinds of demons,
or anything else wonderful, is not able to remain alive.
5.4.11 | He who sees the fire abiding in its natural color as lusterless blue,
or black, or even white, goes to his death on the seventh night.
5.4.12 | Seeing rainbows in a cloudless sky, or clouds in a cloudless sky,
or lightning without clouds, one meets with death.
5.4.13 | He who looks upon the sun or the pure moon as if it were a clay vessel covered by black cloth does not live.
5.4.14 | When one observes an eclipse of the sun or the moon at an improper time—
whether being free from disease or afflicted by it— one's life shall end at that very moment.
5.4.15 | Seeing the sun at night, the moon during the day, smoke rising without fire,
or a lusterless fire at night, one meets with death.

5.4.16 | Desiring to abandon existing states of being, men perceive those states as devoid of power through their own power, and as lacking luster through their own power; they perceive these entities as having altered characteristics.
5.4.17 | At the exhaustion of their lifespan, men perceive forms that are distorted, discolored, appearing in incorrect numbers, and devoid of their usual causes.
5.4.18 | He who sees those things that are truly invisible, and he who does not see those things that are visible—
both of them will undoubtedly soon behold the abode of Yama.
5.4.19 | Furthermore, he who is a listener of that which has no sound, and he who does not perceive sounds—
both of these should be known by the wise as being like those who are dead.
5.4.20 | A wise man should avoid that afflicted person who, when his ears are covered with his fingers, does not hear the sound of a fire. He is one whose life has departed.
5.4.21 | He who perceives the quality or defect of odors in reverse order,
or does not perceive them at all, should be known as one whose life has departed.
5.4.22 | Those skilled in the matter say that a man who does not perceive tastes, or who does not know them in their true nature, is "ripe" [with disease], even if he has no oral ulceration.

5.4.23 | Having touched things that are hot, cold, rough, smooth, soft, or even harsh— once he has touched these various objects— he perceives their difference [from himself] as one who is about to die.
5.4.24 | Without intense austerity or yoga performed according to the prescribed rules,
one who perceives objects excessively through the senses meets his death.
5.4.25 | He who perceives objects of the senses through the senses without the aid of vision, and [perceives] those not born of defects, does not live by means of his senses.
5.4.26 | One should predict death for those who, though healthy, perceive distortions in the objects of the senses due to reversals of their wisdom, and who frequently see what is unreal.
5.4.27 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
He who perceives this sensory cognition exactly as it is,
he alone is a physician worthy of knowing both death and life.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "The Array of the Indriyas," in the Section on the Indriyas (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Five.
5.5.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the Indriya concerning the Prodromal Symptoms (*Pūrvarūpīya*).
5.5.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
5.5.3 | We shall describe, individually and collectively, the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa) of incurable disorders, for the increase of the physicians' knowledge.
5.5.4 | When all the premonitory symptoms of fever manifest in an excessive degree,
death approaches that person, preceded by the onset of fever.
5.5.5 | Furthermore, if the premonitory symptoms of any other disease enter a man in this same manner, his death is certain.
5.5.6 | We shall now describe other very dreadful symptoms which are partial manifestations of the premonitory signs (pūrvarūpa),
by which death follows upon the growth [of the disease] and by which one is bound.
5.5.7 | For one who is addicted to women, whose strength wanes and whose catarrh increases, consumption arises as his end.
5.5.8 | He who, in a dream, travels toward the southern direction on dogs, camels, or even donkeys,
encounters consumption (yakṣman) and relinquishes his life.
5.5.9 | He who drinks liquor together with ghosts in a dream, or is dragged away by a dog,
will encounter a most terrible fever and lose his life.
5.5.10 | He who sees the sky nearby appearing like a garment dyed with lac,
having contracted internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), is led to his end by that very condition.
5.5.11 | He who, in a dream, is carried away by a woman while wearing red garlands, with all his limbs smeared red, dressed in red garments, and laughing repeatedly, perishes upon encountering blood.
5.5.12 | Excessive colic, flatulence, rumbling in the intestines, extreme weakness,
and discoloration of the nails and other parts— this seizure caused by gulma is fatal.
5.5.13 | A cruel thorny creeper that grows within his heart in a dream enters a man for his ultimate destruction as a gulma.
5.5.14 | He whose body, even when touched slightly, breaks apart excessively,
and whose wounds do not heal— him death destroys by means of leprosy.

5.5.15 | In one who is naked, who has poured clarified butter [onto himself], and who offers oblations into a flameless fire, lotuses appear on the chest in a dream; such a person will die of leprosy.
5.5.16 | Even if his limbs are bathed and anointed, he upon whose body flies settle;
having been afflicted by that very same prameha, he is destroyed by it.
5.5.17 | That man who, in a dream, drinks various kinds of unctuous substances together with outcasts (caṇḍālas),
is afflicted by urinary disorder (prameha) and is touched by his own end.
5.5.18 | From that [state of non-attachment] arise meditation, exertion, as well as agitation and delusion arising from inappropriate causes,
restlessness, loss of strength, and death preceded by insanity.
5.5.19 | Seeing one who has developed a loathing for food, whose consciousness is lost, and who is emaciated,
the wise physician should know him to be on the verge of death due to a rapidly progressing insanity.
5.5.20 | Insanity destroys the embodied being who is prone to anger, filled with fear, whose face breaks into laughter at intervals, and who suffers greatly from fainting and thirst.
5.5.21 | He who, while dancing together with hosts of Rākṣasas, sinks into water in a dream,
shall fall into extreme madness upon reaching the world beyond this one.
5.5.22 | He who, while awake, sees non-existent things and hears many kinds of non-existent sounds, is afflicted by epilepsy (apasmāra).
5.5.23 | When a preta seizes a man who is intoxicated and dancing by whirling him around,
death— preceded by epilepsy— seizes him in his dreams.
5.5.24 | For one who has awakened, the jaws, the temples, and likewise the eyes become stiffened;
if this occurs, he will undoubtedly die once the external extension (of the body) has seized him.
5.5.25 | That man who, in a dream, eats fried cakes or even sweetmeats,
if he vomits such things upon waking, he does not live.
5.5.26 | He who correctly understands these premonitory symptoms is capable of knowing their subsequent course and their outcome.
5.5.27 | Furthermore, one should observe these other terrible dreams as portending the destruction or even the great suffering of those who are afflicted by disease.
5.5.28 | He upon whose head bamboos, shrubs, creepers, and the like grow;
he in whom birds settle; and he who becomes bald in a dream.
5.5.29 | He who, in a dream, is surrounded by vultures, owls, dogs, crows, and the like,
or by Rākṣasas, Pretas, Piśācas, women, Caṇḍālas, Draviḍas, and Āndhrakas;
5.5.30 | He who becomes entangled in a thicket of bamboo, cane-sticks, nooses, grass, and thorns in a dream, or who falls while walking; |||
5.5.31 | Furthermore, he who falls asleep on the bare ground, upon a bed of dust, on an anthill, or on ashes; or in a cremation ground, or in a pit—even if he falls [into such places] while dreaming.
5.5.32 | He who sinks in turbid water or mud, or in a well shrouded in darkness,
or who is swiftly carried away by a rapid current;
5.5.33 | Drinking medicated fats, as well as oil massage, emesis, and purgation;
the acquisition of gold, quarrels, and being bound or defeated in a dream.
5.5.34 | The loss of a pair of sandals, falling down, the peeling of the skin from the feet,
experiencing joy in a dream, and being threatened by enraged ancestors.
5.5.35 | If, in a dream, there is the falling or the destruction of one's teeth, the moon, the sun, the stars, deities, lamps, or the eyes; or if there is the splitting of a mountain.
5.5.36 | He who even in a dream enters a forest of red flowers, the earth, a dwelling place of evil-doers, a funeral pyre, or a cave crowded with darkness;
5.5.37 | Wearing a red garland and laughing loudly, naked, he goes toward the southern direction through a dreadful forest in a dream, mounted upon a monkey.
5.5.38 | One does not desire to see in a dream those wearing saffron robes who are ungentle, those who are naked, those carrying staffs, those who are black, or those with red eyes.
5.5.39 | A woman who is black, sinful, devoid of good conduct, with long hair, nails, and breasts,
wearing discolored garlands and garments, is considered Kālaniśā in a dream.
5.5.40 | These are the terrible dreams by which Rohi goes to her death;
one who is healthy may, having fallen into danger, perhaps be released.
5.5.41 | Due to the channels carrying the mind being filled by the three excessively powerful doshas,
one sees terrible dreams at a terrible time.
5.5.42 | A person who is not deeply asleep perceives dreams in many ways— both fruitful and fruitless— through the mind, which is the lord of the senses.

5.5.43 | They know dream to be of seven kinds: that which is seen, heard, or experienced; that which is desired; that which is imagined; that which is based on reality; and that which arises from a physical disorder.

5.5.44 | In that regard, the wise physician should prescribe five types of preliminary [regimens] that are fruitless: sleeping during the day, as well as excessively short or excessively long [sleep].
5.5.45 | A dream seen on the first night shall yield little fruit; however, if one sees it again and does not sleep further, that dream shall immediately become highly fruitful.
5.5.46 | Even after seeing an inauspicious dream, if one should again see something gentle and of auspicious form in that very same [dream], one should know that its fruit will be auspicious.
5.5.47 | Regarding this, there is a verse: The physician who recognizes these premonitory symptoms and these dreadful dreams does not, out of delusion, undertake treatments for incurable diseases.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Prodromal Symptoms," in the Section on the Diagnostic Signs (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Six:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnostic signs concerning which parts of the body [are affected] (*Katamaniśarīriya Indriya*).
5.6.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
5.6.3 | O Great Sage, which bodies are diseased such that a physician should avoid them,
and in which medical treatment does not succeed?
5.6.4 | Thus, having been asked this question by Agniveśa—which was extremely difficult to explain—the venerable Ātreya explained it to him; listen to that.
5.6.5 | When a person speaks, his chest is severely pained above;
food that has been eaten is ejected, and even that which remains undigested does not undergo digestion.
5.6.6 | Strength quickly diminishes, thirst increases excessively, and pain arises in the heart; the physician should avoid treating such a patient.
5.6.7 | To one whose hiccups are deep-seated and who suffers from the discharge of blood in diarrhea,
one should not administer medicine, remembering the instruction of Ātreya.
5.6.8 | When constipation and diarrhea both afflict a weak man who is already diseased,
his survival is difficult to attain.
5.6.9 | Constipation and excessive thirst— when these two afflict a weak man,
his life-breaths abandon him before long.
5.6.10 | He who has a fever occurring in the forenoon and a severe dry cough,
and who is devoid of strength and flesh, is just like a deceased person.
5.6.11 | He whose urine and feces are discharged in a clotted state,
who is devoid of body heat, afflicted with abdominal enlargement, and labored breathing, does not live.
5.6.12 | He whose swelling, located in the abdomen, spreads to the hands and feet,
will bring distress to his circle of kinsmen and be killed by that disease.
5.6.13 | The physician should avoid treating that patient whose swelling is located in the feet, whose two calf-muscles are likewise sagging, and whose two shanks are also sinking.
5.6.14 | A man with swollen hands, swollen feet, and a swollen groin and abdomen,
who has lost his natural complexion, strength, and appetite, should not be treated with medicines.
5.6.15 | One whose chest is afflicted, who has excessive phlegm, and from whom a blue, yellow, or blood-tinged discharge constantly flows from afar— one should avoid such a person.
5.6.16 | A man with bristling body hair, thick urine, swelling, afflicted by cough and fever,
and depleted of flesh, should be avoided from afar by a physician who knows [his condition].
5.6.17 | For one whose three doshas are aggravated and clearly manifest,
and who is emaciated and devoid of strength, there is no cure.
5.6.18 | Fever and diarrhea occurring at the end of swelling, or swelling occurring when those two have subsided—
especially in a weak man— lead to death.
5.6.19 | Pale and exceedingly emaciated, overwhelmed by thirst,
boastful, and breathing with anger— he should be rejected by one who understands.
5.6.20 | One whose jaw, neck, and hands are seized by stiffness, who suffers from excessive thirst and loss of strength,
and whose vital breaths reside only in the chest— such a person one should avoid.
5.6.21 | He faints and stretches out his limbs, finding no comfort whatsoever;
with his flesh and strength wasted away and his food gone, the man is soon to die.
5.6.22 | He whose diseases arise from incompatible origins and require incompatible treatments, and who suffers intensely from these dreadful ailments, is swiftly destroyed.
5.6.23 | Strength, discernment, health, the digestive tract, flesh, and blood—
whosoever’s these are depleted, he is swiftly destroyed.
5.6.24 | For one whose health declines and whose natural constitution deteriorates,
death suddenly and repeatedly carries away their life.
5.6.25 | Regarding this, there is a verse: One should avoid these bodies that are afflicted by disease;
for the wise do not see any success in these cases through medical treatment.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, named "The Chapter on the Body," in the Section on the Sense Organs (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Seven:
5.7.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the sense organ concerning the appearance of a corpse (*pannarūpīyamindriya*).
5.7.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
5.7.3 | One should not desire to treat that man whose vision one would recognize as being like a maiden who has lost her form, consisting merely of a reflection in the eyes.
5.7.4 | He whose reflection appears distorted in moonlight, in sunlight, in a lamp, in water, or even in a mirror,
is likewise a ghost.
5.7.5 | A shadow that is severed, split, agitated, diminished, or even increased;
