one that is lost, thin, divided in two, distorted, or pierced; [is inauspicious].
5.7.6 | These and whatever other loathsome reflections there may be—
all these are to be known as signs of those about to die, provided they are not produced by visible causes.
5.7.7 | He whose shadow is distorted in its shape, size, color, and likewise in its radiance— even if he is healthy— is indeed a ghost.
5.7.8 | Configuration (saṃsthāna) is to be understood as form (ākṛti), which may be symmetrical or asymmetrical.
The measure (pramāṇa) of men is said to be threefold: middling, small, and large.

5.7.9 | That shadow which exists in water, mirrors, sunlight, and so forth, according to the proportions and shapes [of the objects], is a reflection; whereas a shadow is that which rests upon color and luster.
5.7.10 | The reflections of the five beginning with *svā* (the sky) possess various characteristics:
the ethereal (*nābhasī*) reflection is stainless, blue, glossy, and as if radiant.
5.7.11 | That which is dry, dark-brownish, and reddish is the Vāyavī (wind-born) complexion; it is lusterless.
The Āgneyī (fire-born) complexion, however, is pure red, radiant, and pleasing to behold.
5.7.12 | That which is pure like vaidūrya, stainless, and very glossy is considered to be watery (ambhasī).
That which is stable, glossy, dense, smooth, dark, and white is of the earth (pārthivī).
5.7.13 | Among these, the four beginning with the Vāyavī are conducive to happiness;
however, the Vāyavī [alone] leads to ruin or even to great suffering.
5.7.14 | All radiance is fiery (taijasī), and it is recorded as being of seven kinds:
red, yellow, white, dark-brown, green, pale-white, and black.
5.7.15 | Among those [teeth], those that are open, glossy, and broad bring auspicious results;
whereas those that are rough, dirty, and compressed lead to inauspicious outcomes.
5.7.16 | Shadow (chāyā) covers the color, whereas light (bhās) reveals the color;
shadow is perceived when near, while light shines forth when at a distance.
5.7.17 | No one is without shadow or without luster; rather, specific variations of shadow and luster, depending on the time, indicate the arising of good or evil fortune for human beings.
5.7.18 | One whose eyes are jaundiced, whose face is swollen, whose temples have lost their flesh,
and who suffers from palpitations and heat of the body— such a person one should avoid.
5.7.19 | That man who, upon being raised from his bed, repeatedly falls into a state of delusion and does not recover for seven days, is a boaster; he shall not live.
5.7.20 | He in whom diseases are combined and move both in reverse and direct order,
and whose *grahaṇī* is generally impaired, does not live for more than half a month.
5.7.21 | One should avoid that person who, being afflicted by disease, emaciated, and eating little,
nevertheless voids a great deal of urine and feces.
5.7.22 | He who, being weak, eats excessively, or who, being afflicted by disease, eats before his previous meal has been digested,
and whose urine and feces are scanty— he is just like a dead man.
5.7.23 | That man who eats food that is desirable and endowed with [excellent] qualities,
yet constantly declines in strength and complexion, does not live long.
5.7.24 | He who moans, breathes heavily, passes loose stools,
is devoid of strength, afflicted by thirst, and has a parched mouth, does not survive.
5.7.25 | He who breathes out a short breath and whose body trembles excessively— Punarvasu Ātreya declared such a person to be as good as dead.
5.7.26 | Furthermore, the man who breathes out upwards, who is overcome by phlegm,
and whose complexion, strength, and food intake have declined, does not live.
5.7.27 | He whose eyes move upward, whose mind and limbs tremble,
who is devoid of strength, afflicted by thirst, and has a parched mouth— such a person does not survive.
5.7.28 | For one whose cheeks are swollen, who suffers from severe fever and cough, who has colic pain,
and who has an aversion to food— in such a person, the ritual act does not succeed.
5.7.29 | He whose head, tongue, and mouth are distorted, whose eyebrows have fallen away,
and whose tongue is covered with thorns— he is just like a corpse.
5.7.30 | There is excessive swelling, the testicles are greatly distended and protruded;
and the opposite of this, through such deformity, is the sign of one who is like a corpse.
5.7.31 | If one's flesh has been completely consumed so that only skin and bone remain,
and he is emaciated and fasting, his maximum lifespan shall be one month.
5.7.32 | Regarding this, there is a verse: Having recognized these various signs known as *ariṣṭa*, a skilled person attains the designation "knower of Āyurveda."
Thus ends the seventh chapter, named "The Chapter on the Appearance of the Signs," in the Section on the Indicators (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Eight:
5.8.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the indicator concerning the head-downward posture (*Avākśirasīyam Indriya*).
5.8.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
5.8.3 | One whose shadow appears with its head downward, or crooked, or even headless, that person one should not desire to treat.
5.8.4 | If the eyelashes become matted together and the vision is impaired,
the wise physician should not treat that person with medicine.
5.8.5 | He whose eyelids swell and do not close even as he dries up, and whose eyes become coated with a film— he is just like one who is dead.
5.8.6 | If one sees many unprecedented, unmade, and clearly manifest whorls of hair (sīmantāvartakas) on the eyebrows or on the head, one should predict death.
5.8.7 | Sick men live for three days with this sign;
however, for those who are healthy, it is said that this lasts for at most six nights.
5.8.8 | A man who does not perceive his hair being pulled out when it is being plucked—
whether he be healthy or diseased— does not survive beyond six nights.
5.8.9 | A wise man, perceiving that one whose hair, though not anointed with oil, appears as if it were anointed, should know that his life is obstructed and avoid him.
5.8.10 | He whose nasal bridge becomes flattened and wide,
appearing swollen though not actually swollen, should be rejected by one who knows [the truth].
5.8.11 | He whose nose is excessively dilated, or excessively constricted, or crooked, or completely withered, does not live.
5.8.12 | He whose face, ears, lips, teeth, or eyes are white, dark, excessively red,
or discolored through abnormality, does not escape from disease.
5.8.13 | He whose teeth have become white, flower-like, and covered with sordes, shall not suffer from that disease caused by such a transformation; rather, having abandoned it, he attains health.
5.8.14 | It is rigid, insensate, heavy, and excessively covered with thorns;
it is dark-brown, dry, or swollen, resembling the tongue of a corpse, and protruding.
5.8.15 | The wise man, recognizing that a person who, after breathing out long, breathes in short and becomes distressed, has his life-span obstructed, should avoid him.
5.8.16 | When life is at its end, the hands, feet, jaws, and palate become excessively parched; they may also become harsh or even soft.
5.8.17 | He who, being afflicted, repeatedly strikes knee against knee, raises his feet and casts them down,
and throws his face about, does not live.
5.8.18 | By clipping the tips of his nails with his teeth, by pulling out his hair with his nails,
or by scratching the ground with a piece of wood, one is liberated from disease.
5.8.19 | He who gnashes his teeth while awake, crying out or laughing without a cause,
and does not perceive suffering, is not released from disease.
5.8.20 | He who laughs repeatedly, utters loud cries, strikes the bed with his foot,
and frequently probes his own bodily orifices while suffering from illness does not survive.
5.8.21 | One should predict death for one who, weary and longing for pleasure, seeks with those very same objects through which he formerly attained supreme delight when they were all present.
5.8.22 | Neither the neck nor the back supports the head's weight of one who is ill and about to die; nor do the jaws support the morsel held in the mouth.
5.8.23 | Sudden onset of feverish heat, thirst, fainting, loss of strength,
and the loosening of the joints occur in one who is about to die.
5.8.24 | For one whose mouth and other parts exude profuse sweat at the time of the sun's rising,
and who is afflicted by a fever born of toxic application (lepa-jvara), life is difficult to sustain.
5.8.25 | Food does not reach the throat, and the tongue reaches the throat;
as the end of life approaches for a living being, strength also fails away.
5.8.26 | He tosses his head about after painfully releasing his clenched fists;
with sweat flowing from his forehead, he is on the verge of death, his bodily bonds failing.
5.8.27 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
A wise person, being attentive, should observe these signs in men who are about to die;
for some appear and then vanish in an instant, yet there is no sign here that is without result.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, named "The Chapter on the Signs of Impending Death from a Blackish Discoloration," in the Section on the Vital Signs (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Nine. 5.9.1:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the signs of impending death characterized by a blackish discoloration (*yasya-śyāva-nimittīya*).
5.9.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
5.9.3 | When one's vision becomes dark-brown, distorted, or even greenish,
a disease that has arrived for the sake of his end should be recognized by the wise man.
5.9.4 | A wise man, recognizing that one who is unconscious, whose mouth is parched, and who is overwhelmed by diseases, has reached the end of his life, should abandon him.
5.9.5 | That man whose veins are greenish and whose hair follicles are constricted, and who craves sour things, meets his death through pitta.
5.9.6 | The extremities of the body lose their luster, the body itself withers away, and strength declines; he whom Rājayakṣmā afflicts perishes.
5.9.7 | Burning pain in the shoulders, hiccups, vomiting of blood,
abdominal distension, and pain in the flanks occur for the sake of the destruction of the consumptive patient.
5.9.8 | A man suffering from wind-diseases, epilepsy, leprosy, swelling, abdominal enlargement,
abdominal tumors, diabetes, or pulmonary consumption;
5.9.9 | When there is a loss of strength and muscle mass, these become incurable;
the physician should avoid treating them even in cases of other disorders.
5.9.10 | A man who has been purged of flatulence by emetics but is still followed by thirst,
and who distends again after being purged, is just like a corpse.
5.9.11 | A man who is unable to drink even a draught because of the extreme dryness of his throat, mouth, and chest, does not live.
5.9.12 | Having observed the weakening of the voice, the loss of strength and complexion, the increase of disease, and improper conduct, one should predict death.
5.9.13 | A wise man should avoid one who suffers from labored breathing, whose body heat has departed, whose groins are afflicted with pain, and who finds no relief.
5.9.14 | One should avoid from afar a person who speaks with a discordant voice, one who has met his own death, and also one who listens to what is not being said.
5.9.15 | Ātreya considers the life of that man whom a disease suddenly releases while he is weak to be in a state of uncertainty.
5.9.16 | Now, if his kinsmen should entreat him with prostrations,
he may say, "I shall eat with relish," but he should not give him a purgative.
5.9.17 | If no auspicious improvement is seen in him after a month,
and he does not respond to various other medicinal juices, his life is difficult to sustain.
5.9.18 | The wise say that for him whose spittle, excrement, or semen sinks in water, the end of his life has arrived.
5.9.19 | He whose emitted breath appears as various distinct colors,
and who sinks away upon reaching water, is not fit to live.
5.9.20 | When the bile (pitta), following the heat, reaches the temples and becomes obstructed there, that disease is called Śaṅkhaka by name; it destroys life within three nights.
5.9.21 | He from whose mouth blood mixed with foam repeatedly flows,
and whose abdomen is pierced by sharp pains— such a person is to be rejected.
5.9.22 | The patient in whom severe loss of strength and muscle, an increase in disease,
and anorexia are observed does not live beyond three fortnights.
5.9.23 | Regarding this, there are two verses: When death is imminent, these cognitions arise in human beings; one should observe these and others of a similar nature.
5.9.24 | All those [signs] are observed, yet they do not all enter into a human being who is about to perish; therefore, one should be aware of them in every respect.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, named "The Diagnostic Sign of Blackishness," in the Section on the Diagnostic Signs (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Ten:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnostic sign concerning immediate death (*sadyomaraṇīyamindriya*).
5.10.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

5.10.3 | O Agniveśa, I shall now describe separately the various signs of one whose life-breaths (*prāṇas*) are about to depart immediately— those by which a person, when touched [by them], does not survive.
5.10.4 | A fully developed and formidable vātāṣṭhīlā, remaining fixed in the heart,
instantly robs one of life when the person is overwhelmed by thirst.
5.10.5 | Having loosened the collar-bones and bent the nose,
the wind, circulating within the body, instantly robs one of life.
5.10.6 | If one's eyebrows have fallen from their place and there is a terrible internal burning,
the disease causing hiccups will instantly rob him of his life.
5.10.7 | When the blood and flesh are depleted, the wind moving upward courses through both channels equally; such a person's life is instantly snatched away.
5.10.8 | When the wind suddenly moves between the anus and the navel,
seizing the groins of a person who is emaciated, it instantly robs him of his life.
5.10.9 | Expanding the tips of the ribs and seizing the chest,
the wind instantly robs of life the one whose eyes are wide and fixed.
5.10.10 | Having seized both the heart and the rectum, the powerful wind especially robs a weak person of his life instantly.
5.10.11 | When the powerful wind seizes both the groin and the anus,
it produces dyspnea in the living being and instantly robs him of his life.
5.10.12 | When the wind (māruta) severs the umbilical region, the urine, the bladder-head, and the feces,
it produces piercing pain and instantly robs one of life.
5.10.13 | He whose groins are split on all sides by piercing pains of wind (vāta),
and who has diarrhea and thirst, loses his life immediately.
5.10.14 | He whose body here is permeated solely by the vital air (māruta),
and whose excrement is broken up and whose thirst is immediate, shall quickly abandon his life.
5.10.15 | That embodied being whose body is swollen by a swelling caused by Vata,
and who has loose stools and thirst, shall quickly lose his life.
5.10.16 | He in whom there arises a cutting pain originating in the stomach (āmāśaya),
accompanied by diarrhea and thirst, shall lose his life immediately.
5.10.17 | He in whom there occurs a cutting pain arising from the colon (pakvāśaya),
accompanied by thirst and severe constriction of the rectum, shall lose his life immediately.
5.10.18 | Having taken hold of the receptacle of digested food (the colon) and destroyed consciousness,
the wind produces a rattling sound in the throat and instantly takes away life.
5.10.19 | The teeth appear smeared with mud, the face resembles powdered ash, and the limbs become as rigid as wood; these are the signs of one who will die immediately.
5.10.20 | Afflicted by thirst, labored breathing, headache, delusion, distress, weakness, and moaning,
as well as by diarrhea, the patient quickly gives up his life.
5.10.21 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
He who thoroughly understands these signs indeed understands both the life and the death of mortals.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, named "The Signs of Immediate Death," in the Section on the Diagnostic Indicators (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Eleven:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the diagnostic indicator concerning those with "Faint Light" (*Aṇujyotīyam Indriyam*).
5.11.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
5.11.3 | One whose light is minute, who lacks one-pointedness of mind, who is poorly formed, and who is always dejected, finds no delight; he goes to the intermediate state of the other world.
5.11.4 | He whose offered oblation the recipients of the offering do not consume,
he, having gone to another world, consumes the funeral cake (piṇḍa) after a year.
5.11.5 | That person who does not see Arundhatī situated near the Seven Sages shall, at the end of a year, behold the Great One (Mahat).
5.11.6 | He who, through misconduct, attains beauty, prosperity, or wealth without cause— or conversely, suffers a downfall from them— his life lasts only until the end of that period.
5.11.7 | Devotion, character, memory, renunciation, intellect, and strength without cause—
these six qualities depart from one who is about to die within six months.
5.11.8 | He on whose forehead an exceedingly beautiful network of previously unseen veins is visible does not live for six months.
5.11.9 | One whose forehead is covered with lines curved like the crescent moon should be declared to have reached the end of his life within six months.
5.11.10 | Trembling of the body, delusion, gait, and even speech—these are perceived as if in one who is intoxicated; such a person does not live for a month.
5.11.11 | He whose hair, urine, and excrement sink in water is a hater of his own kin; after one month, he sinks into the waters of death.
5.11.12 | He whose hands, feet, and both eyes wither away,
or swell up, apart from the rest of the body, does not live for even one month.
5.11.13 | He upon whose forehead, head, or bladder there appears a dark line curved like the crescent moon, does not deserve to live.
5.11.14 | He on whose body eruptions (masūrikā) arise quickly, resembling coral beads in appearance, and perish before long— he perishes.
5.11.15 | One for whom there is severe pain in the neck, swelling of the tongue, inflammation of the anus, mouth, and throat—
him one should declare to be ripe (for death).
5.11.16 | Agitation, excessive delirium, and the extremely agonizing breaking of bones—
these three occur for one who is ensnared by the noose of Time.
5.11.17 | Fainting, he plucks out his hair;
though weak and impelled by time, the man eats food as if he were healthy, yet he clings to it excessively.
5.11.18 | Bringing his hand with its fingers close to his eyes, he searched;
and the one blinded by Time, whose upward-gazing eyes were unblinking, even smiled.
5.11.19 | Driven by time and deluded, he searches for something unreal in his bed, on his seat, in his limbs, or even in wood or a wall.
5.11.20 | A man who laughs when he should not laugh, who becomes bewildered, who licks the corners of his mouth, and whose feet, hands, and breath are cold— such a man does not live.
5.11.21 | Calling out to his kinsmen or even to people standing nearby,
he whose mind is shrouded by great delusion does not see them, even though he sees them.

5.11.22 | A wise physician, having observed simultaneously the under-activity (ayoga) or over-activity (atiyoga) of the elements beginning with earth (kha) within the body, should not administer medicine.
5.11.23 | Due to the excessive increase of diseases and the depletion of the mind's strength,
the embodied being quickly abandons its dwelling known as the body.
5.11.24 | When there is a decline of *asu*, complexion, voice, food, strength, the faculty of speech, and the strength of the mind diminish; sleep becomes either constant or absent altogether.
5.11.25 | Those who hate their physician, their medicine, their food and drink, or their teacher and friends—
all these should be understood to be under the sway of Yama, the Equal-Dealer.
5.11.26 | In these [cases], disease progresses and medicine is rendered ineffective.
One should not eat the food of these people, nor even touch their water.
5.11.27 | Four feet, though assembled and endowed with the qualities of a practitioner, become useless when life has departed; without substance (wealth), there is no arising of virtue.
5.11.28 | The physician should examine the lifespan of both the healthy person and the diseased patient;
for the entire fruit of knowing the lifespan follows upon one who knows the lifespan.

5.11.29 | Regarding this, there is a verse: When the humors (doṣas), having transcended the path of treatment and pervaded the body alone, manifest signs, that is defined as *ariṣṭa* (the fatal sign).

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Subtle Light" (*Aṇujyotīya Indriya*), in the Section on the Diagnostic Signs (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Twelve.
5.12.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the signs of impending death known as "The Powder of Cow Dung" (*Gomayacūrṇīya Indriya*).
5.12.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
5.12.3 | He upon whose head a powder resembling cow-dung flour appears,
and which falls off along with its oily film, his life lasts for only one month.
5.12.4 | That man who runs about with his shoulders drooping, as if scraping the ground with his feet,
does not dwell long in this world due to his deformity.
5.12.5 | He whose chest dries up excessively first, while all his other limbs remain moist after he has bathed and been anointed, does not live for half a month.
5.12.6 | When a physician, despite striving to administer medicine for the sake of a patient,
is unable to bring about recovery, that person’s life is difficult to preserve.
5.12.7 | Even a medicine that is well-known, proven effective many times, and administered according to the prescribed rules will not succeed for one who lacks proper medical treatment.
5.12.8 | He who, while consuming food properly prepared by a physician,
does not obtain its fruit— for him, life is difficult to maintain.
5.12.9 | We shall now describe, in the section on messengers, the signs of those about to die,
by observing which a wise physician should unhesitatingly refuse to treat them.
5.12.10 | Or if, upon seeing the messenger who has arrived, [the patient] has disheveled hair, or is naked, or is weeping, or is unpurified, the physician should predict death.
5.12.11 | When the physician is asleep, those messengers who come cutting or even breaking [the way]—
the physician should not follow their master.
5.12.12 | They offer oblations into the fire and likewise present funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to the ancestors;
yet the messengers who arrive at the physician’s house seek to destroy him.
5.12.13 | When messengers come to a physician on behalf of men who are about to die, they speak of inauspicious things or think of them again and again.
5.12.14 | Messengers of those about to die visit, speak of, or even mention dead, cremated, or ruined things, as well as other inauspicious matters, in the presence of the physician.
5.12.15 | When a physician sees a messenger who has arrived at a place or time that shares the same qualities as the morbid transformation (vikāra), he should not treat that patient.

5.12.16 | One should recognize as messengers of those about to die: a woman who is wretched, frightened, fleeing, terrified, soiled, or unchaste; and those of the three [degenerate] castes, as well as eunuchs.
5.12.17 | A physician should not go to see a messenger who has suffered a physical injury, one who wears the marks of a religious order, one who is diseased, or one who performs cruel deeds.
5.12.18 | Upon seeing a messenger who has arrived for the sake of a patient riding on a donkey, a camel, or a chariot, the physician should know that the patient’s defeat is at hand.
5.12.19 | Straw, chaff, meat, bone, hair, body hair, nails, teeth,
a broom, a pestle, a winnowing basket, shoes, and a discarded skin.
5.12.20 | Messengers who touch grass, wood, chaff, charcoal, clods of earth,
or stones at the first sight of someone are said to portend that person's imminent death.
5.12.21 | Furthermore, while the messenger is delivering words concerning the patient, if the physician perceives any inauspicious omen, he should not follow after him.
5.12.22 | Likewise, [one should avoid] speaking of a person addicted to vice, a corpse, or even the ornaments of a corpse;
or of something broken, burnt, or destroyed, or words to that effect.
5.12.23 | Whether it be a pungent or intense taste, or a great, corpse-like odor;
or a vast and cruel touch, or whatever else may be inauspicious—
5.12.24 | Having heard the speech previously uttered by messengers, or again at the time of their speaking, a wise man should predict his own death.
5.12.25 | Thus has this entire section on messengers been declared for those about to die, as well as for the families of healthy and diseased persons; now I shall speak again of portents.
5.12.26 | Sneezing, shouting, stumbling, falling,
as well as reviling, striking, forbidding, or censuring;
5.12.27 | [Seeing] garments, turbans, upper cloths, umbrellas, and pairs of shoes;
likewise, seeing the misfortune and the sight of those who have met with death or calamity.
5.12.28 | And the falling of full sacrificial posts, banners, and flags;
the proclamation of the deaths of enemies; and defilement by ashes and dust.
5.12.29 | Furthermore, there may be the blocking of the path by a cat, a dog, or a serpent;
or the cries of cruel beasts and birds directed toward a blazing quarter of the sky.
5.12.30 | Seeing beds, seats, and vehicles turned upside down—
all these the wise declare to be inauspicious.
5.12.31 | A wise physician, observing these [signs] on the way while looking toward the patient's house, or hearing [of them], should not proceed to that dwelling.
5.12.32 | Thus has been described the portents occurring on the road that are censured by physicians;
one should also recognize these signs for those who are about to die while staying at home.
5.12.33 | At the time of entry, there should be the procession of a full pitcher, fire, earth, seeds, fruits, and clarified butter;
and at the time of exit, a bull, a Brāhmaṇa, jewels, food, and deities.
5.12.34 | A physician, upon entering the house of those about to die, sees vessels filled with fire and broken, shattered arrows.
5.12.35 | The people of the house of one who is about to die resort to things that are torn, split, burnt, broken, crushed, and weak.
5.12.36 | For one whose bed, clothing, vehicle, gait, food,
or voice is heard to be inauspicious, there is no cure.
5.12.37 | He whose friends treat his bed, clothing, vehicle, or any other possession as if he were a corpse— he is indeed a corpse himself.
5.12.38 | When food is excessively spoiled and the digestive fire is extinguished—
even as if there were fuel in a windless place— there is no cure for that person.
5.12.39 | If in the house of a patient, vessels break or fall excessively,
his life is difficult to preserve.
5.12.40 | And there are verses on this point: That which has been proclaimed in detail across twelve chapters is the sign of the end of life for those humans who are about to die.
5.12.41 | We shall explain that [subject] in brief, by resorting to another synonym;
for a synonymous expression is indeed appropriate for the comprehension of the meaning.
5.12.42 | Furthermore, this very intention of ours is not enjoined excessively;
it is that which was previously declared in that very same context.
5.12.43 | For embodied beings dwelling in their bodies during their final moments—
who are intensely afflicted and desiring to depart from their bodies for the sake of destruction— [the following occurs].

5.12.44 | For those who endure their cherished life-breaths, who wish to abandon their beloved dwelling, and who, as the mechanical apparatuses of the body break apart, seek to enter into ultimate darkness;
5.12.45 | I shall now describe, according to their enumeration and according to tradition, those forms and various intermediate states that occur here for the sake of destruction.
5.12.46 | The vital breaths are thoroughly tormented, innate knowledge is obstructed,
the limbs vomit up their strength, and all physical movements cease.
5.12.47 | The senses perish, consciousness becomes desolate;
the mind falls into longing, and fear enters even the heart.
5.12.48 | Memory and intelligence desert him; modesty and prosperity withdraw;
evils assail him, and his vigor and splendor perish.
5.12.49 | Character is excessively altered, and devotion is transformed;
reflections are distorted, and shadows undergo a change of form.
5.12.50 | The semen falls from its place, the wind (vāyu) takes an upward course,
the muscles waste away, and the blood also goes to depletion.
5.12.51 | The vital breaths go to dissolution, the joints fall apart,
the odors undergo transformation, and likewise the complexion and the voice are shattered.
5.12.52 | The body assumes a discolored appearance, the orifices of the body become parched,
smoke arises from the head, and the condition known as *dāruṇa* (the dreadful) and *cūrṇaka* (powdery) occurs.
5.12.53 | Those regions of the body which were observed to be constantly vibrating have all become stiffened and do not move in any way whatsoever.
5.12.54 | The qualities of the various parts of the body—cold, hot, soft, and harsh—occur in their respective locations;
however, when they appear in other locations, they behave in the opposite manner.
5.12.55 | Flowers grow upon his nails; mud appears on his teeth;
matted locks grow upon his eyelashes, and parting lines appear even upon his head.
5.12.56 | Medicines do not reach their intended effect according to the desired outcome;
and even those that are obtained, their potency does not succeed.
5.12.57 | Diverse and cruel morbid humors (vikāras), accompanied by various symptoms,
quickly manifest themselves, having struck down both strength and vitality.
5.12.58 | Sound, touch, taste, form, smell, and movement— these, as well as thoughts,
arise only as inauspicious things during the various activities of karmic engagement.
Terrible dreams are seen, wickedness arises,
servants act with hostility, and the appearance of a ghost is manifested.
5.12.60 | The primary nature (prakṛti) declines excessively, while the transformation (vikṛti) increases; every kind of terrible, portentous, and undesirable phenomenon is observed.
5.12.61 These are the characteristics of men who are about to perish, as they have been stated according to their enumeration and in accordance with tradition.
5.12.62 | Even if a physician skilled in diagnosis perceives the signs of death here,
he must not speak of the imminent death unless he has been asked.
5.12.63 | Even when questioned, one must not speak that which is harmful,
if it would cause suffering to the patient or to anyone else.
5.12.64 | A skilled physician, seeing the signs for destruction, should not desire to treat him whose death he does not proclaim.
5.12.65 | Observing signs that are the opposite of those known as indicative of death, the physician should certainly declare that health has been restored.
5.12.66 | By means of messengers, omens, and signs; by observing the patient's family and their surroundings;
and by the characteristics of the patient’s conduct, habits, and the availability of desired medicinal substances.

5.12.67 | A messenger who is of good conduct, cheerful, free from physical defects, renowned, dressed in white garments, neither shaven-headed nor wearing matted hair, and whose caste, dress, and actions are consistent with his status— [such a one should be sent].
5.12.68 | [One should not study] while riding on a camel or a donkey carriage, nor during the twilight hours or when there is an eclipse;
nor under non-cruel constellations, nor under those that are not fierce, nor under the fixed (dhruva) stars.
5.12.69 | Except on the fourth, ninth, and the empty (riktā) dates, nor on the fourteenth; and avoiding midday, midnight, an earthquake, and the appearance of Rāhu.
5.12.70 | The physician should declare that a messenger who has arrived is auspicious if he comes from an auspicious place, lacks inauspicious portents, and is composed.
5.12.71 | [The sight of] curd, unbroken grains, the twice-born, bulls, and a king [brings prosperity].
5.12.72 | Of jewels, of full water-jars, of a white horse,
of celestial banners and flags, of fruits, and of lac-dye;
5.12.73 | Of a maiden, of one increasing in prosperity, of a bound single animal standing still, of the earth being lifted up, and of a blazing fire; |||
5.12.74 | Of sweetmeats, white flowers, sandalwood,
and of a cart filled with pleasing food and drink.
5.12.75 | By means of men, a cow with her calf, a mare, a woman, as well as by a jīvañjīvaka bird, white mustard seeds, a crane, and a sweet-voiced bird—
5.12.76 | Of swans, woodpeckers, blue jays, and peacocks;
likewise of fish, goats, birds, and conchs; of priyaṅgu seeds and of ghee.
5.12.77 | Seeing a necklace, a mirror, white mustard seeds, and yellow pigment (rocanā);
a fragrant scent, a very bright color, and a sweet taste.
5.12.78 | The auspicious and pleasing voices of beasts, birds, and humans;
the raising up of umbrellas, banners, and flags; and their praise.
The sounds of kettledrums, clay drums, and conchs, the auspicious sounds of festive days, the sounds of Vedic recitation, and a pleasant, clockwise-moving breeze [are all favorable omens].
5.12.80 | On the road and upon entering a house, one should recognize the signs of health:
the inhabitants of the house are endowed with auspicious conduct and are accompanied by pleasant fragrances.
5.12.81 | One who is faithful, compliant, and possesses a great accumulation of wealth will attain riches,
power, and happiness, and will easily obtain their desired objects.
5.12.82 | Therein [are described] the application and the successful accomplishment of appropriate materials for houses,
palaces, mountains, elephants, and bulls.
5.12.83 | Mounting horses and men in a dream;
[or seeing] the moon, the sun, fire, the twice-born, cows, and water-bearing clouds.
5.12.84 | Crossing over oceans, prosperity, escaping from a narrow strait,
and being addressed by the gods and the ancestors who are well-pleased in a dream.
5.12.85 | Seeing white garments and a clear lake;
the taking up of meat, fish, poison, impure things, an umbrella, and a mirror.
5.12.86 | Seeing white flowers in a dream is auspicious,
as is riding on horses, cows, or chariots, or traveling toward the northeast;
likewise, weeping, rising from a fall, and the crushing of enemies [are favorable].

5.12.87 | Association with the characteristics of the *sattva* quality, devotion toward physicians and the twice-born, curability, and freedom from despondency— these are the signs of recovery from illness.
5.12.88 | A man endowed with auspicious characteristics obtains health, strength, long life, and great happiness, as well as other desired states of being.

5.12.89 | The signs of death and health have been described in the chapter on cow-dung powder (gomayacūrṇīya), as well as those based on the messenger, dreams, the patient, portents, reasoning, and spiritual attainments.
5.12.90 | Thus has this subject at hand been stated exactly as it is; it should be constantly examined by one who knows medicine,
for in this way one attains success and eternal fame.
Having accomplished his task, he obtains riches.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, named "The Chapter on Cow-Dung Powder," in the Section on the Examiners (*Indriyasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka. The Section on the Examiners is complete. [Now begins] the Section on Therapeutics (*Cikitsāsthāna*) of the *Carakasaṃhitā*.
The First Chapter.
6.1.1.1. The first section on Rasāyana.
Now, therefore, we shall expound the section on Rasāyana concerning Abhayā and Āmalakī.
6.1.1.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

6.1.1.3 | Treatment (cikitsita) is that which removes disease; it is the wholesome regimen, the means of accomplishment, the medicine, the atonement, the pacification, the restoration to the natural state, and the beneficial.
6.1.1.4 | One should know the names of medicinal substances; that medicine is of two kinds:
that which promotes vigor for the healthy, and that which cures disease for the afflicted.

6.1.1.5 | Non-medicine is of two kinds: that which causes affliction and that which causes subsequent affliction. That which promotes vigor in one who is healthy is called *atṛṣya* (non-craving) and is a *rasāyana* (rejuvenative).
6.1.1.6 | Generally, the second [measure] is considered for the pacification of diseases.
For the word "generally" (prāyas) has a specific meaning, as both [the first and second measures] can indeed produce both results.
6.1.1.7 | Long life, memory, intelligence, health, youthfulness,
excellence of radiance, complexion, and voice, as well as supreme strength of body and senses.
6.1.1.8 | One does not obtain mastery of speech, obeisance, or beauty from an elixir (*rasāyana*).
For an elixir is merely a means of acquiring excellent qualities such as [vital] fluids and the like.
6.1.1.9 | That which produces offspring and ensures their continuity, which provides immediate exhilaration,
and by means of which one becomes as strong as a horse and proceeds irresistibly toward women— [that is this].
6.1.1.10 | By whatever means he is nourished, he becomes exceedingly dear to women;
even as he grows old, his semen remains inexhaustible, and he is seen to be fruitful.
6.1.1.11 | Like a great tree with abundant branches, by him a shrine becomes worthy of worship,
highly esteemed by the people, and possesses many offspring.
6.1.1.12 | That which is the root of progeny, by which one enjoys infinity both in this world and after death—
that is indeed aphrodisiac therapy (vājīkaraṇa), which bestows fame, prosperity, strength, and nourishment.
6.1.1.13 | This twofold medicine that promotes vigor for one who is healthy has been described;
that which effects the destruction of disease will be discussed in the section on therapeutics.
6.1.1.14 | The entire purpose of medical treatment for disorders consists of this:
medicinal therapy, the procedure for rejuvenation (rasāyana), and the method for aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa) which follows.
6.1.1.15 | That which is contrary to the medicinal properties [of a drug] should be known as non-medicine; it must not be used. Now, however, I shall describe that medicine which is to be employed.
6.1.1.16 | The sages know two types of application for elixirs (rasāyana):
namely, that which involves entering an enclosed chamber (kuṭīprāveśika) and that which involves exposure to wind and sun (vātātapika).
6.1.1.17 | First, the procedure for the *kuṭīprāveśika* [type of patient] will be taught:
[it concerns those] such as kings, physicians, the twice-born, holy men, and performers of meritorious deeds.
6.1.1.18 | In a city that is safe from fear, auspicious, and well-supplied with necessities,
one should have a small hut constructed on good ground in the north-eastern direction.
6.1.1.19 | It should be endowed with ample width and height, consisting of three inner chambers,
with fine windows, thick walls, pleasant in all seasons, clearly defined, and pleasing to the mind.
6.1.1.20 | [One should choose] a place free from undesirable sounds and the like, inaccessible to women,
provided with desired implements, and where physicians, medicines, and Brahmins are readily available.

6.1.1.21 | Now, during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, at a propitious moment and astrological configuration, having performed a ceremonial shaving;
6.1.1.22 | Having established the strength of fortitude and mindfulness, being full of faith and concentrated,
shaking off the defects of the mind, and contemplating loving-kindness toward all beings.
6.1.1.23 | Having first worshipped the deities and the twice-born, and having circumambulated the gods,
cows, and brahmins, he should then enter that hut.
6.1.1.24 | Once he has been purified by those cleansing therapies, is comfortable, and has regained his strength, he should employ the elixir (rasāyana). I shall now describe that purification.
6.1.1.25 | The powders of *harītakī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *āmalaka*, jaggery (*guḍa*),
*vacā*, *viḍaṅga*, turmeric (*rajanī*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and ginger (*viśvabheṣaja*).
6.1.1.26 | A person who has been prepared with oleation and sudation should drink [the medicine] with warm water;
thereby, for one whose body is purified and who has undergone the process of dietary reintegration, [the medicine shall take effect].
6.1.1.27 | One should consume barley gruel for three nights, or even for five days with clarified butter,
or for seven days of old [grain], until one's bodily luster is purified.
6.1.1.28 | Having ascertained that his digestive tract is purified, one should administer a rejuvenative (rasāyana) therapy,
provided one knows the patient's age, constitution, and suitability, and employs whatever is appropriate for him.
6.1.1.29 | One should know that *harītakī* possesses five tastes, is hot, non-saline, auspicious,
promotes the downward movement of the *doṣas*, is light, and acts as a digestive stimulant and a digestive agent.
6.1.1.30 | It promotes longevity, nourishment, and prosperity; it is supreme for stabilizing youth, pacifies all diseases, and bestows strength upon the intellect and the senses.
6.1.1.31 | It cures leprosy, abdominal tumors, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), consumption, anemia, intoxication, hemorrhoids,
disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa), and chronic intermittent fever.
6.1.1.32 | Heart disease along with diseases of the head, diarrhea, anorexia, cough, urinary disorders, flatulence, splenic enlargement, and acute abdominal dropsy.
6.1.1.33 | Excessive salivation due to phlegm, hoarseness of voice, discoloration of the skin,
jaundice, worms, swelling, asthma, vomiting, exhaustion, and a sense of prostration in the limbs.
6.1.1.34 | Harītakī quickly removes various obstructions of the channels, coatings of the heart and chest, and the delusion of memory and intellect.
6.1.1.35 | Those suffering from indigestion, those who eat dry food, those emaciated by women, wine, or poison,
and those afflicted by hunger, thirst, or heat— these should consume *abhayā*.
6.1.1.36 | One should know that those same qualities and those same actions are present in *āmalakī* as well.
Those [qualities] which were stated regarding the harītakī are, however, the opposite in the case of its potency (vīrya).
6.1.1.37 | Therefore, through such practices, a physician should know that the fruits of *harītakī* and *āmalaka* are like nectar.
6.1.1.38 | The Himalaya, the best of mountains, is the supreme source of medicinal herbs;
therefore, one should cause fruits produced from it to be collected when they are in season.
6.1.1.39 | Their juices and potencies fully developed, they were, from time to time, treated according to the prescribed rules and refreshed by the sun, the wind, shade, and water.
6.1.1.40 | I shall now describe the application and the supreme medicinal action of those fruits which are unchewed, not putrid, free from blemishes, and devoid of disease.
6.1.1.41 | Take ten *pala* measures each of the five groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*),
one thousand *harītakī* fruits, and three times as many fresh *āmalaka* fruits.
6.1.1.42 | One should know Vidārigandhādi to be the group beginning with Vidārigandhā, Bṛhatī, Pṛśniparṇī, and Nidigdhikā, with Śvadaṃṣṭrā as the fifth.
6.1.1.43 | Bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarya, and then pāṭalā;
punarnavā, the two śūrpaparṇīs, balā, and eraṇḍa as well.
6.1.1.44 | Jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, medā, jīvantī, together with śatāvarī,
and likewise the roots of śara, ikṣu, darbha, kāśa, and śāli rice.
6.1.1.45 | One should prepare these five pentads of roots; all that, according to the stated proportions, should be cooked in ten times the amount of water.
6.1.1.46 | One should cause that purified juice, of which one-tenth remains,
to be taken along with all those *harītakī* fruits and all the *āmalaka* fruits.
6.1.1.47 | Having crushed all those boneless fruits with brushes and having strained them into that decoction, one should cause these powders to be added.
6.1.1.48 | Of maṇḍūkaparṇī, pippalī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and plava;
likewise of mustā together with viḍaṅga, and of candana and aguru.
6.1.1.49 | Having taken four-pala portions each of madhuka, haridrā, vacā, and kanaka, as well as of sūkṣmailā and tvac;
6.1.1.50 | One thousand palas of powdered sugar, exceeding one *tulā* in weight,
two *āḍhakas* of oil, and three [palas] of clarified butter should be added therein.
6.1.1.51 | When that entire [mixture] has been cooked in a vessel made of udumbara wood over a gentle fire,
and having ascertained that it is lickable and not burnt, one should mix it with honey once it has cooled.
6.1.1.52 | The quantity of honey should be half that of the oil; all of this, having been mixed together, should be kept in a vessel of ghee. One should administer its dose at the appropriate time.
6.1.1.53 | One should not obstruct the intake of food by even a single measure with respect to one's digestion;
in this regard, sixty-day rice with milk is desired as the meal once [the previous meal] has been digested.
6.1.1.54 | The Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, and others whose wealth is their austerity,
having consumed this elixir, became possessed of immeasurable lifespans.
6.1.1.55 | Having cast off their worn-out bodies, they attained a preeminent and youthful age;
free from lethargy, fatigue, and labored breathing, they were devoid of ailment and composed in mind.
6.1.1.56 Endowed with intelligence, memory, and strength, those whose wealth was austerity practiced for a long time the Brahmanic austerity of celibacy with ultimate perseverance.
6.1.1.57 | One desiring the lifespan of Brahmā should employ this elixir (rasāyana).
He attains a long life, preeminent youth, and his desired objects.
(Thus ends the Brahma-rasāyana.

6.1.1.58 | One thousand *āmalaka* fruits, possessing the qualities as previously described, should be well-steamed by the method of steaming a paste using the heat of milk; once dried in the shade and freed of their seeds, they should be powdered.

Then, one should take a thousand fresh *āmalaka* fruits and soak them in their own juice. To this, one should add a powder consisting of one-eighth part each of *sthirā*, *punarnavā*, *jīvantī*, *nāgabalā*, *brahmanuvarcalā*, *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, *śatāvarī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *pippalī*, *vacā*, *viḍaṅga*, *svayaṅguptā*, *amṛtā*, *candana*, *aguru*, *madhuka*, *madhūkapuṣpa*, *utpala*, *padma*, *mālatī*, *yuvatī*, and *yūthikā*. This mixture should then be soaked in the juice of a thousand palas of *punarnavā* and *nāgabalā*, dried in the shade, and formed into the shape of small balls of jaggery using twice as much clarified butter or honey and clarified butter. These should then be placed in a clean, sturdy [container].

One should place [the powder] in a jar smeared with ghee beneath a heap of ashes underground for a fortnight, after a protective rite has been performed by one learned in the Atharvaveda. Having extracted it at the end of the fortnight, one who consumes it every morning according to the prescribed method—increasing the dose by half a karṣa at a time and mixing it with the powders of gold, silver, copper, coral, and iron in eight parts, while observing the strength of his digestive fire—and who, once it is digested, partakes of ṣaṣṭika rice with milk and ghee, attains the aforementioned benefits.
6.1.1.59 | Furthermore, there are verses on this subject:
This is the Brāhma elixir, practiced by the hosts of great sages;
one who employs it becomes free from disease, long-lived, and possessed of great strength.
6.1.1.60 | He is beloved by his subjects, successful in his aims, and possesses a radiance equal to the moon and the sun;
he retains what he has heard, and the spiritual power of the seers arises within him.

6.1.1.61 | He becomes as strong as the essence of the earth-supporter (the mountain) and equal in prowess to the wind; moreover, poison does not affect him, and even poison turns into non-poison within his body.
(Thus ends the second elixir for Brahman-like longevity.
6.1.1.62 | Bilva, agnimantha, śyonāka, kāśmarya, pāṭali, balā, the four parṇīs, pippalī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and the two types of bṛhatī.
6.1.1.63 | Śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, drākṣā, jīvantī, puṣkara, aguru, abhayā, amṛtā, ṛddhi, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, and śaṭī.
6.1.1.64 | Musta, punarnavā, medā, elā, candana, utpala, vidārī,
vṛṣamūla, kākolī, and kākanāsikā.
6.1.1.65 | One should take five hundred palas of these [drugs] and one hundred palas of *āmalaka*, and boil them together in one *droṇa* of water.
6.1.1.66 | Having ascertained that these medicinal herbs have lost their potency,
and having extracted that juice and that *āmalaka* fruit from its seeds, [one should process them] with oil and clarified butter.
6.1.1.67 | Having fried twelve palas [of the ingredients] and added half a tulā of purified sugar candy (matsyaṇḍikā), the physician should properly prepare it like an electuary (leha).
6.1.1.68 | To this, once it has been prepared and cooled, one should add six palas of honey,
four palas of tugākṣīrī, and likewise two palas of pippalī.
6.1.1.69 | One should add one pala each of cinnamon bark, cardamom, cinnamon leaves, and keśara;
this is declared to be the supreme *rasāyana* known as Cyavanaprāśa.
6.1.1.70 | It is specifically prescribed as a remedy for cough and dyspnea;
it promotes the growth of the body for those who are emaciated or wounded, as well as for the elderly and children.
6.1.1.71 | It removes hoarseness of voice, diseases of the chest, heart disease,
gout, thirst, and the disorders of the urinary and seminal tracts.
6.1.1.72 | One should employ its measure such that it does not obstruct one's eating.
By the use of this, Cyavana, though very old, became young again.
6.1.1.73 | Intelligence, memory, luster, freedom from disease, excellence of lifespan, strength of the sense organs,
supreme delight in women, increase of the digestive fire, clarity of complexion, and downward movement of the wind.
6.1.1.74 | By the application of this elixir (*rasāyana*), even an aged man, through the practice of entering a small chamber (*kuṭīpraveśa*),
casts off all appearance produced by old age and assumes the form of fresh youth.
(Thus ends the Cyavanaprāśa.

By means of this, the great ṛṣis such as Cyavana and others regained their youth and became most beloved by women; they possessed firm, even, and well-proportioned flesh, with compact and stable bodies, and their strength, complexion, and senses were exceedingly clear; they were of unimpeded prowess everywhere and capable of enduring all hardships.

All bodily disorders arise from a diet consisting of sour, salty, pungent, alkaline, dry vegetables, meat, sesame paste, and flour-based foods; from those who consume sprouted grains, new awned cereals, *śamī* beans, incompatible, unwholesome, dry, alkaline, and obstructive substances; from those who eat damp, heavy, putrid, or stale food; from those whose meals are irregular or consumed before the previous meal has been digested; from those habitually sleeping by day, indulging in women, or consuming alcohol; from those whose bodies are agitated by irregular or excessive physical exercise; and from those who abound in fear, anger, grief, greed, delusion, and exhaustion.

For because of this cause, the muscles become flaccid, the joints loosen, the blood becomes vitiated, and a significant amount of fat is discharged; marrow is no longer formed in the bones, semen does not flow, and the vital essence (*ojas*) undergoes depletion. Being in such a state, he becomes exhausted and sinks down; overcome by drowsiness, lethargy, and laziness, he breathes with a lack of vigor and is incapable of physical or mental activities. With his memory, intellect, and complexion destroyed, having become a vessel for diseases, he does not attain the full span of life.

"Therefore, observing all these aforementioned faults and abandoning all unwholesome foods and activities, one ought to employ rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana)," having said this, the Blessed Lord Punarvasu Ātreya spoke again:

Once it is digested, one should eat *śāli* rice and *ṣaṣṭika* grain with milk and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).

By its use, one’s age remains free from decay for a hundred years, what one has heard remains fixed in memory, all diseases are pacified, one attains unimpeded power over women, and one becomes possessed of offspring.

The fourth quarter of the chapter on Rasāyana.
6.1.4.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the quarter on Rasāyana concerning the origin of Āyurveda.
6.1.4.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

6.1.4.3 | At one time, indeed, the sages—both those who lived as householders and those who were wanderers—subsisting on cultivated herbs, became prosperous, indolent in their activities, and generally lacked physical vigor.

Being unable to perform any of their duties and perceiving their own fault to be caused by living in the village, they went to the Himalayas—the source of the Gaṅgā; a place free from the faults of village life due to its former treading; auspicious, meritorious, sublime, and pure; inaccessible to those of unrighteous conduct; frequented by gods, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras; a mass of many jewels with inconceivable and wonderful power; frequented by Brahmanical sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas; the source of divine bathing-places and medicinal herbs; a supreme refuge protected by the Lord of the Immortals—[the sages] Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras.
The great sages Trivasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Agastya, Pulastya, Vāmadeva, Asita, Gautama, and others.
6.1.4.4 | The thousand-eyed preceptor of the immortals, Tānridra, said to them: "Welcome, O Brahmarṣis, knowers of Brahman, whose wealth is knowledge and austerity!

Indeed, you must have experienced exhaustion, loss of luster, loss of voice, and discoloration caused by living among the common folk—misery and its attendant suffering. For life among the common folk is the root of all that is inauspicious. Therefore, it is time for those who perform meritorious deeds to show favor to the people, and it is time for the Brahmarṣis to attend to their own bodies and receive the instruction on Āyurveda."

For the sake of favoring themselves and their progeny, the Aśvins bestowed Ayurveda upon me; Prajāpati bestowed it upon the Aśvins, and Brahmā bestowed it upon Prajāpati. Considering that the lifespan of living beings is short, abounding in old age and disease, unpleasant, and followed by further suffering—and that due to its brevity, there is a deficiency in austerity, self-restraint, observance, charity, and study—you gentlemen ought to listen to and comprehend from me this most meritorious [science], which prolongs life, pacifies old age and disease, bestows vigor, is immortal, auspicious, a refuge, and noble.

And it is for the sake of favoring all creatures that he intends to reveal the Vedic Brahman, as well as his own unsurpassed, noble, and inexhaustible Brahma-merit consisting of friendliness and compassion.
6.1.4.5 | Having heard those words of the Lord of the Gods, all the sages praised the Best of Gods with Vedic hymns; and being greatly delighted, they acclaimed his speech.

6.1.4.6 | Then Indra, having transmitted this Ayurveda, the nectar of immortality, to the sages, said: "All of this must be practiced; this is the auspicious time for elixirs (*rasāyana*), and the divine herbs originating from the Himalayas have attained their full potency."

They are as follows: *aindrī*, *brāhmī*, *payasyā*, *kṣīrapuṣpī*, *śrāvaṇī*, *mahāśrāvaṇī*, *śatāvarī*, *vidārī*, *jīvantī*, *punarnavā*, *nāgabalā*, *sthirā*, *vacā*, *chatrā*, *aticchatrā*, *medā*, *mahāmedā*, and other life-prolonging (*jīvanīya*) plants administered with milk. When perfected through use for six months, they bring about supreme longevity and youthfulness, freedom from disease, excellence of voice and complexion, corpulence, intelligence, memory, supreme strength, and other desired qualities.

(Thus ends the elixir spoken by Indra. 6.1.4.7 | There is a medicinal plant named *brahmasuvarcalā*, which has golden latex and leaves resembling lotuses; a medicinal plant named *ādityaparṇī*, known as *sūryakāntā*, which has golden latex and flowers shaped like the solar disc; a medicinal plant named *nārī*, known as *aśvabalā*, which has leaves resembling *balvaja* grass; a medicinal plant named *kāṣṭhagodhā*, which is shaped like a lizard; a medicinal plant named *sarpa*, which is shaped like a snake; and the king of medicinal plants named *soma*, which has fifteen joints and wanes just like the moon.

And he grows. There is a medicinal herb named Padmā, shaped like a lotus, red as a lotus, and fragrant as a lotus; there is a medicinal herb named Ajā, known as *ajaśṛṅgī*; and there is a medicinal herb named Nīlā, which has blue latex, blue flowers, and is abundant with spreading creepers.

Whichever of these herbs he may obtain, having reached satiety with its fresh juice, he should lie naked upon a covered trough made of moist Palāśa wood that has been saturated with oil. There he dissolves; after six months, he is reborn. Goat's milk is the restorative for him.

Within six months, one becomes like a deity in terms of youth, complexion, voice, form, strength, and radiance; all forms of speech spontaneously manifest within him, he possesses divine sight and hearing, his range of movement extends for a thousand yojanas, and his lifespan is ten thousand years, free from affliction.
6.1.4.8 | And there are verses on this point:
The power of divine medicinal herbs that can be endured by those like you would be impossible to endure for those of undisciplined soul.
6.1.4.9 | By the power of the medicinal herbs, while you remain steadfast in your own duties,
every single and complete prosperity shall accrue to you.
6.1.4.10 | Indeed, these medicinal herbs native to the region can be utilized by forest-dwellers and householders alike, provided they are self-restrained and disciplined in soul.
6.1.4.11 | However, for those [plants] which, due to the qualities of the field and their middling cultivation,
possess weaker potency, the procedure to be known is exactly that same one.
6.1.4.12 | For those who desire happiness but are unable to seek out or employ those [medicines],
this other procedure for elixirs (rasāyana) is recommended.
6.1.4.13 | Of the ten [drugs] that are strengthening (balya), vitalizing (jīvanīya), and nourishing (bṛṃhaṇīya),
as well as those that stabilize the age (vayasaḥ sthāpana), and of khadira and asana—
6.1.4.14 | Of dates, madhūka flowers, musta, and utpala;
of grapes, viḍaṅga, vacā, and citraka.
6.1.4.15 | Of śatāvarī, payasyā, pippalī, and joṅgaka;
and of ṛddhi, nāgabalā, dvāradā, and dhava.
6.1.4.16 | Of triphalā, kaṇṭakārī, vidārī, and candana;
of sugarcane, the roots of śara, śrīparṇī, and tiniśa.

of these, one *pala* portion each should be combined with four times as much cow’s milk.

6.1.4.18 | Two vessels of sesame oil and two of cow’s clarified butter (gavya-sarpiḥ) should be prepared; once all these have been thoroughly cooked together, one should extract the resulting medicated fat (sneha).
6.1.4.19 | In that case, one āḍhaka of amalaka powder, processed a hundred times with its own juice,
should be given along with fresh honey.
6.1.4.20 | One should cause a vessel containing one *prastha* of sugar powder to be provided;
having mixed it together with *tugākṣīrī* and long pepper (*pippalī*), it should be set aside.

6.1.4.21 | For half a month, one should place a dose of this [medicinal oil] equal to the digestive fire in a very clean earthen jar that has been saturated with ghee; thereafter, one should administer it.
6.1.4.22 | Of gold, copper, coral, iron, and crystal;
of pearls, lapis lazuli, and conch shells; and of powdered silver.
6.1.4.23 | Having added the sixteenth measure [of milk] and abstaining from physical exertion and sexual intercourse,
one should eat sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika) whenever it is digested, along with milk and ghee.
6.1.4.24 | It pacifies all diseases, is aphrodisiac, promotes longevity, and is supreme; it bestows strength upon the mind, memory, the bodily fire, the intellect, the senses, and the body.
6.1.4.25 | It is supremely invigorating, as well as bestowing [complexion and] voice;
it pacifies great misfortune and grants mastery over all forms of speech.
6.1.4.26 | Those who desire for their subjects the attainment of their goals, fresh youth, popularity among the people, and fame in the world,
should duly employ this Brahma elixir of noble potency.
(Thus ends another elixir spoken by Indra.
6.1.4.27 | For those who are capable, free from disease, wise, self-controlled,
possessing attendants, and having leisure, entry into a subterranean chamber (*kūṭīpraveśa*) is beneficial.
6.1.4.28 | But for those who act otherwise than this, there is the procedure involving the deities Surya and the Maruts.
Of these two, the former procedure is superior, though it is very difficult to perform.
6.1.4.29 | If diseases should arise due to a failure in the procedure for rejuvenation (rasāyana),
their respective specific medicines should be administered, setting aside the [standard] rejuvenation therapy.
6.1.4.30 | One who speaks the truth, is free from anger, abstains from intoxicants and sexual intercourse,
is non-violent, free from exertion, tranquil, and speaks kindly;
6.1.4.31 | One who is devoted to silent recitation and purification, steadfast, constant in giving, and ascetic;
one who delights in the worship of the gods, cows, Brahmins, teachers, elders, and preceptors.
6.1.4.32 | Always devoted to benevolence, always compassionate by nature,
with equal wakefulness and sleep, and always consuming milk and ghee.

6.1.4.33 | One who knows the measure of place and time, who understands reasoning, who is free from egoism, whose conduct is praiseworthy, who is not confused, and whose senses are inclined toward the inner self;
6.1.4.34 | One should know that man who serves the elders— those who are believers and have conquered their selves—
and who is devoted to the treatises on dharma, as a perpetual elixir.
6.1.4.35 | He who employs the rasāyana with these qualities combined attains all the benefits of rasāyana as they have been described.
(Thus ends the Elixir of Conduct.
6.1.4.36 | Without first eliminating the gross physical and mental defects,
a person can never truly partake of the benefits of the elixirs (*rasāyana*).
6.1.4.37 | For yogas, which serve to prolong life and eliminate old age and disease,
succeed for those of purified mind and body who are self-disciplined.
6.1.4.38 | All this should not be spoken to those whose souls are ruined,
nor to those who are not twice-born, nor to those in whom there is no desire to listen.
6.1.4.39 | Whatever formulations of rejuvenation (rasāyana) and aphrodisiacs (vṛṣya) are considered,
and whatever medicine exists for diseases— all that depends upon the physician.
6.1.4.40 | Therefore, a wise man should honor his physician— who is intelligent and has mastered the Vedas—
to the best of his ability, just as the Lord of the Gods honored the two Aśvins.
6.1.4.41 | The Aśvins are remembered as the physicians of the gods and the bearers of the sacrifice;
for it was by them that the severed head of the sacrifice was restored.
6.1.4.42 | Pūṣan’s teeth were shattered and Bhaga’s eyes were lost;
even the paralysis of the arm of the wielder of the thunderbolt was cured by those two alone.
6.1.4.43 | And the Moon, having been treated for consumption, was seized by the King of Consumption;
the Moon, having fallen under the power of Soma, was made well again by those two.
6.1.4.44 | Bhārgava Cyavana, though aged and having undergone a transformation, being lustful and deprived of his natural complexion and voice, was made young again by those two.
6.1.4.45 | By these and many other such deeds, the two supreme physicians became highly honored by the great-souled ones, beginning with Indra.
6.1.4.46 | The planets, the hymns, the mantras, as well as various sacrificial offerings,
and smoke-colored animals are assigned to those two by the twice-born.
6.1.4.47 | At the morning libation, Śakra partakes of the Soma together with the Aśvins;
and at the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the Blessed One rejoices together with the Aśvins.
6.1.4.48 | Indra and Agni, as well as the two Aśvins, are mostly praised by the twice-born;
indeed, no other deities are praised in the Vedic texts in such a manner.
6.1.4.49 | Thus, the two Aśvins, the physicians, are worshipped by the ageless, immortal, and steadfast gods, together with their lords, as they proceed on their journey.

6.1.4.50 | Furthermore, what could physicians possibly accomplish for mortals who are subject to death, disease, and old age, who are mostly beset by suffering, and who yet seek happiness— unless they possess extraordinary power?

6.1.4.51 | A twice-born man who is virtuous, wise, disciplined, and has mastered the scriptures is to be honored by all living beings like a guru; for he is traditionally known as the teacher of life.
6.1.4.52 | Upon the completion of his studies, the second birth of the physician is proclaimed; for one does not truly attain the title of "Vaidya" by virtue of his previous birth alone.

6.1.4.53 | Upon the completion of his studies, whether it be the Veda, or the Sattva, or even that which belongs to the Ṛṣis, he certainly enters into [the realization of] knowledge; therefore, the twice-born man is remembered as a physician (vaidya).
6.1.4.54 | A wise person, desiring long life, should not harbor ill-will toward the teacher of life, nor should he revile him, nor should he do anything harmful to him.
6.1.4.55 | But that man who, whether having made a formal agreement or not, does not provide treatment for the physician, there is no atonement for him in this world.
6.1.4.56 | A physician, desiring the highest dharma, should protect all patients with diligence as if they were his own children, shielding them from afflictions.
6.1.4.57 | Ayurveda was revealed by the great seers, who were devoted to dharma and desired the eternal state, for the sake of dharma, as well as for the sake of wealth and pleasure.
6.1.4.58 | He who engages in medical practice neither for the sake of wealth nor for the sake of pleasure, but rather out of compassion for living beings, transcends all [worldly bonds].
6.1.4.59 | But those who, for the sake of their livelihood, engage in the trade of selling medical treatments,
abandon a heap of gold and attend instead to a heap of dust.
6.1.4.60 | He who, having severed the nooses of Yama, bestows life upon those being dragged toward the abode of Vaivasvata by dreadful diseases.
6.1.4.61 | A donor of dharma and artha equal to him is not found here;
for indeed, no other gift excels the gift of life.
6.1.4.62 | He who conducts himself with medical treatment, considering that compassion for living beings is the highest dharma, achieves his purpose and enjoys ultimate happiness.
6.1.4.63 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
The origin of Āyurveda, the auspicious method for divine medicines,
and the perfected jewel-elixir (ratnarasāyana), whose qualities are only slightly inferior to nectar (amṛta).
6.1.4.64 | Whatever the Lord of the Immortals spoke to the perfected ones and to the students of sacred knowledge has all been fully revealed in this *Āyurvedasamutthāna*.

Thus ends the fourth quarter on elixirs (rasāyana-pāda), titled "The Origin of Āyurveda," in the chapter on elixirs within the Section on Therapeutics (cikitsā-sthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
This chapter on elixirs is completed.

The first quarter of the chapter on aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa).

The efficacy of aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*), the woman who is the field for him,

6.2.3.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
