Thus ends the fourth quarter on aphrodisiacs, titled "The Man Possessing Arisen Strength and Other Qualities," in the section on therapeutics within the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
This second chapter on aphrodisiacs is completed.
Chapter Three.
6.3.1 | Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of fever.
6.3.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.3.3 | Agniveśa, with palms joined in reverence, questioned Punarvasu— who was free from fever, seated in tranquility in a secluded place, and who had resolved all doubts regarding fevers.
6.3.4 | Fever, which afflicts the body, the senses, and the mind, is the foremost of all diseases and is powerful;
it was declared by the Blessed One of old to be the principal among maladies.
6.3.5 | Regarding that eternal one, the rival of all living beings, at the time of dissolution and emergence,
[he understands] its primordial nature, its activity, its power, and its causes.
6.3.6 | Its preliminary form, its substratum, its power, time, and essential characteristics;
its distraction, the distinction of its rules, and the appearance of that which is separately divided.
6.3.7 | The signs of acute fever, of chronic fever, the medicinal treatment, the sequence of therapeutic procedures,
and the distinct symptoms of the fever as it subsides and becomes pacified.
6.3.8 | One who has been released from fever must be guarded against various factors for a certain period of time,
as well as the causes by which the fever may return even after it has subsided.
6.3.9 | Furthermore, O Blessed One, you ought to explain all those activities that pacify him who has returned [to this world] for the sake of the welfare of the world.
6.3.10 | Having heard those words of Agniveśa, the Teacher said:
"O gentle one, listen to everything that is to be said regarding the chapter on fevers."
6.3.11 | Fever (jvara), morbid alteration (vikāra), affliction (roga), disease (vyādhi), and even distress (ātaṅka)—
these are one and the same thing, designated by various synonymous names.
6.3.12 | Its primary causes are said to be the bodily and mental humors (doṣas);
for fever does not afflict a person who is free from these humors.
6.3.13 | Wasting away, darkness, fever, evil, and death are said to be of the nature of Yama,
arising from the conviction of the five elements in men who are tormented by their own karma.
Thus its origin has been declared; its manifestation, however, arises from grasping, as previously indicated in the *Nidāna* [section], and from the terrible wrath of Rudra.
6.3.15 | For in the second age, the Asuras assailed Śarva, who was established in a vow of non-anger, for a thousand divine years.

6.3.16 | Seeing that he was capable of creating obstacles to the asceticism of the Great-Souled One, Dakṣa Prajāpati, though his own food was being obstructed by those [obstacles], remained indifferent, desiring to create an obstacle to the Great-Souled One's asceticism.
6.3.17 | Furthermore, although being exhorted even by the gods, Dakṣa Prajāpati did not allot a fixed share for Maheśvara in the sacrifice.

6.3.18 | He performed sacrifices devoid of those *ṛc* verses belonging to Paśupati, as well as those *āhuti* offerings prescribed by the followers of Śiva, which are the bestowers of success in sacrifice.
6.3.19 | Then the Lord, having completed his vow and perceiving Dakṣa’s transgression,
Rudra— being a knower of the self— manifested his own fierce nature.
6.3.20 | Having created an eye on his forehead and burnt those Asuras,
the Lord emitted a child scorched by the fire of his wrath, the destroyer of the sacrifice.
6.3.21 | Thereupon that sacrifice was destroyed, and the dwellers of heaven were distressed;
overcome by the agony of burning, the hosts of beings wandered in all directions.
6.3.22 | Then the host of gods, together with the seven seers, praised the omnipresent Lord with Rigvedic hymns as long as Śiva remained absorbed in the state of Śiva.

6.3.23 | Having recognized Śiva as the auspicious one established for the welfare of all beings, Triśiras— armed with ashes, possessing nine eyes, and joined with palms in reverence— stood there in fear.
6.3.24 | Enveloped in garlands of flames, fierce, with short shanks and a protruding belly, the Fire of Wrath said to the God: "What shall I do for you?"
6.3.25 | The Lord said to that Krodha: "In the world you shall become Jvara (Fever);
you shall manifest at birth, at death, and during other disturbances of the humors."
6.3.26 | Fever manifests as burning heat, loss of appetite, thirst, body aches, and pain in the heart; its influence is most intense at birth and at death.
6.3.27 | Nature (prakṛti), onset (pravṛtti), and power (prabhāva) have been demonstrated;
the eight causes previously mentioned are explained here according to their respective divisions.
6.3.28 | Lassitude, tearful eyes, yawning, heaviness, fatigue,
and an uncertain aversion to fire, sunlight, wind, water, and food [are the symptoms].
6.3.29 | A lack of digestion, a bad taste in the mouth, a decline in strength and complexion,
and slight abnormalities of conduct are the premonitory symptoms of fever.

6.3.30 | The body, both alone and with the mind, is said to be the locus of fever; however, its strength and the appropriate time [for treatment] have been demonstrated in the section on etiology (nidāna).
6.3.31 | The specific symptom of fever is heat in both body and mind;
for there is nothing whatsoever that is not tormented by one afflicted with fever.
6.3.32 | Fever is of two kinds according to its classification: physical and mental.
Furthermore, it is observed to be of two types: mild (saumya) or fiery (āgneya).
6.3.33 | Furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: internal movement and external movement;
moreover, it is both natural and modified, as well as curable and incurable.
6.3.34 | Furthermore, fever is seen to be of five types according to the strength or weakness of the humors (doṣas) and the time (kāla):
the continuous (saṃtata), the quotidian (satata), the tertian (anyedyus), the quartan (tṛtīyaka), and the quaternian (caturthaka).
6.3.35 | Furthermore, by way of the distinction of substrates, the elements (dhātus) are considered sevenfold;
moreover, fever is divided into eight types according to the distinction of its causes.
6.3.36 | The bodily [fever] first arises in the body, while the mental [fever] arises in the mind.
Distraction of thought, restlessness, and exhaustion are the characteristics of mental distress.
6.3.37 | Furthermore, a disorder of the sense organs should be known by the symptom of internal burning;
that which consists of bile and heat is characterized by coldness, while that which consists of wind and phlegm is characterized by heat.
6.3.38 | But this fever, possessing mixed characteristics, desires both;
for Vāyu is a "carrier of application" (yogavāha) and, through its conjunction [with other humors], performs the functions of both.
6.3.39 | Endowed with fire, it causes burning; through its reliance on the moon (Soma), it produces coldness. Internal burning, excessive thirst, delirium, labored breathing, and vertigo [arise].
6.3.40 | One should recognize these as the signs of an internal fever: pain in the joints and bones, absence of perspiration, and the suppression of the bodily humors and excrement.
6.3.41 | Excessive external heat, mildness of thirst and other symptoms,
and the outward direction of the force are the signs [of a fever] that is easily curable.
6.3.42 | That which is natural (prākṛta) is easily curable, occurring as it does in spring and autumn.
Pitta, increased by heat during the summer, becomes aggravated in autumn.
6.3.43 | Accumulated [doshas] manifest as kapha during the cold season, and likewise in spring;
in the rainy season, they are aggravated by water and medicinal herbs that have an acid post-digestive effect (vipāka).
6.3.44 | Pitta that has been accumulated and aggravated by the brilliance of the autumnal sun quickly produces fever, and kapha acts as its secondary force.
6.3.45 | By its very nature, there is no danger from fasting in that case;
for the phlegm is accumulated by water and sweet medicinal herbs.
6.3.46 | During the winter, scorched by the sun, that [wind] becomes aggravated in the spring;
therefore, fever arises in the spring due to the phlegm (śleṣman).
6.3.47 | Even during the process of ingestion, wind and bile may follow;
therefore, one should act after discerning the relative strength and weakness of the humors at the beginning, the end, and the middle.
6.3.48 | A learned physician should treat fever according to the seasons of autumn and spring;
natural fever (prākṛta-jvara) is defined with reference to the season and the constitution.
6.3.49 | Generally, [a fever] residing in the wind (vāyu) is difficult to cure; when it occurs at other times, it is morbid.
Its various causes have been fully demonstrated in the section on etiology (nidāna).
6.3.50 | Fever arising from many strong causes, characterized by numerous symptoms, yet occurring when the doshas are weak and without complications, is curable.
6.3.51 | Fever that brings about the end of life, which quickly destroys the sense organs,
[occurs] after seven days, ten days, or likewise twelve days.
6.3.52 | A sharp fever accompanied by delirium, confusion, and labored breathing kills a man;
likewise, a deep-seated fever that persists for many nights in one who is emaciated or swollen.
6.3.53 | A fever that is incurable, severe, and one that creates partings in the hair, wherein the humors have spread through the channels carrying the nutrient fluid (rasa) and become heavy;
6.3.54 | Pervading the entire body and becoming rigid, they cause a continuous fever for ten days,
twelve days, or seven days— a condition that is extremely difficult to endure.
6.3.55 | Because of its rapid action, that [disease] quickly reaches subsidence or it kills;
for the doṣa is constantly equal to the time, the corruptible elements, and the bodily constituents.
6.3.56 | Because it acts without opposition, it should be known as extremely difficult to endure;
just as the wind and other [humors] act upon the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), so too do they act upon urine and feces.
6.3.57 | They manifest simultaneously or successively, according to the rule, in a continuous fever;
whether through the complete purification or non-purification of the *rasa* and the other constituents.
6.3.58 | Within seven days or other such periods, it either subsides or kills;
but when the humors are neither excessively purified nor completely purified.
6.3.59 | These twelve are then declared to be the supports of the continuous [breath];
having performed the emission on the twelfth day, which is characterized by the unmanifest.
6.3.60 | "The subsidence of which is difficult to achieve persists even for a long time";
having understood this, the physician should treat the *santata* fever continuously.
6.3.61 | Generally, in the procedure for the sequence of treatment, one should first employ fasting (apatarpaṇa);
for the doṣa that usually resides in the blood constituent (rakta-dhātu) causes the satata fever.
6.3.62 | One who has an adversary experiences the nature of increase and decrease over time;
one who is constant follows two times throughout day and night.
6.3.63 | Having obtained strength from any one of the factors— time, constitution, or the vulnerable elements (dūṣya)—
the morbid humor (doṣa), having obstructed the fat-carrying channels (medovahāḥ sirāḥ), [causes] a condition that lasts for another day.

6.3.64 | A morbid humor (doṣa) that has reached the bones and marrow, when accompanied by its antagonist, produces fever simultaneously during day and night; it may also cause tertian or quartan fevers.
6.3.65 | The movement [of the dosha] is separated by one interval; otherwise, it is called *anyedyus*.
It may produce a quotidian (*anyedyuṣka*) fever even by resorting to the blood.
6.3.66 | Having entered the channels of the flesh, the dosha produces tertian fever; and having taken refuge in the path of the fat, it produces quartan fever.
6.3.67 | *Anyedyuṣka* occurs every day; *tṛtīyaka* occurs after skipping one day;
that which returns after resting for two days is *caturthaka*.
6.3.68 | Just as a seed lies within the earth and sprouts in due time,
so too does the *doṣa* lie within the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and become aggravated in due time.
6.3.69 | Having reached its full growth and the time of strength, the *doṣa* produces tertian (*tṛtīyaka*) and quartan (*caturthaka*) fevers due to the depletion of opposing forces.

6.3.70 | Having released their force, the humors (malas), their strength exhausted, remain established in their respective locations; yet, increasing again at their own time, they cause fever in the person.
6.3.71 | The tertian fever (tṛtīyaka) is of three types: that which seizes the sacrum due to kapha and pitta; that which seizes the back due to vāta and kapha;
and that which seizes the head due to vāta and pitta.
6.3.72 | The quartan fever manifests its power in two ways:
the phlegmatic type first [affects] the calves, while that arising from wind first [affects] the head.
6.3.73 | Furthermore, there is another type of irregular fever called *caturthaka-viparyaya*.
This occurs when each of the three *dhātus* (humors), situated within two *dhātus*, produces the fever in three ways.

6.3.74 | Fever is generally observed to be of five types arising from the combination [of all three humors]. In a case of combined morbidity (sannipāta), whichever humor is most predominant is designated as the primary disorder.

6.3.75 | Fever assumes its various forms according to the relative strength or weakness of the seasons, days and nights, the humors (doṣas), and the mind, as well as due to the influence of time and the nature of the objective.

6.3.76 | When [the humor] is located in the rasa (plasma), there is heaviness, dejection, agitation, exhaustion, vomiting, and loss of appetite; externally, there is a burning sensation, aching in the limbs, and yawning.
6.3.77 | When [the humor] is located in the blood, there are red and hot pustules, thirst, frequent spitting of blood,
burning sensations, redness, vertigo, intoxication, and delirium.
6.3.78 | Internal burning, fainting accompanied by vomiting, exhaustion,
loose stools, foul odor, and twitching of the limbs occur when the fever is located in the muscle tissue (māṃsa).
6.3.79 | When [the poison] resides in the fat (medas), there is sweating, intense thirst, frequent delirium, repeated vomiting,
intolerance of one's own odor, as well as exhaustion and loss of appetite.
6.3.80 | In fever that has reached the bones (asthigata), there occurs both purgation and emesis, along with breaking pain in the bones,
groaning, tossing of the limbs, and labored breathing.

6.3.81 | Hiccups, labored breathing, cough, and the vision of darkness; cutting pain in the vital organs (marmans), external coldness, and internal burning—these occur when [the poison] has reached the marrow.
6.3.82 | Having reached the seat of semen, having discharged the semen and destroyed it,
that all-pervading lord departs together with the vital breath, wind, fire, and moon.
6.3.83 | That [vāta] which resides in the rasa and rakta is curable; so too that which has reached the medas and māṃsa.
That which resides in the asthi and majjā is difficult to treat, while that residing in the śukra is not cured at all.
6.3.84 | Fever, which was previously described as being of eight types according to its causes and characteristics, has been taught in brief; now hear its characteristics in detail.
6.3.85 | Headache, splitting pain in the joints, horripilation,
dryness of the throat and mouth, vomiting, thirst, fainting, giddiness, and loss of appetite.
6.3.86 | Dreaming of destruction, excessive speech, yawning, symptoms resembling fever caused by vāta and pitta,
coldness, heaviness, drowsiness, a sense of being wrapped in wet cloth, and pain in the joints.
6.3.87 | Headache, catarrh, cough, lack of perspiration,
internal heat, and moderate intensity are the symptoms of fever caused by Vāta and Kapha.
6.3.88 | Intermittent burning, intermittent coldness, frequent obstruction of perspiration,
delusion, cough, loss of appetite, thirst, and the discharge of phlegm and bile.
6.3.89 | A coated and bitter mouth, and drowsiness—these are the manifestations of fever arising from *śleṣman* (phlegm) and *pitta* (bile).
These have been declared to be those born of dual combinations (*dvandvaja*). Now, that which arises from the combination of all three (*sannipātaja*) is described.
6.3.90 | Indeed, following the thirteen types of *sannipāta* fever previously mentioned,
I shall describe their respective characteristics individually.
6.3.91 | Dizziness, thirst, burning sensation, heaviness, and excessive pain in the head—
these should be known as the signs of a fever in which vāta and pitta are predominant and kapha is diminished.
6.3.92 | Coldness, cough, loss of appetite, drowsiness, thirst, burning sensation, pain,
and distress are known as the signs of a disease in which vāta and śleṣman are predominant, while pitta is subordinate.
6.3.93 | Vomiting, coldness, frequent burning sensations, thirst, delusion, and pain in the bones—
these are determined to be the symptoms when wind is mild and pitta and kapha are predominant.
6.3.94 | Pain in the joints, bones, and head, delirium, heaviness, and vertigo occur when Vāta is predominant;
when two [humors] are associated, there is thirst and dryness of the throat and mouth.

6.3.95 | Redness of the blood, feces, and urine; burning sensation, perspiration, thirst, loss of strength, and fainting—these are the signs when all three doṣas are involved and pitta is predominant.

6.3.96 | One should diagnose a *sannipāta* (combined humor) disorder dominated by *kapha* by the presence of laziness, anorexia, nausea, burning sensations, vomiting, aversion to food, giddiness, as well as drowsiness and cough.
6.3.97 | Coryza, vomiting, lassitude, drowsiness, anorexia,
and weak digestion are considered the symptoms when pitta is predominant and kapha is excessive, with vāta being diminished.
6.3.98 | Yellowish urine and eyes, a burning sensation, thirst, vertigo, and loss of appetite—
these are considered the symptoms when vāta is diminished, kapha is moderate, and pitta is predominant.
6.3.99 | Headache, shivering, dyspnea, delirium, vomiting,
and anorexia are the symptoms when pitta is diminished, kapha is moderate, and vāta is predominant.
6.3.100 | Coldness, heaviness, drowsiness, delirium, and excessive pain in the bones and head—
these are known as the signs when pitta is diminished, vāta is moderate, and kapha is predominant.
6.3.101 | Dyspnea, cough, catarrh, dryness of the mouth,
and excessive pain in the flanks are considered the signs when *kapha* is diminished, *pitta* is moderate, and *vāta* is predominant.

6.3.102 | They recognize the following as the signs when kapha is diminished, vāta is moderate, and pitta is predominant: frequent discharge of feces, weakness of the digestive fire, thirst, burning sensation, fever, and vertigo.
6.3.103 | Hereafter, I shall describe the symptoms of sannipāta fever:
burning at one moment and coldness at another, with pain in the bones, joints, and head.
6.3.104 | When the vision is tearful, turbid, bloodshot, or distorted;
when the ears are ringing and painful; and when the throat feels as if it were covered with bristles.
6.3.105 | Lethargy, delusion, delirium, cough, dyspnea, anorexia, vertigo,
a parched and rough-feeling tongue, and extreme flaccidity of the limbs [are the symptoms].
6.3.106 | Spitting of blood and bile mixed with phlegm,
rolling of the head, thirst, loss of sleep, and pain in the heart.
6.3.107 | The delayed and scant appearance of sweat, urine, and feces;
emaciation of the limbs that is not excessive; and constant moaning from the throat.
6.3.108 | The appearance of dark-red pustules and circular patches,
muteness, suppuration of the orifices, and heaviness of the abdomen.
6.3.109 | The delayed maturation of the humors (doṣas) constitutes the clinical form of Sannipāta fever;
when the humors are obstructed and the digestive fire is extinguished, it exhibits all the symptoms in their entirety.
6.3.110 | A fever arising from the combination [of all three doshas] is incurable, whereas one that is otherwise is difficult to cure.
The distinct clinical forms of fever described separately in the section on etiology (Nidāna) are as follows:

6.3.111 | The specific characteristics of combinations (*saṃsarga*) and aggregations (*sannipāta*) have been stated by him [the author]. Furthermore, that which is the eighth, the adventitious (*āgantuka*), is specified as being of four kinds.
6.3.112 | From blows and assaults, from malevolent incantations and curses,
[and injuries caused] by weapons, clods of earth, grass, wood, fists, gems, palms, and teeth.
6.3.113 | When the body is struck by objects of that same nature, a fever born of injury (abhighātaja) occurs.
In that case of fever born of injury, the Vāyu generally vitiates the blood.
6.3.114 | That fever which arises in one afflicted by desire, grief, fear, or anger causes pain, burning sensations, swelling, discoloration, and is accompanied by distress.
6.3.115 | That fever which arises from possession by spirits (bhūtābhiṣaṅga) should be known as *abhiṣaṅgajvara*.
From lust, grief, or fear, the vāyu [is provoked]; from anger, the pitta; thus, all three impurities (malas) are involved.
6.3.116 | Those possessing the common characteristics of the *bhūtas* become agitated due to possession by a *bhūta*.
That eightfold characteristic has been explained in the section on the *bhūtas*.

6.3.117 | Some authorities state that fever arising from the touch of the wind carrying the scent of poisonous trees, as well as from other sources of poison, and even from being possessed by spirits, is called *abhiṣaṅgaja* (fever born of possession).
6.3.118 | That man who is afflicted by the malevolent spells and curses of those possessed of supernatural powers attains peace only through the very antidote that neutralizes poison.

6.3.119 | The *sannipāta* fever is terrible; it should be known as extremely difficult to endure. Whatever symptoms have been described for *sannipāta* fever are recorded as belonging to that [condition].
6.3.120 | There are manifold afflictions of the mind, the senses, and the body, as well as others,
resulting from observing the performance of malevolent spells and indeed curses.
6.3.121 | Having heard it oneself, it is characterized by inference or by tranquility;
for, due to the variety of malevolent spells (*abhicāra*) and curses, it consists of those very elements.
6.3.122 | According to the application of the symptoms, the diagnostic signs may be of various kinds;
in fever caused by passion (kāmajvara), the characteristic signs are known to consist largely of meditation and sighing.
6.3.123 | In [speech] born of grief, there is an abundance of tears; in the fever of fear, it is mostly characterized by terror;
in that born of anger, there is great agitation; but in possession by a spirit, it is non-human.
6.3.124 | In cases of poisoning, there is a predominance of fainting, delusion, intoxication, and exhaustion;
however, for some of these [cases], a burning sensation arises first.

6.3.125 | However, for some authorities, that which has been described as the specific characteristic of fevers arising from desire and so forth— such as those beginning with fever born of passion— is considered equal to [the characteristics of] these [other types of fever].
6.3.126 | This [treatment] is prescribed for diseases born of desire and other such factors, as well as for others;
however, when the mind has been previously afflicted by desire and the like, it does not possess such strength.
6.3.127 | Fever arises from wind and the other [doshas] as long as the body has not yet been corrupted;
once the body has first been assailed by wind and the others, it does not possess such strength.
6.3.128 | Fever occurs as long as the mind is not yet corrupted by desire and the other [mental afflictions].
These [fevers] are initially pure, but later they become characterized by a mixture with their own [specific] symptoms.

6.3.129 | Exogenous fevers (āgantu-jvara) arise from causes such as [poisonous] herbs and specific factors; they occur when the humors (mala), whether combined, aggregated together, or provoked individually, become deranged.
6.3.130 | Having followed the rasa-named constituent (*dhātu*) and having expelled it from its location through digestion,
it [the *agni*] produces the strength of the body's heat by means of its own heat.
6.3.131 | Having obstructed the channels and pervaded the entire body intensely,
they then produce excessive heat within the person's body.
6.3.132 | One whose entire body becomes excessively hot is called "jvarita" (feverish) because of that;
due to the obstruction of the channels, the person does not obtain perspiration.
6.3.133 | When the digestive fire has deviated from its natural seat, there generally occur in acute fever loss of appetite,
indigestion, and heaviness of the abdomen.
6.3.134 | Impurity of the heart, drowsiness, and indeed lethargy;
persistent fever, and the non-elimination of the *doṣas*.
6.3.135 | Salivation, nausea, loss of appetite, a bad taste in the mouth, stiffness, numbness,
and heaviness of the limbs, as well as excessive urination [are the symptoms].
6.3.136 | There is no digestion of undigested food (viḍ-jīrṇā) nor any exhaustion; rather, excessive fever-velocity, thirst, delirium, labored breathing, and vertigo are the symptoms of āma-jvara.
6.3.137 | The onset of waste products (malapravṛtti) and nausea (utkleśa) are the signs of that which is being digested;
likewise, hunger, emaciation, lightness of the limbs, and the subsiding of fever.

6.3.138 | The subsidence of the morbid humors for eight days is the characteristic of fever free from undigested matter (āmaja). In acute fever, one should avoid sleeping during the day, bathing, oil massage, solid food, and sexual intercourse.

6.3.139 | One should avoid anger, exposure to wind, physical exercise, and astringent decoctions (kaṣāya). For fever, fasting alone is prescribed at the beginning, except in the case of *ṛtejvara* (fever occurring without an apparent cause).
1.140 | When the doshas have been reduced to depletion by fasting— arising from exhaustion, turbidity, fear, anger, lust, grief, or fatigue— and the digestive fire has been kindled;
6.3.141 | Freedom from fever, lightness, and hunger arise in him;
one should treat him with fasting that does not conflict with his vital breaths.
6.3.142 | Health, which is the foundation of strength, is the goal for which this sequence of therapeutic procedures is intended:
fasting, sudation, time [for healing], barley gruel, and bitter tastes.
6.3.143 | Purgatives are for undigested doshas in acute fever;
when there is thirst, one should give warm water in fever caused by vata and kapha.
6.3.144 | Furthermore, in cases arising from alcohol or from Pitta, [a decoction] prepared with cooling and bitter substances is beneficial;
for both of these are digestive stimulants, carminatives, and fever-destroyers.
6.3.145 | Mustā, parpaṭaka, uśīra, candana, udīcya, and nāgara are purifying for the channels, strengthening, appetizing, sudorific, and auspicious.
6.3.146 | One should administer water that has been boiled and cooled to alleviate thirst and fever,
[thereby pacifying] the humors (doṣas) located in the stomach (āmāśaya), which are dominated by phlegm (kapha) and are agitated.
6.3.147 | Having identified those things that cause fever, one should eliminate them at the proper time by means of emetics for those who are fit for emesis;
however, emesis is contraindicated in acute fever and in cases where the morbid humors have not yet manifested.
6.3.148 | It intensely produces heart disease, dyspnea, flatulence, and delusion. The *sāma* [doshas] pervading the entire body reside within the tissues (*dhātu*) and are difficult to eliminate.
6.3.149 | The defects of unripe fruits are like their own juices when they are harmful; one should treat the patient who has been made to vomit and fasted with gruels at the proper time.

6.3.150 | From the beginning, the wise physician should administer [the diet] starting with thin gruel (*maṇḍa*) prepared with appropriate medicinal herbs, until the fever becomes mild, or for six days.
6.3.151 | His digestive fire is kindled by them, just as a fire is by fuel-sticks;
and they stimulate the digestive fire because of their medicinal properties and their lightness.
6.3.152 | They facilitate the downward movement of wind, urine, feces, and the bodily humors (*doṣas*);
due to their liquid and warm nature, they serve for inducing perspiration, and due to their liquidity, they alleviate thirst.
Because they serve as food, because they sustain life, because they promote lightness,
and because they are compatible with fever, therefore, at the very beginning, one should treat fevers with peyas (gruels).
6.3.154 | A wise physician should treat fever with [purgatives], except when it arises from alcohol—
specifically in cases of alcoholism, in those habitually addicted to alcohol, during the summer season, or when pitta and kapha are predominant.
6.3.155 | Barley gruel (yavāgū) is not beneficial in cases of upward-moving hemorrhaging (raktapitta) or fever;
in those instances, a satiating drink (tarpaṇa) made from parched grain flour (lājasaktu) should be administered first.

6.3.156 | Then, having consumed the satiation therapy (tarpaṇa) once it is digested, one should eat food combined with fruit juices that alleviate fever, along with honey and sugar, while considering the patient's suitability and strength.
6.3.157 At meal times, one should also provide him with a tooth-cleansing stick (dantadhāvana) along with a thin mung bean soup or the broth of wild game.
6.3.158 | That which is contrary to its taste for the mouth,
and that which is pleasant, produces clarity of the mouth and a longing for food and drink.
6.3.159 | That which, having cleansed itself with the tips of tree branches and having rinsed the mouth repeatedly, bestows an expertise in the various tastes.

6.3.160 | The physician should administer a digestive (pācana) or palliative (śamanīya) decoction (kaṣāya), or have the patient take food with curd, sugarcane juice, wine, and so forth, according to his dietary requirements.
6.3.161 | When six days have passed since the onset of fever, if the patient is fed only light food, the [doshas] become stagnant,
do not undergo digestion, and produce irregular fever (viṣamajvara).
6.3.162 | The doshas bound by a decoction (kaṣāya) due to its astringent quality [should not be used] in acute fever;
however, this does not prohibit the use of a decoction for the purpose of pharmaceutical preparation.
6.3.163 | That which is excessively astringent should be avoided in acute fever;
instead, one should use beneficial soups that are either sour or non-sour, or meat broths from wild animals.
6.3.164 | For ten days one should eat light food for the subsiding of fever;
beyond that, [this applies] when kapha is diminished and vāta-pitta predominate in the fever.
6.3.165 | When the humors (doṣas) have reached maturity, the drinking of clarified butter (sarpiḥ) is like nectar;
even if ten days have not passed since the onset of the disease, it should be administered if one recognizes that kapha is predominant and the patient has not undergone fasting therapy (alaṅghita).

6.3.166 | A physician should not cause him to drink clarified butter; rather, he should treat him with decoctions (kaṣāya). Until lightness [of the body] is achieved, he should give food along with meat broth.
For strength is indeed sufficient for the suppression of the doshas, and it is that which produces strength;
[it is indicated] in a fever characterized by a predominance of vāta and pitta in one overwhelmed by burning sensations and thirst.

6.3.168 | Or, one should conquer a fever that is free from *āma* but characterized by the defects of being either bound or displaced with milk. When the fever does not reach subsidence through these treatments, [then other measures should be employed].
6.3.169 | One whose strength, muscle, and digestive fire are not diminished should pacify that [fever] with purgatives;
however, for one emaciated by fever, neither emesis nor purgation is beneficial.
6.3.170 | However, one may at will remove his impurities with milk or with decoctions;
a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) bestows strength, digestive fire, freedom from fever, joy, and relish for food.
6.3.171 | When administered when the humors (doṣas) have reached maturity, it quickly brings about the removal of pitta,
or kapha-pitta, located in the seat of pitta (pittāśaya).
6.3.172 | Enema (basti) removes the three impurities (malas) situated in the colon (pakvāśaya).
It is indicated for chronic fever, when kapha and pitta have been depleted, and for one with a strong digestive fire.
6.3.173 | One should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) to a patient whose feces are dry and bound,
as well as in cases of heaviness of the head, headache, and obstruction of the sense organs.
6.3.174 | In chronic fever, one should administer head-purgatives (mūrdhavirecana) to stimulate the appetite,
as well as oil massages (abhyaṅga), medicinal pastes (pradeha), affusions (pariṣeka), and immersions (avagāhana).
6.3.175 | Having distinguished between that caused by cold and that caused by heat, the physician should administer [treatment] once the fever has subsided;
by these means, the fever that has moved to the external channels quickly attains pacification.
6.3.176 | Their limbs attain comfort, and their strength and complexion increase;
through the application of fumigations and collyriums, chronic fevers are pacified.
6.3.177 | And for those whose connection with the disease is adventitious and who remain with skin alone [as their only remaining layer],
this sequence of treatment, which destroys fever, has been proclaimed as established.

6.3.182 | One suffering from fever and diarrhea should drink a decoction prepared with *śvadaṃṣṭrā* and *kaṇṭakārī*, which cures fever;

6.3.183 A person should drink the decoction prepared with pṛśniparṇī, balā, bilva, nāgara, utpala, and dhānyaka, along with the drugs of the vidārīgandhādi group, for the purpose of inducing perspiration.
6.3.184 | One suffering from cough, dyspnea, or hiccups, or one afflicted by fever, should drink gruel;

6.3.185 | A patient suffering from fever should drink gruel mixed with clarified butter (sarpiṣmatī) to facilitate the downward movement of the humors (doṣas).

6.3.186 | One should drink a gruel (peyā) prepared with raisins, long pepper root, cavya, emblic myrobalan, ginger, and bilva, in the case of fever accompanied by cutting pain.

6.3.190 | One should know that *karkoṭaka* and *kaṭhilla* are vegetables beneficial for fever. [One should also consume] common quails, grey partridges, antelopes, francolin partridges, and *upacakraka* birds.

6.3.204 | Vatsaka, āragvadha, pāṭhā, ṣaḍgranthā, kaṭurohiṇī,

6.3.258. Now we shall describe the oil known as *Candanādya-taila* (the sandalwood-based oil): [it is prepared from] *candana*, *bhadraśrī*, *kālānusārya*, *kālīyaka*, *padmā*, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, *sārivā*, *madhuka*, *prapauṇḍarīka*, *nāgapuṣpa*, *udīcya*, *nyapodha*, *utpala*, *nalina*, *kumuda*, *saugandhika*, *puṇḍarīka*, *śatapatra*, *bisamṛṇāla*, *śālūka*, *śaivāla*, *śeruka*, *anantā*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *ikṣu*, *darbha*, *śara*, *nala*, the roots of *śāli*, *jambu*, *vetasa*, *vānīra*, *gundrā*, *kakubha*, *asana*, *aśvakarṇa*, *syandana*, *vātapotha*, *śāla*, *tāla*, *dhava*, *tiniśa*, *khadira*, *kadara*, *kadamba*, and the fruit of *kāśmarya*.

R̥jīṣaka, plakṣa, vaṭa, kapītana, udumbara, aśvattha, nyagrodha, dhātakī, dūrvā, itkaṭa, śṛṅgāṭaka, mañjiṣṭhā, jyotiṣmatī, lotus seeds (puṣkarabīja), krauñcādana, badarī, kovidāra, kadalī, saṃvartaka, ariṣṭa, śataparvā, śītakumbhikā, śatāvarī, śrīparṇī, śrāvaṇī, mahāśrāvaṇī, rohiṇī, śītapākī, odanapākī, kālābalā, payasyā, vidārī, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, medā, mahāmedā, madhurasā, ṛṣyaproktā, tṛṇaśūnya, mocarasa, āṭarūṣaka, bakula, kuṭaja, paṭola, nimba, and śālmalī.
One should prepare a decoction of ikṣvāku, kharjūra, mṛdvīkā, priyāla, priyaṅgu, dhanvana, ātmaguptā, madhūka, and other drugs of cooling potency as they are available.
With that decoction, using double the amount of milk and the paste (kalka) of those same drugs, one should cook oil measuring half the quantity of the decoction over a gentle fire.
This oil, through massage, immediately removes burning fever.
One should apply a plaster made from these very same medicinal herbs, finely ground and well-cooled;
and one should employ water boiled with these same herbs and then cooled for the purpose of immersion baths and sprinkling.
Thus ends the oil beginning with sandalwood.
6.3.259 | Sprinkling with honey, fermented gruel, milk, curd, ghee, and water, as well as immersion baths, immediately remove the fever of burning sensation due to their cold touch.
6.3.260 | And there are verses on this point:
[They eat] upon lotus and water-lily petals from the Puṣkara lake that are very cool,
and upon the leaves of plantains, and upon spotless linen cloths.

6.3.265 | Beloved women, who move with graceful, circumambulatory gait, are sprinkled with sandalwood paste and adorned with jewels and pearls; they should console [the king] with supreme objects of desire.

cooling breezes, and the rays of the moon remove the fever of burning heat.

6.3.267 | Now we shall describe the therapeutic procedures, such as massage and others, for those suffering from fever who desire warmth: *aguru*, *kuṣṭha*, *tagara* leaves, *nalada*, *śaileya*, *dhyāmaka*, *hareṇukā*, *sthauṇeyaka*, *kṣemaka*, *elā*, *varaṅga*, *dala*, *purata*, *tamāla* leaves, *bhūtīka*, *rohiṣa*, *sarala*, *śallakī*, *devadāru*, *agnimantha*, *bilva*, *syonāka*, *kāśmarya*, *pāṭalā*, *punarnavā*, *vṛścīra*, *kaṇṭakārī*, *bṛhatī*, *śālaparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *māṣaparṇī*, *mudgaparṇī*, *gokṣuraka*, *eraṇḍa*, *śobhāñjanaka*, *varuṇa*, *arka*, *cirabilva*, *tilvaka*, *śaṭī*, and *puṣkaramūla*.

Aṇḍīra, urubūka, pattūra, akṣība, aśmantaka, śigru, mātuluṅga, pīlu, mūlakaparṇī, tilaparṇī, pīluparṇī, meṣaśṛṅgī, hiṃsrā, dantaśaṭha, airāvataka, bhallātaka, āsphota, kāṇḍīra, ātmaja, ekeṣīkā, karañja, dhānyaka, ajamoda, pṛthvīkā, sumukha, surasa, kuṭheraka, kālamālaka, parṇāsa, kṣavaka, phaṇijjhaka, bhūstṛṇa, śṛṅgavera, pippalī, sarṣapa, aśvagandhā, rāsnā, ruhā, rohiṇī, vacā, balā, atibalā, guḍūcī, śatapuṣpā, śītavallī, nākulī, and gandhanākulī.

One should prepare a decoction of *īṣvetā*, *jyotiṣmatī*, *citrakā*, *adhyuṇḍā*, *amlacāṅgerī*, sesame, *badara*, horse-gram (*kulattha*), black gram (*māṣa*), and other such drugs of hot potency as they may be available; with that decoction and the paste (*kalka*) of those same drugs, one should cook a vessel of oil, adding wine (*surā*), fermented gruel (*sauvīraka*), *tuṣodaka* water, *maireya* liquor, fat (*medaka*), whey (*dadhimanda*), sour gruel (*āranālaka*), and *kaṭvara*.

One should massage the fever patient who desires warmth with that lukewarm oil; thus, the cold fever (śītajvara) is pacified. Furthermore, one should apply a warm poultice (pradeha) made from these same drugs ground finely and mixed with lukewarm water. One should also employ water boiled with these same drugs, used lukewarm for immersion baths (avagāhana) and sprinkling (pariṣeka), for the purpose of pacifying cold fever. This is the Agurvādi-taila. There are also verses on this subject:
The thirteen types of sudation have been demonstrated in the chapter on sudation.
When administered by one who knows the proper measure and timing, it also removes chronic fever.
That hut, that bed, and that covering quickly pacify the cold fever; likewise, thick incense produced from agaru (aloe wood) has the same effect.
6.3.270 | And young women with lovely, well-proportioned limbs, through the heat of their youth,
quickly allay a fever of cold by their embrace.
6.3.271 | Foods and drinks that induce perspiration and those which alleviate vāta and kapha quickly conquer cold fever through the application of their combined properties and potencies.

does not properly cook the rice if it is driven outward by the wind;
6.3.275 | Likewise, when the digestive heat (ūṣman) of men is driven outward from the site of digestion by the humors (doṣas),

6.3.276 | Therefore, for the sake of protecting the digestive fire (*agni-bala*), a regimen beginning with fasting (*laṅghana*) is beneficial;
for within seven days, the impurities (*mala*) residing in the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are indeed digested.

However, this applies especially to one whose *doṣas* have been fully expelled, who has a weak digestive fire, and who eats heavy food at night.

and after having the patient drink a decoction (kaṣāya), one should feed him a meal consisting of meat broth.
6.3.281 | One should employ every therapeutic measure to alleviate chronic fever.

6.3.282 | That which does not reach maturation even in seven days due to mild heat should be treated gradually with the methods previously described, such as fasting and eating small quantities of food.

one should treat with decoctions and other remedies those fevers which are caused by vāta, those born of kapha, and those arising from both kapha and pitta.
6.3.284 | Regarding those [conditions] for which lightening therapy (laṅghana) has been prescribed, it should be applied individually according to each case,
along with emetics, purgatives, and enemas, in their proper sequence.

6.3.285 | A wise physician should treat fevers arising from phlegm, bile, and wind— whether combined in pairs or all three together— by discerning their relative strengths and treating them with corresponding measures.
6.3.286 | One should conquer fevers by means of the aforementioned medicines, taking into account the sequence of the *doṣas*,
either by increasing that which is diminished or by diminishing that which is aggravated.

one should conquer it quickly through bloodletting and the drinking of clarified butter (sarpiḥ).
6.3.289 | For one whose fever is not pacified by plasters that subdue kapha and pitta, nor by nasal drops, gargles, or applications that are cold, hot, unctuous, or dry;

as are those fevers caused by erysipelas (visarpa), trauma (abhighāta), or eruptive boils (visphoṭaka).
6.3.291 | First, in that case, the drinking of clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) is indicated, provided that *kapha* and *pitta* are not predominant;
for when the bodily tissues (*dhātu*) are weakened, a chronic fever (*jīrṇajvara*) persists.
6.3.292 | Therefore, one should treat that [fever] with strengthening and nourishing diets;
one should abandon the general treatment for tertian and quartan fevers.

6.3.293 | For in irregular fever (viṣamajvara), an adventitious factor (āgantuka) is generally the secondary association; [this condition] characterized by a predominance of Vāta should be treated with medicated ghees, enemas, and oil massages (anuvāsana).
6.3.294 | One should pacify irregular fever (viṣamajvara) with unctuous and warm foods and drinks,
as well as by means of purgation with milk processed with clarified butter (sarpiḥ).
6.3.295 | One should conquer fever characterized by a predominance of pitta that is irregular in its onset with bitter and cold [substances],
as well as emesis, digestive stimulants, dry food and drink, and fasting.
6.3.296 | A decoction that is both astringent and hot is recommended for irregular fever (viṣamajvara) when kapha is predominant.
Further formulations that destroy irregular fevers will now be described.
6.3.297 | These should be employed by the wise after distinguishing between their defects and other qualities:
wine with its scum for the purpose of drinking, and the cock for the purpose of food.
6.3.298 | Tittiri and peacock meat should be employed for intermittent fever;
alternatively, one should drink *ṣaṭpala* ghee or administer *abhayā*.
6.3.299 | Or one may take a decoction of triphalā, or the juice of guḍūcī itself,
along with nīlinī, ajagandhā, trivṛt, and kaṭurohiṇī.

6.3.300 | When fever arrives, one who has been prepared with oleation and sudation should drink a large dose of ghee according to the proper method, or alternatively, after drinking it, should induce vomiting again.
6.3.301 | Or, after consuming a large quantity of food and drink, one should vomit it back up again;
or, having drunk a large amount of liquor with food, one should sleep at the onset of the fever.
6.3.302 | One should administer a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) or a sustaining enema (yāpana) in the case of irregular fever (viṣamajvara);
or one should drink the milk of a cat, or its excrement, on that very day.
6.3.303 | A bull [should be fed] with whey (*dadhimaṇḍa*) or wine (*surā*), along with rock salt (*sasaindhava*),
as well as long pepper (*pippalī*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), curd (*dadhi*), buttermilk (*takra*), and clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).
6.3.304 | The administration of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and milk is for intermittent fever; likewise, the consumption of garlic with oil before a meal [is recommended].
6.3.305 | The consumption of fatty substances, hot- potency meats, and [other] animal flesh;
or, alternatively, tiger fat mixed with asafoetida and rock salt used as a nasal drop (nasya).
6.3.306 | Ancient ghee, lion fat likewise, with rock salt;
rock salt, long pepper seeds, rice grains, and realgar.
6.3.307 | Eye-salve ground with oil is recommended for intermittent fever (viṣamajvara).
[The ingredients are] guggulu, nimba leaves, vacā, kuṣṭha, and harītakī.
6.3.308 | Mustard seeds, barley, and clarified butter constitute an incense that destroys fever; likewise, whatever [medicines] serve as smoke-inhalation, nasal drops, or collyrium [are effective].
6.3.309 | Whatever treatment has been prescribed for mental disorders should also be applied in the case of irregular fever (viṣamajvara),
as well as [the use of] gems, medicinal herbs, auspicious objects, and antidotes to poison.
6.3.310 | By wearing amulets and by the use of medicinal herbs, fever shall not arise;
[one should worship] the Lord Soma, together with his attendants, his divine mothers, and his consort.
6.3.311 | Worshipping with self-restraint, one is quickly liberated from irregular fever—
by worshipping Viṣṇu, the thousand-headed, the all-pervading Lord of the moving and unmoving.
6.3.312 | By praising with the Thousand Names, one drives away all fevers—
those caused by Brahmā, the Aśvins, Indra, Agni, and the Himālaya.
6.3.313 | By worshipping the Gaṅgā and the hosts of Maruts with ritual offerings, and by devotion toward one's mother and father as well as by honoring one's teachers, one conquers fevers.
6.3.314 | By celibacy, by austerity, by truthfulness, and by observance of rules;
by the recitation of prayers, by the gift of cows, and by the hearing of the Vedas.
6.3.315 | One is quickly liberated from fever by the sight of the virtuous.
When the fever resides in the rasa (plasma), one should administer emesis and fasting.
6.3.316 | When [the poison] resides in the blood, sprinkling, ointments, and likewise pacifying measures are beneficial;
when it resides in the flesh and fat, purgation along with fasting is recommended.
6.3.317 | Nirūha and anuvāsana enemas should be administered when [the fever] has reached the bones and marrow.
This applies to the fever caused by curses, malevolent spells, or the possession of spirits.
6.3.318 | In that case, all medicinal treatment is held to be dependent on divine intervention;
a fever caused by injury (abhighātajvara) may be cured by the drinking and external application of clarified butter (sarpiḥ).
6.3.319 | Anāha [intestinal obstruction] in those accustomed to wine should be treated with bloodletting, wines, and wholesome meat soups and rice,
along with meals consisting of the essence of *madirā* wine for those accustomed to wine.
6.3.320 | By treating wounds and injuries,
by providing consolation, by the attainment of desired objects, and by the pacification of the bodily wind (vāyu).
6.3.321 | The fevers of desire, grief, and fear are pacified by exhilarating things,
by desirable and pleasing objects, and also by treatments that subdue pitta.
6.3.322 | And by virtuous words, the fever arising from anger is pacified;
the fever of anger is destroyed by desire, and that born of desire is destroyed by anger.
6.3.323 | Furthermore, one who is afflicted by fever suffers when that fever arises from both fear and grief, as he broods over the intensity and the duration of the fever.
6.3.324 | Upon the release from fever, the person moans, vomits, and exerts himself;
panting, discolored, with perspiring limbs, he trembles and repeatedly faints.
6.3.325 | He talks incoherently, his entire body becomes hot and yet his limbs also become cold;
unconscious and afflicted by the force of the fever, he looks as if he were filled with rage.
6.3.326 | A wise physician should recognize these signs at the time of fever's release: the discharge of foul-smelling, liquid feces with forceful urgency.

6.3.327 | Generally, for one with many complications, fever that is recent and severe is very dreadful; however, if it is released through the ripening of the doshas by means of proper treatment, it may leave the patient.

6.3.328 | For those whose fevers persist for a long time, if they gradually subside after having manifested their force due to the influence of the *doṣas*, their release from the fever is not severe.
6.3.329 | One should recognize a person free from fever as being devoid of fatigue and distress, without pain, with pure senses, and endowed with natural vitality.

6.3.330 | One who has a fever, or one who has recently been freed from a fever, should avoid foods and drinks that cause burning sensations, those that are heavy, those that are unwholesome, and those that are incompatible.
6.3.331 | Sexual intercourse, excessive physical exertion, bathing, and overeating—
as well as fever— subside, and once subsided, they do not recur.
6.3.332 | One who has been freed from fever should not engage in physical exertion, sexual intercourse, bathing, or walking about until he has regained his strength.
6.3.333 | If a person who has been freed from fever indulges in that which is to be avoided before his strength has fully returned, the fever will return to him again.
6.3.334 | And when faults among those who are ill-disposed toward him cease,
his life-span extends once again even with only a slight lapse in conduct.
6.3.335 | Having returned, he destroys in a very short time that [enemy] who has been long afflicted, weakened, and deprived of his splendor.
6.3.336. Or else, even when the impurities reach their full maturation within the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) in due order, they do not produce fever; nevertheless, they still cause harm.
6.3.337 | They produce dejection, swelling, lassitude, pallor, loss of appetite for food,
itching, urticaria, and pustules, and they make the digestive fire weak.
6.3.338 | Likewise, other diseases that have recurred also turn back by the non-suppression of the humors, even through slight unwholesome acts in men.

6.3.339 | Even when the fever has subsided, one should eliminate the remaining morbid humors (doṣas) according to the patient's condition, strength, and vital capacity, or bring them to pacification through medicinal applications.
6.3.340 | Mild purificatory treatments for cleansing, palliative enemas, and light soups as well as meat broths from the flesh of wild animals are beneficial.
6.3.341 | Anointing with oil, dry massage, bathing, fumigation, and the application of collyrium are beneficial, as are bitter medicated ghees, in the case of recurrent fever.
6.3.342 | When [the patient] has returned [to health] after eating heavy, obstructive, or unwholesome foods,
the regimen of lightening therapy, warm treatments, and so forth should be carried out as previously described.
6.3.343 | Kirātatiktaka, tiktā, musta, parpaṭaka, and amṛtā,
when drunk habitually, destroy recurring fever (punarāvartaka-jvara).
6.3.344 | In each respective stage, the wise physician,
observing the sequence of treatments for fever, should administer the appropriate therapy.
6.3.345 | Fever is the king of diseases, the end-maker of all beings, and is terrible;
therefore, the physician should especially strive for its pacification.

6.3.346 | Regarding this, there is a verse: Thus has the treatment of fever been explained by Ātreya to Agniveśa, in due order and in response to his questions, out of a desire for the welfare of living beings.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fever," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Four:
6.4.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of hemoptysis (rakta-pitta).
6.4.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.4.3 | Having prostrated before Punarvasu, who dwells with a conquered self at Pañcagaṅgā and possesses the luster of fire, Agniveśa, free from delusion, spoke.
6.4.4 | O Blessed One, the etiology of rakta-pitta has been stated along with its symptoms.
O Teacher, you should now speak that which remains to be said regarding it.
6.4.5 | The Teacher said: One who understands causes and symptoms should treat *raktapitta* quickly, for it is a great disease of great intensity, acting as swiftly as fire.
6.4.6 | Heat, pungent, sour, bitter, and salty [tastes],
as well as exposure to the sun and the burning sensation caused by food, have been previously indicated as its causes.
6.4.7 | By those causes, the aggravated *pitta* reaches the blood;
having reached it, because of their common origin, it increases and vitiates it.
6.4.8 | By its heat, the liquid constituent is secreted from each and every tissue;
through that process of perspiration, it attains further growth.
6.4.9 | Because of its association with blood, its similarity to blood in color and smell,
the wise have designated this pitta as "raktapitta" (blood-bile).
6.4.10 | It exists presiding over both the spleen and the liver;
for the blood-carrying channels are indeed rooted in those two for embodied beings.
6.4.11 | Thick, pale, unctuous, and slimy, it is associated with phlegm;
whereas that which is dark-red, frothy, thin, and dry is associated with wind (vāta).
6.4.12 | Rakta-pitta caused by pitta is tawny, black, resembling cow's urine,
like the smoke of a house-fire, or resembles collyrium.
6.4.13 | That which possesses combined symptoms is the *saṃsarga* type; from the combination [of all three], it is the *sānnipātika* type.
That which follows a single *doṣa* is curable (*sādhya*); that which involves two *doṣas* is said to be palliable (*yāpya*).
6.4.14 | That which arises from all three doṣas is incurable, as is that which occurs in one with weak digestion,
excessive diarrhea, a body emaciated by diseases, the elderly, or one who does not eat.
6.4.15 | The upward and downward courses of rakta-pitta have been shown;
the upward course has seven openings, while the downward course has two.
6.4.16 | There are seven openings in the head and two below; [disease] moving upward is curable, while that moving downward is palliable.
However, when it reaches both pathways, it becomes incurable.
6.4.17 | But when it proceeds from all the apertures and even from the pores of the skin,
they say that its course is dark and leads to the final destination.
6.4.18 | That which flows excessively through both channels,
equal to the smell of a corpse, and is exceedingly red and black;
6.4.19 | That which is combined with both phlegm and wind, which clings to the throat,
and which is further afflicted by all the aforementioned complications;
6.4.20 | That [cough] which is afflicted by yellow, blue, green, or copper-colored tints,
occurring in one who is emaciated and coughing, does not succeed.
6.4.21 | That pitta and blood which follow two doshas, or which, having subsided, becomes aggravated again,
or which moves from one channel to another, is palliable (yāpya).

6.4.22 | Bleeding disorder (raktapitta) that follows a single channel, is present in a strong person, is not excessively rapid, has recently arisen, occurs at a favorable time, and is free from complications is curable.
6.4.23 | Unctuous and hot, as well as hot and dry, are the causes of blood-bile (raktapitta).
For that which moves downward, the latter [causes] generally predominate; for that which moves upward, however, the former [causes] should prevail.
6.4.24 | Moving upward, it is associated with phlegm; moving downward, it is followed by wind. Thus, having two paths, it is bound by both phlegm and wind.
6.4.25 | When blood-bile (raktapitta) occurs in one whose strength and flesh are not diminished, even while eating,
that [condition] is provoked by the vitiated doshas and does not require hemostatic treatment at the outset.
6.4.26 | It [treats] constriction of the throat, putrid nose, fainting, loss of appetite, fever,
abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, flatulence, vitiligo, and difficulty in urination.
6.4.27 | It causes skin diseases, hemorrhoids, erysipelas, loss of complexion, fistula-in-ano,
and impairment of the intellect and the senses, if it is not properly treated from the very beginning.
6.4.28 | Therefore, one who desires success and examines the strength and the defects of the [doshas] should first disregard raktapitta when it has become excessively aggravated by a strong [cause].
6.4.29 | For generally, in embodied beings, when the āma-doṣa is provoked, pitta and blood increase; therefore, that [condition] should first be treated with fasting (laṅghana).
6.4.30 | Having carefully examined the two pathways, the persistence of the doshas, and the etiological factors,
one should administer either fasting or nourishing therapy in cases such as raktapitta.
6.4.31 | One should give water boiled with *hrīvera*, sandalwood, *uśīra*, *musta*, and *parpaṭaka*,
or simply water that has been boiled and then cooled, to one who is thirsty.

6.4.32 | One who knows the time, suitability, and complications, and understands the constitution and its modifications, should first administer a satiating drink (tarpaṇa) when the disorder moves upward, and a thin gruel (peyā) when it moves downward.
6.4.33 | Water boiled with dates, grapes, madhūka, and parūṣaka,
and then cooled, should be administered with sugar for the purpose of satiation.
6.4.34 | One should administer a satiating drink (tarpaṇa) consisting of parched grain flour mixed with ghee and honey;
when drunk at the proper time, it dispels upward-moving hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta).
6.4.35 | For one with weak digestion who is accustomed to sour tastes, the physician should prepare that [milk] even with sour ingredients;
for the sake of acidity, he should cause it to be fermented with pomegranate and āmalaka fruits.
6.4.36 | Śāli, ṣaṣṭika, nīvāra, koradūṣa, praśāntikā, śyāmāka,
and priyaṅgu are the foods for those suffering from raktapitta.
6.4.37 | Mudga, masūra, caṇaka, along with makuṣṭha and the seeds of āḍhakī,
are recommended when prepared as soups or broths for those suffering from raktapitta.
6.4.38 | The tips of the paṭola, nimba, and vetra, the sprouts of plakṣa and vetasa,
the vegetable kirātatiktaka, gaṇḍīra, and kaṭhillaka.
6.4.39 | The flowers of the *kovidāra*, the *kāśmarya*, and the *śālmali*,
as well as whatever other vegetables there may be that alleviate *rakta-pitta*, are used in the preparation of food and drink.
6.4.40 | For those accustomed to vegetables, vegetables intended for that purpose are recommended for those suffering from *rakta-pitta* (hemoptysis/blood-bile),
whether they are steamed, fried in ghee, or cooked like a soup.
6.4.41 | Pigeons, doves, quails, red-eyed partridges,
hares, francolins, antelopes, deer, and black-tailed deer.

6.4.42 | One should know those meat juices (rasa) to be beneficial in cases of raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders); one should administer them, either slightly sour or non-sour, fried in ghee, and containing śaraka.
6.4.43 | When Kapha is the secondary humor, one should administer vegetable soups; when Vata is the secondary humor, one should give meat broths.
Hereafter, the preparation of gruels for Raktapitta will be described.

6.4.44 | The filaments of the lotus and water-lily, pṛśniparṇī, and priyaṅgukā should be boiled in water; a gruel prepared with that decoction is suitable for those suffering from raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
6.4.45 | [One should prepare a decoction] of sandalwood, uśīra, and lodhra with ginger;
and likewise [a decoction] of kirātatikta, uśīra, and musta.
6.4.46 | Or it may be boiled in the decoction of dhātakī, dhanvayāsa, ambu, and bilva;
or in the decoction of masūra and pṛśniparṇī; or else in the juice of sthirā and mudga.
6.4.47 | Or they may be prepared as a liquid extract (rasa) with *hareṇukā* and ghee, or with the juice of *balā*,
or separately in the meat-juice of the pigeon (*pārāvata*) and other such birds.
6.4.48 | Thus have been described the cooling gruels (yavāgū), which destroy raktapitta, when prepared with honey and sugar; this same method of preparation should also be applied to meat broths.
6.4.49 | Rabbit meat with *sāstuka* is recommended for those suffering from *raktapitta* accompanied by constipation;
for those with a predominance of *vāta*, the meat of the *nīttiri* bird boiled in the juice of *udumbara* is beneficial.

6.4.50 | A peacock is beneficial in a decoction of *plakṣa*, and a cock is beneficial in that of *nyagrodha*. In the meat broth of *bilva*, *utpala*, and other such plants, the quail (*vartaka*) and the crane (*krakara*) are wholesome.
6.4.51 | A decoction of fruits prepared with bitter herbs (*tiktaka*) cures thirst,
as does fruit-water prepared with the *vidārigandhādi* group of drugs, or simply boiled and then cooled.
6.4.52 | Having ascertained the two humors (doṣas), the secondary forces (anubalas), and the strength of the food,
one should give water to the thirsty person either after the discharge [of feces] or even in small amounts.
6.4.53 | Whatever has been described as the cause of *rakta-pitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) should not be indulged in by those suffering from *rakta-pitta* who desire life and health.
6.4.54 | Thus has been described the diet and drink for the alleviation of *rakta-pitta* in due order;
now shall be explained the treatment for those with abundant *doṣas* and those who are strong.

6.4.55 | When a strong person whose strength and flesh are not diminished suffers from a severe case of *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) arising from over-nutrition (*saṃtarpaṇa*), [it should be treated as follows].
6.4.56 | At the proper time, for one who is fit for purification,
that [dosha] should be removed without causing complications by means of purgation for the upper part and emesis for the lower part.
6.4.57 | A wise person [should administer] trivṛt, abhayā, or the fruits of āragvadha;
or the root of trāyamāṇā or gavākṣī, or āmalaka fruits.
6.4.58 | One should administer a purgative containing abundant honey and sugar;
among these, meat broth is especially recommended for cases of raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
6.4.59 | A churned drink (mantha) mixed with Madana fruit, honey, and sugar,
or water with sugar, or even the juice of sugarcane itself, causes emesis.
6.4.60 | The fruit of vatsaka, musta, madana, madhuka,
and honey are said to be the best emetic for downward-moving *raktapitta*.
6.4.61 | When [the poison] moves upward, the therapeutic sequence beginning with *tarpaṇa* (satiating drinks) is beneficial for one whose bowels are purified;
when it moves downward, the sequence beginning with *yavāgū* (gruel) is beneficial, provided that the *vāta* (wind humor) is not powerful.
6.4.62 | [One should treat] a woman whose strength and flesh are wasted away, who is emaciated by the burden of grief or by travel,
who is scorched by fire or the sun, or who is weakened by other diseases.
6.4.63 | One should observe that a patient suffering from raktapitta who is pregnant, elderly, or a child, or who eats dry, scanty, or measured food, or who is unfit for emesis or purgation.
6.4.64 | For the pacification of that [disease], treatment with drying (śoṣa) methods—either with or without adjuncts—is recommended for raktapitta; that shall now be explained in detail.
6.4.65 | A decoction of *aṭarūṣaka*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *pathyā*,
mixed with sugar and honey, destroys asthma, cough, and *raktapitta*.
6.4.66 | Having dissolved priyaṅgu, clay, añjana,
lodhra, and honey in a decoction of aṭarūṣaka, one should drink it to alleviate raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
6.4.67 | One should drink padmaka, the filaments of the lotus, dūrvā grass, vāstūka, utpala, nāgapuṣpa, and lodhra according to that same procedure.
6.4.68 | Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, and honey [should be applied] in the juice of horse dung;
or the roots of yavāsa and bhṛṅgaraja in the juice of cow dung.
6.4.69 | Having prepared it, this destroyer of rakta-pitta should be drunk with rice-water;
or one should lick the juice of horse dung mixed with honey and ghee.
6.4.70 | A person suffering from *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) should lick the powdered flowers of *khadira*, *priyaṅgu*, *kovidāra*, and *śālmali* with honey.
6.4.71 | One should lick the powders of śṛṅgāṭaka, parched grain (lāja), musta, dates (kharjūra),
and the filaments of the lotus (padmakeśara) with honey.
6.4.72 | One should have those born in arid lands lick blood with honey; for deer and birds, one should have them lick the dung of a pigeon mixed with honey when the blood is clotted.
6.4.73 | Uśīra, kālīyaka, loghra, padmaka, priyaṅgu, kaṭphala, śaṅkha, and gairika—
each taken in a portion equal to that of sandalwood, mixed with sugar and soaked in rice-washing water.

6.4.74 | When drunk, kirātatikta, kramuka, musta, prapauṇḍarīka, and the two types of lotus (kamala and utpala) immediately pacify blood disorders, pitta, tamaka fever, thirst, and burning sensations.
6.4.75 | The roots of hrībera, the leaves of paṭola, durālabhā, parpaṭaka, and mṛṇāla;
the bark of dhanañjaya, udumbara, vetasa, nyagrodha, śāleya, and yavāsaka.
6.4.76 | Tugālatā, vetasa, taṇḍulīya, sāriva, mocarasa,
and samaṅgā— each of these, when combined with candana according to that same procedure, are beneficial in that case.

6.4.77 | Whether administered at night, or prepared with their own juices, or made into a paste, or crushed, or boiled— these formulations, whether combined as a group or used individually, pacify blood along with bile.
6.4.78 | Mudga beans, along with parched grain, barley, black gram, ushira root, musta grass, and sandalwood— this decoction,
soaked overnight in water, pacifies aggravated blood and bile.

6.4.79 | By drinking water containing vaidūrya, pearl, gem, and red ochre; or water with clay, conch-shell, gold, and *āmalaka*; or honey-water and sugarcane juice, the blood-bile (*raktapitta*) disorder comes to subside.
6.4.80 | The clear supernatant liquid obtained from boiled *uśīra*, *padma*, *utpala*, *candana*, and baked clay,
mixed with sugar and honey and well-chilled, should be administered to alleviate excessive hemorrhaging.
6.4.81 | Water boiled with priyaṅgu, candana, lodhra, sārivā, madhūka, mustā, abhayā, dhātakī, and mṛdvīkā,
together with yaṣṭimadhu-water and sugar, is the supreme remedy for destroying [excessive] blood.

6.4.82 | When the fire is kindled by various prescribed applications of astringents (kaṣāya) and the phlegm (śleṣman) has been conquered, if the blood-bile (raktapitta) does not subside, then wind (anila) must be present; in that case, [treatment] for it should be administered.
6.4.83 | Goat’s milk is the best for administration;
or cow’s milk boiled with five parts water, mixed with sugar and honey, or boiled with the drugs of the Vidārigandhādi group.

6.4.84 | Milk boiled with grapes, or boiled with ginger, or boiled with *balā*, or boiled with *gokṣura*, should be administered along with *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and ghee; or milk boiled with sugar should be used.
6.4.85 | Milk boiled with śatāvarī and gokṣuraka, or likewise milk boiled with the parṇinīs,
quickly destroys blood, especially that which flows painfully from the urinary tract.
6.4.86 | Milk prepared with *mocarasa* is considered especially effective for treating seminal discharge (*viṭpathasaṃpravṛtta*).
Alternatively, it may be prepared with *vaṭāvaroha* (fig-tree roots) or *vaṭaśuṅga* (fig-tree buds), or with *hrīvera*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and *nāgara*.
6.4.87 | Having first drunk decoctions combined with milk, or having eaten *śāli* rice with milk afterwards, one should consume it;
or else, in cases of excessive discharge (*atisrava*), one should drink ghee cooked with these same decoction-formulations.

6.4.88 | Having prepared a decoction of vāsā together with its branches and roots, and having added its flowers and a paste [of its roots], one should cook that ghee; when taken with honey, it quickly destroys [excessive] blood.
Thus ends the Vāsā-ghṛta (6.4.89). One should lick ghee prepared with the fresh juice of *palāśa* shoots and its own paste, mixed with honey as a liquid;
likewise, ghee prepared with the paste of *vatsaka*, or similarly prepared with *samaṅgā*, *utpala*, and *lodhra*.
6.4.90 | This same procedure should be applied to trāyamāṇā, as well as to udumbara and paṭola leaves.
All types of ghee that destroy pitta-fever are recommended for raktapitta.
6.4.91 | Oil massages, medicinal applications, sprinklings, affusions, immersions, beds, and chambers;
cooling regimens and the administration of enemas—these are prescribed as the foremost means for the pacification of Pitta-type fever.
6.4.92 | In cases of raktapitta (hemoptysis or hematemesis), one should administer [these remedies] in their entirety, having first carefully considered the time and the dosage;
for those ghee-confections (sarpirguḍas) which are beneficial for chest wounds (kṣata) also pacify raktapitta immediately.
6.4.93 | This application is indicated when blood, associated with phlegm and bile, has become thickened and obstructed in the throat;
it consists of honey, clarified butter, alkali, and *utpala-nālaja* (lotus-stalk ash), administered according to the proper method.
6.4.94 | Likewise, the alkalis of lotus stalks, lotuses, blue lilies, filaments, as well as of palāśa,
priyaṅgu, madhūka, and aśana, should be employed according to that same procedure.
6.4.95 | A wise physician should cook ghee with four times the amount of milk, having ground together śatāvarī, dāḍima, tintiḍīka, kākolī, medā, madhuka, vidārī, and the root of bījapūraka.
6.4.96 | This ghee cures cough, fever, abdominal distension, constipation, colic, and that [condition known as] raktapitta.
Furthermore, ghee prepared with either the two or the five *pañcamūla* groups performs the same purpose.

Thus ends the *Śatāvaryādi-ghṛta* (6.4.97). The decoction formulations taught here should also be employed by the physician as nasal drops (*avapīḍa*). When the blood flowing from the nose has been drunk and the corrupted humors have been expelled, [the treatment is successful].
6.4.98 | When blood is vitiated, if an avapīḍa bandage is applied, there result malignant coryza and disorders of the head;
the blood becomes purulent, there is a corpse-like odor, loss of the sense of smell, and the presence of harmful worms.

6.4.99 | Blue lotus, combined with red ochre, conch-shell, sandalwood, and white sugar-water, should be used as nasal drops (nasya); likewise, the juice of mango stones, along with *samaṅgā*, *dhātakī*, *mocarasa*, and *lodhra*.
6.4.100 | Nasal therapy (nasya) with grape juice, sugarcane juice, milk, or the fresh juice of dūrvā grass;
likewise, the roots of yavāsa, the root of onion, and water from pomegranate flowers [are used for nasal therapy].
6.4.101 | Priyāla oil, madhuka, and milk;
or ghee prepared from buffalo or goat's milk with mango stones and the like, along with *sārivā*, lotus, and water-lily, should be used as a nasal medication (*nasya*) with milk.
6.4.102 | Bhadraśrī, red sandalwood, prapauṇḍarīka, lotus, and water-lily;
uśīra, vānīra, water, lotus-stalk, sahasravīryā, madhuka, and payasyā.
6.4.103 | The roots of śāli rice and ikṣu sugarcane; the roots of yavāsa, guṇḍrā, nalas, kuśa, and kāśa grasses;
kucandana, śaivala, anantā, kālānusāryā, the root of tṛṇa grass, and ṛddhi.
6.4.104 | The roots and flowers of aquatic plants, as well as the mud from lotus ponds;
Udumbara, Aśvattha, Madhūka, and Lodhra—these are decoction-yielding trees, all of which are cooling.

6.4.105 | When desiring the pacification of blood and bile, the physician should employ the *bhadraśrī* group of drugs in preparations for ointments, as well as in sprinkling treatments, immersions, and the successful processing of clarified butter and oil.
6.4.106 | A fountain-house, an underground chamber, a very cool forest, and a grove cooled by water and breeze;
the touch of vessels made of cat’s-eye, pearl, and gem, and the coolness of water during the heat.
6.4.107 | Leaves and flowers of water-born plants, linen which is cool, and plantain leaves,
as well as the petals of lotuses and water-lilies, are recommended for covering beds and seats.

6.4.108 | During the heat, the touch of beloved and excellent women anointed with priyaṅgu and sandalwood paste is recommended; likewise, cool breezes from fans made of lotus and water-lily petals, moistened with water, are praised.
6.4.109 | All stories concerning rivers, lakes, the Himalayas, mountain caves, moonrises, and lotus ponds— being both agreeable to the mind and cooling— pacify Pitta when it is associated with blood.
6.4.110 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
[The author has described] the cause, the increase, the nomenclature, the location, and the specific signs of each vitiated humor;
as well as the two pathways, the curable, the incurable, the manageable, and the course of treatment.
6.4.111 | Regarding drinks, food, and those things that are desirable as well as those to be avoided, and regarding purification and pacification,
the Teacher has duly explained [these] in the treatment of *raktapitta*.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Raktapitta," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Five:
6.5.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of Gulma.
6.5.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.5.3 | Punarvasu, the refuge of all living beings like a father, the lord of the past and the future,
and the most excellent among those who speak, has proclaimed this proven medical treatment for the purpose of destroying abdominal tumors (gulma).
6.5.4 | Or from excessive discharge of feces, phlegm, or bile; or from being oppressed by those very humors when they have increased;
or by the upward-moving urges being obstructed and driven downward; or by external injuries or excessive pressure.
6.5.5 | By the excessive consumption of dry foods and drinks, or by grief, or by improper medical treatments,
or by irregular and excessive physical activities, the Vāyu becomes aggravated within the digestive tract (koṣṭha).

6.5.6 | That vitiated wind, having agitated both phlegm and bile and obstructed their pathways with them, causes pain in the heart, navel, flanks, abdomen, and bladder; furthermore, it does not move because its path is blocked.

6.5.7 | Located either in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) or in the receptacle of bile and phlegm (pittakaphāśaya), whether independent or dependent on another [tissue], it is called a gulma because it is palpable as a distinct mass; it receives its name according to the specific doṣa involved.
6.5.8 | There are five locations for gulma: in the bladder, the navel, the heart, or the two sides.
I shall now describe its origin from the five [doshas], as well as its symptoms and treatment.
6.5.9 | Dry food and drink, irregular or excessive physical exertion, suppression of natural urges,
grief, injury, excessive loss of blood, and fasting are the causes of *vāta-gulma*.
6.5.10 | That which causes variation in location, shape, and pain; obstruction of feces and flatus; dryness of the throat and mouth;
a dark-red discoloration; a cold fever; and pain in the heart, abdomen, sides, shoulders, and head; |||

6.5.11 | That gulma which increases its provocation excessively when [the food] is digested, and attains mildness after eating, arises from Vata; moreover, in that case, dry, astringent, bitter, and pungent substances do not provide relief.
6.5.12 | Bitter, sour, sharp, hot, burning, and dry substances; anger, excessive wine, exposure to the sun and fire;
internal undigested matter (āma), injury, and vitiated blood—these are declared to be the causes of Pitta-type abdominal tumor (paittika gulma).
6.5.13 | Fever, thirst, discoloration of the face and limbs, severe pain during digestion,
perspiration, a burning sensation, and a tumor that resembles an ulcer and is intolerant to touch— these are the symptoms of a pitta-type gulma.

6.5.14 | Cold, heavy, unctuous, and sedentary behavior, as well as over-satiation and sleeping during the day, are the causes of a gulma arising from kapha; indeed, all these are prescribed as the causes for that which arises from the accumulation [of all three doshas].
6.5.15 | Stiffness, cold fever, lassitude of the limbs, nausea, cough, loss of appetite,
heaviness, coldness, mild pain, and hardness and elevation— these are the symptoms of a gulma of kapha origin.
6.5.16 | Having observed the specific causes and signs in a gulma born of two doṣas, as well as the relative strength and weakness of those doṣas,
one should designate the other three types of gulmas characterized by mixed symptoms for the purpose of determining the appropriate medicinal treatment.

6.5.17 | One should designate as incurable a gulma born of the three doṣas that is characterized by great pain, pervaded by burning sensations, firm and elevated like a stone, quickly suppurating, and dreadful; it robs the mind, the body, and the strength of the digestive fire.
6.5.18 | Due to irregular menstruation, lack of nourishment, fear, emaciation,
suppression of natural urges, and disorders of the womb caused by astringent or scraping treatments, a blood-born gulma (abdominal tumor) arises in a woman.

6.5.19 | That which throbs as a solid mass, not with the limbs, after a long time, accompanied by pain and exhibiting signs identical to those of pregnancy, is a blood-born (raudhira) gulma occurring only in women; it is to be treated once the tenth month has passed.
6.5.20 | Thus, the proven sequence of procedures for destroying gulma in those suffering from it has been established. Hereafter, I shall describe the formulations that eliminate gulma.

6.5.21 | One should first treat with unctuous substances a gulma born of dryness and physical exercise, which is of the vāta type, characterized by intense pain, and associated with the obstruction of feces and flatus.

6.5.22 | After the physician has rendered the patient unctuous with foods, ointments, drinks, non-unctuous enemas, and unctuous enemas, sudation should be administered for the pacification of the gulma.
6.5.23 | Having softened the channels, conquered the aggravated wind,
and broken the obstruction, sudation administered to one who has been lubricated removes the gulma.
