6.5.24 | The internal administration of unctuous substances (sneha-pāna) is beneficial for gulma, especially when it is located above the navel; enemas (basti) are indicated when it has reached the colon (pakvāśaya); and both are recommended when it resides in the abdomen (jaṭhara).
6.5.25 | When the fire is kindled, in cases of vātika gulma, and in the obstruction of flatus and feces,
one should administer nourishing foods and drinks that are unctuous and hot.
6.5.26 | Repeated intake of medicated fats, as well as non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) followed by unctuous enemas (anuvāsana),
should be employed in cases of vāta-gulma by one who protects against the provocation of kapha and pitta.

6.5.27 | If, when the wind (vāta) has been mostly conquered and treatment is being administered, the phlegm (kapha), the bile (pitta), or even the blood (śoṇita) becomes aggravated, [one must act accordingly].
6.5.28 | In that case, the physician’s treatment should be directed toward whichever humor (doṣa) is most aggravated,
while protecting the wind (māruta) at the beginning, the end, and in the middle.
6.5.29 | If, in a case of vātagulma, the increased kapha suppresses the digestive fire and causes anorexia,
nausea, heaviness, and drowsiness, one should treat it with emesis (ullikheta).
6.5.30 | In cases of colic, distension, and constipation, as well as in abdominal tumors (gulma) where vāta and kapha are predominant,
suppositories, pills, and powders that alleviate kapha and vāta are beneficial.
6.5.31 | If pitta is aggravated or if there is a burning sensation in one suffering from vāta-gulma,
he should be purged with unctuous and carminative (ānulomika) substances.
6.5.32 | If a gulma caused by vāta and the other [doshas] does not subside despite being properly treated by a physician, it is pacified by the depletion of blood.
6.5.33 | When a pitta-type gulma arises from unctuous and hot factors, purgation is beneficial;
however, when it is produced by dry and hot factors, clarified butter (ghṛta) is the supreme remedy for its pacification.
6.5.34 | Having ascertained that there is pitta or a pitta-gulma (pitta-type abdominal tumor) located in the colon (pakvāśaya),
one who knows the proper timing should expel it immediately with milk enemas containing bitter herbs.

6.5.35 | Or the physician, considering the strength of the digestive fire, should administer a purgative with milk that is pleasantly warm and mixed with bitter substances, or with *sarpiṣ* (clarified butter) or *tailvaka* oil.
6.5.36 | In cases of gulma accompanied by thirst, fever, burning sensations, colic, perspiration, weak digestion, and loss of appetite,
one should indeed perform bloodletting.
6.5.37 | When their roots are severed, the *gulmas* burn away and go to destruction;
for the blood becomes acidified, and when that [acidification] is absent, there is no pain.
6.5.38 | Once the morbid humors have been removed, the patient has become emaciated, has been nourished with the juices of wild animals,
and has regained his strength though some pain remains, one should again administer medicated ghee.
6.5.39 | If a gulma should undergo suppuration due to the excessive increase of blood and pitta, or because no other treatment has been effective,
then surgical intervention (śastra) is the physician's remedy in that case.
6.5.40 | A Gulma that is heavy, firm in consistency, situated deep within the flesh,
not discolored, and stable is said to be unripe (unmatured).

6.5.41 | One should recognize that gulma is undergoing internal burning (vidāha) by means of burning sensations, pain, distress, agitation, loss of sleep, restlessness, and fever; such a case should be treated with poultices (upanāhana).
6.5.42 | When the gulma is characterized by burning sensations, is elevated and protruding on the outside,
dark-brown with reddish margins, and feels like a bladder upon touch;
6.5.43 | When the mass is pressed, it rises up and becomes rigid; when one lies down, the pain is felt on that very side due to the pressure on its flank;
and when it is localized right there with acute pain, one should diagnose the gulma as being fully matured (suppurated).
6.5.44 | In that regard, the authority for the performance of procedures belongs to the followers of Dhanvantari—
the physicians who have completed their training— in the matters of incision, purification, and healing.
6.5.45 | This is also the characteristic of the internal portion while it is being cooked:
distension of the heart and chest when [the fetus] is situated within, and its emergence through the sides.
6.5.46 | Once matured, the dosha, having moistened the channels, moves either upwards or downwards;
one should allow that self-initiated dosha to pass by means of a wholesome diet.
6.5.47 | For ten or twelve days, the physician should guard against complications;
beyond that period, the beneficial drinking of clarified butter along with purificatory measures [is prescribed].

6.5.48 | For a pure [dosha], medicated ghee with bitter herbs and honey is desired for administration when a gulma caused by kapha has arisen, provided it is treated with cold, heavy, and unctuous substances.
6.5.49 | For one whose digestive fire is weak and whose body is small, one should first administer fasting (laṅghana).
A weak digestive fire, dullness of sensation, and heaviness with stiffness of the abdominal cavity [are the signs].
6.5.50 | He whose vomiting is accompanied by distress and who suffers from abdominal tumors (gulma) is a candidate for emesis;
he should be treated with warm measures after having undergone emesis and fasting.
6.5.51 | And a dietary regimen combined with pungent and bitter medicinal herbs should be employed for a hard,
elevated gulma accompanied by abdominal distension and constipation.
6.5.52 | Having first observed [the patient], the physician should cause them to sweat by appropriate means, and once they have sweated, he should dissolve [the obstruction].
When fasting, emesis, and sudation have been performed, and the digestive fire has been kindled, [one may proceed with purgation].
6.5.53 | A patient suffering from *kapha*-type abdominal tumor (*gulma*) should drink ghee mixed with alkali and pungent substances at the appropriate time;
once it is known that the *kapha*-tumor has been displaced from its site, one should treat it with purgatives.

6.5.54 | Or, when the digestive fire is weak and the wind is obstructed, one should administer purificatory enemas (basti) prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla) along with unctuous substances, after ascertaining that the internal receptacle (āśaya) is unctuous.
6.5.55 | Pills, powders, and decoctions should be administered to those suffering from kaphaja gulma that is deeply rooted,
extensive, hard, immobile, and heavy.
6.5.56 | One should conquer a gulma caused by kapha with alkaline preparations, fermented liquors (ariṣṭas), and thermal cautery (agnikarma),
having understood the combination of the doshas, the patient's constitution, the type of gulma, and the season, when kapha is predominant.
6.5.57 | One who knows the strength of the patient and the dosage of the defect should administer alkali (kṣāra) for a tumor (gulma),
either every other day, every two days, or after resting for three days.
6.5.58 | Expert in the increase and reduction of the body's strength and humors,
[he prescribes] sweet and unctuous phlegm for one who consumes meat, milk, and ghee.
6.5.59 | Having repeatedly cut [the hemorrhoids] from their root, the alkali (kṣāra), due to its corrosive nature, causes them to fall away downward;
this is for those with weak digestive fire, loss of appetite, and for those who eat food that is wholesome and mixed with fat after consuming wine.
6.5.60 | For the purpose of purifying the channels of those with kapha-type gulma, emetic and purgative drugs (ariṣṭas) should be administered,
along with fasting, emesis, sudation, the internal consumption of ghee, and purgation.
6.5.61 | Even with enemas, pills, powders, alkalis, and fermented liquors (ariṣṭas),
a gulma of kapha origin does not subside because it has become firmly established.
6.5.62 | When blood has been removed, cauterization is beneficial for one suffering from delirium due to arrows and other such conditions;
for fire, by virtue of its heat and sharpness, pacifies both phlegm and wind in a gulma.
6.5.63 | From the pacification of those two and from the [pacification of] ama, the formation of the gulma is brought to an end;
regarding the burning sensation, here too lies the strength of the physicians who follow the school of Dhanvantari.

6.5.64 | The strength of physicians who are experts in the science of alkali (kṣāra) lies in the application of alkali. When the doshas are mixed, this very same sequence of treatment is to be applied in a combined manner.
6.5.65 | Hereafter, I shall describe proven formulations for the eradication of gulma (abdominal tumors/lumps),
prepared with trikaṭu, triphalā, dhānyaka, viḍaṅga, cavya, and citraka.
6.5.66 | Ghee prepared with these [three pungents] as a paste, along with milk, cures vātagulma.
This is the Tryūṣaṇādi ghee.
These same substances shall serve as the paste, and the decoction shall be that of the Pañcamūla.
6.5.67 | Or even the ghee prepared with the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūla) is supreme for curing gulma.
Thus ends another formulation, the Tryūṣaṇādi-ghṛta.
(Alternatively, one may drink the six-pala measure of ghee that was prescribed for rājayakṣman.)
6.5.68 | Ghee prepared with clear wine for the sake of milk, or with sour pomegranate juice,
or with whey, should be used to cure wind-induced abdominal tumors (māruta-gulma).
6.5.69 | With asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, cumin, biḍa salt, pomegranate, dīpyaka, puṣkaramūla, the three pungents (vyoṣa), dhanyāka, vetasa, alkali, and citraka;
6.5.70 | Ghee prepared with *śaṭī*, *vaca*, *ajagandhā*, *elā*,
and *surasa*, along with curd, removes colic and flatulence for those suffering from *anila-gulma* (wind-type abdominal tumors).
Thus ends the *hiṅgu-sauvarcalādyam* ghee (6.5.71).
One should cook ghee with *hapuṣā*, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), *pṛthvīkā*, *cavya*, *citraka*, rock salt (*saindhava*), cumin (*ajājī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), and *dīpyaka*.
6.5.72 | This [mixture] of the juice of kola and mūlaka, along with milk, curd, and pomegranate,
is supreme for destroying vāta-gulma and provides relief from colic and abdominal distension.
6.5.73 | This ghee cures disorders of the female reproductive tract, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, dyspnea, cough, anorexia, fever, and pain in the bladder, heart, and flanks.

Thus ends the *hapuṣādyaghṛta* (Ghee with Hapuṣā, etc.). 6.5.74: One *picu* and one and a half [additional] parts of *pippalī*, two *palas* of *dāḍima*, one *pala* of *dhānya*, one *karṣa* of *śuṇṭhī*, and four times as much milk [are the ingredients].
6.5.75 | This ghee, when prepared with these [ingredients], immediately dispels vātagulma (wind-type abdominal tumors),
pain in the female reproductive tract, headache, hemorrhoids, and irregular fever.

Thus ends the Pippalyādya Ghṛta (6.5.76). These medicinal groups of drugs for medicated ghees that have been described are also used as powders, suppositories, and decoctions for those suffering from gulma.
6.5.77 | A gruel (peyā) prepared with kola, pomegranate, warm water,
the scum of surā, sour kāñjika, or the juice of bījapūra, removes colic and abdominal distension.
6.5.78 | One should prepare suppositories or pills from the powders of *mātuluṅga*, saturated with its juice, for the alleviation of the pain of abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and constipation (*ānaha*).
6.5.79 | Asafoetida, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), pāṭhā, hapuṣā, abhayā, śaṭī,
ajamodā, ajagandhā, tamarind, and sour vetasa.
6.5.80 | One should grind together pomegranate, lotus, coriander, cumin, *citraka*,
*vaca*, the two alkalis, the two salts, and *cavya*.
6.5.81 | This powder should be administered in foods and drinks without exception;
it may be taken before a meal, or drunk with wine or warm water.
6.5.82 | In cases of pain in the sides, the heart, or the bladder; in abdominal tumors (gulma) caused by vāta and kapha;
in constipation (ānāha), dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), and pain in the anus or the female genital tract.
6.5.83 | In cases of disorders of the stomach and blood,
in splenic enlargement, jaundice, loss of appetite, constriction of the chest, hiccough, cough, dyspnea, and throat obstruction.
6.5.84 | This powder of *mātuluṅga* should be infused many times with its own juice; pills should then be prepared from it, for they will be more effective than the [powder] itself.
Thus ends the section on the powder and pill of hiṅgu and other ingredients (6.5.85).
The juice of mātuluṅga, hiṅgu, pomegranate, viḍalavaṇa, and saindhavalavaṇa should be drunk with the scum of wine (surāmaṇḍa) to alleviate the pain of vātagulma.
6.5.86 | Śaṭī, puṣkara, hiṅgu, amlavetasa, kṣāra, citraka, dhānyaka,
yavānī, viḍaṅga, saindhava, and vacā.
6.5.87 | Having made a powder of *śaca*, *vyaja*, *pippalīmūla*, *āmajagandhā* along with pomegranate, cumin, and *ajamodā*, one should employ it.
6.5.88 | Again, having prepared a well-ground pill, the size of a jujube fruit, impregnated with the juice of citron or with honey-vinegar;
6.5.89 | It cures abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement (plīhāna), flatulence (ānāha), dyspnea (śvāsa), cough (kāsa), loss of appetite (arocaka),
hiccups (hikkā), heart disease (hṛdroga), hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi), and various types of headache (śiraso ruj).
This pill cures anemia, aggravation of phlegm (kapha), dysentery of all origins,
and pain in the sides, heart, and bladder.
6.5.91 | Having ground half a *pala* of *nāgara* (ginger) and two *palas* of husked sesame,
a man should drink one *pala* of molasses with warm milk.
6.5.92 | It destroys vāta-gulma, udāvarta, and pain in the female reproductive tract.
One should drink castor oil mixed with the scum of vāruṇī wine.
6.5.93 | A person suffering from vātagulma (abdominal tumors due to wind) should drink that same oil with milk;
when kapha is the secondary factor, the former [oil] is beneficial, while the latter [milk] is best when pitta follows.
6.5.94 | One should prepare four palas of clean, dried garlic in eight times as much milk and water; when only the milk remains, the man should drink it.
That milk quickly cures wind-tumors (vātagulma), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), sciatica (gṛdhrasī), irregular fever, heart disease, abscesses, and swellings.

Thus ends the section on garlic and milk (6.5.96). Oil, *prasannā*, cow’s urine, *āranāla*, and *yavāgraja*, when drunk together, will cure abdominal tumors (*gulma*), enlargement of the abdomen (*jaṭhara*), and flatulence (*ānāha*).
Thus ends the group of five oils (tailapañcaka).
6.5.97. One should drink śilājatu with a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūlī) mixed with alkali;
by the use of this, one is liberated from vātagulma.
Thus ends the formulation of *śilājatu*.
6.5.98: Having eaten *vāṭya* with a soup of *pippalī* or with the juice of radishes, one who has been lubricated is freed from upward-moving wind (*udāvarta*) and from *vāta-gulma*.
6.5.99 | One suffering from colic, abdominal distension, and constipation due to vātagulma should be treated with sudation using the methods of nāḍīsveda,
prastarasveda, and saṅkarasveda as described in the chapter on the procedures for sudation.

6.5.100 | One should know that enema therapy (bastikarma) is supreme for destroying abdominal tumors (gulma), for it first conquers the wind (māruta) in its own location and thereby immediately eliminates the tumor.

6.5.101 | Therefore, when administered repeatedly with non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) along with unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), disorders consisting of vāta, pitta, and kapha, as well as abdominal tumors (gulma), are pacified.
6.5.102 | Various enemas proven effective for curing gulma (abdominal tumors) have been described in the section on Siddhis;
furthermore, oils that cure gulma will be discussed in the section on Vāta diseases.
6.5.103 | When administered as drinks, massages, and oil enemas, these [medicines] quickly succeed in treating a gulma born of Vāta; for oil is indeed the supreme conqueror of Vāta.
6.5.104 | This same previously mentioned ghee, combined with the powder of *nīlinī*,
should be administered for purification to one suffering from *vātagulma* accompanied by impurities.
6.5.105 | For the purpose of purification, ghee should be administered together with nīlinī, trivṛtā, dantī, pathyā, kampillaka, along with viḍa salt, kṣāra, and nāgara.
6.5.106 | One should boil one pala each of nīlinī, triphalā, rāsnā, balā, kaṭukarohiṇī,
viḍaṅga, and vyāghrī in one āḍhaka of water.
6.5.107 | With that remainder of one-fourth [of the original quantity], one should cook one *prastha* of ghee,
having added one *prastha* of curd and one *pala* of snuhī-milk.
6.5.108 | Then one should give a pala of ghee mixed with the scum (maṇḍa) of gruel;
once it has been properly digested and the patient has been well-purged, one should feed him a meal of meat broth.
6.5.109 | This ghee cures abdominal tumors, skin diseases, abdominal enlargements, facial freckles, edema, anemia, fever, vitiligo, splenic disorders, and insanity.
Thus ends the *nīlinyādyaghṛta* (6.5.110). Furthermore, chickens, peacocks, partridges, cranes, and quails;
*śāli* rice, wine, and clarified butter—these are the remedies prescribed by physicians for vāta-gulma.
6.5.111 | For those suffering from vāta-gulma, food that is wholesome, warm, liquid, and unctuous is recommended,
along with the drinking of vāruṇī liquor mixed with maṇḍa, or water boiled with coriander seeds (dhānyaka).
6.5.112 | When the digestive fire is weak, the gulma increases; when the fire is kindled, it subsides.
Therefore, one should neither eat to excessive satiety nor practice excessive fasting.
6.5.113 | In every case of gulma, whatever treatment is administered after first applying oleation and sudation attains success; it does not succeed when applied without prior drying therapy.
6.5.114 | Having recognized the condition as urgent, the physician should treat a pitta-type gulma with clarified butter prepared for purgation or with bitter-scented (tikta) ghee.
6.5.115 | One karṣa each of rohiṇī, kaṭukā, nimba, madhuka, and the bark of triphalā,
along with one pala each of trāyamāṇā, paṭola, and trivṛt.
6.5.116 | Two palas of lentils (masūra) should be cooked in eight times their quantity of water;
when boiled down to a remainder equal to [the original weight of] ghee, four palas of clarified butter (sarpiḥ) should be added.

6.5.117 | One should drink it while it is still concentrated; by this, the bilious (paittika) abdominal tumor (gulma) is pacified, as well as fever, thirst, colic, vertigo, fainting, and loss of appetite.
Thus ends the *Rohiṇyādya-ghṛta*.
6.5.118. Four *palas* of *trāyamāṇā* should be boiled in ten times its quantity of water;
when reduced to one-fifth, it should be strained and combined with one *karṣa* each of the following paste ingredients:
6.5.119 | With the pastes of rohiṇī, kaṭukā, mustā, trāyamāṇā, durālabhā, tāmalakī, vīrā, jīvantī, candana, and utpala;
6.5.120 | Having added eight palas each of meat broth, āmalaka fruits, milk, and ghee, one should cook it thoroughly.
6.5.121 | This supreme ghee destroys gulma arising from bile and blood, erysipelas, bilious fever, heart disease, jaundice, and skin diseases.
Thus ends the Trāyamāṇādyam ghee (6.5.122).
One should cook it with the juice of āmalaka and sugarcane, adding one-fourth part ghee and one-fourth part pathyā;
this prepared ghee, when drunk, cures pitta-type gulma.
Thus ends the *Āmalakādya-ghṛta* (6.5.123). One should cook one pala each of grapes, *madhūka*, dates, *vidārī*, *śatāvarī*, *parūṣaka*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
6.5.124 | When one-fourth of a *jalāḍhaka* remains, [one should add] the juice of *āmalaka*,
ghee, sugarcane juice, milk, and a paste of *abhayā* equal to one-fourth [the quantity of the liquids].
6.5.125 | One should prepare that ghee; once prepared, it should be mixed with one-fourth part sugar and honey.
Through its use, it destroys pitta-type gulma and cures all disorders of pitta.
Thus ends the *drākṣādya-ghṛta* (6.5.126). One should crush the *vṛṣa* plant together with its roots and boil it in eight parts of water;
when one-eighth remains, one should add a paste of the flowers of that same plant.
6.5.127 | Ghee prepared with that [decoction], when cooled and mixed with honey, cures pitta-type gulma;
it destroys raktapitta, fever, dyspnea, cough, and heart disease.
Thus ends the Vāsā-ghṛta (6.5.128). Two palas of Trāyamāṇā, boiled in two prasthas of water,
should be drunk while lukewarm and mixed with an equal amount of milk, once reduced to one-eighth of its original volume and strained.
6.5.129 | After that, one should drink warm milk according to one's strength.
By this, when the morbid humors have been expelled, the Pitta-type gulma is pacified.
6.5.130 | In the case of a pitta-type gulma, one should drink the juice of grapes and *abhayā* with jaggery;
or alternatively, for the purpose of purgation, one should lick *kampillaka* mixed with honey as a liquid.
6.5.131 | Anointing with ghee alleviates the burning sensation in those suffering from pitta-type gulma;
likewise, [it is relieved] by anointment with *candanādya* oil or with *madhuka* oil.
6.5.132 | Those milk enemas (kṣīrabasti) that alleviate pitta-fever and contain bitter substances (satikta),
as well as those which will be described in the Siddhisthāna, are beneficial for those suffering from pitta-type abdominal tumors (gulma).
6.5.133 | Śāli rice, the meat of wild animals, cow’s milk, goat’s milk,
clarified butter, dates, āmalaka, grapes, pomegranate, and parūṣaka.
6.5.134 | Water boiled with *balā*, *vidārīgandhā*, and other such herbs should be used for drinking as part of the diet; this constitutes the treatment for *pitta*-type abdominal tumors (*gulma*).

6.5.135 | When there is a family history of *āmānvaya*, or in cases of *pittagulma* with *āma*, or *kapha-vātika* disorders with *āma*, the digestive fire (*agni*)— which has been suppressed by fasting (*vilaṅghita*)— should be stimulated with gruels (*yavāgū*), *khada* soups, or meat broths (*yūṣa*).
6.5.136 | The pacification and provocation of all the *doṣas* depend upon the digestive fire (*agni*).
Therefore, one should always protect the fire and avoid its causes of aggravation.
6.5.137 | One should administer emetics to one who is fit for emesis and suffers from a kapha-type gulma,
once the body has been lubricated and fomented and the gulma has become softened.
6.5.138 | Having wrapped bundles of *balvaja* grass or *kuśa* grass that have been set ablaze,
and having placed them inside a water-pot, the physician should position the tumor at the mouth of the jar.
6.5.139 | When the tumor (gulma) has been grasped, then one should insert a vessel;
having placed a cloth in between, the expert in measurement should then incise the tumor.
6.5.140 | One should press the abdomen according to what is available, avoiding the wrong path, the joints, and the eyes;
one should massage only the mass itself, but must not touch the intestines or the heart.
6.5.141 | Having smeared [the area] with sesame, castor, linseed, and mustard seeds,
the physician should apply fomentation (sveda) using lukewarm iron vessels for a gulma caused by phlegm (kapha).
Ghee boiled with the ten roots (daśamūlī), along with trikaṭu, alkali, salt,
asafoetida, biḍa salt, and pomegranate, quickly conquers kapha-type gulma.

Thus ends the Daśamūlī-ghṛta (6.5.143). Two palas of bhallātaka and one pala each of the five roots (pañcamūla), along with the drugs of the vidārīgandhādi group, should be crushed and boiled in one āḍhaka of water.
6.5.144 | When that soup is deficient in flavor, one should add long pepper,
ginger, sweet flag, embelia, rock salt, asafoetida, barley-alkali, biḍa salt, and costus.
6.5.145 | Having ground one karṣa each of citraka, madhuka, and rāsnā, the physician,
having added a prastha of milk, should cook it with a prastha of ghee.
6.5.146 | This Bhallātaka-ghṛta is supreme for removing kapha-type gulma;
it cures splenic disorders, anemia, dyspnea, grahaṇī disease, and cough.

Thus ends the *bhallātakādya-ghṛta* (6.5.147). One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with one *pala* each of long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), *cavya*, *citraka*, and dry ginger (*nāgara*), along with barley alkali (*yavakṣāra*).
6.5.148 | This ghee, prepared with one prastha of milk, cures gulma caused by kapha;
it destroys malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and removes splenic enlargement, cough, and fever.
Thus ends the *kṣīraṣaṭpalaka* ghee (6.5.149). Having boiled one pala each of *trivṛt*, *triphalā*, *dantī*,
and *kaśamūla* in four times the quantity of water, [one should take] the decoction remaining as one-fourth part.
6.5.150 | One should prepare ghee and oil derived from castor seeds together with milk in a single vessel.
This prepared Miśraka-sneha, when taken with honey, cures Kapha-type abdominal tumors (gulma).

6.5.151 | Miśraka-sneha should be employed in cases of obstruction caused by phlegm and wind, in skin diseases (kuṣṭha), splenic enlargement, and abdominal dropsy, and especially in cases of vaginal pain.

Thus ends the mixed medicated oil (miśraka-sneha). 6.5.152. That Nīlinī-ghṛta which was described as a laxative that destroys Vāta-gulma should be used in double the quantity for the purpose of purgation in those suffering from Kapha-gulma.
6.5.153 | Having licked one karṣa of the powder of Trivṛt, well-impregnated with a liquid of lime-water and milk, mixed with honey and ghee, one is properly purged.
6.5.154 | Twenty-five *abhayā* fruits and as many *pala*s of *dantī* and likewise of *citraka* should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water.
6.5.155 | One should pour in the strained juice when one-eighth remains;
then one should add purified jaggery equal in weight to the *dantī*, as well as those *abhayā* fruits.
6.5.156 | Half a kuḍava of oil, four palas of powdered trivṛt,
and one pala each of powdered pippalī and viśvabheṣaja (ginger).

6.5.157 | That [mixture] is to be prepared like a linctus (leha); when it has cooled, one should add honey equal in measure to the oil, and one pala of the powder consisting of cinnamon, cardamom, cinnamon leaves, and nāgakeśara.

6.5.158 | Then, having licked one pala of this electuary and having eaten one *harītakī*, one who has been treated with oleation is easily purged of a prastha of morbid humors (*doṣa*) without illness.
It cures abdominal tumors, edema, hemorrhoids, anemia, loss of appetite, heart disease, disorders of the duodenum, jaundice, and irregular fevers.

6.5.160 | When consumed, these [drugs] destroy leprosy (kuṣṭha), splenic enlargement (plīhāna), and abdominal distension (ānāha). Its regimen is free from complications, consisting of liquid meat broth and boiled rice.

Thus ends the section on Dantī-harītakī (6.5.161). The Nirūha enemas for those suffering from Kaphaja gulma, proven effective in their respective therapeutic successes, will be described [hereafter]. The proven formulations of Ariṣṭas will also be described in the chapters on the treatment of Grahāṇī and hemorrhoids.

6.5.162 | Those powders and pills prescribed for those suffering from vāta-gulma are beneficial in cases of kapha when they contain double the amount of alkali (kṣāra) along with asafoetida (hiṅgu) and amlavetasa.

6.5.163 | Those very alkalis (kṣāra) which are prescribed for disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī-doṣa) are proven, safe, and recommended for those suffering from kapha-type abdominal tumors (gulma). However, cauterization (dāha) is praised as a final resort.
6.5.164 | Ancient grains, wild animals and birds from arid regions,
soup made of horse-gram or mung beans, and [the preparations] of long pepper and ginger.
6.5.165 | And a broth made from dried radish, as well as from bilva, varuṇa,
the sprouts of cirabilva, yavānī, and citraka.
6.5.166 | One should prepare side dishes with citron, asafoetida, sour vetiver, alkali, pomegranate, buttermilk, oil, and ghee.
6.5.167 | A person suffering from a kapha-type gulma should drink water boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), or aged vāruṇī liquor, or even mature mādhvīka wine, at the appropriate time.
6.5.168 | One should drink buttermilk mixed with powdered yavānī and seasoned with biḍa salt;
it is digestive-stimulant and promotes the downward movement of wind, phlegm, and urine.
6.5.169 | When the gulma has been gradually accumulated, occupying a large area of the abdomen, becoming firmly rooted, bound by vessels, and elevated like the shell of a tortoise;
6.5.170 | That [patient] who is afflicted with weakness, anorexia, nausea, cough, vomiting, aversion to food, fever, thirst, drowsiness, and coryza does not recover.
6.5.171 | Having seized the patient afflicted by fever and dyspnea, and suffering from vomiting and diarrhea,
swelling in the heart, navel, hands, and feet draws away the one suffering from gulma.
6.5.172 | When the time for delivery has passed in the case of a *raudhira* (blood-born) tumor,
one should administer an unctuous purgative (*snehavirecana*) to a woman whose body has been lubricated and fomented.
6.5.173 | Having cooked two vessels of palāśa-alkali and two vessels each of oil and ghee,
one should administer the dose which produces the softening of abdominal tumors (gulma).
6.5.174 | If she should not be divided [from her guilt] in this way, one should administer a purifier for the womb:
either minced meat mixed with alkaline salt, or again, with the milk of the Sudhā plant.
6.5.175 | One should give *kaṭuka-matsyakas* well-impregnated with these two [substances] into the vagina;
or *laktakas* well-impregnated with the bile of a boar (*varāha*) and a fish.
6.5.176 | Or one should administer fermenting agents (kiṇva) mixed with honey, along with downward-moving and upward-moving purgatives,
or with jaggery and alkali, for the purification of the vagina.
6.5.177 | One should have her lick an alkaline preparation that removes *raktapitta* with honey and ghee;
one should also administer garlic, strong liquor, and fish to her.
6.5.178 | When blood is no longer visible, one should administer an enema containing milk, cow’s urine, alkali, and the ten roots (daśamūla) to break up the gulma.
6.5.179 | When the blood is flowing excessively, one should give meat broth with rice,
an ointment of ghee and oil, and fresh *surā* liquor for drinking.
6.5.180 | However, when blood flows excessively, treatments that alleviate *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders) should be administered;
furthermore, for one afflicted by the pain of *vāta*, all *vāta*-alleviating treatments should be applied again.
6.5.181 | And [one should prescribe] sprinklings of ghee and oil, partridges and cock-fowl,
liquor with its scum, and first of all, the drinking of sour clarified butter.
6.5.182 | Or one should administer an enema with the subsequent [medicated] ghee prepared with vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs;
when the bleeding is excessive, an oil enema (anuvāsana) should be given with bitter (tikta) substances.

6.5.183 | Regarding this, there are these verses: For those with Vāta-type Gulma, the treatments are oleation, sudation, medicated ghee, enemas, powders, nourishing therapy, pills, emesis, purgation, and bloodletting.
6.5.184 | Ghee prepared with bitter herbs, milk, purgatives, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha),
bloodletting, and formulations for reassurance and pacification [are indicated].
6.5.185 | Fomentation with medicinal herbs and surgical instruments is for a suppurated internal abscess;
purificatory and palliative treatments are for a *gulma* arising from *pitta*.
6.5.186 | Oleation, sudation, breaking therapy, lightening therapy, emesis, purgation,
ghee, enemas, pills, powders, fermented liquors (arishtas), and alkaline preparations.
6.5.187 | For a kaphaja gulma that has been bled, cauterization is performed at its base;
the therapeutic procedure for a blood-born (raudhira) gulma occurring in women has thus been described.
6.5.188 | The consumption of wholesome food and drink, the avoidance of causes [of disease] according to their respective [nature],
constant maintenance of the digestive fire, and the performance of all therapeutic procedures on one who has been oleated.

The cause, the signs, the successful treatment, the sequence of procedures, the curability, and the non-applicability of therapies— this much has been declared regarding the management of Gulma for Agniveśa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Management of Gulma," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
The Sixth Chapter:
6.6.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of prameha (urinary disorders).
6.6.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

6.6.3 | Free from delusion, pride, and latent tendencies, devoid of desire, and vast in knowledge and austerity, Punarvasu at the proper time spoke to Agniveśa concerning the types of meha along with their symptoms and their pacification.
6.6.4 | The pleasure of sitting, the pleasure of sleep, curd, the tastes of domestic, aquatic, and marshy animals, milk, new grain and drinks,
and preparations of molasses— all these are causes of *prameha* (urinary disorders) and increase *kapha*.
6.6.5 | Kapha, having vitiated the fat, the flesh, and the moisture produced within the body, causes the various types of urinary disorders (meha) when aggravated by hot substances;
and Pitta likewise causes those same disorders after thoroughly vitiating them with hot things.
6.6.6 | When the [other] doshas have been diminished, Vata draws the tissues (dhātus) into the bladder and produces pramehas.
For the dosha, having reached the bladder and vitiated the urine, generates the various types of meha according to its own specific nature.
6.6.7 | Ten types arising from kapha are curable with effort; six born of pitta are palliable; those fourfold [types] arising from vāta are incurable.
This is respectively because they require similar treatments, require dissimilar treatments, and because of their great severity.

6.6.8 | Kapha along with pitta and vāta are the doshas; fat, blood, semen, lymph, muscle-fat, saliva, marrow, plasma, ojas, and flesh are the dūṣyas (vitiated tissues) in those suffering from prameha; thus, there are exactly twenty types of meha.
6.6.9 | Like water, or like sugarcane juice, thick and yet clear on the surface;
white, containing semen, cool, or flowing slowly like saliva, or mixed with sand.
6.6.10 | One should know these ten types of prameha as arising from kapha:
those resembling alkaline water, black, blue, yellow, madder-colored, and red; these six pramehas are said to arise from pitta.

6.6.11 | When the remaining tissues have been depleted, one voids urine that is constantly obstructed by the strength of the marrow, or accompanied by fat, or by lymph; thus, due to Vāta, there are four types [of urinary disorders].
6.6.12 | Prameha assumes its respective color, taste, touch, and smell according to its specific doṣa.
That which is caused by vāta is dusky-red, accompanied by pain, and possesses the qualities of marrow and so forth; it is incurable.
6.6.13 | Excessive perspiration, body odor, looseness of the limbs, and a fondness for the comforts of beds, seats, and sleep;
a coating over the heart, eyes, tongue, and ears; density of the body, and excessive growth of hair and nails.
6.6.14 | A fondness for cold, dryness of the throat and palate, sweetness in the mouth, burning sensations in the hands and feet,
and ants swarming toward the urine are the premonitory symptoms of the disease of meha (urinary disorders).

6.6.15 | One patient with prameha is obese and strong, while another is emaciated and very weak. In that case, nourishing therapy (saṃbṛṃhaṇa) should be administered to the emaciated one, and purification (saṃśodhana) to the one whose doshas are predominant in strength.
6.6.16 | Various unctuous formulations taught in the Kalpa section should be administered for the purification of the impurities (*mala*).
Once the impurity has been eliminated from above and below, nourishing therapy (*saṃtarpaṇa*) alone should be performed in cases of urinary disorders (*meha*).
6.6.17 | By under-nutrition (apatarpaṇa), abdominal tumors (gulma), wasting (kṣaya), pain in the penis and bladder, and urinary retention may occur in a patient suffering from prameha;
therefore, nourishing therapies (paritarpaṇa) should be administered after carefully considering his digestive fire (vahni).
6.6.18 | For that patient suffering from prameha who does not require purification (saṃśodhana), palliative treatment (saṃśamana) should be employed.
Manthas, decoctions (kaṣāya), barley powders, electuaries (leha), and light foods should be used for the pacification of prameha.

6.6.19 | One should eat barley-rice that is dry, or even *vāṭya* porridge, along with the savory juices of wild birds— whether they be those that scratch for food (*viṣkira*) or those that peck (*pratuda*)— as well as flour-mixtures and cakes.

6.6.20 | A patient suffering from prameha should consume old śāli rice with soups of mung beans and the like, or with bitter vegetables, combined with the oils of dantī and iṅgudī; likewise, it may be combined with the oils of atasī and mustard.

6.6.21 | The grain-food for one suffering from prameha should consist of *ṣaṣṭika* rice along with grass-grains, but it should be primarily made of barley. Furthermore, a patient suffering from *kapha*-type prameha should eat various kinds of barley-based foods mixed with honey.

6.6.22 | For those suffering from urinary disorders (prameha), barley gruels prepared with a decoction of triphalā and mixed with honey should be used as nourishing drinks (tarpaṇa). The patient with prameha should drink these, combined with sidhu wine, as a regular regimen specifically for the destruction of the urinary disorder.

6.6.23 | One should eat various kinds of foods, such as barley-grits, cakes with jaggery and salt, and other diverse edibles, prepared from separate portions of barley that have been infused with the decoctions prescribed for *śleṣmameha*.
6.6.24 | To those who maintain donkeys, horses, cattle, swans, and peacocks, as well as barley, various kinds of food should be given;
likewise bamboo-barley and foods made of wheat according to the rules for barley.

6.6.25 | Purification, scraping, and fasting, when administered at the proper time, conquer the kapha-type pramehas; likewise, purgation, nourishing therapy, and palliative measures overcome those originating from pitta.
6.6.26 | A patient suffering from prameha should drink a decoction prepared by boiling dārvī, surāhvā, triphalā, and mustā;
or alternatively, he should drink haridrā mixed with honey along with the juice of āmalaka fruits.
6.6.27 | Harītakī, kaṭaphala, musta, and lodhra; pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, arjuna, and dhanvana;
both types of haridrā, tagara, viḍaṅga, kadamba, śāla, arjuna, and dīpyaka.
6.6.28–29 | Dārvī, viḍaṅga, khadira, and dhava; surāhva, kuṣṭha, aguru, and candana;

dārvī and agnimantha; triphalā with pāṭhā; pāṭhā and mūrvā, as well as śvadaṃṣṭrā; yavānī, uśīra, abhayā, guḍūcī, cavya, abhayā, citraka, and saptaparṇa—these ten decoctions, prepared in four parts [of water] and combined with honey, are prescribed for those suffering from kaphaja prameha.
6.6.30 | Of uśīra, lodhra, añjana, and candana; of uśīra, mustā, āmalaka, and abhayā; of paṭola, nimba, āmalaka, and amṛtā; and of mustā, abhayā, padmaka, and vṛkṣaka.
6.6.31 | Of lodhra-water, kālīyaka, and dhātakī; of nimba, arjuna, āmrātaka, niśā, and utpala;
of śirīṣa, sarja, arjuna, and kesarī; and of priyaṅgu, padma, utpala, and kiṃśuka.
6.6.32 | Ten decoctions prepared from the parts of aśvattha, pāṭhā, āsana, vetasa, kaṭaṅkaṭerī, utpala,
and mustaka are prescribed for urinary disorders of the pitta type, mixed with honey.
6.6.33 | In all types of urinary disorders, however, the two aforementioned decoction-formulations are prescribed;
they may be used in the drinking of *mantha*, in the preparation of barley, in the diet, and separately in the rules for drinking.
6.6.34 | Prepared oils and clarified butters should be administered in cases of urinary disorders (meha) caused by Vāta;
through the application of decoction-formulations and unctuous substances, their fat (medas), phlegm (kapha), and wind (vāyu) are pacified.

6.6.35 | One suffering from urinary disorders caused by *kapha* and *pitta* should lick the powdered flowers of *kampilla*, *saptacchada*, *śāla*, *baibhītaka*, *rauhitaka*, *kauṭaja*, and *kapittha* mixed with honey.
6.6.36 | Furthermore, a person suffering from urinary disorders (mehin) should drink a paste of *āmalaka* fruits, each the size of an *akṣa*, with its juice at the proper time;
once that has been digested, he should eat old grain with the pleasing juices of wild animals.

6.6.37 | Having observed the secondary involvement (anubandha) of wind, phlegm, or bile, the procedure for oleation (sneha-vidhi) should be determined accordingly. In the case of phlegm, oil processed with its own decoctions should be used; in the case of bile, ghee processed with bile-alleviating decoctions should be used.

6.6.38 | With trikaṇṭaka, aśmantaka, somavalka, bhallātaka, ativiṣā, and lodhra; with vacā, paṭola, arjuna, nimba, musta, haridrā, padmaka, and dīpyaka; *Note: The asterisk (*) indicates a line break or a specific formatting marker in the source text.*

6.6.39 | One should cook oil with mañjiṣṭhā, aguru, and all types of candana for urinary disorders (meha) caused by kapha and vāta; however, ghee should be used for those caused by pitta, and a mixture of both for those exhibiting symptoms of all three doṣas.
6.6.40 | Having boiled the three fruits (triphalā), darunishā, viśālā, and mustā, one should drink the decoction along with the paste of niśā,
combined with honey, in all cases of aggravated prameha.
6.6.41 | Lodhra, śaṭī, puṣkara root, elā, mūrvā, viḍaṅga, triphalā, yamānī, cavya, priyaṅgu, kramuka, viśālā, kirātatikta, and kaṭurohiṇī; ||
6.6.42 | Bhaṅgī, nata, the roots of citraka and pippalī, along with kuṣṭha, ativiṣā, and pāṭhā;
kaliṅgaka, keśara, indrasāhvā, nakha, patra, marica, and plava.
6.6.43 | Having boiled one *karṣa* measure of water in a *droṇa* [measure] until it is purified and reduced to a quarter part of water remaining,
one should add half a part of honey to that juice and place it in a vessel of clarified butter for a fortnight.
6.6.44 | This honey-wine (madhvāsava), when administered in a dose of two palas, quickly destroys Kapha-Pitta-type urinary disorders (prameha),
as well as anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya), hemorrhoids (arśas), loss of appetite (aruci), disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa), vitiligo (kilāsa), and various types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

Thus ends the honey-fermented liquor (madhvāsava). 6.6.45. That same decoction, with eight palas of dantī and four palas of bhallātaka, and a specific addition of eight palas of sugar-candy, along with an equal amount of honey—these two are separate fermented liquors (āsava).
6.6.46 | A patient suffering from prameha should drink either sārodaka, or kuśodaka, or madhūdaka, or the decoction of triphalā;
or he may drink plain sidhu, or the finest mādhvīka that has been aged for a long time.
6.6.47 | One should eat roasted meats of wild animals and birds, along with various kinds of barley-based foods and edibles;

by means of purificatory treatments, fermented decoctions (ariṣṭas), medicinal infusions (kaṣāyas), and electuaries (lehās), one should pacify the urinary disorders (pramehas) arising from over-nutrition.
6.6.48 | For one who consumes roasted barley and parched flour (saktu) as a medicinal application, urinary disorders (meha) do not occur;
likewise, through the use of mung beans and āmalaka, vitiligo (śvitra), dysuria (kṛcchra), and skin diseases (kuṣṭha) born of phlegm (kaphaja) do not arise.
6.6.49 | Those formulations which I have taught for diseases arising from over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa) and for those intended to dry up the fat of corpulent persons,
are proven effective for the purpose of drying [excess fluids] in disorders born of kapha and pitta, and they should also be employed in cases of prameha.
6.6.50 | Through various intense physical exercises, vigorous dry massages, bathing, and affusions of water,
as well as by ointments containing *sevya*, *tvak*, *elā*, *nuru*, *candana*, and other ingredients, urinary disorders (*meha*) quickly cease to exist.
6.6.51 | Since increased moisture (*kleda*), fat (*medas*), and phlegm (*kapha*) are observed to be the causes of *prameha*,
the physician should first administer depleting therapies (*apatarpaṇa*) in cases of *meha* arising from *kapha* and *pitta*.
6.6.52 | That treatment previously mentioned for those suffering from vāta-type urinary disorders, which was prescribed for those with a predominance of vāta, should be applied.
For indeed, in those emaciated by other types of meha, the vāyu becomes aggravated; however, regarding those cases that are incurable, there is no concern [to attempt treatment].
6.6.53 | Those causes by which those types of prameha arise are not to be avoided;
rather, just as one avoids a cause, so too is the treatment for a disease that has already arisen.

6.6.54 | One should not diagnose as *prameha* a person who voids urine that is turmeric-colored or blood-red, provided it occurs without the premonitory symptoms of *prameha*; for that is merely the provocation of blood and *pitta*.
6.6.55 | Having observed that the prameha is sweet, slimy, and honey-like, there should be a twofold consideration:
it may be of the nature of vāta when the doṣas are diminished, or it may arise from kapha due to over-nutrition (saṃtarpaṇa).

6.6.56 | Those urinary disorders (mehas) preceded by [the symptoms of] kapha and pitta, as well as those caused by vāta, are incurable; however, those caused by pitta are palliable, provided that the fat (medas) is not excessively vitiated.

6.6.57 | A person born with prameha, or one who is a diabetic (madhumehin), is said to be incurable, for that arises from a defect in the seed (*bījadoṣa*). Furthermore, whatever disorders are hereditary (*kulaja*) are also declared to be incurable.
6.6.58 | Those seven types of carbuncles (*piḍaka*) for those suffering from urinary disorders (*pramehin*), which I have described separately in the section on diseases,
should be treated by skilled surgeons with surgical instruments, as well as with cleansing and healing measures.
6.6.59 | Regarding this, there are these verses:—
The cause, the humor (doṣa), the affected tissue (dūṣya), the prognosis of the pramehas,
the two types of the patient with prameha, the threefold treatment by the physician, and the fault of excessive depletion.

6.6.60 | The first [chapter] contains preparations of meat, manthas that cure urinary disorders, decoctions, formulations of oils, ghees, and electuaries, as well as excellent prepared foods and fermented liquors.
6.6.61 | Various methods of physical exercise, baths, dry massages, and fragrant unguents—
this much has been prescribed in the section on therapeutics for the purpose of pacifying urinary disorders.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Prameha," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Seven:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of Kuṣṭha (skin diseases).
6.7.2 Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.7.3 | O Agniveśa, listen properly and in detail to the cause, the substance, the signs, the substratum, and the pacification of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), specifically those that destroy touch.
6.7.4 | For those who consume incompatible foods and drinks, as well as substances that are unctuous and heavy, and who suppress the urge for vomiting or other natural urges that have arisen;

6.7.5 | For those who indulge excessively in physical exercise, extreme heat, or overeating; and for those who resort to cold things, hot things, fasting, or food without following the proper regimen;

6.7.6 | For those afflicted by the fear of heat and exhaustion who quickly consume cold water, for those who eat when their food is undigested or overeat, and for those who improperly perform the five purificatory therapies (pañcakarma), [the following occurs].
6.7.7 | For those who consume new grain, curd, fish, sesame, salt, and sour things;
and for those who eat black gram, radish, flour-based foods, sesame, milk, and molasses.
6.7.8 | For those who engage in sexual intercourse while food is undigested, those who sleep during the day,
those who insult Brahmins and gurus, and those who perform sinful deeds;
6.7.9 | When the three [doshas], beginning with vāta, are vitiated, they corrupt the skin, blood, flesh, and fat;
this is the collection of the seven substrates (dravya) of the skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
6.7.10 | From this, the skin diseases (kuṣṭhas) arise—seven and eleven in number;
indeed, no skin disease whatsoever is found to be produced by a single doṣa alone.
6.7.11 | Insensitivity to touch, excessive perspiration, or alternatively, discoloration,
elevation, urticaria, horripilation, itching, pricking pain, fatigue, and exhaustion [are the symptoms].
6.7.12 | Excessive pain in ulcers, rapid onset, long duration,
burning sensation, and numbness of the limbs— these are the premonitory symptoms of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

6.7.13 | Hereafter, we shall describe the characteristics of the eighteen types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha): kapāla, udumbara, maṇḍala, ṛṣyajihva, puṇḍarīka, sidhma, kākaṇaka, ekakuṣṭha, carmākhyaka, kiṭima, vipādikā, alasaka, dadru, carmadala, pāmā, visphoṭaka, śatāru, and vicarcikā.
6.7.14 | That which has the appearance of a blackish-red skull, being dry, rough, and thin,
and characterized by excessive pricking pain, is known as the uneven *kāpāla* leprosy.
6.7.15 | They know the *audumbara* type of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) as being pervaded by burning, itching, pain, and redness, with hair that is tawny, and appearing like the fruit of the *udumbara* tree.
6.7.16 | White, red, stable, thick, unctuous, with elevated circular patches,
difficult to cure, and mutually confluent— this is called Kuṣṭha known as Maṇḍala.
6.7.17 | That which is rough, red at the edges, dark-brown within, painful,
and shaped like a deer's tongue is called ṛṣyajihva.
6.7.18 | That which is white with red margins, resembling the petal of a lotus,
elevated, and accompanied by a burning sensation, is called *puṇḍarīka*.
6.7.19 | That thin, white, copper-colored dust which is released when rubbed,
and which is the color of a bottle-gourd flower, is generally known as sidhma, and it usually appears on the chest.
6.7.20 | That leprosy which has the color of a cowrie shell, is unripened, and is accompanied by intense pain, exhibiting the symptoms of all three doshas, is known as Kākaṇa; it is indeed incurable.

Thus end the seven major types of kuṣṭha. 6.7.21. That which is non-sweating, extensive, and resembles the scales of a fish is ekakuṣṭha; that which is thick like an elephant's hide is called carmakīla.
6.7.22 | A dark-brown, rough-to-the-touch, and coarse eruption is known as *kiṭima*.
That which occurs on the feet (*vaipādika*) is characterized by the cracking of the hands and feet and is accompanied by intense pain.
Alasaka is characterized by eruptions covered with itching and redness;
Dadru consists of raised circular patches accompanied by itching, redness, and pustules.
6.7.24 | That which is red, accompanied by itching, eruptions, and pain, and which even cracks upon contact, is called carmadala; it is said to be intolerant of touch.
6.7.25 | Pāmā consists of intensely itchy pustules that are white, reddish, or dark-brown;
visphoṭas are eruptions resembling white or reddish boils with thin skin.
6.7.26 | Rakta (erysipelas) is dark-red, accompanied by burning and pain; śatāru is characterized by many ulcers.
Vicarcikā is itchy, has dark spots, and is marked by abundant discharge and pustules.
Thus, there are eleven minor types of skin diseases (kṣudrakuṣṭha).
When vāta is predominant, one should recognize the kāpāla type; when kapha is predominant, the maṇḍala type;
when pitta is predominant, the audumbara type; and the kākaṇa type arises from all three doṣas combined.
6.7.28 | When vāta-pitta, śleṣma-pitta, or vāta-śleṣman are predominant,
ṛṣyajihva, puṇḍarīka, and sidhma kuṣṭha arise.
6.7.29 | Carma-kustha, ekakustha, kitima along with vipadika,
and alasaka kustha should be known as generally predominant in vata and kapha.
6.7.30 | Pāmā, śatāru, visphoṭa, dadru, and likewise carmadala are generally characterized by an excess of pitta and śleṣman; vicarcikā, however, is predominantly composed of kapha.

6.7.31 | All leprosy (kuṣṭha) arises from the three doṣas; however, the treatment for the various types of leprosy is administered after determining the relative strength or weakness of the doṣas through their respective characteristic signs.

6.7.32 | Whichever humor (doṣa) one observes to have its specific signs excessively aggravated in cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), one should first pacify that very humor, and thereafter treat the secondary association (anubandha).

6.7.33 | By means of the specific types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), the humors (doṣa) are known; and by means of the specific types of humors, the skin diseases are known in turn. Through these, the cause is understood, and it reveals those [causes].
6.7.34 | Dryness, emaciation, pricking pain, aching pain, as well as contraction and stretching,
roughness, a harsh state, horripilation, and a dark-red discoloration [are the signs of vāta].

6.7.35 | In skin diseases (kuṣṭha), the symptoms caused by vāta are [as described]; those caused by pitta are burning sensation, redness, discharge, suppuration, a fleshy odor, moisture, and likewise the falling off of body parts.
6.7.36 | Whiteness, coldness, itching, stability, elevation, heaviness, and unctuousness— these,
along with being eaten by insects and moisture, are the signs of Kapha in skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
6.7.37 | A wise person should avoid blood that possesses all these signs:
when it is accompanied by thirst and burning sensations, when the digestive fire has been extinguished, and when it is infested with worms.
6.7.38 | That which is dominated by vāta and kapha, or that which is aggravated by a single doṣa, is not difficult [to cure].
However, those dominated by kapha and pitta, or pitta and vāta, are difficult to cure.
6.7.39 | In skin diseases (kuṣṭha) where vāta is predominant, ghee is indicated; where kapha is predominant, emesis;
and where pitta is predominant, bloodletting and purgation should be administered first.

6.7.40 | The formulations for emesis and purgation mentioned in the Kalpa-sthāna should be employed for those suffering from skin diseases (kuṣ� scarification is recommended for mild skin disease, while venesection is advised for severe cases.
6.7.41 | A leper with an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas) should be purified repeatedly while carefully protecting his life-force;
for if the humors are removed in excessive measure, the wind (vāyu), finding the patient weak, may quickly destroy him.
6.7.42 | The drinking of unctuous substances is desired when the gastrointestinal tract has been purified and blood has been drained;
for wind quickly enters a weak leprosy patient whose bowels have been cleansed.
6.7.43 | When the heart is afflicted by the humors (doṣas), one should induce emesis in cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) located in the upper parts of the body,
using the fruits of *kuṭaja*, *madana*, and *madhuka*, along with *paṭola* and the juice of *nimba*.
6.7.44 | Cold juices, ripe fruit juices, honey, and madhuka are emetics;
in cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), trivṛtā, dantī, and triphalā are recommended for purgation.
6.7.45 | Sauviraka, tuṣodaka, āloḍana, āsava, and sīdhu liquors are recommended for those who purge downward; the sequence of their use is desired according to the degree of purgation.

6.7.46 | A patient suffering from skin diseases (kuṣṭha) should be administered a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) with dārvī, bṛhatī, sevya, paṭola, picumarda, kṛtamāla, kaliṅga, yava, and musta, along with unctuous substances.
6.7.47 | Having observed that the patient has been purged and given a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), but still has a predominance of vāta and is fit for an unctuous enema (anuvāsana),
one should prepare the oil with *phala*, *madhuka*, *nimba*, *kuṭaja*, and *paṭola*.
6.7.48 | Saindhava salt, dantī, marica, phaṇijjhaka, pippalī, karañja fruit, and viḍaṅga,
used as a nasal medication (nasya), destroy worms, skin diseases, and the provocation of kapha.
6.7.49 | By employing the purgative fumigations described in the section on the chapter of verses (Ślokasthāna),
parasites, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and leucoderma (kilāsa) located in the head are pacified.
6.7.50 | For swellings that are firm, hard, and circular, once they have been fomented by means of beds and channels and rubbed with brushes,
the provocation of blood must be removed.
6.7.51 | One should scarify leprosy (kuṣṭha) that has been fomented and raised with comfortably warm poultices made from the flesh of marsh-dwelling aquatic animals, using a sharp instrument.
6.7.52 | Or, for the purpose of inducing bleeding, one should apply horns or gourds to the kuṣṭha;
or, once the kuṣṭha has been scarified slightly, one should purge it with leeches.
6.7.53 | Those medicinal pastes for leprosy which are applied to those whose blood and humors have been removed,
and whose internal cavities have been purified, achieve success immediately.
6.7.54 | In those cases where the surgical instrument does not penetrate and which would destroy the sense of touch,
alkali (kṣāra) should be applied after draining away the blood and the morbid humors (doṣa).
6.7.55 | When leprosy (kuṣṭha) is as hard as stone, rough, chronic, stable, and long-standing,
an external application (pradeha) with poisons should be administered for one who has already drunk an antidote (agada), followed by an application with antidotes.
6.7.56 | Kuṣṭhas that are rigid, deeply numb, and free from perspiration and itching [should be treated] with brushes made of dantī,
trivṛtā, karavīra, karañja, and kuṭaja.
6.7.57 | Or, having rubbed [the area] with the leaves of *jāti*, *arka*, or *nimba*; or with *śastra* grass; or with sea-foam;
or with cow-dung, one should then apply plasters.
6.7.58 | The treatment prescribed for those with vāta and kapha-type kuṣṭha should be performed for those suffering from pitta-type kuṣṿha;
furthermore, there should be the removal of kapha, pitta, and blood, as well as pacification through bitter and astringent [substances].
6.7.59 | Ghee, bitter substances, and whatever other treatment exists that subdues blood-bile (rakta-pitta)—
that foremost therapy, both external and internal, should be employed for pitta-type skin diseases (pitta-kuṣṭha).

6.7.60 | This treatment for the alleviation of *kuṣṭha*, which has been described according to the specific predominance of the *doṣas*, will now be further explained; for the most part, it is similar in its approach to treating skin disorders (*tvag-doṣa*).
6.7.61 | Either dārvī or rasāñjana, taken with cow’s urine, overcomes kuṣṭha;
or abhayā, administered for a month along with vyōṣa, jaggery, and oil, does so as well.
6.7.62 | One pala each of the root of *paṭola*, likewise of *gavākṣī*, and of the bark of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*);
there should be half a part each of *trāyamāṇā* and *kaṭurohiṇī*, combined with a quarter-part of *nāgara*.
6.7.63 | Likewise, a man should drink one pala of these [drugs] ground together and boiled in water to remove the humors (doṣas).
Once it is digested, he should eat old śāli rice with the meat-juices of wild animals and birds.

6.7.64 | This [formula], through its administration for six nights, destroys skin diseases, swelling, disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, urinary difficulties, and jaundice; it also cures pain in the heart and bladder, as well as irregular fevers.
6.7.65 | Musta, vyoṣa, triphalā, mañjiṣṭhā, dāru, the two pañcamūlis,
the bark of saptacchada and nimba, viśālā, citraka, and mūrvā.
This powder, combined with nine parts of *tarpaṇa* and mixed with honey and clarified butter, is a proven remedy for eradicating skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*); it should be consumed as a regular regimen.
6.7.67 | It cures swelling, anemia, vitiligo, disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, hernia, fistula-in-ano, carbuncles, itching, and urticaria.
Thus ends the *mustādi-cūrṇa* (Musta powder), 6.7.68. [The powder] of triphalā, ativiṣā, kaṭukā, nimba, kaliṅgaka, vacā, paṭola, māgadhikā, the two types of rajanī, padmaka, mūrvā, and viśālā;
6.7.69 | One should take two palas each of bhūnimba and palāśa, and twice that amount (four palas) of trivṛt;
then again, an equal amount of brāhmī. This powder is the supreme remedy for removing numbness.
6.7.70 | The application of *lelītaka* with honey and the juice of *jāti* is supreme;
it destroys the seventeen types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), as does *mākṣikadhātu* with urine.
6.7.71 | A leper should consume mercury that has been properly restrained, combined with sulphur or with gold pyrite, which destroys all diseases and is most excellent.

6.7.72 | A person suffering from leprosy should consume [the medicine] together with *vajraśilājatu* or combined with *yogarāja*, restraining himself and taking it daily, for it pacifies all diseases.
6.7.73 | Having boiled the heartwood of *khadira* and *suradāru*, one should prepare the liquid for the water-portion with that decoction;
it should be added to one *prastha* of honey, and those two [the heartwoods] should each weigh eight *palas*.
6.7.74 | In that [preparation], one should add eight palas of iron powder, as well as these:
one karṣa each of the three myrobalans (triphalā), cardamom (elā), cinnamon bark (tvak), cinnamon leaves (nāgara), cinnamon leaves (patra), and gold (kanaka).
6.7.75 | Sugar-candy, when equal in consistency to honey, was kept for that same length of time in an iron vessel;
for one who consumed it as a honey-wine (*madhvāsava*), his leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and vitiligo (*kilāsa*) were pacified.

Thus ends the honey-fermented liquor (madhvāsava). 6.7.76. Having poured one droṇa of khadira decoction into a jar that has been treated with ghee, six palas each of the following powdered ingredients should be added here:
6.7.77 | Triphalā, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, rajanī, mustā, āṭarūṣaka, indrayava, sauvarṇī, as well as tvak and chinnaruhā— this is the "tanmāsa" [formula].
6.7.78 | One should place it among grain and drink it every morning with the proper method;
in one month it surely destroys major leprosy, but minor types in a fortnight.

6.7.79 | Having drunk the *ariṣṭa* known as Kanakabindu, one becomes free from hemorrhoids, asthma, fistula-in-ano, cough, leucoderma, urinary disorders, and consumption, and attains a golden complexion.
Thus ends the Kanakabindu-ariṣṭa (6.7.80). This should be drunk in cases of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) caused by vāta and kapha, as well as those caused by pitta;
furthermore, this decoction of kṛtamālaka is especially indicated for those caused by kapha.

6.7.81 | A fermented liquor (āsava) made from treacle (gauḍa), combined with the three myrobalans (triphalā), citraka, and kuṣṭha, when joined with the addition of betel nut (kramuka), the ten roots (daśamūla), dantī, varāṅga, and honey, is a destroyer of the disease kuṣṭha.
6.7.82 | One should know that light foods are beneficial for skin diseases (kuṣṭha), as are bitter vegetables;
likewise, foods and ghees combined with bhallātaka, the three myrobalans (triphalā), and nimba are recommended.

6.7.83 | Ancient grains, meats from the arid regions (*jāṅgala*), and mung beans combined with *paṭola* are recommended; however, heavy foods, sour items, milk, curd, [meat from] marshy regions, fish, jaggery, and sesame seeds are not.
6.7.84 | Elā, kuṣṭha, dārvī, śatapuṣpā, citraka, and viḍaṅga;
as well as rasāñjana and abhayā—this is the desired medicinal paste for kuṣṭha.
6.7.85 | Citraka, camelā, bimbī, vṛṣaka, trivṛt, arka, and nāgaraka—
these should be powdered and infused for eight days with the juice of palāśa.
6.7.86 | By means of that alkali produced from the urine of cows, its circular patches (maṇḍalas) are quickly broken and dissolved when smeared with it and heated by the sun.
6.7.87 | A paste consisting of māṃsī, marica, salt, haridrā, tagara, sudhā, soot from a house, urine, bile,
and palāśa-alkali destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
6.7.88 | Tin, lead, iron powder, maṇḍalanut, phalgu, citraka, bṛhatī,
the juice of iguana mixed with salt, devadāru, and urine are a remedy for maṇḍala.
6.7.89 | For meat and for flour-based ferment (*kiṇva*), the functions of water should be performed with the clear liquid obtained from the ash of plantain, palāśa, pāṭala, and nicula.
6.7.90 | Medaka, well-prepared with those fermenting agents (kiṇva), is an excellent external application;
it destroys circular leprosy (maṇḍala-kuṣṭha) when applied while exposed to the sun, and it is also anthelmintic.
6.7.91 | Musta, madana, triphalā, karañja, āragvadha,
kaliṅga, barley, dārvī, and saptaparṇa constitute the bath known as Siddhārthaka.
6.7.92 | This decoction serves as an emetic, a purgative, a cosmetic, and likewise an external rub;
it overcomes skin disorders, leprosy, and swellings, and destroys anemia.
6.7.93 | A plaster consisting of kuṣṭha, karañja seeds, and iḍagaja is a destroyer of skin diseases (kuṣṭha);
so too are prapunnāḍa seeds, rock salt, rasāñjana, kapittha, and lodhra.
6.7.94 | A plaster composed of the root of white karavīra, the fruit of kuṭaja and karañja, the bark of dārvī,
and the sprouts of sumana is proven to remove skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
6.7.95 | A paste of *lodhra*, *dhātakī*, seeds of *vatsaka*, *naktamāla*,
and *mālatī* is used for rubbing and as an ointment in cases of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
6.7.96 | The bark of *śairīṣa*, the flower of *kārpāsī*, the leaves of *rājavṛkṣa*,
and ground *kākamācī*— this is the fourfold external application for curing *kuṣṭha*.
Thus end the ointments (lepāḥ). 6.7.97: [The decoctions] of dārvī, rasāñjana, nimba, paṭola, the heartwood of khadira, āragvadha, vṛkṣaka, triphalā, and saptaparṇa [are used].
6.7.98 | Thus, there are six decoction formulations that destroy skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), along with the seventh from *tiniśa*;
these are beneficial for bathing and drinking, as is the eighth from *aśvamāra*.
6.7.99 | These same decoctions (kaṣāyas) are intended for use as ointments, rubbing powders, and dusting powders,
as well as in the preparation of medicated oils and ghees, for the purpose of pacifying leprosy (kuṣṭha).
6.7.100 | This decoction of triphalā, nimba, paṭola, mañjiṣṭhā, rohiṇī, vacā, and haridrā,
when practiced regularly, destroys skin diseases born of kapha and pitta.
6.7.101 | Ghee prepared with these very same [drugs] overcomes kuṣṭha characterized by a predominance of vāta. This same formulation is also prescribed for khadira, asana, dāru, and nimba.
6.7.102 | Kuṣṭha, arka, tuttha, kaṭphala, mūlaka seeds, rohiṇī, kaṭukā,
the fruit of kuṭaja, utpala, musta, bṛhatī, karavīra, and kāsīsa.
6.7.103 | Eḍagaja, nimba, pāṭhā, kūrālabhā, citraka, viḍaṅga,
the seeds of bitter alābu, kampillaka, sarṣapa, vacā, and dārvī.
6.7.104 | Oil prepared with these [substances] destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha); this formulation is also desired as an ointment, as a rubbing powder, as a friction paste, or as a dusting powder.
6.7.105 | The juice of white oleander (śvetakaravīra), cow’s urine, citraka, and viḍaṅga—
this proven application of oil for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) is approved by physicians.
Thus ends the oil beginning with white oleander (*śvetakaravīra*).
6.7.106. White oleander leaf, root-bark, *vatsaka*, and *viḍaṅga*;
*kuṣṭha*, arka root, mustard, *śigru* bark, *rohiṇī*, and *kaṭukā*.
6.7.107 | Oil prepared with these [drugs] as paste-ingredients (kalka) in a one-fourth portion,
to which four times the amount of cow's urine has been added, destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and itching (kaṇḍū) when used for massage.
Thus ends the oil [formula] beginning with the sprouts of white *karavīra* (6.7.108).
Bitter *alābu* seeds, the two types of *tuttha*, *rocanā*, the two types of *haridrā*,
the fruit of *bṛhatī*, *eraṇḍa*, *viśāla*, *citraka*, and *mūrvā*.
6.7.109 | Kāsīsa, hiṅgu, śigru, tryūṣaṇa, suradāru, tumburu, viḍaṅga, lāṅgalaka,
the bark of kuṭaja, kaṭukā, and rohiṇī.
6.7.110 | Mustard oil should be prepared with these pastes and four times as much urine;
it destroys itching and skin diseases (kuṣṭha) when used for massage, and it subdues vāta and kapha.
Thus ends the oil [recipe] beginning with *tiktekṣvāku*.
6.7.111. *Kanakakṣīrī*, *śailā*, *bhārgī*, the fruits and root of *dantī*, *jātī* sprouts, mustard, garlic, *viḍaṅga*, and the bark of *karañja*.
6.7.112 | Saptacchada, arka-pallava, mūla, tvac, namba, citraka, āsphota, guñjā, eraṇḍa, the roots of bṛhatī, mūlaka, surasa, and the fruits of arjaka.
6.7.113 | Kuṣṭha, pāṭhā, musta, tumburu, mūrvā, vacā, along with ṣaḍgranthā;
eḍagaja, kuṭaja, śigru, tryūṣaṇa, bhallātaka, and kṣavaka.
6.7.114 | Haritāla, avākpuṣpī, tuttha, kampillaka, that which is called amṛtā,
saurāṣṭrī, kāsīsa, the bark of dārvī, and sarjikā-lavaṇa;
6.7.115 | With these pastes, mustard oil— or alternatively, *karavīra* oil— should be prepared with a decoction of the roots and tender leaves of *karavīra*, along with four parts cow’s urine.
6.7.116 | This preparation should be kept in a bitter gourd; once prepared, it quickly breaks up skin eruptions (maṇḍala) when applied as an ointment. Furthermore, it destroys worms and itching.
Thus ends the preparation of Kanakakṣīrī oil (6.7.117).
Take kuṣṭha, tamālapatra, marica, realgar, and iron pyrite;
these, combined with oil, should be kept in a copper vessel for seven days.
6.7.118 | Anointed with that [oil], a case of *sidhma* disappears within seven days for one remaining in the heat;
a new case of *kilāsa* disappears after a month, provided the body is purified by bathing.

Thus ends the plaster for *sidhma*. 6.7.119. They say that the oils of mustard, *karañja*, *koṣātakī*, and *iṅgudī*, as well as the oil of the heartwood of *khadira*, are beneficial in cases of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
6.7.120 | Jīvantī, mañjiṣṭhā, dārvī, kampillaka, payastuttha,
and sarjarasa— this is the preparation for cooking ghee and oil.
6.7.121 | A mixture with beeswax should be applied; by this, *vipādikā* (cracking of the feet) is pacified when massaged.
*Carmadala*, *ekakuṣṭha*, *kiṭibha*, *kuṣṭha*, and *alasaka* are also pacified.
Thus ends the section on ghee and oil for removing *vipādikā* (cracking feet).

6.7.122. A plaster consisting of fermenting agent (*kiṇva*), boar’s blood, *pṛthvīkā*, and rock salt should be applied. A plaster of *kustumburu* and *kuṣṭha* should be used to remove circular skin patches (*maṇḍala*).
6.7.123 | A paste prepared from pūtīka, dāru, jaṭilā, mature surā, honey, and udgaparṇī, along with kākanāsā,
is proven to remove circular skin diseases (maṇḍala-kuṣṭha).
6.7.124 | Citraka, śobhāñjanaka, guḍūcī, apāmārga, devadāru, khadira,
dhava, śyāmā, dantī, and dravantī constitute a medicinal paste.

6.7.125 | Lac, juice of *añjana*, cardamom, and *punarnavā*—these are ointments for those suffering from skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). All of them, when combined with the whey of curd (*dadhi-maṇḍa*), should be applied; they destroy skin diseases caused by the six types of wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*).
6.7.126 | By means of *eḍagaja*, *kuṣṭha*, *sindhu*, *sauvīraka*, *sarṣapa*, and *kṛmighna*,
the skin diseases known as *kṛmi*, *kuṣṭha*, and *maṇḍala*, as well as *dadrū-kuṣṭha*, are pacified.
6.7.127 | Eḍagaja, sarjarasa, and mūlaka seeds— these,
when combined with kāñjika, or used separately, constitute this rubbing powder (udvartana) and ointments for sidhma and kuṣṭha.
6.7.128 | Vāsā, triphalā, bṛhatī, sevya, paṭola, sārivā, and rohiṇī are used for drinking, bathing, dry massage (udvartana), and external application (pralepa).
6.7.129 | Khadira, avaghātaka, kakubha, rohitaka, lodhra, kuṭaja, dhava, nimba, saptacchada, and karavīra are recommended for use in bathing and drinking.
6.7.130 | Water, blue lotus, iron, saffron, leaf, floating plant, and sandalwood, along with lotus stalks,
in increasing proportions by one part each, constitute a prepared ointment for pitta-type and kapha-type skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
6.7.131 | Yaṣṭī, āhva, lodhra, padmaka, paṭola, picumarda, and candana—
these juices, when very cold, are beneficial for those suffering from pitta-type skin diseases (kuṣṭha) in both bathing and drinking.
6.7.132 | Priyaṅgu, hareṇukā, the fruits of vatsaka,
ativiṣā, sevyā, candana, rohiṇī, and kaṭukā should be used as an ointment.
6.7.133 | For burning kuṣṭha lesions, anointment should be performed with bitter ghees or washed ghee,
as well as with oils combined with sandalwood, madhuka, prapauṇḍarīka, and utpala.
6.7.134 | When there is discharge, falling off of the limb, burning sensation, eruption of blisters,
or peeling of the skin, cold plasters and affusions, bloodletting, purgation, and bitter ghee [are indicated].
6.7.135 | Khadira-ghṛta, Nimba-ghṛta, the excellent Dārvī-ghṛta,
and Paṭola-ghṛta are proven remedies prescribed by physicians for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) where blood and bile (raktapitta) predominate.

6.7.136 | Half-pala portions each of the barks of the three myrobalans (triphalā), one karṣa each of patola leaves and the remaining ingredients— katurohiṇī, nimba, yaṣṭyāhvā, and trāyamāṇā— [are to be taken].
6.7.137 | This decoction is prepared by adding two palas of split masūra lentils to one āḍhaka of water;
when one-eighth remains, the strained liquid should be taken.
6.7.138 | And those [drugs] should be boiled with eight palas of decoction and four palas of ghee;
when eight palas remain, it should be drunk while lukewarm.

6.7.139 | This [medicinal formulation] destroys that powerful vāta-pitta kuṣṭha, erysipelas (vīsarpa), and vāta-śoṇita, as well as fever, burning sensations, abdominal tumors (gulma), abscesses (vidradhi), vertigo, and eruptive boils (visphoṭaka).
6.7.140 | One should take half a part each of nimba, paṭola, dārvī, durālabhā, tiktarohiṇī, triphalā, parpaṭaka, and trāyamāṇā.
6.7.141 | When eight parts remain of the decoction prepared from one āḍhaka of water, one should add [the paste] after it has been strained:
sandalwood, kirātatiktaka, māgadhikā, and trāyamāṇā.
6.7.142 | Having made into a paste one karṣa each of musta and the seeds of vatsaka,
this ghee— prepared with six palas of fresh clarified butter— is to be drunk.

6.7.143 | This [preparation] is proven to cure leprosy, fever, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, anemia, and edema; it also removes scabies, erysipelas, pustules, itching, urticaria, and goiters.
Thus ends the Tikta-ṣaṭpala-ghṛta (Ghee with Six Ingredients of Bitter Taste).
6.7.144. [One should take] Saptacchada, Prativiṣā, Śampāka, Tiktarohiṇī, Pāṭhā, Musta, Uśīra, Triphalā, Paṭola, Picumarda, and Parpaṭaka.
6.7.145 | Dhanvayavāsa, candana, upakulyā, padmaka, the two types of haridrā,
ṣaḍgranthā along with viśālā, śatāvarī, and both types of sārivā.
6.7.146 | The wise physician should prepare a paste (kalka) of vatsaka seeds, yāsa, mūrvā, amṛtā, kirātatikta, madhuka, and trāyamāṇā.
6.7.147 | One-fourth part paste, eight parts water, and twice as much juice of amṛtaphala fruits should be added to the ghee; once this is prepared, one should administer that clarified butter.
6.7.148 | Leucoderma, hemorrhagic diseases where blood-pitta is predominant, hemorrhoids with bleeding,
erysipelas, acid dyspepsia, gout, and anemia.
6.7.149 | It [cures] eruptive boils along with scabies, insanity, jaundice, fever, itching, heart disease, abdominal tumors, pustules, menorrhagia, and cervical adenitis.
6.7.150 | This Mahātiktaka ghee, when drunk at the proper time according to one's strength, immediately overcomes even those great disorders that remain unconquered by hundreds of other formulations.
Thus ends the Mahātiktaka-ghṛta (6.7.151). When the doshas have been removed, when the blood has been eliminated, when external and internal pacifying measures have been applied,
and when oleation is administered at the proper time, curable leprosy does not persist.
6.7.152 | Five *tulās* of *khadira*, one *tulā* each of *śiṃśapā* and *asan*,
and half a *tulā* each of all these— *karañja*, *ariṣṭa*, and *vetasa*.
6.7.153 | Parpaṭa, kuṭaja, vṛṣa, and likewise kṛmihara;
the two types of haridrā, kṛtamāla, guḍūcī, triphalā, and trivṛt.
6.7.154 | Seven *saptaparṇa* leaves, crushed, [should be boiled] in ten *droṇas* of water;
one should remove the decoction when eight parts remain.
6.7.155 | One should cook one āḍhaka of ghee with an equal portion of *dhātrī* juice and the paste of the drugs of the Mahātiktaka group, each weighing one pala, as previously described.
6.7.156 | This "Great Khadira" formulation destroys all types of skin diseases through drinking, massage, and application; it is the supreme remedy for various disorders of the skin.
Thus ends the section on Mahākhadira-ghṛta (6.7.157). When the limbs are oozing with lymph, exuding pus, or have been bitten by insects,
neem (*nimba*) and *viḍaṅga* should be used in appropriate measure for bathing, drinking, and as an external application.
6.7.158 | Vṛṣa, kuṭaja, saptaparṇa, karavīra, karañja, nimba, and khadira,
when used with cow’s urine for bathing, drinking, or as an external application, destroy worms and skin diseases.

6.7.159 | Viḍaṅga is preeminent for destroying worms in the preparation of drinks and food, as well as in sprinkling, fumigation, and medicinal plasters; Khadira is preeminent for curing skin diseases.
6.7.160 | Eḍagaja with viḍaṅga, the roots of āragvadha,
uddālana, dog’s teeth, and the teeth of cows, horses, boars, and camels [are used] for skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
6.7.161 | Eḍagaja with viḍaṅga, the two types of niśā, and the root of rājavṛkṣa—
this should be employed as a supreme remedy for the eradication of kuṣṭha, along with pippalī and pākala.
6.7.162 | For those with vitiligo that is particularly severe yet purified on all sides,
the application of *malapūra* mixed with jaggery is desired as the foremost remedy for causing the skin to slough off.

6.7.163 | Having drunk that, one who has been purged should, being well-lubricated, resort to the heat of the sun's rays according to his strength for three days; if thirsty, he should drink thin gruel (peyā).
6.7.164 | One should lance those pustules that arise on a white-leprosy (śvitra) limb with a thorn.
Once the pustules have been drained, one should drink [the remedy] every morning for a fortnight.
6.7.165 | Having boiled *malapū*, *masana*, *priyaṅgu*, and *śatapuṣpā* with water,
or [using] *kṣāra* from the *palāśa* tree mixed with treacle according to one's strength, [one should administer it].
6.7.166 | Whatever else is a destroyer of leprosy (kuṣṭha) is all recommended for vitiligo (śvitra);
or, drinking decoction of khadira combined with khadira-water is the foremost treatment.
6.7.167 | For the purpose of pacifying vitiligo (śvitra), one should apply a plaster consisting of manaḥśilā, viḍaṅga, kāsīsa, rocanā, kanakapuṣpī, and saindhava salt.
