6.7.168 | Or [the powder] made from burnt donkey bone mixed with the alkali of plantain and cow's blood;
or [the powder] of jasmine buds mixed with elephant ichor and alkali.
6.7.169 | Blue lotus with kuṣṭha and rock salt, ground with elephant urine;
or a plaster of radish seeds and avalguja, ground with cow's urine.
6.7.170 | Or *kākodumbarikā* with *avalguja* and *citraka*,
or *manaḥśilā* ground in cow's urine, or combined with peacock bile.
6.7.171 | A medicinal paste consisting of *āvalguja* seeds, lac, cow’s bile,
the two types of collyrium (*añjana*), long pepper (*pippalī*), and iron filings is a destroyer of *kilāsa* (leucoderma).
6.7.172 | White leprosy (śvitra) is cured only in some rare cases by purification, bloodletting, and the administration of parched grain flour (saktu),
provided that the person's sins have been exhausted.
6.7.173 | Dāruṇa, cāruṇa, and śvitra—known by these three names—is to be understood as a threefold disease; it is generally caused by the three doṣas.

6.7.174 | When the *doṣa* is located in the blood, the *śvitra* is red; when it has reached the muscle tissue (*māṃsa*), it is copper-colored; when it has reached the fat (*medas*), it is white. This [condition] becomes increasingly heavy as it progresses to each subsequent layer.
6.7.175 | That which is not distinct from one another, which is extensive and characterized by reddish hair,
and which has arisen over many years— that *śvitra* (leucoderma) is never cured.
6.7.176 | That *śvitra* (leukoderma) which has hair of its natural color, is thin, pale, not long-standing,
and swollen in the center is said to be curable.
6.7.177 | False speech, ingratitude, reviling the gods, and the humiliation of one's teacher;
sinful deeds and actions performed in the past are the causes of leprosy (*kilāsa*), as is food that is incompatible [with one's constitution].

6.7.178 | Regarding this, there are these verses: The etiology, the substances, the various signs, those which are the predominant doshas in each of the skin diseases (kuṣṭhas), the signs of the doshas in kuṣṭhas, and the summary description of the doshas [have been explained].
6.7.179 | Curable, incurable, and difficult-to-cure leprosy (kuṣṭha), the formulations that destroy leprosy,
the proven causes of vitiligo (kilāsa), its symptoms, their severity or mildness, and likewise their pacification.
6.7.180 | Thus has this summary been composed by the Great Sage in the chapter on the destruction of leprosy,
for the sake of increasing the memory and intelligence of his disciple Hutāśaveśa.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Kuṣṭha," in the Cikitsāsthāna of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Eight:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of rājayakṣman (consumption).
6.8.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.8.3 | An ancient tale concerning the Moon, connected with his addiction to passion, was heard by the sages as they were recounting it to the inhabitants of heaven.
6.8.4 | The body of the Moon, who was excessively attached to Rohiṇī and failed to protect his own person,
reached a state of emaciation due to the exhaustion of his essence.
6.8.5 | Because his daughters were not being enjoyed, and because of the remaining [beings],
the anger of Prajāpati issued forth from his mouth in embodied form as a breath.
6.8.6 | For the Moon (Aṃśumān) accepted twenty-eight daughters of Prajāpati as wives, yet he did not behave equally toward all of them.
6.8.7 | Consumed by his preceptor’s curse, unable to control his wife,
and overwhelmed by passion, the weak Śaśin was seized by consumption.
6.8.8 | Overwhelmed by that exceedingly great and heavy wrath, and rendered lusterless,
he went for refuge to his preceptor, accompanied by the gods and celestial sages.
6.8.9 | Then, having perceived the pure intention of the Moon, Prajāpati bestowed his favor; thereupon Soma was treated by the Aśvins.
6.8.10 | Released from the planet's grasp, the moon shone with particular brilliance;
strengthened by the vital energy of the Aśvins, it attained a state of pure essence.

6.8.11 | Anger, consumption (yakṣmā), fever, and disease are synonymous terms for that which is designated as suffering. Because it first afflicted the king, it is therefore considered "royal consumption" (rājayakṣmā).
6.8.12 | That Yakṣman, having been rebuked by the Aśvins, came to the world of men;
having found a fourfold cause, it enters into human beings.
6.8.13 | One should know that undertaking activities beyond one's strength, suppressing natural urges, emaciation,
and irregular eating are the four causes of consumption (yakṣman).
6.8.14 | Through fighting, study, carrying burdens, walking long distances, leaping, and so forth;
or through falls, blows, or other such acts of violence.
6.8.15 | When a person undertakes activities beyond their strength, the chest becomes wounded;
the provoked Vāyu then agitates both Doshas and rushes forward.
6.8.16 | Located in the head, it causes headache; when it has taken refuge in the throat, it causes constriction of the throat, cough, hoarseness of voice, and loss of appetite.
6.8.17 | When located in the sides, it causes pain in the flanks; when situated in the rectum, it causes diarrhea;
when located in the joints, it causes yawning and fever; and when situated in the chest, it causes pain in the chest.
6.8.18 | With a parched chest due to coughing, he spits phlegm mixed with blood;
with a shattered chest, he suffers with difficulty, oppressed by severe pain in the chest.
6.8.19 | Thus the rash disease (yakṣmā) manifests through these eleven forms; therefore, one who knows the self should avoid rashness.
6.8.20 | When a man, out of modesty, or out of disgust, or out of fear, suppresses the impulse that has arisen for flatus, urine, or feces;
6.8.21 | Then, by the obstruction of its momentum, the wind (vāyu), agitating the phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta),
produces disorders in the upward, transverse, and downward directions.
6.8.22 | It cures catarrh, cough, hoarseness of voice,
loss of appetite, pain in the sides, headache, fever, and aching in the shoulders.
6.8.23 | Body aches, frequent vomiting, and diarrhea— these eleven symptoms, characterized by these three features, are by which the great disease known as *yakṣman* (consumption) is described.
6.8.24 | Due to excessive emaciation caused by envy, longing, fear, terror, anger, and grief,
as well as from excessive sexual indulgence and fasting, semen and *ojas* are depleted.
6.8.25 | Thereafter, due to the depletion of the unctuous element (sneha), the aggravated vāyu excites the [other] doshas,
causing coryza, fever, cough, body ache, and headache.
It produces these eleven diseases: dyspnea, diarrhea, loss of appetite, pain in the sides, loss of voice, and burning sensation in the shoulders.
6.8.27 | These eleven symptoms indicate that the great disease Rajayakshma (kingly consumption), which causes the destruction of life through wasting, has arrived.
6.8.28 | When one consumes various kinds of food and drink in an irregular manner,
the Vāyu and other humors become disturbed and produce terrible diseases.
6.8.29 | When the channels of blood and the other elements become irregular due to imbalance, they become obstructed;
this leads to disease, and the bodily tissues (dhātus) can no longer thrive.
6.8.30 | It [treats] catarrh, excessive salivation, cough, vomiting,
loss of appetite, fever, burning pain in the shoulders, and the vomiting of blood.
6.8.31 | One should recognize the symptoms caused by phlegm, bile, and wind respectively as: pain in the sides, headache, and hoarseness of voice.
6.8.32 | Thus, the elevenfold manifestation arising from the causes of the king of diseases— the collection of all maladies— and the fourfold cause have been described.
6.8.33 | Premonitory symptoms include catarrh, debility,
the appearance of morbid humors even when they are not present, and a loathsome appearance of the body.
6.8.34 | There is also a sense of loathing while eating, a wasting away of strength and flesh,
a fondness for women, wine, and meat, and a desire for being veiled.
6.8.35 | Flies, woodworms, hair, and bits of grass frequently fall into food and drink; likewise, there is an excessive growth of hair and nails.
6.8.36 | Being attacked by birds, insects, and beasts of prey;
and in a dream, climbing upon heaps of hair, bones, food, or ashes.
6.8.37 | The sight of reservoirs of water, mountains, forests, and even of celestial bodies, as they wither away, waste away, or fall— this too is such a sight.
6.8.38 | The premonitory symptoms of the multiform disease known as rājayakṣman should be understood;
I shall now describe its specific symptoms along with their remedies, according to their classification.
6.8.39 | Just as the bodily tissues undergo maturation by their respective heat,
so too does each tissue nourish the [subsequent] tissue through its own respective channel.
6.8.40 | Due to the obstruction of the channels, the depletion of blood and other elements,
and the diminution of the bodily tissues and their metabolic heat, consumption (rājayakṣmā) arises.
6.8.41 | At that time, whatever food situated in the stomach is digested by the fire, it mostly becomes waste; only a small portion is fit for the vital essence (*ojas*).
6.8.42 | Therefore, the feces must be preserved, especially in one suffering from rājayakṣman;
for one afflicted by the depletion of all bodily constituents, strength indeed resides in the strength of the stool.
6.8.43 | When the channels are obstructed, the rasa, remaining in its own location, becomes inflamed;
it then flows upward with the force of coughing in many forms.
6.8.44 | Furthermore, from this [state of imbalance], either six or eleven diseases arise;
through their combination, they are designated as *rājayakṣman*.
6.8.45 | Bronchial asthma, lack of heat, loss of voice, fever, pain in the sides and head,
vomiting of blood and phlegm, dyspnea, constipation, and anorexia.
6.8.46 | These are the eleven forms of *yakṣman*, or these six:
cough, fever, pain in the flanks, impairment of voice and stool, and loss of appetite.

6.8.47 | When all three types of signs, or even two, are present due to the depletion of muscle and strength, the patient should be rejected; however, if it is otherwise, he may be treated even if all symptoms are present.
6.8.48 | Phlegm, blood, or even bile situated at the root of the nose flows back toward the wind when the head is distended by the vital air (vāyu).
6.8.49 | Thereafter, a terrible catarrh arises, emaciating the body;
its symptoms are headache, heaviness, and impairment of the sense of smell.
6.8.50 | Fever, cough, aggravation of phlegm, hoarseness of voice, loss of appetite, exhaustion,
and impairment of the sense organs— consumption (yakṣmā) arises from these.
6.8.51 | A patient suffering from consumption coughs up sputum that is slimy, thick, foul-smelling, greenish, or whitish-yellow, accompanied by phlegm.
6.8.52 | Burning pain in the shoulders and sides, heat in the hands and feet,
and fever affecting the entire body— these are the symptoms of rājayakṣman (consumption).

6.8.53 | Hoarseness of voice arises from wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), blood (rakta), the force of coughing, or chronic catarrh (sapīnasa). From wind, the voice becomes dry, thin, and unstable.
6.8.54 | From pitta, there is a burning sensation in the palate and throat, and one is unable to speak;
from kapha, there is a splitting pain, the voice is obstructed, and it makes a "khura-khura" sound.
6.8.55 | In the *sanna* type of hoarseness, the voice issues with difficulty due to the obstruction by blood;
it is harsh from excessive coughing, and associated with phlegm and wind (*kaphavātika*) due to chronic catarrh (*pīnasa*).
6.8.56 | Furthermore, for one afflicted by *yakṣman*, there may be shifting pain in the sides characterized by contraction and expansion,
as well as headache accompanied by a burning sensation and heaviness.
6.8.57 | When the body of a patient suffering from consumption (yakṣman) is afflicted by irregular diet,
blood flows from the throat and phlegm, having been provoked and accumulated, follows suit.
6.8.58 | Because its passage is obstructed, the blood does not reach the muscles and other tissues;
remaining in the stomach and being provoked by its abundance, it rises up to the throat.
6.8.59 | Due to the obstruction of wind and phlegm, the patient suffers from dyspnea;
and when the digestive fire is impaired by the humors, he passes stools mixed with mucus.
6.8.60 | Anorexia arises from the humors (doṣas) individually or combined when they are localized in the tongue and the heart, as well as from mental objects that are disliked regarding food.

6.8.61 | One should recognize that loss of appetite arising from wind (vāta) and the other humors occurs respectively through bitter, astringent, and sweet tastes in the mouth; whereas mental loss of appetite arises from the perception of defects [in food].
6.8.62 | Vomiting that occurs due to loss of appetite, the force of a cough, the provocation of the humors (doṣas), or even fear,
is a complication of other diseases as well.

6.8.63 | Consumption (yakṣmā) arises from all three doṣas; however, the physician, having examined the relative strength and weakness of the doṣas as well as the stage of the disease, should treat the patient suffering from wasting (śoṣin).
6.8.64 | Listen now to the various general therapeutic measures for chronic rhinitis, headache, cough, dyspnea, loss of voice, and pain in the flanks.
6.8.65 | In cases of chronic catarrh (pīnasa), one should employ fomentation, massage, medicated smoking, and external plasters;
as well as affusions, immersions, barley gruel, and barley-based foods.
6.8.66 | One should prepare the savory juices of the common quail, partridge, wild cock, and grey partridge, enriched with fats and made salty, sour, pungent, and hot.
6.8.67 | One should drink the unctuous goat broth, accompanied by long pepper, barley, horse gram,
and ginger, and combined with pomegranate and āmalaka.
6.8.68 | By means of that, the six disorders beginning with chronic catarrh (pīnasa) are eliminated;
or by means of soups prepared from radishes or horse gram (kulattha).
6.8.69 | One should treat the patient with barley, wheat, or rice-based foods according to what is suitable for them;
or they should drink the clear supernatant of *vāruṇī* wine, or water boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūla*).
6.8.70 | Or one may prepare foods with rice cooked in ginger-water, or boiled with *tāmalakī*, or with the four *parṇī* herbs; and with that [decoction], one should prepare the meals.
6.8.71 | With *kṛśara*, *utkārikā*, mung beans (*māṣa*), horse gram (*kulattha*), barley, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
one should treat the throat, sides, chest, and head according to the procedure for mixed fomentation (*saṃkarasveda*).
6.8.72 | One should cause [the patient] to sweat by means of leaf-poultices and sprinkle the head with lukewarm water boiled with *balā*, *guḍūcī*, and *madhuka*.
6.8.73 | Or one should apply tube-sudation (nāḍīsveda) using the heads of a goat or a fish;
or, for the throat, head, and sides, one may use milks mixed with Vāta-alleviating substances.
6.8.74 | One should employ the meat of aquatic and marshy animals, water infused with the five roots (pañcamūla), or sour gruel (āranāla) mixed with fat, for nāḍīsveda (tube-fomentation).
6.8.75 | Of jīvantī, śatapuṣpā, balā, and madhuka;
of vacā, veśavāra, vidārī, and mūlaka.
6.8.76 | Well-prepared poultices made from the meat of aquatic and marshy animals,
combined with the four unctuous substances (catuḥsneha), are recommended for those suffering from pain in the head, sides, and shoulders.
6.8.77 | A plaster consisting of śatapuṣpā, madhuka, kuṣṭha, tagara, and candana,
mixed with ghee, relieves pain in the head and the sides of the body.
6.8.78 | Balā, rāsnā, sesame seeds, ghee, madhuka, blue lotus,
guggulu, devadāru, sandalwood, keśara, and ghee.
6.8.79 | Vīrā, balā, vidārī, kṛṣṇagandhā, punarnavā, śatāvarī, payasyā, kattṛṇa, madhuka, and ghee.

6.8.80 | These four applications (pradehas) have been proclaimed in half-verses; they are recommended for those with mixed humors (doṣas) and for those suffering from pain in the head, sides, and shoulders.
6.8.81 | Nasal drops, medicinal smokes, oleation therapies to be taken after meals,
oils for massage, and likewise enema therapy (basti-karma).
6.8.82 | If blood is vitiated by a horn, a water-lily, or a leech, or by venesection,
one should extract that blood in cases of pain in the head, sides, or shoulders.
6.8.83 | An external application (pradeha) with ghee is desired, made from padmaka, uśīra, and candana;
or alternatively, from dūrvā, madhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, and keśara, saturated with ghee.
6.8.84 | *Prapauṇḍarīka, nirguṇḍī, lotus stamen, blue lotus, kaśerukā, and payasyā, mixed with clarified butter, form a medicinal paste.
Anointing with oil prepared from sandalwood and other ingredients, or with clarified butter washed a hundred times,
as well as sprinkling with milk or water infused with licorice (madhuka), is recommended.

6.8.86 | A sprinkling (pariṣeka) with very cold Māhendraka water, or with water boiled with sandalwood and other [medicinal herbs], should be employed; this is the pacifying treatment (saṃśamanī kriyā).

6.8.87 | For those in whom the humors (doṣas) are predominant, emesis along with purgation is recommended, provided they have been prepared with oleation and sudation; [this applies when] the treatment is unctuous yet not emaciating.

6.8.88 | A person suffering from consumption loses his limbs even from the mere discharge of feces; how much more so one who undergoes purgation, especially when it requires consideration for his weakness?

6.8.89 | These proven formulations should be administered for cough, dyspnea, loss of voice, and pain in the head, flanks, and shoulders, to those whose internal channels have been thoroughly purified by medicinal enemas.

6.8.90 | Clarified butter prepared with balā, vidārigandhā, and others, or with vidārī and madhuka, along with salt, should be used as a nasal medication (nasya); it is excellent for restoring the voice.
6.8.91 | Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, pippalī, bṛhatī, and balā,
prepared with milk and ghee— this excellent nasal medication (nāvana) is beneficial for the voice.
6.8.92 | Ghee taken frequently after meals alleviates pain in the head, sides, and shoulders, and subdues cough and dyspnea.
Ghee prepared with the ten roots (*daśamūla*), milk,
and meat broth, containing *balā* within it, immediately overcomes these diseases.
6.8.94 | Either Rāsnā-ghṛta mixed with milk, or Balā-ghṛta mixed with milk, should be administered over or during the meal, according to the strength of the digestive fire.

6.8.95 | Now hear further concerning linctuses that cure cough, improve the voice, and eliminate dyspnea and hiccups, as well as unctuous preparations that alleviate pain in the head, flanks, and shoulders.
6.8.96 | Ghee combined with dates, raisins, sugar, honey,
and long pepper cures disorders of the voice, cough, dyspnea, and fever.
6.8.97 | The fresh ghee that rises from milk boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla),
taken with long pepper and honey, is the supreme restorer of the voice.
6.8.98 | Ghee prepared with the five groups of five roots (pañcamūlas) destroys pain in the head, sides, and shoulders, and removes cough, dyspnea, and fever.
6.8.99 | Ghee prepared with the decoction of the five groups of five roots (*pañcamūla*) and four times the amount of milk conquers the sevenfold strength of consumption (*yakṣman*).
6.8.100 | Date, long pepper, grapes, chebulic myrobalan, karkaṭa-śṛṅgī, dūrvā,
the three myrobalans, long pepper, musta, water chestnut, jaggery, and sugar.
6.8.101 | Vīrā, śaṭī, the plant known as puṣkara, surasa, sugar, jaggery, nāgara, citraka, parched grain, pippalī, āmalaka, and jaggery.
6.8.102 | One should lick these [medicines] prescribed in half-verse units with honey and clarified butter;
they cure cough and dyspnea, improve the voice, and likewise alleviate pain in the flanks.

6.8.103 | One should have the patient lick a linctus made of sugar-candy, *tugākṣīrī*, long pepper, *bahulā*, and cinnamon bark, each subsequent ingredient being double the quantity of the preceding one, mixed with honey and ghee.
6.8.104 | Or one should have that powder consumed by a patient suffering from dyspnea, cough, and phlegm,
as well as by one with a paralyzed tongue, loss of appetite, weak digestion, and pain in the flanks.
6.8.105 | In cases of burning sensations in the hands, feet, and limbs, as well as in fever, blood disorders, and upward-moving hemorrhages,
ghee prepared with vāsā or with śatāvarī is supremely beneficial.
6.8.106 | Having taken one pala each of durālabhā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, the four types of parṇinī, and balā, as well as one pala of parpaṭaka;
6.8.107 | One should boil [the drugs] in ten times their quantity of water until one-tenth remains;
once the decoction is well-strained, one should add the pastes (kalka) of these substances.
6.8.108 | Of *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *pippalī* and *trāyamāṇā*, of *tāmalakī*, the *kirātas*, *tikta*, and *kuṭaja*;
6.8.109 | Then one should cook one *prastha* of ghee with twice as much milk, along with one *karṣa* each of well-ground fruits and *sārivā*.
This ghee cures fever, burning sensations, vertigo, cough, pain in the shoulders, flanks, and head, as well as thirst, vomiting, and diarrhea.
6.8.111 | Jīvantī, madhuka, drākṣā, and the fruits of kuṭaja;
śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, vyāghrī, gokṣuraka, and balā.
6.8.112 | Having ground blue lotus, tāmalakī, trāyamāṇā, kurālabhā,
and long pepper in equal proportions, the physician should cook ghee with them.
This foremost ghee dispels the elevenfold manifestation that has arisen from this collection of diseases, the Lord of Disease.
6.8.114 | Having prepared a decoction of balā, sthirā, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, and snidigdhikā, one should add cow's milk along with nāgara to that liquid.
6.8.115 | One should employ this [milk] boiled together with grapes, dates, ghee, and long pepper, along with honey; it destroys fever and cough and is beneficial for the voice.
6.8.116 | Likewise, preparations of goat’s meat and milk, as well as the juices of wild animals, are used;
and for the purpose of soups, chickpeas, mung beans, and lentils are prepared.
6.8.117 | That therapeutic procedure for the pacification of fevers which was previously described is recommended,
along with ghee, for the fever and burning sensations of those afflicted by consumption (yakṣman).
6.8.118 | When there is excessive secretion of phlegm, a strong person of phlegmatic constitution should induce vomiting with milk mixed with Madanaphala, or with honeyed meat broth.
6.8.119 | Having been made to vomit with gruel mixed with ghee or prepared with emetic drugs, the patient,
once vomited, should at the time of eating take light food that promotes digestion.
6.8.120 | By consuming barley, wheat, honey-wine (*mādhvīka*), *sidhu*, *ariṣṭa*, *surā*, and *āsava* liquors, as well as roasted meats from arid regions (*jāṅgala*) on spits, one conquers *kapha*.
6.8.121 | Due to excessive secretion of phlegm, the wind (vāyu) expels the phlegm;
the wise physician should conquer that excessive flow of kapha with unctuous and warm treatments alone.
6.8.122 | Whatever treatment is recommended for vomiting is also praised for excessive salivation caused by kapha;
likewise, foods and drinks that are pleasing to the heart, pacify vāta, and are light [are beneficial].
6.8.123 | Generally, due to the impairment of the digestive fire (agni), one suffers from diarrhea accompanied by mucus;
he experiences a bad taste in the mouth and takes no pleasure in food.
6.8.124 | One should prepare formulations that kindle the digestive fire, eliminate diarrhea,
cleanse the mouth, and counteract anorexia.
One should cause [the patient] to drink a prepared gruel (yavāgū) containing long pepper (nāgara) and indrayava with rice-water;
once that has been digested, [he should take it] with cāṅgerī, sour gruel (takra), and pomegranate (dāḍima).
6.8.126 | Pāṭhā, bilva, and yamānī should be drunk combined with buttermilk (takra);
likewise, durālabhā, śṛṅgavera, and pāṭhā should be taken together with wine (surā).
6.8.127 | Jambu, mango, bilva, kapittha, and ginger—
these should be drunk with the scum of gruel (maṇḍa) for the cessation of diarrhea.
6.8.128 | Furthermore, one should have these same three preparations— beginning with the *pāṭha*— prepared as *khaḍas*,
containing pulses and grains, along with fats, sours, and being highly astringent.
6.8.129 | The tender shoots of the *vetasa*, *arjuna*, and *jambu* trees; of *mṛṇālī* and *kṛṣṇagandhā*; and of *śrīparṇī*, *madayantī*, and *yūthikā*.
6.8.130 | One should prepare *khaḍas* from *mātuluṅga*, *dhātakī*, and *dāḍima*, enriched with fats, sours, and salts; these are excellent for checking diarrhea.
6.8.131 | One should cause [the patient] to eat *khaḍa* preparations made from *cāṅgerī*, *cukrikā*, and *dugdhikā*,
combined with curd-whey (*dadhisara*), clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), and pomegranate (*dāḍima*).
6.8.132 | The juices of meats that are easily digested, combined with astringent (saṃgrāhika) substances,
are recommended as side dishes, while red śāli rice is recommended as the main food.
6.8.133 | Water boiled with the five roots beginning with *sthira* is recommended for drinking;
likewise, buttermilk, wine, *cukrikā*, or the juice of pomegranate.
Thus has been described the digestive and astringent medicine for those with loose stools;
now hear about that which is supreme for destroying bad taste in the mouth and for promoting relish.
6.8.135 | One should chew a tooth-cleansing stick and rinse the mouth twice a day;
likewise, one should wash the mouth and hold gargles.

6.8.136 | Thereafter, one should smoke the medicated fumes; then, one should eat wholesome food that is appetizing and promotes digestion, along with medicine, drink, and food that are beneficial and prepared according to one's preference.
6.8.137 | Tvak, musta, and elā; the grains; musta, āmalaka, and tvak; dārvītvaca, yavānī, tejohvā, and likewise pippalī.
6.8.138 | Yavānī and tintiḍīka— these five,
mentioned in the quarters of the verse, are mouth-washes that brighten the face and cleanse the mouth.
6.8.139 | One should hold a pill in the mouth, or cleanse the mouth with powders;
or one should hold gargles made by mixing these [substances] together.
6.8.140 | One should hold in the mouth the desired boluses of *surā*, *mādhvīka*, and *sīdhu* liquors; of oil, honey, and clarified butter; and of milk and sugarcane juice.
6.8.141 | One should prepare one karṣa each of yavānī, tintiḍīka, nāgara, sour vetasa,
pomegranate, and sour jujube.
6.8.142 | One half-kārṣika each of dhānyaka, sauvarcala salt, ajājī, and varāṅga;
one hundred pippalīs and two hundred maricas.
6.8.143 | One should grind four palas of sugar together into a powder;
that powder cleanses the tongue, is pleasing to the heart, and stimulates the appetite for food.
It destroys pain in the heart, spleen, and flanks; it removes constipation and flatulence;
it cures cough and dyspnea; it is astringent; and it alleviates disorders of the digestive tract and hemorrhoids.
Thus ends the Yavānī-ṣāḍava (6.8.145). Tālīśapatra, marica, nāgara, pippalī, and śubhā [are taken] with each succeeding ingredient increased by one part; tvak and elā are each half a part.
6.8.146 | And here, white sugar should be added in eight times the quantity of long pepper;
that powder is an excellent stimulant of digestion and removes cough, dyspnea, and anorexia.

6.8.147 | It cures heart disease, anemia, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, consumption, splenic enlargement, and fever; it destroys vomiting, diarrhea, and colic, and facilitates the downward movement of obstructed wind.
6.8.148 | One should prepare pills by cooking this powder with sugar-candy;
for indeed, through contact with fire, pills are considered lighter than the powder.
Thus ends the section on the Tālīśādya powder and pills (6.8.149). One who knows the proper procedure should administer these to those who are wasting away and whose flesh has been depleted;
in particular, one should give them the flesh of carnivorous animals for nourishment.

6.8.150 | One should give a peacock to a sufferer of consumption, and other birds— vultures, owls, and blue jays— prepared as side dishes according to the rules, using the word "barhis" (sacrificial grass).
6.8.151 | One should give crows under the name of partridges, snakes under the name of "armored" (varmin),
roasted fish under the name of "entrails," and even earthworms.
6.8.152 | A physician should cause foxes, large mongooses, cats, and jackals, when prepared for consumption, to be given under the name of "hares."
6.8.153 | One should offer lions, bears, hyenas, wolves, tigers, and other such flesh-eating animals under the name of "deer," for the sake of increasing the quantity of meat.
6.8.154 | A physician should give the meat of elephants, rhinoceroses, and horses, prepared as *veśavāra*,
under the name of buffalo meat for the purpose of increasing muscle mass.
6.8.155 | For those whose limbs are emaciated by lack of flesh, meat is the supreme means for building up flesh;
it is especially recommended for wild animals and birds because of its sharpness, heat, and lightness.
6.8.156 | Regarding those meats which, due to lack of practice, one finds undesirable to consume, one should apply a preliminary preparation (*upadhā*); for in that way, they can be eaten with ease.
6.8.157 | Knowing [the nature of the meat], one should not eat it while feeling disgust; nor should one vomit it up after it has been eaten.
Therefore, one should cause these meats to be prepared in a concealed manner.
6.8.158 | The meat of the peacock, partridge, and cock, as well as that of swans, boars, camels, donkeys, cows, and buffaloes, is the most effective for increasing flesh.
6.8.159 | Eight types of meat are said to be suitable for food and drink;
having examined them, a learned physician should prescribe these meats for one suffering from consumption.
6.8.160 | Carnivorous animals, land-dwellers, marsh-dwellers, aquatic creatures, and water-fowls should be given in appropriate measure for food to one suffering from consumption caused by Vāta.
6.8.161 | Birds that peck, those that scatter grain, and wild animals and birds born in arid regions should be administered to those afflicted by consumption who are overwhelmed by phlegm and bile.
6.8.162 | One should eat these meats, which have been properly prepared with condiments, and are pleasing, tender, flavorful, and fragrant.
For one who eats only meat, for one who drinks even *mādhvīka* wine,
and for one of uncontrolled and undisciplined mind, life does not long remain in the body.
6.8.164 | Consumption finds no opportunity for an opening in one who constantly drinks the scum of *vāruṇī* wine, who practices external cleansing, and who does not suppress natural urges.
6.8.165 | While eating meats, one should drink, as appropriate for the purpose of a post-prandial draught (anupāna), prasannā, vāruṇī, sīdhu, ariṣṭa, āsava, or honey-wine (madhu).
6.8.166 | Due to its sharpness, heat, clarity, and subtlety, liquor quickly agitates and opens the openings of the channels; through that release, the seven tissues [are affected].
6.8.167 | Because they nourish the bodily tissues (dhātus), consumption (śoṣa) is quickly pacified;
one should employ ghee prepared with the meat-juice of carnivorous animals.
6.8.168 | Ghee prepared with honey and ten times the amount of milk,
or ghee prepared with drugs of the sweet group and decoctions of the ten roots (daśamūla).
6.8.169 | Ghee prepared with milk, meat broth, and [the paste of] pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, and nāgara is the supreme remedy for consumption (śoṣa).
6.8.170 | Ghee prepared with *yavaśūka*, milk, and [the paste of] *rāsnā*, *balā*, *gokṣuraka*, *sthirā*, and *varṣābhū* is a purifier of the channels (*srotas*).
6.8.171 | Ghee extracted from milk containing *jīvantī* and *pippalī* cures consumption;
one should drink an appropriate dose of it with barley gruel or lick it together with honey.
6.8.172 | One should consume these prepared ghees either with food or by themselves; this is the prescribed regimen for their internal administration for those who are emaciated.
6.8.173 | Hereafter, the procedure based on external massage will be described: one should cause the patient, having been well-anointed, to immerse themselves in vats filled with oil, milk, or water.

6.8.174 | For the purpose of releasing the obstruction of the channels and for the sake of strength and nourishment, [the patient] should be treated with mixed unctuous substances after having been lifted up, and then gently massaged with the hands once more.
6.8.175 | One should easily crush the man as he sits comfortably and easily uproot him,
along with jīvantī, śatavīryā, vikasā, and punarnavā.
6.8.176 | Aśvagandhā, apāmārga, tarkārī, madhuka,
balā, vidārī, mustard seeds, kuṣṭha, rice grains, and the fruit of atasī;
6.8.177 | One should grind together all of these— māṣa beans, sesame seeds, and fermenting agent (kiṇva)—
along with three times as much barley flour, and mix it with curd and honey.
6.8.178 | This massage should be performed with a paste of white mustard seeds or with fragrant pastes; it bestows nourishment, complexion, and strength.
6.8.179 | He should bathe in waters pleasant for the season, boiled with life-sustaining herbs;
and he should be adorned with perfumes, garlands, garments, and ornaments.
6.8.180 | Having touched those things that ought to be touched, and having worshipped the deities along with the physicians and the twice-born,
one should partake of food and drink possessing desirable color, taste, touch, and fragrance.
6.8.181 | One should eat the desired food, prepared with desired ingredients, which bestows happiness;
grains that have been stored for a year should be provided for those who are emaciated.
6.8.182 | Those which are light, not deficient in potency, sweet, fragrant,
and exhilarating are indeed most wholesome.

6.8.183 | Furthermore, whatever wholesome regimen is prescribed in the treatment of chest wounds and emaciation should be employed for the patient suffering from consumption, in order to increase strength and flesh.
6.8.184 | By means of oil massages and body rubs, with new and pleasing garments, with baths prescribed for each season, with plunges into water, and with dry cleansings;
6.8.185 | By means of enemas containing milk and ghee, meats, meat soups, and rice;
by means of desired wines and the enjoyment of pleasing fragrances.
6.8.186 | By the sight of friends and beautiful women,
and by the sounds of singing and musical instruments, as well as by things pleasant to hear;
6.8.187 By constantly gladdening and consoling [others], by attending upon one's gurus,
by celibacy, by giving gifts, by austerity, and by the worship of the deities;
6.8.188 | By truthfulness, by the practice of right conduct, by auspicious things, by non-violence,
and by the honoring of physicians and Brahmins, the king of diseases is dispelled.
6.8.189 | One who desires health should perform that sacrifice ordained by the Vedas, by means of which activity the King of Consumption (rājayakṣmā) was formerly conquered.

6.8.190 | Regarding this, there are two verses:— The origin, the causes, the premonitory symptoms, and the manifestation of the form, as well as the medicine for rājayakṣman, have been stated both in brief and in detail.
6.8.191 | Non-treatment due to the cause, incurability, and curability with difficulty—
thus has the entire summary been stated regarding the treatment of *rājayakṣman*.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Rajayakshma (Phthisis)," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agnivesha and redacted by Charaka.
The Ninth Chapter:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of Unmada (insanity).
6.9.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.9.3 | Punarvasu, the abode of Buddhist mindfulness, knowledge, and austerity, and the refuge for all living beings,
being questioned by Agniveśa, explained at the appropriate time the causes, symptoms, and medicines for insanity.
6.9.4 | Incompatible, spoiled, or unclean foods; the assault of gods, teachers, or the twice-born;
mental trauma preceded by fear or joy; and irregular activities—these are the causes of insanity.
6.9.5 | When the impurities of one with little fortitude are provoked, they corrupt the heart— the seat of the intellect— and,
having taken hold of the channels that carry the mind, they swiftly delude the person's consciousness.
6.9.6 | Confusion of intellect, agitation of the mind, a distracted gaze, lack of composure,
incoherent speech, and a vacant heart— these are the general symptoms of the disease of insanity.
6.9.7 | That person of deluded mind finds neither happiness nor sorrow, nor right conduct or duty, much less peace;
with his memory, intellect, and consciousness cast away, he wanders here and there with a distracted mind.
6.9.8 | They say that unmāda (insanity) is a total derangement of the intellect, mind, and memory, arising either from external causes or from one's own [internal] factors.
I shall describe its fivefold origin, as well as its specific symptoms and treatment, separately.
6.9.9 | When vāyu is excessively aggravated by dry, scanty, or cold food, purgation, depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus),
or fasting, it vitiates the heart— which is already afflicted by anxiety and other such factors— and swiftly impairs both the intellect and memory.
6.9.10 | Inappropriate laughter, smiling, dancing, singing, tossing of the limbs, and weeping;
as well as roughness, emaciation, and a reddish complexion—these, along with strength, are the symptoms of [fever] born from Vāta when it has become chronic.
6.9.11 | Pitta, accumulated by foods that are undigested, pungent, sour, burning, and cold, and having its impulse intensified,
quickly brings about extremely violent insanity in one who lacks self-control, taking refuge in the heart as described previously.
6.9.12 | Intolerance, agitation, a state of nakedness, threats, excessive running, heat, and anger;
a desire for shade, cold food, and water; and a yellowish complexion—these are the signs of that which is produced by pitta.
6.9.13 | When kapha, accompanied by heat, increases in a vital organ (marman) due to over-satiation and sluggish physical activity,
it impairs the intellect and memory, deludes the mind, and gives rise to a disorder.
6.9.14 | Slow speech and movement, loss of appetite, a fondness for women and solitude,
excessive sleep, vomiting, salivation, strength, and whiteness of the nails and other parts characterize the [patient] whose nature is dominated by phlegm (kapha).
6.9.15 | That which arises from the combination [of all three doshas], being extremely severe, may occur through all the causes combined;
it manifests all symptoms and, possessing such contradictory therapeutic requirements, must be avoided.
6.9.16 | Assaults by gods, sages, gandharvas, piśācas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and ancestors;
adventitious causes such as violations of rules and vows; and actions performed wrongly in a previous body.
6.9.17 | He whose speech, prowess, heroism, and actions are immortal, who possesses knowledge, higher cognition, strength, and so forth,
and whose onset of madness is unpredictable— that one should be declared a *bhūta-uttha* (possession-induced) case of insanity.
6.9.18 | Without defiling the body of the person, the gods and others enter it by means of their own qualities and powers,
remaining invisible and moving with speed, just as a shadow enters a mirror or light enters a sun-crystal.
6.9.19 | For that period of onset is declared in the *Nidāna* [section] by the gods and others to be the premonitory stage (*pūrvarūpa*).
Now, learn separately the symptoms of insanity (*unmāda*), its duration, and the types of persons susceptible to it.

6.9.20 | For example—one should recognize a person as "god-intoxicated" (devonmatta) if they have a gentle gaze, are profound, unassailable, and free from anger; do not desire sleep, food, or drink; have little perspiration, urine, feces, or wind; possess a pleasant fragrance; and have a face like a blooming lotus. One should recognize a person as intoxicated by [the influence of] gurus, elders, perfected sages (siddhas), or seers (ṛṣis) if their movements, diet, and speech correspond to the curses, malevolent rites, or meditations directed at them by those individuals. One should recognize a person as "intoxicated by the ancestors" (pitṛ-unmatta) if they have a displeased gaze, do not look [at others], are timid, have obstructed speech, have no desire for food, and are overcome by loss of appetite and indigestion.

One should recognize a Gandharva-possessed person as being fierce, reckless, sharp, profound, and unassailable, delighting in mouth-instruments, dancing, singing, food, drink, bathing, garlands, incense, and perfumes, fond of red garments, sacrificial offerings, laughter, and storytelling, and possessing a pleasant fragrance. One should recognize a Yakṣa-possessed person by frequent dreaming, weeping, and laughing, delighting in dancing, singing, instrumental music, recitation, storytelling, food, drink, bathing, garlands, incense, and perfumes, having bloodshot and rolling eyes, reviling Brahmins and physicians, and speaking in secret.

One should recognize a person as being possessed by a *rākṣasa* if they have lost their sleep, loathe food and drink, remain without nourishment yet possess great strength, crave weapons, blood, flesh, and red garlands, and are prone to threats. One should recognize a person as being possessed by a *brahmarākṣasa* if they are preoccupied with laughter and dancing, harbor hatred and contempt for gods, Brahmins, and physicians, recite hymns, Vedic mantras, and treatises, use wood and other materials [as weapons], and inflict injury upon themselves.

One should recognize a person possessed by a *piśāca* as being insane when his mind is unsettled and finds no stability; when he dances, sings, and laughs; when he speaks incoherently or in broken fragments; when he delights in climbing upon heaps of refuse, dirty streets, rags, grass, stones, and wood; when his voice is cracked and harsh; when he runs about naked; when he does not stay in one place; when he manifests various sufferings; and when his memory is lost.

6.9.21 | And therein, the gods generally assail a man who is pure in conduct, skilled in austerity and Vedic study, on the first day (*pratipad*) and the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) of the lunar fortnight, having observed a vulnerability; the seers (*ṛṣis*) generally [assail] one who frequents bathing places, remains pure, and dwells in solitude, and who is proficient in the sentences of the Dharmaśāstras and the Vedas, on the sixth and the ninth days; the ancestors (*pitṛs*) generally [assail] one who serves his mother, father, teacher, elders, perfected ones (*siddhas*), and preceptors, on the tenth and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) days; and the Gandharvas [assail] one who delights in praise, song, and instrumental music.

Yakṣas generally appear on the twelfth and fourteenth lunar days; they are fond of the scent and garlands of others' wives, are clean in their conduct, possess strength, beauty, pride, and valor, and delight in garlands, ointments, and laughter—they are excessively eloquent and active. On the eleventh and seventh lunar days, [they favor] those who take pleasure in self-study, austerity, observances, fasting, celibacy, devotion to the gods and gurus, yet have fallen away from purity—whether they be Brahmins or non-Brahmins—who claim to be Brahmins, consider themselves heroes, and delight in temples and sporting in water. They generally appear at such times.

On the fifth day of the bright fortnight and during the appearance of the full moon, the Brahmarākṣasas [manifest]; whereas the Rākṣasas and Piśācas generally manifest on the second, third, and eighth days toward those of inferior character, the slanderous, the effeminate, the greedy, and the deceitful. Thus, these eight have been explained as the most prominent among the innumerable grahas.

6.9.22 | However, among all those with abnormal movements, one who raises his hands and, out of violent rage, strikes others or himself without hesitation should be known as incurable. Likewise, one whose eyes are filled with tears, from whom blood issues from the urethra, whose tongue is wounded, whose nose is running, whose skin is being torn, whose speech is unimpeded, who constantly groans, who is discolored, afflicted by thirst, and foul-smelling—such a person should be known as one insane with a desire for violence; he should be avoided.

6.9.23 | Having understood that [the patient] is intoxicated by the desire for sexual pleasure and worship through the physician's observation of their intentions and conduct, he should treat them with a procedure involving mantras and medicinal prescriptions mixed with offerings of their limbs and oblations.
6.9.24 | In this regard, we shall explain the therapeutic regimen for both types of insanity—those caused by endogenous factors and those caused by exogenous factors—both in brief and in detail.
6.9.25 | In insanity caused by Vāta, the physician who knows the distinctions should first administer the internal intake of unctuous substances (sneha).
However, if the channels are obstructed, he should perform mild purification (śodhana) combined with unctuous substances.

6.9.26 | Even when [the disease] arises from kapha and pitta, emesis along with purgation should first be administered to one who has been oleated and sudated; once purified, the regimen of gradual dietary restoration (saṃsarjana-krama) should be followed.

6.9.27 | One should then administer a decoction enema (nirūha), an oil enema (snehabasti), and head-purgation (śirovirecana) according to the specific doshas involved; one should repeat these treatments as necessary.
6.9.28 | When the heart, the sense organs, the head, and the internal cavities have been purified by emesis and other such therapies,
one attains clarity of mind and recovers memory and consciousness.
6.9.29 | For one who is pure but has fallen away from right conduct, strong nasal drops, collyrium,
and physical punishment— which causes agitation of the mind, intellect, and body— are beneficial.
6.9.30 | He who is addicted to misconduct should be bound with very firm, comfortable straps—
devoid of iron, wood, and the like— and confined in a dark cell.
6.9.31 | Threatening, frightening, giving, gladdening, consoling, fear, and wonder— these lead the mind back to its natural state by means of causing forgetfulness.
6.9.32 | Local applications, rubbing, massage, medicated smoking, and the internal consumption of ghee should be employed to awaken the mind, intellect, memory, and consciousness.
6.9.33 | For adventitious [mental disorders], the prescribed treatment consists of drinking clarified butter and so forth, as well as the administration of mantras and other such means.
Therefore, hear now the most proven formulations for the destruction of insanity.
6.9.34 | One āḍhaka of ghee, prepared with two palas each of asafoetida, sauvarcala salt,
and the three pungents (vyoṣa) in four times as much cow urine, is a destroyer of insanity.
6.9.35 | Viśālā, triphalā, kauntī, devadāru, elavāluka, sthirā, nata, the two types of rañjanī, the two types of sārivā, and priyaṅgu.
6.9.36 | Blue lotus, cardamom, mañjiṣṭhā, dantī, pomegranate, keśara,
tālīśapatra, bṛhatī, and fresh flowers of mālatī.
6.9.37 | With these twenty-eight paste ingredients— viḍaṅga, pṛśniparṇī, kuṣṭha, candana, and padmaka— each weighing one akṣa;
6.9.38 | One should properly cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much water;
it is used for epilepsy, fever, cough, consumption, weak digestive fire, and wasting.
6.9.39 | In cases of vātarakta (rheumatic condition), coryza, tertian and quartan fevers,
vomiting, hemorrhoids, dysuria, and those afflicted by visarpa (erysipelas);

6.9.40 | And [it is used] for itching, anemia, insanity, urinary disorders, and poisons; for those whose minds are afflicted by spirits, for those with stammering speech, and for those lacking mental clarity.

6.9.41 | This is recommended for women and for those who are barren; it bestows prosperity, longevity, and strength. It destroys misfortune, sin, and demons, and annihilates all malevolent planetary influences.
6.9.42 | This Kalyāṇaka ghee is excellent for use in the puṃsavana rite.
Thus ends the description of Kalyāṇaka ghee.
Having boiled these same [drugs] beginning with sthirā, twenty-one in number, in water—
6.9.43 | One should cook ghee in that decoction with four times as much milk from a cow that has recently calved,
along with vīrā, ārdramāṣa, kākolī, svayaṃguptā, ṛṣabha, and ṛddhi.
6.9.44 | Together with equal parts of the medicinal pastes (kalkas) of Medā, this is the Great Kalyāṇaka;
it is specifically nourishing and is the supreme remedy for the disorder of the three humors (sannipāta).
Thus ends the Mahākalyāṇaka ghee (6.9.45). [One should take] Jaṭilā, Pūtanā, Keśī, Cāraṭī, Markaṭī, Vacā, Trāyamāṇā, Jayā, Vīrā, Coraka, and Kaṭurohiṇī.
6.9.46 | Vayaḥsthā, śūkarī, chatrā, aticchatrā, palaṅkaṣā,
mahāpuruṣadantā, kāyasthā, and the two types of nākulī.
6.9.47 | Having taken kaṭambharā, vṛścikālī, and sthirā, ghee prepared with these [herbs] destroys quartan fever, insanity, possession by grahas, and epilepsy.
6.9.48 | This ghee, named Mahāpaiśācika, is like nectar; it indeed promotes intelligence and memory, and increases the bodily growth of children.
Thus ends the Mahāpaiśācika ghee. (6.9.49) One hundred bulbs of garlic, thirty fruits of abhayā, one pala each of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa),
one prastha of powdered cow-hide, and two āḍhakas each of cow's milk and urine.
6.9.50 | One should employ a *prastha* measure of aged clarified butter prepared with these [ingredients];
once it has cooled, one should add a *pala* of *hiṅgu* powder and a *māṇikā* of honey.

6.9.51 | It quickly destroys unmādas (insanities) arising from those [mental] defects or from exogenous causes, as well as irregular fevers and epileptic seizures, by means of internal potions, external anointments, and nasal drops.
Thus ends the garlic-based ghee (laśunādya-ghṛta).
[6.9.52] One should boil half a *tula* of undecayed garlic, dehusked,
along with half that amount of *daśamūla*, in two *āḍhakas* of water.
6.9.53 | One prastha of ghee, along with the juice of garlic,
and the juices of kola, mūlaka, vṛkṣāmla, mātuluṅga, and ārdraka, [should be cooked] until one-quarter remains.
6.9.54 | One should prepare [the oil] with half as much pomegranate juice, wine, mastu, and sour gruel (kāñjika), along with triphalā, dāru, salt, vyoṣa, and dīpyaka.
6.9.55 | One should drink this [oil] prepared with half-pala each of yavānī, cavya, hiṅgu, and amlavetasa; it destroys colic, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and enlargement of the abdomen.
6.9.56 | It removes bradhna, anemia, splenic disorders, diseases of the female reproductive tract, fever, and worms; it also eliminates all diseases of vāta and kapha, as well as insanity.

Thus ends another ghee preparation beginning with garlic (laśunādya-ghṛta). Ghee prepared with asafoetida (hiṅgu), hingu-parṇī, kāyasthā, and vayaḥsthā is likewise beneficial; so too is that prepared with vayaḥsthā, hiṅgu, and coraka.
6.9.58 | Or one should cause him to drink either pure clarified butter prepared with these [drugs] or ancient (purāṇa) ghee.
Having caused him to drink the maximum dose, one should confine him in a pit or even in a house.
6.9.59 | Furthermore, the physician should have him drink aged ghee;
because it destroys the three doṣas, is purifying, and especially destroys the seizing spirits (grahas).
6.9.60 | Ghee that has been stored for ten years becomes superior in its qualities and actions; it is pungent and bitter in taste, possesses a strong odor, and is aged.
6.9.61 | It resembles the juice of lac, is cooling, and indeed destroys all planetary afflictions;
it is purifying, the foremost among purgatives, and most excellent when very old.
6.9.62 | There is nothing whatsoever that is incurable for him, even if it has persisted for a hundred years;
for that [remedy], when seen, touched, or smelled, removes all seizing spirits.
6.9.63 | These medicinal formulations are especially recommended for those afflicted by epilepsy, possession by spirits, and insanity; or else, they bring such persons under one's control.
6.9.64 | One should employ śirīṣa, madhuka, hiṅgu, laśuna, tagara, and vacā in applications such as collyrium, rubbing, ointments, and nasal drops.
6.9.65 | Kuṣṭha ground with goat's urine should be used as a nasal drop (nāvana) and as a collyrium (añjana).
Likewise, yoṣa, the two types of haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, hiṅgu, and sarṣapa [should be used].
6.9.66 | Śirīṣa seed, when ground together with apāmārga, hiṅgu, āla, and hiṅgupatrikā in equal parts, destroys insanity, possession by spirits, and epilepsy.
6.9.67 | A wick (varti) made from half a part of black pepper and the bile of a cow and a jackal should be prepared;
with it, one should apply collyrium to those afflicted by epilepsy, possession by spirits, insanity, and fever.

6.9.68 | For those afflicted by spirits, those afflicted by the gods, and for humans with eye disease, black pepper is used; for [eye disease] caused by heat, meat mixed with bile is applied as an ointment.
6.9.69 | For one whose memory has been destroyed by the influence of the doshas upon seeing a transformation (vaikṛta), the following should be administered:
siddhārthaka, vacā, hiṅgu, karañja, and devadāru.
6.9.70 | Mañjiṣṭhā, triphalā, śvetā, the bark of kaṭabhī, the three pungents (kaṭutrika), equal parts of priyaṅgu, śirīṣa, and the two types of rajanī; [these should be taken in equal proportions].
6.9.71 | This medicine, ground with goat's urine, is an ointment for the eyes;
it is likewise used as an errhine, a plaster, a bath, and a rubbing powder.
6.9.72 | It removes epilepsy, poison, insanity, malevolent spells, misfortune, and fever;
it destroys fear of spirits and is highly recommended at the royal court.
6.9.73 | Ghee prepared with this [decoction] or with cow's urine serves the same purpose.
In cases of excessive salivation or chronic rhinitis, one should inhale a medicinal smoke made from a wick (varti) prepared with aromatic substances.
6.9.74 | Or with the drugs mentioned for purgative fumigation, such as *śvetā* and others, along with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*),
or with the products derived from the musk deer (*śallaka*), owl, cat, jackal, wolf, and goat.
6.9.75 | One should administer sprinkling, collyrium, blowing [into the nose], nasal medication, and fumigation using urine, bile, feces, hair, nails, and even skins.
6.9.76 | In the case of a disorder characterized by vāta and śleṣman, [the treatments] generally [recommended] for the paittika type are praised;
namely, tikta-ghṛta, jīvanīya-ghṛta, and miśraka-sneha.
6.9.77 | When foods and drinks are cold, sweet, and soft,
the wise physician should release the vein at the junction of the temple and the hairline in cases of fever from birth,
irregular fever, and epilepsy.
6.9.78 | Or, having satiated him with ghee and meat, one should place him comfortably in a windless place;
having abandoned the loss of intellect and memory, and having regained consciousness, he is liberated.
6.9.79 | Or a friend should console him with words consistent with dharma and artha;
or he should speak of the destruction of his beloved, or show him wonders.
6.9.80 | One should place it, bound and smeared with mustard oil, face upwards in the sun;
or else, one should touch it with *kapikacchu* or with heated iron, oil, or water.
6.9.81 | Or, having beaten him with whips, he should confine him well-secured in a solitary house;
for thus his wandering mind attains tranquility.
6.9.82 | He should frighten him with a snake whose fangs have been removed, or with tamed lions and elephants,
or likewise with armed thieves and enemies.
6.9.83 Or else, having led the king’s servant outside with his hands well-bound,
they should terrify him by threatening him with death under the king's command.
6.9.84 | For the fear for one's life is remembered as being greater than the fear of bodily suffering;
by means of that [fear], his mind, which is distracted in every direction, attains tranquility.
6.9.85 | But for one whose mind is afflicted by the loss of a cherished object,
one should bring it to peace through the acquisition of something similar, consolations, and reassurances.
6.9.86 | One should bring to pacification those [afflictions] arising from desire, grief, fear, anger, joy, envy, and greed by means of these very same factors acting as their mutual opposites.
6.9.87 | Having ascertained the location, age, suitability, the [afflicted] humor (doṣa), the time, and the relative strength or weakness [of the patient],
one should apply this medical treatment in cases of insanity caused by a spirit (bhūta-doṣaja).
6.9.88 | However, a wise man should avoid collyrium and other such sharp substances, as well as cruel acts, for one who is possessed by gods, sages, ancestors, or gandharvas.
6.9.89 | In this case, one should administer mild remedies such as the drinking of clarified butter (sarpiṣ),
as well as worship, offerings of strengthening food, and the procedures for mantras and collyrium (añjana).
6.9.90 | He should perform the rites of pacification, the sacrifices, the oblations, the recitations, the auspicious benedictions,
the rules prescribed in the Vedas, and the expiatory ceremonies.
6.9.91 | By constantly worshipping with self-restraint the divine Lord Īśvara, the sovereign of all beings and the master of the world, one conquers the fear born of madness.
6.9.92 | Those who perform worship of the hosts of Rudra known as the Pramathas, who roam the world, are liberated from madness.

6.9.93 | By means of offerings, auspicious rites, burnt oblations, and the wearing of medicinal herbs and antidotes; by truthfulness, right conduct, austerity, knowledge, charity, restraints, and vows.
6.9.94 | By the worship of gods, cows, Brahmins, and teachers,
as well as by means of perfected mantras and medicinal herbs, an affliction coming from outside is pacified.

6.9.95 | Whatever is prescribed in the treatment of epilepsy (apasmāra) should also be performed in cases of insanity (unmāda), because the causes and the affected constituents (dūṣya) are common to both.
6.9.96 | He who has desisted from meat and wine, who eats wholesome food, is self-restrained, and pure—
that man of strong character is not afflicted by innate or adventitious forms of insanity.
6.9.97 | Clarity of the senses and their objects, as well as of the intellect, self, and mind,
and the state of the bodily constituents (dhātus) being established in their natural condition— these are the characteristics of one who is free from insanity.

6.9.98 | Regarding this, there is a verse: The best of physicians has explained the etiology, the symptoms, and the treatment of the various types of insanity— both those caused by internal factors and those caused by external ones.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Insanity," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Ten:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of epilepsy (apasmāra).
6.10.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.10.3 | Medical experts declare apasmāra (epilepsy) to be the loss of memory,
characterized by a state of darkness and loathsome movements, resulting from the agitation of the intellect and the mind.
6.10.4–5 | Due to the excessive aggravation of the humors (*doṣa*), from the consumption of unwholesome and impure food,
and likewise from mental affliction caused by anxiety, desire, fear, anger, grief, agitation, and so forth,
epilepsy (*apasmāra*) arises in men when the mind is struck.
6.10.6 | Indeed, the humors (doṣas) localized in the vessels afflict the heart;
being thus oppressed, the person suffers with a bewildered and deluded mind.
6.10.7 | He sees forms that do not exist; he falls down and even trembles;
with saliva dripping from his tongue, eyes, and eyebrows, he flails his hands and feet.
6.10.8 | When the force of the doshas has subsided, one awakens as if from sleep.
It will be described as being of four types: caused by the doshas individually and by them combined.
6.10.9 | One trembles, bites the lips, froths at the mouth, and even gasps;
moreover, due to wind (vāta), one sees forms that are rough, reddish, or black.
6.10.10 | The person with a bilious (paittika) fever has yellow foam, limbs, face, and eyes; he perceives blood as being yellow in color, and he sees the world as pervaded by thirst, heat, and fire.
6.10.11 | One with white foam, limbs, face, and eyes; who is cold, has horripilation, and feels heaviness;
and who sees white forms—the one with a kapha-dominant fever is released from it after a long time.
6.10.12 | Apasmāra arising from all three doṣas together is to be recognized by all these symptoms combined;
it is incurable when it occurs in one who is emaciated and when it is chronic.
6.10.13 | After a fortnight, or twelve days, or a month, the aggravated humors (malas) produce a paroxysm of epilepsy (apasmāra), with some interval in between.
6.10.14 | At the outset, the physician should effect the awakening of the heart, the channels, and the mind of those obstructed by these [doshas] through sharp procedures such as emesis and the like.
6.10.15 | One should treat epilepsy caused by Vata primarily with enemas, that caused by Pitta mostly with purgatives,
and that caused by Kapha mainly with emetics.
6.10.16 | Now listen to the pacifying formulations for the purpose of liberating one who is completely purified and properly comforted from epilepsy.
6.10.17 | One should drink ghee prepared with equal parts of cow dung juice, sour curd, milk, and urine;
it destroys epilepsy, jaundice, and fever.
Thus ends the section on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and ghee.
6.10.18: The two pentads of roots (pañcamūlī), triphalā, the two types of rajanī, the bark of kuṭaja, saptaparṇa, apāmārga, nīlinī, and kaṭarohiṇī.
6.10.19 | Having boiled two palas each of śampāka, the root of phalgu, pauṣkara, and durālabhā in one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth, [one should use it].
6.10.20 | Bhāgī, pāṭhā, trikaṭuka, trivṛtā, viculā,
śreyasī, āḍhakī, mūrvā, dantī, bhūnimba, and citraka.
6.10.21 | One should grind two parts each of sārivā, rohiṣa, bhūtīka, and madayantikā—each measuring one akṣa—and add them; with this, one should cook one prastha of ghee.
6.10.22 | With equal parts of cow dung juice, sour curd, milk, and urine, that which is known as the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya) is prepared; it is great and like nectar.
6.10.23 | Likewise in epilepsy, insanity, swelling, abdominal enlargements,
abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, anemia, jaundice, and chlorosis.
6.10.24 | This ghee is praised; it should be used day after day.
It destroys misfortune, planetary influences, and diseases, and it eradicates quartan fever.

Thus is the Great Five-Product Ghee (Mahāpañcagavya-ghṛta). 6.10.25. Furthermore, ancient ghee prepared with the juice of Brāhmī, Vacā, Kuṣṭha, and Śaṅkhapuṣpī destroys insanity, misfortune, epilepsy, and sin.
6.10.26 | Ghee prepared with rock salt and asafoetida, along with four times the amount of rainwater and urine,

6.10.27 | Ghee prepared with vacā, śampāka, kaiṭarya, vayaḥsthā, hiṅgu, coraka, and palaṅkaṣā is indicated for disorders characterized by vāta and kapha.
6.10.28 | One *prastha* of oil and one *prastha* of clarified butter should be cooked with one *pala* each of the *jīvanīya* drugs and one *droṇa* of milk; when prepared, it destroys epilepsy.

6.10.29 | One should cook one prastha of ghee with one karṣa each of the eight life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, along with one karṣa each of kaṃsa, milk, sugarcane juice, and the juice of kāśmarya, which is eight times the quantity [of the other liquids].
6.10.30 | It quickly cures epilepsy arising from vāta and pitta.

6.10.31 | A prastha of ghee prepared in the same manner with a paste of two palas of madhuka and one droṇa of āmalaka juice is a remedy for pitta-type epilepsy.
6.10.32 | An oil massage should be performed with mustard oil prepared with four times the amount of goat urine;

6.10.33 | Oil prepared with the decoction of *kaṭabhī*, nimba, *kaṭvaṅga*, and the bark of *madhuśigru*,

6.10.34 | With pālaṅkaṣā, vacā, pathyā, vṛścikālī, arka, and sarṣapa; with jaṭilā, pūtanā, keśī, nākulī, hiṅgu, and coraka;
6.10.35 | With garlic, atirasā, citrā, kuṣṭha, and viḍ salts,

6.10.36 | This prepared medicated oil for massage destroys epilepsy;

6.10.37 | Pippalī, salt, citrā, hiṅgu, hiṅguśivāṭikā, kakkolī,
mustard seeds, kākanāsā, kaiṭarya, and candana.

6.10.39 | An ointment for rubbing [the body] should be prepared from apetarākṣasī, kuṣṭha, pūtanā, keśī, and coraka, ground with urine; likewise, there should be sprinkling with the same urines.
6.10.40 | Likewise with leech excrement, or with burnt goat hairs,
donkey bones, elephant claws, or cow-tail hair.

6.10.43 | From this [mixture], the physician should administer three or six *yoga*s, or five *bindu*s, using *triphalā*, *vyoṣa*, *pītadru*, *yavakṣāra*, and *phaṇijjhaka*.
6.10.44 | Oil prepared with the fruits of *śyāmā*, *apāmārga*, and *kārañja* in goat urine, used as a nasal drop (*nāvana*), destroys epilepsy (*apasmāra*).
6.10.45 | Pippalī, vṛścikālī, kuṣṭha, the salts, and bhārgī should be made into a powder; this is the best for use as a snuff (pradhamana).
6.10.46 | One should prepare suppositories by grinding kāyasthā, śāradamudga, mustā, uśīra, and yava, along with the three pungents (vyoṣa), with goat's urine.

6.10.47 | These [herbs] are like nectar for those afflicted by epilepsy or insanity, those bitten by snakes, those suffering from artificial poisons, those who have ingested poison, and even those who have drowned.
6.10.48 | Musta, vayasthā, triphalā, kāyasthā, hiṅgu, śādvala, vyoṣa, māṣas,
and yavas should be taken with the three types of urine— those of the cow, the goat, and the buffalo.
6.10.49 | Having ground [the ingredients] and made them into a wick (varti), one should employ it in cases of epilepsy (apasmāra),
as well as in skin diseases (kilāsa), insanity (unmāda), and irregular fevers (viṣamajvara).
6.10.50 | The bile of a dog extracted under the Puṣya asterism is an ointment that destroys epilepsy;
that same substance mixed with clarified butter is considered an excellent fumigation.
6.10.51 | The physician should administer fumigation using the beaks, feathers, and excrement of the mongoose, owl, cat, vulture, insects, snake, and crow.
6.10.52 | By these perfected practices, the heart becomes fully awakened;
the channels are also purified, and through that, one regains consciousness.

6.10.53 | If, however, a secondary (āgantuka) factor is observed whose form exceeds the symptoms of the [primary] doshas, then the treatment for that case should be the remedy for exogenous (āgantuka) insanity.
6.10.54 | Immediately thereafter, Agniveśa, with palms joined in reverence, spoke this:
"O Blessed One! In the Section on Verses (Ślokasthāna), the 'Great Disease' was previously mentioned."
6.10.55 | That which is an adherence to what is not reality—its causes and its forms have been treated by the physician.
Since that has not been explained there, I wish to hear it; let it be told here.
6.10.56 | Having heard the words of his disciple who was eager to listen, Punarvasu said:
"O gentle one, listen to the great treatise on diseases, along with their causes, symptoms, and remedies."
6.10.57 | For one who habitually consumes impure food, who suppresses natural urges when they have arisen,
and who excessively indulges in causes such as cold, heat, unctuousness, and dryness;
6.10.58 | Taking refuge in the heart, the vessels carrying the mind and intellect remain there after vitiating the humors (doṣas) of one whose self is shrouded by passion and delusion.
6.10.59 | When the intellect and the mind are shrouded by the increased qualities of rajas and tamas,
and when the heart is agitated by the defects, one then becomes deluded and of feeble consciousness.

6.10.60 | Those who have attained realization call that "adherence to what is not reality" a great malady, for it renders the intellect unbalanced regarding the eternal and the non-eternal, and the beneficial and the harmful.
6.10.61 | Having purified that patient— who has been prepared with oleation and sudation— by means of emesis and other cleansing therapies,
and having administered the gradual dietary regimen (*saṃsarjana*), one should treat him with wholesome foods and drinks.
6.10.62 | That which is called the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya) combined with the fresh juice of Brāhmī,
as well as Śaṅkhapuṣpī and whatever else is purifying and a rejuvenative (rasāyana), should be consumed.
6.10.63 | And his well-wishing friends, who are trustworthy and speak of dharma and worldly prosperity, should endow him with discernment, fortitude, mindfulness, and concentration.
6.10.64 | One should administer garlic with oil, or śatāvarī with milk,
or the juice of brāhmī, or the juice of kuṣṭha, or vacā combined with honey.
6.10.65 | Epilepsy (apasmāra) is indeed difficult to treat when it has persisted for a long time and established its seat;
therefore, one should generally treat it with rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana).
6.10.66 | One should always protect that [patient] from water, fire, trees, mountains, and uneven places, as well as from those who are insane; for these can take life instantly.
6.10.67 | Regarding this, there are two verses:— The aggravated doshas produce apasmāra as their cause; their symptoms and their remedies have been described both collectively and individually.
6.10.68 | The sage [Caraka] has explained, both in detail and in summary, the etiology, symptoms, and treatment of major fevers (mahāgada) and epilepsy (apasmāra).

Thus ends the tenth chapter, named "The Treatment of Epilepsy," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Eleventh Chapter:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of chest wounds and wasting (kṣatakṣīṇacikitsita).
6.11.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.11.3 | The Brahman-sage Ātreya, of noble fame and knower of the ultimate truth,
has declared this medical treatment for the purpose of curing those who are emaciated by wasting diseases.
6.11.4 | For one who strains excessively with the bow, bears a heavy burden,
falls from uneven heights, or fights with those who are strong;
6.11.5 | For one who restrains a running bull, a horse, or another animal to be tamed; or for one who hurls stones, wood, or clods of earth, or strikes down others;
6.11.6 Or for one who is studying while walking very loudly, or traveling a great distance quickly,
or crossing a large river, or running along with horses.
6.11.7 | When [the body] suddenly leaps far away, or dances excessively and rapidly,
or is violently struck by other such cruel actions;
6.11.8 | When the chest is wounded, a powerful disease is provoked,
as is the case for one who is excessively attached to women, or who eats food that is dry, scanty, or measured in excess.
6.11.9 | His chest is afflicted with pain; it feels as if it is being split and then torn apart. Then his sides are oppressed, his limbs wither, and he trembles.
6.11.10 | Gradually, virility, strength, complexion, appetite, and digestive fire decline;
furthermore, fever, pain, mental depression, and diarrhea result from the destruction of the digestive fire.
6.11.11 | The phlegm of one coughing is corrupted, dark-brown, extremely foul-smelling, yellow, knotted, and copious; it is discharged along with blood.
6.11.12 | When that [semen] is injured, it diminishes excessively due to the depletion of semen and ojas;
its unmanifest signs are known as the premonitory symptoms (pūrvarūpa).
6.11.13 | In *kṣata* (wasting due to chest injury), there is specifically chest pain, vomiting of blood, and cough;
in *kṣīṇa* (general wasting), there is blood in the urine and stiffness of the sides, back, and waist.

6.11.14 | A case with few symptoms, occurring in one with a strong digestive fire, who is powerful and whose condition is recent, is curable. One that has persisted for a year is palliable; however, one exhibiting all the symptoms should be rejected as incurable.
6.11.15 | Thinking the chest is wounded, one should immediately drink lac mixed with milk and honey for the sake of healing;
thereafter, one should eat [food] with milk and sugar.
6.11.16 | To one suffering from pain in the flanks and bladder, with diminished bile and digestive fire, this [milk] mixed with wine should be given;
likewise to one with loose stools, it should be taken with Musta, Ativisha, Patha, and Vatsaka.
6.11.17 | Having boiled lac, ghee, beeswax, the group of life-promoting drugs (jīvanīya-gaṇa),
sugar, and *tvakkṣīrī* in milk, one with a stimulated digestive fire should drink it.
6.11.18 | One suffering from a wound should drink milk boiled with *ikṣvālikā*, lotus root fibers, lotus buds, lotus filaments, and sandalwood, mixed with honey, for the purpose of healing.

6.11.19 | Taking powdered barley cooked with milk and saturated with ghee, one should drink it during fever with burning sensations; or alternatively, one should drink parched grain flour (saktu) with sugar, honey, and milk.
6.11.20 | One suffering from cough or pain in the sides and bones should lick a paste of madhūka, madhuka, drākṣā-tvak, kṣīrī, pippalī, and balā, mixed with ghee and honey.
6.11.21 | Half an akṣa each of cardamom and cinnamon bark, half a pala of long pepper,
and one pala each of sugar, licorice, dates, and raisins.
6.11.22 | Having powdered [the ingredients] and mixed them with honey, one should prepare pills. Then, one should consume a single pill, the size of an *akṣa* fruit, day after day.
6.11.23 | Cough, dyspnea, fever, hiccup, vomiting, fainting, intoxication, giddiness,
spitting of blood, thirst, pain in the flanks, and loss of appetite.

6.11.24 | This pill (guṭikā) is nourishing and aphrodisiac; it cures consumption, enlargement of the spleen, disorders of excessive wind, hoarseness of voice, chest wounds, and wasting, as well as hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta).
6.11.25. Ityelādiguṭikā:
When blood flows excessively, one should drink the egg of a cock with vegetable soups or water;
or else the juice of sparrow eggs, or the blood of a goat or wild animal.
6.11.26 | One who spits blood should drink a powder of punarnavā, red śāli rice grains, and sugar,
prepared with grape juice, milk, and ghee.
6.11.27 | Or *taṇḍulīyaka* prepared with honey, *madhuka*, and milk;
for obstructed wind (*mūḍhavāta*), however, goat's fat fried in wine with rock salt [is recommended].
6.11.28 | One who is emaciated, wasted, with a sunken chest, and sleepless due to the presence of strong vāyu should eat boiled milk mixed with honey, ghee, and sugar.

6.11.29 | One who is emaciated, suffering from chest wounds, or physically weak should lick sugar, barley, wheat, *jīvaka*, and *ṛṣabhaka* mixed with honey, followed by the drinking of boiled milk as an after-drink.
6.11.30 | He should drink a decoction of meat from a carnivorous animal, fried in ghee, combined with long pepper and honey; this increases both flesh and blood.
6.11.31 | With *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *śāla*, and *priyaṅgu*; with the pith of the *tāla* tree, the bark of the *jambu*, and *priyāla* along with *padmaka*.
6.11.32 | A man with chest wounds or diminished semen should eat śāli rice with ghee produced from milk boiled with aśvakarṇa.
6.11.33 | Ghee prepared with a decoction of yaṣṭyāhva and nāgabalā, mixed with an equal amount of milk,
and processed with a paste of payasyā, pippalī, and vāṃśī, is beneficial for wounds.
6.11.34 | Likewise, ghee should be prepared by boiling it with eight times its quantity of milk and the juice of *kolala* and *lākṣā*,
along with the paste of *kaṭvaṅga*, the bark of *dārvī*, and the bark and fruit of *vatsaka*.
6.11.35 | Jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, vīrā, jīvantī, nāgara, śaṭī, the four parṇinīs, medā, the two kākōlīs, and the two nidigdhikās.
6.11.36 | Two types of punarnavā, madhuka, ātmaguptā, śatāvarī, ṛddhi, parūṣaka, bhārgī, and likewise bṛhatī.
6.11.37 | Śṛṅgāṭaka, tāmalakī, payasyā, pippalī, and balā; also jujube, walnut, date, vātāmā, and abhiṣuka.
6.11.38 | One should prepare one-karṣa pastes (kalkas) from fruits such as these,
along with the juice of dhātrī, vidārī, sugarcane, goat meat broth, and milk.
6.11.39 | One should prepare [the paste] measuring one *prastha* and cook it with one *prastha* of ghee. When it has cooled, one should add half a *prastha* of honey and half a *tula* of sugar.
6.11.40 | Having infused two karṣas each of patra, elā, hematvak, and narica,
a person should always lick a measured dose of the resulting powder.
6.11.41 | Ghee is the nectar for men; it is called the "consumption of nectar. One who subsists on milk and meat broth should consume this essence of the nectar of ambrosia.
6.11.42 | One should nourish those whose semen is depleted, those suffering from chest wounds, those who are emaciated, the weak, those wasted by disease,
those addicted to women, the thin, and those deficient in complexion and voice.

6.11.43 | It cures cough, hiccup, fever, dyspnea, burning sensation, thirst, and hemorrhagic disorders (asrapitta); it bestows progeny and removes vomiting, fainting, heart disease, gynecological ailments, and urinary disorders.
Thus ends the *Amṛtaprāśa-ghṛta*.
6.11.44: [Take] *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *balā*, *kāśmarya*, *kattṛṇa*, the root of *darbha*, *pṛthakparṇī*, *palāśa*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and *sthirā*.
6.11.45 | One pala of these [drugs] should be cooked in their juice with four times as much milk,
along with a paste (kalaka) of svaguptā, jīvantī, medā, ṛṣabhaka, and jīvaka.
6.11.46 | A *prastha* of ghee prepared with *śatāvarī*, *ṛddhi*, *mṛdvīkā*, sugar, *śrāvaṇī*, and lotus stalks cures vāta and pitta disorders, as well as heart disease and colic.
6.11.47 | It cures dysuria, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, cough, emaciation, and consumption;
it bestows strength and flesh upon those exhausted by archery, women, wine, carrying loads, and travel on foot.

Thus ends the *śvadaṃṣṭrā-ghṛta* (6.11.48). One should cook one *prastha* of ghee in a decoction of eight *palas* of *madhuka* and one *prastha* of *drākṣā*. When the ghee is prepared, one should add eight *palas* of *pippalī* as a paste; once it has cooled, [it may be used].

6.11.49 | One should mix eight palas each of honey and sugar separately; this, combined with an equal amount of parched grain flour (saktu), is beneficial for those suffering from chest wounds (kṣata) and emaciation (kṣīṇa), as well as for uterine tumors (raktagulma).
6.11.50 | A physician should cook seven *prasthas* of ghee with the juices of *dhātrī*, *vidārī*, sugarcane, and the *jīvanīya* group, as well as with the milk of goats and cows.
