6.11.51 | When it has been prepared and cooled, one should add two *prasthas* each of sugar and honey and administer it;
this cures consumption, epilepsy, hemorrhagic disorders, cough, urinary disorders, and wasting.
6.11.52 | Clarified butter stabilizes youth, promotes longevity, and bestows muscle, semen, and strength;
however, one should lick it when pitta is predominant and drink it when vāta is predominant.
6.11.53 | Pitta, when licked, causes cooling; because it is present in small quantity, it does not destroy the digestive fire.
When drunk, it overcomes the Vāyu and obstructs the internal heat.
6.11.54 | For those whose limbs are parched, wasted, and emaciated, these same ghees should be prepared thickened with the powders of *tvakkṣīrī*, sugar, and parched rice.
6.11.55 | Having consumed boluses of ghee and jaggery mixed with honey, one should drink milk afterwards;
by means of these, one shall very quickly attain semen, virility, strength, and nourishment.

Thus ends the section on ghee-and-jaggery preparations (sarpirguḍa). 6.11.56. Balā, vidārī, the small five-roots (hrasvā pañcamūlī), punarnavā, and the leaf-buds of the five milky trees (kṣīrivṛkṣa), each taken in the measure of one handful (muṣṭi).

6.11.57 | One *āḍhaka* of ghee should be cooked with the decoction of these [drugs] mixed with two parts of milk and one part each of the juices of *vidārī* and *āmrātaka*, along with paste (*kalka*) of the *jīvanīya* drugs in the measure of one *akṣa* each.
6.11.58 | When [the decoction] has been strained and cooled, one should add thirty-two palas of sugar,
as well as the powder of wheat, long pepper, vāṃśī, and śṛṅgāṭaka.
6.11.59 | All that, including honey, measured by a *kuḍava*, having been thoroughly stirred with a churning stick,
should be made into solidified *sarpirguḍa* (honey-balls) and wrapped in birch bark.
6.11.60 | Having eaten those *palika* portions, one should drink milk or wine as an after-drink (*anupāna*) in cases of phlegm,
consumption, cough, chest wounds, emaciation, or exhaustion from labor, sexual activity, or carrying heavy loads.
6.11.61 | In cases of spitting blood, fever, chronic catarrh, and when [the disease] is located in the chest;
they are recommended for pain in the sides and head, and for disorders of the voice and complexion.

Thus ends the second group of ghee-and-jaggery preparations (sarpirguḍas). [6.11.62] [These are prepared with] tvakkṣīrī, śrāvaṇī, drākṣā, mūrvā, ṛṣabhaka, jīvaka, vīrā, ṛddhi, kṣīrakākolī, bṛhatī, and kapikacchu.

6.11.63 | One *prastha* of ghee should be cooked with one *pala* each of dates (*kharjūra*) and *medā* fruits ground with milk, along with one *prastha* each of *dhātrī*, *vidārī*, and sugarcane juice.
6.11.64 | Having added half a *tulā* of sugar-candy to the cooled [decoction] along with half a *prastha* of honey,
one should prepare ghee-boluses (*sarpirguḍa*) which remove cough, hiccup, and fever.
6.11.65 | They destroy consumption, asthma, dyspnea, internal hemorrhage, chlorosis,
loss of semen and sleep, thirst, emaciation, and jaundice.
Thus ends the third group of ghee-and-jaggery preparations (sarpirguḍas).
6.11.66. [One should take] fresh āmalaka, drākṣā, ātmaguptā, punarnavā, śatāvarī, vidārī, samaṅgā, and likewise pippalī.
6.11.67 | Take ten *pala* portions each of ginger and eight *pala* of *nāgara*;
two *pala* each of *yaṣṭyāhva* and *sauvarcala*, and one *pala* of black pepper.
6.11.68 | When three āḍhakas of milk, oil, and ghee have been boiled with one hundred palas of sugar, one should add those powders and form boluses of jaggery equal in size to a bilva fruit.
6.11.69 | A man who is emaciated, wounded, or parched should consume them;
by that, through the immediate increase of the bodily fluids (rasa) and so forth, he attains nourishment.

Thus end the fourth [type of] ghee-and-jaggery preparations (sarpirguḍa). 6.11.70. Half an āḍhaka of cow’s milk, one prastha of ghee, one āḍhaka of sugarcane juice, one prastha of the fresh juice of vidārī, and one prastha of the meat-broth of the black partridge (taittira).
6.11.71 | One should administer these ground substances with sugarcane juice; when that has been digested, one should take one kuḍava of madhūka flowers and likewise one kuḍava of priyāla fruit.
6.11.72 | Half a *kuḍava* of *tugākṣīrī*, twenty *kharjūra* fruits,
and separately, four *caturthika* measures each of *bibhītaka* and *pippalī*.
6.11.73 | Thirty palas of sugar candy, one karṣa of madhuka,
and likewise half-pala quantities of the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs should be added here.
6.11.74 | When this [mixture] has been prepared, one should add one *kuḍava* of honey once it has cooled, and then have pills (*modaka*) made,
dusted with a powder of one *pala* each of black pepper and cumin.
6.11.75 | In diseases of wind, blood, and bile; in chest wounds, cough, and wasting;
in those who are emaciated, whose semen is depleted, and when blood is lodged in the chest.
6.11.76 | For those who are emaciated, weak, or aged, for those seeking nourishment, complexion, and strength,
and also for women afflicted by discharges caused by disorders of the female reproductive tract (yoni-doṣa).
6.11.77 | For those women who desire conception, but whose embryo either miscarries or dies,
these [medicines]— which are strengthening, nourishing, and beneficial— are for increasing the semen and the menstrual blood.
Thus end the five ghee-modakas (6.11.78).
When the wind (vāyu) is disordered in the region of the bladder due to excessive sexual indulgence,
one should administer for that patient formulations that are wind-alleviating, nourishing, and aphrodisiac.
6.11.79 | Or one should drink boiled milk mixed with sugar, powdered long pepper (pippalī), ghee, and honey; this cures cough and fever.

6.11.80 | A man exhausted by sexual indulgence should drink this soup, which is sour with fruit, fried in ghee, and boiled in the juice of vidārī and sugarcane; it is life-sustaining and a supreme nourisher.

A person who has been emaciated by chest wounds, who has a keen digestive fire, and who is accustomed to a diet of barley, should drink a churned beverage (mantha) made from flour of parched grain that has been strained through cloth and mixed with honey and ghee.

6.11.82 | Or, for one who is emaciated, one should administer the meat broth of wild animals, prepared with life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, fried in ghee, and mixed with sugar, to be used as a side dish.
6.11.83 | One should feed [the patient] barley-based food with the milk of cows, buffaloes, horses, elephants, and goats,
as well as with meat broths, soups, and sour fruits prepared with ghee.

6.11.84 | This regimen is prescribed when the digestive fire is blazing; when it is sluggish, it should be a digestive stimulant and carminative. For those suffering from consumption (yakṣman), it is ordained as astringent, and it is desired when the stool is broken up.
6.11.85 | One pala of rock salt (saindhava), two palas of ginger (śuṇṭhī), and two palas of black salt (sauvarcala);
one kuḍava each of wood-apple (vṛkṣāmla), pomegranate (dāḍima), and arjaka leaves.
6.11.86 | One *caturthika* each of black pepper and cumin, two *caturthikas* of coriander,
and twelve *palas* of sugar should be added here.
6.11.87 | Having prepared this powder, one should administer the appropriate dose with food and drink;
it is appetizing, digestive, strengthening, and cures pain in the flanks, dyspnea, and cough.
Thus ends the powder of rock salt and other ingredients (6.11.88). One *ṣoḍaśikā* of coriander, two each of cumin and *ajamodā*,
twice that amount each of pomegranate and wood-apple, and one *pala* of black salt (*sauvarcala*).
6.11.89 | One karṣa of dry ginger and five palas from the pulp of the wood-apple (dadhittha)—
one should mix that powder with sixteen palas of sugar.
6.11.90 | This ṣāḍava should be administered as before with food and drinks;
it increases the digestive fire in those suffering from consumption (yakṣman), as well as in cases of weak digestion and diarrhea.

Thus ends the section on the ṣāḍava. 6.11.91: One should drink a pala of the root of *nāgabalā*, increased by half a karṣa each month, combined with milk; for one month, subsisting only on milk and abstaining from solid food.
6.11.92 | This application is supreme for promoting nourishment, longevity, strength, and health;
it is a wholesome preparation of *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, as well as ginger and licorice.
6.11.93 | Whatever food and drink is nourishing, cooling, non-burning, wholesome, and light should be consumed by those suffering from chest wounds and wasting who desire well-being.
6.11.94 | Furthermore, whatever has been stated as wholesome for those suffering from consumption, cough, and hemoptysis,
that one should administer after duly considering the digestive fire, the disease, suitability, and strength.

6.11.95 | When that [wind] has become obstructed, there indeed occurs the secondary complication of consumption (yakṣman). Since it arises even before the onset of that [consumption], one should therefore conquer it with haste.

6.11.96 | Regarding this, there are two verses: [The chapter] on the origin of chest-wounds and wasting, their general and specific characteristics, their incurability, treatability, and incurability, and the successful treatment of those that are curable.

6.11.97 | Punarvasu, who knew the true meaning of reality and was free from the defects of passion and ignorance, spoke thus to his eldest disciple regarding the treatment of wounds and chest ailments.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wasting due to Chest Injury," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, which was not available [in its original form] and has been restored by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Twelve:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of swelling (śvayathu).
6.12.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

6.12.3 | Agniveśa questioned the most excellent physician, the lord of sages and son of Atri, who is honored by gods and perfected beings, regarding the etiology, symptoms, and treatment of swelling (śvayathu), that great disease, exactly as they are.
6.12.4 To him, Atri’s son— the preeminent mountain for causing the ocean of the science of medicine to flow— properly expounded those [remedies] for the threefold disease,
categorized as endogenous (*nija*), exogenous (*anija*), and that arising from both, according to the distinctions of wind (*vāta*) and the other humors.
6.12.5 | For those who are pure, afflicted by disease, emaciated by fasting, or weak, the consumption of alkaline, sour, sharp, hot, and heavy substances,
as well as the intake of curd, raw food, clay, vegetables, incompatible foods, and food contaminated by poison or defilement, [lead to illness].
6.12.6 | Lack of physical activity, lack of bodily purification, injury to the vital organs (marmans), difficult labor,
and improper administration of therapeutic procedures are declared to be the causes of endogenous swelling (nija-śvayathu).
6.12.7 | External trauma (*abhighāta*) caused by wood, stone, weapons, fire, poison, arrows, and so forth, corrupts the external layers of the skin.
Exogenous causes (*āgantuhetu*) are of three types, while endogenous causes (*nija*) are also threefold, based on whether they affect the whole body, half the body, or a specific part or limb.
6.12.8 | When the Vāyu, having reached the external vessels, vitiates the Kapha, blood, and Pitta,
its path being obstructed by them, it then spreads and produces swelling characterized by elevation.
6.12.9 | When the *doṣas* are located in the chest, they cause swelling in the upper part; when situated in their own respective locations (the abdomen), they cause it in the middle;
when pervading all limbs, they cause it throughout the body; and when localized in specific areas, the swelling occurs in those very places, being designated by the name of that location.

6.12.10 | Heat, as well as distress and the stretching of the vessels—these are the premonitory symptoms. This condition involves all three *doṣas*, yet it receives its name and its medical treatment according to the predominant *doṣa*.
6.12.11 | Heaviness, instability, swelling,
a sense of heat, thinness of the veins, horripilation, and discoloration of the limbs are declared to be the general symptoms of swelling (śvayathu).

6.12.12 | Swelling caused by wind (samīraṇa) is mobile, characterized by thin and rough skin, and is reddish or black; it is accompanied by numbness, itching, and pain without apparent cause; it subsides when pressed and rises again when released; and it is more intense during the day.
6.12.13 | Soft, with a specific odor, colored blackish-yellow, accompanied by vertigo, fever, perspiration, thirst, and intoxication;
that which suppurates, causes pain on touch, and brings redness to the eyes—this is a swelling caused by pitta, characterized by intense burning and suppuration.

6.12.14 | A Kapha-type swelling is heavy, stable, pale, and accompanied by anorexia, salivation, drowsiness, vomiting, and weak digestion. It is slow to arise and slow to subside; when pressed, it does not rebound, and it gains strength at night.

6.12.15 | That [hemorrhage] which occurs in one who is emaciated by diseases or weakened by complications such as vomiting, and which follows the vital points (*marmans*), is accompanied by streaks, flows profusely, and spreads throughout the body— this destroys the patient who is already devoid of strength.
6.12.16 | A fresh fever caused by a single dosha in a strong person who has not lost muscle tissue is easy to cure.
One who understands the strength of the dosha and the time of the disease should treat it with measures that reverse the etiology, the dosha, and the season.
6.12.17 | Now, one should first treat the patient with regimens of fasting and digestive (pācana) measures, and with purificatory therapies for aggravated doṣas;
[specifically], those located in the head with head-purgatives (śirovirecana), those below with purgatives (virecana), and likewise those above with emetics (ūrdhvahara).
6.12.18 | One should treat [the patient] with drying measures when the condition arises from unctuousness (sneha), and one should apply the regimen of oleation when it is born of dryness (rūkṣa).

In cases of wind-born (vātaja) constipation of the feces, a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) is indicated; however, in cases of wind-and-bile (pittānilaja) origin, ghee mixed with bitter herbs should be used.
6.12.19 | Milk is desired for one suffering from fainting, thirst, burning sensations, or parchedness; however, for those requiring purification, it should be taken with urine.
One should overcome disorders arising from phlegm by means of alkaline, pungent, and hot substances, combined with urine, buttermilk, and fermented liquors.
6.12.20 | One suffering from edema (śvayathu) should avoid domestic animal meat, marshy meat, weak meat, dried vegetables, fresh grain, preparations of molasses, flour-based foods,

curd, sesame products, slimy substances, sour wine, parched grain, dried meat, eating in equal quantities [of incompatible foods], heavy food, unwholesome food, burning food, sleeping during the night, and sexual intercourse.
6.12.21 | Vyōṣa, trivṛt, tiktakarōhiṇī, and ayōrajas, drunk with the juice of triphalā,
or harītakī with cow’s urine, pacify swelling arising from kapha.
6.12.22 | One should drink either *harītakī*, *nāgara*, and *devadāru* combined with warm water, or all of them together with *punarnavā*.
In all three cases, one should take the medicine with urine; having bathed, one should eat food with milk once the medicine has been digested.
6.12.23 | A wise person should drink one *prastha* of milk with a *karṣa*-measure of the paste of *punarnavā*, *nāgara*, and *musta*;
or, in cases involving wind (*vāta*), one should drink *mayūraka*, *māgadhikā* along with its roots, or *nāgara*.

6.12.24 | Or, for one suffering from wind combined with bile, one should drink milk boiled with half a pala each of dantī, trivṛt, tryūṣaṇa, and citraka, reduced to half its original volume, in a quantity of two prasthas. This removes the morbid humors.
6.12.25 | One should administer ginger with the juice of *pītadru*, or that prepared with *śyāmā*, *urubūka*, and *uṣaṇa*;
or with *tvak*, *dāru*, *varṣābhū*, and *mahauṣadha*; or with *guḍūcī*, *nāgara*, and *dantī*.
6.12.26 | Or else, avoiding food and water, he should drink camel’s milk for seven days or even for a month;
or he may subsist on cow’s milk with its urine, or buffalo’s milk, or likewise the urine of cows, while consuming only milk.
6.12.27 | Or one whose stool is heavy and broken should drink buttermilk with trikaṭu, sauvarcala salt, and honey;
or one whose stool is broken by the presence of morbid humors (doṣa) and is not bound should take jaggery with abhayā, or jaggery with ginger.
6.12.28 | In cases of obstruction of feces and flatus, one should drink castor oil with milk or meat broths before a meal;
in cases of obstruction of the channels and loss of appetite for food, one should drink well-prepared wines and fermented liquors (ariṣṭas).
6.12.29 | One should cook two *prastha*s of *gaṇḍīra*, *bhallātaka*, *citraka*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *viḍaṅga*,
and the two types of *bṛhatī* in one *droṇa* of *kurcikā-mastu* over a fire of cow-dung.

6.12.30 | When one-third remains, it should be well-strained and cooled; then, mixed with one *droṇa* of natural whey (*mastu*) and one hundred pieces of white sugar, it should be placed in a jar smeared with *citraka* and long pepper (*pippalī*).
6.12.31 | Used for ten days while suspended in the air, it destroys swellings,
fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, worms, skin diseases, urinary disorders, discoloration, emaciation, wind-disorders, and hiccups.

Thus ends the *gaṇḍīrādyariṣṭa* (6.12.32). One hundred palas each of the fruits of *kāśmarya*, *dhātrī*, black pepper (*marica*), *abhayā*, *akṣa*, and *drākṣā*, along with long pepper (*pippalī*), and one *tulā* of aged jaggery (*guḍa*), having been finely crushed, should be placed in a jar smeared with honey.

6.12.33 | Having remained for seven days in the heat, or twice that long in the cold, one should drink it mixed with one droṇa of water. This ariṣṭa, known as Aṣṭaśata, destroys swellings and obstructions born of kapha and vāta, and stimulates the digestive fire.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth [chapter], "On Averting Misfortune" (Ariṣṭa).
Having boiled two types of Punarnavā, the two types of Bala, Pāṭhā, Dantī, Guḍūcī, Citraka, Nidigdhikā,
and Triphalā in water until one droṇa remains, one should then take that [decoction].
6.12.35 | Having strained the juice, one should place two *tulās* of old jaggery together with one *prastha* of honey in a vessel of ghee while it is well-cooled;
one should store it for a month in a heap of barley, and after that month [it may be used].

6.12.36 | When that [mixture] has been digested, one should drink it— endowed with fragrance and mixed with honey and ghee— along with the powders of *patra*, cinnamon bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*elā*), black pepper (*marica*), *ambu* (musta), and iron (*loha*), each in the measure of half a *pala*, after carefully considering the strength of the disease.
6.12.37 | It cures heart disease, anemia, severe edema, splenic enlargement, fever, anorexia, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, fistula-in-ano,
various types of abdominal enlargements, cough, dyspnea, malabsorption syndrome, skin diseases, and itching.

6.12.38 | Endowed with complexion, strength, longevity, vigor, and luster, one who eats meat broth and solid food will quickly conquer rheumatic pain in the limbs, constipation, hiccup, vitiligo, and chlorosis.
Thus ends the section on the *ariṣṭas* beginning with *punarnavā*.

6.12.39: One *kuḍava* each of the three fruits (*phalatrika*), *dīpyaka*, *citraka*, long pepper (*pippalī*), iron filings (*loharajas*), and *viḍaṅga*—powdered together—and two parts of honey, along with one *tulā* of old jaggery (*guḍa*).

6.12.40 | One should store it for a month in a vessel of ghee among barley grains; those very same [preparations] destroy diseases. Those which are declared beneficial for hemorrhoids and for those suffering from anemia (pāṇḍu) are also beneficial as *ariṣṭas* for swellings (*śopha*).

Thus ends the Triphalādyariṣṭa (6.12.41). Long pepper, pāṭhā, gajapippalī, nidigdhikā, citraka, ginger, long pepper root, turmeric, ajājī, and musta— this powder, when drunk with warm water, [is beneficial].

A paste of *bhūnimba* and *mahauṣadha*, or iron powder along with the powders of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) and *yāvaśūka*, when drunk with the juice of *triphalā*, destroys swelling caused by the three *doṣas* and that which has been chronic for a long time.
6.12.43 | The two alkalis, the four salts, iron filings, the three pungents (vyoṣa), the three fruits (phalatrika),
along with long pepper root (pippalīmūla), viḍaṅga pith, mustā, ajamodā, amaradāru, and bilva;
6.12.44 | One pala each of Kaliṅgaka, Citraka root, Pāṭhā, Yaṣṭīmadhu, and Ativiṣā; one karṣa of Hiṅgu; and likewise, a fine dry powder of one droṇa each of Mūlaka and Śuṇṭhī.
6.12.45 | That [ash] should be processed with water, stirred until it becomes thick and no longer burns;
once it has solidified, one should form it into a dose the size of a jujube fruit, dry it thoroughly, and administer it according to the prescribed method.
6.12.46 | It dispels splenic enlargement, vitiligo, halīmaka, anemia, jaundice, anorexia, emaciation, edema, cholera,
abdominal tumors, artificial poisons, urinary stones, as well as asthma, cough, and leprosy.
Thus ends the section on alkaline boluses (kṣāraguḍikā).

6.12.47. One should administer fresh ginger (ārdraka) or dry ginger (nāgara), equal in measure to jaggery (guḍa), increasing the dose by half a pala at a time. The maximum dose is five palas. This should be taken for one month. Once it has been digested, milk, vegetable broth, meat broth, and cooked grain should be consumed.
This application overcomes abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, hemorrhoids, edema, urinary disorders, asthma, catarrh, intestinal torpor, indigestion,
jaundice, wasting, mental disorders, cough, and phlegm.
6.12.49 | Likewise, the juice of fresh ginger (*ārdraka-nāgara*) should be drunk; once it has been digested, one should eat food with milk.
Furthermore, *jatvaśmaja* taken with the decoction of *triphalā* forcibly destroys swelling caused by the three *doṣas*.
Thus ends the application of *śilājatu*.

6.12.50 One should boil a *kaṃsa* measure of the decoction of the two *pañcamūla*s along with a hundred *abhayā* fruits and jaggery (*guḍa*). When the electuary (*leha*) is well-prepared, one should then add the powder of *vyoṣa*, the three aromatics (*trisaugandhya*), and *uśīra* once it has been removed from the heat.
6.12.51 | Half a *prastha* of honey, slightly warmed, along with a small amount of the powder of *yavaśūka*,
and having consumed one *abhayā* from this electuary, one destroys even advanced swelling (*śvayathu*) by means of a *śukti* measure.
6.12.52 | It cures dyspnea, fever, anorexia, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, diseases of the three doṣas, abdominal diseases, and anemia;
as well as emaciation, āmavāta, internal hemorrhage, acid gastritis, discoloration, and defects of the urine, wind, and semen.
Thus ends the *Kaṃsaharītakī* formula (6.12.53).
Patola root, amaradāru, dantī, trāyantī, pippalī, abhayā, viśālā,
yaṣṭyāhvaya, tiktakarohiṇī, candana, nicula, and dārvī [should be used].
6.12.54 | A decoction prepared with one karṣa each of these [drugs] should be drunk mixed with one kuḍava of ghee;
it destroys erysipelas, burning sensations, fever, disorders of the three humors (sannipāta), thirst, poisons, and swelling.
6.12.55 | Citraka, coriander, cumin, sauvarcala salt, the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa),
sour vetasa, the fruit of bilva, pomegranate, yavaśūka, long pepper root, and likewise cavya— [these should be used].

6.12.56 | Having ground [the herbs] in the measure of an akṣa and boiled them with one āḍhaka of water, one should then employ one prastha of ghee; this cures hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, edema, and dysuria, and it kindles a bright digestive fire.
One should drink ghee prepared with eight times its weight of water, together with citraka and alkali, which is of great potency;
or else the Kalyāṇaka ghee, or that made with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or the Mahātiktaka, or the Tikta ghee.
6.12.58 | Milk that has turned into curd within a jar smeared with the paste of *citraka* should be thoroughly churned;
the ghee produced from it, containing the root of *citraka*, when prepared with buttermilk (*takra*), is the foremost remedy for edema (*śvayathu*).
6.12.59 | This [preparation] destroys hemorrhoids, diarrhea, wind-disorders, abdominal tumors, and urinary disorders, and it bestows digestive fire and strength.
One should eat solid foods with buttermilk mixed with that same ghee, or otherwise, one should consume gruel (yavāgū) prepared with it.
Thus ends the Citraka-ghṛta (6.12.60). [A preparation] made with jīvanta, ajājī, śaṭī, puṣkarāhva, kāravī, citraka, the pulp of bilva, and yāvaśūka,
each in the quantity of a badara fruit, combined with vṛkṣāmla, and fried in ghee and oil.

6.12.61 | Gruel prepared according to that same method with the five spices (*pañcakola*) is beneficial for hemorrhoids, diarrhea, wind disorders, abdominal tumors, edema, heart disease, and weak digestion; it is exactly equal in its effects to the [gruel] prepared with the aforementioned [five roots].
6.12.62 | A soup of horse gram (kulattha) with long pepper (pippalī), as well as a soup of mung beans (maudga) with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) and barley-ash (yāvaśūka);
likewise, the meat broth of gallinaceous birds and wild animals, including tortoise, iguana, peacock, and pangolin.
6.12.63 | Suvarcalā, gṛñjanaka, paṭola, vāyasī, mūlaka, vetra, and nimba are recommended as vegetables for those seeking greens; likewise, old barley and śāli rice are praised for consumption.
6.12.64 | This internal medicine has been described; now hear duly that which is beneficial externally.
One should administer oleation therapies, poultices, affusions, and sudations for one in whom Vata is predominant.
6.12.65 | With śaileya, kuṣṭha, aguru, dāru, kauntī, tvak, padmaka, elā, ambu, palāśa, musta, priyaṅgu, thauṇeyaka, hema, māṃsī, tālīśapatra, plava, patra, and dhānya;

6.12.66 | For disorders associated with Vāta, they recommend an oil massage prepared from śrīveṣṭaka, dhyāmaka, pippalī, spṛkkā, and nakha, as available; furthermore, a well-ground paste of these same ingredients is recommended for external application.
6.12.67 | Having been fomented with waters prepared from the leaves of vāsā, arka, karañja, śigru, kāśmarya, and arjaka,
and being bathed with lukewarm water heated by the sun, he should be anointed with fragrant unguents.
6.12.68 | The barks of milky trees along with *vetasa*,
*mañjiṣṭhā*, creepers, and lotus stalks, together with *candana*, *padmaka*, and *vālaka*, constitute a poultice (*pradeha*) prepared with oil for the Pitta-type fever.
6.12.69 | For one who has been anointed with that [oil], water heated by the sun, along with sandalwood, abhaya, and padmaka, is beneficial for bathing;
likewise, a decoction of milky trees, milk-water, and the application of sandalwood paste.
6.12.70 | In cases of phlegm (kapha), however, an external application of long pepper (*pippalī*), sand, old oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), *śigru* bark, and hemp (*umā*) is recommended;
as well as sprinkling with water decocted with horse gram (*kulattha*) and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), along with urine, and anointing with *caṇḍā* and *aguru*.
6.12.71 | An application of the pulp from *bibhītaka* fruits is prescribed for all [types of burns] to alleviate burning pain;
for pustules (*piḍakā*), an application consisting of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *mustā*, *kapittha* leaves, and *candana* is recommended.
6.12.72 | Rāsnā, vṛṣa, arka, triphalā, viḍaṅga, the bark of śigru, mūṣikaparṇikā, nimba, ārjaka, vyāghranakha, dūrvā, suvarcalā, and tiktakarohiṇī; ||

6.12.73 | A rubbing paste made of kākāmācī, bṛhatī, kuṣṭha, punarnavā, citraka, and nāgara, ground with urine, is recommended for swellings; likewise, sprinkling with the juice of radish is beneficial.

6.12.74 | Those swellings (śopha) which are located in the limbs and parts of the body are of many varieties due to differences in their location, the tissues affected (dūṣya), their form, and their names. Listen as I speak of some of them for the sake of illustration.
6.12.75 | The three doshas, aggravated by their respective etiological factors, produce a most terrible swelling of the head;
when located within the throat, accompanied by a gurgling sound, it becomes a *śālūka*, which causes obstruction of the breath.

6.12.76 | A swelling at the junction of the throat and the chin, extending to the throat itself, accompanied by constant burning and redness, severe in the respiratory passages, and causing intense pain—this is *biḍālikā*. It becomes fatal if it encircles the throat like a coil.
6.12.77 | There may also be a swelling of the palate (tāluvidradhi), which arises from the three doṣas and is characterized by burning, redness, and suppuration in the palate.
Above the tongue there is upajihvikā, and below it, due to kapha, there is adhijihvikā.

6.12.78 | When suppuration occurs in the gums due to blood and bile, it is designated as *upakuśa*. A swelling in the gums arising from an accumulation of blood caused by *kapha* is known as *danta-vidradhi*.
6.12.79 | A single swelling on the side of the throat is *galagaṇḍa*, while a cluster of many swellings is *gaṇḍamālā*.
These are considered curable; however, they are incurable when accompanied by chronic rhinitis (*pīnasa*), pain in the flanks (*pārśvaśūla*), cough, fever, and vomiting.

6.12.80 | For those [diseases], bloodletting, emesis, head-purgation, medicated smoking, and the drinking of aged ghee are indicated; furthermore, fasting should be employed for those arising in the mouth, as well as rubbing with medicinal powders and gargling.

6.12.81 | In a localized part of the body, there may be a large, pulsating, non-painful (anartiman) tumor arising from muscle tissue caused by Vāta and other humors, while one arising from fat is extremely unctuous and mobile, appearing as if it were maintaining its own natural form through the vessels.
6.12.82 | Once it has been cleansed and fomented, the physician should liquefy the unripened [pus] using stones, wood, or the thumb and a rod;
then, having incised and extracted it along with its capsule, he should cauterize it with a surgical instrument and treat it like a common wound.
6.12.83 | That which is not burnt, but has been slightly left over, grows again slowly;
therefore, having examined the regions of the body, it should be cut away entirely by those who are skilled.
6.12.84 | Once the residual stage has been established, the wound may suppurate due to the process of digestion; from that, erysipelas (visarpa) arising from the injury may spread.
Having carefully considered that complication, the expert physician should treat it with those aforementioned remedies as previously described.

6.12.85 | A physician who knows the procedures should first of all diligently prevent [the occurrence of complications] by applying the specific treatment for each; thereafter, the wound-expert should treat the ulcer with haste according to the prescribed sequence and rules.
6.12.86 | One should avoid [a patient] whose [growth] is located in the sides or the abdomen, as well as one situated in the throat or at a vital point (*marman*);
furthermore, those who are obese or rough-skinned should be avoided, as should those who are children, the elderly, or weak.
6.12.87 | Since there is no distinction between *granthi* (knots) and *arbuda* (tumors) in terms of location, etiology, shape, the involved *doṣas*, and the affected tissues (*dūṣyas*),
the physician who knows the prescribed methods should treat tumors according to the treatment for *granthi*.
6.12.88 | A copper-colored pustule accompanied by pain, with a discharging opening, is called *alajī*.
An ulcerless swelling between the skin and the nail, which vitiates the flesh and blood and suppurates very rapidly, is [also known as] *vidārī*.
6.12.89 | A painless, hard, and elongated mass occurring in the groin or armpit that is accompanied by fever is Vidārikā;
it arises from Kapha and Vāta, and its treatment should be according to the specific Dosha involved.

6.12.90 | For these, bloodletting and poultices on the calf-muscle are indicated; once they have suppurated, treatment is like that for an ulcer. As for eruptive boils (*visphoṭaka*) occurring all over the body—these eruptions are accompanied by fever and thirst.
6.12.91 | Abundant eruptions resembling the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) that arise from pitta and vāta are known as *kakṣā*.
Furthermore, other scattered pustules—whether large, small, or medium-sized—that are born of pitta are also classified as such.
6.12.92 | Small-sized pustules occurring over the entire body, accompanied by fever, burning sensations,
thirst, itching, anorexia, and excessive salivation, are designated as Romāntikā, arising from Pitta and Kapha.

6.12.93 | Those eruptions (masūrikā) the size of lentils that appear on all parts of the body due to pitta and kapha— for them, one should apply the treatment prescribed for the pacification of visarpa (erysipelas), as it is beneficial for both those and for kuṣṭha (skin diseases).
6.12.94 | *Bradhna* (hydrocele) arises from wind and other [humors] in the scrotum; it repeatedly protrudes with its own characteristic signs and re-enters.
One should recognize the swelling as soft and oily if filled with urine, and hard if caused by fat (*medas*).
6.12.95 | For suppurated [abscesses], treatment consists of purgation, massage, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), and topical applications, just as for ulcers.
In cases born of kapha, one should incise, cleanse, and then suture the suppurated area like a wound, following the procedure for an ulcer, along with irrigation using urine.

6.12.96 | From the gnawing of worms on bones, excessive sexual intercourse, straining, or riding on the backs of horses in a gallop, a painful swelling may arise at the sides of the anus; when it becomes suppurated and bursts, it is called bhagaṃdara (fistula-in-ano).
6.12.97 | Purging, probing, and incision should be performed, followed by cauterization with oil on the cleared path.
For the severed [vessel], treatment with well-boiled alkali and urine should be applied, and its management thereafter should be like that of a wound.
6.12.98 | Elephantiasis (ślīpada) occurs in the calves, above the ankles and forefeet, due to the vitiation of muscle, phlegm, and blood;
in that condition, the entire therapeutic procedure for veins and phlegm is prescribed, as well as the application of mustard paste.

6.12.99 | However, when the humors (doṣas) are sluggish yet dominated by pitta and severely vitiated, they produce an extremely intense inflammation of the skin and blood, accompanied by swelling, fever, and thirst; this spreading condition is known as Jālakagardabha.

6.12.100 | One should always prescribe fasting, bloodletting, drying therapies, and purification of the body, as well as the application of *dhātrī* (emblic myrobalan) preparations and cooling plasters for *jālakagardabha*.
6.12.101 | Having thus identified other types of swelling as well by means of the symptoms of vāta and the other [doshas],
one should bring about their pacification with respective applications of ointments, incision, excision, and cauterization, which remove the specific doshas.
6.12.102 | Generally, due to trauma, the wind (vāyu) along with blood produces a reddish swelling;
in that case, one should perform treatments that remove erysipelas, as well as those for wind-blood disorders, and for poison-induced cases, the administration of anti-poisonous measures.

6.12. (103? | Here is a verse on the subject: The signs and the treatment for the two types of swelling—distinguished by the three kinds of humors (*doṣa*), by all [the body], by half [the body], and by individual limbs and members—have been declared.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, named "The Treatment of Swelling" (*śvayathucikitsita*), in the Section on Therapeutics (*cikitsāsthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, which was not recovered [in its original form] and has been restored by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Thirteen:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of abdominal enlargement (*udaracikitsita*).
6.13.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.13.3 | On Mount Kailāsa, which was crowded with perfected Vidyādharas and resembled the Nandana grove,
he was performing intense austerities, standing like Dharma personified.
6.13.4 | Agniveśa spoke these words to Punarvasu, the best among those who know Āyurveda, the founder of the science of medicine, who had conquered his own self.
6.13.5 | O Blessed One, men are indeed seen afflicted by the sufferings of abdominal diseases—
those with parched mouths, emaciated limbs, and distended bellies and flanks.

6.13.6 With their food, strength, and nourishment lost, and powerless in all their activities, they became dejected; due to the absence of any remedy, they gave up their lives like those who are helpless.
6.13.7 | I wish to hear correctly from my preceptor, as it has been properly expounded, their locations, numbers, premonitory signs, forms, varieties, and medicinal treatments.
6.13.8 | Thus urged by his disciple for the welfare of all beings, the sage began to speak words that are beneficial to all beings.
6.13.9 | Due to the defects of fire (agni), various groups of diseases arise in human beings through the increase of impurities (mala); abdominal diseases (udarāṇi) occur especially so.
6.13.10 | When the digestive fire is weak, the consumption of impure food leads to an accumulation of the humors (doṣa) due to their lack of digestion;
having vitiated the prāṇa and apāna breaths, they block the upper and lower passages.
6.13.11 | Having reached the space between the skin and the flesh, it greatly distends the abdomen and produces *udara* (ascites/bloating). Listen now to its cause along with its symptoms.
6.13.12 | From the consumption of excessively hot, salty, alkaline, burning, sour, and artificial (garā) foods;
from improper dietary transitions; and from eating dry, incompatible, or impure food.
6.13.13 | Due to the emaciation caused by splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, and disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), from the derangement of bodily functions,
from the lack of treatment for afflicted conditions, from dryness, and from the suppression of natural urges;
6.13.14 | Due to the corruption of the channels by undigested matter (āma), due to agitation, excessive filling,
obstruction caused by hemorrhoids, hair, or feces, and due to the bursting or tearing of the intestines.
6.13.15 | In those whose humors (doṣas) have been excessively accumulated, who perform sinful deeds,
and especially those with weak digestive fire (mandāgni), abdominal enlargements (udarāṇi) arise.
6.13.16 | There is a loss of appetite; even very sweet, unctuous, and heavy food is digested only after a long time;
everything eaten undergoes acid fermentation (vidāha), and one does not distinguish between what is digested and what is undigested.
6.13.17 | He cannot tolerate excessive satiety, and there is slight swelling in the feet;
his strength constantly diminishes, and he suffers from shortness of breath even with slight exertion.
6.13.18 | An accumulation of feces (*purīṣa-nicaya*) caused by dryness and upward movement of wind (*rūkṣodāvarta-hetuka*) results in swelling;
there is pain and distension at the junction of the bladder (*basti-sandhi*), and it even becomes torn open.
6.13.19 | Even the belly becomes stretched thin from eating very little;
the appearance of lines and the disappearance of wrinkles are the signs of what is to come.
6.13.20 | When the accumulated doshas obstruct the channels that carry sweat and water,
they vitiate the prāṇa, agni (digestive fire), and apāna, thereby producing abdominal enlargement (udara) in men.
6.13.21 | Distension of the abdomen, flatulence, swelling of the feet and hands,
weak digestion, smoothness of the cheeks, and emaciation are the symptoms of *udara*.

6.13.22 | Eight types of abdominal enlargements (udarāṇi) arise from the individual doṣas, from all of them combined, and from splenic enlargement (plīha), intestinal obstruction (baddha), perforation with internal discharge (kṣata-udaka). Listen now to their symptoms individually.
6.13.23 | By means of dry and scanty food, physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and emaciation,
the Vāyu becomes aggravated and moves into the paths of the abdomen, heart, bladder, and anus.
6.13.24 | Having destroyed the digestive fire and having stirred up the phlegm, it then obstructs the channels;
taking refuge between the skin and the flesh, it causes the abdomen of the living being to swell.

6.13.25 | Its symptoms are: swelling of the abdomen, hands, feet, and scrotum; distension of the belly; irregular increase and decrease in size; pain in the abdomen and flanks, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), body ache, breaking pain in the joints, dry cough, emaciation, weakness, anorexia, indigestion, heaviness in the lower body, retention of flatus, feces, and urine, and a dark-red discoloration of the nails, eyes, face, skin, urine, and feces. Furthermore, the abdomen is covered with thin, whitish streaks and a network of visible veins; when struck, it makes a sound like that of a beaten, inflated leather bag.
When the wind moves upward, downward, and transversely, accompanied by pain and sound, one should know this as vātodara (wind-belly).

6.13.26 | By the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, very hot, and sharp foods, by exposure to fire and the sun, and by eating while the previous meal is undigested or by eating before the previous meal has been digested, pitta is quickly accumulated.
6.13.27 | Having reached the wind (vāyu) and phlegm (kapha), obstructing their path and following a wrong course,
they destroy the digestive fire (agni) in the stomach (āmāśaya) and thereby produce abdominal enlargement (udara).

6.13.28 | Its symptoms are: burning sensation, fever, thirst, fainting, diarrhea, and giddiness; a bitter taste in the mouth; and a greenish-yellow discoloration of the nails, eyes, face, skin, urine, and feces. Furthermore, the abdomen is covered with blue, yellow, turmeric-colored, green, or copper-colored streaks and veins; it feels as if it is burning, aching, smoking, becoming hot, perspiring, and moistening, and it becomes soft to the touch and suppurates quickly. This should be known as Pittodara (bilious abdominal enlargement).

6.13.29 | By the excessive indulgence in lack of physical exercise, daytime sleep, and foods that are sweet, very unctuous, and slimy, as well as by the overconsumption of curd, milk, water, and the meat of animals from marshy lands (ānūpa), [the humors become aggravated].
6.13.30 | When the channels are obstructed by aggravated phlegm, the wind (vāyu),
being itself obstructed and afflicting that very [phlegm], may produce abdominal enlargement (udara) as it moves externally along the intestines.

6.13.31 | Its symptoms are: heaviness, anorexia, indigestion, and body aches; numbness; swelling of the hands, feet, calves, and thighs; nausea, drowsiness, cough, and dyspnea; and whiteness of the nails, eyes, face, skin, urine, and feces. Furthermore, the abdomen becomes covered with white streaks and veins, and it is heavy, dull, stable, and hard. This should be known as *śleṣmodara* (phlegmatic abdominal enlargement).
6.13.32 | By unwholesome food, incompatible heavy meals, and those given by women— such as menstrual blood, hair, feces, urine, bones, nails, and the like— the digestive fire becomes weak.
6.13.33 | When the three [doshas], vāta and the others, are provoked by mild poisons,
they gradually accumulate in the digestive tract (koṣṭha) and produce abdominal enlargement (udara) in men.

6.13.34 | Its symptoms are as follows: all the signs of every single dosha are observed together, and all colors appear on the nails and other parts; furthermore, the abdomen becomes covered with streaks and veins of various colors; one should recognize this as sannipātodara (abdominal enlargement caused by the combination of all three doshas).

6.13.35 | Due to excessive agitation after eating, from riding in vehicles or excessive physical exertion, from excessive sexual intercourse, carrying heavy loads, traveling on foot, vomiting, or emaciation from disease;
6.13.36 | The spleen (plīhā), situated on the left side, increases when it has displaced from its natural location;
or blood, having increased from the lymph-chyle (rasa) and other constituents, causes it to grow further.

6.13.37 | In that condition, the spleen becomes hard like a stone at first and grows in the shape of a tortoise; if neglected, it gradually encircles the flanks, the abdomen, and the seat of the digestive fire, thereby producing abdominal enlargement (udara).

6.13.38 | Its symptoms are: weakness, anorexia, indigestion, retention of feces and urine, entry of darkness [into the eyes], thirst, body ache, vomiting, fainting, lassitude of the limbs, cough, dyspnea, mild fever, flatulence, loss of digestive fire, emaciation, bad taste in the mouth, pain in the joints, and colic in the abdomen; furthermore, the abdomen becomes reddish or discolored, marked by blue, green, or yellow streaks. In the same way, the liver situated on the right side may produce similar effects; because its causes, symptoms, and treatments are identical, it is included within the category of *plīhajaṭhara* (splenic abdominal enlargement). This should be known as *plīhodara* (enlargement of the spleen).
6.13.39 | When the anus is obstructed by the ingestion of food along with eyelashes or hair,
or due to upward-moving wind (udāvarta), hemorrhoids, or the twisting of the intestines;
6.13.40 | When the downward-moving wind (apāna) becomes aggravated by the obstruction of its passage, it destroys the digestive fire (agni);
having then blocked the feces, bile, and phlegm, it subsequently produces abdominal enlargement (udara).

6.13.41 | Its symptoms are: thirst, burning sensation, fever, dryness of the mouth and palate, weakness of the thighs, cough, dyspnea, debility, anorexia, indigestion, retention of feces and urine, flatulence, vomiting, sneezing, and pain in the head, heart, umbilicus, and anus; furthermore, there is abdominal enlargement (udara) with obstructed flatus, which is firm and reddish, or marked by blue streaks and covered with a network of veins, generally appearing above the umbilicus like a cow’s tail. This should be known as *baddhagudodara* (intestinal obstruction). 6.13.42 | [It may also be caused] by pebbles, grass, wood, bones, or thorns mixed with food.
When the intestines are ruptured by foods consumed, or by yawning, or by overeating;
6.13.43 | The nutrient essence (rasa) undergoes putrefaction as it flows out through those perforations,
filling the rectum and the small intestine, and thereby produces abdominal enlargement (udara).

6.13.44 | Its symptoms are as follows: below the navel, there generally occurs a progressively enlarging abdominal distension (udakodara), and it manifests the symptoms of the *doṣas* according to their respective strengths. Furthermore, the patient voids stool that is reddish, blue, yellow, slimy, corpse-like in odor, and heavy; he is overcome by hiccups, dyspnea, cough, thirst, urinary disorders, anorexia, indigestion, and weakness. This should be known as *chidrodara* (perforated abdomen).

6.13.45 | In one who has consumed oleaginous substances, whose digestive fire is weak, or who is emaciated or excessively thin, the digestive fire is extinguished by the excessive drinking of water; then the Vāyu becomes localized in the kloman.
6.13.46 | When the channels have their passages obstructed, the phlegm (kapha) and the water, becoming agitated,
cause that very water to increase from its own location and lead to abdominal enlargement (udara).

6.13.47 | Its symptoms are: lack of desire for food, thirst, discharge from the anus, colic, dyspnea, cough, and weakness; furthermore, the abdomen becomes covered with streaks and veins of various colors, and it feels like a water-filled leather bag when shaken or touched. One should recognize this as *udakodara* (water-belly).

6.13.48 | In that regard, one should treat with haste an abdominal enlargement (*udara*) that has arisen recently, is free from complications, contains no fluid, and has not yet reached full development. For if these [conditions] are neglected, the humors (*doṣas*), displaced from their own locations and liquefied by the process of ripening, moisten the joints and the channels (*srotas*). Furthermore, sweat, its movement obstructed within the external channels, remains stagnant and swells that very fluid. Upon the production of fluid (*piccotpatti*), the abdomen becomes circular, heavy, dull, non-resonant to percussion, soft to the touch, devoid of skin markings (*rājīka*), and when pressed, it retracts back toward the umbilicus itself.
Immediately following that, there is the manifestation of water.
Its characteristics are: an excessive enlargement of the abdomen, the disappearance of the veins, and a tactile sensation like the agitation of a leather bag filled with water.

6.13.49 | At that time, complications afflict the patient—namely, vomiting, diarrhea, fainting, thirst, dyspnea, cough, hiccup, debility, pain in the flanks, loss of appetite, hoarseness of voice, and retention of urine; one should recognize such a condition as incurable.
6.13.50 | And there are verses on this point:

The physician should declare that among abdominal enlargements (udara) caused by vāta, pitta, kapha, splenic enlargement (plīhan), the combination of all three (sannipāta), and water, each subsequent one is more difficult to cure than the preceding.
6.13.51 | Furthermore, intestinal obstruction occurring after a fortnight, as well as all cases where ascites has developed,
and perforated bowel, generally lead to the death of men suffering from abdominal enlargement.
6.13.52 | One should avoid a patient who has swollen eyes, a deformed perineum, and moist, thin skin, and whose strength, blood, flesh, and digestive fire have been utterly depleted.
6.13.53 | Swelling arising in all the vital organs (marmans), dyspnea, hiccup, anorexia, thirst,
fainting, vomiting, and diarrhea kill the man suffering from abdominal enlargement (udarin).

6.13.54 | Generally, all types of abdominal enlargement (udara) are considered most difficult to treat from the very moment of their birth; however, that caused by the absence of water (ajātāmbu) in a strong patient, provided it has recently arisen, can be managed with effort.

6.13.55 | It is characterized by the absence of swelling, a reddish hue, and an audible sound; it is not excessively heavy, is constantly accompanied by a rumbling noise (*guḍaguḍāya*), and is covered with a network of visible veins.
6.13.56 | By pressing on the navel and suppressing the urge at the anus, [the disease] perishes.
[Otherwise, there is] pain in each of the heart, navel, groin, hips, and anus.
6.13.57 | The Sṛñjayas [prescribe] a harsh enema when the digestive fire is not too weak,
when the mouth is restless and lacks relish, and when the urine is scanty and the feces are bound.
6.13.58 | Having understood through these signs that the water has not yet been produced,
the physician— who knows the specific distinctions of the humors, strength, and time— should begin his treatment.
6.13.59 | One should first treat vātodara with oleation therapies while the patient still possesses strength;
once the body has been lubricated and fomented, one should administer an unctuous purgative.
6.13.60 | Once the morbid humors have been removed, one should wrap the withered abdomen with a cloth;
thus, due to the lack of space, the wind will not cause it to distend again.
6.13.61 | Due to the excessive accumulation of the *doṣas* and the consequent obstruction of the channels, abdominal enlargement (*udara*) arises; therefore, one should always practice purgation.
6.13.62 | Having mixed pure milk with [the medicine], one should have him drink it for the sake of strength;
however, once strength has been gradually regained, the milk should be discontinued before nausea arises.

6.13.63 | When the digestive fire has been stimulated by soups or meat broths seasoned with mild acids and salts, one should again administer an oil enema (āsthāpana) to the person, after first treating them with oleation and sudation, even if they suffer from udāvarta.
6.13.64 | In cases of throbbing, distension, pain in the joints, bones, sides, back, and the sacrum (trika),
one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) even to a patient who has a strong digestive fire, whose flatus is obstructed, and who is dry.
6.13.65 | For this [condition], a purgative (virūha) combined with strong drugs and daśamūla is indicated;
likewise, an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using castor oil or sesame oil boiled with vāta-alleviating and sour substances [is recommended].
6.13.66 | However, one should recognize that a person who is weak, elderly, or a child; or one who is delicate by nature, has few doshas, or has excessively aggravated vāta, is not to be purged.
6.13.67 | The wise physician should treat that [condition] with pacifying measures, including ghee, vegetable soups, meat broths, rice, enemas, massages, oil enemas, and milk.
6.13.68 | In the case of pitta-type abdominal enlargement (pittodara), one should first administer purgation to a strong patient;
however, for a weak patient, one should first give an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) and then cleanse the system with a milk enema (kṣīrabasti).
6.13.69 | When the strength of the body and the digestive fire have been restored,
one should again administer an unctuous purgative with milk mixed with the paste of *trivṛt*, or with boiled *urubūka* (castor oil plant).

6.13.70 | When kapha is present, [one should treat with] a decoction of sātala and trāyamāṇā, or with āragvadha; when vāta is also present, one should use bitter ghee (tiktasarpiḥ) along with cow's urine.
Furthermore, by consistently and properly applying milk therapy, enema treatment,
and purgation in their proper sequence, one shall surely conquer pitta-type abdominal enlargement.

6.13.72 | A patient suffering from kaphaja abdominal enlargement (kaphodara), once treated with oleation, sudation, and purification, should be nourished with foods that alleviate kapha and are combined with pungent substances and alkalis.

6.13.73 | One should pacify kaphaja udara (ascites) by means of drinking cow's urine and ariṣṭas, as well as powders, iron preparations (ayaskṛti), alkaline substances, and the internal administration of oils.
6.13.74 | In sannipātodara, one should perform all the treatments as previously described;
however, when it has developed complications, a wise physician should declare it incurable.

6.13.75 | One should recognize vāta and the other [doshas] by heaviness, anorexia, and hardness respectively, along with upward movement of wind (udāvarta), pain, swelling, burning sensation, delusion, thirst, fever, and distress.
6.13.76 | Having observed the symptoms of splenic enlargement (*plīhan*) as being predominant, and blood as well through its own specific characteristics,
one should administer treatment according to the dosha and according to the patient's strength.

6.13.77 | Having carefully considered [the patient's condition], one should administer oleation, sudation, purgation, non-unctuous enema (nirūha), or unctuous enema (anuvāsana); or one should perform venesection on either the arm or the leg.
6.13.78 | One should cause [the patient] to drink six palas of ghee, or employ long peppers (pippalī),
or even abhayā with jaggery (guḍa), as well as the groups of alkalis (kṣāra) and fermented liquors (ariṣṭa).
6.13.79 | This sequence of therapeutic procedures has been declared; now hear of the pacifying formulations (yoga).
Long pepper, ginger, danti, and chitraka, with double the quantity of chebulic myrobalan.
One should drink this powder, combined with a portion of viḍaṅga, with warm water.
[Likewise, one may take] viḍaṅga, citraka, śuṇṭhī, rock salt (saindhava), and vacā, along with ghee.

6.13.81 | Having burnt the stalks of *rohītaka* creepers in a skull, one should drink them with milk to cure abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and splenic enlargement (*plīha*). Alternatively, one may take the pieces of the stalks with water of *abhayā*.

6.13.82 | Or one should distill it in urine and drink that which has been left to stand for seven nights; it cures jaundice, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, splenic enlargement, all types of abdominal dropsy, and worms.
6.13.83 | When [the medicine] has been digested, he should eat a meal with the meat-broths of wild animals;
meanwhile, one should take twenty-five palas of the bark of the *rohītaka* tree.
6.13.84 | One should prepare a decoction combined with two *prastha*s of *kola*,
along with one *pala* each of the five *kolas*, and an amount equal to all of those [other ingredients].
6.13.85 | One should cook one *prastha* of ghee with the paste of *rohītaka* bark;
when administered promptly, this quickly pacifies the enlargement of the spleen (*plīhābhivṛddhi*).
6.13.86 | Likewise, in cases of abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, dyspnea, worms, anemia, and jaundice,
the physician should perform cauterization (agnikarma) when vāta and kapha are predominant.
6.13.87 | In the case of Pitta-type [fever], vitalizing (jīvanīya) medicated ghees,
milk enemas (kṣīrabasti), bloodletting, purification therapies (saṃśuddhi), and the drinking of milk are recommended.
6.13.88 | With soups and meat broths combined with digestive stimulants,
all treatment for the liver (yakṛt) is considered identical to that for the spleen (plīha), owing to their similarity.
6.13.89 | The physician should administer light foods mixed together for one suffering from splenic enlargement (plīhodara).
For one with obstructed abdominal enlargement (baddhodara) who has undergone sudation, [the physician should give food] combined with urine and sharp medicinal herbs.
6.13.90 | One should administer a nirūha enema with oil and salt, followed by an anuvāsana enema; likewise, one should prescribe foods that cause laxation and strong purgatives.
6.13.91 | Treatment that removes udāvarta and that which subdues vāta should be administered;
except in the case of chidrodara, one should treat it like śleṣmodara after applying sudation.
6.13.92 | As each portion of fluid is produced, the physician should drain it away;
likewise, he should manage the patient who is afflicted by thirst, cough, and fever, and whose flesh, digestive fire, and food intake have been depleted.
6.13.93 | One should avoid a patient who suffers from labored breathing, as well as one with colic pain or impaired sense organs;
at the outset, one should administer water that removes the humors (doṣas) in cases of abdominal dropsy (udakodara).
6.13.94 | One should treat him with foods that are pungent, combined with urine, containing various types of alkali, and which are digestive stimulants and phlegm-subduing.
6.13.95 | One should treat the abdominal distension caused by liquid substances such as water and so forth in their proper sequence;
for almost all abdominal enlargement is considered to be born from a combination of the humors (doṣas).
6.13.96 | Therefore, one should always employ treatment that pacifies the three *doṣas*;
for when the abdomen is filled by the *doṣas*, the digestive fire attains a state of dullness.
6.13.97 | Therefore, one should eat foods that are wholesome, digestive stimulants, and light—
specifically red śāli rice, barley, mung beans, and the meat of wild animals and birds.
6.13.98 | He should drink milk, urine, *āsava*, *ariṣṭa*, *madhu*, *sīdhu*, and likewise *surā*;
or he may eat gruel (*yavāgū*) or boiled rice (*odana*), along with soups (*yūṣa*) or meat broths (*rasa*).

6.13.99 | Meat from aquatic and marshy animals, vegetables, flour-based preparations, and sesame seeds— prepared with mild sours, fats, and pungents, and processed with the five roots (pañcamūla)— [are beneficial].
6.13.100 | One should avoid physical exercise, walking long distances, sleeping during the day, and traveling in vehicles;
likewise, one should avoid things that are hot, salty, sour, burning, and heavy.
6.13.101 | One suffering from abdominal enlargement should not eat solid foods and should avoid drinking water;
thin buttermilk that is sweet and not too thick is beneficial for drinking.

6.13.102 | A woman suffering from abdominal enlargement due to the accumulation of waste (nicayodari) should drink buttermilk combined with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), alkaline substances, and salts;
one suffering from abdominal enlargement due to Vata (vātodari) should drink buttermilk mixed with long pepper (pippalī) and salts.
6.13.103 | One suffering from pitta-type abdominal enlargement should drink [the decoction] sweetened with sugar and madhuka;
one suffering from kapha-type abdominal enlargement should drink it combined with yavānī, saindhava salt, ajājī, and vyōṣa.
6.13.104 | One should drink slightly warm but not overly thin buttermilk mixed with honey,
along with honey, oil, vacā, ginger, śatāhvā, kuṣṭha, and rock salt.

6.13.105 | One suffering from *plīhodara* (enlargement of the spleen) should take it with *vyoṣa*; one with *udakodara* (ascites) with *vyoṣa* and *tūda*; and one with *baddhodara* (intestinal obstruction) with *hapuṣā*, *yavānī*, *ajājī*, and *saindhava*.
6.13.106 | A woman with a perforated abdomen (śidrodarī) should drink buttermilk combined with long pepper (pippalī) and honey;
this is for those suffering from heaviness, loss of appetite, weak digestion, and diarrhea.
6.13.107 | Buttermilk serves as nectar for those afflicted by wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha).
For those suffering from swelling, abdominal distension, thirst, fainting, and pain, the milk of a young camel is beneficial.
6.13.108 | For those who are pure and emaciated in body, [milk] from cows, goats, or buffaloes [is recommended],
along with [medicinal pastes made from] devadāru, palāśa, arka, hastipippalī, and śigru.
6.13.109 | One should apply a plaster composed of equal parts of vṛścikālī,
vacā, kuṣṭha, pañcamūlī, and punarnavā, along with aśvagandhā and cow’s urine, to the abdomen.
6.13.110 | One should boil bhūtīka, nāgara, and dhānya in water and strain it;
likewise, one should boil palāśa, kattṛṇa, and rāsnā and strain it.
6.13.111 | One should employ these eight types of urine for sprinkling and drinking in cases of abdominal enlargement (udara),
as well as for those who are dry, have an excess of vāta, or desire purification (saṃśodhana).
6.13.112 | We shall describe clarifying ghees that destroy abdominal diseases,
[prepared] with long pepper, long pepper root, chaba pepper, leadwort, and dry ginger.
6.13.113 | One should cook two *prasthas* of ghee with half a *pala* each of alkaline substances,
along with the paste of the two *pañcamūlas* and half a *tulā* of their fresh juice.
6.13.114 | That ghee, when combined with an āḍhaka measure of whey, cures abdominal enlargements;
it destroys swelling, flatulence caused by vāta, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids.
6.13.115 | Having prepared one prastha of nagara and triphalā with one āḍhaka each of ghee, oil, and whey, one should drink this; it removes all types of abdominal enlargement (udara).
6.13.116 | This is recommended for a gulma arising from phlegm and wind:
[one pala] of citraka [root] in four parts water and two parts urine.
6.13.117 | A person suffering from abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara) should drink one prastha of ghee prepared with a paste (kalka), alkali (kṣāra),
and the decoction of barley, jujube, horse gram (kulattha), and the five roots (pañcamūla).
6.13.118 | Or one may drink ghee prepared with *surā* and *sauvīraka*;
once the patient has been lubricated by these, and strength has been restored and the *vāta* pacified.
6.13.119 | When the site of the humors (doṣāśaya) has become relaxed, one should administer a purgative as prescribed in the [relevant] chapter.
[The ingredients are: patola root, turmeric, yellow myrobalan, viḍaṅga, and the bark of triphalā.
6.13.120 | One should powder kampillaka, nīlinī, and trivṛt;
[taking] six of the first [drugs] at one karṣa each, and the last three in two, three, and four times [the quantity respectively].
6.13.121 | Having made a handful of this powder, a person should drink it with cow's urine;
once purged, he should eat a light meal with the juices of wild animals.
6.13.122 | Having drunk the scum and the gruel, a man should drink milk boiled with the three pungents (savyoṣa) for six days;
thereafter, he should drink the powder, and in this manner, repeat it again and again.
6.13.123 | This powder destroys all types of abdominal enlargements, even those accompanied by ascites; it also eliminates jaundice, anemia, and edema.
6.13.124 | This powder, beginning with *paṭola*, is highly esteemed for abdominal enlargements (*udara*).
[It consists of] *gavākṣī*, *śaṅkhinī*, *dantī*, the bark of *tilvaka*, and *vacā*.
6.13.125 | One should drink [the powder of] yavānī, hapuṣā, dhānya, triphalā, and upakuñcikā with grape juice, cow’s urine, or the fermented liquors of kola, karkandhu, and sīdhu.
6.13.126 | Kāravī, pippalīmūla, ajagandhā, śaṭī, vacā, śatāhvā, jīraka, vyoṣa, svarṇakṣīrī, and citraka.
6.13.127 | Two types of alkali, *puṣkaramūla*, *kuṣṭha*, the five salts,
and *viḍaṅga* in equal parts, along with three parts of *dantī*.
6.13.128 | When trivṛt is one part, viśālā two parts, and satalā four parts, this powder is named Nārāyaṇa; it destroys hosts of diseases.

6.13.129 | Diseases do not overcome one who has obtained this [remedy], just as the Asuras could not overcome Viṣṇu. It should be drunk with buttermilk by those suffering from abdominal enlargements, and with a decoction of jujube fruit by those suffering from abdominal tumors.
6.13.130 | In cases of obstructed wind, one should drink it with *surā* liquor; in diseases of wind, with *prasannā*;
in constipation, with whey (*dadhi-maṇḍa*); and in hemorrhoids, with pomegranate juice.
6.13.131 | For cutting pain, with *vṛkṣāmla*; for indigestion, with warm water;
and for fistula-in-ano, anemia, dyspnea, cough, and throat obstruction.
6.13.132 | In cases of heart disease, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), weak digestion, fever, venom from fangs, vegetable poisons, natural poisons, and artificial poisons;
6.13.133 | This purgative should be drunk by one with unctuous bowels as appropriate.
Thus ends the Nārāyaṇa-cūrṇa.
[One should take] hapuṣā, kāñcanakṣīrī, triphalā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
6.13.134 | One should powder together nīlinī, trāyamāṇā, sātalā, trivṛt, vacā, rock salt (saindhava), black salt (kālalavaṇa), and pippalī.

6.13.135 | This [decoction] should be drunk with pomegranate juice, the juice of the pulp of the three myrobalans (triphalā), meat broth, urine, or warm water; it is indicated for all types of gulma, for splenic enlargement (plīhan), and for all abdominal enlargements (udara).
6.13.136 | In cases of vitiligo, painful skin diseases (kuṣṭha), those accompanied by wind (vāta), irregular digestive fire, edema, hemorrhoids, anemia, jaundice, and chlorosis;

6.13.137 | One should quickly pacify vāta, pitta, and kapha by means of purgation. Thus ends the Hapushadya powder. [One should also use] nīlinī, nicula, vyoṣa, the two alkalis (kṣāra), and the salts.
6.13.138 | One should drink the powder of *citraka* with clarified butter to cure abdominal enlargement and gulma.
This is the *nīlinyādyam cūrṇam*.
[One should prepare] curd from one *droṇa* of milk combined with half a *prastha* of *sudhā* (Euphorbia) latex.
6.13.139 | Having churned that [mixture] once it has been produced, one should drink ghee prepared with *trivṛt* according to the prescribed method;
likewise, one should drink one *prastha* of ghee prepared in eight times its quantity of milk.
6.13.140 | With one pala of the paste of snuhī milk and six palas of trivṛt, for the pacification of abdominal tumors (gulma), the effects of administered poisons, and abdominal enlargements (udara).

Thus ends the section on Snuhī-kṣīra-ghṛta (6.13.141). One should drink a dose of one prastha of ghee prepared with one āḍhaka of whey and one pala of the paste of snuhī-kṣīra for the pacification of abdominal enlargement (jaṭhara).
6.13.142 | After these, one should drink gruel, milk, or a savory meat broth.
Once the ghee has been digested, the person who has been purged should drink lukewarm water boiled with ginger.
Then one should drink water, followed by gruel, and then a soup made of *kulattha* beans; thus, being dry, one should drink for three days, or even more, after each meal.
6.13.144 | A skilled physician should administer these prepared medicated ghees again and again, drinking them in that same sequential order.
6.13.145 | For the pacification of gulmas, the effects of poisons, and abdominal enlargements,
ghee prepared with the paste of *pīlu* seeds breaks up flatulence.

6.13.146 | One should drink either the Nīlinī ghee, which destroys abdominal tumors (gulma), or the Miśraka oil. For those whose morbid humors (doṣas) have been gradually eliminated and who subsist on the meat of wild animals, 6.13.147 | I shall hereafter describe formulations for the purpose of eliminating the remaining remnants of the humors.
A man should drink a paste made from *citraka* and *kāmaradāru* with milk.
6.13.148 | Likewise, milk boiled with *hastipippalī*, *viśvabheṣaja*, *viḍaṅga*, *citraka*, *dantī*, *cavya*, and the three acrids (*vyoṣa*) for one month [is beneficial].
6.13.149 | Having drunk a paste made with equal parts of *kola* fruits, one shall conquer increased abdominal enlargement (*udara*).
One should drink a decoction prepared from *triphalā*, *dantī*, and *rohitaka*.
6.13.150 | When digested, one should eat meat with the juices of wild animals combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and alkali;
or, as a meal, meat should be eaten accompanied by the milk and ghee of the Sudhā plant.
6.13.151 | Or one should administer *abhayā* with cow’s urine followed by a draught of milk;
or, while abstaining from solid food, one should drink buffalo urine and milk for seven days.
6.13.152 | For one month, one may consume camel’s milk or goat’s milk mixed with the three pungents (vyoṣa) for three months;
or else, one may consume a thousand myrobalans (harītakī) while subsisting on milk, or consume bitumen (śilājatu).
6.13.153 | One should employ guggulu according to the procedure prescribed for śilājatu; or, a drink consisting of the juice of fresh ginger and ārdraka in equal parts with milk is beneficial.
Oil prepared with that same decoction, or with ten times its quantity,
or oil derived from the fruits of *dantī* and *dravantī*, is beneficial for *dūṣyodara*.

6.13.155 | In cases of colic, abdominal distension, and constipation, [one should administer] gruels, soups, meat broths, and so forth, prepared from the seeds of *saralā*, *madhuśigru*, and *mūlaka*.
6.13.156 | Oils for massage and internal consumption alleviate colic in vāta-type abdominal enlargement (udara), as well as numbness,
anorexia, nausea, weak digestion, and [conditions arising from] alcoholism.

6.13.157 | The excellent physician, having observed the morbid humor (doṣa), should cause non-lethal alkalis (kṣāra) to be administered for the purpose of dissolving the phlegm (śleṣman) in cases of hard, obstructed abdominal enlargement.
6.13.158 | Pippalī, tilvaka, hiṅgu, nāgara, hastipippalī, bhallātaka, the fruit of śigru, triphalā, and kaṭurohiṇī;
6.13.159 | Having prepared devadāru, the two types of haridrā, saralā, ativeṣa, vacā, kuṣṭha, musta, as well as the five salts;
6.13.160 | One should cauterize [the area] with a mixture of curd, ghee, fat, marrow, and oil.
After consuming food, one should then drink alkali with *biḍālaka* salt.

6.13.161 | Heart disease, edema, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, hemorrhoids, and abdominal enlargements [are cured] by means of wine, whey-scum, warm water, *ariṣṭa*, *surā*, and *āsava* liquors.
6.13.162 | It destroys visūcikā, udāvarta, and vātāṣṭhīlā.
One should cook goat-dung alkali that has been strained with urines.
6.13.163 | One karṣa each of pippalīmūla and the five salts,
along with pippalī, citraka, śuṇṭhī, triphalā, trivṛt, and vacā.
6.13.164 | One should drink two types of alkali (kṣāra), sātalā, dantī, svarṇakṣīrī, and viṣāṇikā,
in the form of a pill the size of a jujube fruit (kola), combined with sauvīra.
6.13.165 | In cases of swelling, indigestion, and advanced ascites (dakodara),
one should prepare [a gruel] with sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika) grains soaked in the urine of cows.
6.13.166 | One should feed the person as much as desired gruel prepared with milk,
and he should drink sugarcane juice after it for the cessation of abdominal enlargements.
6.13.167 | In this manner, pitta, kapha, and vāta each return to their respective locations [by means of emetics and purgatives].
[This is accomplished] with the sprouts of śaṅkhinī, snuhī, trivṛt, dantī, cirabilva, and others.

6.13.168 | The physician, knowing the scriptures, should administer vegetables before a meal to one with hard stools; thereafter, for that patient whose humors and feces have become loosened, [he should proceed accordingly].

One should administer milk mixed with urine; it is auspicious for removing residual morbid humors (doṣas), and it also alleviates pain in the flanks, stiffness, and cardiac constriction caused by Vāta.
One should cause him who has fathered [such a child] to drink that oil with the alkali of *bilva*;
likewise, [one should treat it] with [the decoction of] *agnimantha*, *syonāka*, *palāśa*, and the stalks of *tila*.

6.13.171 | Having cooked oil with the filtered alkalis of *balāka*, *kadalī*, and *apāmārga*— each used individually— the physician should administer it for the pacification of abdominal enlargements.
6.13.172 | Furthermore, the cardiac oppression arising from *vāta* in those with abdominal enlargement subsides when the *vāyu* is occluded by *kapha*, or by *pitta*, or by both of them.
6.13.173 | For a strong person, castor oil mixed with its own medicinal herbs is beneficial;
this applies to a man who, having been well-purged, becomes distended again.
6.13.174 | One should treat that person with well-warmed non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) that are sour and salty;
for even if it is supported by other factors, the vāyu may cause a man to suffer from flatulence.
6.13.175 | One should treat that patient with sharp enemas containing alkali and cow’s urine when abdominal enlargement has progressed and the three doṣas remain unsubsided despite treatment.

6.13.176 | Having obtained the permission of his kinsmen, friends, wife, Brahmins, kings, and teachers, the physician should perform the medical procedure while declaring the uncertainty of the outcome.
"Inaction leads to certain death; action brings uncertainty.
Having spoken thus, he was permitted by his circle of friends.
6.13.178 | One should administer poison mixed with his food and drink,
or else one should place the poison on a fruit upon which an enraged serpent has discharged its venom.

6.13.179 | The excellent physician, having carefully considered the case, should feed that patient suffering from abdominal enlargement; by this means, his mass of accumulated morbid humors (doṣas)—which has become fixed, latent, and displaced into wrong channels—[is expelled].

6.13.180 | Because poison acts as a rapid agitator, it causes the hemorrhage to flow out quickly once it has been split open. That [patient], whose morbid humors have been removed by the poison, should be sprinkled with cold water.
6.13.181 | The physician should have [the patient] drink milk or gruel according to their strength,
along with the leaf-vegetables of *trivṛt* and *maṇḍūkaparṇī*, together with barley and *vāstuka*.
6.13.182 | Or he may eat kālaśāka boiled in its own juice and water, free from sourness, salt, and fat, whether it be well-cooked or slightly cooked, while abstaining from all other food.
6.13.183 | Then, for one month, while still thirsty, he should drink fresh juice;
once the morbid humors have been thus eliminated, he should thereafter subsist on vegetables for a month.
6.13.184 | One should administer the milk of a young camel to a weak person;
this, however, is a procedure for surgeons who have mastered their craft.
6.13.185 | Having measured four finger-breadths below the navel on the left side of the abdomen,
the wise physician should incise it with a surgical instrument of appropriate size.

6.13.186 | Thereafter, having incised [the abdomen] and examined the entrails, and having observed the entrails that are constricted or injured, one should anoint the hair and other parts with clarified butter, smooth them down, and release [the entrails].
6.13.187 | One should also release a mantra that has become bewildered by fainting;
moreover, one should cause large ants to bite the perforations of the intestinal tract.
6.13.188 | Having identified and cut away numerous ants that have been gathered,
one should introduce them into the intestine with counter-agents (*pratiyoga*) and then suture the wound with those very creatures.
6.13.189 | Likewise, the physician should puncture all types of ascites (jātodaka);
having inserted a cannula on the left side below the navel, he should drain it.
6.13.190 | After draining [the blood] and massaging it, one should wrap it with a cloth;
likewise, one should wrap everything that has become flaccid due to enemas, purgatives, and so forth.
6.13.191 | When the morbid matter has been expelled, the patient, having undergone the jumping therapy (laṅghana), should drink thin gruel (peyā) that is free from fat and salt;
thereafter, for six months, the man should subsist on a diet of milk.
6.13.192 | For three months he should drink gruel with milk, and for another three months he should eat light food consisting of śyāmāka or koradūṣa grain with milk and without salt.
6.13.193 | By this method, a man may conquer even acquired ascites within a year. After all these applications, one should subsequently administer milk.
6.13.194 | For the sake of guarding against the persistence of the humors (doṣas) and for the sake of strengthening the bodily tissues,
milk is indeed beneficial for those with abdominal enlargements whose limbs have been emaciated by treatment,
just as nectar is for the gods who are afflicted by the depletion of all their vital constituents.
6.13.195 | Regarding this, there are two verses:— The etiology, the premonitory symptoms, and the signs of the eight [types of fever] in detail and in summary;
their complications, their relative severity, and their curability or incurability.
