6.13.196 | In the section on the treatment of abdominal enlargements (udara), the Sage has described the signs of those that have arisen and those yet to arise, as well as their medical treatment, through both concise and detailed explanations.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Abdominal Enlargement," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, which was unavailable and subsequently completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Fourteen:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of hemorrhoids (arśas).
6.14.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.14.3 | Agniveśa questioned Punarvasu, who was seated calmly, having completed his recitation and being ready, regarding the appropriate treatment for hemorrhoids.
6.14.4 | The sage explained to him the causes of provocation, the morphology, the locations, the symptoms, the treatment, and the classification of curable and incurable conditions.

6.14.5 | Indeed, Agniveśa, hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi) here are of two kinds: some are congenital (sahaja), and some arise at a later time after birth. Among these, the seed of the anal folds (gudavali) being afflicted is the site for congenital hemorrhoids. In that regard, the cause for the affliction of the seed is twofold: the improper conduct of the mother and father, and past actions (karma); this is likewise the case for other congenital disorders.
In that context, "congenital" means those born together with the body; "hemorrhoids" refers to disorders of excessive flesh.

6.14.6 | The site for all types of hemorrhoids (arśas) is as follows: within the four-and-a-half-finger-breadth extent of the anus, there are three anal folds (gudavalaya) at intervals of one-third [of that length]; this is the site. However, some teachers prescribe a much larger region for hemorrhoids, namely: the penis, the birth canal, the throat, the palate, the mouth, the nose, the ears, the eyelids, and the skin. This is because they are locations of excessive flesh (*adhimāṃsa*); yet, in this treatise, the specific designation "hemorrhoids" (*arśas*) is applied only to those arising from the anal folds. Furthermore, the substrata for all hemorrhoids are fat, muscle, and skin.

6.14.7 | Among those, the congenital hemorrhoids (ārśāṃsi) are some small, some large, some long, some short, some round, some irregularly spread, some curved inward, some curved outward, some matted together, and some with their openings directed inward; they possess colors according to the specific involvement of the humors (doṣas).

Afflicted by these [factors] from birth onwards, the person becomes extremely emaciated, discolored, wasted, and dejected; he suffers from excessive obstruction of flatus, urine, and feces, and is afflicted with gravel or stones. Furthermore, his stools are irregularly obstructed or passed, and may be digested or undigested, dry or broken, and at intervals he voids stools that are whitish, pale, green, yellow, red, or reddish-brown, thin yet thick and slimy, smelling like a corpse, and undigested. He is accompanied by intense cutting pain in the regions of the umbilicus, bladder, and groin.

He suffers from colic with mucus, dysentery, horripilation, urinary disorders, chronic constipation, intestinal gurgling, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), and a sense of coating over the heart and senses; he has frequent, obstructed, bitter, and sour eructations; he is extremely weak, possesses very feeble digestive fire, has scanty semen, is irritable, and is habituated to painful conduct; he is overcome by cough, dyspnea, fainting, thirst, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, indigestion, catarrh, and sneezing; he suffers from blurred vision, headache, a thin, broken, low, stuck, and hoarse voice, and ear diseases.

His hands, feet, face, and the area around the eyes are swollen; he suffers from fever, body aches, and pain in all the joints and bones; from time to time, he is tormented by seizing pains in the sides, abdomen, bladder, heart, back, and the sacrum; he is preoccupied with brooding and is extremely lethargic.

From birth, the apāna vāyu, being obstructed by the anus being covered with hemorrhoids, moves upward and provokes the samāna, vyāna, prāṇa, and udāna vāyus, as well as pitta and śleṣman. All these five vāyus and pitta and śleṣman, when thus provoked, attack the hemorrhoid and produce these disorders. Thus have the congenital hemorrhoids been described.

6.14.9 | Hereafter, we shall explain the conditions arising at a later time in one who has been born—[resulting] from the consumption of heavy, sweet, cold, obstructive, burning, incompatible, undigested, or insufficient food, as well as unwholesome meals, and the eating of the flesh of cows, fish, boars, buffaloes, goats, and sheep.

From consuming emaciated, dried, or putrid meat; flour-based foods, fine rice, milk, curd-scrum, sesame, molasses, and their derivatives; from the use of bean soup, sugarcane juice, oil-cakes, *piṇḍāluka* tubers, dried vegetables, fermented liquids, garlic, inspissated milk, buttermilk-clots, lotus stalks, lotus fibers, lotus roots, *krauñcādana*, *kaśeruka*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *tarūṭa*, sprouted grains, newly harvested awned grains, *śamī* legumes, raw radishes; from eating heavy fruits, pot-herbs, pungent condiments, green vegetables, *mardaka* beans, animal fat, head-hair, food that has been kept overnight, putrid food, cold food, or contaminated food; and from drinking unfermented or over-matured wine, or from consuming spoiled or heavy substances.

An excessive accumulation of waste products occurs when the digestive fire (*agni*) is impaired by drinking cold water, drinking excessive unctuous substances, failing to undergo purification therapies, errors in the administration of enemas (*basti*), lack of physical exercise, lack of sexual activity, sleeping during the day, and indulging in comfortable beds, seats, and postures; likewise, it occurs from sitting on high, uneven, or hard seats, riding on unstable vehicles or camels, excessive sexual intercourse, improper insertion of the enema nozzle, injury to the anus, and frequent contact with cold water or friction caused by clothes, clods of earth, grass, and the like.

Due to excessive riding, the suppression of the urges of flatus, urine, and feces, the restraint of aroused urges, the miscarriage of immature fetuses in women, pressure on the fetus during pregnancy, and difficult labors, the aggravated *vāyu* (wind) reaches the downward-moving *apāna*; having reached that accumulated waste, it deposits it within the folds of the rectum (*gudavali*), and from that, hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*) manifest therein.

6.14.10 | The shapes of mustard, lentil, black gram, mung bean, kuṣṭhaka, barley, pea, piṇḍī, ṭiṇṭikeraka, ibuka, tinduka, karkandhu, kākaṇantikā, bimbī, badara, karīra, udumbara, date palm, rose-apple, cow’s udder, thumb, śṛṅgāṭaka, śṛṅgī, peacock, cock, parrot, beak, tongue, lotus bud, and pericarp are generally dominated by vāta, pitta, and kapha respectively.

6.14.11 | This is their specific distinction: [the piles] are dry, withered, hard, rough, parched, and dusky; they have sharp tips, are crooked, have split openings, and are irregularly distributed. They are accompanied by piercing pain, convulsions, pricking, throbbing, tingling, and horripilation; they are relieved by unctuous and warm applications. They are characterized by dysentery, flatulence, and severe gripping pain in the penis, scrotum, bladder, groin, and heart, as well as body aches, a sense of fluidity in the heart, and constant obstruction of flatus, urine, and feces. There is pain in the thighs, waist, back, sacrum, sides, abdomen, bladder, and head.

One should recognize that hemorrhoids characterized by a predominance of Vāta cause fear, destruction of the wings [of the nose], eructation, catarrh, cough, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), spasm, emaciation, swelling, fainting, anorexia, bad taste in the mouth, blurred vision, itching, pain in the nose, ears, and temples, and impairment of the voice; furthermore, they cause the nails, eyes, face, skin, urine, and feces to become dusky, reddish-brown, and rough.
6.14.12 | And there are these verses on the subject:
Astringent, pungent, and bitter tastes; dry, cold, and light qualities; eating measured and small amounts of food; and the indulgence in sharp liquor and sexual intercourse.
6.14.13 | Fasting, cold regions and seasons, physical exercise,
grief, and exposure to wind and sun are considered the causes of vāta-type hemorrhoids.

6.14.14 | One should recognize that hemorrhoids characterized by a predominance of Pitta are soft, flaccid, and delicate; unable to tolerate touch; red, yellow, blue, or black in color; accompanied by excessive sweating and moisture; emitting a fleshy, putrid odor and discharging thin, yellowish-red secretions; bleeding; associated with burning, itching, aching, pricking pain, and suppuration; relieved by cold applications; causing the stool to become broken up, yellow, or green; producing abundant yellow, putrid-smelling feces and urine; inducing thirst, fever, tamaka (a type of asthma), delusion, and aversion to food; and resulting in yellowness of the nails, eyes, skin, urine, and feces. These are the signs of hemorrhoids with a predominance of Pitta.
6.14.15 | Pungent, hot, salty, and alkaline substances; physical exercise, fire, sunlight, and glare; unsuitable place and time, lack of coldness, anger, liquor, and envy.
6.14.16 | All drinks, foods, and medicines that are burning, sharp,
and hot should be known as the causes for the provocation of hemorrhoids in those with a predominance of pitta.

6.14.17 | Among those [afflictions], those which possess the following characteristics: they are well-defined, thickened, smooth, tolerant of touch, unctuous, white, pale, and slimy; they are rigid, heavy, numb, deeply asleep, characterized by stable swelling, accompanied by excessive itching, and discharge copious, spreading, reddish-brown, white, or red slimy secretions; they involve heavy, slimy, white urine and feces; they are relieved by dry and hot applications; and they are associated with dysentery, frequent urges, and distension of the groin.

One should know that hemorrhoids caused by an excess of *śleṣman* (phlegm) produce cutting pain, nausea, spitting, cough, loss of appetite, catarrh, heaviness, vomiting, dysuria, emaciation, swelling, anemia, cold fever, urinary stones, gravel, a coating over the heart and senses, sweetness in the mouth, and urinary disorders; they persist for a long time, excessively diminish the digestive fire and cause impotence, are dominated by disorders of undigested matter (*āma*), and result in the nails, eyes, face, skin, urine, and feces becoming white.
And on this point, there are these verses:
Sweet, unctuous, and cold substances; salty, sour, and heavy foods; lack of physical exercise; sleeping during the day; and delight in the comfort of beds and seats.
6.14.19 | Prior indulgence in wind (vāta), cold regions, and disregard for [proper] place and time—
this is declared to be the cause of hemorrhoids (arśas) caused by phlegm (śleṣman).
6.14.20 | One should recognize that conditions characterized by a combination of two [humors] arise from the conjunction of their respective causes.
Every cause for the three doṣas is identical to their innate characteristics.
6.14.21 | Stasis of food, weakness, distension of the abdomen,
emaciation, excessive belching, weakness of the thighs, and scanty stools.
6.14.22 | A suspicion of grahaṇī disorder, anemia (pāṇḍu),
and abdominal enlargement (udara) are specified as the premonitory symptoms for the aggravation of hemorrhoids (arśas).
6.14.23 | Indeed, hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi) do not arise except from the three doshas combined;
however, the specific characteristics of the hemorrhoids are determined by the predominance of a particular dosha.
6.14.24 | The fivefold vital air (māruta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and the three folds of the rectum—
all these indeed become aggravated at the onset of hemorrhoids (gudaja).
6.14.25 | Therefore, diseases are painful, they give rise to many disorders,
they afflict the entire body, and for the most part, they are most difficult to endure.
6.14.26 | He who has swelling in the hands, feet, face, navel, anus, and likewise in the scrotum,
as well as pain in the heart and the sides, is indeed incurable for hemorrhoids.
6.14.27 | Pain in the heart and flanks, delusion, vomiting, body ache, fever, thirst, and inflammation of the anus— these destroy one afflicted by hemorrhoids.
6.14.28 | Those hemorrhoids which are congenital, those caused by the three *doṣas*, and those that arise depending on the innermost fold (*valī*) should be designated as incurable.

6.14.29 | Because some portion of the life-span remains, these [diseases] may be palliated when the patient is endowed with all four pillars of treatment and possesses a strong digestive fire; otherwise, they must be rejected as incurable.
6.14.30 | Those [afflictions] born of dual factors (dvandva), those located in the second stage (valī) of the body,
and those that have persisted for more than a year, they say are curable only with great difficulty.
6.14.31 | Hemorrhoids that have arisen in the outer fold, those aggravated by a single doṣa, and those that are not long-standing are easily curable.
6.14.32 | A wise physician should quickly exert effort to pacify them,
for they, by rapidly obstructing the rectum, may cause *baddhagudodara* (intestinal obstruction).
6.14.33 | Regarding this, some say that excision with a surgical instrument is beneficial for hemorrhoids;
others [recommend] cauterization with alkali, and others likewise cauterization with fire.
6.14.34 | This is true: by a wise man who has seen the results of action and possesses extensive knowledge of the treatises, the threefold action is performed; therein, a lapse is most dreadful.
6.14.35 | Impairment of virility, swelling in the anus, suppression of natural urges,
severe flatulence, sharp pain, distress, and excessive discharge of blood [occur].

6.14.36 | Furthermore, there may be regrowth of healed tissues, suppuration, prolapse of the anus, or even death quickly, due to the mishandling of surgical instruments, alkaline cautery, or thermal cautery.
6.14.37 | We shall now describe that treatment for hemorrhoids which is easy to perform, involves little risk of failure, and is not harsh, for the purpose of eradicating them along with their roots.
6.14.38 | Those who know [the subject] say that dry hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi) are characterized by a predominance of vāta and kapha,
whereas moist and discharging ones are characterized by a predominance of blood and pitta.

6.14.39 | Therein, I shall first describe the treatment for dry hemorrhoids (śuṣkārśas). Those that are stiff, as well as those accompanied by swelling and pain, should first be subjected to sudation (sveda).
6.14.40 | Having anointed [the elephant] with the oil of *citraka*, *kākṣī*, *aralu*, and *bilva*, the wise man [should treat it] with bolsters (*poṭṭala*) made of parched barley,
black gram, horse gram, and shriveled grain.
6.14.41 | With balls of cow, donkey, or horse dung, or with sesame paste and husks,
or with balls of *vacā* and *śatāhvā* mixed with fats and made lukewarm.
6.14.42 Or with balls of unctuous flour-meal mixed with oil and ghee,
or with balls of dried radish, or with balls of *kārṣṇagandhika* root.
6.14.43 Or with comfortably warm boluses of *rāsnā*, or likewise with *hapuṣā* mixed with oil,
or with the leaf-vegetables of *iṣṭakā*, *kharāhvā*, or *gṛñjanaka*.
6.14.44 | Having anointed [the area] with Kuṣṭha oil, one should apply fomentation using cloth-wrapped poultices;
one should also sprinkle it with decoctions of the leaves of vṛṣa, arka, eraṇḍa, and bilva.
6.14.45 | The leaves of the radish, the three myrobalans, the arka, the bamboos, and the varuṇa; and those of the agnimantha, the śigru, and the aśmantaka.
6.14.46 | One suffering from colic should be well-anointed with oil and immersed in water that has been boiled,
or in lukewarm decoctions of *kola*, or in *sauvīraka* or *tuṣodaka* wines.
6.14.47 | Or else, after being well-anointed with oil, one should have him immersed in a lukewarm decoction of *bilva*, or in buttermilk, whey, sour *kāñjika*, or cow's urine.
6.14.48 | One should apply the fat derived from a black snake, a boar, a camel, a bat, and a cat as an ointment; this is beneficial for fumigating hemorrhoids.
6.14.49 | Human hair, the sloughed skin of a snake, the skin of a cat,
the root of the *arka* plant, and the leaves of the *śamī* tree are beneficial as an incense fumigation for hemorrhoids.
6.14.50 | Tumburu, viḍaṅga, devadāru, akṣata, and ghee;
bṛhatī, aśvagandhā, pippalī, surasā, and ghee.
6.14.51 | The excrement of a boar and a bull, as well as roasted grain flour (saktu),
ghee, elephant dung, ghee, and resin (sarjarasa) [are used for fumigation].
6.14.52 | A plaster consisting of milk of the Sudhā plant mixed with turmeric powder;
or long pepper ground with cow-bile and turmeric as a plaster.
6.14.53 | A paste consisting of śirīṣa seeds, kuṣṭha, pippalī, rock salt, jaggery,
the latex of arka, the latex of sudhā, and triphalā [is used for application].
6.14.54 | A plaster composed of long pepper, leadwort, black turpeth, fermenting agent, seeds of the Madana fruit, cock's dung, and jaggery [is used for this purpose].
6.14.55 | A plaster consisting of dantī, śyāmā, amṛtāsaṅga, pigeon dung, jaggery,
elephant bones, nimba, and bhallātaka should be applied.
6.14.56 | A warm plaster, combined with the fat of a spring animal (*vāsantaka*), is sufficient;
or else, one joined with the fat of a monitor lizard (*culūkī*) is effective for removing pain and swelling.
6.14.57 | Milk of the *arka* plant, the stem of the *sudhā* plant, the tender leaves of the bitter *alābu*,
and *arañja* mixed with goat’s urine constitute an excellent external application for hemorrhoids.
6.14.58 | These treatments, beginning with oil massage (abhyaṅga) and ending with medicinal pastes (pradeha), which have been described,
are considered to alleviate stiffness, swelling, itching, and pain in cases of hemorrhoids.
6.14.59 | For hemorrhoids treated with various external applications indeed discharge accumulated vitiated blood; thereafter, the patient becomes comfortable.
6.14.60 | Since a disease is not pacified by cold, hot, unctuous,
or dry treatments when the blood is vitiated, the physician should therefore bleed the blood itself.
6.14.61 | Furthermore, one should repeatedly extract the stagnant blood from hemorrhoids caused by blood using leeches, surgical instruments, or needles.
6.14.62 | One suffering from swelling and pain in the rectum and having weak digestive fire should be made to drink this:
the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), pāṭhā, asafoetida (hiṅgu), and leadwort (citraka).
6.14.63 | Sauvarcala salt, that called puṣkara, ajājī, bilva-peṣikā, biḍa salt,
yavānī, hapuṣā, viḍaṅga, saindhava salt, and vacā.
6.14.64 | Tamarind taken with sour gruel, wine, or warm water likewise frees one from hemorrhoids, disorders of the grahaṇī, colic, and abdominal distension.
6.14.65 | Or one should administer a digestive (pācana) medicine, such as that which was prescribed for diarrhea;
or one should have the patient eat abhayā with jaggery before the morning meal.
6.14.66 | Or one should cause [the patient] to drink the powder of trivṛt combined with the juice of triphalā;
when the morbid humors (doṣas) residing in the rectum have been removed, the hemorrhoids go to destruction.
6.14.67 | One should administer a *harītakī* soaked in cow urine with jaggery,
or one should employ *harītakī* combined with buttermilk, or *triphalā*.
6.14.68 | One should administer Citraka with dry ginger and sidhu wine;
or one should cause [the patient] to drink sidhu mixed with Cavya, Ajāji, and Citraka.
6.14.69 | One should administer wine together with puṣā and apāṭhā, combined with sauvarcala salt;
or it may be combined with dadhittha and bilva, or with cavya and citraka.
6.14.70 Or one should administer a satiating drink of buttermilk combined with *bhallātaka*,
or else combined with *bilva* and *nāgara*, as well as *yavānī* and *citraka*.
6.14.71 | One should give him *citraka*, *hapuṣā*, and *hiṅgu* combined with buttermilk;
or alternatively, one should cause him to take buttermilk mixed with the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*).
6.14.72 | Hapuṣā, kuñcikā, dhānyaka, ajājī, kāravī, śaṭī,
pippalī, pippalīmūla, citraka, and hastipippalī;
6.14.73 | A wise person should place powdered yavānī and ajamodā, mixed with buttermilk and seasoned with mild sourness and pungency, into a vessel smeared with ghee.
6.14.74 | Takrāriṣṭa, which has become manifestly sour and pungent and is pleasant to the mouth,
should be drunk in measured doses at the three times when one is thirsty after eating food.

6.14.75 It stimulates digestion, improves the appetite, enhances the complexion, and facilitates the downward movement of *kapha* and *vāta*. It destroys swelling, itching, and ulcers of the rectum, and increases strength.
Thus ends the section on *takrāriṣṭa*.
6.14.76. Having ground the bark of *citraka* root, one should smear the interior of a jar with it;
the buttermilk or curd produced therein should be drunk to cure hemorrhoids.

6.14.77 | There is no medicine in this world superior to buttermilk for treating hemorrhoids caused by wind or phlegm; it should be administered according to the specific dosha, either with fat or without fat.
6.14.78 | A physician who understands the specific requirements of strength and time should administer buttermilk for seven days, ten days, a fortnight, or even a month.
6.14.79 | One should administer buttermilk to a person whose digestive fire is excessively weak;
or, in the evening, one should give a linctus made from parched grain flour mixed with buttermilk.
6.14.80 | Once the buttermilk has been digested, one should administer buttermilk gruel mixed with rock salt;
thereafter, rice with buttermilk, accompanied by fat, should be given with buttermilk as a post-prandial drink.
6.14.81 | One should feed [the patient] with vegetable soups or meat broths combined with buttermilk;
or, after [the initial treatment], one should feed him with soups or meat broths prepared with buttermilk.

6.14.82 | One who understands the sequence of time should not abruptly discontinue the use of buttermilk (*takra*). It is beneficial to continue the application of buttermilk for up to a month, gradually tapering it off.
6.14.83 | Just as there is an increase [of food], there is no decrease; for one does not withdraw from food.
This is for the sake of attaining strength, for protection, and for the firmness of the digestive fire.

6.14.84 | This sequence is prescribed for the purpose of increasing strength, bulk, and complexion: [the use of] dry ghee, ghee with half its oil extracted, and that from which no oil has been extracted.
6.14.85 | One should administer buttermilk in three ways, according to the state of the humors, the digestive fire, and physical strength.
Indeed, hemorrhoids destroyed by buttermilk do not grow back again.
6.14.86 | Even when poured upon the ground, that buttermilk would burn up the grass and weeds;
how much more so the dry hemorrhoids of a person whose bodily fire is blazing?
6.14.87 | When the channels have been purified by buttermilk, the nutrient essence (rasa) enters them properly;
through that, nourishment, strength, complexion, and exhilaration arise.
6.14.88 | Even a hundred disorders of wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman) are cured;
there is no medicine superior to buttermilk for those diseases born of phlegm and wind.
6.14.89 | Long pepper, long pepper root, leadwort, elephant pepper,
ginger, cumin, black cumin, coriander, and tumburu.
6.14.90 | Having ground bilva, karkaṭaka, and pāṭhā, one should cook a gruel (peyā) with sour fruits and fried in the "yamakas" [ghee and oil]; one should administer that which destroys hemorrhoids.
6.14.91 | One should prepare medicinal powders with these very ingredients, boil water with these,
and likewise prepare clarified butter with these for the alleviation of hemorrhoids.
6.14.92 | Alternatively, one should give a gruel prepared with *śaṭī* and *palāśa*, combined with either *pippalī* or *nāgara*, made sour with buttermilk, and sprinkled with black pepper.
6.14.93 | Or a soup of dried radish, or a soup of horse gram (kulattha),
or a soup of wood apple (dadhittha) and bilva, along with horse gram and akushthaka.
6.14.94 | One should administer goat meat broth mixed with these soups,
or the meat of birds such as the common quail (*lāva*) made sour with fruits and combined with buttermilk and digestive (*grāhin*) substances.
6.14.95 | Red rice, mahāśāli, kalama, lāṅgala, white rice, śārada, and ṣaṣṭika— this is the dietary regimen for those suffering from hemorrhoids.
6.14.96 | Thus has been described the therapeutic procedure for those with hemorrhoids characterized by loose stools;
now I shall explain the remedy for those whose stools are excessively hard.

6.14.97 | One should first eat granulated sugar (matsyaṇḍikā) mixed with dry ginger (nāgara), and then drink clear wine (prasannā) seasoned with salt and combined with unctuous roasted barley flour (śaktu).
6.14.98 | One should have him drink jaggery with ginger and pāṭhā, along with sour fruits;
or one may also administer jaggery combined with ghee and yavakṣāra.
6.14.99 | One should administer yavānī, nāgara, pāṭhā, the juice of pomegranate, jaggery, along with buttermilk and salt, to facilitate the downward movement of flatus and feces.
6.14.100 | Pāṭhā, when combined with even one of the following— duḥsparśaka, bilva, yavānī, or nāgara— destroys the pain of hemorrhoids.

6.14.101 | One should administer the sprouts of *karañja* fried in *yamaka* oil and sprinkled with roasted grain flour (*saktu*) before meals; these facilitate the downward movement of flatus and feces.
6.14.102 Or one may drink wine with salt, or *sīdhu*, or likewise *sauvīraka* sour gruel,
combined with jaggery and ginger, as a pre-meal tonic.

6.14.103 | One should administer ghee prepared with long pepper (pippalī), ginger (nāgara), alkali (kṣāra), caraway (kāravī), coriander (dhānya), cumin (jīraka), and treacle (phāṇita), combined with sour fruits.

6.14.104 | Or one should drink ghee prepared with long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), leadwort (citraka), elephant pepper (hastipippalī), ginger (śṛṅgavera), and barley alkali (yavakṣāra).
6.14.105 Or [one may take] a preparation prepared with *cavya* and *citraka*, combined with jaggery and alkali;
or one prepared with the root of *pippalī*, along with jaggery, alkali, and ginger.
6.14.106 | Ghee prepared with long pepper (pippalī), long pepper root (pippalīmūla), curd, pomegranate (dāḍima),
and coriander (dhānyaka) should be administered to relieve the obstruction of flatus and feces.
6.14.107 | Chavya, trikaṭu, pāṭhā, alkali, kustumburu, yavānī, pippalīmūla, and both viḍa and saindhava salts.
6.14.108 | Having ground together citraka, bilva, and abhayā,
one should cook ghee with four times the amount of curd, for the purpose of restoring the downward movement of flatus once [the medicine] has been produced.
6.14.109 | This ghee cures dysentery, prolapse of the rectum, difficulty in urination, discharge, and pain in the rectum and groin.
6.14.110 | Nāgara, pippalīmūla, citraka,
hastipippalī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, pippalī, dhānya, bilva, pāṭhā, and yavānikā.
6.14.111 | One should cook ghee with the fresh juice of cāṅgerī and these medicinal pastes, along with four times the amount of curd; that ghee alleviates kapha and vāta.
This ghee cures hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), dysuria, dysentery, pain from prolapse of the rectum, and flatulence.
6.14.113 | Having taken three palas each of pippalī, nāgara, pāṭhā, and śvadaṃṣṭrā individually, one should prepare a decoction.
6.14.114 | Having ground gaṇḍīra, pippalīmūla, vyoṣa, cavya, and citraka,
the physician should add two palas of this powder to the strained decoction.
6.14.115 | One should cause forty palas of ghee to be administered therein,
along with an equal amount of the fresh juice of cāṅgerī and six times as much curd.
6.14.116 | Thereafter, it should be prepared over a mild fire; once cooked, one should store the ghee. It should be administered as food and as a drink in the regimen of medicinal applications.
6.14.117 | It destroys disorders of the *grahaṇī* and hemorrhoids, cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and heart disease,
and removes edema, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, flatulence, dysuria, and fever.

6.14.118 | It cures cough, hiccup, anorexia, and dyspnea; it relieves pain in the flanks; it promotes strength and nourishment, improves the complexion, and is a supreme stimulator of the digestive fire.
6.14.119 | One should eat a purgative Harītakī fried in ghee, combined with jaggery and Pippalī,
or likewise combined with Trivṛt and Dantī.
6.14.120 | When feces, flatus, phlegm, and bile have been restored to their natural downward course and have attained equilibrium,
the hemorrhoids are pacified and the digestive fire is greatly increased.

6.14.121 | One should give well-prepared, slightly sour meat broths of the barhin, tittiri, and lāva birds, as well as those of the dakṣa and vartaka birds, in cases of the suppression of feces and flatus.
6.14.122 | One should serve as a vegetable the three— trivṛt, dantī, and palāśa— as well as cāṅgerī and citraka, fried in equal parts of ghee and oil, and accompanied by curd.
6.14.123 | Upodikā, taṇḍulīya, vīrā, sprouts of vāstuka,
suvarcalā with loṇīkā, barley greens, and avalguja.
6.14.124 | Kākamācī, ruhāpatra, mahāpatra, as well as āmlikā,
jīvantī, śaṭi-vegetable, and the vegetable of gṛñjanaka.
6.14.125 | One should cause these vegetables to be served: those prepared with curd and pomegranate, those fried in *yamaka* (a mixture of ghee and oil), and those combined with coriander and ginger.
6.14.126 | One should prepare the juices of the iguana, the young deer, the cat, the porcupine, the camel, and the cow,
as well as those of the tortoise and the pangolin, in the same manner as vegetable soups.
6.14.127 | One should give red śāli rice with those meat broths for the pacification of vāta,
having recognized that the patient suffering from hemorrhoids has a predominance of vāta, is dry, and has weak digestive fire.
6.14.128 | Wine, sugar-cane juice, *sīdhu* liquor, buttermilk, *tuṣodaka*,
*ariṣṭa*, whey, or boiled water cooled to a cold temperature.

6.14.129 | The physician should prescribe as a post-drink (anupāna) either a decoction of kaṇṭakārī or one boiled with ginger and coriander, which facilitates the downward movement of flatus and feces.
6.14.130 | For those afflicted by udāvarta, those who are excessively dehydrated,
those with upward-moving wind (vilomavāta), and those suffering from colic, an oil enema (anuvāsana) is desired.
6.14.131 | Pippalī, madana, bilva, śatāhvā, madhuka, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, citraka, and devadāru.
6.14.132 | Having ground [the herbs], oil should be cooked with twice the amount of milk;
this is the best unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*) for hemorrhoids and for those with obstructed wind (*mūḍhavāta*).
6.14.133 | Protrusion of the rectum, colic, dysuria, tenesmus,
weakness of the waist, thighs, and back, and distension localized in the groin.
6.14.134 | One should conquer the discharge of slimy mucus from the anus, swelling, the suppression of flatus and feces,
and frequent straining by means of an oil enema (anuvāsana).
6.14.135 | One should apply a plaster of finely ground dārvī roots, mixed with unctuous substances and made lukewarm, to hemorrhoids characterized by stiffness and pain.
6.14.136 | When pierced by those poisoned arrows, they quickly discharge a slimy secretion mixed with blood;
itching, stiffness, pain, and swelling subside once the discharge has ceased.
6.14.137 Or one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) containing milk and the ten roots (daśamūla),
combined with urine, fats, salts, and the pastes of the "phala" group and others.
6.14.138 | Half a *prastha* of *harītakī*, one *prastha* of *āmalaka*,
ten *palas* of *kapittha*, and half of that amount of *indravāruṇī* should be taken.
6.14.139 | One should boil two palas each of viḍaṅga, pippalī, lodhra, marica, and elavāluka in four droṇas of water.

6.14.140 | When that liquid has been reduced to the consistency of a paste (droṇa), strained, and cooled, one should add two hundred palas of jaggery; it should then stand for a fortnight in a vessel smeared with ghee.
6.14.141 | After a fortnight, a liquid gruel (peyā) should be given in a dose according to one's strength.
Through the regular use of this Arishta, hemorrhoids (gudaja) go to destruction.
It cures malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia (pāṇḍu), heart disease, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors (gulma), and abdominal enlargements (udara);
it removes skin diseases (kuṣṭha), edema (śopha), and loss of appetite (aruci), while increasing strength, complexion, and digestive fire (agni).
6.14.143 | This proven preparation of abhayā and ariṣṭa destroys jaundice and vitiligo;
it is an ender of worms, tumors, nodules, freckles, pulmonary consumption, and fever.
Thus ends the *Abhayāriṣṭa*. 6.14.144. One should crush one *pala* each of the roots of *dantī*, *citraka*, and both types of *pañcamūla*, and boil them in one *droṇa* of water.
6.14.145 | One should cause three palas of the leaves of triphalā to be added there;
when the decoction is reduced to one-fourth, strained, and cooled, one should add [the remaining ingredients].
6.14.146 | One should place a *tulā* (twelve *śera*) of jaggery in a vessel of clarified butter for half a month;
by drinking it daily in the proper dose, one is completely liberated from hemorrhoids.

6.14.147 | This Dantya-arishta is known to cure malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and anemia (pāṇḍuroga), to facilitate the downward movement of flatus and feces, to stimulate digestion, and to alleviate loss of appetite.
Thus ends the Dantya-ariṣṭa (6.14.148). One *prastha* of *harītakī* fruit, one *prastha* of *āmalaka*, and [one *prastha* each] of *viśālā*, *dadhittha*, *pāṭhā*, and the root of *citraka*.
6.14.149 | Having crushed two palas each [of the ingredients], one should cook them in two droṇas of water;
when the liquid is reduced to one-fourth and strained, one should add [the medicinal paste] to that decoction.
6.14.150 | The physician should place one *tulā* of jaggery in a vessel of ghee; after it has stood for a fortnight, one suffering from disorders of the *grahaṇī* or hemorrhoids should drink it.
6.14.151 | Heart disease, anemia, splenic enlargement, jaundice, irregular fever, obstructions of feces,
urine, and flatus, and weak digestion.
6.14.152 | This Phalāriṣṭa, spoken by Kṛṣṇātreya, cures cough, abdominal tumors (gulma), and upward movement of wind (udāvarta), for it indeed kindles the digestive fire.
Thus ends the section on *phalāriṣṭa*.
6.14.153. One *prastha* each of *durālabhā*, *citraka*, *vṛṣa*, *pathyā*, *āmalaka*, *pāṭhā*, and *nāgara* [should be taken].
6.14.154 | One should boil two-pala portions of each of the dental [herbs] in one droṇa of water;
when reduced to one-fourth, strained, and well-cooled, one hundred palas of sugar [should be added].

6.14.155 | Having cast it into a jar that has been saturated with ghee for half a month, one should place it there after it has been smeared inside with long pepper (pippalī), chavya, priyaṅgu, honey, and clarified butter.
6.14.156 | One should drink a dose of this sugar-based preparation at the proper time according to one's strength,
[to cure] hemorrhoids, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), and loss of appetite.
6.14.157 | One should cure with this [preparation] all cases of turbid feces and urine, belching, constipation, weak digestion, heart disease, and jaundice.

Thus ends the second fatal sign regarding the fruit. 6.14.158: One should take one *tulā* of fresh *āmalaka* that has been crushed into pieces, along with *pippalī*, *viḍaṅga*, and black pepper, each measuring one *kuḍava*.
6.14.159 | One should prepare one pala each of pāṭhā, pippalīmūla, kramuka, cavya, citraka, mañjiṣṭhā, elvāluka, and lodhra.
6.14.160 | One should take half a pala each of kuṣṭha, dāruharidrā, surāhva, the two types of sārivā, indrāhva, and bhadramusta.
6.14.161 | Having prepared four palas of fresh nāgapuṣpa with two droṇas of water, one should remove it [from the fire].
6.14.162 | When one-quarter remains,
it has been strained, and has become cold, one should cause to be added two āḍhakas of cooled grape juice, equal in measure to the decoction.
6.14.163 | One should add two *tulās* of refined sugar that has been broken into pieces,
along with one *prastha* and a half of fresh flower juice.
6.14.164 | Having powdered cinnamon, cardamom, plava, patra, ambu, sevya, betel nut, and keśara, the wise physician should add one karṣa of each of these here.
6.14.165 | One should place all that in a very clean vessel smeared with ghee,
which has been slightly perfumed with the incense of sugar and aguru.
6.14.166 | After a fortnight, this well-known [milk] called Kanaka is ready to be drunk;
it is sweet-tasting, beneficial for the heart, and by its use, it stimulates the appetite for food.
6.14.167 | It [cures] hemorrhoids, disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī), flatulence, abdominal enlargement, fever, heart disease, anemia, edema, abdominal tumors (gulma), and constipation.
It draws away all types of cough and severe diseases caused by phlegm;
it dispels wrinkles, graying hair, and baldness, as well as those conditions arising from the bodily humors.
Thus ends the Kanakāriṣṭa (6.14.169). One should perform cleansing with water infused with leaf-fragments or with warm water.
Thus has been declared this proven treatment for dry hemorrhoids.
6.14.170 | This proven treatment for those with discharging ulcers has been heard;
therein, the secondary complications are of two kinds: those of phlegm (kapha) and those of wind (vāta).
6.14.171 | The stool of those with hemorrhoids (arśas) is dark-brown, hard, rough, and does not pass downward due to the obstruction of wind; the blood is thin, reddish in color, and frothy.
6.14.172 | If there is pain in the waist, thighs, and anus, along with excessive weakness,
and if the cause is dryness, then wind (vāta) is the underlying factor.
6.14.173 | If the stool is loose, white or yellow, unctuous, heavy, and cold;
and if the blood from the hemorrhoids is thick, stringy, pale, and slimy—
6.14.174 | When the anus is slimy, numb, heavy, and unctuous, and when these are the causes,
the wise should recognize that there is an association with kapha in those cases of hemorrhoidal growths (raktārśas).

6.14.175 | Unctuous and cold treatment is beneficial when Vata is predominant, while dry and cold treatment is beneficial when Kapha follows. Therefore, one should apply this therapeutic regimen after due deliberation.
6.14.176 | Considering the condition to be characterized by an excess of pitta and kapha, one should treat it with purification therapies;
or one may overlook the discharge, or manage it with fasting therapies.

6.14.177 | If an unintelligent person suppresses the flow of blood that has begun to issue from the hemorrhoids, it will produce blood disorders, deranged humors, wind disorders, and many other diseases.
It cures internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), fever, thirst, loss of digestive fire,
anorexia, jaundice, edema, and pain localized in the anus and groin.
It causes itching, eruptions, pustules, leprosy, the disease known as jaundice,
the obstruction of flatus, urine, and feces, and pain in the head.
6.14.180 | Stiffness, heaviness of the limbs, and other diseases born of vitiated blood [occur];
therefore, once the corrupted blood has been drained, the retention of blood is beneficial.
6.14.181 | One who knows the causes, symptoms, and timing, and understands strength, blood, and complexion,
should wait for the time until the crisis has passed.
6.14.182 | For the purpose of stimulating the digestive fire, for the collection of blood,
and for the digestion of the humors (doṣas), one should treat the patient primarily with bitter substances.
6.14.183 | However, that blood which persists in one whose [other] doshas have been diminished but in whom vata is predominant,
is to be treated with oleation by means of internal drinking, massage, and unctuous enemas.

6.14.184 | However, that blood which flows excessively due to a predominance of pitta during the hot season should be checked with astringent measures, provided it is not accompanied by vāta and kapha.
6.14.185 | A decoction of *kuṭaja* bark with *nāgara* (ginger) is unctuous, red-colored, and astringent;
likewise, pomegranate bark with *nāgara*, as well as sandalwood juice, have the same properties.
6.14.186 | Candana, kirātatikta, dhanvayavāsa, along with nāgara, boiled together, as well as dārvī,
tvak, uśīra, and nimba, are pacifiers of bleeding hemorrhoids (raktārśas).
6.14.187 | One should administer ativiṣā, the bark and fruit of kuṭaja, and rasāñjana, combined with honey,
to one suffering from thirst who has blood in the stool, using water mixed with rice-washings.
6.14.188 | One hundred palas of fresh Kuṭaja bark should be boiled with rainwater until it has lost its juice;
from that substance, the purified decoction should then be extracted.
6.14.189 | Equal parts each of *mocarasa*, *samaṅgā*, and *phalinī*— these three being taken in equal proportions—
and an amount of powdered *vatsaka* seeds equal to that [total] should be added here.

6.14.190 | That juice, once purified and boiled down until thickened so that it coats the back of a ladle, should be taken. This medicinal extract (*rasakriyā*), when administered in the proper dose and at the right time, conquers hemorrhaging.
6.14.191 | Once the medicine has been digested, one should drink gruel or the scum of gruel with goat's milk according to the strength of one's digestive fire;
and when the medicine is digested, one should eat *śāli* rice with goat's milk.
This medicinal extract (rasakriyā) quickly destroys hemorrhoids with blood, dysentery, and bleeding accompanied by pain; it also conquers even severe hemoptysis and both types of *raktapitta*.
Thus ends the medicinal preparation of the *kuṭaja* group (6.14.193).
Having drunk blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *samaṅgā*, bamboo manna (*mocarasa*), sandalwood, sesame,
and *lodhra* with goat’s milk, one should eat *śāli* rice with that same milk.
Goat's milk, when administered with the juice of *vāstuka*, destroys blood disorders;
likewise does the meat-broth of desert birds and animals, whether it be non-acidic or slightly acidic.
6.14.195 | Pāṭhā, seeds of vatsaka, rasāñjana, ginger, and yavānī, along with bilva— these, ground into a powder, should be drunk by those suffering from hemorrhoids during episodes of pain.
6.14.196 | Dārvī, kirātatikta, musta, and duḥsparśaka are blood-purifying;
when blood flows excessively and there is pain, ghee should be administered.
6.14.197 | A physician should administer ghee prepared with the paste of *kuṭaja* fruit, bark, filaments, blue lotus, *lodhra*, and *dhātakī* for hemorrhoids accompanied by pain and bleeding.
Clarified butter boiled with pomegranate juice and barley-ash (yavaśūka) quickly overcomes bleeding accompanied by pain;
alternatively, it may be prepared with *nidigdhikā* and *dugdhikā*.

6.14.199 | Fried grain (lāja) and thin gruel (peyā), prepared with pomegranate juice and saffron and blue lotus, when drunk, immediately stops the discharge of blood; likewise, [a preparation] with balā and pṛśniparṇī [achieves the same].
6.14.200 | Prepared with a decoction of *hrīvera*, *bilva*, and *nāgara*,
along with fresh butter, and made sour with *vṛkṣāmla*, pomegranate, *amlīkā*, and *kola*.
One should administer a gruel prepared with *gṛñjanaka* and wine, seasoned with *yamaka*,
which suppresses bloody diarrhea, colic, dysentery, and swelling.
6.14.202 | The fruits of the *kāśmarya* and *āmalaka*, along with those of the *karbudāra*, and the sour fruits;
as well as those of the *gṛñjanaka*, the *śālmalī*, the milky trees (*kṣīriṇī*), and the *cukrikā*.
6.14.203 | Furthermore, when excessive bleeding occurs, one should administer pieces of *nyagrodha* shoots and *kovidāra* flowers prepared with curd and cream.
6.14.204 | One should administer cooked onion-vegetable with buttermilk, or upodikā with sour jujube,
and lentil soup with sour buttermilk, in cases of hemorrhaging.
6.14.205 | One should eat a meal consisting of boiled rice, śyāmāka, or kodrava, along with boiled milk,
or soups made of masūra, mudga, āḍhakī, and makuṣṭha, accompanied by sour liquids.

6.14.206 | One should eat a meal consisting of well-prepared meat of the hare, deer, rabbit, grey partridge, and black buck, served with either sour or sweet condiments, or with a small amount of black pepper.

6.14.207 | One whose body is dominated by wind (vāta) should eat the sweet and sour juices of the dakṣa, śikhin, and tittiri birds, as well as those produced from the two-humped camel and the lopāka, when the hemorrhoids are excessively aggravated.
6.14.208 | On its own, or when combined with meat broth, vegetable soup, or gruel, the onion, when consumed,
overcomes excessive bleeding as well as vāta.
6.14.209 | A young goat, cooked with blood and plenty of onions,
seasoned with alternating sweet and sour flavors, should be served when there is a depletion of feces and blood.

6.14.210 | By the habitual consumption of fresh butter and sesame, by the habitual consumption of saffron, fresh butter, and sugar, and by the habitual consumption of the cream of curd after churning, red spots on the skin disappear.
Fresh butter, ghee, goat meat, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice,
along with young *surāmaṇḍa* and fresh *surā*, destroy the blood [disorder].
6.14.212 | Generally, hemorrhoids become dominated by vāta when blood is excessively discharged;
even though kapha and pitta may also be vitiated, vāta should therefore be understood as predominant.

6.14.213 | Having observed that the rakta-pitta is powerful while the symptoms of kapha and vāta are slight, cooling treatments should be employed as previously described, and others will also be stated hereafter.
6.14.214 | One should employ madhuka along with the five barks (pañcavalka), the bark of badarī, udumbara, dhava, and paṭola,
as well as vṛṣaka, kakubha, yavāsa, and nimba, for the purpose of sprinkling (pariṣecana).
6.14.215 | When blood is flowing excessively, and there is burning and discharge,
one should also have the patient immersed in a decoction of madhuka, mṛṇāla, padmaka, candana, kuśa, and kāśa.
6.14.216 | One should have the patient, previously anointed with cold oil, immerse themselves in milk that has been cooled by an infusion of sugarcane juice, madhuka, and vetasa.
6.14.217 | After applying ghee mixed with sugar to the perineal region, the anus, and the sacral area,
a stream of water that is pleasant to the touch due to its coldness should be applied to cause hemostasis.
6.14.218 | Frequent fanning with fresh plantain leaves, lotus leaves sprinkled with cold water,
and petals of red and blue lotuses is desired.
6.14.219 | An application of *dūrvā* grass and clarified butter, as well as clarified butter washed a hundred or even a thousand times,
and very cold fanning with a fan, quickly overcome the discharge of blood.
6.14.220 | With *samaṅgā* and *madhuka*, or with sesame and *madhuka*, or with *rasāñjana* and ghee,
or with *sarjarasa* and ghee, or with *nimba* and ghee, or with honey and ghee.
6.14.221 | With the bark of *dārvī*, ghee, *candana*, blue lotus, ghee, and *abhayā*,
[medicated powders] should be applied as a rubbing treatment for burning sensations, discharge, prolapse of the rectum, and hemorrhoids.
6.14.222 | Or, if his blood does not coagulate despite these cooling treatments,
the wise physician should at the proper time satiate him with unctuous, warm meat broths.

6.14.223 | One should treat him quickly with warm pressed-out ghees (*avapīḍaka-sarpis*), as well as with warm ointments (*abhyaṅga*) containing ghee and oil, and with warm affusions (*sekas*) of milk, ghee, and oil.
6.14.224 | In cases where Vata is predominant, one should quickly administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) with lukewarm scum of ghee;
or, at the appropriate time, one should administer a slimy enema (picchābasti) prepared with that same substance.
6.14.225 | Two palas each of the roots of *yavāsa*, *kuśa*, and *kāśa*, the flowers of *śālmali*,
and the leaf-buds (*śuṅgā*) of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha*.
6.14.226 | One should prepare three prasthas of water and one prastha of milk;
when only the milk remains, the decoction should be strained and mixed with the pastes.
6.14.227 | A paste (kalka) consisting of the resin of *śālmali*, *samaṅgā*, *candana*, *utpala*,
the seeds of *vatsaka*, *priyaṅgu*, and the filaments (*keśara*) of *padma*.
6.14.228 | This picchā-basti (mucous enema), prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, cures dysentery,
prolapse of the rectum, hemorrhaging, and fever.
6.14.229 | Having ground prapauṇḍarīka and madhuka according to the instructions for a picchā-basti,
one should cook an oil for an anuvasana enema with twice the amount of milk.
Thus ends the description of the *picchābasti* (mucilaginous enema).
6.14.230. Hrīvera, utpala, lodhra, samaṅgā, cavya, candana, pāṭhā, ativiṣā, bilva, dhātakī, and devadāru.
6.14.231 | Dārvī-bark, ginger, māṃsī, musta, yava-āgraja alkali,
and citraka— these are to be ground into a paste and cooked with ghee in the fresh juice of cāṅgerī.

6.14.232 | One should prepare all these together as a single compound; that ghee is a supreme medicine for hemorrhoids, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia, fever, and loss of appetite.

6.14.233 | This [preparation], which pacifies the three doṣas, should be employed in cases of dysuria, prolapse of the rectum, distension of the bladder, tenesmus, slimy discharge, and pain from hemorrhoids.

Thus ends the *hrīverādi-ghṛta* (6.14.234). Two *pala* each of *avākpuṣpī*, *balā*, *dārvī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *trikaṇṭaka*, and the leaf-buds (*śuṅgā*) of *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha* [are taken].
6.14.235 | The decoction for these [drugs] should be prepared with the following as paste (peṣyā): jīvantī, kaṭurohiṇī, pippalī, pippalīmūla, nāgara, and suradāru.
6.14.236 | Kaliṅga, śālmali flower, vīrā, candana, utpala, kaṭphala, citraka, musta, priyaṅgu, ativiṣā, and sthirā.
6.14.237 | The filaments of the lotus and water-lily, samaṅgā, sanidigdhikā, bilva, mocarasa, and pāṭhā— these ingredients, each in the measure of one karṣa, [should be taken].
6.14.238 | One should remove the decoction when one prastha remains, having been boiled from four prasthas;
in this context, a prastha should be understood as being thirty-two palas.
6.14.239 | Two *prasthas* each of *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *cāṅgerī*,
and their fresh juice— using all these as specified, one should cook one *prastha* of ghee.
6.14.240 | This [is indicated] in cases of dysentery, diarrhea, bleeding from the rectum arising from the three doṣas,
tenesmus, prolapse of the rectum, and various types of slimy discharges.
6.14.241 | When there is excessive straining, swelling and pain localized in the rectum,
retention of urine, obstructed flatus, weak digestion, and loss of appetite;
6.14.242 | Ghee, which increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire, should be administered according to the rules;
it may be taken alone or with various foods and drinks, as it is entirely free from harm.
Thus ends the *sunipaṇṇaka-cāṅgerī-ghṛta* (6.14.243).
There are also these verses here: One should employ sweet and sour substances, as well as cold and hot ones, in alternation.
One who constantly regards the strength of the digestive fire overcomes diseases caused by hemorrhoids.
6.14.244 | There are three disorders which are generally the causes of one another: hemorrhoids, diarrhea, and the disorder of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa).
6.14.245 | When their digestive fire is weak, there is an increase [of the doshas], and when it is strong, there is a depletion.
Therefore, the strength of the digestive fire must be protected especially among these three.
6.14.246 | One should conquer hemorrhoids through the use of fried vegetables, gruels, soups, meat broths, *khada* preparations,
and various applications of milk and buttermilk.

6.14.247 | Whatever food, drink, or medicinal substance conduces to the downward movement of the wind (vāyu) and increases the strength of the digestive fire (agni), that should be constantly consumed by those suffering from hemorrhoids.
6.14.248 | Whatever is contrary to this, and whatever has been shown in the section on etiology (nidāna),
that should never be indulged in by one afflicted with hemorrhoids (gudaja).

6.14.249 | Regarding this, there are these verses:— The two-fold origin of hemorrhoids, their distinct locations, their sites, shapes, and symptoms, and the determination of which are curable and which are incurable.
6.14.250 | Oil massages, sudation, medicated smokes, immersions, and external applications,
as well as bloodletting, are the formulations that stimulate digestion and promote maturation.
6.14.251 | The foremost rules for drinks and foods that facilitate the downward movement of flatus and feces;
formulations for pacification (saṃśamana), and various medicinal ghees (sarpis).
6.14.252 | Enemas combined with buttermilk, excellent ariṣṭas, and those containing sugar are recommended for dry hemorrhoids,
as are the treatments for bleeding ones.
6.14.253 | For those [hemorrhoids] accompanied by complications, two types of medicine are desired:
decoctions that arrest the flow of blood, and various kinds of medicinal pastes.
6.14.254 | The foremost rules for oleation and diet, as well as medicinal applications for rubbing,
washes, immersions, plasters, and sprinklings.
6.14.255 | Whatever medicine is to be administered for excessively aggravated blood,
all of that has been specified here in the treatment of hemorrhoids (gudaja).
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Hemorrhoids," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Fifteen:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of disorders of the *grahaṇī*.
6.15.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.15.3 | Longevity, complexion, strength, health, enthusiasm, growth, radiance,
vitality, vigor, digestive fire, and the vital breaths are said to be caused by the bodily fire (dehāgni).
6.15.4 When the fire is extinguished, one dies; when it is balanced, one lives long and free from disease;
when it is disordered, one becomes ill. Therefore, fire is called the root.

6.15.5 | That food which nourishes the bodily tissues, vitality, strength, complexion, and so forth—therein, the digestive fire is the cause; for from food that is undigested, the nutrient fluids (rasa) and other elements do not arise.
6.15.6 | Prāṇa, whose function is the taking up of food, draws it into the abdominal cavity;
there, its mass is broken down by liquids and rendered soft by oleaginous substances.
6.15.7 | The internal fire, fanned by the equalizing breath and carrying the wind,
properly digests food eaten at the right time and in equal measure for the increase of life.

6.15.8 | Thus, situated below, the fire digests the food located in the stomach for the sake of the nutrient essence and waste, just as [the fire] in a cooking pot cooks water and rice into boiled rice.
6.15.9 | Immediately after food consisting of the six tastes has been eaten,
as it undergoes digestion, phlegm (kapha) is excited from its sweet nature and emerges in the form of froth.
6.15.10 | However, when [the food] is being digested and becomes partially burnt (vidagdha) due to its sour state,
clear bile is excited as it moves down from its receptacle.
6.15.11 | When it has reached the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) and is being dried by the fire,
the wind (vāyu) arises from the pungent state of that massed, cooked matter.

6.15.12 | For food that is desired and endowed with various desirable fragrances and other qualities gratifies the fragrances and other objects within the body, as well as the sense organs such as the sense of smell.
6.15.13 | The five heats— the terrestrial, the aqueous, the fiery, the windy, and that which is with the ethereal—
digest their respective qualities of the five types of food, beginning with the earthly.
6.15.14 | Within the body, the constituent substances and their qualities nourish their own respective counterparts individually:
the earthly elements nourish only the earthly ones, and the remaining elements nourish the remaining ones in their entirety.
6.15.15 | Furthermore, the seven bodily constituents (dhātus) are of two kinds;
they undergo digestion by their respective fires, resulting in waste (kiṭṭa) and pure essence (prasāda).
6.15.16 | From the essence (rasa) comes blood; from that, flesh; from flesh, fat; from that, bone;
from bone, marrow; from that, semen; and from semen, the embryo is produced from the pure essence (prasāda).
6.15.17 | From rasa [comes] breast milk; from that, blood; from blood, the tendons (kaṇḍarā) and vessels (sirā);
from flesh, fat and the six layers of skin; and from fat, the origin of the ligaments (snāyu).
6.15.18 | The waste product of food is feces and urine; that of the nutrient fluid (rasa) is phlegm (kapha);
that of blood is bile (pitta); that of flesh is the impurities of the orifices (khamala); and that of fat is sweat.

6.15.19 | The waste products (*kiṭṭa*) of the tissues (*dhātu*) resulting from their digestion are as follows: hair and body hair from bone; oiliness from marrow; and tears, feces, and skin from the eyes, respectively.
Thus do the pure essence (*prasāda*) and the waste emerge from the maturation of the elements.
6.15.20 | The succession of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) is mutually supported by moisture;
indeed, the specific potency (*prabhāva*) of aphrodisiacs and similar substances quickly nourishes strength.
6.15.21 | Some maintain that the revolution occurs in six days and nights;
however, the revolution of the nourishing elements occurs through continuity like a wheel.
When the teacher had spoken thus, the disciple questioned him further:
"How is it that blood is produced from lymph, which is of a different nature, within the body?"
6.15.23 | Since there is no coloration in the plasma (rasa), how does it attain redness?
And from that liquid blood, how is firm flesh produced in human beings?
6.15.24 | How can fat arise from the liquid element and from firm flesh?
How does roughness come to the bones from the smooth flesh and fat?
6.15.25 | And by what means do the bones in the donkeys become possessed of marrow, as well as smooth and soft?
If semen is produced through the transformation of the marrow, [how does this occur in them]?
6.15.26 | The wise declare that semen is present throughout the entire body;
likewise, for embodied beings, semen arises from the marrow within the bones.
6.15.27 | "No opening is seen in the bones; how then does that [wind] escape?
Thus addressed by the disciple, the teacher spoke this reply:
6.15.28 | That which is called the essence (*rasa*) of all fiery elements among human beings attains the state of blood (*rakta*) through the coloring of the heat of the bile (*pitta*).
6.15.29 | Combined with wind, water, fire, blood, and heat, it attains stability and becomes flesh; that very flesh is then cooked by its own internal heat.
6.15.30 | Medas is produced when one's own vital energy (tejas), moistened by the quality of water, becomes excessive;
it is a conglomeration of earth, fire, wind, and the other elements, brought about by its own internal heat.
6.15.31 | It produces hardness in him, and from that, bones arise in men;
there, the wind creates cavities within the bones.
6.15.32 | Those [cavities] are filled with fat; from that, marrow is known to arise. Therefore, the oily essence (sneha) of the marrow is produced as semen (śukra).
6.15.33 | Holes are produced in the bones by means of substances such as wind and space;
through those, that semen flows out like water from a new jar.
6.15.34 | It flows from the body through channels that carry semen in all directions,
impelled by joy with force, and by the mental resolve born of desire.

6.15.35 | Melted by the heat of physical exercise and displaced from its location, it collects in the bladder and flows out like water from a high place to a low one, just as clarified butter [flows].
6.15.36 | For the nutrient essence (*rasa-dhātu*) is moved by the *vyāna* wind, whose function is characterized by distribution.
It is always being scattered throughout the body from all sides, simultaneously and incessantly.
6.15.37 | Wherever that rasa, being cast forth due to a deficiency in the channels (*kha*), becomes obstructed,
it produces a morbid transformation there, just as a rain-cloud produces a storm in the sky.
6.15.38 | "In this same way, there may also be a localized provocation of the humors (doṣas).
Thus has been described the function of the elemental tissues, the digestive fire, and the food.
6.15.39 | The digester of food is considered the sovereign of all digesters;
for they are rooted in it, and their increase or decrease is characterized by its own increase or decrease.

6.15.40 | Therefore, one should carefully protect him with wholesome food, drink, and fuel prepared according to the rules; for his life and the stability of his strength depend upon that maintenance.
6.15.41 | For he who eats while disregarding the prescribed rules quickly incurs diseases arising from disorders of the *grahaṇī* due to his greed; these shall be described hereafter.
6.15.42 | From fasting, from eating when the previous meal is undigested, from irregular eating, from consuming unwholesome, heavy, excessive, very dry, or corrupted food;
6.15.43 | From the confusion caused by purgation, emesis, and oleation; from the depletion caused by disease;
from irregularities of place, time, and season; and from the suppression of natural urges.
6.15.44 | The digestive fire becomes impaired; once impaired, it does not digest even light food. Undigested food turns sour and acquires the nature of poison.
6.15.45 | The symptoms of that indigestion (ajīrṇa) are constipation, a sense of exhaustion,
headache, fainting, giddiness, and stiffness of the back and waist.
6.15.46 | Yawning, body aches, thirst, fever, vomiting, tenesmus,
loss of appetite, and indigestion— this is the terrible food-poisoning (annaviṣa).
6.15.47 | Being combined with pitta, it produces burning sensations, thirst, diseases of the mouth,
acid dyspepsia (amlapitta), and other diseases born of pitta.
6.15.48 | Associated with kapha, it produces consumption, chronic rhinitis, urinary disorders, and other diseases born of kapha;
when combined with vāta, it produces many diseases born of vāta.
It causes urinary diseases when located in the urine, abdominal diseases when located in the feces,
and diseases arising from the rasa and other tissues when it is associated with them.
6.15.50 | An irregular fire causes an imbalance of the bodily constituents by digesting them unevenly;
a sharp fire with insufficient fuel dries up the constituents.

6.15.51 | When one who has eaten properly is disciplined and the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) is being digested evenly, a weak person causes the food to burn; that [burnt food] then moves either upwards or downwards.
6.15.52 | When food, whether digested or undigested, flows downwards, it is called the disease of the *grahaṇī*; for almost all his food undergoes internal burning (*vidagdha*).

6.15.53 | That which is excessively discharged or obstructed is designated as *drava* (liquid diarrhea). It is accompanied by thirst, anorexia, a bad taste in the mouth, excessive salivation, and respiratory distress (*tamaka*).
6.15.54 | His hands and feet become swollen, he suffers pain in the bones and joints, vomiting and fever occur,
and a bitter, sour eructation arises from his mouth with a metallic smell of undigested matter (āmadoṣa).
6.15.55 | Its premonitory symptoms are these: thirst, lassitude, loss of strength, burning of the food during digestion, delayed digestion, and heaviness of the body.
6.15.56 | The grahaṇī is considered the seat of the fire for the digestion of food;
situated above the navel, it is supported and nourished by the power of the digestive fire.
6.15.57 | When vitiated and weak in digestive power, it retains undigested food and discharges digested food from the sides; however, when excessively vitiated, it releases even the undigested food.

6.15.58 | That disease may arise from wind (vāta), from bile (pitta), from phlegm (kapha), and indeed from all three combined. Listen now to its causes, symptoms, and distinct clinical forms individually.

6.15.59 | By foods that are pungent, bitter, astringent, excessively dry, and cold; by eating in insufficient quantities, fasting, excessive travel, suppression of natural urges, and sexual intercourse;
6.15.60 | When provoked, the wind (māruta) weakens the digestive fire by enveloping it;
consequently, food is digested with difficulty, resulting in a sour digestion and roughness of the limbs.
6.15.61 | Dryness of the throat and mouth, hunger, thirst, darkness before the eyes, ringing in the ears, pain in the sides,
thighs, groins, and neck, and frequent indigestion (visūcikā).
6.15.62 | Pain in the heart, emaciation, weakness, a bad taste in the mouth, cutting pain in the rectum,
a craving for all flavors, and likewise depression of the mind.
When it has been digested, there is flatulence; while it is being digested, there is discomfort; and after eating, the person returns to a state of health.
Such a man suspects he has vātagulma, heart disease, or splenic enlargement.
Afflicted by cough and dyspnea due to vāta, one passes stool that is delayed in its passage, liquid, dry, thin, scanty, accompanied by sound and froth, and is voided again and again.
6.15.65 | When pitta is aggravated by pungent, undigested, burning, sour, alkaline, and similar substances,
it overwhelms the digestive fire (agni) and destroys it, just as hot water extinguishes a flame.
6.15.66 | Afflicted by indigestion, he passes liquid stools that appear blue or yellow;
he suffers from foul and sour eructations, burning sensations in the heart and throat, loss of appetite, and thirst.
6.15.67 | Aggravated *kapha* destroys the digestive fire due to the consumption of heavy, excessively unctuous, or cold foods, from overeating, or from sleeping immediately after a meal.
6.15.68 | His food is digested with difficulty, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite; there is a coating in the mouth, sweetness in the mouth, cough, spitting, and chronic catarrh.
6.15.69 | One considers the heart region to be constricted, the abdomen to be motionless and heavy;
there is a foul, sweet belch, lassitude, and a lack of desire for women.
6.15.70 | In the kapha-type [dysentery], there is the passage of broken, mucus-mixed, heavy stools;
even in one who is not emaciated, there is weakness and lassitude.
6.15.71 | Furthermore, that fourfold fire previously mentioned in the section on diseases, we shall also describe as the disorder of the *grahaṇī*, excluding the balanced state.

6.15.72 | When there is a combination of causes and symptoms individually specified for vāta and the other [doshas], one should diagnose that as a disorder of all three doshas (tridoṣa); now listen further to their treatment.

6.15.73 | When the humors (doṣas) localized in the grahaṇī are intensified by undigested food (vidagdha-āhāra), they manifest with constipation, excessive salivation, pain, burning sensations, loss of appetite, and heaviness.
6.15.74 | Having observed that it has acquired the symptoms of ripening, one should extract it with lukewarm water,
or else with a decoction of fruits along with long pepper and mustard seeds.
6.15.75 | If the āma is localized or situated in the colon (pakvāśaya), it should be drained with digestive stimulants (dīpana).
When the āma has permeated the bodily rasa, one should employ fasting and digestive treatments (laṅghana-pācana).

6.15.76 | To this person whose internal organs have been purified, one should administer light food such as *peyā* (gruel) boiled with the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*) and others, and further provide digestive stimulants (*dīpana*).
6.15.77 | Having ascertained that the disease of *māruta-grahaṇī* has reached maturity,
the physician should administer clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) combined with digestive stimulants (*dīpanīya*) in small quantities.
6.15.78 | When the fire [of digestion] has been somewhat kindled, but the patient still has obstructed feces, urine, and flatus, one should,
after two or three days of oleation and sudation, administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to the person who has been anointed with oil.
6.15.79 | Then, once the Vāta has been pacified by castor oil, ghee, or Tilvaka oil mixed with alkali, one should administer a purgative to eliminate the displaced Doshas.

6.15.80 | One should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with an appropriate dose of oil processed with digestive stimulants, sour substances, and vāta-alleviating herbs to a patient who has been purified, whose internal channels are dry, and whose bowels are constipated.
6.15.81 | Once the patient has been properly purged,
has undergone a proper oil enema, and has consumed a light meal, one should again administer ghee as a regular practice.
6.15.82 | The two *pañcamūla* groups, *sarala*, *devadāru*, with *nāgara*, *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *citraka*, and *hastipippalī*.
6.15.83 | One should boil hemp seeds, barley, kola fruits, kulattha beans, and likewise suṣavī,
with either fermented rice gruel (āranāla), curd, or sour gruel (sauvīraka).
6.15.84 | When one-fourth remains, one should cook an āḍhaka of ghee with that [decoction],
adding the two alkalis known as svarjikā and yavaśūka in the proper proportion.
6.15.85 | Take two palas each of rock salt (saindhava), sea salt (audbhida), ocean salt (sāmudra), biḍa salt, and romaka salt, along with sauvarcala and pākya salts.
6.15.86 | Having prepared these as a powder, the wise physician should administer one *prasṛta* measure of it.
It kindles the digestive fire, bestows strength and complexion, subdues Vāta, and digests the food already eaten.

Thus ends the *Daśamūlādya-ghṛta* (6.15.87). Having cooked eight palas of ghee with one *bilva*-measure of a paste of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), along with one pala of jaggery, a person with weak digestion should drink a dose of it.
Thus ends the Tryūṣaṇādya Ghṛta (6.15.88).
[The following is] ghee prepared with the five roots (pañcamūla), abhayā, vyōṣa, pippalīmūla, saindhava, rāsnā, the two types of kṣāra, ajājī, viḍaṅga, and śaṭī.
6.15.89 | With the sour juice of mātuluṅga, the fresh juice of ginger,
and the decoctions of dried radish, kola, cukrikā, and pomegranate;
6.15.90 | Cooked with buttermilk, whey, the scum of wine, sour gruel, *tuṣodaka*, and *kāñjika*, it is supreme for kindling the digestive fire.

6.15.91 | Or one should administer clarified butter prepared with the juice of bījapūraka, which removes colic, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, dyspnea, cough, and disorders of wind and phlegm.
6.15.92 | One should employ oil prepared with these [drugs] for the purpose of massage;
or one may drink the powder of these medicinal herbs with lukewarm water.

6.15.93 | When vāta is enveloped by śleṣman, or when kapha is associated with āma, or when kapha is agitated by vāyu, one should administer this powder for the purpose of digestion; it is supreme for kindling the digestive fire.

Thus ends the section on the medicated ghee and powder beginning with the five roots (pañcamūla). 6.15.94: Undigested feces sink in water due to their heaviness, whereas digested feces float, except when they are excessively liquid, compacted, cold, or corrupted by phlegm (śleṣman).

6.15.95 | Having thus previously examined whether the patient has undigested matter (sāma) or is free from it (nirāma), one should treat the one suffering from ama disorders properly according to the prescribed method, either by means of digestive therapy (pācana) or otherwise.
6.15.96 | One should powder together citraka, the root of pippalī, the two types of kṣāra,
the salts, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, ajamodā, and cavya.
6.15.97 | A pill made from *mātuluṅga* with the juice of pomegranate digests undigested matter (*āma*) and quickly stimulates the digestive fire.
Thus ends the *citraka* pill (6.15.98). A decoction of ginger (*nāgara*), ativiṣā, and musta is a digestive for undigested matter (*āma*).
Alternatively, a paste of musta and the end-ingredients, or pathyā and ginger, should be taken with warm water.
6.15.99 | One should drink devadāru, vacā, musta, nāgara, ativiṣā, and abhayā,
fermented in vāruṇī liquor or in lukewarm water, without adding salt.
6.15.100 | In cases of dysentery accompanied by pain, one should drink [the paste of] bilva,
citraka, and nāgara, ground with salt and viḍa, along with pomegranate juice.
6.15.101 | When vāta is associated with āma or kapha and causes pain in the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha), one should drink [a preparation of] kaliṅga, hiṅgu, ativiṣā, vacā, sauvarcala, and abhayā.
6.15.102 | For vomiting, hemorrhoids, tumors, and colic, one should drink the powder of *pathyā*, *sauvarcala* salt, and *ajājī*, combined with black pepper, along with warm water.
6.15.103 | Abhayā, pippalīmūla, vacā, kaṭukarohiṇī,
pāṭhā, vatsakabīja, citraka, and viśvabheṣaja;
6.15.104 | One should drink it by making a powder and boiling it, or with lukewarm water;
this is excellent for removing colic in cases of *grahaṇī* overcome by *pitta* and *kapha*.
6.15.105 | In the case of fever with diarrhea (sāma-sātisāra), one should administer ativiṣā, the three pungents (vyoṣa), salt, alkali, and hiṅgu,
either as a decoction or as a powder made into a paste, with lukewarm water.
6.15.106 | Long pepper, ginger, pāṭhā, sārivā, the two types of bṛhatī,
citraka, seeds of kuṭaja, and the five salts;
A person should drink that powder, along with barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), with curd, warm water, wine, and so forth,
for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire and removing wind from the abdominal cavity.
6.15.108 | One *kuḍava* each of black pepper, *kuñcikā*, *ambaṣṭhā*, and wood sorrel (*vṛkṣāmla*);
ten *palas* of sour cane-sugar (*vetasa-amlaka*), and half a *pala* [of salt].
6.15.109 | Sauvarcala salt, viḍa salt, pākya salt, yavakṣāra, and saindhava salt; śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, hiṅgu, and hiṅguśivāṭikā.
6.15.110 | Having ground all of that together into a fine powder, one should administer it;
it is beneficial for malabsorption (grahaṇī) overcome by Vāta, as well as for loss of appetite (aruci).
Thus ends the powder beginning with *marica*.
6.15.111: One *prastha* each of the four sour substances, three *palas* of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), four *palas* of salts, and eight *palas* of sugar.
Having pulverized it, one should apply it to vegetables, soups, cooked rice, meat gravies, and so forth.
6.15.112 | Cavya, cinnamon bark, pippalī root, dhātakī, vyoṣa, and citraka alleviate cough, indigestion, anorexia, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, and colic.
6.15.113 | Having ground together kapittha, bilva, ambaṣṭhā, śālmalī, hastipippalī,
śilodbheda, and ajājī, in quantities equal to a jujube fruit (badara), [one should apply it].
6.15.114 | Having fried [the grains] in ghee, the physician should prepare a gruel with curd and with the juices of wood-apple (kapittha),
sour hogweed (cukrikā), tamarind (vṛkṣāmla), and pomegranate (dāḍima).

6.15.115 | The soup of the five spices (*pañcakolaka*) and that of radishes with pungent condiments destroy all types of diarrhea, disorders of the *grahaṇī*, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), hemorrhoids, and splenic enlargement.
6.15.116 | A fatty meat broth from wild animals, seasoned with pomegranate and buttermilk,
or the fresh juice of carnivorous animals, is recommended for consumption as it stimulates digestion.
6.15.117 | Buttermilk, fermented gruel, wines, and *ariṣṭas* are for drinking;
however, buttermilk is used in cases of disorders of the *grahaṇī* because it stimulates digestion, is absorbent, and is light.
6.15.118 | It is the best because it has a sweet post-digestive effect (pākaphala) and does not aggravate pitta;
due to its astringent taste, heating nature, expanding quality, and dryness, it is beneficial for kapha.
6.15.119 | Because it is sweet, sour, and thick, buttermilk that is fresh is non-irritating when used for wind disorders;
therefore, there are various applications of buttermilk for abdominal enlargements as well as for hemorrhoids.
6.15.120 | One should employ all these [drugs] prescribed for the disorder of the *grahaṇī*:
*yavānī*, *āmalaka*, *pathyā*, and black pepper, each in a portion of three *palas*.
6.15.121 | One should grind five *pala* portions of salts together into a powder. A person should drink that which has fermented in buttermilk (*takra*) once it has arisen;
this is *takrāriṣṭa*, which stimulates digestion and removes swelling, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, worms, urinary disorders, and abdominal enlargement.

Thus ends the section on *takrāriṣṭa*. 6.15.122. Having recognized that the *pitta* has returned to its own site, become aggravated, and is extinguishing the digestive fire (*agni*), the physician should eliminate it by means of purgation or emesis.
6.15.123 | With foods that do not cause a burning sensation, which are light and combined with bitter [herbs],
as well as with the juices of wild animals, soups of mung beans and the like, and even with *khada* (vinegar-based drinks).

6.15.124 | One should stimulate his digestive fire with powders and bitter ghees that contain pomegranate and sour substances, along with clarified butter, and are combined with appetizers and astringents.
6.15.125 | Sandalwood, padmaka, uśīra, pāṭhā, mūrvā, kuṭannaṭa,
ṣaḍgranthā, sārivā, āsphotā, saptaparṇa, and āṭarūṣaka;
6.15.126 | Two-pala portions each of paṭola, udumbara, aśvattha, vaṭa, plakṣa, kapītana, kaṭukā, rohiṇī, musta, and nimba;
6.15.127 | One should prepare one *prastha* of ghee by boiling it with one *droṇa* of water until one-quarter remains,
adding *kirātatikta*, *indrayava*, *vīrā*, *māgadhikā*, and *utpala*.
6.15.128 | This should be drunk with pastes (kalka) equal to one akṣa each for the disease of pitta-grahaṇī;
and one should also administer that "bitter" (tiktaka) ghee which was prescribed in the chapter on abdominal diseases (kauṣṭhika).
Thus ends the *Candanādya-ghṛta* (6.15.129).
[One should take] ginger, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *dhātakī*, and *rasāñjana*; the bark and fruit of *vatsaka*, *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*.
6.15.130 | One should drink that powder in equal parts with honey and rice-water in cases of pitta-type grahaṇī disorder and when blood is passed in the stool.
6.15.131 | This powder, beginning with ginger (nāgarādyam), honored by Kṛṣṇātreya, conquers hemorrhoids, pain in the anus, and dysentery.
Thus ends the Nāgarādyacūrṇa (6.15.132). One should powder equal parts of bhūnimba, kaṭukā, vyōṣa, mustaka, and indrayava,
along with two parts of citraka and sixteen parts of vatsaka bark.
