6.15.133 | When drunk with cooled water mixed with jaggery, it cures disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī-doṣa) and abdominal tumors (gulma), as well as jaundice, fever, anemia, urinary disorders, anorexia, and diarrhea.
Thus ends the Bhūnimbādyacūrṇa (6.15.134). [The following ingredients are:
Vacā, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, saptaparṇa, rasāñjana, syonāka, udīcya, kaṭvaṅga, vatsakatvak, and durālabhā.
6.15.135 | Dārvī, parpaṭaka, pāṭhā, yavānī, madhuśigruka, paṭola leaves, siddhārtha, yūthikā, and jasmine sprouts.

6.15.136 | One seeking the alleviation of those diseases should administer the inner pulp of *jambu*, mango, and *bilva*, as well as the leaves and fruits of *nimba*, combined with the *bhūnimbādi* group of drugs.
6.15.137 | Kirātatikta, ṣaḍgranthā, trāyamāṇā, the three pungents (kaṭutrika),
candana, padmaka, uśīra, dārvītvak, and kaṭurohiṇī.
6.15.138 | Kaṭaja bark and fruit, musta, yavānī, and devadāru;
paṭola and nimba leaves, elā, saurāṣṭrī, ativiṣā, and tvak.
6.15.139 | The seeds of madhuśigru, as well as mūrvā and parpaṭaka—
this powder should be licked with honey, or drunk with wines or water.

6.15.140 | It destroys heart disease, anemia, disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), abdominal tumors (gulma), colic, loss of appetite, fever, jaundice, disorders of the combined humors (sannipāta), and diseases of the mouth.
Thus ends the Kirātādya powder (6.15.141).
In a case of *grahaṇī* disorder caused by vitiated phlegm (*śleṣman*), after the patient has been properly vomited,
one should increase the digestive fire with pungent, sour, salty, alkaline, and bitter substances.
6.15.142 | Palāśa, citraka, cavya, mātuluṅga, harītakī, pippalī,
pippalīmūla, pāṭhā, nāgara, and dhānyaka.
6.15.143 | Having boiled one karṣa of each [drug] in one prastha of water until reduced to one-fourth,
one should employ it for drinking purposes and prepare gruel with them.
6.15.144 | Alternatively, one should feed light foods with a soup of dried radish or with horse-gram (kulattha), seasoned with pungent, sour, alkaline, and salty flavors.
6.15.145 | One should drink sour buttermilk after [the meal], or else *takrāriṣṭa*;
or likewise *madirā*, *madhvariṣṭa*, *nigada*, or even *sīdhu*.
6.15.146 | One droṇa of madhūka flowers, half that amount of viḍaṅgas,
half of that again of citraka, and likewise one āḍhaka of bhallātaka.
6.15.147 One should boil eight palas of mañjiṣṭhā in three droṇas of water until one droṇa remains;
when it has cooled, it should be combined with half an āḍhaka of honey.
6.15.148 | One should employ that liquor which has been produced and kept for a month in a jar smeared with ela, lotus stalks, aguru, and sandalwood.
6.15.149 | It certainly kindles the digestive fire (*grahaṇī*), is nourishing, and conquers *kapha* and *pitta*.
It destroys edema, skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), leucoderma (*kilāsa*), and urinary disorders (*prameha*).
Thus ends the Madhūka-āsava (6.15.150). One should boil the fresh juice of Madhūka flowers until it is reduced by half,
then add a quarter part honey and, once cooled, store it as previously described.
6.15.151 | Drinking that while eating wholesome food, one may conquer all disorders of the grahaṇī;
likewise, one should drink fermented juices of grapes and dates.
6.15.152 | Two *prasthas* of *durālabhā*, one *prastha* of *āmalaka*,
two handfuls each of *dantī* and *citraka*, and one hundred fresh *abhayā* fruits.
6.15.153 Having boiled four *droṇas* of water down until one *droṇa* remains, once it has cooled,
it should be strained and mixed with two hundred *guḍas* and ten *kuḍavas* of honey.
6.15.154 | Likewise, one should drink [the oil] that has been prepared in a jar of ghee for a fortnight from the powdered seeds of *praiyaṅgu*, *pippalī*, and *viḍaṅga*, each weighing one *kuḍava*.

This [preparation] cures malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), hemorrhoids (arśas), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), erysipelas (vīsarpa), and urinary disorders (meha); it improves the voice and complexion, and alleviates internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta) and phlegm (kapha).
Thus ends the section on Durālabhāsava. 6.15.156. One should boil five-pala portions each of Haridrā, the two Pañcamūlas (major and minor), Vīra, Ṛṣabhaka, and Jīvaka in four droṇas of water.
6.15.157 | When the liquid has been strained and only the dregs remain, the physician should add two hundred palas of jaggery and half-kuḍava portions of powdered [medicinal herbs], along with honey.
One should drink that [decoction] containing *priyaṅgu*, *mustā*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *viḍaṅga*, *madhuka*, *plava*,
and *śābaraka* lodhra, after it has been left to stand for half a month.
6.15.159 | This prepared *mūlāsava* is a digestive stimulant that conquers *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), as well as abdominal distension,
*kapha*-related diseases, heart disease, anemia, and physical exhaustion.

Thus ends the section on Mūlāsava (6.15.160). One should grind one prastha of pippalī and add jaggery, the pulp of bibhītaka, and one prastha of water, then place the mixture in a heap of barley straw.
6.15.161 | Therefore, one should drink one pala of this well-prepared juice combined with a handful of water; for this is the "pinda-āsava," which destroys hosts of diseases.
6.15.162 | Even a person who is healthy should drink this for a month while eating unctuous and flavorful food,
if he desires the non-recurrence of those diseases mentioned here.
Thus ends the Piṇḍāsava.
6.15.163. In a new jar smeared with long pepper and honey and fumigated with agallochum, one should cause an āḍhaka of honey, an equal amount of water, and the following powders to be placed:
6.15.164 | Half a *kuḍava* of *viḍaṅga*, one *kuḍava* of *pippalī*,
and a quarter-part each of *tvakkṣīrī*, *keśara*, and black pepper;
6.15.165 | Take cinnamon, cardamom, cinnamon leaves, *śaṭī*, betel nut, *ativiṣā*, *ghanā*, *hareṇu*, *ilvāluka*, *tejohvā*, long pepper root, and *citraka*.
6.15.166 | One should administer it at the rate of one karṣa per day for a month, and thereafter continue its use.
It kindles a weak digestive fire and makes an irregular fire regular.
6.15.167 | Madhuariṣṭa dispels heart disease, anemia, disorders of the grahaṇī, leprosy, hemorrhoids, edema, fever, and other diseases caused by vāta and kapha.
Thus ends the section on honey-wine (madhvariṣṭa).
6.15.168. One should take long pepper with its roots, the two alkalis, the five salts, citron, chebulic myrobalan, rāsnā, śaṭī, black pepper, and ginger.
6.15.169 | Having made equal portions of these powders, one should drink them in the morning with warm water;
this increases strength, complexion, and digestive fire in cases of *grahaṇī* disorder caused by *kapha*.
6.15.170 | Ghee prepared with these very same medicinal herbs should be drunk when wind (vāta) is predominant;
furthermore, the six-pala ghee and the bhallātaka ghee are prescribed for those suffering from gulma.
6.15.171 | One should burn viḍa salt, kālalavaṇa, sarjikā, yavaśūka, saptalā, kaṇṭakārī, and citraka.
6.15.172 | Having boiled one āḍhaka of ghee with two āḍhakas of this alkaline liquid that has been strained seven times, one should drink it to increase the digestive fire.
Thus ends the alkaline ghee (kṣāraghṛta). 6.15.173. [One should take] long pepper with its root, pāṭhā, cavya, indrayava, ginger, citraka, ativiṣā, asafoetida, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
6.15.174 | One karṣa of vacā, five palas of the five salts, two prasthas of curd, and two kuḍavas each of oil and ghee.
6.15.175 | Having boiled the pieces until the juice has slowly receded within,
one should then burn them with internal smoke (antardhūma), reduce them to powder, and drench it in ghee.
6.15.176 | One should drink a palmful (pāṇitala) of it; once that has been digested, one should eat sweet food.
It destroys all diseases of wind (vāta) and phlegm (śleṣman), as well as poisons and artificial toxins (viṣa-gara).
6.15.177 | One should burn two palas each of bhallātaka, trikaṭuka, triphalā, and the three salts using cow-dung fire while applying the antardhūma technique.
6.15.178 | This alkaline preparation, when drunk with clarified butter or sprinkled over food,
cures heart disease, anemia, disorders of the duodenum, abdominal tumors, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and colic.
6.15.179 | Durālabhā, the two types of karañja, saptaparṇa along with vatsaka,
ṣaḍgranthā, madana, mūrvā, pāṭhā, and likewise āragvadha.
6.15.180 | Having made equal parts of these powders and mixing them with cow urine, one should burn them.
After burning, one should drink that alkali (kṣāra), which increases the strength of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
6.15.181 | One should burn bhūnimba, rohiṇī, tiktā, paṭola, nimba, and parpaṭa with buffalo urine; this alkali (kṣāra) increases the digestive fire.
6.15.182 | Two types of haridrā, vacā, kuṣṭha, citraka, kaṭurohiṇī, and musta—these should be burnt with goat's urine; this alkali increases the digestive fire.
6.15.183 | Four palas from the stem of Sudhā, three palas from the three salts,
one kuḍava of Vārtākī, eight palas from Arka, and two palas from Citraka.
6.15.184 | Pills made from burnt [iron] in the juice of Vārtāku, taken after meals,
quickly digest whatever has been eaten and are beneficial for cough, dyspnea, and hemorrhoids.
6.15.185 | These [pills] also pacify cholera, catarrh, and heart disease.
Thus has this alkali-pill (kṣāraguṭikā) been proclaimed by Kṛṣṇātreya.

Thus ends the description of the alkaline pill (kṣāraguḍikā). 6.15.186. One should grind vatsaka, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, duḥsparśā, hiṅgu, and citraka into a powder and cook it in the alkali of palāśa leaves strained with urine.

6.15.187 | From that thick [mixture], one suffering from disorders of the *grahaṇī*, edema, hemorrhoids, or anemia should drink a *kola* measure with lukewarm water or with fermented liquors (*madya*), using an iron vessel.
Thus ends the fourth alkaline preparation (caturthakṣāra).
6.15.188: Take three palas each of kaṭabhī, cavya, the pulp of bilva, iron filings, rohiṇī, kaṭukā, musta, kuṣṭha, pāṭhā, and hiṅgu.
6.15.189 | Madhuka, the alkalis of muṣkaka and yavakṣāra, trikaṭu, vacā,
viḍaṅga, pippalīmūla, svarjikā, nimba, and citraka.
6.15.190 | One karṣa each of mūrvā, ajamoda, indrayava, guḍūcī, and devadāru,
along with one pala each of the five salts individually.
6.15.191 | Having mixed three kuḍavas of curd with portions of ghee and oil,
one should burn it slowly with internal smoke (antardhūma) and drink one pāṇitala from that.
6.15.192 | One suffering from phlegm, wind, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī),
anemia, splenic enlargement, urinary retention, asthma, hiccups, cough, worms, or fever [should treat them] with ghee.
6.15.193 | Alkali, which generates fire, is excellent for destroying consumption, diarrhea, swelling, urinary disorders, abdominal distension, cardiac oppression, and all types of poison.
6.15.194 | When it has been digested, one should eat with sweet juices or even with milk.
Thus ends the fifth alkali.
In the case of the three doṣas, the wise physician should cause the five purificatory procedures (pañcakarma) to be performed.

6.15.195 | One should administer clarified butter, alkalis, fermented liquors (āsava), and medicinal decoctions (ariṣṭa) that increase the digestive fire, as well as whatever treatments have been prescribed for vāta and the other doshas in the context of grahaṇī.
6.15.196 | One who understands the specific nature of the doshas should perform all these measures either in their regular order or by reversing them:
oleation, sudation, purification, lightening therapy, and digestive stimulation.

6.15.197 | Powders, salts, alkalis, honey, fermented liquors (ariṣṭa), spirits (surā), and distilled spirits (āsava); various preparations with buttermilk, and various kinds of digestive (dīpana) ghees.
6.15.198 | Those suffering from *grahaṇī* disease should utilize [these remedies]; now hear the treatment according to the specific stage:
in the *ślaiṣmika* (kapha-type) condition, expectoration should be treated with dry, digestive-stimulating substances combined with bitter [tastes].
6.15.199 | For one who is emaciated and has an abundance of phlegm, a diet that is once dry and once unctuous is beneficial;
having examined the internal state of the body, it should be combined with unctuous substances to stimulate the digestive fire.
6.15.200 | A digestive stimulant (dīpana) that is bitter combined with sweet is beneficial for one with an excess of bile (pitta);
however, one combined with unctuous substances (sneha), salt, and sour is beneficial for one with an excess of wind (vāta).
In that same way, fire is kindled for them by means of fuel according to the prescribed rules;
one should know that affection alone is the supreme stimulant for a weak fire.
Even very heavy food is not sufficient to pacify the digestive fire that is inflamed by fat,
for one who has weak digestion and passes undigested feces in diarrhea.
6.15.203 | He should drink a measured dose of ghee combined with digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya) herbs;
by means of that, the *samāna* wind becomes tranquil and returns to its proper path.
6.15.204 | Because it moves near the fire, it quickly produces strength;
however, due to its hardness, the person whose feces are [constipated] voids them with difficulty.
6.15.205 | A person suffering from constipation (annāvagraha) should drink ghee mixed with salts.
If the digestive fire is weak due to dryness (raukṣya), one should drink ghee or oil combined with digestive stimulants (dīpana).
6.15.206 | When the digestive fire is weak due to excessive unctuousness, powders, fermented liquors (ariṣṭa), and spirits (āsava) are beneficial;
when it is impaired by the coating of the rectum, oils, wines, and spirits are indicated.
6.15.207 | When the digestive fire is weak due to udāvarta, one should administer nirūha enemas and oil enemas (snehabasti).
However, when the digestive fire is weak due to the increase of the doṣas, the patient, having been purified, should follow the regimen for the respective doṣa.
6.15.208 | When the digestive fire is weak due to the presence of disease, ghee alone is the stimulant for that fire;
when the fire is weakened by fasting, one should drink ghee along with gruels.
6.15.209 | That [milk] which is pressed out while food is still present in the stomach is strengthening, digestive, and nourishing;
however, due to long-term indulgence in it, men who have become emaciated, wasted, and thin [may suffer].
6.15.210 | One should feed [the patient] meat juices from carnivorous animals that are sour;
because they are light, sharp, hot, and purifying, they quickly kindle the digestive fire.
6.15.211 | Because it increases the flesh through the accumulation of flesh, it likewise brings about very rapid nourishment.
The bodily fire is not kindled by fasting, nor is it kindled by overeating.

6.15.212 Just as a fire, whether small or covered by a lack of fuel, [flares up] when provided with various kinds of oils and food-preparations, such as powders, *ariṣṭas*, wines, and spirits; ||| so too does the fire of the body increase through the consumption of diverse substances. ||| Just as a small fire, even if it has no fuel or is covered by a lack of fuel, blazes up when supplied with various types of oils, foods, and preparations, including powders, *ariṣṭas*, wines, and fermented liquors; 6.15.213 | When employed correctly by a physician, the strength of the digestive fire increases;
for just as fire established upon solid wood remains steady for a long time.
6.15.214 | Likewise, by means of oleation therapies and dietary regimens, the internal fire becomes stable;
eating what is wholesome, in moderation, and only after the previous meal is digested, one enjoys long-term health.
6.15.215 | One should strive for the increase of the digestive fire through the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
When the humors (doṣas) are balanced, the heat situated within the body remains moderate and stable.
6.15.216 | When it digests food, it promotes health, nourishment, longevity, and strength;
however, when it is sluggish due to the *doṣas* or excessively increased by them, or when they are irregular, it generates diseases.
6.15.217 | That which was stated regarding the dull-witted has been explained; now that concerning the excessively aged will be told:
when the phlegm (kapha) in a man is diminished, the pitta becomes aggravated, followed by the wind (vāta).
6.15.218 | By its own heat, it bestows strength upon Agni in the seat of fire.
Then, having gained strength in the body, that fire, accompanied by wind, [acts] in the parched [body].
6.15.219 | Overpowering [the other elements], it quickly and repeatedly cooks the food due to its sharpness;
having cooked the food, it then cooks even the bodily constituents (dhātus), such as blood and the rest.
6.15.220 | Thereafter, it brings about weakness, distress, and death for the man. He finds relief after eating food, but as soon as it is digested, he faints away.

6.15.221 | Diseases such as thirst, dyspnea, burning sensations, and fainting arise from excessive digestive fire (atyagni). One should treat that excessive fire with heavy, unctuous, cold, sweet, and slimy substances.
6.15.222 | One should bring him to peace with food and drink, as one quenches a blazing fire with water;
even when his previous meal is not yet digested, one should repeatedly offer him further food.
6.15.223 Just as one who has no fuel might find an opening and thus not destroy [the fire],
so too [one should avoid] milk-rice, rice-and-pulse, oily food, flour-based preparations, and products of molasses.
6.15.224 | He should eat the flesh of aquatic and marshy animals that have been properly prepared,
especially smooth fish and those that dwell in still waters.
6.15.225 | One may eat the meat of a sheep that has been cooked with a very strong fire, which destroys excessive digestive heat;
or, when hungry, one may drink barley-gruel mixed with beeswax or ghee.
6.15.226 | Or, having performed venesection, one should drink a churned drink made from wheat flour;
or milk boiled with sugar, ghee, and life-promoting (jīvanīya) medicinal herbs.
6.15.227 | Soups made from fruits that are sources of oil, as well as those with sugar, produce softness in the digestive fire; likewise, unctuous meat broths do so as well.
6.15.228 | A person should drink ghee mixed with beeswax along with cold water;
or he should drink wheat flour with milk and ghee.
6.15.229 Or, one may take the three fats (snehas), excluding oil, prepared with the juice of meat from marshy animals;
or likewise, a thickened preparation equal in quantity to milk, combined with the three fats.
6.15.230 | One should drink the bark of the *udumbara* tree combined with human breast milk;
or one should eat rice-milk (*pāyasa*) prepared with those two for the pacification of an excessive digestive fire.
6.15.231 | Or one should administer milk boiled with *śyāmā* and *trivṛt* as a purgative;
for the purpose of pacifying *pitta*, one should repeatedly take meals consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).

6.15.232 | Having carefully examined the patient, the physician who knows the rules should, with palms joined in reverence, prescribe whatever food is sweet, unctuous, increases *śleṣman*, and is heavy to digest.
6.15.233 | He who eats all that which is not properly placed on the fire, sleeps during the day,
and consumes fatty foods while his digestive fire is not yet extinguished, [suffers].

6.15.234 | When kapha has increased [but] pitta and vāta have been conquered, one does not suffer misfortune on account of that [increase], but rather attains nourishment; and the digestive fire remains balanced.
6.15.235 | When the bodily constituents (dhātus) are in equilibrium, one digests food for the sake of increasing nourishment, lifespan, and strength.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"In this context, eating wholesome and unwholesome things together is considered 'equal eating' (samaśana)."
6.15.236 | Whether it be unwholesome, or in great or small quantity, eating when the proper time has not yet arrived or when it has passed,
or eating again while there is still a remnant of the previous meal, is considered *adhyashana* (overeating).

6.15.237 | These three [meals], if taken while the previous one is undigested, either bring about death or produce terrible diseases; however, if the morning meal is not yet digested, the evening meal does not cause harm.
6.15.238 | By the sun during the day, the heart awakens like a lotus;
when that [heart] has awakened, all the channels attain clarity in every respect.
6.15.239 | Due to physical exercise, movement about, and the distraction of the mind, his bodily constituents (dhātus) do not undergo moistening during the day; therefore, they remain firm.
6.15.240 | Food poured onto grains that have not become moist does not spoil them,
just as fresh milk mixed with milk that has not yet curdled remains milk.
6.15.241 | Just as [water] does not become corrupted but becomes equal to that very [substance], so too,
when the heart is withered at night and the channels are constricted,
the bodily constituents (dhātus) undergo putrefaction within the abdominal cavity due to being enclosed.
6.15.242 | When other [substances] are poured into uncooked curdled milk, they become spoiled;
when poured into burnt milk, it is like pouring hot milk into [already heated] milk.
6.15.243 | A wise person should not consume food that is from the night or that is undigested;
therefore, one who wishes to preserve his strength and lifespan should eat something else.
6.15.244 | Regarding this, there are these verses:—How the internal fire, possessing its own qualities, sustains the body;
how food is digested; and what the ingested food also produces.
6.15.245 | Those fires by which [beings] are nourished, however many there are, and those whom they cook;
from these very [fires] arises the sequential production of the essences (rasa) and so forth, as well as of the impurities (mala).
6.15.246 | The sequence of the emergence of the bodily constituents (dhātus) according to time is the cause for the swift action of aphrodisiacs;
it is the cause that produces a specific portion of disease, just as the internal fire (antaragni) is predominant.
6.15.247 | How the corrupted [dosha] becomes vitiated, the diseases it produces,
the nature of the grahaṇī, and the symptoms of the disorders of the grahaṇī.
6.15.248 | The premonitory symptoms, the distinct characteristics, the treatment, and likewise the management according to the stages have been specified for each of the four types.
6.15.249 | Furthermore, how atyagni arises and what its treatment is—
all that the sage has stated here in the section on the disorders of the grahaṇī.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Grahani," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, which was not available [in its original form] and has been restored by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Sixteen:
Now we shall expound the treatment of anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
6.16.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.16.3 | Five types of anemia (pāṇḍuroga) are recognized: three caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha;
the fourth by the combination of all three (sannipāta); and the fifth from the ingestion of earth (mṛdbhakṣaṇa).
6.16.4 | When the humors (doṣas), with pitta as the predominant one, become aggravated within the tissues (dhātus), flaccidity of those tissues and heaviness arise.
6.16.5 | Thereupon, complexion, strength, and unctuousness, as well as other qualities of vitality (*ojas*),
undergo extreme depletion due to the severe aggravation of the *doṣas* and the *dūṣyas*.
6.16.6 | He becomes one with diminished passion, little fat, devoid of essence, and with relaxed sense organs; he undergoes discoloration. Listen to the cause of this, along with its symptoms.
6.16.7 | From the consumption of alkaline, sour, salty, excessively hot, incompatible, and unwholesome foods;
and from the habitual use of flat beans, black gram, oil-cakes, and sesame oil.
6.16.8 | From eating food that is improperly digested, from sleeping during the day, from physical exercise, and likewise from sexual intercourse;
from the irregularity of medical treatments, and from the suppression of natural urges.
6.16.9 When bile (pitta) has become aggravated and is situated in the heart, the mind is afflicted by desire, anxiety, fear, anger, and grief.
6.16.10 | Driven by the powerful wind, having reached the ten vessels and entered the entire body, it takes refuge between the skin and the flesh.
6.16.11 | Having vitiated the kapha, vāta, blood, skin, and flesh,
it produces various colors— pale yellow, turmeric-yellow, and green— upon the skin.
6.16.12 | That is called pāṇḍuroga (jaundice). The symptoms of its impending onset are: palpitations of the heart, dryness, absence of perspiration, and fatigue.
6.16.13 | When this [disease] has arisen, the patient will experience ringing in the ears and loss of digestive fire;
he will become weak, dejected, averse to food, and oppressed by fatigue and vertigo.
6.16.14 | A person afflicted with body aches, fever, dyspnea, heaviness,
and loss of appetite feels as if his limbs have been crushed, oppressed, and churned.
6.16.15 | With swollen eye-sockets, greenish in hue, with withered hair and luster lost,
irritable, hating the cold, drowsy, spitting, and speaking little;
6.16.16 | There occur pain and swelling of the calves, thighs, hips, and feet, as well as exhaustion from climbing; its specific characteristics will now be described.
6.16.17 | Vata, aggravated by foods and regimens that increase vata,
produces a dark-pale complexion as well as dryness and a reddish tint of the limbs.
6.16.18 | Body aches, pain, pricking sensations, tremors, pain in the flanks and head,
dryness of the stool, bad taste in the mouth, swelling, abdominal distension, and loss of strength.
6.16.19 | In a person of bilious temperament, the accumulated pitta, having been vitiated by its own specific aggravating factors,
further corrupts the blood and other elements, leading to the development of anemia (pāṇḍuroga).

6.16.20 | That person [afflicted by this fever] has yellowish or greenish urine and stool, is accompanied by fever and burning sensations, and suffers from thirst, fainting, and parchedness; his urine and feces are yellow.
6.16.21 | He perspires, desires cold, and does not take pleasure in food;
his mouth becomes pungent, and he finds no relief in heat or even in sour things.
6.16.22 | When food is improperly digested (vidagdha), sour eructation and a burning sensation arise;
there is also foul odor, diarrhea, weakness, and even darkness before the eyes.

6.16.23 | When *kapha* is increased by *kapha*-generating factors, it causes *pāṇḍu-roga* (anemia/jaundice) as previously described, along with heaviness, drowsiness, vomiting, and a whitish complexion.
Excessive salivation, horripilation, exhaustion, fainting,
giddiness, fatigue, dyspnea, cough, as well as lassitude, anorexia, and impairment of speech and voice.
6.16.25 | Whitish urine, eyes, and feces; a desire for pungent, dry, and hot things;
swelling; and a sweet taste in the mouth—these are the symptoms of anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya) caused by kapha.
6.16.26 | In those who consume all kinds of food, all the corrupted humors (doṣas) produce a disease born of the three humors;
they manifest the symptoms of the three humors and cause the most unbearable anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
6.16.27 | In one who has the habit of eating clay, one or another of the humors becomes aggravated:
the astringent [clay] provokes the wind (vāta), the saline [clay] the bile (pitta), and the sweet [clay] the phlegm (kapha).
6.16.28 | Due to its dryness, it irritates the earthy and watery elements and dries up the food that has been eaten;
moreover, being undigested, it fills and obstructs the channels.
6.16.29 | Having destroyed the strength of the sense organs, as well as their luster, vigor, and vitality,
it quickly causes anemia (pāṇḍuroga), which destroys strength, complexion, and digestive fire.

6.16.30 | With swollen cheeks, eye-sockets, and eyebrows; with a swollen anus, navel, and penis; having worms in the digestive tract, one suffers from diarrhea characterized by stool mixed with blood and phlegm.
6.16.31 | Anemia (pāṇḍuroga) that has been long-standing,
become chronic, or swollen due to the passage of time does not succeed [in treatment], as does one who perceives yellow objects.
6.16.32 | He who suffers from diarrhea characterized by scanty, bound stools mixed with phlegm that is greenish in color;
who is dejected, whose limbs are smeared with white [discharges], and who is afflicted by vomiting, fainting, and thirst.
6.16.33 | That [condition] which arises from the depletion of blood is called *pāṇḍu*, by which one attains a whitish complexion.
Thus has been described the symptomatology of the five types of *pāṇḍuroga*.
6.16.34 | However, when one suffering from anemia excessively indulges in pitta-increasing substances,
that pitta burns the blood and flesh, leading to disease.
6.16.35 | With eyes like turmeric, his skin, nails, and face were intensely yellow;
his excrement and urine were red and yellow, his complexion was like that of a frog, and his senses were destroyed.
6.16.36 | Afflicted by burning sensations, indigestion, weakness, malaise,
and loss of appetite, this *kāmalā* (jaundice), characterized by an excess of *pitta*, is considered to reside in both the visceral cavity (*koṣṭha*) and the peripheral tissues (*śākhā*).
6.16.37 | After some time, it becomes chronic and difficult to treat as Kumbhakāmala;
the person's stool and urine become blackish-yellow, and he suffers from extreme swelling.

6.16.38 | He whose eyes, face, vomit, feces, and urine are blood-stained, who faints, and who is afflicted with burning sensations, anorexia, thirst, oppression in the chest, drowsiness, and delusion;
6.16.39 | One whose digestive fire has lost its function and who suffers from jaundice perishes quickly;
however, I shall now describe the treatment for the other curable types.

6.16.40 | In that regard, one suffering from *pāṇḍu* (anemia/pallor) should be purified with mild, unctuous, sharp, and bitter emetics and purgatives; however, one suffering from *kāmalā* (jaundice) should be purified with purgatives alone.

6.16.41 | To those two whose internal cavities have been thoroughly cleansed, one should administer wholesome foods: aged *śāli* rice along with barley and wheat, served together with vegetable soups.
6.16.42 | One should administer beneficial soups made from mung, āḍhakī, and masūra, as well as the meat-broths of wild animals,
and apply specific medicinal treatments for those two [conditions] according to the respective doṣas.
6.16.43 | One should administer *pañcagavya*, *mahātikta*,
or even *kalyāṇaka* ghee for the purpose of oleation to a patient suffering from jaundice (*kāmalā*) and anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*).
6.16.44 | One *kuḍava* of pomegranate, half a *kuḍava* of coriander, one *pala* each of *citraka*, ginger, and long pepper; this is likewise the "Eightfold Piper" (*pippaly-aṣṭamikā*).

6.16.45 | With these pastes, twenty palas of ghee should be cooked in one āḍhaka of water; when prepared, it cures heart disease, anemia, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, and afflictions caused by vāta and kapha.

6.16.46 | It is an digestive stimulant (dīpana), it cures dyspnea and cough, and it is recommended for obstructed wind (mūḍhavāta). It also bestows conception upon women who have difficult births or those who are barren.
Thus ends the *Dāḍimādya-ghṛta* (6.16.47).
[The following ingredients are: one pala each of *kaṭukā*, *rohiṇī*, *musta*, the two types of *haridrā*, and *vatsaka*;
as well as *paṭola*, *candana*, *mūrvā*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *durālabhā*.
6.16.48 | With one karṣa each of kṛṣṇā, parpaṭaka, nimba, bhūnimba, and devadāru,
one prastha of ghee is prepared with four times the amount of milk.
It destroys internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), fever, burning sensations, swelling, fistula-in-ano,
hemorrhoids, menorrhagia, as well as eruptive boils.
Thus ends the Kaṭukādya-ghṛta (6.16.50).
One *prastha* of ghee prepared with the juice of one hundred *pathyā* fruits and the paste of fifty *pathyā* stalks,
when consumed, cures anemia (*pāṇḍvāmaya*) and abdominal tumors (*gulma*).

Thus ends Pathyā-ghṛta (6.16.51). Similarly, one prastha of ghee prepared with four palas of the juice of dantī and the ground unripe fruits of dantī conquers splenic disorders, anemia, colic, and edema.
Thus ends the Dantī-ghṛta (6.16.52). One prastha of aged ghee prepared with half a prastha of grapes cures jaundice, abdominal tumors, anemia, fever, urinary disorders, and abdominal enlargements.
Thus ends the grape-ghee (drākṣāghṛta). 6.16.53. Buffalo ghee prepared with turmeric, triphalā, nimba, balā, and madhuka, along with milk, is an excellent remedy for jaundice.
Thus ends the *haridrādighṛta* (6.16.54).
[The following preparations are: one prepared with two *akṣa*s of the paste of *dārvī* in twice the amount of cow’s urine;
another, the best, prepared with the paste of *kālīyaka* in a decoction of five *palas* of *dārvī*.
6.16.55 | One *prastha* of buffalo ghee is the first dose; each subsequent dose is double the preceding one.
Having treated the patient with these fats and ascertained that he is sufficiently oleated, one should administer a purgative.
6.16.56 | Boiled with milk mixed with urine, or with milk alone,
and with the juice of *dantī* fruits, it should be prepared while lukewarm with one *añjali* of *kāśmarya*.
6.16.57 | Or, having crushed *krākṣā* with the palms joined together, one should administer it; this cures anemia (*pāṇḍvāmaya*).
A person with a Pitta disorder should drink half a *pala* of powdered *trivṛt* mixed with double the amount of sugar.
6.16.58 | A patient suffering from *kaphaja* anemia (*pāṇḍu*) should take *harītakī* soaked in cow’s urine,
along with *āragvadha*, *rasa* (juice) of sugarcane, and *vidārī* and *āmalaka*.
6.16.59 | A person should drink Bilva leaves with the three pungents (triyūṣaṇa) to cure jaundice;
or alternatively, one should take a paste of half a pala of Danti mixed with double the amount of jaggery and cold water.
6.16.60 | A person suffering from jaundice (kāmalin) should drink *trivṛt* with the juices of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*),
or [the powder of] *viśālā*, *triphalā*, *musta*, *kuṣṭha*, *dāru*, and *kaliṅgaka*.
6.16.61 | One should prepare ativiṣā in portions of one karṣa and half a karṣa, as well as two karṣas of madhurasā; all of this [should be taken] with lukewarm water.
6.16.62 | Having drunk that squeezed and purified juice, one should lick honey after it;
[this cures] cough, dyspnea, fever, burning sensation, anemia, and loss of appetite.
6.16.63 | It destroys abdominal tumors, constipation, āmavāta, and raktapitta.
[One may take] the juice of triphalā, or of guḍūcī, or of dārvī, or of nimba.
6.16.64 | A person afflicted by jaundice (kāmalā) should drink cold milk mixed with honey in the morning;
or he should drink cow’s or buffalo’s milk and urine for a fortnight.
6.16.65 | Or, for seven days, one should take Triphala juice mixed with cow's urine;
or, having extinguished fresh sprouts in cow's urine while they are still burning, one should crush them.
6.16.66 | One should drink that [juice] of mātuluṅga, purified, to remove pale swelling (pāṇḍuśotha).
[One should also take] svarṇakṣīrī, trivṛt, śyāmā, bhadradāru, and nāgara.
6.16.67 | One should drink [the medicine] ground with a handful of cow’s urine, or boiled in urine;
or one may drink milk boiled with these same ingredients to facilitate the downward movement of the humors (doṣas).
6.16.68 | One should drink harītakī with a preparation or with cow’s urine;
once it has been digested, one should eat with milk or with a sweet meat broth.
6.16.69 | Or, for the purpose of pacifying jaundice (pāṇḍuroga), the physician should have the patient drink iron powder that has been infused in cow urine for seven nights, along with milk.
6.16.70 | Equal parts of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), musta, viḍaṅga, and citraka,
along with nine parts of iron powder— this powder should be taken with honey and ghee.
6.16.71 | This powder called Navāyasa, spoken by Kṛṣṇātreya, should be consumed; it removes anemia, heart disease, skin disorders, hemorrhoids, and jaundice.

Thus ends the powder of nine metals (navāyasacūrṇa). 6.16.72. One should prepare pills for a patient suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍuroga) using equal parts by measure of jaggery, ginger, maṇḍūra, and sesame seeds, with long pepper (pippalī) added in double the amount.
6.16.73 | Trikaṭu, triphalā, musta, viḍaṅga,
cavya, citraka, the bark of dārvī, nākṣika mineral, granthika, and devadāru.
6.16.74 | One should prepare these two-pala portions as separate powders;
the purified maṇḍūra, resembling collyrium, should be twice the amount of the powder.
6.16.75 | Having boiled [the ingredients] in eight times the amount of cow’s urine, one should then add that [mixture] to it;
having formed balls (vaṭaka) the size of an udumbara fruit, they should be taken according to one's digestive fire.
6.16.76 | One should consume these with buttermilk, and when they are digested, take food that is wholesome to one's constitution.
Indeed, these Maṇḍūra pills are life-givers for those suffering from anemia.
6.16.77 | It pacifies skin diseases, indigestion, swelling, stiffness of the thighs, disorders of phlegm, hemorrhoids, jaundice, urinary disorders, and splenic enlargement.
Thus ends the section on Maṇḍūra-vatakas (6.16.78).
Take five palas each of tāpya (cinnabar), adrijatu (bitumen), rūpyāya (silver ore), and mala (impurity/iron rust),
together with one pala each of citraka, triphalā, vyoṣa (the three pungents), and viḍaṅga.
6.16.79 | These powders, mixed with eight palas of sugar, drenched in honey, and taken in doses the size of an akṣa,
should be practiced by one who eats wholesome and moderate food once they have been digested.

6.16.80 | By one who avoids horse gram (*kulattha*), black-eyed bean (*kākamācī*), pigeon meat, and the like, there should be three parts of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and three parts of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*).
6.16.81 | One part of the root of *citraka*, and likewise of *viḍaṅga*; five parts of *ajamodana* (realgar), and likewise of silver filings.
6.16.82 | Eight parts of pure honey, as well as eight parts of iron powder and eight parts of sugar— all of this should be finely ground into a powder.
6.16.83 | It should be soaked in honey and kept in a beautiful iron vessel;
one should then eat a dose equal in size to an udumbara fruit, according to one's digestive fire.
6.16.84 | One should employ this day after day; when it has been digested, one may eat as desired, with the exception of horse gram (kulattha), black nightshade (kākamācī), and pigeon meat (kapota).
6.16.85 | This yoga, known as Yogarāja, is like nectar;
it is the most excellent elixir (rasāyana), auspicious, and a remover of all diseases.
6.16.86 | It cures anemia, poisoning, cough, consumption, irregular fever,
skin diseases, indigestion, urinary disorders, wasting, dyspnea, and loss of appetite.
6.16.87 | It specifically destroys epilepsy, jaundice, and hemorrhoids;
thus [ends] Yogarāja.
[It is prepared] with *kuṭaja*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *nimba*, *paṭola*, *ghana*, and ginger (*nāgara*).
6.16.88 | Eight palas of śilājatu, processed for ten days with medicinal juices (rasas) two or three times its own weight, along with an equal amount of white sugar;
6.16.89 | One pala each of tvakkṣīrī, pippalī, dhātrī, and karkaṭākhyā;
one pala of the fruit and root of nidigdhī; and the three aromatics (trigandhaka) in appropriate measure.

6.16.90 | One should prepare honey-balls (*akṣikā*) by mixing three *palas* of honey with the powder; these may be taken with pomegranate juice, water, milk, the broth of birds, wine, or spirituous liquors (*āsava*).
6.16.91 | Having consumed these, one should drink [the decoction] either on an empty stomach or immediately after eating;
it cures anemia, skin diseases, fever, splenic disorders, tamaka-shvāsa, consumption, and fistula-in-ano.
It cures putrid heart-disease, seminal disorders, urinary defects, digestive fire disorders, emaciation, abdominal tumors,
consumption, cough, menorrhagia, internal hemorrhaging, swelling, abdominal lumps, and diseases of the throat.
6.16.93 | These [pills] destroy all ulcers, remove all diseases, and are auspicious.
Thus end the pills of *śilājatu*. [The powder consists of:
*punarnavā*, *trivṛt*, the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), *viḍaṅga*, *dāru*, and *citraka*.
6.16.94 | Kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, triphalā, dantī, cavya, kaliṅgaka, pippalī,
pippalīmūla, and musta— one pala each of these.
6.16.95 | One should cook double the amount of iron rust (maṇḍūra) compared to the powder in two āḍhakas of cow’s urine.
Having formed pills the size of *kola* fruits, a person should drink them stirred with buttermilk (*takra*).
6.16.96 | These [medicines] destroy anemia, splenic enlargement, hemorrhoids, intermittent fever, edema,
disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), leprosy, and likewise worms.

Thus ends the description of Punarnava-maṇḍūra (6.16.97). One suffering from jaundice or anemia should lick a paste of dārvītvak, triphalā, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, and iron powder, combined with honey and ghee.

Equal parts of copper filings, *pathyā*, and turmeric, powdered and mixed with honey and ghee, should be licked by one suffering from jaundice; or alternatively, *abhayā* may be taken with jaggery and honey.
6.16.99 | Triphalā, the two types of haridrā, kaṭurohiṇī, and iron powder— this powder,
when mixed with honey and ghee, is a linctus that removes jaundice.
6.16.100 | Two palas each of tugākṣīrī, nāgara, and madhuyaṣṭikā;
one prastha each of pippalī and krākṣā; and half a tulā of auspicious sugar.
6.16.101 | One should cook one droṇa of the juice of āmalaka fruit with the powder [of the drugs] like a linctus.
When cooled, one should lick a palmful (pāṇitala) of it mixed with one prastha of honey.
6.16.102 | It destroys jaundice, bile disorders, anemia, cough, and chlorosis.
Thus ends the *dhātryavaleha*.
[The following consists of: the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *cavya*, *citraka*, and *devadāru*.
6.16.103 | One should powder viḍaṅga, musta, and vatsaka;
this powder, equal in weight to maṇḍūra, should be cooked in eight times its quantity of cow’s urine.
6.16.104 | Likewise, jaggery (guḍa) should be prepared slowly until it is cooled, in a quantity equal to one karṣa;
these should be consumed according to one's digestive fire, as they remove diseases of the spleen and anemia.
6.16.105 | Those who eat *vāṭya* with buttermilk are known to overcome disorders of the *grahaṇī* and hemorrhoids.
Thus ends the section on *maṇḍūra-vaṭakas*.
[The next formulation: Mañjiṣṭhā, *rajanī*, grapes, the roots of *balā*, and iron filings.
6.16.106 | Lodhra and these [other ingredients] should be used in a molasses-based (gauḍa) ariṣṭa for those suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍuroga).
Thus ends the gauḍa-ariṣṭa.
Sixteen palas of bījaka and twenty palas of triphalā [are required].
6.16.107 | Five parts of grapes and seven parts of lac should be boiled in one droṇa of water;
when reduced to one-fourth and strained, one should add [the following] to the remaining liquid.
6.16.108 | One *tulā* of sugar, one *prastha* of honey,
and one *karṣa* each of the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *vyāghranakha*, *uśīra*, *kramuka*, and *sailavāluka*.
6.16.109 | Madhuka and kuṣṭha—this powder, placed in a vessel of ghee, should be kept among barley for ten nights; twice as long in summer, and in winter.
One should drink that [mixture], which cures disorders of the duodenum (agrahaṇī), anemia (pāṇḍu), hemorrhoids (arśas), edema (śotha), and abdominal tumors (gulma);
it conquers dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra), urinary calculi (aśmarī), urinary disorders (meha), jaundice (kāmalā), and the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta).
6.16.111 | This is proclaimed by Ātreya as *bījakāriṣṭa*. Thus ends the section on *bījakāriṣṭa*. Having pressed two thousand *dhātrī* fruits, one should take that juice.
Combined with one-eighth part honey and half a *kuḍava* of black pepper,
and mixed with half a *tula* of sugar, it should be kept for a fortnight in a smooth jar.
6.16.113 | One who eats wholesome and moderate food should drink [this] in small doses in the morning once it has been digested;
it cures jaundice, anemia, heart disease, gout, and irregular fevers.
6.16.114 | This *ariṣṭa* shall destroy cough, hiccup, anorexia, and dyspnea.
Thus ends the *dhātryariṣṭa*.
Water boiled with the *sthirā* group of drugs is recommended for drinking and in the diet.
6.16.115 | For those suffering from jaundice and those afflicted by *kāmalā*, the juice of *mṛdvīkā* and *āmalakī* has been declared by the Great Sage to be for the purpose of pacifying *pāṇḍu-roga*.
6.16.116 | This should be determined by the physician according to the specific strength of each individual doṣa:
for a vātika condition, it should consist mostly of oil; for a paittika condition, it should be bitter and cold.

6.16.117 | In cases of phlegmatic disorders (*ślaiṣmika*), [the physician should administer] pungent, bitter, and hot [substances]; in cases of combined disorders (*sānnipātika*), a mixture [should be used].
The physician should cause the ingested earth to be expelled from the body.

6.16.118 | A physician who understands the application of methods, having carefully considered the relative strength and weakness [of the patient], should administer strengthening medicated ghees once the body has been purified by sharp cleansing therapies.
6.16.119 | Vyōṣa, bilva, the two types of haridrā, triphalā, the two types of punarnavā,
mustā, iron filings, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, and devadāru.
6.16.120 | Having prepared ghee with equal parts of vṛścikālī and bhārgī along with milk,
a man afflicted by the defects of the earth-element should drink it according to the proper method.
6.16.121 Similarly, for a patient who, out of greed, does not desist from eating earth, [one should administer] keśara, yaṣṭyāhva, pippalī, kṣāra, and śādvala.
6.16.122 | One may certainly give [the medicine] prepared for the sake of one who is disliked, using those [substances] that destroy its defects:
viḍaṅga, elā, ativiṣā, nimba leaves, and pāṭhā.
6.16.123 | For those suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍu-roga), one should administer medicinal treatment using eggplant (vārtāka), kaṭurohiṇī, kuṭaja, or mūrvā, according to the specific humor involved.
6.16.124 | This is considered a specific manifestation of his [disease] due to a particular cause:
the patient suffering from jaundice (kāmalin) who voids stool resembling ground sesame seeds.
6.16.125 | When its path is obstructed by phlegm, one should conquer that pitta with treatments that alleviate kapha,
such as dry, cold, heavy, and sweet substances, physical exercise, and the suppression of natural urges.
6.16.126 | When the powerful Vāyu, agitated by Kapha, displaces Pitta from its site, the person's eyes, urine, and skin become yellowish, while the feces become white.
6.16.127 | There may be a state of distension with flatulence and heaviness of the heart,
accompanied by debility, weak digestion, pain in the flanks, hiccup, dyspnea, anorexia, and fever.

6.16.128 | When pitta is located in the peripheral tissues (śākhā) and is slight, one should administer treatment gradually with the dry, sour, and pungent tastes of the meat of peacock, partridge, and cock.
6.16.129 | One should feed meals with soups made from dried radish and horse gram;
and [one may take] the juice of citron mixed with honey, long pepper, and black pepper.
6.16.130 | One should drink [the bile] with *nāgara* (ginger), so that it returns to its own site;
the treatment also consists of pungent, sharp, hot, salty, and very sour substances.
6.16.131 | It occurs until the bile (pitta) has acquired the color of feces or until the wind (vāyu) has subsided;
when the bile has returned to its own site, the feces become colored by the bile.

6.16.132 | When the complications have subsided, the previously mentioned treatment for jaundice (kāmalika) should be applied; however, when the complexion of the patient becomes pale, greenish, dark-brown, or yellowish, [the following should be done].
6.16.133 | Loss of strength and enthusiasm, drowsiness, dullness of the digestive fire, mild fever, lack of sexual desire for women, body ache, dyspnea, thirst, loss of appetite, and vertigo.
6.16.134 | Then one should recognize that condition as *halīmaka*, arising from wind (*anila*) and bile (*pitta*).
Buffalo ghee prepared with the fresh juice of *guḍūcī* and milk [is the remedy].
6.16.135 | Having been lubricated, he should drink trivṛt with the juice of āmalaka;
once purged, he should consume a diet consisting mostly of sweet substances that alleviate pitta and vāta.

6.16.136 | One should habitually employ the previously mentioned grape electuary (drākṣāleha), sweet medicated ghees (sarpīs), sustaining enemas (yāpana-basti), milk enemas (kṣīra-basti), and oil enemas with unctuous substances (anuvāsana).
6.16.137 | One should drink preparations of *mārdvīkāriṣṭa* with due care for the increase of the digestive fire (*agni*),
as well as the *kāsika* electuary of *abhayā*, and [decoctions of] *pippalī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*.
6.16.138 | One should administer [these] with milk according to the specific disorder and according to the patient's strength.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
The causes, symptoms, and remedies for the five types of *pāṇḍu* (anemia) have been stated.
6.16.139 | Jaundice (kāmalā) is of two types, along with their curability and incurability; and whatever other variant of these there is, namely the great disease halīmaka—
its symptoms and treatment have been stated in brief.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Anemia," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, which was not available [in its original form] and has been restored by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Seventeen:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of hiccups and dyspnea.
6.17.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.17.3 | The wise Agniveśa, with palms joined in reverence, questioned the supreme sage Ātreya— who knew the reality of the worlds of the gods— regarding a doubt.

6.17.4 | Regarding these diseases which have been described as being of two types— those arising from the three *doṣas* and those caused by the three-fold provocation— which among them, having various natures, is the most difficult to conquer?
6.17.5 | Having heard those words of Agniveśa, the best among the wise,
being exceedingly pleased, spoke this determination of the ultimate truth.
6.17.6 | Granted that there are many diseases that take away life,
yet they are not like dyspnea and hiccup, which swiftly cut off the vital breaths.
6.17.7 | Even for a person afflicted by various other diseases,
at the end, hiccups or breathlessness accompanied by intense pain arise.
6.17.8 | These two [types of thirst] are characterized by kapha and vāta, arise from the seat of pitta,
and cause the desiccation of the heart as well as the bodily tissues (dhātus) such as rasa and the rest.
6.17.9 Therefore, these two are considered common [to all] and extremely difficult to conquer;
when treated with falsehood and provoked to anger, they are like two venomous serpents that have been struck.
6.17.10 | These two [types of hemorrhoids] have been specified separately as fivefold in the compendium of diseases. Listen now to their etiology, symptoms, and the physician's treatment.
6.17.11 | From dust, smoke, and wind; from exposure to cold places and the consumption of water;
from physical exercise, sexual intercourse, sacrifices, dry food, and irregular eating; [the eyes become affected].
6.17.12 | From the vitiation of undigested matter (āmadoṣa), from retention of food, from dryness,
from excessive depletion, from weakness, from injury to the vital spots (marmans), from dual humoral combinations, and from excessive purification (śuddhi).
6.17.13 | [It arises] from diarrhea, fever, vomiting, catarrh, chest wounds, consumption, hemoptysis, upward movement of wind (udāvarta),
choleraic pain (visūcī), and intestinal torpor (alasaka).
6.17.14 | These two diseases arise from anemia and from poison,
as well as from the consumption of flattened rice, black gram, oil-cakes, and sesame oil.

6.17.15 | From the consumption of foods that cause constipation, burning sensations, or heaviness— such as ground lotus tubers (śālūka)— and from the habitual use of the meat of aquatic and marshy animals, curd, and the milk of camels or female elephants;
6.17.16 | Due to the application of unctuous treatments, the consumption of phlegm-increasing substances,
the obstruction of the throat and chest, and various types of constipation;
6.17.17 | The Vāyu (wind), having entered the channels that carry the vital breath (prāṇa), becomes aggravated;
situated in the chest and stirring up the phlegm (kapha), it produces hiccup and dyspnea.
6.17.18 | There are five types of terrible afflictions that obstruct the vital breaths of living beings.
Listen now as I describe the premonitory symptoms for both; hereafter I shall speak further.
6.17.19 | Heaviness of the throat and chest, astringency of the mouth,
the prodromal symptoms of hiccups, and distension of the abdomen are [the signs].
6.17.20 | Constipation, pain in the flanks, oppression of the heart,
and upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) are the premonitory symptoms of dyspnea (śvāsa).
6.17.21 | When the wind (vāyu), combined with phlegm (kapha), obstructs the channels that carry breath, water, and food, it produces hiccup (hikkā). Listen now to the specific symptoms of each type.
6.17.22 | When the flesh, strength, vital breath, and radiance are diminished, the wind (vāyu), combined with phlegm (kapha),
suddenly seizes the throat, producing a loud and intense sound.
6.17.23 | Thus, the vital breath (prāṇa), obstructing the channels, the vital points (marman), and the heat itself, constantly produces hiccups that occur singly, in pairs, or in threes.
6.17.24 | It robs one of consciousness, produces stiffness of the limbs,
and blocks the passage of food and drink for one whose memory is impaired.
6.17.25 | Of him whose eyes were overflowing with tears, whose temples were motionless and whose eyebrows were drooping, who was stuck in incoherent chatter and lamentation, and who found no peace—
6.17.26 | Having great roots, great velocity, great sound, and great strength—
known as Mahāhikkā, it is considered to take away the life-breaths of men instantly.

Thus ends the section on severe hiccough (mahāhikkā). 6.17.27: A man who, though emaciated and dejected in mind, suffers from increased hiccoughing, sounding deeply and painfully with his parched chest.
6.17.28 | Yawning, contracting his limbs, and likewise stretching them out,
he pressed both sides of his body together, groaning and afflicted by the pain of stiffness.
6.17.29 | Hiccough arises for him from the umbilical region or even from the colon;
it violently agitates the body and, as if bending it, causes the patient to faint.
6.17.30 | When it obstructs the path of exhalation in one whose strength and consciousness have perished,
that hiccup is called "deep" (gambhīrā) and is considered fatal.
Thus ends the description of the deep hiccup (gambhīrā hikkā). 6.17.31 | That hiccup which arises when the four kinds of food and drink have been eliminated,
and which gains strength again at the end of the digestion of the meal, [is called vyapetā].
6.17.32 | For one afflicted by delirium, vomiting, diarrhea, and thirst, who is disoriented,
yawning, with rolling eyes, a dry mouth, and drooping [of the head], [the physician should act].
6.17.33 | That hiccup which occurs in one who is excessively distended, arising from the base of the collarbones and being continuous,
should be known as the "Vyapeta" hiccup, which obstructs the vital breath.

Thus ends the section on *vyapetā* hiccup (6.17.34). When the minor wind (*kṣudravāta*), agitated by physical exertion, moves from the abdominal cavity and reaches the throat, it produces the *akṣudrā* hiccup.
6.17.35 | That [pain] is not excessively agonizing, nor does it afflict the vital points of the head like a thief;
nor does it stand obstructing the path of inhalation, exhalation, food, or drink.
6.17.36 | It increases as one exerts oneself and becomes soft immediately after eating;
from whatever it first proceeds, from that very same source it ceases.
6.17.37 | Situated in the heart, the kloma, the throat, and the palate,
that mild [hiccup] is known as *kṣudrahikkā* (minor hiccup) and is declared curable in men.

Thus ends [the section on] minor hiccups (kṣudrahikkā). 6.17.38. When the wind (anila) is oppressed by the sudden, excessive consumption of drinks and foods, or by intoxicating liquors that cause extreme intoxication, it moves upward from the abdominal cavity (koṣṭha).
6.17.39 | Likewise, by excessive speaking, walking long distances, laughing, heavy loads, or over-exertion;
or when the air residing in the abdomen is agitated by running, or oppressed by the intake of food and drink.
6.17.40 | Having entered the channel of the chest, it produces hiccup arising from food;
likewise, by sneezing slowly and intermittently, it also causes one to hiccup.
6.17.41 | Hiccough that does not cause pain to the vital organs (marmans) nor afflict the sense organs,
as well as that which arises from food (annajā), subsides after drinking [medicinal liquids] or eating [food].

Thus ends the description of hiccup born from food (annajā hikkā). [6.17.42] It occurs in one whose humors (doṣas) have been excessively accumulated, who is emaciated by the cessation of eating, whose body is wasted by diseases, who is aged, or who has overindulged in sexual intercourse.
6.17.43 | Among these, the hiccup that arises suddenly destroys life quickly,
as does the double hiccup (yamikā) accompanied by delirium, pain, thirst, and confusion.
6.17.44 | For one who is not emaciated, who is not dejected, and whose bodily constituents and sense faculties are stable, the *yamika* [diet] can be successfully accomplished; otherwise, it kills.
6.17.45 | When the wind, preceded by phlegm, obstructs the channels and moves in all directions while being thus confined, it then produces various types of dyspnea.
6.17.46 | A man whose breath is agitated, who suffers with noisy gasping, and being obstructed, pants loudly and incessantly like an intoxicated bull; [this is the condition known as tamaka-śvāsa].
6.17.47 | With his knowledge and discernment lost, and likewise with his eyes wandering,
his eyes and face distorted, his urine and feces suppressed, and his speech faltering;
6.17.48 | His labored breathing is clearly perceived from afar as he becomes distressed;
afflicted by heavy dyspnea, he perishes very quickly.

Thus ends the section on Mahāśvāsa (heavy breathing). 6.17.49: He who breathes deeply upward but cannot draw [the air] back down, his channels of the mouth being obstructed by phlegm and afflicted by the provoked wind (vāyu), [suffers from this condition].
6.17.50 | With his gaze fixed upward, looking about with eyes wandering here and there,
he is bewildered, afflicted by pain, his mouth parched, and tormented by restlessness.
6.17.51 | When the upward breath (ūrdhvaśvāsa) is provoked, the downward breath (adhaḥśvāsa) is obstructed;
as the patient faints and becomes exhausted, that very upward breath destroys his life-breaths.

Thus ends the section on *ūrdhvaśvāsa* (upward breath). 6.17.52: But he who breathes with interruptions, oppressed by all his vital breaths, or does not breathe at all, being afflicted by suffering and tormented by the pain of the cutting of the vital organs (*marmaccheda*).
6.17.53 | Afflicted by abdominal distension, sweating, and fainting due to the burning sensation caused by the enema,
his eyes are rolling, he is emaciated, gasping for breath, and has blood in one eye.
6.17.54 | A man who is disoriented, with parched lips, discolored, and delirious,
being cut off by interrupted breathing, quickly abandons his life-breaths.
Thus ends the section on *chinnaśvāsa* (interrupted breath).
6.17.55: When the wind moves in a contrary direction and enters the channels, seizing the neck and head and agitating the phlegm;
6.17.56 | By that [obstruction], he suffers from chronic catarrh (pīnasa),
as well as a wheezing sound (ghurghuruka) and an extremely violent breathlessness (śvāsa) that afflicts his very life-force.
6.17.57 | Due to the excessive force of the [suppressed] breath, he coughs and feels constricted;
while coughing, he repeatedly falls into a state of fainting.
6.17.58 | When phlegm is not being discharged, one becomes intensely distressed;
but upon its discharge, one obtains happiness for a moment.
6.17.59 | Then his throat becomes constricted; he is able to speak only with great difficulty. Furthermore, afflicted by labored breathing, he finds no sleep even while lying down.
6.17.60 | When he lies down, the wind seizes his side;
while sitting, he finds relief and welcomes warmth.
6.17.61 | With eyes wide open and a forehead profusely perspiring, he suffers intense pain;
his mouth is parched, he breathes repeatedly, and he is frequently gasping for air.

6.17.62 | Tamaka-śvāsa increases due to clouds, rainwater, cold, eastern winds, and substances that increase kapha (śleṣman). It is palliable (yāpya), or it may be curable (sādhya) if it has recently arisen.

Thus ends the section on Tamaka-śvāsa (6.17.63). One should recognize Pratamaka as that [type of asthma] occurring in one overwhelmed by fever and fainting; it arises from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), dust, indigestion, or the obstruction caused by a body saturated with moisture.
6.17.64 | One should recognize *saṃtamaka* as that condition in which [the disease] increases excessively due to darkness and is quickly pacified by cold things,
like one sinking into darkness.
Thus ends the section on *prathamaka* and *saṃtamaka* types of dyspnea.

6.17.65: Dryness and exertion provoke a small amount of *vāta* within the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), giving rise to minor dyspnea (*kṣudraśvāsa*). This does not cause excessive suffering nor does it severely afflict the limbs.
6.17.66 | It does not injure his limbs, nor is it as painful as the others;
nor does it obstruct the normal course of food and drink.
6.17.67 | That which causes neither distress to the sense organs nor any pain whatsoever is said to be curable; all such cases in a strong person are characterized by unmanifest symptoms.
6.17.68 | Thus have the types of dyspnea (śvāsa) and hiccup (hikkā) been described according to their specific characteristics.
Among these, those that are life-threatening should be avoided, for they are terrible and act with great rapidity.
6.17.69 | A physician should quickly treat those conditions that are curable or manageable with medicines; for if neglected, they may consume one just as fire consumes dry undergrowth.
6.17.70 | Since the cause, the site, and the root are one and the same, there is but a single treatment for both; learn from the sages that which has been observed regarding them.
6.17.71 | One should first treat a patient afflicted by hiccup and dyspnea with unctuous sudations, having anointed them with salted oil, using tube-sudation, bed-sudation, and bolus-sudation.
6.17.72 | By these means, his congealed phlegm dissolves within the channels;
the orifices attain softness, and thereafter there is the downward movement of the wind (vāta).
6.17.73 | Just as snow heated by the rays of the sun melts within mountain thickets,
so too does the phlegm, though solid in the body when heated, melt through the perspirations.
6.17.74 | Having recognized that he has sweated, one should then quickly feed him unctuous boiled rice with the broth of fish or pork,
or with the thickened curd-whey (dadhyuttara).
6.17.75 | Thereafter, when the phlegm has increased,
one should cause him to drink an emetic that is not antagonistic to the wind (vāta), combined with long pepper (pippalī), rock salt (saindhava), and honey (kṣaudra).
6.17.76 | When the corrupted bodily mass of phlegm has been expelled, one attains comfort;
and when the channels are purified, the vital air (vāyu) moves unimpeded.
6.17.77 | If a remnant of the morbid humor (doṣa) remains latent, the wise physician should expel it by means of medicinal smokes (dhūma).
[He should use] turmeric, palāśa leaves, castor root, lac, and realgar.
6.17.78 | Having ground devadāru, elā, and māṃsī, one should prepare a wick;
one should inhale the smoke of that wick smeared with ghee, or [use] barley mixed with ghee.

6.17.79 | Having placed beeswax, resin of the *sarja* tree, and clarified butter inside a hollowed-out shell, one should inhale the smoke; or [one may take] the horn, the hair, or the tendon of a cow.
6.17.80 | A tube made of dried syonāka, vardhamāna, or kuśa grass,
or [a paste of] padmaka, guggulu, iron, or śallakī, saturated with clarified butter;

6.17.81 | One should treat hiccup and dyspnea arising from complications such as hoarseness, diarrhea, hemorrhagic disorders, bile disorders, and burning sensations with sweet, unctuous, and cold remedies.

6.17.82 | Those suffering from the pain of pitta and burning sensations, those with excessive bleeding or sweating, those with diminished tissues and strength, the dry, pregnant women, and those of a pitta constitution should not undergo sudation therapy.

6.17.83 | One should, as desired, foment the chest and throat for a moment with lukewarm applications of unctuous substances mixed with sugar, and with mild *utkārikā* poultices and *upanāha* plasters.
6.17.84 | An *utkārikā* prepared with the powders of sesame, linseed, and wheat, along with vāta-alleviating substances, fats, sour liquids, or milk, is beneficial.
6.17.85 | In cases of complications arising from acute fever (navajvara), one should administer dry sudation (rūkṣasveda) and fasting (vilaṅghana);
or, having carefully examined the patient, one may also induce emesis (ullekhana) with salt water.

6.17.86 | Having observed that the vāta has become aggravated by excessive application (atiyoga), the physician should pacify it with vāta-alleviating meat broths and other substances that are neither too cold nor too hot, as well as with oil massages (abhyaṅga).

6.17.87 | Likewise, in cases of upward movement of wind (udāvarta) and flatulence (ādhmāna), food combined with mātuluṅga, amlavetasa, hiṅgu, pīlu, and biḍa salt should be used to facilitate the downward movement of the bowels.
6.17.88 | Indeed, one [type of patient] suffers from hiccup and dyspnea and is strong, while the other is weak;
likewise, one has a predominance of phlegm (kapha), while the other is dry and has an abundance of wind (vāyu).
6.17.89 | When Kapha is predominant and the patient is strong, one should administer emesis along with purgation;
thereafter, for one who eats wholesome food, one should apply pacifying treatments such as medicinal smoking and electuaries.
6.17.90 | One should satisfy those with vāta disorders, the weak, children, and the elderly with vāta-alleviating pacifying agents, such as unctuous soups, meat broths, and the like.

6.17.91 | In those whose kapha is not provoked, who have not undergone sudation, or who are weak, the administration of purification therapies causes the vāyu to gain a foothold; having reached the vital organs (marmans), it quickly dries them up and takes away the life-force.

6.17.92 | Therefore, the physician should purify those who are firm and have abundant kapha after they have been satiated with the juices of marshy and aquatic animals and have undergone sudation; for others, he should provide nourishing therapy.
6.17.93 | Peacock, partridge, and cock, as well as wild animals and birds,
are beneficial when prepared with the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūlī) or in the broth of horse-gram (kaulattha).
6.17.94 | Nidigdhikā, the pulp of bilva, karkaṭa-khyā, durālabhā, trikaṇṭaka, guḍūcī, and kulattha, along with citraka;
6.17.95 | A broth prepared by boiling [vegetables] in water, strained, fried in ghee with long pepper (pippalī),
and combined with dry ginger (nāgara) and salt, is beneficial when consumed as a side dish.
6.17.96 | Having boiled rāsnā, balā, the five roots (pañcamūla), small grains (hrasva), mung beans, and citraka in water,
one should prepare a broth (yūṣa) from that decoction in the same manner as previously described.
6.17.97 | Having boiled the sprouts of the mātuluṅga, nimba, and kulaka,
along with green gram and the three pungents (vyoṣa), one should prepare an alkaline broth (kṣārayūṣa).
6.17.98 | Having added salt, alkali, drumsticks (śigru), and black peppers,
a soup prepared by this method cures disorders of hiccup and asthma.
6.17.99 | A soup made from the leaves of *kāsamarda* and *śobhāñjana*,
as well as a soup of dried radish, prevents hiccup and asthma.
6.17.100 | A soup made from eggplant, seasoned with the six spices and clarified butter, is beneficial;
as are fresh preparations of *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, and barley.
6.17.101 | A gruel prepared with asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, cumin, biḍa salt, puṣkaramūla, citraka,
and karkaṭaśṛṅgī is beneficial for those suffering from asthma and coughing.
6.17.102 | With the ten roots (daśamūlī), śaṭī, rasnā, pippalīmūla, pauṣkara, śṛṅgī, tāmalakī, bhārgī, guḍūcī, nāgara, and water;
6.17.103 | A person should drink gruel prepared according to the prescribed method, or a decoction,
for the alleviation of cough, cardiac oppression, pain in the flanks, hiccups, and dyspnea.
6.17.104 | One should prepare foods and drinks with lotus seeds (puṣkara), śaṭī, the three pungents (vyoṣa), citron, sour vetasa, ghee, biḍa salt, and asafoetida.
6.17.105 | A person suffering from hiccup and asthma who is thirsty should drink either a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) or of devadāru, or even wine.
6.17.106 | Having washed and crushed pāṭhā, madhurasā, rāsnā, sarala, and devadāru, one should place them in the scum of surā.
6.17.107 | Having made that [mixture] with a small amount of salt and measuring one *prasṛta*, the physician should have the patient drink it;
then the hiccup and the dyspnea will be pacified.
6.17.108 | One should drink asafoetida, black salt, jujube, samaṅgā, long pepper, and balā,
ground with the juice of citron or with fermented gruel.
6.17.109 | One should drink sauvarcala salt, nāgara, and bhārgī combined with double the amount of sugar along with warm water; this cures disorders of hiccup and dyspnea.
6.17.110 | One should drink the paste (kalka) of bhārgī and nāgara, as well as that of marica and kṣāra, along with the decoction of pītadru, citraka, āsphota, and mūrvā.
6.17.111 | Madhūlikā, tugākṣīrī, nāgara, and pippalī,
prepared as an *utkārikā* with ghee, are for use in cases of asthma associated with pitta.
6.17.112 | The meat of a porcupine, the flesh of a hare, and the blood of a pangolin,
prepared with long pepper and ghee, are used for asthma associated with a predominance of Vāta.
The juice of *suvarcalā*, milk, and ghee combined with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*),
taken as a post-prandial drink with *śāli* rice, is beneficial for disorders following from *vāta* and *pitta*.
6.17.114 | Alternatively, the fresh juice of śirīṣa flowers or of saptaparṇa,
combined with pippalī and honey, is considered effective for disorders following from kapha and pitta.
6.17.115 | Madhuka, pippalī root, jaggery, the juice of cow and horse dung, ghee,
and honey are beneficial for those suffering from cough, dyspnea, hiccups, and ophthalmia.
6.17.116 | One suffering from excessive phlegm should drink the juice of the dung of a donkey, a horse, a camel, a boar, a sheep, and an elephant, each one separately with honey.
6.17.117 | One should also lick the alkali of aśvagandhā with honey and ghee;
or else, [the alkali of] a peacock’s claw or a piece of śallaka [resin].
6.17.118 | The feathers of a dog, a cock, a wild cock, a blue jay, or a osprey; or the skin, bones, and hooves of horned animals, single-hoofed animals, or cloven-hoofed animals.
6.17.119 | Having burnt all [the ingredients] either individually or together, one should lick the resulting powder mixed with honey and ghee;
this conquers cough, hiccups, and even severe dyspnea.

6.17.120 | For these [fevers] arise from the provocation of the *prāṇa* breath whose movement is obstructed by *kapha*; therefore, linctuses should be administered for the purpose of purifying its passage, provided that *kapha* is not absent.
6.17.121 | A wise physician should administer emetics for cough and hoarseness of voice;
however, for asthma (tamaka), purgatives combined with drugs that alleviate Vāta and Kapha should be used.
Just as water flowing with great force increases even more due to the obstruction of its path,
so too should one constantly clear the passage of that wind.
6.17.123 | Śaṭī, coraka, jīvantī,
vāntī, tvak, musta, puṣkaramūla, surasa, tāmalakī, elā, pippalī, aguru, and nāgara.
6.17.124 | Having made an equal powder of vālaka with eight parts of sugar,
one should employ it in all cases of tamaka-śvāsa (asthmatic breathlessness) and hiccup.
6.17.125 | Pearls, coral, lapis lazuli, conch, crystal,
collyrium, *sāragandha, glass, *arka, small cardamom, and the two types of salt.
6.17.126 | Copper, iron filings, silver, saugandhika, lead, nutmeg, hemp seeds, and the grains of apāmārga;
6.17.127 | The powder of these [drugs] taken in equal parts, when licked with honey and ghee,
quickly subdues hiccup, dyspnea, and cough.
6.17.128 | By its application as a collyrium, it destroys timira, kāca, nīlikā, puṣpaka, and tamaḥ; as well as mala, itching, abhiṣyanda, and even [diseases of] the vital points (marman).
Thus ends the powder beginning with pearl (muktā).
6.17.129: A powder of śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, and āmalaka, or a powder of kālaloha, should be licked together with honey.
One should administer or apply as a nasal drop a mixture of *tāmalakī* with sugar, grapes, the juice of cow and horse dung,
along with equal parts of jaggery and ginger.
6.17.131 | One should cause the root of garlic, or onion, or leek,
or even sandalwood, to be infused with human breast milk.
6.17.132 | One should administer lukewarm clarified butter-scum (ghṛtamaṇḍa) sprinkled with rock salt,
or honey-bee excrement (mākṣikī viṣṭhā) mixed with the juice of lac (alaktaka).
Ghee prepared with cow's milk and the drugs of the sweet group (madhuraka),
when drunk or instilled as nasal drops, immediately subdues hiccup.
6.17.134 | For those with thickened secretions (dhikkina), milk— alternately warm and cold— should be administered once each,
either for drinking or as a nasal therapy (nastaḥkriyā), combined with sugar and honey.
Ghee prepared with the lower parts [of the plants] immediately subdues hiccup;
or else, the juices of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) and *kapittha* (wood-apple), combined with long pepper (*pippalī*) and honey, [achieve the same].
6.17.136 | One should lick a mixture of parched grain, lac, honey, grapes, long pepper, and the juice of horse dung;
or alternatively, a mixture of jujube, honey, grapes, long pepper, and ginger.
6.17.137 | Sprinkling with cold water, sudden fright, causing amazement,
fear, anger, joy, and agitation from pleasant things are considered methods for the expulsion of hiccups.
6.17.138 | That which has been proclaimed as the etiology of the disorders of hiccup and dyspnea should be avoided by those afflicted with hiccup and dyspnea who desire health.
6.17.139 | Those patients who suffer from persistent hiccups and dyspnea, whose chest, throat, and palate are parched,
and whose bodies are naturally dry, should be treated with ghee.

6.17.140 | One should prepare clarified butter in the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla) and the whey of curd (dadhimanda), with long pepper (kṛṣṇā), black salt (sauvarcala), alkali (kṣāra), the "vayaḥsthā" group of drugs, asafoetida (hiṅgu), and coraka.
6.17.141 | By drinking that [mixture] with *kāyasthā*, one should destroy hiccup and dyspnea.
[The powder of] *tejovatī*, *abhayā*, *kuṣṭha*, *pippalī*, and *kaṭurohiṇī* [is also used].
6.17.142 | Bhūtīka, the root of the lotus (pauṣkara), palāśa, citraka, śaṭī, sauvarcala salt, tāmalakī, rock salt (saindhava), and the pulp of the bilva fruit.
6.17.143 | One should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much water and one akṣa each of tālīsapatra, jīvantī, and vacā, along with one-fourth part (pāda) of hiṅgu.
6.17.144 | By drinking this according to one's strength, a person may conquer hiccup and dyspnea,
as well as edema, disorders of wind (vāta), hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and pains in the heart and flanks.
Thus ends the Tejovatī-ghṛta (6.17.145).

One *prastha* of ghee is prepared and beneficial when cooked with one *karṣa* each of realgar (*manaḥśilā*), resin (*sarjarasa*), lac (*lākṣā*), turmeric (*rajanī*), lotus (*padmaka*), madder (*mañjiṣṭhā*), and cardamom (*elā*).
6.17.146 | Or one should lick ghee prepared with life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs along with honey;
or likewise, one should drink ghee prepared with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) and curd, or Vāsā-ghee.
Thus ends the *manaḥśilā-ghṛta* (6.17.147).

Whatever medicine, whether for drinking or as food, is hot, subdues *kapha* and *vāta*, and facilitates the downward movement of *vāta*, is beneficial for one suffering from *śvāsa* (asthma/dyspnea) and *hikkā* (hiccup).

6.17.148 | A substance that produces wind (vāta) may remove phlegm (kapha), and one that produces phlegm may remove wind; therefore, one should not rely exclusively on either of these two, for generally, that which removes wind is more beneficial.

6.17.149 | For in all cases, nourishing therapy (bṛṃhaṇa) is generally mild, feasible, and rarely harmful; whereas in pacifying therapy (śamana), the risk is not excessive, and in reducing therapy (karśana), it is severe and difficult to manage.
Therefore, one should generally treat persons afflicted by hiccup and dyspnea— whether they are pure or impure— by means of pacifying (śamana) and nourishing (br̥ṃhaṇa) therapies.
6.17.151 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
The causes for the difficulty of conquering, the origin, and the unity of treatment,
as well as the signs and the wholesome diet for hiccup and dyspnea, have been shown here.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Hiccups and Dyspnea," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Eighteen:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of cough.
6.18.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.18.3 Endowed with austerity, fame, fortitude, and supreme intelligence,
Ātreya has declared this proven medical treatment for the purpose of pacifying cough.

6.18.4 | There are five types of cough in humans—those born of wind (vāta) and the other [doshas], that born of injury (kṣataja), and likewise that born of wasting (kṣayaja). As these increase, they bring about the destruction of vitality (kṣaya).
6.18.5 | Their premonitory symptoms are a sensation of the throat and mouth being filled with bristles,
itching in the throat, and an aversion to food.
The wind, obstructed below and having ascended to the upper channels,
