attains the state of udāna and becomes fixed in the throat as well as in the chest.
6.18.7 Entering all the apertures of the head and filling them completely,
he broke, shook, and likewise struck the body, the jaw, and the eyes.
6.18.8 | Then, by distorting the eyes, back, chest, and sides, and causing stiffness—
whether dry or accompanied by phlegm— it is called *kāsa* (cough) due to the act of coughing.
6.18.9 | Due to a specific obstruction of that forceful wind,
a particular intensity of pain and sound arises in the coughs.
6.18.10 | Dryness, coldness, astringency, small quantities, fasting, women,
suppression of natural urges, and physical exertion are the factors that initiate vāta-type cough.

6.18.11 | It causes intense pain in the heart, flanks, and chest, as well as hoarseness of voice; it occurs in one whose chest, throat, and mouth are parched, whose hair stands on end, and who faints.
6.18.12 | Dry cough produces hoarseness, dejection, labored breathing, weakness, agitation, and delusion; after expectorating dry phlegm with difficulty, it subsides into mildness.
6.18.13 | It is pacified by the consumption or drinking of unctuous, sour, salty, and hot substances;
however, once the food has been digested, the upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta) becomes forceful.
6.18.14 | Excessive indulgence in pungent, hot, burning, sour, and alkaline substances causes pitta-type cough; so too do anger and the heat generated by fire and the sun.
6.18.15 | Yellowish expectoration, yellow eyes, a bitter taste in the mouth, affliction of the voice,
a sensation of smoke rising from the chest, thirst, burning, delusion, loss of appetite, and vertigo.
6.18.16 | In the Pitta-type [cough], the patient coughs continuously and sees things as if they were glowing lights;
he also spits out phlegm mixed with bile.
6.18.17 | Indeed, when Kapha increases due to heavy, obstructive, sweet, and unctuous foods, as well as sleep and lack of physical activity,
it obstructs the Vata and produces Kaphaja cough.
6.18.18 | Accompanied by weak digestion, loss of appetite, vomiting, catarrh, nausea, heaviness, horripilation,
sweetness in the mouth, moisture, and a sense of exhaustion;
6.18.19 | He expectorates copious, sweet, unctuous, and thick phlegm;
while coughing, though free from pain, he feels as if his chest were filled.
6.18.20 | In one who is dehydrated due to excessive sexual indulgence, heavy loads, travel on foot, battle, or conflict with horses and elephants,
the Vāyu, having seized the chest, brings about cough.
6.18.21 | First he coughs dryly, and then he spits out blood;
his throat is excessively painful, as if his chest were shattered.
6.18.22 | Tormented by the trident-bearer with a spear that was like sharp needles,
he was afflicted by the touch of pain— the agony of being pierced and crushed by the trident.
Afflicted by pain in the joints, fever, dyspnea, thirst,
and loss of voice, he utters plaintive cries like a pigeon due to the force of coughing arising from internal injury.

6.18.24 | When the digestive fire is impaired in men who consume unwholesome or irregular food, engage in excessive sexual intercourse, suppress natural urges, or are full of loathing and grief, the three impurities [vitiate the body].

6.18.25 | When aggravated, they cause cough born of wasting (kṣayaja-kāsa), which brings about the destruction of the body. One should expectorate sputum that is foul-smelling, green, or red, resembling pus.
6.18.26 | Coughing up from his position, he feels as if his heart has been displaced;
suddenly afflicted by heat and cold, he eats much yet becomes weak and emaciated.
6.18.27 | One who has a glossy and clear complexion of the face, eyes that are beautiful to behold,
and smooth palms and soles of the feet, is constantly envious and full of compassion.
6.18.28 | His fever has a mixed manifestation, accompanied by pain in the flanks, coryza, loss of appetite,
stools that are broken or consolidated, and a change in voice without apparent cause.
6.18.29 | Thus, this cough born of wasting (kṣayaja) destroys the bodies of those who are already emaciated;
it may be curable in those who possess strength, whereas that which arises from chest injury (kṣataja) is merely palliable (yāpya) even in such cases.
6.18.30 | These two [conditions] may sometimes be cured when accompanied by the qualities of youth;
however, all coughs caused by old age in the elderly are declared to be merely palliable.
6.18.31 | One should treat the three curable types with wholesome measures and manage those that are palliable. Hereafter, listen to the treatment for the eradication of cough.
6.18.32 | In the case of a cough born of Vāta in a patient who is dry (rūkṣa), one should treat it initially with unctuous substances (sneha),
such as ghee, enemas (vasti), gruels (peyā), meat soups (yūṣa), milk, meat broths, and so forth.
6.18.33 | The wise physician should employ, as appropriate, unctuous substances processed with Vata-alleviating drugs, medicinal smokes, electuaries, massages, affusions, and oleaginous sudations.

6.18.34 | One should conquer obstructed feces and flatus with enemas; dryness and upward movement of wind with [medicated ghees] taken after meals; and [disorders] associated with pitta or kapha with unctuous purgatives.
6.18.35 | A prastha of ghee prepared with thirty palas each of the decoctions of kaṇṭakārī and guḍūcī cures vāta-type cough and stimulates the digestive fire.
Thus ends the Kaṇṭakārī-ghṛta (6.18.36). [The next formulation is prepared] with pippalī, pippalīmūla, cavya, citraka, nāgara, dhānya, pāṭhā, vacā, rāsnā, yaṣṭyāhva, kṣāra, and hiṅgu.

6.18.37 | Having drunk a *caturthikā* prepared from one *kola* measure [of the drug] with one *prastha* of ghee and one *āḍhaka* of the decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūlī*), one should subsequently drink thin gruel (*peyā*) or scum (*maṇḍa*).
6.18.38 | This Pippalyādi ghee, proclaimed by Ātreya, cures dyspnea, cough, constriction of the heart and flanks, disorders of the grahaṇī, and abdominal tumors (gulma).
Thus ends the Pippalyādi-ghee (6.18.39).
[One should take] the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), grapes (drākṣā), kāśmarya fruits, parūṣaka,
the two types of pāṭhā, devadāru, ṛddhi, svaguptā, citraka, and śaṭī.
6.18.40 | Having ground brāhmī, tāmalakī, medā, kākanāsā, śatāvarī,
trikaṇṭaka, and vidārī, [one should add] one karṣa each from each, along with an equal amount of ghee.
6.18.41 | One should drink one *prastha* of this [medicinal oil] prepared with four times as much milk;
it cures cough and removes fever, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), anorexia, splenic enlargement, and pain in the head, heart, and flanks.
6.18.42 This unsurpassed ghee, known as Tryūṣaṇa, cures jaundice, hemorrhoids, wind-disorders, stones, wounds, emaciation, and consumption.

Thus ends the Tryūṣaṇādya-ghṛta (6.18.43). One should prepare [this] in one droṇa of water with rāsnā, daśamūlī, and śatāvarī— each weighing one pala— as well as kulattha, badara, and barley, each weighing one māṇika.
6.18.44 | With half a *tulā* of goat meat and one-fourth part of that [meat] as a remainder,
one should cook one *āḍhaka* of ghee with an equal amount of milk and one *pala* each of the *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) drugs.

6.18.45 | This [oil] is prepared with ten types of pastes; having carefully examined the condition, one should employ it for nasal drops, internal potions, and oil enemas in cases of vāta diseases according to the specific stage of the disorder.

6.18.46 | It conquers the five types of cough, tremors of the head, pain arising from the groin and the female genital tract, diseases affecting the whole body or a single limb, as well as splenic disorders and upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta).
Thus ends the Rāsnā-ghṛta (6.18.47). One should drink either the powder of viḍaṅga, nāgara, rāsnā, pippalī, hiṅgu,
saindhava, bhārgī, and kṣāra, or that same powder mixed with a measured amount of ghee.
6.18.48 | In cough caused by vāta accompanied by phlegm, in cases of dyspnea and hiccups, and in those whose digestive fire is impaired,
[one should use] the two alkalis, the five *kōla* spices, and the five salts.
6.18.49 | One should cause [the patient] to drink either a paste of śaṭī, nāgaraka, and udīcya filtered through a cloth,
mixed with ghee, which destroys cough caused by vāta.
6.18.50 | One should lick a paste of durālabhā, śaṭī, drākṣā, śṛṅgavera, white sugar,
and karkaṭaśṛṅgī with oil in cases of cough caused by vāta.
6.18.51 | One should also have the patient lick a powder of duḥsparśā, pippalī, musta, bhārgī, karkaṭakī, and śaṭī,
mixed with old jaggery and oil.
6.18.52 | By licking a paste of viḍaṅga, saindhava salt, kuṣṭha, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, and manaḥśilā combined with honey and ghee, one shall conquer cough, hiccup, and asthma.
6.18.53 | Citraka, pippalīmūla, vyoṣa, hiṅgu, durālabhā, śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, śreyasī, surasā, and vacā;
6.18.54 | One karṣa each of bhārgī, chinnaruhā, rāsnā, śṛṅgī, and drākṣā,
along with twenty palas of the paste of nidigdhikā, should be added to a decoction of half a tulā [of the former drugs].
6.18.55 | Having added one *kuḍava* each of sugar candy (*matsyaṇḍikā*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one should cook it;
once prepared, it should be cooled and then combined separately with one *kuḍava* each of honey and long pepper (*pippalī*).
6.18.56 | One should add four palas of powdered tugākṣīrī to it;
one should have this licked as a remedy for cough, heart disease, dyspnea, and abdominal tumors.
Thus ends the Citraka-ādi leha (6.18.57).
[One should take] Daśamūlī, Svayaṅguptā, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Śaṭī, Balā,
Hastipippalī, Apāmārga, Pippalīmūla, and Citraka.
6.18.58 | One should boil two-pala portions each of bhārgī and puṣkaramūla, one āḍhaka of barley,
and one hundred harītakī fruits in five āḍhakas of water.
6.18.59 | One should boil that decoction made from steamed barley, having strained it and added one hundred *abhayā* fruits,
along with a *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*) and one *kuḍava* each of ghee and [the other liquids].
6.18.60 | From the oil mixed with powdered pippalī, once it has been prepared and cooled, one should lick honey;
furthermore, one should always consume two abhayā fruits from this rejuvenative (rasāyana) preparation.
6.18.61 | It destroys wrinkles and graying hair, increases complexion, longevity, and strength;
and it cures the five types of cough, consumption, dyspnea, hiccup, and irregular fever.
6.18.62 | It likewise destroys hemorrhoids, grahaṇī, heart disease, anorexia, and chronic rhinitis.
This auspicious elixir (rasāyana), ordained by Agastya, is supreme.
Thus ends the Agastyaharītakī.
6.18.63: [One should take] rock salt (saindhava), long pepper (pippalī), bhārgī, ginger (śṛṅgavera), and durālabhā with sour pomegranate juice;
or bhārgī and ginger with lukewarm water.
6.18.64 | Or one should drink the essence of khadira with wine, sour curd, and whey;
or else, the paste of pippalī fried in ghee and mixed with rock salt.
6.18.65 | When there is pain in the head, discharge from the nose, or exhaustion in the heart,
the physician should administer medicated smoke to those suffering from cough and catarrh.
6.18.66 | Having inserted a tube measuring ten fingers or eight fingers into the hole of a pair of earthen saucers, the wise man should make it curved.
6.18.67 | One suffering from cough should inhale purgative smoke through the mouth alone;
once it has reached the chest, one should expel it again through the mouth alone.
6.18.68 | For that [medicine], by its sharpness, having cut through and extracted the phlegm situated in the chest,
shall pacify the cough arising from wind and phlegm.
6.18.69 | One should inhale smoke made from realgar, orpiment, licorice, spikenard, nut-grass, and ingudi;
thereafter, one should drink lukewarm milk mixed with jaggery.
6.18.70 | This medicated smoke (dhūma) shall destroy coughs arising from individual doṣas, from their combination (sannipāta), or those that are incurable even by hundreds of other formulations.
6.18.71 | Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, śārṅgeṣṭā, manaḥśilā, marica, pippalī, drākṣā, elā, and the flower-cluster of surasa.
6.18.72 | Having prepared a wick wrapped in linen cloth and smeared with ghee, one should inhale the smoke,
followed by milk or even molasses-water.
6.18.73 | With realgar, cardamom, black pepper, alkali, collyrium, and kuṭannaṭa;
with bamboo scrapings, sevyālaka, linen, lac, and rohiṣa grass.
6.18.74 | This smoke is prescribed with its adjuncts according to the previous method;
likewise for realgar and orpiment, along with long pepper and ginger.
6.18.75 | The bark of *iṅgudī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *tālamūlī*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*),
cotton seeds, and *aśvagandhā*— this incense is a destroyer of cough.
6.18.76 | One should feed [the patient] wholesome *śāli*, barley, wheat, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice with the juices of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals,
or with soups made from mung beans (*māṣa*) or *ātmaguptā*.
6.18.77 | With yavānī, pippalī, the pulp of bilva, nāgara, citraka, rāsnā, jājī, pṛthakparṇī, palāśa, śaṭī, and pauṣkara;
6.18.78 | In a disorder born of Vāta, one should drink a prepared gruel (peyā) that is unctuous, sour, and salty;
it destroys pain in the waist, heart, sides, and abdomen, as well as dyspnea and hiccup.

6.18.79 | Likewise, one should administer [the powder] prepared with the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), combined with pañcakola and jaggery; or it may be given with sesame seeds in milk, along with rock salt (saindhava).
A person suffering from cough caused by Vāta should drink a prepared gruel (peyā) enriched with ghee and rock salt, using the meat of fish, chicken, or boar as the source of the broth.
6.18.81 | Vāstuka, vāyasī-vegetable, radish, and suniṣaṇṇaka;
oils and other fats; and foods prepared with milk, sugarcane juice, and molasses.
6.18.82 | Furthermore, the drinking of curd, sour gruel, sour fruits,
and clear wine (prasannā) is recommended for cough caused by vāta, as are sweet, sour, and salty substances.
Thus ends the treatment for cough caused by Vāta (6.18.83). In a cough characterized by Pitta and Kapha, emesis induced with ghee is beneficial,
as is [emesis] with water boiled with Madana, Kāśmarya, and Madhuka.
6.18.84 | Or, with the pastes of the fruits of yaṣṭyāhva combined with the juices of vidārī and sugarcane,
one whose humors have been removed should then follow a cooling and sweet regimen.

6.18.85 | In a cough characterized by pitta and thin phlegm, the physician should administer trivṛt combined with sweet substances; in a case of thick phlegm, it should be given for the purpose of purgation combined with bitter substances.

6.18.86 | When the phlegm is unctuous, cold, and thin, a regimen that is dry and cold should be employed; however, when the phlegm is thick, it is recommended to proceed with foods, fats, and electuaries.
6.18.87 | Śṛṅgāṭaka, lotus seeds, the pith of nīlī, pippalī; pippalī, musta, yaṣṭyāhva, drākṣā, mūrvā, and mahauṣadha.
6.18.88 | Puffed rice, the fruit of immortality (amṛtaphala), grapes, tvakkṣīrī, long pepper, sugar; long pepper, lotus, grapes, and the juice from the fruits of bṛhatī.
6.18.89 | Date palm, long pepper, bamboo manna, and cow-hoof (śvadaṃṣṭrā)— these five,
combined with ghee and honey, are electuaries for those coughing with pitta, as described in the half-verses.

6.18.90 | In cases of pitta-type fever, [a decoction] with sugar, sandalwood, grapes, honey, emblic myrobalan, and blue lotus is used; with musta and black pepper for kapha-type fever; and with ghee added for vāta-type fever.
6.18.91 | One should have the patient lick fifty grains of raisins, thirty long peppers (pippalī), and one pala of sugar with honey; or [one may take] cow's milk and the juice of cow dung.
6.18.92 | With cinnamon, cardamom, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper), raisins, the root of long pepper, lotus seeds;
with parched grain, musta, śaṭī, rāsnā, dhātrī fruit, and bibhītaka;
6.18.93 | A linctus made of sugar, honey, and ghee destroys cough;
it also eliminates dyspnea, hiccup, consumption, and heart disease.
6.18.94 | Having cooked long pepper, emblic myrobalan, grapes, lac, parched rice,
and white sugar in milk until it becomes a solid mass, one should lick it when cold, mixed with a one-eighth part of honey.
6.18.95 | One should drink the juices of vidārī, sugarcane, and lotus stalks, along with milk and white sugar, mixed with honey; this is an excellent remedy for curing pitta-type cough.
6.18.96 | Śyāmāka, yava, and kodrava are wholesome when consumed in moderation with sweet meat-broths from wild animals,
soups made from mung beans and other pulses, and bitter vegetables.

6.18.97 | When phlegm is thick, emollient linctuses (lehas) made of bitter herbs combined with honey should be used; when phlegm is thin, śāli rice and ṣaṣṭika rice, along with meat broths and other such items, should be taken.
6.18.98 | Sugar-water, the juices of grapes and sugarcane, milk, and everything that is sweet, cold, and non-burning is recommended as a post-drink (anupāna).
6.18.99 | For pitta-type cough, one should prepare meat broths, milk, and soups with kākolī, the two types of bṛhatī, the two types of medā, vṛṣa, and nāgara.
6.18.100 | One should drink milk boiled with the decoction of the five roots beginning with śara, as well as pippalī and drākṣā, together with honey and sugar.
6.18.101 | With the pairs of sthirā, asitā, pṛśniparṇī, śrāvaṇī, and bṛhatī;
and with jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, ākāolī, tāmalakī, ṛddhi, and jīvaka;
6.18.102 | A person suffering from cough, fever, burning sensations, or wasting due to chest injury should drink boiled milk;
or the physician should prepare clarified butter (ghṛta) from that milk, mixed with sugarcane juice.

6.18.103 | When the [oil] has been prepared with the sweet fruits such as jīvaka and others, and with the *kalkas* (pastes) of abhiṣuka and others, each weighing one karṣa, one should administer it once it has been strained and cooled.
6.18.104 | Having added the powder of sugar, long pepper, bamboo manna, black pepper, and water chestnut, one should prepare boluses weighing one pala each, with honey as their core.
6.18.105 | One who eats wholesome food should eat jaggery mixed with wheat flour in cases of defects of semen and blood, wasting diseases, cough, and emaciation due to chest wounds.
6.18.106 | Having ground together sugar, ginger, udīcya, kaṇṭakārī, and śaṭī in equal parts,
one should drink the juice strained through a cloth and mixed with ghee.

6.18.107 | One should drink ghee prepared with equal parts of buffalo milk, goat milk, sheep milk, cow milk, and the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) fruits, according to the proper method; this destroys pitta-type cough.
Thus ends the treatment for pitta-type cough (6.18.108). One should first purify a strong patient suffering from kapha-type cough with emetics,
and then treat him with barley-based foods that are pungent, dry, and hot, as well as other kapha-subduing measures.
6.18.109 | One should eat light foods with soups of long pepper, *kṣārika*, horse gram, and radish, or with meat broths seasoned with pungent spices.

6.18.110 | One should drink a decoction of dhanvana, baila, and rasanjana, along with the oils of sesame, mustard, and bilva; or else, one may drink honey, sour gruel, warm water, buttermilk, or even plain wine.
6.18.111 | The roots of *pauṣkara* and *āragvadha*, along with *paṭola*, should be soaked in water overnight;
this water, mixed with honey, should be drunk at the three meal times.
6.18.112 | Kaṭphala, kattṛṇa, bhārgī, musta, dhānyaka, vacā, abhayā, śuṇṭhī, parpaṭaka, karkaṭaśṛṅgī, and surāhvā, boiled in water—
6.18.113 | Honey mixed with asafoetida should be drunk in cases of cough caused by vāta and kapha,
as well as in throat diseases, facial swelling, dyspnea, hiccups, and fever.
6.18.114 | Having ground pāṭhā, śuṇṭhī, mūrvā, gavākṣī, musta, and pippalī,
one should drink it with warm water, combined with hiṅgu and rock salt (saindhava).
6.18.115 | One should drink nagara, ativiṣā, musta, śṛṅgī, karkaṭaka, harītakī, and śaṭī according to that same procedure.
6.18.116 Or one should drink a paste of one akṣa of long pepper fried in oil,
combined with sugar-candy and the broth of horse gram (kulattha), which destroys cough caused by phlegm.
6.18.117 | The juice of *kāsamarda*, horse dung, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and eggplant, taken with honey, destroys cough caused by phlegm; so too does that of *surasā* and black iron.
6.18.118 | Devadāru, śaṭī, rāsnā, karkaṭākhyā, durālabhā, pippalī, nāgara, musta, pathyā, dhātrī, and sitopalā.
6.18.119 | These two electuaries, combined with honey and oil, are for kapha associated with vāta:
pippalī, pippalīmūla, citraka, and hastipippalī.
6.18.120 | Pathyā, tāmalakī, dhātrī, bhadramustā, and pippalī;
devadāru, abhayā, musta, pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja.
6.18.121 | The physician should administer these four linctuses with honey— consisting of viśālā, pippalī, musta, and trivṛt— to cure cough caused by kapha.
6.18.122 | One should drink the powder of sauvarcala salt, abhayā, dhātrī, pippalī, kṣāra,
and nāgara mixed with ghee to alleviate cough caused by vāta and kapha.

6.18.123 | One *prastha* of ghee should be cooked with one *āḍhaka* of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and [the paste of] equal parts of *puṣkaramūla*, *śaṭī*, *bilva*, *surasā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*).
6.18.124 | That drink should be consumed with a liquid after-drink (anupāna) in cases of cough caused by vāta and kapha,
as well as in all diseases of breath (śvāsa) characterized by kapha and vāta.

Thus ends the *Daśamūlādighṛta*. 6.18.125. One *prastha* of ghee should be cooked with one *āḍhaka* of the juice of *kaṇṭakārī*, including its roots, fruits, and leaves, along with *balā*, *vyoṣa*, *viḍaṅga*, *śaṭī*, and *citrika*.
6.18.126 | With sauvarcala salt, yavakṣāra alkali, pippalīmūla, pauṣkara, vṛścīra, bṛhatī, pathyā, yavānī, dāḍima, and ṛddhi;
6.18.127 | One should cook [a decoction] with grapes, punarnavā, cavya, durālabhā, and amlavetasa, along with śṛṅgī, āmalakī, bhārgī, rāsnā, and gokṣuraka.
6.18.128 | This Kaṇṭakārī ghee, prepared with pastes, is recommended for all types of coughs and for hiccup and dyspnea; it indeed destroys diseases caused by phlegm.
Thus ends the Kaṇṭakārī-ghṛta (6.18.129).
Alternatively, one should administer ghee boiled with horse gram soup and the five spices (pañcakola);
this is recommended for cough caused by phlegm, as well as for hiccups and dyspnea.
Thus ends the *kulattha* and other ghees (6.18.130). One should also administer those same medicinal smokes that were prescribed for those suffering from vāta-type cough;
or one may drink the pulp of *kośātakī* fruit mixed with realgar (*manaḥśilā*).
6.18.131 | If Tamaka-kāsa occurs due to an association with pitta in a case of kapha-type cough,
one should apply the therapeutic measures for pitta-type cough according to the specific stage of the disease.
6.18.132 | When wind is associated with phlegm, one should perform treatments that alleviate phlegm;
when wind and phlegm are associated with bile, one should perform treatments that destroy bile.
6.18.133 | In cough caused by vāta and kapha, when it is moist, a drying treatment is indicated; when dry, an unctuous treatment.
In cough born of kapha associated with pitta, food and drink should be combined with bitter substances.

Thus ends the treatment of cough born of phlegm (6.18.134). Considering a cough caused by injury to the chest (kṣataja) to be an emergency, one should treat it with haste using sweet, life-sustaining (jīvanīya), and strength-and-flesh-promoting remedies.
6.18.135 | One karṣa each of ground pippalī and madhuka, along with one pala of sugar-candy;
one prastha each of cow’s milk, goat’s milk, and sugarcane juice.
6.18.136 | Barley, wheat, and grape powder, the juice of āmalaka, and oil—
each of these in the measure of one prasṛta— should all be cooked over a gentle fire.

6.18.137 | This linctus, when taken with ghee and honey, cures cough due to chest injury (kṣatakāsa). It is beneficial for dyspnea (śvāsa), heart disease (hṛdroga), emaciation (kārśya), and in cases of the elderly or those with diminished semen.
6.18.138 | For those overcome by cough due to chest injury (kṣatakāsa), the regimen should be that prescribed for pitta-type cough;
however, when there is a combination of doshas, milk, ghee, and honey should predominate as a specific modification.
6.18.139 | An oil massage with ghee is beneficial for body aches caused by the affliction of vāta and pitta,
as well as for those oppressed by vāyu when using oils that destroy wind-related diseases.
6.18.140 | In cases of pain in the heart and flanks, one should drink *jīvanīya* ghee,
as well as for those with cough and burning sensations who expectorate blood when the digestive fire is strong.
6.18.141 | For those emaciated by lack of meat, the broths of quails and similar birds are beneficial;
for those afflicted by thirst, goat’s milk boiled with the roots of *śara* grass and other such ingredients is recommended.
6.18.142 | When blood has emerged from the channels or from the mouth, ghee produced from milk should be administered as nasal drops,
for drinking, or as gruel— especially when the person is exhausted, emaciated, and their digestive fire is suppressed.
6.18.143 | In cases of stiffness and lameness, one should drink a large dose of ghee,
or administer that which destroys Vata diseases while not aggravating Pitta and blood.
6.18.144 | When the injury to the chest has ceased, but the kapha is increased in a case of chest wound (uraḥkṣata),
the patient who suffers from coughing and feels as if his chest is being torn apart should drink these following medicinal smokes (dhūma).
6.18.145 | Having inhaled the smoke from two types of *meda*, *madhūka*, the two types of *bala*, and *kṣauma* and *lākṣā* rolled into wicks, one should drink *jīvanīya* ghee.
6.18.146 | Having infused *manaḥśilā*, *palāśa*, *ajagandhā*, the bark of milky trees (*kṣīrin*), and *nāgara* [ginger],
one should drink it along with a linen cloth, followed by sugarcane juice and molasses water.
Having ground equal parts of realgar and fresh *vaṭa* sprouts,
one should drink the resulting smoke with clarified butter, followed by a meal of partridge meat.

6.18.148 | Or, one should smoke linen cloth that has been saturated with the drugs of the jīvanīya group mixed with the juice of the eggs of the kuliṅga bird, followed by milk boiled with iron boluses (ayoguḍa).

Thus ends the treatment of cough caused by chest wounds (kṣataja-kāsa). 6.18.149. One should avoid treating a case of cough born of wasting (kṣayaja) that is fully manifested in a weak patient; however, for a strong patient with a recently arisen condition, one should proceed with treatment after informing them of the prognosis.
6.18.150 | For such a person, one should first administer nourishing therapy and stimulate the digestive fire;
for one with an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas), one should give a mild purgative mixed with unctuous substances.
6.18.151 | With śampāka, trivṛt combined with the juice of mṛdvīkā,
with the decoction of tilvaka, and with the fresh juice of vidārī;
6.18.152 | One whose body is emaciated should drink clarified butter prepared as a purificatory agent according to the proper method;
this is considered beneficial for the preservation of both his body and strength.
6.18.153 | [This is especially indicated] when pitta and kapha are diminished and the bodily tissues (*dhātus*) have become greatly depleted.
One should drink ghee prepared with karkaṭakī, milk, and the two types of balā.
6.18.154 | Ghee boiled with vidārī, kadamba, or tāla seeds,
along with milk, [is used] for discoloration of the urine and for difficult urination.
6.18.155 | When the penis is empty yet painful, or when the anus along with the hips and groins is so affected,
one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using the scum of clarified butter mixed with honey, or with a "mixed" (miśraka) preparation.

6.18.156 | For one who has been treated with the meat of wild animals (jāṅgala), birds such as the vartaka and others that dwell in holes, and then gradually carnivorous animals that seize their prey (prasaha), should be administered.

6.18.157 | Due to their heat and their disruptive nature, they dislodge the *kapha* from the channels; once these channels are purified, the nutrient fluid (*rasa*), flowing properly, brings about nourishment.
6.18.158 | With the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūlī), triphalā, cavikā, bhārgī, citraka,
horse-gram (kulattha), pippalī root, pāṭhā, kola, and barley, [one should boil] in water.
6.18.159 | One should cook ghee with equal parts of the boiled decoctions of ginger (nāgara), durālabhā (duḥsparśā), long pepper (pippalī), śaṭī, lotus root (puṣkara), and karkaṭaśṛṅgī.
6.18.160 | When this has been prepared, one afflicted by wasting cough (kṣayakāsa) should drink an appropriate dose after adding two types of alkali and five salts, according to the proper method.
Thus ends the ghee prepared with the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūla) and other ingredients (6.18.161).
[One should take] guḍūcī, pippalī, mūrvā, haridrā, śreyasī, vacā,
nidigdhikā, kāsamarda, pāṭhā, citraka, and nāgara.

Having boiled [the paste] in four times its quantity of water until one-fourth remains, one should drink that prepared ghee in an amount equal to the paste; it cures abdominal tumors (gulma), dyspnea, pain, consumption, and cough.

Thus ends the *guḍūcyādi-ghṛta* (6.18.163). [One should prepare a medicated ghee] with *kāsamarda*, *abhayā*, *musta*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭphala*, and *nāgara*; likewise with *pippalī*, *kaṭukā*, *drākṣā*, *kāśmarya*, and *surasa*.
One should cook one prastha of ghee with six akṣas [of each of the following] in one āḍhaka of milk and grape juice;
this auspicious preparation cures wasting diseases, fever, splenic disorders, and all types of cough.
6.18.165 | Or ghee prepared with *dhātrī* fruits boiled in milk, sprinkled with [powdered] drugs,
and cooked with twice the amount of pomegranate juice combined with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
After a meal, a person should drink either barley-alkali mixed with ghee,
or ghee prepared with long pepper and jaggery, combined with goat’s milk.

6.18.167 | These ghees are for the purpose of increasing the digestive fire in those suffering from wasting and cough; they also serve to purify the channels of the chest and the abdominal cavity when obstructed by the humors.
6.18.168 | One should cook twenty *harītakī* fruits in two *āḍhakas* of a decoction of barley;
once they are softened by boiling, one should press them and add six *palas* of old jaggery (*guḍa*) to that [mixture].
6.18.169 | One should administer one karṣa of realgar and half a karṣa of rasāñjana, along with half a kuḍava of long pepper; this linctus cures asthma and cough.

Thus ends the Harītakī-leha (6.18.170). The burnt spines of a porcupine, taken with ghee, honey, and sugar, cure asthma and cough; or alternatively, the two feet of a peacock taken with honey and ghee [have the same effect].
6.18.171 | Or one should lick the alkali of castor leaves combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa), oil, and jaggery; or, by this same method, that produced from the leaves of *surasā* and castor.
6.18.172 | One should lick a paste of grapes, lotus seeds, eggplant, and long pepper with honey and ghee;
or one may lick the powder of the three pungents (trivṛt, pippalī, marica) with aged jaggery and ghee.

6.18.173 | One should lick a paste of *citraka*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), cumin (*jājī*), *karkaṭākhyā*, the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), and grapes, mixed with honey and ghee; or one may take it with jaggery (*guḍa*).
6.18.174 | One should prepare a fine powder using equal parts of padmaka, triphalā, vyoṣa, viḍaṅga, devadāru, balā, and rāsnā.
6.18.175 | Having thoroughly stirred together honey, ghee, and sugar with all these powders individually, one should lick this beneficial linctus, which cures all types of cough.
6.18.176 | Jīvantī, madhuka, pāṭhā, tvakkṣīrī, triphalā, śaṭī, musta, elā, padmaka, drākṣā, the two types of bṛhatī, and vitunnaka;
6.18.177 | Sārivā, the root of puṣkara, karkaṭākhyā, rasāñjana, punarnavā, iron filings, trāyamāṇā, and yavānikā—
6.18.178 | Bhārgī, tāmalakī, mṛdvī, viḍaṅga,
dhanvayāsaka, kṣāra, citraka, cavya, amlavetasa, vyoṣa, and dāru.
Having reduced these to a powder in equal parts, one should have it licked with honey and ghee. A palmful of this powder dispels the five types of cough.
Thus ends the Padmakādi electuary (6.18.180).
One should lick either powdered black pepper with ghee, honey, and sugar;

Chapter Nineteen.
6.19.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of diarrhea (*atīsāra*).
6.19.2 Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

6.19.3 | Having approached with humility and saluted the Blessed Ātreya—who had completed his daily rites, offered the Agnihotra oblation, and was seated on the northern slope of the Himalayas surrounded by a multitude of sages—Agniveśa said: "O Blessed One, for the sake of favoring all beings, you should explain the primordial origin, causes, symptoms, and treatments of diarrhea."

6.19.4 | Then the Blessed One, Punarvasu Ātreya, having heard those words of Agniveśa, said: "Listen, Agniveśa! All this shall be explained by me in its entirety. In the primordial age, indeed, animals were to be touched [as part of ritual] in sacrifices, but they were not yet subjected to slaughter.

Subsequently, after the sacrifice of Dakṣa, during the rituals of the sons of Manu—such as Nariṣyant, Nābhāga, Ikṣvāku, Nṛga, Śaryāti, and others—animals received the rite of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) because their slaughter was permitted."
Consequently, at a later time, while Pṛṣadhra was performing a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*), due to the failure to obtain [other] animals, he initiated the immolation of cows.

Seeing this, the hosts of living beings were deeply distressed. From the consumption of those cows that had been consecrated for sacrifice—due to their heaviness, heat, unwholesomeness, and because their consumption was inauspicious—their digestive fires were impaired and their minds were afflicted, resulting in the first occurrence of diarrhea during Pṛṣadhra’s sacrifice.

6.19.5 | Furthermore, in a person who is habitually wind-disordered (*vātalas*), due to excessive indulgence in wind-inducing factors, exposure to wind and sun, and physical exercise; who eats food that is dry, small in quantity, or insufficient; who is constantly addicted to strong liquor and sexual intercourse; and who suppresses natural urges—the *vāyu* becomes aggravated and the digestive fire (*paktṛ*) is impaired. That aggravated *vāyu*, while the fire is impaired, draws the urine and sweat into the receptacle of feces (*purīṣāśaya*), liquefies the feces along with those two, and thus brings about diarrhea.

Its symptoms are as follows: the stool is discharged as undigested (*āmam*), disordered (*viplutam*), heavy (*avasādi*), rough (*rūkṣam*), liquid (*dravam*), painful (*saśūlam*), smelling of raw matter (*āmagandham*), and either with sound or silent; it is obstructed in its urine and flatus (*vibaddhamūtravātam*). Furthermore, within the abdominal cavity, the wind moves crookedly, accompanied by sound and pain, and remains obstructed. This is diarrhea due to undigested matter caused by Vata (*āmātisāro vātāt*).

When the stool is digested but obstructed, passed in very small quantities with sound, accompanied by pain, froth, slimy mucus, and cutting pain, while the patient has horripilation, sighs deeply, has a dry mouth, suffers from pain in the waist, thighs, sacrum, knees, back, and sides, and has prolapsed rectum, he voids feces that are repeatedly knotted together due to Vata; some call this condition *anugrathita* (knotted), because the feces are knotted by Vata.

6.19.6 | Furthermore, in one of bilious temperament who excessively consumes sour, salty, pungent, alkaline, hot, and sharp substances; whose body is afflicted by constant heat from fire and the sun as well as hot winds; and who is full of anger and envy—the *pitta* becomes provoked.

That provoked *pitta*, due to its fluidity, overcomes the bodily heat (*ūṣman*); having spread into the receptacle of feces, it breaks through the stool by means of its heat, fluidity, and mobility, thereby causing diarrhea (*atisāra*).

Its symptoms are as follows: the stool is passed as yellow, green, blue, black, or reddish-yellow, accompanied by bilious matter (*rakta-pitta*), being extremely foul-smelling; the patient is overcome by thirst, burning sensations, perspiration, fainting, colic, inflammation of the groin (*bradhna*), and suppuration—this is Pitta-type diarrhea (*pittātisāra*).

6.19.7 | However, in one who is of a phlegmatic constitution (*śleṣmala*), who consumes heavy, sweet, cold, and unctuous foods, who eats until full, who does not reflect, who is devoted to daytime sleep, and who is indolent, the phlegm (*śleṣman*) becomes provoked.

By its very nature—being heavy, sweet, cold, and unctuous—it, having become displaced, impairs the digestive fire (*agni*); then, due to its watery (*saumya*) nature, it afflicts and moistens the receptacle of feces (*purīṣāśaya*), leading to diarrhea (*atisāra*).

Its symptoms are as follows: one passes stools that are unctuous, white, slimy, stringy, heavy, foul-smelling, mixed with phlegm, and accompanied by persistent pain; they are evacuated in small quantities but frequently, along with tenesmus. There is heaviness in the abdomen, anus, bladder, and groin regions; even after defecation, there is a sensation that it has not been done; there is horripilation, nausea, and the patient is overcome by sleep and lethargy, feels exhausted, and has an aversion to food—this is Kaphaja atisāra.

6.19.8 | From the consumption of food that is excessively cold, unctuous, dry, hot, heavy, rough, hard, irregular, incompatible, or unwholesome; from fasting; from eating at improper times; from consuming whatever comes to hand; from drinking spoiled liquor or water; from excessive drinking of liquor; from lack of purification; from the improper application of therapeutic procedures; from lack of care; from excessive exposure to fire, the sun, wind, or water; from lack of sleep or excessive sleep; from the suppression of natural urges; from seasonal abnormalities; from exertion beyond one's strength; and from the excessive presence of fear, grief, or mental agitation.

Or, due to excessive emaciation caused by worms, consumption, fever, or hemorrhoids, the three doshas become aggravated in one whose digestive fire is impaired; having further afflicted the fire and entered the colon (pakvāśaya), they produce diarrhea characterized by the symptoms of all the doshas.
Furthermore, excessively vitiating the bodily constituents such as blood and the rest, they manifest the colors of diarrhea produced by the nature of the corruption of those constituents.

In that condition, when the bodily constituents (dhātus) such as blood and others are excessively vitiated, one passes stools that are colored yellow, green, blue, madder-red, like meat-washings, red, black, or white, resembling the excrement of a boar; these may be accompanied by constant pain or be painless, and may be passed either in their natural order or in reverse order. The stool may be knotted, undigested (āma), or sometimes digested (pakva). This occurs in a patient whose flesh, blood, and strength are not excessively depleted, yet who has weak digestion and impaired taste in the mouth. Such a patient should be known as having a curable disease that is difficult to treat.

One should declare a patient suffering from diarrhea with these colors and accompanied by complications to be incurable; namely: resembling cooked blood, like a piece of liver, similar to fat or muscle-water, resembling curd, ghee, marrow, oil, fat, milk, or meat-broth (vesavāra); excessively blue, excessively red, or excessively black; clear like water, or again, having the luster of a dark-blue gem (mecaka), excessively unctuous, green, blue, or astringent (kaṣāya) in color, variegated, turbid, slimy, fibrous, and undigested.

One should recognize as incurable a case of diarrhea caused by the derangement of all three humors (*sannipāta*) that has reached a fatal stage (*candrakopagata*), smelling like a putrid corpse, pus, raw fish, or being infested with flies; where there is a discharge of many putrid bodily elements, with little or no feces, or where it is being passed as liquid diarrhea (*atisāra*); accompanied by thirst, burning heat, fever, vertigo, fainting, hiccups, and labored breathing; characterized by extreme pain or, conversely, a lack of sensation; where the anus is prolapsed and inflamed, with the anal folds completely displaced and the rectal sphincter released; where strength, flesh, and blood are utterly depleted; where every joint and bone aches; overwhelmed by loss of appetite, restlessness, delirium, and confusion; and where the fatal transformation occurs suddenly. This is *sannipātātisāra*.

6.19.10 | One should treat a tamasic condition that has reached an incurable state by means of a treatment commencing with the most predominant factor, and through an examination of the specific causes, the factors providing relief, and the particular nature of the doshas.

the treatment for these consists of measures that alleviate wind, as well as exhilaration and consolation.

6.19.98 | One should prepare Śatāvarī-ghṛta for him as a linctus;
fresh butter, with sugar added in the amount of half its weight, should be licked.
One who eats wholesome food will quickly conquer that disorder by drinking honey with the tender shoots (śuṅgā) of Nyagrodha, Udumbara, and Aśvattha; these should be crushed and soaked in water.
6.19.100 | One should cook ghee in water that has been heated for a day and night;
one should lick that, mixed with half as much sugar and a quarter part honey.
6.19.101 | Whether blood flows from below or even from above,
he who, being thus weak, out of delusion continues to consume only pitta-aggravating substances;
6.19.102 | Having suffered severe inflammation of the anal folds, he quickly perishes.
In cases of kaphaja diarrhea, fasting and digestive treatments are beneficial at the outset.
6.19.103 | The aforementioned group of digestive stimulants (dīpana-gaṇa) should be employed to cure diarrhea caused by undigested food (āmātisāra).
Furthermore, it does not cease its action even when the sequential regimen of fasting (laṅghana) has been performed.
6.19.104 | If diarrhea is born of kapha, one should treat it with kapha-subduing remedies:
bilva, karkaṭikā, musta, abhayā, and viśvabheṣaja.
6.19.105 | Vacā, viḍaṅga, bhūtīka, dhānyaka, and devadāru;
kuṣṭha, ativiṣā, pāṭhā, cavya, and kaṭurohiṇī.
6.19.106 | One should employ those four formulations consisting of pippalī, pippalīmūla, citraka, and hastipippalī, as prescribed in half-verses.
6.19.107 | Ajāji, asitā, pāṭhā, nāgara, and marica— these, when boiled, increase the digestive fire and strength in cases of kaphaja diarrhea.
6.19.108 | One should give rasāñjana, ativiṣā, and the fruits of kuṭaja, doubled by dhātakī and saturated with the juice of mātuluṅga.
6.19.109 | One should give double the amount of dhātakī to drink, along with honey and ginger;
[the powder of] dhātakī, ginger, bilva, lodhra, and the filaments (keśara) of the lotus.
6.19.110 | Jambū-bark, ginger, coriander, pāṭhā, mocarasa, balā, samaṅgā, dhātakī, the pulp of bilva, and the barks of jambū and āmra.
6.19.111 | Kapittha, viḍaṅga, ginger,
and black pepper— these four, combined with sour cāṅgerī, kola, and buttermilk, [should be used] when phlegm is predominant.
6.19.112 | One should consume *khaḍa* soups prepared with fats and salts as prescribed in the half-verses;
or, having licked the pulp of *kapittha* mixed with *vyoṣa*, honey, and sugar.
6.19.113 | By consuming *kaṭphala* mixed with honey, one is freed from abdominal disease;
likewise, by drinking *pippalī* (long pepper) mixed with honey, or by drinking buttermilk (*takra*) combined with *citraka*.

6.19.114 | By eating young *bilva* fruits, one is freed from abdominal disease. One who suffers from colic and dysentery due to the obstruction of *vāta* should lick a paste of young *bilva*, jaggery, oil, long pepper (*pippalī*), and ginger (*viśvabheṣaja*).
6.19.115 | One should eat food with a decoction of radish and with Vata-alleviating adjuncts, along with soups,
meat broths, and *khada* preparations prescribed for Vata-type diarrhea.
6.19.116 | One should administer either the previously mentioned sour ghee (amlasarpiḥ), or the six-pala preparation according to the patient's strength,
or aged ghee mixed with gruel-scum (yavāgūmaṇḍa).
6.19.117 | In cases of obstruction caused by vāta and kapha, or when phlegm is excessively secreted,
or in the presence of colic or dysentery (pravāhikā), one should administer a slimy enema (picchābasti).
6.19.118 | One should prepare the previously mentioned [mixture] combined with the pastes of pippalī, bilva, kuṣṭha, śatāvarī, and vacā, along with salt.
6.19.119 | When he has returned home, bathed comfortably, and finished his meal at the end of the day,
the wise physician should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) with lukewarm bilva oil.

Alternatively, one who is afflicted by excessive phlegm and wind should have oil cooked with the pastes of *vacā* and other such ingredients and administer it as an unctuous enema (*anuvāsana*); in this way, he shall obtain relief.
6.19.121 | In its own location, the Vata wind necessarily increases when Kapha is diminished. Once it has increased, it may suddenly cause death; therefore, one should conquer it with haste.
6.19.122 | One should conquer the pitta following the vāta, and the kapha following the pitta;
or, among all three, one should first conquer whichever is the strongest.
6.19.123 | Regarding this, there is a verse: The premonitory signs, the causes of onset, the clinical characteristics, the incurability,
the various stages of the action [of treatment], and the established methods for those suffering from diarrhea have thus been specified.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diarrhea," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Twenty:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of vomiting.
6.20.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

6.20.3 | The disciple Agniveśa questioned the son of Atri, Punarvasu— who was illustrious, blazing with the splendor of sacred knowledge and asceticism, possessing a power equal to fire and the sun, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.

6.20.4 | O best among physicians! Please explain correctly, for the benefit of humanity, the treatment along with the etiology and symptoms of those five types of vomiting that were previously mentioned by you in the section on diseases.
6.20.5 | Having heard those words of Agniveśa, the best of physicians, being pleased, spoke this:
"Listen as I describe in detail those five types of vomiting that were previously mentioned by me."

6.20.6 | There are four [types of vomiting] arising from the humors (*doṣa*) individually or from all three combined; a fifth may also occur from contact with an undesirable object. Among these, nausea in the heart and excessive salivation are indeed the premonitory symptoms (*pūrvarūpa*) for the onset of aversion toward food.
6.20.7 | In one who has been excessively emaciated by physical exertion, sharp medicinal drugs, grief, disease, fear,
fasting, and so forth, the wind (vāyu), having increased in the great channel (mahāsrotas), agitates the humors (doṣas) and then drives them upward.
6.20.8 | Furthermore, by aggravating the āmāśaya and afflicting the vital points (marman),
it induces vomiting accompanied by pain in the heart and flanks, dryness of the mouth, distress in the head and navel, cough, hoarseness of voice, and piercing pains.

6.20.9 | Afflicted by wind (vāta), the patient here vomits with great difficulty, with intense retching sounds, accompanied by foam, broken into fragments, blackish, thin, and astringent; though the quantity is small, it is expelled with great force and causes suffering.
6.20.10 | When pitta in the stomach has its force aroused by undigested food, pungent, sour, burning, or cold substances,
it spreads through the nutrient-carrying channels (rasāyanīs), compresses [the channels], reaches the vital points (marmans) above, and causes vomiting.
6.20.11 | Afflicted by fainting, thirst, dryness of the mouth, burning sensations in the head, palate, and eyes, darkness, and giddiness,
one vomits what has been drunk— excessively hot, green, bitter, and smoky— due to *pitta*, accompanied by a burning sensation.
6.20.12 | When kapha is excessively increased by the consumption of unctuous, very heavy, cold, and non-burning foods, as well as by excessive sleep and other such factors,
it obstructs the chest, the head, the vital organs (marmans), and all the nutrient-carrying channels (rasāyanīs), thereby causing vomiting.
6.20.13 | Afflicted by lassitude, sweetness in the mouth, salivation, a sense of satiety, sleepiness, loss of appetite, and heaviness,
one who has been purified of kapha vomits that which is unctuous, thick, sweet, accompanied by horripilation, and with little pain.
6.20.14 | When one constantly consumes all types of tastes and is afflicted by the disorders of undigested food (āma) and the seasonal inversions,
all the humors (doṣas) simultaneously undergo provocation and produce vomiting characterized by the three humors (tridoṣa).

6.20.15 | In men who vomit due to the three doṣas— characterized by continuous colic, indigestion, anorexia, burning sensation, thirst, dyspnea, and profound delusion— the vomitus shall be salty, sour, blue, thick, hot, and blood-stained.
6.20.16 | When the wind, having obstructed the channels that carry feces, sweat, urine, and water, moves upward,
it agitates and draws out from the person's digestive tract (koṣṭha) that accumulated morbid humor (doṣa) which has increased in one whose humors are already aggravated.
6.20.17 | When the stool and urine have a similar color and odor, and the patient is afflicted by persistent thirst, dyspnea, and hiccups, he vomits the corrupted matter with excessive force;
thus tormented by that [vomiting], he quickly meets his destruction.
6.20.18 | That [feeling] which causes one to vomit when encountering objects that are hated, adverse, impure, putrid, unholy, loathsome, foul-smelling, or disagreeable to the sight—
and which agitates the mind through contact with such hateful things— is considered to arise from mental affliction.

6.20.19 | That vomiting which occurs in one who is emaciated, which is excessive, accompanied by complications, and mixed with blood and pus—along with the presence of the *candrikā* (halo)—they declare it incurable; however, one should treat that which is curable and free from complications.

6.20.20 | Since all types of vomiting are considered to arise from the agitation of the stomach (āmāśaya), one should first administer fasting (laṅghana), with the exception of that caused by Vāta; or else, one should perform purification (saṃśodhana) that removes Kapha and Pitta.
6.20.21 | One should lick powders of *abhayā* with honey, or whatever purgatives are pleasing to the heart;
when combined appropriately with wines or milks, they lead downward the morbid humors (*doṣa*) that have risen upward.
6.20.22 | One who is weak and has undergone emesis with preparations such as *vallī* fruits and the like should be treated with palliative measures:
namely, with pleasing meat broths, light foods, dried snacks, various types of edibles, and diverse drinks.
6.20.23 | Well-prepared juices of partridge, peacock, and quail dispel vomiting induced by vāta;
likewise, a soup made with jujube, horse gram, coriander, the roots of bilva and others, sour substances, and barley has the same effect.
6.20.24 | A man suffering from the distress of a fluid-filled heart due to a vāta constitution should drink ghee prepared with rock salt,
as well as with coriander and ginger, along with curd and pomegranate juice.
6.20.25 | Or one should administer a dose of ghee combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa) and the three salts;
likewise, one should provide unctuous and appetizing foods along with meat broths, vegetable soups, curd, and pomegranate-sour preparations.

6.20.26 | In the case of a pitta-dominant condition, trivṛt should be administered with the juices of grapes, vidārī, and sugarcane for the purpose of downward movement. However, if the pitta has increased excessively and is located in the seat of kapha (the stomach), one should eliminate it through the upper route using sweet substances.
6.20.27 | When she has become pure at the proper time, one should cause her to drink a stirred potion (mantha) or a gruel (peyā) made with honey and sugar along with parched grain (lāja);
or else, one should give her boiled śāli rice with the juice of mung beans or with the broths of wild animals.
6.20.28 | One should lick a mixture of sugar, honey, and long pepper, or else kulmāṣa, parched grain, barley flour, and gṛñjana; or the flesh of dates, coconut, grapes, or jujube fruits.
6.20.29 | One should lick with honey either the powders of *srotoñjana*, water-lily (*utpala*), and the marrow of *kola* fruit, along with *abhayā*;
or else the marrow of *kola* seeds, *añjana*, honey, salt, parched grain, sugar, *māgadhikā*, and long pepper (*kaṇā*).
6.20.30 Or one may drink very cold grape juice, or water produced from a clod of earth heated by fire;
or one may drink a very cold decoction made from the tender leaves of the rose-apple and the mango, mixed with honey.
6.20.31 | At night, one should drink water kept overnight in a black vessel, or water with *uśīra* and grains, or chickpea water,
or water with the roots of *gavedhukā*, or *guḍūcī* water, or sugarcane juice, or milk.
6.20.32 | One should drink gold-ore (*kāñcanagairika*) with *bālaka*, or *uttamacandana* with the juice of *dhātrī* and honey, along with rice-wash water; these destroy thirst and vomiting.
6.20.33 | Likewise, a paste of sandalwood, chavya, māṃsī, drākṣā, uttamā, bālaka, and gairika;
or gairika and śāli rice powder with cold water; or likewise mūrvā with rice-washing water.
6.20.34 | In vomiting caused by *kapha*, emesis is recommended using water decocted with long pepper (*pippalī*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), and neem (*nimba*),
combined with *piṇḍītaka* and rock salt (*saindhava*), for the purpose of purifying the seat of *kapha* and undigested matter (*āmāśaya*).
6.20.35 | One should eat old wheat and rice along with barley, using soups prepared from *paṭola*, *amṛta*, and *citraka*;
or soups prepared with *vyoṣa* and *nimba* using buttermilk; likewise, one may eat them with soups that are sour with fruit-acids or pungent.

6.20.36 | He provided juices, meat on spits, and the flesh of wild animals; aged honey-wines, *sīdhu*, and *ariṣṭa* liquors; as well as *rāga* condiments, *ṣāḍava* preparations, and drinks made with grapes, wood-apples, and *phalapūraka* fruits.
6.20.37 | One should lick roasted mung beans, masūra lentils, chickpeas, and peas, combined with ginger and honey;
likewise, one may lick the powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) and *viḍaṅga*, or alternatively, the powder of *viḍaṅga* and *plava*.
6.20.38 | One should lick either jujube fruit with sour jujube powder, or karkaṭaka-śṛṅgī combined with mustā,
or durālabhā mixed with honey, for the purpose of suppressing vomiting caused by phlegm.
6.20.39 | By licking a powder of realgar, citron juice, wood-apple,
and long pepper, combined with honey and black pepper, one may conquer vomiting even when its force is intense.

6.20.40 | This treatment which has been described by me for each [disease] separately should be applied even in cases of combined disorders (*sannipāta*) by synthesizing it through the intellect; one who knows the scriptures should administer it vigilantly, having carefully considered the humors (*doṣa*), season (*ṛtu*), disease (*roga*), digestive fire (*agni*), and strength (*bala*).
6.20.41 | When the mind is afflicted, however, words that are agreeable to the mind—consolations and inspirations;
well-known worldly verses; female companions; and amorous pastimes—are beneficial.
6.20.42 | There were various fragrances pleasing to the mind, such as those from clay, flowers, conch-shells, sour fruits, and the like;
as well as vegetables, foods, drinks, and well-prepared preparations of the six flavors, including savory soups, syrups, and linctuses.
6.20.43 | Soups, meat broths, *kāmbalika* preparations, *khada* dishes, meats, various parched grains, and edible foods,
as well as fruits and roots endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste, conquer vomiting.

6.20.44 | Whatever scent, taste, touch, sound, or form may be pleasing even if it is unwholesome, one should provide that very thing for the sake of her pacification; for a disease born from such [desire] is easily conquered.
6.20.45 | For those who have recovered from vomiting, treatment for the complications should be carried out according to their own specific therapeutic principles;
however, when there is excessive discharge due to over-action of purgation, the measures prescribed for the excessive administration of emetics should be employed.

6.20.46 | Due to the persistence of vomiting, the wind (vāyu) also inevitably increases because of the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu); therefore, when vomiting has been ongoing for a long time, treatments that suppress wind and provide stabilization and nourishment should be administered.
6.20.47 | Medicated jaggery with ghee, milk preparations, the Kalyāṇaka, Tryūṣaṇa, and Jīvana ghees,
as well as aphrodisiac meat broths and electuaries, conquer vomiting that has persisted for a long time.

6.20.48 | Regarding this, there is a verse: The best of sages has declared the etiology, number, symptoms, complications, curability or incurability, and the formulations for the treatment of vomitings, for the purpose of their pacification.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, named "The Treatment of Vomiting," in the Section on Therapeutics (Cikitsā-sthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—where it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Twenty-one:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of erysipelas (visarpa).
6.21.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.21.3 On Mount Kailāsa, which is crowded with kiṃnaras and abounds in springs and medicinal herbs,
there are various lush trees that are always rich in an abundance of flowers.
6.21.4 | [He saw] Ātreya, who was praised by the sages, self-conquered, and wandering about in all directions emitting sweet fragrances, well-adorned with ornaments.
6.21.5 | At the proper time, Agniveśa, with humility, addressed these words to his teacher, who was surrounded by great sages and devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
6.21.6 | "O Blessed One! I perceive a terrible disease, like the venom of a poisonous serpent, spreading through the bodies of embodied beings."
6.21.7 | Suddenly enveloped by that swift-acting one, men perish without even being approached;
regarding this, we have a great doubt.

6.21.8 | By what name is he to be known, and for what reason is he designated? How many divisions does he have, how many elements (dhātus), what is his primary cause (nidāna), and what is his support (āśraya)?
6.21.9 | O Blessed One, how is it known that [a disease] is easily curable, difficult to cure, or incurable? By what characteristics is this known, and what is its remedy?
6.21.10 | Having heard those words of Agniveśa, Punarvasu Ātreya,
the best of sages, explained everything in its entirety and exactly as it is.
6.21.11 | It is known as *visarpa* because it spreads (*sarpati*) in various ways;
or it is called by the name *parisarpa* because it creeps all around (*parisarpaṇāt*).

6.21.12 | That [visarpa] is to be known as sevenfold according to the doshas and consisting of seven dhatus: three are caused by each dosha individually, one is caused by all three together, and three are born from combinations of two doshas.

6.21.13 | There are four types of visarpa: those born of vāta, those born of pitta, those born of kapha, and those born of the combination of all three (sānnipātika). Three others arising from combinations of two humors (dvandvaja) will also be described.
6.21.14 | That which is fiery (āgneya) arises from vāta and pitta; that called a cyst (granthi) is born from kapha and vāta;
while that terrible condition known as kardamaka originates from pitta and kapha.

6.21.15 | Blood, lymph, skin, and flesh are the corrupted tissues (dūṣya); the three doṣas are the impurities (mala). These seven constituents should be known as the sources for the arising of visarpa (erysipelas).
6.21.16 | From the excessive consumption of salty, sour, pungent, and hot tastes,
as well as curd, sour whey, fermented gruel, wine, and sauvīraka;
6.21.17 | From the consumption of excessive wine, hot substances, and *rāga-ṣāḍava* preparations; and from the consumption of green vegetables and other heating (*vidāhin*) foods.
6.21.18 | From the consumption of *kūrcikā*, *kilāṭa*, and *mandaka*; and from the consumption of various types of curd such as *śāṇḍākī* and fermented liquors;
6.21.19 | Of sesame, mung beans, and horse gram; of oils;
of flour-based products; of the meat of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals; and of garlic.
6.21.20 | From the consumption of excessively moist, unwholesome, and incompatible foods;
from overeating, sleeping during the day, eating before the previous meal is digested, and from injury.
6.21.21 | Visarpas arise from the binding of wounds, from falling, from the excessive performance of religious rites,
and from the defects of poison, wind, and fire.
6.21.22 | By these various combined causes, the provoked vāta and other doshas,
having vitiated the corruptible elements such as blood and the rest, spread through those who consume unwholesome food.
6.21.23 | Visarpa (erysipelas) is external, internal, and likewise both;
the strength of these should be known to increase in severity progressively.

6.21.24 | One should know that visarpa (erysipelas) is severe when it relies on both the external and internal pathways, and it is particularly difficult to treat when it is based in the internal [pathway].
6.21.25 | The doshas, when provoked internally, spread within their internal seat;
when provoked externally, they spread externally; and when provoked in both, they spread everywhere.
6.21.26 | From injury to the vital points (marmans), from the obstruction of the channels, from excessive suppression [of natural urges],
and from the improper discharge of the bodily impulses;
6.21.27 | One should recognize the internal type of visarpa (erysipelas) as arising quickly from the depletion of digestive fire and strength;
one should recognize the external type from the opposite conditions and by its own specific characteristics.
6.21.28 | That fever which possesses all the symptoms, whose cause is powerful,
which has severe complications, and which reaches the vital organs (marmans), kills the patient.
6.21.29 | Vāyu, either alone due to dry and hot factors or enveloped by filling [substances], becomes vitiated and,
while corrupting the tissues (dūṣya), spreads according to its strength.

6.21.30 | Its symptoms are: giddiness, distress, thirst, piercing pain, colic, body ache, twisting, tremors, fever, fainting, cough, breaking and loosening of the bones and joints, shivering, anorexia, indigestion, turbidity of the eyes, lacrimation, and a sensation in the limbs as if ants were crawling over them; furthermore, the area where the visarpa spreads appears dark-red in hue, is swollen, and is excessively afflicted by piercing, breaking, colic, stretching, contraction, horripilation, and throbbing.

If it is not treated, it increases with small, rapidly bursting pustules that are reddish or dark-brown, thin, clear, and slightly bloody; the patient's flatus, urine, and feces become obstructed; and the factors mentioned as causes do not alleviate his condition, while their opposites do—this is Vāta-visarpa (erysipelas caused by Vāta).
6.21.31 | Pitta, accumulated through hot regimens and the consumption of burning and sour foods,
spreads by vitiating the tissues and filling the vessels.

6.21.32 | Its symptoms are: fever, thirst, fainting, delusion, vomiting, anorexia, breaking pain in the limbs, excessive perspiration, internal burning sensation, delirium, headache, distress of the eyes, insomnia, restlessness, vertigo, an excessive craving for cold water and wind, and excessively green or yellowish-brown eyes, urine, and feces; as well as the perception of green or yellowish-brown forms, and the area where the visarpa spreads appears coppery, green, yellowish-brown, blue, black, or red.

It nourishes one of the [skin] colors, and it is covered with elevated, excessively burning and bursting pustules that exude fluid of a matching color and take a long time to suppurate; furthermore, the factors mentioned as causes do not alleviate it, while their opposites do—this is Pitta-visarpa.
6.21.33 | Accumulated by the consumption of sweet, sour, salty, unctuous, and heavy foods, as well as by excessive sleep,
the *kapha* vitiation corrupts the bodily tissues (*dūṣya*) and spreads through the limbs with difficulty.

6.21.34 | Its symptoms are: coldness, cold fever, heaviness, drowsiness, languor, anorexia, sweetness of the mouth, coating of the mouth, spitting, vomiting, lassitude, a sense of being wrapped in wet cloth (staimitya), loss of digestive fire, and debility. Furthermore, the area where the visarpa spreads becomes swollen, pale rather than very red, accompanied by oiliness, numbness, stiffness, and heaviness; it is characterized by slight pain, slow suppuration, delayed healing, and eruptions (sphoṭas) with thick coatings of skin.

It is characterized by being bound by white-pale discharges; when it has burst open, it exudes a continuous, unctuous, slimy, fibrous, and thick secretion. Furthermore, it is followed by ulcers that are heavy, firm, webbed, unctuous, and covered with thick skin-like crusts, becoming chronic. There is whiteness of the nails, eyes, face, skin, urine, and feces. The factors mentioned as causes do not alleviate it, whereas their opposites do; this is Kapha-visarpa (Kapha-type erysipelas).
6.21.35 | Vāta and pitta, excessively aggravated by their respective causes and having gained strength from one another, spread through the body while burning it.

6.21.36 | Due to that affliction, the patient feels as if his entire body is being strewn with glowing embers; he is overcome by vomiting, diarrhea, fainting, burning sensations, delusion, fever, respiratory distress, anorexia, breaking pain in the bones and joints, thirst, indigestion, and aching of the limbs. Whichever part of the body the visarpa (erysipelas) creeps into, that region becomes as bright as extinguished embers or excessively red, and it is covered with eruptions resembling those caused by fire. Because of its rapid movement, it quickly follows the course of the vital points (marmans).

When the vital points (marmans) are afflicted, the exceedingly powerful wind (vāyu) excessively tears apart the limbs, causes extreme delusion of consciousness, produces hiccups and dyspnea, and destroys sleep. Deprived of sleep, with his consciousness clouded and his mind distressed, he finds no happiness anywhere. Overcome by restlessness, he desires to move from his standing place or seat to his bed; yet, being mostly afflicted, he quickly falls asleep, and though weak, he wakes up in pain.
One should recognize such a person as incurable when afflicted by Agnivisarpa.
6.21.37 | When kapha and pitta are strongly aggravated by their own respective causes,
they spread over a single region and cause excessive moistening of the embodied being.

6.21.38 | Its complications are: cold fever, heaviness of the head, burning sensation, stiffness, lassitude of the limbs, sleepiness, drowsiness, delusion, aversion to food, delirium, loss of digestive fire, weakness, splitting pain in the bones, fainting, thirst, coating of the channels, dullness of the sense organs, a tendency to sit down as if to die, tossing of the limbs, aching of the limbs, restlessness, and longing; furthermore, the *alasaka* (intestinal obstruction) generally spreads in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), and wherever this spreading disease (*visarpa*) spreads, in that very space—

The site [of the ulcer] appears as if strewn with red, yellow, and pale pustules, yet it is dark, blackish, dirty, moist, hot, heavy, and characterized by dull pain. It is swollen, undergoes deep suppuration, lacks discharge, becomes rapidly moistened, and its skin and flesh become perspired, macerated, and putrid. With little pain, when touched it feels as if being torn apart like pressed mud; it yields an opening, sheds putrid flesh that is excessively moist, reveals veins and sinews, has the odor of a corpse, and destroys consciousness and memory.
One should recognize this as Kardamavisarpa (mud-like erysipelas), which is incurable.

6.21.39 | In those who consume stable, heavy, hard, sweet, cold, and unctuous food and drinks that cause internal obstruction (abhiṣyandi), who avoid physical exercise and similar activities, and who are habituated to neglecting medical treatment, both Kapha and Vata undergo provocation. When these two become vitiated, increased, and exceedingly powerful, they corrupt the bodily tissues (dūṣyas) and lead to the manifestation of Visarpa (erysipelas).

In that condition, the Vāyu, its path obstructed by Kapha, breaks up that very Kapha in various ways and gradually produces a chain of glandular swellings (granthi-mālā) in the seat of Kapha, which are difficult to ripen and hard to cure; or, in one whose blood is increased, it vitiates the blood and produces a chain of glands—whether large or small, long, round, or red—located in the vessels, ligaments, flesh, and skin, accompanied by intense pain.

From the affliction of that [granthi], complications such as fever, diarrhea, cough, hiccup, dyspnea, emaciation, delusion, discoloration, anorexia, indigestion, salivation, vomiting, fainting, breaking pain in the limbs, excessive sleep, restlessness, and lassitude manifest; afflicted by these, he has fallen beyond the scope of all medical treatments and must be abandoned—this is granthivisarpa.

6.21.40 | An *upadrava* (complication), however, is indeed a disease that arises subsequent to the primary disease, is based upon the same site as the disease, and is itself a disease—whether gross or subtle. It is designated as an *upadrava* because it arises after the primary disease. Among these, the primary disease is the principal [condition], while the complication is subordinate to the disease; generally, its subsidence occurs upon the subsidence of the primary disease. Yet, arising later, it becomes more painful because the body is already afflicted by the primary disease; therefore, one should treat the complication with urgency.

6.21.41 | One should know that *sannipāta-visarpa* (the spreading disease arising from the simultaneous derangement of all three humors), which originates in all sense-bases, pervades all symptoms, follows all bodily constituents (*dhātus*), acts with rapidity, and is of great consequence, to be incurable.

6.21.42 | Among these, the three types of visarpa caused by vāta, pitta, and śleṣman are curable. Furthermore, the two known as agni and kardama may attain pacification through the application of standard treatments, provided they do not affect a vital organ (marman) or reach the wasting of vessels, ligaments, and flesh. However, if either of these two is neglected in its treatment, it will quickly destroy the body like a venomous serpent.

Likewise, one should begin the treatment of Granthi-visarpa (creeper-like glandular swelling) provided it is not yet afflicted by complications; however, if it is already overwhelmed by complications, one should avoid it. But that which is born from the derangement of all three humors (Sannipāta) should be known as incurable, because it pervades all the bodily tissues, because it acts with great rapidity, and because its therapeutic measures are mutually contradictory.
6.21.43 | Therein, we shall further explain the means for accomplishing the goals to be achieved.
6.21.44 | Lightening therapy and scraping are recommended, as is the consumption of bitter substances, when the āma is located in the seat of kapha; one should apply ointments that are dry and cold.
6.21.45 | Even when [the disease] has reached the seat of bile (pitta), one should administer this same treatment for the undigested state (āmam),
as well as bloodletting and especially purgation.
6.21.46 | Even when arising from a predominance of vāta, emaciation (virūkṣaṇa) should be applied at the outset;
likewise, even when associated with rakta-pitta, oleation (snehana) is considered not beneficial at the beginning.
6.21.47 | Bitter ghee is recommended for [fevers] dominated by vāta and those caused by pitta;
when the doṣas are mild, it is used, but in cases of pitta with great morbidity, purgation should be administered.
6.21.48 | Ghee should not be administered to one with many morbid humors (*doṣa*) if it does not induce purgation;
for by that [unpurged ghee], the obstructed humor may cook the skin, flesh, and blood.

6.21.49 | Therefore, one should know that for a patient with visarpa, purgation alone is recommended at the outset, as well as bloodletting; for that [blood] is designated as the substratum of this disease.
6.21.50 | Thus has been stated, in brief, the treatment for the cure of visarpa;
this same entire subject shall now be explained again in detail.
6.21.51 | Madana, madhuka, nimba, and the fruits of vatsaka should be administered as an emetic in cases of visarpa caused by kapha and pitta.
6.21.52 | Emesis is recommended for erysipelas using patola, picumarda, pippali, and madana, as well as with indrayava.

6.21.53 | Furthermore, those formulations which I shall describe in the Kalpas for those afflicted by kapha and pitta, as well as for those with erysipelas (visarpa), should be employed; they are auspicious and serve to eliminate the morbid humors.
6.21.54 | A wise physician [should prepare a decoction] from musta, nimba, and paṭola, or likewise from candana and utpala, or from sārivā, āmalaka, uśīra, and musta.
6.21.55 | The physician should administer proven decoctions that destroy visarpa (erysipelas):
kirātatiktaka, lodhra, candana, along with durālabhā.
6.21.56 | One should administer ginger, lotus filaments, blue water-lily, along with bibhītaka, licorice, and nāgapuṣpa for the pacification of visarpa (erysipelas).
6.21.57 | One should drink prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, lotus filaments, utpala, nāgapuṣpa, and lodhra according to that same procedure.
6.21.58 | One should administer grapes, parpaṭaka, ginger, guḍūcī, and dhanvayāsaka,
having been soaked overnight in water, for the alleviation of thirst and erysipelas (vīsarpa).
6.21.59 | One should administer paṭola, picumarda, dārvī, kaṭukarohiṇī,
yaṣṭyāhvā, and trāyamāṇā for the pacification of visarpa (erysipelas).
6.21.60 | Or one should drink a decoction of the *paṭola* group along with *triphalā*;
or one should administer it mixed with ghee and combined with split *masūra* lentils.
6.21.61 | One suffering from visarpa (erysipelas) should be made to drink the juice of paṭola leaves, mung beans, and āmalaka, mixed with ghee.
6.21.62 | Furthermore, that Mahātikta ghee which has been prescribed for the eradication of pitta-type skin diseases (kuṣṭha),
a wise person should also administer it for the pacification of visarpa.
6.21.63 | A wise physician should also administer the *trāyamāṇā-ghṛta* prepared for the treatment of gulma, for the purpose of pacifying erysipelas (*visarpa*).
6.21.64 | Having thoroughly stirred the powder of trivṛt with clarified butter or even with milk,
or having combined it with warm water or with the juice of grapes.
6.21.65 | For the purpose of purgation, one should administer milk prepared with *trāyamāṇā*, which is proven to destroy erysipelas (*vīsarpa*).
Alternatively, one may give milk boiled with *trāyamāṇā* as a purgative.
Clarified butter combined with the juice of triphalā and trivṛt should be administered for the purpose of purgation; it destroys visarpa and fever.
6.21.67 | Or one should administer the juice of āmalaka fruits mixed with ghee;
that same preparation, combined with the powder of trivṛt, is beneficial for one with a heavy digestive tract.
6.21.68 | When the humors have extensively entered the digestive tract (koṣṭha), one should perform this treatment;
however, when the blood is vitiated by the humors, one should first remove the blood itself.
6.21.69 | The physician should extract blood associated with vāta using a horn;
that associated with pitta using leeches; and that associated with kapha using a gourd.
6.21.70 | One should quickly lance the vein nearest to the lesion;
for the putrefaction of skin, flesh, and sinews arises from the putrefaction of the blood.

6.21.71 | When the internal body has been thoroughly purified, but the morbid humor (doṣa) remains localized in the skin and flesh, or when the humors are initially only slight, external treatments will now be described.
6.21.72 | A medicinal paste consisting of udumbara bark, madhuka, lotus filaments,
blue lotus, nāgapuṣpa, and priyaṅgu, combined with ghee, is beneficial.
6.21.73 | Young *nyagrodha* roots combined with the inner core of a plantain tree and lotus-node fibers constitute a paste that should be soaked in clarified butter washed a hundred times.
6.21.74 | Kālīya, madhuka, hema, vanya, candana, padmaka,
elā, mṛṇāla, and phalinī— this should be used as a plaster saturated with ghee.
6.21.75 | A poultice consisting of young grass, lotus stalks, conch-shell, sandalwood, blue lotus,
and the roots of the cane tree, mixed with rice, should be applied.
6.21.76 | Sārivā, lotus stamens, uśīra, blue lotus, mañjiṣṭhā, sandalwood, lodhra, and abhayā constitute a medicinal paste.
6.21.77 | Nalada, hareṇu, lodhra, madhuka,
padmaka, dūrvā, and sarjarasa, combined with ghee, should be used as a medicinal paste.
6.21.78 | Barley meal and roasted grain flour mixed with clarified butter;
a poultice of madhuka and vīrā with ghee, or barley flour with ghee.
6.21.79 | The physician should prepare an ointment consisting of balā, utpala, śālūka, vīrā, aguru, candana, mṛṇāla, and bisā.
6.21.80 | A plaster consisting of barley flour, madhuka, and ghee;
as well as hareṇu beans, lentils, mung beans, and white śāli rice [are recommended].
6.21.81 | Each of these should be used as a separate paste, or all of them together with clarified butter;
or else, cool mud from a lotus pond, or pearl powder ground down.
6.21.82 | Conch shell, coral, pearl-oyster shell, or red ochre soaked in clarified butter—
these external applications are known to be beneficial for those suffering from visarpa (erysipelas).
Prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, balā, śālūka, and utpala [should also be used].
6.21.83 | A plaster consisting of *nyagrodha* leaves and *dugdhikā* with ghee should be applied;
likewise, lotus stalks (*bisāni*), lotus fibers (*mṛṇāla*), and *kaśeruka* tubers with ghee.
