6.21.84 | The tubers of śatāvarī and vidārī, soaked in washed ghee;
śaivāla, roots of nala, gojihvā, and vṛṣakarṇikā.
6.21.85 | Indrāṇī-vegetable with ghee; śirīṣa-bark, balā, and ghee;
and the tender shoots of nyagrodha, udumbara, plakṣa, vetasa, and aśvattha.
6.21.86 | An application of cool pastes made from the barks [of the aforementioned trees] mixed with abundant ghee is beneficial.
All these external applications (*pradeha*) are auspicious when vāta and pitta are predominant.
6.21.87 | Now I shall describe other beneficial plasters (pradeha) for [ulcers] with phlegm (kapha):
triphalā, padmaka, uśīra, samaṅgā, and karavīraka.
6.21.88 | One should prepare a topical paste (pradeha) consisting of Nala roots, Ananta, Khadira, Saptaparṇa, Musta, Āragvadha, and Dhava.
6.21.89 | The physician should apply as an ointment kuraṇṭaka, devadāru,
the leaves of āragvadha, and the bark of śleṣmātaka.
6.21.90 | Indrāṇī-śāka, kākāhvā, śirīṣa flowers,
śauvāla, roots of nala, vīrā, and fragrant priyaṅgu.
6.21.91 | Triphalā, madhuka, vīrā, flowers of śirīṣa,
prapauṇḍarīka, hrībera, the bark of dārvī, madhuka, and balā.
6.21.92 | One should apply these as separate ointments, in pairs, or even all together;
all these poultices (pradehas) should be applied moistened with a small amount of ghee.
6.21.93 | However, those poultices (pradeha) intended for conditions where vāta and pitta are predominant should contain an abundance of ghee;
one should apply them with ghee that has been washed a hundred times, or with pure ghee alone.
6.21.94 | One should sprinkle [the wound] with cold clarified butter-scum, milk, liquorice-water,
or a cold decoction of the five barks.
6.21.95 | For a visarpa characterized by an abundance of vāta, rakta, and pitta, the physician should repeatedly employ those same sprinklings and plasters that are prepared with ghee.
6.21.96 | These powder formulations are for dusting over erysipelas ulcers;
furthermore, ghee prepared with the fresh juice of dūrvā grass serves as a healer of ulcers.
6.21.97 | Dārvī, tvak, madhuka, lodhra, and keśara as a powder; likewise paṭola, picumarda, triphalā, madhuka, and utpala.
6.21.98 | This is the washing with ghee, the powder for the wound, and the ointment;
all these applications must be made as soothing remedies.

6.21.99 | The previously extracted ointment should be applied every moment; however, when the previous application has not been washed off or removed, thick plasters (pradehas) should be applied frequently.
6.21.100 | In cases arising from Kapha, thick plasters (pradehas) should be applied after removing the bandage;
the medicinal paste, ground into a pulp, should be three parts [of the thickness] and the size of a thumb for application as a coating (pralepa).
6.21.101 One should never apply a plaster that is too oily or too dry, nor one that is too solid or too liquid, nor one that is uneven, nor one that has been kept overnight.
6.21.102 | Nor should one ever reapply that same paste;
for due to the absence of heat, it would cause moisture, spreading inflammation, and pain.
6.21.103 | For a plaster applied over a bandage causes the wound to sweat;
pustules born of perspiration and itching arise for that person.
6.21.104 | If a plaster is applied on top of an existing plaster,
it will produce the very same defects as those caused by applying one over a bandage.
6.21.105 | If a paste that is too oily or too liquid is applied,
it does not adhere properly to the skin and likewise fails to pacify the doshas.
6.21.106 | One should not apply it to the body while it is still moist, for once dried, it causes cracking;
furthermore, the medicinal essence does not reach the disease and instead dries up.
6.21.107 | Those very same defects that arise from an insufficiently smeared [unctuous substance] will be produced even more intensely by one that is dried up;
for when applied without oiliness, it causes affliction and disease.

6.21.108 | I shall now describe foods and drinks for the prevention of visarpa (erysipelas). For those who have undergone fasting, a dry *mantha* (barley gruel) mixed with honey and sugar is beneficial.
6.21.109 | Sweet or slightly sour, combined with pomegranate and āmalaka,
along with parūṣaka, grapes, and dates, [this preparation is made] with boiled water.
6.21.110 | With satiating drinks made from barley and *śāli* rice, and with unctuous electuaries (*avalehikā*),
one should eat a meal of aged *śāli* rice with soups once the previous meal has been digested.
6.21.111 | One should prepare soups (yūṣa) using mung beans, lentils, and hemp seeds;
they should be either unsour or soured with pomegranate, along with patola and emblic myrobalan.
6.21.112 | One should prepare for him the juices of the meat of wild animals,
combined with parched grains and *parūṣaka*, *drākṣā*, *dāḍima*, and *āmalaka*.
6.21.113 | Red, white, and large-awned *śāli* rice, along with *ṣaṣṭika* rice— these,
when old and well-strained, are recommended for the purpose of food.
6.21.114 | One should provide barley, wheat, and rice only according to what is suitable;
for those to whom rice is not very accustomed, and for those who have a predominance of phlegm (kapha).

6.21.115 | One should avoid foods and drinks that cause burning sensations, incompatible combinations, sleeping during the day, as well as anger, physical exercise, exposure to the sun, fire, and strong winds.
6.21.116 | From this treatment, one should administer therapies predominantly cooling for the Pitta-type,
predominantly drying for the Kapha-type, and oleaginous for the Vata-type.
6.21.117 | It is beneficial for pacifying vāta and pitta in cases of agnivisarpa (fire-like erysipelas),
while it generally pacifies kapha and pitta in that known as kardama-visarpa.
6.21.118 | Having observed that the glandular erysipelas (granthivīsarpa) is dominated by raktapitta, one should treat it from the outset with drying therapies,
fasting, affusions, and plasters made from the five barks (pañcavalkala).
6.21.119 | One who knows the proper time should treat [the patient] with bloodletting by means of leeches, emetics, and purgatives, as well as with ghees that are astringent and bitter.

6.21.120 | For one who has been purified by upward and downward evacuations and whose blood has been drained, treatments that alleviate Vāta and Kapha are beneficial for those suffering from Granthi and Visarpa.
6.21.121 | For those suffering from glandular swellings (granthi), erysipelas (vīsarpa), or pain, a poultice (upanāha) made of warm *utkārikās* or of unctuous *vaiśeṣika* meat-mince is recommended.
6.21.122 | One should sprinkle [the area] with warm oil prepared with the ten roots (daśamūla),
and also with warm Kuṣṭha oil combined with alkali from burnt bark (pākyakṣāra).
6.21.123 | One should sprinkle [the area] with cow urine, decoctions of leaves, or warm water;
or one should apply a lukewarm paste of ground *aśvagandhā*.
6.21.124 One should apply a warm paste made from dried radish, or from the bark of *naktamāla*, or even from the bark of *bibhītaka*.
6.21.125 | One should prepare a paste for application on a knot using balā, nāgabalā, pathyā, bhūrjagranthi, bibhītaka, bamboo leaves, and agnimantha.
6.21.126 | A plaster composed of the root-bark of *dantī* and *citraka*, the milky sap of *sudhā* and *arka*, jaggery,
the seeds of *bhallātaka*, and *kāsīsa* would split even a rock.
6.21.127 Furthermore, one should break open with these medicinal remedies a cyst located on the external path, especially one arising from phlegm (kapha) that has persisted for a long time.
6.21.128 With soups of radishes and horse gram (kulattha) seasoned with alkali and pomegranate;
or with meals of wheat or barley accompanied by sidhu liquor, honey, and sugar.
6.21.129 | Or with the scum of *vāruṇī* wine mixed with honey and the juice of *mātuluṅga*,
and by the use of *triphalā* combined with long pepper (*pippalī*) and honey.
6.21.130 | By the use of musta, bhallātaka, and parched grain flour, as well as honey,
and by the use of devadāru, guḍūcī, and girija;
6.21.131 | By means of fumigations, head-purgatives, and the previously mentioned methods for breaking up abdominal tumors (gulma),
as well as by the compression of iron, salt, stones, gold, and copper;
6.21.132 | When a knot that is firm and as hard as stone does not subside at all despite these various successful treatments, it is called *balī*.

6.21.133 | Then, cauterization with alkali, or with arrows, or with gold is beneficial for it; or, having caused it to suppurate with drugs that promote suppuration, one should incise it and extract [the foreign body].
6.21.134 | One should repeatedly drain the blood that has become aggravated;
once the blood has been removed, one should administer medicine that conquers vāta and śleṣman.
6.21.135 | Fumigation, purgation of the head, sudation, and massage,
as well as digestive treatment (pācana), are recommended when the morbid humor (doṣa) does not subside.
6.21.136 | When it is moistened by burning and suppuration, the physician should treat it like an ulcer, using both external and internal purifying and healing measures.
6.21.137 | Having ground kampillaka, viḍaṅga, dārvī, and the fruit of kārañjaka, oil should be cooked; this is the treatment for glandular ulcers (granthivraṇa).

6.21.138 | A wise physician, knowing the distinctions of place and time, should also treat erysipelas-born ulcers according to the procedures taught in the chapter on the treatment of two types of ulcers (dvivraṇīya).

Thus ends the treatment of glandular swellings (granthi-visarpa). 6.21.139. The very same procedure prescribed for the eradication of glandular swellings is also for the eradication of goiters (galagaṇḍa) born of phlegm (kapha).
6.21.140 | Those goiters (galagaṇḍa) arising from Vāta that are accompanied by Kapha in men do not recur through the regular practice of ghee, milk, and decoctions.
6.21.141 | All those treatments that have been described here for the cessation of visarpa are on one side, while bloodletting alone is on the other.
6.21.142 | Indeed, erysipelas does not arise without being associated with blood and bile;
therefore, this entire treatment has been described as common to both.
6.21.143 | A specific distinction [of treatment] due to the imbalance of the humors has not been stated in brief;
therefore, a wise physician should administer the treatment as specified both in summary and in detail.

6.21.144 | Regarding this, there are these verses: The etymological derivation, the different names, the morbid humors (doṣas), the affected tissues (dūṣyas), the causes, the locations, the pathways, and the relative severity or mildness of the spreading diseases (visarpa).
6.21.145 | The signs and the complications, the characteristics of each complication, curability and incurability, and the treatment for those conditions that are curable— all this in due order.
6.21.146 | Thus, to the wise Agniveśa who desired to attain perfection,
Punarvasu spoke this treatment for visarpas (erysipelas).
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Visarpa," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Twenty-two:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of thirst (tṛṣṇā).
6.22.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.22.3 | Renowned for his wisdom, tranquility, and asceticism, the son of Atri, who is devoted to the welfare of the world,
has proclaimed a medical treatment for the five [humors] in order to pacify cravings.
6.22.4 | From agitation, fear, exhaustion, grief, anger, leaping over obstacles, intoxication,
and from the consumption of alkaline, sour, salty, pungent, hot, dry, and parched foods;
6.22.5 | By the excessive administration of depletive therapies, emetics, and the like, and by the heat of the sun,
pitta and vāyu become aggravated and dry up the somatic tissues (dhātus).
6.22.6 | Having dried up the rasa-carrying channels that extend from the root of the tongue to the throat and the palate, as well as the kloman,
these two extremely powerful [factors] produce thirst in the bodies of men.
For those emaciated by terrible diseases, even as they drink water again and again, it does not bring relief; rather, that very water becomes a source of further affliction.

6.22.8 | Dryness of the mouth is the premonitory symptom; the specific characteristic is a constant desire for water. Lightness and the disappearance [of other symptoms] are the signs of all types of thirst.
6.22.9 | Dryness of the mouth, hoarseness of voice, vertigo, feverish heat, delirium, rigidity,
roughness of the palate, lips, throat, and tongue, and loss of consciousness.

6.22.10 | Thirst, when it has arisen, produces protrusion of the tongue, loss of appetite, deafness, piercing pain in the vital organs, and exhaustion; hear now its fivefold manifestation according to its symptoms.
6.22.11 | When the aggravated wind dries up the water element residing in the body, the weak person becomes parched as that element dries; then, becoming utterly desiccated, he suffers from thirst.
6.22.12 | Loss of sleep, dizziness of the head, as well as a dry and tasteless mouth, and obstruction of the channels—these are the symptoms of thirst caused by Vāta.
6.22.13 | Pitta is considered to be of fiery nature; when it becomes aggravated, it heats the water-element (ap-dhātu).
Being thus heated, it indeed produces in men a thirst characterized by intense burning.
6.22.14 | A bitter taste in the mouth, burning of the head, a longing for cold things, fainting,
and yellowish eyes, urine, and feces are the clinical features of thirst caused by pitta.

6.22.15 | That thirst which originates from undigested matter (āmaja) is also of the fiery (āgneya) type, because it is produced by āma-pitta. Its symptoms are loss of appetite, flatulence, and excessive salivation due to phlegm (kapha).

6.22.16 | The body is born from the essence (rasa), and that essence is born from water; therefore, upon its depletion, one indeed becomes thirsty, with a feeble voice, fainting, and with the heart, throat, and palate completely parched.

6.22.17 | Indeed, that thirst which arises from the bodily humors (doṣas) is emaciating and painful for those whose bodies are afflicted by fever, urinary disorders, wasting, consumption, dyspnea, and other such ailments.
6.22.18 | All these [signs], when excessively present in those emaciated by disease and afflicted by persistent vomiting,
accompanied by terrible complications, should be known as leading to death.
6.22.19 | For there is no thirst without fire or wind; these two are indeed the causes of drying.
When the water element is excessively increased, yet the water [itself] is diminished, a person indeed suffers from thirst.
6.22.20 | When heavy food, water, and fats, having become fully digested, undergo the stage of burning (vidāha), one who then feels thirsty has his channels obstructed;
in that case as well, Vāyu and Agni are the causes.
6.22.21 | Due to its sharp, hot, and dry qualities, liquor provokes pitta and vāyu;
indeed, these two [doshas] dry up the watery element of those who habitually consume liquor.
6.22.22 | For water poured onto heated sand dries up quickly;
yet for those who are thus tormented, relief comes from drinking cold water.
6.22.23 | The heat of one who has bathed in cold water, being obstructed, enters the digestive tract and causes thirst.
Therefore, one exhausted by the heat should not suddenly resort to cold water.

6.22.24 | Now, the symptoms in all these [types] arise from the depletion of wind (vāyu) and the provocation of bile (pitta). Therefore, I shall explain the treatment for thirsts according to their individual origins.
6.22.25 | For thirst, arising from the depletion of the watery element, may quickly destroy a man by drying him up;
therefore, one should drink Indra’s water (rainwater) mixed with honey, or another liquid possessing similar qualities.
6.22.26 | That which possesses a slightly superior aftertaste, is thin, light, cooling, fragrant, and delicious,
and is non-obstructive to the channels— even if it is of terrestrial origin— should be known as belonging to Indra (the celestial category).

6.22.27 | Or, one may take the decoction boiled and then cooled, mixed with sugar candy and the five roots beginning with śara; or, one may take a churned drink (mantha) made from parched grain flour, barley meal, sugar, and honey, combined with the juice of the aindra plant.
6.22.28 | One should give cold *vāṭya* mixed with honey and sugar to those suffering from fever;
or one should give *peyā* (gruel) made from *śāli* rice, or from *koradūṣa* grain.
6.22.29 | Or, a meal may be prepared with boiled milk mixed with honey and sugar;
or it may be served with the juices of pigeons and other such birds, fried in ghee and seasoned without salt or sourness.
6.22.30 | Jāṅgala meats are well prepared with *tṛṇapañcamūla*, *muñjātaka*, and *priyāla*. Soups made from these, or milk processed with them, are excellent when enriched with sugar and honey.
6.22.31 | Anointed with ghee purified a hundred times, one should drink milk after immersing oneself in cold water;
furthermore, soups made from mung beans, lentils, and chickpeas should be served fried in ghee.
6.22.32 | Milk boiled with sweet, life-promoting (jīvanīya), cooling, and slightly bitter herbs,
combined with honey and sugar, is recommended for drinking, massage, and affusion.

6.22.33 | Or ghee produced from that [milk] is recommended for drinking and massage, and may also be used as nasal drops (nasya). Women's milk with sugar, or camel's milk, or sugarcane juice may likewise be used as nasal drops.
6.22.34 | Gargles made with milk, sugarcane juice, molasses water, sugar candy, honey, rum,
grape wine, vṛkṣāmla, and mātuluṅga destroy dryness of the palate.
6.22.35 | Plasters made from *jambu*, *āmrātaka*, *badarī*, *vetasa*, the five barks (*pañcavalka*), and the five acids (*pañcāmla*),
combined with ghee, applied to the heart, face, and head, alleviate fainting, vertigo, and thirst.
6.22.36 | An application to the head made of pomegranate, wood-apple, lodhra, vidārī,
bījapūraka, and white āmalaka, combined with ghee and sour gruel (āranāla), is beneficial.
6.22.37 | An ointment made of *śaivāla*, mud, lotuses, sour substances, ghee, and parched grain flour; and contact with whey, fermented rice water, wet garments, lotuses, and pearl necklaces.

6.22.38 | The touch of the palms of beloved women—whose breasts are moist with cool water and sandalwood paste, whose bodies are likewise moist, and who wear garments of wet linen—and the touch of their own limbs.
6.22.39 | The remembrance and the stories of the Himalayan caves, forests, rivers, lakes, lotuses, breezes, and the moonbeams— cool with delightful, frigid water— are destroyers of thirst.
6.22.40 | In thirst caused by vāta, food and drink that subdue vāta—being mild, light, and cold—are indicated;
likewise, milk and ghee prepared with drugs that alleviate wasting and cough destroy thirst associated with upward-moving vāta.

6.22.41 | Milk or ghee prepared with *jīvanīya* (vitalizing) drugs should be administered for [fevers] caused by vāta and pitta; for thirst in pitta-type fever, water mixed with grapes, sandalwood, dates, *uśīra*, and honey should be given.
6.22.42 | Red rice, dates, *parūṣaka* fruits, blue lotuses,
grapes, honey, and even a baked clod of earth placed in water should be drunk when it has become cool.
6.22.43 | A prastha measure of red śāli rice, along with lodhra, madhuka, añjana, and utpala, ground together and combined with water from a heated,
cooled clod of earth and honey, should be drunk from an earthen vessel.

6.22.44 | When water has been prepared with the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *mātuluṅga*, and *vetasa* trees, along with the roots of *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass and *yaṣṭyāhva*, one should add black clay or black sand that resembles fire.
6.22.45 | Alternatively, having prepared nine heated potsherds (navakapāla), one should cause [the patient] to drink clear water;
or water boiled with *amṛtavallī* and sugar removes thirst.
6.22.46 | Cold decoctions made from substances rich in milk, sweet,
and cooling, mixed with sugar and honey and combined with roasted earth, destroy thirst caused by pitta.
6.22.47 | A decoction of trikaṭu, vacā, bhallātaka, and tiktaka destroys vomiting caused by undigested matter (āma) and thirst;
furthermore, whatever has been prescribed for vomiting born of kapha should also be performed here.

6.22.48 | Having recognized thirst associated with kapha in cases of stiffness, aversion to food, indigestion, lassitude, and vomiting, emesis is desired using curd, honey, nourishing drinks, salt, and warm water.
6.22.49 | One should administer pomegranate, or other sour fruits, or those that are astringent, or a linctus; or one should give a drink mixed with turmeric and sugar.
6.22.50 | Thirst caused by wasting (kṣayatṛṣṇā) is equal to cough caused by wasting; it is even more serious for men.
Therefore, one should pacify it with medicines beneficial for those suffering from wasting, chest wounds, and consumption (śoṣa).
6.22.51 | One afflicted by thirst from drinking should drink a beverage consisting of half water, enriched with sour and salty aromatics;
one who has bathed in cold water and is thirsty should drink wine-water or molasses-water.

6.22.52 | One who is thirsty due to the obstruction of food, or afflicted by thirst from [excessive] unctuousness, should drink thin gruel; if one is thirsty after a heavy meal, one should eliminate that meal.
6.22.53 | A strong person who is thirsty should vomit by drinking tepid water or water from a bladder;
or, having first cleansed the mouth with *māgadhikā* (long pepper), he should drink a churned beverage (*mantha*) mixed with sugar.
6.22.54 | A strong person with dryness of the palate should drink ghee and consume thirst-inducing foods;
one who is weak should drink milk fried in ghee and eat unctuous meat broths.
6.22.55 | For those who are extremely parched and weak, milk quickly quenches thirst here;
or else, goat’s meat, fried in ghee and served cold, is sweet, pleasing to the heart, and beneficial.
6.22.56 | One should quench with jaggery-water that thirst which occurs after eating unctuous food;
one should destroy the thirst of one afflicted by fainting with remedies that remove blood-bile (raktapitta).

6.22.57 | In cases of thirst, burning sensations, fainting, vertigo, exhaustion, intoxication, hemorrhage, poisoning, and bilious disorders, water that is naturally cold is recommended; in cases of *sannipāta* (combined humoral disorder), water that has been boiled and then cooled is prescribed.
6.22.58 | Hot [drinks] are beneficial for hiccup, asthma, fever, chronic rhinitis, diseases of the flanks and throat treated with ghee,
and for thickened phlegm caused by kapha and vata, as well as for those who have undergone immediate purification.

6.22.59 | Water is not beneficial in cases of anemia, abdominal enlargement, chronic catarrh, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, weak digestion, diarrhea, and splenic enlargement; however, if these conditions are unbearable, one may drink a small amount.
6.22.60 | Previously, while not yet afflicted, being wretched and tormented by thirst, he longed for water;
if he did not obtain it, he would either meet with death or suffer from a chronic illness.
6.22.61 | Therefore, when thirsty, the patient should drink grain-water mixed with sugar and honey;
or whatever else may be suitable for his constitution and the specific disease is likewise recommended.
6.22.62 | When that [craving] has ceased, the affliction born from it is easily conquered.
Therefore, one should first conquer craving, for it is more difficult to overcome than even many diseases.

6.22.63 | Regarding this, there is a verse:— The causes, how fire and wind produce the five types of thirst along with their complications, their individual characteristics, their incurability, and their treatment have been stated.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, named "The Treatment of the Disease of Thirst," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and—where not available—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Twenty-Three:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of poisoning.
6.23.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.23.3 | O Agniveśa, listen to me as I correctly describe the origin, the qualities, the source, the velocities, the symptoms, and the treatments of fever.
6.23.4 | While the ocean was being churned by the gods and asuras for the sake of the nectar of immortality,
a man of terrible appearance was born before the emergence of the amṛta.
6.23.5 | Blazing with splendor, four-fanged, with golden hair and eyes like fire—seeing him, the world became despondent; therefore, he was designated as "Poison" (Viṣa).
6.23.6 | Brahmā ordained that [the seed] in its womb, whether moving or stationary;
therefore, that which arises from those waters is of two kinds and resembles fire.
6.23.7 | It has eight stages, ten qualities, and twenty-four therapeutic approaches;
because it originates from water during the rainy season, it reaches a state of liquefaction like molasses.
6.23.8 | When the clouds have passed away, Agastya moves along and destroys [the poison];
therefore, at the end of the rainy season, the poison becomes weak in its potency.
6.23.9 | Snakes, insects, rats, spiders, scorpions, house-lizards,
leeches, fish, frogs, *kaṇabhas*, and *sakṛtkaṇṭakas*.
6.23.10 | Dogs, lions, tigers, jackals, hyenas, mongooses, and others—
whatever creatures have fangs, their poison arising from the fangs is considered mobile (jaṅgama).
6.23.11 | Mustaka, pauṣkara, krauñca, vatsanābha,
balāhaka, karkaṭa, kālakūṭa, and that which is known as karavīraka.
6.23.12 | Pālakendrayudha, taila, meghaka, kuśapuṣpaka,
rohiṣa, puṇḍarīka, and lāṅgalakyañjanābhaka.
6.23.13 | Saṅkoca, markaṭa, śṛṅgīviṣa, hālāhala,
and likewise other such [poisons] originating from roots and remaining stable.
6.23.14 | Another [poison], known as gara, arises from a combination of [other poisons] and causes disease;
because it ripens over a long period of time, it does not take away life immediately.
6.23.15 | Mobile poison produces sleep, lassitude, exhaustion, burning sensations accompanied by suppuration, horripilation,
swelling, and diarrhea.
6.23.16 | However, the poison in its stationary state may produce fever, hiccups, sensitivity of the teeth, constriction of the throat, frothy vomiting, loss of appetite, dyspnea, and fainting.
6.23.17 | That which is mobile (animal-borne) belongs to the lower category, while that born from roots belongs to the upper category;
therefore, a root-venom destroys the venom of fangs, and a fang-venom destroys the venom of roots.
6.23.18 | Thirst, delusion, horripilation, salivation, vomiting, and exhaustion occur in the first stage;
however, in the second stage, these arise from the corruption of the blood due to the corruption of the rasa (plasma).

6.23.19 | In the third stage of consumption by poisoned meat, there occur discoloration, vertigo, trembling, fainting, yawning, tingling in the limbs, and nausea; in the fourth stage, circular eruptions, itching, swelling, and urticaria appear.
6.23.20 | In the fourth stage, symptoms born of wind and other humors such as burning sensations, vomiting, pain in the limbs, and fainting occur;
in the fifth impulse, there is the vision of blue and other colors, as well as darkness.

6.23.21 | Hiccups occur in the sixth month; a breaking of the shoulder occurs in the seventh, and death in the eighth for men. For quadrupeds, [the prognosis] is fourfold, and for birds, it is threefold.
6.23.22 | In the first stage, he sinks down and wanders; in the second, his four limbs tremble; thereafter he becomes empty.
In the fourth stage, however, having little appetite, he dies indeed from labored breathing.
6.23.23 | In the first stage of the poison's onset, the bird becomes dazed; in the second, it wanders about aimlessly;
and in the third, with its limbs collapsing, it meets its death.
6.23.24 | Light, dry, quick-acting, clear, pervasive, sharp, expansive, subtle, hot,
and with an indefinable taste— these are the ten qualities of poison described by those who know it.
6.23.25 | Due to its dryness it provokes vāta, due to its lack of coldness it provokes pitta, and due to its subtlety it provokes blood;
because its taste is unmanifest, it quickly follows the course of the bodily tissues and the tastes of food.
6.23.26 | Due to its rapid and pervasive nature, it quickly permeates the entire body;
because of its sharpness, it destroys the vital organs (marmans), and because of its expansive quality, it destroys life.
6.23.27 | Due to its lightness and clarity, it is difficult to treat and possesses the defect of moving without obstruction;
having reached the locations of the *doṣas* or the bodily constitution (*prakṛti*), it excites whichever one it encounters.
6.23.28 | In a patient with vātika [hemiplegia], there may be slight symptoms of kapha and pitta in the seat of vāta,
such as thirst, delusion, restlessness, fainting, throat obstruction, vomiting, and frothing at the mouth.

6.23.29 | In one with a predominance of pitta, the poison located in the seat of bile produces thirst, cough, fever, vomiting, exhaustion, burning sensations, fainting, diarrhea, and so forth; it acts similarly for those with a predominance of kapha or vāta.
6.23.30 | When located in the region of phlegm (kapha), it manifests the signs of phlegm and slight signs of wind (vāta) and bile (pitta),
such as dyspnea, throat obstruction, itching, excessive salivation, nausea, and so forth.
6.23.31 | Dūṣīviṣa, however, by vitiating the blood, manifests the symptoms of aruḥ, kiṭima, and koṭha;
having thus corrupted each individual doṣa, it takes away the vital breaths.

6.23.32 | The blood flows out due to the fiery potency of the poison; by obstructing the bodily orifices, it kills the creature. When drunk, it remains in the heart of the deceased; in the case of one bitten or pierced, it should be present at the site of the bite or wound.
6.23.33 | Blue lips, looseness of the teeth, falling hair, breaking and tossing of the limbs;
with cold [substances], there is no horripilation, nor does the line of stripes appear when struck by a staff.
6.23.34 | Blood does not flow from a wound; these are the signs of death.
When they are otherwise, those [wounds] are treatable; hear from me their methods of treatment.
6.23.35 | Mantras, the application of *ariṣṭa*, excision, squeezing, suction, fire cauterization, affusion, immersion,
bloodletting, emesis, purgation, and poultices.
6.23.36 | Eye-salves for the heart-covering [poison], medicinal smokes, electuaries, and pacifying drugs;
antiseptics, antidotes, the restoration of consciousness, and ointments.
6.23.37 | And the Mṛtasañjīvana; these twenty-four are the therapeutic measures. Listen now to how and where each of them should be applied.
6.23.38 | Having bound a tourniquet above the bite of one who has been stung,
the physician should squeeze out the unspread poison from the wound, or else excise it, avoiding the vital spots (*marmans*).
6.23.39 | One should suck that bite with the mouth filled with barley powder and dust;
then, after scarifying, using leeches, or applying venesection, the blood should be drained.
6.23.40 | When the blood is vitiated by poison, the natural constitution (prakṛti) becomes corrupted; consequently, one may lose one's life.
Therefore, blood that does not flow out should be made to flow by means of rubbing and other such methods.
6.23.41 | Trikaṭu, soot, turmeric, the five salts, and gorocana, along with eggplant (vārtāka), should be used for rubbing when there is excessive discharge;
a cooling paste made of the vaṭa-tree group [of herbs] should be applied.

6.23.42 | For blood is the receptacle of poison, just as wind is for fire; by means of cold ointments and affusions, that [blood] flows out, and when it has flowed out, the force of the poison departs.

6.23.43 | Intoxication, fainting, despondency, and the melting of the heart proceed from the force of the poison. One should counteract these with cold applications, and the patient should be fanned until the horripilation ceases.

6.23.44 | Just as poison does not increase after the bite has been excised— like a tree whose roots have been cut— so too are misfortunes [stilled] by sucking out the venom, by bringing water [to the site], and by building a dam.

6.23.45 | Poison located in the skin and flesh burns; it is removed by bloodletting from the blood. When drunk, it is quickly removed by emetics; however, in the second stage, it is removed by purgatives.

6.23.46 | First, the heart must be protected; one should drink its protective covering (the heartwood) as it is available—either with honey, ghee, marrow, and milk, or with red ochre, or the juice of cow dung.
6.23.47 | Or else, having crushed well-ripened sugarcane or a crow, one should quickly drink its juice mixed with *varuṇa; or one should drink the blood of goats and other animals, or ashes, or clay.
6.23.48 | In the third stage, one should administer an alkaline ointment with honey and water, along with scarifying agents that remove swelling;
in the fourth stage, one should use cow-dung juice mixed with wood-apple, honey, and clarified butter.

6.23.49 | On the fifth day, one should administer drops or collyrium made from the fresh juices of *kākāṇḍa* and *śirīṣa*, as well as nasal therapy (*nasya*). Then, on the sixth day, measures for restoring consciousness (*saṃjñā-sthāpana*) should be performed.

6.23.50 | A drink of *rajanī* mixed with cow-bile, along with *mañjiṣṭhā*, black pepper, and long pepper, is for those who have drunk poison; and for those bitten by a venomous creature, one should bite them at the end [of the treatment].
6.23.51 | Palāśa seed combined with half a part of peacock bile is the best antidote for those who have died [from snakebite];
or else, eggplant, treacle, soot, cow bile, and neem.

6.23.52 | Pills made from *surasa*, *granthi*, the two types of *rajanī*, *madhuka*, and *kuṣṭha*, combined with cow-bile, are recommended; they are equal to nectar (*amṛta*), or alternatively, [pills may be made] with the juices of *śirīṣa* flowers and *kākāṇḍaka*.
6.23.53 | With the fruits of *kākāṇḍa*, *surasā*, *gavākṣī*, *punarnavā*, *vāyasī*, and *śirīṣa*,
[one should administer] ointments, medicinal snuffs, and potions for those who have died from hanging, poison, or water.
6.23.54 | Spṛkkā, plava, sthauṇeya, kāṅkṣī, śaileya, rocanā, tagara,
dhyāmaka, kuṅkuma, māṃsī, surasā, aguru, lālā, and kuṣṭha destroy [the poison].
6.23.55 | Bṛhatī, śirīṣa flower, śrīveṣṭaka, padmacāraṭī, viśālā, devadāru, padmakesara, sāvaraka, manaḥśilā, and kauntī.
6.23.56 | Jāti, arka-puṣpa-rasa, the two types of rajanī, hiṅgu, pippalī, lākṣā, jala, mudgaparṇī, candana, madhuka, madana, and sindhuvāra; and also—
6.23.57 | Having collected śampāka, lodhra, mayūraka, gandhaphalā, ākulī,
and viḍaṅga in equal parts under the Puṣya asterism, they should be ground and made into pills.
6.23.58 | It destroys all poisons, brings victory, restores life to those who have died from poison, and subdues fever;
it should be kept in the home for inhalation, as an ointment, as an amulet, or by means of fumigation.
6.23.59 | It destroys spirits, poisons, insects, misfortune, malevolent spells, the most potent mantras, thunderbolts, and enemies;
it wards off bad dreams, the faults of women, untimely death, and fear of water and fire.

6.23.60 | This is the auspicious Mṛtasañjīvana [mantra], ordained by Brahmā before the nectar of immortality was created; it brings success in wealth, grain, and undertakings, and increases fortune, nourishment, and longevity.
Thus ends the "Life-Reviving" medicine (6.23.61). By means of mantras, one should perform the binding of the vessels, cleansing, and self-protection.
Whichever humor (*doṣa*) has the poison located in its seat, that one should be conquered first.
6.23.62 | When [the disease] is located in the site of Vāta, there should be fomentation (sveda), and the drinking of a paste of nata and kuṣṭha with curd.
When it is located in the site of Pitta, there should be the drinking of ghee, honey, milk, and water, as well as immersion baths and affusions.

6.23.63 | When the *dūṣīviṣa* poison has reached the seat of phlegm (*kapha*), one should apply alkaline antidotes (*kṣārāgada*), fomentation (*sveda*), and venesection (*sirāvyadhana*). Furthermore, when it resides in the blood, the fivefold procedure for venesection (*sirākarma*) is indicated.
6.23.64 | Thus, the physician who knows the science must always determine every medicine after careful observation;
for he should first conquer the site [of the disease], and that which is not contradictory to what resides in that site.

6.23.65 | A mortal whose kapha channels are vitiated by poison and whose vital breath is obstructed by the blockage of the channels may breathe as if dead, yet he remains free from the signs of incurability.

6.23.66 | One should apply a paste of the barks of *carmaka* equal in size to a *bilva* fruit upon the "crow's foot" ulcer on the head, and also administer an insufflation (*pradhamana*) of *kaṭabhī*, *kaṭu*, and *kaṭphala*.
6.23.67 | One should place goat, cow, buffalo, or even chicken meat upon that "crow's foot" [mark]; then the poison transfers to it.
6.23.68 | When there is obstruction of the nose, eyes, ears, tongue, or throat,
the procedure should be administered through the nose (nastaḥ) using ground *vārtāku*, *bījapūra*, *jyotiṣmatī*, and other such substances.
6.23.69 | When there is obstruction of the eyes, an ointment (añjana) should be prepared by grinding together catechu (dāru),
the three acrids (vyoṣa), turmeric (haridrā), oleander (karavīra), karanja, nimba, and surasa with goat's urine.
6.23.70 | White vacā, aśvagandhā, hiṅgu, amṛtā, kuṣṭha, rock salt, garlic,
the pulp of the kapittha fruit, ṭuṇṭuka, and karañja seeds.
6.23.71 | Having ground together vyoṣa, śirīṣa flowers, the two types of rajanī, and vaṃśalocana in equal parts with goat’s urine, cow’s bile, and horse’s bile for seven days;
6.23.72 | This [medicine], when administered in reverse order, quickly destroys even poison located in the head,
as well as all fevers, spirits, planetary afflictions, cholera, chronic ailments, fainting, and pains.
6.23.73 | Insanity and epilepsy, cataracts, film over the eye, and disorders of the pupil; dryness of the eyes, ophthalmia, pterygium, tumors, vascular growths, itching, and disorders of the eyelids.
6.23.74 | Furthermore, by its application as an ointment, it destroys consumption, debility, alcoholism, anemia, and fainting;
and by its removal, it neutralizes poisons from wounds inflicted by poisoned weapons, licking, biting, or drinking.
6.23.75 | It is used as a paste for the anus in cases of hemorrhoids with obstruction, as a vaginal application for women,
as a forehead paste for a dead fetus, and for malignant conditions and coryza.

6.23.76 | This medicinal "scented elephant" (agadagandhahastin), when applied as an ointment for scabies, ringworm, leucoderma, eczema, and other such conditions, destroys the diseases caused by poison just as an elephant uproots trees.

Thus ends the medicinal preparation named Gandhahastin. 6.23.77. Leaf-fragrance, aguru, musta, elā, the five exudations, sandalwood, spṛkkā, tvak, nalada, utpala, bālaka, hareṇuka, uśīra, vanya, and nakha.
6.23.78 | Suradāru, kanaka, kuṅkuma, dhānyaka, kuṣṭha, priyaṅgu, tagara,
the five parts (pañcāṅga) of śirīṣa, vyoṣa, āla, manaḥśilā, and jājī.
6.23.79 | White kaṭabhī, karañja, rakṣoghnī, sindhuvārikā, rajanī, surasā, añjana, gaurika, mañjiṣṭhā, and the resin of nimba.
6.23.80 | Bamboo bark, aśvagandhā, asafoetida, wood-apple, amlavetasa,
lac, honey, madhuka, somarājī, vacā, aru, rocanā, and tagara;
6.23.81 | This sixty-ingredient medicine was indeed proclaimed by Tryambaka to Vaiśravaṇa;
it is of unimpeded power and is renowned as the "Great Fragrant Elephant."
6.23.82 | These should be ground with bile and made into pills under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism;
one should accomplish all procedures by means of drinking, collyrium, and external applications.

6.23.83 | It destroys cataracts (pilla), itching, darkness of vision (timira), night-blindness, cataract-like opacity (kāca), tumors (arbuda), and film over the cornea (paṭala) for those men who eat wholesome, moderate, and salutary food and apply it continuously.
6.23.84 | It quickly destroys irregular fevers, indigestion, ringworm, itching, cholera, scabies,
and the poison of all spiders, scorpions, caterpillars, and serpents— indeed,
every poison arising from roots or bulbous roots.
6.23.85 | With his limbs smeared with this, a man can seize snakes and consume poison;
even one overtaken by time lives forever free from affliction.
6.23.86 | An application of the paste to the anus in the case of a retained fetus, as well as an application to the vagina for those with obstructed pregnancies,
and an application to the forehead during fainting and pain, is said to be the most effective treatment.

6.23.87 | A wise person, having smeared drums, mṛdaṅgas, paṭahas, umbrellas, as well as banners and flags with this [ointment], should sound them or display them for the purpose of destroying snake venom.
6.23.88 | Wherever this [mantra] is present, there neither child-seizing spirits nor demons exist;
neither sorcery-necromancers nor Atharvanic spells prevail there.
6.23.89 | Neither malevolent planets nor fire, weapons, kings, or thieves prevail there;
and Fortune dwells where the Great Scent-Elephant resides.
6.23.90 | While this is being ground, one should here recite this perfected mantra: "My mother is named Jayā; my father is named Jaya."
6.23.91 | Thus, I am Jaya, Jayanta, Vijaya, and Jayi. Salutations to Viṣṇu, the lion among men, the architect of the universe.
To Sanātana Kṛṣṇa, to Bhava, and to Vibhava;
he is the manifest splendor of Vṛṣākapi, and the splendor of Brahmā, Indra, and Yama.
6.23.93 | Just as I do not recognize the defeat of Vāsudeva,
nor the taking of my mother's hand in marriage, nor the drying up of the ocean.
6.23.94 | By this word of truth, let this medicine be effective. O Protector, in contact with Hilimili, you who are the best of all medicines, svāhā!
Thus ends the medicinal preparation named Mahāgandhahastin.
6.23.95. Ṛṣabhaka, jīvaka, bhārgī, madhuka, utpala, dhānyaka, keśara, rājā, ghee, sugar, and the marrow of girikola—these, when drunk, remove asthma, fever, and other ailments.
6.23.96 | Asafoetida combined with long pepper, mixed with the juice of wood-apple and the finest salt,
and taken with honey and sugar, destroys fever, hiccups, dyspnea, and cough.

6.23.97 | For vomiting, a linctus made of jujube stones, collyrium, parched grain, blue lotus, honey, and ghee is used; a medicinal wick (dhūmavarti) made from the leaves of the two types of *bṛhatī* and *āḍhakī* destroys hiccup.

6.23.98 | The smoke produced from the feathers of a peacock, the tail-feathers of a peacock, the bones of a crane, mustard seeds, and sandalwood mixed with clarified butter is recommended for use upon houses, beds, seats, garments, and other items to counteract poison.

6.23.99 | This "smoke-antidote" (dhūmāgada), consisting of nata, kuṣṭha, the head of the lord of serpents (snake-head), and śirīṣa flowers combined with ghee, is known to destroy all poisons and remove swelling.

6.23.100 | Soot, *sevya*, leaves, *guggulu*, *bhallātaka*, the flowers of the *kakubha* tree, resin of the *sarja* tree, and white leadwort (*śvetā*) constitute an excellent smoke that destroys snakes, rats, insects, and cloth-dwelling worms.

6.23.101 One should cook the filtered alkali of young *palāśa* leaves together with equal parts of the powdered roots of red ochre (*lohitamṛd*), the two types of *rajanī*, white *surasā*, *mañjarī*, and *madhuka*.
6.23.102 | One should apply a paste of lac, rock salt, māṃsī, hareṇu, asafoetida, the two types of sārivā, kuṣṭha,
the three pungents (vyoṣa), and bāhlīka to the ladle until it is thoroughly rubbed in.
It cures all types of poisoning, swelling, abdominal tumors (gulma), skin diseases, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, and splenic disorders;
as well as edema, epilepsy, worms, possession by malevolent spirits, hoarseness of voice, and anemia.
6.23.104 | These pills, dried in the shade and consumed when they have reached the size of a jujube fruit (kola), destroy weak digestion, cough, and insanity in men.

Thus ends the Alkaline Antidote (kṣārāgada). This has been described as generally applicable for those who have drunk poison, those bitten by venomous creatures, those pierced by poisoned darts, and those smeared with poison. Now, listen duly to the specific instructions according to each individual case.
6.23.106 | A king may face danger from enemies, from his own people, or even from women, arising during matters of food and recreation; therefore, he should examine his servants.
6.23.107 | One who is excessively suspicious, or who speaks much or very little, who has lost his fortune,
and who has undergone a change of natural disposition— such a man should be known as a poisoner.
6.23.108 | Having seen this, one should not hastily consume that food;
rather, one should place it in the fire, for when the fire encounters poisoned food, it undergoes many transformations.
6.23.109 | Its flames variegated with peacock feathers, its eyes sharp, harsh, and corpse-like smoke; it bursts forth with sound, possesses a single whorl, and its radiance is broken.
6.23.110 | Food placed in her vessel becomes discolored, and she kills flies;
she makes the crows thin-voiced, and the eyes of the cakora bird lose their luster.
6.23.111 | In drinking [poison], there is a blue streak, discoloration, and one does not see one's own reflection;
or one sees it distorted, or there is a frothy mass as if smeared with salt.
6.23.112 | From the odor of food and drink containing poison, there arises headache, distress in the heart, and fainting;
from its touch, swelling of the hands, numbness, burning, pricking pain in the fingers, and splitting of the nails.
6.23.113 | A tingling sensation in the lips, swelling of the tongue, numbness, discoloration, loss of the sense of taste, lockjaw, burning in the mouth, salivation, and disorders of the throat occur.

6.23.114 | When [the poison] has entered the stomach (āmāśaya), there occurs discoloration, perspiration, exhaustion, and a sense of moisture; there is obstruction of the vision and the heart, and the body becomes covered with hundreds of spots.

6.23.115 | When the poison has reached the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), there occur fainting, intoxication, delusion, burning sensations, and loss of strength; when it resides in the abdomen (udara), there is drowsiness, emaciation, and paleness.
6.23.116 | When the tooth-cleansing brush frays, and there is swelling of the teeth, lips, and gums;
when there is hair loss, headache, and nodules—these occur when the head-anointing oil is poisoned.
6.23.117 | When the collyrium is vitiated, there occur burning of the eyes, discharge, excessive coating, swelling, and redness;
by vitiated substances that are edible, the internal cavity (koṣṭha) is first affected, while by those that are tangible, the skin is corrupted.

6.23.118 | From the use of contaminated materials for bathing, oil massage, rubbing, clothing, ornaments, and cosmetics, there arise itching, eruptions, pustules, horripilation, tingling sensations, and swellings.
6.23.119 | These [afflictions]— burning and piercing of the hands and feet, exhaustion, and indigestion—
arise from defective royal sandals, horses, elephants, armor, banners, beds, and seats.
6.23.120 | Smoke causes a garland to lose its fragrance and wither, induces headache and horripilation,
obstructs the bodily orifices, and impairs the sense of smell and sight.
6.23.121 | Water from wells, tanks, and other sources that is foul-smelling, turbid, and discolored,
when drunk, causes swelling, skin eruptions, pustules, and even death.
6.23.122 | When [the poison] is first located in the stomach (āmāśaya), the physician should administer emetics; when it resides in the skin, he should apply plasters, affusions, and so forth.
Indeed, the physician should perform the treatment after carefully considering the strength of the doshas.
6.23.123 | Thus the specific varieties of root poisons have been declared; now hear concerning those of mobile origin. Among them, the treatment for snake venom is stated first.

6.23.124 | Here, the three types of snakes— the hooded (*darvīkara*), the circular (*maṇḍalī*), and the striped (*rājimān*)— respectively provoke the wind (*vāta*), the bile (*pitta*), and the phlegm (*śleṣman*).
6.23.125 | The Darvīkara is to be known as having a flat hood; the Maṇḍalī has a circular hood.
A serpent whose body is variegated with spots and lines is called Rājimān.
6.23.126 | Specifically, poison is dry, pungent, sour, hot, sweet, and cold; according to this sequence, it provokes vāta and the other doshas respectively.
6.23.127 | A bite inflicted by a Darvīkaraka snake is characterized by minute fang marks,
is black in color, has its blood arrested, resembles a tortoise in shape, and is considered to cause diseases of the Vata humor.
6.23.128 | A bite inflicted by a Maṇḍalī snake is raised and swollen;
it appears yellowish or yellow-red and produces all the disorders of Pitta.
6.23.129 | The bite inflicted by a *rājimant* [snake] is slimy and causes persistent swelling;
it is glossy and pale, accompanied by thick blood, and provokes diseases of phlegm (*śleṣman*) and wind (*vāyu*).
6.23.130 | A male [serpent] has rounded coils, a large body, hisses, looks upward, has a thick head, and symmetrical limbs; a female, however, is the opposite of this.

6.23.131 | One who is eunuch-like, wears women's clothing, has a downward gaze, lacks vocal resonance, and trembles is considered a man bitten by a female [snake]; one with the opposite of these traits is considered bitten by a male.
6.23.132 | One should declare a man bitten by a neuter snake by these mixed characteristics.
Thus has been described the diagnostic observation of female, male, and neuter snakes.
6.23.133 | A woman who gives birth with a pale face, swollen lips, and dark eyes;
who suffers from yawning, anger, and an upturned tongue; and whose newborn has blood in its urine—[is ill-omened].
6.23.134 | There is a four-footed serpent called the *gauḍheraka*, which is born from a lizard (*godhā*);
it is equal to the black cobra (*kṛṣṇasarpa*), and there may be various hybrid species.

6.23.135 | A bite that is concealed, one where the fang-mark is hidden, one that is pressed down, one where the venom has been injected slowly, and one that causes intense pain—these are the dangerous bites; other types of bites are not so severe.
6.23.136 | Young black snakes, as well as gonasa snakes when old,
and striped snakes in their middle age, become like venomous serpents (āśīviṣa).
6.23.137 | The serpent has four fangs; among them, the lower left fang is white, the upper left fang is yellow, and the lower and upper right fangs are reddish-brown.
6.23.138 | As much as a drop of water falling from a cow’s hair-tip might be,
so much would be the venom of a serpent upon the fang of the lower left [tooth].
6.23.139 | Those whose venom-increments increase by one, two, three, or four parts respectively,
being of the same color, have bites produced by that [venom] which are increasingly severe as the poison increases.
6.23.140 | From the saliva, feces, and urine of snakes, there arise insects considered equal to snakes;
they are briefly regarded as *dūṣīviṣa* (latent-poison) creatures that take away life.
6.23.141 | The limb may be red, white, black, or dark-brown, covered with pustules; it may be accompanied by itching, burning, erysipelas, and suppuration, and likewise become putrid.
6.23.142 | Listen to the signs of a bite by insects with *dūṣīviṣa* poison that takes away life:
just as in a snakebite, the swelling increases and the blood becomes foul-smelling.
6.23.143 | One afflicted by *dūṣīviṣa* poison experiences a bite, heaviness of the eyes, fainting, pain, and labored breathing; he is also overcome by thirst and loss of appetite.
6.23.144 | That which is black or brown in the center of the bite, covered with a network of veins,
resembling a burnt area, excessively suppurating, and accompanied by discharge, swelling, and fever— [is known as a fatal bite].
6.23.145 | One should identify him as being bitten by spiders (*lūtā*) possessing latent poison (*dūṣīviṣa*);
now the symptoms for the bite of all of them are described.
6.23.146 | There is swelling, white, black, red, or yellow pustules, fever,
life-ending dyspnea, burning sensation, hiccup, and stiffness of the head.
6.23.147 | In one afflicted by the poison of the *dūṣī* rat, there occurs pale blood at the site of the bite, circular patches, fever, loss of appetite, horripilation, and a burning sensation.

6.23.148 | Fainting, swelling of the limbs, discoloration, discharge, loss of hearing, fever, heaviness of the head, and vomiting of saliva and blood— these are the symptoms of being bitten by an incurable rat.
6.23.149 | Furthermore, a dark-bluish tint, or blackness, or even various colors,
as well as delusion and diarrhea, occur when one has been bitten by *kṛkalāsaka* lizards.
The venom of a scorpion first burns like fire, then quickly pierces upward; it moves through the site of the sting and remains there afterwards.
6.23.151 | A man bitten [by a snake] who is afflicted in his sight, smell, and taste is incurable;
with flesh falling excessively from him, tormented by pain, he gives up his life-breaths.
6.23.152 | Erysipelas, swelling, pain, fever, and even vomiting occur when one is bitten by a *lakṣṇa* spider; furthermore, the bite site itself falls apart.
6.23.153 | With his hair standing on end like bristling insects and his penis paralyzed,
the person bitten by it experiences intense pain and feels as if his limbs have been sprinkled with cold water.
6.23.154 | Swelling, pain, and a yellowish discoloration caused by the bite of a single-fanged [insect], accompanied by thirst,
vomiting, and drowsiness, are the symptoms of being bitten by poisonous frogs.
6.23.155 | Poisonous fish cause burning, swelling, and pain;
poisonous leeches, however, cause itching, swelling, fever, and fainting.
6.23.156 | The venom of the house-lizard (*gṛhagodhikā*) causes burning, pricking, sweating, and swelling;
the venom of the centipede (*śatapadī*) produces sweating, pain, and burning at the site of the bite.
6.23.157 | There may be itching due to mosquitoes, with slight swelling and mild pain;
a wound caused by mosquitoes is incurable if it resembles that of an insect.

6.23.158 | A bite by flies results in a swelling that exudes pus immediately, is dark-colored, and is accompanied by burning, fainting, and fever; among these, the *sthagikā* variety is the most harmful.
6.23.159 | In cremation grounds, on funeral mounds, in anthills, at sacrificial hermitages, or in temples;
at the junctions of fortnights, at midday, at midnight, and on the eighth lunar days.
6.23.160 | Men bitten by venomous serpents (*āśīviṣa*)— by means of their gaze, breath, impure touch, or poison— do not survive, especially if they are in the dwellings of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*).
6.23.161 | Those bitten on all the vital spots perish quickly, regardless of which snake has caused the bite; this applies to every case.
Poison increases in one who is frightened, intoxicated, weak, or afflicted by heat, hunger, or thirst;
however, when the nature of the poison and the time coincide, even a small amount becomes otherwise [fatal].

6.23.163 | Snakes that have been struck by water, those that are emaciated, those that are frightened, those defeated by mongooses, the elderly, the young, those that have shed their skins, and those with weak venom are considered to be of mild poison.
6.23.164 | Out of anger, a serpent releases the poison that resides throughout its entire body;
yet for the sake of food or out of fear, it does not release that very same poison.
6.23.165 | Generally, *ucciṭiṅga* spiders and scorpions have poison predominant in wind (*vāta*);
insects such as *kaṇabha* and others have wind and bile (*pitta*) predominant; and those such as the *kaṇabha* have phlegm (*śleṣman*) predominant.
6.23.166 | Indeed, whichever specific humor one observes to have an excess of symptoms, one should apply a treatment with medicinal substances possessing qualities opposite to those [symptoms].

6.23.167 | In the case of poison of the Vāta type, there is pain in the heart, upward movement of wind (ūrdhvānila), stiffness, distension of the vessels, pain in the bones and joints, dizziness, cramps, and a dark discoloration of the limbs.
6.23.168 | Loss of consciousness, hot breath, burning in the heart, a bitter taste in the mouth,
tearing at the site of the bite, and swelling that is red or yellow occur in the Pitta-type [poisoning].

6.23.169 | One should recognize poison characterized by an excess of phlegm (śleṣman) through vomiting, loss of appetite, nausea, excessive salivation, distress, heaviness, coldness, and sweetness in the mouth.

6.23.170 | For a wound caused by Vāta, an ointment made with sugar and an oil massage are beneficial; likewise, fomentation using tubes, steam from cooking grains, and nourishing therapies are recommended.
6.23.171 | One should arrest a pitta-type [hemorrhage] with very cold affusions and plasters;
one should conquer a kapha-type [hemorrhage] by means of scraping, excision, fomentation, and emesis.

6.23.172 | Furthermore, in the case of all poisons, whether they have reached any part of the body or are caused by non-scorpion or non-ucchiṭiṅga insects, a cooling treatment is generally beneficial.
6.23.173 | In the case of Vṛścika [poisoning], one should employ fomentation, anointing with ghee and salt,
warm affusions, and food and drink consisting of clarified butter (sarpiḥ).
6.23.174 | This same procedure is also prescribed for Ucciṭiṅga, using powders applied in reverse order,
followed by anointment with lukewarm water and then covering with thick cloths.

6.23.175 | Due to the provocation of the three doṣas and likewise from the derangement of the bodily constituents (dhātus), a dog becomes afflicted with heat in the head, drools saliva, and has its face turned downward.
6.23.176 | Other such venomous creatures are also considered to aggravate kapha and vāta,
and to cause pain in the heart and head, fever, stiffness, thirst, and fainting.
6.23.177 | Itching, pricking, discoloration, numbness, exudation, dryness,
burning sensation, redness, pain, suppuration, swelling, glandular swellings, and contraction [of the limbs].
6.23.178 | Biting, tearing, eruptions, pustules, circular spots, and mandalas, as well as fever, are the symptoms of a venomous [insect]; the opposite, however, indicates one that is non-venomous.
6.23.179 | In that case, all the previously mentioned therapeutic measures should be applied according to the specific condition; now listen as I duly describe another method.

6.23.180 | In cases of burning pain in the heart or excessive salivation, strong purgation and emesis should be administered according to the specific condition; once the patient is purified, the sequential regimen for dietary restoration (saṃsarjana-krama) should be followed.
6.23.181 | When the poison has reached the head, a wise person should administer as an errhine (nastaḥ) the roots of bandhujīva, bhārgī, surasa, and asita.
6.23.182 | When there is a wound in the flesh, blood, or head of a cock, a crow, or a peacock,
it should be applied to the lower part of one who has been bitten from above, or to the feet of one who has been bitten from below.
6.23.183 | Pippalī, marica, kṣāra, vacā, saindhava, and śigruka,
ground together with the bile of a rohita fish and applied as an ointment, destroy [diseases] located in the eye.
6.23.184 | When poison has reached the throat, one should lick raw wood-apple (kapittha) with sugar and honey;
when it has reached the stomach (āmāśaya), one should take a pala of the powder of *nata* with those two.

6.23.185 | When poison has reached the digestive tract (pakvāśaya), a person should drink a paste made by grinding equal parts of long pepper (pippalī), the two types of turmeric (rajanīdvaya), and mañjiṣṭhā with cow bile.
6.23.186 | Dried and powdered blood and meat of the monitor lizard (godhā),
when drunk combined with the juice of wood-apple (kapittha), is beneficial as a potion when the poison has entered the plasma (rasa).
6.23.187 | One should drink the root-bark and the tips of the Śelu, Badara, Udumbara, and Kaṭabhī when [the blood] has reached the blood; one should drink them when it has reached the flesh.
6.23.188 | Khadira, ariṣṭa, and the root of kuṭaja with honey and water;
and for all [these], the two types of bala, madhūka, madhuka, and nata.

6.23.189 | When phlegm has increased, the physician should apply a rubbing paste (pratisāraṇa) consisting of long pepper (pippalī), dry ginger (nāgara), and alkali (kṣāra), mixed with fresh butter (navanīta).
6.23.190 | With māṃsī, kuṅkuma, patra, tvak, rajanī, nata, candana, manaḥśilā, vyāghranakha, and surasa, ground together with water.
6.23.191 | Drinks, snuffs, collyria, and ointments [prepared from these] remove all types of swelling and poison:
sandalwood, tagara, kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, and cinnamon bark.
6.23.192 | Realgar, tamāla, juice,
and saffron, as well as the claw of a tiger, should be finely ground with rice-water.
6.23.193 | White pepper soaked for seven days in the juice of the *śirīṣa* flower destroys all poisons, just as the thunderbolt of Indra destroys the asuras.
6.23.194 | This prepared formulation is beneficial as a nasal drop, a drink, and an eye-salve for those bitten by snakes.
It consists of two palas each of nata and kuṣṭha, along with four palas of ghee and honey.
6.23.195 | This drink also bestows comfort even upon those bitten by Takṣaka:
the root of Sindhuvāra, Śvetā, and Girikarṇikā.
6.23.196 | When bitten by a hooded snake (darvīkara), the potion consists of pākala mixed with honey;
[the nasal medication consists of] mañjiṣṭhā, madhuyaṣṭī, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, and sugar.
6.23.197 | Kāśmarya and the sprouts of the vaṭa tree are the remedy for the poison of maṇḍalins.
Trikaṭu, ativiṣā, kuṣṭha, soot from a house, and hareṇukā [are used against it].
6.23.198 | Tagara, kaṭukā, and honey destroy the poison of *rājīmata* snakes;
likewise do soot from a house, the two types of *haridrā*, and *taṇḍulīyaka* with its roots.
Even one bitten by Vāsuki may drink [the remedy] soaked in honey and ghee;
an ointment made from the bark of milk-exuding trees, applied once the [wound] is purified, removes the poison of insects.
6.23.200 | A plaster of pearls is excellent for removing swelling, burning, piercing pain, and fever;
[so too are] sandalwood, padmaka, uśīra, śirīṣa, and sindhuvārikā.
Kṣīraśuklā, nata, kuṣṭha, pāṭalā, uśīra, and sārivā,
ground with the fresh juice of śelu, constitute a universal remedy for all types of spiders (lūtā).
6.23.202 | (It should be applied as appropriate after careful consideration in ointments and other treatments.
Madhūka, madhuka, kuṣṭha, śirīṣa, udīcya, and pāṭalā, combined with nimba,
sārivā, and honey, form a drink that removes the poison of spiders.
6.23.203 | Safflower, cow’s tooth, golden milk tree,
pigeon dung, danti, trivṛt, and rock salt— these cause the discharge of the ear-wax (karṇikā) from both ears.
6.23.204 | The barks of *kaṭabhī*, *arjuna*, *śairīṣa*, *śelu*, and *kṣīridruma*— used as decoctions,
pastes, or powders— destroy wounds caused by insects and spiders.
6.23.205 | Equal parts of cinnamon bark (*tvac*) and ginger (*nāgara*), finely ground and all taken together, should be drunk with warm water; this destroys the poison of rats.

6.23.206 | This formulation— consisting of the fruit of *kuṭaja* ground with *tagara*, *jālamālinī*, and bitter *ikṣvāku*— is used for drinking, insufflation (*pradhamana*), and other such applications.
6.23.207 | It removes the poison of scorpions, mongooses, spiders, and snakes;
for this [remedy] is equal to nectar, and it destroys both artificial poison and indigestion.
6.23.208 | All non-poisonous remedies should be applied according to the specific humor involved in *kṛkaṇṭaka*.
[The remedy consists of] pigeon dung, *mātuluṅga*, and the juice from the flowers of *śirīṣa*.
6.23.209 | Śaṅkhinī, arka, milk, śuṇṭhī, karañja, honey, and vārścika; the fruit of śirīṣa ground with the latex of snuhī and dārdura.
6.23.210 | The roots of white bhaṇḍī, trikaṭu,
and ghee used for insect bites should all be applied identically to leeches.
6.23.211 | Furthermore, treatment that generally alleviates wind and bile is highly recommended;
for the remedy against the ucciṭiṅga consists of the [flesh] of the vārṣika, the kaṇabha, and the undura.
Vacā, bamboo bark, pāṭhā, nata, the cluster of surasa,
the two types of balā, nākulī, kuṣṭha, śirīṣa, and the two types of rajanī.
6.23.213 | Guhā, atiguhā, śvetā, ajagandhā, śilājatu, kattṛṇa, kaṭabhī, kṣāra, gṛhadhūma, and manaḥśilā.
6.23.214 | Having ground it with the bile of a Rohītaka, this is the supreme medicine;
it is beneficial for nasal drops, collyrium, and ointments applied to those suffering from Viśvambharā and other such ailments.
6.23.215 | Svarjikā, the alkali of goat dung, surasā, and akṣipīḍaka,
when combined with the scum of wine (madirāmaṇḍa), are beneficial against the venom of centipedes.
6.23.216 | Kapittha, akṣipīḍa, arka seeds, as well as trikaṭu, karañja,
the two types of haridrā, and [the remedy for] house-lizard poison shall overcome [poison].
6.23.217 | Taṇḍulīyaka, combined with the juice of the fruit of the crow (kākāṇḍa), is the primary [remedy] for poisons;
likewise is vāyasapīluka with the bile of a peacock.
6.23.218 | This "Five-Śirīṣa" compound, prepared with equal parts of the fruit, root, bark, flower, and leaf of the Śirīṣa tree, is the most excellent for the destruction of poisons.

Thus ends the "Five-Śirīṣa" remedy (6.23.219). Whatever wound caused by the claws or teeth of four-footed or two-footed animals becomes swollen, suppurates, exudes pus, and even causes fever; [it is treated with this remedy].
6.23.220 | Somavalka, aśvakarṇa, gojihvā, and haṃsapadī,
along with the two types of rajanī and red ochre (gairika), constitute a plaster that removes the poison from nails and teeth.

6.23.221 | In deep darkness, for one who has been pierced by someone [with a weapon] under the suspicion that it was poisoned, fever, vomiting, fainting, or even a burning sensation may occur due to the agitation caused by the fear of poison.
6.23.222 | Lassitude, delusion, and diarrhea—this is considered the poison of fear. A wise physician, providing reassurance, should administer this treatment for it.
6.23.223 | White sugar, fragrant substances, grapes, milk, licorice, and honey— these,
along with water purified by mantras for drinking, sprinkling, soothing words, and cheering, [are the remedies].
6.23.224 | Śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, koradūṣa,
and priyaṅgu are recommended for food, and rock salt (saindhava) for seasoning.
6.23.225 | Taṇḍulīyaka, jīvantī, vārtāka,
suniṣaṇṇaka, cucū, maṇḍūkaparṇī, and kulaka vegetables are beneficial.

6.23.226 | For the sake of sourness, one should use *dhātrī* (myrobalan) and pomegranate; soups should be made with green gram (*mudga*) and *hareṇu* lentils; and meat broths should be prepared from the deer, peacock, jackal, common quail, partridge, and spotted antelope.
6.23.227 | Medicinal juices and soups prepared with anti-poisonous herbs,
along with foods that do not cause burning acidity, constitute the physician’s remedy for those afflicted by poison.

6.23.228 | Even one who has been freed from poison should avoid incompatible foods, eating before the previous meal is digested, anger, hunger, fear, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and especially sleeping during the day.
6.23.229 | Repeatedly placing the head down, swelling, drooping of the lips and ears, fever,
stiffness of the eyes and limbs, trembling of the jaw, and aching of the body.
6.23.230 | The falling out of hair, exhaustion, restlessness, trembling, and dizziness—
these are the symptoms here for four-footed creatures that have been bitten.
Devadāru, the two types of haridrā, sarala, candana,
aguru, rāsnā, gorocanā, ajājī, guggulu, ikṣurasa, and nata.
6.23.232 | This powder, consisting of saindhava salt and ananta, combined with cow's bile and honey,
is a universal antidote for animals that have been bitten.
6.23.233 | For the sake of securing good fortune, women provide sweat, menstrual blood, and various bodily impurities, as well as poisons administered by enemies, mixed into their food.
6.23.234 | By these [symptoms], one becomes pale, emaciated, and has weak digestion;
moreover, vomiting arises in him, along with distension from the agitation of the vital organs (marmans) and swelling of the hands and feet.
6.23.235 | Abdominal enlargement, disorders of the digestive tract, consumption, abdominal tumors, wasting, fever,
and likewise the symptoms of other such diseases shall be manifested.
6.23.236 | In dreams, he generally sees cats, jackals, predatory beasts, mongooses, and monkeys, as well as rivers and other waterways, along with trees, all dried up.
6.23.237 | One whose senses are impaired may see himself as dark in a dream when he is actually fair, or as fair when he is dark; or he may even see himself with missing ears or a missing nose.
6.23.238 | Having observed him, the wise physician should ask what was eaten, with what, and when;
having understood this quickly, the physician should administer emetics.
6.23.239 | A fine powder of copper mixed with honey is a purifier of the heart.
Once the heart is purified, one should then administer a *śāṇa* measure of gold dust.
6.23.240 | Gold quickly neutralizes all poisons and artificial toxins (garas).
Poison does not adhere to one whose limbs are adorned with gold, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.
6.23.241 | Ghee prepared from buffalo milk, along with one āḍhaka of cow urine, and processed with nāgadantī, trivṛt, dantī, dravantī, snuhī-milk, and its fruits, is beneficial.
6.23.242 For the pacification of those afflicted by the venom of snakes or insects, or by artificial poisons (gara),
one should use the bark of the śirīṣa tree, the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), sandalwood, and blue lotus.
6.23.243 | Two types of *bala*, *sārivā*, *āsphotā*, *surabhī*, *nimba*, *pāṭalā*,
*bandhujīva*, *āḍhakī*, *mūrvā*, *vāsā*, *asura*, and *vatsaka*.
6.23.244 | Pāṭhā, aṅkola, aśvagandhā, the root of arka, yaṣṭyāhva, padmaka, viśālā, bṛhatī, lākṣā, kovidāra, and śatāvarī.
6.23.245 | Kaṭabhī, dantī, apāmārga, pṛśniparṇī, rasāñjana,
śvetabhaṇḍā, aśvakhuraka, kuṣṭha, dāru, and priyaṅgu;
6.23.246 | Having ground vidārī, the pith of madhuka, the fruit and bark of karañja, the two types of rajanī, and lodhra in equal parts, one āḍhaka of ghee should be prepared [with these].
6.23.247 | Equal quantities of water, goat’s urine, and cow’s urine— three āḍhakas in total— destroy poison, as well as epilepsy,
consumption, insanity, possession by spirits or planets, and abdominal enlargement.
6.23.248 | Anemia, worms, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, stiffness of the thighs, jaundice,
and conditions such as lockjaw and stiffness of the shoulders [are treated] by means of drinking, massage, and nasal drops.
6.23.249 | This supreme ghee, known by the name Amṛta, would kill or even revive men who have died from the bondage of poison; it is the sovereign remedy for all poisons.
Thus ends the section on Amṛtaghṛta (6.23.250). And there are these verses here:
One should wander by night as well as by day, carrying an umbrella and a rattle-drum in hand.
Terrified by its shadow and its sound, the serpents quickly perish.
6.23.251 | As soon as one is bitten, one should immediately bite that snake or even a clod of earth;
one should bind a ligature above the wound, and likewise cut or cauterize the site of the bite.
6.23.252 | Vajra, marakata, sāra, picuka, viṣamūṣikā, karketana, sarpamaṇi, vaidūrya, and gajamauktika.
6.23.253 | One should keep in possession minerals, gems, and excellent medicinal herbs that neutralize poison,
as well as birds such as the maina, the curlew, the peacock, the swan, the parrot, and others.
6.23.254 | Regarding this, there is a verse:

Thus has been described, in detail and in many ways, the medicine for the two types of poison-diseases. Having studied this, understood it, and applied it accordingly, the wise man shall avoid the incurability of poisons.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, named "The Treatment of Poisoning," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Twenty-four:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of alcoholism (madātyaya).
6.24.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.24.3 | She who was formerly worshipped by the gods together with the Lord of the Gods,
she who is offered as an oblation in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice by ritualists, and she who is established [in all things].
6.24.4 | That sacrificial cow by which Śakra, having transgressed against Soma,
was severely overcome by a loss of vigor and possessed by darkness, was rescued from that calamity.
6.24.5 | By high-souled ones performing sacrifices according to the rites ordained in the Vedas,
she is to be seen, touched, and envisioned as the sacrificial object for the successful completion of the sacrifice.
6.24.6 | Though she exists in many ways through specific distinctions such as her place of birth, refinement, name, and so forth,
she becomes of one kind through the common characteristic of intoxication.
6.24.7 | She who, having become the nectar of the gods, and having become the *svadhā* offering for the ancestors,
and having become the *soma*, unites the twice-born with the highest blessings.
6.24.8 | That splendor which belongs to the Aśvins, that strength which belongs to Sarasvatī,
that heroism which belongs to Indra, and that perfection which exists in the Soma and Sautrāmaṇi sacrifices— [all these are present here].
6.24.9 | She who destroys grief, discontent, fear, and agitation, she who is of great power;
she who is joy, she who is delight, she who is speech, she who is nourishment, and she who is bliss.
6.24.10 | That which is called *surā* by the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and humans— because it is a source of delight (*rati*), one should drink that *surā* according to the prescribed rule.
6.24.11 | Having performed the purificatory rites for his body, pure and anointed with the finest perfumes,
he was clothed in spotless garments that were fragrant according to the season.
6.24.12 | Adorned with various and wonderful garlands and decorated with jewel ornaments,
he worshipped the gods and the twice-born and touched the most excellent auspicious objects.
6.24.13 | In a place that was auspicious for the season, strewn with heaps of flowers,
agreeable to the lake, preeminent, and awakened by the fragrance of incense;
6.24.14 | Seated upon a well-spread bed or seat provided with a cushion,
or perhaps reclining on his side, remaining focused on the comfort of his own body.
6.24.15 | He should always drink from vessels made of gold, silver, and likewise of gems, as well as from other pure and well-crafted vessels.
6.24.16 | By women intoxicated by their beauty and youth, especially those highly trained,
adorned with garments, ornaments, and garlands appropriate for each season.
6.24.17 | Being massaged here and there by beloved women who are endowed with purity and affection, he should drink the most excellent wine.
6.24.18 | With various fruits suitable for wine, auspicious green vegetables, salts, and seasonings that reveal their fragrances, as well as snacks appropriate to the season;
6.24.19 | With various kinds of roasted meats of creatures moving on land, in water, and in the air,
and with diverse types of edible foods prepared by the department of kitchen overseers;
6.24.20 | Having worshipped the gods and first offered prayers for blessings,
he gave wine mixed with water to those who sought it upon the surface of the earth.
6.24.21 | A person with a vātika constitution should consume wine after being treated with oil massage, rubbing, bathing, clothing, incense,
and ointments, and after having been nourished with unctuous and warm foods.
One who has been afflicted by pitta does not suffer when drinking liquor if they have been treated with various cooling measures and nourished with foods that are sweet, unctuous, and cold.
6.24.23 | A person of phlegmatic constitution (ślaiṣmika) who eats barley and wheat should drink wine along with non-cool remedies,
meat from animals of the desert (dhanvaja), and black pepper.
6.24.24 | This is the rule for those who possess wealth and for those whose prosperity is yet to come:
they should drink wine in a beneficial measure, according to what is appropriate.

6.24.25 | Wine made from molasses and flour is generally beneficial for those with a predominance of Vāta; however, for those with an excess of Kapha and Pitta, wine made from grapes (Mārdvīka) and that which is produced from Madhūka flowers (Mādhava) are recommended.
6.24.26 | Containing many substances, many qualities, and many actions, and being of the nature of intoxication,
that liquor is characterized by both qualities and defects.

6.24.27 | For one who drinks wine according to the prescribed method, in the proper measure, at the right time, with wholesome food, and in accordance with their strength, while being joyful, it shall be like nectar.
6.24.28 | Furthermore, when wine is drunk by one who habitually indulges in it,
yet lacks moisture and is constantly engaged in physical exercise, it acts upon him like poison.
6.24.29 | Alcohol, having entered the heart, agitates the ten qualities of the *ojas* by means of its own ten qualities, and thereby leads the mind to a state of derangement.
6.24.30 | Alcohol is traditionally said to possess ten qualities: it is light, hot, sharp, subtle, sour, pervasive, quick-acting, dry, expansive, and clear.
6.24.31 | Ojas is traditionally said to possess ten qualities: it is heavy, cold, soft, smooth, thick, sweet, stable, clear, slimy, and unctuous.
6.24.32 | From lightness comes heaviness; from heat, coldness;
from its sour nature, sweetness and softness; and from its lack of impurity, sharpness and clarity.
6.24.33 | Through its dryness it overcomes unctuousness; through its pervasiveness, stability and smoothness;
through its expansive nature, sliminess; and through its clarity, thickness.
6.24.34 | By its subtlety, liquor thus destroys the qualities of *ojo* through its own qualities;
having quickly agitated the *sattva* and that which rests upon it, it produces intoxication.

6.24.35 | The heart is said to be the seat of the channels of rasa, vāta, and the rest; of the mind (sattva), the intellect (buddhi), the sense organs (indriya), and the self (ātman); and of the primary vital essence (ojas).
6.24.36 | By excessively drinking liquor and by the destruction of one's vital energy (ojas),
the heart undergoes morbid transformation, as do the constituent tissues (dhātus) situated therein.
