6.24.37 | When the *ojas* is unimpaired and the heart is awakened, it is the first [type];
when it is slightly impaired, it is the middle; and when it is greatly impaired, it is the lowest.
6.24.38 | Thus, liquor made from flour (paiṣṭika) does not produce such a destruction of vitality (ojas),
for its qualities— expansive, dry, and clear— are not predominant therein.
6.24.39 | When the heart is permeated by the qualities of wine, there arise exhilaration, thirst, passion, and pleasure;
and various transformations according to one's temperament, whether characterized by rajas or tamas.
6.24.40 | From the excessive indulgence in liquor, there arise states ending in the sleep of delusion;
this derangement caused by liquor is known by the name *amada* (intoxication).
6.24.41 | Three stages of intoxication from the wine being drunk are to be recognized: the first, the middle, and the last. We shall describe them according to their characteristics.
6.24.42 | It is exhilarating, producing delight, and revealing the qualities of food and drink;
it is the promoter of instrumental music, song, laughter, and storytelling.

6.24.43 | Neither does it rob one of intellect or memory regarding sense objects, nor is one incapable [of action]; accompanied by pleasant sleep and awakening, this first stage of intoxication is a giver of happiness.
6.24.44 | Memory fluctuates, delusion repeatedly occurs, speech remains indistinct,
there is incoherent prattling about what is relevant and irrelevant, and there is even tossing about.
6.24.45 | One should recognize these signs when one is possessed by the intermediate level of intoxication: the choice of place, drink, food, and conversation, as well as their opposites.
6.24.46 | Having transcended the middle state but not yet reached the highest state of passion (rajas),
men characterized by rajas and tamas perform no action that is not inauspicious.
6.24.47 | What wise man, knowing intoxication to be as dreadful as madness, would pursue such a path, just as a traveler avoids a road that is endless and full of many dangers?
But having reached the third intoxication, one becomes as motionless as a withered log;
with his mind shrouded by intoxication and delusion, he is equal to the dead even while living.
6.24.49 | He perceives neither delightful objects nor his circle of friends;
he finds neither that pleasure for which liquor is drunk, nor that very delight itself.
6.24.50 | What is to be done and what is not to be done, pleasure and pain, and whatever in this world is beneficial or harmful—
that state in which one no longer perceives these, what wise man would enter such a state?
6.24.51 | He is detested by all beings, censurable, and indeed unworthy of being accepted;
because of his addiction, he experiences suffering and disease in the future.
6.24.52 | That which is the highest good both hereafter and in this world, and that supreme good which lies in liberation—
all that depends upon the concentration of the mind for all embodied beings.
6.24.53 | By means of liquor, a great agitation is produced in his mind,
like that of a tree standing on the bank [shaken] by the force of a mighty wind.
6.24.54 | Those overcome by passion and delusion perceive that addiction to intoxicants— which is a great evil and a great disease— as happiness.

6.24.55 | Those whose discernment is impaired by liquor, who are deprived of the qualities of goodness (sattva), are separated from their higher interests; blinded by intoxication and languid with drink, they fall away from what is beneficial.
6.24.56 | Delusion, fear, grief, anger, and death reside in liquor;
as do insanity, intoxication, fainting, epilepsy, and apatanaka.
6.24.57 | Where there is a single lapse of memory, there everything becomes unrighteous;
thus those who know the faults of liquor strenuously condemn liquor.

6.24.58 | It is true that these great evils of liquor have been described, there is no doubt, for when it is drunk in an unwholesome manner, in excessive quantity, and contrary to the prescribed rules.
6.24.59 | However, wine by its very nature is considered to be just like food:
when consumed improperly it leads to disease, but when consumed properly it is like nectar.

6.24.60 | Food is the life-force of living beings; when consumed improperly, it destroys that very life-force. Poison is a taker of life, yet when joined with proper application, it becomes an elixir (rasāyana).
6.24.61 | Wine, when drunk in the proper manner, quickly bestows joy, vigor, delight, nourishment, health, and supreme manliness, while granting pleasant intoxication.
It is brightening, digestive-stimulating, cordial, and clarifies the voice and complexion;
it is pleasing, nourishing, strengthening, and removes fear, grief, and fatigue.
6.24.63 It induces sleep in those who have lost their sleep, restores speech to the mute,
awakens those who are excessively drowsy, and removes obstructions in those who are constipated.
6.24.64 | Furthermore, the lack of awareness regarding the sufferings of slaughter, imprisonment, and affliction,
as well as the diseases arising from liquor, is countered by liquor itself.
6.24.65 | Pleasure in the union with sense objects increases the bond of affection;
even for the elderly, wine brings about the joy of festivals.
6.24.66 | That delight which young men or even the elderly feel toward the five desirable objects during the first stage of intoxication has no equal on earth.
6.24.67 | For this world of living beings, who is struck by manifold sufferings and afflicted by grief, wine, when consumed with moderation, serves as a source of rest.
6.24.68 | Having understood the six triads of food and drink, age, disease, strength, and time, as well as the three doṣas and the three types of temperament (sattva), one should always drink wine.
6.24.69 | The method for these eight triads is now described;
by this method, one drinking wine is not afflicted by the defects of wine.

6.24.70 | Such a man, elevated by the quality of goodness (sattva), enjoys all the qualities of wine as previously described, without causing harm to his virtue (dharma) or his worldly interests (artha).
6.24.71 | Generally, living beings awaken during the first stage of intoxication;
in the second, they reach a state of indistinctness, occurring between the middle and the highest stages.
6.24.72 | Rain causes the awakening of crops; gold reveals its innate nature.
Fire is for all beings, but liquor serves both purposes.
6.24.73 | Just as fire reveals the superior, inferior, and middling forms [of fuel], so does liquor reveal the true nature of sentient beings.
6.24.74 | It was fragrant with the scent of garlands and celestial music, well-arranged and free from confusion; it abounded in delicious food and drink, and its conversations were always sweet.

6.24.75 | A drinking session that is easy to drink from, moderately intoxicating, increasing joy and affection, auspicious in its conclusion, characterized by sattva, and not producing excessive intoxication— [is the best].
6.24.76 | Those of a sattvic nature do not suddenly succumb to impairment through the defects of liquor;
for liquor does not suddenly seize a powerful mind.
6.24.77 | Predominantly consisting of pleasant and unpleasant talk, clear and unclear in an instant,
it was wonderful, fallen into a state of passion, and for the most part agitated by its own end.
6.24.78 | A drinking bout that is devoid of joy and pleasant conversation, lacking satisfaction in food and drink,
and ending in delusion, anger, and sleep, is known as tāmasa.
6.24.79 | Having recognized those at the drinking bout who are of a *sāttvika* nature as well as those who are *rājasa* and *tāmasa*,
one should abandon those companions by whose company one incurs the faults of intoxication after drinking.

6.24.80 | Those who are easy in their character, pleasant in conversation, fair-faced, and esteemed by the virtuous; who are not excluded from the arts, clear-minded, and yet inclined toward the objects of the senses.
6.24.81 | Those who are mutually submissive and whose unity arises from friendship,
who increase the drinking bout with exhilaration, affection, and sweetness;
6.24.82 | Those for whom seeing one another is a greater festival than a festival itself—such companions are pleasant in drinking; drinking with them, one rejoices.
6.24.83 | Those who drink [the nectar] with excellent companions, accompanied by delightful forms, fragrances, tastes, touches, and sounds, are indeed equal to those of virtuous deeds.
6.24.84 | One should drink wine at the proper place and time with a joyful inner self, accompanied by the five desirable objects of the senses that are pleasing to the mind.

6.24.85 | Those whose mental and physical constitutions are stable, who have been accustomed to food since childhood, and who have been habituated to large quantities of liquor, do not become intoxicated all at once.

6.24.86 | Those overcome by hunger and thirst, those who are weak, those with a predominance of wind and bile, those who eat dry, small, or measured amounts of food, those with obstructed digestion, and those with weak mental fortitude;
6.24.87 | Men who are prone to anger, those who are unaccustomed [to drink], those who are emaciated, those who are exhausted, and those whose intoxication has been depleted,
quickly become intoxicated even by a small amount of liquor.
6.24.88 | O Agniveśa! Hereafter, I shall explain in due order the origin, the specific characteristics, and the treatment of intoxication (madātyaya).

6.24.89 | He who is excessively emaciated by grief for a woman, fear, heavy burdens, travel, or physical labor; and he who eats dry, scanty, or measured food, yet drinks [liquor] in excessive measure.
6.24.90 | Dry and aged wine, having disturbed sleep at night,
quickly produces in that person an intoxication characterized primarily by wind (vāta).

6.24.91 | One should recognize a case of alcoholism (madātyaya) dominated by Vāta by the presence of hiccups, labored breathing, trembling of the head, pain in the flanks, insomnia, and excessive delirium.
6.24.92 | He who excessively indulges in sharp, hot, and sour liquor,
who eats sour, hot, and sharp food, who is prone to anger, and who delights in fire and the sun;
6.24.93 | For such a person, alcoholism (madātyaya) arises specifically from pitta;
however, in one where vāta is predominant, it either quickly subsides or kills.

6.24.94 | One should recognize a pitta-predominant alcoholism (madātyaya) by thirst, burning sensations, fever, perspiration, fainting, diarrhea, and giddiness, occurring in one whose complexion has turned greenish-yellow.

6.24.95 | He who drinks [alcohol] in excessive measure— whether it be fresh, predominantly sweet, made from molasses (gauḍa), or from flour (paiṣṭika)— and who consumes food that is sweet, unctuous, and heavy;
One who indulges in lack of physical exertion, sleeping during the day, and the pleasures of beds and seats,
quickly succumbs to intoxication characterized by a predominance of phlegm (kapha).

6.24.97 | One should recognize that a case of alcoholism (madātyaya) characterized by a predominance of phlegm (kapha), accompanied by vomiting, anorexia, nausea, drowsiness, a sense of stiffness, and heaviness, occurs when the patient is overwhelmed by cold.
6.24.98 | Those very qualities observed in poison which provoke the *sannipāta* [disorder] are seen in wine as well; however, they are more powerful in poison.
6.24.99 | For some poison kills quickly, while some conduces to disease;
just as it is with poison, so should the intoxication caused by liquor be understood in its final stage.
6.24.100 | Therefore, the symptoms born of all three doṣas are seen in every case of alcoholism; yet, due to the specific nature of their manifestations, its distinctness is also observed.
6.24.101 | There is intense physical suffering, delusion, pain in the heart,
persistent loss of appetite, thirst, and fever characterized by alternating cold and heat.
6.24.102 | A pain like lightning arises in the joints of the bones of the head and sides;
there occurs excessive yawning, throbbing, trembling, and exhaustion.
6.24.103 | Constriction of the chest, cough, hiccup, dyspnea, insomnia,
trembling of the body, diseases of the ears, eyes, and mouth, and stiffness of the sacrum (trika).
6.24.104 | Vomiting, diarrhea, and nausea arise from vāta, pitta, and kapha;
as do dizziness, delirium, and the perception of non-existent forms.
6.24.105 | With his mind deranged, he imagines that the filling [of the moat] with grass, ashes, creepers, leaves, and dust, as well as the attack by birds, is actually being carried out.
6.24.106 | Furthermore, the visions of agitated and inauspicious dreams—
all these symptoms of alcoholism (madātyaya) are observed.

6.24.107 | One should know that all forms of *madātyaya* (alcoholism) involve all three *doṣas*, though one may be predominant; whichever *doṣa* one perceives as being aggravated in *madātyaya*, one should treat that first.
6.24.108 | In cases of alcoholism (madātyaya), treatment should be administered according to the sequence of the seats of *kapha*,
for alcoholism generally culminates in *pitta* and *vāta*.
6.24.109 | Whatever disease arises from wine that is consumed improperly, deficiently,
or excessively, is pacified by that very same wine when it is consumed in the proper measure.

6.24.110 | When the patient has digested [the previous meal], one should administer wine itself to eliminate the disorder caused by undigested food (āmadoṣa). Once the desire for food and lightness have arisen, whatever is beneficial for him should be given.

6.24.111 | One who knows the proper measure should take it cold, mixed with black salt (*sauvarcala*), biḍa salt, and rock salt (*saindhava*), combined with citron and fresh ginger, and diluted with water.
6.24.112 | By drinking excessively of wine that is sharp, hot, sour, and burning,
the moisture of the food essence becomes digested and turns into an alkaline state.
6.24.113 | It quickly produces internal burning, fever, thirst, delusion, confusion, and intoxication; for its pacification, one should administer wine itself.
6.24.114 | For alkaline substances quickly attain sweetness when combined with sour ones. Wine is the best among sour substances; hear now further of its qualities.
6.24.115 | Four secondary tastes are recorded for liquor, which is sour by nature:
sweet, astringent, bitter, and pungent.
6.24.116 | And the ten qualities previously mentioned— by these fourteen qualities,
wine stands superior to all sour substances.
6.24.117 | When the wind (māruta) is obstructed in the channels by doshas that have been vomited up,
it causes intense pain in the head, the bones, and the joints.

6.24.118 | Indeed, for the purpose of discharging the morbid humors (*doṣa*), wine should be given specifically to him because of its pervasive, sharp, and hot qualities, even when other sour substances are available.

6.24.119 | It relieves the obstruction of the channels, acts as a mild intoxicant, promotes the downward movement of the wind (vāyu), improves the appetite, stimulates the digestive fire, and through regular practice, becomes wholesome to the constitution.
6.24.120 | When the channels are unobstructed and the vital wind (māruta) is moving in its natural direction, his pains cease, his disorders recede, and the effects of intoxication are pacified.
6.24.121 | Combined with citron, vṛkṣāmla, kola,
and pomegranate, and sprinkled with the powder of yavānī, hapuṣā, jīraka, and ginger;

6.24.122 | One should administer liquor made from flour (paiṣṭika), mixed with unctuous roasted grain flour (saktu) and garnished with appetizers (avadaṃśa), along with salt, for the pacification of vāta.
6.24.123 | Having observed the symptoms of a predominance of Vāta, one should treat him with meat soups;
specifically, those of the common quail, partridge, and cock, prepared with unctuous and sour ingredients, as well as those of the peacock.
6.24.124 | With seasoned juices of birds, deer, fish, and marsh-dwellers, as well as of burrowers and predators, along with śāli rice.
6.24.125 With unctuous, hot, salty, and sour veśavāra (minced meat) that is pleasing to the palate,
and with various wheat-based foods combined with the scum of vāruṇī liquor;
6.24.126 One should treat a patient with vāta disorders by means of unctuous cake-rolls filled with fresh meat and ginger, as well as with small cakes made of black gram (māṣa).
6.24.127 | Meat that has been previously described as fatty, neither too oily nor combined with sourness, but prepared with black pepper and fresh ginger, or with the juice of pomegranate.
6.24.128 | One should administer it with warm soups, smeared with meat broth, accompanied by separate portions of trijātaka, coriander, black pepper, and fresh ginger, along with warm cakes.
6.24.129 | After eating, one who is thirsty should be given the scum of *vāruṇī* liquor to drink,
or else the juice of pomegranate, or water boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūla*).
6.24.130 Or water with grain and ginger, or even the whey of curd;
or the scum of sour gruel, or even vinegar-water.
6.24.131 | By this perfected practice, the bodily transformation is pacified;
when applied according to the proper measure and duration, strength and complexion increase.
6.24.132 | With various combinations of meat soups and condiments that stimulate the appetite, with meats, vegetables, flour-based foods, barley, wheat, and rice;
6.24.133 | By means of oil massages, rubbing the body, warm baths, thick coverings,
thick pastes of aguru, and dense incenses produced from aguru;
6.24.134 | By the merciless embraces of women heated with youth,
and by the burdens of their hips, thighs, and breasts, which bring the pleasure of intense pressure and warmth;
6.24.135 | By means of warm beds and coverings, and by pleasant, warm inner chambers,
alcoholism characterized by a predominance of wind (māruta) is quickly pacified.
6.24.136 | Mixed with the juices of bhavya, kharjūra, mṛdvīkā, and parūṣaka,
along with the juice of pomegranate, cooled, and sprinkled with roasted grain flour (saktu).
6.24.137 | One should give sugar-cane juice with sugar, or grape wine, or another [fermented liquid],
with plenty of water, at the proper time for drinking in cases of alcoholism caused by pitta.
6.24.138 | One should consume in one's diet śaśas, kapiñjalas, eṇas, ālāvus, and asitapucchakas, along with sweet and sour rice and ṣaṣṭika grains.
6.24.139 | Or one should prepare goat meat broth mixed with paṭola soup,
combined with satīna and mung beans, and accompanied by pomegranate and āmalaka.
6.24.140 Or one may prepare satiating drinks (tarpaṇas), soups (yūṣas), and various kinds of meat broths using the juice of grapes, emblic myrobalan, dates, and wood-apples.

6.24.141 | Having recognized that in alcoholism (madātyaya), kapha and pitta located in the stomach (āmāśaya) have become aggravated in a patient with abundant morbid humors (bahudoṣa) who is burning with heat and suffering from thirst, [one should treat accordingly].
6.24.142 | Having administered wine, grape juice, water, or even a satiating drink (tarpaṇa), one should induce vomiting until it is complete;
thus, one is quickly freed from the disease.
Furthermore, when the time has arrived and is desired, one should perform the sequence beginning with satiation (tarpaṇa).
By that, his digestive fire is kindled, cooking the remainder of the morbid humors (doṣa) along with the food.
In cases of cough accompanied by expectoration of blood, pain in the flanks and breasts,
thirst with a burning sensation, and distress in the heart and chest;
6.24.145 | Or the physician should administer the juice of *guḍūcī*, *bhadramustā*, or *paṭola* along with dry ginger, followed by a meal consisting of partridge meat.
6.24.146 | When there is excessive thirst and vāta and pitta are greatly aggravated,
one should give grape juice to drink— cold and conducive to the downward movement of the doṣas.
6.24.147 | When that has been digested, one should feed him a meal with goat meat broth seasoned with sweet and sour flavors, and one should have him drink wine without subsequent thirst.
6.24.148 | That is the proper measure for one who is not thirsty, by which the mind is not corrupted;
one who is thirsty should be given wine in very small quantities, mixed with plenty of water.
6.24.149 | That by which thirst may be allayed and intoxication not incurred— namely,
the juice of *parūṣaka* and *pīlu* fruits, or even cold water.
6.24.150 | Or one should drink the cool water of four types of leafy trees;
or one should drink a thirst-quenching juice made from musta, pomegranate, and parched grain.
6.24.151 | A paste made from the juice of *kola*, pomegranate, *vṛkṣāmla*, *cukrīkā*, and *cukrikā*—
known as the "five acids" (*pañcāmlaka*)— applied to the mouth immediately subdues thirst.
6.24.152 | Cool foods and drinks, cool beds and seats,
the touch of cool breezes and water, and cool groves.
6.24.153 | The touch of linen, lotuses, water-lilies, gems, and pearls, as well as the touch of sandalwood water cooled by moonbeams, is as refreshing as the rays of the moon.
6.24.154 | Of vessels made of gold, silver, and bronze filled with cold water, and of leather bags filled with ice, struck by the wind—
6.24.155 | The touch of sandalwood moistened with water and of women accompanied by a gentle breeze,
as well as the scent of the finest sandalwoods, are recommended in cases of pitta-type intoxication (madātyaya).
6.24.156 | Whatever else is of cold potency, one should employ all of that;
[as well as] the petals of the kumuda and utpala lotuses sprinkled with sandalwood water.
6.24.157 | When a burning sensation arises from the consumption of wine, pleasant tactile sensations are beneficial,
as are various stories and the auspicious sounds of peacocks.
6.24.158 | Indeed, the sounds of water-bearing clouds, as well as those of water-machines raining down and wind-machines blowing, pacify the disorder of intoxication (madātyaya).
6.24.159 | The physician should provide cooling water-chambers for the burning sensation,
as well as the fruits of *phalinī*, *sevya*, *lodhra*, water, gold leaf, and *kuṭannaṭa*.

6.24.160 | An ointment combined with *kālīyaka* resin is recommended for burning sensations; likewise, an ointment derived from the tender leaves of the *badarī* tree or produced from *ariṣṭaka* is beneficial.
6.24.161 | An ointment made from the foam of soap-nut (phenilā) is beneficial for application during cauterization;
likewise are fermented liquor with its scum, sour curd, citron juice, and honey.

6.24.162 | For sprinkling and external application, acidic gruels (kāñjika) that destroy burning sensations are recommended, as well as for pouring over the body, immersion baths, and the consumption of side dishes.
6.24.163 | Cold water is recommended for the alleviation of burning sensations and thirst; by means of this treatment applied according to the proper dosage and time, [the affliction] is pacified.
6.24.164 | For an intelligent patient who is compliant with the physician, pitta-type madātyaya is quickly overcome;
one should conquer kapha-type madātyaya through emesis and fasting.
6.24.165 | And if he is thirsty, one should give him water prepared with hrīvera,
or boiled with balā, pṛśniparṇī, or kaṇṭakārī.
6.24.166 | Or water boiled and cooled with all the aforementioned ingredients including *nāgara*,
or with *duḥsparśā* and *mustā*, or with *mustā* and *parpaṭaka*.
6.24.167 | One should also give water boiled with *musta* to digest the morbid humors (*doṣa*).
This very same water is to be used in all cases of alcoholism (*madātyaya*).
6.24.168 | When it has been digested without complication, one should have the patient drink that [milk], which destroys thirst and fever,
is free from undigested matter (āmadoṣa), and is desired at the proper time, mixed with honey.
6.24.169 | [One may take] sugar-cane wine, or aged honey-wine (*madhu*), or *ariṣṭa*, or even *sīdhu*,
combined with parching and nourishing agents, and mixed with *yavānī* and *nāgara*.
6.24.170 | One should feed [the patient] food made from barley or wheat along with unctuousless soup,
or with the juice of well-dried horse gram (kulattha) or radish (mūlaka).
6.24.171 | With a small, light, and thin meal containing pungent and sour flavors and little ghee,
one should consume either the sour soup of *paṭola* or the soup of *āmalaka*.
6.24.172 One should cause [the patient] to be given food with barley that is abundant in pungent and sour [flavors],
or a broth of the three pungents (vyoṣa) that is sour, or a broth with sour vetasa.
6.24.173 | Goat meat broth that is dry and sour, or the broth of wild game,
fried in a pot or on a pan until the liquid has evaporated.
6.24.174 | Eating meat that is pungent, sour, and salty, one may choose honey;
or meat made manifest with black pepper, combined with the juice of mātuluṅga.
6.24.175 | Combined with abundant pungent substances, mixed with *yavānī* and *nāgara*,
fried, soured with the essence of pomegranate, and wrapped in warm bread.
6.24.176 | Just as one might consume fire at the proper time along with abundant slices of fresh ginger,
so too should one drink pure liquor when alcoholism (madātyaya) is predominantly characterized by phlegm (kapha).
Sauvarcala salt, cumin, vṛkṣāmla, āmalaka, and vetasa,
combined with one-quarter part each of cinnamon, cardamom, and black pepper, and joined with an equal portion of sugar.
6.24.178 | This eight-ingredient salt is a supreme stimulant for the digestive fire;
one should administer it in cases of alcoholism (madātyaya) where kapha predominates, as it cleanses the bodily channels.
6.24.179 | Furthermore, this very [preparation], when processed with sweet and sour liquids and fermented,
is an excellent appetizer for wheat-based foods, barley-based foods, and various meats.
6.24.180 | One should grind white grapes that are seedless and combined with pungent substances,
using either the juice of citron or pomegranate.
6.24.181 | This sauce, prepared with sauvarcala salt, cardamom, black pepper, cumin, bhṛṅga, and dīpyaka, combined with honey, is excellent for promoting relish and stimulating digestion.
6.24.182 | One should prepare the *kāravī* preparation according to the same method as that for *mṛdvīkā*.
Combined with fermented gruel (*śukta*) and sugar candy (*matsyaṇḍikā*), it is a sauce (*rāga*) that stimulates digestion and promotes digestion.
6.24.183 | One should prepare separate syrups from the pulps of mango and emblic myrobalan,
seasoned with coriander, sauvarcala salt, cumin, kāravī, and black pepper.
6.24.184 | Food mixed with jaggery and honey, and seasoned with distinct sourness and saltiness, becomes palatable; thus smeared, it is properly relished and digested.
6.24.185 | By means of dry and hot food and drink, by bathing in non-cold water, and through the proper application of physical exercise, fasting, and staying awake.
6.24.186 By means of dry bathing and rubbing powders applied at the appropriate time, and by the use of fragrant unguents that enhance the vitality and complexion of the body.
6.24.187 By the service of garments and even by that of heavy incense,
and by the service of women whose limbs find pleasure in the warmth of the sun's contraction.
6.24.188 | Furthermore, by means of massage performed by women whose hands are well-trained,
alcoholism characterized primarily by an excess of *kapha* is quickly pacified.
6.24.189 | This treatment which has been specified according to the individual strength of each doṣa must be adapted by a learned physician for the ten types of sannipāta.

6.24.190 | He who understands the variations of the doshas, who knows the variations of medicinal drugs, and who discerns the distinction between curable and incurable diseases— he shall successfully treat those diseases that are curable.
Delightful forests, lakes filled with lotuses,
pure food and drink, and cheering companions.
Garlands, fragrant preparations, and spotless garments;
the sounds of music and assemblies dear to the heart.
Clear and engaging conversations, laughter, songs,
and the company of beloved, devoted women destroy the disorder of intoxication.
6.24.194 | For intoxication does not cause *madātyaya* (alcoholism) unless it agitates the mind and impairs the body; therefore, a practice that induces exhilaration should be desired.
6.24.195 | By means of these successful therapeutic measures, alcoholism (madātyaya) subsides;
if this does not occur, one should administer milk to the patient while abstaining from the rules regarding alcohol.
6.24.196 | When the intoxication has been dispelled by means of fasting, digestive stimulants, purificatory treatments for the humors, and palliative measures,
and when the phlegm is diminished and weakness and lightness have arisen;
For one who is impaired by alcohol and has a predominance of wind and bile,
milk is like rain to a tree scorched by the summer heat.
6.24.198 | When the disease has been alleviated by the use of milk and strength has been restored, one should discontinue the administration of milk;
furthermore, one should gradually consume wine in very small quantities.
6.24.199 | If one who has abstained from liquor for a long time suddenly indulges in excessive drinking,
the diseases known as dhvaṃsaka and vikṣaya arise in him.
6.24.200 | For those two [conditions] are most difficult to treat when the body is exhausted by disease;
their symptoms and treatment will now be taught correctly.
Excessive salivation, dryness of the throat and mouth, intolerance of sound,
and excessive drowsiness and sleep are to be known as the symptoms of Dhvaṃsaka.
Heart disease, throat disease, delusion, vomiting, body ache, fever, thirst,
cough, and headache— these are the symptoms of wasting (kṣaya).
6.24.203 | That same treatment which is prescribed for alcoholism caused by wind (vātika) is desired for those two [conditions],
for they indeed arise in one who is weak and whose bodily constituents have been depleted.
6.24.204 | Enemas, the drinking of ghee, the application of milk and ghee,
as well as massage, dry powdering, bathing, and food and drink that alleviate Vata [are recommended].
6.24.205 | By this practice, the wasting disease and consumption are pacified; for one who is disciplined, no disease arising from intoxication occurs today.
6.24.206 | That wise man who has desisted from all intoxicants and has conquered his senses is not afflicted by physical or mental disorders.

6.24.207 | Regarding this, there are these verses: The power of the divine goddess Surā, how she is to be drunk, what substances she consists of, for whom she is intended, what her action is, and the manner in which she requires a specific formulation.
6.24.208 | How intoxication exhilarates, by which qualities the Great Virtue (Mahāguṇa) is endowed,
what intoxication is, and the three distinct types of intoxication each with their own specific characteristics.
6.24.209 | Furthermore, the defects caused by intoxicants, the qualities inherent in intoxication, the three types of drinking bouts, and the characteristics according to one's temperament;

6.24.210 | Those companions who are pleasant during drinking, and those men whose intoxication is slow or rapid, [are mentioned]; as well as the cause of alcoholism (madātyaya), its symptoms, and how it occurs.
6.24.211 | Alcohol, the diseases arising from alcohol, and whatever therapeutic regimen exists—
all that has been explained in its entirety in the treatment of alcoholism (madātyaya).
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Alcoholism," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.
Chapter Twenty-five:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the treatment of the two types of ulcers (dvivraṇīyacikitsita).
6.25.2 Thus indeed said the blessed Ātreya.
6.25.3 | At the proper time, Agniveśa spoke these words with humility to his teacher, Mātreya— who knew both the higher and the lower truths, and who was free from pride and mental distress.
6.25.4 | O Blessed One, bestower of happiness! You previously mentioned two types of wounds in the summary of diseases; you should now describe their symptoms and treatment.
6.25.5 | Having heard these words of Agniveśa, the Teacher said:
"Regarding those two types of ulcers previously mentioned—the endogenous and the exogenous—"
6.25.6 | Listen duly, gentle one! to their symptoms and the remedy. The endogenous [disease] arises from the bodily humors (*doṣa*), while the exogenous is born from external causes.

6.25.7 | Likewise, wounds resulting from slaughter, binding, falling, or injuries caused by fangs, teeth, and claws— whether exogenous or produced by contact with poison, fire, or weapons— are similar [in their treatment].

6.25.8 | By means of mantras, anti-poisonous applications, ointments, and other medicines, as well as by their causes and partial symptoms, they are identified; however, they are the opposite of those [caused by] one's own [intrinsic] ulcers.
6.25.9 For wounds that do not subside— whether endogenous, caused by external factors, or both—
one should administer medicine according to the strength of the involved *doṣas*, just as one treats endogenous wounds.
6.25.10 Just as the vitiated wind, bile, and phlegm of humans, through their respective causes,
resort to external pathways and produce endogenous ulcers.
6.25.11 | A wound arising from wind (māruta) is stiff, hard to the touch, with scanty discharge and extremely intense pain; it pricks, throbs, and becomes darkish in color.
6.25.12 | One should treat a Vata-type ulcer with replenishing therapies, intake of fats (oleation), unctuous fomentations and poultices, as well as with emollient applications and affusions.
6.25.13 | One should recognize a wound caused by *pitta* by thirst, delusion, fever, sweating, burning, corruption, and tearing, as well as by its odors and putrid discharges.
6.25.14 | One should pacify a pitta-type ulcer with cold, sweet, and bitter applications as plasters and affusions, as well as by the drinking of ghee and purgation therapies.
6.25.15 | A wound caused by *kapha* is characterized by abundant pus, heaviness, oiliness, numbness, and mild pain; it is pale in color, has little discharge, and heals slowly.
6.25.16 | One should pacify a Kapha-type ulcer with astringent, pungent, dry, and hot applications as plasters and affusions,
as well as by means of fasting and digestive treatments.
6.25.17 | These two, distinguished by their various types, constitute the twenty wounds. Their examination is threefold; twelve are considered to be vitiated.
6.25.18 | There are likewise eight locations, eight types of odors, fourteen discharges,
sixteen complications, four doshas, and twenty [other factors].
6.25.19 | Likewise, thirty-six established introductory topics have been proclaimed;
hear from me all of these as they have been described in detail.
6.25.20 | It may be excisable or non-excisable, malignant or non-malignant, located in a vital spot or not;
it may be concealed, severe, discharging, poisonous, or situated in a precarious position.

6.25.21 | One should recognize that among these, those located on the lap (*utsaṅgya*) are healed, while those on the opposite side are not. Thus, twenty types of wounds have been defined according to their various distinctions.
6.25.22 | Examination is traditionally held to be threefold: by observation, questioning, and palpation. [The first] is by means of observing the age, complexion, body, and the sense organs.
6.25.23 | The wise should examine the strength of the causes, the seasons, suitability, and the digestive fire based on verbal testimony;
they should also examine softness and coldness through touch, as well as their opposites.
6.25.24 | White, with sunken eyelids, with excessively thick eyelids,
excessively yellowish-brown, blue, dark-brown, with excessive pustules, red, black, and excessively foul-smelling;
6.25.25 | The Ropya and Kumbhīmukha types—these twelve are the severely corrupted ulcers. Indeed, twenty-four [types] have been described according to another classification system.
6.25.26 | Skin, vessels, muscle, fat, bone, ligaments, vital points (marmans), and the internal cavities—
these eight are specified in summary as the locations of ulcers.
6.25.27 | Ghee, oil, muscle fat, pus, blood, dark (śyāva), sour, and putrid—
these eight odors are proclaimed by those who know the scent of wounds as belonging to ulcers.
6.25.28 | They are turbid with lymph, water, pus, and blood; they are yellowish, reddish, and tawny;
they are astringent, blue, green, oily, dry, white, and black.
6.25.29 | Thus, the fourteen types of wound discharges have been described by their characteristics:
erysipelas (visarpa), hemiplegia (pakṣaghāta), stiffness of the vessels (sirāstambha), and facial paralysis (apatānaka).
6.25.30 | Madness, intoxication, wounds, pain, fever,
thirst, lockjaw, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, hiccups, dyspnea, and tremors [arise].
6.25.31 | Sixteen complications of wounds have been described by those who contemplate wounds:
due to the moistening of the ligaments, the moistening of the vessels, depth, and infestation by worms.
6.25.32 | Due to the piercing of bones, the presence of a splinter, being poisoned, or crawling over [the body];
due to the scratching of nails or wood, and from excessive friction against skin and hair.
6.25.33 | From improper bandaging, excessive affection, excessive depletion by medicine,
indigestion, overeating, and the consumption of incompatible or unwholesome food.
6.25.34 | Wounds do not subside due to grief, anger, sleeping during the day, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and likewise from the lack of activity on the part of embodied beings.
6.25.35 | Due to discharge, odor, and the presence of morbid humors along with complications,
wounds with many defects become difficult to treat.

6.25.36 | A wound arising in the skin and flesh, located in a favorable region, occurring in a young person, free from complications, appearing in a wise patient at a suitable time, and being recent, is considered easily curable.
6.25.37 | A wound is considered difficult to treat when it is deficient in any of these qualities; however, one that is devoid of all of them should be known as incurable and beyond treatment.
6.25.38 | From the very beginning, purification of wounds should be performed according to their proximity by means of emetics, purgatives, surgical instruments,
and enemas.
6.25.39 | Indeed, the wounds of those whose bodies have been immediately purified subside. Hereafter, listen in due order to all the therapeutic measures.
6.25.40 | Sixfold is the treatment for swelling: surgical intervention, compression, excision, suturing, sudation, and pacification, as well as probing.
6.25.41 | There are two decoctions for cleansing and healing, along with two for external application; there are two oils with similar properties, one for covering, and two types of bandaging.
6.25.42 | Diet, massage, and the two types of cauterization—
dry and with an unguent— as well as fumigation and ointments that produce firmness or softness, are beneficial.
6.25.43 | It is dusting the wound, coloring it, healing it, and causing hair to grow.
Thus, thirty-six treatments for wounds have been described.
6.25.44 | Having recognized swelling as the premonitory sign of ulcers from the very beginning,
the physician should perform bloodletting for the sake of pacifying the ulcer before it has formed.

6.25.45 | One should purify those with many morbid humors (doṣas), but those with few doṣas one should treat with fasting (vilaṅghana). Alternatively, one should first conquer disorders dominated by Vāta with decoctions and medicated ghees (sarpis).
6.25.46 | A plaster made from the bark of *vyāghra*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and *vetasa*,
mixed with clarified butter, is the best for cooling and subduing swelling.
6.25.47 | Vijayā, madhuka, vīrā, bisagranthi, śatāvarī, nīlotpala, nāgapuṣpa, and candana should be used as a pradeha (a medicinal paste).

6.25.48 | A poultice consisting of roasted grain flour (saktu), licorice (madhuka), and ghee, mixed with sugar, should be applied; furthermore, foods that do not cause burning sensations are the best medicine for swelling.
6.25.49 | If the swelling, despite being treated in this manner, does not subside, then once it has suppurated, surgical incision is said to be beneficial.

6.25.50 | A poultice (upanāha) made of either oil, clarified butter (sarpir), or a combination of both, mixed with balls of roasted grain flour (saktupiṇḍikā) and applied while lukewarm, is recommended for the purpose of ripening an inflammatory swelling (śopha).
6.25.51 | A bolus made of barley meal mixed with sesame, linseed, sour curd,
yeast, kuṣṭha, and salt is recommended for use as a poultice (upanāhana).

6.25.52 | One should diagnose a swelling as being "burnt" (vidagdha) by means of pain, burning sensations, redness, and piercing pricks; one should diagnose it as "fully ripened" (saṃpakva) when its touch is like that of a water-bladder and it rises up when pressed.
6.25.53 | Umā, guggulu, saudha, the milk of the dakṣa and kapota plants, the resin produced from the palāśa tree, kṣāra, hemakṣīrī, and mukūlaka.

6.25.54 | Thus has been described the group of medicinal preparations for incising suppurated swellings; however, for a patient who is delicate or for a difficult case, surgery is said to be the ultimate recourse.
6.25.55 | Incision, puncturing, excision, as well as application [of drugs],
scarification, and suturing— this is the sixfold surgical procedure.
6.25.56 | Fistulous ulcers, suppurated swellings, abdominal enlargement due to a perforated anus,
swellings containing internal foreign bodies, and those of similar nature, are to be incised.
6.25.57 | Ascites that has reached suppuration, all types of abdominal tumors (gulma), those born from blood,
diseases of the blood requiring venesection, erysipelas, carbuncles, and the like [should be treated with bloodletting].
6.25.58 | For ulcers that are protruding, thick-edged, elevated, and hard, as well as for hemorrhoids and similar conditions, the wise physician should treat them by means of excision.
6.25.59 | A wise person should scrape off kilāsa (leucoderma) lesions along with kuṣṭha;
likewise, vātāsṛj, granthi, piḍakā, koṭha, and raktamaṇḍala.
6.25.60 | The physician should scarify skin diseases, a wounded limb, and swellings;
however, that which is deep, such as an incision in the abdomen or the belly, should be sutured.
6.25.61 | Thus, six types of surgical procedures have been described by the wise.
One should apply pressure to those wounds that have narrow openings and possess a cavity.
6.25.62 | Kalāya, masūra, wheat, and hareṇu,
when made into a paste and applied without oil, are highly recommended for the alleviation of pain in ulcers.
6.25.63 | The bark of the śālmalī tree, the root of balā, and likewise the tender leaves of the nyagrodha—
this is designated as the nyagrodhādi group, or alternatively, the balādi group.
6.25.64 | One should know that there is an ointment, an effusion, and an irrigation with these [substances]:
with ghee washed a hundred times, with milk, and with water decocted from madhuka.
6.25.65 | One should soothe with very cold [applications] ulcers in which blood and pitta predominate;
having smeared hanging ulcer-flesh with honey and ghee, one should treat them.
6.25.66 | The physician should join [the bone] evenly and secure it with bandages;
once he knows them to be properly aligned and stable, he should treat them with *phalinī*, *lodhra*, and *kaṭphala*.
6.25.67 | One should dust the area with the powdered *samaṅgā* and *dhātakī*,
or with the powder of the five barks (*pañcavalkala*) combined with the powder of oyster shells.
6.25.68 | Or, by means of the powders of dhātakī and lodhra, those wounds heal;
one should likewise set a fractured bone or a dislocated joint back into its proper alignment.
6.25.69 | Having made it equal with another limb that is equal [in size], the skillful physician,
having established it firmly with bandages of cloth-pads and splints, [proceeds].
6.25.70 | One should bind it firmly and comfortably with strips of cloth soaked in abundant ghee. Furthermore, one should treat the patient with non-burning foods made from flour products.
For exhaustion is not beneficial for him, as it causes the dislocation of joints;
it leads to complications such as erysipelas in those whose limbs have been displaced or injured.

6.25.72 | One who knows the proper time should administer treatment according to the season through one's own medical science. Those ulcers which are dry, intensely painful, stiff, and dominated by Vāta should be treated with sudation using a mixture of *kṛśara* and *pāyasa*.
6.25.73 | A person with an ulcer may likewise find relief through preparations made from village-grown vegetables, lotus stalks, and meat soups, as well as by warm poultices (utkārikā).
6.25.74 | For those ulcers characterized by burning sensations and pain, which are dominated by wind (vāta),
one should apply umā seeds and sesame seeds that have been fried and then soaked in milk.
6.25.75 | Having ground those very same ingredients with milk, the physician should apply it as an ointment.
[The drugs are: balā, guḍūcī, madhuka, pṛśniparṇī, and śatāvarī.
6.25.76 | Jīvantī, sugar, milk, oil, fish fat, and ghee,
prepared together with beeswax, form a "fat-sugar" (sneha-śarkarā) that destroys colic.
6.25.77 | One should perform a sprinkling with lukewarm water decocted with the two groups of five roots (*dvipañcamūla*), or with milk,
or with ghee mixed with oil.
6.25.78 | One should apply a lukewarm plaster consisting of barley powder, madhuka, and sesame seeds, mixed with ghee, for the alleviation of burning sensations and pain.
6.25.79 | A poultice of sesame seeds and mung-bean milk-porridge should be applied;
this procedure is beneficial for alleviating pain and burning sensations in wounds.
6.25.80 | Those ulcers which have narrow openings, profuse discharge, and possess cavities,
provided they do not involve vital spots (marma), are said to benefit from probing (eṣaṇa).
6.25.81 | One should know that the probe (eṣaṇī) is of two kinds: soft and hard.

6.25.82 | In a wound that is deep and fleshy, the physician should know that it is to be probed with a metal probe; however, he should recognize a wound as requiring a director (eṣya) by means of its orifices, and the opposite of this for other types.
6.25.83 | Recognizing wounds that are foul-smelling, discolored, profusely exuding, and highly painful as being impure, one should treat them with purifying measures.
6.25.84 | Triphalā, khadira, dārvī, the group beginning with vaṭa (nyagrodhādi), balā, and kuśa;

6.25.85 | A paste of sesame seeds mixed with salt, the two types of turmeric, trivṛt, ghee,
madhuka, and nimba leaves constitute a topical application that purifies wounds.

6.25.86 | A wound that is neither excessively red, nor excessively pale, nor excessively dark, nor excessively painful; which is neither elevated nor has a raised margin, is pure and ready for healing.
6.25.87 | Nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, kadamba, plakṣa, vetasa,
karavīra, arka, and kuṭaja are astringent decoctions that promote the healing of wounds.
6.25.88 | Sandalwood, lotus filaments, the bark of *dārvī*, blue water-lily, the two types of *medā*,
*mūrvā*, *samaṅgā*, and liquorice are a healing agent for wounds.
6.25.89 | One should apply as a paste to a wound a mixture of prapauṇḍarīka, jīvantī, gojihvā, dhātakī, balā, and sesame seeds, along with ghee, for the purpose of healing.
6.25.90 | Kampillaka, viḍaṅga, vatsaka, triphalā, balā, paṭola,
picumarda, lodhra, musta, and priyaṅgu.
6.25.91 | Having ground khadira, dhātakī, sarja, elā, aguru, and candana, oil should be prepared; that is the supreme healer for wounds.
6.25.92 | Oil prepared with equal parts of prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, the two types of kākoli, and the two types of candana is supreme for the healing of wounds.
6.25.93 | Alternatively, oil prepared with the fresh juice of dūrvā grass, or with kampillaka,
or with a paste of dārvī bark, is a primary healer of wounds.
6.25.94 | By the very same procedure used for oil, one should prepare ghee;
having observed that blood and pitta predominate, the physician should treat the ulcer with healing (ropaṇīya) measures.
6.25.95 | For the covering of wounds, the wise physician should prescribe the leaves of the kadamba, arjuna, nimba, pāṭalī, pippala, and also of the arka plant.

6.25.99 | One should prepare those substances which are galactagogues, vitalizers, and nourishing agents for the purpose of elevating depressed ulcers.
6.25.100 | Bhūrja, granthi, aśmaka, kāsīsa, guggulu, and the lower part [of the plant];

6.25.101 | When blood flows excessively, when the excisable [flesh] has been cut, in cases of excessive granulation tissue (adhimāṃsaka),

6.25.102 | In cases where pus and serum are hidden, where the ulcers are deep and firm,

6.25.103 | One who understands the specific varieties of cauterization should apply heat using beeswax, oil, marrow, honey, fat, or clarified butter, or by means of various heated metals.
6.25.104 | For those ulcers that are dry, delicate, deep-seated, or dominated by vāta, one should cauterize them with fats, beeswax, or metals; otherwise, one should use honey.

6.25.108 | Ulcers become firm when fumigated with fragrant resins;

6.25.113 | With the fruits of *kakubha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *lodhra*, *jambava*, and *kaṭphala*, one quickly obtains skin; wounds sprinkled with the powder of these barks heal swiftly.

6.25.115 | A paste made of iron filings, green vitriol (kasīsa), and the flowers of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) produces blackness instantly on fresh skin.
6.25.116 | A plaster made of kālīyaka, natā, tāmra, asthi, hemakānta, and the best of the arasas, combined with cow-dung juice, is the supreme means for restoring one's natural complexion.
6.25.117 | The roots of the *dhyāmaka*, *aśvattha*, and *nicula* trees; lac; red ochre; gold; *amṛtāsaṅga*; and green vitriol (*kāsīsa*)—these constitute a color-enhancing compound.

6.25.118 | By means of the skin, hair, hooves, horns, bones, and ashes of four-footed animals, the ground, when sprinkled with oil and sprinkled with their powder, becomes possessed of hair once again.
6.25.119 | Furthermore, regarding the sixteen complications that have been described for wounds,

6.25.120 | Regarding this, there are two verses: The two types of wounds, the classifications of wounds, their examination, and their corruption; their locations, odors, and discharges, along with their complications and the therapeutic measures to be employed.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of the Two Types of Ulcers," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Twenty-six:
Now, we shall expound the chapter on the treatment of the three vital organs (marmans).
6.26.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
6.26.3 | Regarding the one hundred and seven vital points (*marmas*) mentioned in relation to the enumeration of the body,

6.26.4 | Because they are the substratum of the vital breaths— for by afflicting them, the winds and other humors afflict the life-breaths themselves—

6.26.15 | A powder of *rakṣoghna*, *tumbī*, *karahāṭa*, and *kṛṣṇā*, or one containing *jīmūtaka* and rock salt,

6.26.16 | When these [complications] arise, the physician should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to one whose body has been well-anointed and properly fomented—

6.26.17 | When wind (vāta) is predominant, [the enema] should be sour and salty with oil; when bile (pitta), it should be with milk; but when phlegm (kapha), it should be with urine.
This quickly removes the obstruction of urine, feces, and wind, and restores the rectum and the vessels to their normal state.

6.26.18 | One should eat barley-based food with the juices of *trivṛt*, sudhā leaves, sesame, and vegetables, as well as those of domestic, aquatic, and marshy animals; these should be prepared so as to promote the free flow of flatus, urine, and feces. One should also drink *prasannā* wine, molasses, and *sīdhu*.
6.26.19 | If there is further persistence [of the disease], the patient should be purged with clear urine, *dadhimanda* (the watery part of curd), and vinegar;

6.26.28 | In cases such as the killing of vultures and cranes, or in wind-diseases (vātaroga) where purgation is indicated,

6.26.29 | Castor oil is recommended when combined with milk, meat broths, or with the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā), vegetable soups, urine, or wine,
according to the association of the involved bodily humors (doṣas).

6.26.30 | Because it is by nature a wind-alleviator, and because it acts as a purgative through its combination [with other drugs], it overcomes diseases of Vāta mixed with fat, blood, pitta, and kapha; therefore, it is a conqueror of such ailments.

6.26.32 | From excessive physical exertion, the use of sharp medicines, dry substances, habitual consumption of wine, constant riding on the back of a horse,

6.26.33 | When the humors (doṣas), either individually provoked by their own specific causes or all together having reached a state of aggravation,

6.26.54 | Alkaline, hot, and pungent medicines, food and drink, sudation, barley-based diet, emesis, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), buttermilk,

6.26.55 | One should drink *vyoṣa*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *truṭi*, and the marrow of *sārasa* bones in the quantity of a *kola*, combined with honey and urine;

6.26.84 | A paste made from puṣkaramūla, phalapūra, mahauṣadha, śaṭī,
and abhayā, mixed with alkali-water, ghee, and salt, destroys vāta-type heart disease and vikartikā.
6.26.85 | A decoction prepared from puṣkara, mātuluṅga, palāśa, bhūtīka, śaṭī, and surāhva, along with nāgara, rājāñjana, vacā, yavānī, and alkali (kṣāra), should be drunk lukewarm and salted.

6.26.86 | A paste made from *pathyā*, *śaṭī*, *pauṣkara*, the five spices (*pañcakola*), and *mātuluṅga*— prepared with equal parts and fried with jaggery, *prasannā* wine, and salt— is used for pain in the heart, the flanks, the back, the abdomen, and the female reproductive organs.
6.26.87 | There should be the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the two myrobalans (triphalā) with pāṭhā, nidigdhikā, gokṣuraka, the two types of balā,
ṛddhi, truṭi, tāmalakī, svaguptā, the two types of medā, madhūka, madhuka, and sthirā.

6.26.88 | A knower of the procedure should cook one *prastha* of ghee with these well-ground ingredients— one *akṣa* each of *śatāvarī*, *jīvaka*, and *pṛśniparṇī*— along with one *prastha* of buffalo curd.
6.26.89 | One should administer it in a dose of one mātrā, a pala, half a pala, or a picu, combined with honey, in cases of asthma,
cough, anemia, jaundice, cardiac distress, and disorders of the duodenum (grahaṇī).
6.26.90 | When the heart is afflicted by pitta, cooling plasters, sprinklings, and purgation are indicated;
once purified, however, food and drink that alleviate pitta should be taken with grapes, sugar, honey, and *parūṣaka*.

6.26.91 | One should also drink a paste made from yaṣṭyāhvā and tiktakarohiṇī with sugar-water. In cases of chest wounds (kṣata), medicated ghees and ghee-jaggery preparations (sarpirguḍas) are beneficial, provided they are properly administered after careful consideration.
6.26.92 | A physician should administer meat juices from desert animals to those who subsist on cow's milk when afflicted by diseases caused by pitta;
by these alone, all pitta-related disorders, even those localized in the blood, are pacified.
6.26.93 | Buffalo ghee prepared with milk and [the following drugs]— raisins, balā, śreyasī, sugar, dates, vīra, ṛṣabhaka, utpala, the two types of kākolī, medā, and jīvaka— is beneficial.
6.26.94 | One should cook kaśerukā, śaivala, śṛṅgavera, prapauṇḍarīka, madhuka, lotus stalks, and their nodes with ghee and milk; this, when combined with honey, removes pitta and cures diseases.

6.26.95 | Ghee prepared with the paste of the *sthira* group of drugs and milk, or with grape juice or sugarcane juice, is beneficial; likewise, very cold juices derived from sweet fruits and sugarcane are wholesome when the heart is afflicted by pitta.
6.26.96 | For one who has undergone sudation, emesis, or fasting, and who suffers from diseases of *kapha* affecting the vital organs (*marmans*), a treatment that subdues *kapha* is indicated:
this includes barley-based foods prepared with the soups of horse-gram (*kulattha*) and other grains, as well as sharp drinks and various mixed preparations (*śaṅkaras*).
6.26.97 | Kaṭphala, śṛṅgavera, pītadru, pathyā, and ativiṣā, boiled in urine, should be administered;
as should the powder of kṛṣṇā, śaṭī, puṣkaramūla, rāsnā, vacā, abhayā, and nāgara.

6.26.98 | A linctus prepared from a decoction of the trees known as udumbara, aśvattha, vaṭa, and arjuna, along with pālāśa, rauhitaka, and khādira, combined with the powder of trivṛt and tryūṣaṇa, destroys kapha when taken with non-cold water.

6.26.99 | Or the physician, remaining vigilant, should administer the substance known as śilājatu according to the prescribed ritual; likewise, he may give the *prāśa*, the *āgastya* linctus, the *brāhma* rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), or that of *āmalakī*.
6.26.100 | In a disease born of the three doṣas, fasting should be performed first; furthermore, food that is beneficial for all [three] should be prescribed.
Having considered whether the condition is mild, excessive, or moderate, the appropriate treatment for all three should be carried out.

6.26.101 | If it is digested after eating, it causes colic; if it remains undigested for a long time, he should drink a decoction of devadāru, kuṣṭha, tilvaka, the two salts (rock salt and sauvarcala), viḍaṅga, and ativiṣā with warm water.
6.26.102 | When [the medicine] has been digested, if there is an excess [of doshas], there should be an unctuous purgative; if it is being digested, one should be purged with fruits.
However, when colic is excessive during all three stages [of digestion], a sharp root-purgative is beneficial.

6.26.103 | Generally, when the movement of the wind (vāyu) is obstructed, it becomes aggravated in the stomach (āmāśaya); therefore, purification (śodhana) must be performed, as well as fasting (laṅghana), digestive treatments (pācana), and all remedies for worms (kṛmighna), in cases of worm-induced heart disease.

Thus ends the treatment of heart disease (hṛdroga). 6.26.104. [Heart disease is caused] by suppression of natural urges, indigestion, dust, excessive speaking, anger, irregularity of the seasons, headache, staying awake at night, excessive sleep, cold water, exposure to dew, sexual intercourse, tears, and smoke.

6.26.105 | When Vāyu increases in the head due to the defect of stagnation (saṃstyāna), it brings about catarrh (pratiśyāya). From this wind arise nasal pain and piercing, sneezing, a watery appearance, discharge, hoarseness, and diseases of the head.
6.26.106 | From pitta arise inflammation of the tip of the nose, fever, dryness of the mouth, thirst, heat, and yellow discharges;
from kapha arise cough, anorexia, thick secretions, excessive salivation, heaviness, and itching in the channels.
6.26.107 | All the symptoms of the humors combined may occur in a case of pīnasa (nasal catarrh) characterized by intense pain and extreme suffering.
When all [the humors] are excessively aggravated due to unwholesome diet, neglected chronic rhinitis becomes a malignant pratiśyāya.
6.26.108 | Thereafter, diseases arise: sneezing, dryness of the nose, nasal obstruction, and discharge;
foul odor of the nostrils, chronic rhinitis (apīnasa), as well as inflammation, swelling, tumors, and the presence of pus and blood.

6.26.109 | From that [vitiation], wounds, diseases of the head, ears, and eyes, baldness, and the greying or whitening of the hair occur; furthermore, thirst, dyspnea, cough, fever, internal hemorrhaging (rakta-pitta), hoarseness, and emaciation arise.

6.26.110 | One should declare that to be corrupted coryza (duṣṭapratiśyāya) in which the nose is afflicted by obstruction, impact, discharge, dryness, or suppuration; where one does not perceive odors;
where the mouth is foul-smelling; and which is frequently aggravated.
6.26.111 | When the Vāyu, situated on its various pathways, touches the vital points (marmans) at the head, it causes sneezing.
When provoked, it dries up the Kapha, resulting in the desiccation of the nasal passages, the *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and the nose itself.
6.26.112 | When phlegm, along with wind, obstructs the passage of exhalation, one should call that condition *pratīnāha*.
When thick, yellowish-green phlegm flows from the brain (*mastuluṅga*), this is indeed *parisrava*.
6.26.113 | Discoloration and foul odor may be disregarded, but putrid rhinitis, swelling, and vertigo [are serious];
for one whose nose becomes constricted, dried up, excessively moist, or emits a smoky smell, [this condition is grave].
6.26.114 | A person who does not perceive smells and tastes, yet persists in his habitual activities, should be diagnosed with apīnasa;
one should declare this disorder to be born of vāta and kapha, possessing symptoms identical to those of pratiśyāya (catarrh).
6.26.115 | From the vitiation of blood and pitta, there occurs a swelling of the nose accompanied by suppuration and discharge, as well as inflammation of the nasal passages (ghrāṇapāka).
Furthermore, the morbid humors (malas), having corrupted the blood and other tissues located in the nose, produce swelling of the nostrils.
6.26.116 | Likewise, by obstructing the passage of exhalation in the nose, tumors may arise due to the corruption of flesh and blood;
or blood mixed with bile, or even pus and blood, may flow from the nose, the ears, or the mouth.

6.26.117 | When vāta, combined with pitta, vitiates the skin and other tissues, it produces ulcers accompanied by suppuration. That disease in which a person's nose feels as if it were on fire is declared to be *dīpta*.
Thus ends the diagnosis of diseases of the nose (6.26.118).
In this condition, due to *vāta*, there is intense pain and throbbing; due to *pitta*, there is burning pain and distress; and due to *kapha*, it becomes heavy.
When all three *doṣas* are involved, or when caused by worms (*krimi*), the head becomes characterized by itching, foul odor, piercing pain, and distress.
Thus ends the diagnosis of diseases of the head (śiroroga).
In diseases of the mouth (mukhāmaya) caused by vāta, there is dryness, roughness, and parchedness, along with shifting pains;
the discharge is blackish-red and cold, accompanied by a sense of sagging, throbbing, pricking, and tearing.

6.26.120 | Thirst, fever, eruptions, burning of the palate, a sensation of fuming, and cracking [of the skin] occur from pitta; there is fainting, various pains, and colors other than white and reddish-brown.
6.26.121 | Itching, heaviness, whiteness, sliminess, oiliness, loss of appetite, numbness, excessive salivation of phlegm,
nausea, weak digestion, drowsiness, and mild pain occur in diseases of the mouth caused by phlegm (kapha).
6.26.122 | When all these symptoms appear together in a disease of the mouth, it is called *sarvaja* (arising from all [doshas]).
Due to differences in their configuration, the affected tissues (*dūṣya*), shape, and names, these [mouth diseases] become sixty-fourfold.
6.26.123 | The causes, symptoms, forms, and treatments for these have been declared in the Śālākyatantra;
now I shall explain the treatment for the four types of oral diseases according to their respective locations.

Thus ends the diagnosis of diseases of the mouth (mukharoga). 6.26.124. Loss of appetite may arise from wind (vāta) and other [humors], as well as from grief, fear, excessive greed, anger, and unwholesome thoughts, tastes, smells, or sights. When accompanied by tingling of the teeth and an astringent taste in the mouth, it is considered to be caused by wind (anila).
6.26.125 | One should know that the mouth is bitter, sour, hot, tasteless, foul-smelling, and salty due to *pitta*;
it is sweet, slimy, heavy, cold, obstructed, and constricted due to *kapha*.

6.26.126 | In anorexia caused by grief, fear, wind, greed, anger, and so forth, as well as by unpalatable food or odors, there may be a natural state of the mouth and a lack of relish; however, in that arising from the three doṣas, the taste shall not be uniform.
Thus ends the etiology of earache (arocaka).
6.26.127: From Vāta arise ringing, excessive pain, dryness of the earwax, thin discharge, and loss of hearing;
from Pitta arise swelling, redness, tearing, burning sensation, and a yellowish, foul-smelling discharge.
6.26.128 | In the case of a discharge caused by *kapha*, there is hearing loss, itching, persistent swelling, white and unctuous secretions, and little pain;
however, in the case of *sannipāta* (the combination of all three *doṣas*), all these symptoms appear, and the discharge has the color of the predominant *doṣa*.
Thus ends the diagnosis of ear diseases.
In eye disease caused by Vāta, there is slight redness, absence of discharge, and a sensation of piercing and splitting pain.
From Pitta, there is burning, intense pain, redness, yellowish discharge, and very hot lacrimation.
6.26.130 | Due to *kapha*, the eye has a white coating, copious slimy tears, heaviness, and itching;
however, when all [humors] are present, there are ninety-six varieties of eye diseases due to their different combinations (*sannipāta*).
6.26.131 | Their manifestation has been fully described in the treatises on ophthalmology (śālākya), as well as their medical treatment.
However, since detailed exposition is not recommended when a subject falls within the domain of another [specialty], we have made no effort here.
Thus ends the diagnosis of eye diseases (Netraroga-nidāna).
6.26.132. When the bodily heat (tejas), together with the wind (anila) and other humors, burns the scalp, it quickly causes baldness (khalati) in a man;
by burning it slightly, however, it produces grey hair (palita) and a tawny (hari) luster of the head-hairs.

6.26.133 | Thus, this section on a portion of the diseases arising above the clavicle has been composed in this treatise so that it is not left empty. Hereafter, learn the compendium of medicines as it is being stated in brief.

Thus ends the diagnosis of the disease of baldness (khālitya). 6.26.134. In cases of cough and hoarseness caused by Vāta, or in chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), one should drink ghee processed with alkali, or warm meat-broth or milk, or indeed, an unctuous medicinal smoke (snaihika-dhūma).
6.26.135 | One should drink a decoction of śatāhvā, tvak, balā, the roots of syonāka, eraṇḍa, bilva, and sāragvadha; or one may use a suppository made from beeswax, muscle fat, and ghee.
Alternatively, the physician should administer smoke therapy to those suffering from acute coryza by placing roasted grain flour mixed with ghee inside a hollowed-out shell and burning it.
6.26.137 | For pain in the temples, the head, or the forehead, one should apply fomentation with the sweat of the hands or poultices.
When the body has been well-anointed, applications such as *saṃkara* (mixed poultices) are used for conditions such as the obstruction of sneezing and nasal discharge.
6.26.138 | And the fragrant substances to be smelled are rohiṣa, ajājī, vacā, tarkārī, and coraka;
or else, powders of tvak, patra, marica, and elā, together with upakuñcikā.
6.26.139 | When there is dryness of the channels, the uvula, the nose, and the eyes, oil should be used as nasal drops (nāvana).
Sesame seeds should be ground with milk and the fat of a white goat, and [the preparation] applied with its own heat.
6.26.140 | One should squeeze the slightly steamed [drugs] along with the powder of yaṣṭyāhvā using that same [juice],
in a decoction of daśamūla, together with a paste of rāsnā and madhuka.
6.26.141 | Oil prepared ten times with rock salt is known as Aṇu-taila;
one should eliminate the morbid humor (doṣa) in vāta-type chronic rhinitis by administering this to a person who has been lubricated with unctuous substances through non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana).
6.26.142 | Light food that is unctuous, sour, and warm, along with the juices of domestic animals and the like, is beneficial;
one should bathe and drink warm water and reside in a windless, warm shelter.
6.26.143 | A wise person, desiring his own welfare, should abstain from anxiety, physical exertion, vocal activity, and sexual intercourse when suffering from a vata-born chronic rhinitis.

In the case of Pitta-type fever, one should drink clarified butter prepared with ginger, or milk boiled with ginger, for the purpose of ripening the doshas; once they have ripened, head-purgation (mūrdhavirecana) should be administered.
6.26.145 | Oil prepared with pāṭhā, virajānī, mūrvā, pippalī, the young leaves of jātī, and dantī should be used as a nasal drop (nasya) for chronic purulent rhinitis (pakvapīnasa).
6.26.146 | Decoctions that cure raktapitta are used for pus and blood, as well as for nasal drops (nāvana).
In cases characterized by suppuration, burning, and dryness, cooling applications (lepa) along with affusions (secanāḥ) should be employed.
6.26.147 | For nasal catarrh with mild pitta, one should employ fragrant nasal treatments, sweet and cooling decoctions, and administer unctuous purgatives.
6.26.148 | Ghee, milk, barley, śāli rice, wheat, the meat-broths of wild animals,
cold and sour items, bitter vegetables, and soups made from mung beans and similar pulses are beneficial.
6.26.149 | In cases of nausea due to heaviness and in kaphaja rhinitis, fasting should be administered first;
once the head has been smeared with clarified butter, fomentations and affusions should be applied to promote suppuration.
6.26.150 | Garlic, combined with powdered mung beans, the three pungents (vyoṣa), alkali, and ghee, should be administered as an emetic;
it is beneficial for one whose phlegm is provoked and who suffers from disorders of kapha.

6.26.151 | In cases of chronic rhinitis (apīnasa), putrid nose (pūtinasya), nasal discharge (ghrāṇasrāva), and when accompanied by itching (sakaṇḍuka), medicated smoking (dhūma) is recommended; likewise, nasal drops (avapīḍa) made from pungent substances are indicated for rhinitis caused by phlegm (kaphapīnasa).
6.26.152 | A powder consisting of namaschila, vacā, vyōṣa, viḍaṅga, hiṅgu,
and guggulu should be administered as a snuff (ghreya), and likewise as a blowing-in treatment (pradhamana) with pungent fruits.
6.26.153 | In urine boiled with bhārgī, madana, tarkārī, surasā, and others, one should add lac, vacā, lambā, viḍaṅga, kuṣṭha, and pippalī.

6.26.154 | Having prepared a paste of karañja, one should cook mustard oil with those [other ingredients]. Once it has cooled after cooking and become thick, this nasal medication (nasya) should be administered for phlegm that resembles fat.
6.26.155 | When the force [of phlegm] has been obstructed in one who has been lubricated, emesis is indicated for cough with excess phlegm,
using a gruel prepared with milk boiled with emetic drugs, sesame, and māṣa beans.

6.26.156 | Soups made from eggplant, kulaka, the three pungents (vyoṣa), horse gram (kulattha), aduki, and mung bean, as well as kapha-subduing food, are recommended; so too is the sprinkling with warm water.

6.26.157 | Sarvajit should be used for corrupted coryza, and Śophajit for swelling; alkali (kṣāra) is indicated for tumors and fleshy growths, while for the remaining conditions, treatment should be determined after careful examination.
Thus ends the treatment for rhinitis and nasal diseases (6.26.158). In cases of Vāta-type head disease, one should administer oleation, sudation, nasal drops (nasya),
drinks, food, and poultices that alleviate Vāta disorders.
6.26.159 | Fomentation with comfortably warm applications of aguru and other substances fried in oil, as well as with the drugs of the jīvanīya group, jasmine flowers, fish, and meat, is recommended.
Oil prepared with *rāsnā*, *sthirā*, and other herbs along with milk,
or alternatively with *rāsnā*, the two types of *kākolī*, and sugar, used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) relieves pain.
6.26.161 Prepared with balā, madhūka, yaṣṭyāhvā, vidārī, candana, utpala, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, drākṣā, and sugar.
6.26.162 | A prastha of oil prepared with milk and half a tula of the meat-juice of wild animals,
used as nasal therapy (nasya), removes all diseases of wind and bile arising above the clavicle.
6.26.163 | Together with the ten roots, balā, rāsnā, triphalā, and madhuka,
one should take a peacock, excluding its wings, bile, intestines, feces, beak, and feet.

6.26.164 | Having boiled one *prastha* of ghee in water, one should cook it with an equal amount of milk and paste (*kalka*) of the drugs of the sweet group (*madhura-varga*), each weighing one *karṣa*. This cures diseases of the head and facial paralysis (*ardita*).
6.26.165 | Known as *māyūra*, it cures diseases of the ears, eyes, nose, tongue, palate, mouth, and throat, and removes ailments above the clavicle.
Thus ends the peacock-ghee (māyūraghṛta).
6.26.166. With this very decoction, one should cook one prastha of ghee with four times as much milk and one karṣa each of these following pastes:
6.26.167 | With jīvantī, triphalā, medā, mṛdvīkā, ṛddhi, parūṣaka, samaṅgā, cavikā, bhārgī, kāśmarī, and suradāru;
6.26.168 | With ātmaguptā, mahāmeda, tāla, and the tops of kharjūra; with mṛṇāla, bisa, śālūka, śṛṅgī, jīvaka, and padmaka;
6.26.169 | With the pairs of śatāvarī, vidārī, ikṣu, bṛhatī, and sārivā;
and with mūrvā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, ṛṣabhaka, śṛṅgāṭaka, and kaseruka;
6.26.170 | With rāsnā, sthirā, āmalakī, sūkṣmailā, śaṭī, pauṣkara, punarnavā, tugākṣīrī, kākolī, and dhanvayāsaka;
6.26.171 | Prepared according to the previous method with these substances— date palms, walnuts, vātāma, muñjāta, and abhiṣuka— as they may be available.
6.26.172 | One should employ it for nasal administration, as a drink, for massage, and likewise for enema,
in all diseases of the head, as well as in cough and severe asthma.

6.26.173 | It is recommended for stiffness of the back, emaciation, hoarseness of voice, facial paralysis, defects of the female reproductive tract, blood disorders, and seminal defects; it bestows sons even upon barren women.
6.26.174 | A woman who has bathed after her menses, having drunk this, gives birth to a son.
This is the Mahāmāyūra ghee, honored by Ātreya.

Thus ends the Mahāmāyūra-ghṛta (6.26.175). Furthermore, a wise person should cook ghee using mice, chickens, swans, and rabbits according to this same procedure; it removes diseases of the upper body.
6.26.176 | In cases of Pitta disorders, ghee, milk, cold affusions, cooling plasters, nasal drops,
vitalizing medicated ghees (jīvanīya-sarpis), and food and drink that pacify Pitta should be employed.

6.26.177 | A medicinal plaster (pradeha) should be made with sandalwood, ushira, licorice, bala, vyaghranakha, and utpala ground with milk; or alternatively, a pouring bath (pariṣecana) should be performed with these same ingredients boiled in water.
6.26.178 | A well-ground paste of cinnamon bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*patra*), and sugar, mixed with rice-water,
should be used as an *avapīḍa* (pressed-out nasal drop), followed by ghee as a nasal medication (*nasya*) in the case of the Pitta-type [headache].
6.26.179 | Ghee prepared with yaṣṭyāhva, candana, anantā, and milk is beneficial;
or, in cases born of pitta, nasal drops (nāvana) made with sugar, drākṣā, and madhūka are likewise recommended.

6.26.180 | In the case of a kapha-born [disease], once the patient has been fomented and purified by means of medicinal smoking, nasal drops, insufflations, and so forth, one should treat them with kapha-subduing plasters, drinks, and foods.
6.26.181 | In cases arising from Kapha and Vata, burning sensations are treated with the drinking of aged ghee and sharp enemas; for the remaining two [doshas], bloodletting is prescribed.
6.26.182 | One should inhale an incense wick (dhūmavartī) made from castor oil, *nalada*, linen, *guggulu*, *aguru*, sandalwood, fragrant substances, as well as *kuṣṭha* and *tagara*.
6.26.183 | In a disease arising from the combination of humors (sannipāta), treatment beneficial for sannipāta should be administered;
and in a case caused by worms (krimija), a strong head-purgative (mūrdhavirecana) should be employed.
6.26.184 | *Tvak*, *dantī*, the claws of a tiger, *viḍaṅga*, *navamālikā*, the fruit of *apāmārga*, the seeds of *naktamāla* and *śirīṣa*,
*kṣavaka*, *aśmantaka*, *bilva*, *haridrā*, *hiṅgu*, and *yūthikā*.

6.26.185 | Oil prepared with these [drugs] along with *phaṇijjhaka*, and four times as much sheep urine and feces, is beneficial when used as nasal drops (*nāvana*) or as a powder for insufflation (*pradhamana*).

6.26.186 | The fruit of *śigru* and *karañja*, along with the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), constitutes an *avapīḍaka*. [These may be prepared as] a decoction (*kaṣāya*), fresh juice (*svarasa*), alkali (*kṣāra*), powder (*cūrṇa*), paste (*kalka*), or an *avapīḍaka*.
6.26.187 | Gargling with sour, bitter, pungent, honeyed, or astringent substances [is prescribed].
Thus ends the treatment for diseases of the head. [The treatments include] medicated smoking, insufflation, purification, purgation, emesis, and fasting.
6.26.188 | In cases of diseases of the mouth, food that is beneficial for the respective doshas should be administered;
[this includes] long pepper (pippalī), agallochum (aguru), the bark of *darvī*, alkali of barley (yavakṣāra), and rasāñjana.
6.26.189 | One should powder pāṭhā, tejovatī, and pathyā in equal parts;
this should be held in the mouth along with honey for all diseases of the oral cavity.
6.26.190 | This is the best method of taking a morsel [of medicine] with sīdhu, mādhava, and mādhvīka wines.
[One should take it with] tejohvā, abhayā, elā, samaṅgā, kaṭukā, and ghana.
6.26.191 | One should powder pāṭhā, jyotiṣmatī, lodhra, dārvī, and kuṣṭha;
this is a tooth-paste that removes bleeding, itching, and pain from the teeth.
6.26.192 | The five spices (pañcakolaka), tālīśa, patra, elā, marica, and tvac, along with the ashes of palāśa and muṣkaka, and yavakṣāra, should be powdered.
6.26.193 | When double the amount of old jaggery has been boiled down,
pills the size of a *karkandhu* fruit are made and kept for seven days in the ashes of the *muṣkaka* tree.
6.26.194 | In all diseases of the throat, these substances—resembling nectar—should be held [in the mouth]:
soot from a house, alkali of barley, pāṭhā, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and rasāñjana.
6.26.195 | Tejohvā, triphalā, lodhra, and citraka— this powder,
when held in the mouth with honey, destroys diseases of the throat.
6.26.196 | That powder named Kālaka cures diseases of the teeth, mouth, and throat. Thus ends the Kālaka powder.
Realgar, barley-alkali, yellow orpiment, and rock salt—
6.26.197 | This powder of dārvītvak, combined with honey and mixed with the scum of ghee (ghṛtamaṇḍa), should be held in the mouth for diseases of the throat.
6.26.198 | Pītaka is proclaimed as the best among treatments for diseases of the mouth.
Thus ends the description of Pītaka powder.
[The ingredients are: Mṛdvīkā, Kaṭukā, Vyoṣa, Dārvītvak, Triphalā, and Ghana.
6.26.199 | One should apply ghee mixed with its scum for throat diseases;
