Chapter Twenty-Seven:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of thigh-stiffness (*ūrustambha*).

or [one may take] *triphalā*, *pippalī*, *musta*, *cavya*, and *kaṭukarohiṇī*.
6.27.39 | A man afflicted by ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs) should lick the powder with honey;
for if the disorder should be caused by under-nutrition (apatarpaṇa), one should treat him with nourishing therapy (saṃtarpaṇa).
6.27.40 | If, through the use of meat from wild animals and aged *śāli* rice prepared with appropriate methods,
there occurs an aggravation of *vāta* characterized by dryness, preceded by insomnia and pain;
6.27.41 | In that case, the sequence of oleation and sudation should be performed to alleviate disorders of Vata;
[the drugs used are] Pīluparṇī, Payasyā, Rāsnā, Gokṣuraka, and Vacā.
6.27.42 | One should cook oil with sarala, aguru, and pāṭhā;
from this, a man should drink one prasṛta or even one añjali, mixed with honey.
6.27.43 | One should cook mustard oil with kuṣṭha, śrīveṣṭaka, udīcya, sarala, devadāru, keśara, ajagandhā, and aśvagandhā.

6.27.44 | One afflicted by *ūrustambha* (stiffness of the thighs) should drink that [mixture] in the proper dose along with honey; thus, being freed from the dryness [that causes] *ūrustambha*, he is liberated from it. 6.27.45 | Two *pala*s of rock salt (*saindhava*), five [pala*s] each of ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *granthika*, and *citraka*.
Two pairs of *bhallātaka* seeds, twenty, and likewise two *āḍhakas*.

6.27.46 | One should cook one *prastha* of oil with fermented gruel (*āranāla*) and these [other] ingredients; it bestows progeny and cures sciatica, stiffness of the thighs, hemorrhoids, dysentery, and all disorders of *vāta*.
6.27.47 | A prastha of oil cooked with two palas each of pippalī root and ginger, along with eight parts of *kaṭvara* and an equal amount of curd, cures sciatica and stiffness of the thighs.

Thus ends the oil for the eight pungent substances (aṣṭakaṭvarataila). This has been described as the internal medicine for ūrustambha; now hear the other external treatment which effects the depletion of phlegm (śleṣman).
6.27.49 | One should perform a vigorous rubbing [of the body] with the powder made from ant-hill earth, the root of the karañja tree, its fruit, its bark, and bricks.
6.27.50 | Or the physician [should use] the roots of *aśvagandhā*, or the roots of *arka*,
or the roots of *picumarda*, or else the roots of *devadāru*.
6.27.51 | In cases of ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs), the physician should perform a firm massage and apply an ointment composed of honey, mustard seeds, and earth from an anthill.
6.27.52 | Furthermore, a wise person [should prepare a decoction] with dantī, dravantī, surasā, and sarṣapa;
and also with tarkārī, śigru, surasā, viśva, vatsaka, and nimba.
6.27.53 | Water boiled with leaves, roots, and fruits, and used warm as a sprinkling;
or ground mustard seeds soaked overnight in urine should be used as an ointment.
6.27.54 | Vatsaka, surasa, kuṣṭha, the fragrant substances (gandhas), tumburu, śigruka, hiṃsrā, the root of arka, earth from an anthill, and kuṭheraka;

6.27.55 | A plaster composed of these [substances] combined with curd and rock salt should be applied by a physician who understands the proper sequence, for the destruction of ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).
6.27.56 | Śyonāka, khadira, bilva, the two types of bṛhatī, sarala, and asana— [these should be used].
Śobhāñjana, tarkārī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, surasā, and arjaka.
6.27.57 | One should sprinkle [the patient] with water boiled with *agnimantha* and *karañja*;
alternatively, an ointment ground with urine is a remedy for preventing *ūrustambha*.
6.27.58 | To reduce phlegm, one should engage in exercises that are possible for him;
at dawn, he should traverse high ground, as well as gravel and sand.
6.27.59 | One should cross a river of cool, auspicious water against the current,
and repeatedly cross a clear, cool lake with still waters.
6.27.60 | Likewise, when his phlegm has been dried up, the seizing pain in the thighs will subside;
one should employ that which effects the depletion of phlegm without provoking the wind.
6.27.61 | All of that should always be employed as the remedy for ūrustambha;
this treatment must be performed while protecting the body, the strength, and the digestive fire.

6.27.62 | Regarding this, there is a verse:— The etiology, the prodromal signs, the symptoms, the cause of functional incapacity, and the two types of medicine have been stated in the treatment of ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs).

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urustambha," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Twenty-Eight:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of Vātavyādhi (wind-disorders).
6.28.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
6.28.3 | Vāyu is life, Vāyu is strength; Vāyu is the sustainer of embodied beings.
Vāyu is this entire universe, and Vāyu is proclaimed as the Lord.
6.28.4 | He whose movement is unimpeded while remaining in his own place and established in his natural state— that person,
free from disease, shall live for more than a hundred years.
6.28.5 | Moving unimpeded through its respective locations, it properly sustains the body in five ways, known as prāṇa, udāna, samāna, vyāna, and apāna.
6.28.6 | The locations of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) are the head, chest, throat, tongue, mouth, and nose;
its functions include spitting, sneezing, belching, breathing, eating, and so forth.
6.28.7 | Furthermore, the locations of udāna are the navel, the chest, and the throat;
its functions are the initiation of speech, exertion, vitality, strength, complexion, and so forth.
6.28.8 | Situated at the sides of the internal fire, the Samāna [vāyu], which bestows strength upon the digestive fire, presides over the channels that carry sweat, waste products, and water.
6.28.9 | Vyāna, moving swiftly among men, pervades the entire body;
it is always active in the functions of movement, extension, contraction, winking, and so forth.
6.28.10 | Located in the lower abdomen, it reaches the testicles, the bladder, the penis, the navel, the thighs, the groins, and the anus;
it resides within the rectum and governs semen, urine, and feces.
6.28.11 | When they are joined and situated in their proper locations, they produce the menstrual flow and the embryo;
they perform their respective functions, and by them the body is maintained free from disease.
6.28.12 | For those who follow wrong paths or are undisciplined, these [factors], along with diseases born from their own station and actions, afflict the body and swiftly take away their lives.

6.28.13 | Indeed, eighty diseases beginning with *nakhabheda* (splitting of the nails) have been shown in the Sūtra as the principal ones among those born from [the humors], which exceed even all calculation.
6.28.14 | Listen as I describe those [disorders] being afflicted by turns, along with their causes and treatments,
whether they affect the wind alone or are obstructed by its movement through various locations.
6.28.15 | By dry, cold, scanty, or light food; by sexual intercourse and excessive staying awake; by irregular treatment; and by excessive bloodletting, [the humors become aggravated].
6.28.16 | By jumping, leaping, excessive travel, physical exercise, and over-exertion;
by the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus); and by the emaciation caused by anxiety, grief, and disease.
6.28.17 | From sleeping or sitting on hard ground, from anger, from sleeping during the day, and even from fear; from the suppression of natural urges, from overeating, from injury, and from fasting.
6.28.18 | Due to the striking of vital points (marmans) and the falling from fast-moving vehicles such as elephants, camels, or horses,
the powerful wind (anila), having filled the empty channels within the body, [causes distress].
6.28.19 | It produces various diseases localized in either the entire body or a single limb;
their unmanifest characteristic is known as the premonitory stage (pūrvarūpa).
6.28.20 | Its manifestation is its own form; moreover, there is decline, lightness, contraction of the joints, stiffness, and even the splitting of the bones and the joints.
6.28.21 | Horripilation, delirium, stiffness of the hands, back, and head;
lameness, deformity of the fingers, and hunchback; emaciation of the limbs and insomnia.
6.28.22 | The destruction of the embryo, semen, and menses; throbbing; numbness of the limbs;
and the distortion of the head, nose, eyes, collarbones, and neck.
6.28.23 | Splitting pain, piercing pain, convulsions, delusion, and exhaustion—
such are the symptoms produced by the provoked vāyu.
6.28.24 | Furthermore, due to the specific nature of the cause and the location, it produces specific diseases.
In that regard, when the vitiated [dosha] is localized in the visceral cavity (koṣṭha), there is suppression of urine and feces.
6.28.25 | It [is indicated] for heart disease caused by *bradhna*, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and pain in the flanks when the wind (*māruta*) is provoked;
and when the wind is agitated throughout the entire body, causing twitching and breaking sensations in the limbs.
6.28.26 | Overwhelmed by these pains, his joints seem as if they are bursting;
there is retention of feces, urine, and flatus, along with colic, flatulence, urinary stones, and gravel.
6.28.27 | When located in the rectum, it causes diseases of the thighs, calves, sacrum, and feet,
as well as wasting, pain in the heart, navel, flanks, and abdomen, thirst, eructation, and visūcikā.
6.28.28 | When located in the stomach (āmāśaya), it causes cough, dryness of the throat and mouth, and dyspnea;
when located in the large intestine (pakvāśaya), it produces rumbling in the intestines, colic, and flatulence.
6.28.29 | Corrupted Vāyu may cause difficulty in passing urine and feces, distension of the abdomen, pain in the three regions [of the body],
and the impairment of the sense organs such as the ears.
6.28.30 | When the *vāyu* resides in the skin (*tvak*), the skin becomes rough, cracked, numb, thin, and black; it is pricked with pain, stretched, reddened, and there is pain in the joints.
When the wind has entered the blood, there are intense pains accompanied by fever, discoloration, emaciation,
loss of appetite, eruptions on the body, and a sense of stiffness after eating.
6.28.32 | When Vāta has entered the muscle and fat tissues, the limbs of the body are excessively pricked, as if struck by a staff or a fist; they are painful and become exceedingly exhausted.
6.28.33 | When the *vāyu* is provoked in the marrow and bones, there is a splitting pain in the joints of the bones, aching at the articulations, loss of muscle strength,
insomnia, and constant pain.
When Vāyu is aggravated and located in the semen (śukra), it may cause the semen to be discharged quickly or to be retained,
or it may even produce a deformity in the embryo.
6.28.35 | When the Vāyu has entered the tendons (snāyu), it causes external and internal contraction, as well as club-foot, hunchback, and diseases affecting the whole body or individual limbs.
6.28.36 | When Vāta has entered the vessels (sirā), the body experiences mild pain and swelling, it withers, and likewise trembles; the vessels become numb, thin, or greatly dilated.
6.28.37 | When the wind (vāyu) has entered the joints, there is swelling with a sensation like that of touching a leather bag filled with air,
along with pain during the processes of extension and contraction.
6.28.38 | (Thus has been described the characteristic of the wind according to its various locations.
When the excessively increased wind enters one half of the body,
it dries up the blood, the arm, the foot, and the knee.
6.28.39 | In that [state], he contracts half his face and makes it crooked;
likewise, he distorts the nose, the eyebrows, the forehead, the eyes, and the jaws.
6.28.40 | Then, food enters his mouth crookedly as if through a curved nose;
his eye becomes fixed, and when he speaks, his sneeze is suppressed.
6.28.41 | His speech becomes faltering, distorted, and interrupted;
his teeth chatter, his ears are oppressed, and his voice breaks.
6.28.42 | Pain in the feet, hands, eyes, calves, thighs, temples, ears, cheeks, or in half of the face, or in the entire face, constitutes that which is known as Ardita (facial paralysis).
6.28.43 | I consider that when the wind, having entered within, resorts to the channels (nāḍīs),
it then causes a stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha) known as antarāyāma.
6.28.44 | The neck is drawn inward and the tendons of the neck (manyā) become severely stiff;
there is gnashing of the teeth, salivation, extension of the back, and stiffness of the head.
6.28.45 | Yawning and the closing of the mouth are also characteristics of *antarāyāma*.
(Thus has *antarāyāma* been described; now *bahirāyāma* is being described.
6.28.46 | Having dried up the external vessels that depend upon the back and the neck, the strong [practitioner]...
The wind (vāyu) may cause a stiffness of the bow (dhanustambha), which is known as external extension (bahirāyāma).
6.28.47 | As he is bent like a bow, his head is drawn backward;
his chest is thrust upward, his neck-tendons become stiff, and his neck is crushed.
6.28.48 | Biting with the teeth, yawning, salivation, and loss of speech— this [disease],
once its force has arisen, either kills or causes deformity.
6.28.49 | When the Vāyu, due to its binding, becomes localized at the root of the jaw, it causes the jaws to become displaced;
or it may cause the mouth to remain open, stiff, and painless.
6.28.50 | Having caused stiffness of the jaw and contraction of the mouth,
the enraged wind known as Ākṣepaka repeatedly convulses the limbs.
6.28.51 | Having dried up the hands and feet, as well as the veins, ligaments, and tendons,
the wind (māruta) causes stiffness in the hands, feet, head, back, and hips.

6.28.52 | When the body is as rigid as a staff, that condition is known as Daṇḍaka and is incurable. One who suffers from Arditā and similar disorders may become healthy when the paroxysm has repeatedly passed away.
6.28.53 | When afflicted by various such pains, the physician should avoid treating them;
for the wind (māruta), having destroyed one side—either the right or the left—[renders the patient incurable].
6.28.54 | For it causes the cessation of movement, pain, and even the paralysis of speech,
having seized half of the body and dried up the vessels and tendons.

6.28.55 | When it causes the contraction of one limb or one hand, producing piercing pain and aching, one should know that as *ekāṅgaroga* (monoplegia); when it arises from the entire body, it is *sarvāṅga* (generalized paralysis).
6.28.56 | Gṛdhrasī seizes the buttocks first, followed by the waist, back, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet in succession; it causes stiffness, pain, and throbbing, and the limb twitches repeatedly.
6.28.57 | Caused by Vāta or by Vāta-Kapha, Khallī is accompanied by drowsiness, heaviness, and anorexia;
it causes a crushing pain in the feet, calves, thighs, and the roots of the arms.
6.28.58 | One should identify the remaining [diseases] by means of signs corresponding to their respective locations;
in all these cases, one should recognize the association with pitta and the other [humors].
6.28.59 | The provocation of wind arises from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus) and from the obstruction of its pathways;
wind, bile, and phlegm circulate through all the channels of the body.
6.28.60 | For it is Vāyu alone, due to his subtlety, who impels those two there; when provoked, he tosses them up and hurls them here and there with maces.
6.28.61 | Because it obstructs the channels, it causes the depletion of the *rasa* and other tissues.
When the *liṅga* (signs) are obscured by *pitta*, there is burning, thirst, colic, giddiness, and darkness before the eyes.
6.28.62 | From pungent, sour, salty, and hot [substances], there is a burning sensation and a desire for cold;
there is coldness, heaviness, and pain, with greater relief from pungent and similar [remedies].
6.28.63 | When [the fever] is covered by kapha, there is a desire for fasting, physical exertion, and things that are dry and hot;
when covered by blood, there is constant burning pain and intense suffering arising from within the skin and flesh.
6.28.64 | The swelling may be accompanied by redness, and circular patches (maṇḍala) arise;
likewise, there are hard, discolored pustules (piḍakā) as well as swelling.
6.28.65 | There is a sensation of ants crawling over the flesh;
the swelling is mobile, glossy, soft, and cold, and there is likewise a loss of appetite for food in the limbs.
6.28.66 | This condition, when covered by fat, should be known as Āḍhyavāta; it is difficult to treat.
When, however, the touch is obstructed by bone, the patient welcomes warmth and pressure.
6.28.67 | It feels as if being split, it sinks down, and it is pricked as if by needles; when the marrow is obstructed, there may be bending, yawning, and a sense of being constricted.

6.28.68 | When the penis is being pressed with both hands, one obtains relief from pain; however, in the case of semen-related disorders, there may be an emission of semen, excessive discharge, or even sterility.
When the wind (vāyu) is obstructed by food, there is pain in the abdomen after eating, which subsides once the food is digested;
when the wind is obstructed by urine, there is non-excretion of urine and distension of the bladder.

6.28.70 | There is excessive obstruction of the vital luster (varcas) below; it causes cutting pain in its own location. The fatty tissue (sneha) quickly undergoes decay, and the person feels bloated after eating.
6.28.71 | After a long time, one voids stool that is difficult to pass due to lack of food, dry, and hard;
there is pain in the hips, groins, and back, and the wind moves in an upward direction.
6.28.72 | When the wind (anila) is obstructed by feces (varcas), the heart becomes unsettled;
there is loosening of the joints, lockjaw, contraction, deformity, and facial paralysis (ardita).
6.28.73 | Impairment of vision, emaciation of the limbs, lameness, khuḍavāta,
stiffness, āḍhyavāta, and those diseases located in the marrow and bones;
6.28.74 | These [qualities] may or may not be accomplished through effort due to the depth of one's position;
however, one should cultivate these nine when they are powerful and free from obstacles.

6.28.75 | Now hear of the proven therapeutic procedure for removing wind diseases (vātaroga), which follows this [diet]. At the outset, one should treat a condition that is purely [wind-based] and without supporting factors (nirupastambha) with unctuous therapies (sneha).

6.28.76 | Thereafter, having comforted the person who has been exhausted by the intake of oil, fat, sesame oil, and marrow, one should again oleate him with milk while administering vāyu [medicinal herbs].
6.28.77 | With soups made from domestic animals, aquatic creatures, or marsh-dwellers, combined with fats;
or with milk-porridges (pāyasa) and rice-and-pulse mixtures (kṛsara), seasoned with sour and salty substances, for the purpose of unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).
6.28.78 | Thereafter, one should foment the patient— who has been well-anointed with very unctuous nasal drops, satiation therapies, and foods—
using tube-fomentation, bed-fomentation, and poultice-fomentation combined with oleaginous substances.
6.28.79 | Likewise, one should treat [the patient] with various other types of sudation as appropriate;
for a limb that has been anointed with oleaginous substances and subjected to sudation may become either bent or stiff.
6.28.80 | It can be gradually bent as desired, like dry wood;
[otherwise there may be] itching, piercing pain, aching, swelling, stiffness, rigidity, and so forth.
6.28.81 | When applied promptly, [fomentation] quickly pacifies the symptoms of one who has been fomented, and softness arises;
furthermore, the oleation, when administered, quickly nourishes the dried-up tissues (dhātus).
6.28.82 | It increases strength, digestive fire, nourishment, and vital breaths;
one should repeatedly treat it with oleation and sudation therapies.
6.28.83 | Likewise, in a digestive tract that is softened by oleation, wind-related disorders do not persist;
yet, if they are not pacified by this procedure due to the persistence of the morbid humors (doṣas), [other measures must be taken].
6.28.84 | One should purify that [wound] with mild medicinal drugs combined with oleaginous substances,
or with ghee prepared with *tilvaka*, or indeed with ghee prepared with *sātala*.
6.28.85 | One should drink either milk or castor oil, which are auspicious and remove the humors;
for the impurity has accumulated through foods that are unctuous, sour, salty, and hot.
6.28.86 | By obstructing the channels, one would block the wind (*anila*); therefore, one should cause it to flow in its natural direction.
One who is weak and unfit for purgation (*avirecya*) should be treated with non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*).

6.28.87 | For a person who has undergone purification (saṃśuddha), once the digestive fire (agni) has been rekindled, oleation (sneha) and sudation (sveda) are again beneficial, administered with foods that are digestive (pācana) or appetizing (dīpanīya), or combined with them.

6.28.88 | Furthermore, one should treat all [of these] continuously with foods that are sweet, sour, salty, and unctuous, as well as with nasal drops (nāvana) and the inhalation of medicinal smoke (dhūmapāna).
6.28.89 | Thus has the general treatment for diseases of wind (vāta) been declared;
specifically, however, when the wind is located in the digestive tract (koṣṭha), a person should drink alkaline preparation (kṣāra).

6.28.90 | One should cause the impurities to be digested by means of digestive (pācana), appetizing (dīpana), or sour (amla) substances. However, when they are located in the rectum or the large intestine (pakvāśaya), treatments that alleviate upward movement of wind (udāvarta) are beneficial.
6.28.91 | When [the dosha] is located in the stomach (āmāśaya) of one who has been purified, treatments that remove the respective dosha should be applied;
when it is provoked throughout the entire body, oil massages and enemas, including those with oily suppositories (anuvāsana), are indicated.
6.28.92 | When [the fever] resides in the skin, [treatment consists of] sudation, oil massage, immersion baths, and strengthening food;
when it resides in the blood, cold poultices, purgation, and bloodletting [are prescribed].
6.28.93 | When [the doshas] reside in the muscle and fat, purgation, decoction enemas (nirūha), and pacifying measures are indicated;
one should conquer those residing in the bone and marrow by means of oleation both externally and internally.
6.28.94 | When [the semen] is located in the semen (śukra), joy, food, and drink that increase strength and semen are beneficial;
or, seeing that the path is obstructed, one should administer a purgative for the semen.
6.28.95 | For one who has been purged and has subsequently eaten, one should perform the previously mentioned treatment;
likewise for those whose fetus has withered due to Vāta, and for children who are wasting away.
6.28.96 | Milk boiled with sugar, kāśmarya, and madhuka is beneficial for inducing vomiting;
milk prepared with aṃśumatī is beneficial when [the doshas] are aggravated in the heart.
6.28.97 | When the abdomen is located in the region of the navel, [cooked] fish prepared with unripe wood-apple fruits (bilva-śalāṭu) should be used;
however, when the body is being constricted by Vāyu, a poultice (upanāhana) should be applied.
6.28.98 | For *saṃkucita*, an oil massage with oil prepared from *māṣa* and rock salt [is indicated];
when it has reached the arms and head, nasal drops (*nasya*) and drinking [of the oil] after meals [are prescribed].

6.28.99 | Enema therapy (basti) is recommended below the navel, as is the use of the avapīḍaka (nasal drops). In cases of facial paralysis (ardita), nasal medication (nāvana), head oil (mūrdhataila), and nourishing treatments (tarpaṇa) are likewise advised.
6.28.100 | Nerve-fomentation (nāḍī-sveda) and poultices (upanāha) made with the flesh of marshy animals are beneficial;
in hemiplegia (pakṣāghāta), sudation combined with oleation and purgation (virecana) are indicated.
6.28.101 | In cases of gṛdhrasī, one should apply venesection between the tendons and the ankle, as well as enema and thermal cautery; however, for khallī, a warm poultice should be applied.
6.28.102 | It is recommended [to administer] milk-porridges, rice-and-pulse mixtures, and meats combined with oil and ghee.
Having opened the mouth wide, one should press the jaw with the two thumbs after it has been fomented.
6.28.103 | By raising [the face] with the two index fingers, elevating the chin is beneficial;
one should restore a sagging [jaw] to its own place and straighten a stiffened [jaw] by means of fomentation.

6.28.104 | One should perform specific treatments for each [condition], such as those affecting the site or the corrupted element (*dūṣya*), including affusions, massages, and enemas using ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow.
6.28.105 | Unctuous sudations, a windless place, coverings,
meat broths, milks, and foods that are sweet, sour, and salty.
6.28.106 | Whatever is nourishing (bṛṃhaṇa) is all recommended for those suffering from disorders of vāta,
[prepared] in the decoction of balā, the five roots (pañcamūla), or the ten roots (daśamūla).
6.28.107 Having separately prepared unctuous meat soups from the flesh of goat, head, lotus, and marshy animals, seasoned with curd, sour substances, and the three pungents (vyoṣa);
6.28.108 | One should feed a man afflicted by wind diseases (vātaroga) with these [meats] made distinctly salty;
and with these very same meats, one should prepare poultices (upanāha).

6.28.109 | For immersion baths, there should be tubs containing a decoction of leaves, milk, oil, and a *droṇa* of oil, prepared with boneless meat that has been crushed, steamed, mixed with ghee and oil, and combined with sour liquids.
6.28.110 | For those suffering from wind disorders (vāta), affusions are recommended after they have been well-anointed with oil;
[these should include] the meat of marshy and aquatic animals, the ten roots (daśamūla), and śatāvarī.
6.28.111 | One should cook horse gram (kulattha), jujube (badara), black gram (māṣa), sesame (tila), vāsā, barley (yava), and balā together with muscle fat, curd, and sour gruel in a large pot.
6.28.112 | One should employ tube-fomentation (nāḍīsveda) and poultices made from these [herbs] ground into a paste;
likewise, ghee and oil prepared with them should be used for massage and even for internal consumption.
6.28.113 | Mustā, kiṇva, sesame seeds, kuṣṭha, surāhvā, salt, and nata,
prepared with curd, milk, and the four fats (catuḥsneha), should be used as a poultice (upanāhana).
6.28.114 | With *utkārikās*, *vesavāra*, milk, *māṣa* beans, sesame, boiled rice, castor seeds, wheat, barley, jujube fruits, *sthira* (śālaparṇī), and so forth;
6.28.115 | Having thickly smeared the painful limb with unctuous substances, the physician should bandage it with castor leaves at night and remove them in the morning.
6.28.116 | Then, having sprinkled it with milk and water and applied it once again,
one should release what was bound during the day while it is night, using skins together with their hair.
6.28.117 | One should apply very cold poultices (pradeha) and compresses (upanāha) made from the fruits that serve as sources of oil, ground with sour liquids,
along with fragrant substances that alleviate vāta.
6.28.118 | One should administer milk-porridges and rice-and-pulse mixtures combined with unctuous substances.
Hereafter, we shall describe the unctuous therapies for those afflicted by dryness and aggravated vāyu.

6.28.119 | One should boil various portions of water in a *droṇa* measure along with four *palas* each of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and various [herbs] that are like nectar for the pacification of diverse diseases.
6.28.120 | With one-prastha measures each of barley, kola, and kulattha,
when reduced to one-fourth as a decoction, it should be mixed with the Jīvanīya drugs ground together with sugar.
6.28.121 | Likewise, one *prastha* of ghee prepared with *svarjūra*, *kāśmarya*, *drākṣā*, *badara*, and *phalgu*, along with milk, cures vāta alone.
6.28.122 | It should be administered without hesitation for drinking, massage, and enemas:
chitraka, ginger, rāsnā, pauṣkara, long pepper, and śaṭī.
6.28.123 | Having ground [the ingredients], one should cook ghee; this is the supreme remedy for diseases caused by Vāta.
One should cook the scum of ghee (ghṛtamaṇḍa) in milk that has been boiled with balā and bilva.

6.28.124 | A dose of one śukti or one prakuñca of this [oil] should be administered as nasal drops (nasya) when the vāyu has reached the head. One should cook the bones of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals in water.
6.28.125 | One should cook that fat again with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), along with jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, āsphotā, vidārī, and kapikacchu.

6.28.126 | Prepared with pastes of wind-alleviating and life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, with two parts of milk, this [oil], when proven effective through nasal drops, massage, as well as oral intake and unctuous enemas, [is beneficial].
6.28.127 | It quickly expels the wind (māruta) located in the vessels, joints, bones, and the visceral cavity;
it is for those whose marrow is diminished and those whose semen and vital energy (ojas) are depleted.
6.28.128 | For them, this [preparation] would be like nectar, providing strength and nourishment;
likewise, the rendered fat (vasā) of crocodiles, fish, tortoises, and porpoises [is beneficial].
6.28.129 | This fresh [mixture], prepared according to this rule, is recommended for administration as nasal drops (nasya) and internal potions (pāna).
One prastha of triphalā and two kuḍavas of kulattha [beans] should be used.
6.28.130 | Five palas each of *kṛṣṇagandhā* and *āḍhakī* should be taken;
two palas each of *rāsnā* and *citraka*, and one pala of the *daśamūla*.
6.28.131 | One should boil one droṇa of water until reduced to one-fourth, adding separately one prastha each of surā,
āranāla, sour curd, saubīraka, and tuṣodaka.
6.28.132 | The juice of *kola*, pomegranate, and *vṛkṣāmla*; oil, muscle fat, ghee, marrow, and milk; and six *pala* measures of the *jīvanīya* (life-promoting) drugs.
Having added a paste, one should properly cook this great unctuous substance (mahāsneha) for cases of vāta located in the vessels,
marrow, and bones, as well as for diseases affecting the whole body or a single limb.
6.28.134 | One should apply it as an ointment for trembling, convulsions, and piercing pains;
having taken the fresh juice from the roots and leaves of nirguṇḍī.

Oil prepared with these [ingredients] in equal proportions is beneficial for sinus ulcers, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and the afflictions of Vāta; it is also suitable for drinking, massage, and filling [the ears] in cases of pāmā and apacī.
6.28.136 | Curd prepared from the juice of cotton seeds and horse gram (kulattha), which cures Vāta,
should be set aside for three days in the juice of radish mixed with an equal amount of milk.
6.28.137 | One should cook one *prastha* of oil with three *prasthas* of that sour liquid (*āmla*),
along with *yaṣṭyāhva*, sugar, *rāsnā*, salt, fresh ginger, and *nāgara*.
6.28.138 | When well-grounded in doses of one pala each, it removes Vāta when drunk or used as an external massage.
Oil-cake from many years old [should be used] with a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla).
Having cooked its juice and strained it, one should boil a *prastha* of oil with eight times as much milk; this cures all disorders of the wind (*vāta*).
6.28.140 | This [diet] is especially recommended when vāta is associated with kapha;
it consists of barley, jujube, horse gram, śreyasī, and dried radish.
6.28.141 | One should cook one handful (añjali) of bilva fruit with sour liquids;
with that decoction, one should likewise prepare oil along with sour fruits and pungent spices.
6.28.142 | One afflicted by severe vātas should apply [this] prepared with flour during the cold season.
Now hear of other oils for all disorders of vāta from another source.
6.28.143 | These four applications promote longevity, strength, and complexion; they cure disorders of the menses and semen, and they facilitate procreation.
One should cook one āḍhaka of oil in the decoction of the weight of sahācara, which is harmless, effective, and a remover of all defects.
6.28.145 | Having added ten palas of milk— four times the amount of the root-paste— to this [decoction],
once it is prepared, the physician should add eighteen palas of powdered sugar.
6.28.146 | Having prepared this, one should administer it for those severe wind-disorders (vāta-vyādhis).
Two *prasthas* of the fresh juice of *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, equal in measure, together with milk—
6.28.147 | Six palas of ginger and eight palas of jaggery,
cooked together with one prastha of oil— this should be administered for all afflictions caused by Vāta.
6.28.148 | When the oil has been digested, the preparation of *peyā* (gruel) with milk is recommended.
[One should take] one hundred parts of *balā*, one-fourth part of *guḍūcī*, and one-eighth part of *rāsnā*.

6.28.149 | Having boiled one *āḍhaka* of oil in one hundred *āḍhakas* of water until the liquid remains as one-tenth of its original volume, one should add equal parts of curd-whey, sugarcane juice, and fermented gruel (*śukta*).
6.28.150 | One should cook [the oil] with half as much goat's milk and these paste ingredients (kalkas) measured at one pala each: śaṭī, sarala, dāru, elā, mañjiṣṭhā, aguru, and candana.
6.28.151 | With padmaka, ativiṣā, musta, sūrpaparṇī,
hareṇu, yaṣṭyāhva, surasa, vyāghranakha, ṛṣabhaka, and jīvaka;
6.28.152 | With the sap of *palāśa*, musk, *nalikā*, and *jātikoṣaka*; with *spṛkkā*, saffron, *śaileya*, *jātī*, *kaṭuphala*, and water;
6.28.153 | With tvacā, kunduru, karpūra, tutuṣka, śrīnivāsaka, lavaṅga, nakha, kakkola, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, and priyaṅgu;

6.28.154 | When the decoction has been prepared with *sthauṇeya*, *tagara*, *dhyāma*, *vacā*, the sprouts of *madana*, and *nāgakeśara*, one should add [the powder] once it has been removed from the heat.
6.28.155 | Then, one should employ that strained leaf-paste according to the prescribed method for [treating] dyspnea,
cough, fever, hiccups, vomiting, abdominal tumors, chest wounds, and consumption.
6.28.156 | This excellent Bala oil destroys splenic enlargement, consumption, epilepsy, and misfortune; it is the foremost destroyer of diseases caused by Vata.
6.28.157 | (Spoken by the teacher Kṛṣṇātreya to Agniveśa:
Thus ends the Bala-oil.
One should boil five *tulās* of *amṛtā* in eight *droṇas* of water.
6.28.158 | One should cook two āḍhakas of oil with an equal amount of milk when one-quarter remains,
along with elā, māṃsī, nata, uśīra, sārivā, kuṣṭha, and candana.
6.28.159 | With balā, āmalakī, medā, śatapuṣpā, ṛddhi, jīvaka,
kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, śrāvaṇī, atibalā, and nakha;
6.28.160 | With mahāśrāvaṇī, jīvantī, vidārī, and kapikacchu; with śatāvarī, mahāmedā, karkaṭa-ākhyā, and hareṇu.
6.28.161 | With vacā, gokṣura, eraṇḍa, rāsnā, kālā, sahācara,
vīrā, śallakī, musta, tvak, patra, ṛṣabhaka, and bālaka;
6.28.162 | With one karṣa each of sahailā, kuṅkuma, spṛkkā, and tridaśāhva;
with three karṣas of mañjiṣṭhā; and with eight palas of madhuka.

6.28.163 | With these pastes, one should restore to their natural state those whose vigor, digestive fire, and strength are diminished, whose minds are deluded, and who are afflicted by insanity, aversion, and epilepsy.
6.28.164 | This foremost oil, called Amṛta, is the best for curing diseases of Vāta;
it was spoken by the preceptor Kṛṣṇātreya and is honored by physicians. Thus ends the Amṛtādya-taila.
6.28.165 | One should cook one droṇa of oil in a decoction of a thousand parts of rāsnā, along with ground Himalayan aromatics and the elādigaṇa; this cures ailments caused by vāta.
6.28.166 | This same procedure applies to aśvagandhā, prasāraṇī, and the two types of balā;
or one may cook [the oil] separately with the decoction, paste, and milk of balā and the others.
Thus ends the Rāsnā oil (6.28.167). One should cook equal parts of radish juice, milk, oil, curd, and sour gruel together with a paste of balā, citraka, and rock salt.
6.28.168 | With pippalī, ativiṣā, rāsnā, cavikā, aguru, śigru, bhallātaka, vacā, kuṣṭha, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and viśvabheṣaja;
6.28.169 | A decoction prepared with *puṣkaramūla*, *śaṭī*, *bilva*, *śatāhvā*, *naṭa*, and *dāru*— when drunk,
it cures even the most severe diseases of a vāta nature.
Thus ends the oil beginning with radish (mūlaka).
6.28.170. One should cook one āḍhaka of oil in a decoction consisting of two hundred roots of vṛṣa and one hundred of guḍūcī, along with one part each of citraka and aśvagandhā.
6.28.171 | This should be administered with milk when [the body] is broken by Vāyu or likewise when it is shattered;
furthermore, this becomes even more effective when prepared with the prior addition of oil.
Thus ends the oil beginning with vṛṣa-mūla (6.28.172). Rāsnā, śirīṣa, yaṣṭyāhva, śuṇṭhī, sahacara, and amṛtā—
6.28.173 | One should prepare a decoction using ten-pala portions each of syonāka, dāru, śampāka, hayagandhā, and trikaṇṭaka.
6.28.174 | Then, with that decoction, along with one karṣa each of all the fragrant substances, and with curd, sour gruel, māṣa-bean water, radish juice, and auspicious sugarcane juice;
One should cook one *prastha* of oil together with one *prastha* each of [the aforementioned substances];
it cures enlargement of the spleen (*plīha*), urinary retention, asthma, cough, and diseases caused by wind (*māruta*).
6.28.176 | This is called Mūlakataila (Radish Oil), which increases complexion, longevity, and strength.
Thus ends the section on Mūlakataila.
[The oil is prepared from] barley, jujube, horse gram, fish, Śigru, and Bilva.
And oil prepared with the juice of radishes, combined with curd and milk.
6.28.177 | Having prepared it, the physician should administer this oil, which cures all wind-related diseases;
this oil, processed with garlic juice and these [other] ingredients, destroys Vāta.
6.28.178 | One should also have these oils drunk by a woman who has bathed after her menses;
for by drinking any one of these, even a barren woman may give birth to a son.

6.28.179 | Furthermore, the oil beginning with aguru which has been prescribed for cold-fever (śītajvara) is also proven effective against hundreds of various types of wind-diseases (vātaroga) when prepared accordingly.
6.28.180 | Those oils which will be described for vātaśoṇita (rheumatic disorders) should also be employed by one desiring success for the purpose of pacifying vāta.
6.28.181 | There is no medicine superior to oil for subduing the wind (māruta).
Due to its pervasive, hot, heavy, and unctuous nature, it becomes even more powerful through processing (saṃskāra).
Therefore, when prepared by means of groups of wind-alleviating [substances] by the hundreds and thousands,
it quickly destroys diseases situated within the subtle channels.
6.28.183 | All therapeutic measures are generally recommended when [the doshas] are combined,
and they are especially indicated when the channels are obstructed by vāta along with pitta and the other doshas.
6.28.184 | In the case of a fever specifically covered by pitta, one should administer cold and hot treatments alternately; furthermore, jīvanīya ghee is recommended.
6.28.185 | Desert meat, barley, śāli rice, nourishing enemas (yāpana),
milk enemas, purgation, drinking milk, and [milk] boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī) and balā.
6.28.186 | One should perform sprinkling with licorice, balā, oil, ghee, and milk,
or with a decoction of the five roots (pañcamūla), or with cold water.
6.28.187 | When [the digestive fire] is obstructed by phlegm (kapha), one should prescribe barley-based foods, meat of wild animals and birds,
strong sudations, non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), emesis, and purgation.
6.28.188 | Old ghee as well as oil derived from sesame and mustard seeds is beneficial.
When [the disease] is associated with both phlegm and bile, one should first subdue the bile.
6.28.189 | Having determined that the *kapha* has reached the stomach (*āmāśaya*), one should administer emesis.
6.28.190 | When pitta is present throughout the body, one should administer purgation for the colon;
likewise, when kapha has been liquefied by sudation and is situated in the colon.
6.28.191 | Or, if pitta manifests its symptoms, one should eliminate it with enemas;
likewise, vāta accompanied by kapha should be removed with warm enemas mixed with cow’s urine.
6.28.192 | One should eliminate [the disorder] associated with pitta by means of purgatives combined with milk;
one should then administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) using oils prepared with sweet medicinal herbs.
6.28.193 | When vata accompanied by phlegm is located in the head, one should administer medicated smoke, nasal drops, and other such treatments.
Once pitta and phlegm have been removed, that vata which follows the channels of the chest [should be treated].
6.28.194 | If a remnant of the disease remains there, treatment consisting solely of purgatives (vātika) should be administered;
if it is covered by blood, one should perform the treatment for vāta-śoṇita (blood-wind disorder).

6.28.195 | One should employ [this treatment] for āmavāta that destroys prameha, vāta, and medas; fomentation, massage, meat broth, milk, and unctuous substances are beneficial when [vāta] is covered by muscle tissue.
6.28.196 | When there is excessive affection (mahāsneha) located in the marrow and bones, it should be treated as before when obstructed by semen;
when obstructed by food, it requires scraping (*ullekha*), digestive treatment (*pācana*), digestive stimulants (*dīpana*), and lightening therapy (*laghu*).
6.28.197 | Diuretic drugs should be used with urine; sudations and urethral enemas (uttara-basti) [should be used];
castor oil with feces; and treatment for unctuous udāvarta should be performed.
6.28.198 | A dosha situated in its own site is strong; one should first conquer it with its own specific medicines, either by emetics, purgatives, enemas, or pacifying therapies.
6.28.199 | (Thus it has been stated regarding the wind being obstructed by pitta and the other doshas as appropriate.
Now listen to the mutual obstruction of the five types of wind among themselves.
6.28.200 | O sinless one, this characteristic, which I am describing both in detail and in brief,
[is that] the prāṇa envelops udāna and the others, and they in turn envelop the prāṇa.
6.28.201 | Likewise, all the others beginning with udāna [are connected] to one another in their proper order;
these twenty coverings are mutually intense.
6.28.202 | One should properly discern those [signs] of the five vital airs (māruta),
having recognized the emptiness of all the sense organs and the decline of memory and strength.
6.28.203 | When the *prāṇa* is obstructed by the *vyāna*, the symptoms there are actions involving the upper part of the neck,
excessive sweating, horripilation, skin disorders, and numbness of the limbs.
6.28.204 | When the vyāna is obstructed by the prāṇa, purgation combined with oleation should be administered there.
When the samāna is obstructed by the prāṇa, there may occur numbness, stammering, and muteness.

6.28.205 | In those cases where the apāna wind is obstructed by a similar [dosha], the application of four types of oleation therapies (sneha), including those for pacification (sayāpana), is recommended; these cure disorders of the grahaṇī, the sides of the chest, and the heart.
6.28.206 | When there is pain in the seat of undigested food (āmāśaya), digestive-stimulating ghee is recommended;
likewise when there is stiffness of the head, catarrh, and obstruction of inhalation and exhalation.
6.28.207 | When the udāna vāyu is obstructed by prāṇa, there occurs heart disease and dryness of the mouth;
in that case, treatments for the upper body and methods of consolation should be employed.

6.28.208 | When the *prāṇa* is obstructed by the *udāna*, there is the destruction of action, vigor, strength, and complexion, or even death; [in that case], one should [sprinkle] him slowly with cold water.
6.28.209 | One should sprinkle him, comfort him, and provide him with ease;
for when the apāna is obstructed by the upward-moving [vāyu], diseases such as vomiting and dyspnea arise.

6.28.210 | In that case of upward-moving *apāna* being obstructed by *vāta*, enemas and the like, as well as food that promotes downward movement, should be administered. There will be fainting, diminished digestive fire, and diarrhea.
6.28.211 | In that case of [excessive] wind, there should be emesis, along with digestive stimulants and constipating food.
[Otherwise, there may arise] vomiting, flatulence, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), abdominal tumors (gulma), pain, and cutting pain in the anal region.

6.28.212 | When the apāna is obstructed by the vyāna, one should treat it with unctuous substances to restore its downward movement. When the vyāna is obstructed by the apāna, there may be obstruction of feces, urine, and semen.
6.28.213 | Even in that case, excessive indulgence is considered to encompass all [the symptoms]:
fainting, drowsiness, delirium, weakness of the limbs, and the loss of digestive fire, vitality, and strength.
6.28.214 | When the vyāna vāyu is obstructed by the samāna vāyu,
there occurs physical exertion, light eating, stiffness, diminished digestive fire, absence of perspiration, loss of activity, and closing of the eyes.
6.28.215 | When Vyāna is obstructed by Udāna, then a diet that is moderate and light is beneficial.
Thus, one should recognize the five mutually obstructed types of Vāta by their respective symptoms.
6.28.216 | The decrease or increase of these respective functions is considered to occur within the *āvaraṇa*.
Thus, this group of eight *āvaraṇas* has been described according to their gross characteristics.
6.28.217 | This medicinal treatment with its specific signs is for the increase of the intellect of the wise,
after having observed the locations of the *vātās* and the increase or decrease of their functions.

6.28.218 | Having observed the other twelve coverings (of the body), the physician should administer oleation, unguents, internal potions, enemas, and so forth, in every respect, as a means of medical victory.
6.28.219 | One should apply [the treatment] either hot or cold in succession by alternating them;
one should direct the udāna upward and facilitate the downward movement of the apāna.
6.28.220 | One should pacify the *samāna* breath and employ the *vyāna* in three ways;
the *prāṇa* must be protected from all four, for its stability is certain in its own place.
6.28.221 | Thus, one should cause those who have strayed onto wrong paths to return to their own proper state.
Fainting, burning sensations, giddiness, pain, a sense of scorching heat, and a desire for cold [are the symptoms].
6.28.222 | When pitta obstructs the vital breath (prāṇa), there is vomiting of undigested matter, spitting,
and the suppression of sneezing, eructation, exhalation, and inhalation.

6.28.223 | When the vital breath (prāṇa) is obstructed by phlegm (kapha), the symptoms are loss of appetite, vomiting, fainting and other such signs, burning sensation in the navel and chest, and exhaustion.
6.28.224 | When the udāna vāyu is occluded by pitta, there is loss of strength (ojas) and exhaustion;
when the udāna is occluded by kapha, there is discoloration and impairment of speech and voice.
6.28.225 | Weakness, heaviness of the limbs, and loss of appetite arise;
as well as excessive perspiration, thirst, burning sensations, fainting, and indeed a lack of relish for food.
6.28.226 | When the samāna vāyu is obstructed by pitta, there occurs an impairment of the body's heat,
as well as absence of perspiration, sluggishness of the digestive fire, and horripilation.
6.28.227 | When the samāna vāyu is obstructed by kapha, there is excessive coldness of the limbs;
but when the vyāna vāyu is obstructed by pitta, there is a burning sensation throughout the body and exhaustion.
6.28.228 | There is a sense of heaviness in the limbs, accompanied by distress and pain;
there is heaviness of all the limbs and pains arising in all the joints and bones.
6.28.229 | When the Vyāna [vital air] is obstructed by Kapha, the symptoms are excessive obstruction of its movement,
as well as yellowish urine and feces, and a burning sensation in the anus and penis.
6.28.230 | When the downward wind (apāna) is obstructed by pitta, there is the excessive discharge of menstrual blood (rajas),
and the passage of stool that is broken up, mixed with phlegm (śleṣman), and heavy.
6.28.231 | When the apāna is obstructed by phlegm (śleṣman), there occurs the onset of kapha-type urinary disorders (kaphameha);
furthermore, there is a mixture of the symptoms of both pitta and kapha.
6.28.232 | Having observed this, the learned physician should declare it to be a mixed condition (miśra-āvaraṇa),
if the other two [doshas] are located in the specific site assigned to that particular vāyu.
6.28.233 | The two [doshas] manifest various diseases according to their own nature,
having obstructed both the prāṇa and the udāna breaths by means of kapha and pitta.
6.28.234 | Physicians whose vision is the scripture perceive [the vital breaths] as being of great importance;
specifically, life depends upon *prāṇa*, while strength is dependent upon *udāna*.
6.28.235 | From the excessive pressure of those two, there would be a loss of both lifespan and strength;
for all these [treatments], if not properly understood, as well as when performed beyond a year, lead to such results.
6.28.236 | Through neglect, these may become incurable or difficult to treat:
heart disease, abscess, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, and diarrhea.
6.28.237 | Complications arise from the neglect of those [obstructed] [doshas];
therefore, the physician should recognize the obstruction of the wind (pavana).

6.28.238 | Having correctly observed the medical treatment for that which consists of the five elements [the body], whether caused by wind (vāta), bile (pitta), or phlegm (śleṣman), the physician should then proceed accordingly.

6.28.239 | With unctuous substances that do not cause secretions, which purify the channels and are not antagonistic to kapha and pitta, one should administer whatever is conducive to the downward movement of vāta.
6.28.240 | Even when all the sites [of the body] are obstructed, that treatment which is beneficial for Vāta should be administered quickly;
generally, sustaining enemas (yāpanā-basti) along with sweet unctuous enemas (sānuvāsana) are recommended.
6.28.241 | Having carefully considered the excess of strength, mild purgatives are beneficial;
indeed, the use of all types of rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana) is highly recommended.
6.28.242 | A man subsisting on milk should practice the linctus prescribed by Bhārgava, made from an abundance of *śailaja*, lac, and *guggulu*, along with milk.

6.28.243 | The eleven hundred preparations with sugar mentioned in the chapter on Abhayāmalakīya are all digestive stimulants and astringents when used for one obstructed by the downward wind (apāna).
6.28.244 | That which facilitates the downward movement of flatus and purifies the colon—
thus has the treatment for those [doshas] that are obstructed been briefly described.
6.28.245 | Having reflected upon this himself, the physician should treat the afflictions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the others accordingly:
when [the breath] is obstructed by pitta, he should use pitta-alleviating measures that do not oppose vāta;
when obstructed by kapha, he should use kapha-alleviating measures that promote the downward movement of vāta.
6.28.246 | Just as the course of wind, sun, and moon in the world is difficult to comprehend,
so too is that of wind, bile, and phlegm within the body.
6.28.247 | Having understood the decrease, increase, equilibrium, and likewise the obstruction of the wind and other humors, the physician does not err in his professional actions.

6.28.248 | Regarding this, there are two verses:— The locations and functions of the fivefold self within the body according to its respective sites; the cause of the provocation of the bodily constituents (dhātus), the provoked state, and the diseases [produced] when it is obstructed or unobstructed in other locations.
6.28.249 | The Lord of Life performs all the functions of living beings; this has been fully explained.
One who follows the tenets of the scripture should apply these [therapies] after considering the locality, suitability, season, and strength.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vāta Diseases," in the Section on Therapeutics (*Cikitsā-sthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala. Chapter Twenty-nine.
6.29.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of *vāta-śoṇita* (blood disorders caused by *vāta*).
6.29.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

6.29.3 | Agniveśa questioned his preceptor, who was seated in the midst of the sages after performing the fire-sacrifice, who was single-mindedly focused, and who possessed the splendor of fire— Punarvasu.
6.29.4 | Then the teacher explained to him the causes, symptoms, and treatments for the combination of wind and blood, which is like the union of fire and wind.
6.29.5 | By the consumption of salty, sour, pungent, alkaline, unctuous, hot, and undigested foods; and by water-soaked or dried meat of aquatic or marshy animals, oil-cakes, and radishes.
6.29.6 | With horse-gram, black gram, flat beans, leafy vegetables, and the like; with meat, sugarcane, curd, sour gruel, sauvīra, vinegar, buttermilk, wine, and fermented liquors;

6.29.7 | By eating incompatible foods, overeating, anger, sleeping during the day, and staying awake at night— these [factors] generally affect those who are delicate and accustomed to eating sweet food and living in comfort.
6.29.8 | Vātaśoṇita (blood vitiated by wind) becomes aggravated in those who have the habit of moving about improperly,
as well as in men when blood is corrupted due to injury or impurity.
6.29.9 | From the consumption of food that is astringent, pungent, bitter, or slightly dry; from fasting; and from riding horses, camels, or vehicles, or from playing in water, bathing, and leaping;

6.29.10 | In heat, from excessive travel over uneven terrain, from sexual intercourse, or from the suppression of natural urges, the wind (vāyu) becomes aggravated; and when it is obstructed on its path by the increased blood, [it causes disease].
6.29.11 | When it vitiates the blood entirely, that should be known as vātaśoṇita (blood vitiated by wind);
it is also called by the names khuḍa, vātabalāsa, and āḍhyavāta.
6.29.12 | Its locations are the hands, the feet, the fingers, and all the joints;
having first established itself in the hands and feet, it spreads through the body as its root.
6.29.13 | Because of its subtlety and its capacity to pervade everything,
as well as the fluidity and mobility of blood, it moves through the channels of the vessels while entering the body.
6.29.14 | Struck during the joints (parvan), the agitated [vāta] remains fixed due to its tortuous nature;
remaining there, combined with pitta and other humors, it produces various types of pain.
6.29.15 | It produces suffering within those very [joints]; therefore, for the most part, various pains arise in the joints of men that are exceedingly difficult to endure.
6.29.16 | Excessive sweating or its absence, blackness of the skin, loss of tactile sensation, excessive pain in wounds,
looseness of the joints, lassitude, malaise, and the eruption of pustules [occur].
6.29.17 | In the knees, shanks, thighs, hips, as well as in the hands, feet, and the joints of the limbs, there is piercing pain,
throbbing, a splitting sensation, heaviness, and numbness.
6.29.18 | Itching in the joints, pain that repeatedly appears and disappears,
discoloration, and the appearance of circular patches are the premonitory signs of vātāsṛj (vātarakta).
6.29.19 | That [fever] is said to be of two kinds: superficial and deep.
That which rests upon the skin and flesh is superficial, while that which rests within is deep.

6.29.20 | The skin on the surface is characterized by itching, burning, pain, stretching, pricking, throbbing, and contraction; it is considered to be dark-brown or reddish, while the underlying layer is copper-colored.
6.29.21 | In the deep type, there is swelling that is stiff, hard, and extremely painful;
it is dark-brown or copper-colored, and is characterized by burning, pricking, throbbing, and suppuration.
6.29.22 | Accompanied by pain and a burning sensation, the forceful Vāyu repeatedly moves within the joints, bones, and marrow,
as if cutting them and causing them to contract.
6.29.23 | Moving throughout the body, it causes lameness or paralysis;
it should be recognized by all its symptoms as being based on both vāta and blood (asṛj).
6.29.24 | In that regard, listen now to the symptoms when Vata is predominant, or when Rakta, Pitta, or Kapha are predominant, or when they are combined, or when all are present together.
6.29.25 | Specifically, there is stretching of the vessels, pain, throbbing, and pricking;
as well as blackness, dryness of the swelling, and its darkening, increase, or decrease.
6.29.26 | When Vāyu is predominant, there is contraction of the vessels, fingers, and joints, seizing pain in the limbs,
excessive pain, flexion, stiffness, and an aversion to cold.
6.29.27 | In the blood [dosa], swelling is accompanied by intense pain, pricking, a coppery hue, and a tingling sensation;
it is not relieved by either unctuous or dry treatments, and is characterized by itching and exudation.
6.29.28 | Burning sensation, pain, fainting, perspiration, thirst, intoxication, giddiness, redness,
suppuration, discharge, and emaciation are said to occur in the Pitta-type [fever].
6.29.29 | In cases of kapha, there is rigidity, heaviness, unctuousness, numbness, and dull pain;
one should recognize those arising from two or three doṣas by the combination of their respective causes and symptoms.
6.29.30 | That which is caused by a single doṣa and is recent is curable; that born from two doṣas is palliable;
that born from three doṣas is incurable, as is that which possesses complications.
6.29.31 | Insomnia, anorexia, dyspnea, putrefaction of the flesh, stiffness of the head,
fainting, intoxication, pain, thirst, fever, delusion, and tremors;
6.29.32 | Hiccups, pricking pain in the limbs, erysipelas, suppuration, piercing pain, vertigo, exhaustion,
curvature of the fingers, eruptions, burning sensations, affliction of the vital points (marmans), and tumors.
6.29.33 | That which is devoid of these complications, or even of delusion alone;
that which is excessively discharging, discolored, rigid, and causes tumors (arbuda).
6.29.34 | One should avoid that which causes contraction and afflicts the senses;
a disease with incomplete complications is palliable, while one without complications is curable.

6.29.35 | When the wind (māruta) settles in the branches and joints, it quickly obstructs the path of the blood; by mutually blocking one another, it carries away the vital breaths through intense pains.
6.29.36 | Therein, one should let out the blood using a horn, leeches, a needle, or a gourd;
or by means of scarifications or venesection, according to the specific humor involved and according to the patient's strength.
6.29.37 | Blood should be let by means of leeches from a part afflicted by pain, burning, piercing, or pricking sensations;
it should be removed with horns or gourds from areas characterized by numbness, itching, or tingling.
6.29.38 | As it moves from one region of the body to another, it should be drained by means of venesection or scarification;
however, it should not be drained when there is exhaustion of the limbs, nor when the condition is dry or dominated by Vāta.
Due to the loss of blood, vāyu produces deep-seated swelling, stiffness, tremors, diseases of the tendons and vessels,
exhaustion, and even contractions.
6.29.40 | Lame gait and other diseases of the wind (vāta), as well as death, may result from excessive bloodletting;
therefore, one should extract blood from the lubricated body in the proper measure.

6.29.41 | Having first administered oleation, one should treat the patient with purgatives combined with unctuous substances, or with mild, non-unctuous purgatives; furthermore, the repeated application of enema therapy is recommended.
6.29.42 | Generally, affusions, massages, ointments, foods, and unctuous substances that do not cause internal burning are recommended for vātarakta; however, listen now to my specific instructions.
6.29.43 | One should treat superficial [fevers] with external applications such as ointments, massages, affusions, and poultices;
one should treat deep-seated [fevers] with purgation, non-unctuous enemas, and the drinking of unctuous substances.
6.29.44 | One should treat a condition dominated by Vāta with the internal administration of ghee, oil, muscle fat, and marrow;
with external massages and enemas; and with comfortably warm poultices.
6.29.45 | One should conquer a case where blood-bile (raktapitta) predominates by means of purgatives, the drinking of ghee and milk, affusions, enemas, and cooling, sedative treatments.
6.29.46 | Mild emesis, not excessive, along with oleation,
affusions, fasting, and lukewarm plasters are recommended in cases of vātarakta where kapha is predominant.
6.29.47 | When vāta-śoṇita is dominated by kapha and vāta, if it is smeared with cold substances,
the increase of burning, swelling, pain, and itching will occur due to the application of an astringent (stambhana) agent.
6.29.48 | When rakta-pitta is predominant, there occurs burning, moistening, and cracking due to hot [applications];
therefore, the physician, having ascertained the strength of the doshas, should perform the treatment.

6.29.49 | One should avoid sleeping during the day, as well as feverish distress, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, pungent and hot foods, heavy and obstructive [to the channels] substances, and salty and sour tastes.
6.29.50 | Ancient grains such as barley, wheat, nīvāra, śāli, and ṣaṣṭika rice,
as well as birds that scatter their food (viṣkira) and those that peck (pratuda), are beneficial for the purpose of food or for providing nutritional essence.
6.29.51 | Āḍhakī, caṇaka, mudga, masūra, and makuṣṭhaka,
prepared as soups with abundant ghee, are recommended for vātaśoṇita (gout).
6.29.52 | Suniṣaṇṇaka, vetrāgra, kākamācī, śatāvarī, vāstuka, upodikā, and likewise sauvarcala as vegetables.
6.29.53 | One should cause him, who is accustomed to vegetables, to be given greens fried in ghee and meat broth as a side dish; likewise, cow’s milk, buffalo milk, and goat’s milk are beneficial.
6.29.54 | Thus, the treatment for vātarakta has been briefly described;
this same matter shall now be explained again in full detail.
6.29.55 | Ghee prepared with equal parts of śrāvaṇī, kṣīrakākolī, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, and madhuka, along with milk, cures vātarakta (gout/rheumatism).
6.29.56 | One should grind together balā, atibalā, medā, ātmaguptā, śatāvarī, kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, rāsnā, and ṛddhi.
Ghee prepared with four times its quantity of milk and these [drugs] cures vātarakta (gout/rheumatism),
and destroys heart disease, anemia, erysipelas, jaundice, and fever.
6.29.58 | One should cook ghee with a decoction of trāyantikā, tāmalakī, the two types of kākolī, śatāvarī, and kaśerukā, along with the pastes of these same ingredients.
6.29.59 | Having added equal amounts of the juices of *parūṣaka*, *drākṣā*, and *kāśmarya*,
as well as the fresh juice of *vidārī* separately, along with four times the amount of milk;
6.29.60 | This medicated ghee, known as Pārūṣaka,
is prescribed for vātarakta, chest wounds, emaciation, erysipelas, and fever of the pitta type.
Thus ends the Pārūṣaka ghee (6.29.61). [Take] the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), Varṣābhū, Eraṇḍa, and Punarnavā;
Mudgaparṇī, Mahāmedā, Māṣaparṇī, and Śatāvarī.
6.29.62 | Having taken two palas each of śaṅkhapuṣpī, avākpuṣpī, rāsnā, atibalā, and balā, one should boil them in one droṇa of water.
6.29.63 | When one-quarter remains, one should add equal quantities of milk, curd, sugarcane juice, and goat's milk,
mix them with one āḍhaka of ghee, and cook slowly over a mild fire.
6.29.64 | Having added the pastes of the two types of Medā, Kāśmarya fruit, Utpala, Tvakkṣīrī, Pippalī, Drākṣā, Padma seeds, and Punarnavā;
6.29.65 | Nāgara, kṣīrakākolī, padmaka, the two types of bṛhatī,
vīrā, śṛṅgāṭaka, bhavya, urumāṇa, and nikocaka.
6.29.66 | Likewise, with dates, walnuts, vātāma, muñjāta, and abhiṣuka—
when one āḍhaka of ghee has been processed with these, one should add honey once it has cooled.
6.29.67 | Having recognized that it has been properly prepared, one should store it well-secured.
Once the ritual for protection has been performed, one should have the patient, who is clean, consume a dose commensurate with his capacity.
6.29.68 | Anemia, fever, hiccup, hoarseness of voice,
fistula-in-ano, pain in the flanks, consumption, cough, splenic enlargement, and gout (vātaśoṇita).

It destroys wasting diseases resulting from injury, epilepsy, urinary calculi, and gravel; it likewise cures all diseases affecting the entire body or a single limb, as well as the retention of urine.
This medicated ghee (sarpis) promotes strength and complexion, bestows prosperity, destroys wrinkles and graying hair, is vitalizing, aphrodisiac, and grants sons even to barren women.
6.29.71 | Or one should drink ghee prepared with grape juice and madhūka-water along with sugar-candy; likewise, one may drink milk boiled in the fresh juice of guḍūcī.
6.29.72 | Jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, medā, ṛṣyaproktā, śatāvarī, madhuka, madhuparṇī, and both types of kākolī.
6.29.73 | Mudgaparṇī, māṣaparṇī, daśamūla, punarnavā,
balā, amṛtā, vidārī, along with aśvagandhā and aśmabheda.
6.29.74 | One should prepare ghee and oil from the decoction and paste of these [drugs], adding fat and marrow as available from wild animals, birds of prey, gallinaceous birds, and waterfowl.
6.29.75 | That [milk] prepared with four times its quantity of milk cures vātaśoṇita (gout) located throughout the entire body, as well as other terrible diseases born of vāta.
6.29.76 | Sthirā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, bṛhatī, sārivā, along with śatāvarī;
kāśmarya, ātmaguptā, vṛścīra, and likewise the two types of bala.
6.29.77 | To the decoction of these [drugs], one should add four parts of milk, along with oil and ghee separately,
together with medā, śatāvarī, yaṣṭi, jīvantī, jīvaka, and ṛṣabha.
6.29.78 | Having cooked this in a quantity of milk three times its own weight with one and a half times as much sugar,
it should be stirred with a churning stick and drunk in cases of vātarakta caused by all three doṣas.
6.29.79 | One should cause [the patient] to drink milk well-blended with oil and sugar;
or one may drink milk mixed with ghee, oil, sugar, and honey.
6.29.80 | A *prastha* of milk boiled with *aṃśumatī* and two *upalas* of sugar is recommended for drinking; likewise, [milk] boiled with *pippalī* and *nāgara* is praised for the same purpose.
6.29.81 | Milk boiled with *balā*, *śatāvarī*, *rāsnā*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *pīlu*, *śyāmā*, castor root (*eraṇḍa*), and *sthirā* destroys the afflictions caused by *vāta*.

6.29.82 | Or one whose Vāyu is obstructed by Pitta and blood should drink milk that is warm from the udder and mixed with urine to facilitate the downward movement of the humors (doṣas), or else milk mixed with the powder of trivṛt.
6.29.83 | A person with an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas) should drink castor oil with milk for the purpose of purgation; once it has been digested, he should eat rice with milk.
6.29.84 | A person should drink a decoction of *abhayā* fried in ghee,
or take the powder of *trivṛt* with milk as an after-drink, or with grape juice.
6.29.85 | One should drink the decoction of kāśmarya, trivṛt, drākṣā, triphalā, and parūṣaka, combined with salt and honey, for the purpose of purgation.
6.29.86 | Or one should drink a decoction of triphalā mixed with honey;
or, if kapha is predominant, a decoction of dhātrī, haridrā, and mustā.

6.29.87 | And one should repeatedly purge that [patient] with mild, oil-impregnated applications prescribed for the [specific] kalpa, once it is known that the vāta is obstructed by waste matter (mala).
6.29.88 | Or one should eliminate his impurity with milk enemas mixed with ghee;
for indeed, there is no treatment for vātarakta equal to the enema.

6.29.89 | Nirūha enemas, along with oil enemas (anuvāsana), are recommended for pain in the bladder, groins, flanks, thighs, joints, bones, and the abdomen, as well as in cases of upward movement of wind (udāvarta).
6.29.90 | A wise physician should administer these oils in enema therapy (bastikarma),
as well as in nasal drops (nasya), massage (abhyañjana), and affusions (seka), for the alleviation of burning sensations and pain.

6.29.91 | One should cook one āḍhaka of oil with an equal quantity of milk in a decoction of one tulā of madhuyaṣṭī reduced to one-fourth, using paste (kalka) of [the following] ingredients measured at one pala each.
6.29.92 | With śatapuṣpā, varī, mūrvā, payasyā, aguru, and candana;
with sthirā, haṃsapadī, māṃsī, the two types of medā, and madhuparṇī;
6.29.93 | With kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, tāmalakī, ṛddhi, padmaka, jīvaka, ṛṣabha, jīvantī, tvak, patra, nakha, and vālaka;
6.29.94 | This oil, prepared with prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, sārivā, aindrī, and vitunnaka, destroys vāta-śoṇita (gout) when applied in four ways.

6.29.95 | It cures fever accompanied by complications, aching in the limbs, and afflictions extending throughout all the body parts; it destroys wind, blood, and bile disorders, as well as burning sensations and pain, and bestows strength and a healthy complexion.
Thus ends the oil of Madhuparṇī and others (6.29.96).
One hundred palas of madhuka, along with grapes, dates, parūṣaka,
madhūka, odanapāki, and one prastha of muñjātaka;
6.29.97 | One āḍhaka of kāśmarya fruit should be boiled in four droṇas of water;
when one-eighth remains and it has been strained, one should cook one āḍhaka of oil in that [decoction].
6.29.98 | Likewise, having added a paste measured at one pala each of āmalaka, kāśmarya, vidārī, and sugarcane juice, along with four droṇas of milk;
6.29.99 | Kadamba, āmalaka, akṣoṭa, padmabīja, kaśeruka,
śṛṅgāṭaka, śṛṅgavera, salt, pippalī, and sugar.
6.29.100 | One should mix [the oil] prepared with the vitalizing (jīvanīya) drugs with one prastha of honey;
it should be employed as nasal drops (nasya), for massage (abhyañjana), for drinking (pāna), and also for enema (basti).
6.29.101 | In all wind-related diseases (vātavyādhi), in stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), lockjaw (hanugraha),
in generalized or localized wind disorders (sarvāṅgaikāṅgavāta), and in wasting due to injury (kṣatakṣīṇa) or fever following injury (kṣatajvara).
6.29.102 | This oil known as Sukumāra destroys disorders of wind and blood, improves the voice and complexion, and bestows health, strength, and nourishment.
Thus ends the *Sukumāraka-taila*. 6.29.103: [One should take] *guḍūcī*, *madhuka*, the small *pañcamūla*, *punarnavā*, *rāsnā*, *eraṇḍa* root, and the *jīvanīya* drugs as they are available.
6.29.104 | Likewise, with five hundred parts of *balā*, one hundred parts of *palāśa*,
and one *āḍhaka* each of *kola*, *bilva*, barley, *māṣa*, and *kulattha* [grains];

6.29.105 | One should boil one *droṇa* of well-dried *kāśmarya* fruits in one hundred *droṇas* of water; once it has been reduced and strained until it is broken down, four *droṇas* of liquid should remain.
6.29.106 | One should cook one droṇa of oil with five times as much milk,
having ground together three palas each of sandalwood, uśīra, and keśara.
6.29.107 | Patra, elā, aguru, kuṣṭha, tagara, madhuyaṣṭikā,
and eight palas of mañjiṣṭhā— this [mixture], when prepared, is suitable for all applications.
6.29.108 | [It is indicated] in cases of vātarakta (gout/rheumatism), wasting from injury, exhaustion from carrying heavy loads,
diminished semen, trembling, convulsions, fractures, and those suffering from diseases of the entire body or a single limb.
This foremost oil, called Amṛta, destroys defects of the womb, epilepsy, insanity, lameness, and paralysis, as well as [difficult] childbirth.
Thus ends the "Amṛtādya" oil (6.29.110). [One should prepare it] with five palas each of lotus, cane, yaṣṭīmadhu, phenilā, padma, and utpala, as well as darbha, balā, candana, and kiṃśuka.
6.29.111 | One should cook one *prastha* of oil with water boiled [with the following], adding an equal measure of *sauvīra* (sour gruel),
along with *lodhra*, *kālīyaka*, *uśīra*, *jīvaka*, *rāsnā*, and *keśara*.
6.29.112 | With the leaves of the *madayantī* creeper, lotus filaments, and *padmaka*,
along with *prapauṇḍarīka*, *kāśmarya*, *māṃsī*, *medā*, and *priyaṅgu*.
6.29.113 | With half a pala of saffron and one pala of mañjiṣṭhā,
this Mahāpadma oil destroys vāta, blood disorders, and fever.
Thus ends the Mahāpadma oil (6.29.114). It should be prepared by boiling a decoction of padmaka, uśīra, yaṣṭyāhva,
and haridrā with the pastes of sarja, mañjiṣṭhā, vīrā, kākoli, and candana.
6.29.115 | This *khuḍḍūkapadmaka* oil alleviates wind-blood disorders (*vātāsra*) and burning sensations. Thus ends the *khuḍḍūkapadmaka* oil.
Ten times the quantity of milk should be prepared with one hundred parts of *yaṣṭimadhuka*.
6.29.116 | Oil prepared with four droṇas of that [oil] and one pala of madhuka,
or with the decoctions of madhuka and kāśmarya, cures vātarakta (gout).
6.29.117 | Having ground one pala of madhuparṇī, one should cook it with one prastha of oil in four times as much milk;
this should be repeated a hundred times, and the same process should be performed a hundred times with madhuka.

6.29.118 | This prepared [mixture] should be administered in cases of the three doṣas; it cures vātarakta, asthma, and cough, and destroys heart disease, anemia, erysipelas, jaundice, and burning sensations.
Thus is the honey-madhu oil processed a hundred times.
6.29.119. One should cook oil with equal parts of milk along with the decoction and paste of bala;
processed a thousand or a hundred times, it cures vātarakta and vāta diseases.
6.29.120 | This is the most excellent elixir (rasāyana), which clarifies the senses,
promotes longevity, provides nourishment, improves the voice, and destroys defects of the semen and blood.
Thus is the Bala oil prepared by a thousand or a hundred decoctions (sahasrapāka or śatapāka).
Oil prepared with the juices of guḍūcī and milk, or with the juice of grapes,
or with the juices of madhuka and kāśmarya, cures vātarakta.
6.29.122 | Oil boiled with one āḍhaka of fermented rice-gruel (āranāla), four palas of resin (sarjarasa),
and a large quantity of water, when churned, is supreme for removing the pain of fever and burning sensations.
6.29.123 | A paste consisting of beeswax, madder, resin of the *sarja* tree, and *sārivā*,
mixed with *piṇḍa*-oil, removes the pain of *vātarakta* when used as an unguent.
Thus ends the section on Piṇḍataila.
6.29.124. Milk boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla) immediately relieves colic;
likewise, an affusion with lukewarm ghee is effective when the condition is predominantly caused by Vāta.
6.29.125 | Or one should sprinkle [the patient] with the four unctuous substances prepared with sweet drugs;
they should be lukewarm for those suffering from stiffness, convulsions, and pain, but cold in cases of burning sensation.
6.29.126 | Likewise, the physician [should treat it] with the milk of cows, sheep, or goats mixed with oil, or with decoctions of the *jīvanīya* group or the *pañcamūla*.
6.29.127 | Grapes, sugarcane juice, wines, curd-whey, sour gruel,
and water mixed with rice, honey, and sugar are recommended for the purpose of irrigation.

6.29.128 | During a burning sensation, sprinkling with cool water containing kumuda, utpala, padma, and other such flowers, as well as pearl necklaces and sandalwood, and physical contact with these items, is beneficial.
6.29.129 | On a bed sprinkled with the water from moonbeams, covered with linen and lotus petals, and fanned by a cool breeze touching the sand;
6.29.130 | Beloved women, with breasts moistened by sandalwood paste, speaking sweetly, cool to the touch and pleasant to embrace, destroy burning heat, pain, and exhaustion.
6.29.131 | In cases of inflammation, pain, and burning, one should drain the blood and apply a paste made of madhuka, the bark of aśvattha, māmsī, vīra, udumbara, and śādvala.
6.29.132 | An ointment made from aquatic plants or barley flour, combined with liquorice, milk, and ghee;
or ghee mixed with the *jīvanīya* drugs ground together, relieves pain and burning sensations.
6.29.133 | A paste made from sesame seeds, priyāla, madhuka, lotus stalks, and the root of vetasa,
ground with goat’s milk, removes burning sensations and redness.
6.29.134 | With prapauṇḍarīka, mañjiṣṭhā, dārvī, madhuka, and candana; with sugar, elā, rākṣā, saktu, masūra, uśīra, and padmaka;

6.29.135 | This plaster alleviates pain, burning sensation, spreading inflammation, redness, and swelling; however, these [prescribed] plasters are for cases where pitta and blood predominate. Now hear of the plasters for cases where vāta predominates.
6.29.136 | Green gram milk-porridge (udgapāyasa), prepared with wind-alleviating (vātaghna) drugs and made unctuous,
or a poultice (upanāha) made of sesamum and mustard pastes, removes pain.
6.29.137 | Aquatic, predatory, marshy, and swampy animals, well-prepared and combined with vitalizing herbs and fats, should be used for poultices (upanāhana).
6.29.138 | Fat, prepared with the life-promoting (jīvanīya) medicinal herbs and milk, destroys stiffness, distension, pain, convulsions, swelling, and rigidity of the limbs.
6.29.139 | Ghee, the root of sahacara, jīvantī, and goat’s milk [form a paste];
likewise, sesame seeds ground and then fried, quenched in milk, [form a paste].
6.29.140 | One should apply a plaster of *umā* ground with milk, as well as the fruits of *eraṇḍa*,
for the cessation of colic, and use *śatāhvā* when the digestive fire is excessive.

6.29.141 | Two prasthas each of ghee, oil, fat, and marrow from marshy animals, wild beasts, and birds, along with two prasthas each of castor oil and its roots, tops, and leaves, should be boiled together in a decoction [of the aforementioned drugs].

6.29.142 | For the purpose of a paste (kalka), one should take the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, cow’s milk, or goat’s milk, along with turmeric, blue lotus, kuṣṭha, cardamom, śatāhvā, and the leaves of aśvahana.

6.29.143 | One should also prepare the flowers of the *kākubha* tree separately in the measure of a *bilva* fruit; once the preparation has been removed from the heat and cooled, one should add eight palas of beeswax.
