6.29.144 | This plaster is recommended for those whose limbs are afflicted by the *śūla* (piercing pain), when the *vāyu* has entered the joints,
and in cases of *vātarakta*, dislocation, fracture, lameness, and kyphosis.
6.29.145 | When this [condition] is characterized by swelling, heaviness, itching, and so forth, and is dominated by Kapha,
oil cooked with urine, alkali, and wine is beneficial for massage.
6.29.146 | Ghee prepared with padmaka, tvak, madhuka, and sārivā,
combined with honey and fermented gruel (śukta), should be used for irrigation and massage when kapha is predominant.
6.29.147 | Alkaline oil, cow’s urine,
and water boiled with pungent [herbs] are recommended for sprinkling in cases of vātarakta where kapha is predominant.

6.29.148 | An ointment made of mustard seeds, nimba, arka, hiṃsrā, milk, and sesame is beneficial; it is excellent when prepared with the bark of kapittha, ghee, milk, and roasted grain flour (saktu).
6.29.149 | A plaster consisting of house-soot, vacā, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā,
and the two types of rajanī relieves pain in vātarakta where vāta and kapha predominate.
6.29.150 | Tagara, bark, śatāhvā, elā, kuṣṭha, musta,
hareṇukā, dāru, and vyāghranakha, when ground with sour liquids, cure disorders of vāta, kapha, and āsra (blood).
Similarly, the seed of *madhuśigru* combined with fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) is beneficial;
having been smeared with acidic substances for a short while, one should sprinkle it upon a condition where vāta and kapha predominate.
6.29.152 | Triphalā, vyoṣa, patra, elā, tvakṣīrī, citraka, vacā, viḍaṅga, pippalīmūla, romaśa, and the bark of vṛṣaka.
6.29.153 | One should grind Ṛddhi, Tāmalakī, and Cavya in equal parts. Having smeared this onto an iron vessel in the early morning, one should then consume it at midday.
6.29.154 | One should avoid curd, fermented acids, milk, and incompatible foods;
however, [milk] is highly beneficial for those afflicted by Vata-blood disorders (vātāsra) and all types of colic (śūla), even when all the doṣas are involved.

6.29.155 | Having understood the specific locations of the doshas and their relative strength or weakness, one who is skilled in reasoning, exclusion, and deliberation should perform this medical treatment.
6.29.156 | When Vāyu is provoked by the obstruction of the channels due to an excessive increase of fat (medas) or phlegm (kapha),
oleation and nourishing therapies are not recommended at the outset.
One should diminish phlegm and fat through physical exercise, purification therapies, the drinking of *ariṣṭa* liquors and urine, purgatives, and the administration of buttermilk and *abhayā*.
6.29.158 One should drink the decoction of the Bodhi tree together with honey;
it quickly conquers vātarakta as well as even severe disorders of the three doṣas.
6.29.159 | By means of ancient barley, wheat, *sīdhu*, *ariṣṭa*, *surā*, and *āsava* liquors;
and by the internal use of *śilājatu*, *guggulu*, and honey.
6.29.160 | If blood is found to have invaded deep [tissues], one should treat it like vāta; subsequently, one should perform treatments that pacify vātarakta.
6.29.161 | However, due to the excessive increase of *rakta-pitta*, it quickly undergoes suppuration;
once burst, it either discharges blood or, if fully digested by heat, pus itself.

6.29.162 | Treatment for these two should be administered through cleansing, excision, and healing; furthermore, one should apply the specific treatment for complications according to their respective medical protocols.

6.29.163 | Regarding this, there are these verses:— The cause, the locations, and the root [of the disease], why it generally becomes aggravated in the joints, its premonitory symptoms, and the two-fold characteristics [of the disease].
6.29.164 | The signs of each distinct type, the predominance of the doshas, complications, the curable, the palliable, and the incurable, as well as the entire course of treatment for the curable.
6.29.165 | Thus has the treatment for vātarakta been described by the Great Sage to Agniveśa, both in summary and in detail, as well as according to its stages.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vātaśoṇita," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—where not extant—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Thirty:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the treatment of disorders of the female reproductive tract (yonivyāpad).
6.30.2 Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
On the sacred slope of the Himalayas, frequented by gods, siddhas, and rishis, which possesses celestial bathing-places and medicinal herbs, and is endowed with variegated minerals and rocks.
6.30.4 | While Punarvasu was dwelling in the practice of austerity, perceiving the truth through the application of yoga and having conquered his own self, Agniveśa questioned him.
6.30.5 | "O Blessed One! Since women are the supreme root of offspring for men, their destruction is being carried out by diseases that have taken refuge in their wombs."
6.30.6 | Therefore, out of a desire to benefit all beings, I wish to hear about their origin, the characteristics of those already born, and the medicinal treatment for them.
6.30.7 | Thus questioned by his disciple, the eminent seer Atri replied:
"Twenty disorders of the female reproductive tract (yoni) have been specified in the Compendium of Diseases."
6.30.8 | Through misconduct, through the vitiated menses of women,
through defects of the seed, and through destiny— listen as I describe these separately.

In a woman who consumes a vāta-aggravating diet and engages in vāta-aggravating activities, the wind (samīraṇa) becomes increased; having taken refuge in the womb, it causes pricking pain and distress in the vagina.
It causes stiffness, a sensation like the crawling of ants, as well as roughness,
numbness, fatigue, and other diseases born of wind (vāta).
6.30.11 | Due to vāta, the menstrual flow (artava) may be accompanied by pain and noise, with frothy and rough characteristics;
due to pitta, it arises from the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, alkaline, and similar substances, resulting in a morbid condition.

6.30.12 | A vagina afflicted by pitta is characterized by burning, suppuration, fever, and heat; the menstrual flow is blue, yellow, or black; and there is a profuse discharge of hot, corpse-like (putrid) matter.
6.30.13 | If the *kapha*, increased by obstructive factors, vitiates the female reproductive tract (*yoni*) of a woman,
it produces a discharge that is slimy, cold, characterized by itching, and associated with mild pain.
6.30.14 | Having vitiated all the bodily fluids, the three impurities (malas) cause the woman to become pale in complexion and to discharge a pale, slimy menses as she consumes all kinds of tastes.
6.30.15 | Those [fetuses] situated in the womb and the uterus cause the woman to contract her birth canal according to their specific characteristics;
she becomes afflicted with burning sensations and pain, and discharges a white, slimy fluid.
6.30.16 | When blood is vitiated by pitta due to factors that cause raktapitta,
it flows excessively from the vagina even when conception has occurred, accompanied by blood.
6.30.17 | If the pitta, located in the womb and the uterus, vitiates the blood,
she is considered to be *arajaskā* (one who has ceased menstruating), which produces extreme emaciation and discoloration.

6.30.18 | Because of not washing the vulva, living organisms born there cause itching. That [woman] would be "itching-footed" (acaraṇā) due to that itching, and because of it, she would long for hell.
6.30.19 | Through excessive sexual intercourse, the wind (vāyu), becoming aggravated, produces swelling, numbness, and pain in the woman's vagina; this condition is known as aticaraṇā.
6.30.20 | In sexual intercourse with one who is too young, the Vāyu, causing pain to the back, waist, thighs, and groins, vitiates the womb; for she has not yet reached the age of menstruation.
6.30.21 | In a pregnant woman, due to the habitual consumption of phlegm-increasing substances, or from the suppression of vomiting and respiration,
the provoked Vāyu brings Kapha to the womb and causes its vitiation.
6.30.22 | When it discharges a pale, painful, or purulent secretion, or flows with white phlegm, that vagina,
pervaded by disorders of phlegm and wind, is known as *upaplutā*.
6.30.23 | In a woman of bilious temperament living in close association with men,
the wind (vāyu), agitated by bile due to the suppression of sneezing and belching, vitiates her womb.
6.30.24 | The swelling is tender to the touch and painful; it bleeds with blue or yellow blood.
It spreads throughout the body as the woman suffers from pain in the hips, groins, and back, and is afflicted by fever.
6.30.25 | The wind (vāyu), by causing the upward reversal of its natural flow, reverses the womb.
Afflicted by pain, she discharges her menses with great difficulty as it has been turned upward.
6.30.26 | When the menstrual flow has been discharged, she attains ease at that very moment;
however, once the flow has ceased, she should be known by the wise as *udāvartinī*.
6.30.27 | When the fetus obstructs the wind during premature labor, that wind,
combined with phlegm and blood, produces a *karṇikā* (polyp) in the vagina.
6.30.28 | Because it obstructs the path of the blood, that [disorder] is considered to be *karṇinī*.
When, due to dryness (*raukṣya*), the wind (*vāyu*) destroys the fetus as soon as it is born, again and again;

6.30.29 | That which arises from vitiated blood in a woman is considered the "son-killer" (putraghnī). It occurs when she engages in sexual intercourse while excessively satiated with food, being oppressed by her meal.
6.30.30 | When the wind is situated in the vaginal canal of a woman whose limbs are improperly positioned,
it causes the mouth of the vagina to become crooked due to pain in the bones, flesh, and wind.
6.30.31 | The vagina is considered to be extremely painful and incapable of sexual intercourse, with its opening turned inward.
In a pregnant woman, the Vayu, becoming aggravated by dryness (raukṣya), vitiates the vagina.
6.30.32 | Due to a defect in the mother, that [fetus] may have a narrow opening like the point of a needle;
at the time of intercourse, the provoked wind (vāyu), obstructing its [the woman's] urges, causes this condition.
6.30.33 | It causes pain from the obstruction of feces and urine, as well as dryness of the vaginal opening;
semen that has entered the uterus [is expelled] after six days or seven nights.
6.30.34 | That which discharges [fluid], whether with pain or without pain, is called *vāminī*;
due to a defect in the seed (*bījadoṣa*), the womb is afflicted by wind (*māruta*) while the fetus is situated therein.
6.30.35 | A woman who hates men and has no breasts is a eunuch (ṣaṇḍhī) and cannot be treated.
Due to sexual intercourse on an uneven bed, the wind (vāyu/anila) becomes aggravated.
6.30.36 | It obstructs the opening of the uterus and the vaginal canal of a woman; with its mouth unobstructed, it causes pain and discharges dry, frothy blood.
6.30.37 | With swollen flesh, a large vaginal opening, and pain in the joints and groin—
by these characteristics, the twenty diseases born of the womb (yoni) are described.
6.30.38 | A womb afflicted by these defects does not retain the semen; therefore, a woman neither conceives nor falls victim to many diseases.
6.30.39 | They cause abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids (arśas), menorrhagia (pradara), and other conditions, as well as excessive affliction by vāta and the other doshas.
Of these [sixteen types], the last four and the first two arise from the vitiation of pitta.
6.30.40 | Pariplutā and vāminī are considered to be of the nature of vāta and pitta;
karṇinī arises from the vitiation of both vāta and kapha, while the remaining types are born of vāta alone.
6.30.41 | Indeed, the bodily humors beginning with Vāta afflict their bodies according to their own specific symptoms.
In cases born of Vāta, one should apply treatments that pacify Vāta, such as oleation, sudation, and enemas.
6.30.42 | A wise physician should administer a cooling treatment that destroys blood and bile for diseases caused by pitta;
however, for those born of kapha, he should perform a treatment that is dry and hot.

6.30.43 | In cases of *sannipāta* (combined humors), one should employ a mixed treatment; likewise, in cases of combined disorders, one should act accordingly. Furthermore, one should restore a displaced vagina that has been lubricated and fomented back to its proper position.
6.30.44 | One should bend the curved tongue with the hand, and lengthen it when it is contracted;
one should cause it to enter when it has protruded, and turn it when it is spread out.

6.30.45 | For the female genital tract, when displaced from its natural position, is considered to be like a foreign body (śalya) for a woman. One should treat every such afflicted genital tract with medical procedures such as emetics and the like.
6.30.46 | One should treat the woman with five mild [measures] after she has been lubricated and sweated;
once she is thoroughly purified in every respect, the remaining procedure is prescribed.
6.30.47 | Treatment that removes wind-related diseases is always beneficial for those afflicted by vāta;
it consists of the meat of aquatic and marshy animals, milk, sesame, and rice.
6.30.48 | One should treat [the patient] with tube-sweats (nāḍīsveda) and jar-sweats (kumbhīsveda) using wind-destroying herbs;
or, having anointed [the body] with salted oil, one should employ stone-sweats (aśmasveda), bed-sweats (prastarasveda), and mixed-sweats (saṅkarasveda).
6.30.49 | When she has sweated and her limbs have been sprinkled with lukewarm water, one should feed her meat broths that subdue Vāta.
In two droṇas of a decoction of balā, one should cook one āḍhaka each of ghee and oil.
6.30.50 | With sthirā, apāmārga, jīvantī, vīra, ṛṣabhaka, and jīvaka;
with śrāvaṇī, pippalī, mudgaparṇī, pīluparṇī, and māṣaparṇī;
6.30.51 | Furthermore, [a gruel] prepared with sugar, kṣīrakākolī, and kākanāsā, ground together with four times the amount of milk, should be drunk according to one's strength.
6.30.52 | Having destroyed diseases caused by vāta and pitta, that [mixture] brings about conception.
[It is prepared] with kāśmarya, triphalā, drākṣā, kāsamarda, and parūṣaka.
6.30.53 | One *prastha* of ghee [should be cooked] with one *akṣa* each of *punarnavā*, the two types of *rajanī*, *kākanāsā*, *sahācara*, *śatāvarī*, and *guḍūcī*.
One should drink this prepared formulation, which destroys disorders of the uterine wind (*yonivāta*) and is supreme for bestowing conception:
long pepper (*pippalī*), cumin (*kuñcikā*), cumin seed (*jājī*), vṛṣaka, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *vacā*.
Having ground together yavakṣāra, ajamodā, sugar, and likewise citraka,
one should fry them in ghee and have the patient drink them with *prasannā wine.
6.30.56 | For the alleviation of pain in the pelvic region, heart disease, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids,
[one should use] vṛṣaka, the roots of mātuluṅga, and madayantikā.
6.30.57 | One should drink [the powder of] pippalī and kuñcikā with salted wines;
likewise, in cases of pain, one should drink milk boiled with rāsnā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, and vṛṣaka.
6.30.58 | One should sprinkle [the area] with decoctions of guḍūcī, triphalā, and dantī;
[and apply] rock salt (saindhava), tagara, kuṣṭha, bṛhatī, and devadāru.
Oil prepared with equal parts of the pastes of *guḍūcī*, *mālatī*, *rāsnā*, *balā*, *madhuka*, and *citraka* should be applied; it removes pain.
6.30.60 | One should cook one *prastha* of oil with one *karṣa* each of *nidigdhikā*, *devadāru*, and *yūthikā*, along with cow’s urine and twice as much milk.

6.30.62 | Warm and unctuous oils that provide oleation should be prepared.

one afflicted by Pitta should use the five barks (pañcavalka); and one suffering from Kapha should use the drugs beginning with Śyāmā.

6.30.63 | For uterine conditions characterized by pitta, cold Pitta-alleviating treatments such as affusions, massages, and the application of cotton swabs (picu) should be performed, as well as the administration of ghees for the purpose of oleation.
6.30.64 | (The physician should likewise prepare preparations with pitta-alleviating herbs.
One should thoroughly macerate four *tulās* of the roots of *śatāvarī*.
6.30.65 | One should cook one āḍhaka of ghee with that juice equal in quantity to milk,
along with the drugs of the jīvanīya group, śatāvarī, mṛdvīkā, and parūṣaka.
6.30.66 | The physician, having prepared a decoction with one-eighth parts of ground priyāla, two yaṣṭis, and madhuka,
should add eight palas each of honey and pippalī once it has cooled.
6.30.67 | Then, one should lick a palmful [of this] mixed with ten palas of sugar;
it destroys defects of the uterine blood and semen, is aphrodisiac, and promotes virility.
6.30.68 | It cures every type of wound, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), cough, asthma, chlorosis (halīmaka),
jaundice, gout (vātarakta), erysipelas (vīsarpa), and stiffness of the heart and head.
6.30.69 | It conquers insanity, aversion to pleasure, and epilepsy caused by vāta and pitta.
This is the *bṛhacchatāvarīghṛta*.
In the same manner, clarified butter prepared with milk and the *jīvanīya* [herbs] is also effective.
6.30.70 | It is the physician’s remedy for those with bile-dominant (pittala) vaginal disorders that cause infertility;

6.30.71 | Prepared with lac-dye repeatedly processed in the bile of a boar,
along with barley powder and rock salt, and processed with the milk of the *arka* plant;

6.30.72 | A wick (varti) should be prepared and held repeatedly; thereafter, it should be sprinkled with lukewarm water [mixed] with long pepper (pippalī), black pepper (marica), māṣa, dill (śatāhvā), costus (kuṣṭha), and rock salt (saindhava).

6.30.73 | A wick, equal in size to the index finger, should be held [in the vagina] as a cleanser of the womb. One *droṇa* of unripe *udumbara* fruits combined with one *adroṇa* of water [should be boiled].
6.30.74 | Having soaked the sprouts of pañcavaktra, kulaka, mālatī,
and nimba in water overnight, one should cook one prastha of oil in that same water.
6.30.75 | One should insert a tampon of oil prepared with the ground exudations of lac, dhava, palāśa, and śālmalī bark into the vagina.
6.30.76 | One should perform irrigation with cool decoctions mixed with sugar for a vagina that is slimy, dilated, affected by the vitiation of time, or severe.
6.30.77 | Within seven days she becomes quickly purified and also conceives offspring,

6.30.79 | With *jambu*, mango, *madhyaka*, *kāsīsa*, *lodhra*, *kaṭphala*, *tinduka*, *saurāṣṭrika*, pomegranate bark, and the tender shoots of the *udumbara* tree;
6.30.80 | One should cook one *prastha* of oil with one *akṣa* each of goat's urine and twice as much milk; then one should apply a cotton swab (*picu*) soaked in it into the vagina.
6.30.81 | One should administer massage to the hips, back, and sacrum, as well as an unctuous enema (snehabasti),

6.30.82 | A swelling that is turned upward, elevated, swollen, and accompanied by pustules and pain may be cured with [a paste of] Karīra,

6.30.83 | Washing with decoctions of *jiṅginī* and the roots of *vṛṣa*, mixed with grape wine (*mārdvīka-sīdhu*), fermented gruel (*śukta*), and honey, destroys vaginal discharges (*yony-āsrāva*).

6.30.84 | One should administer [these] with sour gruel, cow’s urine, vinegar, or the juices of the three myrobalans (triphalā). The applications of long pepper (pippalī), iron powder (ayaḥrajaḥ), and chebulic myrobalan (pathyā) are beneficial when taken with honey.
6.30.85 | For a patient with a predominance of *kapha*, enemas consisting mostly of pungent substances mixed with urine are beneficial;
for *pitta*, those containing sweet substances and milk; and for *vāta*, those combined with oil and sour substances.

6.30.86 | For that which arises from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), the therapeutic action is common [to all]. Furthermore, in the case of *raktayoni*, one should determine the treatment by observing the color of the blood and its associated symptoms.
6.30.87 | Thereafter, one should administer blood-stabilizing medicine according to the specific humor (doṣa):
sesame powder, curd, ghee, molasses, and hog's fat.

6.30.89 | Or curd combined with sugar, honey, liquorice, and ginger; or milk-porridge with blue lotus, lotus-root, lotus-stalk, kālīyaka, and water-lily.
6.30.90 | In cases of *asṛgdara* caused by *pitta*, one should drink [a decoction of] *pāṭhā*, the inner bark of *jambū* and *āmra*, *śilodbheda*, and *rasāñjana*, mixed with milk, sugar, and honey.
6.30.91 | Ambaṣṭhā, śālmalī-śleṣman, samaṅgā,
the bark of vatsaka, bāhlīka, ativiṣā, bilva, musta, lodhra, along with gairika;
6.30.92 | Katvanga, marica, śuṇṭhī, mṛdvīkā, raktacandana,
kaṭphala, vatsaka, anantā, dhātakī, madhuka, and arjuna.
6.30.93 | Having extracted [the plant] under the Puṣya asterism, one should have it made into fine powders of equal measure.

6.30.94 | It destroys hemorrhoids and dysentery, as well as the blood that is passed; it also cures those ailments caused by the bodily humors (doṣas) or external factors (āgantu) which afflict children.
6.30.95 | He forcibly cures the defects of the female reproductive tract, as well as menstrual disorders characterized by white, blue, yellow, dark-brown, or reddish-brown discharges.
6.30.96 | This powder, named Puṣyānuga, is beneficial and honored by Ātreya.

[One may also take] the root of Taṇḍulīyaka with honey and rice-water.
One should drink *rasāñjana* and lac with goat’s milk,
along with the paste of the leaves of *rājādana* and *kapittha* fried in ghee.
6.30.98 | Madhuka, triphalā, lodhra, musta, saurāṣṭrikā, and honey remove pitta and vāta; in cases of pitta disorders, they entirely conquer āsrapitta (hemorrhagic diseases).
6.30.99 | In cases of asṛgdara caused by kapha, one should drink nimba and guḍūcī with alcoholic liquors;

6.30.100 | One should administer that which was prescribed for the management of threatened miscarriage,

6.30.101 | Ghee prepared with the blood of deer, goat, and boar, along with curd, sour fruits, and [other] fats, is beneficial for those with bloody discharges from the womb, those who have ceased menstruating, and those whose sons have died.
6.30.102 | A woman who is free from menstrual discharge (arajaskā) should drink milk processed with the life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs;

6.30.103 | In cases of *kapha* and *vāta*, oil should be administered via an *uttarabasti* (urethral/vaginal enema),

6.30.104 | One should administer yeast powder mixed with honey;
it cures acarana, cleanses the channels, and removes itching, moisture, and swelling.
6.30.105 | A woman who has miscarried prematurely should first be treated with Vata-alleviating oils processed a hundred times,
and she should be administered non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), and sudation (sveda) using Vata-subduing agents.

6.30.106 | By means of oleaginous substances, as well as foods and poultices (upanāha) applied with due method, [one should treat it] with dill, barley, wheat, fermenting agent (kiṇva), costus, and priyaṅgu.

6.30.109 | A medicated oil-soaked plug (sneha-picu) prepared with decoctions (kaṣāya) removes viplutā.
In cases of karṇinī, a wick (vartikā) made from kuṣṭha, pippalī, the tips of arka, and rock salt [should be used].
6.30.110 | A suppository made from goat's urine should be administered, as well as everything that alleviates *śleṣman* (phlegm).
The three-fold unctuous preparation (*traivṛta*), oleation, sudation, and the meat broths of domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals [are also beneficial].
6.30.111 | A milk enema with the ten roots (daśamūla) is for those suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta) and afflictions of vāta;
one should also administer an oil enema with the three sweets (traivṛta), as well as the enema known as uttarabasti.
6.30.112 This very same [treatment] is prescribed when the great vagina (mahāyoni) has prolapsed:
the fat of bears and boars, along with ghee, boiled with sweet [substances].
6.30.113 | Having filled the great vulva, one should bind it with linen and lac;
having lubricated a prolapsed organ with ghee, steamed it in milk, and reinserted it.
6.30.114 | One should administer a bolus of vesavāra starting from the time of urination;
furthermore, one should perform whatever treatment has been prescribed for disorders of vāta.
6.30.115 | In all calamities, especially regarding the great birth-canal, the wise man [should know that] the womb of women is not corrupted except by wind.
6.30.116 | Having pacified that [condition], one should administer the remedy for another disorder.
In the case of pale-colored menorrhagia, one should drink the root-paste of *rohitaka*.
6.30.117 | One should have her lick either the paste of *āmalakī* seeds with water and sugar-honey,
or the powder or juice of *āmalakī* with honey.
6.30.118 | Then one should drink a paste of *lodhra* with a decoction of *nyagrodha* bark;
or, in cases of discharge, one should apply a linen cloth that has been saturated with it.
6.30.119 Or one should apply a bolus made of the powder of *plakṣa* bark mixed with honey;
or, having lubricated the vagina, one should apply [a bolus] of *lodhra*, *priyaṅgu*, and *madhuka*.
6.30.120 A wick (varti) mixed with honey and all types of decoctions (kaṣāya) should be applied;
for the purpose of cutting the discharge, it should be smeared [with oil] or fumigated with substances soaked in ghee.
6.30.121 | With *sarala* resin, *aguru*, and barley; with oil, pungent fish, *kāsīsa*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *kāṅkṣī*, *samaṅgā*, mango stone, and *dhātakī*.
6.30.122 | When there is sliminess, a powder combined with honey produces clarity.
[The ingredients are] the bark of *palāśa*, *sarja*, and *jambū*, along with *samaṅgā*, *moca*, and *dhātakī*.
6.30.123 A paste that is slightly slimy and moistening is desired as a styptic;
it should be applied to parts that are rigid and rough to induce softness.
6.30.124 | One should consume veśavāra, or milk-rice (pāyasa), or likewise kṛśarā;
for those with foul odors, there should be a decoction (kaṣāya) of tuvara, or even a paste (kalka).
6.30.125 | Or a powder of all fragrant substances removes foul odors;
thus, when the wombs are purified, women conceive a fetus.
6.30.126 | When the natural seed is unvitiated and the entry of the life-force has occurred,
even for a person purified by the fivefold medical treatment, the sense organ [may still fail].
6.30.127 | Having examined [the discharge] according to its colors, one should treat that which is vitiated with remedies that destroy those specific defects.
Regarding this, there are verses here:
The disorders of the female genital tract (yoni), along with their symptoms, etiological factors, and treatments, have been described.
6.30.128 | Having been explained correctly and in detail by the sage who perceives the truth,
Agniveśa once again questioned the best of physicians.
6.30.129 | O sinless one, having approached Ātreya,
you have indeed fully enumerated in the chapter on diseases the eight defects of semen in men.
6.30.130 | O best of physicians! [Explain] their cause, the characteristics of the morbid and the non-morbid, the treatment in its entirety, and the four types of impotence.
6.30.131 | Regarding the complications of the female reproductive tract and that which is described as *pradara* (leukorrhea),
[I shall explain] their etiology, symptoms, and treatment in accordance with reality.
"O best of physicians, explain [this] by means of both summary and detail!
To him, who was listening with eager attention, the bull among sages spoke.
6.30.133 | Since the seed, arising from the source of sexual excitement during intercourse, is called "human semen," I shall therefore speak of it; listen to that.
6.30.134 Just as a seed damaged by untimely rain, worms, insects, or fire does not sprout because it is thoroughly corrupted, so too is the semen of embodied beings.

6.30.135 | From excessive sexual intercourse, from over-exertion, and from the consumption of unwholesome things; or from engaging in coitus at the wrong time, or with those who are not the proper partners; ||
6.30.136 | From the consumption of dry, bitter, astringent, excessively salty, sour, and hot foods,
as well as from sexual intercourse with women who lack passion and from old age;
6.30.137 | From anxiety, grief, lack of trust, the confusion caused by weapons, alkaline cautery, or fire;
from fear, anger, malevolent spells, and those emaciated by diseases.
6.30.138 | Due to the obstruction of the natural urges and from injury,
the humors (doṣas)— either individually or collectively— becoming severely aggravated, reach the semen-carrying channels (sirās).
6.30.139 | I shall now describe in detail those things that quickly vitiate the semen:
it becomes frothy, thin, dry, discolored, foul-smelling, and slimy.
6.30.140 | Likewise, the eighth [type] is that which is mixed with other humors,
is putrid, frothy, thin, dry, and is expelled with difficulty and in small quantities due to vāta.
6.30.141 | The semen becomes impaired and is no longer fit for conception if it is bluish or yellowish, excessively hot, or has a foul odor.
6.30.142 | The semen, corrupted by pitta, emerges from the penis with burning;
however, when its passage is obstructed by kapha, it becomes excessively slimy.
6.30.143 | Due to excessive sexual intercourse with women, from injury, or even from a wound,
the semen of a living being generally flows mixed with blood.

6.30.144 | When the semen is obstructed on its path by the suppression of the urge, it is struck by the wind (vāyu) and passes with difficulty as a knotted mass; this is the eighth [type], known as avasādi.
6.30.145 | Thus have the eight defects of semen been fully described along with their characteristics.
[The normal semen] is unctuous, thick, slimy, sweet, and non-burning.
6.30.146 | One should recognize pure semen as white, resembling crystal,
through those beneficial and pleasant applications of aphrodisiac formulations (*vājīkaraṇa*).

6.30.147 | When the semen becomes vitiated by formulations used for curing raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders) as well as those for treating gynecological disorders, one should then treat it accordingly.
Clarified butter, the Jīvanīya group of drugs, Cyavanaprāśa,
and the application of Girija (red ochre) remove defects of the semen.
6.30.149 | Nirūha and anuvāsana enemas are beneficial when semen is associated with Vāta;
and the Rasāyana treatment consisting of Abhayā and Āmalakī is recommended for the Pitta type.
6.30.150 | Māgadhī, amṛta, and loha constitute a rejuvenative (rasāyana) for triphalā;
it destroys seminal disorders arising from kapha, as does bhallātaka.
6.30.151 | Having observed semen that is mixed with other bodily constituents (dhātus), the physician should, according to reason,
apply the remedies for the humors (doṣas) and the constituents as appropriate to each specific humor.
6.30.152 | Ghee, milk, meat broths, śāli rice, barley, wheat, and ṣaṣṭika rice are recommended for disorders of semen, especially when administered via enema therapy (bastikarma).
6.30.153 | Thus has the treatment for the eight defects of semen been declared by the Sage; for impotence arising from defects of the seed is cured only through purification.
6.30.154 | Thereafter, O Agniveśa, I shall explain to you correctly and as it truly is [the causes of impotence]:
through injury to the seed or the penis, through old age, and through the depletion of semen.
6.30.155 | Listen to the general characteristics of his impotence:
he is constantly intent on sexual fantasies, even toward a wife who is dear to him and submissive.
6.30.156 | He does not proceed due to the weakness of his subtle body (liṅga), or even if he should ever proceed,
he is afflicted by labored breathing, his limbs are perspiring, and his resolve and efforts are rendered futile.
6.30.157 | With a withered penis and being seedless—this is the characteristic of impotence.
Indeed, this general characteristic will be explained in detail.
6.30.158 | From eating food that is cold, dry, insufficient, unwholesome, or incompatible,
from indigestion, and from grief, anxiety, fear, terror, and excessive indulgence with women;
6.30.159 | Due to malevolent spells, lack of trust, and the depletion of the bodily fluids (rasa) and so forth;
due to the imbalance of the humors such as wind (vāta), as well as from fasting and exhaustion.
6.30.160 | Due to women's lack of knowledge regarding sexual pleasure and due to the improper performance of the five acts [of coitus],
there occurs damage to the seed (sperm), resulting in a pale complexion and extreme weakness.
6.30.161 | A man [under its influence] will have little vitality and little joy with women; he will be afflicted by heart disease, anemia, consumption, jaundice, and exhaustion.

6.30.162 | Listen now to [the treatment for] impotence caused by the destruction of semen, as well as that caused by the failure of the penis, for one afflicted by vomiting, diarrhea, and colic, and oppressed by cough and fever.
6.30.163 | From the consumption of food that is excessively sour, salty, or alkaline, from incompatible or unwholesome foods,
from excessive drinking of water, from irregular meals, and from eating flour-based foods or heavy meals;

6.30.164 | From the consumption of curd, milk, and the meat of marshy animals; from excessive emaciation; from sexual intercourse with virgins; and even from intercourse with those who are not women (ayoni)—[these lead to the loss of semen].
6.30.165 | A woman who has a chronic disease, one who has long since been abandoned, likewise one who is menstruating,
one who is foul-smelling, one with a diseased womb, and likewise one who suffers from excessive discharge.
6.30.166 | He who, impelled by lust, approaches such a woman out of delusion—
by means of the fourfold approach and the striking of the penis— [incurs the following].
6.30.167 | From not washing the penis, from wounds caused by weapons, teeth, or the sacrificial post, from being struck or crushed by wood, and from excessive indulgence in thorny plants;
6.30.168 | Due to the obstruction of semen, impotence occurs. (I shall hereafter describe the symptoms that arise from it:
swelling and pain in the penis, as well as redness, are observed.
Severe bursting pains arise, and there is even a suppuration of the penis; there is an increase of flesh, and ulcers also quickly appear upon it.
The discharge resembles water mixed with boiled rice-scum, having a dark-red or reddish-brown luster;
furthermore, the constriction becomes firm and forms rings.
Fever, thirst, giddiness, fainting, and vomiting arise in him;
moreover, blood that is black, blue, turbid, or reddish flows forth.
6.30.172 | Like one burnt by fire, there is an intense burning sensation accompanied by pain in the bladder,
the testicles, the perineal seam, or the groins.
6.30.173 | Sometimes the discharge becomes slimy or pale;
a mild swelling arises that is stiff and characterized by slight exudation.
It either takes a long time to ripen, or it ripens quickly and then is released;
worms are born within it, it becomes moist, and it emits a foul odor.
6.30.175 | His jewel (penis) is shattered, as are his penis and testicles;
this is declared to be impotence caused by the collapse of the "flag" (dhvajabhaṅga).
6.30.176 | They declare this fivefold failure of the banner of one’s lineage;
now hear as I describe that which arises from impotence and old age.
6.30.177 | Age is said to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior. In men who are excessively aged, the semen generally diminishes.
6.30.178 | Furthermore, due to the depletion of the bodily fluids (rasa) and so forth, as well as from the failure to consume aphrodisiacs (vṛṣya),
there occurs a gradual wasting away of strength, virility, and the sensory faculties.
6.30.179 | Due to the exhaustion of the lifespan, lack of food, fatigue, and exhaustion,
as well as the onset of old age— by these causes does impotence arise in men.
6.30.180 | By that [excessive discharge], his bodily constituents (dhātus) become exceedingly diminished, and he becomes very weak;
discolored, feeble, and dejected, he quickly succumbs to disease.
6.30.181 | This is indeed the fourth type, born of old age; now hear about that born of wasting.
It arises from excessive anxiety, as well as from grief, anger, and fear.
6.30.182 | That man who constantly succumbs to envy, longing, intoxication, and agitation, or who, being emaciated, consumes dry food, drink, and medicine;
6.30.183 | Furthermore, if one of weak constitution should remain without food,
or due to the consumption of unwholesome food, [the wind] becomes established in the heart.
6.30.184 | For the rasa is the primary constituent; it would quickly diminish, and from that, the blood and other constituents of that embodied being would also diminish.
6.30.185 | Even beyond those [elements], semen is considered the supreme abode;
yet he who, through excessive mental excitement, indulges in sexual intercourse—
6.30.186 | His semen quickly diminishes, and from that he undergoes total depletion;
he contracts a terrible disease or meets his death.
6.30.187 | Therefore, one who desires health should especially protect the semen.
Thus, impotence has been described in its fourfold form according to its etiology and symptoms.
6.30.188 | Some, however, state that there are two types of incurable impotence arising from the collapse of the penis and the wasting away [of semen],
which result respectively from the excision of the glans and the removal of the testicles.
6.30.189 | When, due to defects in the seed of the mother and father, and because of the impurities of one who has not disciplined himself,
the humors reach the semen-carrying channels while the embryo is still in the womb;
6.30.190 | By its rapid depletion, it dries up the semen and also impairs it;
consequently, that man, though possessing all his limbs complete, becomes a non-man (impotent).
6.30.191 | These have been explained as incurable due to the combined aggravation of the humors (sannipāta). Hereafter, listen to the treatment, both in brief and in detail.

6.30.192 | O sinless one, that medicine which has been prescribed by me for defects of the semen should be used to alleviate impotence, as well as whatever is beneficial for those who are emaciated or suffering from chest wounds.
6.30.193 | One should employ all of these: enemas, milk and ghee preparations, those formulations considered aphrodisiacs, and the applications of rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana).

6.30.194 | Having carefully examined the bodily humors, the digestive fire, and the strength, and being knowledgeable regarding the timing of medicine, [one should treat] impotence caused by sexual excess as well as that resulting from the derangement of the tissues (*dhātu*).
6.30.195 | Furthermore, medical treatment based on divine means is for that which arises from malevolent spells;
this has been briefly described as the medicine for the pacification of impotence.
6.30.196 | I shall now explain in detail the remedy for impotence:
for one whose body has been well-fomented and lubricated, a purgative combined with oleation [is prescribed].
6.30.197 | Thereafter, the wise physician should administer food, or alternatively, a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana); then he should give him an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
6.30.198 | Thereafter, one should administer an enema with palāśa, eraṇḍa, mustā, and other such ingredients; furthermore, the aphrodisiac formulations previously described should be employed.
6.30.199 | These [medicines] should be administered by the physician in cases of impotence caused by the impairment of the seed;
having recognized impotence caused by the failure of the penis (dhvajabhaṅga), one should apply the appropriate treatment for it.
One should apply medicinal plasters and affusions, or perform bloodletting; one should also administer internal oleation and purgation with unctuous substances.
6.30.201 | Thereafter, one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) or again a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana).
A wise physician should perform all treatments there according to the procedure for ulcers.
6.30.202 | For impotence caused by old age or by wasting diseases,
purification with unctuous substances is beneficial for one who has been prepared with oleation and sudation.
6.30.203 | Milk, ghee, aphrodisiac formulations, and sustaining enemas (yāpana-basti),
as well as the application of rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana), are said to be the medicine for those two.

6.30.204 | This medicine for those suffering from impotence has been described by me in detail. Now hear concerning that which was previously called *pradara* (uterine disorder), along with its causes and other characteristics.
6.30.205 | That woman who excessively consumes salt, sour, heavy, pungent, burning, unctuous, and meat-based foods;
6.30.206 | When she consumes fatty foods from domestic or aquatic animals, kṛśara, milk-rice,
curd, semen, whey, liquor, and the like, the wind (vāyu) becomes provoked.

6.30.207 Transcending the normal measure of blood, the vessels located within the uterus take recourse in the channels that carry the menses (rajas), and having drawn that blood, they produce that menstrual flow.
6.30.208 | Since it quickly increases the state of pride through its [excessive] essence,
those learned in the treatises call this asṛgdara (menorrhagia).
6.30.209 | Since the *rajas* (uterine blood) flows forth from it, it is therefore known as *pradara*.
Thus has the general cause and the symptom been described.

6.30.210 | It is of four kinds according to its detailed classification: from wind (vāta) and the others, and from their combination (sannipāta). Hereafter, I shall explain its causes, symptoms, and medical treatment.
6.30.211 | But the wind (vāyu), provoked by dry substances and the like, takes up the blood as before and causes pradara; hear from me its symptoms.
6.30.212 It is frothy, thin, dry, dark-brown, or even reddish; it resembles the water of the *kiṃśuka* tree, and may be either painful or painless.
6.30.213 | When the wind (māruta) causes intense pain in the waist, groin, heart, sides, back, and hips, this is known as being of the nature of vāta.
6.30.214 | When pitta is aggravated by sour, hot, salty, and alkaline substances, it causes pradara as previously described; hear now its symptoms according to the paittika type.
6.30.215 | It flows with a bluish, yellowish, very hot, or blackish discharge, or it is intensely red, flowing repeatedly and accompanied by pain.
6.30.216 | Menorrhagia caused by pitta is characterized by burning sensations, redness, thirst, delusion, fever, and vertigo; now, that caused by kapha shall be described.

6.30.217 | When Kapha is aggravated by causes such as heavy foods and other factors, as previously described, it produces Pradara (menorrhagia). Listen now to its symptoms according to their true nature.
The blood flows thick, pale-colored, heavy, unctuous, and cold; it is associated with phlegm (kapha), is dense, and causes little pain.
6.30.219 Accompanied by vomiting, anorexia, nausea, dyspnea, and cough—
here the general cause of defects in breast milk will be explained.

6.30.220 | One should know that asṛgdara (menorrhagia), which possesses the three symptoms and exists in various states, has the same causes as pradarā (leucorrhea), though it arises from the three doṣas.
6.30.221 | When a woman is excessively afflicted and her blood has become depleted,
the wind (vāyu) then becomes greatly aggravated due to the practice of all [the aforementioned] causes.
Through the blood-pathway,
it discharges phlegm that is foul-smelling, slimy, and yellow, being vitiated by the heat of the bile (*pitta*).
6.30.223 | For as long as he takes up the fat and marrow, the forceful one emits through the path of the offspring something resembling clarified butter, marrow, and fat.

6.30.224 | One should avoid that woman who constantly discharges a discharge, who is afflicted by thirst, burning sensations, and fever, whose blood is depleted, and who is weak; she is incurable due to her tamasic nature.

6.30.225 | One should declare the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) to be pure when it is free from sliminess, burning, and pain; when it persists for five nights; and when it is neither too copious nor too scanty.
6.30.226 | One should declare the menstrual flow to be pure when it has the color of a guñjā fruit, resembles lotus-juice or lac, or is like the hue of an indragopaka insect.
6.30.227 | Whatever medicine has been prescribed here for the vaginal channels characterized by Vata and the other doshas,
the physician should administer all of that for the four types of pradara as well.

6.30.228 One should also administer that medicine which has been prescribed for those suffering from bloody diarrhea, for those with blood-bile (rakta-pitta), and for those with hemorrhoids characterized by bleeding.
6.30.229 | The excellence of the wet-nurse’s breast milk has been described in detail previously,
as well as the methods for generating breast milk and the purification of that milk.

6.30.230 | The signs of vitiation by wind and other humors, as well as the treatment for one who is emaciated—all that has been stated; now, those eight defects of breast milk which have been proclaimed shall be described.
6.30.231 | The most skilled physician, whose eye is the scripture, should recognize those [doshas] as residing precisely within vāta and the others;
however, since students are of three types, I shall therefore explain them in detail.
6.30.232 | From eating when the previous meal is undigested, from unwholesome, irregular, incompatible, or excessive food,
and from the consumption of salty, sour, pungent, alkaline, and moistening substances;
6.30.233 | From the affliction of mind and body, from lack of sleep at night due to anxious thought,
from the obstruction of an aroused impulse, and from the provocation of one that has not yet arisen;
6.30.234 | Refined rice with jaggery, kṛśara, and thin curd;
meats that cause secretions, as well as those from domestic, marshy, and aquatic animals.
6.30.235 | From eating excessively and repeatedly, from sleeping during the day, from the excessive consumption of liquor,
from lack of physical exertion, from lack of injury, and from anger and the emaciation caused by disease;
6.30.236 | Having reached the milk-carrying vessels and corrupted the breast milk, the humors further produce eight types [of disorders]; learn from me those according to the humors.
6.30.237 | In the wind-dominant (vātika) type, there is a bad taste, frothy secretions, and dryness; from bile (pitta), there is discoloration, foul odor, unctuousness, sliminess, and heaviness.
6.30.238 | Due to phlegm (kapha), and by its own provocative factors such as dryness (rūkṣa) and so forth, the wind (anila) becomes aggravated;
having reached the receptacle of milk (kṣīrāśaya), it vitiates the essence (rasa) of the breast milk.
6.30.239 | Drinking that milk which has become tasteless and is affected by wind (vāta), one becomes emaciated;
moreover, the milk does not please his palate, and he grows only with great difficulty.
6.30.240 | Likewise, when the wind (vāyu) is aggravated and churns the breast milk within,
it produces a mass of froth, which then issues forth with great difficulty.
6.30.241 | By that [fault], the child becomes weak-voiced, with the binding of feces, urine, and flatus,
and suffers from either wind-born headache or chronic catarrh.
As before, when provoked, the wind dries up the moisture in the breast milk;
as the infant drinks that parched milk, a loss of strength arises from that dryness.
6.30.243 | Pitta, aggravated by hot substances and other factors, floods the receptacle of breast milk and causes discoloration of the milk, such as blue, yellow, black, and so forth.
6.30.244 | The infant’s limbs become discolored and perspiring; he suffers from thirst and passes loose stools. His body is constantly hot, and he takes no pleasure in the breast.
6.30.245 | When pitta is provoked as previously described, the milk becomes foul-smelling;
by drinking that, the child suffers from anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya) and jaundice (kāmalā).
When provoked by the guru and other factors, the phlegm (śleṣman) located in the milk-receptacle of a woman makes her milk excessively unctuous because it is permeated with oiliness.
6.30.247 | By that [dosha], the infant becomes one who vomits, suffers from obstruction, and is prone to salivation;
with his channels constantly smeared [with secretions], he is overcome by sleep and exhaustion.
6.30.248 | When phlegm, overwhelming the breast milk, makes it slimy, the woman is afflicted with dyspnea and cough, accompanied by excessive salivation and a sense of oppression.

6.30.249 | A child drinking that [milk] becomes salivating, with swollen face and eyes, and dull-witted; furthermore, because the *kapha* located in the receptacle of milk is heavy, it causes heaviness of the milk.
6.30.250 | By drinking that [milk], a child makes his teacher guilty; he suffers from heart disease and may incur various other diseases related to the milk.
6.30.251 | When the milk is vitiated by wind (vāta) and the other humors, disorders of that same nature arise.
In that case, first, for the sake of purifying the breast milk, the wet-nurse should be treated with oleation (sneha).
6.30.252 | Having fomented [the patient] according to the rules, the physician should administer emesis using vacā,
priyaṅgu, yaṣṭyāhva, phalavat, vatsaka, and sarṣapa.
6.30.253 | One should induce vomiting with the pastes of nimba and paṭola along with decoctions mixed with salt.
Once she has vomited properly according to the prescribed method, one should then administer the gradual dietary regimen (saṃsarjana).
6.30.254 | Having administered oleation while considering the humors, the season, and the strength [of the patient],
one should then administer a purgative using either Trivṛt or Abhayā combined with the juice of Triphalā.

6.30.255 | The physician who knows the scriptures should cause her to drink *abhayā* mixed with honey, or even *abhayā* alone; or, for the purpose of purgation, he may cause her to drink it combined with urine. 6.30.256 | Once she has been properly purged and has undergone the process of gradual dietary rehabilitation (*saṃsarjana*), the wise physician [should proceed further].
Then, one should treat the patient with food and drink that destroy the remaining traces of the doshas.
6.30.257 | Rice, or sixty-day rice, or śyāmāka grain are beneficial for food;
likewise, priyaṅgu, koradūṣa, barley, and bamboo-seeds are so.

6.30.258 | For the sake of vegetables, one should provide bamboo shoots, cane shoots, and kalāya beans prepared with fats; and for the sake of soups, one should prepare mung beans, lentils, and horse gram.
6.30.259 | One should cause her to drink soups prepared with neem, the tips of rattan, kulaka, eggplant, and āmalaka,
along with trikaṭu and rock salt, for the purification of breast milk.

6.30.260 One should cause to be served hare, *kapiñjala* partridge, and antelope, prepared according to the rules; as well as water boiled with the bark of *śārṅga*, *iṣṭā*, *saptaparṇa*, and *aśvagandhā*.
6.30.261 Or, for the purification of breast milk, one should have her drink a decoction of *rohiṇī* boiled with ginger,
or a decoction of the bark of *amṛtā* and *saptaparṇa* along with ginger.
6.30.262 | One should drink a decoction of *kirātatiktaka* in three doses as prescribed by the quarter-verses;
these three are the general medicine for the purpose of purifying breast milk.
6.30.263 | Having thus described the various defects of breast milk, now learn of another:
one whose milk is tasteless should be made to drink grapes, madhuka, and sārivā.
6.30.264 Having thoroughly stirred together finely ground *payasyā* with lukewarm water,
one should apply a paste to the breasts made from the finely ground *pañcakola* and *kulattha*.
6.30.265 | Having washed her dry [breasts], one should express the milk; thus the breast-milk becomes purified.
One should have that woman drink her own milk, which is like a mass of foam.
6.30.266 | Having ground pāṭhā, nāgara, śārṅgeṣṭā, and mūrvā with lukewarm water [one should apply it];
likewise, añjana, nāgara, dāru, bilva root, and priyaṅgu [are used].
6.30.267 | As before, an ointment for the breasts should be prepared using milk purification.
The physician should boil *kirātatiktaka*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *amṛtā* [to make this].
One should have the wet-nurse drink that decoction, which eliminates defects of the breast milk,

6.30.269 | A woman whose breast milk is dry should drink milk processed with the drugs prescribed in the chapter on the six purgatives (Ṣaḍvirekāśritīya) for the purification of breast milk, or she should drink ghee prepared with those same drugs.

6.30.272 | One should smear her breasts with a paste of grapes and madhuka;

6.30.275 | One should smear her breasts with sārivā, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, śleṣmātaka, and kucandana; or with patra, ambu, candana, and uśīra.
6.30.276 Having ground snigdha-kṣīrā, dāru, musta, and pāṭhā with lukewarm water and drinking them with rock salt,

Or one should drink the roots of *pippalī*, *cavya*, *citraka*, and *nāgara*;

6.30.282 | Thus have been specified those diseases arising from defects of the milk, as well as certain other ailments,

6.30.291 | Even those diseases which have not been specified here due to their great number in terms of name and form— for them as well, this very same treatment should be the remedy after examining the humors and other factors.

6.30.292 | That which is opposite to the humors (doṣa), the affected tissues (dūṣya), and the etiological factors (nidāna) is certainly beneficial; properly administered, it subdues all diseases, whether mentioned or unmentioned.

6.30.293 | Indeed, it is through the proper application of place, time, dosage, and what is wholesome or unwholesome that health is attained; otherwise, even that which is salutary may produce the opposite effect.

Medicine administered through the mouth quickly destroys diseases located in the stomach (āmāśaya); through the nose, those situated in the head; and through the rectum, those residing in the large intestine (pakvāśaya).
6.30.295 | For conditions such as erysipelas and pustules arising from the various parts of the body,

6.30.296 | One should understand the time by observing the day, the patient, the medicine, the disease, the stage of digestion, and the season; specifically, one who observes the day should know it as the forenoon, just as one knows the forest at dawn.
6.30.297 | Just as one who is healthy should drink [medicine] in the morning on an empty stomach when strong,

6.30.298 | The times for medicine are: at the beginning of a meal, in the middle, after, repeatedly, as a "sandwich" (sāmudga) with food, and ten [times] between morsels of food.

6.30.302 | In cases of fever, gruels, decoctions, milk, ghee,

6.30.303 | The subsiding of the urge for hunger, lightness of the body, and purity are the signs that digestion has occurred;

6.30.306 | By repeatedly observing the stage of the diseases and that of the patient, the physician does not become confused in his treatment.

6.30.311 | Diseases caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha are indeed powerful in childhood, middle age, and old age respectively, due to the natural state of human beings at those stages of life.
6.30.312 | Diseases born of Vāta generally gain strength at the end of digestion; those born of Pitta during the process of digestion; and those born of Śleṣman immediately after eating.
A small dose of medicine does not destroy disease, just as a small amount of water cannot extinguish a great fire;

6.30.314 | Therefore, having carefully considered the strength of both the disease and the medicine,

The Vāhlīkas, Pahlavas, Cīnas, Śūlikas, Yavanas,
and Śakas are devoted to meat, wheat, honey-wine, weapons, and fire.

6.30.321 | For many distinctions are recognized based on age, strength, physical constitution, and so forth; likewise, there are differences regarding the internal junctions, pathways, and the humors that move in secret.

6.30.324 | It destroys internal, hidden phlegm; likewise, one should conquer cold with cold things.
Even a thick paste of sandalwood, when finely ground, causes burning when applied as a plaster.

6.30.326 | When substances have been boiled or consumed, a transformation occurs in those very same substances;
therefore, one should examine the ten factors—the defects, the medicines, and so forth—in their true nature.
6.30.327 | A wise person should not treat a disease by means of medicinal applications alone;
even when it has subsided, the disease may recur due to even a slight cause.
6.30.328 | When the body has been worn away and reduced to its path, the remnant is like a subtle fire;
therefore, one should pursue it with a practice that does not abandon it.
6.30.329 | Even when a medicinal preparation has been previously administered for the sake of success and has already proven effective,
a great disorder may become aggravated within due to its hardness or because it was deficient in quantity.

6.30.331 | Having understood this, one should cause the practice to increase;

6.30.332 | By various methods of mental construction, one should again bring about a state of endearment;

There are twenty complications of the female genital tract (yoni), along with their etiology and symptoms.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Gynecological Disorders," in the Section on Therapeutics of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—wherein it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
(30) 6.30.341. In the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka, this sixth section, the Section on Therapeutics, is hereby completed.
The Section on Pharmacopoeia.
Chapter One.
7.1.1: Now, therefore, we shall expound the pharmaceutical preparation of Madana.
7.1.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

7.1.3 | Now, indeed, O Agniveśa, we shall expound the Section on Formulations (Kalpasthāna) for the purpose of preparing emetic and purgative substances by combining them with various other substances that are most pleasant to consume—meaning for their classification, differentiation, and division—as well as for the correct preparation of the methods of administration of those formulations through easy means.

7.1.4 | In that regard, the removal of morbid humors (doṣa) by the upper route is designated as emesis (vamana), and that by the lower route is designated as purgation (virecana); or rather, both receive the designation "purgation" because they purge the impurities of the body.

7.1.5 | In this regard, medicinal substances that are hot (*uṣṇa*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), pervasive (*vyavāyin*), and expansive (*vikāśin*) reach the heart by their own potency, follow the channels (*dhamanī*), and through their fiery nature (*āgneyatva*), liquefy the entire mass of morbid humors (*doṣasaṃghāta*) located in the body via the gross and subtle channels; by their sharpness (*taikṣṇya*), they break them apart. Once broken, [the humor] floats about within the body—which has been prepared by oleation—like honey placed in a vessel smeared with oil, not adhering [to the tissues] due to its subtle and flowing nature; then, propelled by the *udāna* breath, it reaches the stomach (*āmāśaya*).

Because it consists of fire and air, and due to the influence of its upper portion, the medicine is thrown upward; because it consists of water and earth, and due to the influence of its lower portion, the medicine moves downward; and because it possesses both qualities, it acts in both directions.
This is the enumeration of the characteristics.

7.1.6 | In this regard, because it is necessary to grasp the various tastes (*rasa*), potencies (*vīrya*), post-digestive effects (*vipāka*), and specific actions (*prabhāva*) of the fruits of *jīmūtaka*, *ikṣvāku*, *dhāmārgava*, *kuṭaja*, and *kṛtavedhana*; and of *śyāmā*, *trivṛt*, *caturaṅgula*, *tilvaka*, *mahāvṛkṣa*, *saptalā*, *śāṅkhinī*, *dantī*, and *dravantī*—which arise in various regions and seasons; and because [these factors] possess diverse influences upon the body, the *doṣas*, constitution (*prakṛti*), age, strength, digestive fire, dietary preference, suitability (*sātmya*), the stage of disease, and so forth.

For the sake of providing pleasure through the enjoyment of diverse fragrances, colors, tastes, and textures, and in order to demonstrate the various paths of combination even for substances that exist in countless conjunctions, we shall explain six hundred formulations of purgatives.
7.1.7 | Those substances, however, become most capable of performing their functions through the enhancement of their potency by virtue of excellence in place, time, quality, and vessel.
7.1.8 | Indeed, the land is of three types: arid (jāṅgala), marshy (ānūpa), and intermediate (sādhāraṇa).

Therein, the *jāṅgala* region abounds in open space; it is dense with groves of trees such as the *kadara*, *khadira*, *āsana*, *aśvakarṇa*, *dhava*, *tiniśa*, *śallakī*, *sāla*, *somavalka*, *badarī*, *tinduka*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *āmalakī*; it is largely composed of many *śamī*, *kakubha*, and *śiṃśapā* trees; its young shoots are constantly being shaken by the force of the wind blowing over dry, hard ground; it is filled with fine, harsh, and rough sands and pebbles, and is completely shrouded by mirages; and its terrain is frequented by *lāva*, *tittiri*, and *cakora* birds.

One should know that a person with a predominance of *vāta* and *pitta* is generally stable and firm. Now, the marshy (*anūpa*) region is characterized by dense forests of *hintāla*, *tamāla*, coconut, and plantain trees; it is mostly bordered by rivers and the ocean, abounds in cool breezes, and its terrain is reached by rivers whose banks are lined with *vañjula*, *vānīra*, and *ropaṇa* trees. It is adorned with mountain groves, its thickets of trees are fanned by gentle winds, its ground is covered by many rows of flowering forest ranges, and it is enveloped by the lush canopies of trees and creepers.

A region where the trees and branches resound with the cries of swans, ruddy geese, cranes, *nandīmukha* birds, white lotuses, *kādamba* geese, water-fowls, *bhṛṅgarāja* birds, woodpeckers, and intoxicated cuckoos; where the people are delicate; and which is characterized by a predominance of wind and phlegm (*pavana-kapha-prāya*)—such a place is to be known as [the type dominated by] wind and phlegm. A person from these two regions is to be known as "ordinary" (*sādhāraṇa*), being endowed with creepers, forest trees, and large trees, as well as flocks of birds and herds of animals, and possessing stable, delicate, strength, complexion, and firmness, along with common qualities.

7.1.9 | In that region—whether common or arid—which is level, clean, with water flowing clockwise, visited at the proper time by cold, sun, wind, and water; which is free from cremation grounds, sacred trees, temples, assembly halls, pits, pleasure gardens, anthills, and saline soil; which is strewn with *kuśa* and *rohiṣa* grasses; and which possesses soft, black, sweet soil or gold-colored, sweet soil; where medicinal plants have grown on ground not ploughed by the plow and not damaged by other more powerful trees—such plants are praised.

7.1.10 | In that regard, those [medicinal substances] which have been produced in their proper season, have attained full measure, potency, taste, and fragrance; whose fragrance, color, taste, touch, and efficacy have not been impaired by time, sun, fire, water, wind, or living organisms; and which are fresh and situated in the northern direction;

Of these trees, the branches and leaves that have recently sprouted should be taken during the rainy season or spring; the roots during summer or winter when the old leaves have fallen and new ones have grown; the bark, tubers, and milky sap in autumn; the heartwood in late winter; and the flowers and fruits according to their respective seasons. One who observes auspicious conduct, possesses virtuous character, is pure, and wears white garments, having honored the deities, the two Aśvins, cows, and Brahmins, and having observed a fast, should collect them while facing either the east or the north.

7.1.11 | Having taken [the medicines], one should place them in suitable, high-quality vessels kept in store-rooms that have doors facing east or north, in areas sheltered from wind yet with some ventilation, where there is a constant offering of flowers and ritual oblations; these vessels must be inaccessible to fire, water, excessive heat, smoke, dust, mice, and quadrupeds, and should be kept suspended on racks after being well-covered.

7.1.12 | One should administer these [medicines] according to the specific humor (doṣa): with wine, sauvīraka, tuṣodaka, maireya, medaka, fermented grain-water (dhānyāmla), sour fruit juices, sour curd, and so forth, in cases of vāta; with grapes, āmalaka, honey, madhuka, parūṣaka, treacle, milk, and so forth, in cases of pitta; but in cases of kapha, they should be infused and stirred with honey, urine, decoctions, and so forth. This is the summary. We shall explain this in detail by analyzing the substances, the body, the humors, suitability (sātmya), and other factors.
7.1.13 | They declare that among emetic substances, the fruits of the *madana* tree are the very best because they are free from harmful side effects.
One should collect them during the interval between spring and summer, under the asterisms of Puṣya, Āśvayuj, or Mṛgaśiras, during the *maitra* muhūrta.

Those which are ripe, unblemished by spots, not greenish-yellow, pale, free from worms, not putrid, not eaten by insects, and not small—having wiped these clean, tied them in a bundle of *kuśa* grass, smeared them with cow dung, one should place them for eight nights in any one of the following: the chaff of barley, black gram, rice, horse gram, or green gram husks.
Thereafter, having extracted those that have become soft and possess a honey-like fragrance, one should dry them. Once they are thoroughly dried, one should remove the seeds from the fruits.

Having kneaded them with ghee, curd, honey, and sesame paste, and once dried again, one should fill a new jar—well-cleaned, free of sand and dust—to the brim; then, having covered it well and secured it properly, one should suspend it in slings and store it correctly.

7.1.14 | Now, a patient who is to undergo emesis should be treated with oleation and sudation for two or three days. On the day prior to the emesis, his *kapha* should be excited by means of the meat-broth of domestic, marshy, or aquatic animals, milk, curd, black gram (*māṣa*), sesame, vegetables, and so forth. Having stayed overnight with his food digested, and having performed offerings, oblations, auspicious rites, and expiations in the forenoon, he should be given a meal of gruel (*yavāgū*) that is neither too fatty nor too thin, followed by a dose of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Then, one should administer a handful of those *phala-pippalī* fruits—up to as many as one deems appropriate—with the fingernails intact.

Having crushed [the plant] with a decoction of *yaṣṭimadhu*, or with any one of the decoctions of *kovidāra*, *karbudāra*, *nīpa*, *vidula*, *bimbī*, *śaṇapuṣpī*, *sadāpuṣpī*, or *pratyakpuṣpī*, and having let it sit overnight, one should mash it, strain it, and mix it with honey and rock salt. Making it lukewarm, one should fill a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) and consecrate it with this mantra:
*Oṃ! May Brahmā, Dakṣa, the Aśvins, Rudra, Indra, the Earth, the Moon, the Sun, the Wind, and Fire;
the Sages, along with the multitude of medicinal plants and the hosts of elemental beings, protect you!*

"May this medicine be for you like an elixir for the sages, like nectar for the gods, and like fine wine for the noble serpents. Having consecrated it thus, one should have the patient drink it while facing either north or east—specifically those afflicted by phlegm-fever, abdominal tumors, or catarrh—and do so repeatedly until the appearance of bile (pitta), for by that means one vomits properly. However, if the force of the emesis is weak, one should induce it again and again with a paste of long pepper (pippalī), emblic myrobalan (āmalaka), mustard seeds (sarṣapa), and sweet flag (vacā), mixed with salt and warm water, until the appearance of bile.
Thus ends this entire procedure for the application of emetics.

7.1.15 | However, in all emetic procedures, one should employ honey and rock salt (saindhava) for the purpose of dissolving and cutting through phlegm (kapha). There is no contradiction with heat regarding honey when it is used in combination with an emetic, because it returns without being digested and because it expels the morbid humors (doṣas).

7.1.16 | Two parts each of the fruits of *phalapippalī* should be strained through a decoction of *kocidāra* and other [astringent] substances twenty-one times. Having ground a third part with that juice, one should prepare pills (*varti*) equal in size to *harītakī*, *bibhītaka*, or *āmalaka*. One or two of these, having been softened with an *añjali* measure of any of the previously mentioned decoctions, should be administered in cases of severe salivation due to *śleṣman*, glandular swellings, fever, abdominal enlargement, and loss of appetite; the rest is the same as before.

7.1.17 | Milk boiled with *phalapippalī* (long pepper), or milk-gruel (*yavāgū*) prepared with it, is used for downward-bleeding (*raktapitta*), burning in the heart (*hṛddāha*), and for vomiting of phlegm (*kaphacchardi*), fainting (*tamaka*), and excessive salivation (*praseka*). Or, the cream (*uttaraka*) from curd made from that same milk is used for those conditions. Or, one *añjali* of the surface-scum (*santānikā*) from that milk when cooled is used when *pitta* is aggravated and the chest, throat, and heart are coated with thin phlegm; the rest is the same as previously described.

7.1.18 | Butter produced from milk boiled with *phalapippalī*, prepared with the paste and decoction of *phala* and other ingredients, should be administered in the proper dose to one whose digestive fire is overcome by *kapha* and whose body is emaciated; the rest is the same as previously stated.

7.1.19 | With a powder as bright as flower-dust, well-saturated twenty-one times with a decoction of the fruits and other parts of the *phalapippalī*, one should dust a large lotus grown in a pond during the evening. Having let it remain overnight and dusting it again in the morning, one should extract it and have a delicate person—who has agitated *pitta* and *kapha* and who dislikes medicine—inhale it after they have drunk up to the neck any one of the following: turmeric-water, *kṛsara*-rice, milk, or barley-gruel, mixed with rock salt, jaggery, and molasses.
This is the same as the previous [procedure].

7.1.20 | Having boiled the fresh juice of *phalapippalī* strained according to the procedure for *bhallātaka* until it has become like treacle (*phāṇita*) and reached the consistency of a thin thread (*ātantulī*), one should administer it as a linctus; or, once dried in the sun and powdered, one should have the patient drink it with a decoction of *jīmūtaka* and other drugs when the *pitta* has moved into the seat of *kapha*. This is the same as the previous [instruction].

7.1.21 | Powdered fruits and long peppers (*phalapippalī*), processed as before by being strained through the decoction of any one of the six [substances] beginning with *phala*, are made into boluses (*varti*). These are to be drunk as a gruel (*peyā*) with a decoction of the *phala* group as an adjunct; the rest is the same as previously described.

7.1.22 | A linctus prepared with a decoction of any one of the following—*phalapippalī*, *āragvadha*, *vṛkṣaka*, *svādukaṇṭaka*, *pāṭhā*, *pāṭalā*, *śārṅgeṣṭā*, *mūrvā*, *saptaparṇa*, *naktamāla*, *picumarda*, *paṭola*, *suṣavī*, *guḍūcī*, *somavalka*, *dvīpikā*, as well as *pippalī*, *pippalīmūla*, *hastipippalī*, *citraka*, and *śṛṅgavera*—is the same as described previously.

7.1.23 | A *utkārikā* prepared according to the method for *utkārikās*, or *modakas* prepared according to the method for *modakas*, using the decoction of any one of these twenty ingredients—namely, *phalapippalī*, *elā*, *hareṇukā*, *śatapuṣpā*, *kustumburu*, *tagara*, *kuṣṭha*, *tvak*, *coraka*, *marubaka*, *aguru*, *guggulu*, *elavāluka*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *paripelava*, *māṃsī*, *śaileyaka*, *sthauṇeyaka*, *sarala*, *pārāvatapadya*, and *aśokarohiṇī*—should be administered according to the specific humor (*doṣa*) and disease (*roga*), as well as the patient's preference; the rest is the same as previously described.

7.1.24 | Sesame and rice flour, saturated with the juice and decoction of *phalapippalī*, mixed with that [decoction] as a secondary ingredient, may be prepared as *śaṣkulī*s according to the method for *śaṣkulī*s, or as *pūpa*s according to the method for *pūpa*s; the rest is the same as before.

7.1.25 | By this same method, one should prepare [the treatment] with the decoction of any one of the following: sumukha, surasa, kuṭheraka, kāṇḍīra, kālamālaka, parṇāsaka, kṣavaka, phaṇijjhaka, gṛñjana, kāsamarda, bhṛṅgarāja, poṭā, ikṣuvālikā, kālaṅkatika, or daṇḍaira.

7.1.26 | Likewise, one should administer *madanaphala* (emetic nut) mixed with any one of the following—*badara-ṣāḍava*, *rāga*, *leha*, *modaka*, *utkārikā*, *tarpaṇa*, *pānaka*, meat broth (*māṃsarasa*), soup (*yūṣa*), or wine—according to the specific humor (*doṣa*), disease, and the patient's appetite; by these means, one is properly induced to vomit.
7.1.27 | Madana, karahāṭa, rāṭha, piṇḍītaka, and phala are its synonyms; its pharmaceutical preparations are described as follows.

7.1.28 | Regarding this, there are these verses: There are nine formulations in decoctions (*kaṣāya*), eight in measured doses (*mātrā*), five in milk and ghee, two in inspissated juice (*phāṇita*) and powders (*cūrṇa*), one for inhalation (*ghreya*), and six for the preparation of medicinal wicks (*varti*).
7.1.29 | Twenty formulations each are prescribed for electuaries (leha), boluses (modaka), and cakes (utkārikā);
sixteen formulations each are also stated for fried cakes (śaṣkulī) and baked cakes (pūpa).
7.1.30 | Ten others are for the ṣāḍava and other preparations; thus, one hundred and thirty-three formulations have been duly taught by the great seer in this chapter on results.

Thus ends the first chapter, named the "Madana Kalpa," in the Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—wherein it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Two:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the Pharmaceutics of Jīmūtaka.
7.2.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
7.2.3 | Now hear this chapter concerning *jīmūtaka*, based on its fruits and flowers:
*garāgarī*, *veṇī*, and likewise *devatāḍaka*.
7.2.4 | Jīmūtaka, when prepared with appropriate medicinal adjuncts, destroys the three doṣas and should be administered for diseases such as fever, dyspnea, and hiccough.

7.2.5 | For those born in the [proper] region and endowed with the aforementioned qualities, milk should be given when the flowers have appeared; once the fruit has matured, a gruel prepared with milk should be drunk according to the prescribed rule.
7.2.6 | A continuous stream of milk [is produced] from a hairy [cow], while curd is superior from one that is hairless. When boiled milk is mixed with sour curd, it becomes greenish-white.
7.2.7 | One afflicted by vāta and pitta should drink one śukti of the powder of well-dried, aged [drugs], placed in a clean vessel, along with milk.
7.2.8 | Having fermented it in the scum of *surā* liquor and having crushed it,
one should drink the strained liquid in cases of anorexia caused by *kapha*, cough, anemia, and consumption.
7.2.9 | Two or three [pistils] should be crushed from either guḍūcī or madhuka,
or from those beginning with kovidāra, or from nimba, or from kuṭaja.
7.2.10 | Having strained the [decoction] that has been infused with the astringents (kaṣāya), one should drink it according to that same procedure;
or otherwise, one should drink the seven [drugs] beginning with āragvadha as previously described.
7.2.11 | One afflicted by fever caused by pitta or śleṣman should take the decoction of each [drug] individually;
the doses should be like those of the fruits, and they are considered to be the size of a kola fruit.
7.2.12 | One should administer [this] with the juice of jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, ikṣu, or śatāvarī,
in cases of fever caused by pitta and kapha, or in fever caused by vāta and pitta.
7.2.13 | Likewise, one should cook ghee produced from the milk of the jīmūtaka plant with a decoction of the fruits and other [emetic] ingredients; that is considered the best emetic.

7.2.14 | Regarding this, there are two verses: six [recipes] are in milk; one in the scum of wine (*madirāmaṇḍa*); twelve others in the decoction (*kaṣāya*) of *āragvadha* and the rest; and eight in suppositories (*varti*).
7.2.15 | Four formulations beginning with Jīvaka and one with ghee are proclaimed;
in the section on Jīmūtaka, there are thirty-nine formulations.

Thus ends the second chapter, named the *Jīmūtaka-kalpa*, in the Section on Pharmaceutics (*Kalpasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
The Third Chapter.
7.3.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Ikṣvāku-kalpa* (the pharmaceutical preparations of Ikṣvāku).
7.3.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
7.3.3 | Now I shall describe the proven procedure for the Ikṣvākus, which is highly praised for them:
the lambā, the bitter alābu, the tumbī, and likewise the piṇḍaphalā.
7.3.4 | Ikṣvāku and phalinī are said to be its preparation;
it is used for those afflicted by cough, dyspnea, poison, vomiting, and fever, and for those whose *kapha* has been depleted.
7.3.5 | When a person becomes exhausted, this is desired for the purpose of inducing vomiting:
a fistful of sprouts from a tree that has not yet flowered, measuring a span.
7.3.6 | One should administer [the powder] boiled in one prastha of milk in a fever arising from an excess of pitta and kapha.
Furthermore, there are four [preparations] with milk, as in the case of the *jīmūtaka* [group] beginning with *puṣpa*.

7.3.7 | The fifth [type of] *yoga* for those who are greenish-pale is prepared with the scum of wine (*surāmaṇḍa*). It consists of one part of the juice of fruits and is processed with three parts of milk.
7.3.8 | When phlegm is located in the chest, one should administer [this] in cases of hoarseness of voice and chronic rhinitis;
once it has been digested and partially extracted, one should add milk, and when that has turned into curd, [add sugar].
7.3.9 | One should drink that [mixture] when cough with phlegm, asthma, or vomiting has arisen;
one should also soak the seeds in goat’s milk and have them drunk.
7.3.10 | For those afflicted by poison, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, glandular swellings, goiters,
elephantiasis, anemia, skin diseases, or poisoning, one should take the pulp of the fruit mixed with whey.
