7.3.11 | Or, one should drink buttermilk cooked with that [mixture], mixed with honey and salt,
and sprinkled with the dried juice of the fruits and the flowers of the *tumbī*.
7.3.12 | One accustomed to the pleasure of excellent perfumes should vomit after smelling a garland;
or one should eat the pulp of fruit together with molasses and meat paste.
7.3.13 | Or oil prepared from the fruit of the *ikṣvāku* plant, or clarified butter (*ghṛta*) prepared as previously described;
[the fruits and so forth] increase by ten each, up to fifty, in successive order.
7.3.14 | One should drink the seeds after crushing them separately in decoctions for up to one hundred days;
or one should drink a handful (a *muṣṭi*) with the nails tucked inside, using [decoctions] of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *kovidāra*, and so forth.
7.3.15 | The doses of decoctions made from kovidāra and other such plants are prescribed to be like those for fruits.
One should cook one añjali of tumbī seeds with a decoction of bilva roots.
7.3.16 | Of this strained [mixture], there are three parts; a fourth part of inspissated juice (phāṇita);
a part of seeds mixed with ghee; and likewise half-parts of ground flour.
7.3.17 | One should prepare that electuary with mahājālinī, jīmūtaka, kṛtavedhana,
and vatsaka, stirring it with a ladle over a gentle fire.
7.3.18 | As long as a thread dropped into water does not dissolve,
one should lick that electuary in measured doses and subsequently drink the churned decoction.
7.3.19 | This same procedure is prescribed for the group of four beginning with agnimanthā;
alternatively, one may drink a churned drink (mantha) prepared with roasted grain flour (śaktu) saturated with the fresh juice of tumbī.

7.3.20 | In fever born of phlegm, in cough, in diseases of the throat, in loss of appetite, in abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, and excessive salivation, a person should drink a medicinal paste with meat broths;
thus he vomits effectively and does not suffer from weakness.

7.3.21 | Regarding this, there are these verses: Eight preparations with milk, three with the scum of wine, whey, and buttermilk; oil for inhalation with meat-paste, and six preparations with fruits in increasing quantities.
7.3.22 | Ghee alone [is used] among the decoctions; nine others [are used] in the Madhuka and other groups.
There are eight preparations for suppositories (varti), five electuaries (leha), as well as one churned drink (mantha) and one meat broth (rasa).
7.3.23 | Forty-five yogas have been correctly described by the great seer in the *Ikṣvākukalpa*, out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Chapter on Ikṣvāku," in the Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Four:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the Pharmaceutics of Dhāmārgava.
7.4.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
7.4.3 | Karkoṭakī, koṭhaphalā, and mahājālinī,
as well as rājakośātakī, are synonyms for dhāmārgava.
7.4.4 | In cases of poison, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, cough, and when wind (vāta) is situated in the seat of phlegm (śleṣmāśaya),
as well as when phlegm (kapha) is located in the throat and mouth, and in disorders arising from the accumulation of phlegm.
7.4.5 | In these diseases, those [substances] which are stable and heavy should be employed;
one should collect their fruit, flowers, and tender shoots according to the prescribed method.
7.4.6 | Having dried the fresh juice of *pravāla* and made it into separate pills,
they should be drunk with decoctions of *kovidāra* and the like, as well as with that of *madhuka*.
7.4.7 | There are four methods for the application of milk to flowers and other materials, and the fifth is with wine.
As before, the procedure for those that are old and dried will now be explained.
7.4.8 | A fruit extracted from *bīja-laṇṭha* with a decoction of *madhuka*, together with jaggery, should be left to steep overnight; the same applies to those beginning with *kovidāra*.
7.4.9 | One should give it to those suffering from gulma and abdominal enlargements, as well as others afflicted by disorders of phlegm (kapha).
It should be administered combined with food for the pacification of vomiting and heart disease.

7.4.10 | Or, one who has been satiated with meat-broth, milk, gruel, and so forth, may easily vomit after smelling blue lotuses and other flowers that have been repeatedly impregnated with powders [of emetic drugs].
7.4.11 | Having made a wick from the pulverized powder the size of a jujube fruit,
one should dissolve it in the urine of a cow or a horse in a quantity of one añjali and drink it.

7.4.12 | Likewise, the broth made from the dung-juice of the spotted deer, the ṛṣya, the kuraṅga, the elephant, the camel, the mule, the sheep, the dog-toothed animal (śvadaṃṣṭra), the donkey, and the rhinoceros should be drunk.
7.4.13 | Jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, vīrā, ātmaguptā, śatāvarī, kākolī, śrāvaṇī, medā, mahāmedā, and madhūlikā;
7.4.14 | Each of these, ground separately and combined with *dhāmārgava*,
mixed with sugar and honey, form electuaries for those suffering from burning sensations in the heart and cough.
7.4.15 | When kapha is associated with pitta and heat, the paste [of the drugs] should be taken with lukewarm water as an after-drink;
this paste destroys all poisons when taken with a broth made of coriander and *tumburu*.
7.4.16 | Of *jāti*, *saumanasāyinī*, *rajanī*, and *coraka*;
of *vṛścīra*, *mahāsahā*, *kṣudrasahā*, and *haimavata*.
7.4.17 | Having crushed either the *bimbī*, the *punarnavā*, or the *kāsamarda* individually,
or one or two *dhāmārgavas*, in an alkaline solution;
7.4.18 | When mental disorders have been purified, one should drink this excellent emetic:
either ghee produced from boiled milk, or that which has been prepared with the *phala* group of drugs and others.
7.4.19 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
In the fresh sprouts there are nine [formulas], four in milk, one in wine-ferment;
twenty in decoctions, ten in pastes, and twelve in the juice of dung.
7.4.20 | One [formula] is for food, ten for scents, ten for electuaries, and likewise one for ghee;
thus sixty formulations of *dhāmārgava* have been declared by the great seer in this chapter.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, named the *Dhāmārgava-kalpa*, in the Section on Pharmaceutics (*Kalpasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—where it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
The Fifth Chapter.
7.5.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Vatsaka-kalpa*.
7.5.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
7.5.3 | Now I shall proclaim in detail and exactly as it is the names of the Vatsaka, its distinction between male and female, and its ritual procedure (kalpa).
7.5.4 | Vatsaka, kuṭaja, śakra, vṛkṣaka, and girimallikā are synonyms; its seeds are called indrayava as well as kaliṅgaka.
7.5.5 | The Bṛhatphala tree with white flowers and glossy leaves is male;
the Śyāmā tree with reddish flowers and small fruit-stalks is female.
7.5.6 | It destroys blood-bile and phlegm, is harmless for those of delicate constitution,
and is recommended for heart disease, fever, vāta-blood disorders, erysipelas, and similar conditions.
7.5.7 | Having gathered the fruits at the proper time, one should place them in a dry [container].
Having crushed a handful of them inside [the vessel] along with the nails, one should infuse them.
7.5.8 | Having macerated this [powder] overnight in a decoction of madhuka as well as those beginning with kovidāra, one should then mix it with salt and honey.
One should drink that excellent emetic, which subdues pitta and kapha;
one should saturate their powders with milk for eight days using arka.
7.5.10 | Then one should drink a palmful [of the decoction] with a decoction of jīvaka;
likewise separately with those of phala, jīmūtaka, ikṣvāku, and jīvantī.
7.5.11 | The physician should administer an emetic consisting of mustard seeds, madhūka flowers, or salt, mixed with water or combined with kṛśara.

7.5.12 | Regarding this, there is a verse: Nine [preparations] are stated with decoctions, five with powders, three with water, and one should be with kṛśarā; these are remembered as eighteen formulations.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, named the *Vatsaka-kalpa*, in the Section on Pharmaceutics (*Kalpasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—where not available—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
The Sixth Chapter.
7.6.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Kṛtavedhana-kalpa*.
7.6.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
7.6.3 | Learn now the names of Kṛtavedhana and its ritual application (*kalpa*):
it is called Kṣveḍa, Kośātakī, and also Mṛdaṅgaphala.
7.6.4 | Extremely pungent, sharp, and hot [medicines] are desired for deep-seated diseases.
In cases of skin diseases, anemia, splenic disorders, edema, abdominal tumors, artificial poisons, and so forth.
7.6.5 | For milk and the like, as well as for flowers and the like, and for liquor, the procedure is as before.
However, for those that are very dry or aged, one or two [measures] may be used according to one's strength.
7.6.6 | One should drink [the decoction] with the nine astringents beginning with madhuka, like the fruit [preparation].
Having boiled its fruit and strained it, one should have the linctus prepared.
7.6.7 | A portion of *kṛtavedhana* paste, combined with half a portion each of the fruits and other ingredients,
should be separately infused thirteen times with the decoctions of the *āragvadha* group and the others.

7.6.8 | Six types of suppositories (*varti*) are prepared from the powders of the roots of the *śālmalī* tree mixed with ten parts of mucilage (*picchā*), similar to those made from the *phala* group; likewise, there is the medicated ghee (*ghṛta*) from the *phala* group and others.
7.6.9 | One should boil fifty *kośātaka* fruits in the juice of *kovidāra*.
Then, one should again cook that decoction into a linctus (*lehya*) with the pastes (*kalka*) of the [five] fruits and other ingredients.
7.6.10 | In that [preparation], there should be one part of kṣveḍa, while the remaining [ingredients] should each be half a part;
one should thus prepare it separately with decoctions such as those of kovidāra and others.
7.6.11 | Having boiled the decoctions of fruits and other ingredients together with the meat of marshy animals and *kośātakī* separately, one should drink the resulting broth seasoned with salt.
7.6.12 | One suffering from cough should drink the juice of *kṣveḍa* equal in measure to *phalādi-pippalī*,
or likewise drink *kṣveḍa* prepared with sugarcane juice as a mixture.
7.6.13 | Regarding this, there are two verses: Two each in milk, one in wine, twenty-two decoctions,
ten slimy preparations (picchā), one ghee, and six auspicious medicinal wands (varti).
7.6.14 | Eight formulations are for electuaries, seven for meat preparations, and another is for sugarcane juice;
in this section on *kṛtavedhana*, sixty formulations have been proclaimed.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Pharmacopoeia of Kṛtavedhana," in the Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—wherein it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Seven:
7.7.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the pharmacopoeia of Śyāmā-trivṛt.
7.7.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
7.7.3 | Wise men say that the root of Trivṛt is the best for purgation.
Its designation, qualities, function, divisions, and its conceptualization will now be explained.
7.7.4 | Tribhaṇḍī, trivṛtā, śyāmā, kūṭaraṇā,
as well as sarvānubhūti and suvahā— these are the synonymous terms [for it].
7.7.5 | It is astringent, sweet, and dry, and pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka).
It pacifies kapha and pitta, but due to its dryness, it aggravates vāyu.
7.7.6 | Now, when combined with medicinal substances that alleviate wind, bile, and phlegm,
and having attained its specific therapeutic potential (*kalpavaiśeṣya*), it becomes a remover of all diseases.
7.7.7 | Its root, however, is of two kinds: dark and reddish-brown.
Know that of these two, the root which has a reddish luster is the more excellent.
7.7.8 | That [emetic] is auspicious for one who is delicate, a child, an elderly person, or one with a soft bowel;
however, the *śyāmā* [variety], due to its quick action, might cause delusion, emaciation, or fainting.
7.7.9 | Due to its sharpness, it draws [the doshas] from the heart and throat and quickly eliminates the morbid humors;
it is recommended for those with many doshas and for men who have a hard bowel.
7.7.10 | On that auspicious ground, one should extract the root that has grown there;
having fasted, being self-restrained, dressed in white garments, and composed in mind during the bright fortnight.
7.7.11 | That which is deep-seated, smooth, and extends obliquely—one should incise that and extract the fetus; one should cause the dried skin to be set aside.
7.7.12 | One who has been lubricated and fomented, and is to be purged, should comfortably remain for the duration of one meal (*peyā*) before drinking.
Having prepared a bolus of those two [drugs] the size of an *akṣa* fruit, the man should drink it with sour gruel.
7.7.13 | One should drink separately the urine of a cow, sheep, goat, or buffalo, along with sauvīraka,
tuṣodaka, prasannā, and a decoction of triphalā.
7.7.14 | One should drink one part each of the twelve substances beginning with rock salt,
together with ginger and combined with double the amount of trivṛt, as a powder with warm water.
7.7.15 | Pippalī, pippalīmūla, marica, gajapippalī, sarala, kilima, hiṅgu, bhārgī, and likewise tejovatī.
7.7.16 | Musta, haimavatī, pathyā, citraka, rajanī, vacā,
svarṇakṣīrī, ajamodā, and śṛṅgavera— each of these individually [is used].
7.7.17 | One should drink it combined with one-half part of each [ingredient] along with cow’s urine;
or one should drink it combined with half a part of madhuka and mixed with sugar-water.
7.7.18 | Jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, medā, śrāvaṇī, karkaṭāhvayā, the two parṇīs known as mudgaparṇī and māṣaparṇī, and likewise mahatī-śrāvaṇī.
7.7.19 | One should drink kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, indrā, chinnaruhā,
kṣīraśuklā, payasyā, and yaṣṭyāhva according to the prescribed method.
7.7.20 | These [drinks] are beneficial for vāta and pitta, whereas others are for kapha and anila (vāta).
[One may prepare them] separately with milk, meat juice, sugarcane juice, kāśmarya juice, grape juice, or pīlu juice.
7.7.21 | Or one should drink the powder of those two with ghee, adding a half-portion of *abhayā*;
or one should lick it mixed with honey, ghee, and sugar candy.
7.7.22 | Having licked the powder of *ajagandhā*, *tugākṣīrī*, *vidārī*, sugar, and *trivṛt* mixed with honey and ghee, one is effectively purged.
7.7.23 | A person afflicted by the rigidity, burning sensation, and thirst of *sannipāta* fever [should drink] a decoction of *śyāmā* and *trivṛt* with its paste and sugar.
7.7.24 | One should prepare this electuary according to the prescribed method and then lick a palmful of it;
having cooked sugar with honey, one should place it in a new earthen vessel.
7.7.25 | One should cast the powder of trivṛt along with cinnamon, cinnamon leaves, and black pepper into cold water;
one should lick this in the proper dose as a purgative for kings.

7.7.26 | One should prepare [this electuary] by cooking one *kuḍava* each of meat broth, sugarcane juice, small grapes, *pīlu*, and *parūṣaka*, along with one *pala* of white sugar and half a *kuḍava* of honey.
7.7.27 | The physician who knows the scriptures should administer that linctus cold, combined with the powder of trivṛt;
this is a purgative for powerful persons whose pitta has become aggravated.
7.7.28 | One should prepare sugar-candies, sweetmeat balls, medicinal wicks, pills,
and meat-cakes according to this procedure for the purgation of those with a predominance of pitta.

7.7.29 | One should administer a linctus of long pepper (pippalī), ginger (nāgara), alkali (kṣāra), and black turpeth (śyāmā) together with trivṛt and honey as a purgative for those with a predominance of phlegm (śleṣman).
7.7.30 | One should cook the well-fried juices of *mātuluṅga*, *abhayā*, *dhātrī*, *śrīparṇī*, *kola*, and pomegranate in oil, and into that [oil] one should add [the following]:
7.7.31 | From the mango (*sahakāra*) and the wood-apple (*kapittha*), one should take the fruit that is moderately sour;
as before, when it has become thickened, one should add the powder of *trivṛt*.
7.7.32 | This linctus, consisting of the powder of cinnamon, cardamom, saffron, and cardamom seeds mixed with honey in appropriate proportions,
is a purgative for wealthy persons whose bodies are filled with phlegm.
7.7.33 | One should prepare drinks, juices, soups, sweetmeats,
and *rāga-ṣāḍava* preparations according to this method for the purpose of purgation when *kapha* is predominant.

7.7.34 | Equal parts of *bhṛṅga*, *elā*, and *nīlī*, along with three parts of sugar, should be made into a powder; one should drink this as a nourishing draught (*tarpaṇa*) mixed with fruit juice, honey, and parched grain flour (*saktu*).
7.7.35 | For diseases arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha, in those with weak digestive fire,
and in delicate persons, purgation is free from danger.
7.7.36 | A bolus (modaka) made with sugar, triphalā, śyāmā, trivṛt, pippalī,
and honey cures fever caused by the simultaneous aggravation of all three doṣas (sannipāta), as well as upward-moving hemorrhage (ūrdhvarakta-pitta).
7.7.37 | Three śāṇas each of the three myrobalans (triphalā) bark,
and three śāṇas each of powdered viḍaṅga, pippalī, and alkali (kṣāra) are prescribed.
7.7.38 | One should lick a bolus with ghee and honey, or eat it with jaggery;
this should be consumed without restriction, for it is an excellent purgative.
7.7.39 | This [preparation] cures abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement (plīhodara), dyspnea (śvāsa), chlorosis (halīmaka), anorexia, and other diseases caused by kapha and vāta.
7.7.40 | Viḍaṅga, pippalīmūla, triphalā, dhānya, citraka,
marica, indrayava, ajājī, pippalī, and hastipippalī;
7.7.41 | One karṣa each of powdered salts and ajamodā,
along with eight palas each of sesame oil and trivṛt powder.
7.7.42 | Having cooked three *prastha*s of the juice of *dhātrī* fruit together with half a *tulā* of jaggery over a gentle fire, one should eat portions the size of *badara* or *udumbara* fruits.
7.7.43 | Having prepared jaggery (guḍa), there should be no restriction regarding recreation or diet;
it [cures] weak digestion, fever, fainting, dysuria, and anorexia.
7.7.44 | Insomnia, body aches, cough, dyspnea,
vertigo, wasting, leprosy, hemorrhoids, jaundice, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargements, and fistula-in-ano;
7.7.45 | These [medicines] known as Kalyāṇakas destroy malabsorption (grahaṇī) and anemia (pāṇḍuroga), promote virility (puṃsavana), and are suitable for use in all seasons.

Thus ends the section on Kalyāṇaka-guḍa (7.7.46). The physician should administer equal parts of vyoṣa (the three pungents), tvak, patra, musta, elā, viḍaṅga, āmalaka, and abhayā, along with double the amount of mukūlaka.
7.7.47 | Taking eight parts of *trivṛt* and six parts of sugar,
one should make pills of one *pala* each from the powder mixed with honey.
7.7.48 | One should consume it after rising at dawn and drink cold water afterwards,
in cases of dysuria, fever, vomiting, cough, asthma, vertigo, and wasting.

7.7.49 | This formulation is recommended for those who eat without restriction in cases of fever, anemia, and weak digestion; it is considered the best among all remedies for administering purgatives against poisons.
7.7.50 | For diseases born of urine,
two handfuls each of *pathyā*, *dhātrī*, and *urubūka*, along with one *pala* of *trivṛt*, should be administered by one skilled in the procedure.
7.7.51 | One should prepare ten of those modakas as a purgative for lords (or wealthy persons).
Trivṛt, haimavatī, śyāmā, nīlinī, and hastipippalī [are the ingredients].
7.7.52 | One karṣa each of pippalī with its root, musta, ajamodā, and durālabhā;
one pala of nāgara; and twenty palas of jaggery.
7.7.53 | One should make boluses from this powder, resembling the size of udumbara fruits,
seasoned with asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, trikaṭu, yavānī, biḍa salt, and cumin.
7.7.54 | One should envelop the boluses with powders of vacā, ajagandhā, triphalā, cavya, citraka, dhānyaka, along with tumburu and dāḍima.

7.7.55 | [These enemas] are beneficial for those suffering from pain in the three joints, the groins, the heart, the bladder, the abdomen, or the spleen; and for those afflicted by hiccups, cough, anorexia, dyspnea, phlegm disorders, or upward-moving wind (udāvarta).
7.7.56 | Trivṛt, kuṭaja seeds, pippalī, and viśvabheṣaja,
combined with honey and grape juice, constitute this purgative for the rainy season.
7.7.57 | Trivṛt, durālabhā, musta, sugar, udīcya, candana, drākṣā, yaṣṭyāhva, and sātalā,
taken with grape-water at the end of the rainy season [are beneficial].
7.7.58 | One should drink a paste of trivṛt, citraka, pāṭhā, ajājī, sarala, vacā,
and svarṇakṣīrī, prepared with warm water during the winter season.
7.7.59 | Sugar mixed with an equal amount of trivṛt is a purgative for the summer season.
[One may also use] trivṛt, trāyantī, hapuṣā, sātalā, and kaṭurohiṇī.
7.7.60 | Having powdered svarṇakṣīrī, one should macerate it in cow’s urine for three days.
This formulation is suitable for all seasons and removes impurities and defects from those who have been oleated.
7.7.61 | Trivṛt, śyāmā, durālambhā, vatsaka,
hastipippalī, nīlinī, triphalā, musta, and kaṭukā, well-powdered.
7.7.62 | Thereafter, one should drink a palmful of this mixture combined with ghee, meat broth, and warm water;
for this is most pleasant and is recommended even for those who are dry (rūkṣa).
7.7.63 | One karṣa each of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), asafoetida (hiṅgu), and one pala of trivṛt;
half a karṣa of sauvarcala salt, and half a pala of amlavetasa.

One should drink that powder mixed with an equal amount of sugar along with wine or sour gruel; this is proven to cure abdominal tumors (gulma) and pain in the flanks. Once it is digested, one should eat rice with meat broth.
7.7.65 | Having made a powder of trivṛt, triphalā, dantī, saptalā, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and rock salt,
it should be infused for seven days in the juice of āmalakī.
7.7.66 | This [mixture] should be employed in satiating drinks, soups, meat dishes, and preparations with flavoring agents.
Ghee prepared with equal parts of sour substances and a paste of the three types of ghee (trighṛta) is a remedy for abdominal tumors (gulma).
7.7.67 | One should boil the roots of śyāmā and trivṛt together with āmalaka fruits in water;
having cooked ghee with that decoction, a person should drink it.
7.7.68 | One should drink ghee prepared with a decoction of śyāmā and trivṛt; or likewise, milk processed with those two. By this means, one is purged easily.
7.7.69 | One should boil eight fistfuls of *trivṛt*, including the nails, in one *droṇa* of water; when reduced to a quarter, that strained decoction should be combined with one *tulā* of jaggery.
7.7.70 | Having placed it in a greasy jar smeared with honey, long pepper, fruits, and citraka,
one should drink that which has been produced after a month in the appropriate dose.
7.7.71 | It cures malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and destroys abdominal tumors (gulma) and edema (śvayathu).
One may drink liquor (surā) prepared with the fermenting agent (kiṇva) and combined with a decoction of trivṛtā.

7.7.72 | One should drink sauvīraka, which is prepared by soaking boiled kulmāṣa (half-cooked grain) with water for six days in a vessel that has been steamed with a decoction of barley, śyāmā, and trivṛt.
7.7.73 | Or, one should drink barley that has been fried, dehusked, and purified, mixed with its own flour and saturated with water; thus, *tuṣodaka* (barley-wash) is produced.
7.7.74 | Likewise, one should administer the ten types of *ṣāḍava* and other preparations mentioned in the *Madanaka-lpa*,
combined with the powder of *trivṛt*, for the purpose of purgation.
7.7.75 | And Bhava says here:
Purgatives should be administered combined with cinnamon, saffron, hog-plum, pomegranate, cardamom, sugar-candy, honey, citron,
as well as with intoxicating liquors and sour substances that are pleasing to the mind.
7.7.76 | For one who has drunk [the emetic], one should sprinkle the face with cold water to prevent vomiting;
and one should provide pleasant earth, flowers, fruits, and sprouts, as well as sour substances, for the purpose of smelling.
7.7.77 | Regarding this, there are these verses: one with sour substances (amlādi) and others, eight with the ten beginning with rock salt (saindhava),
two with urine, eighteen with liquorice (yaṣṭī), two with the group beginning with Jīvaka, and fourteen [with the group beginning with Vidārī].
7.7.78 | Seven [measures] are used in electuaries beginning with milk; eight in those with sugar; four also in those with sugar;
five in syrups and the like; six in the seasonings; and five in sweetmeats.
7.7.79 | Four [types of drinks] are in ghee, two in milk, likewise two in flour-meal and in satiation-drinks (tarpaṇa);
two in wine, two in sour gruel (kāñjika), and ten others in ṣāḍava and similar preparations.
7.7.80 | In this section on the pharmaceutical preparations of Śyāmā and Trivṛt,
one hundred and ten proven formulations have been proclaimed by the supreme seer.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Pharmaceutics of Śyāmā and Trivṛt," in the Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—wherein it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Eight:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the Pharmaceutics of Caturaṅgula.
7.8.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
7.8.3 | Āragvadha, rājavṛkṣa, śampāka, caturaṅgula,
pragraha, kṛtamāla, karṇikāra, and avaghātaka are synonyms for the same plant.
7.8.4 | For those suffering from fever, heart disease, disorders of wind (vāta), blood (asṛg), upward movement of gases (udāvarta), and similar ailments,
the rājavṛkṣa is especially wholesome, being mild, sweet, and cooling.
7.8.5 | For children, the elderly, those with wounds, the emaciated, and persons of delicate constitution,
the Caturaṅgula [oil] should be employed because it is mild, non-habit-forming, and easily digestible.
7.8.6 | At the time of fruition, one should take that fruit which has ripened;
one should cause the burden of those virtuous ones to be placed upon sands.
7.8.7 | After seven nights have passed, the physician should extract it and dry it in the sun;
then, having extracted the marrow, he should cause it to be placed in a clean vessel.
7.8.8 | One should administer [this] combined with grape juice to a child suffering from burning sensations and upward movement of wind (udāvarta),
from the age of four years up to twelve years.
7.8.9 | One should take four finger-breadths of marrow, or a handful (prasṛta), or even an añjali-measure,
combined with the scum of surā liquor or with kola-sīdhu.
7.8.10 | Having prepared a cold infusion (śītakaṣāya) combined with whey (*dadhimaṇḍa*) or the juice of *āmalaka*, one should drink it, or else with *sauvīraka*.
7.8.11 | Or one should likewise drink the paste of marrow with the decoction of trivṛt;
similarly, it may be taken with a decoction of bilva, combined with salt and honey.
Alternatively, having prepared a linctus by slowly cooking the powder of *trivṛt* with jaggery and the decoction of that same [drug], one should have the person lick it in the appropriate dose.
7.8.13 | Or, one should drink the ghee that arises from milk and other substances prepared with *caturaṅgula*,
having processed it with the paste (*kalka*) of *dhātrī* fruits and their juice.
7.8.14 | One should drink ghee prepared with a decoction of daśamūla, kulattha, and barley, along with the pastes (kalka) of śyāmā and the other [drugs].
7.8.15 | Having added an añjali of the marrow of śampāka, along with jaggery, to a decoction of dantī,
one should administer this arishta after it has been kept for half a month or a full month.
7.8.16 | Whichever drink or food is pleasing to a person— whether it be sweet, pungent,
or salty— one should administer a purgative combined with that.

7.8.17 | Regarding this, there are these verses: [The purgative action of trivṛt] occurs in grape juice, in surā and sīdhu wines, in curd, in āmalakī juice, in sauvīraka, and in the decoction of bilvaka.
7.8.18 | Twelve formulations have been proclaimed in this *Caturaṅgula-kalpa*: two for electuaries (*lehāḥ*), one for *ariṣṭa*, and two for ghee (*ghṛta*), which are gentle and bring about happiness.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, named "The Pharmacopoeia of Caturaṅgula," in the Section on Pharmacopoeia (*Kalpasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
The Ninth Chapter.
7.9.1. Now, therefore, we shall explain the pharmacopoeia of Tilvaka.
7.9.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
7.9.3 | Tilvaka is considered to be lodhra, also known as bṛhatpatra and tirīṭaka;
one should take its dried root-bark, stripped of the inner bark.
7.9.4 | One should powder it after dividing it into three parts; then, one should strain two parts with a decoction of *lodhra* and saturate the third part with that [decoction].
7.9.5 | One should then saturate that portion of the ten roots with their decoction;
having dried it and reduced it to powder once more, one should employ it from that point forward.
7.9.6 | Then one should drink a palmful [of the powder] with curd, buttermilk, the scum of liquor, urine, jujube wine,
or the juice of *āmalaka* fruits.
7.9.7 | When meṣaśṛṅgī, abhayā, kṛṣṇā, and citraka have been boiled in water, one should press the *maruja* [grapes] into it; that which is thus produced is called sauvīraka.
7.9.8 | He should always drink a paste of *lodhra* with *añjali* water;
he should drink wine that has been produced from a *lodhra* decoction and has stood for a fortnight.
7.9.9 | Having boiled one *droṇa* each of *dantī* and *citraka* with one *āḍhaka* of water,
[one should add] one *tulā* of jaggery and one *añjali* of *lodhra*.
7.9.10 | One should add that [powder] after the fortnights; it is a purgative for those who drink liquor, having been well-impregnated ten times with a decoction of kampillaka.
7.9.11 | One should drink a dose of kampillaka with its decoction again;
furthermore, another linctus should be prepared according to the procedure for caturaṅgula.
7.9.12 | A linctus prepared with the decoction of triphalā, along with ghee, honey, treacle,
and lodhra powder, is excellent for purgation.
7.9.13 | A linctus prepared with the decoction and paste of *tilvaka*, together with sugar and ghee, is excellent for purgation.

7.9.14 | One should boil eight handfuls each—counting the nails—of the *trivṛt* and other ingredients separately in one *droṇa* of water until one-quarter remains; then one should cook one *prastha* of ghee in that decoction.
7.9.15 | Then, with those same parts of bilva ground into a paste along with cow's urine and salt, one should drink a dose at the proper time; this is an excellent purgative.
7.9.16 | One should cook ghee with a paste of *lodhra*, along with urine, sour liquids, and salts;
one should also prepare two types of clarified butter according to the procedure for *caturaṅgula*.
7.9.17 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
one [preparation] with curd and the other ingredients, one with *surā* and *sauvīraka*,
one *ariṣṭa*, and likewise one formulation with *kampillaka*.
7.9.18 | Three electuaries with ghee and four more are proclaimed;
these formulations of the roots of *lodhra* are shown in the sixteenth chapter.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, named the *Tilvaka-kalpa*, in the Section on Pharmaceutics (*Kalpasthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
The Tenth Chapter.
7.10.1. Now, therefore, we shall expound the *Sudhā-kalpa* (the pharmaceutical preparation of lime).
7.10.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
7.10.3 | Among all purgatives, sudhā is considered the most potent;
for it quickly breaks up the accumulation of the humors (doṣas), which are otherwise difficult to displace.
7.10.4 | Therefore, this [therapy] should never be administered to one with a delicate digestive tract (*koṣṭha*),
nor when the accumulation of the humors (*doṣa*) is slight, even if the channels (*mārga*) require cleansing.
7.10.5 | In cases of anemia, abdominal enlargement, abdominal tumors, skin diseases,
affliction by latent poison, edema, diabetes, and when the mind is deranged by the humors;

7.10.6 | Having recognized that the patient is afflicted by such diseases yet still possesses vital strength, one should properly administer mahāvṛkṣa; for when it is correctly administered, it [proves effective].
7.10.7 | It immediately removes even a great accumulation of humors (*doṣa*);
it is considered to be of two kinds, by means of either few or many thorns (*kaṇṭaka*).
7.10.8 | The *pravara* has few very sharp thorns, while the *bahukaṇṭaka* has many.
These are known by the names *snugguḍā*, *nandā*, *sudhā*, and *nistriṃśapatraka*.
7.10.9 | A wise physician should incise [the plant] and extract the milky sap with a surgical instrument,
specifically at the end of winter, from a plant that is two or three years old.
7.10.10 | Having prepared equal parts of the decoction of bilva and the others, or of bṛhatī, or likewise of kaṇṭakārī individually, one should dry it over charcoal embers.
7.10.11 | Then one should drink a dose equal in size to a jujube fruit (*kola*) with sour gruel (*sauvīraka*),
or with fermented rice-water (*tuṣodaka*), or with the juice of jujubes, or with that of *āmalaka*.
7.10.12 | With liquor, whey, or the juice of citron,
one should [administer] sātala, kāñcanakṣīrī, the śyāmā group, and the three pungents (kaṭutrika).
7.10.13 | One should macerate [the powder] for seven days with milk and honey as it becomes available;
thereafter, one should drink a dose the size of a jujube fruit (kola) with ghee or with meat broth.
7.10.14 | One should properly prepare a jaggery syrup (guḍapānaka) containing tryūṣaṇa, triphalā, dantī, citraka, and trivṛt, which has been thoroughly saturated with the milk of the snuhī plant.
7.10.15 | Having prepared equal parts of trivṛt, āragvadha, dantī, śaṅkhinī, and saptalā, along with turmeric,
in cow urine, one should then dry them in the sun.

7.10.16 | Having thus processed it for seven days, one should then process it again with the milk of the *snuk* plant for another seven days; once it is dried, it should then be processed with that [milk] as well.
7.10.17 | Having smelled that fragrance and having wrapped themselves in a cloth,
kings with soft bowels are easily and quickly purged.
7.10.18 | Having cooked a linctus with the decoction of *śyāmā* and *trivṛt*, along with the milk of *snuk*, ghee, and treacle,
one should have the person lick it in the appropriate dose for the purpose of purgation.
7.10.19 | A person should drink sudhākṣīra along with soups, meat broths, or clarified butters;
or he may eat dried fish that has been processed [with these], or meat.
7.10.20 | One should cook ghee with milk and *āmalaka* fruits according to the procedure for *caturaṅgula*;
or one should prepare a liquor (*surā*) in milk, or cook ghee as previously described.
7.10.21 | Regarding this, there are two verses:

There are seven formulations with sauvīraka and other [fermented liquids], one with ghee, one with meat broth, one as a drink, one for inhalation, and one as a linctus; and three more formulations with vegetable soups (yūṣa) and so forth.
7.10.22 | Two preparations with dried fish and meat, one with wine, and two with clarified butter—
these twenty formulations of *mahāvṛkṣa* have been described.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, named "The Formulation of Sudhā," in the Section on Formulations (Kalpasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and—where not extant—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Eleventh Chapter:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the formulation of Saptalā and Śaṅkhinī.
7.11.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
7.11.3 | Saptalā, carmasāhvā, and bahuphenarasā;
likewise śaṅkhinī, tiktalā, yavatiktā, and akṣipīḍaka.

7.11.4 | These [purgatives] should be employed in cases of abdominal tumors (gulma), heart disease, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), edema (śopha), abdominal enlargements (udara), and so forth— conditions characterized by expansion, sharpness, and dryness— specifically when kapha is predominant.
7.11.5 | One should take fruit that is not overly dried from the *śaṅkhinī* plant, having removed the husks;
then, having taken the roots of the *saptalā*, one should place them in a vessel.
7.11.6 | One should administer a bolus of the size of an axle-pin (*akṣamātra*), combined with sugar and salt,
for heart disease arising from phlegm and wind (*kaphavāta*) as well as for abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
7.11.7 | With priyāla, pīlu, karkandhu, kola, āmrātaka, and dāḍima;
with drākṣā, panasa, kharjūra, badara, amla, and parūṣaka.
7.11.8 | This same procedure should be applied to *maireya*, whey (*dadhi-maṇḍa*), sour gruel (*sauvīraka*), *tuṣodaka*, and *sīdhu*; it is a pleasant and swift purgative.
7.11.9 | One should cook oil in milk that has been boiled with the drugs of the Vidārigandhādi group,
along with a paste of Saptalā and Śaṅkhinī, containing half a part each of Trivṛt and Śyāmā.
7.11.10 | Having mixed it with whey (dadhimaṇḍa), one should administer that prepared medicine. Two parts of powdered śaṅkhinī and another part of sesame powder [should be used].
7.11.11 | One should drink oil pressed from harītakī with its decoction;
this same procedure applies to linseed, mustard, castor, and karañja.

7.11.12 | From the milk and other liquids of Śaṅkhinī and Saptalā prepared as a siddha-decoction, ghee should be extracted; to the paste-portion of that very ghee, one should add half a part each of Trivṛt and Śyāmā.
7.11.13 | Having stirred it with milk and boiled it thoroughly, one should drink that as a purgative;
this is the procedure for *dantī* and *dravantī*, as well as for *ajaśṛṅgī* and *ajagandhā*.
7.11.14 | Of the kṣīriṇī, the nīlikā, and likewise the two types of karañja,
as well as the masūravidalā and the pratyakparṇī;
7.11.15 | Likewise, ghee should again be prepared with a paste consisting of half a portion each of the two groups [of drugs].
One should also prepare ghee in a decoction of śaṅkhinī, saptalā, and dhātrī.
7.11.16 | And ghee prepared according to the threefold method (*trivṛt-kalpa*), three electuaries (*leha*) like the *lodhra* preparation,
and the formulation of wine (*surā*) and *kampilla* should be made exactly like the *lodhra* preparation.
7.11.17 | According to the method for *dantī* and *dravantī*, *sauvīraka* and *tuṣodaka* should likewise be used as purgatives for *ajagandhā* and *ajaśṛṅgī*.
7.11.18 | Regarding this, there are two verses:
There are sixteen decoctions (kaṣāya), ten in oil, eight in ghee,
five in wine, three electuaries (leha), and likewise one formulation with kampillaka.
7.11.19(? | Thirty-nine yogas have been declared for you by means of both *saptalā* and *śaṅkhinī*; they are proven effective when used together, and each one is also beneficial individually.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on Saptalā and Śāṅkhinī," in the Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, where unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Twelve:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the chapter on the Pharmaceutics of Dantī and Dravantī.
7.12.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
7.12.3 | Dantyudumbaraparṇī, Nikumbha, Mukūlaka,
Dravantī, Citrā by name, Nyagrodhī, and Mūṣikāhvayā [are synonyms].
Likewise, mūṣikaparṇī, upacitrā, śambarī,
pratyakśreṇī, sutaśreṇī, dantī, and raṇḍā are also proclaimed [as such].
Having gathered the roots of these two, which are firm and thick, [one should proceed].
The wise man [observes] the types of ivory that are dark-brown and copper-colored.
7.12.5 | One should steam the [seeds] smeared with long pepper and honey inside a layer of clay and kuśa grass;
then one should dry them in the sun, for fire and the sun destroy their tendency to sprout.
7.12.6 | Substances that are sharp, hot, quick-acting, expansive,
and heavy dissolve the two doṣas and provoke the vāta.
7.12.7 | A bolus the size of a jujube fruit for those two [should be prepared] with curd, buttermilk, the scum of wine,
and likewise with the fermented juices of *priyāla*, *kola*, *badara*, and *pīlu*.

7.12.8 | A man suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) or enlargement of the abdomen (udara), one afflicted by the [three] doṣas, one with anemia (pāṇḍu), one with intestinal worms (kṛmi), one with stomach ulcers (koṣṭha), or one with fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara) should drink [this]. [The meat broth of] cow, deer, and goat [is prescribed].

7.12.9 | One should cook ghee with the paste and decoction of those two (the two types of *saptaparṇa*), combined with the juice of *daśamūla*, for cases of *kakṣyā*, *alajī*, erysipelas (*visarpa*), and burning sensations (*dāha*).

7.12.10 | Oil [is indicated] in cases of urinary disorders (meha), abdominal tumors (gulma), and flatulence with constipation (udāvarta) caused by kapha and vāta; likewise, the "fourfold unctuous substance" (catuḥsneha) is used for the obstruction of feces, semen, and flatus, and for pain caused by vāta.
7.12.11 | A linctus prepared from the juice of dantī and śṛṅgī, combined with jaggery, honey, and ghee,
is effective for purgation and alleviates burning sensations, fever, and urinary disorders.
7.12.12 | In fever caused by wind and characterized by thirst, that same [preparation] should be used with *ajagandhā*.
One should boil the roots of *dantī* and *dravantī* in the juice of *āmalakī*.
7.12.13 | One should fry three parts of that decoction and two parts of treacle in heated ghee or oil, and then add [the remaining ingredients] to it.

7.12.14 | One should administer as a linctus the paste of *dantī* and *dravantī*, along with a portion each of the *śyāmā* group and others; when prepared, this should be consumed, for by it one is easily purged.
7.12.15 | One should likewise cook these electuaries separately in the decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla), in the decoction of bibhītaka, and in the decoction of harītakī.
7.12.16 | A powder of these two [drugs] equal in measure to a bilva fruit, processed with their own juice, combined with sour substances,
is beneficial for undigested food (āma), wind-born disorders, and abdominal tumors (gulma).
7.12.17 | Having split a stalk of sugarcane and smeared its interior with a paste, one should then apply heat and eat it; by this, one is easily purged.
7.12.18 | One should cook the roots of dantī and dravantī together with green gram (mudga);
these broths, prepared with common quail (lāva), grey partridge (vartīra), and other such birds, serve as purgatives.
7.12.19 | Or else, having prepared a gruel with the decoction of those two, or meat broth from wild animals, or a well-prepared bean soup, one should give them; by these, the patient is purged.
7.12.20 | From that decoction, three parts [should be taken], two parts of sugar likewise, and one part of wheat flour; a beautiful *utkārikā* (steamed cake) should then be prepared.
7.12.21 | Or a bolus (*modaka*) should be prepared for him according to the prescribed method, and that [should serve as] the purgative;
furthermore, one should prepare wines for him with the decoction of those two [drugs].
7.12.22 | Having stirred them with a decoction of *dantī* and prepared them with *dantī* oil,
a person should eat various foods seasoned with molasses and salt.
7.12.23 | Danti, dravanti, marica, yavānī,
upakuñcikā, nāgara, hemadugdhā, and citraka— these, when powdered together, [are used].
7.12.24 | Then, for seven days, one should infuse a palmful [of the powder] in cow's urine;
subsequently, one should drink it with fresh ghee, and once purged, one should also take a nourishing draught.
7.12.25 | This powder is the foremost remedy for all diseases, suitable for use in all seasons; because it is never harmful, it is highly esteemed for both children and the elderly.
7.12.26 | It is recommended for indigestion due to improper eating, pain in the sides, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic enlargement, ascites,
scrofula (gaṇḍamālā), vāta disorders, and anemia (pāṇḍuroga).
7.12.27 | One pala each of citraka and danti, twenty of harītakī,
two karṣas each of trivṛt and pippalī, and eight palas of jaggery— this [mixture].
7.12.28 | Having prepared the *modakas*, one should eat eleven of them;
thereafter, one should drink warm water following each meal, on every tenth day.
7.12.29 | These [medicines] are free from contraindications and destroy all diseases;
they remove disorders of the *grahaṇī*, anemia, hemorrhoids, itching, urticaria, and wind (*vāta*).
7.12.30 | A decoction prepared from two palas of dantī and half a prastha of drākṣā is recommended as a purgative for bile-induced cough and anemia.
7.12.31 | One should drink a paste of *dantī* mixed with an equal amount of jaggery and combined with cold water;
this is the most excellent purgative and the best remedy for jaundice.

7.12.32 | A fermented liquor (ariṣṭa) made from the juice of śyāmā and dantī, with jaggery, long pepper, myrobalan, and citraka, and applied [to the skin], removes wind, phlegm, splenic disorders, anemia, and abdominal enlargements.
7.12.33 | Likewise, a jaggery-based preparation should be made from the decoction of dantī and dravantī along with ajagandhā, or with ājaśṛṅgī; this indeed serves as a pleasant purgative.
7.12.34 | Wine produced from the powder, decoction, māṣa-bean water,
and fermenting liquid of that [grain] is used for phlegmatic abdominal tumors (kaphagulma), low digestive fire, and pain in the flanks and waist.
7.12.35 | The two formulations for sauvīraka and tuṣodaka with the decoction of ajagandhā, and for surā and kampillaka, are prescribed to be like those for lodhra.
7.12.36 | Regarding this, there are these verses: *(In the preparations with curd and other items, there are three; in those with *priyāla* and others, five; in the liquid extracts (*rasa*), three;
in the fats (*sneha*), three; in the electuaries (*lehya*), six; and in the powders (*cūrṇa*), there is only one.)*
7.12.37 | There is one [preparation] from sugarcane, likewise three soups (rasa) of mung beans and meat,
three in the case of gruel (yavāgū) and so forth, and that which has been mentioned in the procedure for the *utkārikā*.
7.12.38 | One [part] is in the *modaka*, one in the wine (*madya*), one in its decoction-oil (*kvāthatailaka*),
one again as powder (*cūrṇa*), and five in the *āsava*.
7.12.39 | One [formula] is for *sauvīraka*, then one formula would be for *tuṣodaka*;
one for *sura*, one for *kampilla*, and likewise five are prescribed for *ghṛta*.
7.12.40 | In this chapter on the pharmaceutical preparations of *dantī* and *dravantī*, three sets of sixteen [formulas] have been declared.
Regarding the various types of yogas as remedies for the diseases of the defects of devotion.
7.12.41 | Three hundred and fifty-five formulations for emesis are recorded;
two hundred and ninety-five formulations, however, are for purgation.
7.12.42 | Six hundred [substances] have been described as belonging to the upward-moving (ūrdhvabhāga), downward-moving (anulomabhāga), and both (ubhayabhāga) categories;
these are stated by relying primarily upon fifteen principal substances.

7.12.43 | And there are verses on this point: "Whatever substance is combined with whatever primary [ingredient], that combination is indeed designated by the name of that [primary]; such is the settled conclusion."
7.12.44 | Suras and other beings are subordinate to the principal entities such as fruits;
for they follow them, just as others follow a lord of men.
7.12.45 | Even a contrary potency among these primary factors does not cause obstruction;
for when the potencies are equal, the greater one is recognized as possessing the capacity for action.
7.12.46 | Furthermore, for the sake of desired color, taste, touch, smell, and purpose, there is no disease [arising from their use];
therefore, it is certain that this is the application of substances with mutually contradictory potencies.
7.12.47 Furthermore, their potency should be further enhanced through natural saturations (*svarasabhāvanā*);
for even a small quantity of a substance, when well-saturated, becomes capable of performing many functions.
7.12.48 | Therefore, one should saturate medicinal substances with their own juices or with those of equal potency;
for even a small amount may achieve great results, while a large amount may produce only a minor effect.
7.12.49 | One should perform [the recitation] through the methods of conjunction, separation, time, and refinement;
here, this much—six hundred [recitations] per region—is to be observed.
7.12.50 | One may thus conceive of thousands or even tens of millions by means of one's own intellect;
because there are so many variations of substances, no fixed number of yogas exists.
7.12.51 | Now hear the characteristics of those [arrows] which are sharp, middling, and mild: that which proceeds easily, swiftly, with great velocity, and without obstruction.
7.12.52 | It does not cause excessive exhaustion in the rectum nor pain in the heart; without injuring the internal receptacle, it expels the entire morbid humor (doṣa).
7.12.53 | One should designate that [medicine] as "sharp" (tīkṣṇa) which is a purgative or a non-unctuous enema (nirūha),
provided it has not been touched by water, fire, or insects, and is endowed with the qualities of its place and time.

7.12.54 | A medicine that is combined with ingredients slightly superior [in potency] and well-processed with substances of equal potency attains sharpness in one who has undergone oleation and sudation.
7.12.55 | A medicine that is slightly deficient in these previously mentioned qualities, or in their proper measure, becomes moderate for one who has been properly lubricated and fomented.
7.12.56 | Medication that is weak in potency, dry, deficient in dose,
combined with substances of unequal potency, or mild, will possess only a slow onset.
7.12.57 | Because they do not remove the defects completely, those two [therapies] are impure for those who are very strong;
however, they should be employed by one desiring success for those of middling or inferior strength.
7.12.58 | Disease may be sharp, moderate, or mild, characterized by all, intermediate, or few symptoms;
one should administer medicines that are sharp and so forth, having regard for the patient's strength.
7.12.59 | However, when the previous [dose] has not been expelled, the emetic medicine should be administered again and again after it has been drunk,
generally until the appearance of bile.
7.12.60 | Having observed the threefold strength of the humors and of the patient,
one should administer medicine again, or else abandon it entirely.
7.12.61 | Once the medicine has been eliminated or digested, and the humors have been expelled, the wise physician should administer another remedy, seeking the highest success.
7.12.62 | An unripened emetic expels the morbid humor (*doṣa*), whereas one that is ripening expels it through purgation; therefore, one should not wait for the ripening of the emetic.
7.12.63 | When the medicine has turned yellow, when it has lost its laxative effect without having expelled the humors,
or when it has become old, the wise physician should administer the medicine again after it has been vomited.
7.12.64 | However, for a man with a stimulated digestive fire, many morbid humors, and firm unctuous qualities,
who has not been properly cleansed and has eaten on that day, one should administer [the purgative] again on the following day.
7.12.65 | A person who is weak and has an abundance of morbid humors (doṣas),
yet undergoes purgation slowly due to the ripening of those humors, should be further treated with easily digestible foods.
7.12.66 | For one who has been purified by emetics and purgatives in the proper measure,
one should bring the remaining morbid humors (doṣas) to subsidence through food and post-prandial drinks.
7.12.67 | One should administer a mild medicine to a person who is weak, has been previously purified, has few morbid humors, and whose digestive tract (koṣṭha) is not well known.
7.12.68 | It is better that a mild [emetic] be drunk repeatedly, causing little distress and being free from danger,
rather than one that is excessively sharp, which might quickly bring about a threat to life.
7.12.69 | Even if a person is weak, a great accumulation of morbid humors (doṣas) should be purged frequently in small amounts with mild medicines; for undischarged humors may indeed destroy him.
7.12.70 | If one's [bile] moves downward, mixed with phlegm, and becomes yellow,
one should have that person vomited by means of gargles, purified, lightened, and then administered [the medicine].
7.12.71 | When the humors (doṣas) are obstructed and only a small amount has been discharged after a long time, one should drink warm water;
by that, flatulence, thirst, vomiting, and constipation are pacified.
7.12.72 | If the medicine, obstructed by the bodily humors (doṣas), does not move upward or downward,
one should administer sudation (sveda) for that condition, accompanied by belching and pain in the limbs.
7.12.73 | If the emesis is insufficient, one should quickly induce it with medicine accompanied by eructation;
if there is excessive discharge once the medicine has been digested, the physician should arrest it with very cold substances.
7.12.74 | Sometimes the medicine remains obstructed in the chest by phlegm;
when that phlegm has diminished, it flows out in the evening or at night.
7.12.75 | When the medicine is dry, causes constipation, has been digested, becomes obstructed, or moves upward,
one should drink another medicine that is unctuous and salty.
7.12.76 | If thirst, delusion, vertigo, and fainting occur while the medicine is being digested,
then a pitta-alleviating medicine that is sweet and cold is recommended.
7.12.77 | When [the digestive fire] is obstructed by phlegm (kapha), there is salivation, nausea, constipation, and horripilation;
in that case, sharp, hot, pungent, and other such medicines that subdue phlegm are beneficial.
7.12.78 | One who has been well-oleated but has a hard bowel and has not undergone purgation should undergo fasting;
by this, his phlegm produced by oleation as well as its obstruction are pacified.
7.12.79 | For those who are dry, have a predominance of wind (vāta), possess a cruel digestive tract, engage in physical exercise,
and have a stimulated digestive fire, medicine is digested even without causing purgation.
7.12.80 | Having first administered an enema (basti) to those patients, one should subsequently administer a purgative (virecana).
A purgative quickly removes the morbid humors (doṣa) that have been mobilized by the enema.
7.12.81 | Those men who eat dry food, who are constant in their duties, and whose digestive fire is kindled—
their humors (*doṣa*) go to destruction through [the effects of] karma, wind, heat, and fire.
7.12.82 | They tolerate even the defects of incompatible food, overeating, and indigestion;
they should be treated with oleation to protect them from wind, but one should not purify them when there is no disease.
7.12.83 | One should not administer an unctuous purgative to a person whose body is excessively unctuous;
one should administer a dry purgative to a person whose body has been prepared by oleation.
7.12.84 | Having thus understood the procedure, the wise physician who knows the proper place, time, and dosage,
does not err when administering purgatives to those requiring purification.

7.12.85 | For one whose [digestive fire] is impaired, food acts like poison; therefore, one should not cause him to eat at improper times. Since it must be drunk at the proper times, one should administer it with great care.
7.12.86 | Regarding the dosage of substances that has been stated here for those of middle [constitution], it should be based upon their digestive fire (*koṣṭha*), age, and strength;
having taken that as the foundation, the variation—whether they are greater or less than that—should be determined for each individual.
7.12.87 | Six *dhvaṃśis* make one *marīci*; six *marīcis* make one *sarṣapa* (mustard seed).
Eight of those red *sarṣapas* make one *taṇḍula*, and two of those [make one *liksā*].
7.12.88 | One *dhānyamāṣa* shall be one [unit], two *dhānyamāṣas* make one *yava*,
four of those make one *aṇḍikā*, and four of those make one *māṣaka*.
7.12.89 | Three of those [māṣas] make a *śāṇa*, which is said to be both gold (*hema*) and coriander (*dhānyaka*).
One should know that two *śāṇas* make a *draṅkṣaṇa*, as well as a *kola* and a *badara*.
7.12.90 | One should know that two *drakṣaṇas* make a *karṣa*, as well as a *suvarṇa* and an *akṣa*;
likewise, a *biḍālapadaka*, a *picu*, and a *pāṇitala*.
7.12.91 | One should know that a *tinduka* fruit and a mouthful (*kavalagraha*) are equal;
two *suvarṇas* would be half a *pala*, as would a *śukti* and an *aṣṭamikā*.
7.12.92 | Two half-palas make one pala; [the measures] are muṣṭi, prakuñca, and caturthikā. Bilva, ṣoḍaśikā, and āmra are synonyms for two palas; [the measure] prasṛta is known as vidhu.
7.12.93 | One should know that two *kuḍavas* make one *māṇikā*, which is the eighth measure (*aṣṭamāna*).
One should understand that four times a *pala* is an *añjali*, as is a *kuḍava*.
7.12.94 | Four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*; four *prasthas* make an *āḍhaka*. That same [measure] is known as a *pātra*, and eight *prasthas* likewise constitute a *kaṃsa*.
7.12.95 | Four *kaṃsas* make a *droṇa*, which is also called *ārmaṇa* and *nalvaṇa*. That same measure is known as a *kalaśa*, a *ghaṭa*, and also an *unmāna*.
7.12.96 | A *droṇa* doubled is to be known as a *śūrpa*, and likewise as a *kumbha*. One should know that two *śūrpa*s make a *goṇī*, as well as a *khārī* and a *bhāra*.
7.12.97 | A wise man skilled in measurements should know that thirty-two *vāhas* equal one *śūrpa*,
and he should know that one *tulā* consists of one hundred *palas*.
7.12.98 | This measurement and so forth have been proclaimed for dry substances;
for liquids, double that amount is desired, as it is for substances recently extracted.

7.12.99 | Indeed, when no measure is specified, one should employ that which is called a *māna*, a *tulā*, or a *pala*; however, when a specific measure is not mentioned, it is proclaimed that the measure should be equal [to the preceding].
7.12.100 | Even when a liquid is not specified for a medicinal preparation, water is traditionally prescribed in all such cases;
and because the term "quarter" (pāda) is used as a designation, it refers to one-fourth part.
7.12.101 | Wherever the proportions of water, oil, and medicinal herbs have not been specifically stated,
there the oil should be one part, and the water four times the amount of the oil.
7.12.102 | The cooking of medicated fats (sneha-pāka) is known to be threefold: mild (mṛdu), medium (madhya), and hard (khara).
When the decoction of the drugs is equal in quantity to the paste (kalka), it is considered mild.
7.12.103 | When the juice has been extracted like thickened gruel (*saṃyāva*), the middle [pitch] releases the ladle;
but when the juice is being strained, the rough [pitch] likewise remains present.
7.12.104 | A donkey is prescribed for massage, a crow for nasal treatments,
and one that is moderately cooked should be employed for drinking and enemas.
7.12.105 | They say that measurement is of two kinds: Kāliṅga and Māgadha. Those who know measurement understand that the Māgadha is superior to the Kāliṅga.
7.12.106 | Regarding this, there are two verses: The meaning of the section, purification, nomenclature, the distinct causes for its application,
[the treatment of] the regions and so forth, the fruits and so forth, the qualities, and the six hundred formulations.

7.12.107 | The causes for variations in dosage, the names [of the preparations], the characteristics of the sharp, medium, and mild types, the rules regarding the stages [of administration], the measurement, and the cooking of the unctuous substance have been shown.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, named "The Chapter on Dantī and Dravantī," in the Section on Pharmaceutics (Kalpasthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, where unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
The seventh Section on Pharmaceutics is complete. Now begins the Section on Success (Siddhisthāna).
The First Chapter.
8.1.1: Now, therefore, we shall explain the accomplishment of the preparations.
8.1.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
8.1.3 | What is the conceptualization taught regarding the five types of enemas (bastis), what is their sequence, and what is [the procedure] for those performed and those not performed?
Likewise, what is the sign in cases of excessive administration, what is the number, what are the qualities, and which basti is used for which [conditions]?

8.1.4 | What should be avoided at the time of administering each enema (basti), and once it has been administered, what is the duration of the period of avoidance? By what means does the enema not move forward when being introduced, by what does it move quickly, and by what does it take a very long time?
8.1.5 | Why do some curable diseases not subside when treated with their respective pacifying measures?
Thus was the best of physicians [Punarvasu] properly questioned by Agniveśa, the most excellent of disciples.
8.1.6 | Punarvasu, the knower of the treatise, spoke this to him out of a desire for the welfare of all living beings:
"A person who has undergone oleation therapy should be subjected to sudation for a minimum of three days and a maximum of seven days."
8.1.7 | Beyond this, they do not prescribe further oleation; however, after seven days, it becomes habituated.
Oleation destroys Vāyu, softens the body, and removes the accumulation of impurities.
8.1.8 | In one who has been oleated, the sweat carries away the morbid humor (doṣa) that is hidden within the subtle channels by means of its fluidity;
such a person should be provoked to vomiting with the meat-juices of domestic, aquatic, and marshy animals, along with their flesh and milk.
8.1.9 | One who has an excess of phlegm (*śleṣman*) should be purged with meat juices from wild animals, along with soups that are unctuous and do not increase phlegm;
for such a person vomits without difficulty, whereas one with diminished phlegm is properly purged.
8.1.10 | When kapha is located below and is diminished, one should administer emesis; likewise, when kapha is increased and located above, one should administer purgation.
Emesis should be given to one who has been lubricated (with oleation), and for one who has vomited, the sequential regimen beginning with thin gruel (peyā) should be followed as prescribed.
8.1.11 | For one who has been lubricated and properly sudated, the most appropriate purgative should be administered according to the rules:

[the diet should proceed through] liquid gruel (*peyā*), thick gruel (*vilepī*), unseasoned soup (*akṛta-yūṣa*), seasoned soup (*kṛta-yūṣa*), meat broth (*rasa*), three times, twice, or once [respectively].
8.1.12 | One whose body is purified, having attained purity through superior, middling, and inferior stages, should practice in sequence;
just as a tiny spark of fire, when fanned by grass, cow dung, and other fuels, grows gradually.
8.1.13 | The internal fire of a pure person is great, stable, and likewise capable of digesting everything;
however, for the inferior, middling, and superior types [of patients], four, six, and eight urges are desired respectively in emesis.
8.1.14 | Those same ten [palas], doubled or tripled, constitute the dose for purgation; likewise, a *prastha* increased two, three, or fourfold is used.
Emesis is desired until the end of pitta, while they say that purgation should end with the elimination of kapha, being half the dose of emesis.
8.1.15 | Having expelled two or three urges accompanied by feces, one should measure the [quantity of] medicine in purgation; however, in emesis, it is measured by the drink.
He for whom phlegm, bile, and then wind are expelled in succession is considered to have vomited properly.

8.1.16 | When the purity of the heart, sides, head, sense organs, and channels is observed, as well as lightness of the body, [the emesis is successful]; however, in the case of difficult vomiting, there is the appearance of eruptions, urticaria, itching, impurity of the heart and breath, and heaviness of the limbs.
8.1.17 | In excessive emesis, there may occur thirst, delusion, fainting, provocation of wind (vāta), loss of sleep, strength, and so forth;
whereas [proper emesis results in] purification of the channels, clarity of the sense organs, lightness, vigor, digestive fire, and freedom from disease.
8.1.18 | Furthermore, in one who has been properly purged, there occurs the sequential restoration of the feces, bile, phlegm, and wind;
however, there may also arise the provocation of phlegm, bile, and wind, as well as exhaustion, loss of digestive fire, heaviness, and coryza.

8.1.19 | Drowsiness, vomiting, and anorexia [occur], yet there is downward movement of the wind (vātānulomya) when one has been properly purged; whereas numbness, body aches, fatigue, tremors, and so forth arise from the depletion of kapha, blood, and pitta, or from the provocation of the wind.
8.1.20 | Excessive drowsiness, loss of strength, entry into darkness (fainting), insanity, and hiccups occur when one has been excessively purged.
On the ninth day, one should have him drink ghee mixed with food, or administer an oil enema (anuvāsana).

8.1.21 | Then, after three days have passed and the patient is no longer excessively hungry, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) to him whose body has been anointed with oil. Once the enema has returned, he should be fed with the meat-juice of desert animals, or else according to what is appropriate after considering the strength of the humors (doṣa).
8.1.22 | A man who is fit for an oil enema (anuvāsana) should not be excessively full when entering [the treatment];
he should be given an enema during the cold season and spring by day, and at night during autumn, summer, and the rainy season.
8.1.23 | Having avoided those very same defects that were previously described regarding the drinking of oleaginous substances,
once the oil has returned [to the bowels], food should be given to the patient who is to receive the non-unctuous enema (anuvāsana) on the following day after he has spent the night awake.
8.1.24 | The evening meal should be taken two or three days later; the oil enema (anuvāsana) should be administered on the fifth day.
Or, one may administer the oil enema every third day or even on the fifth day after the decoction enema (nirūha).
8.1.25 | In a disorder born of phlegm (kapha), one or three enemas should be administered; in a disorder of the nature of bile (pitta), five or even seven;
and in that of wind (vāta), nine or eleven. Thus, an expert should apply an odd number of enemas.
8.1.26 | A person who has undergone purgation must certainly avoid the administration of a non-unctuous enema for seven days.
For if one who is purified by a non-unctuous enema undergoes purgation, his already empty body will become further distended.

8.1.27 | Enema establishes youth, promotes a happy life, and bestows strength, digestive fire, intellect, voice, and complexion. It accomplishes all purposes for children, the elderly, and the young; it is free from harm and removes all diseases.

8.1.28 | A Nirūha enema draws out feces, phlegm, bile, wind, and urine; it brings about firmness and bestows semen and strength. By expelling the accumulation of humors (doṣas) situated throughout the body, it pacifies all disorders.
8.1.29 | When the channels have been purified by a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) within the body, the administration of oil provides nourishment and bestows complexion and strength;
indeed, there is no substance superior to the application of oil, especially for those afflicted by Vāta.
8.1.30 | By its unctuousness, oil overcomes the dryness of the wind (pavana), and by its heaviness and heat, it overcomes its coldness;
it quickly bestows clarity of mind, virility, strength, complexion, and nourishment of the digestive fire.
8.1.31 Just as a tree watered at its root becomes possessed of dark foliage and tender sprouts,
and in due time becomes great, yielding flowers and fruit, so too does a man become [prosperous] through the administration of an oil enema (anuvāsana).
8.1.32 | For those who are stiff, as well as those who are contracted, those who are lame, and those who are broken or afflicted by pain—
for those in whose limbs the winds (vātas) circulate, the enema (basti) is especially recommended.
8.1.33 | En cases of flatulence, hard feces, colic, lack of appetite for food,
and other such ailments occurring in the abdomen, the enema (basti) is recommended.
8.1.34 | Furthermore, for women who, due to disorders caused by Vāta, do not conceive even when united with men,
and for those men whose senses are diminished and who are emaciated— for them, the enema (vasti) is highly recommended.
8.1.35 | For those overcome by heat, they prescribe cold enemas; likewise, for those overcome by cold, pleasant-warm ones.
One should apply enemas everywhere after differentiating them according to their application with medicinal drugs that are antagonistic to the specific condition.
8.1.36 | A physician should not administer nourishing enemas (bṛṃhaṇīya) in diseases requiring purification (viśodhana),
such as skin diseases (kuṣṭha), urinary disorders (prameha), and other conditions in obese individuals who require purification.

8.1.37 | One should not administer purification (vishodhana) to those with depleted tissues or wounds, nor to those who are emaciated, nor to those who are extremely weak, nor to those who have fainted,
nor to those who have already been purified, nor to those whose life-span is bound up within the doshas.
8.1.38 | Diseases located in the limbs, those situated in the visceral cavities, and those arising in the vital organs (marmans), the upper body, all parts, or the individual members— of these,
there is indeed no other cause for their birth than Vāyu.
8.1.39 | Since it causes the dispersal and accumulation of the impurities residing in feces, urine, bile, and so forth,
there is no other remedy for its excessive increase than the enema (*basti*).

8.1.40 | Therefore, some say that half of medical treatment consists of enemas; indeed, they claim that every form of treatment is an enema, for it reaches the region of the navel, the waist, the flanks, and the abdomen, and having churned up the accumulation of fecal impurities, [eliminates them].
8.1.41 | That enema (*basti*) by which the body, along with its feces and morbid humors (*doṣa*), having been lubricated, passes properly and easily,
results in the discharge of feces, urine, and flatus, as well as an improvement in appetite, an increase in digestive fire, and lightness of the internal organs.
8.1.42 | The subsiding of disease, restoration to the natural state, and strength—these constitute the signs of a well-settled [enema].
There may be swelling in the regions of the rectum, head, heart, anus, and bladder, as well as coryza and cutting pain.

8.1.43 | Vomiting, retention of flatus and urine, and labored breathing occur when a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) is insufficiently administered. Whatever symptoms arise from excessive purgation, those very same symptoms occur from an excessively administered non-unctuous enema.
8.1.44 | When oil has been properly administered, there occurs clarity of the blood and the sense organs, including the intellect;
the persistence of dreams, lightness, strength, and the natural discharge of bodily urges follow its correct oleation.
8.1.45 | Pain in the lower body, abdomen, arms, back, and sides; a rough and harsh complexion;
and the retention of feces, urine, and flatus—these are the signs of one who has been improperly administered an oil enema (anuvāsana).

8.1.46 | Nausea, delusion, exhaustion, lassitude, fainting, and cutting pain occur for one who has been given an over-abundant unctuous enema; however, that man whose oil continues to circulate for three watches of the day here is one whose body has been thoroughly purified.
8.1.47 | However, another unctuous enema (sneha) should be administered once the patient has recovered; for an enema that does not remain [in the body] does not produce the desired unctuousness.
Thirty enemas are considered the standard course of action; half of that time is for the preparation, and half again is for the administration.
8.1.48 | There are indeed twelve non-unctuous enemas (nirūhas) along with the post-enema unctuous applications (anvāsanas): one unctuous application before, five after;
three at the end, and likewise one before; thus there are six unctuous applications interspersed among the non-unctuous enemas.
8.1.49 | In the case of *yoga*, only three *nirūha* enemas should be administered, and five *sneha* (oleation) enemas at the beginning, middle, and end.
They say that three, five, four, or six *anuvāsana* (oil) enemas should be given for those suffering from *vāta* and the other [doshas].

8.1.50 | Having administered the oleation therapies quickly, the physician should then prescribe non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) for the purpose of purifying the channels. Once the body has been thoroughly cleansed, he should then gradually apply unctuous substances and fomentation (sveda) to the head.

8.1.51 | One should administer purgation three times, twice, or once, having considered the threefold strength of the impurities (*mala*). When the body is properly purified, lightness of the chest and head, clarity of the sense organs, and purification of the channels shall occur.
8.1.52 | In the case of insufficient purging, there is a sensation of a coating in the throat, heaviness of the head, and spitting;
whereas in excessive purification, there is pain and piercing sensations in the head, eyes, temples, and ears, as well as the perception of darkness (timira).

8.1.53 | In that case, the satiation (tarpaṇa) should be mild and liquid; however, for one who has already undergone oleation, it should be sharp, but not repeated in the same application. Thus, this regimen brings happiness to both the patient and the healthy, increases strength and longevity, and destroys diseases.
8.1.54 | The period of time required for the enema and subsequent procedures should be doubled as the period of avoidance;
one must avoid sitting too long, standing, speaking, riding in vehicles, sleeping during the day, sexual intercourse, and the suppression of natural urges.
8.1.55 | One should avoid cold treatments, exposure to the sun, grief, and anger, as well as untimely and unwholesome food,
when the bowels are bound, when the enema has been administered, when the eyes are strained, or when the path is obstructed by hemorrhoids, phlegm, or feces.
8.1.56 | The enema does not enter, nor does it exit easily, if it is obstructed by the *doṣas*, or if it is small in quantity, or lacks potency;
or when the urge for feces, flatus, or urine has arrived; or when the *vāta* is excessively increased; or when the anus is weak.
8.1.57 | A enema that is too hot or too sharp, or one administered into a soft bowel, returns immediately after being introduced.
Furthermore, when the vital air (vāyu) is obstructed by fat and phlegm (kapha), it causes pain, numbness of the limbs, and swelling.
But an ignorant person who applies oleation therapy to such a patient only increases those disorders;
likewise, other diseases that were previously unconsidered may arise when their pathways are obstructed by one another.
8.1.59 | Furthermore, those [diseases] corrupted by other humors do not attain pacification through their own specific medicines;
and every therapeutic action for the alleviation of disease that is deficient, excessive, or performed at an improper time [is likewise ineffective].
8.1.60 | Furthermore, due to improper treatment, even a wholesome regimen (pathya) when administered will not bring that disorder to a state of peace.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
These twelve questions concerning the five therapeutic procedures (pañcakarma) have been presented here in the section on successful formulations (kalpanā).
8.1.61. For the welfare of all beings, the Blessed One, the best of seers, the son of Atri, has correctly proclaimed these great subjects.

Thus ends the first chapter, named "Success through Formulations" (*Kalpanāsiddhi*), in the Section on Success (*Siddhisthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and—where it was missing—completed by Dṛḍhabala.
The Second Chapter.
8.2.1 | Now, therefore, we shall explain the successful application of the five medical procedures (*pañcakarman*).
8.2.2 Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.
8.2.3 | O Agniveśa, I shall fully explain for whom and for what reason one should not have the five types of surgical procedures performed, as well as for whom they should be performed.
8.2.4 | One who is fierce, reckless, timid, ungrateful, and agitated;
one who hates physicians and kings, or is hated by them, and is afflicted by grief.
8.2.5 | One who acts by chance, one who is about to die, one who is deprived of his sense organs,
one who is an enemy, one who is conceited in his knowledge of medicine, one who lacks faith, and one who is deeply suspicious;
8.2.6 | A patient who is disobedient to physicians should not be treated by one who knows the medical science;
by treating such persons, a physician incurs many faults.

8.2.7 | Other than these, men who have been approached by all therapeutic measures will be described [further], after distinguishing their respective stages, as being either to be avoided or to be treated.

8.2.8 | Those for whom [emesis] is prohibited are as follows: those who are emaciated by wounds, those who are excessively obese, those who are extremely thin, children, the elderly, the weak, those exhausted, thirsty, hungry, those afflicted by the burden of work, travel, fasting, sexual intercourse, study, physical exercise, or constant anxiety; those who are pregnant, delicate, or have a constricted bowel; those suffering from difficult vomiting, upward-moving hemorrhage (raktapitta), persistent vomiting, upward-moving wind (ūrdhvavāta), or who have recently undergone non-unctuous or unctuous enemas; and those suffering from heart disease, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), urinary retention, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, abdominal enlargement, prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā), loss of voice, blindness (timira), or pain in the head, temples, ears, or eyes.
