8.2.9 | In that regard, excessive bleeding may occur from further incising a wound; there may be loss of life due to the inability of those who are emaciated, very obese, children, the elderly, or weak to tolerate the strength of the medicine; and the same applies to those who are exhausted, thirsty, or hungry, as well as those afflicted by labor, carrying heavy loads, travel, fasting, sexual intercourse, or study, and those who are wasted by labor, carrying heavy loads, travel, fasting, sexual intercourse, study, physical exercise, or obsessive anxiety.

From dryness, there may be fear of wind-blood disorders (*vātarakta*), cutting, or injury; for a pregnant woman, there is the risk of fetal distress or miscarriage and the onset of severe diseases; for one who is delicate, excessive upward or downward evacuation may cause excessive hemorrhaging from the heart; and in those with a constricted abdomen or those prone to vomiting, the aggravated humors (*doṣas*)—due to excessive purging—produce internal erysipelas (*antardāha*), stiffness, numbness, mental confusion, or death; furthermore, in one suffering from upward-moving blood-bile (*ūrdhvagarakta-pitta*), it may displace the *udāna* breath and take away life.

It would cause blood to flow excessively, as would persistent vomiting; in those who have undergone upward-directed enemas (ūrdhvavāta), non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana), or unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), it would cause an excessive upward movement of wind; in those with heart disease, it would cause oppression of the heart; in those suffering from upward-moving wind (udāvarta), it would produce a more terrible udāvarta that kills more quickly; in those afflicted by urinary retention and similar ailments, it would cause the emergence of more intense pain; in those suffering from blindness (timira), it would increase the blindness further; and in those with headaches and the like, it would increase the pain. Therefore, these persons should not be made to vomit.

However, among all these [causes], even when poison, heavy metals, incompatible foods, or indigestion have not been ingested, [the application of emetics] is not prohibited, because of their extremely rapid action.

8.2.10 | Emaciation (śoṣa) is indeed treatable by emesis (*vamya*), especially in cases of chronic rhinitis, skin diseases, acute fever, pulmonary consumption, cough, dyspnea, throat obstruction, goiter, elephantiasis, urinary disorders, impaired digestion, indigestion from incompatible foods, choleraic poisoning, intestinal torpor, ingestion of poisons or toxins, being bitten or pierced [by venomous creatures], downward hemorrhaging, hemoptysis, salivation, hemorrhoids, nausea, anorexia, indigestion, scrofula, epilepsy, insanity, diarrhea, edema, anemia, stomatitis, vitiated breast milk, and other such kapha-related diseases, as well as those specifically mentioned in the chapter on major diseases.
For among these, emesis is said to be the most important, just as breaking a dam on a field destroys the fault of the non-drying up of rice and other crops.

8.2.11 | However, those who should not be purged by enema are: those with a favorable constitution (*subhaga*), those with an injured anus, those whose rectal canal has been removed, those with downward-bleeding hemorrhoids (*adhobhāga-raktapitta*), those who have undergone fasting therapy (*vilaṅghita*), those with weak sense organs, those with low digestive fire, those recently treated with non-unctuous enemas (*nirūḍha*), those preoccupied with desire and other passions, those suffering from indigestion (*ajīrṇin*), those with acute fever (*navajvarin*), those with alcoholism (*madātyayita*), those with flatulence (*ādhmāta*), those afflicted by foreign bodies (*śalyār dita*), those with trauma (*abhihata*), those who are excessively unctuous, those who are excessively dry, those with a harsh bowel (*dāruṇakoṣṭha*), and those beginning with the wounded up to pregnant women (*kṣatādayaś ca garbhiṇyantāḥ*).

8.2.12 | In that regard, it would cause the aforementioned defect in one who is overly delicate; in one with an injured anus, it would produce pain obstructing the vital breaths in the injured rectum; in one whose stalk has been released, it might kill through excessive discharge; likewise in one suffering from downward-bleeding *raktapitta*; those who have undergone fasting, the weak, those with impaired senses, or those with low digestive fire, if administered as a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), would not withstand the force of the medicine; in one whose mind is distracted by lust and other passions, it would not flow, or if it flows with difficulty, it would produce the defects of improper administration; in one with indigestion, there would be the disorder of undigested matter (*āmadoṣa*); and in one with acute fever...

One should not eliminate morbid humors that have already ripened, nor should one aggravate the Vāta; for in one suffering from alcoholism whose body is depleted by liquor, the Vāyu may obstruct the vital breath (prāṇa). In one who is distended or has undergone purgation, the Vāyu accumulated in the receptacle of the feces, spreading suddenly, may produce severe constipation (ānāha) or even death. In those afflicted by a foreign body, a blow, or a wound, the Vāyu residing in the injury may destroy life. In one who is excessively unctuous, there is the danger of over-action; in one who is dry, the Vāyu may cause the stiffening of the limbs.

In one with a harsh bowel habit (*dāruṇakoṣṭha*), the morbid humors (*doṣas*) expelled by purgation may produce cardiac pain, splitting of the joints, flatulence, body aches, vomiting, fainting, and exhaustion, and thus destroy life; for those starting from those with chest wounds up to pregnant women, the same complications mentioned regarding emesis would occur; therefore, these individuals should not be purged.
8.2.13 | The remaining [diseases], however, are to be treated with purgation;

specifically, those such as skin diseases (kuṣṭha), fever, urinary disorders (meha), upward hemorrhage (ūrdhvaraktapitta), fistula-in-ano (bhagaṃdara), abdominal enlargements (udara), hemorrhoids (arśas), hernia (bradhna), splenic disorders (plīha), abdominal tumors (gulma), tumors (arbuda), goiter (galagaṇḍa), cysts (granthi), cholera (visūcikā), intestinal torpor (ālasaka), urinary retention (mūtrāghāta), intestinal worms (krimikoṣṭha), erysipelas (visarpa), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), pain in the head or flanks (śiraḥpārśvaśūla), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), burning sensations in the eyes, mouth, or heart (netrāsyahṛddāha), heart disease (hṛdroga), freckles (vyaṅga), blue moles (nīlikā), discharge from the eyes, nose, or mouth, chlorosis (halīmaka), dyspnea (śvāsa), cough (kāsa), jaundice (kāmalā), scrofula (apacya), epilepsy (apasmāra), insanity (unmāda), gout (vātarakta), disorders of the female reproductive tract (yonidoṣa), seminal defects (reto-doṣa), blindness (timirya), anorexia (arocaka), indigestion (avipāka), vomiting (chardi), edema (śvayathu), abdominal dropsy (udararoga), eruptive boils (visphoṭaka), and other such diseases characterized by pitta.
And those mentioned in the chapter on major diseases; for among these, purgation is said to be the most important, just as the extinguishing of a fire depends primarily on the house itself.

8.2.14 | Those who should not be subjected to non-unctuous enema (anāsthāpya) are: those with indigestion (ajīrṇin), those who have been excessively oleated (atisnigdha), those who have recently drunk fats (pītasneha), those whose morbid humors (doṣas) are agitated, those with weak digestive fire (alpāgni), those exhausted by travel (yānaklānta), those who are extremely emaciated (atidurbala), those afflicted by hunger, thirst, or fatigue (kṣut-tṛṣṇā-śramārta), those who are very thin (atikṛśa), those who have just eaten (bhuktabhakta), those who have drunk water (pītodaka), those who have undergone emesis (vamita) or purgation (virikta), those who have performed nasal therapy (kṛtanastaḥkarman), those who are angry (kuddha), frightened (bhīta), intoxicated (matta), or fainting (mūrchita), those suffering from persistent vomiting (prasaktacchardi), spitting (niṣṭhīvikā), dyspnea (śvāsa), cough (kāsa), hiccups (hikkā), intestinal obstruction (baddhacchidra), ascites (udakodara), flatulence (ādhmāna), intestinal torpor (alasaka), choleraic diarrhea (visūcikā), premature delivery (amajātā), diarrhea (atīsāra), diabetes (madhumeha), or skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

8.2.15 | In those cases, for one with indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), or who has been excessively unctuous, or who has drunk oil, there may be *dūṣyodara* (abdominal enlargement due to vitiated tissues), fainting, or swelling. For one whose doshas are agitated and whose digestive fire is weak, there is severe anorexia. In one exhausted by travel, the enema, being disturbed by agitation, may quickly dry up the body. In those who are extremely weak, or afflicted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue, the previously mentioned defects would occur. In one who is very emaciated, it may produce further emaciation. In one who has just eaten food and drunk water, the wind (*vāyu*), becoming agitated, may push the enema upward or downward and quickly [produce] terrible [symptoms].

It may produce morbid transformations (*vikāra*); furthermore, in one who has undergone emesis and purgation, the body is parched and a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*) would burn it like caustic on a wound; in one who has undergone nasal therapy (*nastaḥ-karma*), it would cause displacement (*vibhraṃśa*) due to the extreme constriction of the channels; in those who are angry or frightened, the enema fluid might flow upwards; in those who are intoxicated or unconscious, when consciousness is greatly disturbed, complications arise from injury to the mind (*cittopaghāta*); and in those suffering from persistent vomiting, spitting, dyspnea, cough, or hiccups, the upward-moving wind (*vāyu*) would carry the enema fluid upwards.

In those suffering from intestinal obstruction, perforation, ascites, or flatulence, the enema may excessively agitate the doshas and destroy life; in those with intestinal stasis (alasaka), choleraic poisoning (visūcikā), premature delivery, or diarrhea, it would produce disorders caused by undigested matter (āma); and in those with diabetes mellitus (madhumeha) or skin diseases (kuṣṭha), it would cause a recurrence of the disease. Therefore, these individuals are not to be given a non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana).
8.2.16 | The remaining [patients], however, should be treated with enemas (āsthāpana);

specifically those suffering from diseases of the whole body, a single limb, or the abdomen; retention of flatus, feces, urine, or semen; deficiency of strength, complexion, muscle, or semen; disorders of flatulence, numbness of limbs, worms in the intestines, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), diarrhea following purification, pain in the joints, burning sensations, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors (gulma), colic, heart disease, fistula-in-ano, insanity, fever, scrotal swelling (bradhna), pain in the head or ears, stiffness or tremors of the heart, sides, back, or waist, convulsions (ākṣepaka), heaviness or excessive lightness, loss of menses, irregular digestion, and pain in the buttocks, knees, calves, thighs, ankles, heels, forefeet, vagina, arms, fingers, breasts, teeth, nails, or joints.

Bone pain, emaciation, stiffness, intestinal rumbling, cutting pain in the rectum, frequent passing of small amounts of stool with sound, the emergence of a foul odor, and so forth—these are specifically the diseases of Vata, as described in the chapter on major diseases; among these, non-unctuous enema (āsthāpana) is said to be the most important, like the cutting of a tree's root.

8.2.17 | Those who are unfit for the non-unctuous enema (anāsthāpya) are likewise unfit for the unctuous enema (ananuvāsya). Specifically, these include those who have not eaten, those with acute fever (navajvara), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), jaundice (kāmalā), urinary disorders (prameha), hemorrhoids (arśas), coryza (pratiśyāya), anorexia (arocaka), weak digestion (mandāgni), the debilitated (durbala), splenic enlargement (plīha), disorders of kapha in the abdomen (kaphodara), stiffness of the thighs (ūrustambha), diarrhea (varcobheda), those who have ingested poison or artificial poison (viṣagarapīta), those with deranged pitta and kapha (pittakaphābhiṣyanda), those with a heavy digestive tract (gurukoṣṭha), elephantiasis (ślīpada), goiter (galagaṇḍa), scrofula (apacī), and intestinal worms (krimikoṣṭhin).

8.2.18 | In that regard, because the channels are not yet cleared for one who has not consumed food, the unctuous substance (sneha) moves upward. In those suffering from acute fever, anemia, jaundice, or urinary disorders, it would aggravate the humors (doṣas) and produce abdominal enlargement (udara). In one with hemorrhoids, it would cause secretions and flatulence in the hemorrhoids. In one afflicted by anorexia, it would further destroy the desire for food. In those with weak digestion or physical weakness, it would make the digestive fire even weaker. In those with coryza, splenic disorders, and the like, whose humors are already severely aggravated, it would increase the humors even more. Therefore, these individuals should not be given an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).

8.2.19 | Those very patients who are fit for non-unctuous enemas (asthāpya) are also fit for unctuous enemas (anuvāsya); however, those with dry constitutions, sharp digestive fire, and those afflicted solely by diseases of vāta are especially so. For it has been stated that among these, the unctuous enema is the most preeminent, like the watering of the root of a tree.

8.2.20 | Those who are unfit for head-purgation (aśirovirecana) are: one suffering from indigestion; one who has just eaten; one who has recently drunk oils, wine, or water; one who has bathed his head; one desiring to bathe; those afflicted by hunger, thirst, fatigue, intoxication, or fainting; those struck by weapons or staffs; those exhausted by sexual intercourse, physical exercise, or drinking; those with acute fever; those tormented by grief; those who have undergone purgation or oil enema (anuvāsana); pregnant women; those suffering from recent coryza; and during the wrong season or on cloudy days.

8.2.21 | In that regard, administering it to one who has not digested their food or to one who has just eaten obstructs the upward-moving channels (*ūrdhvavaha-srotas*), thereby producing cough, dyspnea, vomiting, and coryza. If administered to those who have consumed fats, wine, or water, or to those desiring to drink, it causes discharge from the mouth and nose, inflammation of the eyes (*upadeha*), visual impairment (*timira*), and diseases of the head. If administered to one who has bathed his head, it causes coryza due to the washing away of the head's natural oils. In one afflicted by hunger, it provokes *vāta*; in one afflicted by thirst, it further increases thirst and causes dryness of the mouth.

In those who are exhausted, distressed, intoxicated, or fainting, it would produce the complications described for non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana). In those struck by weapons or staffs, it would produce more intense pain. In those fatigued by sexual intercourse, physical exercise, or drinking, it would cause affliction of the head, shoulders, eyes, and chest. In those afflicted by acute fever or grief, the heat (ūṣman), following the channels of the eyes, would cause blurred vision (timira) and an increase in fever. In one who has undergone purgation, the Vāyu would cause impairment of the sense organs. In one who has received an unctuous enema (anuvāsana), Kapha [would be aggravated].

It may produce heaviness of the head, itching, worms, and disorders; in a pregnant woman, it may arrest the fetus, causing it to be born one-eyed, with contracted fingers, paralyzed on one side, or as a paraplegic; in one suffering from acute coryza, it may obstruct the channels; and when administered out of season or on a cloudy day, it may produce cold-related disorders, putrid rhinitis, and diseases of the head. Therefore, these individuals are not fit for head-evacuation therapy (śirovirecana).

8.2.22 | The remaining [conditions], however, are treatable (*arha*), especially those affecting the head, teeth, neck-stiffness, throat, jaw, *pīnasa*, uvula, tonsil, *śālūka*, cataract (*timira*), diseases of the eyelids, freckles, sublingual swelling (*upajihvikā*), hemicrania (*ardhāvabhedaka*), diseases of the neck, shoulders, scapulae, mouth, nose, ears, eyes, skull, and head; as well as facial paralysis (*āpatantraka*), convulsions (*apatānaka*), goiter (*galagaṇḍa*), toothache, hypersensitivity of the teeth (*harṣa*), tremors, ophthalmia (*akṣirāji*), tumors (*arbuda*), hoarseness of voice (*svarabheda*), speech impediments (*vāggraha*), stammering (*gadgada*), and wheezing (*krathana*), as well as disorders of the upper part of the body caused by *vāta* and other [humors] when they have reached a state of suppuration.

Among these, head evacuation (śirovirecana) is said to be the most preeminent; for, having entered the head and the upper body, it extracts the morbid humor (doṣa) that causes disorder, just as one pulls out a blade of muñja grass from its sheath.

8.2.23 | One should administer nasal medication (nāvana) during the rainy season, autumn, and spring for urgent diseases, due to the application of artificial qualities [of the drugs]. It should be administered in the forenoon during summer, at midday during the cold season, and on cloudy days during the rains.
8.2.24 | Regarding this, there are these verses: Thus, the fivefold action has been demonstrated in detail—
namely, for whom each action is not beneficial, why it is so, and for whom each action is beneficial.
8.2.25 | A wise person should not become dogmatically attached even to a meaning that has been definitively stated;
in this matter, an intelligent physician should exercise his own critical judgment.
8.2.26 For indeed, there may arise a situation with respect to place, time, and strength,
in which what is to be done would become what is not to be done, and an action that ought to be performed would be avoided.

8.2.27 | Emesis is prescribed in its own treatment for those suffering from vomiting, heart disease, and abdominal tumors; and for leprosy patients, the administration of enemas is indicated upon reaching the appropriate clinical stage.
8.2.28 | Therefore, even when there is an explicit instruction, one should proceed by inferring for oneself through one's own intellect;
for that which is established without reasoning is merely an accidental success.

Thus ends the second chapter, named "The Success of the Five Procedures" (*pañcakarmīyasiddhi*), in the Section on Success (*siddhisthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and—where it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Three:
8.3.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the success regarding the aphorisms on enemas (*bastisūtrīyā siddhi*).
8.3.2 Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

8.3.3 | Having found the opportunity, Agniveśa, standing near the delightful abode of the Lord of Wealth on the excellent mountain and surrounded by throngs of great sages, questioned Punarvasu with palms joined in reverence.

8.3.4 | With what considerations should enemas be administered to men so that they achieve success? Of what material is their nozzle made? What are its dimensions and shape, and what are its qualities? For whom are they intended, and from what source and with what qualities is the bladder (vasti) derived?

8.3.5 | Having heard this— concerning the procedure for non-unctuous enemas (nirūha), their application, dosage, the regimen regarding the patient's bed, and which enemas are beneficial for which conditions— the Great Sage spoke these words in reply.

8.3.6 | Having carefully considered the doshas, the medicines, the place, the time, suitability, digestive fire, temperament, and so forth, as well as age and strength, an enema administered will certainly lead to benefit, and all medical procedures will be successful.
8.3.7 | Net-panels should be made of gold, silver, lead, copper, brass, bell-metal, bone, weapons, wood, bamboo,
ivory, reeds, horns, and various kinds of gems, and they should have three bosses.

8.3.8 | For those born of twenty-six, twelve, and eight years [of age], the apertures should be measured at six, twelve, and eight finger-breadths respectively; they should be capable of passing through mung beans, jujubes, and *satīna* beans, and likewise be plugged with wicks.
8.3.9 | They should be as thick at the base and tip as the thumb and little finger respectively according to age;
they should be straight, shaped like a cow’s tail, smooth, and have rounded ends.
8.3.10 | There should be one *karṇikā* at the fourth part from the tip; two *basti*-bindings should be attached to the base.
The bladder may be that of a goat, a buffalo, a deer, a pig, or even that of a goat.
8.3.11 | Firm-bodied, with the head removed, odorless, reddened by astringent decoctions, very soft, and thoroughly cleansed;
having observed the age of men, it should be applied to the urethras according to what is appropriate, being well-fastened so that urine does not leak.
8.3.12 | If basti materials are unavailable, there may be a bladder made of skin or a very thick cloth with marked measurements;
having examined a person fit for āsthāpana on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, the physician who knows the procedure [should proceed].
8.3.13 | When there is a conjunction of an auspicious lunar mansion and a favorable moment (*muhūrta*), one should begin the treatment with a concentrated mind,

8.3.14 | One should cook eight fruits and half a *tulā* of goat meat in water until one-fourth remains;

8.3.15 | Mixed with medicinal pastes (*kalka*) and combined with jaggery (*guḍa*), honey (*kṣaudra*), ghee (*ghṛta*), and oil (*taila*), [the enema] should be applied lukewarm in the quantity of a *picu*.

8.3.16 | Having placed it in the enema-bag, churned it with a rod, bound it securely, and having pressed out the air so that it is free of wrinkles,
one should cover the opening with the middle of the thumb and remove the wick situated at the tip of the nozzle.
8.3.17 | A person whose body has been anointed with oil, who has voided urine and feces, and who is not afflicted by excessive hunger,
should lie upon a bed that is level or slightly inclined toward the head, neither too high, and provided with a comfortable mattress.
8.3.18 | Having caused him to lie comfortably on his left side with his body straightened and his own arm used as a pillow,
and having drawn up his right thigh while extending his left, one should then apply it [the enema].
8.3.19 | When the anus is lubricated, one should slowly and straightly insert the fourth part of the lubricated nozzle along the spinal column,

8.3.20 | Having pressed it firmly with a single grasp, one should then slowly withdraw the nozzle.

8.3.21 | An enema administered too slowly reaches destruction; one that is squeezed with excessive force runs up into the throat. A cold one causes excessive stiffness, while one that is excessively hot produces a burning sensation, fainting, and distress.

8.3.22 | An unctuous enema causes excessive dullness; a dry one, however, causes wind (vāta). One that is thin, given in small dose, or deficient in salt causes improper action (ayoga). One that is excessive in dose causes over-action (atiyoga). A thick enema, moreover, acts slowly.

8.3.23 | Excessive salt causes burning and diarrhea; therefore, one should administer it properly and in equal measure. First, one should take honey and rock salt, churn them together with a fatty substance, and then add the medicinal paste.
8.3.24 | Having churned it and mixed it again with liquids, one should place that churned substance into the enema bag using a churning rod (*khaja*).
For when there is a disorder localized in the left side, the colon (*grahaṇī*), or the rectum, its application is easily achieved by one standing on the side.
8.3.25 | Thus the coils themselves contract; therefore, one lying on the left side is fit for the administration of an enema.

8.3.26 | With the body lying supine and a pillow provided, his strength likewise enters the body.

8.3.27 | When he has returned, he should be sprinkled with lukewarm water and should eat *śāli* rice with a thin meat broth. Once that is digested, he should be given an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) in the evening for the purpose of nourishment, having eaten a light meal in small quantity.
8.3.28 | Having administered oil prepared with sour substances and drugs that subdue Vāta, in a quantity equal to one-quarter of the *nirūha* enema,

8.3.29 | While the body is supine, one should slightly lift the pair of toes of each foot and rub the soles; with oil, one should also massage the heels, the toes, the calves, and whichever parts of the limbs are afflicted by pain.
8.3.30 | Having crushed them well, one should then comfortably resort to sleep with a pillow provided.
There are five parts of the decoction, while the sixth part is for the oil, when pitta is present or when one is in a state of normal health.
8.3.31 | When vāta is increased, however, the fourth part [of the dose] is used; in nirūhas, the portion for kapha is one-eighth.
The dose of a nirūha is half a prasṛta in the first year, and thereafter it increases by half a prasṛta each year.
8.3.32 | Up to twelve [years], there should be an increase of one *prasṛta*; up to eighteen, [the increase] should be by twelves;
beyond that, up to seventy, that [measure] is prescribed; beyond that, it should be treated like the sixteen-year-old.
8.3.33 | The dosage for a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) is measured by a handful (prasṛta); for children and the elderly, it should be specifically mild.
A bed with a footstool is recommended, neither too high nor with the feet too low.
8.3.34 | The bed should be provided with a primary mattress and a soft coverlet, with the head toward the east and a white cloth as an upper covering.
Furthermore, considering the specific disease, one should likewise provide food consisting of soups, milk, meat broths, and so forth.
8.3.35 | One should know this to be the primary procedure for all [enemas]. Hereafter, I shall describe the subsequent types of enemas:
the decoction of the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), combined with sour liquids, along with goat meat and the aforementioned pastes (peṣya).

8.3.36 | A non-unctuous enema (nirūha) prepared with the three unctuous substances (trisneha), combined with the group of drugs beginning with sthirā, along with balā, paṭola, trāyamāṇā, eraṇḍa, and barley, is declared to be the most excellent for curing all diseases caused by vāyu.
8.3.37 | One *prastha* of meat broth, combined with half a *prastha* of goat’s milk, should again be cooked until it reaches the measure of one *prastha*,
joined with a paste of *priyaṅgu*, black pepper, and *musta*, and mixed with oil, ghee, honey, and rock salt.
8.3.38 | An enema (basti) made with three palas of castor root, one pala of palāśa, and the five minor roots is digestive, bestows muscle mass and strength, and also provides strength to the eyes.

8.3.39 | Take one *pala* each of *rāsnā*, *aśvagandhā*, *atibalā*, *guḍūcī*, *punarnavā*, *āragvadha*, and *devadāru*, together with eight parts of *madana*; boil these in two *droṇas* of water until reduced to one-eighth.
8.3.40 | *Peṣyāḥ* (to be ground): *śatāhvā*, *hapuṣā*, *priyaṅgu*, *pippalī*, *madhuka*, and *balā*;
along with *rasāñjana*, seeds of *vatsaka*, and *musta*, each in a portion of one *akṣa*, combined with a portion of salt.
8.3.41 | An enema consisting of honey, oil, and urine is digestive and scraping for men;
it cures pain in the calves, thighs, feet, sacrum, and back, as well as obstruction by phlegm and suppression of wind.

8.3.42 | When administered, the eraṇḍa enema pacifies the retention of feces, urine, and flatus along with colic, distension, urinary calculi, gravel, constipation, hemorrhoids, and disorders of the grahaṇī.

8.3.43 | Four *pala* of oil and ghee, half a *śata* of goat meat fried therein, along with curd and sour pomegranate juice—this sauce, when ground with spices, bestows strength, flesh, complexion, semen, and digestive fire; it is highly recommended for cataracts and headaches.
8.3.44 | Having boiled eight palas of palāśa in two āḍhakas of water until the decoction remains measuring half an āḍhaka,
it should be combined with a paste made from one pala each of vacā and māgadhikā, and two palas of śatāhvā.
8.3.45 | This non-unctuous enema (nirūha), containing rock salt, honey, and oil, bestows strength and a healthy complexion;
it destroys abdominal distension, diseases of the flanks, disorders of the female reproductive tract, abdominal tumors, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and pain.
8.3.46 | Milk prepared with eight palas of yaṣṭyāhvaya (liquorice), combined with śatāhvā seeds and pippalī,
along with ghee and honey, is a nirūha enema beneficial for vātarakta, hoarseness of voice, and visarpa.

8.3.47 | Milk boiled with yaṣṭī, āhva, lodhra, abhayā, candana, and lotuses— both white and blue— and combined with sugar and honey, when well-cooled and mixed with the jīvanīya group of herbs, destroys diseases caused by pitta.

8.3.48 | Sandalwood, padmaka, riddhi, yaṣṭīmadhu, rāsnā, vṛṣa, sārivā, along with lodhra and mañjiṣṭhā, as well as anantā, balā, sthirādi, and the five roots of grasses (tṛṇapañcamūla), [each weighing] two karṣas.
8.3.49 | Having boiled [the herbs] in water and using that decoction, one should cook half an āḍhaka of milk until the water is evaporated,

8.3.50 | With sugar, long pepper, jīvaka, padmaka-reṇu, prapauṇḍarīka, lotus, and blue water-lily;

8.3.51 | One should administer a cold nirūha enema consisting of flour mixed with ghee, honey, and rock salt (saindhava).

8.3.53 | Milk boiled with grapes and the rest, along with *kāśmarya*, *madhūka*, and *sevya*; with *sārivā*, sandalwood, and *śītapākya*; and with the pastes of *śrāvaṇī*, *mudgaparṇī*, *tugā*, *ātmaguptā*, and *madhuyaṣṭi* [is used for enema].
8.3.54 | One should administer a Pitta-alleviating enema (basti) prepared with wheat flour in the measure of an akṣa, combined with honey, ghee, madhuyaṣṭī,

8.3.55 | It is recommended for men in cases of burning sensations in the heart, navel, flanks, or upper body; when there is internal burning; in cases of difficult urination (mūtrakṛcchra);

Having boiled koṣātakī, āragvadha, devadāru, śārṅgeṣṭā, mūrvā, kuṭaja,
arka, pāṭhā, kṛtavedhana, and bṛhatī in water, there should be ten *prasṛta*s of that decoction.
8.3.57 | These [drugs] should be combined with mustard seeds, cardamom, and madana, along with kuṣṭha, in the measure of one akṣa each, and with one prasṛta each;

8.3.58 | A wise physician should administer a nirūha enema to one suffering from disorders of kapha, as well as to those with weak digestion or an aversion to food,
using water boiled over a fire with paṭola, pathyā, amaradāru, and pippalī.
8.3.59 | A decoction made from the two groups of five roots (dvi-pañcamūla), the three myrobalans (triphalā), and bilva, combined with cow’s urine;
along with a paste of kaliṅga, pāṭhā, and musta fruit, together with rock salt, alkali, and oil.

8.3.60 | The Nirūha-basti is preeminent for destroying disorders born of Kapha, as well as anemia, alasaka, and defects caused by Kāma; likewise, it cures the retention of flatus and urine, as well as even severe abdominal distension (āṭopa).
8.3.61 | With rāsnā, amṛtā, eraṇḍa, viḍaṅga, dārvī, saptacchada, uśīra, surāhvaya, nimba, śampāka,
bhūnimba, paṭola, pāṭhā, tiktā, ākhuparṇī, daśamūla, and musta;
8.3.62 | A decoction made from *trāyantikā*, *āśigru*, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*), combined with water containing *piṇḍītaka* and urine,
along with *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *pippalī*, *phalinī*, *śatāhvā*, *rasāñjana*, white *vacā*, and *viḍaṅga* [is used for this purpose].
8.3.63 | This Nirūha enema, prepared with the pastes of Kaliṅga, Pāṭhā, Ambuda, and Saindhava, mixed with ghee, honey, and oil,
is for those afflicted by worms, skin diseases, urinary disorders, inguinal hernia, abdominal enlargement, indigestion, and disorders of Kapha.
8.3.64 | Even when administered to those who have already been depleted by dry (rūkṣa) medicines, this [ghee], despite these diseases being present,
destroys the Vāta, kindles the digestive fire, conquers the diseases, and bestows strength.

8.3.65 | Punarnavā, eraṇḍa, vṛṣa, aśmabheda, vṛścīra, bhūtīka, balā, palāśa, and the two sets of five roots (the daśamūla) should each be taken in the measure of one pala; these should be crushed and washed, along with eight fruits.
8.3.66 | One *prasṛta* each of bilva, barley, kola, kulattha, and dhānyaphala should be boiled with two *āḍhaka*s of milk and water;
when reduced to the quantity of milk alone, it should be strained through a white cloth.
8.3.67 | [A decoction] prepared with the pastes of vacā, śatāhvā, maradāru, kuṣṭha, yaṣṭyāhva, siddhārthaka, and pippalī,
combined with yavānī and madana, and mixed with jaggery and rock salt, should be neither too hot nor too cold.

8.3.68 | A wise physician should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) according to the prescribed method, consisting of three *prasṛtas* each of honey, oil, and ghee; it destroys diseases caused by all combinations of humors.
8.3.69 | One unctuous and hot enema with meat is prescribed for vāta; two sweet and cold ones with milk for pitta;
and three pungent, hot, and sharp ones with urine for kapha; beyond these, no more nirūha enemas should be administered.
8.3.70 | A supplementary meal (pratibhojana) should consist of meat broth in cases of Vāta, milk in Pitta, and vegetable soups in Kapha.
Likewise, for those requiring oil enemas (anuvāsya), Bilva oil, Jīvanīya oil, and oil prepared with Madanaphala should be used.

8.3.71 | Thus has been declared in its entirety this foremost procedure for the administration of enemas (basti) exactly as it is. The wise man who, having studied this, performs the enema therapy (bastikarma) in this world, attains success.

Thus ends the third chapter, named "The Successful Treatment of Complications Related to Enemas" (*bastisūtrīyasiddhi*), in the Section on Success (*siddhisthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, where unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Four:
8.4.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the successful treatment of complications arising from oleation therapy (*snehavyāpatsiddhi*).
8.4.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
8.4.3 | Now learn of these oil enemas (snehabasti), which alleviate vāta, pitta, and kapha,
as well as the complications arising from improper administration, along with their treatments.
8.4.4 | Daśamūla, balā, rāsnā, aśvagandhā, punarnavā,
guḍūcī, eraṇḍa, bhūtīka, bhārgī, vṛṣaka, and rohiṣa.
8.4.5 | Take one pala each of śatāvarī, sahacara, and kākanāsā;
and one prasṛta each of barley, māṣa, atasī, kola, and kulattha.
8.4.6 | Having boiled one āḍhaka of oil with four droṇas of water until one droṇa remains, one should add an equal amount of milk and one pala each of the drugs of the jīvanīya group.

likewise, the fat (vasā) of marshy animals, prepared with life-promoting (jīvanīya) drugs, has the same effect.

8.4.10 | Having ground svaguptā, kṣīrakākolī, karkaṭākhyā, śaṭī, and vacā,

8.4.12 | Ghee prepared with sandalwood and other [medicinal] powders, with four parts milk and one-fourth part oil,

8.4.13 | Saindhava salt, madana, kuṣṭha, śatāhvā, nicula, vacā,

8.4.15 | One should grind bilva, ajamodā, pippalī, dantī, and rāsnā;

8.4.16 | By means of this oil used as an unctuous enema (anuvāsana), one may destroy bradhna, udāvarta, gulma, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, urinary disorders, excessive wind (āḍhyamāruta), abdominal distension (ānāha), and urinary calculi (aśmarī).
8.4.17 | Or the physician should prepare a kapha-subduing oil using Madana fruits combined with sour substances, or with the Bilvadi group of drugs, or even with other kapha-destroying ingredients.
8.4.18 | Viḍaṅga, eraṇḍa, rajanī, paṭola, triphalā, amṛtā, jātī shoots,
nirguṇḍī, daśamūla, and ākhuparṇikā;
8.4.19 | One should cook oil with a decoction of nimba, pāṭhā, sahacara, śampāka, and karavīra, along with these same ingredients ground into a paste.
8.4.20 | With *phala*, *bilva*, *trivṛt*, black *rāsnā*, *bhūnimba*, *dāru*,
*saptaparṇa*, *vacā*, *uśīra*, *dārvī*, *kuṣṭha*, and *kaliṅgaka*—
8.4.21 | With latā, gaurī, śatāhvā, agni, śaṭī, coraka, and pauṣkara,
that [mixture] cures skin diseases, worms, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, and diseases of the digestive tract.
8.4.22 | When administered as a drink, an external massage, or an oil enema, it quickly dispels impotence, irregular digestion, impurities, and likewise the three humors (doṣas).
8.4.23 | For those whose strength and vitality are depleted by disease, physical exercise, labor, or travel,

8.4.24 | It produces supreme firmness in the feet, calves, thighs, back, shoulders, and hips;

8.4.25 | There are six complications of an unctuous enema (sneha-vasti) when it is obstructed by vata, pitta, kapha, excessive food, or feces, or when it is administered before a meal.

8.4.28 | By means of body aches, fever, flatulence, coldness, stiffness, pain in the thighs,

8.4.29 | One should treat it with unctuous, sour, salty, and hot substances, such as oils of rāsnā and pītadru,
along with sauvīraka, surā, kola, kulattha, and barley.
8.4.30 | One should properly eliminate [the doshas] with enemas prepared from the two *pañcamūla* groups along with cow's urine;

8.4.31 | One should recognize pitta-obstructed [fever] by burning sensations, redness, thirst, delusion, darkness, fever, and impairment; one should eliminate it with enemas containing sweet and bitter substances.
8.4.32 | One should recognize that oil is occluded by kapha through drowsiness, cold, fever, lassitude, salivation, loss of appetite, heaviness, fainting, and exhaustion.

8.4.33 | One should expel that [dosha] by means of enemas prepared with astringent, pungent, sharp, and hot substances, processed with wine and urine, combined with fruit-pastes and oils, and mixed with sour liquids.

8.4.34 | One should recognize that [fever] as being obstructed by overeating when it is accompanied by vomiting, fainting, aversion to food, malaise, pain, drowsiness, body aches, and the symptoms of undigested matter (āma), along with a burning sensation.
8.4.35 | Digestion is promoted by decoctions and powders of pungent and salty substances; mild purgation and the therapeutic measures prescribed for *āmavāta* are beneficial here.

8.4.36 | Having recognized that the unctuous substance (sneha) is obstructed by feces through pain from the retention of feces, urine, and flatus, heaviness, flatulence, and cardiac oppression, one should treat it with oleation, sudation, and suppositories.

8.4.37 | One should properly eliminate [the disorder] with Nirūha and Anuvāsana enemas prepared with the Śyāmā, Bilva, and other groups of drugs, according to the procedure that effectively cures Udāvarta.
8.4.38 | When one has not eaten, or when the rectum is empty, oil that is excessively pressed out by force rushes upward;
from there, it even reaches the upper orifices starting from the throat.
8.4.39 | A decoction prepared with cow’s urine, śyāmā, and trivṛt, containing barley, jujube, and horse gram,
along with oil processed with those same ingredients, is recommended here as both a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) and an unctuous enema (sānuvāsana).
8.4.40 | When [the poison] reaches the throat, its removal should be effected by means of suppression, seizing the throat, emetics, and treatments that counteract vomiting.
8.4.41 | If an unexpelled oil enema (snehabasti) causes no distress—
whether it is entirely retained, partially retained, or obstructed due to dryness— it should be disregarded by the wise physician.

8.4.42 | Having eaten a meal in the proper quantity, one should undergo an oil enema (anuvāsana) every three days; the oil should be mixed with fat, warm, and light, and one should thereafter consume wholesome food.
8.4.43 | A wise physician should administer water boiled with coriander and ginger to one who has fasted overnight,

8.4.45 | Following emesis, purgation, non-unctuous enema (nirūha), and unctuous enema (sānuvāsana),

8.4.46 | One who is dry, has suppressed [urine or stool], possesses a blazing digestive fire, is habituated to physical exercise, and suffers from wind-related diseases,

8.4.47 | The oil of these reaches putrefaction quickly, like water poured upon sand;
for others, however, the fire generally digests the oil within three days.
8.4.48 | One should not administer oil enema (anuvāsana) with the nozzle fully inserted, for it might cause excessive moisture (abhiṣyanda) in the rectum;

8.4.49 | Furthermore, one should not administer unctuous substances immediately after [eating] through either the rectum or the throat;

8.4.50 | One should not habitually employ either the unctuous enema (snehabasti) or the decoction enema (nirūha) exclusively. 8.4.51 | Therefore, one who has undergone purgation (*nirūha*) should be lubricated with oil, and one who has undergone an oil enema (*anuvāsana*) should be purged; thus, through the proper application of oleation and purification, the procedure of enema (*basti-karman*) alleviates the three *doṣas*.

8.4.52 | A dose enema (mātrā-basti) is always recommended for those exhausted by physical labor, exercise, carrying loads, walking long distances, drinking [alcohol], or sexual intercourse, as well as for the weak and those suffering from vāta disorders.
8.4.53 | For one who may eat and act as they please at all times without harm,
a *mātrā-basti* with a small dose of oil will be appropriate.

8.4.54 | This regimen of the proper dose of unctuous substances is strengthening, easy to administer, pleasant, promotes the easy passage of feces, is nourishing, and cures diseases of the wind (vāta).

8.4.55 | There are two verses on this subject: The excellent oil enemas (snehabasti) prescribed for the pacification of vāta and the other doshas; and their complications when administered incorrectly, along with their treatments.
8.4.56 | That which must necessarily precede an unctuous enema (snehabasti), those who are eligible for it, and those who are eligible after three days;
the procedure for the unctuous enema has been stated, as well as the procedure for the measured enema (mātrābasti).

Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "The Successful Management of Complications Arising from Oleation," in the Section on Success (Siddhisthāna) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Five:
8.5.1 Now, therefore, we shall expound the successful management of complications arising from the enema nozzle and the enema bag (*netrabastivyāpatsiddhi*).
8.5.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.

8.5.3 | Now, listen to the contraindications regarding the enema nozzle (*netra*) and the bladder (*vasti*) in clinical procedures, as well as the complications arising from an improperly applied nozzle along with their treatments.
8.5.4 | One should avoid eight types of eyes: those that are too short, too long, too thin, too thick, worn out, with loose joints, with a side-opening, or crooked.
8.5.5 | Non-attainment, excessive passage, agitation, drawing out, cutting, and discharge; anal pain and crooked passage—these are their respective defects in order.
8.5.6 | One should avoid these eight types of enema bags for clinical procedures: those that are uneven, fleshy, torn, thick, net-like, or airy; as well as those that are greasy or damp.

8.5.7 | Irregularity of flow, thinness, leakage, difficulty in grasping, and discharge; as well as frothiness, displacement, and inability to be retained—these may occur in the bladder due to defects of the enema (basti).

8.5.8 | [The faults arising] from the performer are: too relaxed, too hurried, thrown upward, cast sideways, suppressed, and shaken; as well as excessive outward movement, slowness, and excessive speed.
8.5.9 | If [the enema] is administered without allowing the patient to exhale, or while it is still bound [in the nozzle], or if it is given without being completely discharged,
the Vayu, becoming provoked upon entering, will cause piercing pain like a spear.
8.5.10 | In that case, oil massage to the anus, fomentation, and vāta-alleviating foods [are indicated],
when the enema has been rapidly introduced, withdrawn, or suddenly expelled.
8.5.11 | There may be pain in the hips, anus, and calves, stiffness of the bladder, and pain in the thighs;
in that case, food that subdues Vāta, oleation therapies, sudation, and enemas are indicated.
8.5.12 | If the opening is obstructed by a horizontal fold or if it is constricted, the enema does not pass;
in such a case, one should straighten the nozzle, withdraw it, cleanse it, and then reinsert it.
8.5.13 | When the anus is pressed and then released prematurely, the powerful Vayu, being obstructed, may produce pain in the chest and head, as well as weakness in the thighs.
8.5.14 | In that case, an enema containing bilva and other fruits, śyāmā and other roots, and urine should be administered.
If the rectum is struck with a trembling hand, there may be burning, irritation, and swelling.
8.5.15 | In that case, affusions and enemas should be astringent, sweet, and cold;
for [otherwise], due to the injury caused by a nozzle inserted too deeply, the strength [of the patient] is diminished.
8.5.16 | There may be pain, burning, pricking, and the discharge of feces from the anus;
in such cases, an application of ghee-soaked cotton, milk, and a slimy enema (picchābasti) are recommended.
8.5.17 | A fool, however, does not cultivate [the mind], whereas an outsider quickly turns away.
Therefore, one who desires success should properly apply affection (sneha) in that case once again.
8.5.18 | If excessively oppressed [by the enema], it remains in the abdomen or ascends to the throat;
in that case, enemas, purgation, and procedures such as pressing on the throat should be employed.
8.5.19 | Regarding this, there is a verse:
The wise physician who understands these defects of those who apply the nozzle and the enema, along with their remedies, should perform the procedures of enema therapy.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Successful Management of Complications of Eye Treatments and Enemas," in the Section on Success (*Siddhisthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—wherein it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Six:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the successful management of complications arising from emesis and purgation.
8.6.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

8.6.3 | Now, I shall describe the correct procedure for the two types of purification— emesis and purgation— as well as the complications arising from their improper administration, along with their remedies.
8.6.4 | For the summer, the rainy season, and the arrival of winter are characterized by excessive heat, rain, and cold, respectively;
between them are the three intermediate seasons, beginning with the monsoon, which possess moderate qualities.
8.6.5 | Prāvṛṣ and Śuci-Nabhas are to be known as the rainy season; Śarad and Ūrja-Sahas again as autumn; and Tapasya and Madhu as spring, for the purpose of purification.
8.6.6 | Having thus differentiated these seasons, the physician should administer purification,
keeping in mind the regimen for health, but in the case of disease, according to the nature of the disease itself.
8.6.7 | Between and during the intervals of the purificatory procedures such as emesis and the rest, one should employ oleation and sudation; furthermore, one should apply oleation at the very end.
8.6.8 | One should not administer purgation to those suffering from erysipelas, pustules, edema, jaundice, or anemia,
nor to those afflicted by trauma or poison, unless they have been sufficiently oleated.
8.6.9 | One should not administer an unctuous purgative to a person whose body is excessively unctuous;
nor should one administer a dry purgative to a person whose body has been over-saturated with oleation.
8.6.10 | When the medicine has been digested by one who has undergone oleation and sudation,
drinking it in the proper dose with a concentrated mind leads to successful application.
8.6.11 | Just as water is easily pushed out from a vessel that has been lubricated,
so too are phlegm and other humors expelled from the body when it has been treated with oleation, by means of medicinal therapies.
8.6.12 Just as fire causes moist wood to exude moisture from all sides,
so does sudation cause the stable doshas of one who is oleated to flow out.
8.6.13 Just as dirty clothing is cleansed of its impurity by first loosening it with water,
so too is the impurity [of the body] loosened by oleation and sudation and then purified by cleansing therapies.
8.6.14 | When there is indigestion, exhaustion increases and constipation also arises;
even the administered purificatory therapy acts in a contrary manner.
8.6.15 | It is taken in small quantities, possesses great potency, removes many defects, is easy to digest, has a pleasant taste, is nourishing, and destroys disease.
8.6.16 | One should prescribe medicine that is free from alteration even when there is a complication, which does not cause excessive exhaustion,
and which is endowed with appropriate smell, color, and taste, administered in the proper measure.
8.6.17 | Having shaken off the mental defects— desire and the rest— which give rise to inauspiciousness,
that which has been drunk with a one-pointed mind is fit for perfect yoga.

8.6.18 | A person who is to drink an emetic the next day should eat food that increases *kapha*, which is easily digested and predominantly liquid; whereas for a purgative, the meal should be light and not cold.
8.6.19 | For indeed, due to the slight aggravation of phlegm, the morbid humors (doṣas) flow out quickly;
however, once the medicine has been drunk, the physician should observe the signs of purification.
8.6.20 | When pitta is followed by kapha, one should say the doshas have been expelled from above; when feces and pitta are followed by kapha, they have been expelled from below.
One may declare the doshas removed if there is emaciation, weakness, and lightness.

8.6.21 | Thereafter, one should induce emesis for the remainder of the medicine, but not if there is a lack of lightness [of the body]. One should induce emesis even when there is stiffness, obstruction of wind (vāyu), or absence of eructation.
8.6.22 | Because of its lack of heaviness and its thinness, there is no further danger from phlegm after emesis;
indeed, the digestive fire increases and the humors are pacified.

8.6.23 | One who has undergone emesis should undergo fasting (laṅghana) as long as the signs of proper digestion are not observed; however, once those signs are seen, one should follow the sequential regimen beginning with thin gruel (peyā), and no further fasting is required.

8.6.24 | For a person whose body has been purified by the two types of cleansing therapies and whose morbid humors have been removed, the digestive fire tends toward weakness; therefore, one should follow the sequential regimen beginning with thin gruel (peyā).

8.6.25 | When kapha and pitta have been purified, or when there is little [remnant] in those who drink alcohol or those with a vāta-pitta constitution, one should administer the sequence beginning with *tarpaṇa*; for *peyā* would cause excessive secretions (*abhiṣyanda*) in them.
8.6.26 | When the wind moves in its natural direction (anuloma), there is health, hunger, thirst, vigor, mental clarity, lightness,
purity of the senses and eructations, and the characteristic signs that the medicine has been digested.
8.6.27 | Fatigue, burning sensation, malaise of the limbs, giddiness, fainting, headache,
restlessness, and loss of strength— these are the manifestations of residual medicine.
8.6.28 | Medication that is taken at the wrong time, in too small or too large a dose, that is old, not properly processed, or not correctly prepared, will quickly cause harm.
8.6.29 | Distension, cutting pain, discharge, gripping of the heart and limbs,
hemorrhage, displacement, stiffness, complications, and exhaustion.

8.6.30 | These ten complications are considered to arise from improper application (ayoga) or excessive application (atiyoga), as well as from the deficiencies of the attendant, the medicine, the physician, and the patient.
8.6.31 | Proper application (yoga) is correct functioning; excessive application (atiyoga) is over-action;
non-application (ayoga) is action in the reverse direction, or insufficient or no action at all.
8.6.32 | When purgative medicine is drunk during indigestion by one whose *śleṣman* (phlegm) is provoked, it moves upward, being foul-smelling, unpleasant, or excessively copious.
8.6.33 | When a sharp [emetic] is drunk by one afflicted with hunger, having a soft bowel, or whose *kapha* is only slightly agitated,
it remains [in the stomach], becomes disturbed, and results in purgation instead of emesis.

8.6.34 | Because the humors (doṣas) are removed in reverse order and not entirely, they are designated as "non-unification" (ayoga); the humor either moves with difficulty, or it does not move at all, or only slightly.
8.6.35 | If one who has drunk medicine has not been purified, he should drink the medicine again once that [first dose] has been digested;
however, he should not take another medicine while the previous one is undigested, as there would be danger from excessive administration (atiyoga).
8.6.36 | Having ascertained the heaviness of the digestive tract, as well as its lightness and strength,
one should administer either a mild or a sharp medicine in cases of inadequate administration (ayoga).
8.6.37 | One who has difficulty vomiting should not be given emetics, nor one with a difficult bowel (duṣkoṣṭha) a purgative;
for if the medicine is administered again, it would kill those two once more after having been drunk.
8.6.38 | If an emetic medicine is administered to one whose body is neither unctuous nor sudated, and who is dry,
it will be unable to expel the doshas after having merely agitated them, and will instead produce diseases.
8.6.39 | Loss of strength, swelling, hiccup, frequent seeing of darkness,
cramps in the calves, itching, weakness in the thighs, and discoloration.

8.6.40 | If the patient has been lubricated and fomented, or if the digestive fire is excessively strong, or if the medicine has been digested, or if it has been rendered stagnant by cold substances, or if it remains undigested (āma), one should not extract the morbid humors (doṣas) after merely agitating them.
8.6.41 | All that [excessive administration] indeed produces those very same diseases;
therefore, having understood this, the wise physician should perform the treatment as prescribed therein.

8.6.42 | Once he has been anointed with oil and salt and fomented with heated stones and medicinal powders, one should have him drink [a purgative] once that [previous meal] has been digested; or, alternatively, one should administer a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) along with urine.
8.6.43 | After feeding the patient with meat soups seasoned with medicinal herbs,
one should administer an oil enema (anuvāsana) using a measured dose of oil prepared with fruits, māgadhikā, and devadāru.
8.6.44 | One should first lubricate [the patient] with unctuous substances that alleviate Vāta, and then purify [the system] with a sharp [purgative];
however, one should not use an excessively sharp one, for from that an excessive administration may arise.

8.6.45 | An excessively sharp medicine administered to one afflicted by hunger and having a soft bowel habit quickly eliminates the feces, bile, and phlegm, and causes the liquid elements of the tissues (dhātus) to flow out.
8.6.46 | It causes loss of strength and voice, burning sensations, dryness of the throat, vertigo, and thirst;
in such cases, one should administer sweet remedies and purge the remaining morbid matter with emetics.
8.6.47 | If vomiting occurs after purgation, or purgation occurs after vomiting,
one should arrest that [condition] with very cold applications such as sprinkling and immersion baths.
8.6.48 | Likewise, with food, drinks, and medicinal herbs that are astringent, sweet, and cold,
which alleviate hemorrhagic diarrhea and also remove burning sensations and fever.

8.6.49 | One should drink a *mantha* (a churned beverage) consisting of collyrium, sandalwood, *uśīra*, marrow, blood, sugar, water, and parched grain flour; this is the supreme remedy for curing excessive [administration of emetics].

8.6.50 | One should administer a prepared gruel (peyā) made with the shoots of the *vaṭa* tree and others, mixed with honey; likewise, one should provide milk processed with constipating (*varcas-sāṃgrāhika*) drugs and suitable food.

8.6.51 | Or, food with the juices of wild animals is recommended, as is a slimy enema (picchābasti). An oil enema (anuvāsana) should be administered with clarified butter prepared with milk and sweet substances.

8.6.52 | In the case of excessive emesis, however, one who has been sprinkled with cold water should drink a churned beverage (mantha) made with kapha-alleviating ingredients, along with ghee, honey, and sugar.
8.6.53 | In cases of excessive vomiting accompanied by eructations, or in fainting,
one should have the patient lick a powder of coriander and musta mixed with madhuka and honey.
8.6.54 | When the tongue has entered deep inside due to vomiting,
mouthfuls of food made with unctuous, sour, and salty, and pleasing soups, milk, or meat-broths are beneficial.
8.6.55 | Other men should eat sour fruits in front of him;
then, one should cause [the semen] that has been discharged to enter [the vagina], smeared with a paste of sesame and grapes.
8.6.56 | In cases of disorders of speech, seizure, and wind (vāta), the wise physician should administer thin gruel prepared with ghee and meat, as well as oleation and sudation therapies.
8.6.57 | One who has been vomited upon, purged, suffering from weak digestion, or who has undergone fasting therapy,
should follow the sequential regimen beginning with thin gruel (*peyā*) for the purpose of increasing digestive fire and vital strength.
8.6.58 | For one who has many morbid humors (doṣas), is parched, and has weak digestion,
a small dose of medicine causes the humors to become agitated and blocks their natural pathways, resulting in upward-moving wind (udāvarta).
8.6.59 | It causes the navel to become excessively distended, produces pain in the back, sides, and head,
and brings about a severe obstruction of breath, feces, urine, and flatus.

8.6.60 | All therapeutic measures that alleviate udāvarta— including massage, sudation, suppositories, and the like, along with non-unctuous and unctuous enemas— are recommended for one suffering from flatulence (ādhmāna).
8.6.61 | When the patient has a lubricated (snigdha) and heavy abdomen with undigested matter (sāma), a strong medicine [is indicated];
whereas for one who is emaciated (kṣāma), has a soft bowel (mṛdukoṣṭha), is exhausted, or has little strength, [a mild medicine is required].
8.6.62 | Having reached the rectum, the morbid humor (doṣa), along with undigested matter (āma), quickly expelled,
causes a cutting pain (parikartikā) characterized by intense colic and the discharge of slimy blood.
8.6.63 | Fasting and digestive therapy (pācana) are indicated when there is āma; likewise, dry, hot, and light food.
For one who is emaciated, all nourishing (bṛṃhaṇīya) procedures and sweet food that destroys [the āma] are then prescribed.
8.6.64 | If, when the undigested matter (āma) has been digested, a persistent complication remains, then alkaline, sour, and light substances are recommended;
or [the patient should take] sulphate of iron (puṣpakāsīsa) mixed with alkali or salt.
8.6.65 | When vāta is predominant, one should drink ghee prepared with pomegranate juice;
for food and drink, sour curd combined with pomegranate rind should be used.
8.6.66 | Or one should drink a paste of *devadāru* and sesame seeds with warm water;
or milk boiled with *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *kadamba*.
8.6.67 | One should administer either a decoction enema (picchābasti) that is astringent, sweet, and cold,
or alternatively, an unctuous enema (snehāsti) prepared with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka).
8.6.68 | However, a medicine that is too small for a disorder with many complications, having merely agitated the doshas,
causes them to be discharged only in very small amounts, resulting in itching, swelling, skin diseases, and heaviness.

8.6.69 | It may cause weakness of the digestive fire, nausea, a sense of stiffness, loss of appetite, and pallor; that condition is known as parisrāva. One should pacify that disorder or induce emesis.
8.6.70 | Or again, one should administer a sharp purgative after the patient has been oleated;
once purified, one should provide prepared powders, *āsava*, and *ariṣṭa* liquors.
8.6.71 | When the urges of one who has drunk medicinal decoctions are suppressed, the Vāta and other humors become aggravated;
having reached the heart, they cause a terrible cardiac seizure (hṛdgraha).
8.6.72 | He, with hiccup, cough, pain in the flanks, debility, salivation, and rolling of the eyes,
gnaws at his tongue, unconscious, grinding his teeth with a *kiṭikiṭa* sound.

8.6.73 | The physician should not allow the patient to fall into confusion there; he should quickly treat one afflicted by a fainting fit caused by pitta with sweet [substances], and one fainting from kapha with pungent [substances].
8.6.74 | Thereafter, one should digest the remaining morbid humors (doṣa) with digestive (pācanīya) remedies;
then, one should gradually restore his digestive fire (kāyāgni) and strength (bala).

8.6.75 | To one whose heart is oppressed by excessive vomiting due to vāta, one should administer unctuous, sour, and salty [food]; otherwise, if pitta and kapha are involved, one should act differently.
8.6.76 | By the suppression of the urges of one who has drunk medicine, or by phlegm,
or in one who has been excessively purified, the wind (vāta) seizes the limbs.
8.6.77 | In cases of stiffness, trembling, pricking pain, exhaustion, aversion, and twisting,
one should administer all Vata-alleviating treatments, such as oleation and sudation.
8.6.78 | A medicine that is excessively sharp for a person with a soft bowel and mild morbid humors (doṣas),
having expelled the humors and agitated them, carries away the vital essence, the blood.

8.6.79 | One should give food mixed with that [substance] to a crow or even a dog. If it eats it, one should declare the patient to be living; if it does not eat it, one should indicate bile (as the cause of death).
8.6.80 | A white cloth, when soaked and washed with lukewarm water, becomes discolored;
however, it remains pure [in color] when there is pitta or blood.
8.6.81 | For one afflicted by thirst, fainting, or intoxication, one should administer treatment until death—
whatever treatment is beneficial for removing pitta and is also useful in cases of excessive application.
8.6.82 | One should drink the fresh blood of living deer, cows, buffaloes, or goats;
for by that, one's life-force is restored, and the vital breath quickly returns.
8.6.83 | One should administer that same [blood] pressed with *darbha* grass as a blood enema (*raktavasti*).
Milk boiled with *śyāmāka*, *kāśmarya*, *badarī*, *dūrvā*, and *uśīra* [should also be used].
8.6.84 | One should administer a cold enema (basti) combined with the scum of ghee and collyrium;
or a very cold slimy enema (picchābasti), or an oil enema (anuvāsana) using the scum of ghee.

8.6.85 | Having stabilized the prolapsed rectum with astringent decoctions, one should reinsert it; and in the event of loss of consciousness, one should cause the patient to hear the sounds of the Gandharvas along with the Sāman chants.
8.6.86 | When a purgative, having been drunk, remains with the feces at its end,
or an emetic, having been administered, remains with the medicine at its end, it fails to expel the doshas even after having excited them.
8.6.87 | At that time, the aggravated doshas produce diseases such as those beginning with kaṇḍū (itching).
This is considered vibhraṃśa; in that case, the remedy should be according to the specific disease.
8.6.88 | When [emetics] are drunk by one who is unctuous (snigdha), they are accompanied by oiliness (sasneha) and enveloped by the humors (doṣa) due to their softness;
they do not expel the humors, but rather cause those humors that have been displaced to become stagnant in their own locations.
8.6.89 | When there is obstruction of flatus, stiffness of the rectum, and colic, and [the patient] passes [stool] only in small quantities,
he is fit for a sharp enema or purgation, provided he has undergone fasting and digestive treatment.
8.6.90 | A dry purgative, when drunk by one who is already dry or weak,
quickly provokes the Vāyu and may produce terrible complications.
8.6.91 | For one who faints due to severe stiffness and piercing pains in all the limbs,
a regimen that alleviates Vāta, such as oleation and sudation, should be administered.
In a person who has been oleated and possesses a soft bowel, a mild purgative suppresses the phlegm,
bile, and wind, resulting in drowsiness, heaviness, and exhaustion.

8.6.93 | It quickly produces weakness and exhaustion of the limbs; therefore, one should purge it. In this case, fasting, digestive treatments, and purification therapies—both mild and sharp—are indicated.
8.6.94 | Regarding this, there are two verses: Thus have been described these complications of emesis and purgation performed unskillfully upon men, along with their symptoms and treatments.
8.6.95 | Having understood these stages in their true nature,
the wise person who desires health should always administer purification properly to human beings.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Successful Management of Complications of Emetics and Purgatives," in the Section on Success (*Siddhisthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, redacted by Caraka, and—wherein it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala.
Chapter Seven:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the successful management of complications of enemas (*bastivyāpatsiddhi*).
8.7.2 | Thus indeed said the Blessed Ātreya.
8.7.3 | Endowed with humility, the assembly of disciples questioned Punarvasu, who was a treasure-house of wisdom, fortitude, magnanimity, profundity, forbearance, self-restraint, and austerity.
8.7.4 | Having heard these questions—"What are the complications of enema therapy? How many are there? What are their causes and symptoms? And what is the treatment?"—the Teacher spoke to them.
8.7.5 | Excessive application [of emesis] results in exhaustion, flatulence, hiccups, reaching the heart,
upward movement [of wind], dysentery, pain in the head and limbs, cutting pain, and discharge.
8.7.6 | There are twelve complications arising from the improper application of enemas (basti).
Learn now the symptoms and treatment of each one of these individually.
8.7.7 | When the stomach is heavy, dominated by wind (vāyu), dry, or even characterized by an excess of wind,
a meal that is cold, low in salt, lacking oiliness, or consisting mostly of liquids— even if it is thick— is [inappropriate].
8.7.8 | An enema, having agitated that morbid humor (doṣa) but failing to expel it due to weakness,
causes heaviness of the abdomen and the retention of flatus, urine, and feces.
8.7.9 | It causes pain in the umbilicus and bladder, burning sensations, a coating over the heart,
swelling of the anus, itching, eruptions, discoloration, loss of appetite, and weakness of the digestive fire.
8.7.10 | In that case, the drinking of hot *pramathyā* decoctions, various types of sudation,
fruit-suppositories (*phalavarti*), or, having ascertained the proper time, purgation is recommended.
8.7.11 | A enema containing bilva root, trivṛt, devadāru, barley, jujube, and horse gram,
along with wine and other substances, urine, and the paste of the aforementioned drugs, shall bring that [patient] back [to health].
8.7.12 | In one who has been lubricated and fomented, a very sharp and hot [purgative] administered to a person with a soft bowel leads to over-action.
Its symptoms and treatment should be the same as those for excessive purification.
8.7.13 | Having ground pṛśniparṇī, sthirā, padma, kāśmarya, madhuka,
balā, drākṣā, and madhūka, [one should prepare a drink] with milk and rice-wash water.
8.7.14 | Having dissolved grapes, moistened clay,
and licorice in water, one should administer an enema with ghee for burning sensations caused by excessive elimination.
8.7.15 | When the residue of undigested matter (āma) remains, the provoked dosha, if treated with a mild non-unctuous enema (nirūha),
obstructs the pathway of vāta, destroys the digestive fire, and may even cause fainting.

8.7.16 | Excessive dry fomentation may cause exhaustion, a burning sensation, pain in the heart, delusion, convulsions, and heaviness; one should treat such a patient with digestive (pācana) therapies.
8.7.17 | Water boiled with long pepper (pippalī), kattṛṇa, uśīra, devadāru, and mūrvā, mixed with sauvarcala salt, should be drunk; it stimulates digestion and cleanses the heart.
8.7.18 | Vacā, nāgara, śaṭī, and elā, mixed with whey (dadhimanda) or with clear wine (prasannā), or with arishta or asava, should be drunk.
8.7.19 | Having ground together wood-apple (dāru), the three pungents (trikaṭuka), myrobalan (pathyā), palāśa, leadwort (citraka),
and costus (śaṭī), as well as kuṣṭha, one should drink them with urine along with digestive alkaline preparations.
8.7.20 | One should administer an enema for this patient using the ten roots (daśamūla) with urine;
or alternatively, an enema with honey and oil (mādhutailika), containing salt and urine.
8.7.21 | A enema administered when the patient has little strength, great morbidity, dryness, or a cruel disposition (krūrāśaya),
being enveloped by the doshas and its path obstructed, may itself block the vital wind (samīraṇa).
8.7.22 | That wind, having entered an aberrant path, may cause flatulence, affliction of the vital points (marmans),
a burning sensation, heaviness of the abdomen, and pain in the scrotum and groins.
8.7.23 | It constricts the heart with piercing pains and causes one to run hither and thither;
[this is treated] with black fruit (*śyāmāphala*) and others, along with *kuṣṭha*, long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*), salt, and mustard seeds.
8.7.24 | One should insert a wick made from soot, black gram, *vaca*, fermenting agent (*kiṇva*), alkaline powder, and jaggery,
shaped like the thumb with a tapering middle like a barley grain.
8.7.25 | For one whose body has been anointed and fomented, [the enema nozzle] should be smeared with oil and inserted into the lubricated rectum;
or else, it may be prepared with salt, soot, and white mustard seeds.

8.7.26 | There should be a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) prepared with bilva and other drugs, along with pīlu, mustard seeds, and urine; and an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) should be prepared with sarala and amaradāru.

8.7.27 | In a person with a soft bowel and weak constitution, an excessively sharp enema that causes excessive evacuation may produce hiccups; for such a person, hiccup-suppressing and nourishing therapies are beneficial.

8.7.28 | Having cooked oil with balā, sthirā, and the others, along with kāśmarya, triphalā, jaggery, rock salt, prasannā, sour gruel (āranāla), and sour liquids, one should administer an unctuous enema (anuvāsana).
8.7.29 | One should drink one akṣa each of kṛṣṇā and lavaṇa combined with warm water;

Thus ends the seventh chapter, named "The Successful Management of Complications of Enema Therapy" (*bastivyāpatsiddhi*), in the Section on Success (*siddhisthāna*) of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and, being unavailable, completed by Dṛḍhabala.
The Eighth Chapter.

Chapter Nine:
Now, therefore, we shall expound the success regarding the three vital organs (*trimarmīyā siddhi*).
8.9.2 | Thus indeed said the venerable Ātreya.

8.9.3 | There are one hundred and seven vital points (marmas) in this body, Agniveśa, which are situated in the trunks and the branches. When any one of them is afflicted, there occurs an excessive affliction, due to their specific connection with consciousness. Among those, the vital points situated in the trunks are more serious than those situated in the branches, because the branches depend upon them; and even compared to those in the trunks, the heart, the bladder, and the head are the most critical, as they are the roots of the body.

8.9.4 | Therein, in the heart, the ten vessels (dhamanīs), the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the mind (manas), the intellect (buddhi), consciousness (cetanā), and the great elements are established like spokes in the nave; in the head, the sense organs and the channels (srotas) that carry the senses and the vital breaths are situated like rays upon the sun; and the bladder is the reservoir of urine, situated among the large intestine, the scrotum, the perineal raphe (sevanī), and the channels carrying semen and urine, serving as the foundation for all water-carrying channels, just as the ocean is for rivers. And by many...
This body is pervaded by channels known as *marmas*, which have their roots therein, just as the sky is pervaded by the rays of the sun.

8.9.5 | From the injury of even one of these three, the destruction of the body would occur immediately, for when the substratum perishes, that which is supported by it also perishes; moreover, from their impairment, most terrible diseases manifest. Therefore, these must be protected with special care against external injuries, wind, and other such factors.

8.9.6 | In that regard, if the heart is struck, there may occur coughing, dyspnea, loss of strength, dryness of the throat, constriction of the *kloma*, protrusion of the tongue, dryness of the palate, epilepsy, insanity, delirium, loss of consciousness, and so forth; if the head is struck, there may occur stiffness of the neck (*manyā-stambha*), facial paralysis (*ardita*), wandering of the eyes, delusion, convulsions, loss of motor function, coughing, dyspnea, lockjaw, muteness, stammering, closing of the eyes, twitching of the cheeks, yawning, salivation, loss of voice, distortion of the face, and other such symptoms.

Suppression of flatus, urine, and feces causes pain in the groin, penis, and bladder, as well as circular pain (kuṇḍala), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), abdominal tumors (gulma), stiffness (aṣṭhīla), rigidity (upastambha), and obstruction of the navel, abdomen, anus, and pelvis; the symptoms of these conditions when afflicted by Vāta and other humors, along with the rules for their treatment, have been described in the Cikitsā-sthāna.

8.9.7 | However, these [marmans] must be protected especially from vāta, for vāta is the cause for the provocation of pitta and kapha and is the root of prāṇa; it is most effectively treated by enema therapy (basti). Therefore, there is no therapeutic procedure equal to the enema for the protection of the marmans. Having reflected with intelligence upon the six groups of āsthāpana enemas described in the Vimāna [section], as well as the two groups of anuvāsana enemas prescribed here, one should employ them for the purpose of protecting the great marmans and for the treatment of diseases of vāta.

8.9.8 | Furthermore, when the heart is afflicted, one should administer asafoetida powder mixed with the powder of any one of the salts, along with the juice of citron or another sour, heart-tonic liquid. For drinking, one should give the decoction of the *sthirādi* pentad root with sugar, as well as gruel prepared with the decoction of the *bilvādi* pentad root, and the treatments prescribed for heart disease. However, when the head is afflicted by Vāta, one should employ massage, fomentation, poultices, internal oleation, nasal therapy (*nastaḥkarma*), pressed-out nasal drops (*avapīḍana*), medicated smoke (*dhūma*), and so forth.

For the bladder, however, there is pot-sudation (kumbhīsveda), suppositories (vartayaḥ), a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) prepared with *śyāmā* and other herbs in cow’s urine, and one prepared with *surā* liquor using *bilva* and other herbs; a non-unctuous enema containing the paste of *trapusa*, *ervāru*, seeds of *kharāśvā*, *yava*, *ṛṣabhaka*, and *vṛddhi*, along with milk boiled with the roots of *śara*, *kāśa*, *ikṣu*, *darbha*, and *gokṣuraka*; an unctuous enema (anuvāsana) with oil processed with *pītadāru*; and *tailvaka* ghee for the purpose of purgation.

Oil prepared with a decoction of *śatāvarī*, *gokṣuraka*, *bṛhatī*, *kaṇṭakārikā*, *guḍūcī*, *punarnavā*, *uśīra*, *madhuka*, the two types of *sārivā*, *lodhra*, *śreyasī*, and the roots of *kuśa* and *kāśa*, along with four times the amount of milk, and a paste of *balā*, *vṛṣa*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *kharāśva*, *upakuñcikā*, *vatsaka*, the seeds of *trapusa* and *ervāru*, *śitivāraka*, *madhuka*, *vacā*, *śatapuṣpā*, *aśmabheda*, *varṣābhū*, and *madanaphala*, administered as an uttarabasti or a nirūha enema to one who has been purified, lubricated, and fomented, removes pain in the bladder and disorders of the urine.
