An enema consisting of five *prasṛta* measures of a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*) and peacock, swan, and cock, combined with four *prasṛta* measures of oil, ghee, fat (*vasā*), and marrow, and mixed with a paste of *śatapuṣpā*, *musta*, and *hapuṣā*, along with salt, removes diseases of Vāyu affecting the feet, ankles, thighs, knees, calves, sacrum (*trika*), groins (*vaṅkṣaṇa*), bladder, and testicles. 8.12.18-(9).
Enemas should be administered according to this same method for deer, birds, marsh-dwellers, and burrow-dwellers.

(8.12.18–10) An enema consisting of two *prasṛta* measures each of honey and ghee, an equal amount of warm water, half a *pala* of *śatapuṣpā*, and half an *akṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava*) is most aphrodisiac and removes dysuria, pitta, and vāta disorders. (8.12.18–11) An enema consisting of four *prastha* measures each of fresh ghee, oil, muscle fat (*vasā*), and marrow, half a *pala* of *hapuṣā*, and half an *akṣa* of rock salt is most aphrodisiac, removes dysuria and pitta diseases, and acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). (8.12.18–12)

An enema consisting of four *prasṛta* of honey and oil, half a *pala* of *śatapuṣpā*, and half an *akṣa* of rock salt (*saindhava*) is digestive-stimulating, nourishing, bestows strength and complexion, is free from complications, is highly aphrodisiac, acts as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*), and cures worms, skin diseases, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, hernia, splenic disorders, and urinary disorders. (8.12.18–13) Similarly, an enema with equal parts of milk, honey, and ghee, along with the aforementioned paste, bestows strength and complexion, is highly aphrodisiac, is free from complications, cures inflammation and cutting pain of the bladder and penis, dysuria, and diseases of *pitta*, and acts as a rejuvenative. (8.12.18–14)

Similarly, an enema (basti) consisting of honey and ghee in equal parts, with meat broth added in equal measure, combined with *mustā* and *akṣa*, as described previously, cures vāta-balance disorders, cramps in the feet, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and pain in the three corners of the pelvis, the thighs, the knees, the calves, the bladder, the testicles, the penis, the sacrum, and the back. (8.12.18–15) An enema containing seven *prasṛta* measures each of wine (*surā*), fermented grain-water (*sauvīraka*), horse-gram broth (*kulattha-rasa*), meat broth, honey, ghee, and oil, mixed with a paste of *mustā* and *śatāhvā* along with salt, cures all diseases caused by *vāta*. (8.12.18–16)

A decoction of the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūla), triphalā, bilva, and madanaphala, prepared with cow’s urine and mixed with a paste of kuṭaja, madanaphala, musta, and pāṭhā, combined with rock salt, yavaśūka, honey, and oil—this enema should be administered in cases of diseases caused by kapha, flatulence of the bladder, retention of flatus and semen, anemia, indigestion, choleraic disorders, and intestinal torpor.
8.12.19 | Hereafter, we shall describe the most aphrodisiac unctuous substances (*snehas*).

One should take one *prastha* each of the juices of *śatāvarī*, *guḍūcī*, sugarcane, *vidārī*, *āmalaka*, grapes, and dates, having pressed them with a mechanical press; likewise, one should add two *prasthas* each of ghee, oil, and the milk of cows, buffaloes, and goats. Then, one should add a paste (*kalka*) consisting of *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabhaka*, *medā*, *mahāmedā*, *tvakkṣīrī*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *madhūlikā*, *madhuka*, *uccaṭā*, long pepper (*pippalī*), lotus seeds (*puṣkarabīja*), blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *kadamba* flowers, white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), and filaments (*keśara*).

One should prepare [the medicine] by adding one *prastha* each of the meat of spotted deer, hyena, chicken, sparrow, *cakora*, *mattākṣa*, peacock, *jīvañjīvaka*, *kuliṅga*, swan, and eggs, along with fat and marrow. Once it is cooked amidst the sounds of Vedic chanting and the resonance of conchs, kettledrums, and drums, and while shaded by a white umbrella, one should place the Blessed One, the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva), upon the back of an elephant after worshipping him. Then, having mixed that oil with a third part honey, one should administer it as an enema accompanied by auspicious benedictions, hymns of praise, and worship of the deity.

One should know that this is the most wholesome supreme rejuvenative (rasāyana) for men who consort with women and have lost their semen, as well as for those afflicted by wasting diseases, consumption, or irregular fevers; for women with morbid uteri, the barren, those with blood-tumors (raktagulma), those whose children die at birth, those with absent menstruation, and those whose flesh and blood are depleted; it destroys wrinkles and graying hair. 8.12.19–(1)

Having crushed one hundred parts each of *balā*, *gokṣuraka*, *rāsnā*, *aśvagandhā*, *śatāvarī*, and *sahacara*, one should boil them in one hundred *droṇas* of water until one *droṇa* of liquid remains; having strained this decoction through a cloth, one should add one *prastha* each of the fresh juices of *vidārī* and *āmalaka*, as well as the fluids of goat, buffalo, boar, bull, cock, peacock, swan, *kāraṇḍava* duck, and *sārasa* crane, along with one *prastha* each of ghee and oil, and eight *prasthas* of milk.

One should prepare [the decoction] by adding pastes of sandalwood, madhuka, madhūlikā, bark, kṣīrī, lotus root, lotus stalk, blue lotus, paṭola, ātmaguptā, annapāki, the top of the palm fruit, dates, grapes, emblic myrobalan, kaṇṭakārī, jīvaka, ṛṣabhaka, kṣudrasahā, mahāsahā, śatāvarī, medā, long pepper, hrīvera, and cinnamon.
Once prepared according to the prescribed ritual beginning with the chanting of the Veda, one should administer the enema.
By means of this, one may approach a hundred women; furthermore, there is no restriction whatsoever regarding recreation, diet, or physical exercise.

This [milk] is aphrodisiac, strengthening, nourishing, life-prolonging, and a remover of wrinkles and graying hair; it is most wholesome for those afflicted by chest wounds, emaciation, loss of semen, or irregular fevers, as well as for women with vaginal disorders. 8.12.19–(2)

One should boil one hundred palas of sahacara and palāśa in four droṇas of water until one droṇa remains; this well-strained decoction should then be cooked with two prasthas each of vidārī and sugarcane juice, eight times as much milk, and one prastha each of ghee and oil, along with a paste consisting of one akṣa each of balā, madhuka, madhūka, candana, madhūlikā, sārivā, medā, mahāmedā, kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, payasyā, aguru, mañjiṣṭhā, vyāghranakha, śaṭī, sahacara, sahasravīryā, varāṅga, and lodhra—each doubled by the addition of sugar.
Once prepared according to the prescribed ritual beginning with the chanting of the Veda (brahmaghoṣa), one should administer it as an enema (basti).

This is a rejuvenative (rasāyana) that removes all diseases, the best for graceful women moving within the inner apartments; it cures wasting due to injury, disorders of vāta and pitta, pain, dyspnea, and cough. When mixed with one-third part honey, it removes wrinkles and graying hair, and increases complexion, beauty, strength, muscle mass, and semen. These rejuvenative medicated oil enemas (snehabasti), when resources permit, should be prepared by a hundred or a thousand cycles of cooking to impart vigor and strength.
8.12.20 | And there are verses on this point: These enemas and unctuous substances have been described as known as *yāpana*;
they are non-contraindicated for those in good health, for the sick, and for the elderly.
8.12.21 | For those who habitually engage in excessive sexual intercourse, [these preparations] provide semen, muscle tissue, and strength;
they alleviate all diseases and are suitable for use in all seasons.

8.12.22 | It is observed that both oil enemas (sneha-vasti) and decoction enemas (nirūha) serve the purpose of both [fertility and health] for women who have not yet given birth and for men as well, by bestowing offspring.
8.12.23 | Physical exercise, sexual intercourse, wine, honey, cold water,
eating together [with others], and the jolting of a chariot— these are forbidden during enema treatments.
8.12.24 | Regarding this, there are these verses:
Three enemas are prepared from the bile of the peacock, the Indian crane, and the swan;
twenty from gallinaceous birds, thirty from birds that strike with their beaks, and nine from birds that seize their prey by force.
8.12.25 | Twenty and likewise twenty-seven enemas are prepared with aquatic animals,
and nine with fish and similar creatures, as well as with peacock meat.

8.12.26 | Ten enemas [should be prepared] with the meat of crabs and others, along with the paste of tortoise; seventeen with the meat of wild animals (mṛga), nineteen with that of gallinaceous birds (viṣkira), and ten with that of waterfowl (ānūpa). 8.12.27 | Fourteen [enemas] should be prepared with the meat of peacock, cock, and burrowing animals (bhūśaya).
These are, in brief, twenty-nine, together with the unctuous substances.
8.12.28 | These two hundred and sixteen varieties have been described in detail;
when combined with honey, they make a man exceedingly virile.
8.12.29 | They do not produce excessive application nor lack of application, and they do not cause stiffness;
moreover, when these [breaths] are employed, they do not cease because of their gentleness.
8.12.30 | He should be immediately administered sharp non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) along with urine;
[otherwise] swelling, loss of digestive fire, pallor, colic, hemorrhoids, and cutting pain [would occur].
8.12.31 | Fever and diarrhea may arise from the excessive use of *yāpana* enemas.
In such cases, digestive-stimulating (*dīpanī*) treatments using *ariṣṭa*, milk, *sīdhu* liquor, and so forth, are recommended.

8.12.32 | Therefore, one should employ these palliative measures with due reasoning and not through excessive attachment. Thus have been described the complications of loud speaking and similar activities, along with their treatments.
8.12.33 | Having described them individually in detail, one should always protect a person from the complications arising from the improper performance of procedures such as emesis and the others.
8.12.34 | Where the means [of treatment] were described, that is called the Section on Success (Siddhisthāna). Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, spoken by the sage Ātreya.
8.12.35 | This was proclaimed by the wise Agniveśa for the benefit of living beings,
[to attain] long life, fame, health, and the abundant fulfillment of the three goals of human existence.
8.12.36 | By reciting it according to the prescribed rule, one attains unsurpassed success in this world;
he expands what was stated in brief and condenses what is overly prolix.
8.12.37 | The reviser makes the ancient treatise new again;
therefore, this supreme treatise was [revised] by Caraka, who possessed supreme intelligence.
8.12.38 | That [work], refined and complete in its essence, is characterized by three parts;
having propitiated Śaṅkara, the Lord of Beings, he brought it to completion.
8.12.39 | Having gathered a collection of the finest gleanings from many tantras, Dṛḍhabala became the author of the Akhaṇḍārtha in the city of Pañcanada.

8.12.40 | He completed this [work] with the chapters on the seventeen medicinal herbs and their pharmaceutical preparations; it is devoid of any deficiency in word or meaning and is free from the faults of a medical treatise.
8.12.41 | Adorned with twenty-six diverse methodological principles (*tantrayukti*),
therein are the topic (*adhikaraṇa*), the application (*yoga*), the purpose (*hetvartha*), and the meaning of the word (*padārtha*).
8.12.42 | The purpose [of these] consists of: specification (*pradeśa*), general indication (*uddeśa*), detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*), the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*);
as well as instruction (*upadeśa*), designation (*apadeśa*), extension (*atideśa*), presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), and definitive determination (*nirṇaya*).
8.12.43 | Occurrence, the certain and the uncertain, with exclusion, the contrary;
the prima facie argument, the rule, the assent, the explanation, and doubt.
8.12.44 | Consideration of the past and the future, absence of conceptualization,
non-aggregation, illustration, etymological explanation, conjunction, and alternative formulation.
8.12.45 | Rebuttal, as well as extraction, and possibility—
these are indeed the methodological principles (*tantrayukti*) that exist in their entirety within the treatise (*tantra*) as it is set forth both in brief and in detail.

8.12.46 | Just as the sun is seen only in part by a forest of lotuses, or as a lamp is seen [only partially] by a house when its meaning is already expressed by a compound (samāsa), so it is in this case.
8.12.47 | Likewise, the methods of this treatise are for the purpose of awakening and illumination;
for one whose mind has found its footing even in a single scripture here [in this world].

8.12.48 | Because he knows the application of reasoning, he quickly masters even other treatises. A physician who studies the scriptures without the principles of systematics (tantrayukti) does not grasp the meaning of those scriptures, just as one fails to obtain wealth when fortune has run out.
8.12.49 | A scripture poorly grasped surely destroys the ignorant man, like a weapon;
that same scripture and weapon, when well grasped, protects the wise man.
8.12.50 | Therefore, these [topics] shall be explained again in detail in the subsequent section,
for the sake of knowing the true nature of this very tantra, according to its merits and defects.
8.12.51 | He who, having studied this entire work, reflects thoroughly upon its meanings with an undistracted mind and remains constant in its practical application,
becomes a bestower of happiness and life for humanity, and is enriched with fortitude, memory, intelligence, and righteousness.
He in whose heart this twelve-thousand-verse collection resides knows the meaning, he knows how to investigate, and he is skilled in medical treatment.
8.12.53 Why does he not understand their diseases and their treatment—
the medical science of Vāgbhaṭa— concerning the welfare of the healthy and the sick?
8.12.54 | Whatever exists here exists elsewhere; what does not exist here exists nowhere.
In the treatise composed by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka.

8.12.55 | When the eighth section on Success (Siddhisthāna) had been reached by Dṛḍhabala, this section on Success was completed in summary form for the sake of his own accomplishment. Thus ends the twelfth chapter, named "Success regarding the Upper Enema" (Uttarabastisiddhi), in the Section on Success of the treatise composed by Agniveśa, revised by Caraka, and—where it was missing—supplemented by Dṛḍhabala. ||12||
This Caraka-tantra is completed.
